title: Quiz: Zernike moments on the unit disc
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. V_{nm} = R_{nm}(\rho)e^{im\theta} on the unit disc (n - |m| even, |m| \le n); Z_{nm} = \frac{n+1}{\pi}\iint I\,\overline{V_{nm}}; \theta counter-clockwise.

Q1. Which (n, m) are allowed for n = 3? How many zeros does R_{31} have inside the disc (0 < \rho < 1)?






Hint





|m| \le n and n - |m| even; R_{nm} has (n - |m|)/2 zeros.









Answer





m = -3, -1, 1, 3. R_{31} = 3\rho^3 - 2\rho has (3-1)/2 = 1 zero inside: \rho = \sqrt{2/3} = 0.816.




Q2. Why is the radial part orthogonal with the weight \rho, i.e. \int_0^1 R_{nm}R_{n'm}\,\rho\,d\rho, and not with d\rho alone?






Hint





What is the area element in polar coordinates?









Answer





The polynomials must be orthogonal on the disc as an area: dx\,dy = \rho\,d\rho\,d\theta. After the angular integral, the factor \rho remains. A ring of radius \rho has circumference 2\pi\rho, so outer rings count more.




Q3. An image is rotated by 30° counter-clockwise. What happens to Z_{22}, Z_{31} and Z_{40}?






Hint





Z_{nm} \to Z_{nm}e^{-im\alpha}.









Answer





All keep their magnitude. The phase of Z_{22} changes by -60°, of Z_{31} by -30°, and Z_{40} (real, m = 0) does not change at all.




Q4. A real image has Z_{42} = 0.3 - 0.1i. What is Z_{4,-2}? Why is it enough to store the moments with m \ge 0?






Hint





\overline{V_{nm}} = V_{n,-m}.









Answer





Z_{4,-2} = \overline{Z_{42}} = 0.3 + 0.1i. For a real image every Z_{n,-m} is the conjugate of Z_{nm}, so the negative m carry no extra information.




Q5. A classifier uses |Z_{nm}| for n \le 8 to recognise digits in any orientation. Which two digits will it confuse, and why can’t more orders fix it?






Hint





Which digit is another one rotated?









Answer





6 and 9: a 9 is (nearly) a 6 rotated by 180°, and all magnitudes are exactly rotation invariant, at every order. More orders add more invariants, but every one of them is blind to rotation. One needs a non-invariant feature (a phase, or the upright orientation).




Q6. Why should the disc be centred on the object’s centroid before computing Zernike moments?






Hint





What is Z_{11} in terms of m_{10} and m_{01}?









Answer





Zernike moments are only rotation invariant for rotations about the disc’s centre; moving the object changes all of them. Centring the disc on the centroid makes them translation invariant (and Z_{11} = \frac2\pi(m_{10} - im_{01}) = 0). Scaling the radius to the object’s size makes them scale invariant.




Q7. A Zernike reconstruction of a micrograph is very good inside the disc but has a large error over the whole square image. Why?






Hint





Where are the V_{nm} defined?









Answer





The basis lives on the inscribed disc: the corners (21 % of the square) are not described at all, so the reconstruction is 0 there. For a shape that lies inside the disc on a dark background this does not matter; for a crop of a larger image it does.




Q8. Computing R_{40,0}(\rho) with the factorial formula gives values that are wrong by up to 0.015, although every term is computed accurately. Why?






Hint





How large are the individual terms compared with the result?









Answer





The terms alternate in sign and the largest is about 5 \times 10^{13}, while the sum is at most 1. Each term carries a relative rounding error of about 10^{-16}, i.e. an absolute error up to about 10^{-2}, which survives the cancellation. A recurrence in n never forms such large terms.




Q9. (math) Show that \int_0^1 R_{20}R_{00}\,\rho\,d\rho = 0 and compute \int_0^1 R_{20}^2\,\rho\,d\rho.






Hint





R_{20} = 2\rho^2 - 1.









Answer





\int_0^1 (2\rho^3 - \rho)\,d\rho = \tfrac12 - \tfrac12 = 0. \int_0^1 (2\rho^2 - 1)^2\rho\,d\rho = \int_0^1 (4\rho^5 - 4\rho^3 + \rho)\,d\rho = \tfrac23 - 1 + \tfrac12 = \tfrac16 = \frac{1}{2(n+1)} for n = 2.

title: Exercise: Zernike moments on the unit disc
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Zernike polynomials
V_{nm} = R_{nm}(\rho)e^{im\theta}, n \ge 0, \lvert m\rvert \le n, n - \lvert m\rvert even


Small radial polynomials
R_{00} = 1, R_{11} = \rho, R_{20} = 2\rho^2 - 1, R_{22} = \rho^2, R_{31} = 3\rho^3 - 2\rho, R_{33} = \rho^3, R_{40} = 6\rho^4 - 6\rho^2 + 1


Orthogonality
\iint \overline{V_{nm}}V_{n'm'}\,dA = \frac{\pi}{n+1}\delta_{nn'}\delta_{mm'}; radial: \int_0^1 R_{nm}R_{n'm}\rho\,d\rho = \frac{1}{2(n+1)}\delta_{nn'}


Zernike moments
Z_{nm} = \frac{n+1}{\pi}\iint I\,\overline{V_{nm}}\,dA; real image: Z_{n,-m} = \overline{Z_{nm}}


Rotation by \alpha
Z_{nm} \to Z_{nm}e^{-im\alpha}; \lvert Z_{nm}\rvert invariant


Mirror
top–bottom: Z_{nm} \to \overline{Z_{nm}}; left–right: Z_{nm} \to (-1)^m\overline{Z_{nm}}

title: Exercise: Zernike moments on the unit disc
text:
By hand
B1. Orthogonality of the radial polynomials. (a) Compute \int_0^1 R_{20}R_{00}\,\rho\,d\rho and \int_0^1 R_{31}R_{11}\,\rho\,d\rho. (b) Compute \int_0^1 R_{20}^2\,\rho\,d\rho and compare with \frac{1}{2(n+1)}. (c) Where is the zero of R_{20}? Sketch R_{20}, R_{40} and R_{22} on [0, 1].
B2. An image has Z_{22} = 0.3 + 0.4i. (a) What are |Z_{22}| and its phase? (b) The image is rotated by 30° counter-clockwise. Compute the new Z_{22} (magnitude, phase, and as a + bi). (c) The original image is mirrored top–bottom instead. What is Z_{22} now?
B3. Counting. (a) List all (n, m) with n \le 4. How many Zernike polynomials is that, and how many with m \ge 0? (b) How many distinct moments (with m \ge 0) are there up to n = 20? How many real numbers is that (note Z_{n0} is real)?
B4. The disc inscribed in a 64 \times 64 image. (a) What fraction of the pixels lies inside it? (The demo counts 3228 pixel centres.) (b) The image is a crop of a larger micrograph with bright background everywhere. What does a Zernike reconstruction do in the corners? (c) What are the alternatives, and their drawbacks?
B5. Optics. The wavefront error over a round lens pupil is written as W(\rho, \theta) = \sum a_{nm}V_{nm}. (a) Which term is defocus, and what shape does it describe? (b) Which terms describe astigmatism? How many times does the pattern repeat around the pupil? (c) Why is V_{11} (tilt) usually not counted as an aberration of the image?
B6. 6 and 9, b and d. (a) Why do a 6 and a 9 have the same |Z_{nm}| for every n, m? (b) How do the phases of Z_{11} and Z_{22} differ between them? (c) Do b and d have the same magnitudes? Which feature could separate them?
B7. The factorial formula for R_{40,0} has terms up to about 5 \times 10^{13} in size, while |R_{40,0}| \le 1. A double has about 16 significant digits. (a) Estimate the absolute error of R_{40,0} computed with that formula. (b) The demo library compares it with a recurrence: the largest difference on [0, 1] is 1.9 \times 10^{-10} at n = 20, 7.7 \times 10^{-7} at n = 30, 0.015 at n = 40 and 73 at n = 50. Which orders are safe with the factorial formula?

Math questions
B8. (math) Using \int_0^{2\pi}e^{i(m'-m)\theta}d\theta = 2\pi\delta_{mm'} and the radial orthogonality, show \iint \overline{V_{nm}}V_{n'm'}\,\rho\,d\rho\,d\theta = \frac{\pi}{n+1}\delta_{nn'}\delta_{mm'}, and that \hat I = \sum Z_{nm}V_{nm} with the given Z_{nm} is the orthogonal projection.
B9. (math) Show that for a real image Z_{n,-m} = \overline{Z_{nm}}, and that a rotation by \alpha multiplies Z_{nm} by e^{-im\alpha}.
B10. (math) In disc coordinates (x = \rho\cos\theta, y = \rho\sin\theta), express Z_{00}, Z_{11} and Z_{20} in geometric moments m_{pq}. What do Z_{11} and Z_{20} measure?
B11. (math) Show that a left–right mirror x \to -x maps Z_{nm} to (-1)^m\overline{Z_{nm}}.






Solutions





B1. (a) \int_0^1 (2\rho^2 - 1)\rho\,d\rho = \tfrac12 - \tfrac12 = 0. \int_0^1 (3\rho^3 - 2\rho)\rho\cdot\rho\,d\rho = \int_0^1 (3\rho^5 - 2\rho^3)\,d\rho = \tfrac12 - \tfrac12 = 0. (b) \int_0^1 (4\rho^5 - 4\rho^3 + \rho)\,d\rho = \tfrac23 - 1 + \tfrac12 = \tfrac16 = \frac{1}{2 \cdot 3}. ✓ (c) 2\rho^2 - 1 = 0 at \rho = 1/\sqrt2 = 0.707: R_{20} goes from -1 at the centre to +1 at the rim. R_{40} starts at 1, dips to -0.5 at \rho^2 = 1/2 and returns to 1 at the rim (two zeros, at \rho = 0.46 and 0.89). R_{22} = \rho^2 rises from 0 to 1 without a zero.
B2. (a) |Z_{22}| = 0.5, phase 53.1°. (b) The phase changes by -2 \cdot 30° = -60°: magnitude 0.5, phase -6.9°, Z_{22} = 0.496 - 0.060i. (c) Top–bottom mirror conjugates: 0.3 - 0.4i (phase -53.1°), magnitude still 0.5.
B3. (a) (0,0); (1,\pm1); (2,0), (2,\pm2); (3,\pm1), (3,\pm3); (4,0), (4,\pm2), (4,\pm4): 15 polynomials, 9 with m \ge 0. (b) (20 + 2)^2/4 = 121 moments with m \ge 0. Real numbers: the 11 moments with m = 0 are real, the 110 others complex: 11 + 220 = 231 = (N+1)(N+2)/2, the same count as the Legendre moments up to order 20.
B4. (a) 3228/4096 = 78.8\,\% (the continuous value is \pi/4 = 78.5\,\%). (b) The basis is only defined on the disc: the reconstruction is 0 (or undefined) in the corners, a large error there. (c) A circumscribed disc covers the whole square, but a quarter of its area (1 - 2/\pi = 36\,\%) lies outside the image: those parts are treated as 0, which looks like a sharp edge and causes ringing. Or crop/mask the object so that it lies inside the disc on a dark background, which is the usual choice for shape description.
B5. (a) V_{20} = 2\rho^2 - 1: a paraboloid, the wavefront curved like a lens that is too strong or too weak; the constant -1 only shifts it so that its mean over the pupil is 0. (b) V_{2,\pm2} = \rho^2\cos 2\theta and \rho^2\sin 2\theta: a saddle, the focus differs between two perpendicular directions; the pattern repeats twice around the pupil. (c) A tilt of the wavefront moves the whole image sideways without blurring it; it is a shift, not a loss of sharpness.
B6. (a) A 9 is a 6 rotated by 180°, and rotation changes only phases. (b) Z_{11} turns by -180° (sign change), Z_{22} by -360° \equiv 0°: unchanged. In general odd m change sign, even m stay. (c) b and d are mirror images: mirroring conjugates the moments (up to the sign (-1)^m), so the magnitudes are the same. A phase difference, for example the phase of Z_{31} relative to that of Z_{11} (a combination that is rotation invariant but changes under mirroring, like Hu’s \phi_7), separates them.
B7. (a) Relative rounding errors of 10^{-16} on terms of size 5 \times 10^{13}: absolute errors around 5 \times 10^{-3}, consistent with the measured 0.015. (b) Up to about n = 30 (error below 10^{-6}); at n = 40 the error is 1.5 % of the range of R; at n = 50 the result is meaningless.









Solutions (math)





B8. \iint \overline{V_{nm}}V_{n'm'} = \int_0^1 R_{nm}R_{n'm'}\rho\,d\rho\int_0^{2\pi}e^{i(m'-m)\theta}d\theta. The angular integral is 2\pi\delta_{mm'}; for m = m' the radial integral is \frac{1}{2(n+1)}\delta_{nn'}; product \frac{\pi}{n+1}\delta\delta. With an orthogonal basis the projection is \sum \frac{\langle I, V_{nm}\rangle}{\langle V_{nm}, V_{nm}\rangle}V_{nm}, and \frac{\langle I, V_{nm}\rangle}{\pi/(n+1)} = \frac{n+1}{\pi}\iint I\,\overline{V_{nm}} = Z_{nm}.
B9. \overline{V_{nm}} = R_{nm}e^{-im\theta} = V_{n,-m} (R_{nm} depends only on |m|). For real I: Z_{n,-m} = \frac{n+1}{\pi}\iint I\,\overline{V_{n,-m}} = \frac{n+1}{\pi}\iint I\,V_{nm} = \overline{Z_{nm}}. Rotation: I'(\rho, \theta) = I(\rho, \theta - \alpha); substitute \theta = \theta' + \alpha: Z'_{nm} = \frac{n+1}{\pi}\iint I(\rho, \theta')R_{nm}e^{-im(\theta' + \alpha)} = e^{-im\alpha}Z_{nm}.
B10. Z_{00} = \frac1\pi\iint I = \frac{m_{00}}{\pi}. Z_{11} = \frac2\pi\iint I\rho e^{-i\theta} = \frac2\pi\iint I(x - iy) = \frac2\pi(m_{10} - im_{01}): the centroid’s offset from the disc centre (0 for a centred object). Z_{20} = \frac3\pi\iint I(2\rho^2 - 1) = \frac3\pi\big(2(m_{20} + m_{02}) - m_{00}\big): the spread \mu_{20} + \mu_{02} (for a centred object) compared with the disc, i.e. \phi_1 in disguise.
B11. x \to -x maps \theta \to \pi - \theta. Z'_{nm} = \frac{n+1}{\pi}\iint I(\rho, \pi - \theta)R_{nm}e^{-im\theta}; with \theta = \pi - \theta': e^{-im(\pi - \theta')} = (-1)^m e^{im\theta'}, so Z'_{nm} = (-1)^m\frac{n+1}{\pi}\iint I R_{nm}e^{im\theta'} = (-1)^m\overline{Z_{nm}}.

title: Exercise: Zernike moments on the unit disc
text:
Explore: the Zernike polynomials
basis: the real Zernike polynomials for n \le 8 as a pyramid (rows n, columns m; R_{nm}\cos m\theta for m \ge 0, R_{n|m|}\sin |m|\theta for m < 0), red positive, blue negative. Click one for the large view, its radial profile and its name in optics; |V| shows the magnitude |R_{nm}(\rho)|. rotation: a 64 \times 64 test image (a blob, a 6, an F) and a copy rotated by \alpha (optionally mirrored), both drawn from their outlines with partial pixels; the bars compare |Z_{nm}| (n \le 8, m \ge 0) of both, and the dial shows the phase of one Z_{nm} before (orange) and after (blue).



Z1. Preset defocus: read the zero of R_{20} from the profile and compare with B1(c). Click (4, 0) and (6, 0): how many zeros? Where do the rings crowd?
Z2. Switch to |V|. Why do all tiles of the same n and |m| look the same?
Z3. Preset rotate: magnitudes stay (blob, 60°). Read the largest relative difference of |Z_{nm}| and the phase change of Z_{22}. Choose Z_{11} and Z_{33} too. Then try \alpha = 15° and 45°. Explain the differences.
Z4. Preset 6 vs 9. Compare the two images and the bars. Choose Z_{11}, Z_{22}, Z_{31} and read the phase changes. Compare with B6.
Z5. Preset same |Z|, different shape: an F and its mirror image. Are the bars the same? What happens to the phase of Z_{31}? Compare with the rule for a left–right mirror. Untick mirror and set \alpha = 90°: what is the phase change of Z_{31} now?






Solutions





Z1. The profile crosses 0 at \rho \approx 0.71 (1/\sqrt2). R_{40} has 2 zeros, R_{60} has 3; the outer zeros are closer together: the rings crowd towards the rim, where the area (weight \rho) is largest.
Z2. |V_{nm}| = |R_{nm}(\rho)|\cdot|e^{im\theta}| = |R_{nm}(\rho)|: the angular factor has magnitude 1, so only rings remain, the same for +m and -m. (In the cos/sin view, \cos m\theta and \sin m\theta have different magnitudes; their combination e^{im\theta} does not.)
Z3. Largest difference 1.5 % (for moments above 2 % of |Z_{00}|); Z_{22} phase change -120° = -2 \cdot 60°, Z_{11} -60°, Z_{33} -180°. At 15°: 1.9 %, phase change -30°; at 45°: 3.0 %, -90°. The magnitudes would be exactly equal for the continuous shape; the differences come from drawing the rotated outline on square pixels, which is not a rotation of the pixels; how large the effect is depends on how the edges fall on the grid at each angle.
Z4. The rotated 6 is a 9; the bars are identical (difference 0.0 %: a 180° rotation maps the pixel grid onto itself exactly). Z_{11}: -180°, Z_{22}: 0°, Z_{31}: -180°: odd m change sign, even m stay, as in B6. The phases, not the magnitudes, tell 6 from 9.
Z5. The bars are identical (0.0 %). The phase of Z_{31} goes from 41° to 139°: (-1)^1\overline{Z} has phase 180° - 41° = 139°. ✓ With a rotation of 90° instead (no mirror): 41° \to -49°, a change of -90° = -1 \cdot 90°.

title: Exercise: Zernike moments on the unit disc
section: Explore: the disc and the noise
text:
Explore: the disc and the noise
The reconstruction demo of the previous unit; look at the Zernike panel (dashed: the inscribed disc) and the green curve.



E1. Preset Zernike outside the disc (micrograph, N = 20). Compare the four errors. Why is the Zernike error so large, and why does the Zernike curve hardly fall with N?
E2. Choose nucleus and N = 2, 8 and 20. Compare Zernike with Legendre at each. Why can Zernike be better here?
E3. Preset noise in high orders (nucleus, \sigma = 0.3). Find the best N for Zernike and its error, and the error at N = 40. Compare with Legendre and Fourier. Where in the Zernike panel does the noise show most at N = 40?






Solutions





E1. Monomials 0.142, Legendre 0.160, Zernike 0.552, Fourier 0.139. The Zernike reconstruction is 0 outside the disc, and the micrograph is bright there: those 21 % of the pixels carry a large error whatever N is, so the curve stays near 0.55. Inside the disc alone the Zernike error is 0.158, like the others.
E2. N = 2: Zernike 0.571, Legendre 0.685; N = 8: 0.324 and 0.361; N = 20: 0.185 and 0.226. The nucleus is a roundish object in the middle of a dark square: a basis that lives on the disc spends no effort on the empty corners, and its low orders are round blobs, close to the shape.
E3. Zernike is best at N = 18 (0.257); at N = 40 it is 0.421, worse than Legendre (0.340) and Fourier (0.318). The noise shows as speckle concentrated towards the rim of the disc: the high-order radial polynomials oscillate fastest there and fit the noise of the outer pixels.

title: Exercise: Zernike moments on the unit disc
text:
Where this leads
Magnitudes of Zernike moments (or Hu’s invariants) turn a shape into a short vector of numbers. With a training set of labelled shapes, such vectors can be fed to a classifier: nearest class mean, nearest neighbour, or the random forests of day 14, which owns training and testing. Moments describe the mass distribution and are blind to topology and thin branches: the skeleton elective gives the complementary features. In 3D, the same construction gives the 3 \times 3 inertia tensor of a labelled volume and 3D Zernike moments with spherical harmonics as the angular part.

title: Cross-correlation with the FFT
text:
About this lecture
Last unit: slide image B over image A and score every shift; the cross-correlation c(t) = \sum_x A(x+t)\,B(x) for all shifts costs about N^2 operations for N pixels. Today: all shifts at once with three FFTs.

Correlation is a convolution with a flipped image; flipping a real image conjugates its spectrum.
So: FFT both, multiply one spectrum by the conjugate of the other, inverse FFT.
Why it works, in pictures: every wave votes for the shifts at which it agrees.
The FFT assumes the images repeat: circular vs linear correlation, zero-padding.
The cost, worked out, and when brute force still wins. NCC with the FFT.

Recall: complex numbers z = |z|e^{i\varphi}, \bar z = |z|e^{-i\varphi}, z\bar z = |z|^2.
Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: Cross-correlation with the FFT
text:
Three facts from earlier units

Correlation vs convolution (the kernels unit): correlation multiplies the pixels under the kernel as they are; convolution flips the kernel first. Correlating with B is convolving with B flipped.
The convolution theorem (the Fourier unit): convolution in the image is a product of the spectra, one multiplication per frequency.
The FFT (the Fourier unit): the DFT of N samples in about N \log_2 N steps instead of N^2.

One more fact, new today: for a real image, flipping it in space (reading it backwards) gives the complex conjugate of its spectrum: same sizes, opposite phases.

title: Cross-correlation with the FFT
text:
All shifts at once


c(t) for every shift t = inverse FFT of A_k \cdot \overline{B_k}.
Two forward FFTs, one product per frequency, one inverse FFT.
The correlation is a convolution of A with B flipped, and flipping B conjugates its spectrum.

title: Cross-correlation with the FFT
text:
The math: the correlation theorem
Signals of length N, indices modulo N, DFT F_k = \sum_x f(x)\,e^{-2\pi i kx/N}. The circular cross-correlation c(t) = \sum_x f(x+t)\,g(x) has the DFT \hat c_k = \sum_t e^{-2\pi i kt/N} \sum_x f(x+t)\,g(x) = \sum_x g(x)\,e^{2\pi i kx/N} \sum_t f(x+t)\,e^{-2\pi i k(x+t)/N} = \overline{G_k}\;F_k, substituting u = x + t in the inner sum, and using that g is real, so \sum_x g(x)e^{2\pi i kx/N} = \overline{G_k}.
Equivalently: c = f * g^- with g^-(x) = g(-x), and \widehat{g^-} = \overline{G} for real g; then the convolution theorem. The same holds in 2D with kx \to k_x x + k_y y and N \to each side.

title: Cross-correlation with the FFT
section: Why the product works: waves vote
text:
Why the product works: waves vote
Write both images as sums of waves (the Fourier unit). Look at one frequency k:

The wave in A and the wave in B have the same frequency, but each has its own position (phase). A_k \overline{B_k} records how far B’s wave is shifted relative to A’s (the phase difference) and how strong the wave is in both.
The inverse FFT adds all the waves back up. At a shift t, each wave’s contribution is largest if moving by t makes its two copies line up.
At the true shift all waves line up: their votes add up to the peak. Elsewhere they partly cancel.

Strong waves (usually the slow ones) get big votes. Next unit: give every wave the same vote.

title: Cross-correlation with the FFT
section: Try it: FFT vs brute force
text:
Try it: FFT vs brute force




Top left: A and B (32 samples). Top right: c(t), the dots computed directly for every shift, the green line from the FFT; the readout says they agree to about 1e-11. Bottom left: one arrow per frequency k = 1..12, the contribution of that wave at the current shift t; green = pointing right (agrees). Move “shift t” to the true shift 5 and watch the arrows turn right. “waves line up” (N = 16, t = 3) shows it with fewer arrows. “wrap-around fools it”: the circular correlation peaks at −3 (11314) instead of 9 (9966). “padding fixes it”: with zero-padding to 64 the peak is at 9 and the dots (linear, direct) and the line agree again. “by hand: length 4” is the example on the next slide. Bottom right: the cost of the three routes for two n × n images.

title: Cross-correlation with the FFT
text:
By hand: a length-4 example
A = (0, 1, 2, 0) and B = (1, 2, 0, 0): B’s pattern sits one step to the left, so B belongs at t = 1 on A.
Directly: c(t) = \sum_x A(x+t)B(x) with wrap-around: c = (2, 5, 2, 0) for t = 0, 1, 2, 3. Peak at t = 1.

title: Cross-correlation with the FFT
text:
Circular or linear?
The DFT treats each image as one period of a repeating pattern. Shifting B pushes it out on one side and back in on the other: the FFT gives the circular correlation (the “wrap” border rule of the kernels unit).

Two tiles that only partly overlap are not periodic: the wrapped-around part compares pixels that never lie on top of each other.
The circular peak can be wrong, and a shift t cannot be told from t - N.
Zero-pad: put each image into an array of at least 2N - 1 (in practice 2N) filled with zeros. Shifted parts now fall on zeros instead of wrapping: the linear correlation, exactly what sliding computes.

Padding costs FFTs four times as large in 2D. Stitching tools often skip it and test the candidate shifts instead (the stitching unit).

title: Cross-correlation with the FFT
text:
Try it: wrap-around and padding




Seed 1, 32 samples, true shift 9 (dotted green line). Circular: the peak is at −3, where the wrapped-around end of B happens to fit (11314 against 9966 at the truth). Tick “zero-pad to 2N”: the transform length becomes 64, the shifts run from −31 to 31, and the peak moves to 9 (14735). The dots are now the direct linear correlation, and the FFT line still lies on them. Untick “subtract the means” to see how the mean adds a large triangle (more overlap = larger sum) on top of the correlation.

title: Cross-correlation with the FFT
text:
What it costs
Two 1024 \times 1024 tiles, padded to 2048 \times 2048 (M \approx 4.2 \cdot 10^6 samples):

One complex FFT: about 5M\log_2 M \approx 4.6 \cdot 10^8 operations. Three FFTs: 1.4 \cdot 10^9.
Brute force, every shift: 1024^4 multiply-adds \approx 2.2 \cdot 10^{12} operations.
About 1600 times fewer operations: under a second instead of 18 minutes at the same speed (tuned FFTs are faster still).

But with a small search window, brute force is competitive:

\pm 32 pixels: 4.3 \cdot 10^9 multiply-adds, 8.6 \cdot 10^9 operations: only 6 times more than the FFT.
Up to about \pm 12 pixels, brute force needs fewer operations.

The FFT wins when the shift is unknown or large.

title: Cross-correlation with the FFT
text:
The math: counting operations
With N \times N images padded to M = (2N)^2 samples, and \approx 5M\log_2 M real operations per complex FFT: \text{FFT route} \approx 3 \cdot 5M\log_2 M + 6M, \qquad \text{brute force} \approx 2 \sum_{t}(N - |t_x|)(N - |t_y|) = 2N^4. For N = 1024: 1.4 \cdot 10^9 against 2.2 \cdot 10^{12}. The ratio grows like N^2/\log N.
A window |t_x|, |t_y| \le w costs 2\big((2w + 1)N - w(w+1)\big)^2 \approx 2(2w+1)^2N^2; this equals the FFT route at (2w+1)^2 \approx 30\log_2(4N^2), i.e. w \approx 12 for N = 1024.

title: Cross-correlation with the FFT
text:
NCC with the FFT
NCC at shift t needs, over the overlap: the sum of products, the sums of A and B, and the sums of their squares.

Sum of products: a cross-correlation, one FFT product.
Local sums of A and A^2 (and of B, B^2): the sum of the pixels of A that lie under B at shift t is A correlated with a block of ones the size of B. Also a correlation: FFT again.
Then NCC for every shift from these sums, pixel by pixel.

The local sums are box filters; the integral-images elective computes them even faster with summed-area tables. Template matching in the last unit’s demo works this way.

title: Cross-correlation with the FFT
text:
The math: NCC from correlations
With the overlap mask M_B (ones where B has pixels), all sums over the overlap \Omega_t are correlations: S_{AB}(t) = \sum f(x+t)g(x), \quad S_A(t) = \sum f(x+t)M_B(x), \quad S_{AA}(t) = \sum f(x+t)^2 M_B(x), \quad n(t) = \sum M_A(x+t)M_B(x), and likewise S_B, S_{BB} with M_A. Then \mathrm{NCC}(t) = \frac{S_{AB} - S_A S_B/n}{\sqrt{\big(S_{AA} - S_A^2/n\big)\big(S_{BB} - S_B^2/n\big)}}. Six correlations (all zero-padded), each one product of FFTs: still \mathcal O(M\log M). For a template that always lies inside A, n, S_B and S_{BB} are constants.

title: Cross-correlation with the FFT
text:
Summary

Cross-correlation for all shifts = inverse FFT of A_k\overline{B_k}: two FFTs, a product, an inverse FFT.
Each frequency votes with its phase difference and its strength; at the true shift all votes agree.
The FFT gives the circular correlation; for partly overlapping images zero-pad to 2N to get the linear one.
About N\log N instead of N^2 operations: thousands of times faster for megapixel tiles, but a small search window can be cheaper by brute force.
NCC also goes through FFTs: the products and the local sums are all correlations.

title: Quiz: images as landscapes
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. The image is a landscape (grey level = height); water rises from every regional minimum (or only from markers), and a dam is built where two lakes meet.

Q1. You flood an image of bright nuclei on a dark background. Where do the basins start, and what should you flood instead?






Hint





Water collects in valleys.









Answer





The minima are in the dark background, so the basins grow from the background and the dams fall on the bright nuclei: the wrong way round. Flood the inverted image (255 - f, or -f): the nuclei become valleys. Or flood the gradient magnitude, whose valleys are the flat insides of nuclei and background alike.




Q2. A 1D signal has regional minima at samples 4 and 11 and no other minimum between them. The highest sample between them has height 9, at sample 7. Where is the dam, and at which water level is it built?






Hint





When can the two lakes first touch?









Answer





At sample 7, at level 9. Below 9 the two lakes are separated by sample 7; at 9 both reach it. The dam height is the pass between the basins.




Q3. Why does flooding the gradient magnitude put the boundaries on edges, and flooding the intensity not?






Hint





Where is \|\nabla f\| small, and where large?









Answer





The gradient magnitude is small inside regions of nearly constant intensity (valleys) and large on edges (ridges); the dams sit on ridges, so on the edges. Flooding the intensity puts the basins in the dark parts and the dams on the brightest lines between them, which are edges only when the objects are dark valleys separated by bright ridges.




Q4. A noisy image of 20 cells gives 3000 regions after the watershed of its gradient. What went wrong?






Hint





Count the sources.









Answer





Every regional minimum of the landscape starts a basin, and noise makes thousands of tiny minima: oversegmentation. Fewer sources are needed: smooth first, keep only the minima deeper than h (h-minima), or flood from markers.




Q5. A basin has its bottom at 30 and its lowest pass to a deeper basin at 34. Does it survive h-minima with h = 3? With h = 4? With h = 5?






Hint





Its depth is 4. A basin survives when it is deeper than h.









Answer





h = 3: yes (filled to 33, still below its pass). h = 4: no (filled to 34, it reaches the pass and merges). h = 5: no.




Q6. You flood from 3 markers. There are 40 regional minima. How many regions do you get, and what happens to the other 37 minima?






Hint





Only markers are sources.









Answer





3 regions (if every pixel can be reached from some marker). The 37 unmarked minima are not sources: each is filled by water from whichever marker reaches it first, so it becomes part of that marker’s region (it is “drowned”).




Q7. A wide flat ridge (a plateau) separates two basins. Where should the dam go, and why does the order of flooding on the plateau matter?






Hint





Both lakes reach the plateau at the same level.









Answer





In its middle: both lakes arrive at the same level, one at each end, and should spread over the plateau at the same speed. The flooding algorithm achieves this by processing equal heights first in, first out; a different order (e.g. last in, first out) lets one lake run across the plateau and the dam ends up in an arbitrary place.




Q8. (math) For f(x, y) = (x^2 - 1)^2 + y^2, what are the two catchment basins, and what is the height of the pass between the minima?






Hint





Follow -\nabla f; the x component is -4x(x^2 - 1).









Answer





The half-planes x < 0 and x > 0 (the sign of x never changes along the flow); the watershed line is x = 0. The pass is the saddle at (0, 0), height f(0, 0) = 1.

title: Exercise: images as landscapes
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Landscape
grey level f = height; dark = low


Regional minimum
a connected plateau whose neighbours are all higher (in 1D: the samples left and right of the run)


Catchment basin
the points from which water running downhill ends in that minimum


Flooding
water rises from every minimum at the same level; where two lakes meet, a dam is built


Dam height (pass)
the level at which two basins first touch = the highest point on the lowest way between them


Depth of a basin
its bottom subtracted from the lowest pass to a deeper basin


h-minima
fill every basin by h first (the morphology day); basins of depth \le h disappear


Markers
the only sources of water; unmarked minima are drowned



In 1D, a sample on a pass that both lakes reach at the same level is either a dam sample (watershed line) or given to the lake that reached it first. When a question asks for “the basin of every sample”, give it to the basin on its left if both reach it at the same time (this is what the demo and the algorithm of the next unit do here).

title: Exercise: images as landscapes
text:
By hand
The signal (samples 0–11), the same as on the morphology day: f = 7\,1\,4\,3\,4\,6\,5\,1\,6\,4\,2\,3 .
B1. Regional minima and flooding. (a) Mark the regional minima. Name their basins A, B, C, D from left to right. (b) Flood level by level, L = 1, 2, \dots, 7. At each level, which samples are under water, and in which basin? At which levels do two lakes meet, and where? (c) Write the basin of every sample, and the position and height of every dam.
B2. h-minima with h = 2. (a) The h-minima transform (morphology day) is \mathrm{HMIN}_2(f) = 7\,3\,4\,4\,4\,6\,5\,3\,6\,4\,4\,4. Which minima survive? What is the depth of each of the four basins of B1? (b) Flood f again, but only from the surviving minima. Write the basin of every sample and the dams. (c) Which h is the smallest that removes the basin of sample 3? Does h = 1 already do it?
B3. Markers only at samples 3 and 10 (labels A and B). (a) Flood from these markers only. In which order are the samples flooded? (Hint: the water of A spills into the minimum at sample 1 as soon as it reaches sample 2.) (b) Write the basin of every sample and the dam. What happened to the minima at samples 1 and 7?
B4. The step profile f = 1\,1\,1\,1\,5\,5\,5\,2\,2\,2 (samples 0–9). (a) Compute |f'| by central differences, |f(i+1) - f(i-1)|/2, repeating the end samples (f(-1) = f(0), f(10) = f(9)). (b) How many regional minima do f and |f'| have? Flood both. Where are the boundaries in each case? (c) Which of the two do you want if the three flat parts are three different materials?
B5. A noisy flat profile f = 3\,2\,3\,2\,3\,2\,3. (a) How many regional minima, how many regions after flooding? (b) What is the depth of each basin? Which h removes them, and how many regions are left?
B6. A drop of water. On the signal of B1, follow a drop placed on sample 5 (height 6): at each step it moves to the lower of its two neighbours, if that is lower than where it is. Where does it end? Do the same from sample 8. Compare with the basins of B1(c).






Solutions





B1. (a) Minima at samples 1 (height 1), 3 (3), 7 (1) and 10 (2): basins A, B, C, D. (b)

Basins A\,A\,A\,B\,B\,B\,C\,C\,C\,D\,D\,D (samples 2, 5 and 8 sit on the passes; with the rule above they go to the basin on their left). Dams on samples 2, 5 and 8, heights 4, 6, 6. With a watershed line: A\,A\,|\,B\,B\,|\,C\,C\,|\,D\,D\,D.

B2. (a) \mathrm{HMIN}_2 has regional minima at sample 1 (3), sample 7 (3) and the plateau 9–11 (4): three survive. Depths: A: the lowest pass to a deeper basin is 6 (sample 5, towards C; C is as deep as A) and to B 4, but B is shallower; A’s depth is 6 - 1 = 5. B: 4 - 3 = 1 (it overflows into A at 4). C: 5 (pass 6 to A’s side and to D; A is as deep). D: 6 - 2 = 4. Only B has depth \le 2. (b) A\,A\,A\,A\,A\,A\,B\,B\,B\,C\,C\,C (three basins, now called A, B, C): B’s old samples 3 and 4 are taken by A’s water when it passes sample 2 at level 4; sample 5 (6) is reached by A before C. Dams on samples 5 and 8, both height 6. With a line: A\,A\,A\,A\,A\,|\,B\,B\,|\,C\,C\,C. (c) The basin of sample 3 has depth 1: it disappears for every h \ge 1 (a basin survives only if its depth is larger than h). So h = 1 already removes it; \mathrm{HMIN}_1(f) = 7\,2\,4\,4\,4\,6\,5\,2\,6\,4\,3\,3.
B3. (a) The queue starts with the neighbours of the markers: samples 2 (4), 4 (4), 9 (4) and 11 (3). Order of flooding: 11 (3, B), 2 (4, A), then 1 (height 1, A): lower than the current water level 4, so it is flooded immediately: the puddle at sample 1 is drowned; then 4 (A), 9 (B); at level 6: 5 (A), then 6 (5, A) and 7 (1, A), again a drowned puddle; then 8 (6), which both A and B reach: the dam; finally 0 (7, A). (b) A\,A\,A\,A\,A\,A\,A\,A\,B\,B\,B\,B, dam on sample 8 (height 6). The minima at samples 1 and 7 are not sources: they are filled from marker A, so A’s region contains three of the original basins. Two markers, two regions.
B4. (a) |f'| = 0\,0\,0\,2\,2\,0\,1.5\,1.5\,0\,0. (b) f has 2 regional minima (the plateau of 1s, samples 0–3, and the plateau of 2s, samples 7–9); flooding f gives 2 regions, and the bright middle (samples 4–6) is shared between them (A\,A\,A\,A\,A\,A\,B\,B\,B\,B; with a line, the line is on sample 5): the boundary falls in the middle of the bright plateau, not on an edge. |f'| has 3 minima (samples 0–2, sample 5, samples 8–9), so 3 regions; the boundaries are on samples 3–4 and 6–7, where the ridges of |f'| are: on the edges. Without line: A\,A\,A\,A\,B\,B\,B\,C\,C\,C; with line: A\,A\,A\,A\,|\,B\,B\,|\,C\,C. (c) The gradient: it gives one region per flat part, with boundaries on the edges.
B5. (a) Three regional minima (the 2s at samples 1, 3, 5): three regions. (b) Each basin has depth 1 (bottom 2, pass 3). Any h \ge 1 fills all three to 3: the whole signal becomes one plateau at height 3, a single minimum, one region. With h = 0.5 all three survive.
B6. From sample 5 (6): neighbours 4 (4) and 6 (5); the lower is sample 4, then sample 3 (3), whose neighbours (4 and 4) are both higher: it ends in the minimum at sample 3: basin B, as in B1. From sample 8 (6): neighbours 7 (1) and 9 (4): it goes to sample 7, the minimum of basin C, as in B1. On a pass the drop chooses the steeper side; flooding chooses the side that reaches the sample first. Here both agree.




Math questions
B7 (math). In 1D, take two consecutive regional minima a < b (no other minimum between them). Show that flooding builds exactly one dam between them, at the highest sample between a and b, and that its height is \max_{a \le i \le b} f(i).
B8 (math). Let g be strictly increasing. Show that flooding g(f) from the same markers gives the same basins as flooding f (with the same tie-breaking). Is the same true for the h-minima markers with a fixed h? Give an example.
B9 (math). For f(x, y) = (x^2 - 1)^2 + y^2: (a) find all critical points and classify them; (b) solve the gradient flow \dot{\mathbf x} = -\nabla f for the y component and show that the sign of x is preserved for the x component; (c) conclude what the two catchment basins and the watershed line are, and give the height of the pass between the two minima.






Solutions (math)





B7. Between a and b the signal rises from a to its maximum M (at sample t; take the first if several) and falls to b; otherwise there would be another regional minimum between them. Water from a can only move right by flooding samples in order, and it reaches a sample i \in (a, t] when the level is \max_{a \le j \le i} f(j); likewise from b leftwards. Both lakes are below M until the level reaches M, so they cannot meet before; at level M both reach t (or the plateau of Ms), and they meet there: one dam, of height M = \max_{a \le i \le b} f(i), the pass of the minimax formula with a single path.
B8. Flooding only ever compares heights: the queue pops the smallest f (ties by arrival order), and the labels are decided by which neighbours are already labelled. A strictly increasing g preserves every comparison f(p) < f(q) and every tie f(p) = f(q), so the pops come in the same order, with the same decisions: the same basins. h-minima are not invariant: they compare differences of heights (\text{depth} \le h), and g changes differences. Example: f = 3\,2\,3 (depth 1) and g(v) = v^2: 9\,4\,9 (depth 5). With h = 2, the minimum disappears for f but survives for g(f). (Contrast stretching changes which h is right.)
B9. (a) \nabla f = (4x(x^2 - 1),\ 2y), zero at (0, 0) and (\pm 1, 0). Hessian \mathrm{diag}(12x^2 - 4,\ 2): at (\pm 1, 0) it is \mathrm{diag}(8, 2), two minima (f = 0); at (0, 0) it is \mathrm{diag}(-4, 2), a saddle (f = 1). (b) \dot y = -2y gives y(t) = y_0 e^{-2t} \to 0. \dot x = -4x(x^2 - 1): the right-hand side is zero at x = 0, so by uniqueness a solution starting with x_0 > 0 can never cross x = 0; it converges to the stable point x = 1 (for 0 < x < 1, \dot x > 0; for x > 1, \dot x < 0). Likewise x_0 < 0 goes to -1. (c) Basins: the half-planes x > 0 (minimum (1, 0)) and x < 0 (minimum (-1, 0)); watershed line x = 0 (from there the flow runs into the saddle). The pass between the minima is the saddle height f(0, 0) = 1: along x = 0 the function is 1 + y^2 \ge 1, so every path from one minimum to the other has a highest point of at least 1, and the straight path along y = 0 achieves 1.

title: Watershed segmentation of a real image
text:
About this lecture
We have the picture (flood a landscape) and the algorithm (a priority queue). Now a real image: flood the gradient magnitude, so the dams fall on edges.

On the raw gradient every speck of noise is a minimum: thousands of regions.
Three cures, each with its price: smooth more, h-minima, markers.
Region merging: the watershed as a hierarchy of basins.
Where the watershed fails: leakage through a gap in an edge.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: Watershed segmentation of a real image
text:
The landscape: gradient magnitude
g = \big\|\nabla (G_\sigma * I)\big\|

Smooth with a Gaussian of width \sigma, take the derivatives in x and y, combine: the gradient of a Gaussian (the kernels day; Gaussian derivatives at scale \sigma: the edges day).
Inside a region of nearly constant grey level, g is small: a valley. On an edge, g is large: a ridge.
Flooding g puts one basin in every region and the dams on the edges between them. The objects do not need to be darker or brighter than the background, only different.

title: Watershed segmentation of a real image
section: The math: edge and noise after smoothing
text:
The math: edge and noise after smoothing
A step of height J, already blurred by the optics (\sigma_0), and white noise of standard deviation s:

Edge: the gradient of the Gaussian-blurred step peaks at J / \big(\sqrt{2\pi}\, \sigma_{\text{tot}}\big) with \sigma_{\text{tot}} = \sqrt{\sigma_0^2 + \sigma^2} (Gaussians add their variances).
Noise: each derivative component has variance s^2 \sum_k (\partial_x G_\sigma)_k^2 \approx s^2 / (8\pi\sigma^4), so its standard deviation falls like 1/\sigma^2.
Test image (J = 95, \sigma_0 = 1.2, s = 8): \sigma = 1.5: edge 19.7, noise about 0.9 (mean of \|\nabla\|); \sigma = 4: edge 9.1, noise 0.13. The ratio grows from 22 to 73, but the noise dips never reach depth 0.
So: smoothing sets the scale of the edges; the depth of the noise basins must be dealt with separately.

title: Watershed segmentation of a real image
text:
The math: what h removes
Depth (dynamic) of a regional minimum m: \mathrm{dyn}(m) = \min_{\text{paths } m \to \text{deeper minimum}} \max_{\text{path}} g \; - \; g(m): how far the water must rise in m’s basin before it overflows into a deeper one.

The regional minima of \mathrm{HMIN}_h(g) are exactly the minima of g with \mathrm{dyn} > h (morphology day); the deepest minimum always survives.
Scaling: \mathrm{dyn} is a difference of heights, so it scales with the landscape: multiply g by c and the right h becomes ch. A strictly increasing transform of g leaves the flooding unchanged but not the h-minima.
Ordering all minima by dynamic and removing them one by one gives a nested family of segmentations: the hierarchy on the region-merging slide.

Look at what the 8 are: the background together with the inside of the ring cell (the gap!), the touching pair of blobs as ONE region (same intensity, no edge between them: the gradient cannot split them; that is the next unit), four separate blobs, the nucleus in the ring cell, and the dark ring itself. title: Watershed segmentation of a real image
text:
Cure 3: marker-controlled watershed
Decide the markers first, then flood from them only.

One marker per object (and one for the background): the markers decide how many regions; the flooding decides where the boundaries go.
Markers from: user clicks, a threshold of the image, the peaks of another image (the distance transform, next unit), detections.
Equivalent formulation: minima imposition (the morphology day) makes the markers the only minima of g and fills every other basin up to its pass; flooding that image from its minima gives the same boundaries.
This is the usual way the watershed is used in practice: markers from a robust, coarse step; boundaries from the watershed.

title: Watershed segmentation of a real image
section: The math: imposition and flooding from markers agree
text:
The math: imposition and flooding from markers agree
Let M be the markers and g^M the imposed landscape: g^M = R^\varepsilon_{\min(g + 1, f_M)}(f_M), with f_M = 0 on M and \max g + 1 elsewhere (the morphology day).

For every pixel p \notin M: g^M(p) = 1 + d(p), where d(p) = \min_{\text{paths } M \to p} \max_{\text{path}} g is the minimax distance from the markers (reconstruction by erosion computes exactly such minimax values).
Flooding g from M pops the pixels in order of d (previous unit). Flooding g^M from its minima (= M): along the best path to p every pixel q has d(q) \le d(p), so the minimax distance in g^M is 1 + d(p): the same order.
Hence the same labels (up to ties). Imposition is useful when a later step needs the landscape itself; the flooding never needs it.

The touching pair is now split, because each blob has its own marker; the boundary follows the weak dip in the gradient between them. title: Watershed segmentation of a real image
text:
Region merging: a hierarchy
Start from the oversegmentation (every minimum a region), then merge neighbouring regions across their lowest dam, one at a time.

Each merge removes the least significant boundary. The sequence of merges is a tree (a dendrogram) of regions: a hierarchical watershed.
Cutting the tree at a dam height t gives a segmentation; cutting it by dynamics gives exactly the h-minima result. Other criteria (area, volume of the basin) give other cuts of the same tree.
One flooding, many segmentations: the user (or a learned criterion) chooses the level afterwards.

title: Watershed segmentation of a real image
section: Leakage: a gap in an edge
text:
Leakage: a gap in an edge

A dam is only as strong as the lowest point on the ridge around a basin. If the edge has a gap, the lowest pass is in the gap, and two regions merge or meet there at a low level.
With markers on both sides, the boundary across the gap is wherever the two lakes happen to meet: anywhere inside the gap, or far from it, since both lakes flood the flat insides at the same low level.
Typical in microscopy: a faint membrane, a touching cell with the same intensity.
What helps: closing the gap first (closing, the morphology day), a better landscape, more markers; or a method that penalises long boundaries: graph cuts (the graph-cut day; “markers” here, “seeds” there) or level sets (elective).

The micrograph preset (“nucleus + background clicks”) shows the same on a real image: the boundary follows the nuclear envelope on the left and leaks at the bottom and top right.

title: Watershed segmentation of a real image
text:
Summary

Flood \|\nabla (G_\sigma * I)\|: one basin per region of nearly constant grey level, dams on edges.
Raw: thousands of noise minima, oversegmentation.
Smoothing reduces the minima but never removes them, and moves edges. h-minima keep minima deeper than h: one interpretable parameter. Markers fix the number of regions; the flooding places the boundaries.
Merging regions across low dams gives a hierarchy; h-minima is one cut of it.
The watershed leaks through gaps in edges; touching objects of equal intensity have no edge between them: the next unit uses the distance transform.

title: Quiz: the flooding algorithm on a grid
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Meyer’s flooding: a priority queue ordered by height (ties: first in, first out); pop the lowest pixel; label it if its labelled neighbours agree, otherwise it is a line pixel; push its unlabelled neighbours.

Q1. The queue holds (height 3, #7), (height 2, #12), (height 2, #9). Which is popped first?






Hint





Height first, then arrival.









Answer





(height 2, #9): the lowest height, and among the two of height 2 the one that arrived first.




Q2. The water level is 5 and a pixel of height 2 is pushed. When is it popped, and what does that mean in the flooding picture?






Hint





It is lower than everything else in the queue.









Answer





Immediately (next): it is the lowest entry. The water has spilled over a pass into an unmarked dip below the current level, and fills it at once: the dip is drowned and joins the region that reached it.




Q3. A popped pixel has labelled neighbours A, A and B. What happens with a watershed line, and what without one?






Hint





“All labelled neighbours the same?”









Answer





With a line: the labels disagree, so the pixel becomes a line pixel and pushes nothing. Without a line: it takes the label of the neighbour that queued it (the one that reached it first), and pushes its neighbours as usual.




Q4. Why are equal heights popped first in, first out?






Hint





Think of a flat plateau between two lakes.









Answer





On a plateau, height cannot decide; arrival order then makes each lake spread as a wavefront, one ring at a time, so two lakes that reach the plateau at the same level meet in its middle. With last in, first out, one lake would race across the plateau and the dam would end up next to the other lake’s entry.




Q5. Why is a one-pixel diagonal line enough to separate the regions with 4 neighbours, but not with 8?






Hint





Two pixels on either side of a diagonal line touch at a corner.









Answer





Across a diagonal line, pixels of the two regions are diagonal neighbours. With 4 neighbours that is not a contact, so the regions are separated. With 8 neighbours they would touch, so the line must be 4-connected (a staircase), which takes more pixels.




Q6. How many times is each pixel pushed and popped, and what does the flooding of an n-pixel 8-bit image cost with a bucket queue?






Hint





A pixel is marked “queued” when it is pushed.









Answer





At most once each. With one FIFO bucket per grey level, push and pop are constant time (plus at most 256 steps of the bucket pointer per upward sweep), so the flooding costs O(n + 256) = O(n). With a binary heap it is O(n \log n).




Q7. A marker sits halfway up a slope, not at a minimum. Is that a problem?






Hint





Where does its water go?









Answer





No. Its neighbours below it are popped first, so its water runs downhill into the basin below and claims it (any unmarked minimum it reaches is drowned). The region is the same as if the marker had been placed at the bottom, unless another marker’s water gets there first.




Q8. (math) What is the “distance” that Meyer’s flooding computes, and which classical algorithm is it?






Hint





Replace the sum of edge lengths by something else.









Answer





The minimax (bottleneck) distance from the markers: the smallest possible “highest point” on a path from a marker to the pixel. The flooding is Dijkstra’s algorithm with \max in place of +; equivalently, Prim’s algorithm growing a minimum spanning forest from all markers at once.

title: Exercise: the flooding algorithm on a grid
text:
By hand
The 5 \times 5 grid, with marker A at (1, 1) and marker B at (4, 4), 4 neighbours, with a watershed line: f = \begin{bmatrix} 3&2&3&5&6 \\ 2&\mathbf{1}&2&4&5 \\ 3&2&4&3&2 \\ 5&4&3&2&1 \\ 6&5&3&1&\mathbf{0} \end{bmatrix}
B1. The queue. (a) Write the starting queue: every entry as (height, #arrival, pixel), in pop order. (b) Do the first eight pops. For each: the popped pixel, its labelled neighbours, the decision, and the pixels it pushes (with their arrival numbers). (c) Write the queue after the eighth pop. (d) Finish the flooding (you do not need to write every queue). Which pixels end on the watershed line? At which water level does the first line pixel appear?
B2. The same grid and markers with 8 neighbours. Without a full trace: which pixels must now be line pixels, and why does the line get thicker? (Then check with the demo.)
B3. A plateau in 1D: f = 0\,5\,5\,5\,5\,5\,0 (samples 0–6), markers A on sample 0 and B on sample 6, with a watershed line. (a) Trace the flooding with first in, first out among equal heights. Where is the line? (b) Trace it again with last in, first out among equal heights. Where is the line now? (c) Which result would you call correct, and why?
B4. A marker that is not a minimum: f = 5\,3\,1\,2\,4\,6\,4\,2\,0\,2 (samples 0–9), markers A on sample 0 (height 5) and B on sample 8 (height 0), with a watershed line. (a) How many regional minima does f have, and which one has no marker? (b) Trace the pops (pixel, height, water level, decision). What happens to the minimum at sample 2? (c) Write the result.
B5. Cost. A 1024 \times 1024 image with 8-bit heights. (a) Estimate the number of elementary steps for the flooding with a binary heap (\approx n \log_2 n) and with a bucket queue (\approx n + 256). How much faster is the bucket queue? (b) Would you use a bucket queue for a 16-bit image? For the gradient magnitude stored as floating-point numbers?
B6. Why must a line pixel not push its neighbours? Describe what would go wrong on the grid of B1 if (1, 3) pushed (0, 3) and (1, 4) after becoming a line pixel.

B1. (a) A (processed first, in reading order) queues its neighbours up, left, right, down: (0,1) #0, (1,0) #1, (1,2) #2, (2,1) #3, all height 2. B queues (3,4) #4 and (4,3) #5, height 1. In pop order: (1, #4, (3,4)), (1, #5, (4,3)), (2, #0, (0,1)), (2, #1, (1,0)), (2, #2, (1,2)), (2, #3, (2,1)). (b)

Pops 9–14 at level 3 label (4,2) B, (0,0) A, (0,2) A, (2,0) A, (2,3) B, (3,2) B. Pop 15, (1,3) at height 4: its neighbours (0,3) and (1,4) are not yet labelled, (1,2) is A and (2,3) is B: line. Then (2,2) and (3,1) (height 4) are lines too (A and B on both sides). Level 5: (1,4) → B, (4,1) → B, (0,3) → A, (3,0) → A. Level 6: (0,4) and (4,0) are lines. Result (| = line): \begin{matrix} A&A&A&A&| \\ A&A&A&|&B \\ A&A&|&B&B \\ A&|&B&B&B \\ |&B&B&B&B \end{matrix} Five line pixels on the anti-diagonal; the first appears at water level 4 (pop 15). 23 pops in total.

B2. With 8 neighbours, A and B pixels must not even touch diagonally. On the anti-diagonal line of B1, the A pixel (1,2) and the B pixel (2,3) are diagonal neighbours, so a one-pixel diagonal line no longer separates them: the line has to be 4-connected, a staircase. The flooding gives 7 line pixels: (1,3), (1,4), (2,2), (2,3), (3,1), (3,2), (4,1); the corners (0,4) and (4,0) become A. In general the regions and the line use complementary connectivities: 4-connected regions need only an 8-connected line, 8-connected regions need a 4-connected line.
B3. (a) Start: sample 1 #0 (A), sample 5 #1 (B). Pops: 1 → A (pushes 2 #2), 5 → B (pushes 4 #3), 2 → A (pushes 3 #4), 4 → B (3 already queued), 3: neighbours A and B → line. A\,A\,A\,|\,B\,B\,B: the line in the middle. (b) LIFO: 5 (#1) → B, pushes 4 #2; 4 → B, pushes 3 #3; 3: only B labelled → B, pushes 2 #4; 2 → B (its other neighbour, 1, is queued but unlabelled); 1 (#0): neighbours A and B → line. A\,|\,B\,B\,B\,B\,B. (c) FIFO: both lakes reach the plateau at the same level and should spread at the same speed, so the dam belongs in the middle. LIFO lets one lake run across first; where the line ends up depends only on the order of the queue.
B4. (a) Two: samples 2 (height 1) and 8 (height 0). The one at sample 2 has no marker. (b) Start: A queues sample 1 (3) #0; B queues 7 (2) #1 and 9 (2) #2. Pops: 7 (2, level 2) → B, pushes 6; 9 (2, level 2) → B; 1 (3, level 3) → A, pushes 2; 2 (height 1, level 3) → A: lower than the water level, popped at once: the minimum is drowned by A’s water; 3 (2, level 3) → A, pushes 4; 6 (4, level 4) → B, pushes 5; 4 (4, level 4) → A; 5 (6, level 6): neighbours A and B → line. (c) A\,A\,A\,A\,A\,|\,B\,B\,B\,B. A marker does not have to sit at a minimum: its water runs downhill into the nearest basin and claims it.
B5. (a) n = 2^{20} = 1\,048\,576, \log_2 n = 20: heap \approx 2.1 \cdot 10^7, bucket queue \approx 1.05 \cdot 10^6: about 20 times fewer steps. (b) 16-bit: 65 536 buckets is still small compared with the number of pixels, so yes. Floating-point heights: there is no small set of levels; use the heap, or quantise the heights to, say, 256 or 4096 levels first (which merges heights that differ less than one level and changes tie-breaking slightly).
B6. A line pixel has two different labels around it; if it pushed its neighbours, water would cross the dam. (0, 3) would be pushed by a pixel with no label: when it pops, its labelled neighbours might be only A, or (with the “first to reach it” rule) it would get no sensible label at all. The dam must stop the water; only labelled pixels spread.




Math questions
B7 (math). Show by induction over the pops that every region of the result is connected and contains exactly one marker (use 4 or 8 neighbours consistently).
B8 (math). A 1D plateau of k samples (positions 1, \ldots, k, all of the same height) lies between marker A (position 0) and marker B (position k + 1), both lower. Show that with FIFO the fronts advance one sample per round, alternately from the left and the right, and that the line pixel is at position \lfloor k/2 \rfloor + 1. Where is it for k = 5 and k = 4?
B9 (math). Let d(p) = \min_{\text{paths } \pi: \text{marker} \to p} \max_{q \in \pi,\ q \ne \text{marker}} f(q) (the minimax or bottleneck distance). Show that the water level never decreases and that d(p) equals the water level at the moment p is popped. Conclude that pixels are flooded in order of d.
B10 (math). Show that the binary heap version costs O(n \log n) and the bucket queue version O(n + L) for integer heights 0, \ldots, L - 1 (with 4 or 8 neighbours).






Solutions (math)





B7. Invariant after every pop: each label \ell occupies a connected set containing its marker and no other marker. At the start each label is its marker (assume each marker is connected; otherwise each connected piece is its own region). A pop either makes p a line pixel (nothing changes) or gives p a label \ell that a neighbour already carries: the set of \ell grows by a pixel adjacent to it, so it stays connected; p is not a marker (markers are never queued). Other labels are unchanged.
B8. Start: position 1 #0 (pushed by A), position k #1 (by B). Round j (j = 1, 2, \dots) pops position j (A side, pushing j + 1) and then position k + 1 - j (B side, pushing k - j), because entries are popped in arrival order and the arrivals alternate A, B, A, B. This continues while j < k + 1 - j. If k = 2m + 1: after m rounds positions 1..m are A and k - m + 1..k are B; the middle position m + 1 was pushed by A and pops next with neighbours A and B: line at m + 1 = \lfloor k/2 \rfloor + 1. If k = 2m: in round m, A labels position m (position m + 1 is already queued by B), then position m + 1 pops with neighbours m (A) and m + 2 (B): line at m + 1 = \lfloor k/2 \rfloor + 1. For k = 5: position 3 (the exact middle). For k = 4: position 3 (the right one of the two middle samples).
B9. Let \ell be the water level. A pixel q enters the queue when a labelled neighbour r pops; at that moment its best known path cost is \max(d(r), f(q)). If f(q) < \ell, its key is below the current level, so it pops before any pixel of height \ge \ell, while the level is still \ell; its level is \ell = d(r) = \max(d(r), f(q)) (by induction, d(r) = \ell for the pixel r that just popped). If f(q) \ge \ell, it pops when the level reaches f(q), so its level is f(q) = \max(d(r), f(q)). The level never decreases, because it is defined as a running maximum. Optimality: suppose p pops at level \ell but some path \pi from a marker has highest point < \ell. Take the first pixel q on \pi not yet popped; its predecessor on \pi is popped (or a marker), so q is in the queue with f(q) < \ell: it would have been popped before p. Contradiction. So d(p) = \ell, and since \ell never decreases, pixels are flooded in order of d, exactly as in Dijkstra’s algorithm with \max in place of +.
B10. Each pixel is pushed at most once (the “queued” flag) and popped at most once; each pop inspects at most 8 neighbours. Heap: push and pop cost O(\log(\text{queue size})) \le O(\log n), total O(n \log n). Bucket queue: push O(1); pop O(1) plus the pointer moves to the next non-empty bucket. The pointer only moves down when a pixel below it is pushed (at most once per push) and moves up at most L steps plus the total of the downward moves, so all pointer moves together are O(n + L). Total O(n + L).

title: Exercise: the flooding algorithm on a grid
text:
Explore: step through the queue
Cells show their height (darker = higher). Click a cell to raise (upper half) or lower (lower half) it, or choose marker A–D / no marker and click to place or remove markers. step pops one pixel: it gets a red frame, its labelled neighbours a dashed blue frame, and the box above the options writes out the decision. The table is the queue in pop order (height, arrival number, cell); the next pixel to pop is red, the ones just pushed are highlighted; queued cells show their #arrival in the grid. Options: 8 neighbours, watershed line, LIFO ties. next level jumps to the next water level.



P1. Example 5 × 5 (exercise). Check your queue from B1(a), then step through pops 1–8 and compare with B1(b) and (c). Run to the end: how many pops and line pixels? Tick 8 neighbours and compare with B2.
P2. Example plateau between two markers. Run to the end. Where is the line, and how many line pixels? Tick LIFO ties and run again. Then untick watershed line: what happens to the line pixels?
P3. Example two basins. Use next level: how many water levels are there? How many line pixels at the end? Untick watershed line: which basin gets the former line pixels?
P4. Example a marker that is not a minimum. Step through the first six pops. Where does B’s water go, and at which water level does it reach the right-hand minimum? Compare the final result with two basins.
P5. Example every minimum is a marker. How many markers, pops and line pixels? Untick 8 neighbours and press all regional minima as markers: how many markers now, and why more?
P6. On the 5 × 5 grid, lower the height of (2, 2) from 4 to 1 (click its lower half three times). What changes, and why? (Then press reset.)






Solutions





P1. The starting queue is the six entries of B1(a); pops 1–8 and the queue after pop 8 match the tables. 23 pops, 5 line pixels (the anti-diagonal). With 8 neighbours: 7 line pixels, as in B2.
P2. With FIFO the line is the middle column (column 4), 5 line pixels: the two fronts meet in the middle. With LIFO, B’s water snakes across the plateau first; A keeps only its marker, and 3 line pixels sit around it: (1,0), (2,1) and (3,0). Without the line, the middle column goes to whichever lake queued it first (A, with FIFO).
P3. 8 water levels (2 to 9). 8 line pixels, a staircase along the ridge: (0,5), rows 1–4 of column 4, rows 5–7 of column 3. Without the line, each former line pixel takes the label of the neighbour that queued it first: (0,5), (3,4) and (4,4) go to B, the other five to A. The boundary follows the same ridge.
P4. B sits at height 6 on the slope. Pop 3 is (2,6) at height 4 (B), pops 4–6 run downhill: (2,5) height 3, (3,5) height 2, (4,5) height 1, all at water level 4: B’s water reaches the right-hand minimum at level 4 and drowns it. The final result is the same as with the marker in the minimum (two basins).
P5. 5 markers (A–E), 59 pops, 20 line pixels: the grid is just noise, and every minimum makes a region. With 4 neighbours there are 7 regional minima: two pixels that were not minima with 8 neighbours (they had a lower or equal diagonal neighbour) now are.
P6. (2, 2) becomes a regional minimum without a marker: a puddle in the middle of the dam. A reaches it first (it is queued by (1,2) at pop 5) and drowns it at pop 6, at water level 2. A’s region grows by the puddle and the line moves one diagonal towards B: 4 line pixels, (1,4), (2,3), (3,2), (4,1), and the corners (0,4) and (4,0) now go to A.

title: Splitting touching objects with the distance transform
text:
About this lecture
Thresholding nuclei gives one blob for two touching nuclei, and the gradient cannot help: there is no edge between them. The shape of the blob can: two round objects make a blob with a neck.

The distance transform turns the mask into a landscape with one peak per object and a saddle at each neck.
Watershed of -\mathrm{DT} inside the mask: the cut goes through the neck.
When are two discs split? Peaks r, neck \sqrt{r^2 - d^2/4}: split if the neck is deeper than h.
Failure modes: elongated cells (oversplitting), strong overlap (undersplitting), holes, the wrong metric.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Splitting touching objects with the distance transform
text:
The classic problem

Fluorescent nuclei, thresholded (the thresholding day), labelled (the labelling day): nuclei that touch become one component.
The intensity inside the pair is nearly constant: no edge, so no ridge in the gradient (previous unit). Flooding the gradient from h-minima keeps the pair as one region.
But the outline of the pair is not round: it has two bulges and a neck where they meet. The idea: measure, for every pixel of the mask, how far it is from the outside.

title: Splitting touching objects with the distance transform
section: Recall: the distance transform (the morphology day)
text:
Recall: the distance transform (the morphology day)
\mathrm{DT}(p) = \min_{q \notin A} \|p - q\| \qquad (0 \text{ on the background})

A mountain over each object: low at the outline, highest in the middle, with ridges along the centre lines.
Metrics: city-block, chessboard, chamfer 3-4, exact Euclidean; two raster passes for the chamfer ones (the morphology day).
A disc of radius r: a cone with its peak r at the centre.
Two touching discs: two cones, and between them a saddle at the neck, lower than both peaks.

title: Splitting touching objects with the distance transform
text:
Flood the inverted distance transform

Landscape: -\mathrm{DT}, restricted to the mask. The peaks become minima (one per object), the neck becomes a pass.
Markers: the regional maxima of \mathrm{DT}, or better its h-maxima (peaks that rise more than h above the saddle to a higher peak).
Flooding from the markers inside the mask: the dam sits on the saddle line, across the neck.
Result: one label per object, even where objects touch. Count, measure, compare (the measurements day).

Below: the DT along the line through the two centres, with the two peaks, the neck (red), the depth (red bar) and h (orange tick). “two discs: split”: r = 30, d = 40, h = 2: peaks 30.0, neck 23.0, depth 7.02 (the formula gives 7.64), 2 objects. title: Splitting touching objects with the distance transform
text:
When are two discs split?

Two discs of radius 10 with centres 12 apart: the distance transform along the line through the centres.Discs of radius r, centres d apart (d < 2r): peaks of height r; the neck at the midpoint has height \sqrt{r^2 - d^2/4}. With h-maxima markers they are split if and only if the neck depth r - \sqrt{r^2 - d^2/4} > h . Example: r = 10, d = 12: neck 8, depth 2. Split for h < 2, merged for h \ge 2.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Splitting touching objects with the distance transform

title: Splitting touching objects with the distance transform
text:
The math: the neck
Place the centres at (\pm d/2, 0). The background is outside both discs.

The two circles cross at (0, \pm y_c) with y_c = \sqrt{r^2 - d^2/4} (Pythagoras on the triangle centre, midpoint, crossing).
At the midpoint (0, 0) the nearest background points are these two corners, so \mathrm{DT}(0, 0) = y_c. Moving towards a centre along the line, the distance to the corners grows while the distance to the far side of that disc’s circle, r - |x \mp d/2|, takes over: the profile rises to r at each centre.
Depth \delta(d) = r - \sqrt{r^2 - d^2/4}, increasing in d: from 0 (one disc, d = 0) to r (tangent discs, d = 2r).
Split condition \delta(d) > h \iff d > 2\sqrt{r^2 - (r - h)^2} = 2\sqrt{2rh - h^2}. For r = 10, h = 1: d > 8.72.
On a pixel grid the peak and the neck are known only to about one pixel: the demo’s measured depths differ from the formula by up to about 0.9.

With the left disc fixed, the measured depth falls in steps of one pixel: 4.02 at d = 30–33, 3.02 at d = 28–29, 2.02 at d = 27: there they merge (depth ≤ h). The formula predicts the merge at d = 26.15; the grid moves it by about a pixel. Then lower h and pull them further together.

title: Splitting touching objects with the distance transform
text:
Failure modes

Elongated or bean-shaped cells: the DT has a long ridge with small bumps; each bump is a regional maximum. An ellipse with semi-axes 55 and 22 gives 13 objects at h = 0 (Euclidean): oversplitting. A small h (0.5) fixes it.
Strong overlap: the neck is barely lower than the peaks (small d): undersplitting. No h can separate them; their shape no longer says “two”.
Holes in the mask (a dark nucleolus, a threshold too high inside the nucleus): the DT drops to 0 at the hole, and peaks appear all around it. Fill holes first (the morphology day).
Rough outlines (noise at the threshold): small bumps in the DT, again more peaks: smooth the mask or raise h.

title: Splitting touching objects with the distance transform
text:
Combining landscapes

The DT knows the shape, the gradient knows the edges. Use each for what it is good at:

markers from the peaks of the DT (one per object, robust to intensity variations);
flooding on the gradient of the intensity image, inside the mask (the boundary between two touching nuclei follows any faint edge there is).

Other marker sources: h-maxima of the smoothed intensity (bright nuclei), blob detection with the Laplacian of Gaussian (the edges day).
The distance transform can be weighted by intensity, or replaced by any “how deep inside” map; deep learning methods learn such a map (next slide).

text:
Try it: a nuclei image




“nuclei image”: 15 synthetic nuclei (seeded), several touching; threshold 115. The mask has 9 components: labelling alone counts 9. Watershed of −DT with h = 2: 15 objects, exactly one per nucleus. h = 0: 18 (three nuclei split in two by bumps of their DT); h = 1: 15; h = 3: 12 (three touching pairs merged); h = 6: 9 (back to the components). “flood gradient, markers from DT”: the same numbers (the markers decide how many), with boundaries that follow the intensity between touching nuclei. Change the threshold: at 90 or 140 there are 15 objects only at h = 1 (14 at h = 2).

title: Splitting touching objects with the distance transform
text:
Where this goes next

Deep learning (the modern deep learning day): networks for instance segmentation often predict a distance-like map, a boundary class, or a flow field towards each object’s centre, and then split the objects with a watershed-like step. The “how deep inside” idea of this unit, with a learned landscape.
Counting correct splits (the evaluation day): object-level evaluation matches predicted objects to true ones; oversplitting and undersplitting become false positives and false negatives.
Measurements (the next day): once every object has its own label, its area, shape and intensity can be measured.

title: Splitting touching objects with the distance transform
text:
Summary

Touching objects of the same intensity have no edge between them, but their union has a neck.
Distance transform: one peak per object, a saddle at each neck. Watershed of -\mathrm{DT} inside the mask, markers from the h-maxima of \mathrm{DT}: cut through the necks.
Two discs: neck depth r - \sqrt{r^2 - d^2/4}; split iff depth > h. r = 10, d = 12: depth 2.
Use a near-Euclidean metric; fill holes; choose h above the bumps of elongated or rough objects and below the necks of real pairs.
Combine: markers from the DT, boundaries from the gradient.

title: Quiz: 3D images
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Volumes are stored I[z, y, x] with voxel spacing (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z).

Q1. A confocal stack has \Delta x = \Delta y = 0.1 µm and \Delta z = 0.4 µm. A program shows the xz slice with square pixels. What does a round nucleus look like, and why?






Hint





How many rows does the nucleus span in z compared with columns in x?









Answer





Flattened by a factor 4: a nucleus 4 µm across spans 40 columns but only 10 slices, and with square pixels those 10 rows are drawn as tall as 10 columns. The slice must be drawn 4 times taller per row (its physical aspect ratio), or resampled.




Q2. Voxel (0, 0, 0) is at (100, 50, 0) µm and the spacing is (0.2, 0.2, 1) µm. Where is voxel (10, 20, 3)?






Hint





Start at the origin and step along each axis by index × spacing.









Answer





(100 + 10 \cdot 0.2,\; 50 + 20 \cdot 0.2,\; 0 + 3 \cdot 1) = (102, 54, 3) µm.




Q3. How many voxel values does trilinear interpolation use, and what is the result exactly halfway between all of them?






Hint





The point lies in a cube.









Answer





8 (the corners of the surrounding cube). At the centre every weight is \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac18: the mean of the 8 values.




Q4. To compute an oblique slice, why do we go from each output pixel to the volume, and not from each voxel to the plane?






Hint





How many voxels lie exactly on a tilted plane?









Answer





Inverse mapping: every output pixel asks where it comes from and gets one interpolated value. Pushing voxels onto the plane would hit only a few output pixels (almost no voxel lies exactly on the plane), leaving holes. The same reasoning as for rotating a 2D image.




Q5. You want to smooth a stack with \Delta x = 0.2 µm and \Delta z = 0.6 µm by the same physical amount in all directions, \sigma = 0.6 µm. What \sigma in voxels do you use along x and along z?






Hint





Divide the physical \sigma by the spacing of each axis.









Answer





0.6/0.2 = 3 voxels along x (and y), 0.6/0.6 = 1 voxel along z.




Q6. In a MIP along z you count 12 nuclei. Is the true number at most 12, at least 12, or neither?






Hint





What happens to two nuclei at different depths in the projection? Can one nucleus become two?









Answer





Usually at least 12: nuclei at different depths that overlap in x–y merge into one blob in the MIP, so the projection can only undercount by merging. (A strongly curved cell could in principle appear as two blobs, but that is rare; merging is the common error.) Count in 3D.




Q7. Does resampling a stack with \Delta z = 0.5 µm to isotropic voxels of 0.1 µm improve the resolution along z?






Hint





Where do the new values come from?









Answer





No. The new slices are interpolated from the old ones; nothing between the original slices was measured. Resampling makes later steps simpler (cubic voxels, equal neighbourhoods), but costs memory (5 times more voxels here) and adds no detail.




Q8. (math) Write the 4 \times 4 voxel → world matrix for spacing (0.2, 0.2, 0.5) µm and origin (10, 20, 4) µm, and its inverse.






Hint





Spacing on the diagonal, origin in the last column; for the inverse, undo the translation, then the scaling.









Answer





A = \begin{bmatrix} 0.2 & 0 & 0 & 10 \\ 0 & 0.2 & 0 & 20 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.5 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},\qquad A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 & 0 & -50 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & -100 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.

title: Exercise: 3D images
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Volume
values I[z, y, x]: slice z, row y, column x


Voxel spacing
(\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z): distance between neighbouring voxel centres (µm, mm)


Voxel → world
voxel (i, j, k) is at (o_x + i\,\Delta x,\; o_y + j\,\Delta y,\; o_z + k\,\Delta z); in general a 4\times 4 matrix A


World → voxel
\big((x - o_x)/\Delta x,\; (y - o_y)/\Delta y,\; (z - o_z)/\Delta z\big), i.e. A^{-1}


Trilinear
interpolate along x (4 pairs), then y (2 pairs), then z (1 pair)


Oblique slice
output pixel → world point on the plane → A^{-1} → trilinear


MIP
for every (x, y): the maximum over z









The math: the voxel → world matrix





\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf x \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = A \begin{bmatrix} i \\ j \\ k \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad A = \begin{bmatrix} R\,D & \mathbf o \\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix},\quad D = \mathrm{diag}(\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z), with R a rotation (R = I for a microscope stack) and \mathbf o the world position of voxel (0, 0, 0). Trilinear interpolation at fractional position (f_x, f_y, f_z) in a cube with corner values I_{abc}: I = \sum_{a,b,c \in \{0,1\}} I_{abc}\; w_a(f_x)\,w_b(f_y)\,w_c(f_z),\qquad w_0(f) = 1 - f,\ w_1(f) = f.

(c) Yes: at (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) every weight is \tfrac18, so the value is the mean, (10 + 20 + 30 + 60 + 50 + 50 + 90 + 70)/8 = 47.5.
