Math questions
B7. (math) Show that the inverse of A = \begin{bmatrix} RD & \mathbf o \\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix} (R a rotation, D diagonal with positive entries) is \begin{bmatrix} D^{-1}R^\top & -D^{-1}R^\top\mathbf o \\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix}. Check it on B1(c).
B8. (math) (a) Show that the 8 trilinear weights are non-negative and sum to 1. (b) Show that the interpolant is linear along every line parallel to a coordinate axis, but cubic in t along the diagonal (t, t, t). (c) Show that trilinear interpolation reproduces every function a + bx + cy + dz + exy + fyz + gxz + hxyz exactly, and that these 8 functions are as many as there are corners.
B9. (math) The nuclei stack of the demo has 64 \times 64 \times 20 voxels of 0.2 \times 0.2 \times 0.5 µm. (a) How many voxels does it have after resampling to isotropic voxels of 0.2 µm? (b) Show that resampling a function that is linear in z along z reproduces it exactly, and give an example of what resampling cannot recover.






Solutions (math)





B7. Multiply: \begin{bmatrix} RD & \mathbf o \\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} D^{-1}R^\top & -D^{-1}R^\top\mathbf o \\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} RDD^{-1}R^\top & -RDD^{-1}R^\top\mathbf o + \mathbf o \\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} I & \mathbf 0 \\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix}, using RR^\top = I. For B1, R = I: D^{-1}(\mathbf x - \mathbf o) = \big(2.125/0.5,\; 1.75/0.5,\; 3.5/2\big) = (4.25, 3.5, 1.75).
B8. (a) Each weight is a product of three factors in [0, 1]. The sum factorises: \sum_{a,b,c} w_a(f_x)w_b(f_y)w_c(f_z) = \big(w_0(f_x) + w_1(f_x)\big)\big(w_0(f_y)+w_1(f_y)\big)\big(w_0(f_z)+w_1(f_z)\big) = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1. (b) With f_y, f_z fixed, every term is (1 - f_x) or f_x times a constant: linear in f_x. On the diagonal each weight is a product of three factors t or 1 - t, e.g. w_1w_1w_1 = t^3: a cubic. (c) Each of the 8 functions is a product of factors that are linear along each axis separately; trilinear interpolation is exact for 1, x, y, z along each axis and the product structure carries this over (check xyz: corner values abc, interpolant \sum abc\,w_a w_b w_c = f_x f_y f_z). The interpolant is determined by its 8 corner values, and these 8 functions are linearly independent, so they span all trilinear interpolants.
B9. (a) z: 20 \cdot 0.5/0.2 = 50 slices, so 64 \cdot 64 \cdot 50 = 204\,800 voxels instead of 81\,920 (2.5 times more). (b) Along z the resampling is linear interpolation between neighbouring slices, which is exact for a linear function. It cannot recover detail between the original slices: a structure thinner than 0.5 µm that fell between two slices stays missing, and the axial blur of the microscope stays.

title: Exercise: 3D images
text:
Explore: the volume viewer
The demo shows a synthetic stack of nuclei: 64 \times 64 \times 20 voxels of 0.2 \times 0.2 \times 0.5 µm, origin (10, 20, 4) µm, grey values about 10 (background) to 200. Nuclei A and B overlap in x–y at different depths, C is an elongated cell tilted in the x–z plane, D is a small nucleus. The 3D view (drag to rotate) shows the box with the xy slice, the xz slice and the oblique plane; the 2D panels show the slices with their physical aspect ratio and the MIP along z. Click the xy or xz slice to read a voxel. Δz in the header is the spacing the software believes (the true value is 0.5 µm). The readout shows the voxel → world matrix and the number of objects above 100 in the MIP and in 3D.



E1. Preset slices. Set the z slice to k = 6 and click the centre of the large nucleus (near column 23, row 30). Read the world position and check it with the matrix by hand. Which row of A gives the z coordinate?
E2. Preset two nuclei merge in the MIP, not in 3D. How many objects does the readout count in the MIP and in 3D? Which two nuclei merge? Use the xz slice (j = 31) and the oblique panel (here a vertical plane) to see why. At what depths (in µm) are their centres?
E3. Preset ignored z spacing squashes the cell. What changes in the matrix, in the box and in the xz slice? The cell C is tilted by 35° in the true geometry: estimate its tilt in the squashed xz slice, and explain the number with \tan.
E4. Now set Δz in the header to 1.0 µm (too large). What happens to the shape of the box and to the tilt of C?
E5. Preset an oblique slice through the tilted cell. The plane is tilted by −35° about y and passes through C’s centre. How long and how wide is C in this slice (count pixels: the oblique slice has pixels of 0.22 µm)? Move tilt about y to 0°: why does C look shorter?
E6. Preset resample to isotropic. How many voxels does the volume have now, and what does the matrix look like? Do the slices show more detail than before?






Solutions





E1. Voxel (23, 30, 6) has the value 198 (a nucleus) and lies at (10 + 23 \cdot 0.2,\; 20 + 30 \cdot 0.2,\; 4 + 6 \cdot 0.5) = (14.6, 26, 7) µm. The third row of A, (0, 0, 0.5, 4), gives z = 0.5\,k + 4.
E2. MIP 3 objects, 3D 4 objects (threshold 100). Nuclei A and B merge in the MIP: they overlap in x–y, but in the xz slice A sits higher (centre at z = 2.8 µm above the origin, slice 5.6) and B lower (z = 7.2 µm, slice 14.4), with background between them. In the 3D labelling they are separate objects.
E3. The third diagonal entry of A drops from 0.5 to 0.2, the box becomes 4 µm deep instead of 10, and every structure is flattened by 0.4 along z. The cell’s tilt in the xz slice drops from 35° to about 16°: a slope \tan 35° = 0.70 becomes 0.70 \cdot 0.2/0.5 = 0.28, i.e. \arctan 0.28 = 15.6°. Angles, lengths, areas and volumes measured in this geometry are all wrong.
E4. The box becomes 20 µm deep (twice the truth); C now looks steeper: \arctan(0.70 \cdot 1.0/0.5) = 54.5°.
E5. About 33 pixels long and 11 wide, i.e. about 7.2 µm by 2.4 µm: the full length 2 \cdot 3.6 µm and width 2 \cdot 1.2 µm of the cell. At 0° the plane is an xy plane through C’s centre: it cuts the tilted cell at an angle, through its narrow direction, so the section is only about 3.8 µm long (17 pixels).
E6. 64 \times 64 \times 50 = 204\,800 voxels; the matrix has 0.2 on the whole diagonal and the same origin. The slices look the same, slightly smoother along z: resampling interpolates between existing slices and adds no information.

title: Exercise: 3D images
text:
Where this leads
The next unit looks for the boundary of a bright object in 2D: the curve where the image crosses a value c, found with marching squares. The unit after it does the same in 3D (marching cubes), and the last one measures the resulting surfaces. Rendering volumes directly (projections from any direction, volume rendering) is the 3D-graphics day.

title: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering
text:
About this lecture
A CT scan, an MRI or a confocal stack is a volume: a 3D array of values. How do we turn it into one picture?

Rays through the volume, one per pixel, sampled in steps.
Projections along the ray: maximum (MIP), minimum (MinIP), average (an X-ray).
Direct volume rendering: a transfer function decides what to see; light is emitted and absorbed along the ray; compositing front to back.
Speed and artefacts: early termination, opacity correction, step size.
Isosurfaces two ways (ray casting vs a marching-cubes mesh), and polygons vs voxels.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Last unit of the 3D graphics day. It uses the camera matrices of unit 1 (backwards, to make rays) and the “over” compositing of unit 3. Two demos: raycomposite (one ray, by hand) and volview in its “render” mode (the whole image, on the GPU).
crumbs: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering

title: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering
section: Recall: a volume is an array plus a matrix
text:
Recall: a volume is an array plus a matrix
From 3D images (volumes3d, the marching-cubes day):

A volume stores values I[k, j, i] on a grid of voxels with spacing (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z), often anisotropic (\Delta z > \Delta x).
A 4\times4 voxel → world matrix A places it in physical space (the spacing on its diagonal, plus an origin and possibly a rotation); world → voxel is A^{-1}.
Values between voxels: trilinear interpolation. An oblique slice = inverse mapping + trilinear, and a first MIP was shown there.

Today the same inverse mapping is used at every sample of every ray. Our phantom: a synthetic head of 64\times64\times40 voxels of 1\times1\times1.6 mm (skull, brain, ventricles, a thin vessel tree, an air cavity).
crumbs: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering

title: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering
text:
One ray per pixel


For each pixel, a ray from the eye through the pixel (unit 1, run backwards: (PV)^{-1} applied to the pixel at near and far depth). Orthographic: parallel rays.
Clip the ray to the volume’s box, and sample it every \Delta s (in voxels), by trilinear interpolation.
What we do with the samples defines the image. The step \Delta s must be small enough not to miss thin structures (sampling, Fourier unit): about half a voxel.
crumbs: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering

title: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering
text:
Projections: maximum, minimum, average

MIP (maximum-intensity projection): the brightest sample on the ray. Thin bright structures (contrast-filled vessels, fluorescent spots) stand out against everything else; standard in angiography and fluorescence microscopy.
MinIP: the darkest sample within the body: air spaces (airways, sinuses).
Average (or sum): like an X-ray image. A radiograph measures the attenuation summed along the ray (the Beer–Lambert law, owned by the Radon elective); CT reconstructs the volume from many such projections.

All three lose depth: a vessel in front and one behind look the same. One reads them by rotating (a “spinning MIP”) or by combining with slices.
crumbs: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering

title: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering
section: Try it: MIP, MinIP and average
text:
Try it: MIP, MinIP and average




volview in its “render” mode, ray marching on the GPU. “MIP finds the vessels”: the vessel tree (value 230) is the brightest structure on almost every ray through it, the skull (170) gives the bright ring. “MIP has no depth: rotate”: seen from the side, the left and right branches overlap; drag to rotate and they separate. “MinIP finds the air”: the dark cavity below the brain (value 8) inside the head. “average = an X-ray”: a soft, transparent-looking image, as in a radiograph.
crumbs: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering

title: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering
section: Direct volume rendering: the transfer function
text:
Direct volume rendering: the transfer function
Instead of picking one sample, let every sample contribute: a semi-transparent, coloured cloud.

A transfer function maps the value of a sample to a colour c(v) and an opacity \alpha(v). This is where the user chooses what to see.
Opacity 0 for air and soft tissue, high for bone: the skull. Low opacity for soft tissue and high for vessels: a glass head with red vessels.
It is a classification by value only: structures with the same values (contrast-filled vessels and bone in CT) cannot be separated by it.
The editor in the demos: opacity as a piecewise linear function over the histogram of the volume, colours from a colour map (the colour day).
crumbs: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering

title: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering
section: Light along a ray: emission and absorption
text:
Light along a ray: emission and absorption
Picture each sample as a thin slab of glowing fog:

it emits light of its colour, in proportion to its opacity;
it absorbs part of the light coming from behind it.

What reaches the eye is the light of each slab, dimmed by everything in front of it. The fraction of light from depth t that survives to the eye is the transmittance \mathcal T(t): 1 at the eye, falling with every absorbing slab. An opaque wall makes \mathcal T = 0 behind it: nothing there is seen.
The absorption alone is the X-ray picture (Beer–Lambert); emission added makes it a rendering.
crumbs: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering

title: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering
text:
The math: the emission–absorption model
Along the ray, with t the distance from the eye, extinction \tau(t) (absorption per unit length) and colour c(t), the light L travelling towards the eye obeys a linear first-order ODE:
\frac{dL}{ds} = -\tau L + \tau c \qquad (s \text{ pointing towards the eye}).
Solving it (an integrating factor), with the transmittance \mathcal T(t) = \exp\!\big(-\int_0^t \tau(t')\,dt'\big):
L = \int_0^D \mathcal T(t)\,\tau(t)\,c(t)\,dt \;+\; \mathcal T(D)\,L_\text{background}.
Each point contributes its emission \tau c, attenuated by everything between it and the eye. With c = 0 only the background term is left: Beer–Lambert, L = L_\text{background}\,e^{-\int\tau}. For a constant slab of thickness D: L = c\,(1 - e^{-\tau D}) + background \cdot\,e^{-\tau D}.
crumbs: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering

title: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering
text:
From the integral to compositing
Cut the ray into steps of length \Delta s; sample i has colour c_i and opacity \alpha_i = 1 - e^{-\tau_i\Delta s}. Walk front to back, starting with C = 0 and \mathcal T = 1:
C \leftarrow C + \mathcal T\,\alpha_i\,c_i, \qquad \mathcal T \leftarrow \mathcal T\,(1 - \alpha_i).

Example, 5 samples with values 30, 80, 180, 230, 90 and opacities 0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.9, 0.2: \mathcal T goes 1 \to 1 \to 0.8 \to 0.4 \to 0.04 \to 0.032.
This is the “over” operator with premultiplied colours from the texture unit (How graphics cards store colour): each sample is drawn under what is in front.
Back to front (the painter’s order), C \leftarrow \alpha_i c_i + (1 - \alpha_i)\,C from the far end, gives the same final colour, but its partial sums differ, and it cannot stop early.
crumbs: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering

title: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering
section: The math: compositing is the discretised integral
text:
The math: compositing is the discretised integral
Replace the integral by a sum over the steps, with \tau and c constant within step i. The transmittance up to step i is a product, and the step’s own emission is \int_0^{\Delta s} e^{-\tau_i u}\tau_i c_i\,du = (1 - e^{-\tau_i\Delta s})\,c_i = \alpha_i c_i:
L \approx \sum_i \mathcal T_i\,\alpha_i\,c_i, \qquad \mathcal T_i = \prod_{j < i}(1 - \alpha_j).
Front to back computes exactly this, keeping the running product \mathcal T_i. Back to front computes the nested form \alpha_1c_1 + (1-\alpha_1)\big(\alpha_2c_2 + (1-\alpha_2)(\dots)\big); expanding the brackets gives the same sum.
crumbs: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering

title: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering
text:
Try it: compositing one ray




A sagittal slice of the phantom (x = 32 mm) with one ray (E = the eye side; drag the ends). 67 samples at Δs = 1 mm. Plots: value along the ray (dots in the transfer-function colour), α of each sample (red), the transmittance T (blue, falling at the skull and the vessel), the brightness of the accumulated colour C (green). “next sample” from “start”: watch T fall. Switch to “back to front”: the same final colour (0.669, 0.273, 0.299), different partial sums. Tick “early termination”: the ray could stop at sample 62. “opaque wall hides what is behind”: T falls below 0.05 at the first skull crossing, sample 15 of 67; nothing behind it matters. “MIP vs DVR”: the MIP value is the maximum, 209.9, the vessel.
crumbs: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering

title: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering
section: Faster and correct: early termination, opacity correction, step size
text:
Faster and correct: early termination, opacity correction, step size

Early ray termination: front to back, stop when \mathcal T < \varepsilon (say 0.05): what is behind can change the pixel by less than \varepsilon. Rays that hit bone stop at the skull. (In the demo, 345 of 1489 rays stop early and save 45 % of their samples; rays through empty space need empty-space skipping, not covered.)
Opacity correction: a transfer-function opacity is defined for a reference step. Halve the step and you take twice as many samples: with the same \alpha the image gets too opaque. Correct with \alpha' = 1 - (1 - \alpha)^{\Delta s/\Delta s_0}.
Step size: too large a step undersamples thin layers and gives wood-grain rings (aliasing: the Fourier unit). Rule: \Delta s \le half a voxel.
Pre- vs post-classification: interpolate the values and then apply the transfer function (post, sharper), or classify each voxel and interpolate colours (pre, blurrier).
crumbs: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering

title: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering
text:
The math: opacity correction
A step of length \Delta s through a material of extinction \tau lets through e^{-\tau\Delta s} of the light. If the table gives \alpha_0 = 1 - e^{-\tau\Delta s_0} for the reference step \Delta s_0, then
1 - \alpha' = e^{-\tau\Delta s} = \big(e^{-\tau\Delta s_0}\big)^{\Delta s/\Delta s_0} = (1 - \alpha_0)^{\Delta s/\Delta s_0}.
Example: \tau = 0.5 per voxel. One step \Delta s = 1: \alpha = 1 - e^{-0.5} = 0.393. Two steps of 0.5: each 1 - e^{-0.25} = 0.221, and together 1 - 0.779^2 = 0.393: the same. Without correction, two samples of 0.393 give 1 - 0.607^2 = 0.632.
With the correction, a homogeneous slab of thickness D has opacity 1 - e^{-\tau D} for every step size.
crumbs: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering

title: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering
text:
Try it: volume rendering




“semi-transparent soft tissue”: low opacity for soft tissue and brain, a little for bone, nearly opaque vessels. Drag the opacity points in the editor. “only the skull”. “step too large: wood grain”: step 3 voxels, rings on the skull. “no opacity correction”: step 0.25 without correction: the image is much more opaque (mean opacity of the rays 0.334 instead of 0.222); tick the correction. “early termination saves samples”: the heat map of samples per pixel; rays through the skull stop early. “ignored z spacing” (side view): the head is squashed to 40/64 of its height. “isosurface by ray casting”: c = 135, the outer surface of the skull, shaded with the gradient as normal.

title: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering
text:
Isosurfaces two ways
The surface where the volume crosses a value c (the marching-cubes day):

Ray casting: march until a sample crosses c, refine the crossing by linear interpolation between the two samples (the same formula as marching squares), shade with the gradient as the normal (marching-cubes day). Done per pixel, per frame, on the GPU; gives a picture, no geometry.
Extract a mesh with marching cubes, then draw it with units 1–2. Done once per c; gives triangles to measure (area, volume), smooth, export or print.

text:
Polygons or voxels?









volume (voxels)
mesh (polygons)




represents
every point inside
only the surface

512^3 voxels × 2 bytes = 256 MiB
10^6 triangles ≈ 24 MB

Microscopy and medical imaging produce volumes; meshes come from segmenting them (marching cubes) or from surface scanners. Most analysis stays on the voxels; meshes are for looking, measuring surfaces, and modelling.

title: Seeing voxels: projections and volume rendering
text:
Summary

A ray per pixel, sampled every \Delta s with trilinear interpolation.
MIP: vessels and spots; MinIP: air; average: an X-ray. No depth: rotate.
Transfer function: value → colour and opacity: what to see.
Emission–absorption: L = \int \mathcal T\,\tau\,c\,dt; discretised: C \leftarrow C + \mathcal T\alpha c, \mathcal T \leftarrow \mathcal T(1 - \alpha) (front to back = back to front).
Early termination (\mathcal T < \varepsilon), opacity correction 1 - (1 - \alpha)^{\Delta s/\Delta s_0}, step ≤ half a voxel.
Isosurfaces by ray casting (a picture) or by marching cubes (a mesh to measure).

title: Quiz: boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Why must a sliding-window detector have an extremely low false-positive rate per window?






Answer





Because it looks at hundreds of thousands of windows per image (every position and scale), and almost all are background. A false-positive rate of 1 % would give thousands of false detections per image; even 10^{-5} gives several.




Q2. What is a decision stump, and why is it called a weak classifier?






Answer





One feature, one threshold and a direction: “face if the feature is above (or below) \theta”. It is a decision tree of depth 1. Alone it is only somewhat better than guessing; boosting combines many of them into a strong classifier.




Q3. After an AdaBoost round, which training examples get more weight, and why?






Answer





The examples the new stump classified wrongly: their weights are multiplied by e^{\alpha}, the others by e^{-\alpha}. The next stump is chosen by its weighted error, so it must do well on exactly those examples: each round focuses on what is still wrong.




Q4. A stump has weighted error \varepsilon = 0.2. What is its vote \alpha? What would \varepsilon = 0.5 give?






Answer





\alpha = \tfrac12\ln(0.8/0.2) = \tfrac12\ln 4 = 0.69. With \varepsilon = 0.5: \alpha = 0, no vote; the stump is no better than guessing.




Q5. How does boosting select features?






Answer





Each round chooses the single stump, and hence the single feature, with the smallest weighted error out of the whole pool. After T rounds the classifier uses at most T features; the rest of the pool (often over 100 000 features) is never evaluated at detection time.




Q6. A cascade has 5 stages, each with detection rate 0.995 and false-positive rate 0.4. What are D and F?






Answer





D = 0.995^5 = 0.975; F = 0.4^5 = 0.010.




Q7. Why is the first stage of a cascade made as small as possible (one or two features)?






Answer





Every window passes through stage 1, so its cost is paid for every window; later stages are paid only by the few windows that reach them. Most background windows are easy and can be rejected by one or two features.




Q8. Why is each new cascade stage trained on background windows that the earlier stages accepted, rather than on random background?






Answer





Random background is already rejected by the earlier stages; training on it would teach nothing new. The windows that got through are the hard, face-like ones the cascade still gets wrong. Training each stage on those makes the cascade progressively better at exactly the cases that matter.




Q9. How does the detector handle faces of different sizes without an image pyramid?






Answer





It scales the features: in a larger window every rectangle grows by the same factor. With the integral image a larger rectangle costs the same four lookups. Dividing by the window’s standard deviation and the rectangle area keeps the responses comparable across scales.




Q10. A detector trained mostly on faces without glasses misses faces with glasses. Is this a bug in boosting?






Answer





No: boosting chose features and thresholds that fit the training set. If a group of faces is rare or absent there, the chosen features (e.g. “the eyes are dark”) may not hold for it, and the stage thresholds reject it. The fix is in the data: a training (and test) set that covers everyone the detector will be used on, with rates reported per group.




Q11. (math) Show that after reweighting, the stump just chosen has weighted error exactly \tfrac12.






Answer





Before normalising, the wrong examples weigh \varepsilon e^{\alpha} and the correct ones (1-\varepsilon)e^{-\alpha}. With e^{\alpha} = \sqrt{(1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon} both are \sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}, so after normalising each part is \tfrac12.

title: Exercise: boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

find the best decision stump on a small weighted data set, and carry out AdaBoost rounds by hand: weighted error, vote \alpha, new weights,
compute the detection rate, false-positive rate and expected number of features of a cascade,
explain why a cascade is fast, why each stage trains on the background that got through, and what the training set does to the detector,
(math) derive the vote \alpha and the training-error bound.

title: Exercise: boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

find the best decision stump on a small weighted data set, and carry out AdaBoost rounds by hand: weighted error, vote \alpha, new weights,
compute the detection rate, false-positive rate and expected number of features of a cascade,

title: Exercise: boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Stump
one feature, one threshold, one direction: a depth-1 decision tree


Weighted error
$= $ sum of the weights of the misclassified examples (weights sum to 1)


Vote
\alpha = \tfrac12\ln\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}


Reweighting
misclassified: \times e^{\alpha}; correct: \times e^{-\alpha}; then divide by the sum


Strong classifier
sign of \sum_t \alpha_t h_t, with h_t = \pm 1


Training-error bound
\prod_t 2\sqrt{\varepsilon_t(1-\varepsilon_t)}


Cascade
D = \prod d_i, F = \prod f_i; features per window \sum_i n_i \prod_{j<i} p_j

title: Exercise: boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
By hand
B1. AdaBoost on six numbers. One feature with values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and labels -, -, +, -, +, +. Start with equal weights \tfrac16. A stump says “+ if the value is above \theta” (or the opposite direction). (a) Find the best stump: its threshold, direction and weighted error. Compute its vote \alpha_1. (b) Reweight. What are the six new weights? Which example now carries half of the total weight? (c) Find the best stump for round 2 with the new weights, its error and \alpha_2. Compute the score \alpha_1 h_1 + \alpha_2 h_2 of every example. Which examples are still misclassified? (d) Round 3 finds the stump “+ if the value is below 3.5” with weighted error \tfrac29. Is the training error now 0? (Compute the final scores.)
B2. A three-stage cascade. The stages have detection rates 0.99, 0.98, 0.97, false-positive rates 0.5, 0.3, 0.2, and use 2, 5, 20 features. (a) What are the overall detection rate D and false-positive rate F? (b) How many features does a background window need on average? (Use the false-positive rates as the pass rates of background windows.) (c) Without a cascade, one classifier with all 27 features: how many per window? What is the speed-up?
B3. Ten stages. Each stage keeps 99 % of the faces and passes 30 % of the background. (a) Is D \ge 0.9? How small is F? (b) An image has 670 000 windows. How many false detections do you expect? (c) To halve the false detections, would you add a stage or make every stage stricter? What does each cost?
B4. Scales. A feature in the 24 \times 24 base window is a two-rectangle edge with rectangles of 4 \times 8 pixels at position (6, 2). (a) What does it become in a window of 36 \times 36 (scale 1.5)? How many lookups does it cost there? (b) Why divide the response by the window’s standard deviation, and by the rectangle area?
B5. Who is in the training set? A face detector is trained on 5000 faces, almost all without glasses and with light skin. (a) Predict how it behaves on faces with glasses or darker skin, and explain why with the cascade’s per-stage thresholds. (b) Why does a high detection rate on the test set not prove that the problem is absent?






Solutions





B1. (a) Threshold 2.5, “+ above”: only the value 4 (a -) is wrong. \varepsilon_1 = \tfrac16, \alpha_1 = \tfrac12\ln 5 = 0.805. (b) The mistake is multiplied by e^{0.805} = \sqrt5, the others by 1/\sqrt5; after normalising: 0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.5, 0.1, 0.1. The example with value 4 carries half the weight. (c) Threshold 4.5, “+ above”: only the value 3 (a +) is wrong, \varepsilon_2 = 0.1, \alpha_2 = \tfrac12\ln 9 = 1.099. (The old stump at 2.5 would now have error 0.5.) Scores: values 1, 2: -0.805 - 1.099 = -1.903; values 3, 4: 0.805 - 1.099 = -0.294; values 5, 6: +1.903. The value 3 (a +) is still wrong; training error \tfrac16. New weights: 0.056, 0.056, 0.5, 0.278, 0.056, 0.056. (d) \alpha_3 = \tfrac12\ln\frac{7/9}{2/9} = \tfrac12\ln 3.5 = 0.626. The stump says + for 1, 2, 3 and - for 4, 5, 6. Scores: values 1, 2: -1.903 + 0.626 = -1.277; value 3: -0.294 + 0.626 = +0.332; value 4: -0.294 - 0.626 = -0.920; values 5, 6: 1.903 - 0.626 = 1.277. All six correct: training error 0. (The bound is 0.745 \cdot 0.600 \cdot 0.831 = 0.372.)
B2. (a) D = 0.99 \cdot 0.98 \cdot 0.97 = 0.941; F = 0.5 \cdot 0.3 \cdot 0.2 = 0.03. (b) 2 + 5 \cdot 0.5 + 20 \cdot 0.5 \cdot 0.3 = 2 + 2.5 + 3 = 7.5 features. (c) 27 features per window; the cascade is 27/7.5 = 3.6 times faster. With many stages and a tiny first stage the factor grows much larger.
B3. (a) D = 0.99^{10} = 0.904: yes. F = 0.3^{10} = 5.9 \cdot 10^{-6}. (b) 670\,000 \times 5.9 \cdot 10^{-6} \approx 4 false detections per image (before merging). (c) An eleventh stage multiplies F by its own false-positive rate (0.3 would give a factor 3 fewer) and D by its detection rate (0.99): a small loss of faces, and a small extra cost, because few windows reach it. Making every stage stricter lowers D at every stage (ten times the loss) and makes the early stages, which see all windows, more expensive. Adding a stage is usually better.
B4. (a) Rectangles of 6 \times 12 pixels at (9, 3); still 6 lookups. (b) The SD makes the response independent of the contrast of this window (lighting, camera); the area makes responses at different scales comparable (the feature becomes a difference of mean grey levels). Without them, a threshold learnt at scale 1 in one lighting would not fit other scales and lighting.
B5. (a) Each stage’s threshold is set so that almost all training faces pass. Faces that differ systematically from the training faces (glasses hide the dark eyes; different contrasts between eyes, cheeks and skin) get lower scores and are rejected at some stage: they are detected less often. (b) If the test set is drawn from the same population as the training set, it lacks the same faces: the error on the missing groups is never measured. The test set must contain enough faces of every group the detector will meet, and the rates should be reported per group.




Math questions
B6. (math) After round t, AdaBoost multiplies the weights of the misclassified examples by e^{\alpha_t} and the others by e^{-\alpha_t}. Show that with \alpha_t = \tfrac12\ln\frac{1 - \varepsilon_t}{\varepsilon_t} the stump h_t has weighted error exactly \tfrac12 under the new weights. What does that mean for round t + 1?
B7. (math) Let Z(\alpha) = \sum_i w_i e^{-\alpha y_i h(x_i)} (the exponential loss after adding \alpha h). Show that Z(\alpha) = (1 - \varepsilon)e^{-\alpha} + \varepsilon e^{\alpha}, find the \alpha that minimises it, and show that the minimum is 2\sqrt{\varepsilon(1 - \varepsilon)}.
B8. (math) Show for two rounds that the training error of H = \operatorname{sign}(\alpha_1 h_1 + \alpha_2 h_2) is at most Z_1 Z_2 = \prod_t 2\sqrt{\varepsilon_t(1-\varepsilon_t)}. (Use [H(x_i) \ne y_i] \le e^{-y_i F(x_i)} with F = \alpha_1h_1 + \alpha_2h_2, and write the weights after two rounds in terms of F.) Check it on B1.






Solutions (math)





B6. Before normalising, the misclassified examples weigh \varepsilon e^{\alpha} in total and the correct ones (1-\varepsilon)e^{-\alpha}. With e^{\alpha} = \sqrt{(1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon} both equal \sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}. So after normalising, the stump’s error is exactly \tfrac12: under the new weights it is no better than guessing, and round t + 1 must find a stump that carries new information (in B1, the stump at 2.5 has error 0.5 in round 2).
B7. Correct examples have y_i h(x_i) = 1, total weight 1 - \varepsilon; wrong ones -1, total \varepsilon: Z = (1-\varepsilon)e^{-\alpha} + \varepsilon e^{\alpha}. Z'(\alpha) = -(1-\varepsilon)e^{-\alpha} + \varepsilon e^{\alpha} = 0 gives e^{2\alpha} = (1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon, \alpha = \tfrac12\ln\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon} (Z'' > 0: a minimum). Then Z = (1-\varepsilon)\sqrt{\varepsilon/(1-\varepsilon)} + \varepsilon\sqrt{(1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon} = 2\sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}.
B8. Starting from w_i^{(1)} = 1/n, after two rounds w_i^{(3)} = \frac{1}{n}\frac{e^{-y_i\alpha_1h_1(x_i)}e^{-y_i\alpha_2h_2(x_i)}}{Z_1Z_2} = \frac{e^{-y_iF(x_i)}}{nZ_1Z_2}, where Z_t is the normaliser of round t (equal to the minimum of B7). The weights sum to 1, so \frac1n\sum_i e^{-y_iF(x_i)} = Z_1Z_2. A misclassified example has y_iF(x_i) \le 0, so e^{-y_iF(x_i)} \ge 1 \ge [H(x_i) \ne y_i]; hence the training error \le \frac1n\sum_i e^{-y_iF(x_i)} = Z_1Z_2. B1: Z_1 = 2\sqrt{\tfrac16\cdot\tfrac56} = 0.745, Z_2 = 2\sqrt{0.1 \cdot 0.9} = 0.6, bound 0.447 \ge \tfrac16. The same argument works for any number of rounds.

title: Exercise: boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
Explore: boosting and the cascade
The demo trains a detector on 24 \times 24 patches: 300 cartoon faces (random size, pose, lighting, hair; 30 % with glasses) and 600 background patches, with a test set of 200 faces and 400 background patches; switch target to cells for bright cells against debris. The feature pool has 2769 rectangle features (all six templates on a 3-pixel grid, rectangles 2 to 8 pixels). No real people are shown.

boost: add one stump / add 10. Left: the stump shown (slider) on the mean face (white +, black −), and the six examples with the largest weight in that round (orange frame: face, blue: background). Top plot: training and test error and the bound against rounds. Bottom plot: every training example at its score after that round; dot area = its weight for the next round.
cascade: the table lists the stages (stumps, detection and false-positive rate on the stage’s own training set, and the share of random background windows that reach the stage); the bars show how many windows of the test scene reach each stage. The default cascade (8 stages, per-stage detection 0.995 and false positives at most 0.5) is precomputed; build cascade retrains with your settings (a few seconds).
detect: the test scene with merged detections (green: a true face, red: false; dashed: the true faces) and, on the right, every window at the smallest scale coloured by the stage that rejected it.




E1. Preset first two stumps. Which features were chosen (template, position, size)? Read \varepsilon and \alpha of each (move the “show stump” slider). Do larger errors get smaller votes? What are the training and test errors after two rounds?
E2. add 10 until 10 rounds, then until 50. Note the training and test errors at 10 and 50 rounds, and the bound. Why can the training error reach 0 while the test error does not?
E3. Preset boosting focuses on the hard examples (10 rounds). Where are the big dots in the bottom plot? What kind of examples are the six heaviest?
E4. Tab cascade (preset a cascade: few features per window). How many windows does the test scene have, how many does stage 1 reject, and how many pass all stages? How many stumps does the cascade hold, and how many features does a window need on average? Compare with B2.
E5. Tab detect, preset one strong classifier vs a cascade. Compare features per window, faces found and false detections with and without the cascade (untick no cascade). Why does the cascade make fewer false detections, although it evaluates fewer features?
E6. Preset a rotated face is missed. Which face is missed by the cascade? Tick no cascade: what happens? What would you add to the training set?
E7. Preset training set without glasses. Which faces are missed? Compare with B5.
E8. Switch target to cells and look at the boost errors after 10 rounds and at the detection result. Which templates does boosting pick first for cells?






Solutions





E1. Round 1: centre − surround at (0, 3) with cells of 8 \times 2 pixels (a 24 \times 6 band near the top of the window: the hair against the forehead), \varepsilon_1 = 0.069, \alpha_1 = 1.30. Round 2: an edge (left − right) at (0, 15) with rectangles of 4 \times 8: the left side of the face against the background, \varepsilon_2 = 0.132, \alpha_2 = 0.94. Yes: the larger the weighted error, the smaller the vote. After two rounds: training error 6.9 %, test error 8.7 %. (The cartoon faces differ from real ones: here the hairline and the face outline are the most reliable cues; on real faces Viola and Jones found the eye features first.)
E2. 10 rounds: training 0.2 %, test 1.5 % (bound 3.2 %). 50 rounds: training 0.0 %, test 1.0 % (bound below 0.01 %). The training error measures the patches the stumps were chosen on; the test patches are new, and some of them (unusual faces, face-like background) fall on the wrong side of the learnt thresholds.
E3. The big dots lie near the decision boundary at 0 or on the wrong side: background patches with a high score and faces with a low one. The six heaviest examples in round 10 are four background patches and two faces: the examples the first nine stumps found hardest.
E4. 27 750 windows; stage 1 (2 stumps) rejects 20 597 (74 %); 65 windows pass all 8 stages. The cascade holds 37 stumps, but a window needs 3.94 features on average: as in B2(b), the first, tiny stages decide almost every window. Products of the stage rates on their training sets: D = 0.977, F = 2.4 \cdot 10^{-4}.
E5. No cascade (one classifier of 50 stumps, threshold 0): 50 features per window, 7 of 7 faces, 11 false detections. Cascade: 3.94 features per window, 7 of 7 faces, 2 false detections. Each later stage of the cascade was trained on the background windows that the earlier stages wrongly accepted (bootstrapping): hard, face-like background. The single classifier only saw 600 random background patches and never learnt to reject the face-like clutter.
E6. The large face right of the centre, turned by 34°, is missed by the cascade (6 of 7 found). Without the cascade the looser single classifier does find it (7 of 7, but with 11 false detections). Axis-aligned rectangle features expect upright faces; add rotated faces to the training set, use rotated (45°) features, or train separate detectors for several angles.
E7. One of the two faces with glasses is missed (6 of 7 found, no false detections). The glasses’ bright lenses and dark frames replace the dark eyes; trained only on faces without glasses, some stage rejects that window. In B5 terms: the training set decides whom the detector finds.
E8. After 10 rounds: training 0.2 %, test 0.8 %. On the test scene the cascade finds all 9 cells with no false detections (the single 50-stump classifier: 10 false detections). The first stumps are a three-rectangle line (a bright middle band between darker top and bottom), a four-rectangle diagonal and a three-rectangle line across: features that describe a bright round blob with a darker centre.

title: Exercise: boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
Where this leads
The detector is judged by its detection rate and false detections; matching detections to the truth, precision–recall curves and average precision belong to the evaluation day. The random forests day uses the same split search to grow full trees. Modern detectors learn their features with convolutional networks (neural networks, modern deep learning), but the cascade’s principle, spending computation only where it is needed, is still used wherever computation is scarce.

title: The variational autoencoder
text:
About this lecture
An autoencoder gives every image a point z. A variational autoencoder (VAE) gives every image a small cloud, and keeps all clouds near one standard bell shape.

Why: so that every point of the latent space decodes to a plausible image, and we can generate new ones.
How: the decoder is trained on random draws from each cloud (the reparameterisation trick).
The loss has two parts: rebuild the image + stay close to the standard cloud (a KL divergence).

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Concept layer first on every topic, then a “The math” slide that can be skipped. Weaker students should leave with: cloud instead of point, decoder sees random draws, two forces (rebuild vs stay near the prior), and what β does. Reference: D. P. Kingma, M. Welling (2014), Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes, ICLR, arXiv:1312.6114; Rezende, Mohamed & Wierstra (2014) independently.

title: The variational autoencoder
text:
What a plain autoencoder lacks
A plain autoencoder only has to rebuild its training images. It may place them anywhere in z.

Nothing says what lies between two training images: decode a point in a gap and the result can be anything, often a smudge that is no digit at all.
Nothing says where the images are: to generate a new image, which z should we pick?
Each image is one point, with no notion of how sure the encoder is.

We want: similar images nearby, no gaps, and a known region to draw new z from.

Draw on the board: a 2D latent space with a few dots for 1s and 7s scattered with gaps between; pick a point in a gap; the decoder was never trained there. Then draw what we want: the same dots packed into one round region, 1s and 7s side by side, so the point between a 1 and a 7 decodes to something in between.

title: The variational autoencoder
section: A cloud instead of a point
text:
A cloud instead of a point
The encoder outputs, for each image x, a centre \mu(x) and a spread \sigma(x): a Gaussian cloud q(z \mid x) = \mathcal N\big(\mu(x),\ \sigma(x)^2\big).

During training the decoder is handed a random point of the cloud, not the centre, and must still rebuild this image.
So every point near an image must decode to something like it: the space around each image gets trained.
A penalty pulls every cloud towards one standard cloud \mathcal N(0, I), the prior. Clouds overlap, gaps fill.

Two forces: rebuild well (small, separate clouds) against look like the prior (wide, overlapping clouds near 0).

This is the whole idea. The rebuild force alone would shrink each cloud to a point and push them apart: a plain autoencoder. The prior force alone would make every cloud the standard cloud, and the decoder could not tell images apart: every image decoded as the average image. The balance gives a latent space where every region is used and neighbouring points decode to similar images.

title: The variational autoencoder
text:
The result on handwritten digits




A VAE with a 2D latent space trained on 60,000 handwritten digits (MNIST). Dots: the cloud centres of 1000 test digits; orange: the clouds (±2 sd) of six test digits.

Digits of one kind sit together; similar digits (4, 9; 3, 5, 8) are neighbours.
Almost everything lies inside the prior’s dashed circle: no big gaps.
The clouds are small (sd about 0.07): the image says a lot about z.



Real network (784 → 192 → 2, decoder 2 → 192 → 784), trained offline with a fixed seed; the same weights run in the demos. The mean encoder sd over the 10,000 test digits is 0.067. 71.5% of the test centres lie inside radius 2; a standard 2D normal has 86.5% there (1 − e^{−2}). MNIST: Y. LeCun, C. Cortes, C. J. C. Burges; CC BY-SA 3.0 as stated in the Keras documentation.

title: The variational autoencoder
text:
The reparameterisation trick
How do we draw “a random point of the cloud” and still train by walking downhill?
z = \mu + \sigma\,\varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal N(0, 1).

Draw the randomness \varepsilon first, from a fixed bell curve; then shift and stretch it.
Example: \mu = 1, \sigma = 0.5: \varepsilon = -1 gives z = 0.5; \varepsilon = 0.5 gives z = 1.25.
z is now an ordinary formula in \mu and \sigma, so the gradient flows back through it to the encoder.


If we drew z directly from N(mu, sigma²), the draw would be a black box: how does the result change if mu changes a little? Writing z = mu + sigma·eps answers it: dz/dmu = 1, dz/dsigma = eps. In the demo elbo1d the 20 orange dots are z = mu + s·eps with 20 fixed eps; dragging mu shifts them all, dragging s stretches them around mu.

title: The variational autoencoder
section: How far is a cloud from the prior?
text:
How far is a cloud from the prior?
The penalty is the Kullback–Leibler divergence \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p): zero when the two distributions are equal, positive otherwise. For a 1D cloud \mathcal N(\mu, s^2) and the prior \mathcal N(0, 1):
\mathrm{KL} = \tfrac12\big(\mu^2 + s^2 - 1 - \ln s^2\big)

Moving the centre away from 0 costs \tfrac12\mu^2; a cloud much narrower (or wider) than 1 costs too.

The three cases: the prior itself (KL 0); the best cloud of the demo’s default example (mu 1.2, s 0.45: KL 1.12); a narrow cloud away from 0 (mu −1.5, s 0.15: KL 2.53). In 2D (or k dimensions) with independent coordinates, the KLs add. The formula is on this slide so the exercises can use it; the derivation is on the next slide.

title: The variational autoencoder
section: The math: KL of two Gaussians
text:
The math: KL of two Gaussians
\mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p) = \mathbb E_{q}\big[\ln q(z) - \ln p(z)\big]. With q = \mathcal N(\mu, s^2) and p = \mathcal N(0, 1):
\ln q(z) = -\tfrac12\ln(2\pi s^2) - \frac{(z-\mu)^2}{2s^2}, \qquad \ln p(z) = -\tfrac12\ln(2\pi) - \frac{z^2}{2}.
Use \mathbb E_q[(z-\mu)^2] = s^2 and \mathbb E_q[z^2] = \mu^2 + s^2:
\mathrm{KL} = -\tfrac12\ln s^2 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac12(\mu^2 + s^2) = \tfrac12\big(\mu^2 + s^2 - 1 - \ln s^2\big).

\ge 0, with equality only at \mu = 0, s = 1 (since s^2 - 1 - \ln s^2 \ge 0).
Not symmetric: \mathrm{KL}(q\|p) \ne \mathrm{KL}(p\|q) in general.

title: The variational autoencoder
text:
The VAE loss
For every training image x, with z = \mu(x) + \sigma(x)\,\varepsilon:
\text{loss}(x) = \underbrace{\text{reconstruction error of } \text{decode}(z)}_{\text{rebuild this image}} \;+\; \beta\cdot\underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\big(q(z\mid x)\,\|\,\mathcal N(0, I)\big)}_{\text{stay near the prior}}

Reconstruction: squared pixel error (Gaussian pixel noise), or the cross-entropy when the decoder outputs an “ink probability” per pixel, as for digits.
\beta = 1 is the standard VAE. Larger \beta: tidier latent space, blurrier images. Smaller \beta: sharper, but gaps return.
Encoder and decoder are trained together, downhill on the average loss.


Concept slide: the two forces of slide 3 written as one number to minimise. The next slide (math layer) shows where it comes from: with beta = 1 and the right reconstruction term, the loss is minus a lower bound on log p(x), the evidence lower bound (ELBO).

title: The variational autoencoder
section: The math: where the loss comes from (ELBO)
text:
The math: where the loss comes from (ELBO)
Model: z \sim p(z) = \mathcal N(0, I), image x \sim p(x\mid z) (the decoder). We would like to maximise \ln p(x) = \ln\int p(x\mid z)\,p(z)\,dz, but the integral is intractable. For any q(z):
\ln p(x) = \ln \mathbb E_{q}\!\left[\frac{p(x\mid z)\,p(z)}{q(z)}\right] \;\ge\; \mathbb E_{q}\big[\ln p(x\mid z)\big] - \mathrm{KL}\big(q\,\|\,p\big) \;=:\; \text{ELBO}
by Jensen’s inequality (\ln is concave). The gap is exactly \mathrm{KL}\big(q(z)\,\|\,p(z\mid x)\big) \ge 0.

Maximising the ELBO over the decoder makes the images likely; over q it makes q approach the posterior p(z\mid x). The VAE loss is -\text{ELBO} (with \beta = 1).
Gaussian decoder p(x\mid z) = \mathcal N(\text{decode}(z), \sigma_x^2 I): -\ln p(x\mid z) = \frac{\|x - \text{decode}(z)\|^2}{2\sigma_x^2} + \text{const}, the squared error.
“Variational”: q is chosen from a family (Gaussians) to make the bound tight; the encoder outputs it in one pass for every x (“amortised”).


Proof of the gap: ln p(x) − ELBO = E_q[ln q(z) − ln p(z|x)] using p(x|z)p(z) = p(z|x)p(x). So the bound is tight exactly when q is the true posterior. Bayesian reading in one sentence for the concept layer: the standard cloud is the prior, each image’s cloud an approximate posterior.

title: The variational autoencoder
section: A VAE you can solve by hand
text:
A VAE you can solve by hand
One grey value x and a 1D latent z. Decoder: \hat x = w z with w = 1 and pixel noise \sigma_x = 0.5. Observed x = 1.5.

Ignoring the image costs reconstruction; being too sure costs KL. The best cloud sits between the prior and the image.

Rebuild term = ((x − w mu)² + w² s²)/(2 sx²): the expected squared error over the cloud, divided by 2 sx². At the prior: (2.25 + 1)/0.5 = 6.5. Too confident: (0 + 0.0025)/0.5 = 0.005, but KL = ½(2.25 + 0.0025 − 1 − ln 0.0025) = 3.622. Best: mu = 1.2, s² = 0.2. The best cloud is the exact posterior of z given x for this model (math slide after the demo).

title: The variational autoencoder
text:
Try it: the two forces




Start: q = prior, total 6.5. Drag mu towards x: reconstruction falls fast, KL rises slowly. Shrink s: the decoded blue dots gather around x, the reconstruction falls, KL rises. “best cloud” jumps to mu 1.2, s 0.447, total 1.705. Preset “best (β = 5)”: mu 0.667, s 0.745: the cloud is pulled towards the prior; the reconstruction term rises to 2.5. The readout also shows the reconstruction estimated from the 20 draws (what training actually uses): at the prior it is 8.52 instead of 6.5, a noisy estimate of the same number.

title: The variational autoencoder
text:
The math: the best cloud
L(\mu, s) = \frac{(x - w\mu)^2 + w^2 s^2}{2\sigma_x^2} + \frac{\beta}{2}\big(\mu^2 + s^2 - 1 - \ln s^2\big)

\partial L/\partial\mu = 0: \ \mu^* = \dfrac{w\,x}{w^2 + \beta\sigma_x^2}. \qquad\partial L/\partial (s^2) = 0: \ s^{*2} = \dfrac{\beta\sigma_x^2}{\beta\sigma_x^2 + w^2}.
Numbers (w = 1, \sigma_x = 0.5, x = 1.5): \beta = 1: \mu^* = 1.2, s^{*2} = 0.2. \beta = 5: \mu^* = 0.667, s^{*2} = 0.556.
For \beta = 1 this is exactly the Bayesian posterior of z given x (a product of two Gaussians): here the bound is tight. Larger \beta pulls q towards the prior.

title: The variational autoencoder
text:
Summary







Idea
In one line




Cloud
the encoder gives each image a centre \mu and a spread \sigma


Reparameterisation
z = \mu + \sigma\varepsilon: randomness first, so gradients flow


Prior
one standard cloud \mathcal N(0, I) that all clouds are pulled towards


KL
\tfrac12(\mu^2 + s^2 - 1 - \ln s^2) per dimension; 0 only for the prior


Loss
reconstruction +\ \beta\cdotKL; \beta = 1 is the standard VAE


Two forces
rebuild well (small, separate clouds) vs. look like the prior (wide, overlapping)



Next: use the trained decoder to generate, interpolate and detect unusual images.

title: Quiz: generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Short questions on generating, interpolating and using a trained VAE. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. How do you generate a new image with a trained VAE?






Hint





Which part of the network do you need, and where does its input come from?









Answer





Draw z from the prior \mathcal N(0, I) and pass it through the decoder. The encoder is not needed.




Q2. True or false: the latent midpoint of two images always decodes to the pixel average of the two images.






Hint





True for a linear decoder. Is the VAE decoder linear?









Answer





False. A linear decoder (PCA) maps the midpoint to the average, a double exposure. A curved decoder maps it to an in-between shape: a bar halfway, a digit halfway between a 1 and a 7.




Q3. A colleague names the latent axes of a 2D VAE “z_1 = thickness” and “z_2 = slant”. What is the problem?






Hint





Does the loss change if the latent space is rotated?









Answer





The prior \mathcal N(0, I) and the KL penalty look the same after a rotation of the latent space, so the axes have no fixed meaning; another training run could give rotated or flipped axes. Directions should be read from decoded images along them, and need not line up with the axes.




Q4. Why are the images from a VAE blurrier than the training images?






Hint





What single image best matches several different images in squared error?









Answer





Several training images share each region of latent space, and the decoder outputs one image for it. The output that minimises the average squared error is their average, and an average of slightly different sharp images is blurred.




Q5. You use reconstruction error to find unusual cells. Name one kind of unusual cell this will catch and one it may miss.






Hint





What can the decoder draw?









Answer





It catches shapes the decoder cannot draw (a ring, two cells in one crop: large error). It misses unusual cells that happen to look like a normal one in squared error (a square close to a round cell), and small details that change few pixels.




Q6. What does increasing \beta do to generated images and to the latent space?






Hint





Stronger pull towards the prior.









Answer





The latent space gets smoother and better filled, with directions that often follow one factor each; the images get blurrier and more average.

title: Exercise: generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Generate
draw z \sim \mathcal N(0, I), decode


Latent walk
decode z(t) = (1 - t)\,z_A + t\,z_B for t from 0 to 1


Pixel fade
(1 - t)\,x_A + t\,x_B, the images themselves averaged


Reconstruction error
mean squared pixel error between an image and the decoded centre of its cloud


Anomaly score
the reconstruction error; above a threshold set on normal images → “unusual”


Denoising
encode a noisy image, decode the centre of its cloud



The two models of the demo: a 2D VAE trained on MNIST handwritten digits, and a 2D VAE trained on synthetic cell masks (round, elongated, dividing, with a protrusion). Both: 28\times28 images, encoder 784 \to 192 \to 2, decoder 2 \to 192 \to 784.

title: Exercise: generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
By hand

Part A — walks and midpoints
A decoder draws a bright bar on a 3-pixel image: pixel i (i = 0, 1, 2) gets \max(0,\ 1 - |z - i|).
B1. Let z_A = 0 and z_B = 2. Write z(t) for t = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, and decode each.
B2. Compute the pixel fade at t = 0.5. Compare with the decoded latent midpoint. Which one is an image of “a bar”?
B3. A linear decoder (PCA) maps z(t) to the pixel fade exactly. Explain why, using \text{decode}(z) = \bar{\mathbf x} + z\,\mathbf u.


Part B — generating
B4. New images are made by drawing z from the 2D prior \mathcal N(0, I). The probability that a draw lands within radius r of 0 is 1 - e^{-r^2/2}. What fraction of draws lands within radius 1, 2 and 3?
B5. The demo’s “far outside” point is z = (3.3,\ -3.3). How much less probable is a draw near this point than a draw near 0 (ratio of the prior densities)? What does the decoder output there, and should we trust it?


Part C — applications
B6. On 2000 normal test masks of the cell-shape VAE, 95% have reconstruction error below 0.0295 and 99% below 0.0447. You set the threshold at 0.0447. About how many of 2000 normal cells are flagged (false alarms)? Which of these is flagged: a ring (error 0.172), two separate cells in one crop (0.253), a square cell (0.030)?
B7. Explain why the square is not flagged, although no training cell was square. What kind of anomaly can a reconstruction-error detector not see?
B8. Explain in two sentences why decoding a noisy image removes the noise, and what it may remove besides the noise.






Solutions





B1. z(t) = 2t: z = 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, decoded (1, 0, 0), (0.5, 0.5, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, 0.5, 0.5), (0, 0, 1). The bar moves from left to right (smeared over two pixels when it is between them).
B2. Pixel fade at t = 0.5: \tfrac12(1, 0, 0) + \tfrac12(0, 0, 1) = (0.5,\ 0,\ 0.5): two half-bright bars, a double exposure. The latent midpoint decodes to (0, 1, 0): one bar in the middle. Only the latent midpoint is an image of a bar.
B3. \text{decode}\big((1-t)z_A + tz_B\big) = \bar{\mathbf x} + \big((1-t)z_A + tz_B\big)\mathbf u = (1-t)(\bar{\mathbf x} + z_A\mathbf u) + t(\bar{\mathbf x} + z_B\mathbf u), which is the pixel fade of the two decoded images. A linear map preserves straight lines and averages; only a curved decoder can turn a straight latent line into a moving bar.
B4. Radius 1: 1 - e^{-0.5} = 0.393. Radius 2: 1 - e^{-2} = 0.865. Radius 3: 1 - e^{-4.5} = 0.989. About 1 draw in 90 lands outside radius 3.
B5. The density ratio is e^{-(3.3^2 + 3.3^2)/2} = e^{-10.89} \approx 0.00002: about 50,000 times less probable per unit area than near 0. The decoder still outputs an image (for the digits a thin slanted stroke), because it always answers; but almost no training images were encoded there, so nothing says the image is a realistic digit.
B6. 1% of 2000, about 20 false alarms. The ring (0.172) and the two cells (0.253) are flagged; the square (0.030) is not.
B7. A square is close enough to a large round cell that the decoder rebuilds it as one with only a small error (mostly at the corners). The detector only sees anomalies that the decoder cannot draw; an unusual image that happens to look like a normal one in the squared-error sense passes. Anomalies in a small detail (a tiny dark spot) are also hard to see, because they change few pixels.
B8. The decoder can only draw images like those it was trained on, and pixel noise is not among them, so the decoded image is a clean cell. But it is the model’s version of the cell: details it never learned or cannot store in two numbers (a thin protrusion, an exact outline) are replaced by typical ones, and if the noise moves the code to the wrong region, the output is the wrong shape.





Math questions
B9. (math) Several different images x share (almost) the same code z. Show that the single output c minimising \mathbb E\big[\|x - c\|^2\big] is c = \mathbb E[x], and use this to explain why VAE images are blurry.






Solutions (math)





B9. (math) \mathbb E\|x - c\|^2 = \mathbb E\|(x - \mathbb E x) + (\mathbb E x - c)\|^2 = \mathbb E\|x - \mathbb E x\|^2 + \|\mathbb E x - c\|^2 (the cross term has mean zero). Only the second term depends on c, and it is zero at c = \mathbb E x. So the decoder’s best output for a z shared by several images is their average, and the average of differently placed sharp strokes or outlines is a blurred one. Wider clouds (larger \beta) make more images share each z: more blur.

title: Exercise: generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Explore
The demo has two tabs with fixed, pre-trained weights. Left: the latent space with the cloud centres of 1000 test images coloured by class (labels at the class centres) and the prior’s radius-2 circle (dashed). Drag z or click in the map: the large image is decoded from z. Draw an image in the dashed box (or press example ▸) and the encoder places it: the cross is the cloud centre, the orange ellipse its ±2 sd; the error under the encoder input is its reconstruction error. The strip below shows a walk z → z′, draws from the encoder’s cloud, or draws from the prior. noise on input adds noise (fixed seed) to the encoder input.



Data: MNIST handwritten digits (Y. LeCun, C. Cortes, C. J. C. Burges; CC BY-SA 3.0 as stated in the Keras documentation); the 20 example digits are MNIST test images. The cell masks are synthetic, generated by the training script.
E1. Digits. Press example ▸ a few times. Where do the 0s and 1s land, and how big are the clouds? Then draw your own 4 and encode it. Is its reconstruction a 4?
E2. Preset walk 1 → 7, then walk 0 → 1. Describe the strips. Which digits does the 0 → 1 walk pass through, and why?
E3. Press sample from the prior a few times. Are all generated images digits? Then tick decoded grid: where in the map do the images stop looking like digits?
E4. Switch to Cell shapes. Tick decoded grid and describe how the shapes change across the map. Press walk round → dividing.
E5. Cell shapes: step example ▸ through all 15 examples and note the errors. Which kind of normal cell has the largest errors, and what does the reconstruction lose? Which of the three anomalies (examples 13–15) would a threshold of 0.045 flag?
E6. Cell shapes: load example 2 (a round cell), then set noise on input to 0.3. Compare the encoder input, the decoded image and the error. Repeat with example 4 (an elongated cell). Then try the same in the digits tab.






Solutions





E1. The first two examples are 0s, landing at the lower left (centres (-2.48, -1.56) and (-2.19, -2.03)); the 1s land on the right ((2.15, 0.37), (2.00, -0.78)). The clouds are tiny: spreads 0.07–0.13 per axis for these four (the mean over all test digits is 0.067): one image says a lot about its z. Your own 4 depends on your drawing: 4s land in the crowded region around (0.6, 0.35), next to the 9s, and often come back looking like a 9.
E2. 1 → 7: a 1, then a 1 that grows a hook, a 9-like shape, and a 7: every step is digit-like. 0 → 1 passes 0, 6, 2, 5, 9, a faint smudge and 1: the straight line from the 0s (lower left) to the 1s (right) crosses the regions of 6, 2, 5 and 9 on its way. The second-to-last step is faint because it lies in the sparse region below the crowded middle, where few digits are encoded.
E3. Most samples are digits (the first press gives 2, 6, 9, 9, an unclear 7/5-like stroke, 1, 5), but some are blends or blurred, from points between classes. In the grid, the bottom middle (around z_2 < -2, |z_1| < 1) decodes to smudges: almost no test digits are encoded there (1 of the 1000 shown).
E4. Large round cells on the left, smaller and more elongated cells to the right, with the orientation of the long axis changing around the map; dividing cells (dumbbells) along the bottom. Protrusions do not appear as a separate region. The walk round → dividing goes through slightly elongated cells to a waisted dumbbell: a smooth change of shape.
E5. Normal cells: 0.004–0.023. The cells with a protrusion have the largest errors (0.023, 0.016, 0.021): the reconstruction is a round or oval cell without the thin protrusion. Anomalies: ring 0.172 and two cells 0.253 are flagged (their codes, (-6.30, 3.49) and (-4.18, -0.36), lie outside the map; the cross is not visible); the square (0.030) is not.
E6. Example 2 with noise 0.3: the encoder input is speckled, the decoded image is a clean round cell, and the error (against the clean mask) is 0.009, against 0.045 for the noisy input itself. Example 4: the noisy code lands elsewhere and the decoded cell has the wrong orientation: error 0.110, worse than the noisy input (0.047). In the digits tab the decoded image is also free of speckle, but often a different or blurrier digit; in squared error it is usually worse than the noisy input, because the digit reconstructions are blurry even without noise (mean error 0.041 over the test set).

title: Exercise: generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Where this leads

Bigger latent spaces (10–100 dimensions) rebuild far more detail; the 2D maps here are for looking, not for best quality.
Conditional VAEs also give the decoder a label (a digit class, a treatment), so it can generate “a 7” or “a treated cell” on demand.
GANs and diffusion models generate much sharper images; diffusion models learn to remove noise step by step and are behind most current image generators.
Morphology spaces: autoencoder latent spaces of cell and nucleus images are used to compare treatments and find unusual cells in large screens.

title: Segmentation networks
text:
About this lecture
A classification network says what is in an image. For segmentation we want a class for every pixel.

An encoder–decoder: shrink the image to gain context, then upsample back to full size.
Skip connections (the U-Net) bring the fine detail back.
Train with a per-pixel loss: cross-entropy, or a Dice loss when the objects are a small part of the image.
Judge the result with Dice and IoU, by looking at the errors, and on images unlike the training ones.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Suggested demo tour (unetseg): “a typical image” (Dice 0.986), “U-Net vs Otsu on uneven illumination” (0.987 vs 0.349), click the levels of the architecture to see feature maps; “no skips: small nuclei”; “touching nuclei merge”; “dimmer microscope” (domain shift: Dice 0.269, worse than Otsu). Day 6 owns Dice/IoU and the confusion matrix; recall them in one line. Instance segmentation by networks is day 18.

title: Segmentation networks
text:
From “what” to “which pixels”

Output: one class probability per pixel, an image of the same size as the input.
Naive way: classify a patch around every pixel with the network of the last unit. Slow (one network run per pixel), and the patch is small, so the context is small.
Better: a network that is convolutional all the way: no dense layer, so it takes any image size and gives a map out.
The problem: pooling made the maps small (64 \to 16 pixels). We need to get back to full resolution.

title: Segmentation networks
text:
Encoder–decoder


Encoder (left): convolutions and pooling, as in the last unit. The maps get smaller and see more context.
Decoder (right): upsample (each pixel becomes 2 \times 2), then convolutions that sharpen the result. Back to 64 \times 64, one probability per pixel.


The figure is the network of the demo: two levels, 8, 16 and 32 channels, about 30,000 weights. Upsampling by nearest neighbour followed by a 3×3 convolution; the alternative is a transposed convolution, next math slide.

title: Segmentation networks
text:
Upsampling by hand
1D signal (1, 2, 3), upsampled by 2:

Nearest neighbour: (1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3). Blocky; a following convolution smooths it, e.g. with (\tfrac14, \tfrac12, \tfrac14): (0.75, 1.25, 1.75, 2.25, 2.75, 2.25) (zero beyond the ends).
Transposed convolution with stride 2: each input value stamps a weighted copy of the kernel into the output, 2 steps apart. With the kernel (\tfrac12, 1, \tfrac12):

(0.5,\ 1,\ 1.5,\ 2,\ 2.5,\ 3,\ 1.5)
linear interpolation. With a learned kernel the network chooses its own way to upsample.

title: Segmentation networks
text:
The math: transposed convolution

A strided convolution is a matrix A (banded, rows s positions apart): \mathbf y = A\mathbf x maps n to about n/s values.
The transposed convolution applies A^\top: from n/s values back to n. Each input value adds the kernel, scaled by itself, to the output: “stamping”.
Output length (n - 1)s + k - 2p: for n = 3, s = 2, k = 3, p = 0: 7.
It is the same operation that backpropagation uses to send gradients back through a strided convolution. A^\top is not the inverse A^{-1}: it does not undo the convolution, it only goes back to the larger size.

title: Segmentation networks
text:
Skip connections: the U-Net
A decoder that only gets the bottleneck knows what is where, roughly; the exact boundaries were lost in pooling.

U-Net (Ronneberger, Fischer and Brox, 2015): copy the encoder’s feature maps of each size across to the decoder and concatenate them with the upsampled maps.
Context comes from below (deep, coarse maps), detail from the side (shallow, sharp maps).
In the demo network: 32 upsampled channels + 16 copied = 48 channels into the decoder at 32 \times 32; 16 + 8 = 24 at 64 \times 64.

title: Segmentation networks
section: Try it: a U-Net segments nuclei
text:
Try it: a U-Net segments nuclei




Synthetic 64×64 images, generated with the same code as the training set; “new image” draws a new one. Errors: TP white, FP red, FN blue. “U-Net vs Otsu on uneven illumination”: the U-Net Dice 0.987, Otsu 0.349 (the bright right side is all “object”). Click “bottleneck”: 32 coarse maps. “no skips: small nuclei”: 0.936 against 0.954 with skips (same image). On the training distribution skips help little here (validation Dice 0.968 vs 0.965): these smooth blobs are easy to locate from 16×16 maps. “touching nuclei merge”: 7 nuclei, but the mask has 4 connected pieces.

title: Segmentation networks
text:
Per-pixel loss

Cross-entropy per pixel, averaged over all pixels: every pixel is one classification example.
Class imbalance: if nuclei are 5 % of the pixels, “everything is background” is 95 % correct (recall “accuracy lies”, thresholding day). Its cross-entropy is not very large either.
Remedies: weight the object pixels more, or use the Dice loss: $1 - $ soft Dice, computed from the probabilities so that it has a gradient.
Recall (thresholding day): Dice = 2|P \cap G|/(|P| + |G|) of a predicted mask P and the truth G; IoU = |P \cap G|/|P \cup G|.

title: Segmentation networks
section: The math: soft Dice and its gradient
text:
The math: soft Dice and its gradient
With probabilities p_i \in [0, 1] and the true mask g_i \in \{0, 1\}:
D = \frac{2\sum_i p_ig_i}{\sum_i p_i + \sum_i g_i}, \qquad \mathcal L_\text{Dice} = 1 - D, \qquad \frac{\partial D}{\partial p_j} = \frac{2g_j\left(\sum_i p_i + \sum_i g_i\right) - 2\sum_i p_ig_i}{\left(\sum_i p_i + \sum_i g_i\right)^2}

For hard 0/1 predictions D is the usual Dice. The loss depends only on the object pixels and the predicted object area: the background count does not dilute it.
Weighted cross-entropy: -\frac1N\sum_i\big[w_1g_i\log p_i + w_0(1 - g_i)\log(1 - p_i)\big], with e.g. w_c \propto 1/(\text{share of class } c).
(Milletari, Navab and Ahmadi, 2016.)

title: Segmentation networks
text:
Evaluating a segmentation network

Dice and IoU against the ground truth, on held-out images (never seen in training or tuning).
Look at the errors, not only at the number: where are the false positives and negatives? Merged nuclei, missed dim nuclei and boundary pixels are different problems.
The number hides the distribution: a few failed images can disappear in an average over many good ones.
How to build an honest test set, and object-level scores (matched nuclei, F1): the evaluation day (day 16).

title: Segmentation networks
text:
Data: annotation is the bottleneck

Every training image needs a mask drawn by hand: hours per image for dense nuclei.
Small networks and augmentation (flips, rotations, brightness, noise, elastic deformation) go a long way with tens of annotated images: the original U-Net was trained on 30.
Synthetic images with known truth (as in the demo) are good for teaching and testing, but real images differ: blur, debris, textures the generator never made.
A network knows only its training range: a dimmer microscope, more noise, another stain can break it. The demo’s sliders show this; days 16 and 18 come back to it.

title: Segmentation networks
text:
After the mask

Touching nuclei come out as one blob: a semantic mask says “nucleus or not”, not “which nucleus”. Classic fix: a third class “boundary between nuclei”, then labelling or the watershed (days 9–10). Networks that output separate objects directly: day 18.
The probability map is a perfect data term for a graph cut (day 13): D_p(\ell) = -\log p_\ell, plus a smoothness term. The two ideas combine.
The baseline to beat: a random forest on the feature stack (day 14) with a few strokes of annotation. Often it is good enough, and it needs much less data.

title: Segmentation networks
text:
Summary







Idea
In one line




Encoder–decoder
shrink for context, upsample back to one probability per pixel


Upsampling
nearest + convolution, or transposed convolution (“stamping” the kernel)


U-Net
skip connections copy encoder maps to the decoder: context + detail


Per-pixel loss
cross-entropy per pixel; Dice loss or class weights against imbalance


Evaluation
Dice / IoU on held-out images, and look at the errors


Limits
needs annotations; only knows its training range; semantic, not instance masks



Next: evaluation and statistics (day 16): what makes a test set honest, and how to compare methods.

title: Quiz: texture and co-occurrence matrices
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. GLCMs are symmetric and normalised unless said otherwise.

Q1. Why can no feature computed from the histogram of an object tell a fine texture from a coarse one?






Hint





Shuffle the pixels of an object. What happens to its histogram?









Answer





The histogram ignores where the values are: shuffling the pixels changes the texture completely but leaves the histogram, and every statistic computed from it (mean, standard deviation, quartiles), unchanged. Texture is about pairs of pixels at some distance, which is what the co-occurrence matrix counts.




Q2. A GLCM has all its mass on the diagonal. What does that say about the image, and what are its contrast and homogeneity?






Hint





The diagonal means i = j.









Answer





Every pixel has the same (quantised) level as its partner at that offset: the image is constant along that direction, or periodic with the offset as a period. Contrast is 0 and homogeneity is 1.




Q3. White noise and a smooth texture with the same histogram are measured at d = 1 and d = 10. Which one’s contrast changes between the two distances?






Hint





At what distance are the pixels of each texture unrelated?









Answer





The smooth texture: at d = 1 neighbours are similar (low contrast); at d = 10, beyond the grain size, they are unrelated, and the contrast approaches that of white noise. White noise has the same high contrast at every distance, because its pixels are unrelated at any distance.




Q4. A collaborator quantises each cell to 8 levels between its own minimum and maximum before computing texture. A drug makes the cells dimmer and lowers their contrast. Will the texture features show it?






Hint





What does stretching each cell to its own range do to a dim cell?









Answer





Probably not: per-cell min–max quantisation stretches every cell to the full range of 8 levels, which undoes a change in brightness and contrast. Use one fixed range for all cells (and the same L), so that a lower contrast shows up as a lower GLCM contrast.




Q5. Why does L = 256 give unreliable texture features on a nucleus of 300 pixels?






Hint





How many cells does the matrix have, and how many pairs are counted?









Answer





The matrix has 65 536 cells but only a few hundred pairs are counted: almost every cell is 0 or 1. Features such as entropy and ASM then mostly reflect the number of pairs, and two nuclei with the same texture give quite different values. Use 8–16 levels for small objects.




Q6. Two programs report “energy” 0.25 and 0.5 for the same matrix. Can both be right?






Hint





Naming traps.









Answer





Yes: some programs call ASM = \sum p^2 “energy”, others use \sqrt{\text{ASM}}. Here ASM = 0.25 and \sqrt{\text{ASM}} = 0.5. Always check the formula, not only the name.




Q7. Why is the LBP histogram of an object unchanged when the illumination doubles?






Hint





What does an LBP code compare?









Answer





Each bit only records whether a neighbour is at least as bright as the centre. Doubling every value (or adding a constant, or any increasing map) keeps those comparisons, so every code and therefore the histogram stays the same. (Noise in dark, flat regions can still flip bits.)




Q8. (math) Show that for a symmetric GLCM, contrast = 2\sigma^2(1 - \text{correlation}). What is the contrast of a texture with correlation 1? With correlation −1 and \sigma^2 = 0.25?






Hint





Expand E[(I - J)^2] when I and J have the same mean and variance.









Answer





E[(I - J)^2] = \operatorname{var}(I) + \operatorname{var}(J) - 2\operatorname{cov}(I, J) = 2\sigma^2 - 2\rho\sigma^2 (the means cancel because they are equal). Correlation 1: contrast 0. Correlation −1, \sigma^2 = 0.25: contrast 1: the 0/1 checkerboard.

title: Exercise: texture and co-occurrence matrices
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Offset
distance d and angle: 0° = (d, 0) to the right, 45° = (d, -d), 90° = (0, -d) up, 135° = (-d, -d); y points down


Co-occurrence count P(i, j)
number of pixels with level i whose partner at the offset has level j (both inside the image)


Symmetric
P + P^\top: every pair counted both ways


p(i, j)
P divided by its sum


Contrast
\sum (i-j)^2 p


Homogeneity
\sum p / (1 + (i-j)^2)


ASM, energy
\sum p^2, \sqrt{\text{ASM}}


Entropy
-\sum p \log_2 p (bits)


Correlation
\sum (i-\mu)(j-\mu)\,p / \sigma^2 with \mu = \sum i\,p, \sigma^2 = \sum (i-\mu)^2 p (symmetric p)


LBP
8 neighbours clockwise from the top-left, bit 1 if neighbour ≥ centre, read as a binary number (first bit most significant)
