title: Exercise: texture and co-occurrence matrices
text:
By hand
I = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \qquad (L = 3 \text{ levels})
B1. Offset 0°, d = 1 (partner to the right). (a) List the counts of the 12 horizontal pairs and build the symmetric matrix P (3 \times 3, sum 24). (b) Compute contrast, homogeneity and ASM. (c) Compute the entropy. (Use \log_2; a calculator is fine.) (d) Compute \mu, \sigma^2 and the correlation.
B2. Offset 90°, d = 1 (partner above). (a) Build the symmetric matrix. (b) Compute contrast and homogeneity. Which direction has more contrast, and what in the image explains it?
B3. The same image at 45° (d = 1, partner up and to the right) has the symmetric matrix \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix}. Why does it sum to 18 and not 24? Compute its contrast.
B4. Two 4 \times 4 binary images with the same histogram (8 zeros, 8 ones): a checkerboard, and “halves” (every row is 0 0 1 1). (a) Build the symmetric GLCM at 0°, d = 1, for both. (b) Compute contrast and correlation for both. Which features would separate them, which would not? (c) At 90°, what is the GLCM of the halves image?
B5. Vertical stripes with a period of 8 pixels (the value depends only on x, repeating every 8 columns). For which d at 0° is the contrast zero? At 90°? Where is it largest?
B6. The 3 \times 3 neighbourhood \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 2 & 9 \\ 5 & \mathbf 5 & 8 \\ 1 & 4 & 7 \end{bmatrix}. (a) Compute its LBP code. (b) Compute its rotation-invariant code (the smallest of the 8 circular rotations of the bit string). (c) Is it a “uniform” pattern (at most two 0/1 changes around the circle)? (d) Add 10 to every pixel, or double every pixel. What happens to the code?

Math questions
B7. (math) For a symmetric p, show that contrast = 2\sigma^2(1 - \text{correlation}). Check it on B1.
B8. (math) Show that 0 \le \text{entropy} \le \log_2 K where K is the number of non-zero cells, and that K \le \min(L^2, N) for N counted pairs. What does this mean for L = 64 on an object with 200 pairs?
B9. (math) Show that the LBP code is unchanged by any strictly increasing grey-level map g, and that a rotation of the image by 90° about the centre pixel shifts the bit string circularly by 2 positions.
B10. (math) Show that rotating the image by 90° permutes the four standard offsets (up to sign), so the average of a feature over 0°, 45°, 90° and 135° of a symmetric GLCM is unchanged.






Solutions





B1. (a) Rows: (0,0) (0,1) (1,1); (0,0) (0,1) (1,1); (0,2) (2,2) (2,2); (2,2) (2,2) (2,2). Counts: (0,0) 2, (0,1) 2, (1,1) 2, (0,2) 1, (2,2) 5. Symmetric: P = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 10 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \text{sum } 24. (b) Contrast = (4 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 4)/24 = 12/24 = \mathbf{0.5} (cells (0,1), (1,0) differ by 1; (0,2), (2,0) by 2). Homogeneity = (18 + 4 \cdot 0.5 + 2 \cdot 0.2)/24 = 20.4/24 = \mathbf{0.85}. ASM = (16 + 4 + 1 + 4 + 16 + 1 + 100)/576 = 142/576 = \mathbf{0.247}. (c) Entropy = -\big[2 \cdot \tfrac{4}{24}\log_2\tfrac{4}{24} + 2 \cdot \tfrac{2}{24}\log_2\tfrac{2}{24} + 2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{24}\log_2\tfrac{1}{24} + \tfrac{10}{24}\log_2\tfrac{10}{24}\big] = \mathbf{2.37} bits. (d) Row sums 7, 6, 11, so p_x = (7, 6, 11)/24: \mu = (6 + 22)/24 = 1.167, \sigma^2 = \sum (i - \mu)^2 p_x = 0.722. \operatorname{cov} = \sum (i-\mu)(j-\mu) p = 0.472, correlation = 0.472/0.722 = \mathbf{0.654}.
B2. (a) Vertical pairs (lower pixel, upper pixel), columns left to right: column 0: (0,0) (0,0) (2,0); column 1: (0,0) (2,0) (2,2); column 2: (1,1) (2,1) (2,2); column 3: (1,1) (2,1) (2,2). Symmetric: P = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix}. (b) Contrast = (2 \cdot 2 \cdot 4 + 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 1)/24 = 20/24 = \mathbf{0.83}; homogeneity = (16 + 4 \cdot 0.5 + 4 \cdot 0.2)/24 = 18.8/24 = \mathbf{0.78}. More contrast vertically: the boundary between the top rows (0 and 1) and the bottom rows (2) runs horizontally, so vertical pairs cross it more often.
B3. A diagonal pair needs a partner one row up and one column right: only the 3 \times 3 lower-left pixels have one, 9 pairs, 18 counts in the symmetric matrix. Contrast = (2 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 1)/18 = 6/18 = 0.33.
B4. (a) Checkerboard: every horizontal pair is (0,1) or (1,0): P = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 12 \\ 12 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. Halves: per row (0,0) (0,1) (1,1): P = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 4 \\ 4 & 8 \end{bmatrix}. (b) Checkerboard: contrast 1, correlation −1. Halves: contrast 8/24 = 0.33, correlation +0.33. Contrast, homogeneity (0.5 vs 0.83), ASM (0.5 vs 0.28), entropy (1.0 vs 1.92) and correlation all separate them; mean, standard deviation and the histogram do not. (c) Vertically every pair is (0,0) or (1,1): P = \begin{bmatrix} 12 & 0 \\ 0 & 12 \end{bmatrix}, contrast 0, correlation 1.
B5. At 0°: zero for d = 8, 16, 24, \dots (a whole period: each pixel meets its own value). At 90°: zero for every d (the stripes are vertical). Largest at 0° for d = 4, 12, \dots (half a period: each pixel meets the opposite phase). Demo: contrast 24.75 at d = 4 and 12, 0 at d = 8 and 16.
B6. (a) Clockwise from the top-left: 6, 2, 9, 8, 7, 4, 1, 5. Compared with the centre 5: 1 0 1 1 1 0 0 1, so the code is 10111001_2 = \mathbf{185}. (b) The 8 rotations are 185, 115, 230, 205, 155, 55, 110, 220; the smallest is \mathbf{55} = 00110111_2. (c) Around the circle 1 0 1 1 1 0 0 1 changes 4 times: not uniform. (d) Nothing: the code depends only on which neighbours are at least as bright as the centre, which neither an offset nor a gain changes.









Solutions (math)





B7. Let I, J be the levels of a random pair. Symmetry gives the same marginal for I and J, so E[I] = E[J] = \mu and \operatorname{var} I = \operatorname{var} J = \sigma^2. Then \text{contrast} = E[(I - J)^2] = \operatorname{var}(I - J) = 2\sigma^2 - 2\operatorname{cov}(I, J) = 2\sigma^2(1 - \rho). B1: 2 \cdot 0.722 \cdot (1 - 0.654) = 0.50.
B8. Each term -p\log_2 p \ge 0 for 0 < p \le 1, so entropy \ge 0. With K non-zero probabilities, entropy is at most that of the uniform distribution on K cells, \log_2 K (Jensen’s inequality, or Gibbs’ inequality). There are L^2 cells, and N counts can fill at most N of them. With L = 64 and N = 200: entropy \le \log_2 200 = 7.6 bits, far below \log_2 4096 = 12; the value reflects the size of the object as much as its texture (demo: 6.80 bits on a disc of radius 6, against 9.01 on the whole patch).
B9. g strictly increasing means g(a) \ge g(b) \iff a \ge b, so every bit s(n_k - c) is unchanged. A rotation by 90° about the centre maps the neighbour positions top-left → top-right → bottom-right → bottom-left (and the edge neighbours likewise), i.e. each neighbour moves 2 steps around the clockwise ring: the bit string is shifted circularly by 2.
B10. A rotation R by 90° maps (d, 0) \mapsto (0, -d), (0, -d) \mapsto (-d, 0), (d, -d) \mapsto (-d, -d), (-d, -d) \mapsto (-d, d). Since a symmetric GLCM of offset \mathbf d equals that of -\mathbf d, the set \{0°, 45°, 90°, 135°\} is mapped to itself: the GLCM of the rotated image at angle \theta equals the GLCM of the original at another angle of the set (up to the slightly different image border). The average over the set is therefore unchanged.

title: Exercise: texture and co-occurrence matrices
text:
Explore
The demo computes the GLCM of a 64 \times 64 texture patch. The patch is shown quantised to L levels, with three sample pairs at the current offset drawn as yellow arrows. The heat map is the GLCM (rows: level at \mathbf x, columns: level at the partner; the diagonal dashed), with numbers for L \le 4. The table lists the five main features, and the polar plot the contrast against the angle (every 15°, offsets rounded to the grid) at the current d. Choose a second patch B to compare. The disc mask keeps only pairs with both pixels inside a disc; min–max quantises each patch over its own range instead of 0–255.



G1. Preset same histogram, different texture. Compare the two matrices: how many cells are used, and where? Compare the five features. Then set d = 4: which patch changes, and why not the other?
G2. Preset stripes: contrast depends on angle (vertical stripes, period 8, d = 2). Read the contrast at 0°, 45°, 90° and 135°. Why is 45° the same as 0°? Now set the stripe angle to 45° and repeat. Which angle gives zero contrast now?
G3. Preset period = d: contrast vanishes. Move d from 1 to 16 and note the contrast and correlation. Explain the pattern with B5.
G4. Preset fine vs coarse (A: white noise, B: smoothed noise). Read the contrast of both at d = 1, 2, 4, 8. Which one depends on d, and what does the d at which it levels off tell you?
G5. Preset too many levels on a small patch: A and B are two different crops of the same texture, measured in a disc of radius 6 with L = 64. Compare contrast and entropy of A and B. Then set L = 8. Then switch the disc off (radius “off”) at L = 64. What do you conclude?
G6. Preset min–max rescaling hides a brightness difference: B is the same kind of texture as A with half the contrast and darker. Compare A and B with min–max on, then off. Which setting tells you that B is different?
G7. Any stripes preset: untick symmetric. What happens to the number of pairs, and to the contrast? Why can the contrast never change when the matrix is made symmetric?






Solutions





G1. A (smoothed noise): 38 of 64 cells, all near the diagonal. B (the same pixels shuffled): all 64 cells. Contrast 0.51 against 10.59, homogeneity 0.79 against 0.31, ASM 0.058 against 0.016, entropy 4.42 against 6.00 bits, correlation 0.95 against −0.01. At d = 4, A’s contrast rises to 4.51 and its correlation falls to 0.57, while B stays (10.32, 0.02): B has no spatial structure at any distance, A’s grains are a few pixels wide.
G2. Contrast 12.65 at 0°, 45° and 135°, 0 at 90°. The 45° offset at d = 2 is (2, -2): it also moves 2 pixels across the vertical stripes, and moving up does not matter. With the stripe angle at 45° (stripes running along 135°): contrast 8.03 at 0° and 90°, 22.98 at 45°, 0 at 135° (along the stripes).
G3. Contrast 3.79 (d = 1), 12.65 (2), 24.75 (4), 12.34 (6), 0 (8), 24.75 (12), 0 (16); correlation 0.69, −0.02, −0.98, 0.01, 1, −0.98, 1. A full period brings each pixel back to its own value, half a period to the opposite one: contrast and correlation are periodic in d with the period of the texture.
G4. White noise: 10.32, 10.21, 10.34, 10.38: independent of d, because pixels are unrelated at any distance. Smoothed noise: 0.18, 0.36, 0.90, 2.29: it grows with d until pixels become unrelated; the distance at which it levels off (towards the white-noise value) is the size of the grains.
G5. With the disc and L = 64: contrast 14.89 against 6.27, entropy 6.80 against 6.49 bits, and only 200 pairs for 4096 cells. With L = 8: contrast 0.42 against 0.26, entropy 3.28 against 2.35. Without the disc at L = 64: contrast 12.05 against 11.98, entropy 9.01 against 9.01. On a small object the features are noisy (two crops of the same texture disagree by a factor of two in contrast), and with many levels the entropy is limited by the number of pairs. Fewer levels help, a larger region helps more.
G6. With min–max on: A and B look alike (contrast 0.23 and 0.26, ASM 0.141 and 0.125): each patch is stretched to the full range, which undoes B’s lower contrast and offset. With the fixed range 0–255: B has contrast 0.13 and ASM 0.33 against A’s 0.23 and 0.14. Only the fixed range shows the difference; per-object rescaling makes objects incomparable.
G7. The number of pairs halves (7936 → 3968 for d = 2 at 0°); the contrast stays 12.65. (i - j)^2 = (j - i)^2, so adding the transpose adds the same contrast as the original and the normalisation divides it out again. Features that are not symmetric in i and j (for example the row mean of an asymmetric texture) could change.

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
About this lecture
A marching-cubes mesh is not only a picture: it is a measurement. Today: what we can measure from it, how well, and which choices change the answer.

Area and volume from the triangles (the volume by the 3D shoelace formula).
Why counting voxel faces gets the area wrong at any resolution, and marching cubes does not.
Topology: components, holes, cracks, the Euler characteristic.
The choices: the iso-value c, smoothing, anisotropic spacing, surfacing a segmentation, and mesh size.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Last unit of the marching-cubes day. Builds on marching cubes (previous unit), the shoelace formula (isocontour unit; owned by the labelling day) and volumes3d/ (spacing). Choosing thresholds from histograms (Otsu) is the thresholding day’s; here it is one line.

title: Measuring surfaces
section: Area and volume from the triangles
text:
Area and volume from the triangles

Area: the sum of the triangle areas. Each triangle’s area is half the length of the cross product of two of its edges.
Volume: pick any point, e.g. the origin. Each triangle and the origin form a tetrahedron; add up their volumes with sign (+ when the triangle faces away from the origin, − when it faces it). Parts outside the object cancel, and what is left is the volume inside: the 3D version of the shoelace formula.
This needs a closed, consistently oriented mesh (all normals pointing out). A surface that touches the border of the volume is open: pad the volume with background first.
Both are sums over triangles: cheap, even for millions of triangles.

title: Measuring surfaces
section: The math: area and the divergence theorem
text:
The math: area and the divergence theorem
For a triangle with corners \mathbf a, \mathbf b, \mathbf c (counter-clockwise seen from outside):
\text{area} = \tfrac12\,\lVert(\mathbf b - \mathbf a) \times (\mathbf c - \mathbf a)\rVert, \qquad V = \sum_{\text{triangles}} \tfrac16\,\mathbf a \cdot (\mathbf b \times \mathbf c) = \sum \tfrac16 \det[\mathbf a\;\mathbf b\;\mathbf c].

\tfrac16\det[\mathbf a\,\mathbf b\,\mathbf c] is the signed volume of the tetrahedron (\mathbf 0, \mathbf a, \mathbf b, \mathbf c).
Divergence theorem with \mathbf F = \mathbf x/3 (\nabla\cdot\mathbf F = 1): V = \iiint 1\,dV = \oiint \tfrac13\,\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf n\,dA. On a flat triangle, \mathbf x \cdot \mathbf n is constant (= \mathbf a \cdot \mathbf n), and \tfrac13 (\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf n)\cdot\text{area} = \tfrac16\,\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c).
In 2D the same argument with \mathbf F = \mathbf x/2 gives the shoelace formula.
Translating the mesh adds \tfrac16\,\mathbf t\cdot\sum(\ldots) = 0 for a closed mesh: the origin does not matter.

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
One bright voxel, by hand




One voxel of value 1, all neighbours 0, c = 0.5.

Each of the 6 edges to a neighbour is crossed halfway: t = 0.5.
The surface: an octahedron with vertices at distance 0.5 from the centre.
Area \sqrt3 \approx 1.73, volume \tfrac16.
Counting voxels: volume 1, area 6 (the voxel’s faces).

A single voxel is the extreme case; on large objects the two volume estimates agree, the areas do not (next slide).

title: Measuring surfaces
section: Counting voxels: fine for volume, wrong for area
text:
Counting voxels: fine for volume, wrong for area

Volume = number of voxels inside × voxel volume. Errors at the boundary go both ways and cancel: a good estimate for large objects.
Area = number of exposed voxel faces × face area. Always too large: a slanted surface becomes a staircase, and a staircase is longer than the slope.
For a sphere about 1.5 times too large, at any resolution: finer voxels make smaller steps, but just as many of them per unit of area.
In 2D, the pixel-edge perimeter of a disk is 4/\pi \approx 1.27 times too long (for a convex shape it equals the perimeter of its bounding box).
Marching cubes cuts the corners: its area converges to the true area as the voxels shrink.

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
The math: where 1.5 comes from

A small patch of area dA with unit normal \mathbf n, replaced by a voxel staircase, exposes faces whose total area is its projections onto the three coordinate planes: (|n_x| + |n_y| + |n_z|)\,dA.
Averaged over all directions on a sphere, \langle|n_x|\rangle = \tfrac12 (the mean of |\cos\theta| over the sphere), so the staircase area is 3 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac32 times the true area, independent of the voxel size.
In 2D: (|n_x| + |n_y|)\,ds, with \langle|\cos\phi|\rangle = 2/\pi on the circle: 4/\pi.
Weighting voxel configurations cleverly (Lindblad, 2005) reduces the bias to a few per cent without a mesh.

title: Measuring surfaces
section: Try it: voxel faces vs marching cubes
text:
Try it: voxel faces vs marching cubes




Disk and ball of radius R, as a partial-volume grey image (each pixel ≈ the fraction of it inside) or a binary mask. At R = 6: voxel faces 674 against 4πR² = 452.4 (+49 %), marching cubes 449.4 (−0.7 %); pixel edges +27 %. Slide R up to 16: faces stay at +50 %, marching cubes at +0.07 %. Then “binary mask”: marching cubes now runs on 0/1 values, every vertex at an edge midpoint, and the area stays about 8 % too large at every R (terraces); volumes are fine either way.

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
Spacing, slices and topology

Anisotropic voxels: vertex positions use (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z) (forgetting \Delta z scales every volume by \Delta x/\Delta z and distorts areas); gradient normals use them too (forgetting tilts the normals; recall volumes3d/).
Slice planes: the slice of an isosurface is an isocontour: the marching-squares contour of the slice lies on the mesh. A quick check of a surface against the image.
Topology: count connected components, boundary edges (edges with a triangle on one side only: cracks, or the volume border) and the Euler characteristic \chi = V - E + F.
For one closed surface, \chi = 2 - 2g with g the number of holes (handles): a sphere 2, a torus 0. Several components add up. Noise shows up as hundreds of components; a crack as boundary edges.

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
The math: Euler characteristic

Octahedron: V - E + F = 6 - 12 + 8 = 2. Any closed triangulated surface without holes: 2 (Euler’s polyhedron formula).
A torus made from an m \times n grid of quads, each split into 2 triangles: V = mn, E = 3mn, F = 2mn, \chi = 0.
\chi is a topological invariant: refining, decimating or deforming the mesh without tearing does not change it. For a closed surface with g handles \chi = 2 - 2g; for k components \chi = \sum_i(2 - 2g_i).
On a closed triangle mesh every edge has two triangles: 2E = 3F, so \chi = V - F/2 and F \approx 2V for large meshes (the “2 triangles per vertex”).

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
Choosing c

A blurred step edge between a dark level a and a bright level b, blurred symmetrically, passes the half-way value (a + b)/2 exactly at the true edge. Natural choice: c = (a + b)/2, from the two levels (read off the histogram).
On small or strongly curved objects the blur leaks brightness out of the object: at the true boundary the value is below half-way, the surface at c = (a + b)/2 lies inside, and the object looks too small (the partial-volume effect).
Plot the volume against c. A flat plateau: the measurement is robust. A steep curve: the result is mostly your choice of c; report it, or deblur/fit a model instead.
Thresholds from the histogram (Otsu and others) are the thresholding day’s tools; the same reasoning applies.

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
The math: the half-way level

A step from a to b at x = 0, blurred by a symmetric kernel g (e.g. Gaussian): I(x) = a + (b - a)\,G(x) with G the cumulative distribution of g. Symmetry gives G(0) = \tfrac12: I(0) = (a + b)/2.
For a ball of radius R blurred by a Gaussian of width \sigma: at a boundary point, the ball covers less than half of the Gaussian’s weight (the boundary curves away), so I(R) < (a + b)/2. The error grows with \sigma/R.
Sensitivity: \dfrac{dV}{dc} = -\displaystyle\oiint \frac{dA}{\lVert\nabla I\rVert}. A sharp edge (large gradient) gives a flat volume curve; a blurred edge a steep one.

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
Try it: volume against c




A ball of radius 8 voxels (binary), blurred with σ, and the marching-cubes volume as a function of c. σ = 0.5: at c = 0.5 the volume is 2115.5 against the true 2144.7 (−1.4 %), and c ± 0.05 changes it by 2.3 %. “Heavy blur” (σ = 2.5): 1524.5 (−29 %), ± 14 % per ± 0.05 in c: the curve is steep and the partial-volume loss large. Then the nuclei stack (true total 79.2 µm³).

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
Smoothing: before or after?

Before extraction: Gaussian blur of the volume (in physical units, per axis). Removes noise, rounds corners, shrinks small and convex objects, removes thin structures. The surface stays a level set of a (smoothed) image.
After extraction: smooth the mesh, e.g. Laplacian smoothing (move each vertex towards the mean of its neighbours). Removes facets and terraces, but shrinks the whole surface step by step. Taubin’s two-step smoothing alternates a shrinking and an inflating step and keeps the size (mention only).
Either way, report what you smoothed: area is sensitive to it, volume less so.

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
Surfacing a segmentation

The output of thresholding, watershed (day 10) or graph cuts (day 13) is a mask (0/1) or a label image. Marching cubes at c = 0.5 on a mask puts every vertex at an edge midpoint: terraces, staircase normals, and an area that stays several per cent too large at any resolution.
Remedies: blur the mask slightly (σ ≈ 1 voxel) before extraction, or use a signed distance function (positive inside, negative outside, zero on the boundary; what the level-set elective works with): its zero level set is placed with sub-voxel accuracy.
Label images: one surface per label (mask of label \ell, then marching cubes). Two touching labels give two surfaces with a small gap or overlap between them; methods that produce one shared surface exist (multi-label marching cubes, dual methods), pointer only.

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
Mesh size and decimation

Triangles ∝ surface area / voxel area: about 3 per voxel² of area. A skull in a 512³ CT has about 10^6 voxel² of surface: about 3 million triangles.
Storage: shared vertices (1.5 million × 12 bytes + 3 million × 12 bytes ≈ 54 MB) vs a triangle soup with every triangle storing its 3 vertices (108 MB).
Decimation reduces the count where the surface is flat:

vertex clustering: snap vertices to a coarser grid, merge each cell’s vertices into one, drop collapsed triangles. Simple and fast; the topology may break;
edge collapse with quadric error metrics (Garland & Heckbert, 1997): repeatedly merge the two ends of the edge whose removal changes the shape least. The standard; mention only.

Always check area and volume after decimating.

title: Measuring surfaces
section: Try it: binary masks and decimation
text:
Try it: binary masks and decimation




A tilted ellipsoid (semi-axes 16, 9, 11 voxels; true volume 6635) from a grey image, a binary mask, or the mask blurred with σ = 1. “Terraces”: the binary mask gives staircase surfaces and 8.6 % more area than the grey image (1932.9 against 1779.4). “Blurred mask”: smooth again, but 2.3 % too little volume. “Decimate 10×” (cell size 3): 508 triangles instead of 5332, area −2.1 %, volume −4.3 %. At cell size 6 the topology breaks (χ = 4, non-manifold edges).

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
Summary

Area = Σ triangle areas; volume = Σ ⅙ det[a b c] (divergence theorem, the 3D shoelace); needs a closed, oriented mesh: pad first.
Counting voxels gives good volumes; counting voxel faces overestimates area by about 1.5× at every resolution (4/π in 2D). Marching cubes converges.
Use the spacing in positions and normals; check topology with components, boundary edges and \chi = V - E + F.
c: half-way between the levels for a sharp edge; blur and small objects bias the size (partial volume); a volume-vs-c curve shows how much the choice matters.
Masks give terraces: blur slightly or use a signed distance. Decimate big meshes, and re-check area and volume.

title: Quiz: the structure tensor
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Eigenvalues of J: \mu_1 \ge \mu_2 \ge 0.

Q1. Why does averaging the gradient vectors in a window fail to find the orientation of a bright line?






Hint





Which way do the gradients point on the two sides of the line?









Answer





On both sides the gradient points towards the line (towards the brighter middle): on one side in direction \mathbf g, on the other in -\mathbf g. They cancel, and the average is about zero although the orientation is perfectly clear. The outer product \mathbf g\mathbf g^\top is the same for \mathbf g and -\mathbf g, so averaging it does not cancel.




Q2. The structure tensor has two scales, σ and ρ. What does each control?






Hint





One is applied before the products, one after.









Answer





σ is the scale of the gradient (the derivative of a Gaussian): it controls noise and which structures produce gradients at all. ρ is the width of the Gaussian window that averages the products: it controls how large a region is summarised by one tensor. Too small a ρ gives noisy orientations; too large a ρ blurs boundaries between differently oriented regions.




Q3. Classify the window: (a) \mu_1 = 900, \mu_2 = 5; (b) \mu_1 = 600, \mu_2 = 450; (c) \mu_1 = 2, \mu_2 = 1 (noise gives up to about 10).






Hint





How many large eigenvalues?









Answer






An edge or oriented texture (one large eigenvalue, coherence (895/905)^2 = 0.98). (b) A corner (or an isotropic, busy texture): two large eigenvalues, coherence (150/1050)^2 = 0.02. (c) Flat: both within the noise.





Q4. The structure tensor is “the covariance matrix of the gradients”. Describe the gradient point cloud of an edge, a corner and a flat region.






Hint





Plot every gradient in the window as a point (L_x, L_y).









Answer





Edge: the points lie along a line through the origin (all gradients parallel or antiparallel): a long thin ellipse. Corner: points along two different directions: a broad, roundish ellipse. Flat: all points near the origin: a tiny ellipse. The eigenvalues of J are the squared half-axes of the ellipse (up to a factor).




Q5. What is the Harris response \det J - k(\operatorname{tr}J)^2 (with k = 0.05) for J = \begin{pmatrix} 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 8\end{pmatrix} and for J = \begin{pmatrix} 16 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}? Which is the corner?






Hint





Both have the same trace.









Answer





First: 64 - 0.05 \cdot 256 = 51.2, a corner. Second: 0 - 0.05 \cdot 256 = -12.8, an edge (negative). Same trace (total gradient energy), but only the first has it in two directions.




Q6. Why are there no corners at all if the window is switched off (ρ = 0)?






Hint





What is the rank of \mathbf g\mathbf g^\top?









Answer





Without averaging, J = \nabla L\,\nabla L^\top at each pixel has rank 1: \mu_2 = 0 and \det J = 0. A single gradient has a single direction; two directions can only come from different pixels in a window. Every pixel looks like an edge, and the Harris response is never positive.




Q7. Hessian or structure tensor? (a) Find the centre line of a blood vessel. (b) Measure the dominant fibre direction in a patch of collagen. (c) Find points to track between two video frames.






Hint





Second derivatives, signed, at centres; or squared first derivatives, unsigned, in windows?









Answer






Hessian: the vessel’s centre is where the curvature across it is strongest (the gradient is zero there). (b) Structure tensor: orientation and coherence of a texture in a window. (c) Structure tensor: corners (Harris or \mu_2), which can be found again after a shift.





Q8. (math) Show that \mathbf u^\top J\mathbf u is the average of (\nabla L\cdot\mathbf u)^2 over the window, and explain why its maximum over unit vectors is \mu_1.






Hint





(\mathbf g\cdot\mathbf u)^2 = \mathbf u^\top\mathbf g\mathbf g^\top\mathbf u; then the Rayleigh quotient.









Answer





(\mathbf g\cdot\mathbf u)^2 = (\mathbf u^\top\mathbf g)(\mathbf g^\top\mathbf u) = \mathbf u^\top(\mathbf g\mathbf g^\top)\mathbf u; averaging is linear, so \langle(\nabla L\cdot\mathbf u)^2\rangle = \mathbf u^\top\langle\nabla L\nabla L^\top\rangle\mathbf u = \mathbf u^\top J\mathbf u. Writing \mathbf u = \cos\phi\,\mathbf e_1 + \sin\phi\,\mathbf e_2 in the orthonormal eigenvectors of J: \mathbf u^\top J\mathbf u = \mu_1\cos^2\phi + \mu_2\sin^2\phi \le \mu_1, with equality along \mathbf e_1.

title: Exercise: the structure tensor
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Structure tensor
J = G_\rho * \begin{pmatrix} L_x^2 & L_xL_y \\ L_xL_y & L_y^2\end{pmatrix}: gradient at scale σ, window ρ (here, by hand: a plain average over the window)


Eigenvalues
\mu_1 \ge \mu_2 \ge 0; closed form \mu = \frac{a + c}{2} \pm \sqrt{\big(\frac{a - c}{2}\big)^2 + b^2} for \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & c\end{pmatrix}


Orientation
eigenvector of \mu_1 = dominant gradient direction, angle \theta = \tfrac12\operatorname{atan2}(2b, a - c) (image coordinates, y down); the structure runs at \theta + 90°


Coherence
\big(\frac{\mu_1 - \mu_2}{\mu_1 + \mu_2}\big)^2 \in [0, 1]


Verdict
both small: flat; one large: edge / oriented; both large: corner


Harris
R = \det J - k(\operatorname{tr}J)^2, k \approx 0.05: > 0 corner, < 0 edge, ≈ 0 flat

title: Exercise: the structure tensor
text:
By hand
B1. A window contains four gradient vectors: (1, 0), (-1, 0), (1, 0), (-1, 0). (a) What is the average gradient? (b) Compute J as the average of \mathbf g\mathbf g^\top. (c) Eigenvalues, coherence and verdict. What kind of structure could produce these gradients?
B2. The same for (a) (1, 0), (0, 1), (-1, 0), (0, -1); (b) four zero vectors.
B3. A window has J = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{pmatrix}. (a) Compute \mu_1, \mu_2 and the coherence. (b) Compute θ, the angle of the dominant gradient direction in image coordinates. With y down, which way does it point on the screen? At what angle (counter-clockwise on the screen) do the stripes run?
B4. Harris responses with k = 0.05 for J = \mathrm{diag}(10, 0.1), J = \mathrm{diag}(10, 8) and J = \mathrm{diag}(0.1, 0.1). Which is the corner, the edge and the flat region? What does Förstner’s \mu_2 say?
B5. Predict the ellipse glyph of J (shape and orientation) for a window (a) on the straight top edge of a bright square, (b) on its top-left corner, (c) in its flat interior, (d) on vertical stripes, (e) on isotropic noise texture.
B6. You want an orientation map of collagen fibres about 4 pixels apart, in a noisy image, where regions of different fibre direction are about 40 pixels across. Suggest σ and ρ and explain the trade-off in each.






Solutions





B1. (a) (0, 0): the gradients cancel. (b) Each \mathbf g\mathbf g^\top is \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix} (also for (-1, 0)), so J = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}. (c) \mu_1 = 1, \mu_2 = 0, coherence 1: an edge or oriented structure; the gradients are horizontal, so the structure is vertical. Opposite gradients in one window: a vertical line (or vertical stripes), bright or dark. The average gradient said “nothing here”; J says “perfectly oriented”.
B2. (a) Average (0, 0); J = \frac14\big(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{smallmatrix} + \begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix} + \begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{smallmatrix} + \begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\big) = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.5\end{pmatrix}: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = 0.5, coherence 0: two directions in one window, a corner (or isotropic texture). (b) J = 0: flat; coherence undefined (0/0; the demos show 0).
B3. (a) \mu = 3.5 \pm \sqrt{1.5^2 + 2^2} = 3.5 \pm 2.5: \mu_1 = 6, \mu_2 = 1; coherence (5/7)^2 = 0.51. (b) \theta = \tfrac12\operatorname{atan2}(4, 3) = 26.6° in image coordinates: with y down the dominant gradient points to the right and down (−26.6° counter-clockwise on the screen). The stripes run perpendicular to it, at 90° - 26.6° = 63.4° counter-clockwise on the screen (from lower left to upper right, steeply).
B4. \mathrm{diag}(10, 0.1): 1 - 0.05 \cdot 10.1^2 = -4.10, an edge. \mathrm{diag}(10, 8): 80 - 0.05 \cdot 18^2 = 63.8, a corner. \mathrm{diag}(0.1, 0.1): 0.01 - 0.05 \cdot 0.04 = 0.008, flat (tiny). Förstner’s \mu_2: 0.1, 8, 0.1: large only at the corner; it does not distinguish edge from flat, but it does not need to: neither is a corner.
B5. (a) A thin ellipse, long axis vertical (across the edge: the gradients point up or down), short axis ≈ 0. (b) A large, roundish ellipse (gradients up and left). (c) A dot. (d) A thin ellipse with its long axis horizontal (across the stripes). (e) A roundish ellipse whose size reflects the texture’s contrast; coherence near 0.
B6. σ should be smaller than the fibre spacing so that the stripes produce gradients at all, but large enough to suppress pixel noise: σ ≈ 1 to 1.5 (σ = 4 would blur the fibres away). ρ should cover several fibres to average out noise (ρ ≈ 6 to 8, a window of about 25 to 30 pixels), but stay well below the 40-pixel regions, or the boundaries between directions blur into a band of low coherence.




Math questions
B7. (math) Show that \mathbf u^\top J\mathbf u equals the window average of (\nabla L\cdot\mathbf u)^2, and that over unit vectors it is largest along the eigenvector of \mu_1, with value \mu_1.
B8. (math) With \nabla L = r(\cos\phi, \sin\phi), show that J_{xx} - J_{yy} = \langle r^2\cos2\phi\rangle and 2J_{xy} = \langle r^2\sin2\phi\rangle, and that the dominant gradient angle is \tfrac12\operatorname{atan2}(2J_{xy}, J_{xx} - J_{yy}). Why does the doubling make opposite gradients add?
B9. (math) Show that shifting a window by a small \mathbf h changes it by E(\mathbf h) = \sum w\,(I(\mathbf x + \mathbf h) - I(\mathbf x))^2 \approx \mathbf h^\top J\,\mathbf h, and use it to explain why a corner needs \mu_2 large.






Solutions (math)





B7. (\mathbf g\cdot\mathbf u)^2 = \mathbf u^\top\mathbf g\mathbf g^\top\mathbf u, and averaging over the window (with weights w) is linear: \langle(\nabla L\cdot\mathbf u)^2\rangle = \mathbf u^\top\langle\nabla L\nabla L^\top\rangle\mathbf u = \mathbf u^\top J\mathbf u. J is symmetric with orthonormal eigenvectors \mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2; with \mathbf u = \cos\phi\,\mathbf e_1 + \sin\phi\,\mathbf e_2, \mathbf u^\top J\mathbf u = \mu_1\cos^2\phi + \mu_2\sin^2\phi, at most \mu_1, attained at \phi = 0.
B8. L_x^2 - L_y^2 = r^2(\cos^2\phi - \sin^2\phi) = r^2\cos2\phi and 2L_xL_y = 2r^2\cos\phi\sin\phi = r^2\sin2\phi; averaging gives the two identities. From the closed form, the eigenvector of \mu_1 of \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & c\end{pmatrix} has angle \tfrac12\operatorname{atan2}(2b, a - c), i.e. half the angle of the averaged vector \langle r^2(\cos2\phi, \sin2\phi)\rangle. A gradient and its opposite differ by 180° in φ, hence by 360° in 2\phi: they map to the same doubled-angle vector and add instead of cancelling.
B9. First-order Taylor: I(\mathbf x + \mathbf h) - I(\mathbf x) \approx \nabla I(\mathbf x)^\top\mathbf h. So E(\mathbf h) \approx \sum w\,(\nabla I^\top\mathbf h)^2 = \mathbf h^\top\big(\sum w\,\nabla I\nabla I^\top\big)\mathbf h = \mathbf h^\top J\mathbf h. For a fixed shift length |\mathbf h| this ranges from \mu_2|\mathbf h|^2 (shift along \mathbf e_2) to \mu_1|\mathbf h|^2. At an edge, shifting along the edge leaves the window unchanged (\mu_2 \approx 0); a window that changes under every shift, a corner, needs \mu_2 large.
crumbs: The structure tensor: orientation and corners

title: Exercise: the structure tensor
text:
Explore: the structure tensor
Images: synthetic textures (stripes with an angle and a frequency, rotating stripes, a “fingerprint”, two textures meeting at the middle, a checkerboard with a square and a triangle, a single square, isotropic noise) or the micrograph. The left panel shows the image with one ellipse of J per 16-pixel cell, the orientation map (hue = orientation of the structure, saturation = coherence, brightness = energy) or the Harris response with the detected corners. Click a pixel: the window (cyan), its gradient arrows (yellow) and their mean (red), the gradient cloud with the ellipse of J, and the numbers. Average gradients instead shows the naive orientation map from the mean gradient.



E1. Presets edge, corner, flat (square, σ = 1, ρ = 3). Read J, \mu_1, \mu_2 and the coherence in each case, and describe the gradient cloud. Compare with B1, B2 and B5.
E2. Preset averaging gradients cancels (stripes at 30°, naive mode). What does the naive orientation map look like, and why? Compare the mean gradient (red arrow) with \sqrt{\mu_1}. Untick the naive mode.
E3. Preset ρ = 0. Read \mu_2 at the corner (32, 32). Look at the corners tab: how many corners are found? Raise ρ slowly: from which ρ are the four corners of the square detected?
E4. Preset ρ too small or too large (two textures, noise 25, ρ = 1). Describe the orientation map. Then set ρ = 3 and ρ = 8. Read the coherence at (30, 64), (62, 64) (on the boundary) and (96, 64) each time.
E5. Preset rotating stripes. Click across the image at y = 64: x = 16, 32, 64, 96, 112. Read the orientation each time. Does the hue follow?
E6. Preset corners of a checkerboard (ρ = 2). How many corners are found, and where? Raise the corner threshold and lower it; change Harris k. What happens on the triangle’s corners?
E7. Image fingerprint: describe the orientation map. Where is the coherence low, and why?
E8. Preset micrograph (σ = 1.5, ρ = 4). Which regions are oriented (saturated colours), which isotropic (grey)? Click on the nuclear envelope at (94, 126) and inside the nucleus at (150, 150): compare the coherence.






Solutions





E1. Edge (32, 64): J = [740 0; 0 0], \mu_1 = 740, \mu_2 = 0, coherence 1.00, orientation 90° (the edge is vertical): the cloud is a short line along L_x. Corner (32, 32): J = [366 81; 81 366], \mu_1 = 447, \mu_2 = 285, coherence 0.05: the cloud spreads in two directions (a fan from the origin). Flat (64, 64): all zero. As in B1, B2 and B5: one large eigenvalue at the edge, two at the corner, none inside.
E2. The naive map is almost black: the average gradient is near zero everywhere on stripes. At (64, 64) the mean gradient has length 0.48, while \sqrt{\mu_1} = 32.1: the gradients are strong, they just cancel. With J the map is uniformly coloured (orientation 120°, coherence 1.00).
E3. With ρ = 0 the corner pixel has J = [1269 1269; 1269 1269]: \mu_1 = 2539, \mu_2 = 0, coherence 1: an “edge” (one diagonal gradient). The Harris response is never positive, so no corners are found. Already at ρ = 0.5 the four corners are back, at (32, 32), (95, 32), (32, 95) and (95, 95): a window of a few pixels is enough to contain gradients from both edges.
E4. ρ = 1: speckled colours and many grey pixels: each window is too small to average out the noise. Coherence at (30, 64), (62, 64), (96, 64): 0.98, 0.31, 0.97. ρ = 3: clean, uniform colours on both sides: 0.94, 0.05, 0.94. ρ = 8: still clean, but the boundary becomes a wide grey band of low coherence: 0.93, 0.01, 0.92 (the windows near the boundary mix both orientations). ρ trades noise against spatial resolution.
E5. Orientation 106°, 120°, 0°, 60°, 74° at x = 16, 32, 64, 96, 112 (coherence 0.92 to 0.99): the hue changes continuously across the image, following the turning stripes (0° = horizontal stripes in the middle).
E6. 35 corners: the 21 inner corners of the checkerboard (3 columns × 7 rows, where four squares meet), corners along the checkerboard’s right border, the four corners of the square and the three of the triangle. Raising the threshold to 0.5 changes nothing here: all corners of these clean shapes are strong. A larger k penalises the trace more; at k = 0.2 the triangle’s sharp top corner (51°) disappears first (34 corners): its two edges are close to parallel as axes, so \mu_2 is small compared with \mu_1. Right angles and the four-square corners of the checkerboard are the strongest corners.
E7. The colour turns around the centre (the orientation follows the rings), with high coherence (0.95 or more) everywhere except near the centre: 0.00 at the centre, 0.08 four pixels away, 0.49 eight pixels away. There the rings are small and strongly curved, and a window contains every orientation.
E8. Oriented: the membranes, the fibres in the cytoplasm and parts of the nuclear envelope; isotropic: the granular inside of the nucleus and the background texture. At (94, 126) on the envelope the coherence is 0.38 (the envelope is thin and curved, with texture around it); inside the nucleus at (150, 150) only 0.02.

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
About this lecture
Phase correlation gives a spike. Turning it into a usable shift, and many shifts into one consistent picture, takes three more steps.

The four candidates: a circular peak only knows the shift up to the tile size.
Sub-pixel shifts: parabola, centroid, and the upsampled DFT.
Global alignment of a mosaic: pairwise shifts do not add up around a loop; least squares on the graph of tiles.
Drift in a time-lapse and in localisation microscopy; channels; 3D stacks.
The limits: what a shift cannot describe.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Convention as before: the shift t of tile B relative to tile A is where B sits on A, B(x) = A(x + t); for a mosaic it is the position of B minus the position of A. The demos use 128 × 128 tiles cut from the course micrograph enlarged to 384 × 384; with only 256² pixels of real data, the mosaic is a teaching model, honestly labelled.
crumbs: From a peak to a mosaic

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
A peak means four shifts
Without padding, the FFT treats each tile as periodic: a peak at (p, q) only says the shift modulo the tile size N.


t_x \in \{p,\ p - N\} and t_y \in \{q,\ q - N\}: four ways tile B can sit against tile A, with very different overlaps.
Decide by computing NCC on the actual overlap of each candidate and keeping the best; ignore candidates whose overlap is too small to judge.
crumbs: From a peak to a mosaic

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
Resolving the candidates

For each candidate, cut out the overlapping parts of A and B and compute their NCC (the matching unit): a direct, cheap check.
Require a minimum overlap: a few dozen pixels always correlate by chance.
In practice, check the candidates of the few highest peaks, not only the first: on small overlaps, the true peak is not always the highest.
The best NCC is also the pair’s confidence.
Alternative: zero-pad the tiles (the previous unit): no ambiguity, but FFTs four times as large, and the overlap gets a smaller share of the padded image. Stitching programs usually test candidates instead.
crumbs: From a peak to a mosaic

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
Sub-pixel shifts
Stages, drift and chromatic shifts are rarely whole pixels. A drift of 0.3 px matters when single molecules are localised to 0.1 px.

Parabola: fit a parabola through the peak and its two neighbours (in x, and separately in y); its top is the estimate. Cheap, but biased towards whole pixels: pixel locking.
Centroid of the peak and its neighbours: simplest, strongly biased for broad or narrow peaks.
Upsampled DFT: evaluate the inverse DFT of the (normalised) cross-power spectrum on a fine grid (e.g. 1/20 px) near the peak only. This is the exact interpolation of the correlation, without a huge padded FFT (Guizar-Sicairos et al., 2008).

To apply a sub-pixel shift: interpolate (bilinear, the images unit) or multiply the spectrum by a phase ramp (the shift theorem, backwards).
crumbs: From a peak to a mosaic

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
The math: sub-pixel peaks
Parabola. Through (-1, c_{-1}), (0, c_0), (1, c_{+1}): c(\delta) = a\delta^2 + b\delta + c_0 with a = \tfrac12(c_{-1} + c_{+1}) - c_0, b = \tfrac12(c_{+1} - c_{-1}); the vertex is at \delta = -\frac{b}{2a} = \frac{c_{-1} - c_{+1}}{2(c_{-1} - 2c_0 + c_{+1})}. The true shape. For a non-integer shift, the phase-correlation peak is a Dirichlet kernel \frac{\sin(\pi(t - t_0))}{N\sin(\pi(t - t_0)/N)} (the phasecorr unit, B7), not a parabola: hence the bias. Fitting the kernel itself works too (Foroosh et al., 2002).
Upsampled DFT. c(x, y) = \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{k_x,k_y} R_{k_y k_x}e^{2\pi i(k_xx + k_yy)/N} at U \times U points: C = E_y\,R\,E_x^{\top} with small DFT matrices E_x \in \mathbb C^{U\times N}, (E_x)_{jk} = e^{2\pi i k x_j/N}. Cost \mathcal O(N^2U) instead of an FFT of size (UN)^2.
crumbs: From a peak to a mosaic

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
Try it: sub-pixel estimates




B is A shifted by 3.3 px through the Fourier phase ramp, so the truth is exact. Left: the correlation samples near the peak (dots), the parabola through the top three (red dashed), the upsampled-DFT curve (blue); vertical lines: truth (green), parabola, centroid, upsampled. Right: the error of each method for every fraction from 0 to 1. Tour: “parabola: pixel locking” (phase correlation): the parabola’s error is an S-curve, 3.262 instead of 3.300, at most 0.038 px; the centroid’s up to 0.065; the upsampled DFT is within its grid of 1/20 px (0.020). “a broad CC peak”: the parabola fits a broad peak well (0.004), the centroid is terrible (0.47). “upsampling too coarse” (U = 4): the upsampled estimate is quantised to 1/4 px, error up to 0.12. “noise sets the floor”: with noise all methods scatter.
crumbs: From a peak to a mosaic

title: From a peak to a mosaic
section: Many tiles: the mosaic as a graph
text:
Many tiles: the mosaic as a graph
A mosaic of tiles is a graph: one node per tile, one edge per overlapping pair, labelled with the measured shift and its confidence.

Stage positions alone: seams, off by several pixels.
Chaining pairwise shifts along a path: each step adds its error; tiles far down the chain inherit all of them, and one wrong pair moves everything after it.
Around a loop of four tiles, the measured shifts should add up to zero; with noise they do not.
Global alignment: find the tile positions that agree best with all measured shifts at once, weighting each by its confidence. One tile is fixed (the whole mosaic can be moved freely).

Pairs with low confidence (a blank tile, a repetitive pattern) are dropped or down-weighted; a pair whose shift disagrees strongly with the rest (a large residual) is suspicious.
crumbs: From a peak to a mosaic

title: From a peak to a mosaic
section: The math: least squares on a graph
text:
The math: least squares on a graph
Tile positions \mathbf x_1, \ldots, \mathbf x_n, measured shifts \mathbf d_{ij} \approx \mathbf x_j - \mathbf x_i with weights w_{ij}. Minimise, separately in x and in y, E(\mathbf x) = \sum_{(i,j)} w_{ij}\,(x_j - x_i - d_{ij})^2. Setting \partial E/\partial x_m = 0 gives the normal equations L\,\mathbf x = \mathbf b with L_{mm} = \sum_{j \sim m} w_{mj}, \quad L_{mj} = -w_{mj}, \qquad b_m = \sum_{(i,m)} w_{im}d_{im} - \sum_{(m,j)} w_{mj}d_{mj}. L is the weighted graph Laplacian. It is singular: adding a constant to every x_m changes nothing (L\mathbf 1 = 0). Fixing x_1 = 0 (deleting its row and column) makes it invertible when the graph is connected. The graph-cuts day meets the same matrix in normalized cuts.
crumbs: From a peak to a mosaic

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
Try it: stitching a mosaic




3 × 3 tiles of 128², nominal overlap 24 px, stage error up to ±6 px, noise, a brightness change and vignetting per tile. Edges: green = trusted (overlap NCC ≥ 0.7), red dashed = not. Tour: “stage positions: seams”: errors up to 10.1 px (rms 6.4). Default noise: chain 0-1-2-5-4-3-6-7-8 max 1.66 px, global 0.60. “chained pairs: errors add up” (noise 12): max 1.94 at the end of the chain; “global: errors spread”: max 0.83. “an empty tile”: tile 4 is blank, its four pairs are untrusted (NCC 0.27–0.51); the chain runs through it and tiles 3–8 are off by ~130 px; global keeps every other tile within 0.9 px (tile 4 itself cannot be placed from its image). “a wrong pair”: the region shared by tiles 4 and 5 is empty, pair 4-5 measures nonsense (NCC 0.42); its residual after global alignment is 127.7 px, everything else below 0.8 px. “the four candidates”: click any edge to see its surface and candidates. Then blending.
crumbs: From a peak to a mosaic

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
Seams and blending
Even well-placed tiles show seams: each tile has its own brightness (exposure, bleaching) and darker corners (vignetting).

Feathering: in the overlap, blend the tiles with weights that fall off towards each tile’s border; the seam becomes a smooth transition.
Vignetting is better corrected before stitching: divide by a flat-field image (a picture of an empty, even sample).
Vignetting is also a registration hazard: the same dark corners in every tile do not move with the shift, like the border jumps of the phasecorr unit.
crumbs: From a peak to a mosaic

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
Drift in a time-lapse
Frame k is shifted by the drift \mathbf d_k since frame 1. Register every frame, then shift it back.

To the first frame: errors do not accumulate, but late frames may no longer look like the first one (the sample changes, cells move, bleaching makes them dim).
To the previous frame: neighbours look alike, but the drift is a sum of steps; each step’s error is added, and the error grows like a random walk (\sqrt{k} times one step’s error).
Key frames: register to a key frame every few frames, and the key frames to each other: a compromise.

Phase correlation ignores bleaching (a gain) and slow illumination changes; noise and real changes of the sample are the limit.
crumbs: From a peak to a mosaic

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
Try it: drift correction




40 frames (128²) with a random-walk drift of 0.6 px per frame (sd), ending at (6.2, 0.9). “bleaching: no problem”: the last frame keeps 20 % of the brightness, noise 10; to the first frame: max error 0.19 px. The corrected average is sharp, the uncorrected one blurred. “to the previous: errors add up” (noise 30): the error grows from 0.1 to 1.3 px by frame 30 and 5.1 px at the end, where the frames are dim; to the first frame instead: max 0.29. “sample changes: to the first fails” (the field slowly turns into its mirror image): to the first, max 8.4 px at frame 37; “key frames”: 0.44 px; to the previous: 0.76 px.
crumbs: From a peak to a mosaic

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
Localisation microscopy and other uses

Single-molecule localisation: there are no images, only lists of molecule positions over thousands of frames. Render the positions of each time block as an image, correlate all pairs of blocks, and solve for one drift per block by least squares, the same graph problem as the mosaic (redundant cross-correlation). Alternative: fiducial beads.
Colour channels: the channels show different structures, so register a calibration image (beads) instead; chromatic aberration also scales the image, so a shift is only a first approximation.
3D stacks: the same formula with a 3D FFT. Report the shift in µm with the voxel spacing (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z), which is usually larger in z (the 3D images unit of the marching-cubes elective).
Motion estimation: register small windows separately (particle image velocimetry, video coding).
crumbs: From a peak to a mosaic

title: From a peak to a mosaic
section: Try it: drift in localisation microscopy
text:
Try it: drift in localisation microscopy




7981 localisations of three rings and two lines over 4000 frames, precision 0.25 camera px, drift up to 6.2 px. 10 time blocks, 45 block pairs correlated, least squares for the 10 block drifts (block 0 fixed). The rendered image sharpens from a smear to thin rings. Drift error: max 1.57 px, rms 0.74 with 10 blocks (the drift changes within a block); with 40 blocks (780 pairs) max 0.43; with 3 blocks max 2.72. “strong drift” (35 px): blocks of 400 frames are far too long, error up to 15 px.
crumbs: From a peak to a mosaic

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
Limits of a shift

Translation only. Rotation and scale: the Fourier–Mellin method resamples the magnitude spectrum in log-polar coordinates, where they become shifts that phase correlation can find (Reddy & Chatterji, 1996; further reading).
Rigid only. Tissue deforms, cells move independently: non-rigid registration, optical flow and tracking are the Motion elective.
Features instead of pixels: match interest points (the edges day, structure tensor) and fit a transform; robust to large changes.
Empty or repeated texture gives no or many answers: check the confidence, use the stage positions as a fallback.
crumbs: From a peak to a mosaic

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
Summary

A circular peak at (p, q) means four shifts; test them by NCC on the overlap and keep the best (with a minimum overlap).
Sub-pixel: the parabola is quick but locks to pixels; the upsampled DFT evaluates the exact peak on a fine grid at little cost.
A mosaic is a graph; pairwise shifts are combined by weighted least squares (a graph Laplacian), which spreads errors instead of accumulating them and exposes wrong pairs by their residuals.
Drift: register to the first frame, to the previous one, or to key frames; the same graph solution corrects localisation microscopy.
A shift cannot describe rotation, scaling or deformation.
crumbs: From a peak to a mosaic

title: Quiz: stain separation
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Optical density \mathrm{OD}_c = -\log_{10}(I_c/I_{0,c}); with the unit stain vectors as the columns of S, \mathbf{od} = S\mathbf C and \mathbf C = S^{-1}\mathbf{od}.

Q1. Why can’t we unmix brightfield stains directly on the RGB intensities, as we did with fluorescence?






Hint





What happens to the transmitted light when a second stain lies on top of the first?









Answer





Fluorescence adds light; absorbing stains each transmit a fraction, so two stains multiply the transmitted intensity. A product is not a linear mixture. The logarithm (optical density) turns the product into a sum, and the linear model holds in OD.




Q2. A background pixel has I = I_0. What is its optical density, and its stain concentrations?






Hint





\log 1 = 0.









Answer





\mathrm{OD} = -\log_{10}(1) = 0 in every channel, so all concentrations are 0. Unstained glass is the origin of the OD space; that is why I_0 (the white reference) must be right.




Q3. Only the direction of a stain vector matters, not its length. Why?






Hint





What happens to C_k if you double the length of column k?









Answer





\mathbf{od} = \sum_k C_k\mathbf s_k: doubling \mathbf s_k and halving C_k gives the same OD. The concentration is only defined up to that scale, so the vectors are taken as unit vectors and C_k is measured in “OD units along the stain’s direction”.




Q4. With H&E only, why add a third column, and what does its concentration map show?






Hint





How many channels, how many stains? What is perpendicular to both stains?









Answer





Three channels and two stains: to invert a 3 \times 3 matrix we need a third column. The cross product of the two stain vectors is perpendicular to both; its map, the residual, is the part of each pixel’s OD that the two stains cannot explain. Near zero everywhere means the stain vectors fit; structure in it means wrong vectors, a third stain or pigment.




Q5. You deconvolve with the published eosin vector, and the hematoxylin map shows a faint copy of the cytoplasm. What is happening, and what would you do?






Hint





Compare with bleed-through in the first unit.









Answer





Crosstalk: this slide’s eosin differs from the published vector, so part of the eosin OD is attributed to hematoxylin (exactly the bleed-through of a wrong spillover matrix). Estimate the vectors from the image (Macenko), or from single-stained control slides, and check that the residual map drops to noise.




Q6. Very dark nuclei have I = 0 in the red channel. What happens to their optical density, and to the separation?






Hint





-\log_{10}(0).









Answer





-\log_{10}(0) is infinite: the pixel must be clipped (for example at I = 1, OD = \log_{10} 255 = 2.41 for I_0 = 255). The true OD may be higher, and one channel is clipped while the others are not, so the pixel’s OD direction is wrong: the concentrations of saturated pixels are unreliable. Use a shorter exposure or a brighter lamp.




Q7. Why is an amount read from the DAB map not a measure of how much protein is present?






Hint





How is DAB produced?









Answer





DAB is deposited by an enzyme reaction: the amount depends on incubation time and saturates, and DAB scatters as well as absorbs, so Beer–Lambert holds only roughly. The map is a relative signal: fine for “positive or negative” and for comparisons within one batch, not for absolute amounts.




Q8. (math) Show that the OD of a pixel with two stains is the sum of the ODs each would have alone.






Hint





Write I_c = I_{0,c}\,10^{-s_{c1}C_1}\,10^{-s_{c2}C_2}.









Answer





\mathrm{OD}_c = -\log_{10}(I_c/I_{0,c}) = -\log_{10}(10^{-s_{c1}C_1}) - \log_{10}(10^{-s_{c2}C_2}) = s_{c1}C_1 + s_{c2}C_2: the logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms.

title: Exercise: stain separation
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Beer–Lambert
I_c = I_{0,c}\,10^{-\sum_k s_{ck}C_k}: stains multiply the transmitted light


Optical density
\mathrm{OD}_c = -\log_{10}(I_c/I_{0,c}) = \sum_k s_{ck}C_k: linear in the concentrations


Stain matrix
unit stain vectors (R, G, B) as the columns of S; \mathbf{od} = S\mathbf C, \mathbf C = S^{-1}\mathbf{od}


Published vectors
hematoxylin (0.65, 0.70, 0.29), eosin (0.07, 0.99, 0.11), DAB (0.27, 0.57, 0.78) (Ruifrok & Johnston)


Residual column
with two stains: their normalised cross product


Macenko
the plane of the OD cloud (two principal directions), the two extreme angles in it = the stain vectors

title: Exercise: stain separation
text:
By hand
B1. A pixel has I = (80, 120, 200) and the background is I_0 = 255 in every channel. (a) Compute its optical density. (b) Which channel does the stain absorb most? What colour does the pixel look? (c) Deconvolved with the H, E, residual matrix of the lecture, it gives \mathbf C = (0.75, -0.21, -0.09). What does the negative eosin value tell you about this pixel?
B2. Restrict H&E to the red and green channels: hematoxylin (0.65, 0.70), eosin (0.07, 0.99) (columns of a 2 \times 2 S). (a) A pixel has OD (0.5, 1.0). Solve for the two concentrations. (b) A pixel holds 0.4 units of hematoxylin and 0.3 of eosin. Compute its OD, and the OD of each stain alone. Check that they add. (c) With I_0 = 255, compute the transmitted red and green intensities of the three pixels in (b). Check that the two-stain intensity is I_0 times the product of the two single-stain transmissions.
B3. The unit vectors of hematoxylin and eosin are \hat{\mathbf h} = (0.651, 0.701, 0.291) and \hat{\mathbf e} = (0.070, 0.991, 0.110). (a) Compute \hat{\mathbf h} \times \hat{\mathbf e} and normalise it. Check that it is perpendicular to both. (b) The lecture gives S^{-1} for S = [\hat{\mathbf h}\ \hat{\mathbf e}\ \hat{\mathbf r}]. Check that the first row of S^{-1}, (1.482, -0.162, 0.510), times the first column of S gives 1, and times the second column gives 0. (c) Why must the third row of S^{-1} be \hat{\mathbf r} itself?
B4. The angles between the unit stain vectors are H–E 39°, H–DAB 37°, E–DAB 48°. The condition numbers are \kappa = 2.8 for (H, E, residual), 3.0 for (H, DAB, residual), and 3.8 for (H, E, DAB). (a) Which pair of stains is most similar? Which of the three separations amplifies noise most? (b) Why is separating three stains harder than two, even though H–E and H–DAB are about equally far apart?
B5. A nucleus pixel is completely black in red: I_R = 0. What OD do you assign if you clip at I = 1, with I_0 = 255? Why is its hematoxylin value still unreliable?
B6. The true white level is 242, but you analyse with I_0 = 205. (a) What OD does a clean background pixel (I = 242 in every channel) get? (b) The rows of S^{-1} (H, E, residual) sum to 1.83, -0.24 and 0.53. What concentrations does the background pixel get? Which map shows the problem most?
B7. In an H-DAB slide you want to know whether a tumour expresses a protein more than normal tissue next to it. Is comparing the mean DAB map value of the two regions reasonable? Is comparing the same two regions between two hospitals’ slides?

Math questions
B8. (math) Derive the linear OD model from Beer–Lambert, dI/dz = -\mu(z) I along the light path, with \mu = \ln 10 \sum_k s_k\,c_k(z). What is C_k in terms of c_k(z)?
B9. (math) Show that if \hat{\mathbf r} is a unit vector perpendicular to \mathbf s_1 and \mathbf s_2, then for S = [\mathbf s_1\ \mathbf s_2\ \hat{\mathbf r}] the third row of S^{-1} is \hat{\mathbf r}^\top. Conclude that the residual concentration of a pixel is its OD’s component along \hat{\mathbf r}.
B10. (math) In the plane spanned by two stain vectors at angles \varphi_1 < \varphi_2, show that any pixel \mathbf{od} = C_1\mathbf s_1 + C_2\mathbf s_2 with C_1, C_2 \ge 0 (not both zero) has an angle between \varphi_1 and \varphi_2 (assume \varphi_2 - \varphi_1 < 180°). Why does Macenko use percentiles instead of the minimum and maximum angle?






Solutions





B1. (a) \mathrm{OD} = -\log_{10}(80/255,\ 120/255,\ 200/255) = (0.50, 0.33, 0.11). (b) Red (OD 0.50): red light is absorbed, blue passes: a blue-purple pixel, like hematoxylin. (c) The pixel’s OD is not a non-negative mixture of hematoxylin and eosin: it absorbs less green relative to red than hematoxylin does, so the fit needs “negative eosin”. Either a different stain or pigment, or vectors that do not match this slide.
B2. (a) \det S = 0.65 \cdot 0.99 - 0.07 \cdot 0.70 = 0.5945; C_H = (0.99 \cdot 0.5 - 0.07 \cdot 1.0)/0.5945 = 0.715, C_E = (-0.70 \cdot 0.5 + 0.65 \cdot 1.0)/0.5945 = 0.505. (b) H alone: 0.4(0.65, 0.70) = (0.260, 0.280); E alone: 0.3(0.07, 0.99) = (0.021, 0.297); both: (0.281, 0.577), the sum. (c) I = 255 \cdot 10^{-\mathrm{OD}}: H alone (140.1, 133.8), E alone (243.0, 128.7), both (133.5, 67.5). And 255 \cdot (140.1/255)(243.0/255) = 133.5, 255 \cdot (133.8/255)(128.7/255) = 67.5: the transmissions multiply.
B3. (a) \hat{\mathbf h} \times \hat{\mathbf e} = (0.701 \cdot 0.110 - 0.291 \cdot 0.991,\ 0.291 \cdot 0.070 - 0.651 \cdot 0.110,\ 0.651 \cdot 0.991 - 0.701 \cdot 0.070) = (-0.211, -0.051, 0.596), length 0.635, \hat{\mathbf r} = (-0.332, -0.081, 0.940). Dot products with \hat{\mathbf h} and \hat{\mathbf e} are 0 (up to rounding). (b) 1.482 \cdot 0.651 - 0.162 \cdot 0.701 + 0.510 \cdot 0.291 = 0.965 - 0.114 + 0.148 = 1.000; 1.482 \cdot 0.070 - 0.162 \cdot 0.991 + 0.510 \cdot 0.110 = 0.104 - 0.161 + 0.056 = 0.000 (up to rounding). (c) \hat{\mathbf r}^\top S = (\hat{\mathbf r}\cdot\hat{\mathbf h},\ \hat{\mathbf r}\cdot\hat{\mathbf e},\ \hat{\mathbf r}\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}) = (0, 0, 1), which is what the third row of S^{-1} must give (B9).
B4. (a) H–DAB is the most similar pair (37°), H–E almost as similar (39°). The three-stain separation (H, E, DAB) has the largest \kappa (3.8): it amplifies noise most. (b) With three stains, each must be distinguished from the plane spanned by the other two, not just from one other vector, and DAB lies fairly close to the plane of H and E. With two stains the third column is perpendicular by construction, the best possible partner.
B5. \mathrm{OD} = -\log_{10}(1/255) = 2.41. The true OD could be much higher (any value above 2.4 gives I = 0), and only the red channel is clipped, so the pixel’s OD direction is distorted towards green and blue: its hematoxylin is underestimated and some of it leaks into the other maps.
B6. (a) -\log_{10}(242/205) = -0.072 in every channel: negative, “less than no stain”. (b) \mathbf C = S^{-1}(-0.072, -0.072, -0.072)^\top = -0.072 \times (1.83, -0.24, 0.53) = (-0.132, 0.018, -0.038). The hematoxylin map shows it most: the whole background becomes negative. (In the demo, with the slide’s own vectors: -0.13.)
B7. Within one slide, stained in one batch: a reasonable relative comparison (both regions had the same reaction time), with the caveat that DAB saturates in strongly positive regions. Between hospitals: no. Protocols, incubation times and scanners differ, DAB is not stoichiometric, and even the stain vectors differ; compare positive/negative classifications at best, after checking controls.
B8. dI/dz = -\mu I gives I = I_0\exp(-\int\mu\,dz) = I_0\,10^{-\sum_k s_k\int c_k(z)\,dz}, so \mathrm{OD} = \sum_k s_k C_k with C_k = \int c_k(z)\,dz: the amount of stain along the light path (a line integral, as in the Radon elective).
B9. \hat{\mathbf r}^\top S = (\hat{\mathbf r}^\top\mathbf s_1, \hat{\mathbf r}^\top\mathbf s_2, \hat{\mathbf r}^\top\hat{\mathbf r}) = (0, 0, 1) = \mathbf e_3^\top. Multiplying by S^{-1} from the right: \hat{\mathbf r}^\top = \mathbf e_3^\top S^{-1}, the third row. So C_3 = \hat{\mathbf r}^\top\mathbf{od}: the component of the OD perpendicular to the plane of the two stains.
B10. Write \mathbf s_k = (\cos\varphi_k, \sin\varphi_k) in the plane. A non-negative combination of two vectors lies in the (convex) cone between them, so its direction lies between \varphi_1 and \varphi_2 (for an angle difference below 180° the cone is the sector between the two rays). The extreme angles are reached only by (nearly) pure pixels. Minimum and maximum would be decided by single noisy or odd pixels (dust, pigment); the 1st and 99th percentiles are robust extremes.

title: Exercise: stain separation
text:
Explore: separate H&E
A synthetic H&E slide (seeded), rendered by Beer–Lambert from known concentration maps with this slide’s own stain vectors (close to, but not equal to, the published ones), plus detector noise and 8-bit rounding. Right of the image: the stain matrix in use. Below: the three estimated concentration maps (or the true ones). The triangle shows every pixel’s OD divided by its sum (corners: pure red, green or blue absorption); the dashed circles are the true stain directions, the filled circles the vectors in use: drag them. The square is the residual direction (cross product). The heat map T = S^{-1}S_\text{true} says how much of each true stain ends up in each estimated map (the identity = perfect separation). The readout gives \kappa(S), the hematoxylin map’s mean and noise in unstained areas, and, when there are any, the share of pixels with clearly negative concentrations and the number of saturated pixels.



T1. Preset Ruifrok defaults. Read the crosstalk matrix. How much eosin ends up in the hematoxylin map, and how much hematoxylin in the eosin map? What does the residual map show?
T2. Preset the true vectors. What happens to the matrix and the residual map? Where do the pixels lie in the triangle?
T3. Preset wrong eosin vector. Describe the H map and the readout. Then drag the eosin circle yourself onto the end of the pixel cloud.
T4. Preset nearly parallel stains. Compare \kappa and the noise of the H map in unstained areas with T2.
T5. Preset wrong I₀ / saturated pixels. Two problems are combined here (the stain density is raised and I_0 lowered). Use the sliders to separate them: what does each one do?
T6. Preset estimate from the image (Macenko). How close are the estimated vectors to the dashed circles? Compare the crosstalk matrix with T1.






Solutions





T1. The H map contains 0.20 of the true eosin (and 0.92 of the true H); the E map contains 0.10 of the true H (0.81 of the true E). The residual map is not zero: it shows eosin-rich regions (0.20 of the true eosin goes there), because the published eosin vector is 14° away from this slide’s eosin. \kappa = 2.8.
T2. The H and E columns of T become the identity (1.00 and 0.00): perfect separation, and the residual map is zero (up to noise and rounding). In the triangle the pixels lie on the line between the two true directions; the circles sit at its ends. \kappa = 3.7, the H map’s noise in unstained areas has sd 0.007.
T3. The H map contains -0.54 times the true eosin: the cytoplasm becomes negative in the H map (77 % of the pixels have a concentration below -0.05), and the E map overestimates eosin (1.49). \kappa = 5.8. Dragging the eosin circle to the end of the cloud brings the matrix back to near-identity.
T4. \kappa = 10.5 (against 3.7) and the H map’s noise in unstained areas has sd 0.020 (against 0.007): three times noisier. The crosstalk matrix shows large mixed terms (H map -1.48 times the true eosin).
T5. Stain density 2.6 alone: 662 pixels saturate (some channel at I \le 1) in the darkest nuclei; their concentrations are clipped and wrong, the rest is fine. I_0 = 205 alone: the background’s OD becomes negative and the H map’s unstained areas average -0.13 (B6); 86 % of the pixels have a concentration below -0.05.
T6. The Macenko vectors are within 2.0° (H) and 1.1° (E) of the true ones (Ruifrok: 3.7° and 14°). The crosstalk matrix is close to the identity: 1.06 and 0.04 in the H row, -0.07 and 0.96 in the E row. Small deviations remain because no pixel is perfectly pure and the percentiles are robust, not extreme.

title: Exercise: stain separation
text:
Explore: H-DAB, count positive nuclei
The same demo in H-DAB mode: a hematoxylin counterstain, a light eosin, and some nuclei DAB-positive (brown). The maps show H, DAB and E. With count positive nuclei, the DAB map is thresholded with Otsu’s method (the thresholding day) and connected regions of at least 15 pixels are counted.



D1. Preset count positive nuclei. What threshold does Otsu choose, and how many positive nuclei are found? Compare with the truth.
D2. Switch to Ruifrok defaults, then wrong DAB vector and nearly parallel stains. Watch the DAB map, the threshold and the count. Why is the count so robust here, and when would it not be?






Solutions





D1. Threshold 0.27; 14 positive nuclei found; the slide has 14 DAB-positive nuclei among 30.
D2. Ruifrok: threshold 0.29, 14. Wrong DAB vector: 0.39, 14, and the H map gets -0.60 times the DAB (positive nuclei look hematoxylin-poor). Nearly parallel: 0.62, 14, with a noisier DAB map (\kappa = 9.8). The count is robust because the positive nuclei are strongly brown and well separated from the background: crosstalk changes the DAB values (and the threshold) but not which nuclei are above it. Weakly positive nuclei, or touching nuclei, would be miscounted first; the H measurements in DAB-positive nuclei are not robust at all.

Where this leads
Colour deconvolution is the last piece of the day: a fluorescence image, a lambda stack, a hyperspectral scene and a stained slide are all \mathbf y = M\mathbf a.
