title: Active contours (snakes)
text:
About this lecture
A threshold gives a ragged, leaky outline. Often we want something else: one smooth closed curve that sits on the edges of the object. An active contour, or snake (Kass, Witkin & Terzopoulos, 1988), is such a curve that moves by itself until it settles there.

A closed chain of beads: springs between neighbours, plus a pull towards edges.
The beads move downhill on an energy: internal (smooth, short) plus image (on edges).
The force on one bead, by hand: the neighbours’ midpoint, and a straightening term.
What the knobs do: elasticity \alpha, rigidity \beta, smoothing \sigma, step \tau.
What goes wrong: shrinking away, cut corners, stuck on noise, too far away, explosion.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: Active contours (snakes)
section: Find the boundary of this nucleus
text:
Find the boundary of this nucleus


Left: a snake starts as a circle (dashed) around a noisy disk and shrinks onto its edge. Middle: the edge map, bright where the image changes. Right: the same on a micrograph.
A threshold would label pixels; the snake gives a curve: a list of points, smooth, closed, one object. Perimeter, curvature and shape come for free.


Right panel: the nucleus of the course micrograph (128 × 128), start circle centre (74, 57), radius 44, σ = 3, 500 steps: the outline runs along the dark nuclear envelope, with a short cut across at the lower left. The disk: radius 30, start radius 45; after 300 steps the mean radius is 29.79.

title: Active contours (snakes)
text:
Recall: segmentation as energy minimisation
On the graph cuts day (seg-energy/) a segmentation was the labelling with the lowest energy: a data term (fit the image) plus \lambda times a smoothness term (short boundaries).
A snake uses the same recipe with a different unknown:









graph cut
snake




unknown
a label per pixel
the positions of n points on a closed curve


image term
grey level fits the label
the curve lies on edges


smoothness
boundary length, weight \lambda
stretching (\alpha) and bending (\beta)


minimised by
one max-flow, exact
moving the points downhill, step by step, locally



The snake finds a local minimum near where it starts. That is both its weakness (it needs a start) and its strength (it follows what you point it at).

title: Active contours (snakes)
text:
A closed chain of beads
The curve is a polygon of n points \mathbf x_0, \dots, \mathbf x_{n-1}; after the last comes the first again.

Elastic springs between neighbours (weight \alpha): stretching costs energy. Each bead is pulled towards the midpoint of its two neighbours. A chain with springs alone contracts to a point.
Stiffness (weight \beta): bending costs energy. Each bead is pushed to make the chain locally straight; corners are expensive.
The image: low energy on edges. Each bead is pulled uphill on the edge map, towards the nearest strong edge, if there is one nearby.

The snake stops where the three forces balance at every bead.

title: Active contours (snakes)
section: Try it: a snake on a disk
text:
Try it: a snake on a disk




Disk of radius 30 (noise 0.05), start circle radius 45, n = 40, α = 0.1, β = 0.05, σ = 2, w = 2, semi-implicit τ = 1. Press play: the circle shrinks slowly (the elastic force is weak on a smooth circle): mean radius 39.7 after 50 steps, 34.9 after 100; then the edge catches it, and after 200 steps it sits at 29.78 and stays. The energy plot: the internal energy falls from 100.95 to 44.27, the image energy drops from about 0 to −70.9 when the snake reaches the edge. Switch the forces on (default) and the “edge map” view. Drag on the image to place a new circle. Then the presets: “α too large” (α = 1: the springs win, radius 0.2 after 500 steps), “β too large” (square, β = 2: rounded corners), “σ too small” (noise 0.25, σ = 0.5: stuck at radius 37–44), “too far” (α = 0.01: after 300 steps still at radius 53.4), “τ too large” (explicit step, explodes after 55 steps).

title: Active contours (snakes)
section: The forces on a square, by hand
text:
The forces on a square, by hand
Four beads at (1, 1), (-1, 1), (-1, -1), (1, -1), no image.

Elastic (\alpha = 1): bead (1, 1) has neighbours (-1, 1) and (1, -1), midpoint (0, 0). The force is \alpha \times (sum of the neighbours -\,2\times the bead) = (-1,1) + (1,-1) - 2(1,1) = (-2, -2): twice the way to the midpoint.
One step of size \tau = 0.1: (1, 1) + 0.1\,(-2, -2) = (0.8, 0.8). All four beads do the same: the square shrinks to 0.8 and stays a square.
Rigid (\beta = 1): the straightening force at the corner is (-4, -4) (math slide). With \alpha = \beta = 1: (-6, -6), and the step lands at (0.4, 0.4).

On a fine polygon, the elastic force at a bead is the difference with its neighbours: the same [1, -2, 1] as the second-derivative kernel of Filtering & convolution.

title: Active contours (snakes)
section: The math: the snake energy and its force
text:
The math: the snake energy and its force
E = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \Big[\tfrac12\alpha\,|\mathbf x_{i+1} - \mathbf x_i|^2 + \tfrac12\beta\,|\mathbf x_{i-1} - 2\mathbf x_i + \mathbf x_{i+1}|^2 + E_\text{ext}(\mathbf x_i)\Big], \qquad \text{indices mod } n.
E is an ordinary function of 2n numbers. The force on bead i is -\partial E/\partial \mathbf x_i. Point \mathbf x_i appears in two elastic terms and three rigid terms:
-\frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf x_i} = \underbrace{\alpha(\mathbf x_{i-1} - 2\mathbf x_i + \mathbf x_{i+1})}_{\text{elastic}} \;\underbrace{-\,\beta(\mathbf x_{i-2} - 4\mathbf x_{i-1} + 6\mathbf x_i - 4\mathbf x_{i+1} + \mathbf x_{i+2})}_{\text{rigid}} \;-\, \nabla E_\text{ext}(\mathbf x_i).

[1, -2, 1] is the discrete second derivative; [1, -4, 6, -4, 1] = [1, -2, 1] * [1, -2, 1] is the fourth.
Square, \beta = 1, corner (1, 1): \mathbf x_{i\pm2} is the opposite corner (-1,-1), so -\big[(-1,-1) - 4(1,-1) + 6(1,1) - 4(-1,1) + (-1,-1)\big] = (-4, -4).
The internal forces sum to zero over all beads: moving the whole snake costs nothing.

title: Active contours (snakes)
text:
The image term
The snake should sit where the image changes most. Smooth the image with a Gaussian of size \sigma, take the gradient (Filtering & convolution), and square its length: the edge map
f = |\nabla (G_\sigma * I)|^2, \qquad E_\text{ext} = -w\,f \quad (\text{low on edges}).

The image force on a bead is w\,\nabla f: it points uphill on the edge map, towards the ridge of the nearest edge.
Far from any edge f is flat and the force is zero: the snake does not feel the object. How far the pull reaches, the capture range, is a few \sigma.
Small \sigma: sharp, accurate edges, but noise makes its own little edges. Large \sigma: a wide pull, but blurred and slightly shifted edges.


1D check (exercise B5): an edge map f(x) = exp(−(x − 10)²/8) (edge at x = 10, width 2). Its slope f′ is +0.30 at x = 8 (push right, towards the edge), −0.30 at x = 12, and −0.00001 at x = 20: a bead 10 pixels away feels nothing. In the demo the largest inward image force on the disk is 0.69 (w = 2, σ = 2), at radius 31.5.

title: Active contours (snakes)
text:
The math: the continuous snake (Euler–Lagrange)
Let the number of beads grow: a curve \mathbf x(s), s \in [0, L), closed. The sums become integrals:
E[\mathbf x] = \int_0^L \tfrac12\alpha\,|\mathbf x'(s)|^2 + \tfrac12\beta\,|\mathbf x''(s)|^2 + E_\text{ext}(\mathbf x(s))\;ds.
Change the curve a little, \mathbf x + \varepsilon\mathbf h. For the elastic term, integrate by parts (the curve is closed, so the boundary terms cancel):
\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\int \tfrac12\alpha|\mathbf x' + \varepsilon\mathbf h'|^2 ds\Big|_{\varepsilon = 0} = \int \alpha\,\mathbf x'\cdot\mathbf h'\,ds = -\int \alpha\,\mathbf x''\cdot\mathbf h\,ds.
The rigid term, integrated by parts twice, gives +\beta\mathbf x''''. A minimum needs the change to vanish for every \mathbf h: the Euler–Lagrange equation
-\alpha\,\mathbf x'' + \beta\,\mathbf x'''' + \nabla E_\text{ext}(\mathbf x) = 0:\qquad \text{internal force} + \text{image force} = 0.

The discrete stencils are exactly these derivatives with spacing 1. Circle \mathbf x(s) = r(\cos s, \sin s): \alpha\mathbf x'' = -\alpha\mathbf x, a force of size \alpha r towards the centre.

title: Active contours (snakes)
section: Moving the snake: one step at a time
text:
Moving the snake: one step at a time
Start from a curve near the object and repeat: compute the force on every bead, move every bead a little along it.
\text{new position} = \text{position} + \tau \times \text{force}

\tau (the step) small: the snake creeps downhill on the energy and stops where the forces balance.
\tau slightly too large: beads overshoot, the next force overshoots back, and a zig-zag grows until the snake explodes. With \alpha = 0.1, \beta = 0.05 this happens above \tau \approx 1.67.
The image force is read at each bead’s (non-integer) position by bilinear interpolation.

Why exactly 1.67, and a step that never explodes: the next unit.

title: Active contours (snakes)
text:
The math: gradient descent
Stack all bead positions into one vector \mathbf x \in \mathbb R^{2n}. The update is gradient descent on E:
\mathbf x_{t+1} = \mathbf x_t - \tau\,\nabla E(\mathbf x_t) = \mathbf x_t + \tau\,\mathbf F(\mathbf x_t).

For small enough \tau, E(\mathbf x_{t+1}) < E(\mathbf x_t) unless \nabla E = 0 (Taylor: E(\mathbf x - \tau\nabla E) = E - \tau|\nabla E|^2 + O(\tau^2)).
“Small enough” depends on how curved E is: the internal part has curvature up to \lambda_\text{max} = 4\alpha + 16\beta, and the step is stable while \tau\lambda_\text{max} < 2. For \alpha = 0.1, \beta = 0.05: \lambda_\text{max} = 1.2, \tau < 1.67.
A fixed point is a solution of the discrete Euler–Lagrange equation: internal + image force = 0 at every bead.

title: Active contours (snakes)
text:
Reading the knobs








knob
too small
too large




\alpha elasticity
points drift apart; slow to move in flat regions
shrinks off the edge (disk: from \alpha \approx 0.85)


\beta rigidity
follows every corner and noise wiggle
cuts corners: the square comes out rounded


\sigma smoothing
stuck on noise edges
blurred, slightly shifted edges


w image weight
snake ignores the image
stuck on the first weak edge


\tau step
slow
explodes (explicit step)



And independent of the knobs: a snake whose beads are all far from any edge feels no image force at all.

title: Active contours (snakes)
text:
Try it: what goes wrong




“concavity: cannot enter the U”: n = 100, α = 0.03, β = 0.01, resample every 10. The snake wraps the outside of the U and bridges the slot: after 800 steps its deepest point in the slot is at y = 15.6 (the slot ends at y = 77.5). The edge force inside the slot points sideways, at the slot walls, never down into it. Unit 2 fixes this with GVF. “two blobs”: one snake wraps both blobs and bridges the gap (half-height of the bridge 12.6 pixels at the centre): a snake has one outline, whatever the number of objects. “micrograph”: σ = 3, n = 60.

title: Active contours (snakes)
text:
Not covered here, but close

Point spacing: the beads slide along the curve and bunch up in some places. The demo can resample the curve to equal spacing every k steps.
Searching instead of sliding: the greedy snake (Williams & Shah) tries a few positions around each bead and keeps the best. The dynamic-programming snake (Amini et al.) finds the exact best positions within a window for all beads at once: on the dynamic programming day.
Curves that split and merge: an explicit chain of beads cannot. Level sets represent the curve implicitly and can: on the level set day.

title: Active contours (snakes)
text:
Summary

A snake is a closed polygon that moves downhill on an energy: elastic (short), rigid (straight) and image (on edges) terms.
Force on a bead: \alpha pulls it towards its neighbours’ midpoint, \beta straightens, the image pulls it uphill on the edge map |\nabla(G_\sigma * I)|^2.
Balance at every bead = a local minimum = the Euler–Lagrange equation -\alpha\mathbf x'' + \beta\mathbf x'''' + \nabla E_\text{ext} = 0.
Failure modes: shrinks (\alpha), cuts corners (\beta), noise (small \sigma), capture range (too far), explodes (large \tau), concavities, one outline only.

title: Quiz: the snake as a linear system
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A is the snake matrix (internal force = -A\mathbf x), with eigenvalues \lambda_k = 4\alpha\sin^2(\pi k/n) + 16\beta\sin^4(\pi k/n).

Q1. Why does every row of A sum to zero?






Answer





The internal energy depends only on differences between bead positions. Moving the whole snake by the same amount changes nothing, so it creates no force: A\mathbf 1 = 0, and the eigenvalue of the constant mode is \lambda_0 = 0.




Q2. What do the corner entries of A (top right, bottom left) represent?






Answer





The wrap-around of the closed curve: the last bead is a neighbour of the first. Without them A would be banded and describe an open chain with free ends.




Q3. Why are the eigenvectors of A sampled cosines and sines?






Hint





Every row is the same stencil, shifted by one.









Answer





A\mathbf x is a circular convolution of \mathbf x with a fixed stencil. Convolution turns into multiplication in the Fourier basis (Images in frequency space): a wave going k times around the curve comes out as the same wave times a number, \lambda_k.




Q4. \alpha = 0.5, \beta = 0.25. What is the largest step \tau for which the explicit update is stable?






Answer





\lambda_\text{max} = 4 \cdot 0.5 + 16 \cdot 0.25 = 6; stable for \tau\lambda_\text{max} < 2, i.e. \tau < 1/3.




Q5. Which pattern of the beads is the first to explode when \tau is too large, and what does it look like?






Answer





The mode with the largest eigenvalue, k = n/2: alternate beads displaced in opposite directions, a zig-zag. Its factor per step 1 - \tau\lambda_\text{max} drops below -1 first, so it flips sign and grows every step.




Q6. The semi-implicit step costs a linear solve per step. Why is that cheap?






Answer





The matrix A + \gamma I is the same in every step as long as \alpha, \beta, \tau and n do not change: it can be factored (or inverted) once. It is banded with five diagonals plus corners, so a solve costs a few operations per bead, and x and y use the same factorisation.




Q7. A balloon snake inflates nicely inside a cell but escapes where the membrane is faint. Name two things you could change.






Answer





Lower \kappa (but then it may stop early on the strong side or on texture), raise the edge weight w or lower \sigma where the faint edge needs sharpening, switch to GVF without a balloon, or add shape knowledge (a shape model). No single \kappa fits a strong and a weak edge at once.




Q8. What does gradient vector flow add that a larger \sigma does not?






Answer





GVF spreads the edge force into flat regions without blurring the edges themselves: near edges the field stays equal to the sharp edge force. It also points into concavities, where the plain edge force points sideways. A larger \sigma widens the pull but blurs and shifts the edges and merges nearby ones.




Q9. Two touching nuclei, one snake around both. Can GVF or a balloon make the snake separate them?






Answer





No. One snake is one closed curve; no force changes that. It needs two snakes (one started in each nucleus), or an implicit representation that can split (level sets).




Q10. (math) Show that the semi-implicit factor \gamma/(\gamma + \lambda_k) lies in (0, 1] for every \gamma > 0.






Answer





A is positive semidefinite, so \lambda_k \ge 0. With \gamma > 0: 0 < \gamma \le \gamma + \lambda_k, hence 0 < \gamma/(\gamma + \lambda_k) \le 1, with 1 only for \lambda_k = 0 (translation).

title: Exercise: the snake as a linear system
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Snake matrix A
n \times n, row i: \beta,\ -\alpha-4\beta,\ 2\alpha+6\beta,\ -\alpha-4\beta,\ \beta at columns i-2, \dots, i+2 (mod n); internal force = -A\mathbf x


Modes
the sampled waves \cos(2\pi kj/n), \sin(2\pi kj/n): eigenvectors of A


Eigenvalues
\lambda_k = 4\alpha\sin^2(\pi k/n) + 16\beta\sin^4(\pi k/n); \lambda_\text{max} = 4\alpha + 16\beta (n even)


Explicit step
\mathbf x \leftarrow \mathbf x + \tau(-A\mathbf x + \mathbf f): mode k times 1 - \tau\lambda_k


Semi-implicit step
(A + \gamma I)\mathbf x_\text{new} = \gamma\mathbf x + \mathbf f, \gamma = 1/\tau: mode k times 1/(1 + \tau\lambda_k)


Balloon
\kappa\,\mathbf n_i along the outward normal of each bead


GVF
\mathbf v \leftarrow \mathbf v + \Delta t\,[\mu\nabla^2\mathbf v - \lvert\nabla f\rvert^2(\mathbf v - \nabla f)], starting from \mathbf v = \nabla f

title: Exercise: the snake as a linear system
text:
By hand
B1. n = 6, \alpha = 1, \beta = 0. (a) Write A. Which entries come from the curve being closed? (b) Check that A\mathbf 1 = 0. What does that mean for the snake? (c) Check that (1, -1, 1, -1, 1, -1) is an eigenvector. Eigenvalue? Draw what this pattern does to the x coordinates of a hexagon.
B2. Still n = 6. (a) Give all six eigenvalues \lambda_0, \dots, \lambda_5 for \alpha = 1, \beta = 0. Which are equal, and why? (b) The same for \alpha = 1, \beta = 1. Which modes does \beta make most expensive?
B3. Explicit step, n = 6. (a) With \alpha = 1, \beta = 0: what is the largest \tau for which no mode grows? Give the factor per step of modes k = 1, 2, 3 for \tau = 0.1, 0.5 and 1. (b) With \alpha = \beta = 1: largest stable \tau?
B4. Semi-implicit step, n = 6, \alpha = 1, \beta = 0. (a) Factor per step of modes k = 1, 2, 3 for \tau = 1 (\gamma = 1). Compare with the explicit step at the same \tau. (b) What happens to the factors when \tau becomes huge? What does the snake look like after one such step?
B5. Unit 1’s snake: n = 40, \alpha = 0.1, \beta = 0.05, semi-implicit \tau = 1. (a) \lambda_\text{max}, and the largest stable \tau for the explicit step. (b) Mode k = 1 (the overall size of a circle): its eigenvalue and factor per step. About how many steps does it take, without an image, for the circle to shrink to half its radius?
B6. 1D GVF. Seven samples of the edge force g = \nabla f along a line: g = (0, 0, 1, 0, -1, 0, 0) (the edge is at sample 3, counting from 0). Take \mu = 0.25, \Delta t = 1, \mathbf v = g at the start, and at the two ends repeat the end value (so v''_0 = v_1 - v_0). (a) Do one update v_i \leftarrow v_i + \mu(v_{i-1} - 2v_i + v_{i+1}) - g_i^2(v_i - g_i). (b) Do a second update. Where is the force now non-zero that was zero before? Does it point towards the edge? (c) What would the plain edge force do to a bead at sample 0?
B7. Predict, for a balloon started inside a bright disk: (a) \kappa very small; (b) \kappa moderate; (c) \kappa large; (d) moderate \kappa, but the edge of the disk is faint on one side.






Solutions





B1. (a) Rows (2, -1, 0, 0, 0, -1), (-1, 2, -1, 0, 0, 0), …, (-1, 0, 0, 0, -1, 2): the -1 in the top-right and bottom-left corners link bead 0 and bead 5, which are neighbours only because the curve is closed. (b) Every row sums to 2 - 1 - 1 = 0. Moving all beads by the same amount creates no internal force: the snake can be anywhere. (c) Row 0: 2\cdot1 - (-1) - (-1) = 4; row 1: -1 \cdot 1 + 2\cdot(-1) - 1\cdot1 = -4, and so on: A\mathbf v = (4, -4, 4, -4, 4, -4) = 4\mathbf v. Eigenvalue 4. Added to the x coordinates of a hexagon it pushes alternate corners left and right: a zig-zag, the most bent pattern.
B2. (a) \lambda_k = 4\sin^2(\pi k/6): 0, 1, 3, 4, 3, 1. \lambda_k = \lambda_{6-k}: the waves \cos and \sin of the same frequency have the same cost (a wave and its shifted copy). (b) Add 16\sin^4(\pi k/6): 0, 2, 12, 20, 12, 2. Mode 1 goes from 1 to 2, mode 3 from 4 to 20: \beta makes the wiggly modes far more expensive.
B3. (a) \lambda_\text{max} = 4: stable for \tau \le 2/4 = 0.5. Factors 1 - \tau\lambda_k for k = 1, 2, 3: \tau = 0.1: 0.9, 0.7, 0.6. \tau = 0.5: 0.5, -0.5, -1 (the zig-zag flips sign forever, neither growing nor shrinking). \tau = 1: 0, -2, -3: modes 2 and 3 explode. (b) \lambda_\text{max} = 20: \tau \le 0.1.
B4. (a) 1/(1 + \lambda_k): 0.5, 0.25, 0.2, against 0, -2, -3 for the explicit step at \tau = 1. All between 0 and 1: stable, the wiggles shrink fastest. (b) All factors go to 0 except k = 0 (factor 1): after one huge step only the mean position is left, the snake collapses to its centroid. Stable, but the image force must then do all the work in each step.
B5. (a) \lambda_\text{max} = 0.4 + 0.8 = 1.2; explicit stable for \tau < 1.67. (b) \lambda_1 = 0.4\sin^2(\pi/40) + 0.8\sin^4(\pi/40) = 0.00249; factor 1/1.00249 = 0.99751. Half the radius after \ln 2/(-\ln 0.99751) = 278 steps. That is why the snake of unit 1 needed about a hundred steps to shrink from radius 45 to the edge.
B6. (a) v = (0, 0.25, 0.5, 0, -0.5, -0.25, 0). (At sample 2: 1 + 0.25(0 - 2 + 0) - 1\cdot(1 - 1) = 0.5; at sample 1: 0 + 0.25(0 - 0 + 1) - 0 = 0.25.) (b) v = (0.0625, 0.25, 0.8125, 0, -0.8125, -0.25, -0.0625). Samples 0, 1, 5, 6, where g = 0, now have a force, positive on the left (pointing right, towards the edge) and negative on the right: towards the edge. Next to the edge the data term pulls v back towards g (sample 2: from 0.5 up to 0.81). (c) Nothing: g_0 = 0. The bead is outside the capture range of the plain edge force.
B7. (a) It hardly grows: the elastic force (and noise) hold it. (b) It inflates until it reaches the edge, where the edge force balances the balloon. (c) It pushes through the edge and keeps growing. (d) It stops on the strong side but leaks through the faint side: the balloon is the same everywhere, the edge force is not.




Math questions
B8. (math) Show that \mathbf v with v_j = e^{2\pi ikj/n} is an eigenvector of any circulant matrix (row j = row 0 shifted by j), with eigenvalue \sum_m a_m e^{2\pi ikm/n} where a_m is the entry of row 0 in column m. Use it to derive \lambda_k = 4\alpha\sin^2(\pi k/n) + 16\beta\sin^4(\pi k/n).
B9. (math) Show that A is positive semidefinite by writing \tfrac12\mathbf x^\top A\mathbf x as the internal energy (for one coordinate). When is \mathbf x^\top A\mathbf x = 0?
B10. (math) Derive the semi-implicit step from \mathbf x_{t+1} = \mathbf x_t - \tau(A\mathbf x_{t+1} - \mathbf f_t). Show that A + \gamma I is invertible for every \gamma > 0 and that the internal part of the step never increases the internal energy.
B11. (math) Show that the GVF update is gradient descent (up to a factor 2) on \mathcal E(\mathbf v) = \sum_\text{pixels}\mu|\nabla \mathbf v|^2 + |\nabla f|^2|\mathbf v - \nabla f|^2 (finite differences for \nabla\mathbf v). Why is \Delta t \le 1/(4\mu) needed for stability in flat regions?






Solutions (math)





B8. Row j has entry a_{m} in column j + m (mod n). (A\mathbf v)_j = \sum_m a_m v_{j+m} = \sum_m a_m e^{2\pi ik(j+m)/n} = \big(\sum_m a_m e^{2\pi ikm/n}\big) v_j. For the snake, a_0 = 2\alpha + 6\beta, a_{\pm1} = -\alpha - 4\beta, a_{\pm2} = \beta; with c = \cos(2\pi k/n): \lambda_k = 2\alpha + 6\beta - 2(\alpha + 4\beta)c + 2\beta\cos(4\pi k/n). With \cos(4\pi k/n) = 2c^2 - 1 this is 2\alpha(1 - c) + 4\beta(1 - c)^2, and 1 - c = 2\sin^2(\pi k/n) gives 4\alpha\sin^2 + 16\beta\sin^4.
B9. For one coordinate, \tfrac12\mathbf x^\top A\mathbf x = \sum_j\tfrac12\alpha(x_{j+1} - x_j)^2 + \tfrac12\beta(x_{j-1} - 2x_j + x_{j+1})^2 \ge 0 (the gradient of this quadratic is A\mathbf x, and a quadratic form equals half its gradient dotted with \mathbf x). With \alpha > 0 it is zero only when all x_j are equal: the null space is the translations, \lambda_0 = 0.
B10. Moving \tau A\mathbf x_{t+1} to the left: (I + \tau A)\mathbf x_{t+1} = \mathbf x_t + \tau\mathbf f_t; divide by \tau. A is symmetric with eigenvalues \lambda_k \ge 0, so A + \gamma I has eigenvalues \lambda_k + \gamma > 0. Internal part: in the eigenbasis each coefficient c_k becomes c_k/(1 + \tau\lambda_k), with |{\cdot}| \le |c_k|, and the internal energy is \tfrac12\sum_k\lambda_k c_k^2: it cannot increase.
B11. \partial\mathcal E/\partial\mathbf v_p: the smoothness term \mu\sum|\mathbf v_q - \mathbf v_p|^2 over neighbour pairs gives -2\mu(\sum_{q \sim p}\mathbf v_q - 4\mathbf v_p) = -2\mu\nabla^2\mathbf v_p, the data term 2|\nabla f|^2(\mathbf v_p - \nabla f). So -\tfrac12\partial\mathcal E/\partial\mathbf v_p = \mu\nabla^2\mathbf v_p - |\nabla f|^2(\mathbf v_p - \nabla f), the update direction. In flat regions only the diffusion acts: \mathbf v \leftarrow (1 + \Delta t\mu\nabla^2)\mathbf v; the most negative eigenvalue of the 5-point Laplacian is -8 (checkerboard), so the checkerboard is multiplied by 1 - 8\mu\Delta t, which stays \ge -1 only for \Delta t \le 1/(4\mu): the same stability argument as for the explicit snake step.

title: Exercise: the snake as a linear system
section: Explore: the modes of a snake
text:
Explore: the modes of a snake
No image here: a closed polygon of n beads moves under its internal forces only. Drag the beads to make your own shape. The plots show, for each mode k (number of waves around the curve): the eigenvalue \lambda_k (with the explicit limit 2/\tau dashed), the factor per step (green inside \pm1, red outside), and the size of the mode in the current contour (grey bars: at the start; dots: now). show matrix A replaces the contour by A.



S1. Preset n = 6: the matrix by hand. Compare the matrix with B1, the eigenvalues with B2(a), the factors with B3(a) for \tau = 0.2. Add \beta = 1: which entries change?
S2. Preset α only: shrinks to a point (noisy circle, n = 16, \alpha = 0.2, semi-implicit \tau = 1). Step 10 times. Which modes disappear first? Read the factor of mode 1 and estimate after how many steps the circle has half its radius. Check with the demo.
S3. Preset β only. Compare the factors of mode 1 and mode 8 with S2. Which snake keeps its size longer, and which smooths its wiggles faster?
S4. Presets explicit at the limit and explicit just beyond: explodes. Read \tau\lambda_\text{max} and the factor of mode 8. Step and watch the contour and the bottom plot. Then switch the second one to semi-implicit.
S5. Preset semi-implicit, huge τ: still stable (\tau = 50). What does one step do to the noisy circle? Why is that not a useful way to run a snake on an image?
S6. Choose star with n = 32, \alpha = 0.1, \beta = 0, semi-implicit \tau = 1. Which modes carry the star’s points (look at the grey bars)? Play: in which order does the star turn into a circle and the circle into a point?






Solutions





S1. The matrix is B1’s (rows 2, -1, 0, 0, 0, -1 shifted, with the corner entries). The demo’s eigenvalue bars show 0, 1, 3, 4 for k = 0, \dots, 3 (each of 1 and 3 belongs to two waves). With \tau = 0.2 (explicit) the factors are 1, 0.8, 0.4, 0.2. With \beta = 1 the diagonal becomes 2 + 6 = 8, the neighbours -1 - 4 = -5, the second neighbours (two places from the diagonal, including the corners) 1; \lambda_\text{max} = 20 and \tau\lambda_\text{max} = 4: unstable.
S2. The high modes go first (factors 0.71 for k = 4 down to 0.56 for k = 8): after 10 steps the wiggles are gone and a smooth, slightly smaller circle is left. Mode 1 has factor 0.970: half the radius after \ln 2/(-\ln 0.970) \approx 23 steps.
S3. \beta = 0.2: mode 1 has factor 0.995 (half-life 150 steps), mode 8 factor 0.24. Against \alpha = 0.2: 0.970 and 0.56. The \beta-snake keeps its size about six times longer and removes wiggles faster: \beta’s cost grows like k^4, \alpha’s like k^2.
S4. At the limit: \tau\lambda_\text{max} = 1.95, factor of mode 8 is -0.95: the zig-zag flips sign every step and fades slowly. Just beyond: 2.1, factor -1.1: the zig-zag grows by 10 % per step, flipping sign, and after some tens of steps the contour leaves the view and explodes. Semi-implicit with the same \tau = 2.1: mode 8 has factor 1/(1 + 2.1) = 0.32, stable.
S5. All factors except mode 0 are small (mode 1: 0.34, mode 8: 0.02): one step removes the noise and shrinks the circle to a third of its size; a few steps collapse it. With an image, such a step trusts the image force read at the old position for a very long move: the snake can jump over edges. \tau (or \gamma) still sets how far the snake may move per step, it just cannot make it explode.
S6. After mode 1 (the circle itself, size 1.10) the largest grey bars are at modes 4 (0.28) and 6 (0.13): the 5 points ride on the once-around circle, which puts them at 5 - 1 and 5 + 1 waves per turn in the x and y coordinates. Under the internal forces these die within some tens of steps (mode 4: \lambda_4 = 0.4\sin^2(4\pi/32) = 0.059, factor 0.945, half-life about 12 steps; mode 6: factor 0.89), long before mode 1 (\lambda_1 = 0.0038, factor 0.996, half-life about 180 steps): first a smooth roundish shape, then a slowly shrinking circle.

title: Exercise: the snake as a linear system
section: Explore: balloon, GVF and the matrix
text:
Explore: balloon, GVF and the matrix
The snake demo of the previous unit, now with GVF next to the plain edge force, a balloon force \kappa, and the matrix A (explicit) or A + \gamma I (semi-implicit) on the right, with the wrap-around entries framed in orange. Tick field to see the force field the snake uses.



G1. Preset concavity: cannot enter the U, tick field, play. Then preset U: GVF enters the concavity. Compare the two fields inside the slot and the two results. Set resample every to off in the GVF preset and reset: what changes, and why?
G2. Preset balloon from inside (\kappa = 0.3). Play. Then try \kappa = 0.1, 0.6 and 1. Where does each one end?
G3. Preset balloon leaks through the weak edge (\kappa = 0.6). Where does it leak? Lower \kappa until it stops at the edge everywhere. Is there a \kappa that both reaches the edge on the strong side and stops on the weak side?
G4. Preset far start: GVF captures it. Compare with edge force (same start, same \alpha = 0.01). Use field to explain.
G5. Set n = 8 and look at the matrix panel for the explicit and the semi-implicit update (\alpha = 0.1, \beta = 0.05, \tau = 1). Which entries change between the two? Then raise \beta to 1: how does the band change?
G6. Preset two blobs with GVF, and with a balloon from inside one blob. Can any of the new forces separate the two blobs with one snake?






Solutions





G1. The edge force inside the slot points sideways to the walls; with it the snake closes over the mouth (deepest point in the slot y = 15.6 after 800 iterations). The GVF field points down into the slot as well; the GVF snake reaches the bottom of the slot (y = 77.5) after about 800 iterations (40.7 after 100, 53.4 after 400). Without resampling it stops at y = 38: the beads that enter the slot are pulled far apart, and the few beads there cannot follow the long walls; resampling keeps enough beads along the curve.
G2. \kappa = 0.3: it inflates to radius 30.3 and stops on the edge. \kappa = 0.1: 30.0, \kappa = 0.6: 31.1, pushed slightly outward against the edge force. \kappa = 1: it breaks through and keeps growing (radius 256 after 400 iterations).
G3. It leaks through the right-hand side, where the disk fades into the background, and grows on (beads beyond x = 200 after 400 iterations). \kappa = 0.1 stops on the edge everywhere (mean radius 29.8). At \kappa = 0.2 it already bulges out on the weak side (beads up to x = 104); at 0.3 it leaks. No single \kappa fits both sides well: the balloon is the same everywhere, the edge force is not. A weak edge needs a weak balloon, or knowledge of the shape.
G4. With the edge force the snake barely moves (radius 56.4 after 100 iterations): no force reaches it. With GVF it is pulled in at once (radius 39.5 after 50 iterations, 29.85 after 100). The field shows arrows everywhere around the disk pointing towards it: the edge force diffused into the flat background.
G5. The semi-implicit matrix adds \gamma = 1/\tau = 1 to the diagonal (0.5 + 1 = 1.5; off-diagonals -0.3 and 0.05, the same in both); the corner entries are the wrap-around of the closed curve. With \beta = 1 the diagonal becomes 6.2 (explicit) or 7.2, the first off-diagonals -4.1 and the second 1: the band is dominated by \beta, and the explicit step would need \tau < 2/16.4 = 0.12.
G6. No. GVF lets the snake follow the gap between the blobs more deeply, and a balloon in one blob finds that blob only, but one snake is always one closed curve: it either bridges the two blobs or covers one of them. Two objects need two snakes (or a representation that can split: level sets).

title: Exercise: the snake as a linear system
text:
Where this leads
The snake knows only “smooth”: a missing piece of edge is bridged by a straight line, and an outline in clutter can wander off. When the object class is known (hands, leaves, vertebrae, nuclei) we can learn from examples which shapes are plausible: the next unit builds such a shape model, and the one after uses it to search the image.

title: Hit-or-miss and thinning
text:
About this lecture
A thresholded neuron or blood vessel network is a mask. The questions biologists ask about it are how long and how branched, not how much area. For that we want a skeleton: a line one pixel wide, running along the middle of the shape, with the same connections and holes.

Hit-or-miss: a 3 × 3 template that must fit the object and the background at once. Finds end points, isolated pixels, junctions.
Thinning: peel the shape layer by layer with templates, one template at a time.
Simple points: which pixels can go without cutting the shape or opening a hole.
Why end points must be kept.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: Hit-or-miss and thinning
text:
Why a skeleton?

A dendrite 1000 µm long and 2 µm wide, and one 500 µm long and 4 µm wide, have the same area. Area cannot tell them apart; length can.
A skeleton keeps what we want to count: length (pixels along the line), branch points, end points, loops.
Two requirements: thin (one pixel wide) and topology-preserving (the same number of pieces and holes as the shape).
Today: how to get it by local rules on a 3 × 3 neighbourhood. Next units: the skeleton as the middle of the shape (medial axis), then as a graph we can measure.

title: Hit-or-miss and thinning
text:
Recall: erosion asks “does it fit?”
From the morphology day: the erosion A \ominus B keeps the pixels where the structuring element B, placed there, fits inside the object A.

Erosion only looks at object pixels: “are these all 1?”
It cannot ask “are these 0?”. An end point of a line and a pixel in the middle of the line both fit a 1 × 1 element; to tell them apart we must also look at where the background is.

title: Hit-or-miss and thinning
section: Hit-or-miss: fit the object and the background
text:
Hit-or-miss: fit the object and the background
A template on a 3 × 3 grid with three states:

1: this cell must be object,
0: this cell must be background,
· (“don’t care”): either.

The hit-or-miss transform marks every pixel where the template, centred there, fits completely: all its 1-cells on object, all its 0-cells on background.

title: Hit-or-miss and thinning
text:
The math: hit-or-miss
With B_1 = the 1-cells and B_2 = the 0-cells of the template (B_1 \cap B_2 = \emptyset):
A \circledast (B_1, B_2) = (A \ominus B_1) \cap (A^c \ominus B_2).

Two erosions: B_1 must fit in the object, B_2 must fit in the background A^c.
If B_1 \cap B_2 \ne \emptyset, a cell would have to be 1 and 0 at once: the result is empty.
Equivalently (A \ominus B_1) \setminus (A \oplus \check B_2): fits the object, and no background cell hits it.
Pixels outside the image count as background.

title: Hit-or-miss and thinning
text:
Templates for skeleton pixels
On a one-pixel-wide line, the 8 neighbours of a pixel say what it is:

Isolated pixel: centre 1, all 8 neighbours 0.
End point: exactly one neighbour. One template with a 1 above the centre, and its 8 rotations by 45°, find all of them.
Junction: three or more neighbours: T-shaped (left, right, below) and Y-shaped (two diagonals and one straight) templates, with their rotations.
Corner of a blob, edge pixel: templates with a row of 0s on one side and 1s on the other.

The union of the hit-or-miss transforms of all rotations finds every such pixel.

title: Hit-or-miss and thinning
text:
Try it: hit-or-miss




Left: the template editor (click a cell: 1 → 0 → ·) and template presets. Middle: the image (click to edit). Right: the result. Step through: at each object pixel the template is placed, matched cells green, failing cells red. Tour: “find the end points”: end-point template with all 8 rotations: the result is (2, 1) (rotation 3: neighbour to the right) and (3, 5) (rotation 8: neighbour up-left); the isolated pixel at (5, 1) is not an end point. Untick “all 8 rotations”: the single template (neighbour above) finds nothing. Choose the “isolated” template: only (5, 1). “Isolated pixels” preset: the specks are found, the 3 × 3 block is not.

title: Hit-or-miss and thinning
text:
Thinning: peel with templates
Thinning removes, again and again, pixels where an edge or corner template fits, until nothing changes:
A \leftarrow A \setminus (A \circledast T)

Two templates (Golay’s L): L1 an edge pixel (background on one side, object on the other), L2 a corner pixel; each in 4 rotations: 8 templates.
Apply them one at a time: L1, L2, L1 turned 90°, … Each removes its matches before the next one looks.
No template matches a pixel with only one neighbour: end points survive, so lines keep their length.

title: Hit-or-miss and thinning
text:
One template at a time
Why not test all 8 templates on the same image and remove everything at once?


A line two pixels thick: the top row matches “background above”, the bottom row matches “background below”.
Removed in parallel, both rows go and the line is cut away. Each pixel was removable on its own, but not both together.
Sequentially, the top row goes first; then the bottom row has object above it and is kept.

title: Hit-or-miss and thinning
section: Try it: thinning step by step
text:
Try it: thinning step by step




“Thin a rectangle” (3 × 7, the exercise): step through the template applications. Pass 1: L1 removes the top row except its corners (5 pixels), L2 turned 90° removes the bottom-right corner, L1 turned 180° the bottom row except the left corner; pass 2: L2 turned 90° removes (2, 7); pass 3 removes nothing. The skeleton has 9 pixels: a line with a short fork at the left end and one corner pixel kept at the right. The second grid numbers each pixel by the pass that removed it. “Thin an L”: 3 passes (a fourth finds nothing), a skeleton of 18 pixels with short forks at the corners. “Parallel removal cuts the line”: the 2-pixel line disappears in one parallel pass; untick “parallel” and it survives as a line.

title: Hit-or-miss and thinning
text:
Simple points
A pixel is simple if removing it changes neither the number of objects nor the number of holes. Decide it from the 8 neighbours alone:

count the object parts among the 8 neighbours (8-connected),
count the background parts that touch the pixel’s 4 neighbours (4-connected).
Simple exactly when there is one of each.

Examples: a pixel on a straight edge: 1 object part, 1 background part: simple. The middle of a line one pixel thick: 2 object parts (left and right): removing it cuts the line. An interior pixel: no background part: removing it makes a hole. An isolated pixel: no object part: removing it deletes an object.

title: Hit-or-miss and thinning
section: The math: simple points and the Euler number
text:
The math: simple points and the Euler number

Object: 8-connected; background: 4-connected (the pairing that avoids the paradoxes of digital topology, Kong & Rosenfeld 1989).
p is simple iff C_8(N_8(p) \cap A) = 1 and C_4^{p}(N_8(p) \cap A^c) = 1, the second counting only the background parts 4-adjacent to p.
A closed form: Yokoi’s connectivity number \displaystyle N_8(p) = \sum_{k \in \{0, 2, 4, 6\}} \big(\bar x_k - \bar x_k \bar x_{k+1} \bar x_{k+2}\big), \bar x = 1 - x, neighbours numbered around p starting with a 4-neighbour; a border pixel is simple iff N_8(p) = 1.
Removing a simple point keeps the Euler number \chi = (\text{objects}) - (\text{holes}), and more: it keeps every object and hole. Thinning that removes only simple points is topology-preserving.

title: Hit-or-miss and thinning
text:
End points: simple, but kept
An end point has one neighbour: one object part, one background part. It is simple: removing it changes no topology.

Remove simple points until none is left, and a line shortens from both ends; every tree-shaped object shrinks to a single pixel. Only loops survive, because their pixels have two object parts.
So thinning keeps end points on purpose. The L templates do this automatically: none of them fits a pixel with only one neighbour.
Thinning also depends on the order of removal: different (all valid) algorithms give slightly different skeletons.

title: Hit-or-miss and thinning
text:
Try it: simple or not?




“Simple or not?”: five 3 × 3 neighbourhoods (the exercise), centres at columns 2, 7, 12, 17, 22 of row 2. Step to each centre: object parts are filled and lettered a, b, …; background parts touching the pixel are outlined and numbered. Verdicts: vertical line: 2 object parts, not simple; 2 × 2 block corner: simple; interior: not simple; the bent-line corner (neighbours left and above): simple; two diagonal neighbours: 2 parts, not simple. Then “a ring keeps its hole” (simple-point thinning without end points): the ring shrinks to a one-pixel loop and stops. “No end points: a line shrinks”: the 3 × 7 rectangle ends as a single pixel.

title: Hit-or-miss and thinning
text:
Zhang–Suen: a fast parallel variant
The most widely used thinning (Zhang & Suen 1984) removes pixels in parallel, safely, by splitting each pass into two sub-passes:

remove a pixel if it has 2 to 6 object neighbours, exactly one 0 → 1 change around it, and (first sub-pass) its east or south side or north-west corner is background; (second sub-pass) the mirrored conditions.
Each sub-pass only removes from two sides, so a two-pixel line cannot vanish.
Typical artefacts of all thinning methods: lines two pixels thick on some diagonals, small loops or clusters at junctions, corners cut off, and short forks at the ends of wide shapes.

title: Hit-or-miss and thinning
text:
Summary

Hit-or-miss: a three-state template (1, 0, don’t care) must fit object and background at once; it finds isolated pixels, end points (8 rotations), junctions, corners.
Thinning: remove the matches of edge and corner templates, one template at a time, until nothing changes. In parallel, a two-pixel line would be cut.
Simple point: one object part and one background part among the 8 neighbours. Removing simple points keeps the number of objects and holes (the topology).
End points are simple but kept; otherwise every line shrinks to a point.
The result: a one-pixel-wide, connected skeleton, with known artefacts at ends and junctions. Next: where exactly is “the middle” of a shape?

title: Quiz: measuring neurons and vessel networks
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Why is the vesselness thresholded instead of the image itself?






Hint





What does a global threshold do to faint branches on an uneven background?









Answer





The vesselness responds to the tube shape, not to the absolute brightness: faint and bright tubes score alike, and the slowly varying background (which has no strong curvature across) scores near zero. A threshold on the image either cuts faint branches into pieces or lets background and fat bright vessels through.




Q2. How do you choose the range of scales σ for the vesselness filter?






Hint





The best scale grows with the width of the tube.









Answer





From the expected radii: the smallest σ about the radius of the thinnest branches, the largest about that of the thickest vessels. Without the large scales, thick vessels respond only at their two edges and appear hollow (double lines in the skeleton).




Q3. The vesselness fades where two vessels branch. What does that do to the skeleton graph?






Hint





A gap at a junction.









Answer





The mask has a gap at the junction: the branch point is lost, the cut branches get extra end points, and the edges are split. Branch counts drop, end-point counts rise, and a little length is lost. Hysteresis thresholding bridges such gaps if the weak pixels still connect to strong ones.




Q4. A neuron has two primary dendrites; one splits once into two tips, the other does not branch. What are the Strahler orders of the two primary dendrites?






Hint





Tips have order 1; equal orders meeting go up by one.









Answer





The branching dendrite: its two tip branches have order 1 each, equal, so it has order 2. The unbranched one ends in a tip: order 1.




Q5. What does the Sholl profile N(r) count, and how is it read off a skeleton graph?






Hint





Circles around the soma.









Answer





The number of times the arbor crosses a circle of radius r around the soma. On the graph: for each edge path, count how often the distance to the soma centre passes r (a sign change of distance − r between consecutive pixels), and add over the edges.




Q6. A vessel’s radius from \mathrm{DT} on the skeleton is twice its true radius. Name a likely cause.






Hint





Where does \mathrm{DT} come from?









Answer





\mathrm{DT} is computed on the mask, so it measures the mask’s width. A low threshold (of the vesselness or the image), blur, or a large filter scale makes the mask wider than the vessel. The radius estimate is only as good as the segmentation; calibrate it, for example on vessels of known size.




Q7. What is the tortuosity of a half circle, and what does a value of 1 mean?






Hint





Path length over chord.









Answer





A half circle of radius R: length \pi R, chord 2R: \pi/2 = 1.57. A tortuosity of 1 means the edge is straight (its length equals the distance between its ends).




Q8. (math) At a bifurcation a parent vessel of radius 6 splits symmetrically. What radius do the children have according to Murray’s law?






Hint





r_0^3 = r_1^3 + r_2^3.









Answer





r_1 = r_2 = 6 \cdot 2^{-1/3} = 6 \cdot 0.794 = 4.76.




Q9. A measured graph has the right number of branch points, but after matching within 8 pixels, 3 are “missed” and 3 “spurious”. How can that be?






Hint





Matching uses positions.









Answer





Three branch points were found, but more than 8 pixels from their true positions (in narrow forks the skeleton junction slides along the trunk). Each counts once as missed and once as spurious. The tolerance must match the expected position error, and must be reported with the result.

title: Exercise: measuring neurons and vessel networks
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Pipeline
vesselness (edges day) → hysteresis threshold → clean → skeleton → prune → graph


Total length
sum of the edge lengths


Strahler order
tips: 1; at a branch point, if the two child branches have the same order s, the parent has s + 1, otherwise the larger order


Sholl profile
N(r) = number of crossings of the arbor with the circle of radius r around the soma


Radius
\mathrm{DT} on the skeleton; diameter 2\,\mathrm{DT}


Tortuosity
path length / chord of an edge (1 = straight)


Densities
total length / area; branch points / area


Matching
a true and a measured branch point match if they are within a distance d (each used once, closest pairs first); unmatched true = missed, unmatched measured = spurious

Total dendritic length, number of primary branches, branch points and terminal points.
The tortuosity of each edge, and the mean. Which edge is the most tortuous?
The Strahler order of every edge. And the centrifugal order?
The Sholl counts N(r) for r = 20, 50, 65 and 80 µm. Sketch the profile.

B2. Along a vessel centreline the distance transform reads 3.0, 3.2, 3.6, 3.6, 3.2 (pixels). (a) Mean radius and diameter? (b) The best vesselness scale on this vessel is σ = 4.5. On the edges day, a line with a Gaussian profile of width s gave its strongest response at \sigma = \sqrt2\,s. What width does that suggest, and does it agree with (a)? (c) The threshold of the vesselness is lowered. What happens to the mask, to \mathrm{DT} on the skeleton and to the radius estimate? And to the skeleton itself?
B3. True branch points at (20, 30), (45, 32), (60, 70), (80, 40), (95, 90); measured ones at (22, 31), (47, 36), (81, 43), (70, 75), (95, 92), (30, 80) (pixels). Match within 5 pixels. (a) Which pairs match? How many branch points are missed, how many spurious? (b) Precision (matched / measured) and recall (matched / true)? (c) (60, 70) and (70, 75) are 11.2 pixels apart. What might have happened there?
B4. Predict how each problem shows up in the skeleton graph (branch points, end points, edges, length): (a) the vesselness fades where two vessels branch; (b) two vessels run side by side, touching; (c) bright cells sit on a vessel; (d) the noise is high and pruning is off.
B5. A vessel image of 256 × 256 pixels with 2 µm pixels has a total corrected length of 1109 pixels and 12 branch points. (a) The image area in mm², the total length in mm, the length density in mm/mm² and the branching density per mm². (b) Why should densities in physical units, not counts in pixels, be compared between images of different size or pixel size?






Solutions





B1. (a) Total length 30 + 40 + 25 + 20 + 35 + 50 = 200 µm. Primary branches: 2 (S–a, S–b). Branch points: 2 (a, d). Terminal points: 4 (b, c, e, f). (b) S–a 1.071, a–c 1.250, a–d 1.042, d–e 1.053, d–f 1.400, S–b 1.111; mean 1.154. d–f is the most tortuous. (c) Strahler: tips c, e, f, b: order 1; d–e and d–f are both 1, so a–d has order 2; at a, a–c (1) and a–d (2) differ: S–a has order 2; S–b order 1. Centrifugal: S–a and S–b 1; a–c and a–d 2; d–e and d–f 3. (d) N(20) = 2 (S–a, S–b); N(50) = 3 (a–c, a–d, S–b); N(65) = 3 (a–c, d–e, d–f); N(80) = 1 (d–f). The profile rises from 2 to 3, stays at 3 up to about 70, then falls to 1 and to 0 after 90.
B2. (a) Mean \mathrm{DT} = 3.32; diameter 6.64 pixels. (b) s = 4.5/\sqrt2 = 3.18 pixels, close to the radius 3.32 from (a). Both measure the size of the vessel, by different routes: the scale from the filter, the radius from the mask. They agree only roughly, because the vessel’s profile is not exactly Gaussian. (c) A lower threshold makes the mask wider, so \mathrm{DT} on the skeleton grows and the radius is overestimated. The skeleton barely moves (it stays in the middle), but more noise survives, so more spurs. The radius from the mask is only as good as the threshold.
B3. (a) Closest pairs first: (95, 90)–(95, 92) 2.00; (20, 30)–(22, 31) 2.24; (80, 40)–(81, 43) 3.16; (45, 32)–(47, 36) 4.47. Missed: (60, 70). Spurious: (70, 75) and (30, 80). 4 matched, 1 missed, 2 spurious. (b) Precision 4/6 = 0.67; recall 4/5 = 0.80. (c) Probably the same junction, found 11 pixels away from its true place: in a narrow fork the skeleton’s junction moves along the trunk. With a tolerance of 12 pixels it would count as found; the tolerance decides, and must be reported.
B4. (a) A gap at the junction: the side branch is cut off; one branch point lost, two (or three) extra end points, the edges split; a little length lost. (b) The two vessels merge into one wide object: one edge instead of two, branch points lost; length roughly halved there, radius overestimated. (c) A blob on a vessel: vesselness is low on the blob itself (gap) or the mask bulges; the skeleton gets short spurs (spurious branch points and end points). (d) Many short spurs everywhere: spurious branch points and end points, the total length inflated.
B5. (a) Side 256 × 2 µm = 0.512 mm, area 0.262 mm²; length 1109 × 2 µm = 2.218 mm; length density 2.218 / 0.262 = 8.46 mm/mm²; branching density 12 / 0.262 = 45.8 per mm². (b) Counts grow with the imaged area and length in pixels with the resolution; densities in physical units (mm/mm², per mm²) do not, so they can be compared between images, microscopes and studies. Always convert with the pixel size.




Math questions
B6. (math) Murray’s law: at a bifurcation r_0^3 = r_1^3 + r_2^3. (a) For a symmetric split, express r_1 in terms of r_0. (b) A parent of radius 5 gives a child of radius 4. What radius does the other child have? (c) Laminar flow through a tube scales as Q \propto r^3 under Murray’s optimum. Show that the law means the flow is conserved at the bifurcation.
B7. (math) Show that a circular arc of opening angle \varphi has tortuosity \tau = \dfrac{\varphi/2}{\sin(\varphi/2)}. Evaluate it for \varphi = 90°, 120° and 180°. What does \tau tend to for small \varphi?
B8. (math) Prove the rule for the Strahler order of a balanced binary tree: if every branch point has two children of equal order and there are 2^k tips, the root edge has order k + 1.






Solutions (math)





B6. (a) r_0^3 = 2r_1^3, so r_1 = 2^{-1/3} r_0 = 0.794\,r_0. (b) r_2 = (125 - 64)^{1/3} = 61^{1/3} = 3.94. (c) With Q_i = k\,r_i^3: Q_1 + Q_2 = k(r_1^3 + r_2^3) = k\,r_0^3 = Q_0: what flows into the bifurcation flows out.
B7. Radius R: arc length L = R\varphi; the chord subtends the angle \varphi at the centre, so C = 2R\sin(\varphi/2); \tau = R\varphi / (2R\sin(\varphi/2)) = (\varphi/2)/\sin(\varphi/2). \varphi = 90°: (\pi/4)/\sin(\pi/4) = 1.111; 120°: (\pi/3)/\sin(\pi/3) = 1.209; 180°: \pi/2 = 1.571. For small \varphi, \sin x \approx x - x^3/6, so \tau \approx 1 + \varphi^2/24 \to 1: a gentle arc is nearly straight.
B8. By induction over k. k = 0: one tip, its edge has order 1. Step: a balanced tree with 2^{k+1} tips is a root edge whose branch point has two balanced subtrees with 2^k tips each; by induction both have order k + 1; equal orders meet, so the root edge has order k + 2.

title: Exercise: measuring neurons and vessel networks
text:
Explore
A synthetic neuron or vessel network with its known graph. The tabs show the steps: image, vesselness (multi-scale, σ min to σ max), mask (hysteresis threshold of the vesselness; specks below 30 pixels removed, holes up to 20 pixels filled), skeleton (pink: pruned spurs), graph (blue: end points, red: junctions). Overlays: radius (skeleton coloured by \mathrm{DT}), tortuosity (edges coloured, white = straight, red = 1.33 or more), Sholl (the circle at radius r; the plot shows the whole profile, measured and true), truth (the true centreline in cyan; red circles: missed branch points, orange squares: spurious ones; matching within 8 pixels). The table compares the measurements with the truth; length picks the estimator. The generator section changes the tree and the image.



E1. Preset neuron: Sholl profile. Read the measured and true total length, end points, branch points and primary branches. Where is the maximum of the Sholl profile, and how many crossings does it have? Drag the Sholl radius to 30 and 90 and compare with the figure of the lecture.
E2. Same preset, overlay truth. The counts of branch points agree, yet 3 are “missed” and 3 “spurious”. Find them in the image. What happened?
E3. Preset noise: spurs inflate the branch count (noise 14, no pruning). Compare end points and branch points with the truth. Now raise prune k to 8. Which numbers recover? Does the total length change much? Why?
E4. Preset vessels: length and branching density. Compare the three length estimators with the true length (preset pixel counting underestimates length switches to pixel steps). Which is closest, and by how much is pixel counting off?
E5. Same preset, overlay radius. Compare the mean radius from \mathrm{DT} with the true mean radius. Raise threshold low to 0.3 and then 0.5 (and threshold high with it): what happens to the radius, and why? Compare with the mean best σ.
E6. Preset one scale misses the thick vessels (σ = 1 only). Look at the mask of the thick vessels. What happens to length, branch points and loops? Raise σ max to 5: does it recover?
E7. Preset junctions fade: branch points lost. Look at the vesselness tab at the branch points. How many branch points are found, and how many end points? Lower threshold low step by step: from which value are all branch points found?
E8. Preset tortuous vessels. Compare the measured and true mean tortuosity, and the number of loops. Why are there more loops in the measurement than in the truth?






Solutions





E1. Length 1062 (corrected) against 1076; 15 end points, 10 branch points and 5 primary branches, all as in the truth. The measured profile peaks at 15 crossings at r = 100 (truth: 15 at r = 96). At r = 30 the measured profile gives 6 and the truth 7; at r = 90, 12 and 14: near some forks the measured branch point lies on the other side of the circle.
E2. In three narrow forks (two branches leaving at a small angle) the skeleton’s junction lies more than 8 pixels further along the trunk than the true branch point: each such fork counts once as missed (true point unmatched) and once as spurious (measured point unmatched). The number is right, the position is not: a matching tolerance must fit the expected displacement.
E3. Without pruning: 22 end points and 17 branch points (truth: 15 and 10); 10 spurious branch points. With k = 8: 15 and 10 again (3 missed, 3 spurious, the forks of E2). The total length barely changes (1081 → 1074): spurs are short, they distort counts much more than lengths.
E4. True length 1138. Pixel steps 989 (−13 %), 1/√2 1161 (+2 %), corrected 1109 (−2.5 %). The corrected and 1/√2 estimates are close; pixel counting is off by the most. (The remaining error also includes the skeleton ending one radius short of each tip.)
E5. Mean radius 4.27 from \mathrm{DT}, true 2.66: the mask is wider than the vessels, because the vesselness is spread out by the filter’s scale and the low hysteresis threshold (0.15) accepts its outer parts. With threshold low 0.3: 3.73; with high and low at 0.5: 3.18. The best σ (about 3.1) also grows with the vessel size, but it measures the filter’s scale, not the wall: both are proxies that must be calibrated.
E6. With σ = 1 only, the thick vessels become hollow: the filter responds to their two edges, not to the whole tube, and the mask has two parallel lines. Length 1377 against 1138 (+21 %), only 8 of 12 branch points found, the loop lost, radius 1.49. With σ max = 5 the thick vessels fill in again: length 1109, 12 branch points, 1 loop.
E7. At the junctions the vesselness is dark: there both curvatures are large and the filter takes them for blobs. With both thresholds at 0.85, only 2 of 12 branch points are found and there are 30 end points (truth 12); length 989. Lowering threshold low (high still 0.85): 0.8 gives 8 branch points and 20 end points, 0.7 gives 10 and 14, and from 0.65 down all 12 branch points and 12 end points are found (none missed): hysteresis bridges the faint junctions by keeping weak pixels that connect to strong ones.
E8. Mean tortuosity 1.299 measured, 1.341 true. 3 loops measured, 2 true: where a tortuous vessel bends back and touches itself or a neighbour, the mask merges them and creates a cycle that does not exist (failure mode “touching vessels”). Some edges are also split at the false junctions, which lowers their individual tortuosity.

title: Exercise: measuring neurons and vessel networks
text:
Where this leads
The measurements of this day become per-object columns in the labelling day’s table, and their comparison between groups is the subject of the evaluation and statistics day. In 3D, the same pipeline works on stacks with a 3 × 3 Hessian and 3D thinning; the marching-cubes elective covers volumes and voxel spacing. Thin structures are also where segmentation by energy minimisation struggles (the shrinking bias of the graph-cut day), and where learned segmentation (U-Nets) is now often used to produce the mask that is then skeletonised.

title: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction
text:
About this lecture
Thinning gave a one-pixel line, but we never said what “the middle” of a shape is. Today: a geometric definition, and how to compute it.

Grassfire: burn the shape from its boundary; the skeleton is where the fire fronts meet.
Medial axis: the centres of the maximal discs inside the shape.
It is the set of ridges of the distance transform; each axis point carries a radius.
Reconstruction: axis + radii give back the shape exactly.
Lantuéjoul’s formula: the same skeleton from erosions and openings only.
The weak point: boundary noise creates whole new branches.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.
crumbs: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction

title: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction
text:
Grassfire
Blum (1967): set fire to the whole boundary at once, and let the fire burn inwards at the same speed everywhere.

At time t the fire front is the set of points at distance t from the boundary.
Fronts coming from different parts of the boundary meet and quench each other.
The skeleton is the set of meeting points; the time at which a point burns is its distance to the boundary.
A long rectangle of width w: fronts from the two long sides meet on the midline at time w/2; near the ends, fronts from a long side and a short side meet on the diagonals.
crumbs: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction

title: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction
text:
Recall: the distance transform
From the morphology day: the distance transform \mathrm{DT}(p) of an object pixel is its distance to the nearest background pixel, computed in two raster passes (city-block or chessboard steps) or exactly (Euclidean).

\mathrm{DT} is the arrival time of the grassfire.
Thresholding it, \{\mathrm{DT} > r\}, is the erosion by a disc of radius r.
The metric decides what a “disc” is: a diamond (city-block), a square (chessboard), a round disc (Euclidean).
crumbs: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction

title: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction
text:
Maximal discs
Draw a disc inside the shape, centred at p, as large as fits: its radius is \mathrm{DT}(p).

The disc is maximal if no other disc inside the shape contains it.
In the middle of a band, the disc touches both sides: it cannot grow or move without leaving the shape: maximal.
Next to one side only, the disc can slide inwards and grow: it lies inside a bigger disc: not maximal.
The medial axis = the centres of all maximal discs.
crumbs: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction

title: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction
text:
Ridges of the distance transform
Read \mathrm{DT} as a landscape: 0 at the boundary, rising inwards.

Across a band of width w, \mathrm{DT} is a tent: it rises from both sides and peaks at w/2 in the middle.
The medial axis is the ridge line (the crest) of this landscape: where \mathrm{DT} stops rising across the shape.
On the pixel grid: p is on the axis if no neighbour q has a disc that swallows p’s disc, i.e. no neighbour with \mathrm{DT}(q) \ge \mathrm{DT}(p) + d(p, q). With city-block or chessboard distances this is a simple comparison with the 4 or 8 neighbours.
Each axis pixel carries its radius \mathrm{DT}(p): the local half-width of the shape. For a vessel, 2\,\mathrm{DT} on the axis is its diameter.
crumbs: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction

title: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction
section: The math: medial axis and reconstruction
text:
The math: medial axis and reconstruction
For a shape A and a metric d, the disc D(p, r) = \{q : d(p, q) < r\}, \mathrm{DT}(p) = \min_{q \notin A} d(p, q).

D(p, \mathrm{DT}(p)) \subseteq A for every p \in A, and it is the largest such disc at p.
Medial axis S(A) = \{p : D(p, \mathrm{DT}(p)) \not\subset D(q, \mathrm{DT}(q)) \ \forall q \neq p\}.
Reconstruction: A = \bigcup_{p \in S(A)} D(p, \mathrm{DT}(p)). Every disc in A lies in a maximal one, and every point of A lies in its own disc.
On the grid, for city-block and chessboard, it suffices to compare with the neighbours: q’s disc contains p’s iff \mathrm{DT}(q) \ge \mathrm{DT}(p) + d(p, q).
The continuous medial axis of a rectangle a \times b (a > b): a midline segment of length a - b and four diagonals to the corners.
crumbs: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction

title: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction
text:
Try it: the medial axis




Left: DT as colour (iso-lines every 8 steps), the axis in red; drag the white handles. Right: the union of the axis discs (grey), with missing pixels in red. Tour: “a rectangle forks at the ends”: Euclidean maximal discs with λ = 8 (see the bump slide); the disc at (45, 97) near a corner has radius 6. The axis: a midline from x = 75 to 180 and four diagonals; 4 end points, 1 piece. Set λ to “off”: the maximal-disc set breaks into 5 pieces (pixel effects along the diagonals) but reconstructs the rectangle exactly. Switch the metric: city-block gives the same X ends; chessboard (square discs) gives only the midline: a square fits into the corner. Move the grassfire slider: the front (orange) burns in; axis pixels turn red when the fire reaches them.
crumbs: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction

title: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction
text:
Lantuéjoul’s formula: skeleton from erosions
Lantuéjoul (1978) builds the same skeleton with the operations of the morphology day only:

Erode the shape r times by a small element B (3 × 3 cross or square): what is left are the centres of discs of radius r that fit.
Open that result by B: the opening keeps every pixel that lies in a slightly bigger disc.
What the opening removes are the centres of discs of radius r that are maximal: the set S_r.
The skeleton is the union of all S_r; and S_r dilated r times gives back its part of the shape.
crumbs: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction

title: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction
text:
The math: Lantuéjoul’s formula
With rB = B \oplus \dots \oplus B (r times; 0B = the origin):
S_r = (A \ominus rB) \setminus \big((A \ominus rB) \circ B\big), \qquad S(A) = \bigcup_{r \ge 0} S_r, \qquad A = \bigcup_{r \ge 0} S_r \oplus rB.

p \in A \ominus rB: the disc p + rB fits. p is removed by the opening: no disc q + (r+1)B that fits contains p + rB. So p + rB is maximal.
On the grid with B = cross (city-block): S_r = the pixels with \mathrm{DT} = r + 1 that have no 4-neighbour with \mathrm{DT} = r + 2: exactly the maximal-disc test.
A 5 × 5 square: with B = square, S_0 = S_1 = \emptyset, S_2 = the centre; with B = cross, S_0 = the 4 corners, S_1 = 4 diagonal pixels, S_2 = the centre.
Only erosions, openings, set differences and unions: exact reconstruction, but the skeleton is in general not connected.

Practical tools combine both: thin for a connected line, then read \mathrm{DT} along it for the radius.
Both share the same weakness, next slide.

title: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction
text:
Sensitivity to the boundary
The medial axis is not continuous in the shape: a tiny change of the boundary can change it a lot.

A bump of one or two pixels on the boundary gets its own maximal discs: a whole new branch runs from the axis out to the bump.
A rectangle’s axis forks at each end: four branches to the corners, even though the shape “is” a line.
On real masks every pixel step on the boundary is a potential bump: raw skeletons are full of short spurs.
Remedies: smooth or open the mask first; prune short spurs (next unit); or keep only axis points whose two nearest boundary points are far apart, at least λ (the “λ-medial axis”).
crumbs: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction

title: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction
section: Try it: one bump, one branch
text:
Try it: one bump, one branch




“One bump, one branch”: ellipse, thinning, a bump of radius 3 on the lower boundary, right of the middle (position 0.20 along the outline). Without the bump (size 0): 4 end points, 5 branches. With it: 5 end points and 7 branches: one new spur, which also splits the edge it leaves from. Drag the bump position along the boundary: the branch follows. Bump sizes 1 to 3 give one new end point, from 4 on the bump’s own end forks (6 end points). Switch to “maximal discs” with λ off: the Euclidean maximal discs of a curved boundary are a scatter of pieces (every boundary pixel step makes a disc); raise λ to 16: a clean axis, but the reconstruction now misses pixels near the boundary. “The ring keeps its loop” (thinning): one loop. “Reconstruct the star”: Lantuéjoul with the square: exact, but 124 separate pieces.
crumbs: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction

title: Medial axis, distance transform and reconstruction
text:
Summary

Grassfire: burn from the boundary; the skeleton is where the fronts meet; the arrival time is the distance transform.
Medial axis = centres of maximal discs = ridges of \mathrm{DT}; each axis point has a radius \mathrm{DT}.
Reconstruction: the union of the maximal discs is the shape: axis + radii is a lossless shape code.
Lantuéjoul: S_r = (erosion by rB) minus its opening; the union of the S_r is the skeleton, the union of S_r \oplus rB the shape.
Thinning is connected but only approximately centred; the discrete medial axis is centred but often broken. Use thinning for the line and \mathrm{DT} for the radius.
A small bump makes a whole branch: smooth, prune, or use λ.

title: Quiz: from skeleton to graph
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A skeleton pixel has three skeleton neighbours, and two of them also have three. How many nodes is that?






Hint





Do touching junction pixels describe one branch point or several?









Answer





One node: adjacent junction pixels form a junction cluster (a connected component of junction pixels), which represents one branch point. Counting each pixel separately would report several branch points, joined by edges of length 0 or 1.




Q2. How are the edges of a skeleton graph found?






Hint





Remove something, then label what is left.









Answer





Remove the node pixels (end points and junction clusters); the remaining skeleton pixels fall into connected pieces, each a chain of regular pixels. Each piece is an edge, joined to the node(s) its two ends touch. Two node pixels that touch directly (a one-step branch) also form an edge.




Q3. A skeleton graph has 10 edges, 9 nodes and 1 piece. How many holes did the mask have?






Hint





E - V + C.









Answer





10 - 9 + 1 = 2 independent cycles, so 2 holes (as thinning keeps holes, each becomes a loop of the skeleton).




Q4. Two skeleton edges have 40 pixel steps each. One is horizontal, the other diagonal. Are they equally long?






Hint





How long is a diagonal step?









Answer





No. The horizontal one is 40 long, the diagonal one 40\sqrt2 = 56.6. Counting pixels underestimates diagonal lines by up to 29 %, so the measured length would depend on the orientation of the object.




Q5. With weights 1 and √2, a line at about 22.5° comes out 8 % too long. Why?






Hint





Draw the pixel path of such a line.









Answer





The pixel path is a staircase of axial and diagonal steps; each step is measured exactly, but the staircase zigzags around the true line and is longer than it. The weights are exact only for lines at 0° and 45°, which need no zigzag. The corrected estimator lowers the weights slightly and subtracts a little for each corner.




Q6. Why should the pruning length be compared with the local radius of the structure?






Hint





How long is a spur caused by a bump on the wall of a thick vessel?









Answer





A spur from a wall bump starts at the centreline and has to reach the wall, so it is about one radius long. In a thick vessel spurs are long, in a thin one short. A fixed k either leaves the spurs of the thick vessels or deletes real short branches of the thin ones; k = (a factor) × \mathrm{DT} at the junction adapts to both.




Q7. After a spur is removed, its junction has two edges left. What happens to it?






Hint





Is it still a branch point?









Answer





It is no longer a junction (only two edges meet there): it becomes an ordinary point of a line, and its two edges merge into one. This can make a short side branch terminal, so pruning is repeated once.




Q8. (math) Show that for a tree with only end points and degree-3 junctions, the number of end points is the number of junctions plus 2.






Hint





Sum of degrees, and E = V - 1.









Answer





With n end points and J junctions, the degrees sum to n + 3J = 2E, and a tree has E = V - 1 = n + J - 1. So n + 3J = 2n + 2J - 2, i.e. n = J + 2.

title: Exercise: from skeleton to graph
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




End point / regular / junction
a skeleton pixel with 1 / 2 / ≥ 3 skeleton neighbours (8-neighbourhood)


Node
an end point, or a cluster of touching junction pixels


Edge
a piece of regular pixels between two nodes; its path runs from a node pixel to a node pixel


Steps
axial (left, right, up, down) n_e; diagonal n_o; corners n_c = changes of direction


Lengths
pixel steps n_e + n_o; weighted n_e + \sqrt2\,n_o; corrected 0.980\,n_e + 1.406\,n_o - 0.091\,n_c


Pruning with k
delete terminal edges (end point to junction) shorter than k; a junction keeps at least two edges; a node left with two edges merges them


Cycles
E - V + C (edges − nodes + connected pieces) = number of holes

title: Exercise: from skeleton to graph
text:
By hand
B1. A skeleton in a 9 × 9 image (1 = skeleton):

\begin{matrix}

\end{matrix}


Write the number of skeleton neighbours in every skeleton pixel. Which pixels are end points, which are junctions?
Draw the graph: number the nodes, list the edges with the pixels of their paths.
Give each edge’s length by pixel steps and with weights 1 and √2. What is the total length both ways?
Compute E - V + C. Does it match the number of holes?

B2. Prune the skeleton of B1 with k = 2 (weighted lengths). (a) Which edges are removed? Redraw the graph. What happens to the junction at (2, 6)? (b) What is the length of the merged edge from (1, 8) to (4, 4)? (c) And with k = 3? (Remember: a junction keeps at least two edges.)
B3. Straight digital lines, drawn with one pixel per step along the longer axis. (a) From (0, 0) to (50, 50): n_e, n_o, the true length, and the three estimates. Errors in %? (b) From (0, 0) to 100 to the right and 50 down (slope ½): here the steps alternate axial, diagonal, axial, …: n_e = 50, n_o = 50, n_c = 99. True length and the three estimates? Errors? (c) A horizontal line of 100 steps: the three estimates? Which estimator is exact here, and which is not?
B4. Graphs and cycles. (a) A skeleton has 2 junctions joined by 3 separate edges (a “θ” shape) and nothing else. E, V, C? How many holes did the mask have? (b) A skeleton consists of two separate pieces: a ring (no nodes; count it as one node with a loop edge) and a Y. E - V + C? (c) A tree has 7 end points and only junctions with 3 edges. How many junctions does it have, and how many edges?
B5. A vessel of radius 6 pixels has a few bumps on its wall, and a real side branch 30 pixels long. Spurs from the bumps are 5–9 pixels long (measured from the junction on the centreline). (a) Why are the spurs at least about as long as the radius? (b) Which pruning length k removes the spurs and keeps the side branch? What goes wrong with k = 4 and with k = 40? (c) The same image also has thin capillaries of radius 1.5. Why is “k = 1.5 \times \mathrm{DT} at the junction” a better rule than a fixed k?
