Compute the DoG row (σ = 2.4 minus σ = 2). (b) Compute (k - 1)\sigma^2 L_{xx}. How close are they? (c) Where is the DoG most negative, and what does a negative value mean here?

B4. Pyramids. (a) List the side lengths of the Gaussian pyramid of a 1024 × 1024 image down to 1 × 1, and the total number of pixels. Compare with \tfrac43 \cdot 1024^2. (b) A Gaussian blur with σ = 16 (kernel cut at 4σ) applied separably to the full image: how many multiplications? The same smoothing is roughly a σ = 1 blur at level 4 (64 × 64): how many multiplications there? (Building levels 1–4 with σ = 1 blurs costs about 25 million.) (c) Why must each level be blurred before taking every second pixel? What would go wrong with a fine stripe pattern?
B5. Predict. You run blob detection over σ = 1 … 16 on an image, then on the same image enlarged ×2 (each pixel becomes 2 × 2). (a) What happens to the scale and the radius of each detection? To the normalised response values? To the number of detections? (b) What would happen to the raw (unnormalised) response values?
B6. A row of LoG values across an edge: 3.1, 2.4, 0.9, −0.9, −2.4, −3.1 (pixels 0 to 5). Where is the edge (Marr–Hildreth)? Which side is brighter?






Solutions





B1. (a) σ = 3 (48.4) wins: the half-width is 3, as expected for a box (\sigma = a). (b) Half-width 6, so width 12. (c) Divided by σ²: 2.7, 9.7, 5.4, 2.8, 1.0: σ = 2 would win, too small. Without normalisation the curve is pushed towards small σ (here it still has a maximum, at a/\sqrt3 \approx 1.7 for a box; for a disc in 2D at r/2).
B2. (a) r = \sqrt2 \cdot 5 = 7.07 pixels; diameter 14.1 pixels = 2.83 µm. (b) Diameter 10 µm = 50 pixels, radius 25 pixels, so \sigma = 25/\sqrt2 = 17.7: just above the range; σ should go up to about 20 (or the image should be shrunk ×2 first, i.e. one pyramid level down).
B3. (a) DoG: 0.45, −3.15, −5.12, −3.15, 0.45. (b) (k - 1)\sigma^2 = 0.2 \cdot 4 = 0.8, so 0.8\,L_{xx} = 0.64, −3.04, −5.12, −3.04, 0.64. At the centre they agree to two decimals; in the tails the DoG is a little smaller (the approximation has an error of order (k - 1)^2). (c) Most negative at the centre, x = 0: blurring more lowers the peak (the bump flattens), which is what a negative curvature means. With the sign flipped, -\text{DoG} is the Mexican-hat response, largest at the blob’s centre.
B4. (a) 1024, 512, 256, 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1: 11 levels, 1\,398\,101 pixels in total, = \tfrac43 \cdot 1024^2 = 1\,398\,101.3 (the geometric series stops at 1 × 1). (b) σ = 16: 2 \cdot 4 \cdot 16 + 1 = 129 taps, 2 \cdot 129 = 258 multiplications per pixel, 258 \cdot 1024^2 \approx 271 million. At level 4: 9 taps, 18 \cdot 64^2 = 73\,728; with the 25 million for building the levels, about 10 times cheaper, and the other levels come for free. (c) Taking every second pixel can only represent detail coarser than 2 pixels (Nyquist, Fourier unit). Finer detail is not removed but aliased: a fine stripe pattern turns into false coarse stripes (moiré). The blur removes the fine detail first.
B5. (a) Every detection moves to σ × 2 and radius × 2, at position × 2; the normalised responses stay the same (scale invariance), and the number of detections stays the same, provided 2σ is still inside the scale range (detections near σ = 16 drop out; new ones at σ < 2 may appear only from finer detail, of which there is none). (b) Raw values drop by a factor of 4 (second derivatives scale as 1/\text{length}^2): the same blobs would look weaker, which is why the raw LoG cannot compare scales.
B6. The zero crossing is between pixels 2 and 3, halfway (0.9 and −0.9): the edge is at 2.5. The LoG is positive on the dark side and negative on the bright side, so the brighter side is towards pixel 5.




Math questions
B7. (math) (a) For a 1D box of half-width a, show that \sigma^2 L_{xx}(0) = -2\frac{a}{\sigma}\varphi\big(\frac{a}{\sigma}\big) (\varphi = standard normal density) and that its size is maximal at \sigma = a. (b) For a 2D disc of radius r and height 1, use \nabla^2 L(0) = \oint_{|\mathbf u| = r}\nabla G_\sigma\cdot\mathbf n\,ds to show \sigma^2\nabla^2 L(0) = -\frac{r^2}{\sigma^2}e^{-r^2/2\sigma^2}, maximal in size at r = \sqrt2\,\sigma.
B8. (math) Show that the 2D Gaussian G_\sigma(x, y) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2}e^{-(x^2 + y^2)/2\sigma^2} satisfies \partial_\sigma G_\sigma = \sigma\,\nabla^2 G_\sigma, and conclude G_{k\sigma} - G_\sigma \approx (k - 1)\sigma^2\nabla^2 G_\sigma.
B9. (math) A Gaussian blob of width s: I = A\,e^{-(x^2 + y^2)/2s^2}. Show that L = G_\sigma * I = \frac{A s^2}{s^2 + \sigma^2}e^{-(x^2 + y^2)/2(s^2 + \sigma^2)} (semigroup), compute \sigma^2\nabla^2 L(0) and find the σ where it is largest in size.






Solutions (math)





B7. (a) L(x) = \int_{-a}^{a} g_\sigma(x - u)\,du = \Phi\big(\frac{x + a}{\sigma}\big) - \Phi\big(\frac{x - a}{\sigma}\big). Differentiating twice: L_{xx}(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\big[\varphi'\big(\frac{x + a}{\sigma}\big) - \varphi'\big(\frac{x - a}{\sigma}\big)\big] with \varphi'(t) = -t\varphi(t), so L_{xx}(0) = \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\big[-\frac{a}{\sigma}\varphi(\frac a\sigma) - \frac{a}{\sigma}\varphi(\frac a\sigma)\big] and \sigma^2 L_{xx}(0) = -2u\varphi(u) with u = a/\sigma. \frac{d}{du}u e^{-u^2/2} = (1 - u^2)e^{-u^2/2} = 0 at u = 1: \sigma = a. (b) \nabla^2 L(0) = \int_{\text{disc}}\nabla^2 G_\sigma(\mathbf u)\,d\mathbf u (the Gaussian is symmetric), and the divergence theorem turns this into the flux of \nabla G_\sigma through the circle. On the circle \nabla G_\sigma\cdot\mathbf n = \partial_r G_\sigma = -\frac{r}{\sigma^2}\frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2}e^{-r^2/2\sigma^2}, constant, times the length 2\pi r: \nabla^2 L(0) = -\frac{r^2}{\sigma^4}e^{-r^2/2\sigma^2}, so \sigma^2\nabla^2 L(0) = -v\,e^{-v/2} with v = r^2/\sigma^2, largest in size at v = 2: r = \sqrt2\,\sigma.
B8. \partial_\sigma G_\sigma = G_\sigma\big(-\frac{2}{\sigma} + \frac{x^2 + y^2}{\sigma^3}\big). And \partial_{xx}G_\sigma = G_\sigma\big(\frac{x^2}{\sigma^4} - \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\big), likewise in y, so \nabla^2 G_\sigma = G_\sigma\big(\frac{x^2 + y^2}{\sigma^4} - \frac{2}{\sigma^2}\big) and \sigma\nabla^2 G_\sigma = \partial_\sigma G_\sigma. A first-order Taylor step in σ: G_{k\sigma} - G_\sigma \approx (k\sigma - \sigma)\,\partial_\sigma G_\sigma = (k - 1)\sigma^2\nabla^2 G_\sigma.
B9. I = 2\pi s^2 A\,G_s, so L = 2\pi s^2 A\,G_{\sqrt{s^2 + \sigma^2}} = \frac{A s^2}{s^2 + \sigma^2}e^{-r^2/2(s^2 + \sigma^2)}. With v = s^2 + \sigma^2, \nabla^2 e^{-r^2/2v} at r = 0 is -2/v, so \sigma^2\nabla^2 L(0) = -\frac{2As^2\sigma^2}{(s^2 + \sigma^2)^2}. Maximise \sigma^2/(s^2 + \sigma^2)^2: the derivative in \sigma^2 is \frac{(s^2 + \sigma^2) - 2\sigma^2}{(s^2 + \sigma^2)^3} = 0 at \sigma = s, where the value is -A/2.

title: Exercise: scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Explore: a 1D scale space
A 1D signal of 256 pixels: three box bumps of half-widths 2, 6 and 18 (at x ≈ 40, 100, 180); a step and a ramp; a bright line in a dark band; or a line through the micrograph. Top: the signal and its blur at the current σ. Middle: the scale-space image (x across, σ from 0.5 to 32 upwards on a log axis) of L, the slope or the curvature, with features traced as dots. Bottom: the response at the clicked x against σ, normalised (red) and raw (grey). Click the scale-space image to choose both x and σ.



S1. Preset noise lives at small σ (noise 10, L). Count roughly how many dots (extrema of L) there are along the bottom row of the scale-space image and how many survive at σ ≈ 4. Where do the surviving curves lead?
S2. Preset raw LoG prefers small σ (curvature, not normalised, x = 99, the centre of the bump with half-width 6). At which σ does the grey (raw) curve peak, and at which the red (normalised) one? Click the centres of the other two bumps: compare the heights of their raw and of their normalised peaks.
S3. Preset normalised: each bump picks its σ. Read the peak σ for the three bumps and compare with their half-widths 2, 6 and 18.
S4. Preset edges and bumps as curves (step and ramp, slope \sigma L_x). Click on the step (x = 69) and on the middle of the ramp (x = 170). How does \sigma L_x change with σ at each? Why does the step give the same value at every scale?
S5. Preset box kernel creates structure (σ = 8). What happens to the bright line in the blurred signal? Untick box kernel: what does the Gaussian of the same σ do? Find the σ at which the box blur first splits the line.






Solutions





S1. At σ = 0.5 the noisy signal has 143 extrema; at σ ≈ 1, 93; at σ = 2, 45; at σ ≈ 3.9, only 18. The noise extrema form short curves at the bottom that end quickly; the curves that continue upwards belong to the three bumps (and the dips between them). Curves end as σ grows; none starts.
S2. Raw: peak at σ = 3.39 (value 2.57); normalised: σ = 6.14 (value 48.3). Raw peaks are 23.77 (half-width 2), 2.57 (6) and 0.29 (18): the small bump wins by far, although all three have the same height. Normalised peaks are 46.5, 48.3 and 48.6: equal, as they should be for the same shape at different sizes.
S3. σ = 2.00, 6.14 and 17.67, close to the half-widths 2, 6 and 18 (the demo’s 64 scales are spaced by 7 %, so 6 and 18 fall between grid points).
S4. At the step \sigma L_x = 43.3 (σ ≈ 1), 46.9 (2), 47.6 (3.9), 47.8 (8), 47.9 (15.5): constant. A step looks the same at every scale; normalised, its response is 120/\sqrt{2\pi} = 47.9 for a step of 120. At the ramp centre (slope 100/60 per pixel): −1.6, −3.3, −6.5, −13.3, −24.5, i.e. \sigma times the slope, growing until σ is comparable to the ramp’s length (60 pixels). A ramp is an edge at a coarse scale.
S5. With the box (27 pixels wide at σ = 8) the line becomes two bumps with a dip in between (5 extrema instead of 3: at the centre L = 46.7, at x = 118 it is 51.1). The Gaussian keeps one maximum at the centre (54.9). On the demo’s grid of scales the box first splits the line at σ = 8.00 (27 pixels wide); at σ = 7.49 (25 pixels) it still has 3 extrema. The Gaussian never does, at any σ.

title: Exercise: scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Explore: blobs over scales
A 256 × 256 synthetic image (discs of radii 2–20 px, Gaussian spots, a touching pair, an elongated blob, a faint disc, on an uneven background with noise; the truth is known) or the micrograph. The normalised response -\sigma^2\nabla^2 L (or the DoG) is computed for 16 scales σ = 1 … 16. Detections are circles of radius \sqrt2\,\sigma, coloured by scale. The middle panel shows the response at the current σ (0 = grey), the plot below it the response at the clicked pixel against σ. The readout scores detections against the truth (a hit is within max(3, r/2) pixels of a true centre). Pyramid shows the Gaussian and Laplacian pyramids.



E1. Preset one σ finds one size (σ = 4.39, maxima at this σ only). How many detections, how many of the 15 blobs are hit? Which are missed? Move σ to 1.45 and to 9.19: which blobs are found now?
E2. Preset all scales, normalised (threshold 26). How many detections and hits? Which blob is missed, and which false alarms remain? Click the disc at (146, 30) (true radius 6): at which σ does its curve peak, and what radius does that give?
E3. Preset raw LoG: only the small spots (normalise off, threshold 12). At which σ are all detections? Which blobs are found? Click the centre of the disc at (120, 92) and compare the grey and red curves.
E4. Preset radius = √2·σ (truth overlay). Compare the circles with the dashed truth for the discs of radius 3, 9 and 20. Are the radii right? What about the Gaussian spots?
E5. Presets touching blobs and elongated blob. Describe what is detected in each case and why.
E6. Preset low threshold: edges respond too (threshold 18). Where do the extra detections appear, and at which scales? Compare the response of an edge with that of a blob.
E7. Preset DoG matches LoG (k = 1.2). Compare detections with all scales, normalised. Increase k to 1.6: what changes?
E8. Preset uneven background does not matter (σ = 16). Look at the response map: does the bright patch in the lower right (no blobs) give a strong response? Why not?
E9. Preset the pyramid. How many pixels does the Gaussian pyramid hold, and what is the reconstruction error of the Laplacian pyramid? Why is it not exactly 0 in the readout?
E10. Preset dark granules in the micrograph (dark blobs, threshold 50). What is detected? Click the dark granule near (106, 68): at which σ does it respond best?






Solutions





E1. At σ = 4.39: 13 detections, 8 hits, 5 false alarms; missed are the smallest discs (r = 2, 3) and the large ones (r = 12, 16, 20), the elongated blob and the faint disc. All circles have the same radius \sqrt2 \cdot 4.39 = 6.2. At σ = 1.45 only the small blobs are hit (4 hits, 12 detections); at σ = 9.19 the large ones (8 hits, 12 detections) but not the small. One σ finds one size.
E2. 28 detections, 14 hits, 14 false alarms; missed is the elongated blob (its centre is not a maximum; detections lie along it). Of the false alarms, 9 sit along the elongated blob, 2 in the notch of the touching pair, and 3 at the rims of discs. The disc at (146, 30) peaks at σ = 3.65: radius \sqrt2 \cdot 3.65 = 5.2 (true 6; the scales are 20 % apart, and the predicted σ = 4.24 lies between 3.65 and 4.39).
E3. Every detection is at the smallest scale, σ = 1 (radius 1.4): 146 detections, mostly noise, and only 5 hits (the discs of radius 2, 3, 4 and the two small Gaussian spots). At (120, 92) the raw curve is tiny and peaks at σ = 7.64; the normalised one peaks at σ = 11.06 with value 36.1 (radius 15.6, true 16).
E4. Radius 3: σ = 2.09, circle 3.0; radius 9: σ = 6.35, circle 9.0; radius 20: σ = 13.30, circle 18.8. Within one scale step (20 %) of the truth, slightly small for the largest. Gaussian spots of width 2, 4, 7 are found at σ = 2.09, 3.65, 7.64, close to their widths; their dashed circles are drawn at \sqrt2 s.
E5. Touching pair (two discs of radius 10 touching at (54, 215)): two circles at σ = 6.35 (radius 9.0) on the discs, plus one large circle at σ = 11.06 around both (and a small false alarm in the notch): the pair is also a blob at a coarser scale. Elongated blob (26 × 5): a row of small detections along it at σ = 1.2 to 5.3: the LoG fits the width (5), not the length.
E6. 102 detections (88 false alarms): small circles along the rims of the larger discs (35 on the disc of radius 20 alone), along the elongated blob and around the touching pair, almost all at small σ (1.2 to 3.65). The normalised response of a straight edge is at most 0.24 \times its contrast, that of a blob of the same contrast 0.74 \times: about a third. A threshold between the two separates them, as long as blob contrasts are not too different.
E7. At k = 1.2: 21 detections, 13 hits (8 false alarms), nearly the same blobs as the LoG; the smallest disc (r = 2) is missed. At k = 1.6: 17 detections, 12 hits; the faint disc also goes. Larger k smooths over a wider range of scales: fewer false alarms, but the response is less selective and weak or tiny blobs drop below the threshold.
E8. Hardly: at the centre of the patch (180, 192) the noise-free response at σ = 16 is only 5.0, far below the threshold. A smooth background is almost linear over the width of the Mexican hat, and the LoG of a constant or linear function is 0. A global threshold on the image itself would be thrown off by the same patch.
E9. 87 296 pixels for 256² (65 536) and its levels: 4/3 as many. The reconstruction error is about 10^{-6}: exact up to the rounding of 32-bit floating-point numbers (the telescoping sum is exact in real arithmetic).
E10. Dark granules, vesicles and dark spots in the fibrous background: 144 detections at threshold 50 (no truth for this image). The granule near (106, 68) responds best at σ = 3.65 (radius 5.2). The nucleus itself, about 45 pixels in radius, would need σ ≈ 32, outside the range.

title: Exercise: scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Where this leads
The LoG is the trace of the Hessian: it adds the curvatures in two directions and cannot tell a blob from a line. The next unit uses both curvatures separately: blobs, ridges and saddles, and vesselness.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
About this lecture
Linear filters do not know that light is counted in photons. Richardson–Lucy (RL) does.

The RL step in words, and by hand on four pixels.
Why it suits photon counts: never negative, keeps the total light.
The number of iterations is the regularisation parameter (semi-convergence).
3D widefield and confocal stacks, and the missing cone that no method fills.
The PSF you use: too narrow, too wide, and blind deconvolution.
A catalogue of artefacts.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Third unit of the deconvolution day. Recalls: the Poisson (shot) noise model and the camera offset (camera noise unit, day 3); the 3D PSF and the missing cone picture (image formation day); early stopping and filter factors (last unit). Notation: y = observed counts, x = estimate, h = PSF (sums to 1), b = background (counts per pixel), k = iteration.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
Photons are counted

A fluorescence image counts photons (after removing the camera offset): never negative, Poisson noise whose variance equals the mean (camera noise unit).
Wiener and Tikhonov produce negative intensities next to bright objects (the last two units: up to 15 % of the pixels) and treat noise as equally large everywhere.
We want a restoration that keeps every pixel ≥ 0, keeps the total number of photons, and weights the data as Poisson counts.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
Richardson–Lucy in words
Start from a flat guess (every pixel = the mean of the data). Then repeat:

Blur the guess with the PSF: what the microscope would show if the guess were true.
Compare with the data, pixel by pixel, as a ratio data / blurred guess. Where the guess is too dim the ratio is above 1, where it is too bright below 1.
Spread the ratio back with the PSF (mirrored): each object pixel collects the ratios of the image pixels it contributes to.
Multiply the guess by it.

Every factor is positive, so the guess stays non-negative; and (with a PSF that sums to 1) the total stays equal to the total of the data.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
section: The math: RL from the Poisson likelihood
text:
The math: RL from the Poisson likelihood
Model: y_i \sim \text{Poisson}\big((A\mathbf x)_i + b\big), A = convolution with h \ge 0, \sum h = 1, so A^\top\mathbf 1 = \mathbf 1. Log-likelihood (dropping terms without \mathbf x):
\ell(\mathbf x) = \sum_i y_i \log\big((A\mathbf x)_i + b\big) - \big((A\mathbf x)_i + b\big).
Gradient: \nabla\ell = A^\top\!\Big(\dfrac{\mathbf y}{A\mathbf x + b}\Big) - A^\top\mathbf 1. At a maximum with x_j > 0: A^\top\big(\mathbf y/(A\mathbf x + b)\big)_j = 1. RL is the fixed-point iteration
x_j \leftarrow x_j \cdot \Big[A^\top\Big(\frac{\mathbf y}{A\mathbf x + b}\Big)\Big]_j .

It is an EM algorithm (Shepp & Vardi 1982): the likelihood never decreases.
Non-negative: a product of non-negative factors. Flux: \sum_j x_j^{\text{new}} = \sum_i y_i\frac{(A\mathbf x)_i}{(A\mathbf x)_i + b}, which is \sum_i y_i for b = 0.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
section: Try it: RL step by step
text:
Try it: RL step by step




Beads (a 1 : 4 pair, 6 px apart) next to an edge, Gaussian PSF σ = 2 px, Poisson noise with 100 photons at value 1 (the beads peak at 2.5). The iterations are computed in the background; the slider scrubs through ~30 snapshots. Tour: “no noise”: the error keeps falling up to 1000 iterations (1.22 % of the peak), the misfit (Poisson deviance per pixel) drops to almost 0. “Noise: semi-convergence”: best at k = 8 (2.20 %), then rising (10.4 % at 1000); the misfit settles near 1, the noise level. Best Wiener: 2.49 %. “Fewer photons” (20): best at k = 3 (2.56 %). “1000 iterations: speckles” on the cell phantom: 18.7 % error against 2.74 % at k = 5; the background breaks up into bright dots. “RL vs best Wiener” (phantom, 1000 photons): RL 2.18 % at k = 25, Wiener 2.31 %.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
section: The number of iterations is λ
text:
The number of iterations is λ
Recall from the last unit: an iteration from a flat image fills in strong (low) frequencies first and weak (high, noisy) ones last. RL does the same.

Semi-convergence: the error against the truth falls, then rises; the data fit keeps improving.
Fewer photons → stop earlier. In the demo (beads): best k = 40 at 1000 photons, 8 at 100, 3 at 20.
The misfit (Poisson deviance per pixel) reaches about 1 when the blurred estimate explains the data to the noise level: a discrepancy rule for RL.
Alternatives to stopping: add a penalty (e.g. total variation; one line here, the Ising/MRF elective owns TV).
Tomography’s MLEM (Radon elective) is the same algorithm with the projector instead of the PSF.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
section: The math: why stopping early regularises here too
text:
The math: why stopping early regularises here too
Write \mathbf x = \bar x(\mathbf 1 + \boldsymbol\delta) around the flat start \bar x, with small \boldsymbol\delta and b = 0. Then A\mathbf x = \bar x(\mathbf 1 + A\boldsymbol\delta) and
\frac{\mathbf y}{A\mathbf x} \approx \frac{\mathbf y}{\bar x}\big(\mathbf 1 - A\boldsymbol\delta\big), \qquad \mathbf x_{\text{new}} \approx \mathbf x + \mathbf x \cdot A^\top\Big(\frac{\mathbf y - A\mathbf x}{\bar x}\Big).
Near a flat image this is a Landweber step with \omega \approx 1 (in units of \bar x): \mathbf x \leftarrow \mathbf x + A^\top(\mathbf y - A\mathbf x). Per frequency the k-th iterate keeps about 1 - (1 - |H(f)|^2)^k of the inverse: strong frequencies early, weak ones after about 1/|H|^2 iterations.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
Offset and background

RL needs counts: subtract the camera offset first (camera noise unit) but keep the photon scale; a negative pixel breaks the Poisson model.
Most images also have a background: out-of-focus haze, autofluorescence, a few photons per pixel everywhere.
Put it in the model, \mathbf y \approx A\mathbf x + b. If b is left out, RL must explain the background by the object, and it sharpens the background into speckles (the estimate is a sum of bright points).
In the demo (cell phantom, 100 photons at 1, background 30 photons): forgetting b gives at least 27.5 % error at every k; with b in the model 3.18 % at k = 10.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
3D: widefield stacks
Widefield 3D stacks are where deconvolution is most used. Recall (image formation day): the 3D PSF of a widefield microscope is elongated in z: an hourglass of out-of-focus light above and below each point, and its OTF has a missing cone around the k_z axis.

3D RL with the 3D PSF puts out-of-focus light back where it came from: contrast and axial resolution improve a lot. A bead’s axial FWHM in the demo: 1.48 µm blurred, 0.53 µm after 100 iterations.
But the missing cone is not filled: a thin horizontal sheet (all its frequencies along k_z) stays smeared in z: 200 nm thick, 4.7 µm blurred, still 1.3 µm after 100 iterations.
Vertical structures are restored better than horizontal ones.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
The math: the missing cone
The amplitude PSF of a lens is the inverse Fourier transform of the pupil: a cap of the sphere |\mathbf k| = n/\lambda with half-angle α (\sin\alpha = \mathrm{NA}/n). The intensity PSF is its squared magnitude, so the OTF is the autocorrelation of the cap: the set of differences \mathbf k_1 - \mathbf k_2 of two points on it.

The differences fill a torus-like region in (k_r, k_z): up to k_r = 2\,\mathrm{NA}/\lambda laterally.
Near the origin two nearby points on the cap differ in a direction tangent to the cap: at most at angle α to the k_r axis. So for small k_r only |k_z| \lesssim k_r\tan\alpha is reached: a cone around the k_z axis is missing.
A horizontal sheet, uniform in x and y, has only k_r = 0: of all its frequencies only k_z = 0 survives.
Confocal: excitation PSF × detection PSF, so the OTF is the convolution of two widefield OTFs, which fills the cone.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
Try it: a 3D stack




64 × 32 × 32 voxels, 100 nm laterally, 200 nm between planes, NA 0.8 in air, 1000 photons at value 1. Top row: xz slices (drawn to scale), bottom: xy at the middle plane. Right: the OTF magnitude at ky = 0 (log), with the missing cone dashed; then axial profiles. 3D RL costs about 20 ms per iteration here, so 200 iterations take a few seconds. Tour: “widefield” (k = 0): blur above and below every object. “RL restores the bead in z”: bead axial FWHM 1476 nm blurred → 526 nm at k = 100 (444 at 200). “The sheet stays smeared”: 200 nm thick; 4666 nm blurred, 1345 at k = 100, 1111 at 200. “Confocal”: bead 854 → 233 nm, sheet 921 → 282 nm: the cone is filled. “z-steps too large” (800 nm): the bead only goes from 1178 to 808 nm; the stack under-samples the PSF in z.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
Confocal, and depth

Confocal: the pinhole already rejects most out-of-focus light, and its OTF has no missing cone. Deconvolution gains less in contrast, but it works more reliably, and sheets are restored too.
Depth: the 3D PSF must match the depth. Imaging into water with an oil lens (refractive index mismatch) makes the PSF asymmetric in z and change with depth. A PSF measured at the coverslip is wrong 30 µm deeper.
Sampling: the z-step must resolve the PSF axially (Nyquist, image formation day); otherwise deconvolution has nothing to work with.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
The PSF you use








PSF used
result
looks




too narrow
leftover blur, under-restored
safe, but objects too large


right
best



too wide
over-sharpening, dark rims (halos) around bright objects, ringing, objects smaller than they are
crisp, wrong




Measured PSF (beads, image formation day): includes the real aberrations, but noisy and from one depth.
Computed PSF: clean but ideal.
Common compromise: fit a model PSF to measured beads.
In the demo (beads, 1000 photons, k = 100): the single bead’s FWHM is 3.25 px with a PSF 30 % too narrow, 2.63 px with the right one, 2.57 px with one 30 % too wide (truth 1.45 px); the too-wide PSF digs a rim down to 0.013 around it (background 0.05).

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
Blind deconvolution
Estimate object and PSF together: alternate an RL step on the object (PSF fixed) with an RL step on the PSF (object fixed).

Very under-determined: the trivial answer “PSF = a point, object = the blurred image” explains the data perfectly.
So it needs constraints: PSF non-negative, sum 1, limited size, smooth, or a parametric shape (e.g. Gaussian with unknown width).
In the demo (start 50 % too wide, FWHM 7.1 px; true 4.8 px): unconstrained, the PSF width passes the true value near 100 iterations and keeps shrinking (3.3 px at 300). A size limit does not stop this; a Gaussian shape slows it (6.0 px at 300).
Use it when no PSF can be measured (motion, unknown aberration); otherwise prefer a measured or computed PSF.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
section: Try it: the PSF you use
text:
Try it: the PSF you use




Bottom right panel: the true PSF next to the one used (or the current blind estimate). Tour: “PSF too wide” (×1.3, 1000 photons, k = 100): dark rims around the beads; the peak ratio of the 1 : 4 pair is 9.1 instead of 4. “Too narrow” (×0.7): the beads stay round and wide. “Forgot the background”: speckles in the background (up to 0.70 where the truth is 0.05) and the total flux of the estimate equals that of the data including the background. “Ringing at the edge” (Airy PSF, 10 000 photons, 1000 iterations): the profile dips to 0.03 just before the edge (background 0.05) and overshoots to 0.56 after it (true 0.50). “Blind”: watch the PSF estimate shrink (readout: FWHM). “Blind with a Gaussian shape”: slower drift. Blind steps cost three times more, so the run stops at 300 iterations.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
Artefacts

Cell phantom, Gaussian PSF σ = 2 px, 100 photons at value 1. From the left: truth, observed, RL after 5, 25 and 1000 iterations (RMSE against the truth 0.030, 0.039 and 0.205; the observed image 0.050; values 0..1).
Ringing: ripples next to sharp edges and around bright objects.
Speckling: noise turned into bright dots after many iterations (right image).
Halos: dark rims from a PSF that is too wide.
Border artefacts: the periodic FFT; pad and taper (unit 1).
Axial smearing of horizontal structures in widefield 3D: the missing cone.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
Summary

Richardson–Lucy: blur the guess, compare as a ratio, spread the ratio back, multiply. Never negative, keeps the photons, maximises the Poisson likelihood (EM).
Iterations = regularisation: semi-convergence; fewer photons → stop earlier; a misfit of about 1 per pixel means the noise level is reached.
Needs offset-corrected counts and a background term, or the background turns into speckles.
3D: puts out-of-focus light back; restores beads and vertical structures, but the missing cone keeps horizontal sheets smeared. Confocal has no missing cone.
PSF too narrow: leftover blur. Too wide: halos, ringing, objects too small. Blind estimation needs constraints and still drifts towards a point.
Artefacts: ringing, speckles, halos, borders, axial smearing.

title: Quiz: RGB, gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Stored 8-bit sRGB codes are gamma-encoded; “linear” values are proportional to light. Code 128 is 21.6 % of white’s light, code 188 is 50.3 %.

Q1. An image is half black (0) and half white (255), in fine one-pixel stripes. You shrink it by averaging 2 × 2 blocks of the stored codes. What value do you get, and what should it be?






Hint





Average the light, not the codes.









Answer





Averaging codes gives 127.5, i.e. 128, which is only 21.6 % of white’s light. The light averages to 50 %, which is stored as code 188. The naive result is much too dark.




Q2. Why are images stored gamma-encoded at all, if every computation has to undo it?






Hint





Where does the eye need small steps?









Answer





Perceived lightness grows roughly like the cube root of light, so the eye notices small absolute changes in the darks and only large ones in the brights. Encoding spends the 256 codes evenly in perceived lightness: with linear codes the darks would show banding and many bright codes would be wasted.




Q3. Two neighbouring regions, pure red and pure green, are blurred on the stored codes. Why does a dark band appear between them?






Hint





What light does a code of 128 in one channel stand for?









Answer





At the border each channel is about half its code: (128, 128, 0) in codes, which is only about 22 % of full red light plus 22 % of full green light. Blurring the light gives (0.5, 0.5, 0) in light, i.e. codes (188, 188, 0): as bright as its surroundings. Averaging codes loses light wherever values are mixed.




Q4. What do the three columns of the sRGB → XYZ matrix mean, and what does its middle row mean?






Hint





Multiply the matrix by (1, 0, 0).









Answer





Column k is the XYZ of primary k at full drive (the matrix times a unit vector). The middle row gives Y, the luminance: 0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B on linear values, the brightness contributed by each primary.




Q5. A picture of red letters on a green background becomes a blank grey image when converted to luminance. Is the conversion broken?






Hint





What does greyscale keep, and what does it throw away?









Answer





No. The letters and the background have the same luminance, and luminance is a projection of the 3D colour onto one direction: everything else (here the red–green difference) is discarded. Another projection (the channel mean, or the R channel alone) keeps the letters. Choose the greyscale direction that keeps the contrast you need.




Q6. JPEG stores Cb and Cr at half resolution in both directions. Why is that hardly visible, while halving the resolution of Y′ would be obvious?






Hint





Where is the detail of a natural image, and how does the eye see colour detail?









Answer





Edges and texture are mostly changes of brightness, carried by Y′. The visual system resolves fine detail in brightness but only coarse detail in colour differences, so losing three quarters of the chroma samples costs little that we can see. It halves the data (1.5 instead of 3 values per pixel).




Q7. Grey world on a forest scene turns the green leaves grey-magenta. Why?






Hint





What does grey world assume about the scene?









Answer





Grey world assumes the average colour of the scene is grey, and scales the channels until it is. A forest is mostly green, so its average is green; the correction removes green from everything, and the leaves (and any truly grey objects) end up magenta-tinted.




Q8. Why should the white-balance gains be applied to linear values rather than to the stored codes?






Hint





A lamp multiplies light. What does that do to codes?









Answer





The lamp multiplies the light in each channel by a factor, so the right correction is a multiplication of linear values. Codes are a non-linear function of light: multiplying a code by a factor does not multiply the light by a factor, and different brightnesses get different, wrong corrections (the midtones go off while the white comes out right).




Q9. (math) Show that the middle row of the matrix M = (\mathbf p_R\;\mathbf p_G\;\mathbf p_B)\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf s) equals \mathbf s, where each \mathbf p_k = (x_k/y_k, 1, (1 - x_k - y_k)/y_k).






Hint





What is the middle entry of each \mathbf p_k?









Answer





M_{2k} = (\mathbf p_k)_2\,s_k = 1 \cdot s_k. So the luminance weights of the primaries are exactly the scales found from the white point; for sRGB they are 0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722.

title: Exercise: RGB, gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




sRGB decoding
code C \in [0, 1] → light: C/12.92 for C \le 0.04045, else ((C + 0.055)/1.055)^{2.4}


Linear light
values proportional to light; sums and averages of light are meaningful


RGB → XYZ
\mathbf{XYZ} = M\,\mathbf{rgb}_\text{lin}; columns of M = XYZ of the primaries; M(1,1,1)^\top = white


Luminance
Y = 0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B on linear sRGB


Luma
Y' = 0.299R' + 0.587G' + 0.114B' on encoded values


Y′CbCr (JPEG)
C_b = 128 + 0.564(B' - Y'), C_r = 128 + 0.713(R' - Y'), on codes 0–255


White balance
\mathbf c' = D\mathbf c, D diagonal, scales the estimated white to white; on linear values






The sRGB decoding curve: stored code (across) to linear light (up). Code 128 is 21.6 % of white’s light, half of the light is code 188.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
RGB: gamma, linear maps & white balance

title: Exercise: RGB, gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
By hand
B1. (a) Decode the 8-bit codes 0, 128, 188 and 255 to linear light (divide by 255 first). (b) A pixel is the average of a black and a white pixel. What code do you get by averaging the codes? By averaging the light and encoding the result? (c) An image is darkened to half its light. What happens to a pixel with code 200? Is the new code 100?
B2. A toy display has primaries with chromaticities R (0.6, 0.3), G (0.3, 0.6), B (0.2, 0.1) and the white point (1/3, 1/3) (equal energy: X = Y = Z = 1). (a) Write the vectors \mathbf p_k = (x_k/y_k,\; 1,\; (1 - x_k - y_k)/y_k) of the three primaries. (b) Find the scales s_R, s_G, s_B such that s_R\mathbf p_R + s_G\mathbf p_G + s_B\mathbf p_B = (1, 1, 1). (c) Write the matrix M. Check that each row sums to 1. What are this display’s luminance weights?
B3. Compute Y', C_b and C_r (codes 0–255) of (a) pure red (255, 0, 0), (b) mid-grey (128, 128, 128). What happens to C_r of red in 8 bits?
B4. A 1920 \times 1080 image is stored with 8 bits per value. How many bytes does it take as RGB (or Y′CbCr 4:4:4)? With 4:2:0 chroma subsampling? With the luma subsampled 2 × 2 instead, and full chroma?
B5. A photo under a light bulb has linear channel means (\bar R, \bar G, \bar B) = (0.30, 0.20, 0.10). (a) Grey world: find the gains (g_R, g_G, g_B) that make the three means equal to \bar G. (b) Correct the pixel (0.45, 0.30, 0.08). (c) Someone applies the same gains to the stored codes instead. Give one reason why the result is wrong.
B6. The isoluminant test image: letters with linear (R, G, B) = (0.841, 0, 0) on a background (0, 0.25, 0). (a) Compute the luminance of both. (b) Encode both colours to codes (use: 0.841 \to 236, 0.25 \to 137). Compute luma and the channel mean of the codes for both. Which greyscale shows the letters?






Solutions





B1. (a) 0 \to 0; 128/255 = 0.502 \to 0.216; 188/255 = 0.737 \to 0.503; 255 \to 1. (b) Averaging codes: 127.5, about 128, which is 21.4 % of white’s light. Averaging light: 0.5, encoded 1.055 \cdot 0.5^{1/2.4} - 0.055 = 0.735, code 188. The naive average is far too dark. (c) Code 200 is light 0.578; half of that is 0.289, which encodes to code 146, not 100. Code 100 would be only 12.7 % of white, a darkening to less than a quarter of the light.
B2. (a) \mathbf p_R = (2, 1, 1/3), \mathbf p_G = (0.5, 1, 1/6), \mathbf p_B = (2, 1, 7). (b) Solving the 3 \times 3 system gives s_R = 13/60 = 0.217, s_G = 2/3 = 0.667, s_B = 7/60 = 0.117. Check, middle row: 0.217 + 0.667 + 0.117 = 1. (c) M = \begin{pmatrix} 0.433 & 0.333 & 0.233 \\ 0.217 & 0.667 & 0.117 \\ 0.072 & 0.111 & 0.817 \end{pmatrix}, columns s_k\mathbf p_k. Each row sums to 1 because M(1,1,1)^\top is the white (1, 1, 1). The luminance weights are the middle row: 0.217, 0.667, 0.117.
B3. (a) Y' = 0.299 \cdot 255 = 76.2; C_b = 128 + 0.564(0 - 76.2) = 85.0; C_r = 128 + 0.713(255 - 76.2) = 255.5. In 8 bits it is clipped to 255 (the coefficients are rounded; the exact standard gives 255.5 too, and encoders clip). (b) Y' = 128, and B' - Y' = R' - Y' = 0: C_b = C_r = 128. Every grey sits at the centre of the chroma plane.
B4. RGB: 1920 \cdot 1080 \cdot 3 = 6\,220\,800 bytes. 4:2:0: luma 2\,073\,600 plus two chroma planes of 960 \cdot 540 = 518\,400 each: 3\,110\,400 bytes, half. Luma subsampled instead: 518\,400 + 2 \cdot 2\,073\,600 = 4\,665\,600 bytes; it saves less and looks far worse.
B5. (a) g = (0.20/0.30,\; 1,\; 0.20/0.10) = (0.667, 1, 2). (b) (0.45 \cdot 0.667,\; 0.30,\; 0.08 \cdot 2) = (0.30, 0.30, 0.16). (c) The lamp multiplied the light by a factor per channel; codes are a power-law function of light, so multiplying codes by g multiplies the light by about g^{2.2} for midtones and by other factors near black: the cast is removed for one brightness only. (Also, grey world itself assumes an average grey scene.)
B6. (a) Letters: 0.2126 \cdot 0.841 = 0.179. Background: 0.7152 \cdot 0.25 = 0.179. Equal: the luminance image is uniform, the letters vanish. (b) Codes: letters (236, 0, 0), background (0, 137, 0). Luma: 0.299 \cdot 236 = 70.6 against 0.587 \cdot 137 = 80.4: low contrast but visible. Channel mean: 78.7 against 45.7: the letters are clearly brighter. The mean (or the R channel alone) shows them.




Math questions
B7. (math) For a display with primary vectors \mathbf p_k (middle entry 1) and white \mathbf w with Y_w = 1, let M = P\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf s) with P\mathbf s = \mathbf w. Show that M(1,1,1)^\top = \mathbf w and that the middle row of M is \mathbf s^\top, so the luminance weights sum to 1.
B8. (math) Let d(C) be the sRGB decoding function on [0, 1]. Show that d is convex (above the knee it is a power 2.4 of an affine function). Use Jensen’s inequality to show that for any set of codes, d(\text{mean of codes}) \le \text{mean of } d(\text{codes}): averaging codes never gives more light than averaging the light, and gives less unless all codes are equal.
B9. (math) White balance by a full matrix: given n chart colours \mathbf c_i (columns of C, 3 \times n) and their targets \mathbf t_i (columns of T), show that M = TC^\top(CC^\top)^{-1} minimises \sum_i \|M\mathbf c_i - \mathbf t_i\|^2. When is CC^\top invertible?






Solutions (math)





B7. M(1,1,1)^\top = P\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf s)(1,1,1)^\top = P\mathbf s = \mathbf w. Entry (2, k) of M is (\mathbf p_k)_2\,s_k = s_k. The luminance weights sum to \sum_k s_k = (M(1,1,1)^\top)_2 = Y_w = 1.
B8. For C > 0.04045, d(C) = ((C + 0.055)/1.055)^{2.4} has d''(C) = 2.4 \cdot 1.4\,(C + 0.055)^{0.4}/1.055^{2.4} > 0; below the knee d is linear, and at the knee the slope does not drop (1/12.92 = 0.0774 on the left, 2.4 \cdot (0.09545/1.055)^{1.4}/1.055 = 0.0787 on the right), so d is convex on [0, 1]. Jensen: d(\frac1n\sum C_i) \le \frac1n\sum d(C_i), with equality for a strictly convex part only if all C_i are equal. Black and white: d(0.5) = 0.214 < 0.5.
B9. E(M) = \|MC - T\|_F^2 = \operatorname{tr}\big((MC - T)(MC - T)^\top\big). Its gradient with respect to M is 2(MC - T)C^\top; setting it to zero gives MCC^\top = TC^\top, so M = TC^\top(CC^\top)^{-1}. E is a convex quadratic in M, so this stationary point is the minimum. CC^\top (3 \times 3) is invertible iff C has rank 3: the chart colours must not all lie in one plane through the origin (e.g. not only greys, not only two hues).

title: Exercise: RGB, gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
Explore: blur in linear light
The same operation is done twice: on the stored codes (“on encoded values”) and as decode → operate → encode (“in linear light”). Operations: a Gaussian blur with standard deviation \sigma, or block-average downsampling by 2 or 4 (shown at the original size). The plot shows a profile along the dashed row (click or drag on an image to move it): the R′, G′ or B′ code, or the code of the luminance. The readout gives the mean luminance (light) of the input and both results. Show linear values directly puts the linear values on the screen without encoding.



G1. Preset black + white = 128 or 188? What value do the blurred stripes get on codes, and in linear light? Compare with B1. Look at the input from a distance (or squint): which of the two uniform grey patches on the right matches the stripes on your screen?
G2. In the same preset, how much of the image’s light does the blur on codes lose, and how much does the linear-light blur lose?
G3. Preset red meets green: the dark seam. Describe the border in the two results. Look at the luminance profile: how dark does the seam get on codes, compared with the red and green squares?
G4. Preset blurred lights lose their glow. What happens to the small bright lights on codes? How much light is lost? Then try downsample ×4 on the same image.
G5. Preset downsampling darkens fine detail (thin lines, ×4). How much darker is the result on codes? Why does the red/green checker with downsample ×2 show no difference at all?
G6. Tick show linear values directly. Why does everything look too dark and too contrasty?






Solutions





G1. 128 on codes and 188 in linear light, as in B1. On a screen that follows sRGB, the stripes match the lower patch (188), not the upper one (128). (A projector or a mis-set screen may not follow sRGB; that is why the numbers are shown.)
G2. The mean luminance drops from 0.4297 to 0.2883 on codes (−32.9 %); in linear light it is 0.4316 (+0.5 %, an effect of the mirrored border at the edge of the stripes). The blur in linear light keeps the light, as a blur of light must.
G3. On codes the border becomes a dark, muddy olive band (codes about 111, 144, 0 at the border); in linear light it is a bright yellow transition (176, 198, 0). The luminance profile on codes dips to 107, darker than both the red (127) and the green (220); in linear light it never goes below 127.
G4. On codes the lights become small and dim: the largest R′ code drops from 255 to 127 (in linear light 168), and the image loses 62.8 % of its light (linear light: +0.3 %). Downsampling ×4 on codes loses 30.6 %, in linear light nothing.
G5. On codes the mean luminance falls from 0.1645 to 0.0511 (−69.0 %); in linear light it stays 0.1645. With the checker and ×2 the blocks never mix two colours (the 32-pixel squares are aligned with the 2 × 2 blocks), so both methods average equal values: the error appears only where different values are mixed.
G6. The linear values are written to the screen, which then decodes them a second time: every value is darkened by the transfer curve once more (code 0.5 shows as 21.6 % of white). This is why linear data, e.g. from a camera’s raw file or a microscope, must be encoded (or shown with a display transfer) to look natural.

title: Exercise: RGB, gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
Explore: colour as a matrix
The input image (synthetic), the three output channels as grey images, and the recombined result. Y′CbCr: the channels Y′, Cb, Cr (128 = mid-grey); subsample the chroma or the luma by 2, 4 or 8 (one value per block) and rebuild R′G′B′; the readout gives the bytes per pixel and the mean colour difference ΔE*ab to the input (about 2 is just noticeable). Greyscale: weights for R, G, B (normalised to sum 1) on linear or on encoded values; the readout gives the mean grey of the two classes. Any matrix: a 3 \times 3 matrix plus an offset on linear RGB (edit the cells), with the pixels pushed outside [0, 1] shown in white.



M1. Preset Y′CbCr channels. Which channel carries the shapes and the shading? What do Cb and Cr show for the grey card and the table?
M2. Subsample chroma by 4, then subsample luma by 4. Which looks worse? Compare the mean ΔE*ab of the two. Does ΔE*ab capture what you see?
M3. The isoluminant test (greyscale). Check B6 with the luminance, luma, mean and “G only” buttons. Which greyscale would you use to find the letters?
M4. Stained tissue: best single channel. Compare the contrast between nuclei and the rest (the two mean greys) for G only, the channel mean, R only and luminance. Which single channel is best, and why?
M5. sRGB → XYZ (any matrix). What are the row sums, and what do they mean? Then P3 → sRGB: out of gamut: what share of the pixels falls outside [0, 1], and which objects are they?






Solutions





M1. Y′ carries the shapes, the shading and the shadow: it looks like a black-and-white photo. Cb and Cr are flat mid-grey (128) on the grey card and nearly so on the table; they are bright or dark only on coloured objects (Cr bright on the red apple, Cb dark on the yellow fruit, bright on the blue cup), and the shadow hardly shows in them.
M2. Luma ÷4 looks clearly worse (blocky edges everywhere), chroma ÷4 is hard to tell from the input. Yet the mean ΔE*ab is 2.18 for chroma ÷4 and only 1.87 for luma ÷4. A mean colour difference does not weigh errors the way the eye does: the eye is much more sensitive to errors in fine brightness detail (edges) than to colour bleeding across them. Bytes per pixel: 1.125 with chroma ÷4.
M3. Luminance: letters and background both 117.3: the letters vanish. Luma: 70.6 against 80.4 (faint). Mean: 78.8 against 45.7. G only: 0 against 137 (the strongest contrast). To find the letters, use G only (or R only, or the mean), not luminance.
M4. G only: nuclei 88.2, rest 171.7 (difference 83.5). Mean: 139.1 against 217.3 (78.2). R only: 141.5 against 241.2 (99.7). Luminance: 112.6 against 195.4 (82.8). Here the R channel separates best: hematoxylin absorbs red strongly while eosin hardly does, so the nuclei are dark in R and the pink stroma bright. Note that the nuclei are also darker than the stroma in G, but the eosin-stained stroma is darker there too.
M5. Row sums 0.9505, 1.0001, 1.0888: the XYZ of the white R = G = B = 1, i.e. D65 (the middle row sums to 1: white has luminance 1). P3 → sRGB: 2507 of 16 384 pixels (15.3 %) end up outside [0, 1]: the saturated red apple, green leaf, yellow fruit and blue cup. Read as P3 colours they are more saturated than sRGB can show.

title: Exercise: RGB, gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
Explore: white balance
A chart of 24 patches with known (synthetic) reflectance spectra, rendered under a lamp (top left: as captured), corrected (middle), and the truth: the same chart under daylight. The lamp’s spectrum is shown below. Estimate the white by grey world, white patch, a grey card (click a patch of the captured chart) or skip the estimate and fit a full 3 × 3 matrix to the chart. Diagonal scaling applied to: encoded sRGB, linear RGB, cones (von Kries) or the Bradford basis. The readout gives the mean ΔE*ab over the patches against the truth (exposure is matched, so it measures the colour error; about 2 is just noticeable).



W1. Preset tungsten 2800 K (no correction). What is the mean ΔE*ab? Now choose grey card (the third grey of the bottom row is selected) with cones (von Kries), then Bradford, linear RGB and encoded sRGB. Rank the four.
W2. Preset grey world works. Compare grey world with the grey card in the same basis. Why does grey world do almost as well on this chart?
W3. Preset grey world in a forest. What colour cast does the correction produce, and what is the mean ΔE*ab? Choose white patch: better or worse? Why?
W4. Preset white patch fooled by a highlight. What does the white patch estimate as “white”? Compare with the same setting without the highlight, and with the grey card.
W5. Preset narrow-band LED: no diagonal fixes it. How good is the best diagonal (try the bases)? And the 3 × 3 fit? Why can no correction be perfect here?
W6. Choose the grey card with Bradford and move the blackbody temperature: 2000, 4000, 6500 and 10 000 K. Where is the correction easiest, and why?






Solutions





W1. No correction: 44.08. Grey card: Bradford 5.31 < cones 7.61 < linear RGB 11.20 < encoded sRGB 14.99. Scaling codes is the worst (B5c); among the linear bases, the sharper, more cone-like channels work best.
W2. Grey world (cones): 9.01, grey card (cones): 7.61. The chart contains many different hues and a row of greys, so its average is close to grey and the grey-world estimate of the white (0.330, 0.157, 0.036) is close to the grey card’s direction (0.360, 0.159, 0.042).
W3. The leaves turn grey and the bark and sky magenta-pink: mean ΔE*ab 22.62 (worst patch 46.85). The forest’s average is green, and grey world removes it. The white patch (a white flower is in the scene) gives 6.08: the brightest values really are a white surface here.
W4. It takes the clipped highlight as white: estimate (1.000, 1.000, 0.352) instead of about (0.90, 0.40, 0.12); mean ΔE*ab 24.61. Without the highlight the white patch gives 8.19; the grey card gives 7.61 with or without it. A clipped highlight reads “white” whatever the lamp’s colour.
W5. Grey card: 10.62 with cones, 10.36 with Bradford (no correction: 12.81). The 3 × 3 fit: 4.66, with the worst patch at 13.67. Three narrow peaks sample each reflectance at only three wavelengths, and surfaces with different spectra between the peaks collapse onto the same responses (and vice versa): the information is lost before any 3 \times 3 correction, diagonal or not. This is metameric failure on a large scale.
W6. Mean ΔE*ab with grey card and Bradford: 9.06 at 2000 K, 2.47 at 4000 K, 0.71 at 6500 K, 2.16 at 10 000 K. At 6500 K the lamp is close to daylight (the reference), so little correction is needed and the diagonal model’s error is small; the further the lamp from daylight, the more the broad, overlapping channels break the diagonal model.

text:
Where this leads
Linear light and 3 \times 3 matrices are the toolkit for the rest of the day. The next unit asks which space makes a colour segmentation easy: HSV (hue as an angle) and CIELAB (distances that match perception). title: Resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF
text:
About this lecture
Last unit: the optics pass nothing above 2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda. Now the practical consequences:

When are two points resolved? Rayleigh, Sparrow, and why noise decides in practice.
How large may a pixel be? Nyquist for a microscope: \Delta x \le \lambda/4\mathrm{NA}.
In 3D the PSF is longer along the optical axis; widefield images have a missing cone.
How to measure a PSF from beads, and what limits the measurement.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Second unit of the image formation day. Recalls: Nyquist “two samples per cycle” and aliasing (frequency unit, day 1), shot noise and read noise (camera noise unit, day 3). Numbers use λ = 520 nm (green) unless stated. The demo “resolve” has three modes: two points, axial, beads.
crumbs: Resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF

title: Resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF
text:
Two points
Move two equal points closer together: the dip between their peaks shrinks, then vanishes.

Two Airy patterns (grey) and their sum (blue), NA 1.4, λ 520 nm.
Rayleigh: the peak of one point on the first dark ring of the other, d = 0.61\lambda/\mathrm{NA}. The dip is 26 %.
Sparrow: the dip just vanishes, d = 0.47\lambda/\mathrm{NA} (176 nm at NA 1.4).
Resolution is a convention. In practice noise decides: a 26 % dip on top of 2 photons per pixel is invisible.
crumbs: Resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF

title: Resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF
text:
The math: Rayleigh and Sparrow
Two equal points at \pm d/2, profile through both: I(x) = h(x - d/2) + h(x + d/2).

Rayleigh: h is the Airy pattern [2J_1(v)/v]^2 with v = 2\pi\mathrm{NA}\,r/\lambda; put d on its first zero, v = 3.832. At the midpoint each point contributes h at v = 1.916: [2J_1(1.916)/1.916]^2 = 0.367, so I(0) = 0.735 against a peak of about 1: a dip of 1 - 0.735 = 26\,\%.
Sparrow: the midpoint changes from a maximum to a minimum when its curvature changes sign: I''(0) = 2h''(d/2) = 0. The two profiles add up flat at the midpoint exactly when d/2 is at the inflection point of h.
Gaussian PSF h \propto e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}: h'' = 0 at x = \sigma, so Sparrow is d = 2\sigma. With \sigma = 0.21\lambda/\mathrm{NA}: 0.42\lambda/\mathrm{NA}. For the Airy pattern, solved numerically: 0.47\lambda/\mathrm{NA}.
crumbs: Resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF

title: Resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF
section: Try it: two points on pixels
text:
Try it: two points on pixels




Two points imaged by an ideal lens (NA 1.4, 520 nm) on a 2 × 1 µm field. Blue: the optical image (no pixels, no noise); red: the pixel values along the line through both points. Tour: “Rayleigh” (227 nm, 40 nm pixels): dip 26.8 % in the optical image, 25.6 % in the pixels. “Sparrow” (176 nm): no dip. “Rayleigh, 20 photons” (65 nm pixels, noise on): about 2 photons in the peak pixel; the pixel profile is noise, the dip can be anything. Raise the photons to 2000: the dip comes back (23 %). Change λ to 650 nm at d = 227 nm: the dip drops to 0.6 %; at 450 nm it is 51 %.
crumbs: Resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF

title: Resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF
text:
Recall: two samples per cycle
From the frequency unit: a signal must be sampled at least twice per period of its finest component; faster patterns alias to false slow ones. That slide already said: the optics of a microscope should match the pixel size. Now we can say how.

The optics deliver nothing above 2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda: the image is band-limited.
Two samples per period of the finest component: pixel \Delta x \le \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\lambda}{2\mathrm{NA}} = \dfrac{\lambda}{4\mathrm{NA}}. Nyquist for a microscope.
The pixel that counts is the pixel in the sample plane: camera pixel ÷ magnification.

title: Resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF
section: The math: Nyquist from the OTF support
text:
The math: Nyquist from the OTF support
The image is g = f \ast h, so G = FH and G(\mathbf k) = 0 wherever H(\mathbf k) = 0: the image is band-limited to |\mathbf k| \le k_c = 2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda.

Sampling theorem: a band-limited function is determined by samples with spacing \Delta x \le 1/(2k_c) = \lambda/(4\mathrm{NA}) (per axis).
Along the optical axis, the widefield OTF extends to k_z = \dfrac{n}{\lambda}(1 - \cos\alpha), with \sin\alpha = \mathrm{NA}/n. So \Delta z \le \frac{\lambda}{2n(1 - \cos\alpha)}. NA 1.4 in oil (n = 1.518): \cos\alpha = 0.386, \Delta z \le 279 nm. NA 0.8 in air: 650 nm.
For small NA, 1 - \cos\alpha \approx \mathrm{NA}^2/2n^2, so \Delta z \le n\lambda/\mathrm{NA}^2.
crumbs: Resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF

title: Resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF
text:
Oversampling is not free
Smaller pixels than Nyquist add no detail (the optics deliver none), but they cost:

The same photons are spread over more pixels: fewer photons per pixel, a noisier pixel (shot noise \sqrt N, plus read noise per pixel; recall the camera noise unit).
Larger files, slower acquisition, and more bleaching per useful piece of information.

Example (demo): two points 300 nm apart, 500 photons each. With 65 nm pixels the peak pixel holds about 50 photons (noise ±14 %); with 20 nm pixels about 6.5 photons (±39 %).
The usual compromise: 2–3 pixels across the Rayleigh distance. Deconvolution (next day) needs at least Nyquist.
crumbs: Resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF

title: Resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF
text:
The PSF in 3D

Left: widefield PSF in an xz slice (log scale), NA 1.4. Middle: confocal PSF. Right: the widefield OTF in the kx–kz plane: no information in a cone around the kz axis.
The PSF is elongated along the optical axis z. NA 1.4: FWHM 191 nm across, 515 nm along (2.7×); NA 0.8 in air: 335 nm and 1.17 µm (3.5×).
Rule of thumb for the axial extent: 2n\lambda/\mathrm{NA}^2 (for small NA; at NA 1.4 the exact value, 0.56 µm, is smaller than the rule’s 0.8 µm).
Widefield: every plane carries the same total light; out-of-focus light is spread, not removed. The OTF has a missing cone: no optical sectioning.
Confocal: a pinhole rejects out-of-focus light; PSF ≈ (excitation PSF) × (detection PSF): narrower, and the cone is filled.

title: Resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF
text:
Try it: the axial PSF




xz slice of the PSF of an ideal lens (scalar model), computed from the pupil one plane at a time; right panel: the same PSF as a stack with planes every Δz. Tour: “NA 1.4”: lateral FWHM 191 nm, axial 515 nm (2.7×), axial Nyquist 279 nm, z-step 200 nm is fine. “Z-step too large” (1 µm): the planes miss the focus region; the red dots skip the peak. “Out-of-focus light (log)”: the hourglass: light from one point reaches every plane. “Confocal”: lateral 138 nm, axial 369 nm, and the hourglass is gone. “NA 0.5 (air)”: 535 nm and 3.4 µm (6.4×).

title: Resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF
text:
The math: averaging beads

Bead i gives b_i = h + e_i after centring, with independent noise of variance \sigma^2 per pixel. The mean \bar b = h + \tfrac1N\sum e_i has noise variance \sigma^2/N: standard deviation \sigma/\sqrt N. 30 beads: 1/\sqrt{30} = 0.18 of one bead’s noise.
A bead is a uniform sphere of radius R; seen from above, its brightness is the projected thickness \propto \sqrt{R^2 - r^2}. The image is PSF ∗ projection.
Variances add under convolution (for any normalised, centred profiles). Along x, a uniform sphere has variance R^2/5. A Gaussian with that variance has FWHM 2.355\,R/\sqrt5 = 0.53D. Treating the PSF as Gaussian too: \text{FWHM}_\text{meas}^2 \approx \text{FWHM}_\text{PSF}^2 + (0.53\,D)^2.
A 100 nm bead and a 191 nm PSF: \sqrt{191^2 + 53^2} = 198 nm (+4 %). A 200 nm bead: 218 nm (+14 %).

title: Resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF
text:
Try it: beads




Simulated bead slide: 30 beads of 40 nm, NA 1.4, 520 nm, 65 nm pixels, 500 photons per bead, background 10 photons per pixel, seeded Poisson noise. “True PSF” = a point as these pixels record it (FWHM 195 nm; the optical Airy FWHM is 191 nm). Tour: “one bead, noisy”: 204 nm (+4.6 %), lumpy. Slide the number of beads: it scatters between 188 and 206 nm up to 5 beads, then settles: 30 beads give 194 nm. “Forgot the background”: 223 nm (+14.3 %), a pedestal under the curve. “Beads too large” (200 nm beads, 2000 photons): 215 nm.

title: Resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF
text:
Summary

Rayleigh 0.61\lambda/\mathrm{NA} (26 % dip), Sparrow 0.47\lambda/\mathrm{NA} (no dip): conventions. With few photons, noise decides.
Nyquist for a microscope: pixel in the sample plane \le \lambda/4\mathrm{NA} (93 nm at NA 1.4, 520 nm). Undersampling aliases; oversampling costs photons per pixel.
3D: the PSF is about 3–6× longer along z than across; axial Nyquist \lambda/2n(1 - \cos\alpha). Widefield has a missing cone; confocal removes out-of-focus light.
Beads: background subtraction, sub-pixel centring, averaging (\sqrt N), normalisation. Bead size adds about (0.53D)^2 to the squared FWHM.

title: Quiz: from measurements to claims
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. You image 2000 cells from one treated dish and 2000 from one control dish, and a t-test on the cells gives p = 10^{-12}. What is n, and what can you conclude?






Hint





At which level was the treatment applied independently?









Answer





n = 1 per condition: one dish each. The cells share their dish, so the test compares two dishes, and any difference between two dishes (seeding, medium, position in the incubator, imaging day) looks like a treatment effect. Nothing can be concluded about the treatment; repeat the experiment independently several times and compare the dish (or experiment) means.




Q2. Explain a p-value of 0.03 in one sentence, without the word “probability of the hypothesis”.






Hint





Imagine the treatment does nothing.









Answer





If the treatment had no effect, a difference at least as large as the observed one would come up by chance in about 3 % of repeated experiments.




Q3. Why does measuring more cells per experiment hardly shrink the uncertainty of the treatment effect, while more experiments do?






Hint





Which variation do the cells of one experiment share?









Answer





All cells of one experiment share its day-to-day deviation. More cells average out the cell-to-cell variation but not that shared part; the uncertainty levels off at (day-to-day SD) × \sqrt{2/E}. Only more experiments average out the day-to-day variation.




Q4. In a paired design, control and treated are done on the same day in each of 4 experiments. Why is this usually much more powerful than 4 control and 4 treated experiments on 8 different days?






Hint





What happens to the day effect in the difference?









Answer





Within each day, the day effect is the same for both conditions and cancels in the difference treated − control. The paired test compares differences that only contain the (smaller) within-day variation; the unpaired test has to see the effect through the large day-to-day variation.




Q5. You measure 500 features and report the 12 with p < 0.05 as “affected by the treatment”. What is the problem, and what would you do?






Hint





How many hits would chance give?









Answer





With no real effect at all, 0.05 \cdot 500 = 25 features would be expected below 0.05; 12 hits are fully compatible with no effect. Correct for multiple testing: Benjamini–Hochberg to control the share of false discoveries, or Bonferroni (p \le 0.0001) to control the chance of any false hit; and confirm the hits in a new experiment.




Q6. All control wells were imaged on Monday and all treated wells on Tuesday. A colleague suggests a mixed-effects model with day as a random effect. Will it help?






Hint





Can any analysis separate the day from the treatment here?









Answer





No. Day and treatment are confounded: every difference between the conditions is also a difference between the days, and no model can split it. Only the design can: both conditions on every day (and every plate), randomised positions.




Q7. Report A: “p < 0.001”. Report B: “the area increased by 9 % (95 % CI 2 to 16 %), n = 5 experiments”. Why is B more useful?






Hint





What do you want to know about an effect?









Answer





B gives the size of the effect, its uncertainty, and the unit of replication with its n; the reader can judge whether 2–16 % matters biologically. A p-value alone says neither how large the effect is nor whether n counted cells or experiments; with enough cells any tiny difference gives p < 0.001.




Q8. (math) Cells within an experiment have intra-class correlation \rho = 0.1. What is the design effect for 100 cells per experiment, and what is the false-positive rate of a cells-as-n z-test at 5 %?






Hint





Design effect 1 + (m-1)\rho; the z statistic has that variance instead of 1.









Answer





1 + 99 \cdot 0.1 = 10.9. The z statistic has SD \sqrt{10.9} = 3.30, so P(|z| > 1.96) = 2\Phi(-1.96/3.30) = 2\Phi(-0.59) = 0.55: 55 % false positives instead of 5 %.

title: Exercise: from measurements to claims
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

identify the unit of replication in an imaging experiment and analyse at that level,
compute a paired and an unpaired comparison of experiment means by hand, and explain why cells as n misleads,
explain a p-value and a confidence interval in words, and report an effect size with a CI,
count the expected false hits among many features and apply Bonferroni and Benjamini–Hochberg,
recognise a design that is confounded with a batch, and fix the design.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the two demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.
