title: Exercise: from measurements to claims
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Standard error (SE)
the wobble of an estimate between repeated experiments; SD/\sqrt n for a mean of n independent values


p-value
how often chance alone (no effect) gives a result at least this extreme


95 % CI
estimate \pm\, t_{0.975}\cdotSE (about ± 2 SE): the effects compatible with the data


Unit of replication
the level at which the treatment was applied independently (experiment, animal, well)


Pseudoreplication
treating dependent measurements (cells of one dish) as independent replicates


Paired design
both conditions in every experiment; compare within each


Bonferroni
reject when p \le \alpha/m (m tests)


Benjamini–Hochberg
sort the p-values; the largest k with p_{(k)} \le k\,q/m; reject the k smallest



Critical values of the t-distribution, t_{0.975}: 4.30 (2 degrees of freedom), 2.78 (4 df), 2.07 (22 df), 1.96 (very many).

title: Exercise: from measurements to claims
text:
By hand
B1. Three experiments (days), four cells per condition each:




control
treated




day 1
10, 11, 12, 11
12, 13, 14, 13


day 2
14, 15, 13, 14
15, 16, 14, 15


day 3
8, 9, 7, 8
10, 9, 11, 10




Compute the experiment means, and the paired differences treated − control per day.
Paired analysis: mean difference, SD of the differences, SE, t. Is it significant at 5 % (2 df)? Give the 95 % CI.
Unpaired analysis of the experiment means (3 against 3): the two means, their SDs, the SE of the difference and t (4 df). Significant?
Cells as n (12 against 12): the pooled two-sample test gives t \approx 1.65 (22 df). Now imagine 100 cells per experiment with the same spread: t becomes about 8.6. Which analyses are right, which is wrong, and why does the paired one win?

B2. 200 features, none with a real effect, each tested at \alpha = 0.05. (a) How many “hits” do you expect? (b) What is the probability of at least one (independent tests)? (c) What is the Bonferroni threshold?
B3. Ten sorted p-values: 0.001, 0.004, 0.012, 0.02, 0.03, 0.2, 0.4, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9. How many hits at \alpha = 0.05 (a) uncorrected, (b) with Bonferroni, (c) with Benjamini–Hochberg at q = 0.05?
B4. A plate: controls in columns 1–2, treatment A in columns 3–12, imaged from left to right over two hours while the focus drifts slowly. (a) What could go wrong? (b) How would you lay out and image the plate instead?
B5. Rewrite the sentence “Treated cells were significantly larger (p < 0.0001, n = 2400)” into a good report. What extra information do you need?






Solutions





B1. (a) Control means 11, 14, 8; treated 13, 15, 10. Differences 2, 1, 2. (b) Mean difference 5/3 = 1.67, SD 0.58, SE = 0.58/\sqrt3 = 0.33, t = 5.0 > 4.30: significant (p = 0.038). 95 % CI: 1.67 \pm 4.30 \cdot 0.33 = 0.23 to 3.10. (c) Means 11 and 12.67 (difference 1.67); SDs 3.0 and 2.52; SE of the difference \sqrt{(9 + 6.33)/3} = 2.26; t = 0.74 < 2.78: not significant. (d) Right: the paired analysis (the design is paired: both conditions every day), and the unpaired analysis of experiment means (valid, but it throws away the pairing). Wrong: cells as n. Its t = 1.65 is not “nearly significant evidence”; it treats 12 cells as 12 independent replicates. With 100 cells per experiment the same data would give t \approx 8.6 and a tiny p-value, although nothing about the evidence changed (still three days). The paired analysis wins because the day-to-day differences (means 8 to 14) are much larger than the treatment effect; comparing within each day removes them.
B2. (a) 200 \cdot 0.05 = 10. (b) 1 - 0.95^{200} = 0.99996: practically certain. (c) 0.05/200 = 0.00025.
B3. (a) Five p-values \le 0.05. (b) Bonferroni threshold 0.005: 0.001 and 0.004, 2 hits. (c) BH lines k \cdot 0.005: 0.005, 0.010, 0.015, 0.020, 0.025, … The largest k with p_{(k)} \le its line: k = 4 (0.02 \le 0.020; 0.03 > 0.025, and no later p-value is below its line). 4 hits.
B4. (a) The treatment is confounded with the plate position (edge columns, evaporation) and with time (focus drift, bleaching, cells changing during two hours): any difference between columns 1–2 and the rest could be position or time, not treatment. (b) Spread controls over the whole plate (e.g. in every row, also in the middle), randomise or balance the positions of the conditions, avoid or fill the edge wells, and image in a randomised (or interleaved) order; replicate on several plates and days, with controls on every plate.
B5. For example: “Treated cells were 12 % larger than controls (95 % CI 4 % to 20 %; mean of per-experiment medians, n = 4 independent experiments, 600 cells each; paired t-test, p = 0.02).” Needed: the effect size and its CI; the unit of replication and its n (experiments, not cells); how values were aggregated; the test; the number of features tested if this was one of many (and the correction).




Math questions
B6. (math) In the two-level model y_{ec} = \mu + u_e + \varepsilon_{ec} (E experiments, m cells each, u_e \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2), \varepsilon_{ec} \sim N(0, \sigma^2), independent), derive the variance of the grand mean and the design effect 1 + (m-1)\rho with \rho = \sigma_u^2/(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2). What is n_{\text{eff}} for m = 500, \rho = 0.2, E = 3?
B7. (math) Derive the false-positive rate of the cells-as-n z-test under no effect, 2\,\Phi\big(-1.96/\sqrt{1 + (m-1)\rho}\big), and evaluate it for m = 10, 100, 1000 at \rho = 0.1.
B8. (math) Show that the paired difference of experiment means does not contain u_e. When does pairing lose power compared with the unpaired test of experiment means?
B9. (math) Prove that Bonferroni controls the family-wise error rate without any independence assumption. Show with B3 that Benjamini–Hochberg can reject a hypothesis with p > \alpha/m.






Solutions (math)





B6. \bar y_e = \mu + u_e + \bar\varepsilon_e with \text{Var}(\bar\varepsilon_e) = \sigma^2/m, so \text{Var}(\bar y_e) = \sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2/m. The grand mean \bar y = \frac1E\sum_e \bar y_e averages E independent experiment means: \text{Var}(\bar y) = \sigma_u^2/E + \sigma^2/(Em). If all Em cells were independent with variance \sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2, it would be (\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2)/(Em). Ratio: \frac{m\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2}{\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2} = 1 + (m - 1)\frac{\sigma_u^2}{\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2} = 1 + (m-1)\rho. With m = 500, \rho = 0.2: design effect 1 + 499 \cdot 0.2 = 100.8; n_{\text{eff}} = 1500/100.8 = 14.9 cells’ worth of information, close to the limit E/\rho = 15. 1500 cells from 3 experiments are worth about 15 independent cells.
B7. Under no effect, \bar y_1 - \bar y_0 has variance 2(\sigma_u^2/E + \sigma^2/(Em)) = \frac{2(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2)}{Em}\,(1 + (m-1)\rho) by B6. The cells-as-n statistic divides by \sqrt{2(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2)/(Em)}, so z \sim N(0, 1 + (m-1)\rho). It rejects when |z| > 1.96: P = 2\,P\big(Z > 1.96/\sqrt{1 + (m-1)\rho}\big) = 2\Phi\big(-1.96/\sqrt{1 + (m-1)\rho}\big). At \rho = 0.1: m = 10: \sqrt{1.9} = 1.38, 2\Phi(-1.42) = 0.155; m = 100: \sqrt{10.9} = 3.30, 2\Phi(-0.594) = 0.553; m = 1000: \sqrt{100.9} = 10.04, 2\Phi(-0.195) = 0.845.
B8. With both conditions in experiment e: \bar y_{e,T} = \mu + \tau + u_e + \bar\varepsilon_{e,T} and \bar y_{e,C} = \mu + u_e + \bar\varepsilon_{e,C}; the difference is \tau + \bar\varepsilon_{e,T} - \bar\varepsilon_{e,C}, without u_e, with variance 2\sigma^2/m instead of 2(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2/m). Pairing loses only when \sigma_u is about 0 (nothing to remove): then it has E - 1 degrees of freedom instead of 2E - 2, a larger critical value (t_{0.975} = 4.30 instead of 2.78 for E = 3), and slightly less power. It also loses if the “pairs” do not really share a day effect.
B9. Let N be the set of true null hypotheses, |N| \le m. Each null p-value is uniform, so P(p_i \le \alpha/m) = \alpha/m. P(\text{any false hit}) = P\big(\bigcup_{i \in N}\{p_i \le \alpha/m\}\big) \le \sum_{i \in N} \alpha/m \le \alpha, by the union bound, which needs no independence. In B3, BH rejects p = 0.012 and p = 0.02, both above \alpha/m = 0.005.

title: Exercise: from measurements to claims
text:
Explore: cells, experiments, pairs
A simulated experiment with two conditions: E experiments, m cells per experiment and condition, a day-to-day SD (shared by all cells of an experiment), a cell-to-cell SD and a true effect. Designs: independent (each experiment does one condition), paired (both conditions in every experiment), confounded (all treated experiments in a later batch, shifted by the batch shift). The SuperPlot shows cells as small dots coloured by experiment (at most 80 drawn per experiment) and experiment means as big markers. Three analyses: cells as n, experiment means as n, paired experiment means, each with the estimate, 95 % CI and p. The bars show the share of p < 0.05 over 1000 repetitions (the false-positive rate when the true effect is 0, the power otherwise). The last plot shows the SE of the effect against m: the true one, and what cells-as-n claims.



P1. Preset 1000 cells, no effect. Read the estimate, CI and p of the three analyses, and the shares of p < 0.05. Which analysis would you believe?
P2. Keep everything but set the cells per experiment to 10, then 100. Read the false-positive rate of cells as n. Compare with the formula of B7: here \rho = 1/(1 + 4) = 0.2.
P3. Preset more cells does not help (true effect 1, 1000 cells per experiment), then more experiments does (10 experiments of 20 cells). Compare the power of the experiments-as-n analysis, and look at the SE plot.
P4. Preset paired design wins. Compare the paired and the unpaired analysis of the same experiment means (p and CI), and their power over 1000 repetitions. What do the lines in the SuperPlot show?
P5. Preset confounded with the day: no treatment effect, but every treated experiment was done in a later batch. Read the estimate and the p-values. Increase the number of experiments to 10: does it help? What would?
P6. With the independent design and no effect, set the day-to-day SD to 0. What happens to the false-positive rate of cells as n? Why is this no excuse to analyse cells as n?






Solutions





P1. Cells as n: estimate 0.65 [0.54, 0.75], p = 2.6 \cdot 10^{-31}. Experiments as n: the same estimate, CI −2.27 to 3.57, p = 0.49. Over 1000 repetitions with no effect, cells as n gives p < 0.05 in 89 % (88.5 %) of them, experiments as n in 4.0 %. Believe the experiment-level analysis: the estimate is the same, but only its CI reflects the day-to-day variation.
P2. m = 10: 25 % false positives (25.1 %); m = 100: 69 % (68.8 %); m = 1000 (P1): 89 %. The formula with \rho = 0.2: 0.24, 0.67 and 0.89. It fits well even with only 3 experiments per condition.
P3. 1000 cells per experiment, 3 experiments per condition: power 12.5 %. 10 experiments of 20 cells (far fewer cells in total): 46 %. In the SE plot the true SE flattens out at about 0.82 beyond ~100 cells (for 3 experiments), while cells as n claims 0.06 at 1000 cells.
P4. Paired: estimate 0.87, CI 0.30 to 1.45, p = 0.023. Unpaired experiment means: the same estimate, CI −1.90 to 3.64, p = 0.43. Power over 1000 repetitions: 84 % paired, 14 % unpaired. The lines join the control and treated means of each experiment: they all go up by about the same amount, although the experiments sit at very different levels. Pairing compares the slopes, not the levels.
P5. Estimate 2.53 (no real effect; the batch shift is 1.5 and this run is a little lucky), and even the experiment-level analysis gives p = 0.029. Over 1000 repetitions it rejects in about 21 % of them instead of 5 %, and the estimate is always biased by the batch shift. More experiments do not help: with 10 experiments the estimate is 1.51 (the batch shift, now measured precisely), p = 0.005, and the experiment-level test rejects in 88 % of repetitions. More data make the batch difference more certain, not the treatment effect. Only the design helps: every batch must contain both conditions (or pair within a batch).
P6. With day-to-day SD 0, cells as n rejects in about 4 % of the null experiments, like the experiment-level test: cells are then really independent. But you cannot know beforehand that days do not differ (in practice they nearly always do), and aggregating first costs little when they do not. Analyse at the level of the unit of replication.

title: Exercise: from measurements to claims
section: Explore: many features on a plate
text:
Explore: many features on a plate
A 384-well plate (or 96), half treated, half control, with m features measured per well. A share of the features carries a real treatment effect (in SDs). Plate effects: a left–right and a top–bottom gradient and edge wells, which each feature feels with its own sensitivity. Layouts: treated on the left half, random, or random per row. Left: the plate map of one feature (treated wells outlined). Middle: the histogram of all p-values (grey: the null features). Right: the sorted p-values against their rank on log axes, with the uncorrected line \alpha, the Bonferroni line \alpha/m and the BH line k\alpha/m; green dots are real features, red dots null features (known from the simulation). The table counts the hits of each method and how many are false.



F1. Preset 300 null features. Read the hits of each method. Describe the histogram of p-values.
F2. Set m to 50 and to 500. How many uncorrected hits, and how many does \alpha m predict?
F3. Preset 10 % real: BH finds most. Read hits, false hits and true hits for each method. Where are the real features in the rank plot?
F4. Preset gradient + treated on the left. Read the hits. Look at the plate map of the smallest-p feature. Why does Bonferroni not help?
F5. Preset randomised layout fixes it (the same gradient). Read the hits. Then try random per row.
F6. Preset edge wells, row-blocked layout: edge effect, a top–bottom gradient and 10 % real features, with a balanced layout. How do the three methods do? Then untick 384 wells (96 wells, same settings): what happens, and why?






Solutions





F1. Uncorrected 15 hits (all false), Bonferroni 0, BH 0. The histogram is flat at about m/20 = 15 per bin: under no effect every p-value is equally likely.
F2. m = 50: 1 hit (\alpha m = 2.5); m = 500: 27 hits (\alpha m = 25). The number of false hits grows in proportion to the number of features.
F3. 30 real features. Uncorrected: 43 hits, 14 false, 29 true. Bonferroni: 13 hits, all true. BH: 24 hits, 2 false, 22 true. The real features have the smallest p-values (green dots at low ranks, below the BH line); the null ones continue as the uniform curve. BH finds most real features with few false ones; Bonferroni is safe but misses more than half.
F4. 281 of 300 features “significant” uncorrected, 249 after Bonferroni, 281 with BH; none of them real. The plate map shows the left–right gradient, and the treated wells are all on one side. Every feature that feels the gradient differs between the halves; the p-values are tiny, so no correction for the number of tests can remove them. The problem is bias (confounding), not chance.
F5. Random layout: 37 uncorrected hits, 0 after Bonferroni or BH. The gradient now hits both conditions alike on average; it only adds noise (and a little chance imbalance, which pushes many features together, hence 37 instead of 15 uncorrected). Random per row: 13 uncorrected hits, 0 corrected.
F6. 384 wells: uncorrected 32 hits (8 false), Bonferroni 8 (all true), BH 19 (1 false). With 96 wells: uncorrected 19 hits (6 false, 13 true); Bonferroni and BH find only 1. With a quarter of the wells the SE of each comparison doubles, and an effect of 0.35 SD hardly stands out from 300 tests.

title: Exercise: from measurements to claims
text:
Where this leads
The evaluation of a method (units 1–3) and the analysis of an experiment (this unit) share one lesson: count what is independent, and decide before you look. The modern deep learning day reuses the object matching and AP of unit 1 for detection.

title: Neighbours, parents and children
text:
About this lecture
So far every column described one object on its own. Many questions are about relations: how crowded is a cell, which nucleus does a spot belong to, are the cells clustered?

Three definitions of neighbour, three different answers.
Per object: number of neighbours, percent touching, first and second closest, the angle between them.
Population: the nearest-neighbour distance against a random pattern (Clark–Evans), and the border problem.
Parents and children: spots in nuclei, nuclei in cells; assignment by overlap or by centroid, and the cases in between.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Third unit of the measurements day. Two kinds of “between” measurements: between objects (this unit) and between channels (next unit). Both need a rule for which pixels or objects are paired, and both are easy to over-interpret. Region adjacency was met on the labelling day; the distance transform and its feature transform are the morphology day’s.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Neighbours, parents and children
text:
Who is my neighbour?
Three common definitions, applied to the same 40 nuclei (demo, random placement):

Adjacent: the segmented objects share a boundary (4- or 8-neighbouring pixels). Here the cell bodies, grown 9 px from the nuclei: 1.15 neighbours on average.
Within distance r: the closest pixels of the two objects are at most r apart. Nuclei, r = 10 px: 0.45; r = 20: 1.45; r = 30: 2.45.
Expand until adjacent: grow every object into the background until it meets another, so the whole image is divided among them. 4.90.

The answer is a property of the definition as much as of the cells. Report it with the number.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Neighbours, parents and children
text:
Expand until adjacent
Give every background pixel to the nearest object (the distance transform of the morphology day, keeping which object was nearest):

The result tiles the image: a Voronoi tessellation of the objects. The boundaries are the midlines between objects, the same picture as the watershed of the distance transform (watershed day).
Neighbours = objects whose regions touch. Every object gets some, however far apart the objects are.
In the interior of a large random pattern the average is close to 6 (demo: 5.62 for interior objects).
Cheap to compute: one exact distance transform with nearest-object labels.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Neighbours, parents and children
text:
The math: Voronoi neighbours
The region of object k: V_k = \{\mathbf x : d(\mathbf x, O_k) \le d(\mathbf x, O_j)\ \forall j\}, with d(\mathbf x, O) = \min_{\mathbf y \in O} \lVert \mathbf x - \mathbf y \rVert.

The feature transform gives, for every pixel, its nearest object pixel \mathbf y^*(\mathbf x), and the label at \mathbf y^* is the region. Same cost as the distance transform.
For points as objects, the regions are convex polygons and the neighbour graph is the Delaunay triangulation, a planar graph. Euler’s formula V - E + F = 2 with every face a triangle gives E \le 3V - 6, so the mean degree 2E/V < 6.
Regions at the image border are cut off, so border objects have fewer neighbours: a bias towards lower counts.

Percent touching tells a cell in a dense sheet (close to 100 %) from one with a free edge. Distances are between centroids here; boundary-to-boundary distances are another choice.
The neighbour graph: objects as nodes, neighbours as edges. It was the region adjacency graph on the labelling day; the graph cuts day uses graphs of pixels the same way.

title: Neighbours, parents and children
text:
Clustered, random or regular?
Compare the mean nearest-neighbour distance \bar d with what a random (Poisson) pattern of the same density would give: the Clark–Evans ratio
R = \frac{\bar d_{\text{observed}}}{\bar d_{\text{random}}}, \qquad \bar d_{\text{random}} = \frac{0.5}{\sqrt{\rho}},\ \rho = \frac{\text{number of objects}}{\text{area}}.

R < 1: clustered; R \approx 1: random; R > 1: regular (cells avoid each other).
Demo (40 nuclei in 256 × 256 px, \bar d_{\text{random}} = 20.2 px): clustered 0.73, random placement 1.11, regular 1.86.
Why 1.11 and not 1: nuclei cannot overlap, so very short distances never occur. Real objects are never exactly Poisson.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Neighbours, parents and children
section: The math: the Poisson nearest neighbour
text:
The math: the Poisson nearest neighbour
Points scattered independently with density \rho: the number in a disc of radius r is Poisson with mean \rho\pi r^2.

P(D > r) = P(\text{no other point within } r) = e^{-\rho \pi r^2}, so the density of the nearest-neighbour distance is f(r) = 2\pi\rho r\, e^{-\rho\pi r^2} (the curve in the demo).
E[D] = \int_0^\infty P(D > r)\,dr = \int_0^\infty e^{-\rho\pi r^2} dr = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt\rho}.
For n points the standard error of \bar d is \approx 0.26136/\sqrt{n\rho}, which gives a z-test for R = 1 (Clark & Evans, 1954).
Edge effect: near the border the true nearest neighbour may be outside the image, so observed distances are too long and R is biased upwards.

title: Neighbours, parents and children
text:
Objects at the image border
Objects near the edge have fewer neighbours (part of their surroundings is not in the image), and their nearest neighbour may be outside.

Demo (60 nuclei, expansion): interior objects 5.69 neighbours, objects whose region touches the border 4.29.
Remove border objects before measuring: their neighbours lose a neighbour, and the new outer layer is biased instead.
Guard zone: measure only objects whose centroid is at least g from the border, but let all objects count as neighbours. Unbiased, at the cost of fewer measured objects (43 of 60 here, mean 5.63).

The same idea as the unbiased counting frame of the labelling day: decide which objects are measured separately from which ones exist.

title: Neighbours, parents and children
text:
Parents and children
Objects of one kind inside objects of another: spots in nuclei, nuclei in cells, cytoplasm = cell minus nucleus.

Parent of a child = the parent label with the largest overlap, or the label at the child’s centroid.
Per parent: child count (“spots per nucleus”), the mean or sum of a child feature, distances of children to the parent’s centre or edge (normalised as in the radial rings of the first unit).
Explicit cases: children outside any parent (spots in the cytoplasm when the parents are nuclei), children across two parents.
Overlap of two objects A and B: the share of A inside B, the share of B inside A, and the Jaccard index |A\cap B|/|A \cup B| (the thresholding day). Matching objects of two segmentations by overlap is the evaluation day.

title: Neighbours, parents and children
text:
The math: assignment
Child c with pixels C, parents P_1, \dots, P_m:
\text{overlap rule: } \operatorname{parent}(c) = \arg\max_k |C \cap P_k| \ (\text{none if all are } 0), \qquad \text{centroid rule: } \operatorname{parent}(c) = L_P(\operatorname{round}(\bar{\mathbf x}_C)).

Both rules need one pass over the pixels: accumulate |C \cap P_k| in a sparse table indexed by (child, parent).
Child count per parent = number of children assigned to it; per-parent aggregates (mean child intensity, total child area) are sums over the same table.

title: Neighbours, parents and children
text:
Summary

“Number of neighbours” depends on the definition: adjacent boundaries, closest pixels within r, or expansion until adjacent (a Voronoi tessellation, about 6 neighbours inside a random pattern).
Percent touching, the closest objects and the angle between them are per-object relation columns.
Clark–Evans R compares the mean nearest-neighbour distance with a random pattern: < 1 clustered, > 1 regular.
Border objects lose neighbours: use a guard zone, not removal.
Children get a parent by largest overlap or by centroid; count, aggregate, and flag the children outside or across parents.

title: Quiz: regularisation
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A restoration minimises data term + λ · penalty; σn is the noise standard deviation.

Q1. In “data term + λ · penalty”, what does each of the three parts express?






Hint





One is about how the image was made, one about the object, one about trust.









Answer





The data term measures how well the blurred estimate explains the data (the forward model and the noise). The penalty measures how implausible the estimate is as an object (prior knowledge: small, smooth, non-negative, piecewise constant). λ sets how much the prior counts relative to the data.




Q2. A restoration with the roughness penalty turns a sharp step into a smooth S-curve. Which penalty would keep the step, and what would it do to a gentle ramp?






Hint





Which penalty charges a jump by its size rather than its square?









Answer





Total variation, \sum|x_{i+1} - x_i|: a single sharp step costs the same as a ramp of the same height, so it has no reason to round the step. But it prefers flat pieces, so a gentle ramp is turned into a staircase of small flat steps (and small bright spots are shrunk).




Q3. With the discrepancy principle the RMS residual should equal σn. What does it mean if the residual is much smaller than σn?






Hint





The residual is data minus the blurred estimate. What is left in it if it is smaller than the noise?









Answer





The estimate explains part of the noise as if it were signal: it is over-fitted, λ is too small. A good estimate leaves behind about the noise itself.




Q4. The noise level doubles. Should the best λ grow or shrink? By roughly what factor, according to the MAP reading?






Hint





λ = σn² / τ².









Answer





It should grow: the data deserve less trust. In the MAP reading λ = σn²/τ², so doubling σn multiplies λ by 4 (if the prior stays the same).




Q5. What are the two branches of the L-curve, and where is the good λ?






Hint





Log residual norm across, log penalty up.









Answer





For small λ the penalty explodes (noise is fitted) for almost no improvement of the fit: a steep, vertical branch. For large λ the fit gets worse for almost no gain in smoothness: a flat, horizontal branch. The good λ is at the corner where the two meet.




Q6. Tikhonov with λ = 0.01: what fraction of a frequency with blur gain s = 0.1 is kept? And with s = 0.5?






Hint





\varphi = s^2/(s^2 + \lambda).









Answer





s = 0.1: 0.01/(0.01 + 0.01) = 0.5. s = 0.5: 0.25/0.26 = 0.96. The roll-off sits where s^2 \approx \lambda, here s \approx 0.1.




Q7. An iterative restoration is run for 10 000 iterations “to be sure it has converged”. Why can that be worse than stopping at 30?






Hint





Which frequencies does the iteration add last?









Answer





Starting from a flat image, the iteration first restores the strong (low) frequencies and only later the weak (high) ones, which carry mostly noise. Running to convergence approaches the inverse filter, which amplifies that noise. The error against the truth is U-shaped in the number of iterations (semi-convergence): the number of iterations acts like λ.




Q8. (math) Show that for a Landweber step \mathbf x_{k+1} = \mathbf x_k + A^\top(\mathbf y - A\mathbf x_k) from \mathbf x_0 = 0, the component along the i-th singular vector is multiplied by 1 - (1 - s_i^2)^k compared with the inverse.






Hint





Write x_{k,i} = \mathbf v_i^\top\mathbf x_k and use A^\top A\mathbf v_i = s_i^2\mathbf v_i.









Answer





With c_i = \mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y: x_{k+1,i} = (1 - s_i^2)x_{k,i} + s_i c_i. The fixed point is c_i/s_i (the inverse); the distance to it shrinks by (1 - s_i^2) per step, from c_i/s_i at k = 0. So x_{k,i} = (1 - (1 - s_i^2)^k)\,c_i/s_i.

Idea

Restoration
minimise \lVert A x - y\rVert^2 + \lambda\cdot\text{penalty}(x)


Penalties
energy \lVert x\rVert^2; roughness \lVert D^2 x\rVert^2; total variation \sum\lvert x_{i+1} - x_i\rvert; constraint x \ge 0

From λ = 1 to 100, ρ almost doubles (0.303 to 0.561) while η falls only by 3: a flat, horizontal branch. The corner lies around λ = 0.01 to 1. (The demo’s corner is λ = 0.18.)
B5. (A) total variation, (B) energy (it shrinks everything towards 0, including the mean), (C) roughness (smooth, but nothing stops the undershoots), (D) roughness + non-negativity.
B6. (a) It grows: the target residual σn is larger, and the residual grows with λ. (b) Earlier: the noise appears in the iterates sooner. (c) Smoothed noise has little power at high frequencies, so the estimate can only explain it at low frequencies: the residual cannot reach σn until the estimate is very smooth. The discrepancy principle assumes white noise. (In the demo: λ = 11.7 instead of the best 0.32.)




Math questions
B7. (math) With the SVD A = U\Sigma V^\top, show that the Tikhonov solution of \min\|A\mathbf x - \mathbf y\|^2 + \lambda\|\mathbf x\|^2 is \hat{\mathbf x} = \sum_i \frac{s_i^2}{s_i^2 + \lambda}\frac{\mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y}{s_i}\mathbf v_i. With \mathbf y = A\mathbf x + \mathbf n, what noise does term i carry?
B8. (math) Show that the squared residual \|A\hat{\mathbf x}_\lambda - \mathbf y\|^2 of B7 increases with λ (so the discrepancy equation has one solution).
B9. (math) Gaussian noise of variance σn² and a Gaussian prior D\mathbf x \sim \mathcal N(0, \tau^2 I): show that the most probable \mathbf x given \mathbf y is Tikhonov’s with λ = σn²/τ².
B10. (math) Show that for small s^2, Landweber after k steps keeps about the same fraction as Tikhonov with λ = 1/k: compare 1 - e^{-ks^2} with s^2/(s^2 + 1/k) at s^2 = 1/k and for s^2 \ll 1/k and s^2 \gg 1/k.






Solutions (math)





B7. The normal equations (A^\top A + \lambda I)\mathbf x = A^\top\mathbf y become, with A^\top A = V\Sigma^2V^\top and A^\top\mathbf y = V\Sigma U^\top\mathbf y, and \mathbf x = V\mathbf z: (s_i^2 + \lambda)z_i = s_i\,\mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y. So z_i = \frac{s_i}{s_i^2 + \lambda}\mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y = \frac{s_i^2}{s_i^2 + \lambda}\frac{\mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y}{s_i}. With \mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y = s_i x_i + n_i, term i is \varphi_i x_i + \varphi_i n_i/s_i: the noise n_i is multiplied by \varphi_i/s_i = s_i/(s_i^2 + \lambda) \le 1/(2\sqrt\lambda), bounded however small s_i is.
B8. A\hat{\mathbf x} - \mathbf y = \sum_i (\varphi_i - 1)(\mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y)\mathbf u_i plus the part of \mathbf y outside the range of A (independent of λ). So \|A\hat{\mathbf x} - \mathbf y\|^2 = \sum_i\big(\frac{\lambda}{s_i^2 + \lambda}\big)^2(\mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y)^2 + \text{const}, and each \frac{\lambda}{s_i^2 + \lambda} increases with λ.
B9. p(\mathbf x\mid\mathbf y) \propto p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x)\,p(\mathbf x) \propto \exp\!\big(-\|A\mathbf x - \mathbf y\|^2/2\sigma_n^2\big)\exp\!\big(-\|D\mathbf x\|^2/2\tau^2\big). Maximising it = minimising \frac{1}{2\sigma_n^2}\|A\mathbf x - \mathbf y\|^2 + \frac{1}{2\tau^2}\|D\mathbf x\|^2; multiply by 2\sigma_n^2: \|A\mathbf x - \mathbf y\|^2 + \frac{\sigma_n^2}{\tau^2}\|D\mathbf x\|^2.
B10. (1 - s^2)^k = e^{k\ln(1 - s^2)} \approx e^{-ks^2} for small s^2. At s^2 = 1/k: Landweber 1 - e^{-1} = 0.63, Tikhonov 0.5. For s^2 \ll 1/k both are \approx ks^2; for s^2 \gg 1/k both are \approx 1. The two curves have the same position and similar shape (Landweber’s step is a little sharper).

title: Exercise: regularisation
text:
Explore
A 1D profile (256 samples) is blurred with a Gaussian (σ = 3 samples) and noise σn = 0.02 is added (fixed seed). Top left: truth (dashed), data (thin blue), estimate (red). Top right: the residual (data − blurred estimate) with the ±σn band, or (choose show) the filter factors with the blur’s |H|. Bottom left: the L-curve (penalty against residual norm, log–log) with the current λ (red), the corner (orange) and the discrepancy λ (green). Bottom right: error against the truth (orange) and RMS residual (blue) for 37 values of λ, with σn dashed; vertical lines: current, discrepancy and corner. Restore by switches between λ and stopping Landweber after k iterations. Total variation and non-negativity are computed iteratively; their curves fill in after a moment.



E1. Presets λ too small and λ too large. For each, give the error and the residual from the readout, and compare the residual with σn. Look at the residual panel: where does the residual of the large λ show structure?
E2. Presets discrepancy principle and L-curve corner. Which λ does each choose, with which error? Which λ is best on the path, and how much better is it?
E3. Preset the two rules disagree (correlated noise). Read the discrepancy λ, the corner λ and the best λ with their errors. Which rule is closer to the best, and why does the other fail?
E4. Presets roughness keeps the mean, energy shrinks it, TV keeps the step, staircases the ramp, TV shrinks the narrow peak and non-negativity removes the dips. For each, write one sentence on what the penalty kept and what it destroyed, with a number from the readout or the plot.
E5. Preset iterations as λ: semi-convergence. At which k is the error smallest? Give the error at k = 100, 1000 and 10 000. Which k does the discrepancy rule choose? Watch the filter factors while you move k.
E6. Set the penalty to energy (profile step and ramp, no correlated noise). Compare the discrepancy λ, the corner λ and the best λ, with their errors. Which rule does well here?






Solutions





E1. λ = 10⁻⁶: error 2.29, residual 0.0151, below σn = 0.02: the estimate fits the noise and oscillates wildly. λ = 100: error 0.0767, residual 0.0351, above σn; the residual shows bumps at the step edges and at the top and foot of the ramp: image structure the over-smooth estimate failed to explain.
E2. Discrepancy: λ = 2.57, error 0.0588. Corner: λ = 0.178, error 0.0539. Best on the path: λ = 0.1, error 0.0537. Both rules land near the best error; the corner is almost optimal, the discrepancy principle slightly over-smooths (9 % more error).
E3. Discrepancy λ = 11.7 (error 0.0651), corner λ = 0.056 (error 0.0611), best λ = 0.316 (error 0.0586). The corner is closer here. The discrepancy principle assumes white noise; correlated noise has little high-frequency power, so the residual stays below σn until the estimate is very smooth.
E4. Energy (λ = 0.3) shrinks the whole profile: mean 0.256 against 0.331 in the truth (factor 1/1.3); roughness keeps the mean (0.333). TV (λ = 0.01) keeps the step sharp and flat at 0.80 but turns the ramp into small flat steps; its error 0.0219 is far below the best roughness error (0.0537), because this profile is mostly flat pieces. TV on the narrow peak (λ = 0.02): the peak of height 1.0 comes out at 0.31; TV pays for every jump, and a narrow spot has two jumps for little area. Non-negativity: roughness with λ = 10⁻⁴ dips to −1.16 (error 0.323); adding x ≥ 0 removes the dips (minimum 0) and the error falls to 0.109.
E5. Smallest error at k = 32 (0.0542). At k = 100: 0.0586, at 1000: 0.143, at 10 000: 0.375 (semi-convergence). The residual keeps falling all the time. The discrepancy rule stops at k = 6: early, a little blurred, but safe. The filter-factor step moves from high |H| (low frequencies) towards low |H| as k grows.
E6. Discrepancy λ = 0.0189 (error 0.0552), corner λ = 0.0056 (error 0.0635), best λ = 0.0178 (error 0.0553). Here the discrepancy principle is almost exactly right and the corner too far to the left: the rules have no guarantee, and checking with a known-truth test is the honest way.

title: Exercise: regularisation
text:
Where this leads
The next unit takes the probabilistic reading seriously for photon counts: Richardson–Lucy maximises the Poisson likelihood with an iteration that keeps every pixel non-negative, and its number of iterations is the regularisation parameter, exactly like Landweber’s here. The same “data + λ · penalty” pattern returns on the graph-cut day (with labels instead of intensities) and in the electives on Markov random fields (total variation) and wavelets (sparsity).

title: Region properties and moments
text:
About this lecture
The last unit turned a mask into a label image. Now we measure each object: one row per label, one column per property.

Area, centroid, bounding box: sums over the pixels of the object.
Perimeter: three ways to count it, and why the simplest one is 27 % too long at any resolution.
Second moments: the covariance matrix of the pixel coordinates, its eigenvectors (orientation) and the equivalent ellipse: PCA of one object.
The Euler number: objects minus holes, counted from 2 × 2 patterns without labelling.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Coordinates: x = column (right), y = row (down), pixel centres at integers. Angles are given counter-clockwise as seen on the screen (the course convention). PCA is recalled from the pca/ unit of day 1, not re-taught. The covariance is divided by n, as in pca/.

title: Region properties and moments
section: One scan, one row per object
text:
One scan, one row per object
Everything on this slide is a sum over the pixels \Omega_k of object k, so a single raster scan computes it for all labels at once.

Area A = number of pixels (times the pixel area for µm²).
Centroid (\bar x, \bar y) = mean pixel position: the balance point of the object.
Bounding box: smallest and largest x and y. Extent = area / box area (1 for an axis-aligned rectangle, \pi/4 for a disc).
Touches the border: box reaches the image edge (truncated object, see the last unit of the day).

title: Region properties and moments
text:
The math: moments
Raw moments of object \Omega: \quad m_{pq} = \sum_{(x,y)\in\Omega} x^p y^q.

m_{00} = A, centroid \bar x = m_{10}/m_{00}, \bar y = m_{01}/m_{00}.
Central moments \mu_{pq} = \sum_{\Omega} (x - \bar x)^p (y - \bar y)^q do not change when the object is moved.
From the raw moments, without a second scan: \mu_{20} = m_{20} - m_{10}^2/m_{00}, \mu_{11} = m_{11} - m_{10} m_{01}/m_{00}, \mu_{02} = m_{02} - m_{01}^2/m_{00}.
These are the integrals \iint x^p y^q \, dx\,dy over the shape, turned into sums with one sample per pixel.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Region properties and moments
text:
Perimeter: three estimates


Edge count (left): pixel edges between object and background. A staircase is as long as its two legs, so a digital disc gets about 8r instead of 2\pi r: 27 % too long, at every resolution.
Chain code (right): walk the boundary pixel centres with steps 1 and \sqrt 2: a few per cent off, depending on the direction.
Crofton: count crossings of the boundary with lines in 4 directions: within about 1 % for large objects. (Better step weights, or a sub-pixel contour, also work.)
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Region properties and moments
text:
The math: where 4/\pi comes from
A boundary segment of length \ell at angle \varphi is replaced by a staircase of \ell|\cos\varphi| horizontal and \ell|\sin\varphi| vertical pixel edges. For a closed convex curve all directions occur equally, so
\frac{P_{\text{edges}}}{P} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} \big(|\cos\varphi| + |\sin\varphi|\big)\,d\varphi = \frac{4}{\pi} \approx 1.273.
Finer pixels make the staircase finer but not shorter: the error does not go away.
Cauchy–Crofton: P = \tfrac12 \int_0^\pi \int n(\theta, s)\,ds\,d\theta, with n the number of crossings of the line at angle \theta and offset s. With rows, columns and both diagonals (spacing 1 and 1/\sqrt2): P \approx \tfrac{\pi}{8}\big(n_0 + n_{90} + (n_{45} + n_{135})/\sqrt2\big).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Region properties and moments
section: Second moments: an object is a cloud of points
text:
Second moments: an object is a cloud of points
Recall from the PCA unit (day 1): for a cloud of points, the covariance matrix S holds the spreads; it is symmetric, its eigenvalues \lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge 0 (descending) are the variances along its orthogonal eigenvectors, the principal axes.
The pixels of an object are a cloud of points (x, y):
S = \frac{1}{A}\begin{pmatrix}\mu_{20} & \mu_{11}\\ \mu_{11} & \mu_{02}\end{pmatrix}.

\mathbf v_1: the direction in which the object is longest (the orientation); \mathbf v_2 perpendicular to it.
\sqrt{\lambda_1}, \sqrt{\lambda_2}: the spread of the pixels along these axes.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Region properties and moments
text:
The equivalent ellipse

The ellipse with the same area, centroid and second moments as the object: semi-axes a = 2\sqrt{\lambda_1}, b = 2\sqrt{\lambda_2} along \mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2.

Eccentricity \sqrt{1 - \lambda_2/\lambda_1}: 0 for a disc, near 1 for a rod. Elongation \sqrt{\lambda_1/\lambda_2} = ratio of the axes.
Major and minor axis length 4\sqrt{\lambda_1}, 4\sqrt{\lambda_2}.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Region properties and moments
section: The math: orientation and the ellipse
text:
The math: orientation and the ellipse
Orientation. For S = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & c\end{pmatrix} the eigenvalues are \lambda_{1,2} = \frac{a + c}{2} \pm \sqrt{\big(\frac{a-c}{2}\big)^2 + b^2}, and \mathbf v_1 = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta) with
\theta = \tfrac12 \operatorname{atan2}(2b,\ a - c) = \tfrac12\operatorname{atan2}(2\mu_{11}, \mu_{20} - \mu_{02})
(from \tan 2\theta = 2b/(a - c), the condition that the off-diagonal entry vanishes after rotating by \theta). With y pointing down, \theta turns from x towards y, i.e. clockwise on screen; the orientation counter-clockwise on screen is -\theta.
Ellipse. A solid ellipse with semi-axes a, b has variance \frac{1}{\pi ab}\iint u^2 = a^2/4 along its major axis. So matching \lambda_1 = a^2/4 gives a = 2\sqrt{\lambda_1}. Check with a disc of radius r: \lambda = r^2/4, a = r.

title: Region properties and moments
section: Try it: moments of a shape
text:
Try it: moments of a shape




The shape (a polygon) is digitised on the pixel grid; the slider sets the pixel size. Overlays: centroid, box, the equivalent ellipse (orange), v1 (red, length 2√λ1) and v2 (green). The table compares the digitised values with the exact values of the outline. Tour: “rotate the ellipse”: λ1 = 121.25, λ2 = 24.88, θ = 28.8°; drag the shape around: nothing changes but the centroid. On the exercise page you can rotate in 15° steps: S changes completely, λ1 and λ2 stay (120.5, 25.3), θ follows. “a square”: λ1 = λ2: no orientation. “the L”: the ellipse is not the shape. “a ring”: Euler number 0. “a digital disc”: the edge count stays at 1.27 × the true perimeter at every pixel size (plot).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Region properties and moments
section: What the moments do and do not tell
text:
What the moments do and do not tell

Rotation of the object rotates the eigenvectors and leaves the eigenvalues unchanged: S = Q\Lambda Q^\top becomes (RQ)\Lambda(RQ)^\top. Area, eigenvalues, eccentricity: rotation invariant.
Equal eigenvalues (a disc, but also a square, a regular hexagon, a plus sign): every direction is a principal axis. The orientation is undefined, and noisy for nearly round objects: do not report it.
The ellipse is a summary, not the shape: an L, a ring and a solid ellipse can share it.
Invariants, in one line each: central moments (translation), normalised moments \mu_{pq}/m_{00}^{1+(p+q)/2} (scale), eigenvalues and Hu’s seven invariants (rotation). Higher moments and invariants: the moments elective.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Region properties and moments
text:
The Euler number
Euler number E = number of objects − number of holes (objects 8-connected, holes 4-connected).

A disc: 1; a ring: 0; the digit 8: −1; two discs: 2.
Counted by labelling: the objects, and the background components that do not touch the border (or via fill holes from the morphology day).
Surprise: E is local. Count the 2 \times 2 windows with exactly one object pixel (Q_1), with three (Q_3), and the diagonal pairs (Q_D): E = (Q_1 - Q_3 - 2Q_D)/4. One scan, no labelling (Gray, 1971).
Thinning (skeleton elective) must keep E: it may not cut objects or open holes. In 3D, E = objects − tunnels + cavities.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Region properties and moments
section: The math: why the bit-quads count E
text:
The math: why the bit-quads count E
Think of each object pixel as a closed unit square, and count corners (V), edges (E_d) and squares (F) of the union: Euler’s formula \chi = V - E_d + F gives objects − holes.

Each 2\times2 window is centred on one grid corner. A corner belongs to the union if any of its 4 squares is in the object; its contribution to V - E_d + F depends only on the window: +\frac14 for Q_1, 0 for Q_2 and Q_4, -\frac14 for Q_3.
A diagonal pair Q_D is the ambiguous case: with 8-connected objects the two squares are joined at the corner (-\frac12); with 4-connected objects they are not (+\frac12).
Sum over all windows (pad with background): E_8 = \tfrac14(Q_1 - Q_3 - 2Q_D), E_4 = \tfrac14(Q_1 - Q_3 + 2Q_D).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Region properties and moments
text:
Summary

One scan gives a row per object: area, centroid, box, extent, raw and central moments.
Perimeter depends on the estimator: edge count \approx 4/\pi too long at any resolution; chain code a few %; Crofton \approx 1\,\%.
S = covariance of the pixel coordinates: PCA of one object. Eigenvectors: orientation; eigenvalues: spread; equivalent ellipse with semi-axes 2\sqrt{\lambda_i}.
Rotation changes S, not \lambda_1, \lambda_2; with \lambda_1 = \lambda_2 there is no orientation.
Euler number = objects − holes, from 2 × 2 patterns.
Next unit: shape beyond moments (convex hull, Feret diameters, form factor).

title: Quiz: rectangle features
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A two-rectangle feature (left − right) is placed on a flat region of grey level 120. What is its response? And on a region that is 120 on the left and 80 on the right, with rectangles of 10 \times 10 pixels?






Answer





Flat: 100 \cdot 120 - 100 \cdot 120 = 0. Edge: 100 \cdot 120 - 100 \cdot 80 = 4000 (a mean difference of 40 grey levels).




Q2. Two rectangle sums cost 4 lookups each. Why does the two-rectangle feature need only 6?






Answer





The two rectangles share a side, so two of their corners are the same table entries. Their coefficients are added (giving \pm 2) and each shared entry is read once: 8 - 2 = 6.




Q3. Which template would you use to find (a) a thin bright vertical line, (b) a horizontal edge, (c) a round dark spot of about 10 pixels?






Answer






The three-rectangle line template across, with the centre rectangle about as wide as the line (positive response). (b) The two-rectangle edge template top − bottom. (c) Centre − surround with a centre box of about 10 pixels: a strongly negative response (the centre is darker than its surroundings).





Q4. Why is the feature response divided by the standard deviation of the detection window?






Answer





To remove the effect of contrast (lighting, camera gain): with twice the contrast every difference doubles, and so does the SD. Dividing makes the response the same. A brightness offset needs no correction, because the weights of every template sum to zero.




Q5. A 24 \times 24 window holds about 160 000 rectangle features but only 576 pixels. Is the feature set a basis? Does that matter for detection?






Answer





No: the features are far more numerous than the pixels, so they are linearly dependent (overcomplete), and the image cannot be uniquely rebuilt from them in a stable way. For detection that does not matter: the aim is to discriminate faces from background, not to reconstruct. The redundancy offers many candidate features; learning picks the useful few.




Q6. How do the 2D Haar wavelets differ from Haar-like features?






Answer





Haar wavelets use only dyadic sizes (powers of two) at fixed grid positions and form an orthonormal basis (the transform is invertible, useful for compression). Haar-like features take every size and position: an overcomplete set, with no inverse, for detection.




Q7. In a box feature stack, why does the box SD at 16 px cost the same as at 1 px?






Answer





Both come from four lookups in the table of I and four in the table of I^2, whatever the window size. Computed directly, the 16 px box (33 \times 33, 1089 pixels) would read 121 times as many pixels per window as the 1 px box (3 \times 3, 9 pixels).




Q8. (math) An edge feature of two w \times h rectangles (left − right) lies on the ramp I(x, y) = 3x + 40. What is its response divided by the area of one rectangle?






Answer





The response is -a w^2 h = -3w^2h; divided by wh: -3w, the slope times the distance w between the centres of the two rectangles.
