title: Exercise: rectangle features
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Rectangle feature
weighted sum of rectangle sums; the weights sum to zero


Edge (two rectangles)
sum(white) − sum(black), side by side or one above the other: 6 lookups


Line (three rectangles)
2\cdotsum(centre) − sum(left) − sum(right): 8 lookups


Diagonal (four rectangles)
top-left + bottom-right − top-right − bottom-left: 9 lookups


Centre − surround
sum(small box) − sum(large box)/9 (large = 3 × 3 small): 8 lookups


Lookups
the distinct table corners with a non-zero coefficient; shared corners are read once


Normalisation
divide by the window’s standard deviation (contrast) and by the rectangle area (size)


Box feature stack
box mean, box SD, centre − surround, edge across, edge down, at scales 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 px



As before, pixels are numbered from 1, x = column, y = row, and S(x, y) is the sum over columns 1..x and rows 1..y (zero for x = 0 or y = 0).

title: Exercise: rectangle features
text:
By hand
The 6 \times 6 image (row y = 1 on top) and its integral image:
I = \begin{bmatrix} 1&1&1&5&5&5 \\ 1&2&1&6&5&5 \\ 1&1&2&5&6&5 \\ 2&1&1&5&5&6 \\ 1&1&1&5&5&5 \\ 1&2&1&5&6&5 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
S = \begin{bmatrix} 0&0&0&0&0&0&0 \\ 0&1&2&3&8&13&18 \\ 0&2&5&7&18&28&38 \\ 0&3&7&11&27&43&58 \\ 0&5&10&15&36&57&78 \\ 0&6&12&18&44&70&96 \\ 0&7&15&22&53&85&116 \end{bmatrix}
(S has rows y = 0..6 and columns x = 0..6.)
B1. An edge feature, left − right, over rows 2–5: the left rectangle is columns 2–3, the right one columns 4–5. (a) Write each rectangle sum with four lookups. (b) Combine them. Which corners are shared, and what coefficients do they get? How many distinct lookups remain? (c) Compute the response and check it by adding the pixels. What does its sign say about the image?
B2. A line feature, 2\cdotcentre − left − right, over rows 2–5 with one column per rectangle: left = column 3, centre = column 4, right = column 5. (a) List the 8 lookups with their coefficients. (b) Compute the response and check it directly.
B3. Which template? A 6 \times 6 image is 1 everywhere except columns 3 and 4, which are 9 (a bright vertical bar). Four features cover the whole image: (i) edge across (columns 1–3 minus 4–6), (ii) edge down (rows 1–3 minus 4–6), (iii) line across with rectangles 2 columns wide (2\cdotcolumns 3–4 − columns 1–2 − columns 5–6), (iv) diagonal with 3 \times 3 quarters. Predict which respond, then compute all four responses.
B4. Counting. (a) How many edge-across features (two rectangles of w \times h side by side, any w, h \ge 1, any position) fit in an 8 \times 8 window? (b) The same window has 64 pixels. Why does a detector want so many more features than pixels?
B5. Lighting. A face is photographed twice, the second time with twice the contrast and 50 grey levels brighter. What happens to the raw response of the eyes-versus-cheeks feature? What happens after dividing by the window’s standard deviation?
B6. Scales for free. A box feature stack has 5 feature types at 5 scales (1 to 16 px) on a 1000 \times 1000 image. About how many table lookups does the whole stack take? How would the cost of the box mean at 16 px compare if it were computed directly (33 \times 33 window)?






Solutions





B1. (a) Left: S(3,5) - S(3,1) - S(1,5) + S(1,1) = 18 - 3 - 6 + 1 = 10. Right: S(5,5) - S(5,1) - S(3,5) + S(3,1) = 70 - 13 - 18 + 3 = 42. (b) Left − right = 2S(3,5) - 2S(3,1) - S(1,5) + S(1,1) - S(5,5) + S(5,1). The corners S(3,5) and S(3,1) on the shared side appear in both sums and get coefficients +2 and -2: 6 distinct lookups. (c) 36 - 6 - 6 + 1 - 70 + 13 = -32. Directly: left 2+1+1+1 + 1+2+1+1 = 10, right 6+5+5+5 + 5+6+5+5 = 42, difference -32. Negative: the right side is brighter, a dark-to-bright edge from left to right.
B2. (a) Corners lie at x = 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = 1, 5: S(2,5) - S(2,1) - 3S(3,5) + 3S(3,1) + 3S(4,5) - 3S(4,1) - S(5,5) + S(5,1). At x = 3 the left rectangle’s right side (-1) meets the centre’s left side (-2): coefficient \mp 3; at x = 4 the centre’s right side (+2) meets the right rectangle’s left side (+1): \pm 3. Eight lookups. (b) -54 + 9 + 12 - 2 + 132 - 24 - 70 + 13 = 16. Directly: column 3 rows 2–5: 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 5; column 4: 6 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 21; column 5: 5 + 6 + 5 + 5 = 21; 2 \cdot 21 - 5 - 21 = 16.
B3. Only (iii) responds. (i): both halves contain one bright column (column 3 left, column 4 right): 0. (ii): the bar runs through both halves equally: 0. (iv): each quarter contains the same amount of bar: 0. (iii): centre columns 3–4: 12 pixels of 9 = 108; each side 12 pixels of 1 = 12; 2 \cdot 108 - 12 - 12 = 192, positive: a bright line on a dark background.
B4. (a) Rectangle width w = 1..4 (the feature is 2w wide), height h = 1..8: \sum_w (9 - 2w) \cdot \sum_h (9 - h) = (7 + 5 + 3 + 1)(8 + 7 + \dots + 1) = 16 \cdot 36 = 576, nine times the number of pixels. (b) The detector does not know in advance which differences of regions matter. A large, redundant pool contains features tuned to every part, size and orientation of the object; the learning step then picks the few that discriminate.
B5. The raw response doubles (twice the contrast); the offset of 50 does not change it, because the weights sum to zero. After dividing by the window SD (which also doubles) the response is the same in both photos.
B6. 25 maps of 10^6 pixels each, each with 4 lookups for a box mean (8 for an SD, which uses two tables; 8 for centre − surround, 6 for an edge): roughly 25 \times 6 \times 10^6 \approx 1.5 \cdot 10^8 lookups, the same at every scale. The box mean at 16 px directly: 33^2 = 1089 pixels per window, about 270 times the 4 lookups.




Math questions
B7. (math) Show that the edge feature needs 6 distinct corners and the diagonal feature 9, by adding the corner coefficients (+1, -1, -1, +1 times the rectangle’s weight) of all its rectangles. Why does the centre − surround feature need 8 and not fewer?
B8. (math) Let I(x, y) = ax + b. Show that the edge feature “left − right” with two w \times h rectangles gives -a w^2 h, independent of its position and of b. What does an edge feature “top − bottom” give on the same image?
B9. (math) Show that the number of placements of a template of a \times b cells in a W \times H window is \sum_{w=1}^{\lfloor W/a\rfloor}\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor H/b\rfloor}(W - aw + 1)(H - bh + 1), and compute it for the edge across (a = 2, b = 1) in 24 \times 24.






Solutions (math)





B7. A rectangle with weight c puts +c at its top-left and bottom-right corners and -c at the other two. Edge: on the shared side x = x_0 + w, rectangle 1 (c = +1) contributes its top-right (-1) and bottom-right (+1) corners, and rectangle 2 (c = -1) its top-left (+c = -1) and bottom-left (-c = +1) corners. The shared corners get -2 (top) and +2 (bottom): they do not cancel, and with the four outer corners there are 6. Diagonal: the corners form a 3 \times 3 grid. Each outer corner belongs to one rectangle (\pm 1); each edge midpoint to two rectangles of opposite weight, whose contributions have the same sign (\pm 2); the centre to all four, each contributing +1: +4. All 9 are non-zero. Centre − surround: the small box lies strictly inside the large one, so they share no corner: 4 + 4 = 8.
B8. Pair each pixel (x, y) of the left rectangle with (x + w, y) of the right one: their difference is -aw. There are wh pairs, so the response is -aw \cdot wh = -aw^2h; b cancels and the position does not appear. “Top − bottom” pairs pixels with the same x: every difference is 0, so the response is 0. The feature responds to the component of the gradient across its two rectangles.
B9. For cell sizes w (width) and h (height) the template covers aw \times bh pixels and its top-left corner can be at W - aw + 1 horizontal and H - bh + 1 vertical positions; w ranges over 1..\lfloor W/a\rfloor and h over 1..\lfloor H/b\rfloor. For a = 2, b = 1, W = H = 24: \sum_{w=1}^{12}(25 - 2w) = 144 and \sum_{h=1}^{24}(25 - h) = 300, product 43\,200.

title: Exercise: rectangle features
text:
Explore: rectangle features on images
Drag the template over the image: inside it to move it, the yellow handle to resize it. White rectangles count +, black -; the dots are the table entries read (green +, red -), numbered, and the readout lists their coefficients, the response (also per pixel of one rectangle), the number of lookups and the number of pixels a direct sum would add. response at every position shows the response with its centre at each pixel (red positive, blue negative).



E1. Preset eyes are darker than cheeks. Read the response, the response per pixel, the lookups and the pixels a direct sum adds. Drag the feature down over the mouth, then onto the background. What happens to the sign and size?
E2. Preset eyes darker than the bridge of the nose. How many lookups? Compare with B2. Explain the sign of the response.
E3. Choose each template in turn and count the dots. Do they match 6, 8, 9 and 8?
E4. Preset vertical edge on a cell boundary. In the response map, where are the strongest red and blue responses? Switch the template to edge — (top − bottom): which membranes light up now?
E5. Preset centre − surround finds cells of its size. Which cells give the strongest red response? Make the template smaller (resize to about half) and then larger. Which objects respond now?






Solutions





E1. Response -13\,230, per pixel -9.8 (the eye band is about 10 grey levels darker on average); 6 lookups instead of 2700 pixels. Over the mouth the upper band (cheeks) is brighter than the lower one (mouth): the sign flips to positive (about +18.6 per pixel 40 pixels lower). On flat background the response is small (about 3 per pixel).
E2. 8 lookups (three rectangles in a row, corners at four x positions and two y positions, as in B2). The response is large and positive (+59\,329, 114 per pixel): the centre rectangle, on the bridge of the nose between the eyes, is bright skin, the two side rectangles contain the dark eyes.
E3. Edge across and edge down: 6; both line templates: 8; diagonal: 9; centre − surround: 8.
E4. The strongest responses lie along nearly vertical boundaries: the left and right sides of the nucleus and the dark membranes of the cytoplasm, red where the left side is brighter, blue where the right side is. With top − bottom the vertical boundaries fade and the upper and lower boundaries of the nucleus and the horizontal membranes light up.
E5. With a 16 \times 16 centre box (48 × 48 in all) the strongest red responses sit on the centres of the larger bright cells, whose size matches the centre box (52 per pixel on the cell under the template). Smaller templates respond to small bright debris and to the bright rims inside cells; larger ones only to the biggest cells, and more weakly. Like the difference of Gaussians on the edges day, centre − surround is a blob detector tuned to one size.

title: Exercise: rectangle features
text:
Explore: a box feature stack
The 25 thumbnails are the box group of a feature stack: rows box mean, box SD, centre − surround, edge across, edge down; columns scales 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 px. Paint pixels of class A (orange) and B (blue) on the image. The scatter plot shows the painted pixels in two features: click a thumbnail to choose x (red frame); tick y and click to choose y (green frame). The slider puts a threshold on x; the readout counts A and B on each side and gives the best share any single threshold on x gets right. inspect shows the 25 features of one pixel (as z-scores over the image) in the bar plot.


E6. Preset nucleus or cytoplasm? (x = box mean at 4 px, y = box SD at 2 px). How well does a single threshold on x separate the classes? Look at the image: is the nucleus darker or brighter than the cytoplasm?
E7. Click through the thumbnails as x and note the best single-threshold share. Which feature and scale separates best? Why does the scale matter so much here?
E8. Preset cell or background? on the synthetic cells. Find a feature that separates perfectly. Is that problem easier or harder than E6, and why?
E9. Use inspect on a pixel in the nucleus and one in the cytoplasm. Which groups of bars differ most?






Solutions





E6. Poorly: the best threshold on the box mean at 4 px gets 82 % right (at the slider’s 50 % position only 61 %). The nucleus is on average a little brighter than the cytoplasm around it, but the grey levels overlap; so do the clouds along x.
E7. The box SD at 16 px is best (99.2 %), followed by the box SD at 8 px (92.6 %) and centre − surround at 16 px (91.6 %); the box SD at 4 px gets 86.5 %. The nucleus is uniformly fine-grained, the cytoplasm is full of membranes and vesicles; that difference in texture shows only when the window is large enough to contain several membranes. With the integral image the 16 px features cost exactly as much as the 1 px ones.
E8. The box mean at 8 px separates the painted cell and background pixels perfectly (100 %), as do several others: the synthetic cells are much brighter than their surroundings. Easier: here the mean grey level differs; in E6 only the texture does.
E9. For example at (140, 120) in the nucleus and (80, 30) in the cytoplasm: the box SD at 8 and 16 px is low in the nucleus (z about -1.5 to -1.9) and higher in the cytoplasm; centre − surround at 16 px is near 0 in the nucleus and strongly negative in the cytoplasm (-2.3); the box means differ less. The edge features are small and change sign from pixel to pixel.

title: Exercise: rectangle features
text:
Where this leads
Out of about 160 000 rectangle features in a 24 \times 24 window, which should a detector compute? The next unit lets boosting pick a few, one at a time, and arranges them in a cascade so that most windows are rejected after one or two of them.

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
text:
About this lecture
Last unit: every vertex gets a pixel position and a depth. Now the triangles in between.

Rasterisation: which pixel centres lie inside a triangle (edge functions).
Barycentric coordinates: interpolating colours, depths, normals across a triangle; and why perspective needs a correction.
The z-buffer: which surface is in front; why depth precision is uneven.
Shading: Lambert, Phong, Blinn–Phong; flat, Gouraud or per pixel; why normals transform with M^{-\top}.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Second unit of the 3D graphics day. Both demos are drawn by a software rasteriser written for the course (the same algorithm a GPU runs in hardware), so every step can be inspected.

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
section: Which pixels does a triangle cover?
text:
Which pixels does a triangle cover?
After the viewport transform a triangle is three points \mathbf a, \mathbf b, \mathbf c in pixel coordinates (with a depth each). A pixel is drawn if its centre lies inside.
The test, for each edge: on which side of the line \mathbf a \to \mathbf b is the pixel centre \mathbf p?
E_{ab}(\mathbf p) = (b_x - a_x)(p_y - a_y) - (b_y - a_y)(p_x - a_x)

E_{ab} > 0: \mathbf p is to the left of \mathbf a \to \mathbf b; < 0: to the right; = 0: on the line.
For a counter-clockwise triangle, inside = all three edge functions positive.
E is linear in \mathbf p: one pixel to the right changes it by a constant. And every pixel is tested independently: thousands of pixels at once, which is why GPUs are fast at this (Pineda, 1988).

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
section: The math: edge functions are areas
text:
The math: edge functions are areas
E_{ab}(\mathbf p) is the 2\times2 determinant \det[\mathbf b - \mathbf a,\ \mathbf p - \mathbf a]: twice the signed area of the triangle \mathbf a, \mathbf b, \mathbf p (positive when counter-clockwise).
Linear: E_{ab}(\mathbf p + (1, 0)) = E_{ab}(\mathbf p) - (b_y - a_y) and E_{ab}(\mathbf p + (0, 1)) = E_{ab}(\mathbf p) + (b_x - a_x): a rasteriser walks along a row with one addition per edge.
The three edge functions at \mathbf p split the triangle into three sub-triangles:
E_{bc}(\mathbf p) + E_{ca}(\mathbf p) + E_{ab}(\mathbf p) = E_{ab}(\mathbf c) = 2\,\text{area}(\mathbf a, \mathbf b, \mathbf c),
so their ratios to the whole area are the barycentric coordinates (next slide). Example: \mathbf a = (1, 1), \mathbf b = (7, 2), \mathbf c = (3, 6) has E_{ab}(\mathbf c) = 28; at \mathbf p = (4.5, 3.5) the three values are 4, 12.5, 11.5, summing to 28.

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
text:
Barycentric coordinates: interpolation from areas
b_a = \frac{E_{bc}(\mathbf p)}{E_{ab}(\mathbf c)}, \qquad b_b = \frac{E_{ca}(\mathbf p)}{E_{ab}(\mathbf c)}, \qquad b_c = \frac{E_{ab}(\mathbf p)}{E_{ab}(\mathbf c)}, \qquad b_a + b_b + b_c = 1.

b_a is the share of the area of the sub-triangle opposite \mathbf a: 1 at \mathbf a, 0 on the far edge.
Any value given at the vertices (colour, depth, normal, texture coordinate) is interpolated as f(\mathbf p) = b_a f_a + b_b f_b + b_c f_c.
Inside the triangle all three are positive (the inside test again).
The same idea as bilinear interpolation (images unit): weights from areas that sum to one. A square split into two triangles is interpolated differently: there is a crease along the diagonal.

Example: at \mathbf p = (4.5, 3.5) in the triangle above, (b_a, b_b, b_c) = (0.143, 0.446, 0.411); with depths 0.2, 0.6, 0.4 at the corners the pixel gets depth 0.461.

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
section: Try it: a rasteriser, pixel by pixel
text:
Try it: a rasteriser, pixel by pixel




The grid is 32 × 24 pixels, y up, pixel centres at the dots. “one triangle”: 437 pixel visits (the bounding box), 178 drawn. Press “start”, then “next pixel”: the readout gives the three edge functions, inside or outside, the barycentric coordinates and the depth test. Click a pixel, e.g. (10, 10): E = 166.5, 57, 132.5, barycentrics 0.468, 0.160, 0.372. Switch the view to “barycentrics” (the RGB colours are the weights) and to “edge function E_ab” (a linear ramp, zero on the edge). Drag a vertex. Then “a shared edge” (16 × 12): no pixel is drawn twice; untick “top-left rule”: 4 pixels on the diagonal are now covered by both. “flipped winding is culled”: the right triangle is clockwise and disappears with back-face culling.

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
text:
Shared edges and back faces

Shared edges: a pixel centre exactly on the edge between two triangles must be drawn once, not twice (double blending) and not zero times (a crack). The top-left rule: it belongs to the triangle for which the edge is a “top” or “left” edge.
Back-face culling: after projection, a triangle seen from behind has the opposite winding: its area E_{ab}(\mathbf c) is negative. For a closed, consistently wound mesh these triangles are hidden anyway, so they are skipped: about half the work saved.
A mesh with inconsistent winding (previous unit) gets holes when culling is on.

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
text:
The z-buffer
Several triangles can cover the same pixel. Which one is in front?

Keep a second image, the depth buffer (z-buffer, Catmull 1974), one depth per pixel, initially “far”.
For each covered pixel: interpolate the triangle’s depth; draw the pixel only if it is nearer than the stored depth, and store the new depth.
The result does not depend on the drawing order (for opaque surfaces), and intersecting triangles come out right, pixel by pixel.
Transparency breaks it: a half-transparent surface must be blended with what is behind it, so order matters again (compositing: the texture and volume units).
Two surfaces at (almost) the same depth flicker between each other: z-fighting.

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
text:
Depth precision is uneven
Depth after the projection is z_\text{ndc} = A + B/z (previous unit): it changes fast near the camera, slowly far away.

The depth buffer stores it with a fixed number of bits (24-bit integers, or 32-bit floats: see the floating-point unit). Equal steps of z_\text{ndc} are tiny steps in distance near the camera and large steps far away.
The near plane decides how much is wasted: with n = 0.01 and f = 100, half of the depth range is used up within 0.02 units of the camera; with n = 1, within 2 units.
Two surfaces at distances 50 and 51: with n = 0.01 they are 0.26 steps of a 16-bit buffer apart (same stored value: z-fighting); with n = 1, 26 steps.
Rule: push the near plane out as far as you can; the far plane matters much less.

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
text:
The math: depth resolution
With z_\text{ndc} = A - B/d in terms of the distance d = -z > 0 and B = 2fn/(f - n):
\frac{dz_\text{ndc}}{dd} = \frac{B}{d^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \Delta d \approx \frac{d^2}{B}\,\Delta z_\text{ndc} \approx \frac{d^2}{2n}\,\Delta z_\text{ndc} \quad (f \gg n).
A buffer with k bits has \Delta z_\text{ndc} = 2/(2^k - 1). The smallest separable distance grows with d^2 and shrinks only with n: ten times larger n gives ten times finer depth everywhere; f hardly matters.
Example: n = 0.01, f = 100: z_\text{ndc}(50) = 0.9998000 and z_\text{ndc}(51) = 0.9998078, a difference of 7.8\cdot10^{-6}, while a 16-bit step is 3.1\cdot10^{-5}.

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
text:
Perspective-correct interpolation
Barycentric weights measured on the screen are not the weights in 3D: the far half of a receding triangle is squeezed into fewer pixels.

Interpolating a texture coordinate with screen weights bends straight lines: a receding checkerboard made of two triangles kinks along the diagonal.
The fix: on the screen, 1/w and f/w (attribute divided by w) are linear. Interpolate both, then divide: f = \frac{b_a f_a/w_a + b_b f_b/w_b + b_c f_c/w_c}{b_a/w_a + b_b/w_b + b_c/w_c}.
Example: an edge from w = 1 (u = 0) to w = 3 (u = 1). At the screen midpoint: affine gives u = 0.5; correct is \tfrac{0.5\cdot0 + 0.5\cdot\frac13}{0.5 + 0.5\cdot\frac13} = 0.25.
Orthographic views (w = 1) need no correction; depth z_\text{ndc} itself is already linear on the screen.

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
section: The math: why 1/w is linear on the screen
text:
The math: why 1/w is linear on the screen
A triangle lies in a plane \alpha x + \beta y + \gamma z = \delta in view space (\delta \ne 0 unless the plane passes through the eye). A point on it projects to x_s = x/w, y_s = y/w with w = -z. Divide the plane equation by w:
\alpha x_s + \beta y_s - \gamma = \frac{\delta}{w} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac1w = \frac{\alpha x_s + \beta y_s - \gamma}{\delta}:
affine in the screen coordinates. An attribute that is affine in 3D, f = \mathbf g\cdot\mathbf x + h, gives f/w = \mathbf g\cdot(x_s, y_s, -1) + h/w: also affine on the screen. So screen-space barycentrics interpolate 1/w and f/w exactly, and their ratio is f.

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
section: Try it: affine vs perspective-correct, and depth precision
text:
Try it: affine vs perspective-correct, and depth precision




“affine vs perspective-correct”: a floor seen in perspective, two triangles with a checkerboard texture. With “perspective-correct” off the checks bend at the diagonal; tick it and they are straight. View “barycentrics” shows the screen weights vs the 3D weights. Then “near plane 0.01 vs 1”: two triangles at distances 8–9 and 8.5, depth buffer of 14 bits. With n = 0.01 the orange triangle is visible on 119 pixels instead of 61: the wrong surface wins on 58 pixels, in a jagged band; set n to 1: correct. The small plot shows z_ndc(d) with the vertex depths: with n = 0.01 all of them are near 1.

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
text:
Clipping and jagged edges

Clipping: a triangle that crosses the near plane is cut there in clip space, before the divide (vertices behind the camera have w < 0). The cut polygon is drawn as a fan of triangles. The other sides of the view need no clipping: pixels outside the screen are simply never visited.
Edge aliasing: one sample (the centre) per pixel makes edges staircase-like and lets thin triangles vanish between centres. Multisampling tests several points per pixel and averages coverage (the sampling of the Fourier unit).

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
section: Shading: how bright is a surface?
text:
Shading: how bright is a surface?
A light from direction \mathbf l, a surface with unit normal \mathbf n, the eye in direction \mathbf v (all unit vectors pointing away from the surface):

Lambert (matte): brightness k_d \max(0, \mathbf n\cdot\mathbf l). A tilted roof catches less light: the light falling on it is spread over a larger area, by the factor \cos\theta = \mathbf n\cdot\mathbf l.
Ambient k_a: a constant for all the light bounced around by the scene (a crude stand-in).
Specular (shiny): a highlight where the mirror direction of the light points at the eye. Phong: k_s \max(0, \mathbf r\cdot\mathbf v)^s; Blinn–Phong: k_s \max(0, \mathbf n\cdot\mathbf h)^s with the half vector \mathbf h between \mathbf l and \mathbf v. The shininess s makes the highlight small and sharp.
Physically based shading (energy conservation, measured materials) refines this; not covered.

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
text:
The math: Phong and Blinn–Phong
Mirror direction and half vector:
\mathbf r = 2(\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf l)\,\mathbf n - \mathbf l, \qquad \mathbf h = \frac{\mathbf l + \mathbf v}{\lVert \mathbf l + \mathbf v\rVert}.
\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf v = 1 exactly when \mathbf h = \mathbf n: both models peak in the mirror configuration. Away from it, the angle between \mathbf n and \mathbf h is about half the angle between \mathbf r and \mathbf v, so Blinn–Phong’s highlight is wider for the same s (roughly s_\text{Phong} \approx s_\text{Blinn}/4 gives similar highlights).
Example: \mathbf n = (0, 0, 1), \mathbf v = (0, 0, 1), \mathbf l = (1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2, k_a = 0.1, k_d = 0.8, k_s = 0.5, s = 20. Diffuse: 0.1 + 0.8\cdot0.707 = 0.666. Phong: \mathbf r\cdot\mathbf v = 0.707, 0.5\cdot0.707^{20} = 0.0005. Blinn–Phong: \mathbf n\cdot\mathbf h = \cos 22.5° = 0.924, 0.5\cdot0.924^{20} = 0.103.

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
text:
Where to evaluate the lighting

Flat: once per triangle, with the face normal. Facets are visible; right for a cut gem, wrong for a sphere.
Gouraud (1971): at the vertices, with vertex normals; the colours are interpolated across the triangle. Cheap, smooth, but a highlight that falls inside a triangle is missed (and highlights look star-shaped).
Per pixel (Phong 1975): interpolate the normal, renormalise, light every pixel. What GPUs do today.
Vertex normals of a mesh: the area-weighted average of the normals of the faces around the vertex (the sum of the un-normalised cross products), unless the mesh has a known exact normal (a sphere) or a crease that should stay sharp.

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
text:
Try it: shading




Drawn by the same software rasteriser, 360 × 360. “Gouraud misses the highlight”: a level-1 icosphere (80 triangles), light from the left so that the mirror point is the centre of a triangle: with Gouraud there is no highlight at all (every vertex gets a specular term below 0.001); switch to “per pixel”: a bright spot. “facets vs smooth”: the low-poly gem, flat, with the normals drawn. “squashed sphere: wrong normals”: squash 0.4, normals by M: the lighting looks wrong (normals off by up to 46.4°); switch to M⁻ᵀ. “Phong vs Blinn–Phong at grazing light”: the light almost from the side; Phong’s highlight is cut off and small, Blinn–Phong’s is wider for the same shininess.

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
text:
Transforming normals

A normal is defined by being perpendicular to the surface. Under a rotation or a uniform scale, M\mathbf n stays perpendicular. Under a non-uniform scale it does not: squash a circle into an ellipse, and M\mathbf n leans the wrong way.
The right transform is M^{-\top} (the inverse transpose), applied to the normal and then renormalised. For a rotation M^{-\top} = M; for \mathrm{diag}(2, 1, 1) it is \mathrm{diag}(\tfrac12, 1, 1).

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
section: The math: why the inverse transpose
text:
The math: why the inverse transpose
A tangent \mathbf t (a direction along the surface) transforms like any direction: \mathbf t' = M\mathbf t. The normal must satisfy \mathbf n^\top\mathbf t = 0 before and \mathbf n'^\top\mathbf t' = 0 after, for every tangent. Try \mathbf n' = G\mathbf n:
\mathbf n'^\top\mathbf t' = \mathbf n^\top G^\top M\,\mathbf t = 0 \text{ for all } \mathbf t \perp \mathbf n \quad\Longleftarrow\quad G^\top M = I \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G = M^{-\top}.
Example: M = \mathrm{diag}(2, 1, 1), the plane x + y = 1 with \mathbf n = (1, 1, 0) and tangent \mathbf t = (1, -1, 0). M\mathbf t = (2, -1, 0); M\mathbf n = (2, 1, 0) gives M\mathbf n\cdot M\mathbf t = 3 \ne 0; M^{-\top}\mathbf n = (\tfrac12, 1, 0) gives 1 - 1 = 0.
(Only the 3\times3 part matters: normals are directions, w = 0. Any scalar multiple of M^{-\top} works, since the normal is renormalised.)

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
text:
The GPU pipeline, conceptually


Vertex stage (a small program per vertex): P V M\mathbf x, normals by M^{-\top}, per-vertex lighting for Gouraud.
Fixed hardware: clipping, divide by w, viewport, culling, rasterisation (edge functions, barycentrics, perspective correction).
Fragment stage (a small program per covered pixel): per-pixel lighting, texture reads (next unit).
Output: the depth test against the z-buffer, then writing or blending (transparency) into the image.

title: From triangles to shaded pixels
text:
Summary

Edge functions (twice signed areas) decide which pixel centres are inside; the top-left rule settles shared edges; negative area = back face, culled.
Barycentric coordinates = area ratios; they interpolate any vertex attribute.
Perspective-correct: interpolate f/w and 1/w, then divide.
z-buffer: draw a pixel only if it is nearer. Depth A + B/z is crowded near the camera: keep the near plane far out.
Lambert \mathbf n\cdot\mathbf l; Phong/Blinn–Phong highlights; lighting per face, per vertex (Gouraud) or per pixel.
Normals transform with M^{-\top}.

title: Quiz: RANSAC
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. w is the inlier fraction, s the sample size, N the number of samples, \varepsilon the inlier distance.

Q1. Why does a least-squares line fit fail when 30 % of the points are outliers?






Hint





How much does one point 30 px from the line cost?









Answer





Least squares minimises the sum of squared distances. A point 30 px away costs 900, as much as 900 points 1 px away, so a few far outliers dominate the sum and pull the line towards them. Every point has a say, including the ones that do not belong to the line.




Q2. Why does RANSAC fit its sample with the smallest possible number of points (2 for a line)?






Hint





What must be true of the sample for the guess to be good?









Answer





A guess is only good if every point in the sample is an inlier. The probability of that is w^s, which falls quickly with s: with w = 0.5, 0.25 for 2 points, 0.125 for 3, 0.03 for 5. The smallest sample that determines the model maximises the chance of a clean sample.




Q3. How many samples are needed for a 99 % chance of at least one all-inlier sample, for a line with half the points inliers? And for a circle?






Hint





N = \log(1 - p)/\log(1 - w^s), rounded up.









Answer





Line: \log 0.01/\log 0.75 = 16.0, so 17. Circle (s = 3): \log 0.01/\log 0.875 = 34.5, so 35. The number of points does not enter.




Q4. Why is the best model refitted by least squares at the end, and why only on its inliers?






Hint





How many points determined the best model?









Answer





The best model passes exactly through its 2 (or 3) sample points, which are noisy, so it is only roughly right. Least squares on all its inliers averages their noise and gives a more precise model. Only the inliers, because including the outliers would bring back the very problem RANSAC solves.




Q5. Two parallel lines lie 8 px apart, and \varepsilon is set to 6 px. What does RANSAC find?






Hint





How wide is the band of a model halfway between the lines?









Answer





A line between the two: its band of ±6 px contains both lines (each 4 px from it), so it has more inliers than either true line and wins. \varepsilon must be smaller than half the distance between models you want to keep apart, but larger than the noise of the inliers.




Q6. The inlier fraction drops from 0.5 to 0.2. By what factor does the required number of samples grow for a line? Why is the Hough transform not hurt in the same way?






Hint





For small w^s, N \approx 4.6/w^s.









Answer





From 17 to 113, about 6.6 times; for small w, N \approx 4.6/w^2, so roughly (0.5/0.2)^2 = 6.25. The Hough transform lets every point vote once per angle, whatever the fraction of outliers: the true line still collects its votes in one bin, while the outliers’ votes spread over many bins. As long as the peak stands above the floor, it is found, with a fixed amount of work.




Q7. Which method would you use to fit an affine transform (6 parameters) to 200 matched point pairs of which 40 % are wrong, and why?






Hint





How large is a 6D accumulator? How many samples does RANSAC need?









Answer





RANSAC. An affine transform is determined by 3 point pairs, so s = 3, w = 0.6: N = \log 0.01/\log(1 - 0.216) = 19 samples for 99 %. A Hough accumulator with only 20 steps per parameter would have 20^6 = 64 million cells.




Q8. (math) Show that the total-least-squares line through a set of points passes through their centroid and has as its normal the eigenvector of the scatter matrix with the smaller eigenvalue.






Hint





Minimise \sum_i (\mathbf n^\top \mathbf p_i - \rho)^2 first over \rho, then over unit \mathbf n.









Answer





The derivative with respect to \rho is -2\sum_i(\mathbf n^\top\mathbf p_i - \rho) = 0, so \rho = \mathbf n^\top\bar{\mathbf p}: the centroid is on the line. Substituting, the cost is \sum_i (\mathbf n^\top(\mathbf p_i - \bar{\mathbf p}))^2 = \mathbf n^\top S\,\mathbf n with S = \sum_i(\mathbf p_i - \bar{\mathbf p})(\mathbf p_i - \bar{\mathbf p})^\top. For unit \mathbf n this Rayleigh quotient is smallest at the eigenvector of the smallest eigenvalue: the normal points in the direction of least spread, and the line along the direction of largest spread (the first principal component).

title: Exercise: RANSAC
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

run a few RANSAC iterations by hand: fit a minimal sample, count inliers, choose,
compute the number of iterations for a given inlier fraction and sample size,
choose \varepsilon and predict what goes wrong when it is too small or too large,
decide between voting (Hough) and hypothesise-and-verify (RANSAC) for a problem,
(math) derive the iteration formula and the least-squares refits for lines and circles.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo.

title: Exercise: RANSAC
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

title: Exercise: RANSAC
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Minimal sample
the fewest points that determine the model: s = 2 (line), 3 (circle), 3 pairs (affine transform)


Inliers
points within distance \varepsilon of the model


RANSAC
repeat N times: sample, fit exactly, count inliers; keep the best; refit on its inliers


Success probability
P = 1 - (1 - w^s)^N, w = inlier fraction


Iterations
N = \log(1 - p)/\log(1 - w^s), rounded up


Line distance
|x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta - \rho| for a line in normal form

title: Exercise: RANSAC
text:
By hand
B1. Eight points: (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (4, 4.2), (5, 1), (1, 4), (4, 0). Use \varepsilon = 0.5. (a) Sample 1 is \{(0, 0), (3, 3)\}. Give the line through them in normal form and the distance of every point to it. How many inliers? (b) Sample 2 is \{(5, 1), (1, 4)\}. Show that the line through them is 3x + 4y = 19, i.e. normal (0.6, 0.8) and \rho = 3.8. Distances and inliers? (c) Which model does RANSAC keep? Which points are used in the refit, and roughly where will the refitted line be?
B2. Iterations for a 99 % chance of at least one all-inlier sample: (a) a line with w = 0.5; (b) a circle with w = 0.5; (c) a line with w = 0.2; (d) a circle with w = 0.3. (e) With w = 0.2 and only the 17 iterations of (a), what is the chance of success?
B3. Voting or guessing? Explain your choice. (a) A single straight filament in an image where 90 % of the edge points are clutter. (b) Fitting an affine transform (6 parameters, 3 point pairs per sample) to matched points of two images, with 40 % wrong matches. (c) Finding all 20 straight edges of a building facade.
B4. The inliers of a line scatter with a standard deviation of 0.8 px. (a) Suggest \varepsilon. (b) A second line runs parallel, 8 px away. What is the largest \varepsilon that keeps the two lines apart, and what happens above it?






Solutions





B1. (a) The line y = x: normal (\cos 135°, \sin 135°) = (-0.707, 0.707), \rho = 0 (any sign convention: distance |x - y|/\sqrt2). Distances: 0, 0, 0, 0, 0.14, 2.83, 2.12, 2.83. 5 inliers: the first five points. (b) The direction from (5, 1) to (1, 4) is (-4, 3), so the normal is (3, 4)/5 = (0.6, 0.8); \rho = 0.6 \cdot 5 + 0.8 \cdot 1 = 3.8, i.e. 3x + 4y = 19. Distances |3x + 4y - 19|/5: 3.8, 2.4, 1.0, 0.4, 1.96, 0, 0, 1.4. 3 inliers: (3, 3), (5, 1), (1, 4). (c) Sample 1 (5 inliers). The refit uses (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (4, 4.2): the total-least-squares line through their centroid (2, 2.04), at about 46.1° (slightly steeper than 45°, pulled by (4, 4.2)). The three outliers play no part.
B2. (a) \log 0.01/\log(1 - 0.25) = 16.0: 17. (b) \log 0.01/\log(1 - 0.125) = 34.5: 35. (c) \log 0.01/\log(1 - 0.04) = 112.8: 113. (d) w^3 = 0.027: \log 0.01/\log 0.973 = 168.2: 169. (e) 1 - 0.96^{17} = 0.50: a coin toss.
B3. (a) Hough. RANSAC with w = 0.1, s = 2 needs \log 0.01/\log 0.99 = 459 samples; the Hough transform with gradient voting handles a 90 % clutter fraction with a fixed amount of work, as long as the filament’s peak stands above the floor. (b) RANSAC: w = 0.6, s = 3: \log 0.01/\log(1 - 0.216) = 19 samples; a 6D accumulator with 20 steps per parameter has 20^6 = 64 million cells. (c) Hough: 20 instances of a 2-parameter model, all found in one pass; RANSAC would need 20 sequential runs, the first ones with a small inlier fraction (w \approx 1/20 per line among the edge points).
B4. (a) 2 to 3 times the noise: \varepsilon \approx 2 px (the demo uses 2). (b) A model halfway between the lines is 4 px from each; with \varepsilon \ge 4 its band contains both lines, so it beats each true line and the two merge. Keep \varepsilon well below 4 (2 is fine).




Math questions
B5. (math) Derive N = \log(1 - p)/\log(1 - w^s). Show that for small w^s, N \approx 4.6/w^s when p = 0.99. By what factor does N grow when w halves, for a line and for a circle?
B6. (math) Show that the total-least-squares line (minimising the sum of squared perpendicular distances) passes through the centroid and that its normal is the eigenvector of the scatter matrix S with the smaller eigenvalue. Check with B1(c): the five inliers have centroid (2, 2.04); is the refitted line close to y = x?
B7. (math) Write the algebraic circle fit as a linear least-squares problem in (a, b, c) with c = r^2 - a^2 - b^2. Set up the system for the four points (5, 0), (0, 5), (-5, 0), (0, -5) and solve it. What quantity does the algebraic fit minimise, and why is it not exactly the geometric distance?






Solutions (math)





B5. A sample is all-inlier with probability w^s; samples are independent, so all N fail with probability (1 - w^s)^N. Requiring (1 - w^s)^N \le 1 - p and taking logarithms (both negative, so the inequality flips when dividing): N \ge \log(1 - p)/\log(1 - w^s). For small q = w^s, \log(1 - q) \approx -q, so N \approx -\log(0.01)/q = 4.6/w^s. Halving w multiplies w^s by 2^{-s}, so N grows about 4 times for a line and 8 times for a circle.
B6. \partial/\partial\rho \sum_i(\mathbf n^\top\mathbf p_i - \rho)^2 = -2\sum_i(\mathbf n^\top\mathbf p_i - \rho) = 0 gives \rho = \mathbf n^\top\bar{\mathbf p}. The remaining cost is \mathbf n^\top S\,\mathbf n with S = \sum_i(\mathbf p_i - \bar{\mathbf p})(\mathbf p_i - \bar{\mathbf p})^\top; over unit vectors its minimum is the smallest eigenvalue, attained at its eigenvector (Rayleigh quotient). For B1(c): the deviations from the centroid are (-2, -2.04), (-1, -1.04), (0, -0.04), (1, 0.96), (2, 2.16); S has a dominant eigenvector at 46.1° and the normal at 136.1°: close to y = x, tilted by 1.1° towards (4, 4.2).
B7. (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2 \iff x^2 + y^2 = 2ax + 2by + c. Each point gives one row: [2x_i \;\; 2y_i \;\; 1]\,(a, b, c)^\top = x_i^2 + y_i^2. For the four points: rows (10, 0, 1), (0, 10, 1), (-10, 0, 1), (0, -10, 1), right-hand side 25 each. The normal equations A^\top A = \operatorname{diag}(200, 200, 4), A^\top \mathbf z = (0, 0, 100) give a = b = 0, c = 25, r = \sqrt{25} = 5. The fit minimises \sum_i (x_i^2 + y_i^2 - 2ax_i - 2by_i - c)^2 = \sum_i (d_i^2 - r^2)^2 = \sum_i (d_i - r)^2(d_i + r)^2, with d_i the distance of point i from the centre: the geometric error (d_i - r) weighted by (d_i + r)^2, so points outside the circle count more than points inside. For exact or nearly exact data it agrees with the geometric fit; it is linear and needs no starting guess.

title: Exercise: RANSAC
text:
Explore
The point set: inliers on a line (or a circle) with noise of 0.8 px, plus uniform outliers, all from a fixed seed. Click to add a point, click a point to remove it, drag to move it. One sample draws a minimal sample (red, with its band of ±\varepsilon) and counts its inliers; run all finishes the iterations and shows the best model refitted on its inliers (blue; green points are its inliers). Orange, dashed: least squares on all points. Top right: the inlier count of each sample (bars) and the best so far (blue). Middle right: the chance of at least one all-inlier sample against N, with the current iteration (red dot) and the 99 % value. Optional: a second model (sequential RANSAC, purple) and the line Hough accumulator of the same points (its peak drawn purple, dotted).



R1. Preset least squares fails (30 % outliers). The true line is \theta = 63°, \rho = 58. What does least squares on all points give? Press run all: what does RANSAC give, with how many inliers, and how many of them are true inliers?
R2. Preset RANSAC: 17 iterations (w = 0.5). Press restart, then one sample 17 times. Which samples are all-inlier (the readout says so), how many inliers do they get, and which one becomes the best? Compare the refit with least squares.
R3. Still on that preset, try seeds 1 to 10. In how many runs is the refitted line right? Is that consistent with the 99 % on the curve?
R4. Preset 80 % outliers (100 points, 17 iterations, Hough accumulator on). What is the chance of success after 17 samples? What does RANSAC find with seed 1, and what does the Hough transform find? Now set the iterations to 113. What changes? Look at the all-inlier samples in the readout as you step: why do some of them get only a few inliers?
R5. Preset ε too large: two lines merge (two parallel lines 8 px apart, \varepsilon = 6). Where is the RANSAC line, and how many inliers does it have? Set \varepsilon = 2.
R6. Preset two lines: sequential. What does least squares give? What do the first and the second RANSAC model give? Compare with the true lines \theta = 131.8°, \rho = -10 and \theta = 71.6°, \rho = 62.
R7. Preset circle (true centre (52, 48), r = 28). How many iterations are needed for 99 %? Compare the RANSAC refit with the least-squares circle on all points. Which parameter does least squares get most wrong, and why?
R8. Back to RANSAC: 17 iterations, set \varepsilon = 0.5. What happens to the inlier counts and the refit? Why?






Solutions





R1. Least squares: \theta = 68.6°, \rho = 59.1, visibly tilted by the outliers. RANSAC (refit): \theta = 62.9°, \rho = 58.0, with 41 inliers, all of them true inliers (42 points are on the line).
R2. Samples 2, 3 and 14 are all-inlier, with 29, 29 and 30 inliers; the best is sample 14 (30). Mixed samples get 3 to 16. The refit uses 31 inliers (29 true, 2 outliers that happen to lie within 2 px): \theta = 63.4°, \rho = 58.1, against \theta = 75.8°, \rho = 56.4 for least squares.
R3. In all ten runs at least one sample is all-inlier, and the refit lands within about 1° of 63° and 0.3 of 58 (for example seed 4: the very first sample is all-inlier). That fits 99 %: a failure is expected in about 1 run in 100.
R4. 50 % (1 - 0.96^{17}). With seed 1 no sample is all-inlier; the best is a chance alignment of 10 points (4 true inliers) at \theta = 85.9°, \rho = 53.2: wrong. The Hough peak is at \theta = 63°, \rho = 58.2 with 22 votes: right. With 113 iterations the best model appears at iteration 18 (22 inliers), and the refit is \theta = 62.1°, \rho = 58.7 with 24 inliers (18 true). The all-inlier samples (iterations 91 and 93) get only 8 and 7 inliers: their two points are close together, so the noise of 0.8 px tilts the line through them a lot. A sample with a long baseline (even one containing an outlier that happens to lie near the line, as at iteration 18) fits better.
R5. The refit is \theta = 74.1°, \rho = 54.6, with 42 inliers: halfway between the two lines (\rho = 50 and 58), with both inside its band. With \varepsilon = 2: \theta = 76.4°, \rho = 50.9, 24 inliers, all true: one of the two lines.
R6. Least squares: \theta = 163.1°, \rho = -28.9, a line that fits neither. First model: \theta = 131.8°, \rho = -10.2 (21 inliers); second, after removing those: \theta = 71.4°, \rho = 62.2 (21 inliers). Both match the true lines.
R7. 35 iterations (s = 3, w = 0.5). RANSAC refit: centre (51.8, 48.4), r = 27.8. Least squares on all points: centre (51.5, 48.2) but r = 34.8. The outliers are spread evenly around the circle, so they barely move the centre, but on average they lie farther out than the circle, so the radius grows.
R8. With \varepsilon = 0.5 (smaller than the noise of 0.8) most true inliers fall outside the band: the best model has only 10 inliers (9 true), and the refit \theta = 64.4°, \rho = 58.2 rests on few points. The counts are small and noisy, so the choice of the best model is close to chance. \varepsilon should be 2 to 3 times the noise.

title: Exercise: RANSAC
text:
Where this leads
RANSAC returns the best model and its inliers; with matched feature points between two images the same loop estimates the transform that aligns them, which is the subject of the planned Motion elective. The other days of the Detection group take a different route to finding objects: integral images make box filters so cheap that a detector can test millions of windows.

title: Projections and the sinogram
text:
About this lecture
An X-ray image overlays everything the beam passed through: ribs, heart and spine end up on top of each other. Computed tomography (CT) gets a clean slice instead. The idea of the day: take many X-ray profiles from all around the object, then undo the overlaying.

What an X-ray detector measures: a line integral of the attenuation.
Lines described by an angle and a distance, (\theta, \rho).
A projection = all parallel line integrals at one angle; stacked over angles they form the sinogram.
A point becomes a sinusoid; shifts, sums and the 180° symmetry of sinograms.

This unit is about the measurement. The next three invert it: back-projection, filtered back-projection, and reconstruction as a linear system.
Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Day plan: radon (this unit), backprojection, fbp, algebraic-recon. If the Hough elective was taken first, the (ρ, θ) slide is a recall: the Hough day draws the same sinusoids by voting, this day integrates grey values along lines and then inverts. Open with a real chest X-ray and a CT slice if you have licensed images at hand (none are bundled with the course); the question “how does CT get a slice?” carries the day.

title: Projections and the sinogram
text:
What the detector measures
A narrow beam of I_0 photons crosses the body; I arrive at the detector.

Every centimetre of material removes a fixed fraction of the photons that reach it. That fraction per cm is the attenuation coefficient \mu: higher for bone than for soft tissue, about 0.2 cm⁻¹ for water-like tissue.
Fractions multiply along the path: through 20 cm of tissue with \mu = 0.2 cm⁻¹, I/I_0 = e^{-4} \approx 0.018. Under 2 % of the photons get through.
Taking -\ln(I/I_0) turns the product into a sum: -\ln(I/I_0) = \mu_1 \Delta s + \mu_2 \Delta s + \dots, the sum of \mu along the ray (times the step). In the limit: a line integral.

So after a logarithm, each detector reading is “how much stuff lies on this line”. That number is what CT reconstructs from.

title: Projections and the sinogram
text:
The math: Beer–Lambert
Along the ray (arc length s) the beam loses photons in proportion to how many there are and to the local attenuation:
\frac{dI}{ds} = -\mu(s)\,I(s) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad I = I_0 \exp\Big(-\int_{\text{ray}} \mu(s)\,ds\Big), \qquad -\ln\frac{I}{I_0} = \int_{\text{ray}} \mu(s)\,ds.

Assumes a monochromatic beam (one photon energy). Real tubes emit a spectrum; low energies are absorbed first (“beam hardening”), which bends this straight line slightly.
Two layers: 18 cm of tissue (\mu = 0.2) and 2 cm of bone (\mu = 0.5): -\ln(I/I_0) = 3.6 + 1.0 = 4.6, I/I_0 = e^{-4.6} = 0.010. The order of the layers does not matter: a sum.

title: Projections and the sinogram
section: Other machines that measure line integrals

title: Projections and the sinogram
text:
Lines as (\theta, \rho)
Coordinates: origin at the image centre, x right, y up, angles counter-clockwise.

A line is the set of points with x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = \rho.
\theta \in [0°, 180°): the direction of the line’s normal; \rho: the signed distance of the line from the centre.
\theta = 0°: vertical lines x = \rho. \theta = 90°: horizontal lines y = \rho.
The same convention as the Hough elective (there: lines found by voting; here: grey values summed along lines).

A projection at angle \theta is the profile p_\theta(\rho): the line integrals of all parallel lines, one per detector bin. At \theta = 0° the rays run vertically and p_0 is the column sums of the image; at 90° it is the row sums.

title: Projections and the sinogram
section: Try it: projections and the sinogram
text:
Try it: projections and the sinogram




Left: the object, the rays of the current angle (yellow, arrow = beam direction) and the detector (blue bar); the coloured dots on the detector are where each point lands. Middle: the projection. Right: the sinogram filling in up to the current angle, with each point’s sinusoid drawn over it. Tour: “three points by hand” at 45°: read ρ in the readout (22.6, 11.3, −22.6 px = 1.41, 0.71, −1.41 units). Press +45° to 90°. Then play from 0°. “The centre does not move”: the point at the centre is a flat line. “Shepp–Logan sinogram”, “a real image”. Click into the image to add points: each new point is a new sinusoid.

title: Projections and the sinogram
text:
The sinogram
Stack the projections side by side: \theta across, \rho up. This picture is the sinogram: it is all the scanner measures.

A point at radius r and direction \varphi traces \rho = r\cos(\theta - \varphi): a sinusoid, hence the name.
Amplitude = distance from the centre; phase = the point’s direction: the curve peaks at \theta = \varphi.
The centre of rotation is the only point that stays put: a flat line at \rho = 0.
Where two sinusoids cross, the two points lie on the same ray: they hide behind each other at that angle. A and B cross at \theta = 63.4°.


The Shepp–Logan phantom (a standard test object for CT) and its sinogram, 180 angles.

title: Projections and the sinogram
text:
Four properties of every sinogram

Linearity: the sinogram of two objects is the sum of their sinograms. Overlapping sinusoids add.
Shift: moving the object by \mathbf t = (t_x, t_y) moves every point’s curve by t_x\cos\theta + t_y\sin\theta: the sinogram is bent by a sinusoid, it does not just slide.
Symmetry: the ray (\theta + 180°, \rho) is the ray (\theta, -\rho) walked the other way, so p_{\theta + 180°}(\rho) = p_\theta(-\rho). Half a turn is enough for parallel beams.
Mass: every projection sums to the same number, the total of the image.

A real sinogram that breaks one of these tells you something went wrong in the scanner: a moving patient, a wrong centre of rotation, a dead detector element.

title: Projections and the sinogram
text:
The math: the Radon transform
\mathcal R f(\rho, \theta) = \iint f(x, y)\,\delta(x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta - \rho)\,dx\,dy = \int f(\rho\,\mathbf n_\theta + s\,\mathbf n_\theta^\perp)\,ds,
with \mathbf n_\theta = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta), \mathbf n_\theta^\perp = (-\sin\theta, \cos\theta) (Radon, 1917).

Linear: \mathcal R(af + bg) = a\,\mathcal R f + b\,\mathcal R g.
Shift: f(\mathbf x - \mathbf t) \mapsto \mathcal R f(\rho - \mathbf t\cdot\mathbf n_\theta, \theta) (substitute \mathbf x = \mathbf x' + \mathbf t).
Symmetry: \mathcal R f(-\rho, \theta + \pi) = \mathcal R f(\rho, \theta), since \mathbf n_{\theta + \pi} = -\mathbf n_\theta.
Mass: \int \mathcal R f(\rho, \theta)\,d\rho = \iint f\,dx\,dy for every \theta (the change of variables (\rho, s) is a rotation).
Uniform disc of radius R, value \mu: \mathcal R f(\rho, \theta) = 2\mu\sqrt{R^2 - \rho^2} for |\rho| \le R (the chord length). An ellipse has a closed form too, which is why test phantoms are built from ellipses: their sinograms are exact.

title: Projections and the sinogram
text:
On a pixel grid
A computer image is a grid of numbers, not a function. To integrate along a ray we walk along it and read the image between pixel centres by linear interpolation (the images unit’s bilinear interpolation, in one direction).

One detector bin per pixel width, rays through the bin centres.
Rays steeper than 45° take one sample per image row, the others one per column; each sample is weighted by the path length per row or column.
The result is close to the exact integral: for the demo’s Shepp–Logan phantom the RMS difference from its exact sinogram is 1.4 % of the largest value.
Only what lies inside the circle seen at every angle is measured at every angle: the demos keep objects inside that field of view.

title: Projections and the sinogram
section: Can you tell which image it was?
text:
Can you tell which image it was?
Two projections of a 3 \times 3 binary image: row sums (1, 2, 1) and column sums (1, 2, 1).
\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&1\\0&1&0\end{bmatrix} \qquad \begin{bmatrix}0&1&0\\1&0&1\\0&1&0\end{bmatrix} \qquad \dots
Five different binary images have exactly these sums. Two projections do not determine the image; swapping a 2 \times 2 checkerboard pattern inside it changes no row or column sum.
More angles add more equations and remove ambiguity. How many are enough, and how to turn the numbers back into an image, is the subject of the rest of the day.

title: Projections and the sinogram
text:
Summary

After -\ln(I/I_0), an X-ray measurement is a line integral of the attenuation \mu (Beer–Lambert).
Lines are (\theta, \rho): normal direction and signed distance from the centre.
A projection collects the parallel line integrals at one angle; the sinogram stacks them over \theta \in [0°, 180°).
A point traces a sinusoid \rho = r\cos(\theta - \varphi); sinograms are linear, shift by a sinusoid, are symmetric after 180°, and every projection has the same total.
Two projections leave many images possible: reconstruction needs many angles.

title: Quiz: quantisation and bit depth
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A camera has a 12-bit ADC and a monitor shows 8 bits per channel. How many camera levels fall on one monitor level if the whole camera range is shown?






Answer





2^{12} / 2^8 = 4096 / 256 = 16 camera levels per monitor level. The monitor cannot show the difference between them, but the data still contain it: measure on the 12-bit numbers, not on the screenshot.




Q2. You reduce an image from 8 to 7 bits. By what factor does the RMS quantisation error grow, and what happens to the SNR in dB?






Hint





How does the step \Delta change when you remove one bit?









Answer





The step doubles (from 1/255 to 1/127 of the range, almost exactly a factor 2), so the RMS error \Delta/\sqrt{12} doubles too. The SNR drops by 20\log_{10}2 \approx 6 dB.




Q3. Why is banding easy to see in a picture of a clear blue sky, and hard to see in a picture of grass, even with the same bit depth?






Answer





In the sky, brightness changes slowly over many pixels, so many neighbouring pixels round the same way and the steps line up into visible contour lines. In the grass, the brightness changes a lot from pixel to pixel; the rounding error is different for each pixel and looks like (invisible) noise. The texture acts as a natural dither.




Q4. Adding random noise before rounding (dithering) makes the RMS error larger. Why do we do it anyway?






Answer





Without dither, the error follows the image: it forms bands that look like edges that are not there, and a value between two levels is always pushed the same way (a bias). With dither, the error is independent of the image and has mean zero for every grey value, so averaging over a region (or by the eye) recovers grey values between the levels. Structured error is worse than a slightly larger random error.

title: Exercise: quantisation and bit depth
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute the number of levels and the step for a given bit depth, and quantise values by hand,
predict where banding appears and explain what dithering changes,
predict how the rounding error and the SNR change with the bit depth (about 6 dB per bit).

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the interactive part. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: quantisation and bit depth
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

predict where banding appears and explain what dithering changes,
predict how the rounding error and the SNR change with the bit depth (about 6 dB per bit).

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the interactive part. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: quantisation and bit depth
text:
By hand
B1. How many grey levels do a 10-bit and a 14-bit sensor have? By about what factor is the step of a 12-bit image finer than that of an 8-bit image, if both cover black to white?
B2. Quantise the row of values (as fractions of the full range) 0.10,\quad 0.22,\quad 0.37,\quad 0.55,\quad 0.81 to 2 bits, i.e. to the levels 0, \tfrac13, \tfrac23, 1. Give the codes k \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}, the stored values and the errors. What is the largest error that rounding can ever make here?
B3. A flat region has the value 0.25 everywhere and is quantised to 2 bits. (a) Without dither, what does every pixel become, and what is the error? (b) With random dither, a pixel rounds up to \tfrac13 with some probability and down to 0 otherwise. Predict that probability, and the average over many pixels.
B4. A smooth ramp from black to white is quantised to 6 bits and to 10 bits. Use the rule “about 6 dB per bit” to predict the SNR of the rounding in each case, and give the RMS error \Delta/\sqrt{12} as a fraction of the range. How many times smaller is the 10-bit error?






Solutions





B1. 2^{10} = 1024 and 2^{14} = 16\,384 levels. The steps are 1/255 and 1/4095 of the range: the 12-bit step is 4095/255 \approx 16 times finer.
B2. Multiply by 3 and round: 0.30 \to 0, 0.66 \to 1, 1.11 \to 1, 1.65 \to 2, 2.43 \to 2. Stored values 0, \tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac23, \tfrac23. Errors (stored − true): -0.100, +0.113, -0.037, +0.117, -0.143. Rounding never moves a value by more than half a step, \Delta/2 = \tfrac16 \approx 0.167.
B3. (a) 0.25 \times 3 = 0.75 rounds to 1: every pixel becomes \tfrac13, an error of +0.083 everywhere. The whole region is too bright by the same amount: no average can fix that. (b) The value is 75 % of the way from level 0 to level 1, so a pixel rounds up with probability 0.75: three quarters of the pixels become \tfrac13, one quarter 0. The average is 0.75 \cdot \tfrac13 = 0.25, the true value.
B4. About 6 \cdot 6 = 36 dB and 6 \cdot 10 = 60 dB (exactly 20\log_{10}63 = 36.0 and 20\log_{10}1023 = 60.2 dB). RMS error \frac{1}{63\sqrt{12}} = 0.0046 and \frac{1}{1023\sqrt{12}} = 0.00028 of the range: 1023/63 \approx 16 times smaller, 2^4 for 4 more bits.




Math questions
B5. (math) Let the rounding error e be uniform on [-\Delta/2, \Delta/2]. Show that \operatorname{Var}(e) = \Delta^2/12. A signal spread evenly over the full range R = (2^b - 1)\Delta has variance R^2/12: show that the SNR is 20\log_{10}(2^b - 1) \approx 6.02\,b dB, and evaluate it for b = 4.
B6. (math) Random dither: in units of \Delta, x = k + f with 0 \le f < 1 and u uniform on [-\tfrac12, \tfrac12). Show that \mathbb E[\operatorname{round}(x + u)] = x, and that the mean squared error, averaged over f uniform on [0, 1), is \Delta^2/6. By what factor is the RMS error larger than without dither?






Solutions (math)





B5. \mathbb E[e] = 0 by symmetry, so \operatorname{Var}(e) = \int_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2} e^2 \tfrac{1}{\Delta}\,de = \tfrac{1}{\Delta}\cdot\tfrac{2}{3}\left(\tfrac{\Delta}{2}\right)^3 = \tfrac{\Delta^2}{12}. Then \text{SNR} = 10\log_{10}\frac{R^2/12}{\Delta^2/12} = 20\log_{10}(2^b - 1) \approx 20\,b\log_{10}2 = 6.02\,b dB. For b = 4: 20\log_{10}15 \approx 23.5 dB (6.02 · 4 = 24.1 is the large-b approximation). The demo’s ramp at 4 bits shows exactly 23.5 dB.
B6. x + u reaches the rounding threshold k + \tfrac12 when u \ge \tfrac12 - f, with probability f; then the output is k + 1, otherwise k. So \mathbb E = (1-f)k + f(k+1) = x. The error is 1 - f (probability f) or -f (probability 1-f): \mathbb E[e^2] = f(1-f)^2 + (1-f)f^2 = f(1-f), and \int_0^1 f(1-f)\,df = \tfrac12 - \tfrac13 = \tfrac16. In units of \Delta^2: \Delta^2/6, twice \Delta^2/12, so the RMS error is \sqrt2 \approx 1.41 times larger. (The demo: 0.0272 vs 0.0192 on the ramp at 4 bits, a ratio of 1.42.)

title: Exercise: quantisation and bit depth
text:
Explore

Quantising an image
The demo rounds an image to b bits and shows the rounding error (0 = grey, \pm\Delta = white/black) and its histogram. Images: a ramp, smooth blobs, and the 8-bit micrograph.



E1. On the ramp, step the bits from 8 down to 1. Compare the RMS error with \Delta/\sqrt{12} in the readout. How much does the SNR change per bit?
E2. Click 4 bits: banding, then 4 bits + dither. What happens to the contour lines, to the error histogram, and to the RMS error? Which picture looks closer to the original?
E3. Micrograph at 2 bits: compare no dither and error diffusion. Which has the larger RMS error? Which shows the cell better? What does that tell you about RMS error as a measure of image quality?
E4. Micrograph at 8 bits: the RMS error is 0. Why?






Solutions





E1. They agree to the 4th decimal at every bit depth (e.g. 0.0192 at 4 bits, 0.0046 at 6 bits): on a ramp the error is exactly uniform. The SNR goes 23.5, 29.8, 36.0 dB for 4, 5, 6 bits: about 6 dB per bit.
E2. The contour lines disappear and become fine grain. The histogram changes from a box on \pm\Delta/2 to a triangle on \pm\Delta, and the RMS error grows from 0.0192 to 0.0273, about \sqrt2 times. Yet the dithered image looks closer to the original from a distance: its error has no structure, and the eye averages it away.
E3. Error diffusion has the larger RMS error (0.1200 against 0.0968), but it shows far more of the cell: with only 4 grey levels, the local average of the diffused pixels follows the true grey value. The RMS error compares pixels one by one and ignores what the eye does, which is to average neighbours. A small number is not always a better picture.
E4. The micrograph is stored with 8 bits already, so every value is exactly one of the 256 levels and rounding changes nothing. Quantising can only lose information; it cannot add the bits that were never measured.

title: Exercise: quantisation and bit depth
text:
Where this leads
Rounding is only one source of error in a pixel value. The next unit, camera noise, asks where the numbers come from: a camera counts electrons, the count is noisy, and that noise, not the rounding, usually decides how many bits are worth storing. It also defines the SNR and PSNR used in the rest of the course.

title: Image formation and the point spread function
text:
About this lecture
A microscope does not deliver the object; it delivers a blurred, sampled, noisy version of it. Today we write down what it does, step by step:

The imaging chain as a forward model: object → optics → pixels → noise.
The image of a point, the point spread function (PSF): image = object ∗ PSF.
Its Fourier transform, the OTF: how much contrast survives at each frequency.
Diffraction: a lens passes nothing above 2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda. Resolution in nanometres.
Other blurs: defocus (contrast can reverse) and motion (the OTF has zeros).

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

First unit of the image formation day (day 4). It owns the PSF, the OTF and the forward model. Recalls (one slide each, no re-teaching): convolution (filtering unit, day 1), the convolution theorem (frequency unit, day 1), noise and quantisation (bit depth and noise day, day 3). Notation: f = object, h = PSF, g = image, H = OTF, n = noise. Wavelength λ in nm, NA = numerical aperture. Restoration (deconvolution) is the next day; this day ends with the diagnosis only (third unit).

title: Image formation and the point spread function
text:
The imaging chain

A micrograph treated as the true object (40 nm pixels), through an ideal lens with NA 0.8, sampled with 160 nm pixels, about 20 photons per pixel, and 8 grey levels.
Optics blur: every point becomes a small blob.
Sampling: the pixel grid records one number per pixel.
Noise: photons arrive at random, the camera adds read noise.
Quantisation: a finite number of grey levels.

This chain is the forward model: what the instrument does to the truth. Analysis that wants to measure the object has to know it.

Image: transmission electron micrograph of a mesenchymal stem cell, Robert M. Hunt, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons. It is itself already a blurred image; here it plays the role of the “true object”. Emphasise the order: blur happens in the continuous world before the pixels; noise is added per pixel after sampling.

title: Image formation and the point spread function

Recall: the last two steps
From the bit depth and noise day:

Noise (the camera noise unit): photon counts are Poisson, \text{SNR} = \sqrt{N} for N photons; the camera adds read noise and an offset.
Quantisation (the quantisation unit): a finite bit depth rounds every value to a grey level.

Today is about the first steps: the optics, and (next unit) the pixels. The noise comes back at the end of the day, where it decides what can be undone.

title: Image formation and the point spread function
text:
The image of a point
A lens cannot focus light to a point. The image of a point is a small blob: the point spread function, h.

Fluorescence is incoherent: the images of different points add up in intensity.
So the image is a sum of shifted copies of the PSF, each weighted by the brightness of its point: a convolution, image = object ∗ PSF.
This is the convolution of the filtering unit, with a kernel made by physics. A blur kernel is a PSF.

title: Image formation and the point spread function
section: The math: convolution and the OTF
text:
The math: convolution and the OTF
Object f, PSF h, noise n:
g(\mathbf x) = (f \ast h)(\mathbf x) + n(\mathbf x) = \int f(\mathbf y)\,h(\mathbf x - \mathbf y)\,d\mathbf y + n(\mathbf x).
Fourier transform (capital letters), by the convolution theorem:
G(\mathbf k) = F(\mathbf k)\,H(\mathbf k) + N(\mathbf k).

H is the optical transfer function (OTF); |H| is the modulation transfer function (MTF).
A PSF normalised to \int h = 1 has H(\mathbf 0) = \int h(\mathbf x)\,e^{0}\,d\mathbf x = 1: the mean brightness passes unchanged.
A PSF that is symmetric, h(-\mathbf x) = h(\mathbf x), has a real OTF; it can still be negative.
A grating 1 + \cos(2\pi \mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x) is imaged as 1 + H(\mathbf k)\cos(2\pi\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x) (symmetric PSF): its contrast is multiplied by H(\mathbf k).
crumbs: Image formation and the point spread function

title: Image formation and the point spread function
text:
Recall: blur in frequency space
From the frequency unit: convolution = multiplication of spectra. So the optics act frequency by frequency.

The PSF’s Fourier transform, the OTF, says how much of each frequency (each stripe pattern) survives.
Its magnitude, the MTF, is the contrast kept: 1 at frequency 0 (the mean brightness), falling towards 0 for fine detail.
Example (numbers on the next slides): a grating with period 500 nm keeps 54 % of its contrast through an NA 1.4 objective, one with period 250 nm 15 %, one with period 150 nm nothing.
crumbs: Image formation and the point spread function

title: Image formation and the point spread function
section: Diffraction: a hard edge in frequency
text:
Diffraction: a hard edge in frequency
The objective collects only a cone of light with half-angle \alpha. Its numerical aperture is \mathrm{NA} = n\sin\alpha (n: refractive index, 1.518 for immersion oil).

Left: the PSF of a perfect lens (Airy pattern), log scale. Middle: its profile, with the Gaussian approximation. Right: the OTF, zero beyond 2NA/λ.
The OTF is exactly zero beyond the cut-off frequency 2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda: the microscope is a low-pass filter with a hard edge.
Detail finer than the cut-off is not just blurred: it is gone from the image.
The PSF of a perfect lens is the Airy pattern: a central disc, radius 0.61\lambda/\mathrm{NA}, and faint rings.
crumbs: Image formation and the point spread function

title: Image formation and the point spread function
section: The math: the pupil and the Airy pattern
text:
The math: the pupil and the Airy pattern
The lens passes the plane waves inside the cone: in frequency space a disc of radius \mathrm{NA}/\lambda, the pupil P.

Coherent (amplitude) PSF: a = \mathcal F^{-1} P. Incoherent (intensity) PSF: h = |a|^2 = |\mathcal F^{-1}P|^2.
Then H = \mathcal F h = P \star P, the autocorrelation of the pupil: the overlap of the disc with a copy shifted by \mathbf k. It is zero once the shift exceeds the pupil diameter: cut-off |\mathbf k| = 2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda.
Overlap of two discs, s = |\mathbf k|/k_c: \displaystyle H(s) = \tfrac{2}{\pi}\big(\arccos s - s\sqrt{1 - s^2}\big) for s \le 1, else 0.
Circular pupil: h(r) \propto \left[\dfrac{2J_1(v)}{v}\right]^2, v = \dfrac{2\pi\,\mathrm{NA}\,r}{\lambda} (J_1: Bessel function). The first zero of J_1 is at v = 3.832, so the dark ring is at r = \dfrac{3.832}{2\pi}\dfrac{\lambda}{\mathrm{NA}} = 0.61\dfrac{\lambda}{\mathrm{NA}}.
Width: \text{FWHM} = 0.51\lambda/\mathrm{NA}; the Gaussian with \sigma = 0.21\lambda/\mathrm{NA} matches the central disc.

title: Image formation and the point spread function
text:
Other blurs, other PSFs

Defocus: the PSF widens; far out of focus it becomes a ring. Its OTF goes negative at some frequencies: stripes there appear with reversed contrast (bright where the object is dark).
Motion during the exposure (length L): the PSF is a short line. Its OTF along the motion is a sinc with exact zeros at 1/L, 2/L, \dots: those stripe patterns vanish completely. L = 1 µm: zeros at 1, 2, 3 cycles/µm.
Gaussian with \sigma = 0.21\lambda/\mathrm{NA}: the convenient approximation of the in-focus PSF (no rings, no hard cut-off). The scale of the optics, \sigma = 78 nm at NA 1.4: spot detectors (edges, blobs and ridges day) should be tuned to it.
Also blurs: scattering in tissue, the pixel’s own area, atmospheric turbulence for telescopes.
crumbs: Image formation and the point spread function

title: Image formation and the point spread function
text:
The math: defocus and motion
Defocus by z: each plane wave in the pupil travels a slightly different optical path. A phase \phi(\rho) = 2\pi z\big(\sqrt{(n/\lambda)^2 - \rho^2} - n/\lambda\big) is added at pupil frequency \rho; close to the axis this is \approx -\pi\lambda z\rho^2/n, a quadratic phase.
h_z = \big|\mathcal F^{-1}\big(P\,e^{i\phi}\big)\big|^2, \qquad H_z = (P e^{i\phi}) \star (P e^{i\phi}).
The phases interfere in the autocorrelation; the overlap can sum to a negative number.
Motion at constant speed over a length L along x: h(x) = \tfrac1L\mathbf 1_{[-L/2,\,L/2]}(x), and
H(k) = \frac1L\int_{-L/2}^{L/2} e^{-2\pi i k x}\,dx = \frac{\sin(\pi L k)}{\pi L k} = \mathrm{sinc}(Lk),
zero at k = 1/L, 2/L, \dots, most negative -0.217 between the first two zeros.

title: Image formation and the point spread function
section: Try it: defocus and motion blur
text:
Try it: defocus and motion blur




“Defocus: contrast reversal” (NA 0.7 in air, 2 µm out of focus, signed OTF, contrast stretched): the PSF is a ring of 826 nm FWHM. The OTF is negative from about 0.55 to 2.3 cycles/µm (most negative −0.057 at 0.68); on the star, the spokes between about 1.1 and 4.6 µm from the centre are reversed: follow one bright spoke inwards and it turns dark. “Motion blur” (1 µm along x): the signed OTF image shows vertical blue and white stripes; the curve has zeros at 1 and 2 cycles/µm and dips to −0.143; the vertical spokes of the star lose and reverse contrast, the horizontal ones do not. Change the angle. “Gaussian approximation” (beads, log PSF): FWHM 186 nm vs 192 nm for the Airy PSF; the curves agree up to about 4 cycles/µm, but the Gaussian has no rings and no hard cut-off.

title: Image formation and the point spread function
text:
Summary

The forward model: image = sample(object ∗ PSF) + noise. Restoration tries to run it backwards (end of the day; the deconvolution day does it).
PSF = image of a point; incoherent light: image = object ∗ PSF.
OTF = Fourier transform of the PSF = contrast kept per frequency; H(0) = 1.
Diffraction: OTF = 0 beyond 2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda; finer detail is gone. Airy disc radius 0.61\lambda/\mathrm{NA}: 227 nm at NA 1.4, 520 nm.
Defocus: wider PSF, negative OTF lobes, reversed contrast. Motion: a line PSF, OTF zeros at k/L.
The Gaussian \sigma = 0.21\lambda/\mathrm{NA} is a good approximation of the in-focus PSF.

title: Quiz: closed boundaries in polar coordinates
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. The image is unwrapped around a centre c: angle across, radius down; the boundary is one radius r_k per angle, with |r_{k+1} - r_k| \le \delta and a penalty \alpha|r_{k+1} - r_k|.

Q1. What does “star-shaped around c” mean, and why does polar DP need it?






Answer





Every ray from c leaves the object exactly once. Then the boundary is a function: one radius per angle. Polar DP chooses exactly one radius per angle, so it can only describe star-shaped boundaries; where a ray crosses the boundary several times, all but one crossing are lost.




Q2. Why does the unwrapping use bilinear interpolation?






Answer





The sample points c + r(\cos\theta, \sin\theta) almost never fall on pixel centres. Bilinear interpolation reads a value between the four surrounding pixels (inverse mapping, as for any geometric transform), so the polar image is smooth and does not depend on rounding.




Q3. A dark cell on a bright background. Which polarity should the cost have, going outward from the centre? What goes wrong with the other one?






Answer





Dark inside, bright outside: dark → bright, cost = -\partial P/\partial r (low where the intensity rises). With bright → dark the real boundary costs extra, and the path settles on whatever falls in intensity going outward: noise, or a dark neighbour’s far edge.




Q4. What happens with \delta = 0? And with a very large \delta and \alpha = 0?






Answer





\delta = 0: the radius cannot change: the result is a circle around c (the radius with the lowest total cost). A large \delta with \alpha = 0: every angle chooses its own best radius almost independently, and the boundary jumps between edges, noise and neighbouring objects.




Q5. Why does the plain DP table not give a closed curve, and what does the exact method do about it?






Answer





The table treats angle 0 and angle K-1 as the two ends of an open path; nothing links them, so the radii at the two ends can differ by more than \delta (a jump at 0°). The exact method fixes the start radius, runs DP, and accepts only ends within \delta of the start; it does this for every start radius and keeps the best closed path.




Q6. Unrolling: why does running DP over three copies of the angles and keeping the middle copy usually give a closed curve? Is it guaranteed?






Answer





The middle copy is far from the free ends of the long path, so it is (usually) where the path has “settled” into the same route as in its neighbouring copies; then the middle copy ends where the next copy starts, at about the same radius. It is not guaranteed: the path may enter the third copy at another radius, and then the middle copy does not close; and even when it closes it need not be the cheapest closed path.




Q7. Compared with a snake started near the boundary, what is the advantage of polar DP, and what is its price?






Answer





Polar DP finds the global optimum of its energy: it is not trapped by a weak edge near the start, and needs only a centre, not a starting curve. The price is the restriction to star-shaped boundaries around a known centre; a snake can describe any closed curve (but only finds a local minimum).




Q8. (math) With K angles, R radii and steps up to \delta, how many operations does one DP run take, and how many does the exact closure take?






Answer





One run: K \cdot R cells with up to 2\delta + 1 candidates, about KR(2\delta + 1). Exact closure: one run per start radius, about KR^2(2\delta + 1): for K = 360, R = 100, \delta = 3, 252 000 and 25.2 million.

title: Exercise: closed boundaries in polar coordinates
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Star-shaped around c
every ray from c leaves the object once; the boundary is a radius r(\theta) per angle


Unwrapping
P(\theta_k, r) = I(c_x + r\cos\theta_k,\ c_y + r\sin\theta_k), read by bilinear interpolation; y points down, so \theta turns clockwise on the screen


Cost
from the radial derivative \partial P/\partial r: +\partial P/\partial r for a bright → dark edge, -\partial P/\partial r for dark → bright


Smoothness
\lvert r_{k+1} - r_k\rvert \le \delta, plus a penalty \alpha\lvert r_{k+1} - r_k\rvert


Recursion
M(k, r) = C(k, r) + \min_{\lvert d\rvert \le \delta}\big(M(k-1, r+d) + \alpha\lvert d\rvert\big)


Closure
also \lvert r_0 - r_{K-1}\rvert \le \delta: try every start radius (exact) or unroll the angles three times (heuristic)
