B8. (math) DP snakes. Each of n snake points may move to one of m positions in a window. (a) With an elastic term \alpha|v_i - v_{i-1}|^2 and an image term, write the recursion and show that one pass costs O(nm^2). (b) With a bending term \beta|v_{i+1} - 2v_i + v_{i-1}|^2, explain why the states must be pairs of positions and show the cost O(nm^3).
B9. (math) Show that for a bright disc of radius \rho and contrast h on a dark background, smoothed with a Gaussian of scale \sigma \ll \rho, the radial derivative along any ray from the centre is most negative at r \approx \rho, with value about -h/(\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma). What happens to the minimum if the centre is moved by a small offset?






Solutions (math)





B6. Every closed path has a start radius s. For fixed s the run with only s allowed at angle 0 computes, by the principle of optimality, the cheapest path from (0, s) to every (K-1, r); adding the closing step \alpha|r - s| and allowing only |r - s| \le \delta gives the cheapest closed path starting at s. The minimum over s is the cheapest closed path. Work: R runs of K R (2\delta + 1) operations: 100 \cdot 360 \cdot 100 \cdot 7 = 25.2 million, against 252\,000 for one open run (100 times more), still a fraction of a second.
B7. |r(0°) - r(270°)| = |4 - 2| = 2 > 1: not closed. Its cost with the closing step ignored: 2 + 1 + 0 + 3 = 6. The best closed path (trying all starts as in B1) costs 7. The open path through three copies is optimal as a whole, but nothing forces it to pass the “seam” between two copies at the same radius at both ends of the middle copy: the cheapest way through the third copy may enter it at a different radius than the middle copy was entered from the first. Usually the copies agree (the middle is far from the free ends), but not always, and when it closes it is not guaranteed to be the cheapest closed path.
B8. (a) M_i(v) = E_{\text{img}}(v) + \min_{u \in W_{i-1}}\big(M_{i-1}(u) + \alpha|v - u|^2\big): m states, m candidates each, so m^2 per point and O(nm^2) per pass (times m for the exact closure of a closed snake). (b) The bending term at point i involves v_{i-1}, v_i, v_{i+1}; a recursion over single positions would need v_{i-2} when choosing v_i, which is not in the state. With the state (v_{i-1}, v_i): M_i(v_{i-1}, v_i) = E_{\text{img}}(v_i) + \alpha|v_i - v_{i-1}|^2 + \min_{v_{i-2}}\big(M_{i-1}(v_{i-2}, v_{i-1}) + \beta|v_i - 2v_{i-1} + v_{i-2}|^2\big): m^2 states with m candidates each, O(nm^3).
B9. Near the boundary a disc of radius \rho \gg \sigma looks like a straight step of height h across the ray. The smoothed step is h\,\Phi\big((\rho - r)/\sigma\big) (with \Phi the normal distribution function), whose derivative in r is -\frac{h}{\sigma}\varphi\big((r - \rho)/\sigma\big), most negative at r = \rho with value -h/(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma). From an offset centre the ray meets the boundary at an angle \gamma to the normal; the radial derivative is the directional derivative along the ray, about \cos\gamma times the normal one, so the minimum stays at the boundary but is weaker where the ray is oblique: another reason to centre well.

title: Exercise: closed boundaries in polar coordinates
text:
Explore
Left: the image with the centre (drag it, or click to move it), every few rays (red: angle 0°), the allowed annulus [r_{\min}, r_{\max}] (dashed) and the boundary found. Middle: the unwrapped image, angle across and radius down, with the path; cost shows the cost table (blue = cheap) and table M the cumulative table of the DP. The readout gives the gap |r(0°) - r(\text{last})|, whether the curve closes, the path cost (lower is better), the number of operations and the time.



E1. Preset nucleus: done (K = 120, \delta = 1, \alpha = 0.1, bright → dark, exact). Read the gap and the cost. Look at the lower left of the nucleus, where its edge is a weak, wide ramp: how does the boundary get across? Switch the middle view to cost and find the weak part there.
E2. Same preset, closure open, then unroll ×3, then exact. Compare gap, cost and operations. Which ones close?
E3. Preset no smoothness (\delta = 8, \alpha = 0). Where does the boundary go at 0°, and is its cost higher or lower than in E1? What does that tell you about the energy? Now raise \alpha to 0.3: what happens?
E4. Preset open path: jump at 0°. How large is the jump? Switch to exact: where does the path change?
E5. Preset bad centre (the bean, centre in its left lobe). Which part is missing, and why can no smoothness setting recover it? Press centre → centroid of the contour a few times. Does it converge to a good boundary? Then choose the image bean (its default centre is in the middle, below the dent): what happens at the dent, with \delta = 1 and with \delta = 8?
E6. Preset wrong polarity (dark → bright on a bright nucleus). Where does the path go, and what is its cost? Try either.
E7. Preset micrograph nucleus (dark-line cost, \delta = 2). Where does the boundary follow the nuclear envelope, and where does it go wrong? Explain with the “brighter edge on the same ray” failure mode.






Solutions





E1. Gap 0 px (closes), cost -58.67 with 3 618 020 operations. In the lower left (angles around 145°) the cost is only weakly negative over a wide band of radii; the smoothness limit (\delta = 1 per 3°) and the penalty make the path continue at the radius of the neighbouring rays, about 40 px, until the strong edge returns. In the cost view the weak part is the pale stretch of the blue band.
E2. Open: gap 7 px, does not close (the readout’s closed cost -58.72 includes the closing step; the open path itself costs -59.42), 35 819 operations. Unroll ×3: gap 0, cost -58.67, 108 059 operations (3 runs). Exact: gap 0, cost -58.67, 3 618 020 operations (one run per start radius). Here the unroll heuristic finds the same closed path as the exact method, 33 times faster.
E3. At 0° the path jumps out to the outer edge of the brighter neighbour, radius 94 px, and comes back on the other side of it (the jumps of up to 8 px per angle make that possible). Its cost is lower: -69.99 against -58.67. The energy prefers the neighbour’s outer edge, which is a stronger bright → dark edge; the optimiser is doing its job, the model (cost and smoothness) is what decides. With \alpha = 0.3 the detour becomes too expensive: the boundary returns to the nucleus (largest radius 51 px), cost -50.53.
E4. The gap is 15 px: the open path starts at radius 52 px at 0° and ends at 37 px at the last angle. With exact the gap becomes 0: both ends now meet at the same radius, and the path near 0° changes so that the curve closes.
E5. The right lobe is missing: from a centre in the left lobe, the rays towards the right lobe cross the dent of the bean, so they leave the object, cross background and enter it again. A radius per angle can describe only one crossing; no smoothness setting changes that. Pressing centre → centroid moves the centre to (84, 139), (88, 142) and then (92, 145), where it stays: the contour still only covers the left part, so its centroid stays there too. Iterating does not escape. Dragging the centre to the middle of the bean below the dent (the image’s default centre (128, 140); choose the image bean again) gives a boundary around both lobes, but it bridges the dent at a radius of about 61 px instead of dipping into it: the walls of the dent run almost along the rays, and with \delta = 1 (or even 4) and \alpha = 0.1 going 45 px down and back up costs more than the dent’s edge gains. With \delta = 8 the path follows the dent (radius 16 px straight up, at 270°). Star-shaped is necessary, but steep parts of the boundary also need a large enough \delta.
E6. With dark → bright the boundary of the nucleus is the wrong sign and costs extra. The path stays close to the centre (radius 8–14 px), following noise, with cost -3.05: nearly nothing is found. Either finds the nucleus again (cost -60.39).
E7. At the top, right and bottom the boundary follows the thin dark envelope of the nucleus. On the left it runs outside the envelope, along the parallel dark cell membrane a few pixels further out: on those rays the membrane is an equally good (or better) dark line, and \delta = 2 lets the path reach it. A tighter annulus (r_{\max}) or a larger \alpha helps here; a different centre changes which line each ray sees first.

title: Exercise: closed boundaries in polar coordinates
text:
Where this leads
Polar DP needs an order: angle after angle. A boundary between two points that may wander in any direction, in any image, has no such order. The next unit drops the fixed order and lets the algorithm discover it: Dijkstra’s algorithm and live-wire segmentation.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
text:
About this lecture
Paint a few strokes on an image, “this is nucleus, this is background”, and let a forest label every pixel: semantic segmentation without deep learning.

Every pixel becomes a point in feature space; the painted pixels are the training set.
The feature stack: filters at several scales describe each pixel’s neighbourhood.
The interactive loop: paint, train, look at the result and the uncertainty, correct.
The traps: neighbouring pixels are not independent, label imbalance, painting only the easy cases.
From probabilities to objects.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

This unit owns the pixel feature stack and the paint – train – correct loop for the course. The SVM, integral-images and neural-network days recall it. The demo works on a synthetic test image with ground truth (so we can measure honestly) and on the course micrograph.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
text:
Every pixel is a point

Thresholding asked one question of one number: is the pixel bright?
Instead, describe each pixel by many numbers: its brightness at several blurs, how strong the edges near it are, whether it sits in a blob, a line or a texture.
The painted pixels, with their classes, are training points in this feature space.
The forest colours the whole feature space, and with it every pixel of the image.

Why not intensity alone? Two kinds of cell in the test image have the same mean brightness: smooth nuclei and granular cells. Only their texture differs: exactly the situation of the eight pixels in the decision-trees unit.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
text:
The feature stack

Each filter family at each scale \sigma gives one image, a channel; a pixel’s feature vector is its value in every channel. Above (test image, left to right, top row then bottom): smoothed at \sigma = 1 and 5, gradient magnitude (\sigma = 1.6), Laplacian of Gaussian (\sigma = 5), Hessian eigenvalue and structure-tensor eigenvalue (\sigma = 1.6).

Scales used in the demo: σ = 0.7, 1, 1.6 (small) and 3.5, 5, 10 (large). Five families: intensity (1 channel per σ), edges (1), blobs (1), ridges (2), texture (2): 7 channels per σ, 42 in all. The granular cells light up in the gradient and structure-tensor channels at small σ; the LoG at σ = 5 is a “blob of this size” detector.

The filters come from the filtering unit (Gaussian, derivatives, Laplacian) and the edges, blobs and ridges day (LoG, Hessian, structure tensor). The forest takes the whole pile as it is: no scaling, and redundant channels do no harm. Box means and local variances are the cheap cousins (integral-images day).

title: Pixel classification with a forest
section: The math: the stack as formulas

title: Pixel classification with a forest
section: The loop: paint, train, look, correct
text:
The loop: paint, train, look, correct

Paint a few strokes per class.
Train the forest on the painted pixels (seconds, or less).
Look at the segmentation and at the uncertainty map (1 − the largest vote fraction).
Correct: paint where the result is wrong or uncertain, and train again.

Few strokes go a long way, because each stroke holds hundreds of pixels and the features describe their neighbourhoods. Interactive pixel-classification programs implement exactly this loop.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
text:
Try it: paint and classify




Synthetic test image: background (uneven illumination, brighter to the right), smooth nuclei (some dim), granular cells as bright as the nuclei. Tour: “two strokes” (nucleus + background): 87.4 % of the pixels right; the granular cells are called nucleus (8.5 % of the image). “intensity only” (three classes painted): 91.3 %, granular cells partly nucleus. “full stack”: 96.3 %, Dice nucleus 0.85, granular 0.86. “uncertainty”: without a granular stroke the granular cells are classified confidently as nucleus — the uncertainty map shows the object rims and the brighter background on the right, not the granular cells. Then “micrograph: nucleus” and “+ cytoplasm”.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
section: Trap 1: neighbouring pixels are near copies
text:
Trap 1: neighbouring pixels are near copies

The pixels of one stroke are almost identical in every channel (the filters even mix them).
OOB error assumes independent samples. A pixel left out of a tree’s bootstrap sample has its neighbour inside it: the “unseen” pixel is not new. OOB accuracy is close to 100 % almost regardless of the result.
Honest evaluation: a held-out region (or another image) with its own labels: the confusion matrix and Dice of the thresholding day.
Even then: your strokes sit where labelling was easy. Accuracy on painted pixels overrates the result; a full annotation of a region is the honest test.

Rule: split by image or region, never by pixel. The evaluation day treats leakage and object-level evaluation in full.

“OOB vs held-out region”: training strokes only left of the yellow line. OOB accuracy 100.0 %; the held-out region’s painted pixels 99.8 % right (650 pixels); against the full ground truth in that region 95.9 %.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
section: The math: why OOB fails here
text:
The math: why OOB fails here
The bootstrap treats the n painted pixels as n independent draws. Pixels along a stroke are strongly correlated: the effective number of independent samples is close to the number of strokes, not the number of pixels. A tree that saw pixel p + 1 has, in effect, seen pixel p, so the OOB vote on p is not a prediction for new data. The OOB error is then an estimate of the error on pixels next to the strokes. Leaving out whole strokes (or regions) restores independence: the SVM day’s by-stroke cross-validation does exactly that.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
text:
Trap 2: label imbalance

A big background stroke has thousands of pixels; a nucleus stroke a few dozen.
Ambiguous pixels (dim nuclei, object rims) fall into leaves dominated by background: the probabilities lean towards the big class.
Fix: balance: weight each class by 1/n_c (or sample the same number of pixels per class).
Balancing moves errors from the small classes to the large one: the small classes are found more often, the background a little less. It cannot invent information the strokes lack.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
text:
The math: class weights = resampling
With weight w_k for every sample of class k, the class shares in a node become p_k = \frac{w_k n_k}{\sum_l w_l n_l} , the same as if each sample of class k were copied w_k times. So weighted Gini picks the same splits as Gini on the resampled data. Balancing weights w_k = \dfrac{n}{K\, n_k} give every class the same total weight n/K. Example: 400 background and 20 nucleus pixels: w = 0.525 and 10.5 (ratio 20). A leaf with 8 background and 2 nucleus pixels: P(\text{nucleus}) = 0.2 unweighted, 0.83 weighted.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
section: Trap 3: the forest knows only what it was shown
text:
Trap 3: the forest knows only what it was shown

Paint only the bright nuclei, and the dim ones look like nothing the forest knows: part of them become background.
Leave out a whole class (the granular cells) and its pixels are forced into the classes that exist, often confidently: the uncertainty map flags rims and new illumination, but not “something else that looks like a nucleus”.
Scale: channels much larger than the structures blur across boundaries; with only small scales the result is speckled and loses context.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
text:
From probabilities to objects

Threshold the probability map of the class you want (0.5, or chosen with the ROC or precision–recall curve of the thresholding day).
Clean up with morphology: opening, filling holes, removing small pieces.
Or smooth with a graph cut: use -\log P(\text{class} \mid \text{features}) as the data term (the graph-cuts day).
Then label the connected components and measure them, and the measurement table may go into another forest (previous unit).

title: Pixel classification with a forest
section: Forests, SVMs and networks on the same pixels
text:
Forests, SVMs and networks on the same pixels

A forest on a hand-made stack is the strong baseline that works from a few strokes: no scaling, little tuning, fast.
An SVM on the same stack needs standardised features and a search over its settings (the SVM day plugs into the same demo).
A convolutional network (U-Net, the neural-networks day) learns its own filters instead of the stack, and needs many more labelled pixels.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
text:
Summary

Pixel classification = classification in a feature space whose axes are filter responses at several scales.
The feature stack: intensity, edges, blobs, ridges, texture; the forest needs no scaling.
The loop: paint, train, look at segmentation and uncertainty, correct.
OOB is optimistic for pixels (neighbours are near copies): evaluate on a held-out region with full labels.
Imbalance: weight or resample; the forest knows only what it was shown.
Probabilities → threshold, morphology or graph cut → objects.

title: Quiz: SVMs for pixel classification
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. The pixel classifier of the random forests day: paint strokes, compute a feature stack, train, look, correct; here with an SVM.

Q1. Why does an RBF SVM need standardised features while a random forest does not?






Hint





What does each method compute with the feature values?









Answer





The RBF kernel function depends on the distance between feature vectors, which is dominated by the features with the largest numbers; features with small ranges become invisible. A forest only compares one feature at a time with a threshold, and a threshold works the same in any units.




Q2. You standardise with the mean and standard deviation of all pixels of the image, including the held-out region you evaluate on. What is wrong with that?






Hint





Which data may influence the model?









Answer





The held-out pixels then influence the model (through \mu_j, s_j): information leaks from the evaluation data into training, and the measured error can be optimistic. Compute the statistics on the training pixels (in cross-validation: on the training folds) and apply them unchanged to everything else.




Q3. Cross-validation with folds by pixel reports 0% error; with folds by stroke 19%. Which do you report, and why do they differ?






Hint





Where are the neighbours of a held-out pixel?









Answer





By stroke. With folds by pixel, each held-out pixel’s neighbours (nearly identical, from the same stroke) are in training, so even memorising gets it right. With folds by stroke the held-out pixels come from strokes the SVM has not seen, as new parts of the image will be.




Q4. A cross-validation map over (C, \gamma) is worst in the corner with the largest C and \gamma. Explain.






Hint





Unit 3: what does an RBF SVM with large \gamma and large C do to the training points?









Answer





Large \gamma: each bump covers only its own training pixel; large C: no violation is tolerated. The SVM builds an island around every training pixel and calls everything else by the default value b: it memorises (zero training error) and fails on held-out strokes. Overfitting.




Q5. A one-vs-rest SVM gives a pixel f_1 = -0.5, f_2 = -0.2, f_3 = -0.9. Which class, and how sure is it?






Hint





How many classifiers claim the pixel?









Answer





Class 2 (the largest f), but none of the three SVMs claims the pixel: it lies in a region that each SVM assigns to “the rest”. The decision compares uncalibrated values and is unreliable; the pixel is a good place to paint.




Q6. How many SVMs does one-vs-one train for 4 classes? And one-vs-rest?






Hint





One per pair; one per class.









Answer





One-vs-one: 4 \cdot 3/2 = 6. One-vs-rest: 4.




Q7. Nuclei are only 5% of the painted pixels and the SVM misses many of them. Name two remedies that do not need more painting.






Hint





One changes the training, one the decision.









Answer





Class weights: a larger penalty C for nucleus violations (e.g. balancing weights n/(k\,n_c)). Or keep the SVM and lower the threshold on f for the nucleus class, trading precision for recall (an ROC curve shows the trade-off).




Q8. When would you choose an SVM over a random forest for pixels, and when a neural network?






Hint





How many labels, and where do the features come from?









Answer





An SVM: few labelled pixels and a good hand-made feature stack, when you are willing to standardise and cross-validate (C, \gamma); it is about as accurate as a forest there, but slower to predict and more work to tune. A neural network: many labelled images, when the features themselves should be learnt (the neural networks day). The forest remains the low-effort baseline.

text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

explain why an RBF SVM needs standardised features and a forest does not, and standardise by hand,
choose (C, \gamma) from a cross-validation map, and explain why folds must be by stroke,

title: Exercise: SVMs for pixel classification
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Feature stack
per pixel: intensity, edges, blobs, ridges, texture at several scales (the random forests day)


Standardisation
z_j = (x_j - \mu_j)/s_j per feature, with \mu_j, s_j from the training pixels


(C, \gamma) grid
cross-validated error on a log grid; small values underfit, large values overfit


Folds by stroke
all pixels of a stroke go into the same fold; folds by pixel are optimistic


Class weights
penalty C_c per class; balancing weights n/(k\,n_c)


One-vs-rest
K SVMs (class k vs the rest), take the largest f_k


One-vs-one
K(K-1)/2 SVMs (one per pair), majority vote
