Which (C, \gamma) do you pick? What do you do next?
Explain the corner with small C and small \gamma, and the row \gamma = 10.
With folds by pixel the same grid shows 0–2% for most cells with \gamma \ge 0.1. Why?

B4. You painted 2000 background pixels and 100 nucleus pixels. (a) Give the balancing weights n/(k\,n_c) for the two classes, and the ratio C_{\text{nucleus}}/C_{\text{background}} they imply. (b) Instead of retraining, how could you make the SVM find more nucleus pixels? What do you trade?
B5. In which order would you do these steps, and which must be repeated inside each cross-validation fold? (i) compute \mu_j, s_j; (ii) standardise; (iii) train the SVM; (iv) choose (C, \gamma); (v) report the error on the test region.

Math questions
B6 (math). K = 5 classes, 200 training pixels each. How many SVMs, of which sizes, do one-vs-rest and one-vs-one train? If training costs about (size)² operations, which is cheaper, and by what factor?
B7 (math). Show that a linear SVM trained on features scaled by a diagonal matrix D (\mathbf x' = D\mathbf x) is not the same classifier as the one trained on \mathbf x, even though any line in \mathbf x can be written as a line in \mathbf x'. (Hint: what happens to the penalty \|\mathbf w\|^2?)






Solutions





B1. (a) \boldsymbol\mu_A = (2000, 0.25), \boldsymbol\mu_B = (2100, 0.85). Distances of the test pixel: to A \sqrt{80^2 + 0.05^2} = 80.0, to B \sqrt{20^2 + 0.55^2} = 20.0: class B, decided by the intensity alone. (b) Intensity: mean 2050, standard deviation 906.9. Texture: mean 0.55, standard deviation 0.304. z-scores: \boldsymbol\mu_A \to (-0.055, -0.986), \boldsymbol\mu_B \to (0.055, 0.986), test pixel \to (0.033, -0.822). (c) Distances in z-scores: to A 0.187, to B 1.809: class A. The z-scores are more believable: the intensity hardly differs between the classes (both span 1000–3000), while the texture separates them cleanly, and the test pixel’s texture (0.3) is that of class A. In raw units, a difference of 80 grey levels outweighs any texture difference.
B2. p: class 1 (only f_1 > 0; clear). q: f_1 and f_2 are both positive: two classifiers claim it; the largest is f_2 = 0.6: class 2, ambiguous. r: no classifier claims it (all negative); the largest is f_3 = -0.2: class 3, ambiguous. s: class 2 (only f_2 > 0; clear). The ambiguous decisions compare f values of different SVMs, which were never trained to be comparable.
B3. (a) C = 10, \gamma = 0.1 (11%). Then train on all training pixels with these settings and evaluate once on the test region (the 11% itself is slightly optimistic, being the minimum of 16 estimates). (b) Small C, small \gamma: almost a straight boundary that tolerates many violations: underfitting (31%). \gamma = 10: a length scale shorter than the distance between strokes; each training pixel has its own island, and the held-out strokes fall outside all islands: overfitting, whatever C. (c) With folds by pixel, every held-out pixel has its neighbours from the same stroke in training; those are nearly identical, so even an SVM that only memorises (large \gamma) gets them right. The by-pixel error measures memory, not generalisation to new places in the image.
B4. (a) n = 2100, k = 2: background 2100/(2 \cdot 2000) = 0.525, nucleus 2100/(2 \cdot 100) = 10.5. Ratio 20: a nucleus violation costs 20 times as much as a background violation, so both classes count the same in total. (b) Lower the threshold on f (classify as nucleus when f > \theta with \theta < 0). More nuclei are found (higher recall) at the price of more background pixels called nucleus (lower precision); sweeping \theta traces the ROC curve.
B5. Inside each fold: (i) on the training folds only, (ii) both training and held-out fold with those numbers, (iii) train, then measure the error on the held-out fold. Repeat for every cell of the grid; then (iv) choose (C, \gamma); then (i)–(iii) once more on all training pixels; finally (v) once, on the test region. Computing \mu_j, s_j on all pixels before splitting lets the held-out pixels influence training.
B6. One-vs-rest: 5 SVMs, each on all 1000 pixels: 5 \times 1000^2 = 5\,000\,000. One-vs-one: 5 \cdot 4/2 = 10 SVMs, each on 2 \times 200 = 400 pixels: 10 \times 400^2 = 1\,600\,000. One-vs-one is about 3.1 times cheaper, despite twice as many SVMs.
B7. A line \mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x + b equals \mathbf w'\cdot\mathbf x' + b with \mathbf w' = D^{-1}\mathbf w, so the set of possible classifiers is the same. But the SVM minimises \tfrac12\|\mathbf w'\|^2 + C\sum hinge in the new coordinates, and \|\mathbf w'\|^2 = \|D^{-1}\mathbf w\|^2 = \sum_j w_j^2/D_{jj}^2 \ne \|\mathbf w\|^2. Shrinking a feature (small D_{jj}) makes its weight expensive, enlarging it makes it cheap: the margin is measured differently, so the optimum differs. Only a forest (thresholds on single features) is fully indifferent to scaling.

title: Exercise: SVMs for pixel classification
section: Explore: an SVM in the pixel classifier
text:
Explore: an SVM in the pixel classifier
The pixel-classification demo of the random forests day, with the SVM selected (switch to the random forest to compare). Paint with the mouse; the classifier retrains when you lift it. The SVM’s settings are sliders: kernel function (0 linear, 1 RBF), C, \gamma, standardise (0 no, 1 yes), and one-vs-rest or one-vs-one. The panel SVM: settings and cross-validation at the bottom has one-click settings, and runs a cross-validation over a (C, \gamma) grid on the painted pixels, with folds by stroke or by pixel; use the best copies the best cell to the SVM. The readout gives the accuracy, Dice and the confusion matrix against the ground truth of the test image. (Training uses a random subset of about 500 painted pixels; prediction fills in row by row and takes a few seconds when there are many support vectors.)



P1. Preset full stack. Compare the SVM and the random forest: accuracy, Dice per class, and how long the prediction takes.
P2. Press unscaled features in the panel. What happens to the accuracy, the nucleus Dice and the number of support vectors (in the readout)? Switch to the forest: does it care? Press standardised to go back. Explain with B1.
P3. Press γ = 10 (too large). Accuracy? How many of the training pixels are support vectors? What has the SVM learnt? Then try linear.
P4. Back to the defaults (reload the preset). Run the cross-validation with folds by stroke, then with folds by pixel. Compare the two maps and the best cells. Which one would you trust, and why is the other so low?
P5. Switch between one-vs-rest and one-vs-one. Does the accuracy change much on this image?
P6. Preset intensity only with the SVM, then with the forest. Which class suffers, and why can no classifier fix that?






Solutions





P1. SVM: accuracy 96.4%, Dice 0.99 (background), 0.87 (nucleus), 0.85 (granular cell), with 60 support vectors. Forest: 96.3%, Dice 0.99, 0.85, 0.86. Practically the same on a good feature stack. The SVM’s prediction is noticeably slower: every pixel needs the kernel function with every support vector, while a tree needs a few comparisons.
P2. Unscaled: accuracy 82.0%, nucleus Dice 0.06, granular 0.02: nearly everything becomes background. 410 of the 505 training pixels are support vectors. A few channels with large numbers (standard deviation over 200, against below 1 for others) dominate every distance, so with \gamma = 0.01 even nearby pixels look dissimilar and the SVM memorises. The forest is unaffected (96.3%): its thresholds do not depend on units. As in B1, the classes are separated by channels whose numbers are small.
P3. \gamma = 10: accuracy 81.8%, and all 505 training pixels are support vectors: the SVM has memorised the painted pixels and calls everything else background (the value far from all bumps). Linear: 96.2%, with 27 support vectors: on this stack a linear boundary is already good.
P4. By stroke: errors between about 19% and 30% everywhere; the best cell is C = 1, \gamma = 0.001 with 18.7%. By pixel: 0% in many cells (best C = 10, \gamma = 0.001). The by-pixel estimate is optimistic: held-out pixels have their stroke neighbours in training. The by-stroke map is the honest one, but here it is also pessimistic: there is only one granular-cell stroke (and two nucleus strokes), so when it is held out the training data contain no granular cell at all. Paint more strokes per class before trusting a by-stroke map.
P5. One-vs-one 96.4%, one-vs-rest 96.2%: little difference with three well-separated classes; the ambiguous regions of one-vs-rest are small here.
P6. Intensity only (6 channels): SVM 91.4%, forest 91.3%; the granular cells suffer most (Dice 0.52 with the SVM, 0.68 with the forest), confused with nuclei. Granular cells have the same mean brightness as bright nuclei; they differ in texture, which intensity channels do not describe. No classifier can separate classes that coincide in the feature space: that needs better features, not a better classifier.

title: Exercise: SVMs for pixel classification
section: Explore: training error, test error and cross-validation in 2D
text:
Explore: training error, test error and cross-validation in 2D
The 2D SVM demo in cross-validation mode: the filled points are the training set, the hollow points a test set from the same source. Below, the training and test error against C (or against \gamma, with the other fixed at its slider value); the dashed line marks the current value. 5-fold CV over (C, γ) computes the cross-validated error of the training points on a grid; use the best applies its best cell.



C1. Preset noisy moons: train vs test (\gamma = 1). Read the training and test error at C = 0.01, 1 and 1000 from the curve or the readout. Describe the shape of both curves.
C2. Switch to error against γ (C = 1). Where is the test error lowest? What happens to the training error at \gamma = 10 and above, and to the test error?
C3. Press 5-fold CV over (C, γ). Which cell is best, with which CV error? Press use the best: what is the test error now? Did cross-validation (which never saw the test points) find a good setting?
C4. Preset overlapping blobs: train vs test. Repeat C3. Why is a small \gamma best here?






Solutions





C1. C = 0.01: training 45%, test 48% (underfitting: a nearly constant f). C = 1: training 13%, test 13%. C = 1000: training 1%, test 28%. The training error falls steadily with C; the test error first falls, then rises again: a U-shape with its minimum near C = 1 (12% at C = 0.56).
C2. The test error is lowest around \gamma = 0.3–1 (12–13%). At \gamma = 10 the training error is 3% but the test error 32%; at \gamma = 20 the training error is 0% and the test error 35%. Small bumps memorise the training points, including the mislabelled ones.
C3. Best cell: C = 10, \gamma = 0.1, CV error 13%. With it, the test error is 14.0%, close to the best the test curves showed (12%). Cross-validation used only the training points and still found a setting near the best for new data.
C4. Best cell: C = 1, \gamma = 0.01, CV error 11%; test error 12.0%. The two blobs overlap and the best boundary is a straight line; a small \gamma (length scale 10, wider than the data) gives an almost linear boundary, while a large \gamma only fits the noise in the overlap (at \gamma = 100 the CV error is about 50%).

title: Exercise: SVMs for pixel classification
text:
Where this leads
The day’s other half of “more learning” is the Gaussian mixtures day: generative models of each class, fitted even without labels. For pixels with many labels, the neural networks day learns the features themselves instead of using a hand-made stack. Detection of objects with a sliding window and a linear SVM on gradient-direction histograms is a classic application of this unit (not covered here).

title: Meshes, coordinate spaces and projection
text:
About this lecture
A 3D object is stored either as a surface (polygons) or as a volume (voxels). Today: how each becomes an image on a screen. This unit and the next follow polygons; then textures (how the graphics card stores and samples images); then voxels.

A mesh: vertices, an indexed list of triangles, winding and normals.
Coordinate spaces: model → world → view → clip → screen, one 4\times4 matrix each.
The camera as a change of basis, and perspective from similar triangles.
Conventions: those of OpenGL/WebGL (the camera looks down -z, depth after projection in [-1, 1]; some systems use [0, 1]).

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

An elective day of the 3D group, after the marching-cubes day. Everything is linear algebra the students know (homogeneous coordinates, change of basis, inverses); the only new matrix is the perspective projection. Demo tour at the “Try it” slide.

title: Meshes, coordinate spaces and projection
text:
Surfaces as meshes
A mesh is two arrays:

a vertex array: a position (x, y, z) per vertex, plus optional attributes (normal, colour, texture coordinate);
a triangle list: three vertex indices per triangle.

A cube: 8 vertices, 12 triangles. Stored as a “triangle soup” (three positions per triangle) it needs 36 positions; indexed, 8 positions and 36 small integers.

A closed mesh has about twice as many triangles as vertices: 10^6 triangles share about 5\cdot10^5 vertices.
Why triangles? Three points are always flat and convex, and a value given at the corners has one natural interpolation inside (next unit).

title: Meshes, coordinate spaces and projection
text:
Winding, normals, manifolds

The order a, b, c of a triangle’s indices is its winding. Seen from the front, the corners go counter-clockwise.
The face normal \mathbf n = (\mathbf b - \mathbf a)\times(\mathbf c - \mathbf a) points out of the front side (right-hand rule).
Consistent orientation: neighbouring triangles use their shared edge in opposite directions. Then all normals point outwards, and “inside” is defined.
Manifold: every edge belongs to exactly two triangles, and the triangles around a vertex form one disc. Not manifold: three triangles on one edge; two cubes touching at a corner.

Tools need this: smooth normals, inside/outside tests, the volume formula of the marching-cubes day, and back-face culling (next unit) all assume a consistent, closed mesh.

title: Meshes, coordinate spaces and projection
section: The math: why a closed mesh has F \approx 2V
text:
The math: why a closed mesh has F \approx 2V
Euler’s formula for a closed surface without holes (a sphere-like mesh): V - E + F = 2.
Each triangle has 3 edges and each edge belongs to 2 triangles, so 3F = 2E. Substituting E = \tfrac32 F:
V - \tfrac32 F + F = 2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad F = 2V - 4.
For a surface with g handles (a torus has g = 1), V - E + F = 2 - 2g and F = 2V - 4 + 4g: still about 2V.
Memory of an indexed mesh with 32-bit floats and indices: 12V + 12F \approx 12V + 24V = 36V bytes (plus 12V for normals).

title: Meshes, coordinate spaces and projection
text:
From 3\times3 to 4\times4
Recall the images unit: in 2D, \mathbf x' = A\mathbf x + \mathbf t became one 3\times3 matrix by adding a coordinate 1. In 3D the same trick gives 4\times4 matrices:
\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf x' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} A & \mathbf t \\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf x \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.

Points get w = 1; directions (normals, light directions) get w = 0: translation does not move a direction.
A chain of moves is a product, applied right to left. “Rotate 90° about z, then move by (1, 0, 0)” is T R, and sends the point (1, 0, 0) to (1, 1, 0). In the other order, R T sends it to (0, 2, 0).
Rotations do not interpolate linearly (the average of two rotation matrices is not a rotation); animation uses quaternions, not covered here.

title: Meshes, coordinate spaces and projection
text:
A chain of coordinate spaces


Model space: the object’s own axes (the house’s floor centred at the origin).
World space: the scene. The model matrix M places, turns and scales the object.
View space: the camera’s axes; the view matrix V.
Clip space, then NDC: the projection P, then division by w.
Screen: the viewport scales [-1, 1] to pixels.

All the vertices of one object get the same product P\,V\,M: one matrix per object per frame, the same work for every vertex.

title: Meshes, coordinate spaces and projection
section: The camera as a change of basis
text:
The camera as a change of basis
A camera has a position \mathbf e (eye), looks at a target \mathbf g, and has an “up” direction. Its own axes:

forward \mathbf f = from the eye towards the target; right \mathbf r = perpendicular to forward and up; up \mathbf u' = perpendicular to both.
View space writes every point in these axes, with the eye at the origin: right = +x, up = +y, and forward = -z (the camera looks down -z).

The view matrix does what the camera’s placement undoes: if a matrix C puts a camera into the world, then V = C^{-1}. Moving the camera left is the same as moving the whole world right.
Orbiting the camera = rotating \mathbf e about \mathbf g: the drag in every 3D demo of the course.

title: Meshes, coordinate spaces and projection
text:
The math: the look-at matrix
\mathbf f = \frac{\mathbf g - \mathbf e}{\lVert \mathbf g - \mathbf e\rVert}, \qquad \mathbf r = \frac{\mathbf f\times\mathbf u}{\lVert \mathbf f\times\mathbf u\rVert}, \qquad \mathbf u' = \mathbf r\times\mathbf f.
The rows of R are \mathbf r^\top, \mathbf u'^\top, -\mathbf f^\top (orthonormal), and
V = \begin{bmatrix} R & -R\,\mathbf e \\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad V\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf e\\1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf 0\\1\end{bmatrix}.
The camera’s placement is C = \begin{bmatrix} R^\top & \mathbf e \\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1\end{bmatrix} (its columns are the camera’s axes in world coordinates, and its position). Since R^{-1} = R^\top for an orthonormal R, C^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} R & -R\mathbf e\\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1\end{bmatrix} = V.
Example: \mathbf e = (0, 0, 5), \mathbf g = \mathbf 0, \mathbf u = (0, 1, 0) gives \mathbf f = (0, 0, -1), \mathbf r = (1, 0, 0), \mathbf u' = (0, 1, 0), R = I and V = translation by (0, 0, -5).

title: Meshes, coordinate spaces and projection
text:
Perspective by similar triangles

A point at depth -z in front of the eye lands on an image plane at distance n at
x_s = \frac{n\,x}{-z}, \qquad y_s = \frac{n\,y}{-z}.
Twice as far away = half as big. Dividing by z is not linear, so no matrix can do it. The trick: the matrix copies -z into the fourth coordinate w, and the hardware divides by w afterwards (the perspective divide).

title: Meshes, coordinate spaces and projection
text:
The math: the perspective matrix
We also need a depth for hiding surfaces (next unit). After the divide every coordinate has the form (row of P)·\mathbf x / (-z), so the new depth must be z_\text{ndc} = A + B/z. Choose A, B so that the near plane z = -n goes to -1 and the far plane z = -f to +1:
A - \frac{B}{n} = -1, \quad A - \frac{B}{f} = 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad A = \frac{f + n}{f - n}, \;\; B = \frac{2fn}{f - n}.
With a vertical field of view \theta and aspect ratio a (width/height), let s = 1/\tan(\theta/2):
P = \begin{bmatrix} s/a & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & s & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -\frac{f+n}{f-n} & -\frac{2fn}{f-n} \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad w_\text{clip} = -z.
Example: n = 1, f = 3: A = 2, B = 3, so z_\text{ndc} = 2 + 3/z; the point at z = -2 gets depth 0.5, past the middle. Depth is not linear in distance.

title: Meshes, coordinate spaces and projection
section: Try it: follow a vertex through the spaces
text:
Try it: follow a vertex through the spaces




Left: the world from far away, with the camera (pink pyramid) and its view frustum. Right: the selected space. Under it M, V, P. The readout follows vertex 9 (the front end of the roof ridge; click another vertex to change it). Tour: in view space vertex 9 is at (−0.044, 0.769, −3.190): 3.19 in front of the camera, and its clip w is 3.190 = −z. Switch to clip → NDC: the frustum has become the cube; the house is squashed towards the far side. “orthographic vs perspective”: w = 1 for every vertex, parallel edges stay parallel. “dolly zoom”: distance 9, field of view 18.4°: the house keeps its size on the screen but looks flatter. “near plane too close”: all NDC depths between 0.972 and 0.982. “a vertex behind the camera”: vertex 9 (view x = −0.730, to the left, and z = +0.107, behind) has w = −0.107; after the divide its NDC x is +14: flipped to the right. The screen still shows a sensible picture because triangles are clipped at the near plane first. “non-uniform scale”: M has 2.165 in its corner.

title: Meshes, coordinate spaces and projection
text:
Orthographic projection
Orthographic: drop the depth instead of dividing by it. P just scales and shifts a box [l, r]\times[b, t]\times[-n, -f] to the cube [-1, 1]^3; w stays 1.

Parallel lines stay parallel; size does not depend on distance.
Used where measurements matter: technical drawings, most microscopy viewers, and maximum-intensity projections (unit 4).
Dolly zoom: move the camera back and narrow the field of view together. The subject keeps its size (d\tan(\theta/2) constant: from d = 4, \theta = 40° to d = 9, \theta = 18.4°), but the background grows: perspective depends on the distance, not on the zoom. Far away with a narrow field of view approaches orthographic.

title: Meshes, coordinate spaces and projection
text:
Clip space and the frustum
What the camera sees is a truncated pyramid, the view frustum, between the near and far planes. After P (before the divide) it is the region
-w \le x \le w, \qquad -w \le y \le w, \qquad -w \le z \le w,
and after the divide it is the cube [-1, 1]^3 (NDC, normalised device coordinates).

Triangles outside are dropped; triangles crossing the boundary are clipped. This happens in clip space, before the divide.
Why before: a vertex behind the camera has w < 0; dividing flips it to the other side of the screen. The near plane cuts the triangle first (next unit).
The viewport then maps x_\text{ndc} \in [-1, 1] to [0, \text{width}] pixels (and y likewise).

title: Meshes, coordinate spaces and projection
text:
From pixels back to rays
Run the chain backwards: a pixel is not a point but a ray from the eye through the pixel.

(P V)^{-1} applied to the pixel at NDC depth -1 and at +1 gives two points on the ray. Volume rendering (unit 4) and picking a vertex with the mouse both start like this.
One camera cannot tell how far along the ray a point is: depth is lost. Two cameras can (stereo, epipolar geometry): the inverse problem of reconstructing geometry from images, an elective of its own.

title: Meshes, coordinate spaces and projection
text:
Summary

A mesh = vertices + indexed triangles; winding gives the front side and the normal (\mathbf b - \mathbf a)\times(\mathbf c - \mathbf a); closed meshes have F \approx 2V.
4\times4 homogeneous matrices: points w = 1, directions w = 0; products apply right to left.
model \xrightarrow{M} world \xrightarrow{V} view \xrightarrow{P} clip \xrightarrow{\div w} NDC \xrightarrow{\text{viewport}} screen.
The view matrix is the inverse of the camera’s placement (a change of basis to the camera’s axes).
Perspective = divide by distance; the matrix puts -z into w. Depth after the divide is A + B/z: not linear.
Orthographic: w = 1, no shrinking with distance.

title: Quiz: phase correlation
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Phase correlation divides every A_k\overline{B_k} by its size and takes the inverse FFT.

Q1. Why does the cross-correlation of two micrographs usually have a broad peak?






Hint





Which waves are strongest in a typical image, and how fast does their vote change with the shift?









Answer





Most of an image’s strength is in the slow waves (smooth brightness changes). Their votes are the largest, and a slow wave still agrees at shifts a few pixels away from the true one. The sum is a wide hill rather than a spike.




Q2. Which property of the Fourier transform makes phase correlation work?






Hint





What does a shift do to the sizes and to the phases of the waves?









Answer





The shift theorem: shifting an image multiplies each F_k by a phase factor e^{-2\pi i k t/N}; the sizes |F_k| do not change. All the information about the shift is in the phase differences, so the sizes can be thrown away.




Q3. Image B is a perfect circular shift of A by t_0. What does the phase-correlation surface look like?






Hint





After normalising, every frequency is a pure phase ramp.









Answer





A single spike of height 1 at t_0 and zero everywhere else: the inverse DFT of e^{-2\pi i kt_0/N} for all k is a delta.




Q4. B is A with twice the contrast and 50 grey levels brighter. How does the phase-correlation surface change? And the cross-correlation?






Hint





Which B_k does the offset change, and what does the gain do to the phases?









Answer





Phase correlation: not at all. The gain multiplies every B_k by 2 (same phase), the offset only changes B_0, and after normalisation R_0 has size 1 whatever B_0 is. Cross-correlation: the surface doubles (gain) and the mean term changes (offset); with the means subtracted, only the factor 2 remains, but an uneven brightness change would move CC’s peak.




Q5. Why does phase correlation suffer more from noise than cross-correlation?






Hint





Where in the spectrum is the noise as strong as the signal?









Answer





At high frequencies the image signal is weak and the noise is about as strong: the phase differences there are random. Cross-correlation gives these frequencies small votes (they are weak); phase correlation gives them the same vote as the strong low frequencies. Many random votes make a noisy floor that can be higher than the spike.




Q6. Name two ways to make phase correlation more robust to noise.






Hint





Change the weights of the frequencies.









Answer





Multiply the normalised spectrum by a low-pass weight that fades out the highest frequencies; or normalise only partly, dividing by |A_k\overline{B_k}|^p with 0 < p < 1, which keeps some of the strength information. (Also: an \varepsilon in the denominator, averaging or smoothing the images first.)




Q7. Without a taper, phase correlation of two crops often shows a false peak at shift (0, 0) and a bright cross in the spectrum. Why?






Hint





What does the DFT assume happens at the border of a crop?









Answer





The DFT treats each crop as periodic, so the left border meets the right one (and top meets bottom), usually with a jump in brightness. These jump lines produce strong waves along the axes (the cross) and they are at the same place in both crops: they do not move with the shift, so they vote for zero shift. A Hann taper brings both crops smoothly to zero at the border and removes the jumps.




Q8. Two tiles give a phase-correlation peak of 0.08 and a peak ratio of 1.05. What do you conclude?






Hint





What do the height and the ratio measure?









Answer





Do not trust this shift. A ratio of 1.05 means the second-best shift is almost as good; a height of 0.08 means very little shared content (or a lot of noise). Typical reasons: a nearly empty tile, a periodic texture, a very small overlap. A mosaic program should drop this pair or give it a small weight.

title: Exercise: phase correlation
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute a short phase correlation by hand and explain why it is a spike,
show why gain and offset do not matter, and predict the effect of uneven illumination,
predict how noise affects phase correlation and choose a remedy (low-pass weight, exponent p),
explain the taper and read the peak height and peak ratio as a confidence.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo.

title: Exercise: phase correlation
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute a short phase correlation by hand and explain why it is a spike,
show why gain and offset do not matter, and predict the effect of uneven illumination,
predict how noise affects phase correlation and choose a remedy (low-pass weight, exponent p),
explain the taper and read the peak height and peak ratio as a confidence.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo.

title: Exercise: phase correlation
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Cross-power spectrum
A_k\overline{B_k}: phase difference and strength of wave k in both images


Phase correlation
R_k = A_k\overline{B_k}/|A_k\overline{B_k}|, then the inverse FFT; a pure circular shift gives a spike of height 1


Exponent p
divide by |A_k\overline{B_k}|^p: p = 0 is cross-correlation, p = 1 phase correlation


Low-pass weight
multiply R_k by a smooth weight that fades out the highest frequencies


Hann taper
w(n) = \tfrac12\big(1 - \cos\frac{2\pi n}{N-1}\big): 0 at both ends, 1 in the middle; in 2D w(x)w(y)


Peak height
about the fraction of content shared by the two images


Peak ratio
highest peak / second-highest peak; near 1: ambiguous

title: Exercise: phase correlation
text:
By hand
B1. A = (0, 1, 2, 0), B = (1, 2, 0, 0), A_k\overline{B_k} = (9, -5i, -1, 5i) (the previous unit). (a) Normalise every entry to size 1. (b) Take the inverse DFT, r(t) = \tfrac14\sum_k R_k\,i^{kt}. (c) Compare with the cross-correlation (2, 5, 2, 0).
B2. Same A, but B' = 2B + 1 = (3, 5, 1, 1). (a) Compute B'_k and compare with B_k = (3, 1 - 2i, -1, 1 + 2i). (b) Show that the normalised cross-power is the same as in B1. (c) What does the cross-correlation of A and B' look like (no means subtracted)?
B3. Two images share only one strong vertical edge (a long straight boundary, dark on the left, bright on the right); the rest is noise. Predict the shape of the phase-correlation surface. What can you measure, and what not?
B4. Two 128 \times 128 crops of one image, B’s frame (21, 13) pixels right and down of A’s, no noise. (a) What fraction of A’s pixels have a partner in B? Predict the phase-correlation peak height. (b) The same shift with 64 \times 64 crops? (c) Why does a Hann taper raise the peak a little in (a)?
B5. The Hann taper. (a) Write down w(n) for N = 5 and N = 8. (b) A 128 \times 128 tile overlaps its neighbour only in its last 24 columns. What is the average taper weight in those columns? What does that mean for registering mosaic tiles with a taper?
B6. A lattice of blobs 18 pixels apart is shifted by (21, 13). Which shifts give a high phase-correlation peak? What is the peak ratio likely to be?






Solutions





B1. (a) Sizes (9, 5, 1, 5): R = (1, -i, -1, i). (b) r(0) = \tfrac14(1 - i - 1 + i) = 0; r(1) = \tfrac14(1 + (-i)(i) + (-1)(-1) + (i)(-i)) = \tfrac14(1 + 1 + 1 + 1) = 1; r(2) = \tfrac14(1 + i - 1 - i) = 0; r(3) = \tfrac14(1 - 1 + 1 - 1) = 0. A delta at t = 1. (c) The cross-correlation (2, 5, 2, 0) has its peak at 1 too, but with neighbours of 40 % of the peak; phase correlation leaves only the spike.
B2. (a) B'_k = (10, 2 - 4i, -2, 2 + 4i): for k \ne 0 exactly 2B_k; only B'_0 is not doubled (10 = 2\cdot3 + 4, the offset adds 4 \cdot 1 to the constant term). (b) For k \ne 0, A_k\overline{B'_k} = 2A_k\overline{B_k}, which has the same phase; for k = 0, A_0\overline{B'_0} = 30, normalised to 1 as before (9 → 1). So R and the delta are unchanged. (c) c'(t) = \sum_x A(x+t)(2B(x) + 1) = 2c(t) + \sum A = (4 + 3, 10 + 3, 4 + 3, 0 + 3) = (7, 13, 7, 3): same peak, twice as high, on a raised floor.
B3. A ridge: a line of high values along the edge direction. Shifting B along the edge (vertically) does not change how the edges line up, so every t_y scores the same for the right t_x. The horizontal shift is measured; the vertical shift is not determined at all (the “aperture problem”). In practice the noise picks a random point on the ridge.
B4. (a) (128 - 21)(128 - 13)/128^2 = 107 \cdot 115/16384 = 0.75: a peak of about 0.75, less in practice because the parts without a partner add noise; the demo gives 0.62. (b) (64 - 21)(64 - 13)/64^2 = 43 \cdot 51/4096 = 0.54; the demo gives 0.32, and the floor is relatively higher. (c) The taper weights the middle of each crop most; with a moderate shift, the middle of A is inside the overlap, so the shared fraction as weighted is higher (the demo: 0.67 instead of 0.62).
B5. (a) N = 5: (0, 0.5, 1, 0.5, 0). N = 8: (0, 0.19, 0.61, 0.95, 0.95, 0.61, 0.19, 0). (b) The average of w(n) over the last 24 of 128 samples is 0.10 (at most 0.29), against 0.5 over the whole tile: the overlap, the only part that the two tiles share, is almost switched off. Tapering is fine for crops that overlap mostly (drift, channels), but for mosaic tiles with small overlaps it removes the information: stitching registers the tiles without a taper and resolves the consequences (the four candidates) separately.
B6. Every shift that moves the lattice onto itself: (21 + 18m, 13 + 18n) for integers m, n, e.g. (3, -5), (3, 13), (-15, -5), (21, 13). All of these give about equally high peaks; which one wins depends on the crop borders and the noise. Peak ratio close to 1: ambiguous.




Math questions
B7. (math) (Sub-pixel shifts.) In 1D, let the normalised cross-power be an exact phase ramp for a non-integer shift t_0: R_k = e^{-2\pi i k t_0/N} for k = -\frac{N-1}{2}, \ldots, \frac{N-1}{2} (N odd). Show that r(t) = \frac1N\sum_k R_k e^{2\pi i kt/N} = \frac{\sin\big(\pi(t - t_0)\big)}{N\sin\big(\pi(t - t_0)/N\big)}, the Dirichlet kernel (“periodic sinc”) centred at t_0. What are the two largest samples for t_0 = 0.5 and large N?
B8. (math) (a) Show that the exponent p = 0 gives the cross-correlation. (b) Show that phase correlation of f and g equals the cross-correlation of the whitened images \tilde f, \tilde g with \tilde F_k = F_k/|F_k|, \tilde G_k = G_k/|G_k|. Why is whitening an edge-enhancing filter for typical images, whose |F_k| falls off with |k|?
B9. (math) Let g(x) = f(x + t_0) + \eta(x) with noise spectrum H_k. Write G_k = e^{2\pi i kt_0/N}(F_k + H'_k) with |H'_k| = |H_k|. Show that the phase error of R_k satisfies |\sin\delta_k| \le |H_k|/|F_k| when |H_k| < |F_k|. Where in the spectrum is the error large for a typical image with white noise?






Solutions (math)





B7. r(t) = \frac1N\sum_{k=-m}^{m}e^{2\pi i k(t - t_0)/N} with m = (N-1)/2, a geometric sum with ratio q = e^{2\pi i(t - t_0)/N}: \sum_{k=-m}^{m}q^k = \frac{q^{m+1/2} - q^{-m-1/2}}{q^{1/2} - q^{-1/2}} = \frac{\sin(\pi(t - t_0))}{\sin(\pi(t - t_0)/N)}, since (m + \tfrac12)\cdot\frac{2\pi(t - t_0)}{N} = \pi(t - t_0). Dividing by N gives the formula; at t = t_0 it is 1 (limit). For large N, N\sin(\pi u/N) \approx \pi u and r(t) \approx \operatorname{sinc}(t - t_0) = \sin(\pi(t-t_0))/(\pi(t - t_0)). For t_0 = 0.5 the samples at t = 0 and t = 1 are equal, \approx 2/\pi = 0.64: the spike is split between two pixels. Fitting this shape locates t_0 (the stitching unit).
B8. (a) |A_k\overline{B_k}|^0 = 1: nothing is divided, the inverse FFT of A_k\overline{B_k} is the cross-correlation. (b) \tilde F_k\overline{\tilde G_k} = \frac{F_k\overline{G_k}}{|F_k||G_k|} = \frac{F_k\overline{G_k}}{|F_k\overline{G_k}|}, so the cross-correlation of the whitened images (the correlation theorem) is the phase correlation. Whitening divides each wave by its size; when |F_k| falls off with |k|, the high frequencies are amplified relative to the low ones, like a sharpening filter: what remains are edges, lines and texture.
B9. R_k \propto (F_k + H'_k)\overline{F_k}\,e^{-2\pi i kt_0/N}, whose phase differs from the ideal -2\pi kt_0/N by \delta_k = \arg\big(1 + H'_k/F_k\big). The point 1 + z with |z| = |H_k|/|F_k| < 1 lies in a disc of radius |z| around 1, so its angle satisfies |\sin\delta_k| \le |z|. White noise has about the same |H_k| at every frequency, while |F_k| of a typical image falls off with |k|: the error is small at low frequencies and large (random phase) at high frequencies, exactly where a low-pass weight helps.

title: Exercise: phase correlation
text:
Explore
Left: the micrograph with frame A (blue) and frame B (red); drag frame B, or set the shift with the sliders. Middle: the two crops (B with its degradations) and a small panel with the spectrum of A or the phase of A_k\overline{B_k} as a colour. Right: the correlation surface with shift (0, 0) in the centre; green ring: the true shift, cyan cross: the highest peak, white circles: the next ones. p blends from cross-correlation (p = 0) to phase correlation (p = 1). uneven light brightens the whole field from one corner to the other (both crops); ramp on B only crop B. brute force computes NCC for every shift directly and times it.



E1. Preset same image, shifted: delta: B is A rolled around by (21, 13). Read the peak height and the peak ratio. Show the cross-power phase panel: what pattern do you see, and how does it change if you change the shift?
E2. Preset CC: broad peak, then phase: sharp peak. Compare the peak heights, the next-highest peaks and the peak ratios. Which shift is second best for CC?
E3. Preset illumination ramp on B (CC, a ramp of 500 grey levels across B). Where is CC’s peak? Switch the method to phase, then to NCC. Which finds the shift? Then set the ramp to 0, gain 0.5 and offset 80 with phase correlation: does anything change?
E4. Preset noise: phase peak drowns (σ = 120 on both crops). Where is the highest peak, and how high is the surface at the true shift? Then preset noise + low-pass weight. Also try p = 0.5 without low-pass, and CC.
E5. Preset no taper: false (0, 0) peak (CC, uneven light 600, no taper). Where is the peak? Look at the spectrum panel, then tick Hann taper. Then untick the taper again and choose phase correlation: where are the false peaks now?
E6. Preset periodic texture. Where is the highest peak, and what is the value at the true shift? Explain with B6.
E7. Preset phase: sharp peak. Switch the crop size to 64. How do the peak height and the ratio change? Compare with B4.
E8. Preset overlap NCC, then press brute force. Compare the result, the number of multiply-adds and the time with the FFT route.






Solutions





E1. Height 1.00, peak ratio ∞ (everything else is zero up to rounding). The phase of A_k\overline{B_k} is a set of parallel stripes running through the whole spectrum: a phase ramp -2\pi(k_xt_x/128 + k_yt_y/128), wrapping around every 2\pi. Their direction and spacing are set by the shift: a larger shift gives more, narrower stripes.
E2. CC: peak at (21, 13), 4.03\cdot10^6; the second best (20, 10) still has 2.81\cdot10^6 (70 %), ratio 1.44. Phase: peak 0.67, next peaks 0.03 (at (-23, -6) and (-33, 16)), ratio 23.3.
E3. CC’s peak is at (54, 1): wrong. Phase correlation finds (21, 13) with the same height 0.67 and ratio 23.0. NCC (on the overlap) fails too, at (62, -57): NCC removes a constant offset and gain, not a ramp. With gain 0.5 and offset 80 the phase-correlation surface is exactly the same as without (0.671, ratio 23.26).
E4. The highest peak is at (-6, 7) (0.043, ratio 1.03), the true shift only 0.033: the spike has drowned. With the low-pass weight (sd 0.08 cycles per pixel) the peak is back at (21, 13), ratio 1.54. p = 0.5 gives (21, 14), CC also (21, 14): one pixel off, still close. The low-pass weight keeps the reliable low frequencies with equal votes and removes the noisy ones.
E5. The peak is at (0, 0) (the next ones on the line t_y = 0): the jumps at the crop borders do not move with the shift. The spectrum shows a bright horizontal and vertical cross. With the taper the cross disappears and CC finds (21, 13) (ratio 1.31). Phase correlation without taper finds (21, 13) (0.62), but the next peaks are at (15, 0) and (12, 0): still the axis line, only weaker.
E6. The highest peak is at (3, -5) (0.15), one lattice period from the truth in both directions; (3, 13) (0.10) and (-15, -5) (0.09) follow, and the true shift (21, 13) scores only 0.03. Peak ratio 1.58: not convincing. Every shift by a whole number of periods matches the lattice; only the crop borders make one of them a little better.
E7. At 64 \times 64 the peak drops from 0.67 to 0.32 and the ratio from 23 to 5.2: the shared fraction drops from 75 % to 54 % (B4), and there are fewer frequencies to vote, so the floor is relatively higher.
E8. NCC (through FFTs) finds (21, 13) with NCC 1.000; its second peak (20, 10) has 0.69. Brute force finds the same shift with 268 million multiply-adds and takes around a second or two in the browser (1.6 s in a test run), against tens of milliseconds for the FFT route; the readout shows the times on your machine.

title: Exercise: phase correlation
text:
Where this leads
The spike sits on whole pixels, and the circular FFT only knows the shift up to the size of the image. The next unit turns a peak into a usable shift (the four candidates, sub-pixel estimation), combines many pairwise shifts into a consistent mosaic, and corrects drift.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
About this lecture
The Fourier unit rewrote an image in a fixed basis of waves. PCA finds a basis from the data: the directions in which a set of images (or patches, or pixels) actually varies.

Many small images are a cloud of points: one axis per pixel.
Centre the cloud, then find the direction of most spread: the first principal component.
The covariance matrix holds all the spreads; its eigenvectors are the principal components.
Keep a few scores, rebuild the rest: projection and reconstruction, and how many components to keep.
Image examples: two-pixel images, 8×8 patches, colour pixels.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

This is the course’s PCA unit: every later day that needs PCA (the region’s principal axes, shape models, colour decorrelation, compression, unmixing, autoencoders) recalls it from here. Linear algebra needed: dot product, unit vectors, eigenvectors of a symmetric 2 × 2 matrix. The covariance is divided by n throughout (as in the autoencoder unit); with n − 1 the eigenvectors are the same and the eigenvalues scale by n/(n − 1).

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Two pixels, one point




Take two neighbouring pixels of a smooth image: a tiny image with two grey values (p_1, p_2). Draw it as a point, pixel 1 across, pixel 2 up.

150 such pairs make a cloud. The two pixels are almost equally bright, so it lies along the diagonal.
The cloud is long in one direction (overall brightness of the pair) and thin in the other (the small difference, a tiny edge).
One number, the position along the blue line, almost describes each pair. Red: what that one number misses.

A 28 \times 28 image is a point with 784 coordinates. Same idea; we just cannot draw it.


The data are the “neighbouring pixels” preset of the demo (and of the autoencoder unit’s demo): brightness uniform in [0.15, 0.85], difference ±0.06 (normal), fixed seed. Ask the class first: if the pixels were far apart in the image, what would the cloud look like? (Rounder: far-apart pixels are less related.)

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Step 1: centre the cloud
Subtract the mean image \bar{\mathbf x} (the average of each pixel) from every image.

The cloud now sits around the origin. Directions are measured from the centre of the data, not from black (0, 0).
Without centring, the “best direction” through (0, 0) mostly points at the mean: it describes how bright the images are on average, which we already know, instead of how they differ.
Every later step works on the centred images \mathbf x - \bar{\mathbf x}; the mean is added back at the end.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Spread along a direction
Pick a direction: a unit vector \mathbf u (length 1). Each centred image gets one number, its score:
s = \mathbf u \cdot (\mathbf x - \bar{\mathbf x}) \qquad \text{(how far along } \mathbf u \text{ the image lies)}

The scores of all images have a variance: the spread of the cloud along \mathbf u.
Turn \mathbf u: the variance changes. For the neighbouring pixels it is largest along the diagonal, smallest across it.
PC1 (first principal component) = the direction of largest variance. PC2 = the largest among the directions perpendicular to PC1 (in 2D: simply the perpendicular).

title: Principal component analysis
section: Try it: the shape of a point cloud
text:
Try it: the shape of a point cloud




Start at u = 0° (keep pixel 1 only): variance 0.0406, error 0.0414. Drag u round: the blue curve peaks at the orange tick (PC1, 45.3°, variance 0.0762), the red error curve bottoms out there (0.0058 = λ2). Blue + red is always tr S = 0.0820. Then “four images” (the next slides’ example). Then “one outlier”: a single hot pixel turns PC1 and drops PC1’s share from 93 % to 70 %. Then “no centring”: the line through (0, 0) is far worse than PCA. Drag dots to make the cloud round, or long in another direction.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
The covariance matrix, by hand
Four two-pixel images: (0.2, 0.4), (0.4, 0.2), (0.6, 0.8), (0.8, 0.6).

Mean image (0.5, 0.5). Centred: (-0.3, -0.1), (-0.1, -0.3), (0.1, 0.3), (0.3, 0.1).
Average the products, over the 4 images:

S = \begin{pmatrix} \overline{y_1^2} & \overline{y_1 y_2} \\ \overline{y_2 y_1} & \overline{y_2^2} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.05 & 0.03 \\ 0.03 & 0.05 \end{pmatrix}

Diagonal: the variance of each pixel (0.05 each). Off-diagonal: the covariance, positive because the pixels tend to be bright together.
The variance along any unit vector \mathbf u follows from S alone (math slide). Along the diagonal \mathbf u = (1, 1)/\sqrt2: 0.08. Across it, (1, -1)/\sqrt2: 0.02. Along pixel 1, (1, 0): 0.05.


y = x − mean. Products for the off-diagonal: 0.03, 0.03, 0.03, 0.03, average 0.03. This is the demo’s “four images” preset: the readout shows the same S. The total variance (sum of the diagonal) is 0.10; it is the same in every orthogonal pair of directions: 0.05 + 0.05 = 0.08 + 0.02.

title: Principal component analysis
section: The math: the best direction is an eigenvector
text:
The math: the best direction is an eigenvector
Centred images \mathbf y_i = \mathbf x_i - \bar{\mathbf x}, covariance S = \frac1n\sum_i \mathbf y_i\mathbf y_i^\top (symmetric, d \times d). The variance of the scores along a unit vector \mathbf u:
\frac1n\sum_i (\mathbf u^\top\mathbf y_i)^2 = \frac1n\sum_i \mathbf u^\top\mathbf y_i\,\mathbf y_i^\top\mathbf u = \mathbf u^\top S\,\mathbf u.
Maximise \mathbf u^\top S\mathbf u subject to \mathbf u^\top\mathbf u = 1. With a Lagrange multiplier \lambda, setting the gradient of \mathbf u^\top S\mathbf u - \lambda(\mathbf u^\top\mathbf u - 1) to zero:
2S\mathbf u - 2\lambda\mathbf u = 0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S\mathbf u = \lambda\mathbf u, \qquad \text{and then } \mathbf u^\top S\mathbf u = \lambda.

So the stationary directions are the eigenvectors of S, and the variance along each is its eigenvalue. The largest eigenvalue \lambda_1 gives PC1.
S is symmetric, so (spectral theorem) its eigenvectors can be chosen orthonormal, and all \lambda_k \ge 0. Order them descending: \lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_d.
For S = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}: eigenvectors (1, \pm1)/\sqrt2, eigenvalues a \pm b. The example: 0.05 \pm 0.03.

title: Principal component analysis
section: Principal components: new axes for the data
text:
Principal components: new axes for the data
The eigenvectors \mathbf u_1, \mathbf u_2, \dots of S, ordered by eigenvalue (largest first), are the principal components.

They are perpendicular to each other: a rotated set of axes, fitted to the cloud.
The eigenvalue \lambda_k is the variance of the scores along \mathbf u_k.
In the new axes the scores are uncorrelated: the cloud’s tilt is gone.
Nothing is lost by rotating: the total variance (sum of the pixel variances) equals \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \dots. In the example 0.05 + 0.05 = 0.08 + 0.02.
Share of PC1: 0.08 / 0.10 = 80\,\%. For the 150 neighbouring pixel pairs: 93\,\%.


In the demo, the ellipse is the 2-SD contour of a Gaussian with covariance S: its axes are the PCs and its half-lengths are 2√λ. Sign: −u is as good as u; programs may return either.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Projection and reconstruction
Keep only the first k scores, s_j = \mathbf u_j \cdot (\mathbf x - \bar{\mathbf x}), and rebuild:
\hat{\mathbf x} = \bar{\mathbf x} + s_1\mathbf u_1 + \dots + s_k\mathbf u_k.
The example, k = 1, image (0.2, 0.4), \mathbf u_1 = (1, 1)/\sqrt2:

Score s_1 = \big((-0.3) + (-0.1)\big)/\sqrt2 = -0.283: the pair is darker than average.
Rebuilt: (0.5, 0.5) + s_1\,\mathbf u_1 = (0.5, 0.5) - (0.2, 0.2) = (0.3, 0.3): same brightness, the difference is gone.
Error (0.2, 0.4) - (0.3, 0.3) = (-0.1, 0.1), squared length 0.02. All four images lose 0.02: the mean error is \lambda_2 = 0.02, the variance that was dropped.

With all components the reconstruction is exact: rotate, rotate back. The saving comes from keeping few.

title: Principal component analysis
section: The math: the error is the sum of the dropped eigenvalues
text:
The math: the error is the sum of the dropped eigenvalues
Write a centred image in the PC basis: \mathbf y = \sum_{j=1}^d s_j\mathbf u_j with s_j = \mathbf u_j^\top\mathbf y. Keeping the first k terms leaves \mathbf y - \hat{\mathbf y} = \sum_{j > k} s_j\mathbf u_j, and since the \mathbf u_j are orthonormal,
\|\mathbf y - \hat{\mathbf y}\|^2 = \sum_{j > k} s_j^2, \qquad \frac1n\sum_i\|\mathbf y_i - \hat{\mathbf y}_i\|^2 = \sum_{j > k}\lambda_j = \operatorname{tr}S - \sum_{j \le k}\lambda_j.

For one direction \mathbf u (not necessarily a PC): mean error = \operatorname{tr}S - \mathbf u^\top S\mathbf u (Pythagoras for each image). Smallest error ⇔ largest variance kept: the same \mathbf u_1.
More generally (Eckart–Young): no k-dimensional flat subspace through the mean fits the images better in squared error than the first k PCs.
The scores are uncorrelated: \frac1n\sum_i s_{ij}s_{il} = \mathbf u_j^\top S\mathbf u_l = \lambda_l\,\mathbf u_j^\top\mathbf u_l = 0 for j \ne l.

title: Principal component analysis
section: How many components? The scree plot
text:
How many components? The scree plot


Plot the eigenvalues, largest first (a scree plot), or the cumulative share of the variance.
Keep components up to the “elbow”, or until a target share is reached (90 %: here 11 of 64 numbers per patch).
The small eigenvalues are often mostly noise: dropping them also denoises.


Numbers computed with NumPy from the course micrograph (cell256.png, values scaled to [0, 1]): all 62 001 overlapping 8 × 8 patches, covariance divided by n. Shares: 68.5, 6.2, 4.3, 2.5, 2.1 % for PC1–5; cumulative 89.3 % at 10 components, 90 % needs 11, 95 % needs 24, 99 % needs 50. Rebuilding the image from non-overlapping patches with 1, 4 and 10 components gives RMS errors 0.131, 0.100 and 0.076. There is no universal rule for k: the elbow, a share, or what the next step (classification, display, compression) needs.

title: Principal component analysis
section: PCA and Fourier: two changes of basis
text:
PCA and Fourier: two changes of basis
Both rewrite an image (or patch) as a weighted sum of basis images, with orthonormal basis vectors: rotate, keep the important coefficients, rotate back.









Fourier (DFT/DCT)
PCA




basis
fixed waves, the same for every image set
learned from the data: eigenvectors of S


order
by frequency
by variance in these data


best for
any image; fast to compute
the data it was fitted on: fewest components for a given error




On the micrograph’s patches, the PCs look like waves: flat, then slow ramps, then faster patterns. PC1–3 match the three lowest cosine waves (overlap 0.97 or more). For images whose statistics are the same everywhere, PCA and cosines nearly agree, which is why JPEG can use the fixed cosines.
On a special data set (faces, cell shapes, one kind of tissue) the learned basis wins.


“Overlap” is |dot product| of the unit-length PC and the best-matching 8 × 8 DCT basis image: 0.999 (PC1, the flat patch), 0.981 (PC2), 0.973 (PC3); PC4 and PC5 are mixtures (0.76). Same NumPy computation as the scree figure. The theorem behind “PCA ≈ Fourier”: for a stationary process the covariance of a patch is (nearly) a convolution matrix, and convolution matrices are diagonalised by the Fourier basis (the convolution theorem of the Fourier unit). PCA under the name Karhunen–Loève transform is the optimal (but data-dependent) transform coder.

title: Principal component analysis
section: Colour pixels: three numbers per pixel
text:
Colour pixels: three numbers per pixel
A colour pixel (R, G, B) is a point in 3D; the pixels of a photograph are a cloud.

In most scenes the three channels rise and fall together (light and shadow change all three). PC1 points close to (1, 1, 1)/\sqrt3: brightness, carrying most of the variance.
PC2 and PC3 are colour differences (e.g. red against blue, green against magenta), with much less variance.
That is why image formats store brightness plus two colour differences, and give the differences fewer bits or fewer pixels: the decorrelation PCA would find, fixed in advance.
For a stained tissue section the PCs follow the stains, not the screen colours: a starting point for separating them.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
When PCA misleads

Outliers: variance is a sum of squares, so one hot pixel or one bad image can turn PC1 (demo: “one outlier”).
Units: mix a cell area in µm² with an intensity in [0, 1], and PC1 is simply “area”. Standardise each feature (divide by its standard deviation) first when units differ.
Nearly equal eigenvalues: a round cloud has no preferred direction; the PCs swing when one point moves. Report the subspace, not the individual axes.
Curved clouds: PCA fits flat subspaces. Images of a moving spot lie on a curve; one PCA score folds it. A nonlinear autoencoder can follow it (the VAE units).
PCA finds directions of variance, not of meaning: the largest spread may be lighting, not biology.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Summary







Idea
In one line




Image as a point
one axis per pixel; a set of images is a cloud


Centre
subtract the mean image first


Covariance S
pixel variances on the diagonal, covariances off it


Principal components
eigenvectors of S, largest eigenvalue first; perpendicular; scores uncorrelated


Eigenvalue
the variance along that component; they add up to the total variance


Reconstruction
mean + scores × components; error = the dropped eigenvalues


Scree plot
how many components carry most of the variance


vs Fourier
both a change of basis: Fourier fixed, PCA learned from the data

title: Quiz: choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Class 0 is background (i \le t), class 1 is object; \omega_k, \mu_k, \sigma_k^2 are the class weights, means and variances.

Q1. Why is minimising the within-class variance the same as maximising the between-class variance?






Hint





What happens to the total variance when t moves?









Answer





Total = within + between, and the total variance of all pixels does not depend on t. Whatever the within part loses, the between part gains.




Q2. Two splits have class means 40 and 200. In split A the classes hold 50 % and 50 % of the pixels; in split B 99 % and 1 %. Which has the larger \sigma_B^2, and by how much?






Hint





\sigma_B^2 = \omega_0\omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2.









Answer





A: 0.25 \cdot 160^2 = 6400. B: 0.0099 \cdot 160^2 = 253. A is about 25 times larger: Otsu prefers splits where both classes are substantial.




Q3. One isodata step: the current split has class means 60 and 140. Where does the threshold go next? When does isodata stop?






Hint





Midpoint.









Answer





To (60 + 140)/2 = 100. It stops when the new midpoint gives the same split as before: every pixel is then nearer to its own class mean (a fixed point, as in k-means with k = 2).




Q4. Objects are rare (5 % of the pixels) and both classes have the same spread. Is the minimum-error threshold above or below the midpoint of the two means?






Hint





At the midpoint, which class is more likely for a pixel?









Answer





Above (towards the object mean). At the midpoint both densities are equal, but background is 19 times more common, so a pixel there is probably background. The boundary moves towards the rarer class until the weighted densities are equal.




Q5. Why can the minimum-error rule with unequal variances label a pixel object when it is darker than the background mean?






Hint





Compare the tails of a narrow and a wide normal curve.









Answer





If the object class is much wider, its density decays more slowly than the narrow background peak, so far below the background mean the object density is larger again. The weighted curves cross twice, and the Bayes rule says “object” in both tails. (In practice that dark tail holds very few pixels.)




Q6. A fluorescence image has a huge dark background peak and a faint tail of a few bright spots, with no valley. Which method would you try first, and why does Otsu fail?






Hint





Otsu needs both classes to be substantial.









Answer





The triangle method (or maximum entropy): it is made for a unimodal histogram with a long tail and puts t where the peak ends. Otsu’s \sigma_B^2 barely rewards separating a 1 % class, so it splits the background peak instead.




Q7. Two classes overlap so much that the best possible threshold misclassifies 20 % of the pixels. Will a cleverer histogram method do better?






Hint





What information does any histogram method use?









Answer





No. The Bayes threshold is already the best rule that looks at one grey level at a time. To do better you need more information than the grey level of a single pixel: its neighbours (smoothing, graph cuts) or other features.




Q8. (math) Show that \mu_0 - \mu = \omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1).






Hint





\mu = \omega_0\mu_0 + \omega_1\mu_1 and \omega_0 = 1 - \omega_1.









Answer





\mu_0 - \mu = \mu_0 - (1 - \omega_1)\mu_0 - \omega_1\mu_1 = \omega_1\mu_0 - \omega_1\mu_1 = \omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1).

title: Exercise: choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute Otsu’s threshold by hand from a small histogram, and check that total = within + between,
run isodata by hand, and recognise when it stops at a different split than Otsu,
find the minimum-error (Bayes) threshold of two normal classes, and say which way it moves from the midpoint,
predict from the shape of a histogram which method is biased, and in which direction.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the three demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute Otsu’s threshold by hand from a small histogram, and check that total = within + between,
run isodata by hand, and recognise when it stops at a different split than Otsu,
find the minimum-error (Bayes) threshold of two normal classes, and say which way it moves from the midpoint,
predict from the shape of a histogram which method is biased, and in which direction.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the three demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Background







Symbol
Meaning




Class 0, class 1
grey levels i \le t (background) and i > t (object)


\omega_0, \omega_1
class weights: fractions of the pixels; \omega_0 = P(t)


\mu_0, \mu_1; \sigma_0^2, \sigma_1^2
class means and variances


\sigma_W^2
within-class variance \omega_0\sigma_0^2 + \omega_1\sigma_1^2


\sigma_B^2
between-class variance \omega_0\omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2; \sigma_T^2 = \sigma_W^2 + \sigma_B^2


Otsu
$t^* = $ the t with the largest \sigma_B^2


Isodata
repeat t \leftarrow (\mu_0 + \mu_1)/2


Bayes threshold
where \omega_0 f_0(t) = \omega_1 f_1(t); equal variances: t = \frac{\mu_0 + \mu_1}{2} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu_1 - \mu_0}\ln\frac{\omega_0}{\omega_1}

title: Exercise: choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
By hand
The worked example of the lecture: grey levels 0–7 with counts h = (2, 5, 3, 1, 1, 2, 4, 2), N = 20, \mu = 3.3, \sigma_T^2 = 5.81.
B1. Otsu’s table. (a) Compute \omega_0, \mu_0, \mu_1 and \sigma_B^2 = \omega_0\omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2 for t = 2, t = 3 and t = 4. (b) Given \sigma_B^2 = 1.21, 3.60, \cdot, \cdot, \cdot, 3.94, 1.52 for the other t, which t does Otsu choose? Which pixels are object?
B2. Isodata on the same histogram. (a) Start at t = 5.5 (class 0 = levels 0–5). Compute \mu_0, \mu_1 and the new t. Do one more step. (b) Where does it stop? Compare with B1.
B3. Three groups: counts h = (9, 0, 0, 8, 7, 0, 0, 5) for levels 0–7 (29 pixels). (a) Run isodata from t = 6.5. Where does it stop? (b) Compute \sigma_B^2 for the split \{0\} \mid \{3, 4, 7\} and for \{0, 3, 4\} \mid \{7\}. Which one does Otsu choose? (c) Run isodata from t = 0.5. What does this tell you about isodata?
B4. Two classes with normal grey levels: background \mu_0 = 50, objects \mu_1 = 150, both \sigma = 20; objects are 10 % of the pixels. (a) Compute the Bayes threshold. Does it lie above or below the midpoint 100? Explain in words why. (b) What is the threshold when the objects are 50 % of the pixels? (c) Isodata and Otsu ignore the weights. Which way would you expect them to err for 10 % objects, and why?
B5. Unequal widths: background \mu_0 = 80, \sigma_0 = 12; objects \mu_1 = 150, \sigma_1 = 40, \omega_1 = 0.4. The weighted densities cross at 40.8 and 105.4. (a) Sketch the two weighted curves. Which class wins (has the larger weighted density) below 40.8, between 40.8 and 105.4, and above 105.4? (b) Is a single threshold the best possible rule here? What is the best rule?
B6. For each histogram shape, name a method that suits it and one that fails: (a) two well-separated peaks of similar size and width; (b) a large dark background peak and a small, long bright tail (a few fluorescent spots); (c) three peaks (background, cytoplasm, nucleus); (d) two peaks that overlap so much that there is no dip between them.






Solutions





B1. (a) t = 2: class 0 has 2 + 5 + 3 = 10 pixels with sum 0 + 5 + 6 = 11: \omega_0 = 0.50, \mu_0 = 1.10; class 1 has 10 pixels with sum 66 - 11 = 55: \mu_1 = 5.50; \sigma_B^2 = 0.5 \cdot 0.5 \cdot 4.4^2 = 4.84. t = 3: 11 pixels, sum 14: \omega_0 = 0.55, \mu_0 = 1.27; class 1: 9 pixels, sum 52, \mu_1 = 5.78; \sigma_B^2 = 0.55 \cdot 0.45 \cdot 4.51^2 = 5.02. t = 4: 12 pixels, sum 18: \omega_0 = 0.60, \mu_0 = 1.50; class 1: 8 pixels, sum 48, \mu_1 = 6.00; \sigma_B^2 = 0.6 \cdot 0.4 \cdot 4.5^2 = 4.86. (b) The largest is 5.02 at t^* = 3: object = grey levels 4–7, 9 pixels.
B2. (a) Class 0 = levels 0–5: 14 pixels, sum 28, \mu_0 = 2.00; class 1 = levels 6–7: 6 pixels, sum 38, \mu_1 = 6.33; new t = 4.17. Next: class 0 = levels 0–4: 12 pixels, \mu_0 = 1.50; class 1: \mu_1 = 6.00; t = 3.75. (b) Then class 0 = levels 0–3: \mu_0 = 1.27, \mu_1 = 5.78, t = 3.53, which gives the same split again: it stops at 3.53, the split \{0..3\} \mid \{4..7\}, the same as Otsu.
B3. (a) From 6.5: class 0 = \{0, 3, 4\}: 24 pixels, sum 0 + 24 + 28 = 52, \mu_0 = 2.17; class 1 = \{7\}: \mu_1 = 7; t = 4.58. The split is the same, so it stops at 4.58. (b) \mu = (24 + 28 + 35)/29 = 3.00. Split \{0\} \mid rest: \omega_0 = 9/29 = 0.31, \mu_0 = 0, \mu_1 = 87/20 = 4.35: \sigma_B^2 = 0.31 \cdot 0.69 \cdot 4.35^2 = 4.05. Split \{0, 3, 4\} \mid \{7\}: \omega_0 = 24/29 = 0.83, \sigma_B^2 = 0.83 \cdot 0.17 \cdot (7 - 2.17)^2 = 3.33. Otsu chooses \{0\} \mid \{3, 4, 7\}. (c) From 0.5: class 0 = \{0\}, \mu_0 = 0, \mu_1 = 4.35, t = 2.17; the split is the same, so it stops at 2.17, the Otsu split. Isodata finds a fixed point near its start: a local optimum. With two clear groups there is only one; with three groups there are several.
B4. (a) t = 100 + \frac{20^2}{100}\ln\frac{0.9}{0.1} = 100 + 4 \cdot 2.197 = 108.8, above the midpoint. Near the midpoint, a grey level is equally far from both means, but a random pixel is 9 times more likely to be background; the boundary moves towards the rarer class until the two weighted densities are equal. (b) \ln 1 = 0: t = 100, the midpoint. (c) They put t near the middle of the two class means, or lower: the large background class dominates, and a split that cuts into its tail barely changes \mu_0. They err towards the background (too low t), so many background pixels become object. (On these curves Otsu chooses 98.5.)
B5. (a) Below 40.8 the wide object class wins (its tail decays much more slowly than the narrow background peak), between 40.8 and 105.4 the background wins, above 105.4 the objects win. (b) No. The Bayes rule labels object both below 40.8 and above 105.4. A single threshold at 105.4 misses the (tiny) object tail below 40.8; in practice that tail is so small that the single threshold is nearly as good, but the rule is an interval, not a threshold.
B6. (a) Otsu, isodata and minimum error all work and agree; nothing fails badly (the triangle method is not made for this and lands lower). (b) Triangle or maximum entropy (or minimum error if the tail is roughly normal); Otsu and isodata fail, dragged into the big peak. (c) Multi-level Otsu with three classes; any two-class method has to merge two of the classes. (d) Every histogram method fails: the grey level alone cannot separate the classes. Smooth first, or use neighbours (graph cuts).




Math questions
B7. (math) Prove \sigma_T^2 = \sigma_W^2 + \sigma_B^2 (add and subtract the class mean inside the square), and then \sigma_B^2 = \omega_0\omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2. Check both at t = 3 in the worked example (\sigma_0^2 = 0.744, \sigma_1^2 = 0.840).
B8. (math) With P = P(t) and M = M(t), show that \mu_1 - \mu_0 = (\mu P - M)/(P(1 - P)) and hence \sigma_B^2(t) = (\mu P - M)^2/(P(1 - P)).
B9. (math) Show that for continuous grey levels every stationary point of \sigma_B^2(t) satisfies t = (\mu_0 + \mu_1)/2 (Otsu’s optimum is an isodata fixed point).
B10. (math) Derive the equal-variance minimum-error threshold t = \frac{\mu_0 + \mu_1}{2} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu_1 - \mu_0}\ln\frac{\omega_0}{\omega_1} from E'(t) = 0. Then show that for unequal variances the condition is a quadratic equation in t.
B11. (math) Show that the average negative log-likelihood of the pixels, each assigned to its own side of t with a fitted normal distribution, is \tfrac12\ln 2\pi + \tfrac12 + \sum_k\omega_k\ln\sigma_k - \sum_k\omega_k\ln\omega_k (the Kittler–Illingworth criterion up to constants).






Solutions (math)





B7. \sum_{i \in k}(i - \mu)^2 p_i = \sum_{i \in k}\big((i - \mu_k) + (\mu_k - \mu)\big)^2 p_i = \sum_{i \in k}(i - \mu_k)^2 p_i + 2(\mu_k - \mu)\sum_{i \in k}(i - \mu_k)p_i + (\mu_k - \mu)^2\sum_{i \in k}p_i. The middle sum is \omega_k\mu_k - \mu_k\omega_k = 0. Summing over k: \sigma_T^2 = \sum_k \omega_k\sigma_k^2 + \sum_k\omega_k(\mu_k - \mu)^2. With \mu = \omega_0\mu_0 + \omega_1\mu_1 and \omega_0 + \omega_1 = 1: \mu_0 - \mu = \omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1), \mu_1 - \mu = \omega_0(\mu_1 - \mu_0), so \sigma_B^2 = \omega_0\omega_1^2 d^2 + \omega_1\omega_0^2 d^2 = \omega_0\omega_1 d^2 with d = \mu_0 - \mu_1. At t = 3: \sigma_W^2 = 0.55 \cdot 0.744 + 0.45 \cdot 0.840 = 0.787, \sigma_B^2 = 5.023, sum 5.81 = \sigma_T^2.
B8. \mu_0 = M/P and \mu_1 = (\mu - M)/(1 - P) (the total first moment is \mu). Then \mu_1 - \mu_0 = \frac{P(\mu - M) - M(1 - P)}{P(1 - P)} = \frac{\mu P - M}{P(1 - P)}, and \sigma_B^2 = P(1 - P)(\mu_1 - \mu_0)^2 = \frac{(\mu P - M)^2}{P(1 - P)}.
B9. With density p: P' = p(t), M' = t\,p(t), D = \mu P - M, D' = (\mu - t)p(t). \frac{d}{dt}\frac{D^2}{P(1 - P)} = \frac{2DD'P(1 - P) - D^2(1 - 2P)p}{P^2(1 - P)^2} = 0 gives (for p(t) \ne 0, D \ne 0) 2(\mu - t)P(1 - P) = D(1 - 2P). With D = P(1 - P)(\mu_1 - \mu_0): t = \mu - \frac12(1 - 2P)(\mu_1 - \mu_0), and inserting \mu = P\mu_0 + (1 - P)\mu_1 gives t = P\mu_0 + (1 - P)\mu_1 - \frac12(\mu_1 - \mu_0) + P(\mu_1 - \mu_0) = \frac12(\mu_0 + \mu_1).
B10. E'(t) = -\omega_0 f_0(t) + \omega_1 f_1(t) = 0. With normal densities, take logs: \ln\omega_0 - \ln\sigma_0 - \frac{(t - \mu_0)^2}{2\sigma_0^2} = \ln\omega_1 - \ln\sigma_1 - \frac{(t - \mu_1)^2}{2\sigma_1^2}. For \sigma_0 \ne \sigma_1 the t^2 terms have different coefficients: a quadratic at^2 + bt + c = 0 with a = \frac1{2\sigma_1^2} - \frac1{2\sigma_0^2}. For \sigma_0 = \sigma_1 = \sigma they cancel: (t - \mu_1)^2 - (t - \mu_0)^2 = (\mu_0 - \mu_1)(2t - \mu_0 - \mu_1) = 2\sigma^2\ln\frac{\omega_1}{\omega_0}, so t = \frac{\mu_0 + \mu_1}{2} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu_1 - \mu_0}\ln\frac{\omega_0}{\omega_1}.
B11. -\sum_i p_i\ln\big(\omega_k f_k(i)\big) = -\sum_k\sum_{i \in k}p_i\Big(\ln\omega_k - \ln\sigma_k - \tfrac12\ln 2\pi - \frac{(i - \mu_k)^2}{2\sigma_k^2}\Big). Use \sum_{i \in k}p_i = \omega_k and \sum_{i \in k}p_i(i - \mu_k)^2 = \omega_k\sigma_k^2: = -\sum_k\omega_k\ln\omega_k + \sum_k\omega_k\ln\sigma_k + \tfrac12\ln 2\pi + \sum_k\frac{\omega_k\sigma_k^2}{2\sigma_k^2}, and the last sum is \tfrac12.

title: Exercise: choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Explore: Otsu by hand
The eight bars are a histogram; drag a bar up or down to change its count (0–9). The threshold t (slider, or click a row of the table) colours class 0 blue and class 1 orange; the dots under the bars are the class means. The table lists \omega_0, \mu_0, \mu_1 and \sigma_B^2 for every t (★ = Otsu). The bar below the plot splits the total variance into within and between. isodata step moves the isodata threshold (dashed) to the midpoint of the class means.



P1. Preset the worked example. Check your B1 table. Move t from 0 to 6: what happens to the total, the within and the between part?
P2. Press isodata step three times and compare with B2. Then preset isodata stuck: press isodata step until it stops, and compare with B3.
P3. Preset two equal peaks. Where is Otsu’s threshold, and why? Now drag the bar at level 7 up to 9. Does t^* move?
P4. Preset a tiny object class: the objects are the 2 pixels at level 7. Which split does Otsu choose? Is that the split you want? What does isodata give from 5.5?






Solutions





P1. The table matches B1: t^* = 3 with \sigma_B^2 = 5.02. The total stays at 5.81 for every t; the within part is smallest (0.79) exactly where the between part is largest (5.02), and both trade off as t moves.
P2. From 5.5: 4.17, 3.75, 3.53, then it stops at the split of t = 3, as in B2. Stuck: 6.5 → 4.58, and then 4.58 again: it stops at split 4 with \sigma_B^2 = 3.33, while the star (Otsu) is at t = 0 with 4.05 (the rows t = 0, 1, 2 tie, because levels 1 and 2 are empty).
P3. t^* = 3, with \sigma_B^2 = 3.27: the histogram (1, 4, 6, 2, 2, 6, 4, 1) is symmetric about 3.5, so the best split is in the middle. Raising h_7 to 9 makes the histogram asymmetric, but t^* stays at 3 (\sigma_B^2 = 4.29, just ahead of 4.26 at t = 4): the extra bright pixels raise \mu_1 for every split, and the middle remains the best place to cut.
P4. Otsu splits at t = 3: levels 4–7 (6 pixels: three 4s, one 5 and the two 7s) are called object. It cuts into the tail of the big peak, because a class of 2 pixels out of 32 contributes little to \sigma_B^2 (at t = 6, \sigma_B^2 = 1.45 against 1.84 at t = 3). Isodata from 5.5 goes to 4.52 and stops at 4.13 (split 4): also inside the big peak.

title: Exercise: choosing the threshold from the histogram
section: Explore: two Gaussians and six thresholds
text:
Explore: two Gaussians and six thresholds
The image (right) is drawn from a two-class model: a blob-shaped object mask covering a fraction \omega_1 of the pixels, and for each pixel a grey level drawn from its class’s normal distribution \mathcal N(\mu_k, \sigma_k^2). Top left: the histogram of the image (grey), the weighted class densities \omega_0 f_0 (blue) and \omega_1 f_1 (orange), and the thresholds of Otsu, isodata, min-error (Kittler–Illingworth), triangle, Kapur (maximum entropy) and the Bayes boundary of the true model (dashed; the selected method solid). The shaded areas are the selected method’s errors: orange = object pixels it calls background, blue = background pixels it calls object. Below: the selected method’s criterion as a function of t. The table gives each method’s threshold and its error rate under the model; the caption above the image gives the wrong pixels in this image.



E1. Preset equal, well separated. Which methods agree, and on what threshold? Which one does not, and why?
E2. Preset unequal weights (\omega_1 = 0.1). Read Otsu’s threshold and error, and the Bayes threshold and error. Which way did Otsu move, and how does that match B4? Which histogram method comes closest to Bayes? Now raise \omega_1 to 0.3 and 0.5.
E3. Preset unequal variances. Where are the two Bayes crossings? Select min-error and Otsu: compare their thresholds and errors.
E4. Preset small object (3 %). Is the histogram bimodal? Compare the errors of Otsu, triangle, Kapur and min-error with Bayes. Select triangle and look at its criterion curve.
E5. Preset heavy overlap. What is the smallest possible error? What do the masks look like?
E6. Back to unequal weights: set the image size to 32² (1024 pixels) and to 256². Which methods change their threshold, and by how much?






Solutions





E1. Otsu, isodata and min-error choose 125 and Kapur 124, all at the Bayes threshold 125.0 (error 0.1 %). The triangle method chooses 109 (error 1.2 %): it draws its line from the background peak to the end of the histogram and assumes a unimodal histogram with a tail, which this is not.
E2. Otsu: 85 with an error of 19.9 %; Bayes: 114.6 with 3.4 %. Otsu moved down, into the large background class, by about 30 grey levels, as predicted in B4. Min-error chooses 123 (4.1 %), Kapur 108 (3.9 %), triangle 105 (4.5 %): Kapur is closest in error here, min-error is the only one on the correct side of Bayes. At \omega_1 = 0.3: Otsu 97 (7.5 %) against Bayes 105.6 (6.0 %); at \omega_1 = 0.5 every method except the triangle chooses 100, the Bayes threshold (6.7 %).
E3. The weighted densities cross at 40.8 and 105.4; below 40.8 the wide object class wins again (B5). Min-error chooses 112 (7.2 %), close to the Bayes error of 6.2 %; Otsu chooses 125 (10.8 %): it ignores that the object class is wide and puts the threshold too far into it.
E4. No: the 3 % object class is a small shoulder on the right of one big peak. Otsu chooses 62, inside the background peak, with a disastrous 40.6 % error; isodata 64 (34.4 %). Triangle 91, Kapur 93 and min-error 98 all have about 1.4–1.5 %, close to Bayes (94.1, 1.4 %). The triangle criterion is the distance below the line from the peak to the end of the tail; it is largest where the background peak ends and the object tail begins.
E5. Bayes: 120.4 with 21.9 % error, the best any threshold can do: more than a fifth of the pixels are wrong whatever t is. Otsu and isodata (113, 23.2 %) and Kapur (123, 22.1 %) are close to it; min-error (173) and triangle (149) fail badly because the histogram is one hump. Every mask is speckled: the grey level of a single pixel simply does not tell the classes apart. Neighbouring pixels must help (smoothing, or graph cuts).
E6. At 32² the histogram is ragged: Otsu stays at 85, isodata 85, but the triangle method jumps from 105 to 85 (19.9 %), Kapur from 108 to 103 and min-error from 123 to 121. At 256² the curves are smooth: Otsu 84, triangle 114 (3.4 %), Kapur 107, min-error 123. Methods that look at the shape of the histogram (triangle, Kapur) need many pixels; Otsu’s means are stable even for small images (but biased).

title: Exercise: choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Explore: Otsu on the micrograph
The same demo as in the last unit, now with Otsu’s criterion \eta(t) = \sigma_B^2(t)/\sigma_T^2 (between 0 and 1) on the lower plot, and the option of three classes (two thresholds t and t_2; multi-level Otsu).



C1. Untick 3 classes and press t = Otsu. What is Otsu’s threshold for the micrograph, and how large is \eta there? What does the mask separate?
C2. Tick 3 classes and press t = Otsu. Give t_1 and t_2. What do the three classes contain? Can any threshold separate the nucleus from the cytoplasm?
C3. Untick 3 classes, choose synthetic blobs, set noise σ to 20, and press t = Otsu. Compare Otsu’s Dice with the best Dice you can find by hand.






Solutions





C1. t^* = 163 with \eta = 0.76: the split explains 76 % of the grey-level variance. It separates the bright empty background (above 163) from everything else (45.2 % of the pixels are at or below 163): the cell and the dark material around it.
C2. t_1 = 120, t_2 = 188. Darkest class (purple): membranes, dense granules and the darkest parts of the cell; middle class (orange): cytoplasm and nucleus together; brightest: empty background. The nucleus and the cytoplasm have overlapping grey levels, so no threshold separates them; their difference is texture and position, which the histogram does not see.
C3. Otsu chooses t = 106 with Dice 0.946; the best threshold is about 112 with Dice 0.951. With 25 % objects Otsu is slightly biased into the background, but the loss is small when the peaks are well separated.

title: Exercise: choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Where this leads
Every method here looks at one pixel at a time and at one global histogram. The next unit drops both assumptions: the threshold may vary over the image (local thresholds), and a pixel’s decision may depend on its neighbours (hysteresis). The Bayes two-class model returns in graph cuts (day 13): its data term is exactly this unit’s -\log(\omega_k f_k), with a smoothness term added.
