title: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction
text:
About this lecture
All moments determine an image. Can we get the image back from the moments up to order N?

With monomials it is a linear system, and a badly conditioned one: x^8 and x^{10} look almost the same.
Gram–Schmidt turns 1, x, x^2, \dots into orthogonal Legendre polynomials.
Legendre moments: the same information, better coordinates. Reconstruction becomes a projection, like truncating a Fourier series.
What pixels do to it: sampled polynomials are not quite orthogonal; integrate, or use discrete orthogonal polynomials.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Third unit of the moments elective. Linear algebra assumed: inner product, orthogonal projection, Gram–Schmidt on vectors, condition number (one line of recall). From the Fourier unit (day 1): a coefficient is an inner product with a basis function, and low-pass filtering = truncating the expansion. Coordinates are mapped to [−1, 1] throughout.
crumbs: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction

title: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction
text:
Getting the image back
The moments are inner products: m_{pq} = \langle I, x^p y^q\rangle. Suppose we look for the polynomial \hat I = \sum_{p+q \le N} a_{pq}\, x^p y^q with the same moments as I (the best polynomial approximation, see below).

Each moment condition is one linear equation in the unknowns a_{pq}: a linear system G\,a = m.
The matrix G holds the inner products of the basis functions with each other: the Gram matrix, G_{jk} = \langle x^j, x^k\rangle in 1D.
If the basis functions were orthogonal, G would be diagonal and each coefficient would be one division. Monomials are far from orthogonal.
crumbs: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction

title: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction
text:
Monomials look alike

On [-1, 1], x^8 and x^{10} are almost the same curve: the cosine of the angle between them (as vectors of a function space) is 0.994. Their moments carry almost the same information, and telling their contributions apart is like solving for two nearly parallel vectors.
crumbs: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction

title: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction
section: The math: the Gram matrix and its condition
text:
The math: the Gram matrix and its condition
Inner product of functions on [-1, 1]: \langle g, h\rangle = \int_{-1}^{1} g(x) h(x)\,dx (a sum \sum_i g_i h_i \Delta x on a grid).

Monomials: G_{jk} = \int_{-1}^{1} x^{j+k}\,dx = \frac{2}{j+k+1} if j + k is even, else 0. On [0, 1]: \frac{1}{j+k+1}, the Hilbert matrix.
\cos\angle(x^8, x^{10}) = \frac{2/19}{\sqrt{(2/17)(2/21)}} = 0.994.
Condition number \kappa(G) (largest / smallest eigenvalue): about \log_{10}\kappa digits are lost when solving G a = m.

title: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction
text:
Gram–Schmidt: make them orthogonal
Linear algebra: take the vectors one by one and subtract from each its projections onto the ones already made orthogonal. The same with functions:

P_0 = 1.
x is already orthogonal to 1 on [-1, 1] (odd times even): P_1 = x.
x^2 has a component along 1: its average \tfrac13. Subtract it: x^2 - \tfrac13, scaled so that P_2(1) = 1: P_2 = \tfrac12(3x^2 - 1).
And so on: P_3 = \tfrac12(5x^3 - 3x), …

These are the Legendre polynomials. Each new one has exactly one more zero; they look like waves that get faster, and none is close to another.
crumbs: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction

title: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction
text:
The math: Legendre polynomials

Gram–Schmidt: q_n = x^n - \sum_{k<n} \frac{\langle x^n, q_k\rangle}{\langle q_k, q_k\rangle} q_k, then P_n = q_n / q_n(1).
Three-term recurrence (no projections needed): (n+1)P_{n+1}(x) = (2n+1)\,x\,P_n(x) - n\,P_{n-1}(x).
Orthogonality: \int_{-1}^{1} P_m P_n\,dx = \frac{2}{2n+1}\delta_{mn}.
P_n is even for even n, odd for odd n, P_n(1) = 1, and it has n zeros in (-1, 1), crowded towards the ends.

title: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction
section: Try it: monomials and Legendre in 1D
text:
Try it: monomials and Legendre in 1D




Top: the basis functions up to degree N, and their Gram matrix as cosines (1 = same direction) with the condition number. Bottom: a signal on [−1, 1] (400 samples) fitted with degree N by both bases, and the error against N. Tour: “monomials look alike” (N = 10): the Gram matrix is full of cosines near 1, κ = 9.5 × 10⁶. Click Legendre: the identity, κ = 21 (only the different lengths 2/(2n+1), from 2 down to 2/21). “Gram–Schmidt to P₃”: step through with the button; the top-left block of the Gram matrix becomes diagonal one row at a time. “fit a step”: with 64-bit arithmetic both fits are identical up to N ≈ 20 (error 0.1749 at N = 12). “monomials break down” (bump, N = 24): monomials 0.147, Legendre 0.017. Switch to 32-bit: the monomial fit stops improving already at N ≈ 13.
crumbs: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction

title: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction
text:
Legendre moments
Use P_p(x)P_q(y) instead of x^p y^q, on the image mapped to the square [-1, 1]^2:
a_{pq} = \frac{(2p+1)(2q+1)}{4} \iint P_p(x)\,P_q(y)\, I(x, y)\,dx\,dy.

Same information as the monomial moments: P_p is a combination of 1, x, \dots, x^p, so each a_{pq} is a fixed combination of the m_{kl} with k \le p, l \le q (a triangular change of basis).
Better coordinates: each a_{pq} is just the coefficient of P_p P_q in the image. No system to solve.
crumbs: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction

title: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction
section: The math: from geometric to Legendre moments
text:
The math: from geometric to Legendre moments
Write P_p(x) = \sum_{k \le p} \beta_{pk} x^k (from the recurrence). Then
a_{pq} = \frac{(2p+1)(2q+1)}{4} \sum_{k \le p}\sum_{l \le q} \beta_{pk}\beta_{ql}\, m_{kl}.
Example: P_2 = \tfrac32 x^2 - \tfrac12, so a_{20} = \tfrac54\big(\tfrac32 m_{20} - \tfrac12 m_{00}\big).
The triangular matrix (\beta_{pk}) is invertible: the a_{pq} with p + q \le N and the m_{pq} with p + q \le N determine each other. What changes is only how the numbers are conditioned.
crumbs: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction

title: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction
text:
Reconstruction is a projection
\hat I_N(x, y) = \sum_{p + q \le N} a_{pq}\, P_p(x)\, P_q(y).

This is the orthogonal projection of I onto the polynomials of total degree \le N: the best such polynomial in the least-squares sense.
Adding an order never changes the coefficients already computed (it would with monomials: every a_{pq} of the system changes when N grows).
The same as truncating a Fourier series (the low-pass of the Fourier unit), with a different basis: the error looks different (next slide).
crumbs: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction

title: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction
section: Try it: rebuild an image from its moments
text:
Try it: rebuild an image from its moments




64 × 64 inputs. Panels: monomials (least squares through the Gram system), Legendre, Zernike (next unit) and a Fourier low-pass with the same number of coefficients; error = relative RMS against the input. Display range: the input’s range ± 30 %, so overshoots show. Tour: “low orders = blurry ellipse” (nucleus, N = 2, 6 coefficients): a blurry blob, Legendre error 0.685. Move N up: at N = 20 (231 numbers) the dent is back, error 0.226. “monomials explode” (letter E, N = 14, monomial coordinates in [0, 1]): monomial error 2.43 against 0.366 for Legendre; switch the coordinates to [−1, 1]: 0.365, the same as Legendre (at 64 × 64 it departs only from N ≈ 25). “Legendre vs Fourier ringing” (square, N = 16): errors 0.254 and 0.227; compare the ripples.
crumbs: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction

title: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction
text:
Ringing and compression

A sharp edge cannot be a low-degree polynomial: the projection overshoots next to it (Gibbs-like ringing), as in the Fourier low-pass.
Legendre ripples follow the image border and crowd towards it (the zeros of P_n crowd towards \pm 1). Fourier ripples are evenly spaced and wrap around the border: the Fourier basis is periodic.
Moments as compression: up to N = 20 there are 231 Legendre moments; a 128 \times 128 image has 16384 pixels (1.4 %). Low orders keep the coarse shape, like the low frequencies.
crumbs: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction

title: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction
section: Pixels: sampled polynomials are not orthogonal
text:
Pixels: sampled polynomials are not orthogonal
On a grid of pixels the integrals become sums, and the sampled P_n are only approximately orthogonal. The error grows with the order.

Integrate per pixel: use the average of P_n over each pixel (exact for an image that is constant on each pixel).
Discrete orthogonal polynomials (Tchebichef, Krawtchouk; Mukundan 2001): polynomials of degree n that are exactly orthogonal on the points 0, 1, \dots, W-1 (Gram–Schmidt on the sampled monomials, or a discrete three-term recurrence).

In the demo, the micrograph (bright edges) at N = 40: sampled Legendre error 0.349 and rising; pixel-integrated 0.099; discrete 0.094.
crumbs: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction

title: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction
section: The math: projection and discrete orthogonality
text:
The math: projection and discrete orthogonality
Best approximation. For an orthogonal basis \{b_k\} of a subspace V, \hat f = \sum_k \frac{\langle f, b_k\rangle}{\langle b_k, b_k\rangle} b_k satisfies \langle f - \hat f, b_j\rangle = 0 for every j. For any g \in V: \|f - g\|^2 = \|f - \hat f\|^2 + \|\hat f - g\|^2 \ge \|f - \hat f\|^2 (Pythagoras).
On a grid. With \langle g, h\rangle = \sum_i g(x_i)h(x_i)\Delta x the sampled Legendre polynomials have \langle P_m, P_n\rangle \ne 0 for m \ne n (the midpoint rule is not exact for polynomials of degree m + n \ge 2). Discrete orthogonal polynomials T_n satisfy \sum_i T_m(x_i)T_n(x_i) = \delta_{mn} exactly; projection with them is the exact least-squares fit on the grid, which the monomial Gram system also computes, if the arithmetic were exact.
crumbs: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction

title: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction
text:
Summary

Reconstructing from monomial moments is a linear system with the Gram matrix; monomials are nearly parallel, the system is ill-conditioned (\kappa \approx 10^7 at degree 10 on [-1, 1], 10^{14} on [0, 1]).
Gram–Schmidt gives the Legendre polynomials: P_0 = 1, P_1 = x, P_2 = \tfrac12(3x^2 - 1), three-term recurrence.
Legendre moments carry the same information as m_{pq}; reconstruction is an orthogonal projection: best in least squares, earlier coefficients never change.
Ringing at edges as in Fourier, with a different pattern; on pixels, integrate or use discrete orthogonal polynomials.

title: Quiz: matching objects
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. IoU = overlap / union of two objects; matching is one to one at an IoU threshold \tau; TP = matched pairs, FP = unmatched predictions, FN = unmatched true objects.

Q1. Why is there no “true negative” when we count objects, and what does that mean for accuracy and ROC curves?






Hint





What would a true-negative object be?









Answer





A true negative would be “background correctly not predicted as an object”, but the background is not made of countable objects. So object-level scores use only TP, FP and FN: precision, recall, F1, matching accuracy. Accuracy (TP + TN)/\text{all} and the false-positive rate FP/(FP + TN) of a ROC curve are undefined; precision–recall curves take their place.




Q2. A nucleus of radius 3 px is predicted one pixel off; a nucleus of radius 20 px too. Which prediction is more likely to fail at \tau = 0.5, and why?






Hint





Compare the lost overlap with the area of the object.









Answer





The small one. A one-pixel shift loses a strip of about one pixel times the diameter: a large fraction of a small object (IoU about 0.65 for radius 3 px) and a small fraction of a large one (about 0.94 for 20 px). With a little extra outline error the small object falls below 0.5. Small objects need a lower \tau or a different criterion (e.g. distance between centres).




Q3. At \tau = 0.6, can one true object have two predictions with IoU \ge \tau?






Hint





How much of the true object must each of them cover?









Answer





No. IoU above 0.5 means the prediction overlaps more than half of the true object. Two non-overlapping predictions cannot both cover more than half of it. So above 0.5 every object has at most one candidate, and the matching is forced: no greedy-versus-optimal question.




Q4. A true nucleus is split by the method into two halves, each with IoU 0.4 with it. What are its contributions to TP, FP and FN at \tau = 0.5? And at \tau = 0.3?






Hint





One to one: at most one half can be matched.









Answer





At \tau = 0.5: no half matches, so 0 TP, 2 FP, 1 FN. At \tau = 0.3: one half matches (TP), the other is an FP: 1 TP, 1 FP, 0 FN.




Q5. Method A has F1 0.92 at \tau = 0.5 and 0.30 at \tau = 0.8; method B has 0.80 and 0.75. Which would you use to count cells, and which to measure their areas?






Hint





What does a high \tau demand?









Answer





A finds more objects (better at 0.5) but with sloppy outlines (collapses at 0.8): better for counting. B’s outlines are tight (holds up at 0.8), but it misses or merges more objects: better for measuring areas and shapes of the objects it finds. One F1 at one \tau would have hidden this.




Q6. A method predicts 20 objects with scores; 4 low-scored specks at the end of the list are false positives. Why does removing them change F1 but hardly change AP?






Hint





Where in the sorted list are they, and what happens to recall there?









Answer





F1 counts all predictions at the chosen cut-off: 4 fewer FP raise precision and F1. AP is the area under the precision–recall curve built by walking down the list by score; the specks come after all true objects are found, so they do not increase recall and add (almost) no area. AP rewards a good ranking; a method can have a high AP and still need a good score cut-off.




Q7. Paper X reports “AP_{0.5} = 0.80” for nucleus segmentation, paper Y “AP_{0.5} = 0.88” for detection. Can you conclude that Y is better?






Hint





The same name is used for two quantities.









Answer





No. Cell-segmentation papers often write AP for TP/(TP + FP + FN) at one \tau (the matching accuracy in this course); detection papers mean the area under a precision–recall curve of scored predictions. The two numbers are on different scales even for the same result (in the lecture’s example: 0.5 versus 0.69). Besides, they are measured on different data.




Q8. (math) Show that the object F1 equals 2\,TP/(n_G + n_P), where n_G and n_P are the numbers of true and predicted objects. Why does this make F1(\tau) non-increasing?






Hint





Every predicted object is either TP or FP.









Answer





n_P = TP + FP and n_G = TP + FN, so 2\,TP + FP + FN = n_G + n_P, which does not depend on \tau. Raising \tau removes allowed pairs, so the number of matches can only stay or drop; F1 is that number divided by a constant.

Background







Word
Meaning

title: Exercise: matching objects
text:
By hand
B1. On a pixel grid: (a) Two 4 \times 4 squares, one shifted by one pixel to the right. Compute the IoU. (b) Two 2 \times 2 squares, shifted the same way. Compute the IoU. (c) Which loses more for the same one-pixel error? What does that mean when you evaluate small objects (spots, small nuclei) at \tau = 0.5?
B2. An IoU table with 3 true objects and 4 predictions:

Match at \tau = 0.5. Give TP, FP, FN, precision, recall and F1.
The same at \tau = 0.3 and at \tau = 0.7.
What kind of error is G2? Sketch shapes that could give its row.
Sketch F1 as a function of \tau from 0 to 1. Where are the steps?

B3. Greedy and optimal matching at \tau = 0.3:

Match greedily: take the largest IoU first, then the largest among the objects still free. How many matches?
Find the matching with the most matches. What is its total IoU, compared with the greedy one?
Draw two true objects and two predictions that could give this table.
Could this happen at \tau = 0.55? Why not?

B4. Four true objects. A method predicts five objects; sorted by score they are TP, TP, FP, TP, FP (at \tau = 0.5). (a) Write down recall and precision after each prediction, and draw the precision–recall curve. (b) Make the precision non-increasing from the right and compute the area under it: the average precision. (c) Compute the matching accuracy TP/(TP+FP+FN) and the F1 for all five predictions. A paper reports “AP 0.5” for this method. Is it wrong? (d) A sixth prediction with the lowest score is added; it is an FP. What happens to AP, to precision and to F1?
B5. Predict, then explain. (a) A method finds every nucleus but every predicted outline is one pixel too large. Sketch its F1-vs-\tau curve. What happens to the pixel Dice? (b) A perfect method, except that one pair of touching nuclei is merged into one object. Sketch its F1-vs-\tau curve. Which is worse for counting cells, (a) or (b)? (c) Why can a method with pixel Dice 0.97 have a lower object F1 than a method with Dice 0.86?






Solutions





B1. (a) Overlap 3 \times 4 = 12 pixels, union 16 + 16 - 12 = 20: IoU = 0.6. (b) Overlap 1 \times 2 = 2, union 4 + 4 - 2 = 6: IoU = 1/3. (c) The small square loses far more: a one-pixel error is a large fraction of a small object. At \tau = 0.5 the 2 \times 2 prediction is already an FP plus an FN. For small objects either use a lower \tau (or a distance between centres instead of IoU), or report the F1-vs-\tau curve so the reader sees it.
B2. (a) Pairs with IoU \ge 0.5: G1–P1 (0.82) and G3–P4 (0.62). TP 2, FP 2 (P2, P3), FN 1 (G2). Precision 2/4 = 0.5, recall 2/3 = 0.67, F1 = 4/(4 + 2 + 1) = 4/7 = 0.57. (b) \tau = 0.3: G2–P2 (0.45) also matches (P3 cannot, G2 is taken). TP 3, FP 1, FN 0: precision 0.75, recall 1, F1 = 6/7 = 0.86. \tau = 0.7: only G1–P1. TP 1, FP 3, FN 2: precision 0.25, recall 0.33, F1 = 2/7 = 0.29. (c) G2 is split into P2 and P3: two predictions that each cover part of it (IoU 0.45 and 0.38). For example a nucleus cut in two by a wrong watershed line, slightly unequal halves. (d) F1 = 6/7 for \tau \le 0.45, 4/7 for 0.45 < \tau \le 0.62, 2/7 for 0.62 < \tau \le 0.82, and 0 above 0.82. A staircase, stepping down at the IoU values of the matched pairs.
B3. (a) Greedy takes G1–P1 (0.60). G2’s only candidate P1 is taken, and P2’s only candidate G1 is taken: 1 match, total IoU 0.60. (b) G1–P2 and G2–P1: 2 matches, total IoU 0.40 + 0.35 = 0.75, more matches and also more IoU. (c) Two touching nuclei G1 (left) and G2 (right); P1 is a large object between them, covering most of G1 and part of G2; P2 is a smaller object inside the left part of G1. (The lecture’s figure has this geometry, with IoUs 0.44, 0.39, 0.31.) (d) No: above 0.5 every object has at most one partner (the lecture’s math slide), so each row and column has at most one allowed pair and there is no choice to get wrong. Here only G1–P1 would be allowed at 0.55.
B4. (a) Recall: 0.25, 0.5, 0.5, 0.75, 0.75; precision: 1, 1, 0.67, 0.75, 0.6. (b) Interpolated precision: 1, 1, 0.75, 0.75, 0.6. Recall increases by 0.25 at predictions 1, 2 and 4: AP = 0.25 \cdot 1 + 0.25 \cdot 1 + 0.25 \cdot 0.75 = 0.6875. (c) TP 3, FP 2, FN 1: matching accuracy 3/6 = 0.5; F1 = 6/9 = 0.67. The paper is not wrong if it means the matching accuracy, but its “AP” is a different number from the area under the PR curve (0.69). Compare only numbers with the same definition. (d) AP does not change: the new FP does not raise recall, so it adds an area of width 0. Precision drops to 3/6 = 0.5, F1 to 6/10 = 0.6.
B5. (a) A one-pixel dilation lowers the IoU of every object a little (more for small ones), but all IoUs stay well above 0.5: F1 = 1 up to a fairly high \tau (around 0.8 for nuclei of radius ~10 px), then it drops to 0 within a short range of \tau, because all objects have about the same IoU. The pixel Dice drops somewhat (every boundary pixel ring is an FP). (b) F1 is a little below 1 at every \tau: the merged object can match at most one of the two nuclei. If it matches one (IoU \ge \tau): 1 FN; otherwise 2 FN + 1 FP. The curve is a lower, flat plateau. For counting, (b) is worse: the count is wrong, while (a) counts correctly. (c) Pixel Dice weighs big objects and boundary pixels; it barely notices a merge (almost every pixel is right). Object F1 counts objects: every merge costs a TP. Many merges with tight outlines: high Dice, low F1. Sloppy outlines without merges: lower Dice, higher F1 at \tau = 0.5.




Math questions
B6. (math) Prove that IoU(A, B_1) > \frac12 and IoU(A, B_2) > \frac12 is impossible for disjoint B_1, B_2. Is it still impossible with IoU exactly \frac12? Give an example with IoU \ge \frac13 for both.
B7. (math) Write the matching of B3 as an assignment problem with unknowns x_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}. List all feasible x (row and column sums \le 1, only pairs with IoU \ge 0.3) and find the optimum (a) of the total IoU, (b) of “number of matches first, then IoU”. Do they agree here?
B8. (math) (a) Show that with every object matched or unmatched, F1 = 2\,TP/(n_G + n_P), where n_G, n_P are the numbers of true and predicted objects. (b) Show that F1(\tau) is non-increasing in \tau for the forced matching above 0.5. (c) Show that greedy matching has the same property at any \tau. (d) Show that the matching accuracy equals F1/(2 - \text{F1}).






Solutions (math)





B6. IoU(A, B) > \frac12 gives |A \cap B| > \frac12|A \cup B| \ge \frac12|A|. If both held, |A \cap B_1| + |A \cap B_2| > |A|; but A \cap B_1 and A \cap B_2 are disjoint subsets of A, so their sizes add to at most |A|. Contradiction. At exactly \frac12 it is possible: cut A into two equal halves B_1, B_2; then |A \cap B_i| = \frac12|A| and |A \cup B_i| = |A|, IoU = \frac12 for both. The same example has IoU \ge \frac13 for both; so does A cut into halves with each B_i a little larger than its half.
B7. Allowed pairs: G1–P1 (0.60), G1–P2 (0.40), G2–P1 (0.35). Feasible matchings: none (0); \{G1–P1\} (0.60); \{G1–P2\} (0.40); \{G2–P1\} (0.35); \{G1–P2, G2–P1\} (0.75). (\{G1–P1, G2–P1\} uses P1 twice, \{G1–P1, G1–P2\} uses G1 twice.) (a) Maximum total IoU: \{G1–P2, G2–P1\} with 0.75. (b) Most matches: the same, 2 matches. They agree here; they would differ if, say, G1–P1 were 0.80: total IoU would then prefer the single pair (0.80 > 0.75), “matches first” still the two pairs.
B8. (a) Every predicted object is TP or FP: n_P = TP + FP; every true object TP or FN: n_G = TP + FN. So 2\,TP + FP + FN = n_G + n_P. (b) For \tau > \frac12 the matched pairs are exactly the pairs with IoU \ge \tau (forced). Raising \tau can only remove pairs, so TP(\tau) is non-increasing, and with the fixed denominator n_G + n_P so is F1. (c) Greedy sorts all pairs by IoU and walks down the list. At a higher \tau it walks the same list but stops earlier; every decision it makes before stopping is the same, so its matches are those of the lower \tau with IoU \ge \tau: a subset. (d) acc = TP/(TP + FP + FN) = TP/(n_G + n_P - TP). With f = 2\,TP/(n_G + n_P): f/(2 - f) = 2\,TP/(2(n_G + n_P) - 2\,TP) = TP/(n_G + n_P - TP).

title: Exercise: matching objects
text:
Explore
The image is a synthetic fluorescence image of 16 nuclei (6 touching pairs, 3 dim nuclei). True outlines are white. Predicted objects are filled green (TP) or red (FP) at the current \tau; true objects without a match get a dashed orange outline (FN). The error generator turns the truth into predictions: boundary jitter, an outline bias (too large or too small), merging of touching pairs, splitting, missing dim nuclei, and specks; every prediction gets a score (low for specks and dim nuclei). Edit by hand freezes the predictions as ellipses you can move, resize, rotate, add, delete, split and merge. The IoU table shows the objects near the yellow marker (click the image to move it): matched cells boxed, cells below \tau grey. The right panel shows F1 against \tau (with the pixel Dice as a dashed line) or the precision–recall curve at \tau.



E1. Preset a typical result (\tau = 0.5). Read TP, FP, FN, precision, recall, F1 and the pixel Dice. Which kinds of error do you see in the image, and how many of each?
E2. Preset Dice high, count wrong. Compare the pixel Dice with F1. How many merges are there, and how many nuclei does the method count? Explain why Dice hardly notices.
E3. Preset sloppy outlines. Read F1 at \tau = 0.5 and at \tau = 0.8 (move the slider, or read the curve). Compare with E2 at the same two thresholds. Which method is better, and for what purpose?
E4. Preset one split. Find the split nucleus (label “split”) and put the marker on it. Read its row in the IoU table. How does one split change TP, FP and FN?
E5. Preset greedy loses a match (\tau = 0.3). Read the IoU table at the marker. Compare TP with greedy and optimal matching. Then move \tau to 0.35 and to 0.4: what happens to the difference, and why?
E6. Preset specks. Read precision, recall and F1, then open the PR curve tab. What are AP at \tau and AP over 0.5–0.95? Set specks to 0: which numbers change and which do not? Why?
E7. Preset vs a second annotator. The grey curve is the F1 of annotator B against annotator A (the truth); the band above it is out of reach of any honest claim. Where does the prediction’s curve lie? At which \tau do the two annotators start to disagree strongly?
E8. In a typical result, choose edit by hand, click a correctly found nucleus and press split. Predict the change of TP, FP and FN at \tau = 0.5 before you look. Then try merge with nearest on another one, and move an ellipse until its IoU drops just below \tau.






Solutions





E1. 16 true, 14 predicted objects: TP 12, FP 2, FN 4; precision 0.857, recall 0.750, F1 0.800, matching accuracy 0.667; pixel Dice 0.864. Two merges: each merged object matches the larger of its two nuclei (IoU 0.57) and leaves the other one unmatched (2 FN). Two dim nuclei are missed (2 FN), and the two specks are the 2 FP. The count is 14 instead of 16, and two of the 14 are not nuclei.
E2. Pixel Dice 0.971, but F1 0.692 at \tau = 0.5 (TP 9, FP 1, FN 7). Every touching pair is merged: 5 merged objects (one of them a chain of three nuclei), so the method counts 10 objects instead of 16. Almost every pixel is labelled correctly (only the thin gap between the nuclei of a pair is wrong), so Dice is high; but each merge loses one or two true objects.
E3. Sloppy outlines: F1 0.875 at 0.5, 0.250 at 0.8 (Dice 0.857). Merges (E2): 0.692 at 0.5, 0.385 at 0.8. For counting the sloppy method is better (it finds the objects); for measuring shapes and areas neither is good, and at strict \tau the merging method with tight outlines does better. One number at one \tau hides this.
E4. One nucleus is cut into two halves with IoU 0.41 and 0.40 with it (below 0.5). Its row has two non-zero cells, neither boxed. TP 15, FP 2, FN 1 (F1 0.909): one split costs one TP and adds two FP and one FN. The pixel Dice is still 0.978.
E5. At the marker: G1–P1 0.376 (largest), G1–P2 0.335, G2–P1 0.339. Greedy takes G1–P1 and leaves G2 and P2 unmatched: TP 15 (F1 0.938). Optimal pairs G1–P2 and G2–P1: TP 16 (F1 1.000). At \tau = 0.35 the pairs G1–P2 and G2–P1 are no longer allowed (both below 0.35), so both methods give TP 15; at 0.4 also G1–P1 drops out and both give TP 14. Greedy can only lose when there is a choice, which needs several allowed pairs in a row or column.
E6. Precision 0.571, recall 1.000, F1 0.727 (16 TP, 12 FP). AP at \tau = 0.5 is 1.000 and AP over 0.5–0.95 is 0.821. With specks set to 0: precision and F1 become 1.000, AP stays 1.000 and AP over 0.5–0.95 stays 0.821. The specks have the lowest scores, so they come last in the list, after all true objects are found; they do not raise recall, so they add no area. AP measures the ranking; F1 at a fixed cut-off (all predictions) does not use the scores.
E7. Up to \tau = 0.8 the prediction’s curve (F1 1.000) lies above annotator B’s curve (0.968), i.e. in the band; at 0.85 it drops to 0.875, below B (still 0.968), and at 0.9 both fall (0.625 and 0.710). Annotator B left out one disputed dim nucleus and draws slightly different outlines; above \tau = 0.85 the two annotators disagree strongly. The prediction was generated from annotator A, so “better than a human” here means “closer to annotator A”. On real data a score above the inter-annotator agreement says “as good as a human”, not “better”.
E8. A correctly found nucleus split into halves with a 2-pixel gap: each half has IoU just under 0.5 with it, so TP −1, FP +2 (net predicted objects +1), FN +1. Merging two correctly found separate nuclei: the merged object matches at most one of them; usually it is too large for either (IoU < 0.5): TP −2, FP +1, FN +2. Moving an ellipse: when its IoU crosses \tau its pair stops being a TP and becomes one FP plus one FN.

title: Exercise: matching objects
text:
Where this leads
The same matching and AP are used for detection with boxes on the modern deep learning day. The next unit asks how good the truth is, and what to do when the outline or the count matters more than the match: boundary distances and agreement plots.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
text:
About this lecture
A neural network is a function with many adjustable numbers, fitted to examples. This unit opens the neural-networks day with the smallest networks we can draw.

One neuron = a weighted sum, then a bend: it draws a line through feature space. It can do AND and OR, but not XOR.
A network is matrix × vector, then a bend, repeated. You have done the matrix part since the first unit.
Without the bend, any number of layers collapses to one matrix.
With the bend, simple hinges add up to curves, and lines add up to any boundary.
Many classes: one output per class, turned into probabilities by softmax.
Training = walking downhill on an error, one small step at a time.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

No machine learning is assumed. The aim is to demystify the words network, layer, hidden unit, ReLU, weight, training, learning rate, so that the rest of the neural-networks day (and later the autoencoder units) can use them freely. Later units of the day write the layers as W^{(1)}, W^{(2)}: here A = W^{(1)}, C = W^{(2)}. Adapted from “Beyond linear models” in the 3MB00A course. Keep it light: the picture and the demo carry the unit, the algebra is a few lines.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
section: Recall: a classifier draws a line
text:
Recall: a classifier draws a line
Thresholding (day 6) decides “nucleus if intensity > t”: a cut on one measurement. Day 14 put objects as points in a feature space and let a classifier carve it up.

Two measurements per object (say area and mean intensity): each object is a point in the plane.
The simplest rule that uses both: a straight line, w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + b > 0 means “nucleus”.
The numbers w_1, w_2, b are what we will learn from examples.


One slide of recall from thresholding and from the random-forest day, which owns feature space and the train/test vocabulary. A forest carves feature space into boxes; a neuron cuts it with a line; a network combines many lines.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
text:
One neuron


A neuron adds its inputs with weights, adds a bias, then bends the result with an activation \varphi:
\text{out} = \varphi(w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + b)

Step \varphi: a hard yes/no, the perceptron (1958).
Sigmoid \varphi(s) = 1/(1 + e^{-s}): a probability between 0 and 1.
ReLU \varphi(s) = \max(0, s): the workhorse of today’s networks.

The weights point across the line, to the positive side; the bias moves the line.


\mathbf w = (2, 1), b = -4: (2, 1) and (3, 0) are positive.


Compute two points with the class: (1, 1) gives 2 + 1 − 4 = −1, negative; (2, 1) gives +1, positive. With the sigmoid the outputs are 0.27 and 0.73: a neuron with a sigmoid is exactly logistic regression. Doubling w and b keeps the line but makes the probabilities sharper.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
section: The math: a neuron is a half-plane
text:
The math: a neuron is a half-plane
\text{out} = \varphi(\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x + b)

The decision boundary \mathbf w^\top\mathbf x + b = 0 is a line (a hyperplane in \mathbb R^n) with normal \mathbf w.
Its distance from the origin is |b|/\|\mathbf w\|; the signed distance of a point is (\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x + b)/\|\mathbf w\|.
With the sigmoid, the output is an S-shaped function of that signed distance times \|\mathbf w\|: larger \|\mathbf w\|, steeper transition, same line.
Example: \mathbf w = (2, 1), b = -4: distance 4/\sqrt5 = 1.79.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
text:
AND, OR, but not XOR
Inputs x_1, x_2 \in \{0, 1\}, step activation (1 if the sum > 0):




AND
OR
XOR




weights, bias
1, 1, -1.5
1, 1, -0.5
none exists


corners that are 1
(1,1)
all but (0,0)
(1,0) and (0,1)




XOR wants (1,0) and (0,1) on one side, (0,0) and (1,1) on the other: no single line does that.
This observation (Minsky and Papert, 1969) stalled neural networks for a decade. The answer: more than one neuron.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
text:
Two hidden units solve XOR
h_1 = \text{ReLU}(x_1 + x_2), h_2 = \text{ReLU}(x_1 + x_2 - 1), \ \text{out} = h_1 - 2h_2:



(x_1, x_2)
(0,0)
(1,0)
(0,1)
(1,1)




h_1, h_2
0, 0
1, 0
1, 0
2, 1


out
0
1
1
0




Each hidden unit is a neuron with its own line; the output combines them.
The hidden layer has turned the four corners into points that one line can separate.


Do the table on the board. In the playground, preset “2 hidden units solve XOR” shows the two hidden units as two half-planes (thumbnails) and the output region as the band between two lines.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
text:
A layer: matrix, then bend

\mathbf h = \text{ReLU}(A\mathbf x + \mathbf b), \qquad \text{out} = C\mathbf h + d, \qquad \text{ReLU}(s) = \max(0, s)

Each line in the picture is one number of A or C (a weight).
The bend (ReLU) acts on each entry separately: negatives become 0.
The entries of \mathbf h are the hidden units: every row of A is one neuron.
Later units write W^{(1)} for A and W^{(2)} for C: layer l computes \mathbf a^{(l)} = \varphi(W^{(l)}\mathbf a^{(l-1)} + \mathbf b^{(l)}).


A layer is the matrix–vector product of the first unit plus a shift. The only new thing is the ReLU, applied entry by entry. Older networks used an S-shaped curve instead of ReLU; the choice matters much less than having a bend at all. For images, x is the whole image as one long vector: 784 numbers for a 28 × 28 image.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
section: One input through the network, by hand
text:
One input through the network, by hand
A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \mathbf b = \mathbf 0, C = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, d = 0, input \mathbf x = (1, 2).

Matrix: A\mathbf x = (1 + 2,\ 1 - 2,\ -1 + 4) = (3,\ -1,\ 3)
Bend: \text{ReLU} \to (3,\ 0,\ 3)
Matrix: \text{out} = 1\cdot 3 + 2\cdot 0 + 1\cdot 3 = 6

Without the bend: 1\cdot 3 + 2\cdot(-1) + 1\cdot 3 = 4. The bend changed the answer.

Do this on the board. Every step is a dot product except step 2, which only clips negatives.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
text:
Without the bend, layers collapse
Applying A and then C is applying the single matrix CA:
C(A\mathbf x) = (CA)\,\mathbf x, \qquad CA = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
Check: (2, 1)\cdot(1, 2) = 4, the “no bend” answer.

2 or 100 layers with no bend in between are one matrix: a straight-line (linear) map.
The bend between the matrices is what lets a network draw curves.


Composition of linear maps is matrix multiplication, as in Images as arrays & geometric transforms. With shifts, C(Ax + b) + d = (CA)x + (Cb + d): still a plane. We will meet this again: a linear autoencoder is PCA, and only the bend makes an autoencoder more than PCA.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
text:
Hinges add up to curves

A line scan across two nuclei. One input (position), three hidden units, one output.

Each hidden unit is a hinge: flat, then a straight rise (or the reverse), at its own position.
The output adds the hinges with weights: a bent line through the data.
More units → more hinges → any curve, as closely as we like.


The figure is made with the same code as the demo (3 units after 3000 training steps). The orange curves are each hidden unit’s contribution (its ReLU times its output weight, plus the output shift); the triangles mark where each hinge bends. Ask: how many hinges would you need for the two plateaus and four edges? Roughly two per edge, so about 8; the demo shows 12 gets close to the noise level.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
section: Training: walk downhill on the error
text:
Training: walk downhill on the error
How do we find the weights? Measure how wrong the network is (the loss, e.g. the mean squared error over the data), then nudge every weight a little in the direction that lowers it. Repeat thousands of times.

Picture the loss as a landscape over the weights: training walks downhill.
The learning rate is the step length: too small takes forever, too large overshoots to the other side of the valley.
The walk can stop in a dip that is not the deepest one: two trainings from different starts can give different networks.


Concept layer: students must take away “downhill on the error, step size matters, the result depends on the start”. The next slide is the math layer and can be skipped.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
text:
The math: one gradient step
Step against the gradient: \mathbf w \leftarrow \mathbf w - \eta\, \nabla_{\mathbf w} L.

One weight, L(w) = (y - wx)^2 with x = 2, y = 3, start w = 0: L'(w) = -2x(y - wx), so L'(0) = -12. With \eta = 0.1: w \to 1.2, and L drops from 9 to 0.36.
Distance to the best w = 1.5 after one step: w_\text{new} - 1.5 = (1 - 8\eta)(w - 1.5). Converges for 0 < \eta < 0.25; \eta = 0.5 makes L grow to 81.
For a network, \nabla L comes from the chain rule applied layer by layer, from the output back to the input (backpropagation).


Show the parabola L(w) and the step on the board. The exercise does the four step sizes 0.1, 0.125, 0.25, 0.5 (new w 1.2, 1.5, 3, 6; loss 0.36, 0, 9, 81). In the demo the steps use Adam, a variant that adapts the step length per weight; the idea is the same.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
section: Try it: a network classifies points
text:
Try it: a network classifies points




Tour: “one neuron, by hand”: drag the handle and the tip, read the loss (lower when the line separates the blobs and w is long). “one neuron on XOR fails”: play, the loss stays at 0.69 (= ln 2, a coin toss), accuracy 50 %. “2 hidden units solve XOR”: play, the two thumbnails become two half-planes, loss below 0.01 after a few hundred steps; “new start” with other seeds often gets stuck at 75 %: the start matters. “no nonlinearity: still a line”: 8 units, no bend, the circle cannot be separated (74 %). “circle: 3 ReLU units”: a triangle-like region. “spiral needs depth”: 8 + 8 units. “3 classes with softmax”.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
text:
Many classes: softmax
One output score z_k per class; turn the scores into probabilities:
p_k = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}

All p_k are positive and sum to 1; the largest score gets the largest probability.
Scores (2, 1, 0) → probabilities (0.67, 0.24, 0.09). The predicted class is the largest.
Two classes with softmax are the same as one sigmoid output.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
text:
The math: softmax

Adding a constant to all scores does not change p: e^{z_k + c}/\sum_j e^{z_j + c} = e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j}. So (102, 101, 100) gives the same (0.665, 0.245, 0.090), and computers subtract \max_k z_k first to avoid overflow.
Two classes: p_1 = e^{z_1}/(e^{z_0} + e^{z_1}) = 1/(1 + e^{-(z_1 - z_0)}), the sigmoid of the score difference.
Universal approximation (Cybenko 1989 for sigmoids; the same holds for ReLU): one hidden layer with enough units approximates any continuous function on a bounded region as closely as we like. It says nothing about how many units, or whether training finds them.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
section: Try it: fit a line scan
text:
Try it: fit a line scan




Press “train 500 steps” a few times: the hinges move to the edges of the nuclei and the loss falls. Presets: “one hinge” can only make one bend (loss 0.059); “3 hinges” 0.020; “12 hinges” 0.0019, close to the noise variance 0.0009. “no bend”: 12 units, but the fit stays a straight line (0.065, barely better than the flat mean line, 0.073). “learning rate too large”: the loss jumps around and then every unit ends up flat (all hinges off the data): the fit is the flat mean line, loss 0.073. That is a “dead” network.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
text:
Images are long vectors
A 28 \times 28 image is a vector in \mathbb R^{784}. A layer from the image to 100 hidden units has
784 \times 100 + 100 = 78{,}500 \text{ numbers.}

Image networks easily have hundreds of thousands of weights. Training adjusts all of them at once, with the same downhill steps.
Many weights need many training images, or the network memorises instead of learning.
Such a layer has no idea that neighbouring pixels belong together: shift the digit by one pixel and almost every input changes. The convolutional networks of this day fix exactly that.


A 784 → 100 → 10 classifier has 78,500 + 1,010 = 79,510 numbers. Count with the class: the full VAE of the VAE day (784 → 192 → 2 means + 2 log-variances, and 2 → 192 → 784) has 303,380 numbers. Overfitting is the same phenomenon as fitting a high-degree polynomial through a few points; the defences are more data, a penalty, and checking on images not used for training.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
text:
Summary







Idea
In one line




Neuron
weighted sum + bias, then a bend: a line in feature space


XOR
needs a hidden layer: no single line separates it


Layer
matrix × vector + shift, then ReLU on each entry


No bend
stacked matrices collapse to one matrix: a linear map


Hidden unit
one hinge; hinges add up to curves


Loss
how wrong the network is, e.g. mean squared error


Training
step against the gradient, \mathbf w \leftarrow \mathbf w - \eta\nabla L, many times


Softmax
scores → class probabilities that sum to 1


Learning rate
step size: too small is slow, too large overshoots



Next: how training really works (losses, gradients, backpropagation), then networks whose input is a whole image.

title: Quiz: spectral partitioning and normalized cuts
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. W is the symmetric matrix of affinities, D the diagonal matrix of degrees d_p = \sum_q w_{pq}, and L = D - W.

Q1. Why is \mathbf{1} (the vector of all ones) always an eigenvector of L, and with which eigenvalue?






Hint





Compute row p of L\mathbf{1}.









Answer





Row p of L\mathbf{1} is d_p - \sum_q w_{pq} = 0. So L\mathbf{1} = 0 \cdot \mathbf{1}: eigenvalue 0. Since \mathbf{x}^\top L\mathbf{x} = \sum w_{pq}(x_p - x_q)^2 \ge 0, no eigenvalue is negative, so 0 is the smallest.




Q2. A graph consists of two separate pieces with no edges between them. What is \mu_2, and what does the Fiedler vector look like?






Hint





Find a second vector with \mathbf{x}^\top L\mathbf{x} = 0.









Answer





\mu_2 = 0. Any vector that is constant on each piece has \mathbf{x}^\top L\mathbf{x} = 0, for example +1 on one piece and -c on the other, chosen orthogonal to \mathbf{1}. Its sign splits the graph exactly into the two pieces. The number of zero eigenvalues is the number of connected pieces.




Q3. For \mathbf{x} \in \{\pm 1\}^n, why is \mathbf{x}^\top L\mathbf{x} equal to 4 times the cut?






Hint





\mathbf{x}^\top L\mathbf{x} = \sum_{\text{edges}} w_{pq}(x_p - x_q)^2.









Answer





For an edge inside a part, x_p = x_q and the term is 0. For an edge across the cut, x_p - x_q = \pm 2 and the term is 4 w_{pq}. Summing gives 4 \sum_{\text{across}} w_{pq} = 4\,\text{cut}(A, B).




Q4. Why does minimising the plain cut without seeds give a useless answer, and how does Ncut avoid it?






Hint





What does it cost to cut off a single node, in cut and in Ncut?









Answer





Cutting off one node costs only the weights of its own edges, usually less than any real boundary, which crosses many edges. In Ncut that same cut is divided by the node’s volume, which is exactly those weights: \text{cut}/\text{vol}(A) = 1. A balanced split with weak edges between large groups has \text{Ncut} \ll 1, so Ncut prefers it.




Q5. What is the relation between L\mathbf{x} = \mu D\mathbf{x} and an ordinary symmetric eigenproblem?






Hint





Substitute \mathbf{x} = D^{-1/2}\mathbf{y} and multiply by D^{-1/2}.









Answer





L D^{-1/2}\mathbf{y} = \mu D^{1/2}\mathbf{y}, and multiplying on the left by D^{-1/2}: D^{-1/2}LD^{-1/2}\,\mathbf{y} = \mu\,\mathbf{y}. The matrix D^{-1/2}LD^{-1/2} (the normalized Laplacian) is symmetric, so it has real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors; \mathbf{x} = D^{-1/2}\mathbf{y} recovers the generalized eigenvector.




Q6. The Fiedler vector has real entries, not \pm 1. How do you get a segmentation from it, and why is the result not guaranteed to be the minimum Ncut?






Hint





What did the relaxation change?









Answer





Threshold it: at 0, or at the split point along the sorted vector that gives the smallest Ncut. The eigenvector is the exact solution of the relaxed problem (real values), not of the original one (two values). Rounding it back can be far from the true optimum on some graphs; in practice it is usually good when the graph has a clear two-group structure.




Q7. In an image graph, what happens to the Fiedler vector when \sigma_I, the intensity scale of the affinity, is made very large?






Hint





What does w_{pq} then depend on?









Answer





All intensity factors become close to 1, so w_{pq} depends only on the distance between pixels: the graph is just the pixel grid. Its Fiedler vector is a slowly varying wave across the image (like a lowest-frequency cosine), and the split is geometric (left/right or diagonal), regardless of the image content.




Q8. Name one advantage of graph cuts over normalized cuts, and one the other way round.






Hint





Think of what each needs as input and what each guarantees.









Answer





Graph cuts find the exact minimum of their energy, and the user can steer the result with seeds. Normalized cuts need no seeds or intensity model and take the whole image into account at once; they find the dominant grouping, but only approximately (relaxation and thresholding), and the result may not be the object you wanted.

title: Exercise: spectral partitioning and normalized cuts
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

write down the degree matrix and the Laplacian L = D - W of a small graph,
evaluate the quadratic form \mathbf{x}^\top L\mathbf{x} and relate it to the cut,
verify an eigenvector, and split a graph by the sign of its Fiedler vector,
compute Ncut and explain why it prefers balanced splits to the minimum cut.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the interactive part.

title: Exercise: spectral partitioning and normalized cuts
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

write down the degree matrix and the Laplacian L = D - W of a small graph,
evaluate the quadratic form \mathbf{x}^\top L\mathbf{x} and relate it to the cut,
verify an eigenvector, and split a graph by the sign of its Fiedler vector,
compute Ncut and explain why it prefers balanced splits to the minimum cut.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the interactive part.

title: Exercise: spectral partitioning and normalized cuts
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Affinity
w_{pq} = w_{qp} \ge 0: how strongly p and q belong together


Degree, volume
d_p = \sum_q w_{pq}; \text{vol}(A) = \sum_{p \in A} d_p


Laplacian
L = D - W; \mathbf{x}^\top L\mathbf{x} = \sum_{\text{edges}} w_{pq}(x_p - x_q)^2


Cut
\text{cut}(A, B) = \sum_{p \in A, q \in B} w_{pq}; for x = \pm1: \mathbf{x}^\top L\mathbf{x} = 4\,\text{cut}


Fiedler vector
eigenvector of the second-smallest eigenvalue of L (unnormalized), or of L\mathbf{x} = \mu D\mathbf{x} (normalized)


Normalized cut
\text{Ncut}(A, B) = \text{cut}/\text{vol}(A) + \text{cut}/\text{vol}(B)

title: Exercise: spectral partitioning and normalized cuts
text:
By hand
B1. A path of 4 nodes, 1 - 2 - 3 - 4, all weights 1. (a) Write W, D and L. (b) Check that \mathbf{1} is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 0. (c) Check that \mathbf{v} = (1,\ \sqrt2 - 1,\ 1 - \sqrt2,\ -1) is an eigenvector of L with eigenvalue 2 - \sqrt2. Which split does its sign give?
B2. Same path. Compute \mathbf{x}^\top L\mathbf{x} for \mathbf{x} = (1, 1, -1, -1) and \mathbf{x} = (1, -1, 1, -1), once with the matrix and once with \sum_{\text{edges}}(x_p - x_q)^2. Which cuts do the two vectors describe, and what are their costs?
B3. Same path, now the normalized problem L\mathbf{x} = \mu D\mathbf{x}. (a) Check that \mathbf{x} = (1, \tfrac12, -\tfrac12, -1) solves it with \mu = \tfrac12. Check that \mathbf{x}^\top D\mathbf{1} = 0. (b) Compute Ncut for the splits \{1, 2\} \mid \{3, 4\} and \{1\} \mid \{2, 3, 4\}. Which is better?
B4. Seven nodes: a triangle 1, 2, 3 and a triangle 4, 5, 6, all triangle edges with weight 1; an edge 3 - 4 with weight 0.1; and a node 7 attached only to node 6, with weight 0.05. (a) Compute the degrees and the total volume. (b) What is the minimum cut over all splits? Which split is it? (c) Compute Ncut for \{7\} against the rest, for \{1, 2, 3\} against the rest, and for \{6, 7\} against the rest. Which split does Ncut prefer?
B5. Show that if a graph has two connected components A and B, the eigenvalue 0 of L has (at least) two independent eigenvectors. Give one that is orthogonal to \mathbf{1}. What does its sign do?






Solutions





B1. (a) W = \begin{bmatrix} 0&1&0&0\\1&0&1&0\\0&1&0&1\\0&0&1&0 \end{bmatrix}, D = \operatorname{diag}(1, 2, 2, 1), L = \begin{bmatrix} 1&-1&0&0\\-1&2&-1&0\\0&-1&2&-1\\0&0&-1&1 \end{bmatrix}. (b) Every row of L sums to 0, so L\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{0}. (c) Write a = \sqrt2 - 1, so \mathbf{v} = (1, a, -a, -1). Row 1: 1 - a = 2 - \sqrt2, and \mu v_1 = 2 - \sqrt2. Row 2: -1 + 2a + a = 3a - 1 = 3\sqrt2 - 4, and \mu v_2 = (2 - \sqrt2)(\sqrt2 - 1) = 2\sqrt2 - 2 - 2 + \sqrt2 = 3\sqrt2 - 4. Rows 3 and 4 follow by symmetry (they are rows 2 and 1 with the signs flipped). The sign splits \{1, 2\} \mid \{3, 4\}, in the middle. (All eigenvalues: 0, 2 - \sqrt2 = 0.586, 2, 2 + \sqrt2 = 3.414.)
B2. \mathbf{x} = (1, 1, -1, -1): L\mathbf{x} = (0, 2, -2, 0), \mathbf{x}^\top L\mathbf{x} = 0 + 2 + 2 + 0 = 4; edge sum: (1-1)^2 + (1+1)^2 + (-1+1)^2 = 4. The cut \{1, 2\} \mid \{3, 4\} crosses one edge: cut 1, and 4 = 4 \cdot 1. \mathbf{x} = (1, -1, 1, -1): L\mathbf{x} = (2, -4, 4, -2), \mathbf{x}^\top L\mathbf{x} = 2 + 4 + 4 + 2 = 12; edge sum 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. The cut \{1, 3\} \mid \{2, 4\} crosses all 3 edges: cut 3, and 12 = 4 \cdot 3.
B3. (a) L\mathbf{x} = (1 - \tfrac12,\ -1 + 1 + \tfrac12,\ -\tfrac12 - 1 + 1,\ \tfrac12 - 1) = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12, -\tfrac12, -\tfrac12) and \mu D\mathbf{x} = \tfrac12(1, 1, -1, -1): equal. \mathbf{x}^\top D\mathbf{1} = 1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot \tfrac12 - 2 \cdot \tfrac12 - 1 \cdot 1 = 0. (b) \{1, 2\} \mid \{3, 4\}: cut 1, volumes 1 + 2 = 3 and 3: Ncut = \tfrac13 + \tfrac13 = 0.667. \{1\} \mid \{2, 3, 4\}: cut 1, volumes 1 and 5: Ncut = 1 + 0.2 = 1.2. The balanced split is better, although both cut one edge of weight 1.
B4. (a) d = (2, 2, 2.1, 2.1, 2, 2.05, 0.05), total volume 12.3. (b) The minimum cut is 0.05: \{7\} against the rest. (Separating the triangles costs 0.1; any split through a triangle costs at least 2.) (c) \{7\}: cut 0.05, volumes 0.05 and 12.25: Ncut = 1 + 0.004 = 1.004. \{1, 2, 3\}: cut 0.1, volumes 6.1 and 6.2: Ncut = 0.0164 + 0.0161 = 0.0325. \{6, 7\}: cut 2 (edges 4 - 6 and 5 - 6), volumes 2.1 and 10.2: Ncut = 0.952 + 0.196 = 1.149. Ncut prefers separating the two triangles, by a factor of 30; the minimum cut prefers cutting off node 7. (Computed numerically, the normalized Fiedler vector of this graph is negative on nodes 1–3 and positive on 4–7, with \mu_2 = 0.031: its sign gives the triangles.)
B5. The indicator vectors \mathbf{1}_A (1 on A, 0 on B) and \mathbf{1}_B both satisfy L\mathbf{x} = 0: each row of L only involves nodes of one component, and on that component the vector is constant. A combination orthogonal to \mathbf{1}: \mathbf{x} = |B|\,\mathbf{1}_A - |A|\,\mathbf{1}_B (sum |A||B| - |A||B| = 0). Its sign is + on A and - on B: it splits the graph exactly into its components, at cut 0.









The math: the Laplacian quadratic form





Show that \mathbf{x}^\top L\mathbf{x} = \sum_{\text{edges}} w_{pq}(x_p - x_q)^2 for any graph. (Write \mathbf{x}^\top D\mathbf{x} = \sum_p d_p x_p^2 and \mathbf{x}^\top W\mathbf{x} = \sum_{p,q} w_{pq}x_p x_q, and expand (x_p - x_q)^2.) Conclude that all eigenvalues of L are \ge 0.
Solution: \sum_{\text{edges}} w_{pq}(x_p - x_q)^2 = \tfrac12\sum_{p,q} w_{pq}(x_p^2 - 2x_px_q + x_q^2) (the double sum counts each edge twice). The first and last terms each give \tfrac12\sum_p d_p x_p^2, together \mathbf{x}^\top D\mathbf{x}; the middle term gives -\sum_{p,q} w_{pq}x_p x_q = -\mathbf{x}^\top W\mathbf{x}. So the sum is \mathbf{x}^\top(D - W)\mathbf{x}. It is a sum of non-negative terms, so \mathbf{x}^\top L\mathbf{x} \ge 0 for every \mathbf{x}; for an eigenvector, \mathbf{x}^\top L\mathbf{x} = \mu\|\mathbf{x}\|^2, hence \mu \ge 0.









The math: the normalized eigenproblem





Show that L\mathbf{x} = \mu D\mathbf{x} is equivalent to D^{-1/2}LD^{-1/2}\mathbf{y} = \mu\mathbf{y} with \mathbf{y} = D^{1/2}\mathbf{x}, and that the constraint \mathbf{y} \perp D^{1/2}\mathbf{1} is the same as \mathbf{x}^\top D\mathbf{1} = 0.
Solution: Put \mathbf{x} = D^{-1/2}\mathbf{y} into L\mathbf{x} = \mu D\mathbf{x}: LD^{-1/2}\mathbf{y} = \mu D^{1/2}\mathbf{y}. Multiply on the left by D^{-1/2}: D^{-1/2}LD^{-1/2}\mathbf{y} = \mu\mathbf{y}. All steps can be reversed when every d_p > 0. The constraint: \mathbf{y}^\top D^{1/2}\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{x}^\top D^{1/2}D^{1/2}\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{x}^\top D\mathbf{1}.

title: Exercise: spectral partitioning and normalized cuts
text:
Explore
The demo builds a graph on points (affinity w = e^{-d^2/2\sigma^2} between every pair) or on the pixels of a 32 \times 32 image (neighbours within 2 pixels, affinity from the grey-level difference with scale \sigma and from the distance). It computes the Fiedler vector of L\mathbf{x} = \mu D\mathbf{x} (normalized) or of L\mathbf{x} = \mu\mathbf{x}, colours the nodes by it (blue negative, orange positive) and splits them at the threshold (red lines: the cut edges; for images, a black line). The top plot shows the vector sorted; the bottom plot shows Ncut (purple) and the cut (green, scaled) for every split along the sorted vector, with the best Ncut marked. Show the minimum cut shows the smallest cut without balance instead (for points the exact one, for images the smallest along the sorted vector). Points can be dragged.



E1. Two blobs (\sigma = 0.08). Read \mu_2, the split at threshold 0, its cut and its Ncut. Tick show the minimum cut: is it the same split? Now raise \sigma to 0.15. What does the minimum cut do now, and what does the normalized cut do?
E2. Blobs + outlier. Which split does the normalized Fiedler vector give? Untick normalized: what does the unnormalized Fiedler vector look like, and which split does threshold 0 give now? Compare with B4.
E3. Three blobs. How does the Fiedler vector split the three blobs? How would you get all three?
E4. Two rings (\sigma = 0.05). Are the rings separated? Raise \sigma to 0.12 and use the best Ncut button. What happens, and why?
E5. Image: shapes (\sigma = 30). Which region does the split separate? Tick show the image to compare. Then raise \sigma to 60. What kind of split do you get, and why? Why is the square never separated as a third region?
E6. Image: micrograph (\sigma = 30). Does the split find the nucleus? Press best Ncut. What does the best normalized cut separate, and what does this tell you about unsupervised segmentation?






Solutions





E1. \mu_2 = 0.0135; threshold 0 splits 25 | 25 (the two blobs), cut 2.19, volumes 173 and 185, Ncut 0.0245, which is also the best Ncut on the sweep. The minimum cut (any split) is the same here: 2.19, 25 | 25, because the blobs are well separated at this \sigma. At \sigma = 0.15 the blobs are more strongly connected: the minimum cut now cuts off a single point (cut 9.84, 1 | 49), while the normalized cut still splits the two groups (24 | 26, Ncut 0.143).
E2. Normalized: the two blobs are split (25 | 26: the outlier, almost unconnected, goes with one of them), Ncut 0.0245, as before. Unnormalized: \mu_2 = 4.3 \cdot 10^{-7}; the vector is +1 at the outlier and almost 0 everywhere else, and threshold 0 gives 50 | 1: the outlier alone, Ncut 1.00. That is also the minimum cut (cut 4.2 \cdot 10^{-7}). Without normalisation, cutting off a weakly connected node is cheap, exactly as for node 7 in B4. (The sweep still finds the blob split as the best Ncut, at k = 25, because the tiny differences between the blob values order the points correctly.)
E3. \mu_2 = 9.5 \cdot 10^{-4} and the split is 40 | 20: one blob against the other two (the two that are closest together stay together). For three segments, split again: compute the Fiedler vector of the subgraph of the 40 points. (Or use the third eigenvector as well.)
E4. At \sigma = 0.05 the rings are separated: 20 | 44, \mu_2 = 6.6 \cdot 10^{-6}; the cut between them is tiny (2.1 \cdot 10^{-4}), because the gap is many \sigma wide. At \sigma = 0.12 the affinity reaches across the gap. Threshold 0 now cuts both rings in half (32 | 32), and the best Ncut along the sweep (40 | 24, Ncut 0.214) does not follow the rings either: the “two rings” structure is no longer the dominant one at this scale. \sigma decides what counts as close.
E5. At \sigma = 30 the split is 875 | 149: the bright disk against everything else. (Ncut 6.4 \cdot 10^{-4}.) At \sigma = 60 the grey-level differences matter much less (the disk edge, 190 - 60 = 130, is only about 2\sigma), and the split becomes geometric, roughly in half (527 | 497), like the Fiedler vector of a plain grid. The square is never a third region because one eigenvector gives one split; it would take a second split of the background part (or more eigenvectors).
E6. No: at threshold 0 the image is split diagonally (434 | 590), into the lower left and the upper right. The best Ncut along the sweep (242 pixels, Ncut 0.021) separates the bright white area in the upper right from the rest. Normalized cuts find the dominant grouping of the whole image, here bright versus dark, not necessarily the object you are interested in. To get the nucleus you need more information: seeds (graph cuts), a model, or further splits.

title: Exercise: spectral partitioning and normalized cuts
text:
Where this leads
Spectral partitioning is the basis of spectral clustering, used far beyond images, and of several superpixel methods that over-segment an image into many small coherent regions as a first step. Graph cuts and normalized cuts both treat the image as a graph; other segmentation methods follow image gradients (watershed) or evolve a contour (level sets).

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
About this lecture
A binary image was corrupted by noise. We want the clean image back, using what we know about noise (the likelihood) and about images (the Ising prior).

Bayes: posterior \propto likelihood \times prior; its negative log is an energy.
Two answers: the single most probable image (MAP) and the most probable value of each pixel (MPM).
Four ways to compute them: ICM, simulated annealing, mean field, and the exact minimum cut.
What goes wrong: local minima, and a prior weight \lambda that is too large.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

From this unit on the prior weight is λ (= 2J), as on the graph-cut day; J appears only in the math slides that connect to units 1–2. The demo is mrfdenoise: a 128 × 128 binary image, noise, six methods, and an energy plot.

Bayesian denoising with an Ising prior

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
The problem


Truth \mathbf x: a binary image (here a disc, a square, a 1-pixel and a 3-pixel line, a small square).
Observed \mathbf y: each pixel flipped with probability \varepsilon = 0.2. Taking \mathbf y as the answer leaves 3321 of 16 384 pixels wrong.
Right: two estimates from this unit. The exact best image under the model has 242 wrong pixels, but the 1-pixel line is gone. Why, and what else could we have done?
crumbs: Ising model and Markov random fields
Bayesian denoising with an Ising prior

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
Recall: Bayes’ rule and energies
From the thresholding day (the two-class Bayes rule) and the graph-cut day (seg-energy/, “the probabilistic view”):
\underbrace{p(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf y)}_{\text{posterior}} \;\propto\; \underbrace{p(\mathbf y \mid \mathbf x)}_{\text{likelihood: the noise}}\;\underbrace{p(\mathbf x)}_{\text{prior: what images look like}}

Taking -\log turns the product into a sum: posterior energy = data term + prior term.
Most probable image = lowest energy. That is the graph-cut day’s energy minimisation, now with a probabilistic meaning for every term.
crumbs: Ising model and Markov random fields
Bayesian denoising with an Ising prior

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
The model: noise + Ising prior
Labels L_p \in \{0, 1\} (1 = object), as on the graph-cut day:
E(L \mid \mathbf y) = \sum_p D_p(L_p) + \lambda\sum_{(p,q)}[L_p \ne L_q]

Data term from the noise. With flip noise, a label that disagrees with y_p costs \log\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon} more than one that agrees: \log 4 = 1.39 for \varepsilon = 0.2. Rare flips make disagreeing expensive.
Prior from the Ising model: every disagreeing neighbour pair costs \lambda (= 2J).
\lambda = 0 is thresholding: every pixel keeps its observed value.
With Gaussian noise on two grey levels (the camera-noise model of cameranoise/, day 3), D_p(\ell) = (y_p - \mu_\ell)^2/2\sigma_n^2: grey values near the middle are uncertain, values far out are sure.
crumbs: Ising model and Markov random fields
Bayesian denoising with an Ising prior

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
section: The math: likelihood, field and posterior
text:
The math: likelihood, field and posterior
Flip noise, independent per pixel: p(y_p \mid x_p) = 1 - \varepsilon if y_p = x_p, else \varepsilon. In spins (x_p, y_p = \pm 1):
\log p(y_p \mid x_p) = \tfrac12\log\big(\varepsilon(1 - \varepsilon)\big) + h\,x_py_p, \qquad h = \tfrac12\log\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon}.
With the Ising prior p(\mathbf x) \propto \exp(J\sum x_px_q) the posterior is again an Ising model, with a pixel-dependent field h_p = h\,y_p:
E(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf y) = -J\sum_{(p,q)}x_px_q - \sum_p h_px_p \;(+\text{ const}), \qquad p(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf y) \propto e^{-E(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf y)}.
In label form (unit 1): D_p(1) - D_p(0) = -2h_p, \lambda = 2J. Gaussian noise with levels \mu_0, \mu_1: D_p(\ell) = (y_p - \mu_\ell)^2/2\sigma_n^2, so h_p = \frac{D_p(0) - D_p(1)}{2} is linear in y_p (the squares y_p^2 cancel). The model’s own temperature is T = 1; a T in an algorithm below is a knob of the algorithm.

Bayesian denoising with an Ising prior

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
Two answers: MAP and MPM
The posterior is a distribution over images. Which single image do we report?

MAP (maximum a posteriori): the one most probable image = the lowest energy. All pixels are decided jointly.
MPM (maximum of the posterior marginals; Marroquin, Mitter & Poggio, 1987): for each pixel separately, the value it has in most of the posterior’s probability mass.
MPM gets, on average, the fewest wrong pixels. MAP is the best guess of the whole image.
Marginals come from sampling at T = 1: run a Gibbs sampler, count how often each pixel is 1. The marginal is also an uncertainty map: 0.5 = don’t know.
Three pixels: p(L_2 = 1) = 0.64, p(L_1 = 1) = 0.75, so MPM is also 111, but with a clear warning that the middle pixel is uncertain.
crumbs: Ising model and Markov random fields
Bayesian denoising with an Ising prior

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
section: The math: which estimate minimises which loss?
text:
The math: which estimate minimises which loss?
For an estimate \hat{\mathbf x} and the unknown truth \mathbf x (distributed as the posterior):

0–1 loss (“right only if every pixel is right”): \mathbb E[1 - [\hat{\mathbf x} = \mathbf x]] = 1 - p(\hat{\mathbf x} \mid \mathbf y), minimised by the MAP.
Number of wrong pixels: \mathbb E\sum_p[\hat x_p \ne x_p] = \sum_p\big(1 - p(x_p = \hat x_p \mid \mathbf y)\big). Each term depends on one pixel: minimised pixel by pixel by \hat x_p = \arg\max_v p(x_p = v \mid \mathbf y), the MPM.

The marginal p(x_p = v \mid \mathbf y) = \sum_{\mathbf x: x_p = v}p(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf y) sums over 2^{n-1} images: no closed form. A Gibbs sampler at T = 1 estimates it as the fraction of samples (after burn-in) with x_p = v.
crumbs: Ising model and Markov random fields
Bayesian denoising with an Ising prior

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
Finding the MAP: ICM
Iterated conditional modes (Besag, 1986): the Gibbs sampler at T = 0.

Visit the pixels in turn; give each the label with the lower energy given its neighbours. Repeat until nothing changes.
Fast (a few sweeps), and the energy never increases.
But it stops in the nearest local minimum, and the result depends on the order of visits.
Three pixels from \mathbf y = (1, 0, 1), left to right: pixel 1 sees a background neighbour and switches to 0 (1.39 < 2); pixel 2 stays 0, pixel 3 switches for the same reason: 000, energy 2.77, a local minimum. Visiting the middle pixel first gives 111, the MAP.
crumbs: Ising model and Markov random fields
Bayesian denoising with an Ising prior

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
Annealing and mean field

Simulated annealing (unit 2): Gibbs sampling while T falls from T_0 towards 0, then ICM. Slow cooling approaches the lowest energy; a quench behaves like ICM.
Mean field: replace each neighbour by its average value and iterate: every pixel holds a number between 0 and 1 instead of a label. Deterministic and smooth; an approximation of the marginals (often over-confident). Thresholded at 0.5, it gives an estimate.
crumbs: Ising model and Markov random fields
Bayesian denoising with an Ising prior

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
The math: mean field
In spin form, keep for each pixel a mean m_p \in [-1, 1] and replace the neighbours in the local field by their means:
m_p \leftarrow \tanh\Big(\frac{J\sum_{q \sim p}m_q + h_p}{T}\Big), \qquad p(x_p = +1) \approx \frac{1 + m_p}{2}.

This is the mean of the local conditional p(x_p \mid \text{neighbours}) (unit 2) with the neighbours frozen at their means. Iterated pixel by pixel, it reaches a fixed point.
It is exact when the pixels are independent (J = 0: m_p = \tanh(h_p/T)). Otherwise it ignores correlations between neighbours and tends to be too sure.
Mean field minimises a “free energy” over factorised distributions (variational inference, also behind the VAE day): pointer only.
crumbs: Ising model and Markov random fields
Bayesian denoising with an Ising prior

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
section: The exact MAP: one minimum cut
text:
The exact MAP: one minimum cut
For binary labels and \lambda \ge 0 this energy is the graph-cut day’s segmentation energy. One max-flow gives its exact minimum (Greig, Porteous & Seheult, 1989; recalled from maxflow/ and graphcut-seg/).

In the demo it is computed once per parameter change (128 \times 128: about 50 ms) and drawn as the dashed reference line.
So for binary images the optimiser is not the problem: we can always compare with the true minimum.
For more labels the exact MAP is in general NP-hard (graph-cut day, α-expansion).

Bayesian denoising with an Ising prior

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
section: Try it: denoising a binary image
text:
Try it: denoising a binary image




Panels: noisy input, current estimate, and truth / errors (red: false object, blue: missed object, grey: correct object) / marginal p(object). Energy plot: log sweep axis, dashed = exact minimum (min-cut). Tour, ε = 0.2: “ICM: fast, stuck” (λ = 0.8): 14 sweeps, energy 5171.6 against the exact 5121.2; 427 wrong pixels against 242. “Slow cooling” (1000 sweeps): energy 5124.2, 235 wrong: annealing almost reaches the min-cut energy. “Quench” (10 sweeps): 5161.2, like ICM. “MAP vs MPM” (λ = 1.2): Gibbs at T = 1 for 300 sweeps; MPM 276 wrong, MAP 314; switch the third panel to p(object): uncertain pixels along every edge and on the 3-pixel line. “λ too large” (λ = 3): the exact MAP removes both lines and the small square: 602 wrong. “the exact MAP is not the best image” (λ = 1.6): exact 469 wrong, ICM 401, mean field 207.
crumbs: Ising model and Markov random fields
Bayesian denoising with an Ising prior

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
Lessons from the comparison

ICM is fast but stuck: its energy stays clearly above the minimum. Slow annealing gets close to the min-cut energy; a quench does not.
The exact MAP is not always the best image. Greig et al. (1989) found that for large \lambda the exact MAP was worse than approximate solutions. In the demo at \lambda = 1.6: exact MAP 469 wrong pixels, ICM 401, mean field 207. The fault is the prior (it charges for every boundary pixel, so thin structures are “improbable”), not the optimiser.
The posterior’s best image and the true image are different things. Compare methods by energy to judge the optimiser, and by errors against a known truth to judge the model.
crumbs: Ising model and Markov random fields
Bayesian denoising with an Ising prior

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
Choosing \lambda

Too small: noise survives. An isolated wrong pixel has 4 disagreeing neighbours; it is removed only if 4\lambda > \log\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon}: \lambda > 0.35 for \varepsilon = 0.2. Below that, the MAP is the thresholded image.
Too large: structures vanish, thin ones first. A clean line of width k is removed once 2\lambda > k \log\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon} (two boundaries against k data costs per unit length): the shrinking bias of the graph-cut day.
\varepsilon can be estimated from the noise (e.g. in a flat region); \lambda by trial on a synthetic image with known truth, or by pseudo-likelihood (Besag, 1974): named only.
crumbs: Ising model and Markov random fields
Bayesian denoising with an Ising prior

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
Summary

Posterior energy = data term from the noise model + \lambda\cdot(number of disagreeing neighbours). \lambda = 0 is thresholding.
MAP: the most probable image (lowest energy). MPM: per pixel, the most probable value; fewest expected wrong pixels; comes with an uncertainty map from sampling.
ICM is greedy and gets stuck; annealing gets close to the minimum if cooled slowly; mean field is a fast deterministic approximation; the minimum cut gives the exact MAP for binary images.
A better optimiser does not fix a poor prior: for large \lambda the exact MAP loses thin lines and small objects.

title: Quiz: reconstruction and h-extrema
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Reconstruction R_A(M): dilate the marker M one step, clip it to the mask A, repeat until nothing changes. Grey levels: the same with max/min; \mathrm{HMAX}_h(I) = R_I(I - h), \mathrm{HMIN}_h(I) = R^{\varepsilon}_I(I + h).

Q1. A mask contains 30 cells and many specks. You put one seed pixel in each of 5 cells and reconstruct. What is the result?






Hint





How far can the marker grow, and where must it stop?









Answer





Exactly the 5 seeded cells, complete and unchanged; the other 25 cells and all specks are gone. The marker grows through every pixel connected to a seed inside the mask, and cannot leave the mask.




Q2. Why does an opening by reconstruction keep thin bridges and protrusions that an ordinary opening removes?






Hint





What role does the erosion play in each case?









Answer





In the ordinary opening, the erosion result is dilated back by the SE: only what the SE reaches comes back, so thin parts stay lost. In the opening by reconstruction, the erosion is only a marker: it says which components contain a part the SE fits into. The reconstruction then floods each such component completely, bridges and protrusions included.




Q3. How do you remove all objects that touch the image border with a reconstruction? And how do you fill holes?






Hint





Choose the marker and the mask.









Answer





Clear border: marker = object pixels on the frame (the outermost rows and columns), mask = the objects; the reconstruction is the set of objects touching the border; subtract it from the mask. Fill holes: marker = background pixels on the frame, mask = the background; the reconstruction is the background reachable from outside; everything else (the holes) becomes object. Use 4-connected steps for the background, 8-connected for objects.




Q4. In 1D, what is R_I(M) for I = 3\,5\,2\,6\,1 and a seed only at the 6, i.e. M = 0\,0\,0\,6\,0?






Hint





Each step: max over the 3-window, then min with I.









Answer





Step 1: 0\,0\,6\,6\,6 \to clipped: 0\,0\,2\,6\,1. Step 2: 0\,2\,6\,6\,6 \to 0\,2\,2\,6\,1. Step 3: 2\,2\,6\,6\,6 \to 2\,2\,2\,6\,1. Step 4: no change. Result 2\,2\,2\,6\,1: the seed’s hill is kept, and to the left the flood can only pass at the level of the pass, 2.




Q5. A noisy image of nuclei has thousands of regional maxima. How does the h-maxima transform reduce them, and what does h mean in grey levels?






Hint





How deep must you go down from a maximum to reach a higher one?









Answer





\mathrm{HMAX}_h lowers every peak by h and flattens every peak whose dynamic (the descent needed to reach a higher point) is at most h. Noise bumps have dynamics of a few noise standard deviations; a nucleus rises far above the background. With h above the noise bumps but below the nucleus contrast, one regional maximum per nucleus remains. (Touching nuclei separated by a shallow neck may still merge.)




Q6. What does \mathrm{HMIN}_h do to a basin of depth 5 and to one of depth 2, for h = 3?






Hint





Water up to h above the bottom, but never above the spill level.









Answer





The basin of depth 5 is filled by 3: its bottom rises by 3, it remains a regional minimum (2 deep). The basin of depth 2 is filled to its spill level and merges with its neighbour: it is no longer a minimum. This is how the watershed day removes noise basins before flooding.




Q7. Why is reconstruction by iterated geodesic dilation slow on a large image, and what does the fast algorithm do differently?






Hint





How many pixels change in one iteration?









Answer





Each iteration visits every pixel, but only the pixels on the moving front change; a flood across a 200-pixel object needs about 200 iterations, so the cost is (number of pixels) × (number of iterations). The fast algorithm keeps a first-in-first-out queue of front pixels and only processes those; each pixel is handled a small number of times, so the cost is linear in the number of pixels.




Q8. (math) Does R_A(M) depend on the SE used in each geodesic step? Compare the 3 \times 3 square with the 5 \times 5 square (clipping after each step in both cases).






Hint





Characterise the result as the components of A that meet M. Can a step with the 5 \times 5 square cross a one-pixel gap?









Answer





With the 3 \times 3 square the result is the union of the 8-connected components of A that meet M: the marker spreads to every pixel connected to it inside A, and never leaves a component. With the 5 \times 5 square the marker can jump over a one-pixel gap of background, so it can enter a different component of A that is 2 pixels away: the result can be larger. So it does depend on the SE: the SE defines the connectivity. Larger steps give the same result only if the components of A are at least as far apart as the SE reaches.

Background







Idea
What it means




Marker, mask
M \subseteq A (binary) or M \le I (grey)


Geodesic dilation
dilate M by one step (3-window in 1D, 3 \times 3 square in 2D), then clip: \min(M \oplus B, I)


Reconstruction R_I(M)
repeat until nothing changes; binary: the components of A that contain a seed


Geodesic erosion, R^{\varepsilon}_I(M)
for M \ge I: erode one step, then \max(\cdot, I); repeat


Opening by reconstruction
R_A(A \ominus B)


Clear border / fill holes
A \setminus R_A(A \cap \text{frame}) / complement of R_{A^c}(A^c \cap \text{frame}) (background 4-connected)


h-maxima / h-minima transform
\mathrm{HMAX}_h(I) = R_I(I - h) / \mathrm{HMIN}_h(I) = R^{\varepsilon}_I(I + h)


Regional maximum (minimum)
a plateau whose neighbours are all lower (higher)


Minima imposition
R^{\varepsilon}_G(M) with M = 0 on the markers, \max I + 1 elsewhere, and G = \min(I + 1, M)

The basins at samples 1 and 7 were filled up to their spill levels (5 and 7), and the passes between the markers kept their heights.
B5. (a) The flood of the background from the frame reaches every background pixel except row 4, column 4, the hole inside the ring; the last pixels are reached at the 3rd geodesic dilation (row 2, column 2, through the gap between the two objects). Filled result: the ring becomes a solid 3 \times 3 block (one pixel added). (b) The top-left object touches the frame at row 0, columns 0–1 and row 1, column 0; one geodesic dilation reaches its other 3 pixels (row 1, columns 1–2 and row 2, column 1), after which nothing changes. 6 pixels are removed.
