Sum 256 + 24 + 48 + 128 + 96 = 552, and 552/24 = 23. With complement: “rotate, then complement” fixes a case when every cycle alternates above/below, which needs every cycle to have even length; then each cycle has 2 alternating patterns. The identity, the 120° rotations (cycles of length 1 and 3) fix nothing; 90° rotations fix 2^2 = 4 each (24), face 180° fix 2^4 = 16 each (48), edge 180° fix 16 each (96): 168 in total. (552 + 168)/48 = 720/48 = 15.
B9. For a curve \mathbf x(s) in the level set, \frac{d}{ds}I(\mathbf x(s)) = \nabla I \cdot \mathbf x'(s) = 0, so \nabla I is perpendicular to all tangent directions. \nabla I points to increasing I; inside a bright object I > c, so +\nabla I points inwards and -\nabla I outwards. Where \nabla I = 0 the level set need not be a smooth surface (a saddle or a plateau) and the direction is undefined: normalising divides by (nearly) zero, and noise decides the result.
B10. The barycentric weights are the solution of the linear system \mathbf x = \sum\lambda_i\mathbf p_i, \sum\lambda_i = 1, so they are affine functions of \mathbf x, and so is f: f(\mathbf x) = \mathbf a \cdot \mathbf x + b. Its level set \mathbf a \cdot \mathbf x = c - b is a plane (if \mathbf a \ne 0). A plane splits the 4 corners into two groups (1 + 3 or 2 + 2) and cuts the 3 or 4 edges between the groups: a triangle or a quadrilateral, convex as the intersection of two convex sets. The trilinear interpolant on a cube contains the terms xy, yz, xz, xyz: its level sets are curved (hyperbolic on the faces), and can be disconnected inside one cube, so the corner signs do not determine the topology.

title: Exercise: marching cubes
text:
Explore: one cube
One marching-cubes cell, drawn with the corner numbering of the figure above (drag to rotate; front, side, top and 3/4 view buttons). Click a corner to flip it to the other side of c (orange = above) and select it; the first slider sets the selected corner’s value. The readout gives the bits, the case index, the class among the 15 and the 23 and the rotation to the class representative (rotate to its representative animates it). Ambiguous faces are tinted purple; the face rule decides how they are cut. 5 / 6 tetrahedra show the tetrahedral split and its triangles. Neighbour cube adds a second cube on the +x side with its own face rule; cracks are drawn in red.



C1. Preset one corner. Read the case and class. Click corner 1: what are the case and the class now? Click rotate to its representative and describe the rotation.
C2. Preset values: vertices slide. Which corners are above c = 0.5, and what is the case? Check the vertex on edge 0–1 by hand (I_0 = 0.9, I_1 = 0.35) and the one on edge 0–4 (I_4 = 0.45). Move c up to 0.55: which vertex moves furthest along its edge, and why?
C3. Preset the 15 classes: step through all of them. Which classes have 4 triangles? Find the class whose single loop is a hexagon. Which classes have an ambiguous face?
C4. Preset an ambiguous face (case 9). How many triangles do separate and join give? What does decider choose, and why exactly that? Now click corner 0 twice (it flips and flips back, and is selected) and set its value to 0.9: what does the decider do now?
C5. Preset a crack. How many crack edges are there? Set the neighbour’s rule to separate; then set both cubes to decider. When is the surface closed?
C6. Preset tetrahedra instead (case 9 with 6 tetrahedra). How many triangles? Switch to 5 tetrahedra and to marching cubes. Then load one corner and compare the three algorithms again (B4).






Solutions





C1. Case 1, class 1 of 15 and of 23 (already the representative). With corner 1 also above: case 3, class 2 (representative 3 itself, so no rotation). (Other edges need a rotation: with corners 1 and 3 above, case 10, the demo turns the cube by 120° about a body diagonal to reach case 3; a 90° turn about the z axis would do as well, B2.)
C2. Corners 0 (0.9) and 2 (0.6): case 1 + 4 = 5, the edge class (2 of 15), 2 triangles. Edge 0–1: t = (0.5 - 0.9)/(0.35 - 0.9) = 0.727, vertex (0.73, 0, 0). Edge 0–4: t = (0.5 - 0.9)/(0.45 - 0.9) = 0.889, vertex (0, 0, 0.89). At c = 0.55 the case stays 5; a vertex moves by \Delta t = \Delta c/|I_b - I_a|, so the one on the edge with the smallest difference of values moves furthest: edge 2–6 (0.6 → 0.3), from t = 0.33 to 0.17. Edge 0–1 moves only from 0.73 to 0.64.
C3. Classes 9 to 14 have 4 triangles (with the “separate” rule). Class 9 (case 23: corner 0 and its three neighbours 1, 2, 4) has a single hexagonal loop. Classes 3, 6, 7, 12, 13, 14 (representatives 6, 22, 25, 30, 60, 105) have at least one ambiguous face: 6 of the 15.
C4. Separate: 2 triangles (two corner pieces). Join: 4 triangles (one band across the cube). The decider computes f^\ast = (0.8 \cdot 0.8 - 0.2 \cdot 0.2)/(0.8 + 0.8 - 0.2 - 0.2) = 0.5 = c, the borderline, and does not join (it joins only for f^\ast > c): 2 triangles. With I_0 = 0.9: f^\ast = (0.72 - 0.04)/1.3 = 0.523 > 0.5: it joins, 4 triangles.
C5. 4 crack edges (red). With the neighbour on “separate” (the same as the left cube) the crack closes: 0. With both on “decider” it closes too. The surface is closed whenever both cubes cut the shared face the same way, which a rule that depends only on the face’s own values guarantees.
C6. Case 9 with 6 tetrahedra: 8 triangles; with 5 tetrahedra: 2; with marching cubes (“separate”): 2. For one corner (case 1): marching cubes 1, 5 tetrahedra 1 (corner 0 is cut off by one corner tetrahedron), 6 tetrahedra 6. The count depends on how the corners sit relative to the split.

title: Exercise: marching cubes
section: Explore: marching cubes on a volume
text:
Explore: marching cubes on a volume
Marching cubes on a whole volume (48³ voxels, or the nuclei stack), recomputed on every change; drag to rotate. Choose the volume, c (slider or histogram), blur \sigma (voxels) and noise; face normals shade each triangle flat, gradient normals use -\nabla I; ignore the z spacing treats the voxels as cubes; cubes / 6 / 5 tetrahedra switch the algorithm; the face rule (decider, separate, complement as in the 15-case table) applies to cubes. Red lines are boundary edges (cracks). Show an xy slice adds a slice with its marching-squares contour at the same c. The readout gives vertices, triangles, area, volume, components and the Euler characteristic \chi = V - E + F (2 for each closed surface without holes, 0 for a torus; more in the next unit).



M1. Preset two blobs merge (c = 0.6). How many components? Lower c in steps of 0.01. At which c do the two surfaces become one? What happens to \chi? (The blobs are two Gaussians with value 1 at their centres, 20 voxels apart, \sigma = 6: what is the value halfway between them?)
M2. Preset a torus has a hole. Read \chi and the number of components. Compare the area and volume with the true torus (tube radius 5.5, centre-line radius 13: area 4\pi^2 R r, volume 2\pi^2 R r^2). Switch to 6 tetrahedra: how many triangles, and how does the area change?
M3. Preset noise: many tiny surfaces. How many components and triangles? Compare the area with the noise-free sphere (switch noise to 0). Then preset blur first: what happens to components, area and volume? Why is the blurred volume smaller than the true \frac43\pi \cdot 15^3?
M4. Preset faceted vs gradient normals. With wireframe on, switch between face and gradient normals. Are the triangles different? Explain what the gradient normals add.
M5. Preset wrong z spacing (an ellipsoid sampled with \Delta z = 2.5 voxels). Compare area and volume with “ignore the z spacing” on and off. By what factor does the volume change, and why exactly that factor?
M6. Preset cracks from inconsistent faces. How many cracks are there with the complement rule? Switch to decider and to separate. Then try 6 tetrahedra.
M7. Preset a slice is a contour (torus). How many contours does the slice show, and how do they relate to the surface? Move the slice to the top of the torus and above it.
M8. Preset nuclei stack (the volume of volumes3d/, values scaled so that background ≈ 0.05 and nuclei ≈ 1). How many components are there, and what is the total volume in µm³? (The true volumes of the four ellipsoids add up to 79.2 µm³.) Lower c to 0.3: what happens to the volume?






Solutions





M1. 2 components (\chi = 4: two sphere-like surfaces). At c = 0.50 still 2, at c = 0.49 one component with \chi = 2. Halfway between the centres each Gaussian has the value e^{-10^2/(2 \cdot 36)} = 0.249, together 0.499: the saddle value, where the two surfaces touch.
M2. \chi = 0, 1 component: a closed surface with one hole. Area 2816.0 and volume 7698.4 (voxel units) against the true 4\pi^2 \cdot 13 \cdot 5.5 = 2822.7 and 2\pi^2 \cdot 13 \cdot 5.5^2 = 7762.4: −0.2 % and −0.8 % (the tube’s edge is a smooth ramp, which shifts the half-way level slightly). With 6 tetrahedra: 24 216 triangles instead of 7680 (3.2 times), area 2828.8, still \chi = 0.
M3. Noise: 4324 components and 56 054 triangles; the area is 7351.7 against 2824.6 without noise (the true sphere: 2827.4): the many tiny surfaces and the roughness add area. Blur first (\sigma = 1.5): 1 component, area 2772.3, volume 13 670.9 against \frac43\pi \cdot 15^3 = 14\,137.2. Blurring a convex object moves its half-way level inwards (a curved edge loses more brightness to the outside than it gains), so the surface shrinks; the effect grows with \sigma and with the curvature.
M4. The triangles are identical; only the normals used for shading differ. Face normals are constant per triangle (facets visible); gradient normals vary smoothly from vertex to vertex because they come from the image, so the same coarse mesh looks like a smooth sphere.
M5. With the correct spacing: area 1976.7, volume 7608.9 (true \frac43\pi \cdot 17 \cdot 9 \cdot 12 = 7690.6). Ignoring it: area 1184.6, volume 3043.6. The volume changes by exactly 1/2.5 = 0.4: every vertex’s z is scaled by 1/2.5, and volume scales with the product of the three scale factors. The area changes by a factor between 0.4 and 1 (here 0.60), depending on how the surface is oriented.
M6. Complement rule: 296 crack edges (red), and many more components and a jumpy \chi. Decider and separate: 0 cracks. 6 tetrahedra: 0 cracks, but about 3 times the triangles.
M7. Two closed contours, the outer and the inner circle of the torus’ cross-section in that plane: the slice of an isosurface is an isocontour, and the yellow curve lies on the surface. Moving up, the two circles approach each other (the ring-shaped cross-section gets thinner) and vanish together at the top of the tube; above the torus, none.
M8. 4 components (A, B, C, D), volume 77.8 µm³ (area 146.6 µm²), against 79.2 µm³ for the ideal ellipsoids. At c = 0.3: 95.9 µm³, larger, because the surfaces move out into the blurred edges. Which c is “right” is the subject of the next unit.

title: Exercise: marching cubes
text:
Where this leads
The mesh is a measurement instrument: the next unit computes areas and volumes from it, compares them with counting voxels, and looks at the choice of c, smoothing, anisotropic voxels and mesh size. Rendering the mesh (projection, rasterisation, Lambert and Phong shading) is the 3D-graphics day.

title: Least-squares unmixing
text:
About this lecture
Last unit: two dyes, two channels, compensation with M^{-1}. A spectral detector records 8–32 channels per pixel, a lambda stack: more equations than unknowns, and with noise they never all hold.

Take the mixture closest to the measured spectrum: least squares, a projection.
One pseudo-inverse for the whole image.
The residual shows where the model is wrong (a missing component).
Conditioning: how much similar spectra amplify noise.
Photon noise and weighted least squares.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Second unit of the spectral unmixing day. Linear algebra needed: least squares and the normal equations, which the students know from linear algebra; here they get a physical meaning. The noise model (Poisson, variance = mean) is recalled from the camera-noise unit (day 3).

title: Least-squares unmixing
section: A lambda stack: every pixel is a spectrum
text:
A lambda stack: every pixel is a spectrum

A spectral microscope records one image per wavelength band (here 16 bands of about 14 nm between 480 and 700 nm). Each pixel is a short measured spectrum.
The cell has four components: nucleus, mitochondria, membrane, and a diffuse autofluorescence with a broad spectrum.
Job: explain each pixel’s spectrum as a sum of the four reference spectra, \mathbf y \approx M\mathbf a, with M now 16 × 4.
The same problem everywhere: multiplexed immunofluorescence, hyperspectral remote sensing (a field pixel = soil + crop + water), Raman and hyperspectral histology.

title: Least-squares unmixing
section: More equations than unknowns: take the closest mixture
text:
More equations than unknowns: take the closest mixture


Three channels, two dyes. All the pixels the model can explain, M\mathbf a for any \mathbf a, form a plane through the origin, spanned by the two columns.

A noisy pixel lies a little off the plane: no \mathbf a fits exactly.
Least squares picks the point of the plane closest to the pixel: drop a perpendicular.
The perpendicular part is the residual: what the model cannot explain.
With as many channels as dyes the plane is the whole space and least squares is M^{-1}: last unit was a special case.

title: Least-squares unmixing
text:
A 3 \times 2 example by hand
M = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.2 \\ 0.5 & 0.5 \\ 0.1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, a pixel \mathbf y = (1.3,\ 0.9,\ 1.2).
M^\top M = \begin{pmatrix} 1.26 & 0.55 \\ 0.55 & 1.29 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad M^\top \mathbf y = \begin{pmatrix} 1.87 \\ 1.91 \end{pmatrix}.

Solve the 2 \times 2 system: \hat{\mathbf a} = (1.029,\ 1.042). (The pixel was made from (1, 1) plus noise.)
Fit M\hat{\mathbf a} = (1.238,\ 1.036,\ 1.145), residual \mathbf r = (0.062,\ -0.136,\ 0.055).
Check: M^\top\mathbf r = (0, 0): the residual is perpendicular to both columns.

title: Least-squares unmixing
text:
The math: the normal equations
Minimise E(\mathbf a) = \|\mathbf y - M\mathbf a\|^2 = (\mathbf y - M\mathbf a)^\top(\mathbf y - M\mathbf a):
\nabla E = -2M^\top(\mathbf y - M\mathbf a) = \mathbf 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad M^\top M\,\hat{\mathbf a} = M^\top\mathbf y .

Same thing geometrically: the residual is orthogonal to every column, M^\top \mathbf r = \mathbf 0.
If the columns are independent, M^\top M is invertible: \hat{\mathbf a} = M^+\mathbf y with the pseudo-inverse M^+ = (M^\top M)^{-1}M^\top (K \times N).
M^+M = I; for square M, M^+ = M^{-1}.

title: Least-squares unmixing
section: One matrix for the whole image
text:
One matrix for the whole image

M^+ depends only on the reference spectra: compute it once (K \times N, here 4 × 16).
Unmixing the image is one matrix product: \hat A = M^+ Y (abundances × pixels = (K \times N)(N \times \text{pixels})).
Each abundance map is a weighted sum of the channels, with weights from one row of M^+ (some negative).
The fitted image M\hat A and the residual Y - M\hat A come for free.

title: Least-squares unmixing
section: The math: least squares is a projection
text:
The math: least squares is a projection
P = MM^+ = M(M^\top M)^{-1}M^\top maps a pixel to its fit.

P^2 = M(M^\top M)^{-1}(M^\top M)(M^\top M)^{-1}M^\top = P and P^\top = P: an orthogonal projection onto the column space.
The residual (I - P)\mathbf y is the projection onto the orthogonal complement: N - K dimensions the dyes cannot reach.
With the SVD M = U\Sigma V^\top (thin): M^+ = V\Sigma^{-1}U^\top. A small singular value \sigma_i becomes a large 1/\sigma_i.

title: Least-squares unmixing
section: Try it: unmix a lambda stack
text:
Try it: unmix a lambda stack




Synthetic cell, four components, 16 channels, 400 photons for a pixel of abundance 1 (all channels together), Poisson noise. Top: true merge, unmixed merge, residual in units of the expected noise. Bottom: the four abundance maps (red = negative). Right: the spectra and the 16 bins; below, the clicked pixel: dots = measured, black = fit, coloured bands = each component’s share. Tour: “one channel per dye”: each map is the dye’s brightest channel; the autofluorescence map shows the whole cell (RMSE 0.30) and the mitochondria map contains some of the nucleus. “Least squares removes it”: RMSE 0.017–0.06, the maps are clean. Click the nucleus and a mitochondrion and show the stacked contributions. “Two dyes 6 nm apart”: nucleus and mitochondria maps become grainy (noise × 4.9 and 5.1). “32 channels”: hardly better. “Forgot the autofluorescence”: residual lights up in the cytoplasm. “Add it as a component”. “Photon-starved”.

title: Least-squares unmixing
section: The residual: where the model is wrong
text:
The residual: where the model is wrong
The residual map shows, for each pixel, how far its spectrum is from the best mixture, in units of the expected photon noise. About 1 everywhere means “noise only”.

Leave the autofluorescence out of M: the cytoplasm’s residual rises to 1.37 times the noise (the nucleus stays at 1.04). The broad spectrum cannot be made from the three narrow ones.
And the missing light goes somewhere: the other maps absorb it (mitochondria RMSE 0.023 → 0.054).
Add the spectrum as an extra column and the residual drops back to noise (0.99).
An offset (dark level) is a component with a flat spectrum: subtract it, or give it a column.

title: Least-squares unmixing
text:
Similar spectra amplify noise
Two near-parallel columns (1, 0.9, 0.5) and (0.9, 1, 0.5):

Their sum is well determined, their difference is not: the data barely change when you trade one dye for the other.
A unit error in channel 1 moves the abundances by (5.2,\ -4.8). For well-separated columns (1, 0.1, 0.5) and (0.1, 1, 0.5): by (0.88,\ -0.23).
Picture: the cloud of possible estimates is an ellipse, long along “dye 1 minus dye 2”.
Condition number \kappa = \sigma_\text{max}/\sigma_\text{min}, the ratio of the largest and smallest stretch of M: 20.3 for the near-parallel pair, 1.45 for the separated one.

title: Least-squares unmixing
section: The math: noise of the estimate
text:
The math: noise of the estimate
With independent channel noise of variance \sigma_n^2, \operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf y) = \sigma_n^2 I and \hat{\mathbf a} = M^+\mathbf y:
\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf a}) = M^+(\sigma_n^2 I)M^{+\top} = \sigma_n^2 (M^\top M)^{-1}.

Near-parallel pair: M^\top M = \begin{pmatrix} 2.06 & 2.05 \\ 2.05 & 2.06 \end{pmatrix}, eigenvalues 4.11 and 0.01 (eigenvectors (1, 1) and (1, -1)).
\operatorname{sd}(\hat a_1 + \hat a_2) = 0.70\,\sigma_n, \operatorname{sd}(\hat a_1 - \hat a_2) = 14.1\,\sigma_n: the small eigenvalue sits in the difference direction.
Singular values of M are the square roots: \sigma_1 = 2.03, \sigma_2 = 0.10, \kappa = 20.3. The noise of the worst combination is 1/\sigma_\text{min} times the channel noise.

title: Least-squares unmixing
text:
More channels, better filters
In the demo, with nucleus and mitochondria 6 nm apart (same photons in total), the noise on those two maps is multiplied by:



channels
8
16
32




noise × (vs the dye alone)
5.7, 5.9
4.9, 5.1
4.7, 4.9




Finer bins help a little: the shapes are sampled better. They add no photons and cannot separate identical shapes.
What helps: dyes further apart (45 nm: 1.3 and 1.7), more photons, filters placed where the spectra differ (choose them to minimise \kappa, or the noise on the abundance you care about).

title: Least-squares unmixing
text:
Photon noise: weighted least squares
Recall the camera-noise unit (day 3): photon counts are Poisson, variance = mean. A bright channel is noisier in absolute terms than a dim one.

Ordinary least squares trusts every channel equally. Weighted least squares divides each squared error by the channel’s expected variance: weight w_c = 1/\text{expected count}.
Bright pixels (hundreds of counts): little difference. Photon-starved pixels (a few counts per channel): WLS helps. In the demo at 20 photons the RMSE drops by 6–10 % (e.g. mitochondria 0.105 → 0.095).
Maximum likelihood with the exact Poisson model does better still (pointer: the same idea as Richardson–Lucy on the deconvolution day).

title: Least-squares unmixing
section: The math: WLS is maximum likelihood
text:
The math: WLS is maximum likelihood
Approximate channel c as Gaussian with variance v_c (Poisson: v_c \approx the expected count). The log-likelihood of \mathbf a is, up to constants,
-\tfrac12 \sum_c \frac{(y_c - (M\mathbf a)_c)^2}{v_c} = -\tfrac12 (\mathbf y - M\mathbf a)^\top W (\mathbf y - M\mathbf a), \quad W = \operatorname{diag}(1/v_c).
Setting the gradient to zero: M^\top W M\,\hat{\mathbf a} = M^\top W\mathbf y, so \hat{\mathbf a} = (M^\top WM)^{-1}M^\top W\mathbf y. The expected counts come from a first ordinary fit (the demo does one such iteration).

title: Least-squares unmixing
text:
Negative abundances in dim pixels

Least squares does not know that abundances cannot be negative. In dim pixels the noise is as large as the signal and many estimates go below zero: 18 % of all abundance values in the demo.
A negative abundance is not a measurement error to ignore: it says the pixel lies outside the set of physically possible mixtures.
The next unit adds the constraints (non-negative, sum to one) and their geometry: cones and simplices.
Afterwards, an abundance map is an ordinary image: threshold it (day 6) to find the positive cells, measure it, or compare it between conditions.

title: Least-squares unmixing
text:
Summary

A lambda stack: each pixel is a spectrum; \mathbf y \approx M\mathbf a with more channels than components.
Least squares = the closest mixture = an orthogonal projection onto the column space; \hat{\mathbf a} = M^+\mathbf y, one M^+ for the whole image; square case = M^{-1}.
The residual is perpendicular to every spectrum; a residual above the noise shows a missing component (autofluorescence, an offset).
Similar spectra: a small singular value, a large condition number \kappa, noise amplified in the difference of the abundances. More channels help a little; more photons and better-separated dyes help more.
Poisson noise: weighted least squares, weights 1/expected count.
Unconstrained least squares gives negative abundances in dim pixels.

title: Quiz: prediction, dictionaries and lossless formats
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Neighbours: a left, b up, c up-left; residual e = x - \hat x.

Q1. Why can the decoder of a predictive coder rebuild the image exactly, although it never sees the predictions \hat x?






Hint





From what is \hat x computed?









Answer





\hat x is computed only from pixels that are already decoded (left, up, up-left). The decoder has those same pixels, so it computes the same \hat x and adds the stored residual: x = \hat x + e. Nothing is rounded or thrown away.




Q2. The pixel histogram of an image is wide, the histogram of its residuals is narrow and centred at 0. Which one has the lower entropy, and what does that mean for the file size?






Hint





Fewer likely values means less information per value.









Answer





The narrow residual histogram: most residuals are a few small values, so each carries few bits. An entropy coder spends about H bits per pixel, so coding the residuals instead of the pixels makes the file smaller (in the demo’s smooth image 3.3 instead of 7.1 bits per pixel).




Q3. Where in an image are the residuals of a good predictor large?






Hint





Where do neighbours fail to predict a pixel?









Answer





At edges and fine texture (the neighbour lies on the other side of a change), and everywhere there is noise. The residual image looks like an edge map: the left-neighbour residual is a finite-difference derivative.




Q4. You add noise to an image. Does lossless compression get better or worse? Can it get worse than storing the noisy pixels without prediction?






Hint





Can a neighbour predict the noise at this pixel?









Answer





Worse: noise is new, unpredictable information at every pixel, so the residual is at least as wide as the noise. On pure noise (a flat image plus noise), prediction even makes it worse: the residual of the left predictor contains the noise of two pixels, twice the variance, about 0.5 bit more per pixel.




Q5. A vertical edge runs between c, a (left, dark) and b, x (right, bright). Which of the predictors left, up, average and MED gets x right?






Hint





Which neighbour lies on the same side of the edge as x?









Answer





b (up) is on the same side as x. Up predicts b: right. Left predicts a: wrong. Average predicts halfway: wrong. MED: c (dark) \le \min(a, b), so it predicts \max(a, b) = b: right. MED detects which side of the edge the pixel is on.




Q6. Why does PNG apply a prediction filter before DEFLATE, instead of DEFLATE alone?






Hint





What does LZ77 need to find?









Answer





LZ77 replaces exact repeats by pointers, and noisy grey values rarely repeat exactly. After prediction, smooth regions become runs of small residuals (many 0, ±1, ±2), which repeat far more often and have a narrower histogram for the Huffman stage of DEFLATE.




Q7. A 16-bit microscope image compresses losslessly by a factor of 2.3. Its owner hopes for 10. Is that realistic? What limits it?






Hint





What is the information that no lossless method can remove?









Answer





No: lossless ratios for noisy scientific images are typically 1.5–3. The camera noise is new information in every pixel; a lossless code must keep it exactly. Only removing information (lossy compression, or binning) gets to 10, and then the measurements may change (last unit of the day).




Q8. (math) The residual of a predictor has an approximately Gaussian histogram with standard deviation 4 grey levels. Estimate its entropy. How many bits do you save by halving the standard deviation?






Hint





For a Gaussian with standard deviation \sigma on integers: H \approx \log_2(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi e}).









Answer





H \approx \log_2 4 + \log_2\sqrt{2\pi e} = 2 + 2.05 = 4.05 bits. Halving \sigma subtracts \log_2 2 = 1 bit per pixel.

title: Exercise: prediction, dictionaries and lossless formats
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Neighbours
a = left, b = up, c = up-left of the pixel x; all already decoded


Residual
e = x - \hat x; the decoder computes the same \hat x and adds e back


Left, up, average
\hat x = a, b, \lfloor (a+b)/2 \rfloor


Planar
\hat x = a + b - c (exact on a plane)


Paeth (PNG)
of a, b, c the one closest to a + b - c (ties: a, then b)


MED (JPEG-LS)
\min(a,b) if c \ge \max(a,b); \max(a,b) if c \le \min(a,b); else a + b - c


Cost
about H(e) bits per pixel; a spread \sigma costs about \log_2 \sigma + 2.05 bits


LZ77
a repeat becomes (go back d, copy \ell); DEFLATE = LZ77 + Huffman

title: Exercise: prediction, dictionaries and lossless formats
text:
By hand
B1. The row 100 102 104 103 105 107 106 108, predictor: left neighbour, the first value stored as it is. (a) Write the residuals. (b) Compute the entropy of the 8 pixel values and of the 7 residuals after the first. (c) Decode the residuals 50, 1, 1, 0, −2, −2, 1 (first value stored as it is).
B2. Predict x with Paeth and with MED for these neighbours (a, b, c): (a) (100, 120, 110), (b) (50, 60, 100), (c) (10, 30, 12).
B3. A vertical edge: the pixels left of column 5 are 40, from column 5 on they are 100. For a pixel in column 5 (not in the top row), give a, b, c and the predictions of left, up, average, planar and MED. Which predictors are exact? Repeat for a horizontal edge (rows above row 5 are 40, from row 5 on 100, a pixel in row 5).
B4. A flat region of grey level 128 with independent noise of standard deviation \sigma = 10. (a) What standard deviation does the residual of the left predictor have? Of the average predictor? (b) Using “a spread \sigma costs about \log_2 \sigma + 2.05 bits”, estimate the bits per pixel of the pixels themselves and of the two residuals. Does prediction help?
B5. A 12-bit camera image stored in 16-bit words has a residual entropy of 7.2 bits per pixel. What is the best lossless compression ratio you can expect from a coder that reaches the entropy? How large is a 2048 × 2048 frame raw and compressed?
B6. LZ77: encode ABABABABAB as literals and (go back, length) pairs. Then explain why the noisy row 101 99 100 102 98 101 100 99 has almost no repeats, but its residuals might.






Solutions





B1. (a) (100), 2, 2, −1, 2, 2, −1, 2. (b) 8 different values, each once: \log_2 8 = 3 bits. Residuals: 2 five times, −1 twice: H = -\tfrac57\log_2\tfrac57 - \tfrac27\log_2\tfrac27 = 0.347 + 0.516 = 0.86 bits. (c) 50, 51, 52, 52, 50, 48, 49.
B2. (a) a + b - c = 110; distances to a, b, c: 10, 10, 0: Paeth takes c = 110. MED: c lies between 100 and 120, so a + b - c = 110. (b) a + b - c = 10; distances 40, 50, 90: Paeth a = 50. MED: c = 100 \ge \max = 60, so \min(a, b) = 50. (c) a + b - c = 28; distances 18, 2, 16: Paeth b = 30. MED: 12 is between 10 and 30: 28.
B3. Vertical edge, pixel in column 5: a = 40 (left of the edge), b = 100 (above, same column), c = 40; x = 100. Left 40, up 100, average 70, planar 40 + 100 - 40 = 100, MED: c = 40 \le \min(a, b), so \max(a,b) = 100. Up, planar and MED are exact. Horizontal edge, pixel in row 5: a = 100, b = 40, c = 40: left 100, up 40, average 70, planar 100, MED 100: left, planar and MED are exact. MED (and planar) find the right side of the edge in both cases; left and up only in one each; average never.
B4. (a) Left: e = n_i - n_{i-1}, variance 2\sigma^2, sd \sqrt2 \cdot 10 = 14.1. Average: e = n_x - (n_a + n_b)/2, variance \sigma^2 + \sigma^2/2, sd 12.2 (ignoring the rounding). (b) Pixels: \log_2 10 + 2.05 = 5.37 bits; left residual: \log_2 14.1 + 2.05 = 5.87; average: \log_2 12.2 + 2.05 = 5.66. Prediction makes it worse: pure noise cannot be predicted, and every predictor adds the noise of its neighbours.
B5. Ratio 16/7.2 = 2.2. Raw: 2048^2 \cdot 2 bytes = 8.4 MB; compressed about 2048^2 \cdot 7.2/8 = 3.8 MB. (Four of the 16 stored bits are always zero; most of the gain comes from them.)
B6. A, B, then (go back 2, copy 8): the copy may overlap what it is writing, so one pair produces the whole repetition. The noisy row has no exact repeat of length ≥ 2 that pays for a pointer. Its left residuals are −2, 1, 2, −4, 3, −1, −1: still small and irregular, but they come from a narrow range, so their Huffman code is short; in smooth or flat images residuals also repeat more often than pixel values (many 0s and ±1s), which LZ77 can use.




Math questions
B7. (math) Show that the decoder reconstructs every pixel exactly, by induction over the raster order, for any predictor that uses only pixels before x in raster order.
B8. (math) Show that the planar predictor a + b - c is exact for every image x(i, j) = \alpha + \beta i + \gamma j, and that MED is the median of a, b and a + b - c.
B9. (math) A smooth signal s plus independent noise n of variance \sigma^2: x = s + n. Show that no predictor \hat x that depends only on earlier pixels can make the residual variance smaller than \sigma^2. What is the residual variance of the left predictor if s is constant?






Solutions (math)





B7. The first pixel is predicted from nothing (a constant), so x_1 = \hat x_1 + e_1 is known. Suppose all pixels before x_k in raster order are decoded exactly. The encoder computed \hat x_k from those same pixels, so the decoder computes the same \hat x_k, and x_k = \hat x_k + e_k exactly (integer arithmetic, no rounding differences). Hence all pixels are exact.
B8. a = x(i, j-1), b = x(i-1, j), c = x(i-1, j-1): a + b - c = \alpha + \beta i + \gamma(j-1) + \alpha + \beta(i-1) + \gamma j - \alpha - \beta(i-1) - \gamma(j-1) = \alpha + \beta i + \gamma j. MED: if c \ge \max(a,b) then a + b - c \le \min(a,b), so the median of \{a, b, a+b-c\} is \min(a,b); if c \le \min(a,b) then a + b - c \ge \max(a,b) and the median is \max(a,b); otherwise a + b - c lies between a and b and is the median.
B9. e = s + n - \hat x, where \hat x depends only on earlier pixels, hence on s and earlier noise values, all independent of n at this pixel. So \operatorname{Var}(e) = \operatorname{Var}(s - \hat x) + \sigma^2 \ge \sigma^2 (taking s as given, its variance is that of -\hat x; the cross term vanishes because n is independent with mean 0). For constant s and the left predictor: e = n_i - n_{i-1}, variance 2\sigma^2.

title: Exercise: prediction, dictionaries and lossless formats
text:
Explore: prediction
The demo shows an image x, the residual e = x - \hat x of a predictor (white = 0, red positive, blue negative), a scatter of each pixel against its left neighbour, and the histograms of pixels (blue) and residuals (orange) on one axis. The readout gives the entropy of pixels and residuals, the ideal size H \cdot N / 8 bytes, and the real DEFLATE size of the raw pixel bytes and of the residual bytes, made by the browser’s own compressor. added noise sd adds Gaussian noise (fixed seed). Click a pixel to see its neighbours a, b, c, the prediction and the residual.



P1. Preset smooth image (left predictor). Note the entropies, the ideal sizes and the DEFLATE sizes. DEFLATE stores the pixels in fewer bytes than their ideal size H \cdot N/8. How can it beat the entropy?
P2. Still on the smooth image, try all seven predictors. Which one gives the smallest residual entropy, which the largest (apart from none)? Explain with B4: what dominates the residual of a smooth image with a little noise?
P3. Preset left neighbour on the cell. Compare pixel and residual entropy, and find the best predictor. What lossless compression ratio does the best DEFLATE size give? Look at the residual image: why is so little gained?
P4. Preset smooth image again, then raise the noise to 5, 10 and 20. Note the residual entropy (left) and the pixel entropy each time. What happens to the gain from prediction?
P5. Choose flat field and set the noise to 10. Compare pixel and residual entropy for the left and the average predictor, and check your estimate of B4.
P6. Preset MED at an edge (shapes, MED predictor). Click the pixel at (121, 190), just right of the dark rectangle’s right edge, and note the prediction. Switch to average: what is predicted now? Which predictor wins overall on this image, and why is that not MED?
P7. Preset binary mask. How large is the DEFLATE file of the raw mask, and why is it so small? Compare the residual DEFLATE sizes of left and up.
P8. Preset 12-bit spots (MED). Compare the ideal residual size with the DEFLATE residual size. Why does DEFLATE do so much worse here than on the 8-bit images?






Solutions





P1. Pixels: H = 7.08, ideal 58 014 B, DEFLATE 44 457 B. Residuals: H = 3.28, ideal 26 909 B, DEFLATE 31 212 B. DEFLATE beats the histogram entropy of the pixels because the entropy treats pixels as independent, while LZ77 finds repeated byte strings (neighbouring rows of a smooth image repeat). The entropy is a bound only for independent symbols. On the residuals, which have little exact repetition left, DEFLATE’s byte-wise Huffman is above the ideal size.
P2. none 7.08, left 3.28, up 3.41, average 3.11 (best), planar 3.66 (worst), Paeth 3.33, MED 3.28. The image is smooth, so the residual is mostly the noise (sd 1.5) of the pixels involved. Average subtracts half the noise of two neighbours (variance 1.5\sigma^2), left the noise of one (2\sigma^2), planar the noise of three (4\sigma^2): the more neighbours a predictor adds or subtracts at full weight, the more noise it adds.
P3. Pixels 7.68 bits, left 6.78, best average 6.45 (MED 6.55). DEFLATE: 61 552 B raw, 54 034 B for the average residuals: a ratio of 65\,536/54\,034 = 1.21. The residual image is full of fine grain: the electron micrograph has texture and noise at the pixel scale that no neighbour predicts.
P4. Residual entropy (left) for noise 0, 5, 10, 20: 3.28, 4.95, 5.89, 6.87 bits; pixel entropy 7.08, 7.13, 7.21, 7.37. The gain from prediction shrinks from 3.8 bits to 0.5 bits: the noise is new information in every pixel and sets the floor.
P5. Pixels 5.37 bits, left 5.87, average 5.66: both residuals are worse than the pixels, by about 0.5 and 0.3 bits, as estimated in B4 (5.37, 5.87, 5.66).
P6. At (121, 190): a = 69 (the half-covered edge pixel), b = 100, c = 68, x = 102. MED: c \le \min(a, b), so it predicts \max(a,b) = 100, residual 2. Average predicts 84, residual 18. Along the rectangle’s vertical edges the mean |residual| is 1.9 for MED against 12.3 for average. Overall the average predictor still wins on this image (3.27 bits against 3.36 for MED): edges are a small part of the image, and in the flat regions, which dominate, averaging two neighbours reduces the noise.
P7. The raw mask DEFLATEs to 791 bytes (from 65 536, 83 times smaller): long runs of exactly equal bytes are what LZ77 is made for. Left residuals: 833 B, up residuals: 659 B: both are zero except at the shape outlines, and all three sizes are tiny. For a mask the dictionary coder alone already does the job; prediction adds little.
P8. Ideal residual size 59 728 B, DEFLATE 79 341 B (raw 131 072 B, DEFLATE of the raw pixels 82 742 B). DEFLATE codes bytes: each 16-bit residual is split into a low byte (noisy) and a high byte (0 or 255 depending on the sign), and the Huffman stage of DEFLATE cannot see that the two belong together. Lossless formats for 16-bit data therefore predict on the values themselves and code the residuals with their own entropy coder, or regroup the bytes before DEFLATE (the “shuffle” filters of chunked array formats, last unit).

title: Exercise: prediction, dictionaries and lossless formats
text:
Where this leads
Prediction removes the inter-pixel redundancy one pixel at a time, and it is exact. The next unit takes a different route: a change of basis (the DCT) that packs the image into a few large coefficients, which can then be quantised. That step is lossy, and it is how JPEG reaches 10 to 20 times smaller files. JPEG reuses the prediction idea once: the DC coefficient of each block is coded as the difference from the previous block.

title: When one threshold is not enough
text:
About this lecture
The last two units chose one threshold for the whole image from its histogram. That fails as soon as the image is not two clean classes.

When a global threshold cannot work: uneven illumination, few small objects, faint objects, noise.
Remedy 1: correct the background, then threshold globally.
Remedy 2: local thresholds T(x) from a window: mean − C, Niblack, Sauvola; the window size.
Remedy 3: hysteresis: two thresholds, and connectivity to sure seeds.
When noise is the problem: let neighbours agree (graph cuts, MRFs).

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Convention in this unit: the synthetic test image is bright-field-like, dark objects on a bright background, because the local methods are published in that form (text on paper). Object where I < T. For bright objects, apply everything to the inverted image. Recalls: box and Gaussian filters (kernels, day 1); hysteresis inside Canny (edges day, day 2); connected components (labelling day, day 9).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: When one threshold is not enough
text:
When a global threshold fails

Left: dark discs, lit by a light that is dim on the left and bright on the right (plus a darker rim, vignetting). Middle: the best global threshold (Otsu); object in black. Right: a local threshold (Sauvola).

Uneven illumination: the background on the left (about 79) is darker than the objects on the right (about 90). No single t can be above every object and below every background pixel.
Unimodal histogram: a few small objects make no peak of their own.
Small or faint objects: blur mixes them with the background (partial volume).
Noise: single pixels cross any threshold; no rule on single pixels fixes that.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: When one threshold is not enough
section: The threshold must follow the background
text:
The threshold must follow the background

One row of the image (grey), the global threshold (red, dashed) and a local threshold T(x) (orange).

The background level changes along the row; the objects are dips relative to it.
A global threshold is below the background on the right but above it on the left: it calls the whole left side object.
A threshold that follows the local background separates every dip from its own surroundings.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: When one threshold is not enough
text:
Remedy 1: correct the background
Estimate the smooth background B(x), remove it, then threshold the corrected image globally.

B(x): a heavily blurred copy of the image (blur much larger than the objects), or a plane or quadratic surface fitted by least squares to the background pixels.
Illumination multiplies the image: divide, I(x)/B(x). An additive offset (glow, stray light): subtract, I(x) - B(x).
In the test image: objects are about 0.5 \times their background on both sides (39/79, 90/202). After dividing, one threshold (e.g. 0.75) works everywhere.
The top-hat of the morphology day (day 8) estimates the background without being pulled by the objects. A flat-field image (the same optics without a sample) measures the illumination directly.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: When one threshold is not enough
text:
The math: dividing or subtracting
Model: I(x) = L(x)\,R(x) + O(x) + n(x), with illumination L, the true reflectance or stain R, an additive offset O and noise n.

Multiplicative illumination (O = 0): I/L = R + n/L. Dividing makes the object contrast the same everywhere, but amplifies the noise where L is small (dark corners).
Additive offset (L constant): I - O = LR + n.
A fitted plane B(x, y) = a + bx + cy: least squares over background pixels, \min_{a,b,c} \sum_j (I_j - a - bx_j - cy_j)^2, solved by the normal equations A^\top A\,\boldsymbol\beta = A^\top \mathbf I with rows (1, x_j, y_j).
A blur as estimate: B = G_s * I contains the objects too; with dark objects covering a fraction f of the window, B is pulled down by about f times the object contrast.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: When one threshold is not enough
section: Remedy 2: a threshold for every pixel
text:
Remedy 2: a threshold for every pixel
Compute the threshold from a window W around each pixel: T(x) depends on what is near x.

mean − C: T(x) = m_W(x) - C, the local mean minus a margin. A pixel is object if it is clearly darker than its surroundings.
The local mean m_W is a box filter (the filtering unit, day 1): a moving average over the window.
In flat background m_W \approx the background, so T follows the illumination by construction.
The margin C must exceed the noise (or background speckle becomes object) and be smaller than the object contrast everywhere, including the dim side.

By hand: profile 100, 110, 80, 130, 140, 150, 160, 130, 180, 190 on a rising background, window 3, C = 10: object at positions 3 and 8 only. A global t = 125 takes positions 1–3 instead.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: When one threshold is not enough
section: Niblack and Sauvola: adapt to the contrast
text:
Niblack and Sauvola: adapt to the contrast
Use the local standard deviation s_W too: it is small in flat regions and large where there is an edge.

Niblack (1986): T = m + k\,s with k \approx -0.2. Near an object, T drops a little below the mean. In empty background, s is just the noise, and T is barely below the mean: 42 % of the background pixels fall below it. Speckle everywhere.
Sauvola (2000): T = m\,\big(1 + k(s/R - 1)\big), R = 128, k \approx 0.2–0.5. In flat regions (s \ll R), T \approx m(1 - k): well below the mean, so background stays background. Near objects s is large and T rises towards m.
Both scale with the window statistics; Sauvola’s T \propto m also scales with multiplicative illumination.

(Published for dark text on white paper. For bright objects, apply them to the inverted image.)
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: When one threshold is not enough
section: The math: Niblack and Sauvola in numbers
text:
The math: Niblack and Sauvola in numbers
Flat background with mean \mu_b and Gaussian noise \sigma_n: m \approx \mu_b, s \approx \sigma_n.

Niblack: object if I < \mu_b + k\sigma_n, i.e. \frac{I - \mu_b}{\sigma_n} < k: probability \Phi(k) = \Phi(-0.2) = 0.42, independent of the noise level.
Sauvola, \mu_b = 200, \sigma_n = 6, k = 0.3: T = 200\,(1 + 0.3(6/128 - 1)) = 142.8, more than 9 noise standard deviations below the background: no false pixels.
At an object edge, m = 150, s = 50: T = 150\,(1 + 0.3(50/128 - 1)) = 122.6; an object at 90 is below, the background at 200 above.
With R = 128 (the largest standard deviation of 8-bit data), s/R \le 1 and T \le m.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: When one threshold is not enough
text:
The window size
The real parameter of every local method.

Larger than the objects: if the window fits inside an object, the local mean is the object, and the object’s centre is no darker than its surroundings: discs come out hollow (only a rim).
Smaller than the illumination change: a window as large as the image is a global threshold again.
Rule of thumb: about twice the largest object diameter. In the test image (discs up to 45 pixels across, light changing over 256 pixels): 11 \times 11 hollows the discs, 51 \times 51 to 81 \times 81 work, 241 \times 241 is nearly global.
The same trade-off returns for the size of the structuring element of a top-hat (day 8).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: When one threshold is not enough
section: Local mean and variance are box filters
text:
Local mean and variance are box filters
m_W = \text{box}(I) and s_W^2 = \text{box}(I^2) - \text{box}(I)^2: two box filters and a subtraction.

A box filter with running sums costs the same for any window size: add the pixel that enters, subtract the one that leaves. Two 1D passes for 2D.
The integral image gives any rectangle sum from four lookups; it is taught on the integral-images elective.
So local thresholds cost O(N) for an image of N pixels, however large the window.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: When one threshold is not enough
section: The math: variance from two box filters
text:
The math: variance from two box filters
For the n pixels I_1, \dots, I_n in the window: s^2 = \frac1n\sum_j (I_j - m)^2 = \frac1n\sum_j I_j^2 - 2m\,\frac1n\sum_j I_j + m^2 = \text{box}(I^2) - m^2 .

Numerically fragile when s \ll m (two large, nearly equal numbers are subtracted): use doubles, or subtract a rough offset first.
Running sum along a row, window 2r + 1: S(x + 1) = S(x) + I(x + r + 1) - I(x - r). Two passes (rows, then columns) give the 2D box sum.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: When one threshold is not enough
text:
Try it: local thresholds




Left: the image with the mask (orange); click to move the profile row (blue). Top right: I and T along the row, with the true discs shaded. Bottom: the threshold surface T(x). Readout: Dice against the ground truth, false positives and negatives. Tour: “global Otsu fails”: t = 127, Dice 0.701, the whole left side is object. “divide by the background”: Dice 0.982. “window too small” (11 × 11, mean − C): the large discs are hollow, Dice 0.602. “window too large” (241 × 241): nearly global again on the left, Dice 0.897. “Niblack in empty background”: speckle, 3180 false pixels. “Sauvola fixes it”: Dice 0.976, 12 false pixels.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: When one threshold is not enough
text:
Remedy 3: hysteresis

Two thresholds t_\text{low} < t_\text{high} (the edges day used this inside Canny, on edge strength):

Pixels above t_\text{high} are sure: seeds (red).
Pixels above t_\text{low} are kept only if they are connected to a seed (orange); the others are rejected (blue).
The fading structure survives to its faint end; isolated noise above t_\text{low} does not. But the faint separate bump on the right has no seed: it is lost.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: When one threshold is not enough
text:
Hysteresis on a grid
Connected = linked by a chain of neighbouring pixels that are all above t_\text{low}.

4-connectivity: neighbours share a side. 8-connectivity: corners count too. A one-pixel-wide diagonal line is connected only with 8.
Foreground with 8-connectivity is the convention of the following days.
The result is a connected-components question: keep every component of the low mask that contains a seed. How that is computed (reconstruction, labelling) is on days 8 and 9.
Good for thin, faint, continuous structures: vessels, filaments, edges. Useless for separate faint objects without a bright spot.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: When one threshold is not enough
text:
Try it: hysteresis




Top: the 1D picture; drag either line. Bottom left: hysteresis on a 128 × 128 image of faint filaments that fade from one end to the other; bottom right: the two single thresholds. Tour: “high alone breaks the filament” (621 pixels, only the bright halves); “low alone keeps noise” (1412 pixels, with speckle); “hysteresis keeps both ends” (1311 kept, 101 rejected); “4- vs 8-connectivity”: 11 more pixels rejected with 4. Lower t_low to 50: the speckle around the filaments starts to connect (752 rejected, but 1670 kept). Finally the edge strength of the micrograph.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: When one threshold is not enough
section: When noise is the problem: let neighbours agree
text:
When noise is the problem: let neighbours agree

Every method so far decides each pixel by its own grey level (and a threshold that may vary). Isolated wrong pixels survive.
Smoothing first helps, but blurs edges.
The principled fix: an energy with a data term (how well the grey level fits each class: this unit’s Bayes model) plus a smoothness term that charges for neighbours with different labels.
Graph cuts (day 13) minimise it exactly; thresholding is the special case with no smoothness term (\lambda = 0). The Ising/MRF elective gives the probabilistic view.

title: When one threshold is not enough
text:
Summary

One global threshold fails under uneven illumination, for few small or faint objects, and with noise.
Correct the background first: divide by (or subtract) a smooth estimate, then threshold globally.
Local thresholds T(x) from a window: mean − C, Niblack m + ks (speckle in empty background), Sauvola m(1 + k(s/R - 1)) (background stays background).
The window must be larger than the objects and smaller than the illumination changes. Local mean and variance are box filters: O(N) for any window.
Hysteresis: seeds above t_\text{high}, keep what is connected above t_\text{low} (4- or 8-connectivity).
For noise, make neighbours agree: graph cuts.

title: Quiz: Dijkstra and live-wire
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Pixels are nodes of a grid graph; a path pays the costs of the pixels (or links) it uses; Dijkstra repeatedly makes the unfinished pixel with the smallest tentative cost final.

Q1. Why can the row-by-row DP table not find the cheapest path when moves in all four directions are allowed?






Answer





The table needs an order in which every value is computed after the values it depends on. With moves in all directions, the best path to a pixel may come from a pixel below it (or to its right), which the row order computes later, and that pixel may in turn depend on the first one. No fixed order works in general.




Q2. Why is the unfinished pixel with the smallest tentative cost already final?






Hint





Where must any other path to it leave the set of final pixels, and what does that cost?









Answer





Any other path to it must leave the final pixels through some unfinished pixel, which already has a tentative cost at least as large; the rest of that path can only add cost (all costs are non-negative). So no other path can be cheaper.




Q3. After Dijkstra has run from a seed, how do you get the cheapest path to a pixel the mouse points at? Why is that fast?






Answer





Follow the stored predecessors from the pixel back to the seed (backtracking) and reverse. It takes as many steps as the path is long: no new shortest-path computation, so the live-wire can follow the mouse in real time. The expensive part, the tree, is computed once per seed.




Q4. Name the three terms of the live-wire local cost and what each one rewards.






Answer





Gradient magnitude: strong edges are cheap. Laplacian zero crossing: the centre of the edge (where the second derivative changes sign) is cheap, so the wire sits on the edge, not beside it. Gradient direction: running along the edge direction is cheap, cutting across it is expensive; this keeps the wire smooth and on one edge.




Q5. The wire cuts across the inside of a cell instead of following its faint boundary. Why, and what do you do?






Answer





The cost is a sum along the path: a long path along a weak edge can cost more than a short path across a uniform region. Place an anchor on the boundary (shorter pieces), or make the edge terms count more relative to the constant per-pixel cost.




Q6. Why does Dijkstra need non-negative weights, and why is that no problem for live-wire?






Answer





With a negative weight, a later detour could lower the cost of a pixel that was already declared final, so “smallest is final” breaks. The live-wire cost terms (gradient, zero crossing, direction, plus a small constant) are all \ge 0 by construction.




Q7. Dijkstra and watershed flooding use the same priority queue. What is the difference in what they minimise?






Answer





Dijkstra minimises the sum of the costs along a path. Watershed flooding minimises the maximum height along a path (the lowest pass between a pixel and a marker). Both process pixels from the queue in increasing order of their value.




Q8. (math) What is the running time of Dijkstra on an n \times n image with 8 neighbours and a binary heap?






Answer





N = n^2 pixels and about 8N edges; each pop and each update costs O(\log N): O(N \log N) = O(n^2 \log n).

B2. (a) d(1,1) = 10 (from the left: 2 + 8), d(1,2) = 17 (from (1,1)), and d(1,3) = 20: its best path now comes from below, from (2,3) with d = 15, a step up. The other distances do not change. When the pass reaches (1,3), the pixel (2,3) below it has not been computed yet: the best path to (1,3) comes from below, against the scan order. All other pixels are correct.
B3. Follow the channel: down column 1 to row 5, right along row 5 to column 3, up column 3 to row 2, right along row 2 to column 6, down column 6 to the bottom: 19 pixels of cost 1, total 19 (the best monotone path costs 24). Dijkstra makes pixels final in order of their distance: (5,1) has distance 6 (six 1s from the top), while (2,3) in the channel is reached only via row 5 and has distance 11. Pixels are not processed by row but by cost, so the far end of the detour comes later even though it is higher up.
B4. Dijkstra makes s final (0), then a with the smaller tentative value 2, then b with 3; when b is final, a is already final and is not updated. Result: d(a) = 2. True: s \to b \to a costs 3 - 2 = 1. The argument “any other route passes through an unfinished node that already costs at least as much and can only add” fails: the route through b costs 3 at b and then decreases.
B5. (a) 60 px of boundary cost 60 \cdot 0.40 = 24; the chord costs 40 \cdot 0.88 = 35.2: the wire follows the boundary. 100 px of boundary cost 40 > 35.2: the wire takes the chord. (b) Break-even at 40 \cdot 0.88 / 0.40 = 88 px. The user can add an anchor in the middle of the boundary (each piece is then much shorter than its chord’s alternative), increase the edge weights relative to the constant part, or smooth less so that the edge is stronger.
B6. (3, 4): 4 neighbours 3 + 4 = 7; 8 neighbours 3\sqrt2 + 1 = 5.243 (three diagonal steps and one straight); Euclidean 5. (5, 5): 10, 5\sqrt2 = 7.071, 7.071: on the exact diagonal 8 neighbours are exact, but between the axes and the diagonals they overestimate, and 4 neighbours overestimate by up to 41%. The next unit removes this error.




Math questions
B7. (math) Prove that Dijkstra’s algorithm is correct when all weights are non-negative: when a node is made final, its tentative value equals the true shortest distance. Point out where non-negativity is used.
B8. (math) Show that with a binary heap Dijkstra takes O((N + E)\log N) time for N nodes and E edges. What is that for an n \times n image with 8 neighbours? (The demo pushes a pixel again when its value improves, instead of decreasing its key; why is that still O(E \log E)?)
B9. (math) Suppose every edge goes from row i to row i + 1 (moves only downwards). Show that the rows give an order in which every Bellman equation can be evaluated once, that this order is a topological order of the graph, and that Dijkstra and the row-by-row DP table give the same distances.
B10. (math) Watershed-style flooding minimises the largest pixel value along a path (the lowest pass), d(v) = \min_{u \sim v} \max\big(d(u), C(v)\big). Show that the Dijkstra argument still works for this “bottleneck” cost.






Solutions (math)





B7. Induction over the pops. Suppose all final values are correct, and v is the unfinished node with the smallest tentative value \tilde d(v), which is the cost of an actual path (through final nodes), so d(v) \le \tilde d(v). Take any path P from s to v and let y be its first node outside the final set, entered from a final x. When x was made final, y was updated: \tilde d(y) \le d(x) + w(x, y). The rest of P from y to v has non-negative weight (here non-negativity is used), so \text{cost}(P) \ge d(x) + w(x, y) \ge \tilde d(y) \ge \tilde d(v). Hence d(v) = \tilde d(v).
B8. Each node is popped once as final and each edge relaxed at most once (from its final end): N pops and at most E decrease-key operations, each O(\log N) on a heap: O((N + E)\log N). An n \times n image with 8 neighbours: N = n^2, E \approx 8n^2, so O(n^2 \log n). With re-insertion instead of decrease-key, the heap holds at most one entry per successful relaxation, at most E + 1 entries; each push and pop costs O(\log E) = O(\log N) (since E \le N^2), and stale entries are skipped when popped.
B9. Every edge goes from a lower row index to a higher one, so evaluating row by row, every right-hand side d(u) (with u in the previous row) is final before it is used: a topological order (every edge points forward in it). The DP table computes exactly the Bellman equations in this order, so it gives the true shortest distances; Dijkstra also gives the true shortest distances (B7), so the two agree. (The test file of the demos checks this on random grids.)
B10. Replace “d(x) + w(x, y) + \text{rest}” by “\max(d(x), C(y), \dots)”. The cost of a path never decreases when the path is extended (\max with something can only grow or stay), which is all the argument needs: for the first non-final node y on any path to v, \text{cost}(P) \ge \max(d(x), C(y)) \ge \tilde d(y) \ge \tilde d(v). So the smallest tentative value is final, and the priority queue processes pixels in order of the flooding level, as in the watershed day.

E5. Preset weak edge: the wire short-cuts. Compare the wire’s length with the straight line. Now click an anchor on the left part of the envelope, near (103, 110) in image pixels (about the middle of the left edge), and drag the handle back to the bottom. Compare the total cost of the two-piece contour with the single short-cut. What does that tell you?
E6. Preset no smoothing: noise wins (\sigma = 0.5, along the weak lower-left arc of the synthetic nucleus). Describe the wire. Raise \sigma to 1.5 and 3. Which value would you use, and what is the price of a large \sigma?
E7. Preset the neighbour steals the path. Where does the wire go? Fix it in two ways: (a) with one anchor at the contact between the two nuclei, (b) without anchors, by changing a weight. Which works better?
E8. Preset measure along a neurite (bright-line cost). How long is the neurite between the two tips, compared with the straight line? Switch to the edges cost: what happens?






Solutions





E4. Closed, 4 segments, 362.7 px, cost 289.08. Without the last anchor, the wire follows the envelope only while the handle stays close to the previous anchor; moved further around, it soon takes a short-cut through the textured interior (as in E5) or runs along other dark lines nearby. The distance map grows slowly across the textured inside and quickly along the dark envelope: the iso-lines are stretched along the envelope.
E5. The wire is 143.4 px long against a straight line of 135.3 px: it cuts straight through the nucleus (cost 134.89). With an anchor at (103, 110) the contour follows the left envelope: 69.9 px (cost 60.81) to the anchor plus 99.2 px (cost 78.10) to the bottom, 169.1 px with a total cost of 138.91: more than the short-cut. The energy itself prefers the short-cut: a sum over a long path along a weak, interrupted line costs more than a short path across. The anchor is the user’s knowledge that the cost function lacks.
E6. At \sigma = 0.5 the wire zig-zags through the noise inside the wide, faint ramp of the weak arc, up to about 10 px from the true boundary (56.7 px, cost 19.63). At \sigma = 1.5 it is smooth and within about 4 px of the boundary (61.8 px, cost 22.79). \sigma = 1.5 to 2 is a good choice here; a large \sigma blurs nearby edges into each other (the contact with the neighbour) and rounds corners.
E7. The wire runs around the outer edge of the brighter neighbour: 195.2 px for a straight distance of 68.2 px, cost 24.14. Its edge is stronger than the nucleus edge, so it is cheaper per pixel even though the detour is long. (a) An anchor at the contact (the nucleus boundary at angle 0°, near (150, 128)) splits the wire into 45.3 px and 48.9 px pieces along the nucleus. (b) Raising w direction to 1 makes the turns of the detour expensive: the wire gets much shorter (94.9 px) but still bulges about 9 px off the nucleus boundary. The anchor works better: it is a hard constraint.
E8. 240.1 px along the neurite (through the soma), against a straight line of 188.4 px: a measurement along the structure, with steps of 1 and \sqrt2 as on the skeleton day. With the edges cost the wire follows the sides of the thin neurite (its edges) and wanders: 260.8 px. For thin lines, a line (ridge) cost is the right one.

title: Moving a curve: the level set equation
text:
About this lecture
Last unit: a curve is the zero level of \phi. Now we make it move: every point of the curve travels along its normal with a speed F. Instead of moving points, we change the image \phi a little at every time step.

Why moving the points of a polygon goes wrong.
The level set equation \phi_t + F|\nabla\phi| = 0, first in 1D.
One time step on the grid: forward Euler in time, upwind differences in space.
How large a step may be: the CFL condition, seen in the demo first.
Speeds: constant (grass fire) and curvature flow.
Merging and splitting for free; reinitialisation to keep \phi healthy.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

The densest unit of the day. Prerequisites: the previous unit (implicit curves, signed distance), forward differences and Taylor from Filtering & convolution. No PDE theory: the equation is “a rule for how each pixel value of φ changes per time step”. Stability is shown in the demo before the condition is stated.

title: Moving a curve: the level set equation
section: The task: move a curve along its normal
text:
The task: move a curve along its normal
Every point of the curve moves with speed F along its outward normal (F > 0: outward, F < 0: inward).


Explicit (left): move each point of a polygon along its normal. At the dents the points converge, the curve crosses itself and forms loops (“swallowtails”); elsewhere the points spread apart. Two curves that meet would need surgery to merge.
Implicit (right): the same motion as a moving zero level. No loops, corners where the fronts meet, and the topology may change.
crumbs: Moving a curve: the level set equation

title: Moving a curve: the level set equation
section: The idea: change φ, not the points
text:
The idea: change φ, not the points

Let \phi depend on time. At each pixel, how fast must \phi change so that its zero level moves with speed F?
Picture a slope: where \phi rises steeply, a small decrease of \phi shifts the zero crossing only a little; where it is shallow, the same decrease shifts it far.
To move the crossing outward by F per unit time, \phi must drop by F times its slope: \phi_t = -F\,|\nabla\phi| \qquad\text{the level set equation.}
Only the speed along the normal matters: sliding points along the curve does not change the curve.
