For example column 4: slope (8 - 2)/2 = 3, curvature 2 + 8 - 2 \cdot 5 = 0. The slope is largest at column 4, the middle of the ramp. The curvature is positive where the ramp starts (column 3, the brightness bends upwards), negative where it ends (column 5), and passes through 0 at column 4. Both point to column 4; the zero crossing of the curvature is the sharper criterion, because it is a sign change rather than a broad maximum. (The Laplacian finds edges this way.)
B10. x^2: one-sided 4 - 1 = 3, central (4 - 0)/2 = 2: the central difference is exactly right, the one-sided one is off by 1. x^3: one-sided 8 - 1 = 7, central (8 - 0)/2 = 4, true value 3: the central difference is much closer. The one-sided difference measures (roughly) the slope halfway between the two pixels, at x = 1.5, not at x = 1; the central difference is centred on the pixel, so its errors on the two sides cancel. That is why derivative kernels such as Sobel compare the right neighbour with the left one and skip the centre. Curvature: 4 - 2 + 0 = 2 for x^2 (exact) and 8 - 2 + 0 = 6 for x^3 (exact as well).





Math questions
B11. (math) Use the Taylor expansions of f(x+1) and f(x-1) around x to show that f(x+1) - 2f(x) + f(x-1) = f''(x) + \mathcal{O}(h^2) (here h = 1; keep track of which terms cancel). Then show that adding the 1D kernel [1\;\;-2\;\;1] in the x direction and in the y direction gives the Laplacian kernel. What is the error term of the one-sided difference f(x+1) - f(x) as an estimate of f'(x), and why do Sobel kernels skip the centre column? (Compare with B10.)






Solutions (math)





B11. f(x \pm h) = f \pm hf' + \tfrac{h^2}{2}f'' \pm \tfrac{h^3}{6}f''' + \tfrac{h^4}{24}f'''' + \dots Adding the two, the odd terms cancel: f(x+h) + f(x-h) = 2f + h^2 f'' + \tfrac{h^4}{12}f'''' + \dots, so \big[f(x+h) - 2f(x) + f(x-h)\big]/h^2 = f'' + \mathcal{O}(h^2). In 2D, [1\;-2\;1] along a row plus [1\;-2\;1] along a column puts 1 at the four direct neighbours and -2 - 2 = -4 in the centre: the Laplacian \nabla^2 I = I_{xx} + I_{yy}. The one-sided difference: f(x+h) - f(x) = hf' + \tfrac{h^2}{2}f'' + \dots, so \big[f(x+h)-f(x)\big]/h = f' + \mathcal{O}(h), an error of first order. The central difference \big[f(x+h) - f(x-h)\big]/2h cancels the f'' term and is accurate to \mathcal{O}(h^2); that is why Sobel compares the right column with the left one and gives the centre column weight 0.

title: Exercise: filtering with 3×3 kernels
text:
Explore
The demo shows the input image, the editable kernel and the output, side by side. Type a weight (press Enter afterwards) or use − and +. Divide by the sum divides the weighted sum by the sum of the weights. Apply × repeats the kernel. A click on either image selects a pixel; the grey box then shows its 3 × 3 neighbourhood, the weights, the products and the sum. Show the output chooses how numbers become grey levels: as is (below 0 is black, above 255 is white), |value| (the size, stretched so the largest is white) or 0 = grey (negative darker, positive brighter). Blur input first applies the Gaussian twice before your kernel.



E1. With the cell and Gaussian, read the selected pixel (row 129, column 129) in the grey box. Check one row of products by hand, and check that the sum divided by 16 gives the output. Then choose box blur and raise apply × to 5. What happens to the fine texture of the nucleus, and to the dark nuclear envelope?
E2. With box blur, untick divide by the sum. What happens to the output, and why? Read the range in the last line of the grey box. Then tick it again and set the centre weight to 0: what is the sum now, and does the blur still keep the brightness?
E3. Choose the test pattern, then Sobel x and Sobel y. Which of the thin lines light up in each? On the bright disk, which side is bright and which is dark with Sobel x (0 = grey)? Then switch to |value|: what changes?
E4. Set noise to 30 and choose the Laplacian. Can you still see the outlines? Tick blur input first. What changes, and what happens to the 1-pixel lines and the checkerboard? Repeat with Sobel x.
E5. Choose shift and set apply × to 5. Which way does the image move, and by how much? Then choose box blur, apply × 5, and switch between copy edge and zeros: look at the border of the output.






Solutions





E1. The products in the grey box are each pixel times the weight on top of it, for example the middle row 99 × 2 = 198, 116 × 4 = 464, 127 × 2 = 254. The nine products add up to 1759, and 1759 ÷ 16 = 109.94, shown as grey level 110. With the box blur applied 5 times, the grainy texture inside the nucleus is smoothed into a soft grey; the nuclear envelope survives as a broad, faint dark band. Fine detail is lost first, large structures last.
E2. Without dividing, every output pixel is the plain sum of 9 pixels, about 9 times too bright: almost everything is white. The grey box shows the whole output ranging from 44 to 2295, 9 times the blurred range 4.9 to 255. With the centre weight set to 0, the sum is 8 and the output is divided by 8: it is still an average (of the 8 neighbours), so a flat region keeps its brightness.
E3. Sobel x lights up the vertical lines and the left and right sides of the disk and letters; Sobel y lights up the horizontal lines and the top and bottom sides. With 0 = grey and Sobel x, the left side of the bright disk is bright (the image gets brighter to the right there) and the right side is dark (it gets darker). With |value|, both sides look bright: the sign, that is the direction of the change, is lost, and only the strength remains.
E4. At noise 30, the Laplacian output is dominated by speckle; the outlines are hard to see. With the input blurred first, the speckle is much weaker and the outlines of the disk, the letters and the square appear clearly; the output range shrinks from about ±600 to below ±100, because most of that range was noise. The price: the 1-pixel lines become faint and the checkerboard loses contrast, because blurring removes fine detail along with the noise. Sobel x behaves the same way but less extremely, since it already averages over three rows.
E5. The shift kernel copies each pixel’s left neighbour, so the image moves to the right, one pixel per pass, so 5 pixels in total. A thin strip on the left edge repeats the edge pixels (copy edge) or turns black (zeros). With the box blur ×5 and zeros outside, a dark frame a few pixels wide appears around the output, because the missing pixels count as black. Copy edge has no such frame.

title: Exercise: filtering with 3×3 kernels
text:
Where this leads
A 3\times3 kernel can only see structures a few pixels across. Larger Gaussian kernels (and the Laplacian of Gaussian) let you choose the scale of what you detect. For large kernels it becomes cheaper to filter in the Fourier domain, the topic of the next unit.

title: Kernel functions and the kernel trick
text:
About this lecture
Last unit: the max-margin line. Many problems need a curve (unit 1: XOR, a ring around a blob). This unit gets curves while keeping the line, by working in a bigger feature space, and then never writing that space down.

Lifting: add features such as x_1^2 + x_2^2; a plane up there is a curve down here.
The SVM needs only dot products between data points.
Replace them by a kernel function k(\mathbf x, \mathbf z): the kernel trick.
The RBF kernel function and its length scale 1/\sqrt\gamma; what large \gamma and large C do.
What makes a valid kernel function.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Course convention: “kernel” alone is a convolution kernel (the filtering unit). Here it is always “kernel function”, a similarity between two feature vectors. The dual is in the math layer; the concept layer needs only “f is a weighted sum of similarities to the support vectors”.
crumbs: Kernel functions and the kernel trick

title: Kernel functions and the kernel trick
section: Lift the points, cut with a plane
text:
Lift the points, cut with a plane
A ring around a blob: no line separates them in (x_1, x_2).

Add a third coordinate x_3 = x_1^2 + x_2^2 (the squared distance from the centre). Every point is lifted onto a paraboloid: the inner points sit low, the ring sits high.
Now a flat plane x_3 = r^2 separates them.
Seen from above, the plane cuts the paraboloid in a circle: a curved boundary in 2D from a linear classifier in 3D.

General plan: map \mathbf x \mapsto \varphi(\mathbf x) to more features, fit the max-margin plane there. (On this day \varphi is the feature map; on the neural networks day \varphi was the activation function.)
crumbs: Kernel functions and the kernel trick

title: Kernel functions and the kernel trick
text:
Try it: lift and cut




WebGL. Left: the points and the boundary in 2D; right: the lifted points, the lifted surface and the plane of a linear SVM in 3D, with its cut through the surface (black). Drag the 3D view to rotate. Tour: “ring → plane”: rotate to the side view: inner points low, ring high, the plane between. “XOR needs x₁x₂”: the saddle map lifts one diagonal up and the other down; switch to the paraboloid map: it does not help. “Two rings”: a band in the middle height; no single plane works. “(x₁², √2x₁x₂, x₂²)” is the map of the next slides.
crumbs: Kernel functions and the kernel trick

title: Kernel functions and the kernel trick
text:
The cost of explicit features
Lifting works, but the number of features explodes:

All products of two features (the quadratic map) of a pixel with 20 features: 20 + 20 + 190 = 230 coordinates (x_i, x_i^2, x_ix_j).
All monomials up to degree 5: 53 130 coordinates.
The Gaussian (RBF) similarity below corresponds to infinitely many.

We need a way to fit the max-margin plane in such a space without computing \varphi(\mathbf x).
crumbs: Kernel functions and the kernel trick

title: Kernel functions and the kernel trick
section: The SVM only needs dot products
text:
The SVM only needs dot products
A fact from the math layer (next slides): the max-margin solution is a weighted sum over the support vectors,
f(\mathbf x) = \sum_{i} \alpha_i y_i\, \mathbf x_i\cdot\mathbf x + b, \qquad \alpha_i > 0 \text{ only for support vectors},
and the weights \alpha_i are found from the dot products \mathbf x_i\cdot\mathbf x_j of the training points alone.

Training: needs \mathbf x_i\cdot\mathbf x_j for all pairs. Prediction: needs \mathbf x_i\cdot\mathbf x for the support vectors.
In a lifted space: replace every \mathbf x_i\cdot\mathbf x_j by \varphi(\mathbf x_i)\cdot\varphi(\mathbf x_j). If that number can be computed directly from \mathbf x_i, \mathbf x_j, we never need \varphi.
crumbs: Kernel functions and the kernel trick

title: Kernel functions and the kernel trick
text:
Kernel functions: the kernel trick
A kernel function computes the dot product in a lifted space directly: k(\mathbf x, \mathbf z) = \varphi(\mathbf x)\cdot\varphi(\mathbf z).
By hand. \varphi(\mathbf x) = (x_1^2,\ \sqrt2\,x_1x_2,\ x_2^2), \mathbf x = (1, 2), \mathbf z = (3, 1):

Lifted: \varphi(\mathbf x) = (1,\ 2\sqrt2,\ 4), \varphi(\mathbf z) = (9,\ 3\sqrt2,\ 1), dot product 9 + 12 + 4 = 25.
Directly: \mathbf x\cdot\mathbf z = 3 + 2 = 5, and (\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf z)^2 = 25. The same, with 2 multiplications instead of 6.

So k(\mathbf x, \mathbf z) = (\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf z)^2 is a dot product of quadratic features. The polynomial kernel function (\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf z + c)^p covers all monomials up to degree p at the cost of one dot product.
The SVM with f(\mathbf x) = \sum_i \alpha_i y_i\, k(\mathbf x_i, \mathbf x) + b is the max-margin plane in the lifted space: the kernel trick. (Not a convolution kernel: “kernel” alone in this course means the filter.)
crumbs: Kernel functions and the kernel trick

title: Kernel functions and the kernel trick
text:
The math: Lagrange multipliers
Recall (equality constraints): at the optimum of \min g(\mathbf u) subject to h(\mathbf u) = 0, the gradients are parallel, \nabla g = \alpha\nabla h; equivalently, \mathbf u is a stationary point of the Lagrangian g - \alpha h. (Multipliers are called \alpha here: \lambda is the prior weight course-wide.)
For inequality constraints h_i(\mathbf u) \ge 0 the multipliers must be \alpha_i \ge 0, and complementary slackness holds: \alpha_i\,h_i(\mathbf u) = 0. In words: a multiplier is non-zero only where its constraint is tight (holds with equality).
For the SVM, constraint i is y_i f(\mathbf x_i) - 1 \ge 0. It is tight exactly for the points on the edge of the street. So \alpha_i > 0 only for support vectors.
crumbs: Kernel functions and the kernel trick

title: Kernel functions and the kernel trick
text:
The math: the dual problem
Hard margin. Lagrangian L = \tfrac12\|\mathbf w\|^2 - \sum_i\alpha_i\left[y_i(\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x_i + b) - 1\right], \alpha_i \ge 0. Stationarity:
\frac{\partial L}{\partial\mathbf w} = 0 \Rightarrow \mathbf w = \sum_i \alpha_i y_i\mathbf x_i, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = 0 \Rightarrow \sum_i \alpha_i y_i = 0.
Substituting back eliminates \mathbf w and b:
\max_{\boldsymbol\alpha}\ \sum_i\alpha_i - \tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_j y_iy_j\,\mathbf x_i\cdot\mathbf x_j \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0,\quad 0 \le \alpha_i \le C.

The data enter only through \mathbf x_i\cdot\mathbf x_j: replace by k(\mathbf x_i, \mathbf x_j).
Soft margin: the same, with the extra bound \alpha_i \le C (from the slack multipliers). \alpha_i = C: inside the street or wrong; 0 < \alpha_i < C: on the edge.
b from any edge point: y_i f(\mathbf x_i) = 1. Then f(\mathbf x) = \sum_i\alpha_iy_i\,k(\mathbf x_i, \mathbf x) + b.
crumbs: Kernel functions and the kernel trick

title: Kernel functions and the kernel trick
section: The math: how it is solved
text:
The math: how it is solved

The dual is a quadratic program in n variables with box constraints and one equality: convex, one optimum.
SMO (sequential minimal optimisation; Platt, 1998): change two \alphas at a time. Two, because \sum_i \alpha_iy_i = 0 forces any change in one to be balanced by another. For a pair the optimum is a 1D quadratic, solved in closed form and clipped to the box [0, C].
Which pair? The two that violate the optimality conditions most (with a second-order rule: Fan, Chen & Lin, 2005). Stop when no pair violates them by more than a tolerance.
The kernel matrix K_{ij} = k(\mathbf x_i, \mathbf x_j) is computed once (n^2 numbers): fine for a few thousand training points. The demos use this solver.
crumbs: Kernel functions and the kernel trick

title: Kernel functions and the kernel trick
text:
The RBF kernel function
The most used kernel function: the Gaussian or RBF (radial basis function)
k(\mathbf x, \mathbf z) = e^{-\gamma\|\mathbf x - \mathbf z\|^2}.

A similarity: 1 for identical points, falling to 0 with distance.
1/\sqrt\gamma is a length scale: how far one training point’s influence reaches.
f(\mathbf x) = \sum_i \alpha_iy_i\,e^{-\gamma\|\mathbf x_i - \mathbf x\|^2} + b: a signed sum of Gaussian bumps on the support vectors. Red bumps up, blue bumps down; the boundary is where they balance.
Seen before: the graph-cut n-link weight and the normalized-cuts affinity e^{-\Delta^2/2\sigma^2} (the graph cuts day) are this function with \gamma = 1/(2\sigma^2). The kernel matrix K_{ij} is that day’s affinity matrix W.
Unlike a Gaussian mixture’s bumps (the Gaussian mixtures day), the weights are signed and fitted to separate, not to describe the density.
crumbs: Kernel functions and the kernel trick

title: Kernel functions and the kernel trick
text:
Two bumps by hand




Support vectors (0, 0) with \alpha y = +1 and (2, 0) with \alpha y = -1, b = 0, \gamma = 1:

f(0.5, 0) = e^{-0.25} - e^{-2.25} = 0.779 - 0.105 = 0.673: class +1.
f(1, 0) = e^{-1} - e^{-1} = 0 and f(1, 1) = e^{-2} - e^{-2} = 0: on the boundary, the line x_1 = 1.
At (0.5, 0) with \gamma = 0.1: 0.177 (wide, flat bumps); with \gamma = 10: 0.082 (narrow bumps, almost nothing reaches).
crumbs: Kernel functions and the kernel trick

title: Kernel functions and the kernel trick
text:
Try it: kernel functions in 2D




The same demo as the last unit, with a kernel-function menu. Tour: “ring”: linear: w ≈ 0, 21 errors; polynomial degree 2: a closed curve, 0 errors, 13 support vectors; RBF (γ = 0.32): 0 errors, 15 support vectors. Tick “show the RBF bumps”: circles of radius 1/√γ. “XOR: degree 2”: linear 38 errors of 80, polynomial degree 2: 0 errors. “γ too large”: 79 of 80 points are support vectors, an island around each; lower γ to 1: 35 support vectors, 1 error. “γ too small”: the boundary is almost a line (10 errors, like the linear one). Tick “show the kernel matrix”: blocks by class; with a large γ it becomes the identity.
crumbs: Kernel functions and the kernel trick

title: Kernel functions and the kernel trick
text:
\gamma and C together









small C
large C




small \gamma (long length scale)
almost a straight line, wide street: underfits
still smooth; a few more bends


large \gamma (short length scale)
bumps too narrow to interact, many support vectors
an island around every training point: overfits, memorises




Large \gamma: each bump reaches only its own point; with large C every training point is classified correctly, and new points between them get the background value b.
In practice both are chosen by cross-validation on a log grid (next unit).
crumbs: Kernel functions and the kernel trick

title: Kernel functions and the kernel trick
section: What makes a valid kernel function?
text:
What makes a valid kernel function?
A kernel function must behave like a dot product somewhere.

Every kernel matrix K_{ij} = k(\mathbf x_i, \mathbf x_j) must be symmetric with no negative eigenvalues (positive semidefinite): a negative eigenvalue would be a “negative squared length”.
Example of an invalid “similarity”: two points with k(\mathbf x, \mathbf x) = k(\mathbf z, \mathbf z) = 1 and k(\mathbf x, \mathbf z) = 2. The matrix \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2\\2 & 1\end{bmatrix} has eigenvalues 3 and -1. The “squared distance” would be k(\mathbf x, \mathbf x) + k(\mathbf z, \mathbf z) - 2k(\mathbf x, \mathbf z) = -2: impossible.
Building new ones: sums and products of kernel functions, and positive multiples, are kernel functions.
A valid kernel function keeps the training problem convex: one optimum.
crumbs: Kernel functions and the kernel trick

title: Kernel functions and the kernel trick
text:
The math: Mercer’s condition

Mercer: k is a dot product \varphi(\mathbf x)\cdot\varphi(\mathbf z) in some (possibly infinite-dimensional) space \iff for every finite set of points the kernel matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite. (Stated, not proven.)
The RBF kernel function’s space is infinite-dimensional: e^{-\gamma\|\mathbf x - \mathbf z\|^2} = e^{-\gamma\|\mathbf x\|^2}e^{-\gamma\|\mathbf z\|^2}\,e^{2\gamma\,\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf z}, and the Taylor series e^{2\gamma\,\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf z} = \sum_{p \ge 0} \frac{(2\gamma)^p}{p!}(\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf z)^p contains polynomial kernel functions of every degree.
The squared distance in the lifted space is \|\varphi(\mathbf x) - \varphi(\mathbf z)\|^2 = k(\mathbf x, \mathbf x) + k(\mathbf z, \mathbf z) - 2k(\mathbf x, \mathbf z), computable without \varphi.
crumbs: Kernel functions and the kernel trick

title: Kernel functions and the kernel trick
text:
Summary

A curved boundary = a plane in a lifted feature space \varphi(\mathbf x).
The SVM needs only dot products; a kernel function k(\mathbf x, \mathbf z) = \varphi(\mathbf x)\cdot\varphi(\mathbf z) computes them without \varphi: the kernel trick. f(\mathbf x) = \sum_i \alpha_iy_i\,k(\mathbf x_i, \mathbf x) + b, a sum over the support vectors.
Polynomial (\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf z + c)^p; RBF e^{-\gamma\|\mathbf x - \mathbf z\|^2} with length scale 1/\sqrt\gamma (the graph-cut affinity with \gamma = 1/2\sigma^2).
Small \gamma: almost linear. Large \gamma and C: islands, overfitting.
Valid kernel functions give positive semidefinite kernel matrices.
crumbs: Kernel functions and the kernel trick

title: Quiz: the JPEG pipeline, artefacts and quality metrics
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Pipeline: Y′CbCr and 4:2:0 → 8 × 8 blocks → DCT → quantise q = \operatorname{round}(c/Q) → zigzag → DC difference, (run, size) symbols, Huffman.

Q1. Which steps of JPEG lose information, and which are exactly reversible?






Hint





Which steps round or throw away values?









Answer





Lossy: chroma subsampling (4:2:0 averages colour over 2 × 2 pixels) and quantisation (rounding c/Q). Reversible: the colour conversion (up to tiny rounding), cutting into blocks, the DCT, zigzag order and the entropy coding.




Q2. Why are the quantisation steps larger at the bottom right of the table than at the top left?






Hint





Which frequencies does the eye notice least?









Answer





The bottom right holds the highest frequencies: fine detail that the eye barely sees, and that natural images contain little of. Large steps there turn most of those coefficients into zeros, which cost almost nothing to store, while the low frequencies (the visible shading) keep fine steps.




Q3. A coefficient has the step Q = 24. What is the largest error it can have after decoding? And the block’s pixels?






Hint





Rounding error, and the DCT is orthonormal.









Answer





At most Q/2 = 12 for the coefficient. Its basis image has unit length, so the squared pixel error caused by this coefficient is at most 12^2 = 144, summed over the 64 pixels of the block; spread over the block it is a pattern with an amplitude of a few grey levels.




Q4. Why is the DC coefficient coded as the difference from the previous block?






Hint





How different are the averages of two neighbouring blocks, usually?









Answer





Neighbouring blocks have similar averages, so the differences are small numbers with a narrow histogram: they cost fewer bits than the DC values themselves. It is the prediction of the lossless unit, applied to block averages.




Q5. At low quality, the sky in a photograph turns into a mosaic of squares. Explain in two sentences.






Hint





What survives quantisation in a smooth block, and is the next block coded with it?









Answer





In a smooth block only the DC (the block average) survives a coarse quantisation, so the block decodes as a flat square. Each block is quantised on its own, so neighbouring squares have different rounded averages and meet with a visible step: blocking.




Q6. Image A has a brightness shift of 10 grey levels, image B has random noise with standard deviation 10. Compare their PSNR and SSIM.






Hint





What is the MSE of each? What does SSIM compare?









Answer





Both have MSE 100 and PSNR 28.1 dB. SSIM of A is close to 1 (the local structure is unchanged, only the mean differs slightly); SSIM of B is clearly lower, because the noise destroys local structure, most of all in flat areas. PSNR cannot tell them apart.




Q7. You save a JPEG at quality 75, open it, and save it again at quality 75 without changes. Then you crop 4 pixels from the left and save again. Which save loses more?






Hint





Where are the 8 × 8 blocks after the crop?









Answer





The second save (same grid, same table) loses almost nothing: the decoded image is already nearly on the quantisation grid. After the crop the 8 × 8 grid lies in a different place, the new blocks’ coefficients are not quantised yet, and the save loses again: generation loss.




Q8. (math) Show that halving all quantisation steps improves the PSNR by about 6 dB.






Hint





The error variance of a uniform quantiser with step \Delta is \Delta^2/12.









Answer





The MSE (the same in coefficients and pixels, by Parseval) goes from \Delta^2/12 to \Delta^2/48 per coefficient: a factor 4. \Delta\text{PSNR} = 10\log_{10} 4 = 6.02 dB. (Coefficients that were quantised to 0 and stay 0 do not improve; hence “about”.)
crumbs: The JPEG pipeline, artefacts and quality metrics

title: Exercise: the JPEG pipeline, artefacts and quality metrics
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

take one block through quantisation, zigzag, run-length symbols and Huffman bits by hand,
scale a quantisation table for a quality factor and give the largest possible error per coefficient,
relate the quantisation step to rate and distortion (6 dB per bit),
recognise blocking, ringing, colour bleeding and generation loss,

title: Exercise: the JPEG pipeline, artefacts and quality metrics
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

take one block through quantisation, zigzag, run-length symbols and Huffman bits by hand,
scale a quantisation table for a quality factor and give the largest possible error per coefficient,
relate the quantisation step to rate and distortion (6 dB per bit),
recognise blocking, ringing, colour bleeding and generation loss,
compute PSNR and SSIM for small examples and explain why they can disagree.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demos.

title: Exercise: the JPEG pipeline, artefacts and quality metrics
text:
Background







Step
What happens




Colour
Y′CbCr; 4:2:0 keeps the colour channels at half resolution in both directions


Blocks
8 × 8, pixel values − 128


DCT
64 coefficients per block (previous unit)


Quantise
q = \operatorname{round}(c/Q), decoded qQ; error \le Q/2


Quality factor
s = 5000/q (q < 50) or 200 - 2q (q \ge 50); Q' = \lfloor (Q s + 50)/100 \rfloor, between 1 and 255


Zigzag
read diagonally from the top left: low frequencies first


DC
difference from the previous block’s DC; Huffman code of its size + the value’s bits


AC
(run of zeros, size) Huffman-coded + the value’s bits; EOB ends the block


Size of a value
number of bits of |v|: 1 → 1, 2–3 → 2, 4–7 → 3, …; negative values: bits of v - 1 in that size, e.g. −3 → 00


PSNR
10 \log_{10}(255^2/\text{MSE}) dB for 8-bit images


SSIM
\frac{(2\mu_x\mu_y + C_1)(2\sigma_{xy} + C_2)}{(\mu_x^2 + \mu_y^2 + C_1)(\sigma_x^2 + \sigma_y^2 + C_2)}, C_1 = (0.01 \cdot 255)^2 = 6.50, C_2 = (0.03 \cdot 255)^2 = 58.5



Excerpt of the standard luminance Huffman tables: DC sizes 0: 00, 1: 010, 2: 011, 3: 100. AC symbols (run, size): (0,1) 00, (0,2) 01, (0,3) 100, (1,1) 1100, (1,2) 11011, EOB 1010.

title: Exercise: the JPEG pipeline, artefacts and quality metrics
text:
By hand
B1. A block’s DCT coefficients are (row, column of the coefficient table): c_{00} = 190, c_{01} = -33, c_{10} = 25, c_{20} = -15, c_{11} = 5, c_{02} = 9; all others are smaller than half their step. The table at quality 50 has Q_{00} = 16, Q_{01} = 11, Q_{10} = 12, Q_{20} = 14, Q_{11} = 12, Q_{02} = 10. (a) Quantise. How many of the 64 values are non-zero? (b) Dequantise and give the error of each of the six coefficients. Is it always at most Q/2?
B2. Continue with B1. The zigzag order starts (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (2,0), (1,1), (0,2), (0,3), … (a) Write the zigzag sequence up to the last non-zero value. (b) The previous block had DC 9. Write the DC difference and the AC symbols (run, size) value, ending with EOB. (c) Count the bits with the table excerpt. How many bits per pixel is that?
B3. Scale the table entries Q_{00} = 16 and Q_{77} = 99 for the qualities 10, 25, 75 and 100. What is the largest possible error of a decoded c_{00} at quality 25?
B4. You halve every quantisation step. Roughly how do the mean squared error, the PSNR and the number of bits change?
B5. A 3 × 3 8-bit image is decoded with the errors 2 −1 0 / 0 3 0 / −2 1 0. Compute the MSE and the PSNR.
B6. Two image patches: y = x + 10 everywhere (a brightness shift), with local mean \mu_x = 100 in a window. Compute the MSE, the PSNR, and the SSIM of the window. Then think of a distortion with the same MSE that you would see immediately.
B7. A 256 × 256 colour image has 3 values per pixel. How many values are left after Y′CbCr with 4:2:0 subsampling? Which of the artefacts on the lecture’s list does subsampling cause?
B8. Name the artefact: (a) a sky becomes a mosaic of slightly different flat squares; (b) a black text line on white gets faint grey copies parallel to it; (c) a red object on a blue background gets a purple seam; (d) an image saved, cropped by 3 pixels and saved again, ten times, gets steadily worse.






Solutions





B1. (a) 190/16 = 11.9 \to 12; -33/11 = -3; 25/12 = 2.08 \to 2; -15/14 = -1.07 \to -1; 5/12 = 0.42 \to 0; 9/10 = 0.9 \to 1; all others 0. Five non-zero values out of 64. (b) Decoded: 192, −33, 24, −14, 0, 10. Errors: 2, 0, 1, 1, 5, 1, all within Q/2 = 8, 5.5, 6, 7, 6, 5.
B2. (a) 12, −3, 2, −1, 0, 1. (b) DC difference 12 - 9 = 3 (size 2). AC: (0,2) −3, (0,2) 2, (0,1) −1, (1,1) 1, EOB. (c) DC: 011 + 11 = 5 bits; (0,2) −3: 01 + 00 = 4; (0,2) 2: 01 + 10 = 4; (0,1) −1: 00 + 0 = 3; (1,1) 1: 1100 + 1 = 5; EOB 1010 = 4. Total 25 bits for 64 pixels: 0.39 bits per pixel (raw 8).
B3. Quality 10: s = 500: Q_{00} = 80, Q_{77} = 495 \to 255 (the maximum). Quality 25: s = 200: 32 and 198. Quality 75: s = 50: 8 and 50. Quality 100: s = 0: both 1 (the minimum). At quality 25 the decoded c_{00} is off by at most 32/2 = 16, i.e. the block mean by at most 16/8 = 2 grey levels.
B4. The squared error per coefficient (\approx \Delta^2/12) drops to a quarter, the PSNR rises by 10\log_{10} 4 = 6 dB, and every coefficient that is not zero needs about one more bit (and some that were zero become non-zero).
B5. Squared errors 4 + 1 + 9 + 4 + 1 = 19, MSE = 19/9 = 2.11, PSNR = 10\log_{10}(65\,025/2.11) = 44.9 dB.
B6. MSE = 100, PSNR = 28.1 dB, which sounds poor. SSIM: the contrast–structure term is exactly 1 (y - \mu_y = x - \mu_x); the luminance term is \frac{2 \cdot 100 \cdot 110 + 6.5}{100^2 + 110^2 + 6.5} = 0.995. The image looks the same, only brighter. The same MSE as noise of standard deviation 10, or as strong blocking, is clearly visible: PSNR does not see the difference, SSIM does.
B7. 256^2 \cdot 3 = 196\,608 values before; after 4:2:0: 65\,536 + 2 \cdot 128^2 = 98\,304, half. Subsampling causes colour bleeding at sharp colour edges.
B8. (a) Blocking. (b) Ringing (mosquito noise). (c) Colour bleeding. (d) Generation loss; the crop moves the 8 × 8 grid, so each save quantises different blocks.




Math questions
B9. (math) Show that the error of a uniform quantiser with step \Delta, if it is uniformly distributed on [-\Delta/2, \Delta/2], has variance \Delta^2/12. Why does this error appear unchanged in the pixels of the decoded block?
B10. (math) A coefficient is spread uniformly over a range R \gg \Delta. Show that one more bit (halving \Delta) improves the PSNR by 6.02 dB.
B11. (math) Show that the luminance term of SSIM, \frac{2\mu_x\mu_y + C_1}{\mu_x^2 + \mu_y^2 + C_1}, is at most 1, with equality iff \mu_x = \mu_y. Do the same for the contrast–structure term, using the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality |\sigma_{xy}| \le \sigma_x \sigma_y.






Solutions (math)





B9. \int_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2} e^2 \frac{de}{\Delta} = \frac{1}{\Delta} \cdot \frac{2}{3}\big(\tfrac{\Delta}{2}\big)^3 = \frac{\Delta^2}{12} (the mean is 0). The decoder applies the inverse DCT X = D^\top C D, which is orthonormal: the pixel error is D^\top E D for the coefficient error matrix E, and \|D^\top E D\|^2 = \|E\|^2. So the summed squared error is the same in both domains, and the mean squared pixel error of a block is the mean of the coefficient error variances.
B10. MSE = \Delta^2/12; with \Delta/2 it is \Delta^2/48, a factor 4. PSNR changes by 10\log_{10} 4 = 6.02 dB. The number of levels R/\Delta doubles: one more bit.
B11. \mu_x^2 + \mu_y^2 - 2\mu_x\mu_y = (\mu_x - \mu_y)^2 \ge 0, so the numerator is at most the denominator (both positive thanks to C_1 > 0), with equality iff \mu_x = \mu_y. Similarly 2\sigma_{xy} \le 2\sigma_x\sigma_y \le \sigma_x^2 + \sigma_y^2; equality needs \sigma_x = \sigma_y and \sigma_{xy} = \sigma_x\sigma_y, i.e. y - \mu_y = x - \mu_x in the window.

title: Exercise: the JPEG pipeline, artefacts and quality metrics
text:
Explore: JPEG
Original | decoded | difference (×4, mid grey = 0) or SSIM map (white = 1). quality scales the standard table; chroma 4:2:0 (colour card only) halves the colour resolution; flat table (same size) replaces the standard table by one equal step, chosen to give about the same file size; generations recompresses the decoded image again and again, optionally with the 8 × 8 grid moved by 4 pixels each time; zoom ×4 shows the 64 × 64 pixels around the selected block (click an image to choose a block). The tabs show one block through the pipeline, the quantisation table, and the rate–distortion curves (PSNR and SSIM against bits per pixel for qualities 5, 10, …, 100). The size is the exact number of Huffman-coded bits plus the file header; “browser encoder” is the size of the browser’s own JPEG of the same image and quality, as a cross-check.



J1. Preset quality 90: invisible. Note size, ratio, PSNR and SSIM. Can you see any difference? Lower the quality to 50, 25 and 10 and note the same numbers. At which quality do you first see something, and where?
J2. Preset quality 10: blocking. Open the one block tab and click a block in the white background. How many quantised values are non-zero? What does the block look like after decoding, and why do neighbouring background blocks differ?
J3. Choose a block of the micrograph and compare its tab at quality 10 and 90: the zigzag sequence, the number of symbols and the bits. Where do the zeros come from?
J4. Preset ringing at an edge (test card, quality 25). Where does the error appear? Switch to SSIM map. Then lower the quality to 10 and look at the gradient at the top of the card.
J5. Preset colour bleeding (4:2:0). Toggle chroma 4:2:0 off and on: what changes in the image, the size and the PSNR? Why does the SSIM not change?
J6. Preset flat table, same size. Compare PSNR and SSIM with the standard table at quality 50 (untick the flat table). Which wins on the numbers? Look at the difference image: where does each table put its error? Why does JPEG use the non-flat table anyway?
J7. Preset recompress 10× (quality 75, grid moved 4 pixels each time). Compare 1 and 10 generations. Then untick move grid: what happens now, and why?
J8. rate–distortion tab, micrograph and test card. At 1 bit per pixel, which image has the higher PSNR? Why are the curves so different?






Solutions





J1. Quality 90: 34 681 bytes, 1.9 : 1, PSNR 36.5 dB, SSIM 0.985; no visible difference. Quality 50: 14 373 bytes (4.6 : 1), 26.7 dB, 0.891; quality 25: 9 219 bytes (7.1 : 1), 24.8 dB, 0.827; quality 10: 5 021 bytes (13.1 : 1), 22.6 dB, 0.719. Around quality 25–50 the fine grain starts to be smoothed and the background shows faint blocks; at 10 the blocks are obvious.
J2. In the white background only the DC (and perhaps one or two low frequencies) survives: each block decodes to a flat square at its own mean. Neighbouring blocks have slightly different means (and their DCs are rounded to a step of 80/8 = 10 grey levels at quality 10), so the flat squares do not match at the borders: blocking.
J3. At quality 10 a block of the cell has a handful of non-zero values at the start of the zigzag and then EOB; at quality 90 there are dozens of non-zero values (45 per block on average) and long symbol lists, about 270 bits per block on average. The zeros come from quantisation: high-frequency coefficients are smaller than half their (large) step.
J4. Next to the thin dark lines and edges: ripples parallel to them, in the blocks that contain an edge; flat blocks without an edge are almost error-free. The SSIM map is dark in exactly those blocks. At quality 10 the steep ramps at the top become staircases of flat 8 × 8 blocks (PSNR 27.1 dB, SSIM 0.949).
J5. At quality 75: 4:4:4 gives 5 230 bytes and PSNR 41.7 dB; 4:2:0 gives 3 567 bytes and 33.9 dB. The colour channels now cost a third of what they did; the red/blue edge gets a purple fringe a pixel or two wide. The SSIM is computed on the brightness (Y′) only, which is identical in both (0.996).
J6. Flat table (step 42): 14 257 bytes, PSNR 27.1 dB, SSIM 0.900; standard table at quality 50: 14 373 bytes, 26.7 dB, 0.891. The flat table wins on both numbers at the same size: for squared error, an equal step for all coefficients is the better strategy. The standard table spends its bits on low frequencies and throws away more fine detail, which the eye notices less than noise in smooth areas; JPEG is tuned for viewers, not for MSE. (For data analysis that tuning is not necessarily what you want: next unit.)
J7. One generation: 29.8 dB; ten generations with the grid moved: 25.1 dB (SSIM 0.883). Without moving the grid it stays at 29.8 dB: quantising the same blocks with the same table again changes almost nothing (the decoded image is already almost on the quantisation grid). A shifted grid sees new blocks, whose coefficients are not quantised yet: every save loses again.
J8. At 1 bpp the test card is at about 41 dB (between quality 75: 0.88 bpp, 37.2 dB, and quality 90: 1.14 bpp, 46.3 dB), the micrograph at about 24 dB (between quality 10: 0.61 bpp, 22.6 dB, and quality 25: 1.13 bpp, 24.8 dB). The card is flat regions and a few edges, which few coefficients describe; the micrograph is grainy texture everywhere, which costs bits at every quality.

title: Exercise: the JPEG pipeline, artefacts and quality metrics
text:
Explore: same MSE, different quality
The cell (or the test card) distorted five ways, each tuned to the same MSE: a brightness shift, a contrast change, Gaussian noise, a blur, and JPEG (with a continuously scaled table). Each panel shows its parameter, MSE, PSNR and SSIM. show SSIM maps replaces the images by their SSIM maps (white = 1).



S1. MSE 144. Rank the five distorted images by how good they look to you. Then rank them by SSIM. Do the rankings agree?
S2. Show the SSIM maps. Where does each distortion lose structure?
S3. Set the MSE to 25 and to 400. How does the SSIM of the brightness shift change, and that of the blur?
S4. Choose the test card at MSE 144. Which distortion is now the worst by SSIM, and which is barely affected? Why is this different from the cell?






Solutions





S1. PSNR is 26.6 dB for all. SSIM: brightness shift 0.996 (darker by 12.2), contrast change 0.973, JPEG 0.888, noise 0.884, blur 0.877 (σ = 0.66). Most viewers rank the shift and the contrast change as almost perfect and the other three as clearly degraded, like SSIM; MSE cannot tell them apart.
S2. Shift and contrast: almost white everywhere (structure kept). Noise: uniformly grey, worst in flat regions where the noise is large compared with the local contrast. Blur and JPEG: darkest in the fine-textured regions, where the small structures are smoothed away; JPEG also in a block pattern.
S3. Brightness shift: 0.999 at MSE 25, 0.987 at MSE 400. Blur: 0.981 at MSE 25, 0.629 at MSE 400 (σ = 1.22). The shift never hurts structure; the blur removes ever more of the fine texture.
S4. Noise is now by far the worst (SSIM 0.613): the card is mostly flat, and noise is clearly visible there. Blur (0.975) and the brightness shift (0.991) are barely affected: the card has few fine details to blur. JPEG 0.947. Which distortion is “worst” depends on the image content, not only on the error energy.

title: Exercise: the JPEG pipeline, artefacts and quality metrics
text:
Where this leads
PSNR and SSIM measure what a viewer would notice. A scientist needs something else: are the numbers still right? The next unit runs a spot-counting and intensity measurement on compressed fluorescence images, and shows that a JPEG that looks perfect can still shift the intensities of dim spots by several percent. It also introduces JPEG 2000 (wavelets instead of blocks) and the formats that keep data intact.

title: Level sets and marching squares
text:
About this lecture
A threshold tells us which pixels belong to a bright object. Today we draw its boundary as a curve with sub-pixel precision, in 2D; the next unit does the same in 3D.

The boundary at level c: the level set \{I = c\}, an isocontour.
Marching squares: each 2 \times 2 cell on its own, 16 cases, crossing points by linear interpolation.
The two saddle cases, and the asymptotic decider that resolves them.
Measuring a contour: length, and the enclosed area by the shoelace formula.
Real images: noise, blur, and the choice of c.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

This unit owns marching squares for the whole course: the level-set elective draws its zero contours with the same code (lib/marching.ts) and only recalls the idea. Prerequisites: bilinear interpolation from “Images as arrays”; thresholds (one line here; the thresholding day owns them).

title: Level sets and marching squares
section: A boundary is where the image crosses a value
text:
A boundary is where the image crosses a value

A bright object on a dark background: inside I > c, outside I < c. The boundary is where I = c.
The set of points \{(x, y) : I(x, y) = c\} is the level set of I at level c. In 2D it is a set of curves, an isocontour: the contour lines of a height map, with I as the height. In 3D it is a surface (next unit).
Thresholding at c labels whole pixels (the thresholding day). The level set lies between the pixel centres: where exactly between a pixel of 40 and one of 200 does I pass 120?
One c gives one boundary; a different c moves it, merges or splits pieces. Choosing c comes back in the last unit of the day.

title: Level sets and marching squares
section: We only know the image at the pixels
text:
We only know the image at the pixels
Treat pixel centres as grid points and look at one cell of 2 \times 2 pixels at a time.


Mark each corner above (orange, I > c) or below c. Four corners, two states: a 4-bit case index, 2^4 = 16 cases. Corners 0, 1, 2, 3 = top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left, bit k = corner k.
An edge whose two corners disagree is crossed by the contour, exactly once. The case says which edges are crossed and how to connect them.
Cases 0 and 15: no contour. Cases 5 and 10: four crossings, two ways to connect them (later).

title: Level sets and marching squares
text:
Where on the edge?
Along an edge from corner a (value I_a) to corner b (value I_b), assume I changes linearly. It reaches c at the fraction
t = \frac{c - I_a}{I_b - I_a}
of the way from a to b.

Example: I_a = 40, I_b = 200, c = 120: t = 80/160 = 0.5. With c = 80: t = 0.25, closer to the dark pixel.
Midpoint rule (t = \tfrac12 always): the contour of the thresholded image. It only knows above/below, so it is blocky, with steps of half a pixel.
Linear interpolation uses the grey values: a smooth contour, accurate to a fraction of a pixel when the image is smooth.

title: Level sets and marching squares
text:
The math: the crossing point
The straight line through (0, I_a) and (1, I_b) is f(t) = I_a + t\,(I_b - I_a). Setting f(t) = c:
t = \frac{c - I_a}{I_b - I_a} \in (0, 1)\quad\text{when } c \text{ lies strictly between } I_a \text{ and } I_b.

The point is \mathbf p = \mathbf p_a + t\,(\mathbf p_b - \mathbf p_a).
Computed from the same two values, it is the same point whichever of the two neighbouring cells computes it.
Along a cell edge the bilinear interpolant of images/ is this straight line, so the crossing points lie exactly on the level set of the bilinear interpolant.

title: Level sets and marching squares
section: Marching: every cell on its own
text:
Marching: every cell on its own

Visit the cells one by one (“marching” over the grid). Each cell needs only its 4 corners: no global step, every cell could be processed in parallel.
Two neighbouring cells share an edge, so they compute the same crossing point there: the segments join up. The result is a set of closed curves, or curves that end at the image border.
Pad the image with a frame of background pixels, and every contour closes.
Orientation: connect each segment so that the bright side is always on the same side. Then outer boundaries run one way round and the boundaries of holes the other way: that sign is what makes the area formula work.

title: Level sets and marching squares
section: Try it: marching squares by hand
text:
Try it: marching squares by hand




An 8 × 8 grid of values (one bump, maximum 9.1); case numbers in the cells, the selected cell’s arithmetic in the readout. Tour: move c from 5 down to 3 and up to 8: one closed contour that grows and shrinks. Click a cell on the contour, e.g. (2, 2): corners 4.7, 6.1, 8.8, 6.7, case 14, one crossed edge pair. Drag a corner value up or down and watch the crossing points slide. “All 16 cases”: find all of them; 5 and 10 are drawn in purple. “Midpoint vs linear” at c = 3: the midpoint contour is an octagon-like staircase; the dashed red curve is the exact level curve of the bilinear interpolant.

title: Level sets and marching squares
text:
Saddle cells: two valid answers


Case 5 (corners 0 and 2 above) and case 10 (corners 1 and 3): diagonal corners above, the other two below. Four crossings, two ways to pair them:

separate the two bright corners (two small bright pieces), or
join them through the cell (one bright band, the dark corners cut off).

The corners alone cannot decide. A fixed rule (always separate) still gives closed, consistent curves, but sometimes the wrong topology: two objects where there is one, or the reverse.

title: Level sets and marching squares
text:
The asymptotic decider
Use the values, not only the signs. The bilinear interpolant inside the cell (from images/) has curved level lines: hyperbolas. In a saddle cell it has a saddle point with value f^\ast:

if f^\ast > c, the middle of the cell is above c: the bright corners are joined;
if f^\ast < c, the middle is below c: they are separated.

Example (corners clockwise from top-left: 8, 4, 7, 3, c = 5): f^\ast = (8 \cdot 7 - 4 \cdot 3)/(8 + 7 - 4 - 3) = 44/8 = 5.5 > 5: join. With 6 instead of 8 and 6.5 instead of 7: f^\ast = 27/5.5 = 4.91 < 5: separate.
Two neighbouring cells never disagree: the decision is made inside one cell (Nielson & Hamann, 1991).

title: Level sets and marching squares
section: The math: the saddle of the bilinear interpolant
text:
The math: the saddle of the bilinear interpolant
On the cell [0, 1]^2 with corner values I_{00}, I_{10}, I_{01}, I_{11} (first index x):
f(x, y) = I_{00}(1-x)(1-y) + I_{10}\,x(1-y) + I_{01}(1-x)\,y + I_{11}\,xy = A + Bx + Cy + Dxy,
with D = I_{00} + I_{11} - I_{10} - I_{01}. Setting \partial_x f = B + Dy = 0 and \partial_y f = C + Dx = 0 gives the saddle at x^\ast = -C/D, y^\ast = -B/D, with value
f^\ast = A - \frac{BC}{D} = \frac{I_{00}I_{11} - I_{10}I_{01}}{I_{00} + I_{11} - I_{10} - I_{01}}.

f - f^\ast = D\,(x - x^\ast)(y - y^\ast): the level lines are hyperbolas with asymptotes x = x^\ast and y = y^\ast (hence the name).
In a saddle case the two bright corners lie in opposite quadrants around (x^\ast, y^\ast); they are connected inside the cell exactly when the region \{f > c\} contains the centre point of the hyperbolas, i.e. when f^\ast > c.

title: Level sets and marching squares
text:
Measuring a contour

Length: the sum of the segment lengths.
Enclosed area: the shoelace formula (from the labelling day’s shape features, restated here): for a closed polygon (x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_n, y_n), A = \tfrac12 \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i\,y_{i+1} - x_{i+1}\,y_i), \qquad (x_{n+1}, y_{n+1}) = (x_1, y_1).
Example: the diamond (1, 0), (2, 1), (1, 2), (0, 1): \tfrac12\big[(1 - 0) + (4 - 1) + (1 - 0) + (0 - 1)\big] = 2.
Signed: one direction round gives +, the other -. With the orientation of marching squares, holes count negative automatically; summing over all contours gives the bright area.
Compare: counting pixels above c gives almost the same area, but the pixel boundary (a staircase) has the wrong length.

title: Level sets and marching squares
section: The math: why the shoelace works
text:
The math: why the shoelace works

Each term \tfrac12(x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i) = \tfrac12\det\begin{bmatrix} x_i & x_{i+1} \\ y_i & y_{i+1}\end{bmatrix} is the signed area of the triangle (origin, \mathbf p_i, \mathbf p_{i+1}). Summed around the polygon, the parts outside cancel.
Equivalently, Green’s theorem: A = \oint \tfrac12(x\,dy - y\,dx), evaluated exactly on straight segments.
This is the 2D version of the divergence theorem. The last unit of the day uses the 3D version to get the volume of a closed surface from its triangles.

title: Level sets and marching squares
text:
Real images: noise and blur

Noise: every pixel that noise pushes across c starts a tiny contour of its own, and the boundary becomes ragged. Lengths explode; areas are almost unaffected (the specks inside and outside roughly cancel).
Blur first (Gaussian, kernels/): the noise is averaged away, contours become smooth and few. Too much blur rounds corners, moves the contour of small objects, and breaks or closes thin necks.
c decides the topology: two blobs joined by a valley are one contour below the valley’s height and two above it.

title: Level sets and marching squares
section: Try it: contours of an image
text:
Try it: contours of an image




128 × 128 test image (two Gaussian blobs, two discs joined by a 3-pixel neck, background 30) or the micrograph. Tour: “noise” (σ_n = 25, c = 120): 141 contours (111 outer, 30 holes), total length 935 px, yet enclosed area 2138 px² against 2212 pixels above c. “Blur first” (σ = 1.5): 3 contours, length 385 px. Raise the blur to 2.5: the neck breaks and the dumbbell falls apart (4 contours). “Two blobs merge as c drops”: lower c from 140; the two blobs join at about c = 96 (their saddle value). Then the micrograph.

title: Level sets and marching squares
text:
Summary

The boundary at level c is the level set \{I = c\}: curves in 2D, surfaces in 3D.
Marching squares: per cell, 4 corners → case index (16 cases) → crossed edges → segments. Shared edges make the curves close up.
Crossing points by linear interpolation t = (c - I_a)/(I_b - I_a); the midpoint rule gives the blocky boundary of the thresholded image.
Saddle cases 5 and 10 are ambiguous; the asymptotic decider joins the bright corners when the bilinear saddle value exceeds c.
Length by summing segments, area by the shoelace formula; noise makes many tiny contours, blur first.

title: Quiz: energy and probability
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Spins s_p = \pm 1, energy E(\mathbf s) = -J\sum_{(p,q)} s_ps_q - h\sum_p s_p, Gibbs distribution p(\mathbf s) = e^{-E(\mathbf s)/T}/Z.

Q1. Two images differ only in one pixel. The first has energy 3 units lower. At T = 1, how much more probable is it? Do you need Z?






Hint





Take the ratio of the two probabilities.









Answer





e^{3} \approx 20 times more probable. Z cancels in the ratio: only the energy difference is needed.




Q2. What happens to the Gibbs distribution as T \to 0? As T \to \infty?






Hint





Compare e^{-E/T} for two different energies when T is tiny, and when it is huge.









Answer





As T \to 0, all probability goes to the lowest-energy states (the ground states): sampling becomes energy minimisation. As T \to \infty, e^{-E/T} \to 1 for every state, so all states become equally likely and the energy no longer matters.




Q3. In a 2 \times 2 lattice with J = 1, h = 0, how many states have energy 0, and why can the level E = 0 be more probable than the level E = -4 although each of its states is less probable?






Hint





A level’s probability is (number of states) \times (probability of one state).









Answer





12 states: all except the 2 aligned states and the 2 checkerboards. The level has 12 states against 2, so at high enough T (e.g. T = 4: 0.66 against 0.30) the many slightly worse states together outweigh the two best ones.




Q4. What does a positive field h do to the two ground states “all +1” and “all -1”?






Hint





Without a field the two have the same energy.









Answer





It lowers the energy of “all +1” by nh and raises that of “all -1” by nh. Their probability ratio becomes e^{2nh/T}: the field breaks the tie, and “all +1” becomes the single most probable state. In an image model the field is the data term.




Q5. Why can we not compute the probability of one particular 256 \times 256 binary image under an Ising model?






Hint





What is needed besides e^{-E/T}?









Answer





We need Z, a sum over all 2^{65536} \approx 10^{19728} states. It cannot be computed by listing, and in 2D there is no general shortcut. Energies and ratios of probabilities are easy; absolute probabilities are not.




Q6. For pixels on a line, Z can be computed quickly. What is the trick, and which algorithm from the graph-cut day does it resemble?






Hint





Go along the line one pixel at a time.









Answer





Sum from left to right, keeping the total weight of all partial chains that end in +1 and in -1; each new pixel updates these two numbers with a 2 \times 2 table (the transfer matrix). It is dynamic programming on a chain, as in segchain, with “minimum” replaced by “sum”: n steps instead of 2^n terms.




Q7. On the graph-cut day the smoothness weight was \lambda. Which Ising parameter is it, and what plays the role of the data term?






Hint





Write s_p = 2L_p - 1.









Answer





\lambda = 2J: a disagreeing pair costs 2J more than an agreeing one. The field is the data term: D_p(1) - D_p(0) = -2h_p, with a pixel-dependent field h_p when the data differ between pixels. The minimum cut is the Ising ground state.




Q8. (math) Show that p \propto e^{-E/T} is unchanged when a constant is added to every energy.






Answer





e^{-(E + c)/T} = e^{-c/T}\,e^{-E/T}. The factor e^{-c/T} is the same for every state, so it multiplies Z too and cancels in e^{-(E + c)/T}/Z'. Only energy differences matter.

title: Exercise: energy and probability
text:
By hand
B1. The 2 \times 2 lattice has 4 neighbour pairs and 16 states. (a) Group the 16 states by energy: how many have E = -4, E = 0 and E = +4? Draw one of each. (b) Write Z as a function of T and evaluate it at T = 1 and T = 4. (c) What is the probability of the energy level E = -4 at T = 1 and at T = 4? Of one particular aligned state? (d) At T = 4, which energy level is most probable? Which single state is most probable? Explain the difference.
B2. Same 2 \times 2 lattice at T = 1, now with a field h = 0.5. (a) Compute the energies of “all +1” and “all -1”. (b) By what factor is “all +1” more likely than “all -1”? Answer without computing Z. (c) With Z = 427.20, give both probabilities. Where has the probability of “all -1” gone?
B3. Temperature. For the 2 \times 2 lattice, describe without computing what happens to p(\text{all } +1) as T \to 0 and as T \to \infty. What do the two limits correspond to in image analysis?
B4. Negative coupling. Take J = -1, h = 0 on the 2 \times 2 lattice at T = 1. Which states are now most probable, and with what total probability? (Use B1: what happens to the energy of each state when J changes sign?)
B5. From spins to labels. A row of 4 pixels has the Ising energy E = -J(s_1s_2 + s_2s_3 + s_3s_4) - h(s_1 + s_2 + s_3 + s_4), with J = 1, h = 0.5. (a) Compute E for \mathbf s = (+, +, -, -) and for (+, -, +, -). (b) With labels L_p = (s_p + 1)/2, write the energy as \sum_p D_p(L_p) + \lambda\sum[L_p \ne L_q] + \text{const}. What are \lambda, D_p(1) - D_p(0) and the constant? (c) Check (b) on the two states of (a).
B6. How many states? How many states has a 4 \times 4 lattice, a 16 \times 16 lattice, a 256 \times 256 image? If a computer evaluates 10^9 energies per second, how long does Z take for the 4 \times 4 and for the 16 \times 16 lattice?






Solutions





B1. (a) Two aligned states (all pairs agree): E = -4. Two checkerboards (all pairs disagree): E = +4. The other 12 states have two agreeing and two disagreeing pairs: E = 0. (One -1 among three +1: the -1 disagrees with its two neighbours and the other two pairs agree; two -1 side by side: the two pairs across the middle disagree.) (b) Z = 2e^{4/T} + 12 + 2e^{-4/T}. T = 1: 109.196 + 12 + 0.037 = 121.23. T = 4: 5.437 + 12 + 0.736 = 18.17. (c) Level E = -4: 109.20/121.23 = 0.901 at T = 1; 5.437/18.17 = 0.299 at T = 4. One aligned state: half of that, 0.450 and 0.150. (d) At T = 4 the level E = 0 has probability 12/18.17 = 0.660: most probable. But each of its 12 states has only 1/18.17 = 0.055, less than an aligned state (0.150). A single low-energy state is always the most probable state; a level with many states can still win because of their number.
B2. (a) All +1: E = -4 - 4 \cdot 0.5 = -6. All -1: E = -4 + 2 = -2. (b) e^{-(-6) + (-2)} = e^{4} = 54.6. (c) p(\text{all } +1) = e^6/427.20 = 0.944, p(\text{all } -1) = e^2/427.20 = 0.017. Without the field both had 0.450; the field moved almost all the probability of “all -1” to “all +1”. The field breaks the tie between the two ground states.
B3. As T \to 0 the two ground states share all the probability: p(\text{all } +1) \to \tfrac12 (and with any small h > 0 it goes to 1). As T \to \infty every state gets \tfrac1{16}. The first limit is energy minimisation (graph cuts find the ground state); the second is “the prior means nothing”: every image equally plausible.
B4. With J = -1 every energy changes sign: the two checkerboards now have E = -4, the aligned states +4. The 12 others stay at 0. So Z is the same, 121.23, and the two checkerboards carry 0.901 of the probability together. An antiferromagnet prefers disagreeing neighbours.
B5. (a) (+, +, -, -): pairs +1 - 1 + 1 = 1, field sum 0: E = -1. (+, -, +, -): pairs -3, field 0: E = +3. (b) \lambda = 2J = 2; D_p(1) - D_p(0) = -2h = -1 (take D_p(1) = -1, D_p(0) = 0); constant = \sum_p h - 3J = 2 - 3 = -1. So E = -(\text{number of object pixels}) + 2 \cdot (\text{number of boundaries}) - 1. (c) (+, +, -, -): 2 object pixels, 1 boundary: -2 + 2 - 1 = -1. (+, -, +, -): 2 object pixels, 3 boundaries: -2 + 6 - 1 = 3. Both agree with (a).
B6. 2^{16} = 65\,536 (well under a millisecond), 2^{256} \approx 1.2 \cdot 10^{77} (about 10^{68} seconds, far longer than the age of the universe, 4 \cdot 10^{17} s), 2^{65536} \approx 10^{19728}. Exact Z is out of the question for any real image.




Math questions
B7. (math) Show that adding a constant c to every energy leaves the Gibbs distribution unchanged, and that p(\mathbf a)/p(\mathbf b) depends only on E_a - E_b. Show that for two lattices that do not interact, E = E_1 + E_2, the Gibbs distribution factorises and Z = Z_1Z_2.
B8. (math) Derive the general translation of B5: with s_p = 2L_p - 1 and m neighbour pairs, show that E_{\text{Ising}} = \sum_p(-2h_p)L_p + 2J\sum_{(p,q)}[L_p \ne L_q] + \sum_p h_p - mJ.
B9. (math) Transfer matrix. For a ring of n spins with h = 0, show that Z = \operatorname{tr}(M^n) with M = \begin{bmatrix} e^{J/T} & e^{-J/T} \\ e^{-J/T} & e^{J/T}\end{bmatrix}, find the eigenvalues of M, and evaluate Z for n = 3, J = 1, T = 1. Check by listing the 8 states. What fraction of Z comes from the larger eigenvalue for n = 3, n = 10 and n = 100?






Solutions (math)





B7. e^{-(E + c)/T}/\sum e^{-(E' + c)/T} = e^{-c/T}e^{-E/T}/(e^{-c/T}\sum e^{-E'/T}): the factor cancels. p(\mathbf a)/p(\mathbf b) = e^{-E_a/T}/e^{-E_b/T} = e^{-(E_a - E_b)/T}; Z cancels. With E = E_1(\mathbf s_1) + E_2(\mathbf s_2): e^{-E/T} = e^{-E_1/T}e^{-E_2/T} and Z = \sum_{\mathbf s_1}\sum_{\mathbf s_2}e^{-E_1/T}e^{-E_2/T} = Z_1Z_2, so p(\mathbf s_1, \mathbf s_2) = p_1(\mathbf s_1)\,p_2(\mathbf s_2).
B8. s_ps_q = 1 if L_p = L_q and -1 otherwise, so s_ps_q = 1 - 2[L_p \ne L_q] and -Js_ps_q = 2J[L_p \ne L_q] - J; summed over m pairs: 2J\sum[L_p \ne L_q] - mJ. And -h_ps_p = -h_p(2L_p - 1) = -2h_pL_p + h_p. Adding gives the result.
B9. e^{-E/T} = \prod_i e^{Js_is_{i+1}/T} = \prod_i M_{s_is_{i+1}}; summing over s_1, \dots, s_n is the matrix product \sum M_{s_1s_2}M_{s_2s_3}\cdots M_{s_ns_1} = \operatorname{tr}(M^n). M has eigenvectors (1, 1) and (1, -1) with eigenvalues e^{J/T} \pm e^{-J/T} = 2\cosh(J/T),\ 2\sinh(J/T), and \operatorname{tr}(M^n) = \mu_1^n + \mu_2^n. n = 3: 3.0862^3 + 2.3504^3 = 29.39 + 12.98 = 42.38. Listing: 2 aligned states with E = -3 and 6 states with one spin different (E = +1): 2e^3 + 6e^{-1} = 40.17 + 2.21 = 42.38. Fraction from \mu_1^n: 0.694 (n = 3), 0.938 (n = 10), 1 - 1.5 \cdot 10^{-12} (n = 100): for long chains only the largest eigenvalue matters.

title: Exercise: energy and probability
text:
Explore
The demo lists every state of a 2 \times 2 (16 states) or 3 \times 3 (512 states) lattice. Click a spin to flip it (orange +1, blue -1). Bonds are green where the pair lowers the energy and red where it raises it; dashed stubs are the wrap-around pairs of the periodic boundary (the 3 \times 3 torus has 18 pairs, the free 3 \times 3 lattice 12). The readout gives E (split into pairs and field), e^{-E/T}, Z and the probability of the state shown. The bars are the probabilities of the energy levels (number of states above each bar; orange: the level of the current state), or of the magnetisation m.



E1. Preset 2×2 by hand. Check B1: read Z and p of the aligned state at T = 1. Flip one spin: what are E and p now? Move T to 4 and compare the bars with B1(c, d).
E2. Choose 3 \times 3, periodic, T = 2. How many energy levels are there, and how many states does the lowest one have? What is the probability of the two ground states together? Why does the level E = -2 have so many states and so little probability?
E3. Preset T → 0 and then T → ∞. Describe the two bar charts. In the second, why are the bars nearly proportional to the number of states?
E4. Preset a field breaks the tie (T = 1.5, h = 0.3, magnetisation tab). Read p(m = 1) and p(m = -1). Which is larger: p(m = -1) or p(m = 7/9)? Explain.
E5. Preset J < 0: checkerboards win (free boundary). Read the probability of the lowest level. Now switch to periodic. What is the lowest energy now, and how many states have it? Why can a 3 \times 3 torus not be a perfect checkerboard?






Solutions





E1. Z = 121.2, p = 0.450 for all +1. One flipped spin: E = 0, p = 0.00825 = 1/Z. At T = 4: Z = 18.17; the bars are 0.299 (E = -4), 0.660 (E = 0), 0.040 (E = 4), as in B1.
E2. Six levels: E = -18, -10, -6, -2, 2, 6 with 2, 18, 48, 198, 144, 102 states; Z = 20\,438. The two ground states carry 0.793 together (0.396 each). The level E = -2 has 198 states, but each one has weight e^{1} against e^{9} for a ground state: 198e^{1} = 538 against 2e^{9} = 16\,206, so it gets only 0.026.
E3. At T = 0.3 the two ground states carry all the probability (1.000); every other level is invisible. At T = 100 every state has almost the same weight, so a level’s probability is its share of the 512 states: E = -2 (198 states) 0.394, E = 2 (144) 0.275, E = 6 (102) 0.187, and the ground states only 0.005. Counting states, not energy, decides.
E4. p(m = 1) = 0.941 and p(m = -1) = 0.026. p(m = 7/9) = 0.027 is (slightly) larger than p(m = -1): “all -1” is a single state with the lowest pair energy, while m = 7/9 has 9 states (one spin down), each with 8 more units of pair energy but a better field term. At this temperature the 9 states together just beat the lone state on the wrong side.
E5. Free 3 \times 3 (J = -1, T = 1): the two checkerboards have E = -12 (all 12 pairs disagree) and carry 0.890. Periodic: the lowest energy is E = -6, shared by 102 states (0.974 together). Each row and column of the torus is a ring of 3 spins: around an odd ring at least one pair must agree. So no state can make all 18 pairs disagree (this is called frustration); many states share the best compromise.

title: Intensity inside an object
text:
About this lecture
A segmentation gives a label image; a measurement turns it into a table: one row per object, one column per property. The size and shape columns were the labelling day. Today: what the pixel values inside an object tell us.

Statistics of the values: integrated, mean, spread, median, quartiles, MAD.
Which numbers survive a background offset, a gain, a mask one pixel too large, saturation.
Where the signal is: edge intensity, mass displacement, radial distribution.
From a table to numbers you can compare: units, aggregation per well, normalisation.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

This is the first of four units of the measurements day: intensity (this), texture, relations between objects, colocalisation between channels. The day is a practical catalogue; theory owned by other days (perimeter estimators, moments, convex hull, the distance transform, PCA, the statistics of measurements) is recalled in one line with a pointer. Coordinates: x = column, y = row (down), pixel centres at integers.

title: Intensity inside an object
text:
Same mask, same total signal

Six synthetic cells: identical mask (6521 px), identical sum of the pixel values (652 100). Uniform, bright rim, one off-centre spot, punctate, gradient, nuclear.

Area, shape and the total are the same. A biologist would call these six different phenotypes.
Which numbers separate them? Spread, extremes, where the signal sits relative to the centre and the edge.


The cells are the patterns of the intensityfeat demo (160 × 160, an ellipse with semi-axes 52 and 40, blurred by a Gaussian of σ = 1.2 px to mimic the optics, scaled so that the mean inside the mask is 100). Ask the class which of them they could tell apart with “mean intensity” alone: none.

Statistics of the pixel values

Integrated intensity = their sum: proportional to the amount of dye (DNA content: G2 nuclei have twice the integrated DAPI of G1 nuclei).

title: Intensity inside an object
text:
The math: intensity statistics
For the values I_1, \dots, I_n of the pixels of \Omega:
S = \sum_k I_k, \qquad \mu = \frac{S}{n}, \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{\frac1n \sum_k (I_k - \mu)^2}.

\sigma divides by n: the pixels are the whole object, not a sample (tools differ; n - 1 changes little for n in the hundreds).
Quantiles q_p by sorting: position h = (n-1)p in the sorted list, linear interpolation between neighbours. Median q_{0.5}, quartiles q_{0.25}, q_{0.75}.
\mathrm{MAD} = \operatorname{median}_k |I_k - q_{0.5}|. For normal data \mathrm{MAD} = \sigma\,\Phi^{-1}(0.75) = 0.6745\,\sigma, so 1.4826 \cdot \mathrm{MAD} estimates \sigma.
Sorting costs O(n \log n) per object; sums cost O(n), for all objects in one scan.

title: Intensity inside an object
text:
The math: offset and gain
Write the measured image as J = g\,I + b (gain g > 0, offset b).

Sum: \sum_\Omega J = g \sum_\Omega I + b\,n. Mean: \mu_J = g\,\mu_I + b. Every quantile moves the same way: q_p(J) = g\,q_p(I) + b (sorting is unchanged by an increasing map).
Spread: \sigma_J = g\,\sigma_I and \mathrm{MAD}_J = g\,\mathrm{MAD}_I: differences cancel b.
A ratio of two means \mu_1/\mu_2 (edge / mean, nucleus / cytoplasm) cancels g but not b: \frac{g\mu_1 + b}{g\mu_2 + b} moves towards 1 as b grows.
So subtract the background before any ratio, and divide by a reference after.

title: Intensity inside an object
text:
Local background
The offset is rarely constant across an image. Measure it next to each object:

A ring around the object: skip a gap of a few pixels (the blurred edge), then take a band of a few pixels; leave out pixels that belong to other objects.
Background = the median of the ring (robust to a neighbour’s edge or debris).
Subtract it from every pixel of the object, then compute the statistics.

The ring is “distance to the object between gap and gap + width”: a threshold of the distance transform of the background (morphology day).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Intensity inside an object
text:
Edge intensity
The edge band = the object minus its erosion by one pixel (the cross): the object pixels that have a 4-neighbour outside (morphology day).

The same statistics on the band: edge mean, edge integrated, …
Edge / mean separates rim staining (a membrane marker) from filled staining.
Demo: bright rim 2.43, uniform 0.66 (not 1: the optics blur the edge, so the outermost pixels are darker), nuclear 0.28.
It is sensitive to the mask: one pixel inwards or outwards moves the band to a very different place in the edge profile.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Intensity inside an object
text:
Mass displacement
Two centres of an object:

the geometric centroid: mean pixel position (labelling day);
the intensity-weighted centroid: each pixel counts with its value, the “centre of mass” of the signal.

Mass displacement = the distance between them (in px, or µm with the pixel size).

0 for a uniform or a rim-stained cell (by symmetry), large when the signal is polarised: demo off-centre spot 8.9 px, gradient 10.6 px.
Noise and a background offset pull the weighted centroid towards the geometric one: subtract the background first.

title: Intensity inside an object
section: The math: the first intensity moment
text:
The math: the first intensity moment
Intensity moments are the region moments of the labelling day with weights I(\mathbf x):
M_{pq} = \sum_{(x,y)\in\Omega} I(x,y)\, x^p y^q, \qquad \bar{\mathbf x}_I = \Big(\frac{M_{10}}{M_{00}}, \frac{M_{01}}{M_{00}}\Big), \qquad \bar{\mathbf x} = \Big(\frac{m_{10}}{m_{00}}, \frac{m_{01}}{m_{00}}\Big).

Mass displacement = \lVert \bar{\mathbf x}_I - \bar{\mathbf x} \rVert.
With I = c constant, M_{pq} = c\,m_{pq} and the two centroids coincide.
With J = I + b: \bar{\mathbf x}_J = \frac{M_{00}\,\bar{\mathbf x}_I + b\,n\,\bar{\mathbf x}}{M_{00} + b\,n}, a weighted average that slides towards \bar{\mathbf x} as b grows.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Intensity inside an object
text:
Radial distribution
Divide the object into k rings that follow its shape, from the centre to the edge.

For each pixel: d_c = distance to the centre point, d_e = distance to the edge (the distance transform). Normalised position \rho = d_c/(d_c + d_e): 0 at the centre, close to 1 at the edge, whatever the shape.
Ring j holds the pixels with \rho in [\tfrac{j-1}{k}, \tfrac{j}{k}).
FracAtD: the share of the object’s total intensity in ring j.
MeanFrac: FracAtD divided by the share of the object’s pixels in ring j: 1 = as expected for uniform staining, > 1 enriched, < 1 depleted.
RadialCV: how unequal the ring is around the circle (coefficient of variation over 8 angular sectors).

Demo, 4 rings: nuclear MeanFrac 3.26, 2.62, 0.45, 0.42; bright rim 0.52, 0.52, 0.52, 1.61; uniform about 1.

title: Intensity inside an object
text:
The math: rings
For pixel \mathbf x \in \Omega with centre \mathbf c: \rho(\mathbf x) = \dfrac{\lVert \mathbf x - \mathbf c\rVert}{\lVert \mathbf x - \mathbf c\rVert + \mathrm{DT}(\mathbf x)}, ring r(\mathbf x) = \min(k, \lfloor k\rho \rfloor + 1).
\mathrm{FracAtD}_j = \frac{\sum_{r(\mathbf x) = j} I(\mathbf x)}{\sum_\Omega I}, \qquad a_j = \frac{\#\{r(\mathbf x) = j\}}{n}, \qquad \mathrm{MeanFrac}_j = \frac{\mathrm{FracAtD}_j}{a_j}.

\sum_j \mathrm{FracAtD}_j = \sum_j a_j = 1, and \sum_j a_j\,\mathrm{MeanFrac}_j = 1: enrichment in one ring is paid for in another.
\mathrm{MeanFrac}_j = \bar I_j / \bar I: the ring’s mean over the object’s mean, so the gain cancels; an offset pulls every MeanFrac towards 1.
The centre \mathbf c matters: the centroid, the intensity maximum, or a parent object such as the nucleus (nuclear vs peripheral signal; translocation assays).

title: Intensity inside an object
text:
Try it: intensity features




Tour: “background offset” (offset 40, noise 4): mean, median and integrated move, std barely (noise adds a little), MAD becomes non-zero. Then “polarised cell”: the arrow is the mass displacement (8.9 px); switch the rings to the intensity maximum. “nuclear: radial bins”: MeanFrac 3.3 in ring 1, 0.4 at the edge. “dilated mask”: offset 10 and the mask 2 px too large: the mean drops from 110 to 104.3 and edge / mean collapses. “saturation”: the max is clipped at 300. The Δ column compares with the ideal measurement of the same cell (no offset, gain 1, no noise, exact mask).

title: Intensity inside an object
section: Per object, per image, per well
text:
Per object, per image, per well

Per-image columns use the same statistics over the whole image: total intensity, fraction of saturated pixels, a focus score. They are quality control: flag images before trusting their objects.
Units: lengths × pixel size (µm), areas × pixel size² (µm²), 3D voxels × \Delta x\,\Delta y\,\Delta z (often anisotropic: the 3D images unit). Intensities stay in the stored units: compare only images acquired and stored the same way. Ratios are dimensionless.
Aggregate objects per image or per well: the median (robust), the mean, counts and fractions (“% of cells with more than 3 spots”).
Redundant columns: area, perimeter, equivalent diameter, convex area and maximum Feret move together. Keep one per group, or summarise with PCA (day 1).

title: Intensity inside an object
text:
Normalisation: plates and batches
Wells on different plates or days differ in gain and offset (batch), and within a plate in smooth row/column gradients (edge evaporation, illumination, timing).

z-score against the control wells: (x - \text{mean}) / \text{sd}.
Robust z: (x - \text{median}) / (1.4826 \cdot \text{MAD}) of the controls: one outlying control well does not inflate the scale.
Robust z removes a plate’s offset and gain, not a gradient across it. A gradient needs a row/column correction first (subtract row and column medians: “median polish”); the scale then comes from the robust spread of all wells.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Intensity inside an object
text:
Try it: two plates




Plate demo: two plates of 4 × 6 wells, each well the median of 40 simulated cells, controls in the outer columns, four treated wells (+40). “plate offset: robust z”: raw plate B is brighter (controls 149 to 169 against 94 to 103 on plate A: gain 1.4, offset 20); robust z puts both on the same scale and finds the four treated wells (|z| > 3) and nothing else. “plate gradient hides it” (12 units per column): the controls now spread from 64 to 133 on plate A, the robust scale grows, and no treated well reaches |z| = 3 (largest 1.4). “row/column correction”: subtract row and column medians first, then a robust z over all wells; the four hits come back (z 6.8 to 9.8 on plate A) and no other well passes |z| > 3.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Intensity inside an object
section: The math: robust z and median polish
text:
The math: robust z and median polish
Controls c_1, \dots, c_m: \quad z_i = \dfrac{x_i - \operatorname{median}(c)}{1.4826\,\operatorname{MAD}(c)}.

Under x \mapsto g x + b the median moves to g\,\mathrm{med} + b and MAD scales by g: z is unchanged. That is why it removes batch gain and offset.
Breakdown: up to half the controls can be wild before the median and MAD follow them; one wild value moves the mean and sd without bound.
Median polish fits x_{rc} \approx m + a_r + b_c by alternately subtracting row medians and column medians; the residuals x_{rc} - a_r - b_c keep the treated wells (few per row and column) and lose the smooth gradient. A column made only of controls loses its spread in the polish, so the scale is taken from the MAD of all residuals (this is the idea of the “B-score”).

title: Intensity inside an object
text:
Summary

An object’s pixel values give location (mean, median, quartiles), spread (std, MAD) and amount (integrated).
A background offset moves the location and the integral, not the spread; a gain scales all but ratios; a mask that is too large dilutes the mean; saturation clips the top.
Where the signal is: edge / mean, mass displacement, and radial rings in normalised distance (FracAtD, MeanFrac).
Comparable numbers need units, a robust aggregate per well, and normalisation: robust z against controls for batches, a row/column correction for gradients.

title: Quiz: integral images
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. S(x, y) is the sum of all pixels in columns 1..x and rows 1..y, with a zero row and column at index 0.

Q1. The running totals of a row are 0, 2, 7, 7, 10, 18. What are the pixel values? What is the sum of pixels 2 to 4?






Hint





Neighbouring differences give the pixels; a range sum is one difference.









Answer





Pixels: 2, 5, 0, 3, 8. Pixels 2–4: S(4) - S(1) = 10 - 2 = 8 (= 5 + 0 + 3).




Q2. Why do we pad the table with a zero row and column?






Hint





What would S(x_0 - 1, \cdot) be for a rectangle that starts in column 1?









Answer





So that the four-corner formula works for every rectangle, including those touching the top or left border: the corner just outside the rectangle is then a real table entry with value 0. Without padding, every border case would need its own formula.




Q3. For the rectangle with corners A (above-left, outside), B (above-right), C (below-left), D (its bottom-right pixel), why is S(A) added, not subtracted?






Hint





Which pixels are in both S(B) and S(C)?









Answer





S(D) contains the rectangle plus the strip above it, the strip to its left, and the block above-left. Subtracting S(B) removes the strip above and the block; subtracting S(C) removes the strip to the left and the block again. The block has been removed twice, so S(A), which is exactly that block, is added back once.




Q4. How many additions does the sum over a 64 \times 64 window take directly, and with the integral image? Does the answer with the table change for a 256 \times 256 window?






Hint





Adding n numbers takes n - 1 additions.









Answer





Directly 64^2 - 1 = 4095 additions. With the table 3 (four lookups), and still 3 for 256 \times 256 (directly 65\,535). The cost does not depend on the size of the rectangle.




Q5. You need the sum over a single 3 \times 3 window of a 2000 \times 2000 image, once. Should you build the integral image?






Hint





What does building the table cost?









Answer





No. Building it takes about 3 \times 4 \cdot 10^6 additions; the direct sum takes 8. The table pays off only when many sums are needed (a window at every pixel), when the windows are large, or when windows of many sizes are needed.




Q6. Fill in: the running total is to a row of pixels what the ______ is to a function, and taking differences of neighbouring entries corresponds to ______.






Answer





The antiderivative (integral from the start up to x); taking differences corresponds to differentiation, which gives the function back. The range sum S(b) - S(a-1) is the discrete \int_a^b f = F(b) - F(a).




Q7. In what order must the table entries be filled with the recursion S(x,y) = I(x,y) + S(x{-}1,y) + S(x,y{-}1) - S(x{-}1,y{-}1)? Could you fill it column by column instead?






Hint





Which entries must already be known?









Answer





Each entry needs its left, upper and upper-left neighbours, so any order that visits those first works: row by row (left to right) is the usual raster order, but column by column (top to bottom) works just as well. A random order does not.




Q8. (math) How many table lookups does a box sum in a 4-dimensional table need (e.g. a 3D video, x, y, z, t)? What sign does the corner with all four coordinates at the lower end get?






Answer





2^4 = 16 lookups. A corner with u coordinates at the upper end gets the sign (-1)^{4 - u}; the all-lower corner has u = 0, sign (-1)^4 = +1.
