title: Exercise: integral images
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Running total
S(i) = f(1) + \dots + f(i), S(0) = 0; built with one addition per entry


Range sum
f(a) + \dots + f(b) = S(b) - S(a-1): one subtraction


Integral image
S(x, y) = sum of the pixels in columns 1..x and rows 1..y; S(0, y) = S(x, 0) = 0


Recursion
S(x, y) = I(x, y) + S(x-1, y) + S(x, y-1) - S(x-1, y-1), filled row by row


Rectangle, columns x_0..x_1, rows y_0..y_1
S(x_1, y_1) - S(x_1, y_0{-}1) - S(x_0{-}1, y_1) + S(x_0{-}1, y_0{-}1)


Cost
building: about 3 additions per pixel; each rectangle: 3 additions, whatever its size



Pixels are numbered from 1; x is the column (across), y the row (down). Throughout, the 5 × 5 image is
I = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 & 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 5 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 & 4 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & 0 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}
(row y = 1 on top). The demo’s preset exercise image is the same image.

title: Exercise: integral images
text:
By hand
B1. The row f = (3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6). (a) Write down the running totals S(0), \dots, S(8). (b) Compute the sums of pixels 3–7, 2–5 and 1–8 from the table. How many additions would each need directly? (c) What is S(6) - S(5)? What does a difference of two neighbouring entries give in general?
B2. (a) Build the 6 \times 6 integral image of I (with the zero row and column), row by row with the recursion. Check: the last entry must be the sum of all 25 pixels. (b) Compute the sum over the inner 3 \times 3 block (columns 2–4, rows 2–4) with four lookups. Name the four entries and their signs. Check by adding the nine pixels. (c) The same for columns 3–5, rows 2–5. (d) Get the single pixel I(3, 3) back from four table entries.
B3. A rectangle that touches the border: columns 1–3, rows 1–2. Which of the four lookups fall in the zero row or column? Do you need a special case?
B4. Counting. A 100 \times 100 image; we want the sum of the k \times k window at every position where the window fits inside the image. (a) k = 3: how many windows are there? How many additions directly, and how many with the table (building it, plus 3 per window)? (b) The same for k = 31. (c) When is the table not worth it?
B5. You change one pixel of the image, I(2, 2), from 4 to 6. Which entries of the table change, and by how much?






Solutions





B1. (a) S = 0, 3, 4, 8, 9, 14, 23, 25, 31. (b) Pixels 3–7: S(7) - S(2) = 25 - 4 = 21 (directly 4 + 1 + 5 + 9 + 2: 4 additions). Pixels 2–5: S(5) - S(1) = 14 - 3 = 11 (3 additions). Pixels 1–8: S(8) - S(0) = 31 - 0 = 31 (7 additions). With the table: always 1 subtraction. (c) S(6) - S(5) = 23 - 14 = 9 = f(6). The difference of neighbouring entries gives back the pixel: differencing undoes summing.

(row y down the side, column x across the top). Example: S(3, 3) = I(3,3) + S(2,3) + S(3,2) - S(2,2) = 5 + 11 + 10 - 7 = 19. The last entry 48 is the sum of all pixels. (b) S(4,4) - S(4,1) - S(1,4) + S(1,1) = 31 - 6 - 6 + 2 = 21. Directly: 4 + 2 + 0 + 1 + 5 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 4 = 21. (c) S(5,5) - S(5,1) - S(2,5) + S(2,1) = 48 - 7 - 17 + 2 = 26. (d) I(3,3) = S(3,3) - S(3,2) - S(2,3) + S(2,2) = 19 - 10 - 11 + 7 = 5.
B3. S(3, 2) - S(3, 0) - S(0, 2) + S(0, 0) = 10 - 0 - 0 + 0 = 10 (= 2 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 4 + 2). Three lookups fall in the zero row or column. No special case: the zeros do the work, which is the point of padding.
B4. (a) 98^2 = 9604 windows. Directly 9604 \times 8 = 76\,832 additions. With the table: building 3 \times 10\,000 = 30\,000, plus 3 \times 9604 = 28\,812: 58\,812 in total. A modest saving. (b) 70^2 = 4900 windows; directly 4900 \times 960 = 4\,704\,000; with the table 30\,000 + 14\,700 = 44\,700, about 100 times fewer. (c) For small windows and few of them: building the table costs about 3 additions per pixel, which a single 2 \times 2 window (3 additions) never pays back. It pays off for large windows, many windows, or windows of many different sizes.
B5. S(x, y) changes by +2 for every entry with x \ge 2 and y \ge 2: the 4 \times 4 block of entries from (2,2) to (5,5), 16 entries. Every other entry stays the same. (A single changed pixel can change a quarter of the table: the table is cheap to read, but not cheap to update.)




Math questions
B6. (math) Prove the corner formula of the Background from the definition S(x, y) = \sum_{x' \le x}\sum_{y' \le y} I(x', y'): count how many times each pixel of the image is included in the four terms. Then show that the recursion is the corner formula for a single pixel.
B7. (math) A volume (or a video, with time as the third axis) has a 3D table S(x, y, z) = sum over x' \le x, y' \le y, z' \le z. (a) How many lookups does the sum over a box need, and with which signs? (b) Write the recursion that builds S in one pass.
B8. (math) Show that the integral image can be built with two passes of 1D running totals: first along every row, R(x, y) = \sum_{x' \le x} I(x', y), then along every column of R. How many additions per pixel does that take?






Solutions (math)





B6. Let the rectangle be columns x_0..x_1, rows y_0..y_1. Each pixel (x', y') is in S(x, y) if x' \le x and y' \le y. Split the image into regions by whether x' < x_0, x_0 \le x' \le x_1 or x' > x_1, and the same for y'. A pixel with x' > x_1 or y' > y_1 is in none of the four terms. For the others, count the terms +S(x_1, y_1) - S(x_1, y_0{-}1) - S(x_0{-}1, y_1) + S(x_0{-}1, y_0{-}1) that contain it:

inside the rectangle: 1 - 0 - 0 + 0 = 1;
left of it (x' < x_0, y_0 \le y' \le y_1): 1 - 0 - 1 + 0 = 0;
above it (x_0 \le x' \le x_1, y' < y_0): 1 - 1 - 0 + 0 = 0;
above-left (x' < x_0, y' < y_0): 1 - 1 - 1 + 1 = 0.

So the sum contains exactly the pixels of the rectangle, once each. With x_0 = x_1 = x, y_0 = y_1 = y: I(x, y) = S(x, y) - S(x, y-1) - S(x-1, y) + S(x-1, y-1), which rearranged is the recursion.
B7. (a) 8 lookups, one per corner of the box. With lower corner (x_0{-}1, y_0{-}1, z_0{-}1) and upper (x_1, y_1, z_1): a corner with u upper coordinates has sign (-1)^{3 - u}: + for the all-upper corner, - for the three corners with two upper coordinates, + for the three with one, - for the all-lower corner. (b) S(x,y,z) = I(x,y,z) + S(x{-}1,y,z) + S(x,y{-}1,z) + S(x,y,z{-}1) - S(x{-}1,y{-}1,z) - S(x{-}1,y,z{-}1) - S(x,y{-}1,z{-}1) + S(x{-}1,y{-}1,z{-}1): the single-voxel box solved for its all-upper corner.
B8. \sum_{y' \le y} R(x, y') = \sum_{y' \le y}\sum_{x' \le x} I(x', y') = S(x, y). Each pass is one addition per pixel, so 2 additions per pixel, one fewer than the recursion (which uses 3). The two-pass form is also easier to run in parallel: all rows at once, then all columns.

title: Exercise: integral images
text:
Explore
The demo has two modes. In 1D (first), the top plot shows a row of pixel values (drag the bars up or down), the bottom plot their running total as a staircase. The sliders a and b choose a range: its bars are shaded, and the red and green dots mark S(a-1) and S(b). smooth replaces the bars by a curve f and the staircase by its antiderivative F.



In 2D (below), the left grid is the image and the right grid its table, with the zero row and column in grey. step fills one more table entry: the orange cell is the one being filled, the green + cells are added, the red − cell subtracted. fill all completes the table. Drag across the image to choose a rectangle: its four corner entries are marked with their signs, the readout writes out the sum, and a counter adds up the additions “direct” and “table” over all rectangles you have tried. edit pixels lets you change pixel values (upper half of a cell: +1, lower half: −1).


E1. In 1D, preset exercise row: check B1(b) by moving a and b. Then make pixel 6 equal to 0 (drag its bar down). Which entries of the running total change? Which range sums change?
E2. In 1D, preset one spike. Describe the staircase. Where is it steep, and where flat? Tick smooth: where does F rise fastest?
E3. In 2D, preset exercise image: press step until the cell S(3, 3) is filled. Check the four numbers in the readout against your B2(a).
E4. Fill the table, then drag the rectangles of B2(b) and B2(c). Compare with your answers. After both, what does the counter say for “direct” and “table”? Now drag the whole image: how many additions directly, and with the table?
E5. Preset one pixel, four lookups and preset rectangle at the border: compare with B2(d) and B3.
E6. Preset 1 × 8 row = 1D. Which two of the four lookups are always 0? Why is the 2D formula then the same as the 1D one?
E7. Switch to edit pixels and add 2 to the pixel at x = 2, y = 2 (exercise image, filled table). Which table entries change? Compare with B5.






Solutions





E1. With f(6) = 0, the running totals S(6), S(7), S(8) all drop by 9 (to 14, 16, 22); S(0) to S(5) stay. Every range that contains pixel 6 changes by -9 (e.g. 3–7 becomes 12); ranges that end before 6 or start after 6 do not.
E2. The staircase rises by 1 at every pixel (flat-ish, slope 1) and jumps by 9 at the spike (position 7). It is steep where the pixels are bright. With smooth, F rises fastest at the peak of f: the slope of F is f.
E3. Filling cell 13 (row 3, column 3): S(3,3) = I(3,3) + S(2,3) + S(3,2) - S(2,2) = 5 + 11 + 10 - 7 = 19.
E4. Inner 3 \times 3: 31 - 6 - 6 + 2 = 21. Columns 3–5, rows 2–5: 48 - 7 - 17 + 2 = 26. Counter after these two: direct 8 + 11 = 19, table 3 + 3 = 6. The whole image: S(5,5) - 0 - 0 + 0 = 48, directly 24 additions, with the table 3 (the counter adds them to the running totals).
E5. One pixel: 19 - 10 - 11 + 7 = 5, as in B2(d): 0 additions directly, 3 with the table, so for one pixel the table loses. Border: 10 - 0 - 0 + 0 = 10, as in B3.
E6. The two lookups in row 0 (the zero row): S(x_1, 0) and S(x_0 - 1, 0). What is left, S(x_1, 1) - S(x_0 - 1, 1), is exactly the 1D rule S(b) - S(a-1). For pixels 4–8: 31 - 8 = 23.
E7. All 16 entries with x \ge 2 and y \ge 2 grow by 2 (e.g. S(5,5) from 48 to 50); row 1, column 1 and the zero row and column stay the same.

title: From masks to objects
text:
About this lecture
The network says “nucleus” for every nucleus pixel. Which pixels belong to which nucleus?

A semantic mask is not a set of objects: touching cells come out as one blob.
A network has no fixed number of outputs, so it predicts a map that makes separation easy, and a classical step makes the objects.
Four such maps: a boundary class, a distance map, star-convex polygons, flow fields; what each one gets wrong.
Detection (boxes) as another output, and panoptic segmentation.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

This unit builds on the U-Net unit of the neural networks day (pixel probabilities), the watershed day (distance transform + markers + flooding), the labelling day (connected components) and the evaluation day (matching objects at an IoU threshold, F1). It recalls them and does not re-teach them. All network outputs in the demo are simulated: the exact training target plus controllable errors, so that every failure can be switched on and off.

title: From masks to objects
section: Recall: a U-Net gives a class per pixel
text:
Recall: a U-Net gives a class per pixel
The U-Net unit of the neural networks day: a probability “nucleus” per pixel, thresholded to a mask. Its “touching nuclei merge” preset: two touching nuclei become one connected blob.

Semantic segmentation: a class per pixel (“nucleus”, “background”).
Instance segmentation: an object identity per pixel (“nucleus 7”).
Panoptic segmentation: both at once. Every pixel gets a class; countable things (nuclei, cells) also get an identity, uncountable stuff (background, stroma) does not.

Counting, measuring, tracking: all need instances.

title: From masks to objects
text:
Why post-processing is unavoidable

A convolutional network does the same thing at every position (translation equivariance) and produces a fixed set of output maps.
The number of objects in an image varies from 0 to 1000.
So the network cannot output “object 1, object 2, …” directly. It outputs a map that makes separation easy, and a classical step turns the map into objects: labelling, watershed, suppression, following arrows.

The question for every method: which map, and which classical step?

title: From masks to objects
text:
Route 1: a boundary class
Train with three classes: background, cell interior, cell boundary (a thin ring around every cell, also between touching cells).

Label the connected interiors (the labelling day), then grow each one back over its boundary pixels.
Touching cells are separated by the boundary class between them.
Fails when the boundary is missed in one place: a one-pixel bridge connects two interiors and they merge. Thin structures are hard to predict, especially exactly where two cells touch.

title: From masks to objects
text:
Route 2: a predicted distance map
Train the network to predict, for every cell pixel, its distance to the cell’s border (scaled to 1 at the centre of each cell).

Then exactly the watershed day’s pipeline: threshold for the mask, h-maxima as markers, flood -D inside the mask.
Better than the distance transform of a mask: the network has seen the image, so it can put a deep neck between two cells even where the mask has none.
Fails on elongated cells: the distance has a long flat ridge, and small errors make several peaks on it: one cell is split.

title: From masks to objects
section: Try it: four maps on one image
text:
Try it: four maps on one image




Simulated network output: the exact target of the chosen route, plus the error sliders. Tour: “semantic mask merges”: 11 objects for 14 cells, three merges (M). “boundary: gaps merge”: with contact bias 0.5 the boundary class fades exactly where cells touch: the same three merges. “distance separates”: same contact bias, the distance route finds all 14. “elongated: oversplit”: noise 0.2 and h = 0.1: the rod splits into 3, the C-shaped cell into 5 (S). Raise h to 0.3: all 14 again. Point at the map panel each time: the errors are visible in the map before they are visible in the labels.

title: From masks to objects
text:
Route 3: star-convex polygons
For every pixel, the network predicts an objectness (how central the pixel is in its cell) and the distances to the border along n fixed rays (e.g. 32 directions).

Each pixel thus proposes a polygon for “its” cell; pixels near the centre propose good ones.
Overlapping proposals are pruned by non-maximum suppression: keep the best, delete those that overlap it by more than t, repeat (next unit).
Works well for round and oval nuclei. Fails by construction on shapes that are not star-convex: a C-shaped or kidney-shaped cell has no point from which all of its border is visible along straight rays.

title: From masks to objects
text:
The math: the four targets
Cell O, pixel p \in O:

Boundary class: p is boundary if one of its 4 neighbours is not in O; loss: cross-entropy over the 3 classes.
Distance: D(p) = \min_{q \notin O}\|p - q\| \,/\, \max_{p' \in O}\min_{q \notin O}\|p' - q\|; loss: squared or absolute error.
Star-convex rays: \mathbf u_k = (\cos\tfrac{2\pi k}{n}, \sin\tfrac{2\pi k}{n}), r_k(p) = \max\{r : p + s\,\mathbf u_k \in O \ \ \forall s \in [0, r]\}; objectness = D(p).
O is star-convex with respect to c if the segment from c to every point of O lies in O; then the ray distances from c describe O exactly (up to the angular sampling). Every convex set is star-convex with respect to each of its points.
Flows (next slides): \mathbf v(p) = \nabla h(p)/\|\nabla h(p)\|; loss: squared error on \mathbf v.

title: From masks to objects
text:
Route 4: flow fields
For every cell pixel, the network predicts a small arrow pointing along a path inside the cell towards its centre.

Training targets: put a heat source at the cell’s centre and let heat diffuse inside the cell only; the arrows point uphill in temperature. The paths bend around corners, so they follow a C-shape or a bent cell.
To segment: every pixel follows the arrows for a number of steps. Pixels that end in the same sink form one object.
Handles long, bent, irregular cells. Fails when the predicted arrows are noisy (spurious sinks: splits) or when two touching cells share one smooth field (merge).

title: From masks to objects
text:
The math: following the flow
Heat target: h solves the diffusion (heat) equation inside O with a source at the centre c and no flow through the border; in practice h \leftarrow average of its neighbours in O, plus 1 at c, repeated. Flow \mathbf v = \nabla h/\|\nabla h\|.
Following the flow = Euler steps of the ODE \dot{\mathbf x} = \mathbf v(\mathbf x):
\mathbf x_{j+1} = \mathbf x_j + \eta\,\mathbf v(\mathbf x_j), \qquad \eta = 1 \text{ pixel}.
Along the path \frac{d}{dt}h(\mathbf x(t)) = \nabla h \cdot \mathbf v = \|\nabla h\| > 0: h only increases, so a path can only end at a maximum of h. If h has a single maximum in O (the source), every path ends there: one sink per cell. Noise in \mathbf v can create extra fixed points (sinks) where the arrows point at each other.

title: From masks to objects
section: Try it: flows follow the bend
text:
Try it: flows follow the bend




“flows follow the bend”: all 14 cells, including the C-shape and the bent cell. Press “animate”: the particles (white) run to their sinks. Click a pixel of the C on the map: its path bends around the arc. Then “C-shape: no polygon fits”: the clicked pixel’s 32 rays and polygon (red) cover only part of the C; the C is split into 2 (S), F1 0.97. Set rays n to 8: 19 objects. “noisy flows: many sinks”: noise 0.7 gives 22 objects, splits in the rod, C and a round cell. Finally “contact bias: merges” on the distance route: 11 objects, three merges; switch route to flows: 12 objects.

Whatever the route: look at the predicted map, not only at the final labels. Errors in the map turn into object errors (merges, splits, missed dim cells) that the evaluation day’s matching counts.

title: From masks to objects
text:
Detection: objects as a list
The other big family predicts a list of objects instead of a map: a box and a score per object, optionally a small mask inside each box (“detect, then segment inside the box”).

A box is 4 numbers; good for counting, tracking and cropping; poor for long diagonal objects.
The detector proposes many overlapping boxes, removed by non-maximum suppression: the next unit.
Star-convex polygons are the same idea with a polygon instead of a box.

title: From masks to objects
text:
Panoptic segmentation
A semantic head (stuff and thing classes for every pixel) and an instance head (identities of the things), merged by a rule: on “thing” pixels the instance label wins.
Tissue example: nuclei are things (counted, measured one by one); stroma, lumen and background are stuff (area only).

title: From masks to objects
text:
The math: panoptic quality
Match predicted and true segments one to one at IoU > 0.5 (the evaluation day’s matching: above 0.5 the matching is unique). With TP matched pairs, FP unmatched predictions, FN unmatched truths:
\mathrm{PQ} = \underbrace{\frac{\sum_{(p,g) \in TP}\mathrm{IoU}(p,g)}{|TP|}}_{\text{segmentation quality SQ}} \times \underbrace{\frac{|TP|}{|TP| + \tfrac12|FP| + \tfrac12|FN|}}_{\text{recognition quality RQ} \,=\, F_1}
Example: 3 matches with IoU 0.9, 0.8, 0.7, one FP and two FN: SQ = 0.8, RQ = 3/4.5 = 0.67, PQ = 0.53. Computed per class and averaged over classes.

title: From masks to objects
text:
Recall: counting the errors
From the evaluation day: match predicted to true objects one to one at IoU \ge \tau (here \tau = 0.5), count TP, FP, FN objects; F1 = 2\,TP/(2\,TP + FP + FN); matching accuracy = TP/(TP + FP + FN); a merge is a predicted object covering two true ones, a split a true object covered by two predictions.
The demo shows these numbers for every route and every error setting.

title: From masks to objects
text:
Summary

A semantic mask is not a set of objects; instance segmentation needs a map plus a classical step.
Boundary class + labelling: one missed boundary pixel merges two cells.
Distance map + watershed: separates round touching cells; oversplits long ones.
Star-convex polygons + suppression: great for round nuclei; cannot describe a C-shape.
Flows followed to their sinks: follow bends; noisy flows make extra sinks.
Panoptic = things with identities + stuff with classes. Always look at the predicted map.

title: Image analysis
text:
A course on the mathematics and methods of digital image analysis, for students who have studied linear algebra and calculus. Most of image analysis turns out to be linear algebra and calculus in disguise: an image is a matrix, a geometric transform is a matrix acting on coordinates, a filter is a linear map, and the Fourier transform is a change of basis.
The course is built around interactive demos: change the input, and see what happens. Every unit has one; the demo gallery lists them all.

title: Image analysis
text:
How each unit works
Work through the sidebar from top to bottom. Each unit has:

a lecture (slides, green in the sidebar),
a quiz (blue): short questions to check your understanding,
an exercise: questions to do by hand, then an interactive demo (orange) with questions to explore.

Do the pen-and-paper questions first, then use the demo to check and extend them.
The material comes in two layers. The ideas (pictures, demos, plain explanations and small examples with numbers) are complete on their own. The math (formulas, derivations, proofs) is clearly marked: slides titled The math with a “math layer” badge, and questions tagged (math). On a first pass you can skim the math and still follow every idea; come back to it when you want the full story.

title: Image analysis
text:
Topics
The course is organised in five parts of one-day topics, plus electives.

Part I: Images as numbers: images, filters, frequencies and principal components; edges, blobs and ridges; bit depth and noise; image formation; deconvolution.
Part II: From pixels to objects: thresholding, colour, morphology, labelling, watershed and measurements.
Part III: Aligning images: registration in frequency space (FFT registration).
Part IV: Segmentation as optimisation: graph cuts (energy minimisation, maximum flow, graph-cut segmentation, normalized cuts).
Part V: Learning from examples: random forests, neural networks, evaluation and statistics, variational autoencoders and modern deep learning.
Electives, each taken after a core day: Objects (skeletons, moments), Curves and energies (snakes and active shape models, level sets, dynamic programming, Ising models and Markov random fields), Detection (Hough transform, integral images), More learning (support vector machines, Gaussian mixtures), Transforms (wavelets, image compression, Radon transform and tomography), Spectral (spectral unmixing) and 3D (marching cubes, 3D graphics).

title: Curves as level sets
text:
About this lecture
A snake stores a boundary as a list of points. Today we store it in a completely different way: as the place where a function on the image grid is zero. This is the starting point of level set methods (Osher & Sethian, 1988).

Two ways to store a curve: explicit (points) and implicit (the zero level of \phi(x, y)).
Inside and outside from the sign; union and intersection with min and max.
Topology belongs to the slice, not to the function: one contour can become two.
Normal and curvature read directly from \phi.
The signed distance function: the most convenient \phi.
On a pixel grid, \phi is just an image.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

First unit of the level-set day (elective, “Curves and energies”: snakes → level sets → dynamic programming). Prerequisites: partial derivatives and the gradient; finite differences from Filtering & convolution (day 1). The distance transform is owned by the morphology day, marching squares by the marching-cubes day; both are only recalled here.

title: Curves as level sets
section: Two ways to store a curve
text:
Two ways to store a curve


Explicit: a list of points (x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2), \dots along the curve, or a parametric curve \mathbf C(s). This is a snake.

Easy to draw, easy to measure the length.
But: one list is one curve. Two objects need two lists; a curve that splits needs surgery.


Implicit: a function \phi(x, y) on the whole image, and the curve is where \phi = 0.

Think of a height map: the coastline is the zero level of the height. The map stores heights everywhere; the coast is read off where the height crosses sea level.
We fix the sign once: \phi < 0 inside, \phi > 0 outside.


Same coast, two descriptions. Raise the sea level and the coastline moves, and islands may appear or merge, without anyone redrawing the coast by hand.

text:
Curves from formulas

To test whether a point is inside, evaluate \phi there and look at the sign. No search along a list of points.
The circle: at (1, 0) with r = 1.5, \phi = 1 - 1.5 = -0.5: inside, and half a unit from the edge.
Many functions have the same zero set: x^2 + y^2 - r^2 also describes the circle. They differ away from the curve.

title: Curves as level sets
Curves as level sets
section: Topology is a property of the slice
text:
Topology is a property of the slice

Cut the surface z = \phi(x, y) of the two circles with horizontal planes z = c. Below c = 0.2 the cut is two curves, above it one. The function did not change at all; only the height of the cut did.

This is the central picture of the day. Unit 2 moves the curve by changing φ a little at every step; when the zero level passes a saddle of φ, the topology of the curve changes, and nothing special has to be done. Ask: at what c do the two contours touch? (0.2, the value of φ at the saddle point, the origin.)

title: Curves as level sets
text:
Try it: slicing a surface




Left: the surface φ as a mesh (drag to rotate; front/top/3/4 buttons), the orange plane at height c and the two contours drawn on the surface. Right: the top view, blue inside, red outside, thin level lines every 0.5, solid black φ = 0, dashed orange φ = c. Tour: “one becomes two” starts at c = 0.4 (one contour); slide c down past 0.2: two contours (the readout says 2 pieces). Then “egg crate” (sin(πx/2) sin(πy/2)): many pieces; move c and watch blobs appear and merge. Click a point in the top view to see the normal arrow and the curvature circle (next slides).

title: Curves as level sets
section: Normal and curvature, read from φ
text:
Normal and curvature, read from φ

The gradient \nabla\phi points uphill, from inside to outside, and is perpendicular to the level line. So the outward normal is \mathbf n = \nabla\phi / |\nabla\phi|.
Curvature \kappa: how fast the normals spread out as you move along the curve. A circle of radius r has \kappa = 1/r: small circles bend a lot, a straight line has \kappa = 0.
With our sign convention, \kappa > 0 where the inside is convex (a bump), \kappa < 0 in a dent.
Both come from \phi at one point, with derivatives: no neighbours along a list of points are needed.

title: Curves as level sets
text:
The math: normal and curvature
Normal. Along a level line \phi(\mathbf C(s)) = c. Differentiate with the chain rule: 
abla\phi \cdot \mathbf C'(s) = 0. The gradient is perpendicular to the tangent, so \mathbf n = 
abla\phi/|
abla\phi| (pointing to larger \phi, outward).
Curvature is the divergence of the unit normal field, 
abla\cdot\mathbf v = \partial_x v_1 + \partial_y v_2 (“how much the arrows spread out”): \kappa = 
abla\cdot rac{
abla\phi}{|
abla\phi|} =  rac{\phi_{xx}\phi_y^2 - 2\phi_x\phi_y\phi_{xy} + \phi_{yy}\phi_x^2}{(\phi_x^2 + \phi_y^2)^{3/2}}.
Circle. \phi = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} - r, ho = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}: 
abla\phi = (x, y)/ho, so \mathbf n = (x, y)/ho and 
abla\cdot\mathbf n = \partial_x(x/ho) + \partial_y(y/ho) = 	frac{y^2}{ho^3} + 	frac{x^2}{ho^3} = 	frac{1}{ho}. On the curve, \kappa = 1/r.

title: Curves as level sets
text:
Signed distance functions
The most convenient \phi: |\phi(\mathbf x)| = the distance from \mathbf x to the curve, with a minus sign inside.

It is the distance transform of the morphology day, with a sign: distance to the boundary, negative inside the object.
Walking straight away from the curve, \phi grows by exactly 1 per unit: |\nabla\phi| = 1 everywhere (except on the “ridge” in the middle of a shape, where two nearest points compete).
Then the normal is simply \mathbf n = \nabla\phi, and the curvature is the Laplacian, \kappa = \phi_{xx} + \phi_{yy}: the Laplacian kernel of Filtering & convolution.
And \phi tells you how far away the curve is, which unit 2 will use to keep time steps safe.

text:
The math: why |∇φ| = 1 simplifies everything

If |
abla\phi| = 1, then \mathbf n = 
abla\phi and \kappa = 
abla\cdot
abla\phi = 
abla^2\phi.
Not every \phi with the right zero set is a distance. For the circle, \phi = x^2 + y^2 - r^2 has 
abla\phi = 2(x, y), so |
abla\phi| = 2ho: 3 on the curve if r = 1.5. Its normal and the curvature of its level lines are still correct (they do not depend on the scaling), but 
abla^2\phi = 4 everywhere: the Laplacian shortcut is wrong.
Scaling \phi by 3 changes nothing about the curve, \mathbf n or \kappa; it triples |
abla\phi|. Distances read from \phi would be off by a factor 3.
At corners the signed distance has kinks (inside a square, along the diagonals): there \phi is not differentiable and finite differences give a huge \kappa.

title: Curves as level sets

“same curve, different φ”: circle of radius 1.5 with φ = 3d, point (1.2, −0.9) on the curve: |∇φ| = 3.00, κ = 0.67 = 1/1.5. Switch to “distance d”: the black contour stays where it is, the surface becomes a cone of slope 1, |∇φ| = 1.00, κ unchanged. “d + d²/2R” is (x² + y² − R²)/(2R) for the circle: same contour, a bowl instead of a cone; click (0.6, −0.45) inside: |∇φ| = 0.50, while the distance gives 1.00; κ = 1.33 in both. Then “corner: κ blows up”: square, point (1.6, −1.6) just outside a corner: κ = 7.08 (the level line is an arc of radius 0.14 around the corner). Click (1, 1) on the inside diagonal: κ is over 200, the kink of the distance function.

title: Curves as level sets
section: On a pixel grid, φ is an image
text:
On a pixel grid, φ is an image

Store \phi at the pixel centres: an image of the same size as the data, with negative values inside.
Inside/outside of a pixel: the sign. Derivatives: differences of neighbours (Filtering & convolution).
The curve itself lies between pixels: on every pixel edge where the sign changes, interpolate linearly to find the crossing, and join the crossings cell by cell. This is marching squares; the case table, the ambiguous saddle cells and the by-hand work belong to the marching-cubes day (isocontour/).
Every contour drawn in today’s demos is computed this way.

title: Quiz: images as arrays & geometric transforms
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Questions marked (math) use the formulas from the math slides; the others need only the ideas.

Q1. A 16-bit greyscale microscopy image has 2048 × 2048 pixels. How many different grey levels can a pixel take, and how many bytes does the image need (uncompressed)?






Answer





2^{16} = 65\,536 grey levels (0 to 65 535). Each pixel needs 2 bytes, so 2048 \cdot 2048 \cdot 2 = 8\,388\,608 bytes, i.e. 8 MiB.




Q2. Without multiplying anything out: what does A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1\\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} do to an image? And B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}?






Hint





Read the columns: where do (1, 0) and (0, 1) go? Then look at the determinant.









Answer





A sends (1,0) \to (0,1) and (0,1) \to (-1,0): a rotation by 90° counter-clockwise, \det A = 1. B swaps the two axes, (1,0) \leftrightarrow (0,1): a reflection in the line y = x, \det B = -1, so the image is mirrored.




Q3. You scale an image by a factor 3 by sending every input pixel to its new position. Why does the result look like a grid of isolated dots, and how do you avoid it?






Answer





Forward mapping sends the N^2 input pixels to N^2 positions spread over an area 9 times larger, so 8 of every 9 output pixels receive nothing. Use inverse mapping: for every output pixel \mathbf{x}', look up the input at A^{-1}\mathbf{x}' and interpolate.




Q4. A transform has \det A = 0.25. What happens to the area of a cell in the image? Can you undo the transform?






Answer





Every area is multiplied by 0.25, so the cell covers a quarter of its original area (for example, scaling both axes by 0.5). It is invertible, since \det A \neq 0, so geometrically yes. But when you shrink an image onto the same pixel grid, detail finer than the new pixel spacing is lost, and transforming back cannot restore it.




Q5. (math) Why does rotating about the image centre need a 3 \times 3 matrix, while rotating about the origin needs only a 2 \times 2 one?






Answer





A 2\times2 matrix always keeps the origin fixed, A\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}. Rotating about another point \mathbf{p} needs a translation: shift \mathbf{p} to the origin, rotate, shift back. Translation is not linear, but it becomes a matrix product in homogeneous coordinates, which are 3\times3.




Q6. A label image stores an object number in every pixel: 0 for the background, 1, 2, 3, … for the cells. You rotate it by 30°. Why should you use nearest-neighbour interpolation, not bilinear?






Hint





What does bilinear interpolation give halfway between a pixel of cell 2 and a pixel of cell 4?









Answer





Bilinear interpolation averages neighbouring values. Halfway between cell 2 and cell 4 it gives 3: the number of a different cell, and along every cell boundary it invents values that are not labels of anything there (0.5 between background and cell 1, and so on). Nearest neighbour only ever copies existing values, so every output pixel is still a valid label.

title: Exercise: images as arrays & geometric transforms
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

read what a 2\times2 matrix does to an image from its columns and determinant,
compute a geometric transform backwards, with nearest-neighbour and bilinear interpolation,
rotate about a point other than the origin, and explain why the order of transforms matters,
(math) build an affine transform from homogeneous 3\times3 matrices.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the interactive part. Questions marked (math) ask for derivations; do the others first.

title: Exercise: images as arrays & geometric transforms
text:
By hand
B1. Sketch what the shear H = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2\\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} does to the unit square with corners (0,0), (1,0), (1,1), (0,1). What is \det H, and what does that say about the area?
B2. For each matrix, say whether the result is a mirror image, and give the factor by which areas change: (a) \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0\\ 0 & 0.5\end{bmatrix} (b) \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0\\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} (c) \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0\\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} (d) \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1\\ 0.5 & 0.5\end{bmatrix}
B3. The image is scaled by A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0\\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} about the origin. Which input position does the output pixel at \mathbf{x}' = (3, 5) come from?
B4. Bilinear interpolation. Four neighbouring pixels have the values I(0,0) = 10, I(1,0) = 20, I(0,1) = 30, I(1,1) = 60 (written as I(x, y)). Estimate I(0.25, 0.5): first interpolate along x on the rows y = 0 and y = 1, then along y. What does nearest-neighbour give?
B5. Rotate by 90° counter-clockwise about the point \mathbf{p} = (2, 1), without matrices: shift \mathbf{p} to the origin, turn a quarter turn, shift back. Where do the points (3, 1) and (2, 3) go? Check your answers with a sketch.
B6. Let S stretch the image by 2 along x (keep y), and R rotate it by 90° counter-clockwise about the centre. Where does the point (1, 0) go if you apply S first and then R? And if you apply R first and then S? A square image: is it tall or wide afterwards, in each case?






Solutions





B1. H keeps (1, 0) and sends (0, 1) to (2, 1): horizontal lines stay horizontal and every point slides sideways by twice its height. The square becomes a parallelogram with corners (0,0), (1,0), (3,1), (2,1). \det H = 1: the area is unchanged.
B2. (a) \det = 1: twice as wide, half as tall, area unchanged, not mirrored. (b) \det = -1: mirrored left–right, area unchanged. (c) \det = 1: a rotation by 180°, not a mirror image. (d) \det = 0.5 - 0.5 = 0: the columns are parallel, the whole image is squashed onto a line; area 0, not invertible.
B3. A^{-1} = \tfrac12 I, so \mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{x}' = (1.5, 2.5): between pixels, so we must interpolate.
B4. Along x at y = 0: 10 + 0.25\,(20 - 10) = 12.5. At y = 1: 30 + 0.25\,(60 - 30) = 37.5. Along y: 12.5 + 0.5\,(37.5 - 12.5) = 25. Nearest neighbour: (0.25, 0.5) is equally far from (0, 0) and (0, 1), so it depends on the tie-breaking rule: 10 or 30. (Rounding 0.5 up gives (0, 1), value 30.)
B5. (3, 1): shifted, it is (1, 0), one step to the right of \mathbf{p}; a quarter turn takes it to (0, 1); shifting back gives (2, 2), one step above \mathbf{p}. (2, 3): shifted, (0, 2); turned, (-2, 0); shifted back, (0, 1), two steps to the left of \mathbf{p}. The point \mathbf{p} itself stays where it is.
B6. S then R: (1, 0) \to (2, 0) \to (0, 2). R then S: (1, 0) \to (0, 1) \to (0, 1): the stretch along x no longer touches it, because it now points up. The square stretched first becomes wide, then the quarter turn stands it up: tall (twice as tall as wide). Turned first, it is still a square, then stretched along x: wide. The two orders give different images, so the order of transforms matters.




Math questions
B7. (math) Write the 3\times3 homogeneous matrix that rotates by 90° counter-clockwise about the point \mathbf{p} = (2, 1), as a product T_{\mathbf{p}}\,R\,T_{-\mathbf{p}}. Check it: where does \mathbf{p} go? Where does (3, 1) go? Compare with B5.
B8. (math) Show that in bilinear interpolation it does not matter whether you interpolate along x first (as in B4) or along y first: both give (1-\alpha)(1-\beta)\,I_{00} + \alpha(1-\beta)\,I_{10} + (1-\alpha)\beta\,I_{01} + \alpha\beta\,I_{11} at the point (\alpha, \beta). Check it on the numbers of B4, interpolating along y first.






Solutions (math)





B7. T_{\mathbf{p}}RT_{-\mathbf{p}} =
\begin{bmatrix}1&0&2\\0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}0&-1&0\\1&0&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}1&0&-2\\0&1&-1\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix}0&-1&3\\1&0&-1\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}. Check: (2, 1) \mapsto (0\cdot2 - 1 + 3,\; 2 + 0 - 1) = (2, 1), so \mathbf{p} stays fixed. (3, 1) \mapsto (-1 + 3,\; 3 - 1) = (2, 2): the point one step to the right of \mathbf{p} ends up one step above it, a quarter turn counter-clockwise, as in B5.
B8. Along x first: the two rows give (1-\alpha)I_{00} + \alpha I_{10} and (1-\alpha)I_{01} + \alpha I_{11}; interpolating these along y with weights 1-\beta and \beta gives the four terms above. Along y first: the two columns give (1-\beta)I_{00} + \beta I_{01} and (1-\beta)I_{10} + \beta I_{11}; interpolating along x with weights 1-\alpha and \alpha gives the same four products, in a different order. With the numbers of B4 (\alpha = 0.25, \beta = 0.5): along y at x = 0: 10 + 0.5\,(30 - 10) = 20; at x = 1: 20 + 0.5\,(60 - 20) = 40; then along x: 20 + 0.25\,(40 - 20) = 25, the same as before.

title: Exercise: images as arrays & geometric transforms
text:
Explore
The same ideas on a picture: a drawn cell (with an “F” in the corner, so mirror images are easy to spot), centred on the origin. Drag the red and blue handles (the columns of A) or use the presets and the rotation slider.



E1. Drag the blue handle to make the shear H from B1. Does the frame (solid outline) look like your sketch?
E2. Before clicking, predict each preset from its columns: Rotate 30°, Scale, Reflect, Misaligned. Which one gives a mirror image? Then set the rotation slider to 180°: is that a mirror image too?
E3. Click Collapse, then slowly drag the blue handle away from the red one. When exactly does the cell become a line?
E4. Click Scale and look closely at the edges of the cell and the F. The demo uses nearest-neighbour lookup. What would bilinear interpolation change?






Solutions





E1. The red handle stays at (1, 0); put the blue one at (2, 1). Horizontal lines stay horizontal and every point slides sideways by 2 times its height: the x-axis stays put, the top edge of the frame (height 1.5) slides 3 units to the right and the bottom edge 3 units to the left, so the corners leave the view. The lean is the same as in the B1 sketch, where the top of the unit square (height 1) slides 2 units.
E2. Rotate 30°: columns (0.87, 0.5) and (-0.5, 0.87), the picture turns counter-clockwise. Scale: columns (2, 0) and (0, 0.5), twice as wide, half as tall. Reflect: column 1 is (-1, 0), so the picture is mirrored left–right and the F reads backwards. Misaligned: tilted and skewed, as two images of the same sample often are before registration. Rotating by 180° turns the F upside down, but it is not a mirror image: turn your head (or the screen) and it reads normally again. Only the reflection flips it (\det = -1).
E3. Exactly when the two columns lie on one line through the origin, i.e. when \det A = 0. Then every point x\cdot\text{col 1} + y\cdot\text{col 2} is on that line, so the whole picture is squashed onto it. As soon as the columns point in different directions, the picture is a (thin) parallelogram again.
E4. In the horizontal direction each input pixel now covers two output pixels, so edges look blocky and staircase-like. Bilinear interpolation would blend neighbouring values, giving smooth ramps instead of steps, at the price of introducing grey levels that were not in the input (bad for label images, where every value is an object ID).

title: Exercise: images as arrays & geometric transforms
text:
Where this leads
Finding the matrix that aligns two images (registration) is an optimisation problem over the entries of A and \mathbf{t}; this unit only applies a given transform. Next: changing pixel values using their neighbours.

title: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem
text:
About this lecture
We know the forward model and the PSF. Can we get the object back from the image?

Undo the blur by dividing by the OTF: inverse filtering. Perfect without noise.
With noise it explodes where the OTF is small, and has nothing to divide beyond the cut-off.
Invisible objects: different objects can give exactly the same image.
Blur is a matrix; undoing it is solving a badly conditioned linear system: an ill-posed problem.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Short closing unit of the image formation day (about 45 minutes with the exercise). It shows why restoration needs more than the forward model, and names no cure: Wiener, Tikhonov, regularisation, Richardson–Lucy and denoisers belong to the deconvolution day (tomorrow). The demo is the deconvolution day’s lab in its inverse-only mode. Notation as before: g = f ∗ h + n, G = FH + N.
crumbs: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem

title: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem
text:
The question
The forward direction is well behaved: one object gives one image. The inverse problem runs it backwards: from the image (and the PSF) to the object.

Forward: object → blur → sample → add noise → image. Every step is known.
Backward: image → ? The blur averaged neighbours together; the noise added something we do not know.
Is there one object that explains the image? Can we find it? Does a tiny change in the image make a tiny change in the answer?
crumbs: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem

title: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem
text:
Divide by H
In frequency space the blur is a multiplication: G = F \cdot H. So divide: \hat F = G / H. This is inverse filtering.

Without noise, and where H \ne 0: \hat F = FH/H = F, exactly the object.
Each frequency is multiplied by the gain 1/H: weakly transmitted frequencies are amplified strongly.

title: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem
text:
With noise
The image is G = FH + N. Dividing:
\hat F = \frac{G}{H} = F + \frac{N}{H}.

The noise is spread over all frequencies, about equally (white noise). The signal is not: at high frequencies FH is tiny.
Where H is small, N/H is huge: the restored image is dominated by amplified noise at the finest frequencies.

Small example. The blur (1, 2, 1)/4 multiplies the three waves of the frequency unit (constant, period 4 pixels, period 2 pixels) by 1, 0.5, 0. The inverse multiplies them by 1, 2, ∞. Noise at period 4 doubles; noise at period 2 cannot be divided at all.
crumbs: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem

title: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem
text:
Try it: the inverse filter




The deconvolution day’s lab, inverse-only mode, 128 × 128 cell phantom. Panels: truth, observed, inverse-filtered, error. Plot: blue |H|, red 1/|H|, dashed the noise floor. Tour: “no noise: inverse is perfect” (Gaussian σ = 1.5 px): RMSE 6e-9 — but the readout’s largest gain is 1.1e9. “0.1 % noise: inverse explodes”: RMSE 4.8e4, half the pixels negative. Lower the PSF width to 0.5 px: largest gain 3, and at 0.1 % noise the inverse now beats the observed image (RMSE 0.0018 against 0.0057); at 1 % it does not (0.018 against 0.011). “Motion blur: zeros” (9 px, star, 1 % noise): RMSE 0.96, streaks along x. “An invisible grating”: next slide.
crumbs: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem

title: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem
text:
Invisible objects

Object B is object A plus a grating of period 160 nm, finer than the cut-off of an NA 1.4 objective (λ/2NA = 186 nm). Their images are identical.
A grating finer than the cut-off gives exactly the same image as no grating at all (H = 0 there).
So adding it to any object changes nothing in the image: the data cannot tell these objects apart.
No method can recover what the optics never transmitted. A restoration that shows such detail has invented it.
crumbs: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem

title: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem
text:
Ill-posed
A problem is well-posed if an answer exists, is unique, and depends stably on the data. Deblurring fails all three:

Existence: noise puts energy at frequencies where H = 0; no object, blurred, gives exactly that image.
Uniqueness: invisible objects can be added freely.
Stability: a tiny change in the image (noise of 0.1 %) changes the answer enormously (gains of 10^9).

The forward model alone does not determine the object. Something else must.
crumbs: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem

title: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem
section: The math: blur is a circulant matrix
text:
The math: blur is a circulant matrix
On a periodic 1D signal of n pixels, blur by a kernel is \mathbf g = A\mathbf f with a circulant matrix: each row is the kernel shifted by one. For (1, 2, 1)/4 and n = 4:
A = \frac14\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}.

Every circulant matrix has the Fourier waves \mathbf w_k = (e^{2\pi i k j/n})_j as eigenvectors, with eigenvalues H(k), the DFT of the kernel. Here H = (1, 0.5, 0, 0.5) for k = 0, 1, 2, 3.
So the convolution theorem is the diagonalisation A = W^{-1}\,\mathrm{diag}(H)\,W (the DFT is a change of basis).
For a symmetric kernel A is symmetric; its singular values are |H(k)|. Condition number: \kappa(A) = \frac{\max_k |H(k)|}{\min_k |H(k)|} = \frac{1}{\min_k |H(k)|}, infinite as soon as some H(k) = 0 (this A is singular: \mathbf w_2 = (1, -1, 1, -1) is in its null space).
crumbs: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem

title: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem
text:
The math: ill-posedness

Hadamard (1902): a problem is well-posed if a solution exists, is unique, and depends continuously on the data.
For \mathbf g = A\mathbf f: the null space of A (the waves with H(k) = 0; for a lens, all frequencies past 2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda) can be added to any solution: not unique. Data with a component outside the range of A have no exact solution.
Stability: for A(\mathbf f + \delta\mathbf f) = \mathbf g + \delta\mathbf g with invertible A, \frac{\|\delta\mathbf f\|}{\|\mathbf f\|} \le \kappa(A)\,\frac{\|\delta\mathbf g\|}{\|\mathbf g\|}. A relative error of 10^{-3} in the image can become 10^{-3}\kappa in the object.
Two-pixel blurs: \begin{bmatrix}0.75 & 0.25\\0.25 & 0.75\end{bmatrix} has eigenvalues 1 (sum) and 0.5 (difference), \kappa = 2; \begin{bmatrix}0.55 & 0.45\\0.45 & 0.55\end{bmatrix} has 1 and 0.1, \kappa = 10. An error of 0.01 in the difference grows to 0.02 and to 0.1.
crumbs: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem

title: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem
text:
What must we add?

The same blurred image (Gaussian σ = 1.5 px, 0.1 % noise) restored two ways.The data alone cannot decide. Restoration only works if we add what we know:

about the object: it is smooth, or mostly piecewise constant, and never negative;
about the noise: how large it is, and what kind (Poisson, Gaussian).

Tomorrow (the deconvolution day): how to add it, and how to choose how much.
crumbs: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem

title: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem
text:
Other forward models
The same diagnosis appears whenever we measure something through an instrument:

Tomography (the Radon elective): the forward model takes line integrals instead of a convolution with a PSF; reconstructing the object from them is ill-posed in the same way.
Missing frequencies, small gains and noise: the vocabulary of today carries over.
crumbs: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem

title: Running the model backwards: an ill-posed problem
text:
Summary

Inverse problem: from the image back to the object. Inverse filter: \hat F = G/H.
Without noise and with H \ne 0: exact. With noise: \hat F = F + N/H explodes where H is small.
Beyond the cut-off H = 0: invisible objects; nothing can bring them back.
Blur = circulant matrix, eigenvectors = Fourier waves, eigenvalues = OTF; condition number 1/\min|H|.
Ill-posed: existence, uniqueness and stability all fail. We must add knowledge about the object and the noise: the next day.

title: Quiz: Hough transform for lines
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Lines are written in normal form x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = \rho, \theta \in [0°, 180°), origin at the image centre, y up.

Q1. What does a single edge point become in the (\theta, \rho) parameter space, and what does that curve represent?






Hint





Which lines pass through the point?









Answer





A sinusoid \rho(\theta) = x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta. Each point of the curve is one line through the edge point: the curve is the set of all lines that pass through it.




Q2. Why is the slope–intercept form y = mx + c a poor choice of parameters for a Hough accumulator?






Hint





What are m and c of a vertical line?









Answer





The slope is unbounded: a vertical line has m = \infty, and nearly vertical lines have very large m and c. A finite grid of bins over (m, c) cannot contain all lines. The normal form has \theta \in [0°, 180°) and |\rho| at most half the image diagonal, so a finite grid covers every line.




Q3. A line is drawn as a dashed line: only every other group of 10 pixels is present. Compared with the solid line, what happens to its peak in the accumulator?






Hint





Each point votes independently.









Answer





The peak stays at the same (\theta, \rho) and has about half the height (half as many edge points vote for it). The gaps themselves do not matter; only the number of points on the line does. If half the height is still above the threshold, the line is found.




Q4. Without non-maximum suppression, a single straight edge gives several detections. Why?






Hint





Do all votes of one line land in exactly one bin?









Answer





Edge positions are rounded to pixels and slightly noisy, and the grid is discrete, so the votes of one line spread over a few neighbouring (\theta, \rho) bins. Several of them exceed the threshold, and each becomes a nearly identical line. NMS keeps only the bin that is the maximum in its neighbourhood.




Q5. You make the bins ten times finer to measure the angle of a line more precisely, and the line is no longer detected. What happened?






Hint





How many votes does each small bin get?









Answer





The edge points of a real line are not exactly collinear. With very small bins their votes spread over many bins, so no single bin reaches the threshold: the peak dissolves. Bins should be about as large as the scatter of the votes (about 1 px in \rho and a fraction of a degree to a degree in \theta). For more precision, refine the peak afterwards, for example by fitting a line to the points that voted for it.




Q6. An edge point has gradient direction 30°. With gradient voting, for which lines does it vote? Why does this reduce false detections in clutter?






Hint





How is the gradient related to the direction of the edge?









Answer





The gradient is perpendicular to the edge, so it is the normal of the line the point lies on: the point votes only for \theta \approx 30° (within a small window), at its own \rho. A random clutter point now casts a few votes instead of one per angle, and for a bin to collect many votes the points must be collinear and have gradients perpendicular to that line. Chance alignments of clutter rarely satisfy both.




Q7. (math) Show that the curves of two different points (x_1, y_1) and (x_2, y_2) cross at the \theta whose normal is perpendicular to (x_2 - x_1, y_2 - y_1).






Hint





Subtract the two equations \rho = x_i\cos\theta + y_i\sin\theta.









Answer





At a crossing both give the same \rho: (x_1 - x_2)\cos\theta + (y_1 - y_2)\sin\theta = 0, i.e. (\cos\theta, \sin\theta) \cdot (\mathbf p_1 - \mathbf p_2) = 0. The normal is perpendicular to the difference of the points, so the line with this normal and \rho = x_1\cos\theta + y_1\sin\theta contains both points. In [0°, 180°) there is exactly one such \theta.




Q8. How are the Hough transform for lines and the Radon transform related?






Hint





What is the integral of a binary edge image along a line?









Answer





The Radon transform integrates an image along every line (\theta, \rho). For a binary edge image this integral counts the edge pixels on the line, which is the number of votes in the Hough bin (\theta, \rho). The Hough accumulator is a discretised Radon transform of the edge map; the Hough transform looks for its peaks, while the Radon day uses it for reconstruction.

title: Exercise: Hough transform for lines
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Normal form
a line is \{x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = \rho\}, \theta \in [0°, 180°), \rho signed; origin at the image centre, y up


A point’s curve
\rho(\theta) = x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta: a sinusoid; all lines through the point


Accumulator
bins (\theta_j, \rho_k); each edge point adds one vote per \theta_j, in the bin of its \rho


Peak
a bin with many votes = many collinear points; votes ≈ length of the line in pixels


Threshold, NMS
keep bins with ≥ t votes that are the largest in a window around them


Gradient voting
vote only for \theta within a small window of the point’s gradient direction (taken modulo 180°)


Segments
edge points within ~1 px of a detected line, split at gaps > g, pieces shorter than L_\text{min} dropped

title: Exercise: Hough transform for lines
text:
By hand
B1. The points (2, 0), (1, 1), (0, 2). (a) Compute \rho = x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta for each point at \theta = 0°, 45°, 90°, 135° (two decimals). (b) Fill a 4 \times 5 accumulator: rows \theta = 0°, 45°, 90°, 135°, columns \rho = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 (round each \rho to the nearest integer). Which bin has the most votes? (c) Which line is it? Write it as x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = \rho and as y = \dots.
B2. Predict, then explain: (a) A straight line of 120 edge pixels gives a peak of 120 votes. The same line is now dashed: 10 pixels on, 10 off. Where is the peak and how high is it? (b) Half of the line’s pixels are moved by one pixel, at random, to either side. What happens to the peak with \Delta\rho = 1, and with \Delta\rho = 3?
B3. Two parallel lines 3 px apart, \rho_1 = 10 and \rho_2 = 13 at the same \theta, each 100 px long. The bins have \Delta\rho = 4 and the NMS window is ±1 bin.
