The bin (45°, 1) has 3 votes; every other bin has at most 1. (c) x\cos 45° + y\sin 45° = \sqrt2 (the bin holds \rho = 1.41), i.e. x + y = 2, or y = 2 - x. The bin centre \rho = 1 is only accurate to half a bin; the exact value comes from the points themselves.
B2. (a) Same position, about half the height: 60 votes. Each present pixel still votes for the same bin; the missing ones simply do not vote. (b) With \Delta\rho = 1, a pixel moved by one changes its \rho by about 1 (times |\cos| of the angle between the move and the normal), so up to half the votes move to the neighbouring bins: the peak drops towards 60 and two or three neighbouring bins rise. With \Delta\rho = 3 most moved pixels stay in the same bin and the peak stays near 120, at the price of a coarser \rho.
B3. (a) Bins [8, 12), [12, 16): the lines vote into neighbouring bins (100 votes each). Bins [10, 14): both lines vote into the same bin, 200 votes. (b) First case: two neighbouring bins with 100 votes each; NMS with a window of ±1 keeps only one of them (the first in scan order at a tie): one detection. Second case: one bin, one detection, with twice the votes. To separate lines 3 px apart, use \Delta\rho \le 1.5 (so they are at least two bins apart) and an NMS window smaller than their distance in bins (for \Delta\rho = 1: window ±1 or ±2).
B4. (a) 180° / 0.5° = 360 angles. The diagonal is 512\sqrt2 = 724 px, so \rho runs over \pm 362: 725 bins. In total 360 \times 725 = 261\,000 bins, about 1.04 MB. (b) 10\,000 \times 360 = 3.6 million votes. (c) 10\,000 \times 5 = 50\,000 votes; with one bin per point 10\,000. The memory is the same; the work drops by a factor 72 or 360.
B5. (a) A rotation by \Delta\theta moves a point at distance d by about d\,\Delta\theta. With $d = $ half the diagonal: 192\sqrt2/2 = 136 px, so \Delta\theta = 1/136 rad = 0.42°; for 512 × 512: 362 px, \Delta\theta = 0.16°. (b) 0.5\sqrt2/100 = 0.0071 rad = 0.41°. Bins of 1° are a bit coarser than the uncertainty, so the votes of the segment fall into one or two angle bins: a robust peak, with an angle known to about half a degree. Much finer bins (0.1°) would split the peak over several bins.




Math questions
B6. (math) Show that the sinusoids of (x_1, y_1) and (x_2, y_2) cross at \tan\theta = (x_2 - x_1)/(y_1 - y_2), and that the line with these parameters passes through both points. Check it for (2, 0) and (0, 2).
B7. (math) Show that x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = A\cos(\theta - \varphi) with A = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} and \varphi = \operatorname{atan2}(y, x). What are the amplitude and the position of the maximum of the curve of (1, 1)? Which points have the flattest curves, and why does that make sense?
B8. (math) Show that (\theta + 180°, -\rho) describes the same line as (\theta, \rho). Why does the accumulator only need \theta \in [0°, 180°), and what does that imply for non-maximum suppression near \theta = 0° and \theta = 180°?






Solutions (math)





B6. Equal \rho: (x_1 - x_2)\cos\theta + (y_1 - y_2)\sin\theta = 0, so \tan\theta = -(x_1 - x_2)/(y_1 - y_2) = (x_2 - x_1)/(y_1 - y_2). The equation says (\cos\theta, \sin\theta) \perp \mathbf p_1 - \mathbf p_2, so with \rho = \mathbf n \cdot \mathbf p_1 also \mathbf n \cdot \mathbf p_2 = \mathbf n \cdot \mathbf p_1 + \mathbf n \cdot (\mathbf p_2 - \mathbf p_1) = \rho: both points are on the line. For (2, 0), (0, 2): \tan\theta = (0 - 2)/(0 - 2) = 1, \theta = 45°, \rho = 2\cos 45° = \sqrt2.
B7. Write x = A\cos\varphi, y = A\sin\varphi (polar coordinates of the point). Then x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = A(\cos\varphi\cos\theta + \sin\varphi\sin\theta) = A\cos(\theta - \varphi). For (1, 1): A = \sqrt2 = 1.41, \varphi = 45°: the maximum is \rho = 1.41 at \theta = 45°. Points near the origin have small amplitude, so flat curves: every line through a point near the origin passes close to the origin, so |\rho| is small for all \theta.
B8. x\cos(\theta + 180°) + y\sin(\theta + 180°) = -(x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta), so the equation for (\theta + 180°, -\rho) is the same equation multiplied by -1: the same set of points. Every line therefore has exactly one representative with \theta \in [0°, 180°). A line with \theta just below 180° is a neighbour of the line with \theta just above 0° and the opposite \rho: the accumulator wraps around with \rho mirrored, and NMS must compare bins across that seam (the demos do), or a nearly vertical line can be detected twice.

title: Exercise: Hough transform for lines
text:
Explore: points and their curves
The left panel is the image plane (x right, y up, origin in the middle). Drag the points, click on empty space to add one (up to 8), right-click a point or use remove last to delete. The right panel is parameter space: one curve per point, in the normal form (sinusoids in (\theta, \rho)) or in slope–intercept form (straight lines in (m, c)). Grey dots mark where the curves of two points cross; a green ring marks a crossing shared by all curves, and the green line is that line in the image. Click anywhere in parameter space to draw that line (red, dashed). Accumulator shows the binned votes behind the curves, with bin sizes \Delta\theta, \Delta\rho.



D1. Preset three collinear points. Read the common (\theta, \rho) from the readout and compare with B1. Click on the curves at \theta = 0° and \theta = 90°, at the height of the blue curve: which lines are these in the image, and why do they pass through the blue point?
D2. Drag the point (0, 2) to (0, 3). What happens to the common crossing? How far is the farthest point from the best-fitting line now (readout)?
D3. Preset towards vertical, in slope–intercept form. Where do the three lines meet, and why can you not see it? Switch to the normal form: what are \theta and \rho of the line? Now drag the middle point to (0.6, 0) and the top point to (0.6, 3), so that the three points are on a vertical line: what happens in each form?
D4. Preset two lines. How many grey crossings would six points in general position give? Where do they pile up here, and which lines are the two piles?
D5. Preset noisy collinear (6 points close to a line). Switch on the accumulator with \Delta\theta = 15°, \Delta\rho = 1.5, then 10° and 1, then 5° and 0.5, then 2° and 0.25. Note the number of votes in the highest bin each time. Explain the trend.






Solutions





D1. \theta = 45.0°, \rho = 1.41. At \theta = 0° the blue curve (point (2, 0)) has \rho = 2: the vertical line x = 2; at \theta = 90° it has \rho = 0: the horizontal line y = 0. Both pass through (2, 0), because every point of the blue curve is a line through the blue point.
D2. The three curves no longer meet in one point: there are three separate pairwise crossings (grey dots), and the readout says “not collinear”. The best-fitting line has \theta = 33.0°, \rho = 1.57, and the farthest point is 0.18 from it.
D3. The lines meet at m = 7.5, c = -7.5, far outside the panel (|m| \le 4). In the normal form the line has \theta = 172.4°, \rho = -0.99: well inside the panel. With all three points at x = 0.6 the line is vertical: in slope–intercept form the three lines c = y_i - 0.6\,m become parallel (all have slope -0.6) and never meet (m = \infty); in the normal form the crossing simply moves to \theta = 180° \equiv 0°, \rho = 0.6.
D4. Six points give 6 \cdot 5/2 = 15 pairs, so 15 crossings. Here the three pairs within each line coincide: one pile at \theta = 108.4°, \rho = -0.63 (the line through (-4, -2), (-1, -1), (2, 0), i.e. y = (x - 2)/3) and one at \theta = 56.3°, \rho = 0.83 (through (-3, 3), (0, 1), (3, -1), i.e. y = 1 - 2x/3). The other 9 crossings are lines through one point of each line, spread out.
D5. Highest bin: 6 of 6 votes (15°, 1.5), 3 (10°, 1), 3 (5°, 0.5), 4 (2°, 0.25). With coarse bins all six slightly scattered curves fall into one bin; with finer bins the near-crossings no longer share a bin and the peak splits. The noise (the points are up to 0.14 off the best line) sets how small the bins can usefully be. (The small rise at 2° comes from where the bin edges happen to fall.)

title: Exercise: Hough transform for lines
text:
Explore: line detection
Three panels: the edge points (Canny from the edges day, orange; the edges buttons choose fine, medium or smooth settings), the accumulator (\theta across from 0° to 180°, \rho up; brightness is the square root of the votes; detected peaks are ringed), and the detected lines or segments. Click an edge point to see its votes (cyan) in the accumulator; click the accumulator to draw that bin’s line dashed on the image. The readout gives the number of edge points, the votes cast, the peaks, and the time.



E1. Preset clean lines. How many edge points and how many votes? Explain the ratio. How many lines are detected, and how many votes has the strongest? Click an edge point on the long side of the triangle and follow its curve to the peak.
E2. Still on clean lines, set the threshold to 30, then 60. How many lines are detected each time? Which sides of the shapes are lost first, and why?
E3. Preset no NMS: clusters. How many detections are there now, and what do they look like? Set the NMS window back to ±4.
E4. Preset bins too fine (noise 18, \Delta\theta = 0.25°, \Delta\rho = 0.5). How many lines are found, and how strong is the strongest peak? Now set \Delta\theta = 1°, \Delta\rho = 1 px (same noise). Then preset bins too coarse on the window grid: what goes wrong there?
E5. Preset clutter raises the floor (threshold 30). How many lines are detected? Compare with the same scene without clutter (clutter 0). Then preset gradient voting: votes per point, total votes, and detections. Finally widen the gradient window to ±15°: what changes?
E6. Preset segments with gaps (road, g = 6, L_\text{min} = 12). How many segments are drawn? Is the dashed centre line among them? Set g = 30: what appears, and what else appears? Which g would you choose for lane markings?
E7. Preset deskew the page. What dominant angle does the readout give, and what tilt? Why is the dominant angle near 90° rather than near 0°?
E8. Preset filaments (gradient voting, segments). How many filaments are found? Switch gradient voting off: how many detections now, and why?






Solutions





E1. 815 edge points and 146,700 votes: every point votes once for each of the 180 angles (815 \times 180). 8 lines above the threshold of 40; the strongest has 114 votes, at \theta = 148°, \rho = 35: the long left side of the triangle (about 140 px, partly hidden by the quadrilateral). The clicked point’s sinusoid passes through that peak, as do the sinusoids of all other points on the side.
E2. Threshold 30: 11 lines (every side of the three shapes); threshold 60: 3 lines. The threshold is a minimum length in pixels: the short sides of the quadrilateral and the partly hidden sides go first, the long sides of the triangle remain.
E3. 22 detections instead of 8: each strong line comes as a bundle of nearly identical lines (neighbouring bins of the same peak are all above the threshold).
E4. Fine bins: 3 lines, strongest peak 63 votes. With 1° and 1 px at the same noise: 9 lines, strongest 110. The noisy edge points of one side spread their votes over many small bins, so the peaks drop below the threshold. Coarse bins (5°, 8 px) on the window grid: 21 detections; each bin covers several neighbouring window edges, so lines from different rows and columns merge, and the detected lines run at the wrong angles between them.
E5. 32 lines with clutter, 11 without. The clutter blobs add about 1300 edge points whose curves raise the whole accumulator (the 99th percentile of the non-empty bins goes from 17 to 27 votes), so chance alignments of blob edges pass the threshold. Gradient voting: 7 votes per point (±3° in 1° bins), 14,826 votes instead of 381,240, and 5 detections: the blob edges point in all directions and no longer pile up. With ±15°: 31 votes per point, 65,658 votes and 9 detections: a wider window lets clutter back in.
E6. 7 segments: the horizon, the two sides of the road (road edge and lane line fall into the same peak), and four short pieces of accidental alignments; the dashed centre line is not among them: its peak has 50 votes, but each dash is only 10 px long, shorter than L_\text{min}, and the gaps (10 px) are longer than g. With g = 30: 10 segments; the centre line appears as one segment of 117 px, but the four accidental diagonals also grow into long false segments (52 to 95 px), because points scattered along them are now joined. A gap just above the dash spacing (about 12 px) joins the dashes without bridging larger empty stretches; the false diagonals are better removed with a higher threshold.
E7. \theta = 97.0°, a tilt of 7.0°. The text lines are nearly horizontal; the normal of a horizontal line points up, \theta = 90°. A page tilted by 7° counter-clockwise has normals at 97°.
E8. 6 peaks, 7 segments (one filament is split by a gap): the six filaments. Without gradient voting: 22 peaks and 14 segments; the clutter blobs and noise create chance alignments, and the two sides of each filament (about 2.5 px apart) can also give separate peaks.

title: Exercise: Hough transform for lines
text:
Where this leads
A circle has three parameters instead of two; the same voting idea gives the circle Hough transform in the next unit, where the gradient direction saves even more work. For any shape without a formula, the generalised Hough transform stores the shape as a table. And when voting needs too many bins, RANSAC guesses and checks instead.

title: Hough transform: circles
text:
About this lecture
The line unit let every edge point vote for all lines through it. Circles work the same way, with one more parameter (Kimme, Ballard & Sklansky, 1975).

A circle has three parameters: centre (a, b) and radius r.
Known radius: every edge point votes for a ring of possible centres; the rings meet at the true centre.
Unknown radius: a 3D accumulator, and what each extra parameter costs.
The gradient direction points at the centre: two votes per radius instead of a whole ring.
Applications, failure modes, alternatives, and ellipses briefly.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Second unit of the Hough day; builds on the line unit (voting, accumulator, peaks, NMS, gradient voting). Coordinates here are pixel coordinates (column, row): the centre of a circle is a pixel position, and the centre accumulator looks like the image.

title: Hough transform: circles
text:
Circles: three numbers
A circle is the set of points at distance r from a centre (a, b):
(x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2.

Three parameters, so the parameter space is 3D: one axis for each of a, b, r.
An edge point (x, y) is on every circle whose centre is at distance r from it.
For a fixed r those centres form a circle of radius r around the edge point.

title: Hough transform: circles
text:
Known radius: rings of votes

Left: with a known radius, each edge point (dots) votes for all centres at distance r: a ring around it. All rings pass through the true centre (+). The accumulator is a 2D image of the same size as the input, with a peak at every centre.

title: Hough transform: circles
text:
Try it: circles of votes




Panels: image with edge points (orange) and detections (cyan), the accumulator slice at the radius on the slider, the maximum over all radii. Values are votes / (2πr): the fraction of a full circumference that voted. Tour: “one radius” (r = 12): the edge point at the top of the upper-left disc is selected; its votes are the dashed ring in the slice. Two discs have r = 12: peaks 0.85 and 0.80; the others give rings of votes but no sharp peak. “wrong radius” (r = 15, no disc has it): highest value 0.25, nothing detected; the slice shows bright rings and blurred spots. Then “scan the radius” (r = 5–24, next slides): all 7 discs found, 1.37 million votes.

title: Hough transform: circles
text:
The math: a ring-shaped kernel
With a known radius, the accumulator at a candidate centre \mathbf c counts the edge pixels at distance r:
H_r(\mathbf c) = \sum_{\mathbf p} E(\mathbf p)\,K_r(\mathbf p - \mathbf c), \qquad K_r(\mathbf d) = \big[\, \big|\,\|\mathbf d\| - r\,\big| < \tfrac12 \,\big],
with E the binary edge map and K_r a ring of radius r and width one pixel. This is a correlation of the edge map with a ring (a convolution, since the ring is symmetric): the kernels unit’s weighted sum, with a ring as the kernel (Filtering & convolution). The ring has about 2\pi r pixels (a digital ring slightly fewer: 56 for r = 10), so dividing by 2\pi r gives the fraction of the circumference that is present.

title: Hough transform: circles
text:
Unknown radius: a 3D accumulator
Repeat for every radius in a range: one (a, b) slice per radius, stacked into a 3D accumulator (a, b, r). Each edge point now votes for a cone of centres (rings growing with r).

A circle is a peak in 3D: the right centre and the right radius.
NMS in 3D: largest in a window in a, b and r.
Cost: a 256 × 256 image with 40 radii has 2.6 million bins. With 5000 edge points and radii 5 to 40, each point casts \sum 2\pi r \approx 5100 votes: about 25 million votes.
Every extra parameter multiplies the bins and the votes by the number of steps along it.

title: Hough transform: circles
section: The math: the cost of each parameter
text:
The math: the cost of each parameter

With n steps per parameter and d parameters, the accumulator has n^d bins: lines n^2, circles n^3, ellipses n^5.
Full voting: each edge point votes along a (d-1)-dimensional surface of parameter space (a curve for lines, a cone for circles): O(n^{d-1}) votes per point.
Gradient voting fixes one more parameter per point: for circles, the gradient fixes the direction from the point to the centre, leaving only r free: O(n) votes per point instead of O(n^2).
Memory can be cut by keeping only a 2D centre map (votes summed over r), then estimating r per detected centre from a radius histogram of its edge points.

title: Hough transform: circles
section: The gradient points at the centre
text:
The gradient points at the centre
On a circle, the gradient of the image is radial: it points straight towards the centre, or straight away from it.

Bright disc on a dark background: the gradient points inward, the centre is at \mathbf p + r\,\mathbf u (\mathbf u the unit gradient).
Dark disc on a bright background: outward, the centre is at \mathbf p - r\,\mathbf u.
Unknown polarity: vote for both, two votes per radius. Known polarity: one.

Example: radius 5, edge point (3, 4), unit gradient (0.6, 0.8): candidate centres (3, 4) \pm 5\,(0.6, 0.8) = (6, 8) or (0, 0).
From 2\pi r votes per radius to 1 or 2: for radii 5 to 40, from about 5100 to 36 or 72 votes per point.

title: Hough transform: circles
section: Try it: gradient voting and a range of radii
text:
Try it: gradient voting and a range of radii




“gradient voting”, bright on dark, radii 5–24: 15,437 votes instead of 1,370,005 (full voting, preset “scan the radius”); all 7 discs found, but peaks are lower (0.40 to 0.74 instead of 0.68 to 0.99): the gradient direction is not exact, so the votes for large radii scatter. The selected point at the top of the r = 18 disc votes one dot per radius (magenta) along its gradient; at r = 18 it hits the centre. Switch polarity to “dark on bright”: no disc is found (maximum 0.06): every vote goes the wrong way. “either”: 30,203 votes, same detections. Click a centre in the slice: the votes at that centre against r (radius histogram), peak at the true radius.

title: Hough transform: circles
text:
Applications

Nuclei, round cells, vesicles: bright or dark discs of a known range of radii. Gradient voting with the right polarity.
Colonies on an agar plate: many discs, different radii.
Wells of a multi-well plate: a known radius (one slice) and a regular grid. (Demo: “plate wells”: all 42 wells, dark on bright.)
Powder diffraction rings: concentric circles around a known centre. Then only r is unknown: the accumulator is a 1D histogram of radius at that centre. (Demo: “diffraction rings”: click the centre.)
A detected centre as the starting point of a boundary search in polar coordinates (the dynamic-programming elective).

title: Hough transform: circles
text:
When circles go wrong

Not quite circles: an ellipse or an irregular cell has no single centre. Its votes smear over several centres and radii; the peak is low and wide. (Demo: “ellipse”.)
Touching or overlapping cells: a shared or missing boundary removes votes from both; parts of two circles can add up to a weak extra peak.
Low threshold: any curved piece of boundary has a centre of curvature and collects some votes there. (Demo: “low threshold: false circles”: the ellipse gives two false circles of radius 9 near its ends.)
Wrong radius range: a circle outside the range is never found; a range that is too wide costs time and invites false peaks.
Strong straight edges nearby: their votes form bright lines in the accumulator.

title: Hough transform: circles
text:
Alternatives for round objects

Distance transform peaks (the morphology day): from a binary mask, the centre of a disc is the pixel farthest from the background; touching discs give two peaks. They also make markers for the watershed (the watershed day).
Blob detection with the Laplacian of Gaussian at scale \sigma \approx r/\sqrt2 (the edges day): a region-based cousin that uses the inside of the disc, not its edge.
Circle Hough: works on edges, tolerates gaps and partial occlusion, and gives the radius.

title: Hough transform: circles
text:
Ellipses, briefly
An ellipse needs five parameters: centre (2), the two semi-axes (2) and an angle (1). A full 5D accumulator is impractical: with 50 steps per parameter that is 312 million bins.
Two ways out:

Find the centre first: two edge points with parallel gradients on an ellipse lie symmetrically about its centre; their midpoints vote for the centre in 2D. Then find the remaining three parameters.
Hypothesise and verify: fit an ellipse to 5 random edge points and count how many others agree (the RANSAC unit).

title: Hough transform: circles
section: The math: conics have five degrees of freedom
text:
The math: conics have five degrees of freedom
Every ellipse (and every conic) is the zero set of a quadratic:
A x^2 + B xy + C y^2 + D x + E y + F = 0, \qquad B^2 - 4AC < 0 \text{ for an ellipse}.
Six coefficients, but multiplying all of them by the same non-zero number gives the same curve: 5 degrees of freedom, so five points in general position determine a conic (one linear equation per point, a 5 \times 6 system with a one-dimensional null space). A circle is the special case B = 0, A = C: three degrees of freedom, as in (a, b, r).

title: Hough transform: circles
text:
Summary

A circle has 3 parameters; an edge point votes for a ring of centres per radius (a cone over all radii).
Known radius: a 2D accumulator, the edge map correlated with a ring.
Unknown radius: 3D, and the cost grows with every parameter.
The gradient points at the centre: 1 or 2 votes per radius, depending on whether the polarity is known.
Watch for non-circular objects, touching objects, the radius range and the threshold.
Ellipses (5 parameters) need the centre first, or hypothesise-and-verify.

title: Quiz: histograms and a global threshold
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Object pixels are those with I(x) > t; p_i is the normalised histogram and P(t) the cumulative histogram.

Q1. An image has N = 10\,000 pixels, and 400 of them have grey level 200. What is p_{200}? What does it mean in words?






Hint





Divide by the number of pixels.









Answer





p_{200} = 400/10\,000 = 0.04: a pixel chosen at random has grey level 200 with probability 4 %.




Q2. P(120) = 0.85. Which fraction of the image does the threshold t = 120 call object?






Hint





P(t) counts the pixels at or below t.









Answer





1 - P(120) = 0.15: 15 % of the pixels are brighter than 120 and become object.




Q3. Two images have exactly the same histogram. Must a histogram-based threshold give masks of the same shape? Of the same area?






Hint





What does a histogram remember about the pixels?









Answer





Same area, yes: the threshold is the same and the area is 1 - P(t). Same shape, no: the histogram forgets where the pixels are, so one image may contain round blobs and the other scattered noise with the same grey levels.




Q4. The valley of a histogram is deep and wide between 90 and 140. Why does it hardly matter where in the valley you put t?






Hint





When t moves up by one grey level, which pixels change label?









Answer





Only the pixels with grey level exactly at the threshold change label, and in a deep valley there are almost none. The mask (and its area) stays nearly the same for every t in the valley.




Q5. You add noise to a bimodal image. What happens to the two peaks and the valley, and what does the mask look like?






Hint





Each pixel moves up or down by a random amount.









Answer





Both peaks get wider, overlap, and the valley fills up. Pixels whose noise pushes them across t are misclassified one by one: isolated wrong pixels (salt and pepper) in the object and in the background.




Q6. A 5 \times 5 mean filter is applied before thresholding. By which factor does it reduce the noise, and what is the price?






Hint





An average of n independent values.









Answer





It averages 25 pixels, so the noise standard deviation drops by \sqrt{25} = 5. The price: edges are blurred over about 5 pixels, so boundary pixels become mixtures (partial volume), small objects lose contrast, and the boundary of the mask is less precise.




Q7. A 16-bit image from a 12-bit camera uses grey levels 100–3900. Why is a histogram with 256 bins over 0–65 535 a poor choice?






Hint





Compute the bin width.









Answer





Each bin is 256 grey levels wide, so all the data fall into about 15 bins: the peaks merge and the valley is invisible. Use bins over the range of the data (e.g. 256 bins over 100–3900) or one bin per grey level.




Q8. (math) Show that the mean grey level of the image equals \sum_i i\, p_i.






Hint





Group the pixels by grey level.









Answer





\frac1N \sum_{\text{pixels } x} I(x) = \frac1N \sum_i i \cdot h_i = \sum_i i\,\frac{h_i}{N} = \sum_i i\,p_i: summing over pixels is the same as summing over grey levels, each counted h_i times.

compute a histogram, its normalised and cumulative versions, and threshold a small image by hand,

explain why a threshold in a deep valley is robust and one in a shallow valley is not,

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: histograms and a global threshold
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Binary mask
B(x) = 1 (object) where I(x) > t, else 0 (background)


Histogram
h_i = number of pixels with grey level i (or in bin i)


Normalised histogram
p_i = h_i / N, N = number of pixels; \sum_i p_i = 1


Cumulative histogram
P(t) = \sum_{i \le t} p_i: the fraction of pixels a threshold at t calls background


Mask area
1 - P(t)


Percentile threshold
the t with P(t) = 1 - q: keep the brightest fraction q


Ground truth
the true mask (known for synthetic images, drawn by hand for real ones)
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Exercise: histograms and a global threshold
text:
By hand
B1. A 5 \times 5 image with grey levels 0–7: I = \begin{bmatrix} 0&1&1&2&1\\ 1&6&7&6&2\\ 1&7&5&6&1\\ 2&6&6&3&0\\ 1&2&1&0&4 \end{bmatrix} (a) Draw the histogram h_i, the normalised histogram p_i and the cumulative histogram P(t). (b) Threshold at t = 3 and at t = 4 (object where I > t). How many object pixels does each give, and which pixels change? Why is the change small? (c) Compare t = 1 with t = 2. Which threshold would you trust more, and why?
B2. A 256 \times 256 image: background grey level 50 (75 % of the pixels), objects 110 (25 %), plus Gaussian noise with standard deviation \sigma_n = 20. The threshold is t = 80. (a) Which fraction of the background pixels ends up above t, and of the object pixels below t? How many wrong pixels is that in total? (A normal variable lies more than 1.5 standard deviations above its mean with probability 0.0668.) (b) The image is smoothed first with a 3 \times 3 mean. What is the noise now, and roughly how many wrong pixels remain? (More than 4.5 standard deviations: probability 3.4 \cdot 10^{-6}.) (c) Which pixels does (b) ignore, that will in fact be wrong after smoothing?
B3. A 12-bit camera stores its images in a 16-bit container (grey levels 0–4095 out of 0–65 535). (a) You make a histogram with 256 equal bins over 0–65 535. How many bins contain data? (b) Suggest two better choices of bins.
B4. In a 512 \times 512 fluorescence image, spots cover about 2 % of the pixels. The cumulative histogram gives P(100) = 0.950, P(110) = 0.968, P(120) = 0.980, P(130) = 0.988. (a) Which threshold keeps the brightest 2 %? How many pixels is that? (b) In the next image of the series the cells are more active and spots cover 4 %. What does the same percentile rule do now?
B5. In the demo’s synthetic image (25 % objects) the mask area is 25.8 % at t = 100 and 22.3 % at t = 130. After adding strong noise (\sigma_n = 35) it is 33.8 % and 20.5 %. (a) How many pixels per thousand change label per grey level of t in each case? (b) Which image’s segmentation depends more on the exact choice of t, and by what factor? What does that tell you about its histogram between 100 and 130?
B6. A 3 \times 3 window of a dark background contains one hot pixel: 50, 52, 48, 51, 250, 49, 50, 53, 47 (the 250 in the centre). (a) Compute the mean and the median of the window. (b) The image is thresholded at t = 60 after a 3 \times 3 mean. What happens around the hot pixel? And after a 3 \times 3 median?
B7. You shuffle the pixels of an image to random positions. Which of these change: the histogram, the mask area at t = 100, the shape of the mask, the best threshold according to a method that uses only the histogram?






Solutions





B1. (a) Counts h = (3, 8, 4, 1, 1, 1, 5, 2) for grey levels 0–7 (sum 25). Normalised: p = (0.12, 0.32, 0.16, 0.04, 0.04, 0.04, 0.20, 0.08). Cumulative: P = (0.12, 0.44, 0.60, 0.64, 0.68, 0.72, 0.92, 1.00). (b) t = 3: the 9 pixels with grey level 4–7 (the 3 \times 3 bright block except the 3, plus the 4 in the bottom-right corner). t = 4: 8 pixels; only the single 4 in the corner changes. The change is small because there is only one pixel at grey level 4: t moves inside the valley of the histogram (levels 3, 4, 5 have one pixel each). (c) t = 1 gives 14 object pixels, t = 2 gives 10: the four 2s change, the edge of the dark peak. A threshold in the valley (3 or 4) is more trustworthy: moving it by one changes one pixel, not four.
B2. (a) 80 is 1.5 standard deviations from both means: 6.68 % of each class is wrong. That is 0.0668 \cdot 49\,152 = 3284 background pixels and 0.0668 \cdot 16\,384 = 1095 object pixels: about 4378 wrong pixels, scattered as salt and pepper. (b) The mean of 9 independent noise values has \sigma = 20/3 = 6.7. Now 80 is 4.5 standard deviations away: 3.4 \cdot 10^{-6} \cdot 65\,536 \approx 0.2, so essentially no pixel inside the objects or the background is wrong. (c) The pixels near the edges: their 3 \times 3 window contains both object and background, so their mean lies between 50 and 110 (partial volume). Those near 80 can go either way; the boundary becomes less precise.
B3. (a) The bin width is 65\,536/256 = 256, so 0–4095 fall into the first 4096/256 = 16 bins; the other 240 bins are empty. The histogram has 16 coarse bars: any valley is invisible. (b) One bin per grey level over 0–4095 (4096 bins), or 256 bins over the actual range of the data [\min, \max] (width 16 for the full 12-bit range). With few pixels per bin, prefer fewer bins.
B4. (a) P(t) = 1 - 0.02 = 0.98 at t = 120. That keeps 0.02 \cdot 262\,144 \approx 5243 pixels. (b) It still keeps the brightest 2 %, i.e. about half of the spot pixels: the threshold rises into the spots. The percentile rule assumes the object fraction, so it is only safe when that fraction is known and stable.
B5. (a) Clean: (25.8 - 22.3)\,\% / 30 = 0.117\,\%, i.e. 1.2 pixels per thousand per grey level. Noisy: (33.8 - 20.5)\,\% / 30 = 0.443\,\%, i.e. 4.4 per thousand. (b) The noisy one, 3.8 times as sensitive. The change of the area per grey level is the histogram at t: the clean histogram has a deep valley between 100 and 130, the noisy one has pixels everywhere there.
B6. (a) Mean 650/9 = 72.2, median 50. (b) After the mean, every window that contains the hot pixel (the 9 windows around it) has a mean near 72: a 3 \times 3 object appears around the hot pixel. The mean spreads the outlier instead of removing it. After the median every window gives about 50: the hot pixel disappears.
B7. Unchanged: the histogram (the same grey levels), hence the mask area at any t and the threshold of any histogram method. Changed: the shape of the mask, which becomes scattered pixels instead of blobs.




Math questions
B8. (math) Show that \sigma^2 = \sum_i (i - \mu)^2 p_i = \sum_i i^2 p_i - \mu^2. Compute \mu and \sigma^2 for the image of B1.
B9. (math) Noise values n_1, \dots, n_n are independent with variance \sigma^2, and \bar n = \sum_k w_k n_k with \sum_k w_k = 1. Show that \operatorname{Var}(\bar n) = \sigma^2 \sum_k w_k^2, and that among all weights with \sum_k w_k = 1 the equal weights w_k = 1/n make it smallest.
B10. (math) Let A(t) = 1 - P(t) be the mask area. Show that A(t) - A(t + 1) = p_{t+1}, and for continuous grey levels with density p(x) that A'(t) = -p(t). Use it to explain B5.






Solutions (math)





B8. Expand: \sum_i (i - \mu)^2 p_i = \sum_i i^2 p_i - 2\mu \sum_i i\,p_i + \mu^2 \sum_i p_i = \sum_i i^2 p_i - 2\mu^2 + \mu^2. For B1: \mu = \sum_i i\,p_i = 72/25 = 2.88; \sum_i i^2 p_i = 352/25 = 14.08; \sigma^2 = 14.08 - 2.88^2 = 5.79.
B9. For independent variables the variances add: \operatorname{Var}(\sum_k w_k n_k) = \sum_k w_k^2 \operatorname{Var}(n_k) = \sigma^2 \sum_k w_k^2. Minimise \sum_k w_k^2 subject to \sum_k w_k = 1: the Lagrange condition 2w_k = \lambda makes all weights equal, w_k = 1/n, with \sum_k w_k^2 = 1/n. (Or by Cauchy–Schwarz: 1 = (\sum_k w_k)^2 \le n \sum_k w_k^2.)
B10. A(t) = \sum_{i > t} p_i, so A(t) - A(t + 1) = \sum_{i > t} p_i - \sum_{i > t + 1} p_i = p_{t+1}. Continuously, A(t) = \int_t^\infty p(x)\,dx and A'(t) = -p(t) by the fundamental theorem of calculus. In B5 the average slope between 100 and 130 is the average histogram height there: 1.2 per thousand per grey level for the clean image, 4.4 for the noisy one.

title: Exercise: histograms and a global threshold
text:
Explore
The demo shows an image (left) with the mask in orange, its histogram (top right) and the mask area 1 - P(t) as a function of t (bottom right). Drag the threshold on either plot, or use the slider. The synthetic image has bright blobs covering exactly 25 % of the pixels on a dark background; its ground truth is known, so the readout gives the Dice coefficient (1 = the mask is perfect; defined in the evaluation unit). noise σ adds Gaussian noise; median 3×3 and blur σ smooth the image before the histogram is made; bins sets the number of histogram bins; P(t) adds the cumulative histogram to both plots; dark objects makes the mask I \le t.



E1. Preset clean bimodal. Read the mask area and Dice at t = 120. Move t to 100 and to 130: how much do the mask area and Dice change? Find the t with the highest Dice.
E2. Tick P(t). Where does the cumulative curve rise steeply, and where is it flat? Relate this to the peaks and the valley of the histogram.
E3. Preset noise fills the valley. Where is the valley now? Read Dice at t = 110, and find the best t. Then preset blur restores it: Dice at t = 110? Instead of the blur, try median 3×3 (blur σ = 0), then blur σ = 3. Which works best, and why is σ = 3 worse than σ = 1.5?
E4. Preset too few bins (8 bins). Can you see two peaks? Raise the bins to 32 and 256. Which number of bins shows the structure best for this 256 \times 256 image? Tick log scale: what does it reveal?
E5. Preset percentile: brightest 25 % (noise 35). Which t does it choose, and how does its Dice compare with the best you found in E3? Why does this work here, and when would it fail?
E6. Preset the micrograph (an electron micrograph: the cell is darker than the empty background, so dark objects is on). Describe the histogram. Is there a clear valley? What does the mask contain at t = 150?






Solutions





E1. At t = 120: mask area 23.7 % (truth: 25 %), Dice 0.974. At t = 100: 25.8 %, Dice 0.983; at t = 130: 22.3 %, Dice 0.942. Thirty grey levels move only 3.5 % of the pixels, because t is in the valley. The best Dice is 0.991 at t = 108.
E2. P(t) rises steeply through each peak (most steeply in the background peak around 60, where 75 % of the pixels sit) and is almost flat in the valley between about 90 and 140 and above 190. Its slope is the histogram, and the mask area is its mirror image 1 - P(t).
E3. With noise 35 the two peaks merge into one broad hump with a shoulder; there is no valley. Dice at t = 110 is 0.813; the best is 0.823 at t = 119. After a Gaussian blur with σ = 1.5 the valley is back and Dice at t = 110 is 0.970. The 3 \times 3 median gives 0.960, a bit worse here (the noise is Gaussian, which averaging handles best). With σ = 3 the best Dice falls to 0.949 (0.936 at t = 110): the blur now smears the edges of the blobs over several pixels, and these partial-volume pixels fill the valley again.
E4. With 8 bins (width 32) the histogram is a staircase: a big bar for the background and a falling tail, with no visible second peak. With 32 bins both peaks and the valley appear; 256 bins also show them, but more ragged (about 256 pixels per bin on average). 32–64 bins are a good compromise here. The log scale makes small counts visible: the long tails of the peaks and the few pixels in the valley.
E5. It chooses t = 119 (the smallest t with P(t) \ge 0.75), with Dice 0.823, the same as the best threshold of E3. It works because the objects really cover 25 % of this image. In an image with a different object fraction it would keep the wrong number of pixels, however clear the valley is.
E6. The histogram is broad: it rises from about 50 to a plateau between 100 and 200 and has a peak near 240, the empty background. There is no deep valley; the cell (cytoplasm, nucleus, dark membranes) spreads over most grey levels. At t = 150 the mask holds 39.7 % of the pixels: the cell, its dark membranes and the dark material outside it, with a ragged boundary where texture crosses the threshold. A single threshold cannot pick out the nucleus: it has the same grey levels as the cytoplasm.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
text:
About this lecture

Scientific and medical images have 12 or 16 bits per pixel. Screens show 8.
How the numbers are stored: containers, alignment, packing, signed and unsigned types.
How arithmetic on them breaks: wrap-around, saturation, and why we compute in a wider type.
How to show them: windows, CT window/level, contrast stretching, colour maps.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

The previous unit said how many bits are worth measuring. This one is about the daily life of those bits: the black image that is not black, the background subtraction that turns the background white, the CT window. All of it is simple, and all of it causes real errors in real projects.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
section: Where high bit depths come from
text:
Where high bit depths come from

A memory container comes in 8, 16 or 32 bits. A 12-bit value sits in a 16-bit box with 4 bits to spare.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
text:
The black image
A 12-bit camera writes values 0…4095 into a 16-bit file. A viewer that assumes the full 16-bit range maps 0 → black and 65 535 → white:
4095 \;\mapsto\; 255 \cdot \tfrac{4095}{65\,535} \approx 16 \text{ of } 255.
The brightest pixel is shown as a dark grey: the image looks black, but nothing is wrong with the data. Only the display range is wrong.

LSB-aligned: the 12 bits are the low bits; values 0…4095. The usual case.
MSB-aligned: the 12 bits are shifted to the top (value × 16); values 0…65 520, every 16th value used. Displays fine, but the histogram is a comb.
Packed: two 12-bit pixels in 3 bytes, no wasted bits (25 % smaller); must be unpacked before use.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
text:
Try it: show a 12-bit image




Starts with the window 0–65535: black. Switch histogram axis between type range and data range. Click 0–4095: the cells appear. min–max is almost the same here (the data reach 4095 because two spots saturate). Percentiles 0.5–99.5 % gives a much better picture: the saturated spots no longer set the scale. Show hi-lo: blue and red mark what is clipped. Then MSB-aligned with data-range histogram: a comb, every 16th value. Keep the subtraction presets for the next slide.

text:
Integer types

Signed integers use two’s complement: −1 is stored as all ones (0xFFFF in 16 bits), −30 as 65 506.
The same 16 bits mean 65 506 as uint16 and −30 as int16. The bits do not know their type; the file header or your program decides.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
section: When the result does not fit
text:
When the result does not fit
Subtract a background of 160 from a pixel of 150, in uint16:

Same trap when averaging: in uint16, (40\,000 + 30\,000)/2 gives 2232 instead of 35 000, because the sum wraps before the division.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
section: The math: wrap-around is arithmetic modulo 2^n
text:
The math: wrap-around is arithmetic modulo 2^n
An n-bit unsigned integer stores every result modulo 2^n:
a \ominus b = (a - b) \bmod 2^n, \qquad 150 \ominus 160 = -10 + 65\,536 = 65\,526.
Two’s complement uses the same rule to store negatives: -x is stored as 2^n - x. That is why addition and subtraction circuits do not care whether a number is signed: only the interpretation of the top half of the range differs (2^{n-1} \dots 2^n - 1 means -2^{n-1} \dots -1).
Saturation is \min(\max(a - b, 0), 2^n - 1): not modular, and not linear either; \mathbb E[\max(X, 0)] > \mathbb E[X] when X has noise around 0.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
text:
Rules for arithmetic

Compute in a wider type: convert to float (or int32) before subtracting, adding, averaging, filtering. A filter with negative weights needs signed results anyway.
Convert back on purpose, with an explicit scale and clip, and only for storage or display.
Watch the conventions: some programs scale floats to [0, 1], others keep raw counts. Converting 4095 (uint16) to a “[0, 1] float” can give 4095/65\,535 \approx 0.0625, not 1.
Summing frames: 16 frames of a 12-bit camera fit in uint16 (16 \cdot 4095 = 65\,520); the 17th does not.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
section: Showing 12–16 bits on an 8-bit screen: windows
text:
Showing 12–16 bits on an 8-bit screen: windows
A window [\ell, h] maps raw values linearly to the 256 display levels and clips the rest:

v \le \ell → black, v \ge h → white, in between a linear ramp.
Window/level: width W = h - \ell, centre L = (\ell + h)/2.
A narrow window spreads a small range of values over all display levels: more contrast, more clipping.
Auto-contrast: set \ell and h to percentiles (say 0.5 % and 99.5 %), so a few saturated or dead pixels do not set the scale.

The window changes only the display. Measure on the raw values.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
text:
The math: the window formula
The display level of a raw value v is the straight line through (\ell, 0) and (h, 255), clipped and rounded:
d(v) = \operatorname{round}\!\left(255 \cdot \operatorname{clip}\!\left(\frac{v - \ell}{h - \ell},\; 0,\; 1\right)\right).
With width W = h - \ell, one display level covers W/256 raw values: for W = 4096, 16 raw values share one grey on screen. A LUT (look-up table) generalises this: any function from raw value to colour, stored as a table. The window is the linear LUT.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
text:
CT: Hounsfield units and windows
CT measures X-ray attenuation \mu and reports it relative to water, in Hounsfield units (HU): air −1000, fat ≈ −100, water 0, soft tissue 20–80, bone several hundred to 2000+.
Soft tissue differs by tens of HU, but the image spans 4000 HU: no single window shows everything. Radiologists switch between standard windows:

Files often store HU + 1024 as unsigned numbers, with the offset in the header; forget it and every window is 1024 HU off.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
text:
The math: Hounsfield units
\text{HU} = 1000 \cdot \frac{\mu - \mu_\text{water}}{\mu_\text{water} - \mu_\text{air}}.
Water is 0 and air is −1000 by construction; one HU is 0.1 % of the attenuation of water. A stored value s becomes HU through a linear rescale, \text{HU} = a\,s + c (often a = 1, c = -1024), recorded in the file header.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
text:
Try it: CT windows


Synthetic slice: body, fat layer, lungs with vessels, a vertebra at the back, an organ between the lungs with a faint lesion 20 HU brighter than its surroundings. Soft tissue: organs visible, lungs black, bone white. Lung: vessels in the lung, everything else white. Bone: the cortical rim. Narrow W150 L70: the lesion appears. Then “uint16 HU+1024” with the soft-tissue preset: everything white, because the window was meant for HU, not for stored numbers.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
section: Colour maps, HDR and tone mapping
text:
Colour maps, HDR and tone mapping

A LUT can map grey values to colours. A “hi-lo” LUT marks clipped pixels (blue below, red above): use it to set a window honestly. Perceptual colour maps are on the colour day.
High dynamic range (HDR) scenes span 10^5 : 1 or more. A linear window either loses the shadows or the highlights.
Tone mapping compresses the range with a non-linear curve (e.g. logarithmic, or x/(1 + x)), globally or adapted to the neighbourhood. Good for looking, bad for measuring: it changes the ratios between pixels.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
text:
Summary

12-bit data in a 16-bit container look black when shown as 0…65 535: the display range, not the data, is wrong.
Integer arithmetic wraps (modulo 2^n) or saturates; both are wrong for negative results. Compute in float or a wider type.
A window maps a range of raw values to the 256 display levels; CT uses standard windows in Hounsfield units.
Displays, LUTs and tone mapping are for looking; analysis uses the raw numbers.

title: Quiz: the Hessian
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Eigenvalues are ordered |\lambda_1| \le |\lambda_2|; bright = high.

Q1. What do the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the Hessian at a pixel tell you, in words?






Hint





Think of the image as a landscape.









Answer





The eigenvalues are the strongest and weakest curvature (bending) of the brightness surface at that pixel; the eigenvectors are the two perpendicular directions in which they occur. Negative means bending down (a bright structure), positive bending up (a dark one).




Q2. At a pixel \lambda_1 = -0.5 and \lambda_2 = -12. What structure is this? In which direction does it run?






Hint





One strong curvature, one weak.









Answer





A bright ridge (line): it bends down strongly across one direction (\lambda_2) and hardly at all along the other. It runs along the eigenvector of \lambda_1.




Q3. Classify: (a) \lambda = (-8, -10); (b) \lambda = (6, -9); (c) \lambda = (0.2, 11); (d) \lambda = (0.1, -0.3) when the noise gives |λ| up to about 1.






Hint





Signs, and the ratio of the sizes.









Answer






Bright blob (both strongly negative, similar size). (b) Saddle (opposite signs, both large). (c) Dark ridge (one strong positive curvature, the other ≈ 0). (d) Flat (both within the noise).





Q4. Why can the Laplacian of Gaussian not tell a blob from a line, while the determinant of the Hessian can?






Hint





Trace and determinant in terms of the eigenvalues.









Answer





The LoG is the trace \lambda_1 + \lambda_2. A blob with λ = (−10, −10) and a line with λ = (0, −20) both give −20. The determinant \lambda_1\lambda_2 is 100 for the blob and 0 for the line: it is large only when both curvatures are large.




Q5. What does the Hessian report at a step edge?






Hint





Where is the second derivative across a step zero?









Answer





On the edge itself the curvature across it is zero (it is the zero crossing of the second derivative), so the pixel looks flat. Just inside the bright side the brightness bends down (a weak bright half-ridge), just outside it bends up (a weak dark half-ridge). The Hessian finds the centres of lines and blobs; edges are the gradient’s job.




Q6. Vesselness has two knobs, β and c. What happens if you make β very large? If you make c very large?






Hint





Look at which ratio each one divides.









Answer





β divides the blob ratio R_B = \lambda_1/\lambda_2: with a large β the blob penalty disappears and blobs score as high as lines. c divides the structure strength S: with a large c almost every structure counts as “weak”, so all vesselness values become small (only the strongest lines remain visible).




Q7. Why is vesselness computed at several σ and normalised by σ²? What fails at a junction of two vessels?






Hint





Which σ fits a thin line, and which a thick one?









Answer





Each line responds best at a σ matched to its width; a single σ misses thick lines (or broadens thin ones). Normalising by σ² makes the responses at different σ comparable, so the maximum over σ picks each line’s own scale. At a junction two lines cross: both curvatures are large, the pixel looks like a blob, and vesselness drops exactly where branches meet.




Q8. (math) Show that the curvature \mathbf u^\top H\mathbf u along a unit vector \mathbf u is largest and smallest along the eigenvectors of H.






Hint





Write \mathbf u in the eigenvector basis.









Answer





H is symmetric, so it has orthonormal eigenvectors \mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2. Write \mathbf u = \cos\phi\,\mathbf e_1 + \sin\phi\,\mathbf e_2. Then \mathbf u^\top H\mathbf u = \lambda_1\cos^2\phi + \lambda_2\sin^2\phi, a weighted average of the two eigenvalues with weights summing to 1. It lies between them and reaches them exactly at \phi = 0 and \phi = 90°, i.e. along the eigenvectors.

title: Exercise: the Hessian
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Hessian
H = \begin{pmatrix} L_{xx} & L_{xy} \\ L_{xy} & L_{yy}\end{pmatrix} of the image smoothed at scale σ; x right, y down


Eigenvalues
the extreme curvatures, ordered \lvert\lambda_1\rvert \le \lvert\lambda_2\rvert; eigenvectors = their directions (perpendicular)


Closed form
\lambda = \frac{a + c}{2} \pm \sqrt{\big(\frac{a - c}{2}\big)^2 + b^2} for \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & c\end{pmatrix}


Classes
(\lambda_1, \lambda_2) both ≪ 0: bright blob; \lambda_2 \ll 0, \lambda_1 \approx 0: bright ridge; opposite signs: saddle; both ≈ 0: flat; dark = signs flipped


Trace, determinant
\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 (= LoG), \lambda_1\lambda_2


Vesselness
\mathcal V = e^{-R_B^2/2\beta^2}\big(1 - e^{-S^2/2c^2}\big) if \lambda_2 < 0 (else 0), R_B = \lambda_1/\lambda_2, S = \sqrt{\lambda_1^2 + \lambda_2^2}


Second differences
L_{xx} \approx [1\;-2\;1] along a row, L_{yy} along a column, L_{xy} \approx \tfrac14\big[f(1,1) - f(1,-1) - f(-1,1) + f(-1,-1)\big]

B5. A Hessian at a pixel is \begin{pmatrix} -20 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{pmatrix}. Compute the eigenvalues, the class, and the vesselness for β = 0.5, c = 15. What happens to the vesselness if β = 0.1? If c = 50?






Solutions





B1. (a) H = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}: \lambda_1 = 0, eigenvector (0, 1) (along y); \lambda_2 = -2, eigenvector (1, 0). A bright ridge running vertically (along y). (b) H = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{pmatrix}: \lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = -2, every direction is an eigenvector. A bright blob (hilltop). (c) H = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{pmatrix}: \lambda = 2 (eigenvector (1, 0)) and -2 (eigenvector (0, 1)), equal in size; a saddle: brightness rises left and right, falls up and down. (d) f = -(x^2 + 2xy + y^2), H = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2\end{pmatrix}: \lambda_1 = 0 with eigenvector (1, -1)/\sqrt2, \lambda_2 = -4 with eigenvector (1, 1)/\sqrt2. A bright ridge along the line x + y = 0; with y down, (1, -1) points up and to the right on the screen.
B2. (a) L_{xx} = 5 - 18 + 5 = -8; L_{yy} = 5 - 18 + 5 = -8; L_{xy} = \tfrac14(9 - 1 - 1 + 9) = 4. (b) \lambda = -8 \pm 4: \lambda_1 = -4, \lambda_2 = -12. The eigenvector of -4: \begin{pmatrix} -8 & 4 \\ 4 & -8\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1\end{pmatrix} = -4\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1\end{pmatrix}, so (1, 1)/\sqrt2. (c) |\lambda_1/\lambda_2| = 1/3: one curvature three times the other, both negative: a bright ridge (with this ratio threshold of ½), running along (1, 1), i.e. from top left to bottom right. The patch indeed has its bright values (9) on that diagonal.

B4. At σ = 2 (much smaller than the disc): centre flat (λ ≈ 0: the inside of the disc is flat at this scale); 8 px: bright ridge (λ = −5.2, −22.9: the brightness starts to fall towards the rim); 12 px: dark ridge (λ = −3.4, +23.0: it bends up as it reaches the dark floor); 20 px: flat. With β = 0.1 the blob penalty becomes strict: e^{-0.137^2/0.02} = 0.39, \mathcal V = 0.24. With c = 50 the structure counts as weak: 1 - e^{-20.42^2/5000} = 0.080, \mathcal V = 0.08.




Math questions
B6. (math) Derive the closed-form eigenvalues of \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & c\end{pmatrix} from the characteristic polynomial, and show that they are always real. When are they equal?
B7. (math) Show that trace and determinant of the Hessian do not change when the image is rotated. (Hint: rotating the image by R turns H into R^\top H R.)
B8. (math) A bright line with a Gaussian profile of width s: I(x, y) = A\,e^{-x^2/2s^2}. (a) Show that after smoothing with G_\sigma, L(x) = \frac{As}{\sqrt{s^2 + \sigma^2}}e^{-x^2/2(s^2 + \sigma^2)}. (b) Compute \sigma^2 L_{xx}(0) and find the σ where its size is largest. (c) What does this mean for reading the width of a vessel from the best scale?






Solutions (math)





B6. \det\begin{pmatrix} a - \lambda & b \\ b & c - \lambda\end{pmatrix} = \lambda^2 - (a + c)\lambda + (ac - b^2) = 0, so \lambda = \frac{a + c}{2} \pm \sqrt{\frac{(a + c)^2}{4} - ac + b^2} = \frac{a + c}{2} \pm \sqrt{\big(\frac{a - c}{2}\big)^2 + b^2}. The square root is of a sum of squares, so it is real. The eigenvalues are equal only if a = c and b = 0, i.e. H is a multiple of the identity (a perfectly round blob or a flat pixel).
B7. If L'(\mathbf x) = L(R\mathbf x), the chain rule gives H' = R^\top H R. Then \operatorname{tr}(R^\top H R) = \operatorname{tr}(H R R^\top) = \operatorname{tr}H (cyclic property, RR^\top = I), and \det(R^\top H R) = \det R^\top \det H \det R = \det H. Equivalently, H' has the same eigenvalues as H; only the eigenvectors rotate.
B8. (a) In x the profile is A\sqrt{2\pi}\,s\,g_s(x); convolving with g_\sigma gives A\sqrt{2\pi}\,s\,g_{\sqrt{s^2 + \sigma^2}}(x) (semigroup), which is the stated expression. (b) With v = s^2 + \sigma^2: L_{xx}(0) = -\frac{As}{\sqrt v}\cdot\frac1v, so \sigma^2 L_{xx}(0) = -As\,\frac{\sigma^2}{v^{3/2}}. Setting the derivative with respect to \sigma^2 to zero: v^{-3/2} - \tfrac32\sigma^2 v^{-5/2} = 0 \Rightarrow v = \tfrac32\sigma^2 \Rightarrow \sigma^2 = 2s^2, \sigma = \sqrt2\,s. (c) The best scale is proportional to the width, so multi-scale vesselness measures vessel width: width s \approx \sigma_\text{best}/\sqrt2 for this normalisation. (Other normalisations, \sigma^{2\gamma} with \gamma = 3/4, make the best scale equal s; the factor depends on the convention, the proportionality does not.)
crumbs: The Hessian: blobs, ridges and saddles

title: Exercise: the Hessian
text:
Explore: the Hessian per pixel
Images: an editable quadratic f = ax^2 + bxy + cy^2 (with contours; its Hessian is shown in the units of f), a test scene (a bright blob, a thin and a thick bright line, a dark line, a saddle of two bright and two dark spots, a step edge at the bottom left; noise 3), curved lines, or the micrograph (256 × 256). Tabs show the class map, λ1, λ2, trace, determinant, vesselness and the best scale. Click a pixel: the glyph shows the eigenvector axes (length ∝ |λ|, red = negative curvature), the readout the matrix, the eigenvalues and the verdict; its point is circled in the (λ1, λ2) plane.



E1. Presets hilltop, ridge, saddle: check your answers to B1(a)–(c) in the readout. Then set a = c = -1, b = -2 for B1(d). Where does the glyph point, and what does the image look like?
E2. Preset an edge is not a ridge (test scene, σ = 3). Click on the step at (25, 114), then one pixel to the left and one and three pixels to the right. Read λ1, λ2 and the class each time. Compare the size of λ2 with that of the thin line at (86, 27).
E3. Preset LoG cannot tell blob from ridge; det can. Compare the trace and then the determinant at the blob (28, 28) and on the thin line (86, 27). Look at the whole trace and determinant images: which structures light up in each?
E4. Preset vesselness: blob suppressed (σ = 3). Read the vesselness at the blob, the thin line and the thick line (30, 70). Untick bright lines: what lights up now? Change β and c and describe their effect.
E5. Preset one σ misses the thick line (σ = 1.5), then multi-scale. Compare the vesselness of the thick line in both. Which σ wins for the thin and for the thick line (best σ tab)? Compare with B8.
E6. Image curved lines, multi-scale, vesselness tab. Where does the vesselness drop along the lines? Why?
E7. Preset membranes in the micrograph (dark lines, σ = 2, c = 20). Which structures get high vesselness? Click on the nuclear envelope at (94, 126). What else responds, and how could you reduce it?






Solutions





E1. Hilltop: H = [−2 0; 0 −2], λ = (−2, −2), bright blob. Ridge: H = [−2 0; 0 0], λ = (0, −2), bright ridge; the glyph is one red bar across the ridge (the λ1 axis has length 0). Saddle: H = [2 0; 0 −2], λ = (2, −2), a blue and a red bar of equal length. With a = c = -1, b = -2: H = [−2 −2; −2 −2], λ = (0, −4), a bright ridge running from lower left to upper right; the red bar points across it, along (1, 1).
E2. At σ = 3: on the step (25, 114) λ = (−0.15, −3.87): flat (|λ2| below the threshold 4). One pixel left (24, 114): λ = (−0.02, +4.25): a weak dark ridge. One pixel right (26, 114): (−0.27, −10.76), three right (28, 114): (−0.39, −14.52): a bright ridge. The edge appears as a weak dark half-ridge outside, a bright half-ridge inside and nothing on the edge; λ2 there (−14.5) is half that of the thin line (−28.65), although the edge has the same contrast class.
E3. Trace: −31.3 (blob), −28.8 (thin line): almost the same. Determinant: 245 (blob), 2.7 (line). In the trace image all bright structures (blob, lines, the bright side of the edge) are dark (negative) and all dark structures bright; in the determinant image only the blob and the saddle’s spots stand out (the saddle centre itself is strongly negative, −96).
E4. Blob 0.10, thin line 0.84, thick line 0.40. With dark lines selected, the dark line lights up and the bright structures vanish; the dark side of the edge and the dark spots of the saddle respond a little. Larger β lets blobs through (the blob brightens); smaller β darkens everything that is not perfectly line-like. Larger c darkens weak structures first; smaller c brings up the noise.
E5. At σ = 1.5 the thick line scores only 0.06 (the kernel sees the flat top of the line); at σ = 3, 0.40; multi-scale (σ = 1 … 8) gives 0.70, won at σ = 5.94. The thin line wins at σ = 2.44 (0.87). The thick line has width 4.5 and the thin one 1.5: √2 × 4.5 = 6.4 and √2 × 1.5 = 2.1, both close to the winning σ on the 8-level grid, as B8 predicts.
E6. Vesselness drops where two lines cross or meet: there both curvatures are large, R_B approaches 1 and the blob penalty switches the response off. It also drops at line ends, and where a thin line passes near a thick one (they blend at the larger scale).
E7. The nuclear envelope and the membranes and fibres of the cytoplasm, which are dark thin lines; at (94, 126) the vesselness is 0.97. The dense granular texture inside the nucleus and the fibrous background also respond at σ = 2. A larger σ (or the multi-scale maximum with σ ≥ 2) and a larger c suppress the fine texture; but the Hessian alone cannot know which dark lines are “membranes”: that needs a classifier (random-forest day) or a model of the shape.

title: Exercise: the Hessian
text:
Where this leads
The Hessian measures second derivatives and finds the centres of blobs and lines. The next unit uses first derivatives, squared and averaged over a window: the structure tensor, which measures orientation and finds corners.

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
text:
About this lecture
The Fourier transform rewrites a signal as a sum of waves. Every wave runs over the whole signal, so the spectrum says which frequencies are present but not where. Today: a basis whose functions are short.

A spike and a step in the Fourier basis: every coefficient is busy.
The short-time Fourier transform, and why one window size cannot serve all frequencies.
The wavelet idea: short windows for high frequencies, long windows for low ones.
The Haar transform by hand: averages and differences, level by level, and back.
The Haar basis is orthonormal, and piecewise-constant signals are sparse in it.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

First unit of the wavelets elective (group “Transforms”; the compression day follows and builds on it). Prerequisites: the Fourier unit (change of basis, orthogonality, Parseval) and the kernels unit (convolution). Everything today is on 1D signals of 8 to 256 samples; images come in unit 3.
crumbs: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
section: Recall: the Fourier basis is global
text:
Recall: the Fourier basis is global
From Images in frequency space (day 1): the DFT is a change of basis to waves e^{2\pi i k n/N}, each of which extends over the whole signal. It is orthogonal, so nothing is lost and energies add up (Parseval).
That is perfect for signals that are periodic or smooth everywhere. Images are not: they are flat in most places, with edges and spots at a few positions.
crumbs: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
section: A spike and a step in the Fourier basis
text:
A spike and a step in the Fourier basis


A spike: every Fourier magnitude is exactly 1. Where the spike is lives only in the phases, spread over all coefficients.
A step: the magnitudes fall off slowly, like 1/k. Keep the 6 largest of 64 and the result rings everywhere (Gibbs).
6 coefficients in the Haar basis of this lecture (dashed blue) do much better: 12.5 % and 5.5 % error instead of 90 % and 19 %.


N = 64, spike at position 23, step from position 23 (positions from 0). Left: the signal; middle: |X_k| for k = 0..32 (the rest mirror these); for the step the dashed curve is 64/(πk), the envelope for small k. Right: keeping the 6 largest coefficients in a real orthonormal Fourier basis (cosines and sines) and in the Haar basis (6 levels). Relative errors: spike 90 % (Fourier) vs 12.5 % (Haar), step 19 % vs 5.5 %. In the Haar basis both signals have only 7 nonzero coefficients (log2 64 + 1), so 6 of them miss one small one. Ask: why can a single wave never say “here”?
crumbs: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
section: The math: spectra of a spike and a step
text:
The math: spectra of a spike and a step
DFT X_k = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x_n e^{-2\pi i k n/N}.

Spike at n_0, x_n = [n = n_0]: \;X_k = e^{-2\pi i k n_0/N}, so |X_k| = 1 for every k. The position n_0 is only in the phase -2\pi k n_0/N.
Box of m ones starting at n_0 (a step up and a step down): a geometric sum, |X_k| = \left|\sum_{n=n_0}^{n_0+m-1} e^{-2\pi i k n/N}\right| = \left|\frac{\sin(\pi k m/N)}{\sin(\pi k/N)}\right| \approx \frac{N}{\pi k}\,|\sin(\pi k m/N)| \quad (k \ll N).
So the coefficients of a jump decay only like 1/k: the energy beyond frequency K is \sum_{k > K} 1/k^2 \approx 1/K, which falls slowly. Cutting them off leaves an overshoot near the jump of about 9 % of the jump height that does not shrink as K grows (Gibbs phenomenon).
crumbs: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
text:
Fix 1: the short-time Fourier transform
Cut out a piece of the signal with a smooth window (the tapers of the Fourier unit), take its DFT, slide the window along.

Now each coefficient belongs to a position (the window) and a frequency: a tile in the position–frequency plane.
A narrow window locates the step well, but a few samples contain too few cycles of a slow wave to tell its frequency.
A wide window resolves low frequencies, but smears the step over the whole window.
One window size serves either the edges or the slow variations, not both.
crumbs: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
text:
The math: the uncertainty relation
For a window w(t) with \int |w|^2 dt = 1, define its spread in time and in (angular) frequency: \Delta t^2 = \int (t - \bar t)^2 |w(t)|^2 dt, \qquad \Delta\omega^2 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int (\omega - \bar\omega)^2 |\hat w(\omega)|^2 d\omega.

Heisenberg–Gabor: \Delta t\,\Delta\omega \ge \tfrac12, with equality only for a Gaussian window (Gabor 1946).
Squeezing the window in time by a factor s, w(t) \to \sqrt{s}\,w(st), multiplies \Delta t by 1/s and \Delta\omega by s: the area of a tile is fixed, only its shape can change.
The STFT uses the same tile shape everywhere. Wavelets change the shape with the frequency: \Delta t \propto 1/\omega, so each tile holds about the same number of cycles.
crumbs: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
text:
Fix 2: the wavelet idea
Short windows for high frequencies, long windows for low frequencies.

High frequencies (edges, spots, noise) change quickly: we want to know exactly where they are.
Low frequencies (slow shading) are spread out anyway: a long window gives their frequency precisely, and their position does not matter much.
So: tall, thin tiles at high frequency; short, wide tiles at low frequency (right panel of the tiling figure).

The simplest way to build such tiles is to keep halving the signal: pairs, then pairs of pairs, … This is the Haar transform (Haar, 1910).
crumbs: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
text:
The Haar transform by hand
Replace each pair (a, b) by its average and half-difference: s = \frac{a + b}{2}, \qquad d = \frac{a - b}{2}. Keep the ds; repeat on the ss. For x = (4, 6, 10, 12, 8, 6, 5, 5):



level
averages s
differences d (kept)




1
5,\ 11,\ 7,\ 5
-1,\ -1,\ 1,\ 0


2
8,\ 6
-3,\ 1


3
7
1



Result (coarse to fine): (7 \mid 1 \mid -3,\ 1 \mid -1,\ -1,\ 1,\ 0). Eight numbers in, eight out: 1 overall average + 1 + 2 + 4 details, each detail tied to a place and a scale.

Do this on the board first, then with the demo. Point out that the level-1 details are small where the signal is locally flat (the last pair 5, 5 gives 0), and read the level-3 detail: the left half averages 8, the right half 6, so the left half lies 1 above the overall average 7 and the right half 1 below.
crumbs: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
section: Try it: the Haar transform step by step
text:
Try it: the Haar transform step by step




Board example, N = 8. Press step three times: the brackets show which pairs are combined next; the grey blocks are the current averages drawn over the signal; the lower panel the coefficients coloured by level. Readout: Σx² = 446 but Σc² = 63 with the 1/2 normalisation. Switch to s = (a+b)/√2: now Σc² = 446. Keep K = 3 (orthonormal): kept 19.80, 2.83 and −6; the reconstruction (orange) is (5, 5, 11, 11, 6, 6, 6, 6), squared error 10 = sum of the dropped squared coefficients. Presets: spike (4 nonzero coefficients), step (a jump inside a pair: 4 nonzero), ramp (details everywhere: Haar only knows constants), constant (one coefficient). “Show basis” draws the transform matrix.
crumbs: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
text:
Going back: nothing is lost
Each step can be undone: from s and d, a = s + d, \qquad b = s - d.
Board example backwards: 7 \pm 1 \to (8, 6); 8 \pm (-3) \to (5, 11), 6 \pm 1 \to (7, 5); then 5 \pm (-1) \to (4, 6), … back to x.

The Haar transform is a change of basis, like the DFT: the same signal, described by different numbers.
The coefficient of a basis vector says how much of that pattern the signal contains. Which patterns?
crumbs: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
text:
The Haar basis vectors




Each coefficient multiplies one pattern; the signal is their sum.

One constant (the overall average),
one +/- square wave over the whole signal,
two over half the signal, four over a quarter.

Short patterns for fine detail, long ones for coarse: the wavelet tiling. They are all the same shape, shifted and squeezed: that shape is the Haar wavelet.
With 1/\sqrt2 in place of 1/2 at each step the patterns all have length 1 and are perpendicular: an orthonormal basis.
crumbs: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
section: The math: the Haar matrix is orthogonal
text:
The math: the Haar matrix is orthogonal
Normalised step: s = (a + b)/\sqrt2, d = (a - b)/\sqrt2, i.e. each pair is multiplied by \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}, an orthogonal matrix (a rotation by 45° and a reflection).

One level on N samples is block-diagonal in these 2 \times 2 blocks (after reordering): orthogonal. A product of orthogonal matrices is orthogonal, so the whole transform c = Hx has H H^\top = I.
N = 4: \;H = \begin{pmatrix} \tfrac12 & \tfrac12 & \tfrac12 & \tfrac12 \\ \tfrac12 & \tfrac12 & -\tfrac12 & -\tfrac12 \\ \tfrac1{\sqrt2} & -\tfrac1{\sqrt2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \tfrac1{\sqrt2} & -\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\end{pmatrix}, rows of length 1, mutually perpendicular.
Hence Parseval: \|c\|^2 = x^\top H^\top H x = \|x\|^2, and the inverse is the transpose, x = H^\top c.
With 1/2 the rows are still perpendicular but have lengths 2^{-j/2}: invertible, not orthonormal. Board example: \|x\|^2 = 446, but \sum c^2 = 63 with 1/2 and 446 with 1/\sqrt2.
crumbs: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
text:
Why this pays off: sparsity
A coefficient is zero when its pattern sees a flat signal.

A piecewise-constant signal has nonzero details only where a jump falls inside a pattern: at most one per level, near each jump.
A spike touches only the patterns that contain it: one per level plus the average, \log_2 N + 1 coefficients (4 of 8, 9 of 256).
A ramp gives nonzero details everywhere: Haar patterns only see constants as “nothing to report”. Better wavelets in the next unit.

Few large coefficients and many (near-)zero ones = sparse. Keeping only the large ones then loses little.
crumbs: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
section: Try it: sparsity in two bases
text:
Try it: sparsity in two bases




256 samples; Haar with 5 levels (periodic). One slider K keeps the K largest coefficients in both bases. Tour: “step”: at K = 8 Fourier has 16.5 % error, Haar 2.8 %; 1 % error needs 176 Fourier and 11 Haar coefficients. “spike”: Fourier needs 247 of 256, Haar 6 (5 levels + the approximation). “sine”: one Fourier coefficient; Haar needs 218. “Doppler” (frequency changes along the signal): both need many, Fourier 231 and Haar 196. Switch the lower-left panel to “wavelet coefficients by level”: the large coefficients sit where the signal jumps.
crumbs: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
section: The math: error of keeping K coefficients
text:
The math: error of keeping K coefficients
Orthonormal basis \{\mathbf u_i\}, coefficients c_i = \mathbf u_i^\top x, so x = \sum_i c_i \mathbf u_i. Keep a set S of K indices: \hat x = \sum_{i \in S} c_i \mathbf u_i. Then \|x - \hat x\|^2 = \Big\|\sum_{i \notin S} c_i\mathbf u_i\Big\|^2 = \sum_{i \notin S} c_i^2.

The error is the sum of the dropped squared coefficients (Pythagoras), so the best S keeps the K largest |c_i|.
The error curve against K depends only on the sorted magnitudes |c|_{(1)} \ge |c|_{(2)} \ge \dots: a basis is good for a signal when they fall fast.
This only holds in an orthonormal basis. With the 1/2 normalisation, coefficients at different levels are not comparable: a level-j coefficient counts 2^j times in the error.
crumbs: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
text:
Summary

The Fourier basis is global: a spike or a step spreads over all coefficients, and truncation rings.
A window trades position against frequency resolution; one window size cannot fit all frequencies. Wavelets use short windows for high frequencies, long for low.
Haar transform: pairwise averages and differences, repeated on the averages; inverse a = s + d, b = s - d.
With 1/\sqrt2 it is an orthonormal change of basis: energy is preserved, and the error of dropping coefficients is the sum of their squares.
Piecewise-constant signals are sparse in the Haar basis; ramps are not: next unit, wavelets with more vanishing moments.
crumbs: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform

title: Quiz: graph-cut segmentation
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. The graph has one node per pixel, s = object, t = background; t-links s \to p with capacity D_p(0) and p \to t with D_p(1); n-links \lambda w_{pq} in both directions.

Q1. A pixel ends up on the source side of the cut. Which of its t-links is cut, and what does that cost correspond to?






Hint





Only edges from S to T count.









Answer





p \in S means L_p = 1 (object). The edge p \to t goes from S to T and is cut, at cost D_p(1): the data cost of labelling p object. The edge s \to p lies inside S and costs nothing.




Q2. Why is each n-link added in both directions?






Hint





Which pixel of a disagreeing pair is on the source side?









Answer





The boundary cost \lambda w_{pq} must be paid whether p is object and q background, or the other way round. With p \in S, q \in T the edge p \to q is cut; with q \in S, p \in T the edge q \to p is. Exactly one of the two counts, so the cut pays \lambda w_{pq} once.




Q3. Two neighbours have grey levels 100 and 160, and \sigma = 20. What is w_{pq}? What if they were 100 and 105?






Hint





w_{pq} = \exp(-(I_p - I_q)^2/2\sigma^2).









Answer





60^2/(2 \cdot 400) = 4.5, so w = e^{-4.5} = 0.011: a boundary there is almost free. For 100 and 105: 25/800 = 0.031, w = e^{-0.031} = 0.97: almost the full cost.




Q4. How does an object seed force a pixel to be object? Why not simply set its label after the cut?






Hint





A seed also affects its neighbours.









Answer





Its t-link s \to p gets a capacity larger than any cut could cost (and p \to t capacity 0), so no minimum cut puts it on the background side. Setting the label afterwards would not do the same: the seed must take part in the optimisation, so that its neighbours, through the n-links, are pulled towards the object label too.




Q5. Why does a graph cut with a large \lambda tend to remove thin structures, but keep large blobs with the same intensity?






Hint





Compare how data gain and boundary cost grow with size.









Answer





The data gain of keeping a structure grows with its area, the boundary cost with its perimeter. A thin line of length \ell has area \ell and perimeter about 2\ell: its gain per unit boundary is small. A disk of radius r has area \pi r^2 and perimeter 2\pi r: the gain per unit boundary grows with r. This preference for short boundaries is the shrinking bias.




Q6. Segmented with a 4-neighbourhood, a round cell comes out with flat sides and diagonal corners cut off. Why, and what helps?






Hint





How much does a diagonal boundary cost per unit length with 4 neighbours?









Answer





With 4 neighbours the boundary cost is the city-block length: a diagonal boundary costs \sqrt2 \approx 1.41 times as much per unit of true length as a horizontal or vertical one. The cut therefore prefers axis-aligned boundaries (metrication). An 8-neighbourhood with suitable weights (here \tfrac12 for sides and \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt2} for diagonals) makes the cost nearly the same in every direction.




Q7. Object seeds are placed on a nucleus and background seeds only on the white space around the cell. The result includes the cytoplasm. Why, and how do you fix it?






Hint





What does the intensity model learn from these seeds?









Answer





The model only knows “nucleus grey” (object) and “white” (background). The cytoplasm is grey too, so its data term says object, and nothing in the energy says otherwise. Add background seeds on the cytoplasm: the background model then includes its grey levels, and where nucleus and cytoplasm overlap in intensity, the seeds and the contrast weights at the nuclear envelope decide.




Q8. Can a graph cut minimise an energy that rewards boundaries, V(L_p, L_q) = -[L_p \ne L_q]?






Hint





Check the submodularity condition V(0,1) + V(1,0) \ge V(0,0) + V(1,1).









Answer





No: V(0,1) + V(1,0) = -2 < 0 = V(0,0) + V(1,1), so it is not submodular. The n-links would need negative capacity, and adding a constant does not help because it does not depend on whether the labels differ. Such energies are NP-hard in general (maximum cut).

title: Exercise: graph-cut segmentation
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

build the graph of a small image: t-links from the data term, n-links from the smoothness term,
check that the cost of a cut equals the energy of its labelling, and find the minimum,
compute contrast-sensitive weights and see how they change the result,
use seeds, and explain the shrinking bias and metrication.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the two demos.
