title: Exercise: graph-cut segmentation
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Nodes
one per pixel, plus s (object) and t (background)


t-links
s \to p with capacity D_p(0), p \to t with capacity D_p(1)


n-links
p \to q and q \to p, each with capacity \lambda w_{pq}, for 4-neighbours p, q


Labelling from a cut
L_p = 1 (object) if p is on the source side, else 0


Cut = energy
c(S, T) = \sum_p D_p(L_p) + \lambda \sum w_{pq}[L_p \ne L_q] = E(L)


Contrast weights
w_{pq} = \exp\!\big(-(I_p - I_q)^2/2\sigma^2\big); \sigma = \infty means w_{pq} = 1


Seeds
an object seed gets s \to p with infinite capacity; a background seed p \to t



Throughout, grey levels are 0 to 3 with \mu_0 = 0, \mu_1 = 3 and D_p(\ell) = (I_p - \mu_\ell)^2, so D_p(0) = I_p^2 and D_p(1) = (3 - I_p)^2. This is what the first demo uses.

title: Exercise: graph-cut segmentation
text:
By hand
B1. The 1 \times 3 image I = (3, 1, 3), with w_{pq} = 1. (a) Draw the graph: 5 nodes, 6 t-links, 2 pairs of n-links. Write every capacity for \lambda = 1. (b) List all 8 cuts (labellings) with their cost. Which is the minimum? Which labelling does thresholding give? (c) Repeat (b) for \lambda = 2. At which \lambda does the minimum change?
B2. Same image, now with contrast weights, \sigma = 1. (a) Compute w_{12} and w_{23}. What is w_{pq} for a grey-level difference of 1, and of 3? (b) Compute the energy of 101 and 111 for \lambda = 2 and \lambda = 5. Up to which \lambda does the dark pixel stay background? (c) Is that what you want if the dark pixel is noise? If it is a real gap between two objects?
B3. The 2 \times 2 image \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, 4-neighbours (4 pairs of n-links), w_{pq} = 1, \lambda = 2. Write labellings as top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right, e.g. 1100 = top row object. (a) Give the t-link capacities of the four pixels. (b) Compute the cost of the cuts 1100, 1000, 1110, 1111 and 0000. Then argue (or check by listing all 16) which cut is the minimum.
B4. Same 2 \times 2 image and \lambda, but the bottom-left pixel (grey level 1) is an object seed. Which capacities change? What is the minimum cut now, and its cost (counting the seed’s data cost D(1) = 4)?
B5. Shrinking bias. A 6 \times 6 image is 0 everywhere except column 2, which is a vertical line of grey level 2, and columns 4–6, a band of grey level 2 that touches the right border. Use w_{pq} = 1. (a) How much data cost does the line save by being object rather than background? How many n-links does labelling it object cut? Above which \lambda does the minimum drop the line? (b) The same for the band. (Its right side lies on the image border: no n-links there.) (c) Generalise: a long strip of width k pixels and data gain g per pixel. Above which \lambda is it removed?
B6. Metrication. Consider a long straight boundary in a large image with w_{pq} = 1. (a) With 4-neighbours, how many n-links does a horizontal boundary of length \ell cut? And a 45° staircase boundary of the same Euclidean length? (b) With 8-neighbours, horizontal and vertical n-links get weight \tfrac12, diagonal ones \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}. Compute the cost per unit length of a horizontal and of a 45° boundary. (c) Which neighbourhood gives the more “round” results, and why?
B7 (math). Show that the pairwise term V(L_p, L_q) = \lambda w_{pq}[L_p \ne L_q] with \lambda w_{pq} \ge 0 satisfies V(0,1) + V(1,0) \ge V(0,0) + V(1,1). Which pairwise term in a segmentation energy would violate it?






Solutions





B1. (a) D(0) = 9, 1, 9 and D(1) = 0, 4, 0: t-links s \to 1: 9, s \to 2: 1, s \to 3: 9; 1 \to t: 0, 2 \to t: 4, 3 \to t: 0. n-links 1 \leftrightarrow 2 and 2 \leftrightarrow 3: capacity \lambda = 1 each way. (b) Writing data + boundaries:

At \lambda = 1 the minimum is 101 (cost 3), the same as thresholding. (c) At \lambda = 2 the minimum is 111 (cost 4). 101 costs 1 + 2\lambda, 111 costs 4: they tie at \lambda = 1.5.
B2. (a) w_{12} = w_{23} = e^{-2^2/2} = e^{-2} = 0.135. For a difference of 1: e^{-0.5} = 0.607; of 3: e^{-4.5} = 0.011. (b) E(101) = 1 + \lambda \cdot 2 \cdot 0.135: 1.541 at \lambda = 2, 2.353 at \lambda = 5. E(111) = 4. The dark pixel stays background as long as 1 + 0.271\lambda < 4, i.e. up to \lambda = 11.08. (c) Contrast weights make a boundary across a large intensity jump almost free. That protects a real gap between two objects, but it also protects a noise pixel that differs strongly from its neighbours. \sigma should be larger than typical noise differences and smaller than the jumps at real edges.
B3. (a) Grey levels 3, 2, 1, 0: s \to p: 9, 4, 1, 0; p \to t: 0, 1, 4, 9. (b) 1100: data 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 2, n-links cut: top-left–bottom-left and top-right–bottom-right, 2, cost 2 + 2 \cdot 2 = 6. 1000: data 0 + 4 + 1 + 0 = 5, 2 n-links, cost 9. 1110: data 0 + 1 + 4 + 0 = 5, 2 n-links, cost 9. 1111: data 0 + 1 + 4 + 9 = 14, cost 14. 0000: data 9 + 4 + 1 + 0 = 14, cost 14. The minimum is 1100 with cost 6: it has the smallest possible data cost (each pixel takes its cheaper label, total 2), and any labelling with both labels cuts at least 2 n-links, so no labelling with a boundary can beat 2 + 4 = 6; the two without a boundary cost 14. Listing all 16 confirms it; the next best are 1000 and 1110 (9).
B4. The seed’s t-links become s \to p: \infty, p \to t: 0 (and its data cost D(1) = 4 is paid in any allowed labelling). Only labellings with bottom-left = 1 are allowed. The best is 1110: data 0 + 1 + 4 + 0 = 5, 2 n-links (top-right–bottom-right and bottom-left–bottom-right), cost 5 + 4 = 9. Next: 1010 (12) and 1111 (14). The seed pulls its pixel into the object, and the boundary moves to the right of it.
B5. (a) Each line pixel saves D(0) - D(1) = 4 - 1 = 3; 6 pixels save 18. As object, the line cuts 6 n-links on each side, 12 in total (top and bottom are the image border): cost 12\lambda. Dropped when 12\lambda > 18, i.e. \lambda > 1.5. (b) The band: 18 pixels save 54; it cuts only the 6 n-links on its left side: dropped when 6\lambda > 54, i.e. \lambda > 9. Same intensity, 6 times more robust. (c) Per unit length, a strip of width k gains kg and its two sides cost 2\lambda: it is removed for \lambda > kg/2. Thin structures go first.
B6. (a) Horizontal: \ell vertical n-links, cost \ell, i.e. 1 per unit length. A 45° staircase of Euclidean length \ell goes \ell/\sqrt2 steps right and \ell/\sqrt2 down and cuts one n-link per step: \sqrt2\,\ell, i.e. 1.41 per unit length. (b) Horizontal: per unit length, one vertical n-link (\tfrac12) and two diagonal ones (2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}): \tfrac12 + \tfrac1{\sqrt2} = 1.207. At 45°, per step of length \sqrt2: one horizontal and one vertical n-link (\tfrac12 + \tfrac12) and two diagonals across the boundary (\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}; the diagonals along the boundary are not cut): (1 + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2})/\sqrt2 = 1.207 per unit length. The same. (c) 8-neighbours: the boundary cost no longer depends on direction (at least for these two directions), so the cut has no reason to prefer axis-aligned edges. With 4-neighbours, diagonal boundaries are 41% more expensive and shapes come out blocky.
B7. V(0,1) + V(1,0) = 2\lambda w_{pq} \ge 0 = V(0,0) + V(1,1). A term that rewards disagreement, V(0,1) < 0 (or that charges more for equal labels than for different ones), violates it; for example a term that wants neighbouring pixels to differ, as in a checkerboard pattern.

title: Exercise: graph-cut segmentation
section: Explore: the graph of a small image
text:
Explore: the graph of a small image
The demo draws a small image as its graph. Pixels show their grey level (0–3) and are framed orange (object) or blue (background) according to the minimum cut. Small images (1 × 3, 2 × 2) show the whole graph with every capacity, and the cut edges dashed red. The 6 × 6 images show the t-links as two bars inside each pixel (left: s \to p, right: p \to t; the cut one is solid), and n-links as lines whose width is \lambda w_{pq}. Click a pixel to change its grey level, or choose label (your cut) and click pixels to make your own labelling; the table then compares its energy with the minimum.



P1. Check B1 and B2 in the demo: the 1 × 3 image at \lambda = 1 and \lambda = 2, then \sigma = 1 at \lambda = 2. Do the cut costs and the max flow match your table?
P2. Choose 2 × 2 (\lambda = 2) and label (your cut). Make the labellings of B3(b) one by one and compare their costs with yours.
P3. Choose 6 × 6 blob (\lambda = 1.5). Which pixels does the minimum cut label differently from thresholding (set \lambda = 0 to see thresholding)? Check that E = data + \lambda \cdot \Sigma w in the table.
P4. Choose thin vs thick and raise \lambda. At which \lambda does the line disappear, and at which the band? Compare with B5.
P5. Choose noisy edge (\lambda = 1, \sigma = 1). One noise pixel in the dark half is labelled object. Why does the cut keep it? Set \sigma = \infty: what happens to it, and to the energy?






Solutions





P1. At \lambda = 1, \sigma = \infty: labelling 101 with cost 3 (data 1, \Sigma w = 2), max flow 3. At \lambda = 2: 111, cost 4. With \sigma = 1 at \lambda = 2: the n-links around the middle pixel shrink to 0.27 each (\lambda w = 2 \cdot 0.135), and 101 is the minimum again with cost 1.54 (shown as data 1, \Sigma w 0.27, \lambda \Sigma w 0.54).
P2. 1100: 6 (the minimum, the demo’s own cut), 1000 and 1110: 9, 1111 and 0000: 14. Every cut you make has cost = energy, and none is below 6.
P3. Thresholding (\lambda = 0) labels 13 pixels object with energy 5: it leaves the dark pixel (grey level 1) inside the blob as background and takes the two isolated pixels of grey level 2 (right of the blob and at the right edge) as object. At \lambda = 1.5 the minimum cut fills the hole and drops both isolated pixels: 12 object pixels, the block of 4 rows and 3 columns. The table shows data 14, \Sigma w 14, E = 14 + 1.5 \cdot 14 = 35 = max flow.
P4. The line disappears at \lambda = 1.5 (at exactly 1.5 the two labellings tie, and the solver drops the line), the band at \lambda = 9 (again a tie). As computed in B5: the band has 9 times the data gain per row but only half the boundary.
P5. The pixel (row 4, column 2, grey level 2) has dark neighbours (0), so with \sigma = 1 each of its 4 n-links has weight e^{-2} = 0.135: isolating it costs only 4 \cdot 0.135 = 0.54, less than the data it saves (4 - 1 = 3). The contrast weights protect it as if it were a real edge. With \sigma = \infty all weights are 1, isolating it costs 4, and the cut drops it; the energy rises from 12.5 to 23, because every boundary is now expensive, including the real one between the halves.

title: Exercise: graph-cut segmentation
text:
Explore: interactive segmentation
A 128 \times 128 image: a synthetic test image (a bright disk with a thin arm, with noise) or a micrograph of a cell. Paint seeds with the mouse: object (red) or background (blue); erase and clear remove them. The intensity model is estimated from the seeds: a Gaussian per label, or a histogram. The large image shows the graph-cut result (orange, with a yellow boundary), the small one thresholding with the same model (\lambda = 0). The table gives the energy of both, the number of object pixels, and, for the test image, the number of wrong pixels compared with the truth. 4 / 8 chooses the neighbourhood; \sigma the contrast weights (\infty: none).



G1. Preset noise (\lambda = 1.5). Compare thresholding and graph cut: wrong pixels, data term and total energy. Which has the smaller data term? Check that the max flow equals E.
G2. Still on noise, move \lambda. Which \lambda gives the fewest wrong pixels? At which \lambda does part of the thin arm disappear, and when is it almost completely gone? Explain with B5.
G3. Preset thin arm lost (\lambda = 6). Now set \sigma = 50. What happens to the arm and to the number of wrong pixels? Why?
G4. Preset blocky (4 neighbours). Describe the shape of the disk. Switch to 8 neighbours. What changes, and what happens to the number of wrong pixels?
G5. Preset nucleus (micrograph, histograms, \lambda = 10, \sigma = 25). Where does the segmentation leak outside the nucleus? Paint a background seed there and see the result update. Then set \sigma = \infty: how does the boundary change?
G6. Preset overlapping intensities: the same object seeds, background seeds only on the white areas. What is segmented, and why? Fix it with a few background strokes on the grey cytoplasm around the nucleus.






Solutions





G1. Thresholding: 2587 wrong pixels, graph cut: 55. The data term of thresholding is smaller (69111.6 against 71491.9): by definition it is the smallest possible data term. But its boundary is enormous (\Sigma w = 7351.0 against 335.6), so its total energy at \lambda = 1.5 is 80138.2, against 71995.3 for the cut. The max flow is 71995.3 = E. (The large numbers come from the constant \log s in the Gaussian data term, the same for every labelling.)
G2. The fewest wrong pixels are at \lambda = 1.5 (55); from \lambda \approx 1 to 1.6 it stays between about 55 and 110. At \lambda = 1.7 the outer half of the arm disappears (wrong pixels jump to 102), at \lambda = 2.75 most of it (137), and from \lambda = 4.7 only a stub of a few pixels is left. The arm is 3 pixels wide: as in B5, its data gain per unit length is about 3g while its two long sides cost 2\lambda (times the 8-neighbour weight 1.21), so it goes long before the disk is affected.
G3. With \sigma = 50 the arm comes back (almost all of it), but the number of wrong pixels rises from 138 to 247. The n-links across the arm’s edges now have small weights (the jump from 80 to 170 is large compared with \sigma), so cutting along the arm is cheap. But noise also produces large differences between neighbours, so noisy pixels are cheaper to cut out as well: more specks survive. Contrast weights help only when edges are larger than the noise.
G4. With 4 neighbours (noise 90, \lambda = 6) the disk comes out as a rounded square with flat horizontal and vertical sides: 457 wrong pixels. With 8 neighbours it is round again and the error falls to 217. With 4 neighbours a diagonal boundary costs 41% more per unit length (B6), so the cut trades the diagonal parts of the circle for axis-aligned ones.
G5. With these seeds the nucleus is found along its envelope (3152 object pixels), with a leak into dark material at the right edge of the image. A background stroke there removes it. With \sigma = \infty (no contrast weights) the boundary no longer follows the dark nuclear envelope: at \lambda = 10 it takes short cuts and the object shrinks to 1779 pixels. The contrast weights make the envelope the cheapest place for the boundary.
G6. The whole cell and its neighbours are segmented (6239 object pixels): the cytoplasm and the other dark material are included. The background model has only seen white, so every grey pixel looks more like the object than like the background; nucleus and cytoplasm have overlapping grey levels, and the data term cannot tell them apart. A few background strokes on the cytoplasm add its grey levels to the background model; with the contrast weights at the envelope the result approaches the nucleus preset.

title: Exercise: graph-cut segmentation
text:
Where this leads
Graph cuts need seeds or a given intensity model, and they find the exact best labelling of a restricted energy. The next unit drops the seeds: normalized cuts look for a balanced split of the whole graph, using an eigenvector of the graph Laplacian.

title: How graphics cards store colour
text:
About this lecture

An image in memory is one long row of bytes. Where is pixel (x, y), channel c?
Layouts: interleaved or planar, channel order, row padding, byte order.
A graphics card (GPU) stores images as textures in a choice of formats: normalised integers, plain integers, floats, packed bits, sRGB. What does each keep, and what does it cost?
The GPU also interpolates (filters) between pixels in hardware. Which formats allow it, and why the stored numbers must be “linear” for it to be right.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Unit 3 of the 3D graphics day (elective, 3D group), after the units on the transformation pipeline and rasterisation, and after the bit-depth day (core): that day was about how many bits a value needs and how floats behave. This one is about how values are laid out and encoded, using the GPU as the example because it makes the choices explicit: every texture has a declared format. The concepts (layout, stride, normalised vs float, filtering) apply to any image file or array. No graphics programming is needed or taught.

title: How graphics cards store colour
section: An image is a row of bytes
text:
An image is a row of bytes
A 4 × 2 RGB image, 8 bits per channel:







layout
bytes in memory




interleaved (RGBRGB…)
R G B R G B R G B R G B · R G B … (row 0, then row 1)


planar (RRR…GGG…BBB…)
all R of the image, then all G, then all B




Interleaved keeps one pixel’s channels together: what screens, cameras and textures use.
Planar keeps one channel together: convenient when each channel is processed alone (e.g. a microscope with one image per fluorescent dye).
Channel order is a convention: RGBA or BGRA (common in camera drivers and on Windows). Swap it by mistake and red and blue trade places.

title: How graphics cards store colour
text:
Rows are padded: the stride
Hardware likes rows that start at a multiple of 4 (or more) bytes. Each row may end with unused padding bytes.

Stride (pitch) = bytes from the start of one row to the start of the next, including padding.
An RGB image 1001 pixels wide: 3 \cdot 1001 = 3003 bytes of data per row, padded to a stride of 3004.
Read it with the wrong stride (3003) and row y is read starting y bytes too early: the image is sheared by a third of a pixel per row, and the colours cycle from row to row (each byte is read as the wrong channel).

Always ask an image buffer for its stride; do not compute it from the width.

title: How graphics cards store colour
section: Bytes in a multi-byte number: endianness
text:
Bytes in a multi-byte number: endianness
A 16-bit value occupies two bytes. Which comes first?

Little-endian (almost all CPUs and GPUs today): low byte first. 1000 = 0x03E8 is stored as E8 03.
Big-endian (some file formats, network order): high byte first, 03 E8.
Read little-endian data as big-endian and 1000 becomes 0xE803 = 59 395: a smooth image turns into noise-like garbage, because the low byte changes fastest.

Image file formats state their byte order in the header; 8-bit images do not have the problem.

title: How graphics cards store colour
section: The math: where is a pixel?
text:
The math: where is a pixel?
For an image of width w, height h, C channels of B bytes each, and row stride s \ge w C B, the byte offset of pixel (x, y), channel c is
\text{interleaved: } \; y\,s + x\,C B + c\,B, \qquad \text{planar: } \; c\,(h\,s_1) + y\,s_1 + x\,B,
where s_1 \ge w B is the stride of one plane. The total size is h\,s (interleaved) or C\,h\,s_1 (planar). The matrix index (i, j) of earlier units is (row y, column x); memory is “row-major”: a row is contiguous.

title: How graphics cards store colour
section: Texture formats: what a stored number means
text:
Texture formats: what a stored number means
A GPU texture has a declared format. Three families:









family
stored
the shader reads
example




normalised
integer k, b bits
k/(2^b - 1), a number in [0, 1]
8 bit per channel (RGBA8)


integer
integer k
k itself
16-bit unsigned integer


float
IEEE float
the float
half float (16 bit), float32




Normalised formats make “8 bits” and “10 bits” look the same to the program: both give [0, 1], only the step differs.
Integer formats are exact (labels, raw camera counts), but the hardware cannot interpolate them.
Float formats keep values outside [0, 1], and precision relative to the value (floating-point unit).

title: How graphics cards store colour
text:
Packed formats: bits shared out
When memory or bandwidth is tight, channels get unequal numbers of bits in one 16- or 32-bit word:

5-6-5: red 5 bits, green 6, blue 5 = 16 bits per pixel. Green gets the extra bit because the eye is most sensitive to green (colour day). A grey ramp gets tinted steps, because green steps at different places than red and blue.
10-10-10-2: 10 bits per colour, 2 bits of alpha = 32 bits, the same memory as 8 bits per channel, but 4 times finer steps. Used for HDR displays and medical monitors.

title: How graphics cards store colour
section: Try it: the same data in different formats
text:
Try it: the same data in different formats




The same ramp of values 0.20–0.24 is uploaded twice; the shader stretches 0.20–0.24 to black–white so every stored step shows. 8 bit: 11 bands. 10 bit: 42 bands, much smoother. “565 tint”: coloured bands, because red/blue and green step at different values. “darks: sRGB” on the very dark ramp: linear 8 bit only has codes 0 and 1, sRGB 8 bit has 17 codes there. “half vs float” on the very dark ramp: both smooth. “filter an int”: the integer texture with linear filtering is black. Click a texel to show the stored bits.

title: How graphics cards store colour
section: sRGB storage: more codes for the dark
text:
sRGB storage: more codes for the dark
Light intensities and perceived brightness are not proportional: we notice small differences in dark tones much more than in bright ones.

An sRGB-encoded 8-bit value is not proportional to light: the 256 codes are spaced closely in the dark and widely in the bright. Most 8-bit photos and screenshots are stored this way.
A linear value of 0.005 is code 1 in plain 8 bit, but code 16 in sRGB 8 bit.
An sRGB texture format tells the GPU so: it decodes to linear values when the shader reads the texture, before filtering or blending.
Why the curve has its shape, and why averaging must happen on linear values, is the subject of the colour day. Here: sRGB is a storage encoding, and the GPU undoes it for you if you declare it.

title: How graphics cards store colour
text:
Filtering in hardware
When a texture is drawn larger or smaller than its pixels, the GPU interpolates for free:

Each pixel gets texture coordinates (u, v), interpolated perspective-correctly across its triangle (previous unit), and the texture is sampled there.
nearest: take the closest texel (blocky); linear: bilinear interpolation of the 4 nearest texels (as in the images unit).
Normalised and float formats can be filtered. Integer formats cannot: a texture with linear filtering and an integer format is “incomplete” and reads as black. (Interpolating label 3 and label 7 to give 5 would be wrong anyway.)
Some GPUs cannot filter 32-bit float textures; half floats always can.
Filtering is a weighted average, so it is only right on values proportional to light: hence the sRGB decode first, and premultiplied alpha.

title: How graphics cards store colour
text:
Premultiplied alpha
Alpha \alpha is opacity: 1 = opaque, 0 = fully transparent. A transparent pixel’s colour is meaningless but still stored.

Straight alpha stores (R, G, B, \alpha). Average an opaque red texel with a transparent green one: (0.5, 0.5, 0, 0.5): a half-transparent olive. Green leaks in from a pixel you cannot see: dark or coloured fringes around cut-out objects.
Premultiplied alpha stores (\alpha R, \alpha G, \alpha B, \alpha). The transparent green becomes (0, 0, 0, 0), and the average is (0.5, 0, 0, 0.5): half-transparent red, correct.
So filtering, blending and resizing images with transparency should work on premultiplied values.

title: How graphics cards store colour
section: The math: compositing and filtering with alpha
text:
The math: compositing and filtering with alpha
Drawing a source over a destination (“over” operator, Porter–Duff), with premultiplied colours \mathbf c = \alpha\,\mathbf C:
\mathbf c_\text{out} = \mathbf c_\text{src} + (1 - \alpha_\text{src})\,\mathbf c_\text{dst}, \qquad \alpha_\text{out} = \alpha_\text{src} + (1 - \alpha_\text{src})\,\alpha_\text{dst}.
Both lines have the same form, so premultiplied values are filtered and blended with the same linear formula in every channel. A filter with weights w_i gives \sum w_i \alpha_i \mathbf C_i and \sum w_i \alpha_i; dividing, the true colour is the opacity-weighted average \sum w_i \alpha_i \mathbf C_i / \sum w_i \alpha_i, in which transparent texels have no say. Straight alpha would weight every \mathbf C_i equally.

title: How graphics cards store colour
text:
Mipmaps and memory

A mipmap stores the texture at full, half, quarter, … size, down to 1 × 1. When the texture is drawn small, the GPU reads a pre-shrunk (pre-blurred) level instead of skipping pixels, which would alias (Fourier unit). Cost: +1/3 memory.
Memory = width × height × bytes per texel:




format, 4096 × 4096
bytes/texel
memory
with mipmaps




RGBA 8 bit
4
64 MiB
85.3 MiB


RGBA half float
8
128 MiB
170.7 MiB


RGBA float32
16
256 MiB
341.3 MiB




Compressed texture formats store 4 × 4 blocks in 4–8 bits per pixel, lossy, decoded in hardware.

title: How graphics cards store colour
section: The math: why mipmaps cost a third
text:
The math: why mipmaps cost a third
Each level has a quarter of the texels of the one before:
1 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac1{16} + \dots < \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 4^{-k} = \frac{1}{1 - 1/4} = \frac43.
For a 2^n \times 2^n texture the chain has n + 1 levels and \sum_{k=0}^{n} 4^{k} = (4^{n+1} - 1)/3 texels, just under \tfrac43 \cdot 4^n.

title: How graphics cards store colour
text:
Summary

An image in memory: interleaved or planar, a channel order, a stride per row (with padding), and a byte order for multi-byte values. Get one wrong and the image is sheared, recoloured or scrambled.
Texture formats: normalised (k/(2^b - 1)), integer (exact, not filterable), float, packed (5-6-5, 10-10-10-2), sRGB (decoded by the GPU).
Hardware filtering is a weighted average: it needs linear, premultiplied values.
Memory = texels × bytes per texel (× 4/3 with mipmaps).

title: Quiz: quadratic smoothing and total variation
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Energy E(\mathbf x) = \tfrac12\sum_p(x_p - y_p)^2 + \lambda\sum_{(p,q)}\rho(x_p - x_q) with \rho(d) = d^2/2 (quadratic) or \lvert d\rvert (TV).

Q1. Why is quadratic smoothing “just a linear system”, while TV is not?






Hint





Differentiate the energy.









Answer





With \rho(d) = d^2/2 every derivative of E is linear in \mathbf x: setting the gradient to zero gives (I + \lambda L)\mathbf x = \mathbf y. With \lvert d\rvert the derivative is \pm1 (and undefined at 0), so the optimality conditions are not linear; TV needs a special algorithm (in 1D an exact one).




Q2. A noisy image has a sharp edge of height 100. Why does quadratic smoothing blur it, while TV keeps it sharp?






Hint





Compare the prior cost of one jump with many small steps.









Answer





A quadratic prior charges d^2: one jump of 100 costs \tfrac12 \cdot 10^4, the same rise in 10 steps of 10 costs \tfrac12 \cdot 1000: ten times less. So it spreads the edge into a ramp. TV charges the total height (100) however it is spread, so nothing is gained by blurring and the data, which say “sharp”, win.




Q3. In what sense is quadratic smoothing a low-pass filter?






Hint





What does the solution do to a wave +1, -1, +1, \dots, and to a constant?









Answer





On a long signal it multiplies each frequency \omega by 1/(1 + \lambda(2 - 2\cos\omega)): 1 for a constant, 1/(1 + 4\lambda) for the fastest oscillation. High frequencies (noise, but also the sharp part of edges) are damped, low ones pass.




Q4. What are staircasing and contrast loss in TV denoising?






Hint





What shapes do TV solutions consist of?









Answer





TV solutions are made of flat runs. A smooth ramp in noisy data is therefore turned into a series of flat steps (staircasing). Each run is pulled towards its neighbours by about \lambda/\text{width}, so small or narrow features (a thin bright line, a small spot) lose contrast and eventually vanish.




Q5. When would you prefer the Huber penalty over TV?






Hint





Huber is quadratic for small differences.









Answer





When the image has both smooth gradients and sharp edges. Huber treats small differences quadratically, so ramps stay smooth (no staircases), and large differences linearly, so edges are not blurred.




Q6. Samples from the TV prior look like rough random walks, not like flat plateaus. Why then are TV estimates piecewise constant?






Hint





Which single image does the estimate pick from the posterior?









Answer





The estimate is the minimum of the energy (the MAP), not a typical sample. The kink of \lvert d\rvert at 0 makes “exactly equal neighbours” a common place for the minimum to sit, although typical samples almost never have equal neighbours. The look of the estimate is a property of the optimisation, not of what the prior believes images look like.




Q7. How does the noise level enter the quadratic smoothing system?






Hint





Start from the posterior with noise standard deviation \sigma_n.









Answer





The posterior energy is \frac1{2\sigma_n^2}\sum(x_p - y_p)^2 + \frac{\lambda'}2\sum(x_p - x_q)^2; multiplying by \sigma_n^2 gives our form with \lambda = \lambda'\sigma_n^2. More noise means a larger effective \lambda: the data are trusted less and the image is smoothed more.




Q8. (math) Why does (I + \lambda L)\mathbf x = \mathbf y always have exactly one solution?






Answer





\mathbf x^\top(I + \lambda L)\mathbf x = \|\mathbf x\|^2 + \lambda\sum_{(p,q)}(x_p - x_q)^2 > 0 for every \mathbf x \ne 0 (with \lambda \ge 0): the matrix is positive definite, hence invertible. Equivalently the energy is strictly convex.

title: Exercise: quadratic smoothing and total variation
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

set up and solve the linear system of quadratic (Gaussian MRF) smoothing for a few pixels,
explain with numbers why a quadratic prior blurs edges and total variation keeps them,
solve small TV problems by hand with the plateau rule, and predict staircasing and contrast loss,
read quadratic smoothing as a low-pass filter,

title: Exercise: quadratic smoothing and total variation
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Energy
E(\mathbf x) = \tfrac12\sum_p(x_p - y_p)^2 + \lambda\sum_{(p,q)}\rho(x_p - x_q), neighbours on a line or grid


Quadratic
\rho(d) = d^2/2; minimum solves (I + \lambda L)\mathbf x = \mathbf y


Path Laplacian L
diagonal 1, 2, …, 2, 1; -1 for each neighbour pair


Gain
quadratic smoothing multiplies frequency \omega by 1/(1 + \lambda(2 - 2\cos\omega))


Total variation (TV)
\rho(d) = \lvert d\rvert


Plateau rule (TV, 1D)
the solution is made of flat runs; each sits at the mean of its data, moved by \lambda/\text{width} towards each neighbouring run that is higher or lower


Huber
\rho(d) = d^2/2 for \lvert d\rvert \le \delta, \delta(\lvert d\rvert - \delta/2) beyond
crumbs: Ising model and Markov random fields

title: Exercise: quadratic smoothing and total variation
text:
By hand
B1. Quadratic, three pixels. \mathbf y = (0, 3, 0). (a) Write I + \lambda L for \lambda = 1 and solve (I + L)\mathbf x = \mathbf y. (b) Repeat for \lambda = 2. What happens to the sum x_1 + x_2 + x_3? (c) Compute the energy of your solution for \lambda = 1, and of \mathbf y itself and of (1, 1, 1). Is the solution really the best of the three?
B2. Ramps and jumps. A signal must go from 0 to 3. Compute the prior cost \sum\rho(d) of doing it in one jump, in 3 equal steps, and in 30 equal steps, for the quadratic and the absolute penalty. Which shape does each prior prefer? What does this predict for an edge in a noisy image?
B3. TV, a step. \mathbf y = (0, 0, 3, 3). (a) Use the plateau rule to find the TV solution for \lambda = 1. Check that its energy is lower than that of \mathbf y. (b) For which \lambda does the step disappear completely? What is the solution then? (c) Compare with quadratic smoothing at \lambda = 1: \hat{\mathbf x} = (0.43, 0.86, 2.14, 2.57). Describe the difference in words.
B4. TV, a narrow peak. \mathbf y = (0, 3, 0). (a) Find the TV solution for \lambda = 0.5 and for \lambda = 1. (b) A peak of width w samples and height a on a flat background: about how much does TV lower it? For which \lambda does it vanish, roughly? Which features of an image does TV therefore remove first?
B5. Low-pass. For quadratic smoothing: (a) Compute the gain at \omega = \pi (the pattern +1, -1, +1, \dots) for \lambda = 1 and \lambda = 10. (b) For \lambda = 10, at which frequency (in cycles per sample, \omega/2\pi) is the gain \tfrac12? (c) Why does any low-pass filter blur a step edge?
B6. Which prior? Choose quadratic, Huber or TV, and explain: (a) a fluorescence image of cells with flat interiors and sharp boundaries; (b) an estimate of the slowly varying illumination of a microscope; (c) a gel image with smooth gradients and sharp bands.






Solutions





B1. (a) I + L = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}. By symmetry x_1 = x_3 = a, x_2 = b: 2a - b = 0, -2a + 3b = 3, so b = 1.5, a = 0.75. (b) I + 2L: 3a - 2b = 0, -4a + 5b = 3: \hat{\mathbf x} = (0.857, 1.286, 0.857). The sum stays 3: quadratic smoothing preserves the mean (the rows of L sum to 0). (c) E(\hat{\mathbf x}) = \tfrac12(0.75^2 + 1.5^2 + 0.75^2) + \tfrac12(0.75^2 + 0.75^2) = 1.6875 + 0.5625 = 2.25. E(\mathbf y) = 0 + \tfrac12(9 + 9) = 9. E(1, 1, 1) = \tfrac12(1 + 4 + 1) + 0 = 3. Yes, 2.25 is the lowest.
B2. Quadratic: \tfrac12 \cdot 9 = 4.5; 3 \cdot \tfrac12 = 1.5; 30 \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot 0.01 = 0.15. Absolute: 3 in all three cases. The quadratic prior strongly prefers spreading the change over many small steps (a ramp); TV is indifferent to how a monotone change is spread. Prediction: under a quadratic prior an edge is smeared out; under TV the data decide, and they say the edge is sharp.
B3. (a) Two plateaus of width 2, data means 0 and 3. The left one has a higher neighbour: up by \lambda/2 = 0.5; the right one down by 0.5: \hat{\mathbf x} = (0.5, 0.5, 2.5, 2.5). Energy: data 4 \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot 0.25 = 0.5, TV \lambda \cdot 2 = 2: total 2.5, against 0 + 3 = 3 for \mathbf y. (b) The plateaus meet at the mean 1.5 when \lambda/2 = 1.5: \lambda = 3. For \lambda \ge 3 the solution is (1.5, 1.5, 1.5, 1.5). (c) TV keeps one sharp jump, just smaller (2 instead of 3): contrast is lost but the edge stays where it is and stays sharp. Quadratic smoothing replaces the jump by a ramp over all four samples.
B4. (a) The peak (width 1, two lower neighbours) drops by 2\lambda, each side (width 1, one higher neighbour) rises by \lambda: \lambda = 0.5: (0.5, 2, 0.5). At \lambda = 1 they would meet at 1: (1, 1, 1), the mean. (b) It is lowered by about 2\lambda/w (a little less in practice, because the background rises too). It disappears for \lambda around aw/2. Small and narrow features lose contrast first and then vanish, even if they are bright: TV shrinks small structures.
B5. (a) \omega = \pi: 2 - 2\cos\pi = 4; gain 1/5 = 0.2 (\lambda = 1) and 1/41 = 0.024 (\lambda = 10). (b) 1 + 10(2 - 2\cos\omega) = 2: \cos\omega = 0.95, \omega = 0.318, i.e. 0.051 cycles per sample (a period of about 20 samples). (c) A step is a sum of waves of all frequencies (its Fourier transform falls off only like 1/\omega); damping the high frequencies removes the parts that make it sharp. A linear filter cannot distinguish a high frequency belonging to an edge from one belonging to noise.
B6. (a) TV: flat regions with sharp boundaries are exactly what its solutions look like (some contrast loss at small cells). (b) Quadratic (and a large \lambda): illumination has no edges, and the linear system is fast. (c) Huber: quadratic for the small differences of smooth gradients (no staircases), linear for the large jumps at bands (no blurring).




Math questions
B7. (math) Show that \sum_{(p,q)}(x_p - x_q)^2 = \mathbf x^\top L\mathbf x, that the gradient of E for the quadratic prior is (\mathbf x - \mathbf y) + \lambda L\mathbf x, and that I + \lambda L is positive definite, so the minimum is unique.
B8. (math) On a ring of n samples, show that \mathbf f with f_p = e^{i\omega p}, \omega = 2\pi k/n, is an eigenvector of L with eigenvalue 2 - 2\cos\omega, and derive the gain of B5.
B9. (math) Derive the plateau rule for 1D TV from the optimality condition x_p - y_p + \lambda(g_{p-1} - g_p) = 0, g_p \in \operatorname{sign}(x_{p+1} - x_p) (with g_p \in [-1, 1] where x_{p+1} = x_p, and g = 0 beyond the ends).
B10. (math) With Gaussian noise of standard deviation \sigma_n and the prior p(\mathbf x) \propto \exp(-\frac{\lambda'}2\mathbf x^\top L\mathbf x), show that the posterior is Gaussian, that its MAP solves (I + \lambda'\sigma_n^2L)\mathbf x = \mathbf y, and that MAP and posterior mean coincide.






Solutions (math)





B7. \mathbf x^\top L\mathbf x = \sum_pd_px_p^2 - \sum_{p,q}W_{pq}x_px_q = \sum_{(p,q)}(x_p^2 + x_q^2 - 2x_px_q) = \sum_{(p,q)}(x_p - x_q)^2 (each edge once). \nabla\tfrac12\|\mathbf x - \mathbf y\|^2 = \mathbf x - \mathbf y and \nabla\frac\lambda2\mathbf x^\top L\mathbf x = \lambda L\mathbf x (L symmetric). \mathbf x^\top(I + \lambda L)\mathbf x = \|\mathbf x\|^2 + \lambda\sum(x_p - x_q)^2 > 0 for \mathbf x \ne \mathbf 0: positive definite, so E is strictly convex with one minimum.
B8. (L\mathbf f)_p = 2e^{i\omega p} - e^{i\omega(p-1)} - e^{i\omega(p+1)} = (2 - e^{-i\omega} - e^{i\omega})e^{i\omega p} = (2 - 2\cos\omega)f_p; on the ring p \pm 1 wraps around, which works because e^{i\omega n} = 1. Then (I + \lambda L)\mathbf f = (1 + \lambda(2 - 2\cos\omega))\mathbf f, and solving the system divides the \mathbf f-component of \mathbf y by this number: the gain.
B9. On a plateau x_a = \dots = x_b = c with different values outside, add the conditions for p = a, \dots, b: the terms \lambda(g_{p-1} - g_p) telescope to \lambda(g_{a-1} - g_b), so \sum_{p=a}^b(c - y_p) = -\lambda(g_{a-1} - g_b) and c = \bar y_{[a,b]} - \lambda(g_{a-1} - g_b)/(b - a + 1). g_{a-1} = +1 if the left neighbour is lower (-1 if higher), g_b = +1 if the right neighbour is higher (-1 if lower). A higher neighbour on one side and a lower one on the other: g_{a-1} = g_b, no shift. A local maximum: g_{a-1} = 1, g_b = -1, shift -2\lambda/w. A plateau at the end of the signal with one higher neighbour: +\lambda/w.
B10. -\log p(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf y) = \frac1{2\sigma_n^2}\|\mathbf x - \mathbf y\|^2 + \frac{\lambda'}2\mathbf x^\top L\mathbf x + \text{const}, a quadratic form in \mathbf x with Hessian A = I/\sigma_n^2 + \lambda'L (positive definite): the posterior is Gaussian with covariance A^{-1}. Gradient zero: (\mathbf x - \mathbf y)/\sigma_n^2 + \lambda'L\mathbf x = 0, i.e. (I + \lambda'\sigma_n^2L)\mathbf x = \mathbf y. A Gaussian has its maximum at its mean, and each marginal is a Gaussian centred at the same point: MAP = mean = MPM.

title: Exercise: quadratic smoothing and total variation
text:
Explore
A profile of 200 samples with Gaussian noise (fixed seed): step · ramp · peak (a step at 40, a ramp from 2 down to 0 over 80–140, a 4-sample peak of height 2 at 166–169), plateaus, or a line across the micrograph. Choose the prior and \lambda (and \delta for Huber). The plot shows the noisy data (grey dots), the truth (dashed) and the estimate; the readout splits the energy into data and prior terms and gives the error (RMSE) against the truth. Tabs: prior samples (five random walks from the quadratic and from the TV prior, with the same step variance, and the two step distributions), and the matrix (I + \lambda L for 10 samples, and the gain of quadratic smoothing against frequency).



E1. Preset quadratic blurs the step (\lambda = 10). Read the RMSE of the estimate and of the noisy data. Over how many samples is the step spread? How high is the peak? Now find the \lambda with the smallest RMSE for the quadratic prior. What do you see at that \lambda?
E2. Preset TV keeps the step (\lambda = 1). Compare the step, the RMSE and the energy split with E1. What happened to the ramp and to the peak?
E3. Preset TV staircases the ramp (\lambda = 3, zoomed on the ramp). Describe the estimate on the ramp. Is the RMSE better or worse than at \lambda = 1?
E4. Preset TV shrinks the narrow peak (\lambda = 2, zoomed on the peak). Read the peak height of the estimate at \lambda = 1, 2 and 3 and compare with B4(b) (w = 4, a = 2).
E5. Preset Huber in between (\lambda = 5, \delta = 0.1). Compare step, ramp, peak and RMSE with the best quadratic and the best TV result (find the best \lambda for TV).
E6. Choose the plateaus profile. Compare quadratic (\lambda = 10) and TV (\lambda = 1). Why does TV do especially well here?
E7. Tab prior samples. Which draws look more like the profiles we denoise: the quadratic or the TV ones? Do the TV draws have flat plateaus? Compare the two step distributions in the lower plot.
E8. Tab the matrix. For \lambda = 10, read the entries of I + \lambda L and compare with the Background table. Read the gain at 0.05 and at 0.5 cycles per sample, and check with B5.






Solutions





E1. RMSE 0.240 against 0.291 for the noisy data. The step rises from 10 % to 90 % over about 15 samples, and the peak reaches only 0.90 (true height 2). The best quadratic \lambda is about 1.2 (RMSE 0.190): the step is a little sharper (about 13 samples) and the peak higher (1.53), but much of the noise is back. Quadratic smoothing trades noise against blur and cannot win both.
E2. The step stays sharp (from 0.25 to 2.04 within two samples), RMSE 0.137, energy 7.30 (data) + 6.81 (prior). The ramp is cut into flat steps (staircasing), and the peak is lowered to 1.36.
E3. The ramp becomes a staircase of about a dozen flat steps. RMSE 0.268, worse than at \lambda = 1 (0.137): the plateaus also lose more contrast (the peak is down to 0.36).
E4. Peak 1.36 (\lambda = 1), 0.86 (\lambda = 2), 0.36 (\lambda = 3). The rule 2\lambda/w = \lambda/2 predicts 1.5, 1.0, 0.5: the same trend, each a bit lower because the noise and the rising background also count. It vanishes around \lambda = aw/2 = 4.
E5. Huber (\lambda = 5, \delta = 0.1): sharp step, smooth ramp without stairs, peak 1.72, RMSE 0.128. The best quadratic gets 0.190 (\lambda \approx 1.2), the best TV 0.125 (\lambda \approx 0.55; small noise plateaus remain in the flat parts, and the ramp is still a staircase). Huber and TV are about equally good by RMSE; Huber looks better on the ramp.
E6. Plateaus: quadratic RMSE 0.227, TV 0.104. The profile is piecewise constant, which is exactly the shape of a TV solution: TV’s prior assumption is right here, so it removes noise without blurring the jumps.
E7. Neither looks like a profile with steps: both are rough random walks drifting up and down. The TV draws have no flat plateaus. Their step distribution (Laplace) has a sharper peak at 0 and heavier tails than the normal one: more tiny steps and more big ones. The flat plateaus of TV estimates come from minimising the energy, not from the prior’s typical samples.
E8. Diagonal 1 + 10 = 11 at the two ends and 1 + 20 = 21 inside, -10 next to the diagonal, zeros elsewhere: tridiagonal. Gain 0.505 at 0.05 cycles per sample and 1/41 = 0.024 at 0.5: as in B5.

title: Exercise: quadratic smoothing and total variation
text:
Where this leads
The same two priors return when the image is also blurred: the deconvolution day adds a point-spread function to the data term (Tikhonov = quadratic, and TV). In 2D, TV denoising keeps object boundaries in microscopy images, and its binary cousin, the boundary length, is the smoothness term of graph cuts, of the Ising model and of the Chan–Vese level-set model.

title: Mixtures on images
text:
About this lecture
We can fit a mixture of Gaussians to any cloud of points with EM. Now the points are pixels and objects.

Grey-level mixtures: K classes from the histogram; labels and probability maps.
Colour and feature-space segmentation: why a full covariance keeps a shadowed object whole.
Populations: fractions of cells or spots from the component weights.
Anomalies: pixels or objects that no component explains.
Mixtures as the data term of a graph cut (GrabCut).

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: Mixtures on images
section: Recall: two Gaussians and a threshold

title: Mixtures on images
text:
A mixture of grey levels


Every pixel’s grey value is a point in 1D. Fit K Gaussians with EM: each class gets a mean, a width and a weight (its share of the pixels).
EM on the histogram: pixels with the same grey value have the same responsibilities, so each of the 256 bins is one point with weight = its count. One iteration costs 256 \times K evaluations, whatever the image size.
Synthetic image above: three classes (background, cytoplasm, organelles; 49 %, 39 %, 12 % of the pixels). EM finds weights 0.49, 0.40, 0.12 and the Bayes boundaries at grey values 100 and 160.

title: Mixtures on images
section: The math: EM on a weighted histogram
text:
The math: EM on a weighted histogram
Grey values g_j (bin centres) with counts h_j, n = \sum_j h_j. All pixels in bin j have the same responsibilities r_{jk}, so every sum over pixels becomes a sum over bins with weight h_j:
N_k = \sum_j h_j r_{jk}, \qquad \pi_k = \frac{N_k}{n}, \qquad \mu_k = \frac{1}{N_k}\sum_j h_j r_{jk}\,g_j, \qquad \sigma_k^2 = \frac{1}{N_k}\sum_j h_j r_{jk}\,(g_j - \mu_k)^2,
\log p(\mathcal D) = \sum_j h_j \log\sum_k \pi_k\mathcal N(g_j \mid \mu_k, \sigma_k^2).
The result is identical to EM on all pixels (exactly, for integer grey values). For numerical safety compute \log\sum_k e^{a_k} as a_{\max} + \log\sum_k e^{a_k - a_{\max}} (log-sum-exp): a pixel far from every mean would otherwise give \log 0.

title: Mixtures on images
text:
Labels, probability maps, boundaries

Label image: every pixel gets its most probable class. Because the label depends only on the grey value, it is a multi-level threshold at the Bayes boundaries.
Probability map: the responsibility of one class at every pixel, a soft segmentation. Values near 0.5 mark pixels the model cannot decide on (edges, overlapping classes).
K = 2 with free variances: the minimum-error threshold again, now found by EM.
Equal variances (tied): the boundaries are halfway between neighbouring means, shifted by the weights. Close to multi-level Otsu (thresholding day), which also assumes equally wide classes.
The weights matter: a rare class gets a smaller region; its boundary moves towards its own mean.

title: Mixtures on images
text:
The math: the two-class boundary
Two classes with \sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma: the boundary \pi_1\mathcal N_1(x) = \pi_2\mathcal N_2(x) is
x^* = \frac{\mu_1 + \mu_2}{2} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu_2 - \mu_1}\ln\frac{\pi_1}{\pi_2},
the thresholding day’s equal-variance formula. With \sigma_1 \ne \sigma_2, taking logs gives a quadratic equation in x,
\frac{(x - \mu_1)^2}{\sigma_1^2} - \frac{(x - \mu_2)^2}{\sigma_2^2} = 2\ln\frac{\pi_1\sigma_2}{\pi_2\sigma_1},
with two roots: the narrower class wins only between them (unit 2). Example: the synthetic image’s small bright class has \pi_3 = 0.04 against \pi_2 = 0.48: x^* = 155 + \frac{13^2}{51.5}\ln 12 \approx 163 instead of the midpoint 155.

title: Mixtures on images
text:
Try it: a histogram mixture




Course micrograph, 128 × 128. “K = 3 on the micrograph”: weights 0.50, 0.34, 0.16; means 122, 204, 240; Bayes boundaries 173 and 229. “K = 2”: boundary 183, multi-level Otsu 164: the dark class is much wider (σ 39 against 22), so the minimum-error boundary moves towards the narrow bright class. Synthetic image “equal variances: Otsu-like”: boundaries 101 and 160, Otsu 100 and 155; 97.4 % of pixels as in the truth. “K too large”: K = 6 splits the background peak into three; press BIC: smallest at K = 3. “noise”: noise 22, 85.7 % correct, salt-and-pepper labels. “small bright class”: π3 = 0.04, posterior view; the boundary is at 163.

title: Mixtures on images
section: The histogram forgets where pixels are
text:
The histogram forgets where pixels are
A label that depends only on the grey value cannot use the neighbours:

with noise, the classes overlap in the histogram and the label image is speckled (single wrong pixels everywhere);
a smooth intensity gradient (uneven illumination) shifts the classes and no single mixture fits the whole image.

Fixes that keep the mixture as the data term and add the neighbours:

graph cuts with a smoothness term (graph-cut day);
a hidden Markov random field (a Potts prior on the labels), with the mixture re-estimated by EM: the Ising elective.

title: Mixtures on images
section: Colour: a feature space with shape
text:
Colour: a feature space with shape
A colour pixel is a point in 3D (RGB or L*a*b*). The colour day segmented colours with thresholds and distances (and one slide of k-means); a mixture adds shape.

A shadowed object is not a ball of colours: its pixels lie along a line from bright to dark (in RGB, towards black; in Lab mostly along L*).
k-means describes every group by a round blob: to cover the long shadow line it splits the object, and to make room it merges two other colours.
A full-covariance component is a long ellipse along the shadow line: the object stays whole.
More features: colour + local mean (texture), or colour + position (x, y) with a weight: groups become spatially compact regions.

title: Mixtures on images
text:
Try it: colour segmentation




Synthetic scene: a red ball lit from the left, a green block, a blue ellipse on a beige table; features RGB, K = 4. “shadowed ball”: k-means (start 5) splits the ball into two clusters and merges the green block with the blue ellipse (Dice green 0.68, blue 0.00; J = 1.086 × 10⁶). “best of 6 starts”: k-means’ best J is this split (1.086 × 10⁶, against 1.462 × 10⁶ for the correct grouping): the split is what k-means wants. Switch to “Gaussian mixture” (full): from start 5 it keeps the ball whole and finds all four objects (Dice 1.00), log p = −137 740; best of 6 starts: the same. Spherical covariances split the ball again. “RGB vs Lab”: in Lab, k-means is already right (the shadow mostly changes L*). “add position”: Lab + xy, K = 6: the table breaks into compact patches.

title: Mixtures on images
text:
Relatives: mean shift and superpixels

Mean shift: put a small Gaussian on every point (a kernel density estimate); move every point uphill to the nearest peak of the density. Points that reach the same peak form a group. K is not chosen; the kernel width is.
SLIC superpixels: k-means on (colour, x, y) with many small groups (K in the hundreds), each centre searching only a local window. The result is an over-segmentation into compact, colour-coherent patches.
Superpixels make later steps cheaper: a graph cut on 500 superpixels instead of 250 000 pixels.

title: Mixtures on images
text:
Populations: counting by mixture weights
The points are objects now (one point per nucleus or spot), with features from the measurements day.

DNA content (integrated nuclear intensity): cells in G1 have one copy (2N), in G2 two copies (4N), in S phase something in between. The histogram is a mixture of a G1 peak, a G2 peak at twice the intensity, and an S-phase plateau. The fitted weights are the fractions of cells in each phase.
Spot brightness: a spot holds 1, 2 or 3 fluorophores, so its intensity is a mixture of peaks at 1×, 2×, 3× the single-molecule brightness. The weights count the molecules.
Constraints help: tie the G2 mean to twice the G1 mean, or the spot means to multiples of one brightness. EM still works (the M-step changes).

title: Mixtures on images
text:
Anomalies: what no component explains
Fit a mixture to “normal” pixels or objects. A new point is an anomaly when

its density p(\mathbf x) is below a threshold \tau, or
its Mahalanobis distance is above (say) 3 to every component.

Examples: dust or debris in a field of cells, an out-of-focus object, a rare cell type, a stain artefact.

Unlike a classifier, this needs no examples of the anomalies: it only knows what normal looks like.
The threshold is a trade-off: for a Gaussian in 3D, 1 normal point in 150 lies beyond d_M = 3.5 anyway (1 in 34 beyond 3, 1 in 6600 beyond 4.5).
The VAE day uses the reconstruction error of an autoencoder for the same purpose.

title: Mixtures on images
text:
Try it: an odd object




The scene with a small yellow object; Lab, K = 4, full covariances, start 2. The four mixture components describe the table, ball, block and ellipse (Dice 0.99–1.00). View “d_M > t to all” with t = 4.5: 119 pixels are flagged, the 113 pixels of the odd object and 6 noise pixels. Lower t to 3.5: many more noise pixels on the table. Other starts may give a component to the yellow object: then it is no longer an anomaly, but a class.

title: Mixtures on images
text:
Mixtures as data terms: GrabCut
The graph-cut day’s energy needs a data term D_p(\ell) = -\log P(I_p \mid \ell): how well pixel p’s value fits label \ell. A fitted mixture per label provides it.
GrabCut (Rother, Kolmogorov & Blake, 2004), for colour images:

The user draws a box: outside = background, inside = unknown.
Fit a colour mixture (about 5 components) to the background pixels and one to the current object pixels.
Graph cut with these data terms and contrast-sensitive smoothness.
Refit the mixtures to the new labels; cut again; repeat until it settles.

The same loop as EM: a labelling step and a model-fitting step, alternating.

title: Mixtures on images
text:
Summary

Histogram mixtures: EM on the bins, weighted by their counts; K classes, labels = multi-level thresholds at the Bayes boundaries; responsibilities = probability maps.
K = 2: the minimum-error threshold; equal variances: close to multi-level Otsu; weights move the boundaries.
The histogram ignores neighbours: noise gives speckle (fix: graph cuts, hidden MRF).
In colour, a full covariance follows a shadow; k-means splits it.
Weights count populations; low likelihood or large Mahalanobis distance flags anomalies.
Fitted mixtures are the data terms of graph cuts: GrabCut alternates fitting and cutting.

title: Quiz: the generalised Hough transform
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. The R-table stores, for each gradient-direction bin, the vectors from the template’s edge points to its reference point.

Q1. What is stored in the R-table, and why is it indexed by the edge direction?






Hint





What does an edge point in a new image know about itself?









Answer





For each edge point of the template, the vector from the point to the reference point, filed under the point’s gradient direction. In a new image an edge point knows only its position and its direction; the direction narrows down where on the shape it can be, and so which vectors can lead to the reference point.




Q2. A direction bin of the R-table holds 20 vectors. An edge point of the scene falls into that bin. How many votes does it cast, and how many of them can be correct?






Hint





The point lies at one place on the shape.









Answer





20 votes, one per vector. If the point belongs to a copy of the shape, at most one of them (the vector of its own position on the boundary, or a few if several template points are very close) lands on the reference point; the others land elsewhere. Only the correct votes of many points pile up; the wrong ones spread out.




Q3. Why is the circle Hough transform with gradient voting and a known radius a special case of the generalised Hough transform?






Hint





Build the R-table of a disc with its centre as the reference point.









Answer





On a disc each gradient direction occurs at one point of the boundary, and from there the centre is at distance r along the gradient. So the R-table has one vector per direction, of length r along the direction; voting with it puts one vote at \mathbf p + r\mathbf u, which is exactly circle voting with a known radius and polarity.




Q4. The template is a key; in the scene the key is rotated by 60°. Without a rotation search it is not found. Why not?






Hint





Two things change under a rotation.









Answer





The gradient directions of the rotated key are all 60° larger, so its edge points look up the wrong bins; and even with the right bin, the stored vectors point in the unrotated directions. Its votes scatter instead of meeting. A rotation search shifts the bin index and rotates the vectors for each tried angle.




Q5. Searching 36 rotations and 5 scales: how much more work and memory than translation only?






Hint





One accumulator slice per pose.









Answer





36 \times 5 = 180 poses: 180 lookups per edge point instead of 1, and 180 accumulator slices instead of 1. That is why the search is done coarse to fine: all poses on a small image, then only the best ones at full resolution.




Q6. A third of a copy is hidden behind another object. Is it still found?






Hint





Which votes are lost?









Answer





Usually yes: the visible two thirds still vote for the same reference point, giving about two thirds of the full peak. It is found if that is above the threshold; the threshold works as a minimum visible fraction of the boundary.




Q7. Why can a shape that is merely similar to the template (say, a key with a longer shaft) be reported as a detection?






Hint





How many of its edge points vote correctly?









Answer





Large parts of its boundary coincide with the template’s after a shift: those points vote for (nearly) the same reference point and produce a peak that may reach a third or more of a full match. With a low threshold it is accepted. A higher threshold, or checking the whole outline afterwards, rejects it.




Q8. (math) Show that with a single direction bin the generalised Hough transform is the correlation of the scene’s edge map with the template’s edge map.






Hint





Write the votes at \mathbf c as a double sum and substitute \mathbf q = -\mathbf v.









Answer





With one bin, every edge point votes with every vector: H(\mathbf c) = \sum_{\mathbf x}\sum_{\mathbf v \in T} E(\mathbf x)[\mathbf x + \mathbf v = \mathbf c] = \sum_{\mathbf v \in T} E(\mathbf c - \mathbf v). With \mathbf q = -\mathbf v, the template edge points relative to the reference point: H(\mathbf c) = \sum_{\mathbf q} E(\mathbf c + \mathbf q)E_T(\mathbf q), the correlation of E with E_T. The direction bins restrict each sum to points of the same direction, which makes the match selective.

title: Exercise: the generalised Hough transform
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Reference point
any fixed point of the template (here: its centre)


R-table
for each gradient-direction bin: the vectors from the template’s edge points in that bin to the reference point


Voting
an edge point \mathbf p with direction \theta votes at \mathbf p + \mathbf v for every \mathbf v in bin \theta


Pose search
for each rotation \phi and scale s: look up bin \theta - \phi, vote at \mathbf p + sR(\phi)\mathbf v; one accumulator slice per pose


Score (demo)
edge points voting within 1 px of a cell, divided by the number of template edge points



Coordinates are pixel coordinates (x, y) with y down. For a bright shape on a dark background the gradient points into the shape.

title: Exercise: the generalised Hough transform
text:
By hand
B1. A bright square with corners (0, 0), (4, 0), (4, 4), (0, 4), reference point (2, 2). Its edge points are the integer points on the sides, without the corners: three per side. Use 4 direction bins: gradient pointing down, up, right, left. (a) Which side has its gradient pointing down? Write the R-table: for each bin, the three vectors. (b) A copy of the square has corners (10, 5) and (14, 9). Its top side has edge points (11, 5), (12, 5), (13, 5). Where do these three points vote? (c) Without writing all votes: how many votes do the 12 edge points of the copy cast in total? Which position gets the most, and how many? How many does its best competitor get?
B2. Rotations of the square. (a) The copy is rotated by 90°. Which table entries does a rotated table need? Does the unrotated table still find it? Why is the square special? (b) The copy is rotated by 45° (a diamond). What are its gradient directions, and does the unrotated 4-bin table find it?
B3. Cost of a pose search. A scene of 160 × 160 pixels has 721 edge points. The template’s R-table has 182 entries in 36 bins. (a) Translation only: how many table lookups? About how many votes? (b) With 36 rotations and 5 scales: how many lookups, how many accumulator slices and cells? (c) The demo reports 649,388 votes for (b). Is that consistent with your estimate?
B4. A key is detected with score 0.90 when fully visible. A disc hides about a third of its boundary. What score do you expect? What is the largest threshold that still finds it?






Solutions





B1. (a) The top side (y = 0): the square is below it, so the gradient (towards bright) points down. Vectors = reference − point:

(2, 1), (2, 0), (2, -1)


left
right, (4, 1), (4, 2), (4, 3)
(-2, 1), (-2, 0), (-2, -1)




Each looks up “down” and adds the three vectors: (11, 5) votes at (12, 7), (11, 7), (10, 7); (12, 5) at (13, 7), (12, 7), (11, 7); (13, 5) at (14, 7), (13, 7), (12, 7). So (12, 7) gets 3, (11, 7) and (13, 7) 2 each, (10, 7) and (14, 7) 1 each.
12 \times 3 = 36 votes. The centre (12, 7) gets 3 from each side: 12. The best competitors, (11, 7), (13, 7), (12, 6), (12, 8), get 4 each (2 from each of two sides). The votes form a cross through the centre, as in the demo’s “square, 4 bins” preset.

B2. (a) Rotating by 90° turns each gradient direction into the next one (down → right → up → left, counter-clockwise on the screen) and rotates each vector by 90°: the rotated table holds for “right” what the original table holds for “right”, and so on. A square rotated by 90° is the same square, so the unrotated table finds it without any rotation search: shapes with a rotational symmetry need only part of the angle range. (b) The diamond’s sides have gradients at 45°, 135°, 225°, 315°: exactly between the 4 bins. Each lands in some neighbouring bin, whose vectors belong to a side at a different angle, so the votes scatter: not found. A rotation search (in steps of a few degrees) and finer bins are needed.
B3. (a) 721 lookups; on average 182/36 = 5.1 vectors per bin, so about 721 \times 5.1 \approx 3600 votes (the demo: 4,682; bins are not equally full, and the key’s long straight sides fill a few bins heavily). (b) 721 \times 180 = 129{,}780 lookups; 180 slices of 160 \times 160 = 4.6 million cells. (c) 129{,}780 \times 5.06 \approx 656{,}000: close to 649,388 (votes that land outside the image are not counted).
B4. About two thirds of 0.90: roughly 0.6. Any threshold below about 0.6 still finds it (the demo, preset “occluded copy still found”: 0.58, found at threshold 0.5).




Math questions
B5. (math) The template is rotated by \phi (counter-clockwise on the screen) and scaled by s about its reference point. Show that the rotated copy’s R-table is: bin \theta + \phi holds the vectors sR(\phi)\mathbf v for \mathbf v in the original bin \theta. Write the vote of a scene point for the pose (\phi, s) using only the original table.
B6. (math) Show that with a single direction bin the GHT computes H(\mathbf c) = \sum_{\mathbf q} E(\mathbf c + \mathbf q)\,E_T(\mathbf q): the correlation of the scene’s edge map E with the template’s edge map E_T (relative to the reference point). Why do more direction bins reduce false peaks?
B7. (math) Does the choice of reference point change which copies are found (translation only)? With a rotation search in steps of \Delta\phi, a copy is rotated by up to \Delta\phi/2 from the nearest tried angle. How far do the votes of an edge point at distance d from the reference point miss? What does that say about where to put the reference point?






Solutions (math)





B5. A template edge point \mathbf x_T with gradient direction \theta and vector \mathbf v = \mathbf c_T - \mathbf x_T moves to \mathbf x = \mathbf c + sR(\phi)(\mathbf x_T - \mathbf c_T), and its gradient direction becomes \theta + \phi (a rotation turns all directions; scaling does not change them). Its vector to the new reference point \mathbf c is sR(\phi)\mathbf v. So the rotated table has sR(\phi)\mathbf v in bin \theta + \phi. A scene point \mathbf p with direction \theta' looks up the rotated bin \theta', i.e. the original bin \theta' - \phi, and votes at \mathbf p + sR(\phi)\mathbf v for each \mathbf v there; no rotated table needs to be stored.
B6. With one bin every point votes with every vector: H(\mathbf c) = \sum_{\mathbf x} E(\mathbf x)\sum_{\mathbf v \in T}[\mathbf x + \mathbf v = \mathbf c] = \sum_{\mathbf v \in T} E(\mathbf c - \mathbf v). The template edge points relative to the reference point are \mathbf q = \mathbf x_T - \mathbf c_T = -\mathbf v, so H(\mathbf c) = \sum_{\mathbf q} E(\mathbf c + \mathbf q) E_T(\mathbf q). With direction bins, the sum only pairs scene and template points of the same direction: an edge in the scene supports a template point only if it has the same orientation, so random edges and other shapes match far less often.
B7. For translation only, no: moving the reference point by \mathbf d adds \mathbf d to every vector, so every vote and every peak moves by \mathbf d; the same copies are found. Under a rotation error \delta \le \Delta\phi/2, a vote along a vector of length d misses by about d\,\delta (an arc). Points far from the reference point miss most, so the reference point should be central (for example the centroid), which keeps the largest d small; equivalently, the angle step must satisfy d_\text{max}\,\Delta\phi/2 \lesssim 1 px.

title: Exercise: the generalised Hough transform
text:
Explore
Left: the template with its edge points (found with the same edge detector as the scene) and the R-table drawn as arrows to the reference point (+), coloured by direction bin; drag a vertex or the reference point. Below it the table itself. Middle: the scene with its edge points and the detections (cyan outlines at the found position, angle and scale). Right: the accumulator, the maximum over all searched poses. Click a scene edge point to see its votes (magenta) for the pose of the strongest detection. The readout gives lookups, votes and the detections as (reference point) angle, scale: score.



G1. Preset square, 4 bins. How many entries has the table, and how many per bin? What do the scores of the two squares come out as? Describe the accumulator around each square and compare with B1(c).
G2. Preset translation only (the key, 36 bins). Scores of the two keys? Drag the reference point (+) to a corner of the template: what happens to the detections, the peaks, the scores?
G3. Still on translation only, set the direction bins to 4, then 8, then 72. Note the scores of the two keys, the number of votes, and the strongest false peak (lower the threshold to see it). Explain the trade-off.
G4. Preset occluded copy still found. What is the score of the occluded key? Increase the occlusion until it is lost: at roughly which setting?
G5. Presets rotated: missed and rotation search: found. Compare lookups, votes and detections. At which angle is the second key found, with which score? What are the weaker peaks in the accumulator?
G6. Preset scale search (copies at 0.8 and 1.2). Which scores? Why is the small copy’s score lower, even though it is a perfect copy?
G7. Preset similar shape: false positive. What is detected, and with which scores? What threshold would remove the false positive, and what would that cost?
G8. Preset circle template = circle Hough. How many vectors per bin, and how long are they? Explain why this is circle detection with gradient voting.






Solutions





G1. 120 entries: 29, 30, 31 and 30 in the four bins (about 30 edge points per side of a 30-px square). Scores 1.00 and 0.99. Around each square the accumulator shows a bright cross: each side’s 30 vectors spread its points’ votes along a line through the centre, and the four sides’ lines cross at the centre, which gets all of them. B1(c) is the same picture with 3 points per side.
G2. 0.90 and 0.74. The copies are identical; the difference comes from the clutter and the noise: a clutter blob overlaps part of the second key’s boundary, and noise breaks a few edges (with clutter and noise set to 0 both score 1.00). Moving the reference point moves the peaks and the yellow dots with it; the cyan outlines stay on the keys and the scores stay nearly the same: the reference point is arbitrary for translation.
G3. 4 bins: 0.99 and 0.96, 30,495 votes, strongest false peak 0.29. 8 bins: 0.99 and 0.95, 16,739 votes, false 0.34. 36 bins: 0.90 and 0.74, 5,826 votes. 72 bins: 0.85 and 0.66, 4,116 votes. Few bins put many vectors in each bin: more votes and more accidental agreement (higher false peaks), but tolerant of small errors in the edge direction. Many bins are selective and cheap, but a direction error of a few degrees moves a point into the neighbouring bin, which has other vectors, so the true peak drops.
G4. 0.58 (instead of 0.90 unoccluded). Its score falls to 0.54 at occlusion 0.6, 0.50 at 0.7 and 0.47 at 0.75: with the threshold at 0.5 it is lost between 0.7 and 0.75, when its score has dropped to about half of the unoccluded 0.90.
G5. Without rotation search: 721 lookups, 4,682 votes, only the upright key (0.90). With 36 rotations: 25,956 lookups (36 times), 129,925 votes, both keys found; the rotated one at 60° with 0.91. The weaker peaks (0.31 to 0.40) are other poses of the same keys: rotated by 90°, 180°, 270° the key’s long straight sides still line up with part of the template.
G6. 0.93 at scale 1.2 and 0.54 at scale 0.8. The score divides by the number of template edge points; a copy at 0.8 has only about 0.8 times as many edge points, and its small teeth (3 px) are smoothed away by the edge detector. A score relative to the expected number of points at that scale would correct for the first effect.
G7. The true key at 0.90 and the stretched key at (108, 112) with 0.31: a false positive (the shaft and the bow partly coincide with the template). A threshold above 0.31, e.g. 0.4, removes it; the cost is that a key with more than about half its boundary hidden would also be missed.
G8. 2 to 5 vectors per bin (136 in total over 36 bins), all of length 18, pointing along the bin’s direction. A disc’s edge point with gradient direction \theta looks up vectors of length 18 along \theta: one vote at \mathbf p + 18\mathbf u, exactly circle voting with r = 18, bright on dark. Scores 0.93 and 0.92.

title: Exercise: the generalised Hough transform
text:
Where this leads
Voting needs one accumulator dimension per parameter: two for a line, three for a circle, four for a shape with rotation and scale. The last unit of the day, RANSAC, avoids the accumulator altogether: guess a model from a few points and count how many others agree.

title: Edge-based segmentation: geodesic active contours
text:
About this lecture
We can now move a curve with any speed F. To segment an image, let the image decide the speed: fast where nothing happens, almost zero on edges. The front then stops on object boundaries, and it can split around several objects on its own.

Recall: snakes, and what they could not do.
The edge-stopping function g: the image turned into a speed.
Stage 1: a balloon that brakes at edges.
Stage 2: geodesic active contours: the shortest curve in an image-weighted metric, with a pull into the edge.
What the knobs do, and the typical failures: leaking through weak edges, getting stuck in concavities and noise.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Prerequisites: the previous two units (implicit curves, the level set equation with upwind differences), Gaussian smoothing and the image gradient (Filtering & convolution, Edges day). The snakes day (previous in this elective chain) is recalled on one slide only.

title: Edge-based segmentation: geodesic active contours
text:
Recall: snakes (snakes day)
A snake is an explicit closed curve that moves downhill on an energy: internal (elasticity \alpha, rigidity \beta: short and smooth) plus image (large edge strength |\nabla I|^2 is attractive).

It works, given a good start: it refines a curve you place near the object.
Fixed topology: one snake, one curve. Two objects need two snakes; it cannot split or merge.
Points bunch up or spread out and must be re-sampled; nothing prevents self-intersection.
A balloon force helps it reach far edges, and leaks through weak ones.

Level sets keep the idea (an energy, a pull towards edges, a balloon) and drop the points.

title: Edge-based segmentation: geodesic active contours
text:
The image as a speed
Make a function that is about 1 in flat regions and about 0 on edges: g = \frac{1}{1 + |\nabla I_\sigma|^2 / k^2}, \qquad I_\sigma = \text{the image smoothed with a Gaussian of width } \sigma.

|\nabla I_\sigma|: the edge strength, from Gaussian smoothing and differences of neighbours (Filtering & convolution, the edges day).
k sets what counts as an edge: where |\nabla I_\sigma| = k, g = 0.5; at 3k, g = 0.1.
\sigma suppresses noise: without smoothing every noisy pixel looks like a small edge.
