Detail of a polynomial x_n = \sum_{q < p}\beta_q n^q: \;d_k = \sum_n g_n x_{2k+n} = \sum_q \beta_q \sum_n g_n (2k+n)^q. Expanding (2k+n)^q binomially gives only sums \sum_n n^m g_n with m \le q < p: all zero.
Smooth x: Taylor around 2k with remainder of order p: d_k = \mathcal O\big(\max|x^{(p)}|\big) over the filter’s support, small where x is smooth.
db2: g = (h_3, -h_2, h_1, -h_0) with h = (1+\sqrt3,\ 3+\sqrt3,\ 3-\sqrt3,\ 1-\sqrt3)/(4\sqrt2): \sum g_n \propto (1 - \sqrt3) - (3 - \sqrt3) + (3 + \sqrt3) - (1 + \sqrt3) = 0, and \sum n g_n \propto -(3 - \sqrt3) + 2(3 + \sqrt3) - 3(1 + \sqrt3) = 0.
crumbs: Multiresolution, filter banks and Daubechies wavelets

title: Multiresolution, filter banks and Daubechies wavelets
text:
Daubechies wavelets




dbp: the shortest orthogonal filters with p vanishing moments, 2p taps (Daubechies 1988). db1 = Haar.

More moments: smoother, sparser on smooth parts.
But longer: each edge touches more coefficients.
Symlets (sym4): nearly symmetric variants.
Orthogonal and symmetric is impossible except Haar; JPEG 2000 uses biorthogonal wavelets (CDF 9/7, LeGall 5/3; the compression day).



φ and ψ computed by the cascade algorithm: iterate the two-scale relation, starting from a single 1 (the demo’s “basis functions” view does it one iteration at a time). db2 is continuous but has corners (it is Hölder ≈ 0.55); db8 is visibly smooth. Supports: [0, 2p − 1].
crumbs: Multiresolution, filter banks and Daubechies wavelets

title: Multiresolution, filter banks and Daubechies wavelets
section: Try it: smoother wavelets, sparser coefficients
text:
Try it: smoother wavelets, sparser coefficients




HeaviSine: a smooth wave with two jumps. For 1 % error: Fourier 145, Haar 184, db2 54, db4 34, db8 40 coefficients. db8 is smoother than db4 but longer, so the two jumps spread over more coefficients. Step: Haar 11, db2 24, db4 39, db8 55: for a pure jump the short Haar filter wins. Doppler: Haar 196, db4 75, db8 69, Fourier 231.
crumbs: Multiresolution, filter banks and Daubechies wavelets

title: Multiresolution, filter banks and Daubechies wavelets
text:
Borders
A finite signal ends; a filter of length L near the end needs samples that do not exist. The same choices as for any convolution (Filtering & convolution, border rules):

Periodic (wrap): simple, exactly orthogonal, N coefficients. But the jump from the last sample to the first is a false edge and gives large details at the end.
Symmetric (mirror): no jump, so far fewer border artefacts; the usual choice for images. Keeps a few extra coefficients, (N + L - 2)/2 per branch.
Zero padding: a jump to 0 at both ends, also extra coefficients.

With all coefficients kept, every rule reconstructs exactly; they differ in how sparse the border is.

Demo, filter-bank view, db4 on the ramp (64 samples): periodic: largest detail inside 1e-16, at the border 0.48; symmetric: 0.001; zero: 0.48. Coefficient counts: periodic 32 + 32, symmetric and zero 35 + 35.
crumbs: Multiresolution, filter banks and Daubechies wavelets

title: Multiresolution, filter banks and Daubechies wavelets
text:
Summary

The Haar transform is a multiresolution analysis: V_{j+1} = V_j \oplus W_j, approximation + detail at each scale, with \varphi and \psi defined by two filters h, g.
DWT = filter bank: low-pass and high-pass, keep every second sample; synthesis upsamples, filters and adds. Aliasing of the two branches cancels; reconstruction is exact.
The cascade on the low-pass branch costs \mathcal O(N) and gives exactly N coefficients.
Vanishing moments: polynomials of degree < p give zero details, smooth signals tiny ones. Daubechies dbp: shortest such filters; smoother but longer as p grows.
Borders: periodic, symmetric or zero extension; periodic adds a false edge.
crumbs: Multiresolution, filter banks and Daubechies wavelets

title: Quiz: filtered back-projection and sampling
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. What does the ramp filter do to the spectrum of a projection, and why is that the right correction?






Hint





Think of the spokes of the Fourier slice theorem.









Answer





It multiplies the projection’s 1D spectrum by |\omega|: low frequencies down, high ones up. Every projection contributes a spoke through the centre of the 2D spectrum, so the spokes crowd near the centre; weighting each spoke by its distance from the centre (in proportion to the gap it must cover) gives every frequency its fair share. It undoes the 1/|\omega| of plain back-projection.




Q2. Why does the filtered projection of a point have negative values, and what are they for?






Answer





A ramp suppresses the low frequencies, so the filtered profile has zero (or almost zero) total and must dip below zero beside the peak. Back-projected, the negative dips form dark bands along each smear; around the point they cancel the positive tails of the smears from other angles, which removes the 1/r halo.




Q3. A reconstruction from a low-dose scan is grainy. Which filter would you choose instead of the ramp, and what do you lose?






Hint





Where is the noise in frequency?









Answer





A tapered ramp (Hann, cosine, or Shepp–Logan), possibly with a lower cutoff. The noise sits mostly at high frequencies, which the ramp amplifies most; the taper turns them down. The price is resolution: edges and small details blur.




Q4. Your projections have 256 bins. Roughly how many angles over 180° should you acquire? What happens with 60?






Answer





About \tfrac{\pi}{2}\cdot 256 \approx 400. With 60 the spokes far from the centre of the spectrum are much more than one frequency step apart: streaks radiate from high-contrast edges.




Q5. Why must each projection be zero-padded before filtering it with an FFT?






Answer





Multiplying DFTs is circular convolution: the kernel’s tail that sticks out at one end of the projection reappears at the other end. Padding with zeros to at least twice the length gives the tail room, so the result equals ordinary (linear) convolution. Without padding, values near the edges of the object are wrong (for a large object: darker towards its rim).




Q6. An electron tomography tilt series covers \pm 65°. What is missing from the data, and how does a round particle look in the reconstruction?






Answer





A wedge of 180° - 130° = 50° around the beam direction in the 2D spectrum is never measured. The particle is elongated along the beam direction and its edges facing the beam are blurred: it looks like a lemon. No filter can restore the missing frequencies; only prior knowledge can partly fill them in.




Q7. With a fixed number of photons for the whole scan, why is it usually better to take many noisy views than a few clean ones with FBP?






Answer





The noise in the reconstruction depends mostly on the total number of photons, however they are shared. Too few views add a different error, streaks from missing spokes, that more photons per view cannot fix. Spreading the dose avoids the streaks at little cost in noise.




Q8. (math) Where does the |\omega| in FBP come from mathematically?






Answer





From the Jacobian of polar coordinates: writing the 2D inverse Fourier transform with \boldsymbol\omega = \omega\,\mathbf n_\theta gives d\boldsymbol\omega = |\omega|\,d\omega\,d\theta. With the slice theorem the inner integral becomes the inverse 1D transform of |\omega|P_\theta(\omega), and the outer integral over \theta is back-projection.




Q9. (math) The noise variance of FBP scales as \omega_c^3. By how much does the noise standard deviation grow if the cutoff is raised from 0.25 to 0.5 cycles per pixel?






Answer





Variance \times 2^3 = 8, standard deviation \times\sqrt8 \approx 2.8.

title: Exercise: filtered back-projection and sampling
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

filter a projection with a (truncated) ramp kernel by hand and explain the negative sidelobes,
explain why the filter is a ramp, why it amplifies noise, and what a tapered ramp trades,
use the angle rule N_\theta \approx \tfrac{\pi}{2}N and predict streaks,
predict the missing wedge of a limited tilt range and its effect on an object.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the two demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: filtered back-projection and sampling
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

filter a projection with a (truncated) ramp kernel by hand and explain the negative sidelobes,
explain why the filter is a ramp, why it amplifies noise, and what a tapered ramp trades,
use the angle rule N_\theta \approx \tfrac{\pi}{2}N and predict streaks,
predict the missing wedge of a limited tilt range and its effect on an object.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the two demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: filtered back-projection and sampling
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




FBP
filter every projection with a ramp, then back-project, times \pi/N_\theta


Ramp
multiplies the projection’s 1D spectrum by |\omega|; as a kernel (Ram–Lak): h[0] = \tfrac14, h[k] = -1/(\pi k)^2 for odd k, 0 for even k \ne 0


Taper
Shepp–Logan, cosine, Hann: multiply the ramp so it rolls off to 0 at the cutoff


Zero padding
extend each projection with zeros to at least twice its length before filtering by FFT


Angle rule
N detector bins need about \tfrac{\pi}{2}N angles over 180°


Missing wedge
a tilt range of \pm\alpha leaves a wedge of 180° - 2\alpha in the spectrum empty

title: Exercise: filtered back-projection and sampling
text:
By hand
B1. The truncated ramp kernel (-0.1,\ 0.25,\ -0.1). (a) Filter the box projection (0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0) (zeros outside). Where is the result largest, where negative? (b) Filter the wider box (0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0). What happens inside a wide object? (c) Explain in words how the negative values just outside the object remove the glow of plain back-projection.
B2. The full Ram–Lak kernel. (a) Compute h[0], h[1], h[2] and h[3]. (b) The sum of the kernel over |k| \le K is \tfrac14 - 2\sum_{k \text{ odd} \le K}\frac{1}{\pi^2k^2}. Compute it for K = 1 and K = 3. What is the limit, and why must it be so for a ramp? (c) Why is the three-tap kernel of B1 not quite right for a wide, flat object?
B3. The angle rule. (a) How many angles over 180° does a detector with 512 bins need? With 256? (b) A scan of a 256-bin detector uses 90 angles. What artefact do you expect, and where in the image is it strongest?
B4. An electron microscope records a tilt series from -60° to +60° in steps of 2°; the beam is vertical at 0° tilt. (a) How many images are recorded? Which sector of the 2D spectrum stays empty, and how wide is it? (b) The same with a range of \pm 70°.
B5. Same tilt series as B4. Sketch what a thin horizontal line and a thin vertical line look like after reconstruction. Which one suffers, and why? What happens to a disc?
B6. Noise. (a) The noise variance of FBP grows like the cube of the cutoff frequency. By what factor does the noise standard deviation change if you halve the cutoff? (b) By what factor does it change if you double the number of photons per ray (shot noise: the variance of a line integral is about 1/counts)? (c) Why is it expensive in dose to halve the pixel size?






Solutions





B1. (a) (0,\ -0.1,\ 0.15,\ 0.05,\ 0.15,\ -0.1,\ 0). Largest at the two edges of the box (0.15), smaller inside (0.05), negative just outside (−0.1). (b) (0,\ -0.1,\ 0.15,\ 0.05,\ 0.05,\ 0.05,\ 0.15,\ -0.1,\ 0): the interior is flat at 0.05; only the edges are emphasised. (c) Back-projected, the negative values make a negative band along both sides of each smear. Around the object the smears from all the other angles leave a positive glow there; the negative bands cancel it. Inside, the positive centre parts add up to the object’s value.
B2. (a) h[0] = 0.25, h[1] = -1/\pi^2 = -0.101, h[2] = 0, h[3] = -1/(9\pi^2) = -0.011. (b) K = 1: 0.25 - 0.203 = 0.047; K = 3: 0.25 - 0.225 = 0.025. The limit is 0 (with \sum_{\text{odd}} 1/k^2 = \pi^2/8). The ramp is 0 at frequency 0, so a constant input must give 0: the kernel must sum to 0. (c) The three taps sum to 0.05, not 0: every flat part keeps 0.05 times its value, a low-frequency error that the far-reaching small negative taps would remove. For a wide object that leftover is a slow bump in the reconstruction.
B3. (a) \tfrac{\pi}{2}\cdot 512 = 804, about 800 angles; for 256 bins about 400. (b) Far too few (about a quarter): streaks radiating from high-contrast edges, strongest around dense or bright structures and towards the edge of the field of view, where neighbouring spokes are farthest apart.
B4. (a) (60 - (-60))/2 + 1 = 61 images. The spokes cover 120°; a 60° wedge around the beam direction (the vertical frequency axis) stays empty. (b) 71 images; the empty wedge is 40° wide.
B5. The horizontal line suffers: its spectrum lies along the vertical frequency axis, inside the missing wedge, so it is smeared out along the beam (vertically) and loses contrast, or nearly vanishes. The vertical line’s spectrum lies along the horizontal axis, which is measured: it stays sharp. A disc is stretched along the beam and its top and bottom edges blur: a lemon.
B6. (a) Variance \times 1/8, standard deviation \times 1/\sqrt8 = 0.35 (2.8 times smaller). (b) Variance halves, standard deviation \times 1/\sqrt2 = 0.71. (c) Half the pixel size needs twice the cutoff frequency (8 times the variance) and each detector bin collects half the photons (another factor 2): 16 times the variance at the same dose, or 16 times the dose for the same noise.




Math questions
B7. (math) Derive FBP: write f(\mathbf x) = \iint F(\boldsymbol\omega)e^{2\pi i\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\mathbf x}d\boldsymbol\omega in polar coordinates \boldsymbol\omega = \omega\mathbf n_\theta with \omega \in \mathbb R, \theta \in [0, \pi), and use the Fourier slice theorem.
B8. (math) Derive the Ram–Lak kernel: h[k] = \int_{-1/2}^{1/2}|f|\,e^{2\pi ifk}\,df.
B9. (math) For the untapered ramp with cutoff \omega_c, compute \int_{-\omega_c}^{\omega_c}|\omega|^2\,d\omega. For the Hann taper W(\omega) = \tfrac12(1 + \cos(\pi\omega/\omega_c)), show that the integral is still proportional to \omega_c^3.
B10. (math) Derive the angle rule: the detector has N bins (spacing 1), so the spectrum is sampled out to |\omega| = \tfrac12 in steps of 1/N. Require the arc between neighbouring spokes at the outer ring to be at most one step.






Solutions (math)





B7. d\boldsymbol\omega = |\omega|\,d\omega\,d\theta (each point of the plane is covered once by \omega \in \mathbb R, \theta \in [0, \pi)). So f(\mathbf x) = \int_0^\pi\int F(\omega\mathbf n_\theta)|\omega|e^{2\pi i\omega\,\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf n_\theta}d\omega\,d\theta. By the slice theorem F(\omega\mathbf n_\theta) = P_\theta(\omega), so the inner integral is the inverse 1D Fourier transform of |\omega|P_\theta(\omega) evaluated at \rho = \mathbf x\cdot\mathbf n_\theta: the ramp-filtered projection q_\theta(\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf n_\theta). The outer integral is back-projection.
B8. |f| is even, so h[k] = 2\int_0^{1/2}f\cos(2\pi fk)\,df. For k = 0: 2 \cdot \tfrac18 = \tfrac14. For k \ne 0, integrate by parts: \int_0^{1/2}f\cos(af)df = \big[\tfrac{f\sin af}{a} + \tfrac{\cos af}{a^2}\big]_0^{1/2} with a = 2\pi k; \sin(\pi k) = 0, so h[k] = 2\,\frac{\cos(\pi k) - 1}{4\pi^2k^2} = \frac{(-1)^k - 1}{2\pi^2k^2}: -1/(\pi^2k^2) for odd k, 0 for even.
B9. \int_{-\omega_c}^{\omega_c}\omega^2d\omega = \tfrac23\omega_c^3. With \omega = \omega_c u: \int_{-\omega_c}^{\omega_c}\omega^2W(\omega)^2d\omega = \omega_c^3\int_{-1}^1 u^2\,\tfrac14(1 + \cos\pi u)^2du, a fixed number times \omega_c^3. Any taper that only scales with the cutoff gives the same cube law.
B10. Neighbouring spokes differ by \pi/N_\theta in angle; at radius \tfrac12 the arc between them is \tfrac{\pi}{2N_\theta}. Requiring \tfrac{\pi}{2N_\theta} \le \tfrac1N gives N_\theta \ge \tfrac{\pi}{2}N.

title: Exercise: filtered back-projection and sampling
text:
Explore: filters, dose and padding
The demo of the previous unit, now with the filters. Middle panel: the filter’s frequency response (red; dashed: the ideal |f|) and the current projection before (grey) and after (red) filtering, both scaled to height 1. Show filtered sinogram colours the filtered sinogram (red positive, blue negative). Photons per ray adds shot noise; the readout gives the RMSE against the phantom and the mean and standard deviation in a flat 8 \times 8 region (the noise).



E1. Preset one point: ramp cancels the star (16 angles). Describe the filtered projection in the lower plot. Press clear and add angles one by one: what does one filtered smear look like? Set angles in the scan to 180: what remains of the halo?
E2. Preset ramp: sharp. Read the RMSE and the flat-region values. Switch to none: what changes?
E3. Preset ramp, low dose: grain (1000 photons per ray). Read the noise (flat-region std) for ramp, Shepp–Logan, cosine and Hann. Rank the filters by noise and explain with the shape of their frequency responses.
E4. Still with the ramp, set the photons per ray to 10^4 and 10^5. How does the noise change per factor 10 in dose? Compare with B6.
E5. Hann filter at 1000 photons: lower the cutoff from 0.5 to 0.25. How do the noise and the RMSE change? What do you see in the image? Compare the noise ratio with the cube law.
E6. Preset forgot to pad (a large disc, no zero padding). Look at the reconstruction towards the rim of the disc. Tick zero padding. What was wrong, and why?






Solutions





E1. The filtered projection is a sharp positive peak with negative dips on both sides. One filtered smear is a bright stripe with dark (negative) borders. At the point all stripes add; around it the dark borders of each stripe cancel the bright tails of the others. With 180 angles the halo is gone: a clean point (RMSE 0.002). With 16 angles some star-shaped streaks remain far from the point.
E2. Ramp: RMSE 0.039, flat region mean 0.200 (the true value) with std 0.003. With none (plain back-projection) the image glows and its values are on a different scale (flat region mean 62.6): no RMSE is given.
E3. Noise std: ramp 0.048, Shepp–Logan 0.038, cosine 0.023, Hann 0.016. The ramp keeps all high frequencies; the Shepp–Logan taper lowers them a little, the cosine more, and Hann goes smoothly to 0 at the cutoff. The more a filter suppresses the high frequencies, where the noise is, the smoother the image, and the softer its edges (RMSE: ramp 0.059, Hann 0.075).
E4. 10^3: 0.048, 10^4: 0.017, 10^5: 0.005. Each factor 10 in dose divides the noise by about 3 (\sqrt{10} = 3.2): shot noise.
E5. Noise falls from 0.016 to 0.005 (ratio 3.2; the cube law predicts \sqrt8 = 2.8), but the RMSE rises from 0.075 to 0.116: the image is smooth but visibly blurred, the small ellipses smear out.
E6. Without padding the disc gets darker towards its rim (about 0.79 instead of 1 near the edge; the centre 0.98). The FFT filter is circular: the kernel’s negative tail reaching beyond one end of the projection wraps around to the other end, where the disc’s projection is large, and subtracts there. With zero padding the projection has room and the disc is flat.

title: Exercise: filtered back-projection and sampling
text:
Explore: how much data?
One phantom, reconstructed by FBP with the Hann filter. Sliders: number of angles, angular range (a tilt series from -range/2 to +range/2; at 180° the full half turn), detector bins (each bin integrates 1, 2 or 4 pixel widths) and photons per ray; with fixed total photons the photons are shared over the views (slider value × 180 photons per ray in total, e.g. 10^3 \times 180). Panels: reconstruction, error, and the spectrum of the reconstruction with the measured spokes in orange. The note under the angle slider gives the angle rule for the current detector.



E7. Preset enough angles (200). Read the RMSE. Then 18 angles: streaks. Where are the streaks, and how does the spectrum panel explain them? Find the number of angles below which you start to see streaks.
E8. Preset ±60°: missing wedge and ±60°: a disc becomes a lemon. Where is the empty sector in the spectrum? In which direction is the disc stretched? Compare with B4 and B5.
E9. Preset few bins: blur (32 bins). Compare the RMSE for 128, 64 and 32 bins. What does the angle rule say for 32 bins?
E10. Presets equal photons: many noisy views… and …or few clean ones. Compare the RMSE, then try 15 views. With a fixed photon budget, is it better to take many noisy views or few clean ones?






Solutions





E7. 200 angles: RMSE 0.074 (most of it is the Hann filter’s softening of the skull edge). 18 angles: 0.109, with streaks radiating from the bright skull out into the background. In the spectrum only 18 spokes are drawn; far from the centre the gaps between them are many frequency steps wide. Streaks become visible somewhere below about 90 angles and obvious below 45, although the RMSE barely changes until then (0.074 at 90, 0.075 at 45): RMSE is not a good judge of streaks.
E8. The empty sector is around the vertical axis of the spectrum (the beam direction, vertical at 0° tilt), 60° wide. The phantom and the disc are stretched vertically: the disc (diameter 61 pixels) comes out about 58 wide and 70 tall, with blurred top and bottom edges. RMSE 0.132 for the phantom, 0.233 for the disc.
E9. 128 bins: 0.074; 64: 0.126; 32: 0.164. Wide bins average the projection over 2 or 4 pixels: fine detail is lost before reconstruction, so the image is blurred. For 32 bins the angle rule asks only for about 51 angles: with fewer bins, fewer angles suffice.
E10. 180 views with 10^3 photons each: RMSE 0.075; 30 views with 6 \times 10^3 each: 0.083; 15 views with 1.2 \times 10^4: 0.128. With FBP, spreading the photons over many views wins: noise falls with the total number of photons either way, but streaks from too few views do not go away with more photons per view.

title: Exercise: filtered back-projection and sampling
text:
Where this leads
FBP needs many angles and enough photons, and it cannot use anything we know about the object. The next unit writes reconstruction as a linear system A\mathbf x = \mathbf b, solves it iteratively (ART, SIRT), and adds priors (non-negativity, total variation), which is how low-dose CT and electron tomography cope with few views and missing wedges.

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
text:
About this lecture
Dijkstra finds the cheapest path on the pixel graph. But the graph’s distances are not the distances of the plane: on a flat image the distance from a point grows in diamonds (4 neighbours) or octagons (8 neighbours), not circles.

The arrival time of a front that starts at a seed and moves with a given speed.
Fast marching: Dijkstra’s order, with a better update from two neighbours at once (Sethian, 1996).
One update by hand; why it approximates the Euclidean distance.
Costs from the image, and minimal paths by descending the arrival time.
How it relates to live-wire, geodesic active contours and watershed.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

This unit moved here from the level-set day (it closes this day’s arc: grid DP → polar DP → Dijkstra → fast marching). Prerequisites: Dijkstra (previous unit); the level set equation (previous day of this chain) is recalled on one slide; the Euclidean distance transform is owned by the morphology day.

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
section: Distances on the grid are not round
text:
Distances on the grid are not round

The same flat cost (1 per pixel of length), the same seed: lines of equal distance every 10 pixels.

4 neighbours: the city-block distance. At 45° a point 100 px away gets 141: 41% too far.
8 neighbours: steps of 1 and \sqrt2. Exact on the axes and diagonals, up to 8% too far in between (at 22.5°).
Fast marching: circles, within about 1–2% here.

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
section: The arrival time of a front
text:
The arrival time of a front
Light a fire at the seed. It spreads in every direction, with a speed that may depend on the place: fast on cheap pixels, slow on expensive ones.

T(x) = the time at which the fire reaches the point x. Lines of equal T are the successive fronts.
With speed 1 everywhere, T is the Euclidean distance from the seed: the fronts are circles.
With the speed low on edges, the fronts slow down there: T becomes a distance that “costs more” across edges.
Running time is a cost per unit of length: P = 1/\text{speed}. T is the cheapest total cost of a continuous path, measured along its length, not counted in pixel steps.

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
text:
The math: the Eikonal equation
Where the front passes x moving with speed F(x) > 0, it travels a distance F\,\Delta t in time \Delta t along the normal, so
|\nabla T(x)|\, F(x) = 1, \qquad \text{or}\qquad |\nabla T| = P,\quad P = 1/F, \qquad T = 0 \text{ at the seeds}.
This is the Eikonal equation. With P = 1 its solution is the Euclidean distance to the seeds (the distance transform of the morphology day, from the seed set). T(x) is also the minimal weighted length \min_\gamma \int_\gamma P\, ds over all curves \gamma from a seed to x.
Recall from the level-set day: a front moving with normal speed F is the zero level of \phi with \phi_t + F|\nabla\phi| = 0. When F never changes sign, each point is passed once, and \phi(x, t) = T(x) - t solves it: the arrival time is a level-set function that never needs to be updated in time.

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
section: Fast marching: Dijkstra with a better update
text:
Fast marching: Dijkstra with a better update
Keep everything of Dijkstra:

tentative values in a priority queue, the smallest is made final, then its neighbours are updated.

Change one thing, the update:

Dijkstra: d(v) = \min_u \big(d(u) + \text{cost}\big): the front arrives along one grid edge.
Fast marching: use the final neighbour along x and the final neighbour along y together, and solve for the time at which a straight front passing both would arrive. A front crossing the pixel diagonally is now seen as diagonal.

The values still only grow along the front, so “the smallest is final” still holds.

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
text:
The math: the upwind update
At pixel v (spacing 1), let a = the smaller final value of its left and right neighbours, b = the smaller final value of its upper and lower neighbours (∞ if none is final). Discretise T_x^2 + T_y^2 = P^2 with one-sided (“upwind”) differences towards the known side:
(T - a)^2 + (T - b)^2 = P^2, \qquad T \ge \max(a, b).
If |a - b| < P: \displaystyle T = \frac{a + b + \sqrt{2P^2 - (a - b)^2}}{2}. Otherwise (only one useful neighbour): T = \min(a, b) + P, which is Dijkstra’s update.
Each T is larger than both a and b, so values never decrease along the front, and Dijkstra’s argument gives the order. Work O(N \log N), as Dijkstra.

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
text:
One update by hand
A pixel with known neighbours T = 2 on its left and T = 2.5 above, flat cost P = 1:

Dijkstra (4 neighbours): \min(2, 2.5) + 1 = 3.
Fast marching: |2 - 2.5| = 0.5 < 1, so T = \big(4.5 + \sqrt{2 - 0.25}\big)/2 = 2.911.
With only the left neighbour known: 2 + 1 = 3; with 2 and 3.2: too far apart, again 3.

From a seed at (0, 0): T(1, 0) = T(0, 1) = 1, then T(1, 1) = \big(2 + \sqrt 2\big)/2 = 1.707, against \sqrt2 = 1.414 exactly and 2 for 4-neighbour Dijkstra. Next to a point seed the first-order update is crude; implementations set the pixels within a few pixels of the seed to their exact distance first (the demo uses 3 px). Far from the seed the error is small.

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
section: Try it: fronts on a grid
text:
Try it: fronts on a grid




Left: fast marching, right: Dijkstra on 4 or 8 neighbours, same cost P and same seeds; colour = arrival time, white lines = fronts at equal time steps. Click places a target (or a seed, after “add seed”); orange = gradient descent on T, blue = Dijkstra’s pixel path. Tour: “flat cost”: circles against diamonds. “Dijkstra 4-nbr vs fast marching”: from the bottom-left to the top-right: T = 277.3 for a straight line of 275.8, Dijkstra 390.0 (city block); with 8 neighbours 275.8 on the exact diagonal. “two seeds”: the fronts meet on the perpendicular bisector (a Voronoi boundary). “neurite”: cost low on bright lines: the path follows the neurite. “edge cost”: P = 1 + (|∇I|/k)², the fronts slow down and bunch up at the nucleus boundary.

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
text:
Costs from the image
As for live-wire, the cost P comes from the image:

Slow at edges: P = 1/g with the edge-stopping function g = 1/\big(1 + (|\nabla I|/k)^2\big) of the level-set day: P \approx 1 in flat regions and large on strong edges. A front from a seed inside a nucleus fills it quickly and then stalls at its boundary.
Fast along lines: P small on a bright thin structure (a neurite, a vessel): the front runs along it, and T measures the cost along the structure.
k (contrast) sets which edges count, like \sigma in the contrast weights of the graph-cut day.

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
section: Minimal paths: descend the arrival time
text:
Minimal paths: descend the arrival time
T has a single minimum, at the seeds, and no other local minima. So from any target:

Gradient descent on T (small steps against \nabla T) runs down to a seed. The curve it traces is the minimal path, at sub-pixel precision, not restricted to grid steps.
Dijkstra’s path follows the pointers: grid steps only, so a straight line at 30° becomes a staircase, longer than the line.

Same principle as before: compute the “table” (T) once, then read off any path by backtracking.

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
text:
Three relatives









path
optimum




Live-wire (previous unit)
discrete, on the pixel graph
global (for its graph)


Fast marching + descent (today)
continuous
global (up to the discretisation)


Geodesic active contours (level-set day)
continuous
local, from a starting curve



The geodesic active contour minimises the same kind of weighted length \int g\, ds, but by moving a curve downhill: it can stop in a local minimum. Fast marching computes the global minimal path between two points directly, as live-wire does on the grid.

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
text:
Fronts, flooding and watershed
Recall from the watershed day: flooding from markers also processes pixels in the order of a priority queue, and the basins meet at the watershed lines.

Fast marching with several seeds: each pixel is reached first by one seed’s front; the fronts meet where the arrival times from two seeds are equal (with P = 1, the perpendicular bisector: a Voronoi diagram).
Watershed flooding uses the maximum height along the way, not the accumulated time; its basins meet at the ridges of the image.
Same machinery, different “cost of a path”: sum (Dijkstra, live-wire), integral of P (fast marching), maximum (watershed).

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
text:
Summary

Dijkstra’s grid distances are blocky: diamonds with 4 neighbours, octagons with 8.
The arrival time T of a front with speed 1/P solves |\nabla T| = P; with P = 1 it is the Euclidean distance.
Fast marching = Dijkstra’s order + the upwind update from the smaller known neighbour along x and along y; O(N\log N); nearly round fronts.
Costs from the image (slow at edges, fast along lines); minimal paths by gradient descent on T, at sub-pixel precision.
The day’s arc: DP table (fixed order) → polar DP (closed curves) → Dijkstra (order found on the fly) → fast marching (continuous fronts).

title: Quiz: information, entropy and entropy codes
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Information I = -\log_2 p, entropy H = -\sum_k p_k \log_2 p_k bits per symbol.

Q1. An 8-bit image uses all 256 grey levels equally often. What is its entropy, and how much can an entropy coder save?






Hint





What is H for a flat histogram of K values?









Answer





H = \log_2 256 = 8 bits per pixel, exactly what the raw image uses: an entropy coder that treats pixels independently saves nothing. Only a method that uses the neighbours (prediction, transforms) can help, and only if the neighbours are related.




Q2. Which carries more information: a grey level that occurs in 50% of the pixels, or one that occurs in 1%? By how much?






Hint





-\log_2 0.5 and -\log_2 0.01.









Answer





The rare one: -\log_2 0.01 = 6.64 bits against -\log_2 0.5 = 1 bit, 5.64 bits more. A good code therefore gives the common grey level a short code word and the rare one a long one.




Q3. You shuffle the pixels of a micrograph at random. What happens to the entropy of its grey-level histogram? And to the size of a file compressed with a method that looks at neighbouring pixels?






Hint





Does shuffling change the histogram?









Answer





The entropy stays exactly the same: the histogram does not change. The compressed file grows, because neighbouring pixels are no longer alike (in the lecture’s example from 44 457 to 58 519 bytes). The histogram entropy is a lower bound only for coding pixels independently; neighbours carry extra structure that it ignores.




Q4. Is the code {A = 0, B = 01, C = 11} prefix-free? Can the bit string 011 be decoded uniquely?






Hint





Is any code word the beginning of another?









Answer





No: 0 (A) is the beginning of 01 (B). Here 011 can only be read as A C (0 11), because 01 followed by 1 leaves an incomplete word; but the decoder has to look ahead to see that: after the first 0 it cannot tell an A from the start of a B. With a prefix-free code (every symbol a leaf of the tree) each symbol is known as soon as its last bit arrives.




Q5. In a Huffman code, why is the code word of the most probable symbol never longer than that of a less probable symbol?






Hint





Which symbols are merged first, and what does each merge add to their code words?









Answer





Every merge adds one bit to all code words below it. The least probable trees are merged first, so their symbols take part in the most merges and get the longest code words; the most probable symbol joins late and gets a short one. If a more probable symbol had a longer word, swapping the two words would lower \bar L, so the code would not be optimal.




Q6. A binary mask has 99% background pixels. Its entropy is 0.08 bits per pixel. What is the best a Huffman code on single pixels can do, and what would you use instead?






Hint





How short can a code word be?









Answer





1 bit per pixel: each pixel needs a code word of at least one bit, more than 12 times the entropy. Better: run-length coding (code the lengths of the long background runs), Huffman on blocks of pixels, or arithmetic coding, which spends about -\log_2 0.99 = 0.015 bits on a background pixel.




Q7. Name the three redundancies of an image and say which kind of codec removes each.






Hint





Coding, between pixels, and what the eye does not need.









Answer





Coding redundancy (all values get the same number of bits): removed by entropy codes such as Huffman or arithmetic coding. Inter-pixel redundancy (neighbours are alike): removed by prediction, transforms or dictionary methods. Psychovisual redundancy (detail the eye does not see): removed by quantisation. Lossless codecs remove only the first two; only lossy codecs remove the third.




Q8. (math) Show that for two symbols with probabilities p and 1 - p the entropy is largest at p = \tfrac12. What is its value there?






Hint





Differentiate h(p) = -p \log_2 p - (1-p)\log_2(1-p).









Answer





h'(p) = -\log_2 p - \frac{1}{\ln 2} + \log_2(1 - p) + \frac{1}{\ln 2} = \log_2 \frac{1-p}{p}, zero at p = \tfrac12; h''(p) = -\frac{1}{\ln 2}\big(\frac1p + \frac1{1-p}\big) < 0, so it is a maximum: h(\tfrac12) = 1 bit.

title: Exercise: information, entropy and entropy codes
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute the information of an outcome and the entropy of a histogram by hand,
say what entropy measures and what it ignores (neighbours),
run-length encode a binary row,
build a Huffman code by hand, check that it is prefix-free, and compare its average length with the entropy,
explain why a Huffman code needs at least one bit per symbol and how arithmetic coding gets around that.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: information, entropy and entropy codes
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute the information of an outcome and the entropy of a histogram by hand,
say what entropy measures and what it ignores (neighbours),
run-length encode a binary row,
build a Huffman code by hand, check that it is prefix-free, and compare its average length with the entropy,
explain why a Huffman code needs at least one bit per symbol and how arithmetic coding gets around that.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: information, entropy and entropy codes
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Information
I = -\log_2 p bits for an outcome of probability p


Entropy
H = -\sum_k p_k \log_2 p_k, the average information per symbol


Bounds
0 \le H \le \log_2 K for K symbols; flat histogram: \log_2 K; constant: 0


Shannon
no lossless code of independent symbols averages fewer than H bits per symbol


Fixed-length code
\lceil \log_2 K \rceil bits per symbol


Run-length coding
runs of equal values as (value, length)


Huffman
merge the two least probable trees until one is left; 0/1 on the branches


Prefix-free
no code word is the beginning of another: decoding needs no separators


Average length
\bar L = \sum_k p_k L_k; Huffman: H \le \bar L < H + 1


Arithmetic coding
the message narrows [0, 1) to width \prod p: about \sum I bits in total



Useful values: \log_2 3 = 1.585, \log_2 5 = 2.322, \log_2 10 = 3.322.

title: Exercise: information, entropy and entropy codes
text:
By hand
B1. How many bits of information are in: (a) heads of a fair coin, (b) a six on a fair die, (c) one grey level drawn from 256 equally likely ones, (d) a background pixel that is white with probability 0.9, (e) the rare case that it is not white? Which of (d) and (e) should get the shorter code word?
B2. A source has five symbols A–E with p = (0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1). (a) Compute H. (b) How many bits per symbol does a fixed-length code need?
B3. Build a Huffman code for the source of B2. When two trees have the same probability, take the one that was created first (leaves before merged trees). (a) Draw the tree, write the code word of each symbol and check that the code is prefix-free. (b) Compute \bar L and compare with H and the fixed-length code. (c) Encode the message CAD and decode the bit string 0011100 (with your code).
B4. Build the Huffman tree of B2 again, but now among equal probabilities take the tree created last. (a) Give the code lengths and \bar L. (b) Both codes are optimal. Which one has the larger spread of code lengths? For the 16-symbol message CCADACAACDAAABAB, how many bits does each code need?
B5. Run-length encode the binary row 0000000111100000 as (value, run) pairs and as plain run lengths starting with a run of zeros. What happens to the row 0101010101010101?
B6. A 4 × 4 image has the rows 10 10 20 20, 10 10 20 20, 30 30 40 40, 30 30 40 40. (a) Compute the entropy of its grey-level histogram. (b) Now shuffle the 16 pixels randomly. What is the entropy of the shuffled image? Which of the two images is easier to describe in words, and why does H not show it?
B7. A binary mask is 95% background (0) and 5% object (1). (a) Compute H and the average Huffman code length per pixel. Why can Huffman not do better? (b) Suggest two ways to get below 1 bit per pixel.
B8. Arithmetic coding with p(A) = 0.6, p(B) = 0.3, p(C) = 0.1 (in this order on [0, 1)). Narrow the interval for the message AAB step by step. How wide is the final interval, and about how many bits are needed? Compare with a Huffman code for the same three symbols.






Solutions





B1. (a) -\log_2 \tfrac12 = 1 bit. (b) \log_2 6 = 2.585 bits. (c) \log_2 256 = 8 bits. (d) -\log_2 0.9 = 0.152 bits. (e) -\log_2 0.1 = 3.32 bits. The common outcome (d) should get the short code word: it carries little information.
B2. (a) H = 0.4 \cdot 1.322 + 2 \cdot 0.2 \cdot 2.322 + 2 \cdot 0.1 \cdot 3.322 = 0.529 + 0.929 + 0.664 = 2.122 bits. (b) 5 symbols need \lceil \log_2 5 \rceil = 3 bits.
B3. (a) Merge D + E (0.2). Now B, C and DE all have 0.2: take B and C (created first): BC (0.4). Now DE (0.2) is the smallest, then A and BC tie at 0.4: take A (a leaf, created first): A–DE (0.6). Finally BC + A–DE (1.0). With 0 for the first tree taken in each merge: B = 00, C = 01, D = 100, E = 101, A = 11. No code word begins another one: prefix-free. (b) \bar L = 0.4 \cdot 2 + 0.2 \cdot 2 + 0.2 \cdot 2 + 0.1 \cdot 3 + 0.1 \cdot 3 = 2.2 bits: H = 2.122 \le 2.2 < 3. (c) CAD → 01 11 100 = 0111100. 0011100 → 00 B, 11 A, 100 D: BAD. (A different 0/1 assignment gives different code words but the same lengths; that is fine.)
B4. (a) After D + E, take the newest tree DE together with C (newer than B): CDE (0.4). Then B (0.2) with the newest 0.4-tree, CDE: BCDE (0.6). Then A + BCDE. Lengths A 1, B 2, C 3, D 4, E 4; \bar L = 0.4 + 0.4 + 0.6 + 0.4 + 0.4 = 2.2 bits, the same. (b) The second code has the larger spread (lengths 1 to 4; variance of the length 1.36 against 0.16). The message has 8 A, 2 B, 4 C, 2 D: the first code needs 8 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 2 + 4 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 3 = 34 bits, the second 8 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 2 + 4 \cdot 3 + 2 \cdot 4 = 32 bits. On average over many messages they are equal; on one message either can win.
B5. (0, 7) (1, 4) (0, 5), or run lengths 7 4 5: three numbers instead of 16 bits. The alternating row has 16 runs of length 1: 16 numbers, more than the 16 bits of the row itself. RLE helps only when runs are long.
B6. (a) Four grey levels, 4 pixels each: H = \log_2 4 = 2 bits/pixel. (b) Still 2 bits: shuffling does not change the histogram. The original is “four 2 × 2 squares”, a very short description; the shuffled image has no such structure. H of the histogram treats the pixels as independent and does not see the neighbours.
B7. (a) H = -0.95 \log_2 0.95 - 0.05 \log_2 0.05 = 0.070 + 0.216 = 0.286 bits. Huffman gives the two symbols the code words 0 and 1: \bar L = 1 bit, 3.5 times H. A Huffman code gives every symbol a whole number of bits, at least 1. (b) Run-length coding (code the lengths of the long background runs), coding blocks of several pixels as one symbol (e.g. 4 pixels: 16 symbols, and the all-background block gets a short code), or arithmetic coding, which spends -\log_2 0.95 = 0.074 bits on a background pixel.
B8. Start [0, 1): A = [0, 0.6), B = [0.6, 0.9), C = [0.9, 1). After A: [0, 0.6). After A again: [0, 0.36). After B: the B part of [0, 0.36) is [0.216, 0.324), width 0.108 = 0.6 \cdot 0.6 \cdot 0.3. About -\log_2 0.108 = 3.21 bits = 2 \cdot 0.737 + 1.737 (the information of the three symbols). A Huffman code for p = (0.6, 0.3, 0.1) has lengths 1, 2, 2: AAB costs 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 bits. (Over long messages Huffman averages 1.4 bits per symbol here, arithmetic coding approaches H = 1.295.)




Math questions
B9. (math) Show that H \le \log_2 K for a histogram of K symbols, with equality only for the flat histogram. (Hint: Jensen’s inequality for the concave \log, or Gibbs’ inequality with q_k = 1/K.)
B10. (math) (a) Prove the Kraft inequality \sum_k 2^{-L_k} \le 1 for the code word lengths of a prefix code. (b) Using Gibbs’ inequality -\sum_k p_k \log_2 q_k \ge -\sum_k p_k \log_2 p_k, show that every prefix code has \bar L \ge H.
B11. (math) Show that the lengths L_k = \lceil -\log_2 p_k \rceil satisfy the Kraft inequality, and that their average is below H + 1. Why does this prove \bar L < H + 1 for the Huffman code?
B12. (math) When is \bar L = H for a Huffman code? Show that it happens for p = (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac1{16}, \tfrac1{16}).






Solutions (math)





B9. H = \sum_k p_k \log_2 \frac{1}{p_k} \le \log_2 \sum_k p_k \frac{1}{p_k} = \log_2 K by Jensen (the sum runs over the K symbols with p_k > 0, at most K of them). Equality in Jensen needs 1/p_k constant, i.e. the flat histogram. With Gibbs: H \le -\sum_k p_k \log_2 \frac1K = \log_2 K, equality iff p = q.
B10. (a) Let L = \max_k L_k. A code word of length L_k is the start of exactly 2^{L - L_k} of the 2^L binary words of length L. For a prefix code these sets are disjoint (if two overlapped, one code word would start the other), so \sum_k 2^{L - L_k} \le 2^L. (b) Let S = \sum_j 2^{-L_j} \le 1 and q_k = 2^{-L_k}/S. Then \bar L = \sum_k p_k L_k = -\sum_k p_k \log_2 (q_k S) = -\sum_k p_k \log_2 q_k - \log_2 S \ge H - \log_2 S \ge H.
B11. L_k \ge -\log_2 p_k gives 2^{-L_k} \le p_k, so \sum_k 2^{-L_k} \le \sum_k p_k = 1: a prefix code with these lengths exists. L_k < -\log_2 p_k + 1, so \sum_k p_k L_k < H + 1. The Huffman code has the smallest average length of all prefix codes, so its \bar L is at most that of this code, hence < H + 1.
B12. By B10 equality needs S = 1 and q_k = p_k, i.e. p_k = 2^{-L_k}: every probability a power of \tfrac12 (dyadic). For p = (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac1{16}, \tfrac1{16}) Huffman merges the two sixteenths, then \tfrac18 with \tfrac18, and so on: lengths 1, 2, 3, 4, 4 = -\log_2 p_k, and \bar L = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12 + \tfrac38 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac14 = 1.875 = H.

title: Exercise: information, entropy and entropy codes
text:
Explore: build a Huffman code
The demo shows a histogram of up to 12 symbols (drag a bar to change its count; + and − add or remove a symbol), the Huffman tree, the code table with p, the information -\log_2 p, the code word and its length, and bars comparing the entropy H, the Huffman average length \bar L and the fixed-length code. next merge adds one merge: the two lightest trees (green, dashed) become one (orange). build all finishes the tree, restart removes all merges. ties chooses which tree is taken first among equal counts. Below, a 16-symbol message drawn from the histogram is encoded with the code (code words in alternating colours) and decoded by walking the tree; new message draws another one.



E1. Preset worked example (counts 8, 4, 4, 2, 2). Press next merge four times and compare each merge with your tree from B3. Then switch ties to newer first and compare with B4. Do the code lengths and \bar L match?
E2. Preset flat: no gain and preset dyadic: L = H. Note H, \bar L and the fixed-length code for both. Why is there nothing to gain in the first, and why is \bar L exactly H in the second?
E3. Preset one dominant symbol and preset binary mask. Note H and \bar L. How far is \bar L above H in each case? Relate it to B7.
E4. Preset prediction residuals: the histogram of the differences between neighbouring pixels of a smooth image (next unit), and preset cell grey levels: the grey levels of the cell micrograph in 12 bins. Compare H, \bar L and the fixed length for the two. Then try both tie rules on the residuals: what changes, and what does not?
E5. Start from worked example, remove one symbol with − and drag the bars to make counts 8, 4, 2, 2. Predict H and the code lengths before you look. Then make a two-symbol histogram where H is about 0.5 bits: what is \bar L?
E6. Back to worked example with older first. Read the 16-symbol message and its bit count. Count the symbols in the message and check the bit count with the code table. Switch to newer first: why does the same message now need a different number of bits although \bar L is the same?






Solutions





E1. Older first: D + E (4), B + C (8), DE + A (12), then the root (20); lengths 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, \bar L = 2.200. Newer first: D + E, then C with DE (8), then B with CDE (12), then A: lengths 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, also \bar L = 2.200. Both match B3 and B4 (H = 2.122, fixed 3 bits).
E2. Flat (8 symbols of count 5): H = \bar L = 3 = fixed length. Every symbol is equally likely, so no symbol deserves a shorter word. Dyadic (16, 8, 4, 2, 2, i.e. p = \tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac1{16}, \tfrac1{16}): H = \bar L = 1.875 bits against 3 fixed: every -\log_2 p is a whole number, and Huffman uses exactly those lengths (B12).
E3. One dominant symbol (p = 0.9, 0.05, 0.025, 0.025): H = 0.619, \bar L = 1.150, 0.53 bits above H (almost twice H). Binary mask (47 : 3, p = 0.94): H = 0.327, \bar L = 1, three times H. In both a single symbol has p \gg 0.5 but cannot get a code word shorter than 1 bit. This is the gap of B7; run lengths or arithmetic coding close it.
E4. Residuals: H = 3.237, \bar L = 3.288, fixed 4 bits. Cell grey levels: H = 3.279, \bar L = 3.323, fixed 4. Both are close to H (within 0.05 bits): with many symbols and no very large p, Huffman is nearly ideal. With the other tie rule the residual code lengths change (e.g. the 0 residual gets 2 bits instead of 3 and the extreme ones 6 instead of 5), but \bar L stays 3.288. (Remember the residuals here are only the central part of the histogram; the next unit computes the full entropy of the residuals.)
E5. p = (0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125) is dyadic: H = \bar L = 1.75, lengths 1, 2, 3, 3. A two-symbol histogram always gets \bar L = 1; H \approx 0.5 for p \approx 0.89 : 0.11 (e.g. counts 9 : 1 give H = 0.469, counts 8 : 1 give 0.503). One bit per symbol is twice the entropy.
E6. The message is CCADACAACDAAABAB with 34 bits (fixed code: 48): it has 8 A, 2 B, 4 C, 2 D, so 8 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 2 + 4 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 3 = 34. With newer first the same message needs 32 bits (8 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 2 + 4 \cdot 3 + 2 \cdot 4). \bar L is an average over the probabilities; this message has more A (8 of 16 = 0.5 instead of 0.4) and no E, and the second code favours A. (B4 again.)

title: Exercise: information, entropy and entropy codes
text:
Where this leads
Entropy is the yardstick for the rest of the day: the next unit, prediction, turns an image into residuals whose histogram has a much smaller entropy; the DCT unit does the same with a change of basis; JPEG ends with exactly the Huffman coding built here, with run lengths of zeros. Entropy also comes back outside compression: information gain in decision trees (random forests), texture entropy (measurements) and the cross-entropy loss of neural networks.

title: Endmembers: the geometry of mixtures
text:
About this lecture
Least squares (last unit) needs the spectra in advance and allows negative abundances. Both problems have a picture: the pixels form a cloud in channel space, and every physically possible mixture lies in a cone.

Pixels as points; the cone, and the simplex after normalising.
Constraints: non-negative (NNLS) and sum to one, and what they cost.
How many components? The singular values of the pixels.
Finding the spectra: vertices of the simplex, and NMF, with its non-uniqueness.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Third unit of the spectral unmixing day, the densest one. The cone/simplex geometry is needed for the vertex methods anyway. Recall PCA (day 1, pca/) in one slide; KKT conditions and the NMF update stay in the math layer.

title: Endmembers: the geometry of mixtures
text:
Pixels live in a cone


Every pixel is a point in channel space (3 channels: a point in 3D).

One unit of dye k lands at its spectrum \mathbf m_k. Mixtures a_1\mathbf m_1 + a_2\mathbf m_2 + \dots with non-negative amounts fill the cone spanned by the spectra.
Pure pixels lie on the cone’s edges; dim pixels near the origin; mixtures inside.
Without noise, every pixel is inside the cone. The cone is the set of physically possible pixels.

title: Endmembers: the geometry of mixtures
section: Normalise: the cone becomes a simplex
text:
Normalise: the cone becomes a simplex
Divide every pixel by its total (sum over channels): brightness disappears, only the colour of the spectrum remains.

Every ray of the cone becomes one point: the cone becomes a simplex, a triangle for three components (a segment for two, a tetrahedron for four).
A mixture lies inside the triangle; its position gives the fractions of the components (barycentric coordinates).
Same picture as the chromaticity diagram of the colour day: mixtures of two lights lie on the straight line between them.

title: Endmembers: the geometry of mixtures
text:
The math: cone and simplex
\text{cone}(M) = \{M\mathbf a : \mathbf a \ge 0\}, \qquad \text{simplex} = \{M\mathbf a : \mathbf a \ge 0,\ \textstyle\sum_k a_k = 1\}.

If every column is scaled to sum 1 (fractions of the light), then \sum_c (M\mathbf a)_c = \sum_k a_k: normalising a pixel by its total is the same as asking the abundances to sum to one.
Barycentric coordinates: for vertices \mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \mathbf e_3 and a point \mathbf p in the triangle, solve \sum_k a_k \mathbf e_k = \mathbf p, \sum_k a_k = 1.

title: Endmembers: the geometry of mixtures
section: Try it: the cloud, the cone and the triangle
text:
Try it: the cloud, the cone and the triangle




Three channels, three components of the day’s cell (nucleus, mitochondria, membrane); drag the cloud to rotate. Tour: “noise-free”: every point inside the cone (grey faces), the three arms are the pure structures. “Noise: LS goes negative”: a dim pixel is picked automatically; LS (red) reaches it exactly but with a negative abundance, NNLS (orange) lands on a face. “Normalise”: the cone collapses onto the triangle; the right panel is the same triangle flat. Dim pixels scatter far: little light, much noise. “A wrong endmember”: the membrane corner is dragged inward; real membrane pixels fall outside, and the constrained methods hide it (the residual readout grows). “Fourth component”: granules with a spectrum outside the triangle: a fourth corner.

title: Endmembers: the geometry of mixtures
text:
Noise pushes pixels outside: NNLS
A dim pixel with noise can land outside the cone. Unconstrained least squares then reports a negative abundance.

Two channels, spectra (1, 0.2) and (0.3, 1), pixel (0.1, 0.9), just outside: LS gives (-0.18,\ 0.94).
NNLS (non-negative least squares) takes the closest point in the cone. Here it lies on the edge of spectrum 2: (0,\ 0.85).
The projection lands on a face or an edge; the components “behind” it get exactly zero. The active-set method (Lawson & Hanson) guesses which components are zero, solves least squares for the rest, and repairs the guess until no component wants to go negative or come back.

title: Endmembers: the geometry of mixtures
section: The math: NNLS and its optimality conditions
text:
The math: NNLS and its optimality conditions
\min_{\mathbf a}\ \|\mathbf y - M\mathbf a\|^2 \quad\text{subject to}\quad \mathbf a \ge 0 .
A convex quadratic programme. With \mathbf w = M^\top(\mathbf y - M\mathbf a) (minus half the gradient), \hat{\mathbf a} is optimal if and only if (KKT):
\hat a_k \ge 0, \qquad w_k \le 0, \qquad \hat a_k\, w_k = 0 \quad\text{for every } k.

A component in use (\hat a_k > 0) has zero gradient; a component at zero (\hat a_k = 0) would make the error worse if increased (w_k \le 0).
Example above: \hat{\mathbf a} = (0, 0.853), \mathbf w = (-0.147,\ 0). Both conditions hold.

title: Endmembers: the geometry of mixtures
section: Sum to one, and the price of constraints
text:
Sum to one, and the price of constraints
Fully constrained least squares: non-negative and summing to one: the closest point in the simplex (for normalised pixels, or fractions).

Honest costs: in dim regions the noise is clipped at zero from below but not from above: a positive bias (the mean of a clipped noisy zero is above zero).
A wrong endmember puts real pixels outside the simplex, and the constraint projects them back in silence: the error moves into the residual, not into a negative abundance. Always look at the residual.

title: Endmembers: the geometry of mixtures
text:
The math: the sum-to-one constraint
Without the sign constraint, minimise \|\mathbf y - M\mathbf a\|^2 subject to \mathbf 1^\top\mathbf a = 1 with a Lagrange multiplier:
\hat{\mathbf a} = \hat{\mathbf a}_\text{LS} + (M^\top M)^{-1}\mathbf 1\ \frac{1 - \mathbf 1^\top\hat{\mathbf a}_\text{LS}}{\mathbf 1^\top(M^\top M)^{-1}\mathbf 1}.

Both constraints together (Heinz & Chang): add a row \delta(1, \dots, 1) to M and the value \delta to \mathbf y, with \delta large, and solve NNLS. The extra row is an “equation” that must hold almost exactly.

title: Endmembers: the geometry of mixtures
text:
What unmixing is not

Clustering (k-means on pixel colours, the colour day; Gaussian mixtures): each pixel belongs to one class. Unmixing: each pixel is a mixture, how much of each. Different questions about the same cloud.
Non-linear mixing: quenching, energy transfer (FRET), absorption inside the sample, saturated pixels: the cloud bends and straight edges no longer fit.
Neighbouring pixels have similar abundances: a spatial prior (a smoothness term, as in the Ising/MRF elective) can stabilise noisy maps. Not covered here.

title: Endmembers: the geometry of mixtures
text:
How many components?
Best case: reference spectra from single-stained controls (the crosstalk unit). Often not possible: spectra shift inside cells, autofluorescence is unknown, a remote-sensing scene’s materials are unknown.

First question: how many components? Stack the pixels as the columns of Y (channels × pixels) and take its singular values (PCA without centring, recall the PCA unit of day 1).
K components without noise: exactly K non-zero singular values. With noise: K stand out above a floor.
The day’s cell, 16 channels, 4 components: \sigma_i/\sigma_1 = 1,\ 0.65,\ 0.51,\ 0.12,\ 0.070,\ 0.066, \dots: four above the floor (the fourth, the dim autofluorescence, only just).

title: Endmembers: the geometry of mixtures
text:
PCA axes are not spectra

The principal axes are orthogonal and have negative entries; spectra are neither.
A triangle-shaped cloud: its principal axes point along its spread, its corners point at the pure components. Only the corners are spectra.
PCA tells you how many and the subspace (the plane of the triangle); finding the spectra needs more: the corners, or non-negativity.

title: Endmembers: the geometry of mixtures
section: Pure pixels: the vertices are the spectra
text:
Pure pixels: the vertices are the spectra
If some pixels contain only one component, they are the corners (vertices) of the normalised cloud.

Vertex finding (the idea behind VCA): take the most extreme pixel, project it out, repeat. Each step finds one corner.
N-FINDR: the K pixels that span the simplex of largest volume.
No pure pixels: the cloud’s corners lie inside the true simplex, and vertex methods undershoot: found spectra are mixtures. In the demo: 3–5° from the true spectra with pure pixels, 7–11° without.
Macenko’s stain estimate (next unit) is the two-component case.

title: Endmembers: the geometry of mixtures
section: The math: volume and the best rank-K approximation
text:
The math: volume and the best rank-K approximation

Simplex volume: for K vertices \mathbf e_k in K-1 dimensions, V = \frac{1}{(K-1)!}\left|\det\begin{pmatrix} 1 & \cdots & 1 \\ \mathbf e_1 & \cdots & \mathbf e_K \end{pmatrix}\right|. N-FINDR swaps pixels in and out to maximise it.
Eckart–Young: the truncated SVD U_K\Sigma_K V_K^\top is the best rank-K approximation of Y in the Frobenius norm. Projecting the pixels onto the first K left singular vectors removes the noise outside the signal space before looking for vertices.

title: Endmembers: the geometry of mixtures
text:
Try it: finding the spectra




The same cell, 16 channels, Poisson noise. Top left: singular values (log scale). Bottom left: the normalised bright pixels projected onto their two main principal directions, true spectra as circles, found ones as squares. Right: true (dashed) and found spectra, the found abundance maps. Tour: “count the components”: four bars above the floor; the PCA axes as spectra have negative lobes. “Pure pixels”: three steps of vertex finding land on the corners (angles 4.5°, 3.8°, 2.6°). “No pure pixels”: the cloud shrinks to three clusters inside the true triangle; vertex finding returns mixtures (11°, 7°, 10°). “NMF from two seeds”: seed 1, then seed 2: different spectra, same error. “Three spectra known”: the fourth still has dips at the known dyes’ peaks.

title: Endmembers: the geometry of mixtures
text:
NMF: factorise without pure pixels
Non-negative matrix factorisation: Y \approx WH with both W (spectra, channels × K) and H (abundances, K × pixels) non-negative.

Start from a seeded positive guess; alternately improve H and W with multiplicative updates. The error never increases.
Not unique: any cone that contains all the data and lies inside the positive orthant fits equally well. Without pure pixels, two seeds give two answers with the same error (demo: 3.195 and 3.201, the true spectra give 3.199; seed 1 lands 4.5°, 3.2°, 9.1° from the true spectra, seed 2 10.2°, 7.4°, 8.9°).
Remedies: pure pixels, smallest volume, sparse abundances, known spectra. Even with three of four spectra known, a broad fourth one is found only up to “minus a bit of the known ones” (dips at their peaks).

title: Endmembers: the geometry of mixtures
text:
The math: the NMF updates
Minimise \|Y - WH\|_F^2 over W, H \ge 0. Lee & Seung’s multiplicative updates (element-wise \odot, \oslash):
H \leftarrow H \odot (W^\top Y) \oslash (W^\top W H), \qquad W \leftarrow W \odot (Y H^\top) \oslash (W H H^\top).

Gradient descent with a step chosen per entry, \eta = H \oslash (W^\top W H): non-negative stays non-negative, and the error never increases.
Non-uniqueness: WH = (WR^{-1})(RH) for any invertible R that keeps both factors non-negative (scalings and permutations always do; others sometimes).
With Poisson noise, the Kullback–Leibler version of NMF is the maximum-likelihood estimate (pointer).

title: Endmembers: the geometry of mixtures
text:
Validation without ground truth

The residual at the noise level everywhere (unit 2).
Non-negativity: abundances clearly below zero mean the model or the spectra are wrong.
Agreement with a control: a found spectrum should match a single-stained control where one exists.
Stability: the same answer from different seeds, subsets of the image, or neighbouring numbers of components.

title: Endmembers: the geometry of mixtures
text:
Summary

Pixels form a cloud; without noise it lies in the cone of the spectra; normalised, in their simplex.
Noise pushes dim pixels outside: LS goes negative; NNLS projects onto the cone (components behind the face get zero); fully constrained onto the simplex. Costs: a positive bias, and wrong endmembers hidden in the residual.
How many components: singular values above the noise floor. PCA axes are not spectra.
Pure pixels: spectra = vertices (vertex finding, largest simplex). No pure pixels: vertex methods undershoot.
NMF needs no pure pixels but is not unique; constrain it, and validate with residual, signs and controls.

title: Quiz: fitting a mixture with EM
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. E-step: responsibilities r_{ik}; M-step: N_k = \sum_i r_{ik}, \pi_k = N_k/n, weighted means and covariances.

Q1. In one sentence each: what does the E-step compute, and what does the M-step compute?






Hint





One step uses the parameters to get labels, the other the labels to get parameters.









Answer





E-step: with the current parameters, the responsibility of every component for every point (soft labels, by Bayes’ rule). M-step: with these responsibilities as weights, new weights \pi_k, means and covariances (a weighted fit of each Gaussian).




Q2. Three points x = 0, 1, 10 have responsibilities r_{i1} = 1, 0.5, 0 for component 1. What are N_1, \mu_1 and \pi_1 after the M-step?






Hint





Weighted mean with weights r_{i1}.









Answer





N_1 = 1.5, \mu_1 = (1 \cdot 0 + 0.5 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 10)/1.5 = 0.33, \pi_1 = 1.5/3 = 0.5.




Q3. What do you have to change in EM to get exactly k-means?






Hint





Labels, covariances, weights.









Answer





Make the labels hard (each point fully to its nearest centre), give every component the same round covariance \sigma^2 I (not re-estimated) and equal weights (not re-estimated). Equivalently: equal round covariances with \sigma \to 0, where the soft responsibilities become 0 or 1 by themselves.




Q4. The log-likelihood plot of your EM run shows a drop between two iterations. What can you conclude?






Hint





What does the theory say about EM’s log-likelihood?









Answer





Something is not plain EM: a bug, a numerical problem (for instance a variance clipped at a floor in a way the M-step does not account for), or a modified algorithm (hard assignments, fixed weights). Exact EM never decreases the log-likelihood.




Q5. Two runs of EM on the same data end with log-likelihoods −1520 and −1384. Which do you keep, and why can this happen?






Hint





Local maxima.









Answer





Keep the run with −1384 (higher likelihood). EM only finds a local maximum, which depends on the start; the other run got stuck, for example with two components sharing one group.




Q6. One component of your fit has a variance of 10^{-9} and sits on a single pixel value, and the log-likelihood is huge. What happened, and how do you prevent it?






Hint





What is the density of a Gaussian at its centre when σ → 0?









Answer





The component collapsed onto one data point: its density there grows like 1/\sigma, so the likelihood is unbounded, although the fit is useless. Prevent it with a variance floor (add \varepsilon to every variance), by restarting collapsed components, or with a prior on the covariances. Many identical values (e.g. saturated pixels) make it especially likely.




Q7. Adding a fourth component raises \log p(\mathcal D) from −2050 to −2046 on n = 500 points; it adds 6 parameters. Does BIC accept it? Does AIC?






Hint





Compare 2 \times the gain in log-likelihood with p\ln n and with 2p.









Answer





-2\log p drops by 8. BIC adds 6\ln 500 = 37.3: worse by 29.3, rejected. AIC adds 12: worse by 4, also rejected. (With a gain of 10 in \log p, i.e. 20 in -2\log p, AIC would accept and BIC still reject.)




Q8. Why is the log-likelihood alone useless for choosing the number of components?






Hint





What happens with one component per point?









Answer





More components (or more flexible covariances) can only fit the same data at least as well, so the maximum likelihood never decreases with K; with one component per point it is even infinite. A penalty for the number of parameters (BIC, AIC), or a test on held-out data, is needed.




Q9. (math) Show that for any distribution q(k) over the components, \log p(\mathbf x) \ge \sum_k q(k)\log\frac{\pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x)}{q(k)}, with equality when q(k) = r_k(\mathbf x).






Hint





Jensen’s inequality for the concave \log: \log E[Y] \ge E[\log Y].









Answer





\log p(\mathbf x) = \log\sum_k q(k)\,\frac{\pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x)}{q(k)} = \log E_q[Y] \ge E_q[\log Y] with Y = \pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x)/q(k). For q(k) = r_k(\mathbf x) = \pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x)/p(\mathbf x), Y = p(\mathbf x) for every k: a constant, so both sides equal \log p(\mathbf x).

title: Exercise: fitting a mixture with EM
Exercise: fitting a mixture with EM
Exercise: fitting a mixture with EM
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




E-step
r_{ik} = \pi_k\mathcal N(\mathbf x_i \mid \boldsymbol\mu_k, \Sigma_k) / \sum_j\pi_j\mathcal N(\mathbf x_i \mid \boldsymbol\mu_j, \Sigma_j)


M-step
N_k = \sum_i r_{ik}, \pi_k = N_k/n, \boldsymbol\mu_k = \frac1{N_k}\sum_i r_{ik}\mathbf x_i, \Sigma_k = \frac1{N_k}\sum_i r_{ik}(\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu_k)(\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu_k)^\top


Log-likelihood
\log p(\mathcal D) = \sum_i\log\sum_k\pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x_i); never decreases under EM


Collapse
a component on one point with \sigma \to 0: \log p(\mathcal D) \to \infty


Variance floor
add \varepsilon to every variance after the M-step


BIC, AIC
-2\log p(\mathcal D) + p\ln n and -2\log p(\mathcal D) + 2p; smaller is better

title: Exercise: fitting a mixture with EM
text:
By hand
B1. Data 1, 2, 4, 7, 9, 10 (the k-means example). Start \mu = (2, 8), \sigma^2 = (4, 4), \pi = (0.5, 0.5). (a) Show that with equal variances and weights r_1(x) = 1/(1 + e^{-a}) with a = [(x - 8)^2 - (x - 2)^2]/8. Compute r_1(4) and r_1(7). (The others are 1.00, 0.99, 0.00, 0.00 for x = 1, 2, 9, 10; more precisely 0.998, 0.989, 0.002, 0.001.) (b) M-step: compute N_1, \mu_1, \mu_2 and \pi_1. (c) Compare with the k-means result (2.33, 8.67). Which point is “shared”, and how does that show in \mu_1 and \mu_2? (d) The log-likelihood over the first iterations is -14.94, -14.22, -14.03, -13.99. What would a decrease tell you?
B2. A smaller example: points 0, 2, 3; start \mu = (0, 4), \sigma^2 = (1, 1), \pi = (0.5, 0.5). (a) E-step: compute all responsibilities. (Use r_1(x) = 1/(1 + e^{-a}) with a = [(x - 4)^2 - x^2]/2.) (b) M-step: N_k, \mu_k, \sigma_k^2, \pi_k.
B3. Two groups of points overlap in the middle. A point lies exactly halfway between the two current means; both components have the same variance and weight. (a) What does k-means do with it, and what does EM do? (b) In the M-step, how much does the point pull on each mean in k-means, and in EM?
B4. BIC and AIC. You fitted 1D mixtures to n = 1000 pixel intensities and got \log p(\mathcal D) = -4210, -4020, -4012, -4010 for K = 1, 2, 3, 4. (a) Give the number of parameters p for each K. (b) Compute BIC and AIC. Which K does each choose? (c) Explain in words why they differ.
B5. Choosing the covariance type. Two components fitted to n = 200 points in 2D give \log p(\mathcal D) = 273.0 with diagonal covariances and 274.7 with full covariances. Compute both BICs. Which model does BIC prefer, and what does that say about the shape of the groups?
B6. Predict and explain: you start EM with one component placed exactly on an outlier point, far from the rest, with a small variance. What happens in the next few iterations? What would you see in the log-likelihood plot? How do you fix it?






Solutions





B1. (a) With equal \sigma^2 and \pi, the constants cancel: r_1 = \frac{e^{-(x-2)^2/8}}{e^{-(x-2)^2/8} + e^{-(x-8)^2/8}} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-[(x-8)^2 - (x-2)^2]/8}}. At x = 4: a = (16 - 4)/8 = 1.5, r_1 = 0.82. At x = 7: a = (1 - 25)/8 = -3, r_1 = 0.05. (b) N_1 = 0.998 + 0.989 + 0.818 + 0.047 + 0.002 + 0.001 = 2.85; \mu_1 = (0.998 + 2 \cdot 0.989 + 4 \cdot 0.818 + 7 \cdot 0.047 + \dots)/2.85 = 2.31; N_2 = 3.15, \mu_2 = 8.39; \pi_1 = 2.85/6 = 0.48. (Variances: \sigma^2 = (1.87, 2.83).) (c) The point 4 is shared: 82 % of it goes to component 1, 18 % to component 2. It pulls \mu_2 down from 8.67 to 8.39 and \mu_1 slightly down (2.31 instead of 2.33, since 4 counts only 0.82 while 7 adds a little). After convergence EM ends at (2.34, 8.66): close to k-means, because the groups are well separated. (d) A bug (or a modified algorithm): exact EM can never decrease the log-likelihood.
B2. (a) x = 0: a = 8, r_1 = 0.9997. x = 2: a = 0, r_1 = 0.5. x = 3: a = -4, r_1 = 0.018. (b) N_1 = 1.518, N_2 = 1.482; \mu_1 = (0 + 1 + 0.054)/1.518 = 0.69, \mu_2 = (0.001 + 1 + 2.946)/1.482 = 2.66; \sigma_1^2 = 0.94, \sigma_2^2 = 0.23; \pi = (0.51, 0.49).
B3. (a) k-means gives it fully to one of the two (whichever wins the tie). EM gives it responsibility 0.5 to each. (b) k-means: weight 1 on one mean, 0 on the other. EM: weight 0.5 on each; it pulls both means a little towards the middle.
B4. (a) p = 3K - 1: 2, 5, 8, 11. (b) BIC = -2\log p + p\ln 1000 (\ln 1000 = 6.91): 8433.8, 8074.5, 8079.3, 8096.0: K = 2. AIC = -2\log p + 2p: 8424, 8050, 8040, 8042: K = 3. (c) Going from 2 to 3 components improves -2\log p by 16 at the cost of 3 parameters. AIC charges 2 \times 3 = 6 and accepts; BIC charges 3 \times 6.91 = 20.7 and refuses. BIC’s penalty grows with n, so for large data sets it prefers simpler models.
B5. p = 9 (diagonal: 1 + 4 + 4) and p = 11 (full: 1 + 4 + 6); \ln 200 = 5.30. BIC: -546.0 + 47.7 = -498.3 (diagonal) and -549.4 + 58.3 = -491.1 (full). BIC prefers the diagonal model: the two extra covariance numbers improve the fit by only 1.7 in \log p. The groups are (close to) axis-aligned ellipses; their correlations are not needed.
B6. The component owns the outlier with responsibility close to 1 and almost nothing else. The M-step puts its mean on the outlier and its variance becomes (almost) zero; its density at the outlier explodes and the log-likelihood shoots up to a huge value in one or two iterations, then stays there (in practice limited by a numerical minimum variance). The plot shows a sudden jump, not a gentle rise. Fix: a variance floor, removing or restarting the component, starting from k-means(++) or from several starts, or a robust model (heavy-tailed components).




Math questions
B7. (math) Starting from \log p(\mathcal D) = \sum_i\log\sum_k\pi_k\mathcal N(\mathbf x_i \mid \boldsymbol\mu_k, \Sigma_k), derive the M-step for \boldsymbol\mu_k (set the gradient to zero) and for \pi_k (with a Lagrange multiplier for \sum_k\pi_k = 1).
B8. (math) Prove Jensen’s bound \log p(\mathbf x_i) \ge \sum_k q_i(k)\log\frac{\pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x_i)}{q_i(k)} for any distribution q_i, show that it is tight for q_i(k) = r_{ik}, and use it to show that one EM iteration cannot decrease \log p(\mathcal D).
B9. (math) Take \Sigma_k = \sigma^2 I for all k, fixed, and \pi_k = 1/K, fixed. Show that as \sigma \to 0 the responsibilities become 0 or 1 (for points with a unique nearest centre), and that EM becomes k-means.
B10. (math) Show that the likelihood of a 1D mixture with two components is unbounded: put \mu_2 = x_1 and let \sigma_2 \to 0 while component 1 is fixed. Why does this not happen with a single Gaussian (unless all points are equal)?






Solutions (math)





B7. \partial/\partial\boldsymbol\mu_k of \log\sum_j\pi_j\mathcal N_j(\mathbf x_i) is \frac{\pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x_i)}{\sum_j\pi_j\mathcal N_j(\mathbf x_i)}\Sigma_k^{-1}(\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu_k) = r_{ik}\Sigma_k^{-1}(\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu_k). Summing over i and setting to zero (multiply by \Sigma_k): \sum_i r_{ik}(\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu_k) = 0, so \boldsymbol\mu_k = \sum_i r_{ik}\mathbf x_i/N_k. For \pi_k: \partial/\partial\pi_k[\log p(\mathcal D) - \lambda(\sum_j\pi_j - 1)] = \sum_i\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x_i)/p(\mathbf x_i) - \lambda = \sum_i r_{ik}/\pi_k - \lambda = 0, so \pi_k = N_k/\lambda; \sum_k\pi_k = 1 and \sum_k N_k = n give \lambda = n. The r_{ik} depend on the parameters, so these are fixed-point equations; EM iterates them.
B8. \log is concave, so \log\sum_k q_k y_k \ge \sum_k q_k\log y_k for weights q_k \ge 0 summing to 1 (Jensen). With y_k = \pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x_i)/q_i(k), the left side is \log p(\mathbf x_i). For q_i(k) = r_{ik}, y_k = p(\mathbf x_i) for all k, and both sides are \log p(\mathbf x_i). Write \mathcal L(q, \theta) = \sum_i\sum_k q_i(k)\log\frac{\pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x_i)}{q_i(k)}. E-step: q = r^{\text{old}}, so \mathcal L(q, \theta^{\text{old}}) = \log p(\mathcal D \mid \theta^{\text{old}}). M-step: \theta^{\text{new}} maximises \mathcal L(q, \theta) over \theta (only \sum_i\sum_k q_i(k)[\log\pi_k + \log\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x_i)] depends on \theta: weighted one-Gaussian fits). Then \log p(\mathcal D \mid \theta^{\text{new}}) \ge \mathcal L(q, \theta^{\text{new}}) \ge \mathcal L(q, \theta^{\text{old}}) = \log p(\mathcal D \mid \theta^{\text{old}}).
B9. r_{ik} = \frac{\exp(-\lVert\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu_k\rVert^2/2\sigma^2)}{\sum_j\exp(-\lVert\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu_j\rVert^2/2\sigma^2)} (the constants and equal weights cancel). Divide numerator and denominator by the term of the nearest centre k^*: r_{ik} = 1/\sum_j\exp(-(d_j^2 - d_k^2)/2\sigma^2). For k = k^* all other exponents are negative and \to -\infty: r_{ik^*} \to 1; for k \ne k^* the term j = k^* has a positive exponent \to +\infty: r_{ik} \to 0. The M-step mean with 0/1 weights is the mean of the points nearest to \boldsymbol\mu_k: exactly k-means’ update.
B10. p(x_1) \ge \pi_2\mathcal N(x_1 \mid x_1, \sigma_2^2) = \pi_2/(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma_2) \to \infty, and for i \ne 1, p(x_i) \ge \pi_1\mathcal N_1(x_i) > 0, a fixed positive number. So \prod_i p(x_i) \to \infty. With one Gaussian, shrinking \sigma to fit x_1 makes every other point’s density go to zero (like e^{-(x_i - \mu)^2/2\sigma^2}, much faster than 1/\sigma grows), so the likelihood goes to 0, not infinity; its maximum is at the sample variance, which is positive unless all points are equal.

title: Exercise: fitting a mixture with EM
text:
Explore: EM step by step
The demo shows 6–12 points on a line (drag them) and the current mixture: each weighted component \pi_k\mathcal N(x \mid \mu_k, \sigma_k^2) dashed, their sum in black, the means as vertical lines. Points are coloured by their responsibilities. The tables give r_{ik} for every point and N_k, \mu_k, \sigma_k^2, \pi_k per component; the readout gives \log p(\mathcal D) after every M-step. E-step and M-step do one half-step each. Options: hard assignments, equal variances and weights, and a variance floor \varepsilon = 0.1.



P1. Preset the by-hand example. Do one E-step and one M-step and compare the tables with B1. Then alternate until nothing changes. Is \log p always increasing? Where does it end?
P2. Preset an ambiguous point in the middle. What is the responsibility of the point 5.5 at the start and at the end? Why does it not change?
P3. Preset collapse: one component on one point. Alternate E and M. Write down \log p after each M-step. What happens to \sigma_2^2? Now tick variance floor and repeat (reset first).
P4. Preset hard EM = k-means. Run to convergence. Compare the means with B1 of the k-means unit. Untick hard assignments (keep equal variances and weights), reset and run again: does the result change?






Solutions





P1. After the E-step: r_{i1} = 1.00, 0.99, 0.82, 0.05, 0.00, 0.00; after the M-step N = (2.85, 3.15), \mu = (2.31, 8.39), \sigma^2 = (1.87, 2.83), \pi = (0.48, 0.52). \log p: -14.94 \to -14.22 \to -14.03 \to -13.99, always increasing, and it converges at -13.99 with \mu = (2.34, 8.66), \sigma^2 = 1.57 for both, \pi = (0.5, 0.5).
P2. 0.50 at the start and 0.50 at the end. The data and the start are symmetric about 5.5 (points 1, 2, 3 and 8, 9, 10; means 2 and 9; equal variances and weights), so every iteration keeps the symmetry: the point is always exactly halfway, with equal densities and equal weights. EM ends at \mu = (2.50, 8.50), \sigma^2 = 2.08 for both.
P3. Without the floor: \log p = -16.59 \to -14.58 \to -14.24 \to -12.97 \to -2.13. Component 2 sits on the single point 10; its variance shrinks from 8 to 10^{-10} (the demo’s numerical minimum) and the spike makes \log p jump.
