With a smaller numerical minimum the jump would be larger still: the likelihood is unbounded. With the floor \varepsilon = 0.1: -16.59 \to -14.59 \to -14.27 \to -13.20 \to -12.50, and \sigma_2^2 stops at 0.1: still a narrow component on one point, but with finite likelihood. (Is one point a “group”? Unit 4 calls such points anomalies.)
P4. The means end at (2.33, 8.67), exactly the k-means answer. \log p goes -29.41 \to -16.40 \to -15.27 \to -13.99. With soft assignments (equal variances and weights still fixed to be equal) EM ends at (2.34, 8.66), \log p = -13.99: almost the same here, because the groups are well separated; it takes more iterations (13 M-steps instead of 4), since the start (1, 2) makes both components share all points at first.

title: Exercise: fitting a mixture with EM
text:
Explore: EM in 2D
The main demo of the day. The points come from a dataset (seeded); click to add points, drag them, or remove them. Choose K, the covariance type (spherical, diagonal, full, tied) and the start (random points, k-means, k-means++ seeds, or by hand: drag the centres). E-step, M-step, step and run fit the mixture; points are coloured by their responsibilities, ellipses are 1σ (solid) and 2σ (dashed), and the background shows the regions of the most probable component (or the density). Right: \log p(\mathcal D) per iteration (a red ring would mark a decrease), 20 restarts (histogram of the final \log p), BIC / AIC for K = 1..6, and the variance floor \varepsilon. k-means (hard) switches to Lloyd’s algorithm for comparison.



E1. Preset well separated. Press run. What are the final \log p and weights? Press 20 restarts: do all runs end at the same value?
E2. Preset elongated: k-means fails, full GMM works. It starts in k-means mode: run and describe the groups. Switch to EM (soft) and run. Compare the groups, and look at the ellipses.
E3. Preset one big, one small: weights matter. Run. Where is the boundary (background) compared with the k-means bisector? What are the weights?
E4. Preset bad start: local maximum. Run. What is the final \log p, compared with E1 (same data)? Describe the solution. Press new start, then run.
E5. Preset collapse (floor off). Run and watch the \log p plot and the readout. Then set the floor to 10^{-4} (reset and run). Compare.
E6. Preset K too large: BIC says no. Read the BIC and AIC bars. Which K does each choose? Relate to B4.
E7. Presets diagonal is enough and diagonal is not enough. In each, compare the BIC values for diagonal and full covariances (switch Σ and press BIC / AIC). When are the extra parameters worth it?
E8. Preset heavy overlap: soft labels near 0.5. Run. Which points have mixed colours? Would a hard label be trustworthy there?






Solutions





E1. \log p(\mathcal D) = 179.7 with weights 0.33, 0.33, 0.33 (three blobs of 50 points). (The log-likelihood is positive because the points live in the unit square, where densities are larger than 1.) Of 20 restarts from k-means, 19 end at 179.7 and one at 140.4, a local maximum.
E2. k-means cuts across both cigars (J = 3.079; only 125 of 160 points grouped as in the cigars). EM with full covariances ends at \log p = 245.6 with two long, thin, tilted ellipses, one per cigar: 146 of the 160 points are grouped as in the two cigars. The covariance lets each component follow the shape of its group.
E3. Weights 0.80 and 0.20; the wide component’s region extends around the small, tight group, and the boundary lies close to the small group, not halfway between the centres. All 150 points get the label of the group they came from (k-means: 138).
E4. \log p = 123.4, far below 179.7: one component covers two blobs (weight 0.67), the other two share one blob (0.08 and 0.25). No single EM step can move a component across the empty gap. A new start (k-means) finds 179.7 again.
E5. Without a floor the third component sits on the outlier at (0.88, 0.15): after one iteration \log p jumps from -62.0 to 203.1 and then 203.9; its variance is at the numerical minimum 10^{-10}, and the readout reports a collapse. With \varepsilon = 10^{-4}, \log p = 190.1 and the component is a small circle (variance 10^{-4}, i.e. σ = 0.01) on the outlier: finite, and visibly an “outlier component” with weight 0.01.
E6. BIC is smallest at K = 2 (the two blobs), AIC at K = 4. As in B4, AIC’s penalty (2 per parameter) is smaller than BIC’s (\ln 100 = 4.6 per parameter), so AIC accepts extra components that improve the fit only slightly.
E7. Diagonal is enough (axis-aligned clouds): BIC at K = 2 is -498.3 for diagonal and -491.0 for full: the two correlations are not worth their cost. Diagonal is not enough (tilted cigars): with diagonal covariances BIC is smallest at K = 4 (-361.1): it needs a staircase of axis-aligned blobs to cover each tilted cigar. With full covariances BIC is -439.9 at K = 1 and -435.3 at K = 2: far better than any diagonal model, and one tilted ellipse (or two) suffices. (BIC slightly prefers one big ellipse around both cigars here: the cigars are close together.)
E8. The points in the overlap region, between the two centres, have mixed colours: 26 of the 100 points have responsibilities between 0.3 and 0.7. A hard label there is close to a coin toss; the soft label says so honestly.

title: Exercise: fitting a mixture with EM
text:
Where this leads
EM fits mixtures to any points: pixels in a feature space, or objects in a feature table. Unit 4 applies it to images: mixtures of grey levels (the thresholding day’s minimum-error threshold for K classes), colour segmentation, populations of cells, and anomalies.

title: The 2D wavelet transform and sparsity of images
text:
About this lecture
The last two units transformed 1D signals. Images are 2D, and the 2D wavelet transform is the 1D one applied twice.

Separable: transform every row, then every column. One level gives four subbands: LL, H, V, D.
A 2 \times 2 block by hand, and which band an edge lights up.
Repeat on LL: the subband pyramid.
How sparse a real image is in a wavelet basis, and “keep the K largest” against Fourier and the 8 \times 8 block DCT.
Shift variance: move the image by one pixel and the coefficients change a lot.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Third unit of the wavelets elective. Uses the filter bank of the previous unit, the 2D DFT’s separability from the Fourier unit, and PSNR from the camera noise unit. The subband names LL / H / V / D are the course convention (also on the compression and integral-image days).

title: The 2D wavelet transform and sparsity of images
text:
Separable: rows, then columns
As for the 2D DFT (Images in frequency space): a 2D transform built from 1D ones.

Run one level of the 1D filter bank on every row: left half = low-pass along x, right half = high-pass along x.
Run it on every column of the result: top = low-pass along y, bottom = high-pass along y.

Four quarter-size subbands:









low-pass along x
high-pass along x




low-pass along y
LL: approximation, a half-size thumbnail
V: vertical edges


high-pass along y
H: horizontal edges
D: diagonal detail

title: The 2D wavelet transform and sparsity of images
text:
One level on an image


LL looks like the image at half size.
V responds where the image changes along x: the vertical bar’s sides. H responds to changes along y: the horizontal bar’s top and bottom. The diagonal bar changes along both axes, so it shows up in V, H and D.
Flat regions give 0 in every detail band (white).


128 × 128 synthetic image, one level of orthonormal 2D Haar. Detail bands in a diverging map (blue negative, red positive), each scaled to its own largest value; LL in grey. The sign tells the direction of the change (dark to bright or bright to dark).
crumbs: The 2D wavelet transform and sparsity of images

title: The 2D wavelet transform and sparsity of images
text:
The math: naming the bands
Write the 1D analysis as two operators: L (low-pass h, keep every second sample) and H (high-pass g, keep every second). With the image X as a matrix (rows = y, columns = x), one level is X \;\mapsto\; \begin{pmatrix} L \\ H \end{pmatrix} X \begin{pmatrix} L \\ H \end{pmatrix}^{\!\top} = \begin{pmatrix} L X L^\top & L X H^\top \\ H X L^\top & H X H^\top\end{pmatrix}.

Two-letter names, first letter = filter along x (columns of X), second = along y: LXL^\top = LL, LXH^\top = HL (high along x) = our V, HXL^\top = LH = our H, HXH^\top = HH = D.
Books disagree on whether “LH” means “low along x” or “low along y” (and on which band is called “horizontal”). This course uses LL / H / V / D by what they show; in the math layer, first letter = x.
If the 1D transform W = \binom{L}{H} is orthogonal, so is X \mapsto W X W^\top: \|WXW^\top\|_F = \|X\|_F.

The subband pyramid
Repeat on LL only (the cascade of the last unit, in 2D):

Each level splits the current LL into a quarter-size LL and three detail bands.
Drawn in place, this is the Mallat layout: the smallest LL in the top-left corner, then the bands of the coarsest level around it, then finer and finer bands outwards.

How sparse is a real image?

title: The 2D wavelet transform and sparsity of images
section: The math: K-term approximation and PSNR
text:
The math: K-term approximation and PSNR
For an orthonormal transform (all orthogonal wavelets, the orthonormal DCT, the DFT scaled by 1/N): \mathrm{MSE} = \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{i,j}(x_{ij} - \hat x_{ij})^2 = \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{\text{dropped}} |c|^2, \qquad \mathrm{PSNR} = 10\log_{10}\frac{255^2}{\mathrm{MSE}}.

PSNR as defined in Camera noise, SNR and PSNR (peak 255 for 8 bits).
So the PSNR-vs-K curve follows from the sorted coefficient magnitudes alone, as in 1D. A basis is good for an image class when its sorted magnitudes fall fast.
For piecewise-smooth images with edges (smooth regions bounded by smooth curves), the squared error of the best K-term wavelet approximation falls like K^{-1}, the Fourier one only like K^{-1/2} (Mallat 2009, ch. 9): the edge costs Fourier coefficients at all frequencies.
CDF 9/7 is biorthogonal, not orthonormal: the formula is then only approximate.
crumbs: The 2D wavelet transform and sparsity of images

title: The 2D wavelet transform and sparsity of images
text:
Coefficients are not bits
Keeping 5 % of a 256 \times 256 image is 3277 numbers, but a decoder also needs to know where they are:

value (say 8 bits) + position (16 bits for one of 65 536 places): 3277 \times 24 = 78\,648 bits against 524\,288 for the raw image, a ratio of 6.7, not 20.
Real codecs do much better: they quantise the values, code the positions cleverly (most large coefficients sit under each other across levels), and use entropy coding.
JPEG 2000 = 2D CDF 9/7 (or LeGall 5/3) DWT + quantisation + bit-plane coding. That is the subject of the compression day, the next day of this elective.

title: The 2D wavelet transform and sparsity of images
text:
Shift variance
Shift the image by one pixel and transform again:

The Fourier magnitudes do not change at all (a shift is only a phase).
The decimated wavelet coefficients change a lot: for a square, 68 % (relative change of all detail coefficients, Haar, 2 levels); for the micrograph, 92 % (db4, 3 levels).
Why: keeping every second sample makes the transform depend on where an edge falls relative to the even–odd grid (Haar unit, B5: a jump between pairs gives fewer details than a jump inside a pair).
The energy per band changes little; the individual coefficients do. For denoising this causes artefacts tied to the grid, and the fix (averaging over shifts) comes in the next unit.

2D DWT = 1D filter bank on rows, then columns: four subbands LL (approximation), V, H, D (vertical, horizontal, diagonal detail). An edge lights the band of its orientation.

title: Quiz: decision trees
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A tree has three questions: “x \le 0.5?”, then on both sides “y \le 0.3?”. Into how many regions does it cut the plane, and what shape are they?






Hint





Each question cuts one region in two, along an axis.









Answer





Four regions (one per leaf), all axis-aligned rectangles: left-bottom, left-top, right-bottom, right-top. Here both sides happen to use the same threshold on y, so the four rectangles form a 2 \times 2 grid.




Q2. A node holds 6 nuclei and 2 background pixels. What is its Gini impurity? What would a pure node have?






Hint





G = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2.









Answer





G = 1 - 0.75^2 - 0.25^2 = 0.375. A pure node (one class only) has G = 0; the most mixed two-class node has G = 0.5.




Q3. Why does the split search only try thresholds between neighbouring values of a feature?






Hint





What changes when the threshold moves between two neighbouring values?









Answer





Moving the threshold between two neighbouring values does not move any training point from one side to the other, so the split and its impurity stay the same. Only n - 1 distinct splits exist per feature for n distinct values; taking the midpoint is a convention.




Q4. A tree grown until every leaf is pure has 0 % training error. Why is that not good news?






Hint





What does it do with a mislabelled or noisy training point?









Answer





It has memorised the training data, including its noise: every mislabelled point gets its own small region. On new data those regions are wrong, so the test error is higher than for a shallower tree. Zero training error says nothing about new data.




Q5. You tried ten depths and chose the one with the smallest test error. What is wrong with reporting that test error?






Hint





What role did the test set play in the choice?









Answer





The test set was used to choose a setting, so it has become a validation set and its error is optimistic (the best of ten noisy numbers). Choose on a validation set or by cross-validation, then evaluate once on a test set that played no role in any choice.




Q6. In 5-fold cross-validation, how often is each training example used for validation, and how many trees are grown per setting?






Hint





Each fold takes its turn.









Answer





Each example is validated exactly once (when its fold is held out) and used for training in the other 4 rounds. Five trees are grown per setting, one per round; their 5 validation errors are averaged.




Q7. One feature is an area in µm², another an intensity from 0 to 4095. Do you have to rescale them before growing a tree?






Hint





Does a split depend on the size of the numbers or on their order?









Answer





No. A split only depends on the order of the values along one feature; rescaling (or any increasing transformation) moves the thresholds but keeps the same splits. Methods based on distances (nearest neighbour, the SVM) do need comparable scales.




Q8. A regression tree with 4 leaves is fitted to a smooth intensity ramp. What does the fit look like?






Hint





What does a leaf predict?









Answer





A staircase of 4 flat steps: each leaf predicts the mean of its points, so the fit is piecewise constant. A smooth ramp needs many leaves to be approximated well.




Q9. (math) Show that for two classes the Gini impurity is 2p(1-p), where p is the share of one class.






Hint





p_1 = p, p_2 = 1 - p.









Answer





G = 1 - p^2 - (1-p)^2 = 1 - p^2 - 1 + 2p - p^2 = 2p - 2p^2 = 2p(1-p). Equivalently \sum_{k \ne l}p_kp_l = p(1-p) + (1-p)p.

title: Exercise: decision trees
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Feature space
one axis per feature; each pixel or object is a point


Decision tree
nodes ask “feature j \le t?”; leaves hold a class (or class shares)


Gini impurity
G = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2: chance that two random points of the node have different classes


Entropy
H = -\sum_k p_k \log_2 p_k (almost the same splits as Gini)


Impurity decrease
\Delta = I(\text{parent}) - \tfrac{n_L}{n}I(L) - \tfrac{n_R}{n}I(R); the best split has the largest \Delta


Overfitting
training error keeps falling with depth, test error rises again


Validation / test
the validation set chooses settings; the test set is used once, at the end


k-fold cross-validation
k rounds, each fold validates once; average the k errors


Regression tree
leaves hold the mean; splits reduce the sum of squared errors









The math: why the impurity decrease is never negative





The parent’s class shares are the weighted mean of the children’s: p_k = \tfrac{n_L}{n}p_k^L + \tfrac{n_R}{n}p_k^R. Gini and entropy are concave functions of the shares, so (Jensen) I(\text{parent}) \ge \tfrac{n_L}{n}I(L) + \tfrac{n_R}{n}I(R), i.e. \Delta \ge 0. Equality holds when both children have the parent’s shares: such a split is useless.

Math questions
B8. (math) Show that 1 - \sum_k p_k^2 = \sum_{k \ne l} p_k p_l. For two classes with shares p and 1 - p, show that both G and H are largest at p = 1/2, and give their maxima.
B9. (math) Show that the impurity decrease of a split is \ge 0 when the impurity is a concave function of the class shares. When is it exactly 0?
B10. (math) 400 points of class A and 400 of class B. Split 1 gives children (300 A, 100 B) and (100 A, 300 B); split 2 gives (200 A, 400 B) and (200 A, 0 B). Compute the decrease of the misclassification impurity M = 1 - \max_k p_k and of Gini for both. Which split does each prefer, and why is M a poor splitting criterion?
B11. (math) For a regression split of n values into n_L and n_R with means \bar y_L and \bar y_R, show that the decrease in the sum of squared errors is \frac{n_L n_R}{n}(\bar y_L - \bar y_R)^2. Check it on B6.






Solutions (math)





B8. 1 = (\sum_k p_k)^2 = \sum_k p_k^2 + \sum_{k \ne l} p_k p_l. Two classes: G = 1 - p^2 - (1-p)^2 = 2p(1 - p), derivative 2 - 4p = 0 at p = 1/2, maximum G = 0.5. H = -p\log_2 p - (1-p)\log_2(1-p), derivative \log_2\frac{1-p}{p} = 0 at p = 1/2, maximum H = 1 bit. Both are 0 at p = 0 and p = 1.
B9. With w = n_L/n, the parent’s shares are \mathbf p = w\,\mathbf p^L + (1 - w)\,\mathbf p^R. Concavity of I gives I(\mathbf p) \ge w\,I(\mathbf p^L) + (1-w)\,I(\mathbf p^R), i.e. \Delta \ge 0. For a strictly concave I (Gini, entropy) equality holds only if \mathbf p^L = \mathbf p^R: both children have the parent’s class mix.
B10. Parent: M = 0.5, G = 0.5. Split 1: both children have M = 0.25, so \Delta M = 0.5 - 0.25 = 0.25; G = 2 \cdot 0.75 \cdot 0.25 = 0.375 each, \Delta G = 0.125. Split 2: M(200, 400) = 1/3, M(200, 0) = 0; \Delta M = 0.5 - \tfrac34 \cdot \tfrac13 - 0 = 0.25. G(200, 400) = 4/9, \Delta G = 0.5 - \tfrac34\cdot\tfrac49 = 0.167. M cannot tell them apart; Gini prefers split 2, which makes a pure child that needs no further questions. M is piecewise linear (not strictly concave), so it misses such progress, and in a node where every candidate child keeps the parent’s majority class it gives \Delta M = 0 for every split and the growth stops too early.
B11. Write S = \sum (y_i - \bar y)^2. With \bar y = (n_L\bar y_L + n_R\bar y_R)/n, the split of the total sum of squares gives S_P = S_L + S_R + n_L(\bar y_L - \bar y)^2 + n_R(\bar y_R - \bar y)^2. Since \bar y_L - \bar y = \frac{n_R}{n}(\bar y_L - \bar y_R) and \bar y_R - \bar y = -\frac{n_L}{n}(\bar y_L - \bar y_R), the last two terms are \frac{n_L n_R^2 + n_R n_L^2}{n^2}(\bar y_L - \bar y_R)^2 = \frac{n_L n_R}{n}(\bar y_L - \bar y_R)^2. B6: \frac{3 \cdot 3}{6}(11 - 31)^2 = 600 = 604 - 4.

E1. Preset two blobs: one stump. Which question does the root ask, with which impurity decrease? What is the best cut along y, and why does the tree not use it? How many training points are wrong? Press grow fully: how many leaves, and what happens to the training and test errors (tick show test points)?
E2. Preset XOR: first split looks useless. Read the best impurity decrease along x and y at the root and compare with the decrease in E1. Press next split four times and note the training error after each. What does this say about greedy growth?
E3. Preset diagonal: staircase. How many leaves does the full tree have? Tick show test points: what is the test error? Set min leaf size to 5: leaves and test error now? Why can a tree only approximate this boundary?
E4. Preset one mislabelled point. Find the point of class 2 inside the class-1 cloud. How does the full tree handle it? Set min leaf size to 3. What changes in the picture, in the training error and in the test error?
E5. Preset noisy overlap: error vs depth. Read the training and test errors at depth 1, 3 and 12 from the curve. Which depth would you choose, and how would you choose it without a test set?
E6. Back to two blobs, choose misclass. and press grow fully. How many splits does the tree make now, and why does it stop? Compare with Gini.
E7. Preset regression: a cell edge. Read the leaf means of the depth-2 tree. Using the error-vs-depth curve, give the training and test MSE at depths 1, 2, 3 and 6. Which depth fits the edge best?






Solutions





E1. The root asks x \le 0.48, with impurity decrease 0.480 (of a possible 0.5: the children are almost pure). The best cut along y is y \le 0.475 with decrease 0.328: the blobs overlap more in y. 1 of 100 training points is wrong. Grown fully: 3 splits, 4 leaves, depth 3, training error 0, but the test error rises from 2.5 % (stump) to 3.5 %: the two extra splits only chase one point.
E2. Root: best decrease 0.024 along x (at 0.453) and 0.013 along y, against 0.48 in E1: no single cut separates a chessboard. Training errors: 47/120 after one split, 20/120 after two, 1/120 after three, 0 after four. A useless-looking first question can be the start of a perfect tree; greedy growth works here only because it keeps going.
E3. 13 leaves (depth 7), training error 0, test error 7.7 %. With min leaf size 5: 7 leaves (depth 4), training error 2.7 %, test error 10.0 %. Each split is horizontal or vertical, so a diagonal line can only be approximated by a staircase; finer steps need many leaves and many points.
E4. The point at (0.27, 0.40) belongs to class 2 but sits among class 1. The full tree (4 leaves, depth 3) cuts a thin horizontal strip around it: training error 0, test error 1.0 %. With min leaf size 3 a leaf may not hold a single point, the strip disappears, the point is simply misclassified (training error 1/81 = 1.2 %), and the test error drops to 0.8 %.
E5. Depth 1: training 22.5 %, test 22.8 %. Depth 3: 17.5 % and 20.9 % (the lowest test error). Depth 12: 0.5 % and 28.9 %. Choose depth 3 (or 4, 21.0 %). Without a test set: cross-validation on the training points, or a separate validation set; the test set is then used once to report the error.
E6. With misclassification the tree stops after 1 split (training error 1/100). The further splits under Gini isolate a single point inside a child where the other class is the large majority; the majority class of each child does not change, so the misclassification impurity does not decrease (\Delta M = 0) and the growth stops. Gini still sees the purer child (as in B10).
E7. Depth 2: four plateaus with means 40, 75, 129 and 158 (left to right). MSE (training / test): depth 1: 262.8 / 264.8; depth 2: 124.7 / 141.4; depth 3: 88.0 / 130.1; depth 6: 31.8 / 224.2. Depth 3 has the lowest test error; deeper trees follow the noise of the training samples.

title: Exercise: decision trees
text:
Where this leads
One deep tree is unstable: small changes of the data give a different tree. The next unit grows many trees on slightly different data and lets them vote: bagging and random forests. Later units use forests on tables of object measurements and on stacks of filtered images.

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
About this lecture
Many image problems ask for the cheapest path: a boundary along dark pixels, a seam through an image, an alignment of two signals. There are far too many paths to try them all. Dynamic programming (DP) finds the best one exactly, with a table and a few additions.

The question: the cheapest path from the top row to the bottom row of a cost image.
Why trying all paths fails, and why the greedy choice fails.
The key idea: an optimal path is made of optimal sub-paths.
Fill a table row by row, then backtrack to read off the path.
The general recipe, and two old friends that are the same recursion: the two-label chain of the graph-cut day and the distance transform.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

This is the first unit of the dynamic-programming day (elective group “Curves and energies”, after snakes and level sets). Everything here is sums, minima and a table; no probability. The next units turn the same table sideways (closed boundaries in polar coordinates), drop the fixed order (Dijkstra, live-wire), and go continuous (fast marching).

The question
A small cost image: each pixel has a cost (light = cheap). Find the cheapest path from the top row to the bottom row that moves one row down per step, one column left, straight or right.

The cost of a path is the sum of its five pixels. Try to guess the best path before the next slide.

Give the class a minute. Most people start at the 3 in the top right (the cheapest first pixel) or look for the column of small numbers. The answer is 10, along columns 1, 0, 1, 1, 1; the “start at the cheapest pixel and keep going downhill” path costs 19.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
Why not try all paths?

From each pixel there are 3 ways down (2 at the image border). A path through n rows has n - 1 steps, so there are about m \cdot 3^{n-1} paths in an image with m columns.
5 \times 5: 259 paths (405 without the border effect). Still possible by hand, barely.
100 \times 100: about 1.5 \cdot 10^{49} paths.
256 \times 256: about 10^{124} paths, more than the roughly 10^{80} atoms in the observable universe.

Trying them all is hopeless. We need a way to reuse work: the paths overlap almost everywhere.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
Greedy fails
The obvious shortcut: start at the cheapest pixel of the top row and always step to the cheapest of the three pixels below.

In the example: start at 3 (top right), then 2, 6, 2, 6: 19.
The best path costs 10: 4, 2, 1, 1, 2. Its first pixel (4) is not the cheapest one.

A cheap first step can lead into an expensive region. To decide the first step well, we must know what comes later. Dynamic programming turns this around: it works out the best way to reach every pixel, so no decision is made too early.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
The key idea: optimal sub-paths
Suppose the best path to the bottom passes through pixel p. Then its part from the top to p must be the best path to p: if there were a cheaper way to reach p, we could swap it in and get a cheaper path to the bottom.
So we only ever need to remember one number per pixel:

M(p) = the cost of the cheapest path from the top row to p.

and, for pixel p in row i, it is known as soon as row i - 1 is known:

M(p) = cost of p + the smallest M among the (up to) three pixels above it.

This is Bellman’s principle of optimality (1957).
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
The math: the Bellman recursion
Cost image C(i, j), rows i = 0, \dots, n-1, columns j = 0, \dots, m-1. A path is j_0, j_1, \dots, j_{n-1} with |j_{i} - j_{i-1}| \le 1, cost \sum_i C(i, j_i).
M(0, j) = C(0, j), \qquad M(i, j) = C(i, j) + \min_{d \in \{-1, 0, 1\}} M(i-1, j+d) \quad (i \ge 1),
with M = \infty outside the image. Store the minimising d as a pointer B(i, j). The optimal cost is \min_j M(n-1, j); the path follows the pointers back from that cell.
Why it is correct (by induction on i): every path to (i, j) comes from one of the three cells above, and its cost is C(i, j) plus the cost of its part up to row i - 1, which is at least M(i-1, j+d). The recursion takes the best of these lower bounds, and it is reached by extending the optimal path to that cell.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
Filling the table, then backtracking


Row 0 of M copies the costs. Row 1: M(1,0) = 2 + \min(7, 4) = 6; M(1,1) = 9 + \min(7, 4, 8) = 13; …
Each cell also remembers which cell above gave the minimum: a pointer.
At the end, the smallest M in the last row is 10. Follow the pointers back up: columns 1, 0, 1, 1, 1.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
section: Try it: the table step by step
text:
Try it: the table step by step




Left: the costs; right: the table M. “step” fills one cell: the candidates in the row above are outlined, the chosen minimum is shaded green and an arrow points back to it. “next stage” fills a whole row, “fill all” the table, “backtrack” follows the arrows from the best cell of the last row; the last frame adds the greedy path (red “g”). Tour: by-hand grid (10 against greedy 19; 52 operations against 259 paths). “greedy fails”: 9 against 20. “two equal optima”: both mirror paths cost 9; the table keeps one pointer per cell (on a tie: straight, then left, then right), so it reports one of them. “a detour”: the cheap channel turns back upwards; no monotone path can follow it (cost 24). That is the cliffhanger for the live-wire unit. Click the upper half of a cost cell to raise it, the lower half to lower it.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
What it costs

Each cell looks at (at most) 3 cells above: one addition and one comparison each. An n \times m image needs about 3nm operations.
5 \times 5: 52 operations instead of 259 paths. 256 \times 256: about 195 000 operations instead of 10^{124} paths.
Memory: the whole table and the pointers to recover the path; if only the cost is wanted, the previous row is enough.

The trick is the overlap: the cheapest way to each pixel is computed once and reused by every path that continues from it.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
section: The math: counting paths and operations
text:
The math: counting paths and operations
Let N(i, j) be the number of paths from row 0 to (i, j). Then N(0, j) = 1 and N(i, j) = \sum_{d} N(i-1, j+d): the same recursion with (+, \text{sum}) in place of (+, \min).

Every cell has between 2 and 3 cells above it (for m \ge 2), so m \cdot 2^{n-1} \le \sum_j N(n-1, j) \le m \cdot 3^{n-1}: exponential in n.
The table needs one candidate per (cell, step): (n-1)(3m - 2) evaluations (the two border cells of each row have 2 candidates). Linear in the number of pixels.
With 2\delta + 1 allowed steps instead of 3: O(nm\delta) work, about m(2\delta+1)^{n-1} paths.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
The recipe
Dynamic programming in four steps:

Stages and states: here the rows are the stages and the column of the path is the state.
A recursion: the best value of a state from the best values of the previous stage.
An order in which every right-hand side is known before it is needed: here, row by row.
Backtracking: store where each minimum came from, and follow it back from the best final state.

Step 3 is the condition that matters later: if no such order exists, plain DP does not work (the live-wire unit).
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
section: Same recursion, other states: the two-label chain
text:
Same recursion, other states: the two-label chain
Recall from the graph-cut day (unit Segmentation as energy minimisation): the best labelling of a 1D profile, E(L) = \sum_p D_p(L_p) + \lambda\,\#\{p : L_p \ne L_{p+1}\}, solved exactly by DP.

Stage = pixel p, state = its label 0 or 1. The table has two numbers per pixel.
Transition cost \lambda when the label changes: a “path” through a 2-column grid with a step penalty.
This is the Viterbi algorithm; the same idea decodes signals and aligns speech.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
Try it: the two-label chain




The demo is the graph-cut day’s own demo, embedded unchanged. Only make the link: two states per stage instead of m, and a penalty λ on a “sideways” step. The exercise (B3) fills the two-state table for the graph-cut day’s 1 × 5 example.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
Same recursion, other steps
The recursion does not care what the steps are, as long as each one goes back in the filling order.

One row down, up to \delta columns sideways, with a penalty \alpha |d| for a step of d columns: smoother paths. The next unit uses this for closed boundaries.
Right or down (top-left to bottom-right): M(i, j) = C(i, j) + \min\big(M(i-1, j),\ M(i, j-1)\big). Fill row by row, left to right. In the demo: moves → ↓. Adding the diagonal step gives the table used to align two signals (dynamic time warping).
Seams through an image (seam carving) are the ↙↓↘ case on an energy image.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
section: Same recursion, other order: the distance transform
text:
Same recursion, other order: the distance transform
Recall from the morphology day: the two-pass (chamfer) distance transform. Its first pass is
D(i, j) = \min\big(D(i, j),\ D(i-1, j) + 1,\ D(i, j-1) + 1\big)
in raster order: a Bellman recursion where the “previous stage” is the pixel above and the pixel to the left.

One pass is not enough: a pixel whose nearest background lies below or to the right gets the wrong value. A second pass in the opposite order fixes this case.
So what happens when the best path may go up, down, left and right, and no fixed order works at all? That is the live-wire unit: let the algorithm discover the order.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
When is DP exact?

DP is exact when the problem is a chain (one state per stage, each stage talks only to the next) or a tree, so that there is an order in which everything needed is already known.
A 2D labelling with neighbours in both directions is not a chain: the grid has loops. The graph-cut day solves binary 2D labellings exactly in another way (max-flow, for submodular energies).
A boundary that can be written as one value per stage (one column per row, one radius per angle) is a chain, so DP finds the global optimum, however many local minima the image has.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
Summary

The cheapest path through a cost image cannot be found by trying all paths (\sim 10^{124} for 256 \times 256) or greedily.
Principle of optimality: the best path to the end is made of best paths to its intermediate pixels.
Fill the table M = cost + the smallest M above, row by row; store pointers; backtrack from the best final cell.
About 3nm operations, exact.
The recipe (stages, states, recursion, order, backtracking) also gives the two-label chain (Viterbi) and the passes of the distance transform.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: Quiz: diffusion models and generated detail
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. In the forward process, what happens to an image as \tau goes from 0 to 1, and what does the noise schedule decide?






Hint





Signal \sqrt{\bar\alpha}, noise \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha}.









Answer





The signal is shrunk and Gaussian noise is added until only noise is left (\bar\alpha \approx 0). The schedule decides how fast: how much signal remains at each time.




Q2. Why is training a denoiser “supervised learning with free labels”?






Hint





Who added the noise?









Answer





We take clean training images and add noise ourselves, so the correct answer (the noise, or the clean image) is known for every training example without any annotation.




Q3. At very high noise, what does the best possible denoiser output?






Hint





What is the best guess when the noisy image says almost nothing?









Answer





The average of all clean images compatible with the noisy one; at the highest noise, the average of the whole training set: a blurry mean image, not a sample.




Q4. Why does sampling with very few steps give blurry or “in-between” results?






Hint





Q3.









Answer





Each step jumps towards the denoiser’s estimate, which at high noise is an average of many images. With few steps the sample ends near such an average (between modes); many small steps let the estimate refine at lower noise levels, where it follows one mode.




Q5. A diffusion model was trained to perfection on 50 images. What will its samples be?






Hint





What distribution does a perfect denoiser of 50 images describe?









Answer





Copies of the 50 training images: the perfect denoiser of a finite set generates exactly that set. Real networks generate new images because they are imperfect (they smooth between examples).




Q6. What does a strong guidance weight do to conditional samples?






Hint





Typical versus diverse.









Answer





They become more typical of the condition and less diverse: samples move to where the condition is most certain and away from anything that might also fit another condition.




Q7. A restoration’s posterior mean and one posterior sample: which has the higher PSNR on average, and which looks more realistic?






Hint





Averaging removes uncertain detail.









Answer





The mean has the higher PSNR (it minimises the expected squared error; a sample has twice the error for a Gaussian posterior). The sample looks more realistic: it is sharp everywhere, but its uncertain details come from the prior.




Q8. A generatively restored image shows two nucleoli in a cell whose nucleoli are smaller than the blur of the raw image. May you report “two nucleoli”?






Hint





Where does detail below the resolution come from?









Answer





No. Below the resolution of the measurement the detail comes from the prior (the training images). Count on the raw data, or validate the count on images with ground truth, and check whether several samples agree.




Q9. Why is a prior that has never seen a rare phenotype dangerous for restoration?






Hint





What does the posterior do with something it cannot explain?









Answer





It explains the measurement with the closest normal training images, so the rare phenotype is “corrected” to normal. The result looks convincing, and even samples agree on it, so nothing warns you.




Q10. (math) x_0 = 3, \sqrt{\bar\alpha} = 0.6, \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha} = 0.8, \varepsilon = 0.5. Compute x_\tau and its variance given x_0.






Hint





x_\tau = \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha}\,\varepsilon.









Answer





x_\tau = 1.8 + 0.4 = 2.2. Given x_0 the variance is 1 - \bar\alpha = 0.64.

title: Exercise: diffusion models and generated detail

By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute a forward noising step, and say what the noise schedule controls,

title: Exercise: diffusion models and generated detail
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Forward process
x_\tau = \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha}\,\varepsilon, from data (\bar\alpha = 1) to noise (\bar\alpha \approx 0)


Denoiser
predicts the noise \varepsilon (or x_0) from x_\tau; the best one returns the average of the compatible clean images


Sampling
start from noise, denoise a little at a time; stochastic or deterministic


Conditioning
the denoiser also gets a label or a measurement; guidance w pushes harder


Posterior mean
the average of all restorations compatible with the measurement


Posterior sample
one such restoration, drawn at random






Left: 500 points sampled from noise in 100 steps land on the two moons (one path in orange); right: the noise schedule. Below: a heavily blurred cell restored with a generative prior: the posterior mean is smooth, the samples are sharp and disagree about the nucleoli.





A heavily blurred cell restored with the exact posterior of a generative prior: truth, measurement, classical, posterior mean, four samples, disagreement and the most trusted training cells.

title: Exercise: diffusion models and generated detail
text:
By hand
B1. One forward step: x_0 = 2, \sqrt{\bar\alpha} = 0.8, \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha} = 0.6, \varepsilon = -1. (a) Compute x_\tau. (b) If the whole training set is the single value x_0 = 2, which \varepsilon must a perfect denoiser report for this x_\tau? (c) At a later time \sqrt{\bar\alpha} = 0.1. What is left of x_0 in x_\tau, and what does x_\tau look like whatever x_0 was?
B2. Data: x_0 = +1 or -1, equally likely. Noising: x_\tau = 0.6\,x_0 + 0.8\,\varepsilon. You observe x_\tau = 0.5. (a) Which x_0 is more likely? Using the formula from the lecture, the best estimate of x_0 is \tanh(0.6 \cdot 0.5/0.64): compute it. (b) Why is the best estimate not +1? (c) A sampler does not stop at this estimate. What does it do instead, and where do its samples end?
B3. Sampling with few steps. Two blobs of data at -1.2 and +1.2 (in 1D, equally likely). (a) What is the average of the data? Where does a single denoising step from pure noise put every sample? (b) Why do many small steps give samples in the blobs instead?
B4. A prior made of two training images: a cell with one nucleolus and a cell with two. A heavily blurred measurement is equally compatible with both. (a) What does the posterior mean look like? How many nucleoli would a threshold count on it? (b) What do posterior samples look like? What is the probability that a sample shows the wrong count if the truth has one nucleolus? (c) Which of the two images is “better” for the PSNR against the truth, and which looks more like a real cell?
B5. A restoration network with a generative prior was used on 200 blurred images. For each measurement, may you report it from the restored images? (a) the nucleus area; (b) the number of nucleoli per nucleus, where the nucleoli are about the size of the blur; (c) the mean intensity of each cell; (d) the length of thin protrusions. What would you need to check first?
B6. A prior trained only on healthy cells is used to restore images of a mutant whose nuclei are ring-shaped. What will the restored images show, and why is this the most dangerous failure?






Solutions





B1. (a) x_\tau = 0.8 \cdot 2 + 0.6 \cdot (-1) = 1.0. (b) With one training value, x_0 = 2 is known, so \varepsilon = (x_\tau - 0.8 \cdot 2)/0.6 = (1 - 1.6)/0.6 = -1: the true noise. (c) 0.1\,x_0: one tenth of the signal; x_\tau is almost pure noise with variance 1 - 0.01 = 0.99; it looks like \mathcal N(0, 1) for any data.
B2. (a) +1 (the observation is positive). Estimate \tanh(0.469) = 0.44. (b) x_\tau = 0.5 could also come from x_0 = -1 with a positive noise; the best estimate under squared error is the average of +1 and -1 weighted by their probabilities: P(+1 \mid x_\tau) = 0.72, P(-1 \mid x_\tau) = 0.28, average 0.72 - 0.28 = 0.44. (c) It moves a little towards 0.44, adds back some noise, and denoises again at a lower noise level; as the noise shrinks, the estimate is pushed to one of the two values. Its samples end at +1 (about 72 % of the time from this point) or at -1, never at 0.44.
B3. (a) Average 0. One step from pure noise returns the average of all data: every sample lands at 0, between the blobs. (b) Each small step only commits a little; at lower noise levels the denoiser’s average is taken over the data near the current point, which lies in one blob: the samples end in the blobs.
B4. (a) The average of the two images: one nucleolus at full brightness where they share it, plus a half-bright spot where only the second has one; a threshold for “bright” may count 1 (or 0, if the shared one is also blurred). (b) Each sample is one of the two cells (sharp), each with probability 0.5. If the truth has one nucleolus, a sample shows the wrong count with probability 0.5. (c) The mean has the lower error (higher PSNR) on average; a sample looks more like a real cell, but its details are a coin flip.
B5. (a) Probably: the outline is large compared with the blur and is fixed by the data; check on images with ground truth. (b) No: structures of the size of the blur are exactly where the prior decides; the counts would come from the training set. (c) Probably, if the restoration preserves intensities (check: a restoration may sharpen and redistribute intensity); better measure it on the raw image. (d) No, not without validation: thin protrusions are below the resolution; the prior can add or remove them. First: restore images with known truth (synthetic, or high-quality acquisitions), compare the measurements, not only PSNR, and look at the disagreement between samples.
B6. The prior has never seen a ring; the posterior explains the measurement with the closest training cells: normal, filled nuclei. The phenotype you are looking for is “corrected” away, the restored images look healthy and convincing, and nothing in them warns you. A disagreement map may not either, since all samples agree on the wrong answer.




Math questions
B7. (math) Show that n forward steps x_t = \sqrt{1 - \beta_t}\,x_{t-1} + \sqrt{\beta_t}\,\varepsilon_t give x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon with \bar\alpha_t = \prod_{s \le t}(1 - \beta_s), and that x_t \to \mathcal N(0, 1) in distribution if \bar\alpha_t \to 0.
B8. (math) Derive the \tanh of B2: for x_0 = \pm 1 with probability \tfrac12 each and x_\tau = a\,x_0 + b\,\varepsilon, show \mathbb E[x_0 \mid x_\tau] = \tanh(a\,x_\tau/b^2).
B9. (math) Scalar Gaussian prior x \sim \mathcal N(0, 1), measurement y = x + n, n \sim \mathcal N(0, 0.25). Derive the posterior mean and variance. Show that a posterior sample has twice the expected squared error of the posterior mean, and compute both errors.
B10. (math) Prove Tweedie’s formula for a Gaussian prior: x_0 \sim \mathcal N(\mu, s^2), x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha}\,\varepsilon. Compute \nabla\log p(x_t) and check that (x_t + (1 - \bar\alpha)\nabla\log p(x_t))/\sqrt{\bar\alpha} equals the posterior mean of x_0.






Solutions (math)





B7. By induction: suppose x_{t-1} = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\eta, \eta \sim \mathcal N(0, 1) independent of \varepsilon_t. Then x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \beta_t}\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\eta + \sqrt{\beta_t}\,\varepsilon_t; the last two terms are independent Gaussians with total variance (1 - \beta_t)(1 - \bar\alpha_{t-1}) + \beta_t = 1 - \bar\alpha_t. So x_t \mid x_0 \sim \mathcal N(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0, 1 - \bar\alpha_t). If \bar\alpha_t \to 0, the mean \to 0 and the variance \to 1 for every x_0 (and the data have finite variance), so x_t \to \mathcal N(0, 1).
B8. p(x_\tau \mid x_0 = \pm 1) \propto \exp(-(x_\tau \mp a)^2/2b^2). Ratio of posteriors: \frac{P(+1 \mid x_\tau)}{P(-1 \mid x_\tau)} = \exp\!\big(\frac{(x_\tau + a)^2 - (x_\tau - a)^2}{2b^2}\big) = \exp(2ax_\tau/b^2). With u = ax_\tau/b^2: P(+1) = e^{u}/(e^u + e^{-u}), and \mathbb E[x_0] = P(+1) - P(-1) = \tanh u. B2: a = 0.6, b^2 = 0.64, x_\tau = 0.5: \tanh(0.469) = 0.437.
B9. p(x \mid y) \propto \exp(-x^2/2)\exp(-(y - x)^2/0.5): Gaussian with precision 1 + 4 = 5, variance v = 0.2, mean 4y/5 = 0.8y. Mean estimate error: \mathbb E[(0.8y - x)^2 \mid y] = v = 0.2. A sample \tilde x = 0.8y + \sqrt v\,\xi independent of x given y: \tilde x - x = (0.8y - x) + \sqrt v\,\xi, two independent terms each with variance v: error 2v = 0.4.
B10. x_t \sim \mathcal N(\sqrt{\bar\alpha}\mu, \bar\alpha s^2 + 1 - \bar\alpha); write c = \bar\alpha s^2 + 1 - \bar\alpha. \nabla\log p(x_t) = -(x_t - \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\mu)/c. Tweedie: \frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha}}\big(x_t - \frac{(1 - \bar\alpha)(x_t - \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\mu)}{c}\big) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha}}\cdot\frac{\bar\alpha s^2 x_t + (1 - \bar\alpha)\sqrt{\bar\alpha}\mu}{c} = \frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha}s^2x_t + (1 - \bar\alpha)\mu}{c}. The posterior of the linear Gaussian model x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha}x_0 + \text{noise} (as in B9, with gain \sqrt{\bar\alpha} and noise variance 1 - \bar\alpha) has mean \mu + \frac{s^2\sqrt{\bar\alpha}}{\bar\alpha s^2 + 1 - \bar\alpha}(x_t - \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\mu) = \frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha}s^2x_t + (1 - \bar\alpha)\mu}{c}: the same.

title: Exercise: diffusion models and generated detail
text:
Explore: diffusion in 2D
The data are 2D point clouds made of Gaussian blobs (grey), so the exact best denoiser is known at every noise level. Forward: 500 data points melt into noise as \tau goes from 0 to 1; the small plot shows the schedule (signal \sqrt{\bar\alpha}, noise \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha}). Reverse: 500 points (blue) start as pure noise and are denoised step by step; the arrows show where the denoiser pushes at the current noise level; one path is drawn in orange. Choose the number of steps, a stochastic or deterministic sampler, the exact score or a small learned denoiser (trained briefly or long), and a condition with guidance w.



D1. Preset forward: data melts into noise. Read \sqrt{\bar\alpha} and \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha} at \tau = 0.4; check that their squares add to 1. At which \tau can you no longer see the moons? Switch to the linear schedule: earlier or later?
D2. Preset noise in, data out. Where do the samples end? Use back to noise and step: describe the arrows at the start and near the end.
D3. Preset too few steps: between the blobs (2 deterministic steps). Where are the samples, and what fraction is off the data? Increase the steps to 5, 20, 100. Explain with B3.
D4. Preset learned score: the rare blob (the briefly trained network). Which fraction of the samples lands in the rare blob, against 5 % in the data? Switch to learned: long and to the exact score.
D5. Preset perfect score of 20 points: copies. Where do the samples end? Why is this “perfect” denoiser a bad generator?
D6. Presets conditioning on one blob and strong guidance (ring of 8, condition “upper half”, w = 4). Count the samples per blob for w = 0 and w = 4 (the readout lists them from 0°, anticlockwise). Which blobs gain, and why?






Solutions





D1. \sqrt{\bar\alpha} = 0.805, \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha} = 0.594; 0.648 + 0.353 = 1.00. The moons are hard to see from about \tau = 0.6 (cosine schedule: \sqrt{\bar\alpha} = 0.70 at \tau = 0.5, 0.38 at 0.75). The linear schedule removes the signal earlier: its \bar\alpha falls quickly in the first half.
D2. On the two moons: 48 % and 52 % (data 50/50), 0 % off the data. At the start the arrows all point towards the middle of the whole cloud (at high noise the denoiser only knows “the data are somewhere around here”); near the end they point onto the nearest moon, short and local.
D3. The samples lie on a line between the two blobs; 38 % are off the data (each blob still gets 50 %). With more steps the samples move into the blobs: one or two steps return averages (B3), many small steps follow the local structure.
D4. 1 % in the rare blob (data 5 %), 7 % off the data: the briefly trained network has not learned the small, rare blob, so it is almost never generated. With the long-trained network and with the exact score the rare blob gets 6 % (off the data: 1 %), close to the data’s 5 % (500 samples). A model can only generate what it has learned well; rare phenotypes are the first to go.
D5. Every sample lands on one of the 20 training points (100 % within 0.05). The perfect denoiser of a finite set is the training set: it only copies. Generalisation comes from imperfection (smoothing between training examples).
D6. w = 0: 135, 123, 124, 118 in the four upper blobs (0°, 45°, 90°, 135°), none below. w = 4: 55, 195, 195, 55. The blobs at 45° and 90° gain: they are farthest from the lower half, where the condition is most certain. Guidance favours the most typical members of the condition and reduces diversity: the blobs at the border of the condition (0°, 135°) lose most of their samples.

title: Exercise: diffusion models and generated detail
text:
Explore: which details are real?
A 32 \times 32 synthetic cell (truth, which in practice you never have) is measured with blur and noise, or with holes (click the measurement to add or remove a hole). The prior is made of 300 training cells (one nucleus outline of six, 0–2 nucleoli, some with a protrusion, some dividing), each the centre of a narrow Gaussian, so the posterior is computed exactly. Panels: the classical restoration (Wiener, or smooth filling of holes), the posterior mean, four posterior samples, the disagreement (pixel standard deviation over 32 samples) and the training cells the posterior trusts most. Under each image: the number of nuclei and nucleoli and the area found by thresholds, and the PSNR against the truth.



G1. Preset mild blur: everything agrees. Compare the counts of truth, classical, mean and samples. What does the disagreement map show? Which restoration has the best PSNR?
G2. Preset heavy blur: samples invent nucleoli (σ 3.5, noise 0.08). How many nucleoli does the truth have, and how many do the mean, the classical restoration and the 32 samples show? Which has the best PSNR? Where is the disagreement large?
G3. Still on heavy blur, press resample a few times and look at the four samples. Would you count nucleoli on any single sample? On the mean?
G4. Preset prior without dividing cells. What is the truth, and what do the mean and the samples show? Which training cell does the posterior trust? Switch the prior to all kinds.
G5. Preset unusual nucleus: made normal (a ring-shaped nucleus). Compare the truth, the classical restoration, the mean and the samples. What does the disagreement map tell you here?
G6. Preset three nucleoli: one is lost. How many nucleoli do the samples show? Which PSNR is highest, and which count is right?
G7. Preset inpainting: what is in the hole? The hole covers the inside of the nucleus. What do the samples put there? What does the classical filling do?






Solutions





G1. Truth 1 nucleus, 2 nucleoli; classical, mean and all 32 samples also 1/2. The disagreement map is dark (max sd 0.03): all samples agree. Classical 34.2 dB, mean 32.1 dB, first sample 30.2 dB: with mild blur the cautious Wiener filter is already excellent.
G2. Truth 2 nucleoli. Mean: 0 (a smooth bright nucleus: the average of cells with nucleoli in different places), PSNR 30.5 dB. Classical: 1 nucleolus, 25.1 dB. Samples: 10 show 1 nucleolus, 22 show 2; each looks like a sharp, real cell; the first one 24.9 dB. The disagreement (max sd 0.15) is inside the nucleus, where the nucleoli may be. The mean has the best PSNR and the least detail.
G3. Each resample shows cells with nucleoli in different places and in different numbers: the detail comes from the training cells the posterior trusts (32 %, 15 %, 10 %, … of the weight). No single sample can be counted. The mean cannot be counted either (it shows none); the honest answer is “the measurement does not resolve the nucleoli”.
G4. The truth is a dividing cell (2 nuclei). Mean and all samples: 1 nucleus (area 174), PSNR 18.9 dB: the posterior trusts a single training cell with a protrusion (100 %), the closest thing to two touching nuclei that it knows. The classical restoration shows one blurred blob (25.9 dB). With all kinds, the dividing training cells explain the measurement and the division comes back.
G5. The truth is a ring-shaped nucleus (area 114). The classical restoration keeps the measured shape (area 114, 26.7 dB). The mean and the samples show a normal, filled nucleus (area 150), PSNR 26.0 dB: the prior has never seen a ring, so the posterior uses normal cells (the top six training cells get 11 % each). The disagreement map is dark (max sd 0.03): the samples agree on the wrong answer. A low disagreement does not prove correctness when the prior lacks the phenotype.
G6. All 32 samples show 2 nucleoli (truth 3), the mean shows 2 with the best PSNR (30.9 dB), the classical restoration 1 (27.4 dB). The posterior puts 90 % on one training cell with two nucleoli: no training cell has three. The best-PSNR image has the wrong count.
G7. The samples fill the hole with 0, 1 or 2 nucleoli (16, 11 and 5 of 32); the truth has 1. The mean shows a smooth nucleus (0), the best PSNR (31.9 dB). The classical filling interpolates smoothly from the edge of the hole and leaves a dim patch (area 89 instead of 150). Whatever is shown inside the hole is the prior’s guess.

title: Exercise: diffusion models and generated detail
text:
Where this leads
This is the course’s introduction to diffusion models; an elective day on diffusion models goes deeper (score matching, samplers, latent diffusion, diffusion priors for inverse problems). The rules for what may be measured on a restored image return in the unit on images as evidence (bit depth day).

title: Finding objects as boxes
text:
About this lecture
How does a network output “there are 12 cells, here”, when the number is not known in advance?

Boxes: the simplest object description; IoU of two boxes in closed form.
Where candidate boxes come from: anchors (template boxes on a grid) or centre heat maps (peaks = objects).
Every object gets many candidates: non-maximum suppression (NMS) keeps one, and what it gets wrong in a crowd.
How detections are scored: recalled from the evaluation day.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

This unit follows “From masks to objects” (instances/), which previewed NMS for star-convex polygons. The matching of predictions to truth, F1, matching accuracy and average precision are owned by the evaluation day (object-eval/); here they are only readouts. The demo’s detector is simulated (jittered boxes around the true cells, with scores), so the effect of NMS can be seen without any trained network.

title: Finding objects as boxes
text:
Boxes
A box = centre, width, height (4 numbers), plus a class and a score (how sure the detector is).

Enough for counting, tracking, cropping each object for a second network.
Poor for long diagonal objects: a box around a diagonal rod is mostly background (in the demo’s rod: the rod fills 16 % of its box).
A mask per object can be predicted inside each box afterwards.

title: Finding objects as boxes
text:
IoU of two boxes
The evaluation day’s overlap measure, intersection over union: \mathrm{IoU} = |A \cap B| / |A \cup B|. For two axis-aligned boxes the intersection is a box again.

A = [0, 4] \times [0, 4], B = [2, 6] \times [2, 6]: intersection [2, 4] \times [2, 4], area 4; union 16 + 16 - 4 = 28; \mathrm{IoU} = 4/28 = 0.14.
The same 4 \times 4 box shifted by one pixel to the right: 12/20 = 0.6. Shifted by one pixel right and down: 9/23 = 0.39.
For small objects one pixel matters a lot.

title: Finding objects as boxes
section: The math: IoU of boxes in closed form
text:
The math: IoU of boxes in closed form
A = [a_0, a_1] \times [b_0, b_1], B = [c_0, c_1] \times [d_0, d_1]:
w = \max(0, \min(a_1, c_1) - \max(a_0, c_0)), \quad h = \max(0, \min(b_1, d_1) - \max(b_0, d_0)),
\mathrm{IoU}(A, B) = \frac{wh}{|A| + |B| - wh}.

Scale invariant: scaling both boxes by s multiplies every area by s^2; the ratio is unchanged.
1 - \mathrm{IoU} as a training loss gives no gradient when the boxes do not overlap (w = 0 or h = 0 on a whole region): the loss is flat at 1 however far apart they are. Hence the regression losses on the box coordinates (next slides).

title: Finding objects as boxes
text:
Recall: scoring detections
From the evaluation day, unchanged:

Match predictions to true objects one to one at IoU \ge \tau (often \tau = 0.5): TP, FP, FN objects; F1 and matching accuracy TP/(TP + FP + FN).
Rank the scored detections, walk down the list: a precision–recall curve; its area is the average precision (AP). Detection benchmarks often average AP over \tau = 0.5, 0.55, \dots, 0.95.

This unit is about what happens before the evaluation: where the scored boxes come from, and how duplicates are removed.

title: Finding objects as boxes
text:
Where candidates come from: anchors
The network looks at every position of a coarse grid (a feature map, e.g. every 16 pixels; the neural networks day) and guesses there.

At each grid cell: a few anchors, template boxes of preset sizes and shapes (e.g. 1:1, 2:1, 1:2).
For each anchor the network predicts “is there an object?” (a score) and a small correction of the box.
An object is learned only by anchors that overlap it well (IoU \ge 0.5 during training). Objects much smaller, larger or more elongated than every anchor match no anchor and are never learned.

A 4 \times 4 cell and a 10 \times 10 anchor with the same centre: IoU = 16/100 = 0.16: not matched.

title: Finding objects as boxes
section: The math: boxes relative to an anchor
text:
The math: boxes relative to an anchor
Anchor centre (x_a, y_a), size (w_a, h_a); the network predicts
t_x = \frac{x - x_a}{w_a}, \quad t_y = \frac{y - y_a}{h_a}, \quad t_w = \log\frac{w}{w_a}, \quad t_h = \log\frac{h}{h_a}.

Dividing by the anchor size makes the targets the same for small and large objects.
The log: a box twice too wide and one half as wide are equally wrong (\pm\log 2); the predicted width w_a e^{t_w} is always positive; and an error in t_w is a relative error in w.
Training: a cross-entropy for the score of every anchor (most anchors are background, so easy background examples are down-weighted, e.g. by a factor (1 - p)^\gamma, the focal loss), and a squared or absolute error on (t_x, t_y, t_w, t_h) for the matched anchors.

title: Finding objects as boxes
section: Where candidates come from: centre heat maps
text:
Where candidates come from: centre heat maps
Anchor-free: the network outputs a heat map of object centres (a small bump at every centre) and, at every pixel, the size of the box centred there.

Objects = local maxima of the heat map: a pixel that is the largest in its 3 \times 3 (or larger) window and above a threshold.
No preset shapes. Two problems remain: two objects whose centres are too close give one peak; a noisy heat map gives two peaks in one object.
This is the peak picking of the Hough accumulator (the Hough day), applied to a learned map.

title: Finding objects as boxes
section: The math: heat-map targets and peaks
text:
The math: heat-map targets and peaks
Training target for objects with centres c_k:
Y(p) = \max_k \exp\!\Big(-\frac{\|p - c_k\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big),
with \sigma growing with the object size; loss: a pixelwise (focal) cross-entropy.
Peaks: p is a detection if Y(p) = \max_{q \in W(p)} Y(q) over the window W(p) (a grey-level dilation with a square, compared with the map) and Y(p) \ge \theta. A larger window removes noise peaks but also merges close objects.

title: Finding objects as boxes
text:
Many candidates per object
Whatever proposes the boxes, every object gets several overlapping candidates: neighbouring anchors, neighbouring pixels of a peak, jittered guesses.
Greedy non-maximum suppression: sort by score; keep the best box; delete every remaining box with IoU > t with it; repeat with the best remaining box.
Five boxes: b_1 = [0,10]^2 (0.9), b_2 = [1,11] \times [0,10] (0.8), b_3 = [8,18] \times [0,10] (0.7), b_4 = [9,19] \times [1,11] (0.6), b_5 = [20,26]^2 (0.3). Two true cells: under b_1 and under b_3.

title: Finding objects as boxes
text:
The math: greedy NMS

Sort the candidates by score, highest first; K = \emptyset.
Take the first remaining candidate b; add it to K.
Remove every remaining candidate c with \mathrm{IoU}(b, c) > t.
Repeat from 2 until no candidate remains; output K.

At most n rounds, each comparing with up to n boxes: O(n^2) IoUs. The result depends only on the order of the scores and on t. It is not an optimisation of any global criterion; it is a rule. The same rule with polygon IoU prunes the star-convex polygons of the previous unit.

title: Finding objects as boxes
text:
Try it: boxes and suppression




The detector is simulated: 5 jittered boxes per true cell with scores from their IoU, plus 3 false boxes. Tour: “IoU of two boxes”: drag B, watch 4/28 = 0.143 change. “duplicates removed”: sparse image, t = 0.5, 48 candidates → 12 boxes, all 9 cells found (3 FP are the false boxes). Step through: the first kept box removes 4 duplicates. “touching cells”: two palisades of elongated touching cells at ±45°, whose boxes overlap their neighbours by about 0.3. With t = 0.2: 10 boxes, 4 cells have no box left. “threshold too high” (t = 0.75): 46 boxes, 34 false positives (duplicates). Find the best t (about 0.4). Then “diagonal rod”, “small cell: no anchor matches” (anchors: 1 of 5 objects matched) and the two heat-map presets.

title: Finding objects as boxes
text:
What NMS gets wrong

In a crowd of touching cells, the box of a true neighbour overlaps the kept box by more than t: it is deleted (a missed cell). The fix “raise t” lets duplicates of the same cell survive.
One threshold cannot do both when neighbours overlap as much as duplicates do. In the demo’s palisade (neighbour IoU about 0.3): t = 0.2 loses 4 of 12 cells; t = 0.75 keeps 34 duplicates; the best, t = 0.4, still has 3 false positives.
Hence for dense cells the map-based routes of the previous unit are usually preferred over boxes.

title: Finding objects as boxes
text:
Three meanings of “non-maximum suppression”








Where
What is suppressed
Neighbourhood




Canny (the edges day)
gradient values that are not the largest across the edge
the two neighbours along the gradient direction


Hough accumulator (the Hough day)
accumulator cells that are not a local peak
a window in parameter space


Detection (here)
boxes that overlap a better box by more than t
IoU with the kept boxes



A centre heat map’s peak picking is the Hough version; box NMS is a different rule with the same name.

title: Finding objects as boxes
text:
Summary

A box is 4 numbers + score; IoU of boxes has a closed form; poor for diagonal or long objects.
Candidates come from anchors (template boxes: objects that match no anchor are never learned) or from peaks of a centre heat map (no templates; close objects or noise are the risk).
Every object gets many candidates; greedy NMS keeps the best and deletes overlaps above t.
In crowds, one t cannot both remove duplicates and keep touching neighbours.
Scoring (matching, F1, AP) comes from the evaluation day.

title: Quiz: denoising and what you may measure
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Method noise = noisy − denoised; PSNR uses peak 255.

Q1. A camera has a few hot pixels (always 255) in an otherwise good image. Which denoiser removes them without blurring edges, and why does a Gaussian not?






Hint





Which statistic ignores a single extreme value in a window?









Answer





The median: a hot pixel is one extreme value among nine (3 × 3), so the median of the window is a normal value. A Gaussian averages it in, spreading a bright blob over the neighbourhood, and blurs every edge as well.




Q2. A 5 × 5 median filter is applied to an image of 1-pixel-wide filaments. What happens to them?






Hint





How many of the 25 window values belong to the filament?









Answer





They disappear: a straight 1-pixel filament covers only 5 of the 25 window values, far from a majority, so the median is the background. A median removes structures thinner than about half its window.




Q3. Why does the bilateral filter keep an edge between grey levels 50 and 150 when the noise is σn = 5, but fail when σn = 60?






Hint





Compare the edge height with σr and the noise.









Answer





With small noise, σr can be chosen between the noise (5) and the edge (100), say 20: neighbours across the edge differ by 100 and get weight e^{-100^2/800} \approx 0, while noisy neighbours on the same side are averaged. With σn = 60 the noise differences are as large as the edge: a σr small enough to protect the edge also protects the noise, and a σr large enough to average the noise also averages across the edge.




Q4. Non-local means works very well on an image of a regular crystal lattice, and badly on a single small bright particle. Why?






Hint





How many similar patches does each find?









Answer





In a lattice, every patch has many near-identical copies in the search window, so the average over them removes noise without blurring the pattern. A unique particle has no similar patch; the weights go to dissimilar patches (if h is large enough to give any weight), and the particle is averaged away.




Q5. The method noise of a denoiser shows the outlines of all the cells in the image. What does that tell you?






Hint





What should noisy − denoised contain ideally?









Answer





The filter removed signal at the cell boundaries: it blurred the edges. Ideally the method noise is pure noise, with no structure. Choose an edge-preserving filter or a weaker setting.




Q6. After 200 iterations of Richardson–Lucy, a bead looks twice as bright at its peak relative to its neighbour as in the raw image. Is the ratio of their brightness now more accurate?






Hint





Which quantity does RL keep?









Answer





Not necessarily. RL keeps the total intensity (flux) of each object, if integrated over a region larger than the PSF, but moves light into the peak in a way that depends on the object, the noise and the number of iterations. Compare integrated intensities over masks, preferably on the raw image; never peak values after restoration.




Q7. Two images of the same sample were deconvolved, one with 20 and one with 100 iterations. Can you compare the sizes of the objects in them?






Hint





What happens to the FWHM of a small object with the iterations?









Answer





No: sizes of objects near the resolution limit shrink with the iterations, towards a floor set by the method and the noise rather than by the object. Different settings give different sizes for the same object. Process all images with identical settings, and validate sizes with beads or a phantom of known size.




Q8. (math) Show that the median m of x_1, \dots, x_n (n odd) minimises \sum_i |x_i - m|.






Hint





Differentiate where no x_i = m.









Answer





For m not equal to any x_i, \frac{d}{dm}\sum_i|x_i - m| = \#\{x_i < m\} - \#\{x_i > m\}. Below the median there are more values above m than below: the sum decreases as m grows. Above the median it increases. The function is convex and piecewise linear, so its minimum is at the median, where the slope changes sign.

title: Exercise: denoising and what you may measure
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Gaussian
weighted mean of the neighbours by distance; linear


Median
middle value of the sorted window; a rank filter


Bilateral
weights e^{-\lVert p - q\rVert^2/2\sigma_s^2}e^{-(I_p - I_q)^2/2\sigma_r^2}: close and similar


Non-local means
weights e^{-d^2/h^2}, d^2 = mean squared difference of two patches


Method noise
noisy − denoised; should look like pure noise


Flux
total intensity; kept by RL, by roughness-penalised Tikhonov; shrunk slightly by Wiener


Restored image
an estimate: detect on it, measure on the raw image, validate, report the settings

Every window containing the 50 has two 10s: the median is 10 everywhere. The line is erased.

B2. (a) For the 10s: e^0 = 1 (both the centre and the left neighbour). For the 50: e^{-40^2/(2 \cdot 10^2)} = e^{-8} = 0.000335. (b) (10 + 10 + 50 \times 0.000335)/(1 + 1 + 0.000335) = 10.007. The mean is (10 + 10 + 50)/3 = 23.3: the bilateral filter does not average across the step. (c) e^{-1600/(2\sigma_r^2)} = 0.5: \sigma_r^2 = 1600/(2\ln 2) = 1154, \sigma_r = 34.
B3. (a) Median (3 × 3); avoid Gaussian, which spreads each outlier into a blob. (b) Bilateral, or non-local means with a small patch and h; avoid a median larger than the filament (it erases it) and a wide Gaussian (it blurs it into the background). (c) Non-local means: many similar patches; avoid a wide Gaussian. (d) None of the edge-preserving filters works well: the bilateral either keeps the noise or blurs the edges (cartoon); a modest Gaussian or Wiener is the honest choice, or better data.
B4. (a) kept (RL keeps flux; the mask is larger than the PSF); (b) changed (peaks rise with the iterations); (c) kept, approximately (both fluxes are kept); (d) changed (shrinks towards a floor set by the method); (e) changed or unknown (biased when the dip between them is weak; validate); (f) unknown (speckles can add false beads, merged pairs remove some; depends on the threshold and the iterations).
B5. (a) It removed noise only: good. (b) It blurred the edges (removed signal there). (c) It averaged the lattice partly away: the filter is too strong for the texture (or uses too large patches or h).
B6. Wiener’s gain at f = 0 is 1/(1 + 1/\mathrm{SNR}) = 1/1.01 = 0.990: the total intensity drops by 1 %. Tikhonov with the roughness penalty has gain exactly 1 at f = 0: unchanged.




Math questions
B7. (math) Show that the median minimises \sum_i |x_i - m|, while the mean minimises \sum_i (x_i - m)^2. Move one value of B1’s row from 200 to 2000: what happens to the mean and to the median of the window?
B8. (math) Non-local means with patch (2P + 1)^2 and search window (2S + 1)^2 on an n-pixel image. Count the operations of the direct method and of the per-offset method with integral images.
B9. (math) Show that RL keeps the total intensity at every iteration, and that a linear filter multiplies it by its gain at f = 0.






Solutions (math)





B7. \frac{d}{dm}\sum_i(x_i - m)^2 = -2\sum_i(x_i - m) = 0 gives m = \bar x. For the absolute deviations see Q8 of the quiz: the slope \#\{x_i < m\} - \#\{x_i > m\} changes sign at the median. Window (10, 2000, 10): the mean jumps from 73.3 to 673.3; the median stays 10, because the extreme value only counts as “one above”.
B8. Direct: for each of the n pixels and each of the (2S + 1)^2 candidates, a patch distance over (2P + 1)^2 pixels: n(2S + 1)^2(2P + 1)^2 operations. Per offset: for each of the (2S + 1)^2 offsets, the squared differences (n), their integral image (n) and one box sum per pixel (4 lookups): about n(2S + 1)^2 \cdot c with a small constant c, independent of P. For P = 2, S = 5: 25 times fewer.
B9. RL: \sum_j x_j^{\text{new}} = \sum_j x_j\sum_i A_{ij}\frac{y_i}{(A\mathbf x)_i} = \sum_i\frac{y_i}{(A\mathbf x)_i}(A\mathbf x)_i = \sum_i y_i. Linear filter: the total \sum_j x_j is the Fourier coefficient at f = 0; the filter multiplies each coefficient by its gain, so the total becomes W(0)\sum_j g_j (and with H(0) = 1 the data total equals the object total).

title: Exercise: denoising and what you may measure
text:
Explore: denoisers
A 128 × 128 test image (top left a step, top right a ramp crossed by a 1-pixel line, bottom left a dot lattice, bottom right a flat area with one unique spot) or a crop of the micrograph, with Gaussian, Poisson or salt-and-pepper noise (fixed seed). Panels: noisy, denoised, method noise (noisy − denoised; blue negative, red positive) and the error against the truth. Compare with shows a second method (with its own last settings) next to the first. The plot shows the marked row (orange ticks in the noisy image); the readout gives the PSNR (peak 255).



E1. Preset Gaussian blurs the step (σn = 20, σ = 2). Read the PSNR of the noisy and the denoised image. Why is the denoised one worse? Find the σ with the best PSNR.
E2. Preset salt and pepper: median wins. Compare the median (3 × 3) with the Gaussian (σ = 1): PSNR and look.
E3. Preset median eats the thin line. Find the line in the profile (x = 96). What is its value before and after, and what does the PSNR do? Does a 3 × 3 median keep it?
E4. Preset bilateral keeps edges: compare with the Gaussian. Then bilateral at high noise: cartoon: describe the ramp.
E5. Preset non-local means on texture: compare it with the bilateral filter overall and on the lattice. Then non-local means smears the unique spot: what happens to the spot (row 98)?
E6. Preset method noise shows the removed edge (Gaussian σ = 3). What do you see in the method noise? Switch to the bilateral filter (σs 2, σr 30) and compare.
E7. Preset best PSNR, wrong look (micrograph crop, σn = 25). Compare the PSNR of the two methods and the images. Which would you use to show membranes, and what does that say about PSNR?






Solutions





E1. Noisy 22.1 dB, Gaussian σ = 2: 21.6 dB, worse than doing nothing. The dot lattice (period 6 px) is wiped out and every edge blurred: the error there outweighs the noise removed elsewhere. The best Gaussian is σ ≈ 0.6 (25.8 dB): it can only remove a little noise without destroying the lattice.
E2. Median: 15.3 → 22.7 dB, the image is clean with sharp edges. Gaussian σ = 1: 21.9 dB, but every hit pixel becomes a grey smudge.
E3. The line (true value 211 on the ramp at row 32) drops to 133 after the 5 × 5 median: it is erased; PSNR falls from 34.1 dB (noisy, σn = 5) to 21.6 dB. A 3 × 3 median erases it too (133): a 1-pixel line is only 3 of the 9 values.
E4. Bilateral (σs 2, σr 30) at σn = 15: 33.7 dB, edges sharp; Gaussian σ = 2: 21.7 dB. At σn = 50 with σr = 100 the ramp becomes a few flat patches with steps between them (a cartoon), and the lattice turns into blotches; 21.9 dB.
E5. Non-local means (patch 3 × 3, search 15 × 15, h = 25): 29.5 dB against 27.0 dB for the bilateral filter; on the lattice quarter 26.7 dB against 23.2 dB (noisy: 20.1 dB): the dots are kept because every dot has many similar copies. With patch 5 × 5 and h = 45, the unique spot (true value 220) falls to 129: it has no similar patch and is averaged with flat ones.
E6. The method noise shows the step as a bright and dark double line (up to +72 and −58 at the edge), the ramp’s line and the lattice; in flat regions it is plain noise (RMS 9.9, about σn = 10). The bilateral filter’s method noise has almost no edge in it.
E7. Wiener (SNR 3): 23.4 dB; bilateral (σs 1.5, σr 50): 23.3 dB. The Wiener result is blurred overall; the bilateral keeps the membranes and edges sharper but leaves flat patches. The PSNR prefers the blurred one by a hair: it measures pixel-wise error, not whether structures look right. Look at the images (and the method noise), not only at a number.
