is best for both \lambda. Moving a boundary by one pixel costs about 15.5–17.7: the grey level 2 does not belong with 6 and 7, nor 6 with 1.

B2. Grey level 4: 6.25 - 7.5625 = -1.31, negative: joins the inside. Grey level 2: 20.25 - 0.5625 = 19.69: outside. The two squared distances are equal at (c_1 + c_2)/2 = 3.875.
B3. (a) \{4, 5, 7\}: c_1 = 6, c_2 = 1.4, data 0 + 3.2, 4 boundary points: E = 3.2 + 4\lambda. \{4, 5, 6, 7\}: c_1 = 5.25, c_2 = 1, data 6.75 + 0, 2 boundary points: E = 6.75 + 2\lambda. (b) Equal at 3.2 + 4\lambda = 6.75 + 2\lambda: \lambda = 1.775. Above it, filling in is cheaper. (A brute-force check over all 256 labellings confirms that these are the best for \lambda = 0, 1 and for \lambda = 2, 4.) (c) The model cannot tell: only \lambda decides how much boundary a deviating pixel is worth. A small \lambda keeps real gaps and also noise; a large one removes both.
B4. (6.5 + 1.25)/2 = 3.875: above are pixels 4–7 (6, 7, 7, 6), below the rest. The class means are again 6.5 and 1.25: nothing changes. B1(a) is a fixed point of isodata, and the Chan–Vese minimum for \lambda = 0.
B5. \nu\cdotArea adds 0.5 \cdot 4 = 2 to (a) and 0.5 \cdot 5 = 2.5 to (b): (a) stays best. A large \nu makes every inside pixel expensive: the inside shrinks or vanishes (\nu < 0: it grows). Since inside and outside are interchangeable in the data term, \nu mainly matters when one region should be preferred.
B6. (a) Chan–Vese: the means differ by 0.4 and the noise averages out; edge detection on noise with standard deviation 0.3 is hopeless without strong smoothing. (b) Chan–Vese: the means still differ, but the gradient of a 10-pixel blur is small, so g hardly drops and a geodesic contour leaks. (c) Edge-based: the disk’s edge is still a local step, but no single background mean fits: at the bright end the background is as bright as the disk and is labelled inside. (d) Chan–Vese with two phases puts the 0.5 object with whichever mean is closer; with c_2 \approx 0.1 and c_1 \approx 0.7 (the mean of both objects) the threshold is about 0.4, and both objects are found, but the model fits neither object well; more phases or local models are needed. Edge-based methods find both edges.




Math questions
B7. (math) Show that for a fixed curve the minimising c_1, c_2 are the means. Then write E with H(\phi) and derive \phi_t (constant c_1, c_2, data weights \lambda_1, \lambda_2).
B8. (math) Show that at a fixed point of Chan–Vese with \lambda = \nu = 0 (and \lambda_1 = \lambda_2) the split is a threshold at (c_1 + c_2)/2 with c_1, c_2 the class means: the isodata condition. What changes with \lambda_1 \ne \lambda_2?
B9. (math) For a signed distance function \phi of a circle of radius r and a sharp \delta, compute \int\delta(\phi)|\nabla\phi|\,dx\,dy. With \delta_\varepsilon(x) = \varepsilon/(\pi(\varepsilon^2 + x^2)), what is \int\delta_\varepsilon(\phi)\,dx\,dy for a large image (assume r \gg \varepsilon)?






Solutions (math)





B7. \partial/\partial c_1 \sum_{\text{in}}(I - c_1)^2 = -2\sum_{\text{in}}(I - c_1) = 0 gives the mean; the other terms do not contain c_1. Level set form: E = \int\lambda_1(I - c_1)^2(1 - H) + \int\lambda_2(I - c_2)^2H + \lambda\int\delta(\phi)|\nabla\phi| + \nu\int(1 - H). Varying \phi: H' = \delta, and the variation of the length term is -\lambda\delta(\phi)\nabla\cdot(\nabla\phi/|\nabla\phi|) = -\lambda\delta\kappa. So \delta E/\delta\phi = \delta(\phi)[-\lambda_1(I - c_1)^2 + \lambda_2(I - c_2)^2 - \lambda\kappa - \nu] and \phi_t = \delta(\phi)[\lambda\kappa + \nu + \lambda_1(I - c_1)^2 - \lambda_2(I - c_2)^2].
B8. At a fixed point the bracket has the sign that keeps each pixel where it is: inside pixels have (I - c_1)^2 \le (I - c_2)^2, outside pixels the reverse. With c_1 > c_2 this is I \ge (c_1 + c_2)/2 inside: a threshold at the midpoint of the means, where the means are those of the two classes. That is the isodata condition. With \lambda_1 \ne \lambda_2 the dividing grey level is where \lambda_1(I - c_1)^2 = \lambda_2(I - c_2)^2, i.e. |I - c_1|/|I - c_2| = \sqrt{\lambda_2/\lambda_1}: no longer the midpoint; for \lambda_1 > \lambda_2 it moves towards c_1 and the inside shrinks.
B9. In polar coordinates \phi = \rho - r, |\nabla\phi| = 1: \int\delta(\rho - r)\,\rho\,d\rho\,d\theta = 2\pi r, the length. For \delta_\varepsilon: \int_0^\infty\delta_\varepsilon(\rho - r)\,2\pi\rho\,d\rho \approx 2\pi r\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_\varepsilon(s)\,ds = 2\pi r when r \gg \varepsilon, plus a correction from the slowly decaying tails (\delta_\varepsilon \sim \varepsilon/(\pi s^2), so far pixels still contribute: the reason a wide \delta_\varepsilon reaches the whole image).

title: Exercise: Chan–Vese
text:
Explore: regions instead of edges
The left image shows the result: the inside (\phi < 0) tinted, the contour in yellow. Next to it: the image thresholded at (c_1 + c_2)/2 with the current means, \phi itself (blue < 0), the histogram with c_1 (inside), c_2 and the threshold, and the energy E against the iteration. Grey levels run from 0 to 1. Start: a grid of small blobs, one large circle, a circle around the ring, or a small circle in the ring’s hole. Speed: Chan–Vese, or the edge-based flow of the previous unit on the same image, shrink-wrapping from a box near the border (\sigma = 2, k = 8 on the 0–255 scale, balloon -0.3, \varepsilon = 0.3, advection 5; switching restarts). The readout gives the iteration, the means, the energy terms, how many pixels differ from the threshold image, and (test images only) the number of wrong pixels, counting the brighter region as object, also for the threshold. math layer shows the slider for the data weights \lambda_1/\lambda_2.



E1. Preset noise: regions work (noise 0.3, \lambda = 0.2, grid start). Play for 300 iterations. Read c_1, c_2 and the wrong pixels, and compare with the threshold. Does E decrease? Then choose edge-based and play until the front stops moving (about 2000 steps). What happens?
E2. Preset λ = 0 is thresholding (noise 0.15). Watch “≠ threshold” over time (100, 300, 1000 iterations). What does it go towards, and why? Look at the histogram: where is the threshold?
E3. From the default settings (noise 0.15, grid start), compare \lambda = 0.1, 0.5, 1 and 2 (reset each time, 300 iterations). Which objects disappear first? Explain with the quiz’s Q4.
E4. Preset a hole appears (one circle around the ring, \varepsilon = 1). At about which iteration does the ring’s hole open? Repeat with \varepsilon = 0.1 and \varepsilon = 3. Explain.
E5. Preset bad start (a small circle in the ring’s hole, \varepsilon = 0.1). What happens to the curve, and what is the final energy? Compare with the grid start under the same settings.
E6. Preset gradient background. How many pixels are wrong, and which? Compare with the threshold. Switch to edge-based and play until it settles: better or worse?
E7. Preset micrograph (\lambda = 0.05). After 300 iterations, which region is “inside” (look at c_1 and c_2)? What has been separated from what? Try \lambda = 0.3 and \lambda = 1.
E8. (math) Reset the default (noise 0.15, \lambda = 0.1), run 300 iterations, then tick math layer and set \lambda_1/\lambda_2 = 2 without resetting. Run 300 more iterations and watch the area. Then try 0.5. Compare with B8.






Solutions





E1. After 300 iterations: c_1 = 0.698, c_2 = 0.304 (the true levels 0.7 and 0.3), 371 wrong pixels; the threshold at (c_1 + c_2)/2 with the same means has 4312. E drops steeply in the first 30–50 iterations and then levels off (1555). Edge-based (shrink-wrap from a box): the noise makes g small almost everywhere, the front sticks in it and is still one ragged curve after 2000 steps (3966 wrong pixels). Even the plain threshold is not much worse.
E2. “≠ threshold” falls from 172 (100 iterations) to 115 (300) and 72 (1000): towards 0. With \lambda = 0 every pixel eventually moves to the side of the nearer mean, which is the threshold at (c_1 + c_2)/2. The threshold sits at about 0.44, not at 0.5: there are 3.6 times as many background as object pixels, so many noisy background pixels lie above 0.44 and pull the inside mean down, while the outside keeps only the darker part of the background, so its mean drops below 0.3. The two means are 0.62 and 0.26: the isodata fixed point of this histogram, with 2775 wrong pixels after 300 iterations (and about as many for the threshold).
E3. \lambda = 0.1: 183 wrong pixels, all six objects (the ring counts as two curves). \lambda = 0.5: 537, the thin bar and the small disk are gone (4 curves left). \lambda = 1: 712; \lambda = 2: 902, with the remaining objects more rounded. Thin and small objects have the most boundary per area: they go first.
E4. With \varepsilon = 1 the hole’s centre leaves the inside at about iteration 200; with \varepsilon = 3 at about 250; with \varepsilon = 0.1 only at about 350. With a narrow \delta_\varepsilon the pixels in the hole, far from the start curve, are updated very little: the hole must wait until the curve gets near. (The very wide \varepsilon = 3 is not faster here, because it also weakens the update near the curve: \delta_\varepsilon(0) = 1/(\pi\varepsilon).) By iteration 600 with \varepsilon = 1 all objects are found (273 wrong pixels).
E5. The circle contains only background: c_1 \approx c_2, the data hardly push, and the curve shrinks and vanishes within 100 iterations. E = 762.2 (the whole image as one region). From the grid start: 430. A local minimum: Chan–Vese only goes downhill from where it starts.
E6. About 4370 wrong pixels: the brighter right part of the background is labelled as object, because it is closer to the object mean (0.62) than to the background mean (0.23). The threshold makes the same mistake (4383). The edge-based flow only looks at local differences: the slow ramp is no edge, and it wraps the objects with 1463 wrong pixels (4 curves; the blurred disk’s soft edge and the thin bar are the hard parts). Here edges win.
E7. c_1 = 0.81 (inside) and c_2 = 0.43: the inside is the bright background between the cells; the outside is the darker cell, nucleus and cytoplasm together. Chan–Vese splits into the two best-fitting grey levels, and these are “light” and “dark”, not “nucleus” and “the rest”. \lambda = 0.05: 46 curves, a ragged boundary; \lambda = 0.3: 7; \lambda = 1: 3 smooth curves.
E8. With \lambda_1/\lambda_2 = 2 the inside (the objects, c_1 = 0.68) shrinks from 3563 to 3399 pixels; with 0.5 it grows to 3677. A heavier weight on the inside data makes a pixel need to be closer to c_1 to join (B8). (From a grid start, unequal weights can tip the whole image to one side before the means separate; that is why we change them only after convergence here.)

title: Exercise: Chan–Vese
text:
Where this leads
Chan–Vese fits two constants. Real images need more: several phases (more level set functions), colour (a mean vector per region), shading (smoothly varying grey levels), and knowledge of the expected shape (shape priors from the snakes day’s shape models). The same energy on a pixel graph can be minimised globally with graph cuts (graph cuts day). The next day of this elective chain, dynamic programming, finds optimal curves in another way: as minimal paths, exactly and globally, for curves that can be ordered.

title: Edges: Gaussian derivatives and Canny
text:
About this lecture
The filtering unit ended with “smooth first, then differentiate”. Today we make that precise, and build the classic edge detector on top of it (Canny, 1986).

The Gaussian of width σ: one knob for how much to smooth.
Separable: a 2D Gaussian is two 1D passes.
Derivative of a Gaussian: smoothing and differentiating in one kernel.
Gradient magnitude and direction at every pixel.
Canny in four steps: smooth, gradient, non-maximum suppression, hysteresis.
How to choose σ and the two thresholds.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

This unit owns Gaussian derivatives, the gradient direction convention and Canny for the whole course; the Hough elective recalls the edge list from here, the thresholding day recalls hysteresis. Convention throughout: x to the right, y down (rows), Ly = change going down; angles are counted counter-clockwise as seen on the screen.

title: Edges: Gaussian derivatives and Canny
text:
Recall: derivatives amplify noise

From the filtering unit: a derivative is a difference of neighbours, and noise is exactly “a pixel that differs from its neighbours”. Smooth first, then differentiate: one clean bump at the edge.

The synthetic step goes from 50 to 170 with noise of standard deviation 10. The finite difference has noise of about ±7 everywhere and a peak of 60 at the edge; after a Gaussian of σ = 2 the noise almost disappears and the peak is still about 24. The rest of the unit makes the “how much smoothing” precise.

title: Edges: Gaussian derivatives and Canny
text:
The Gaussian of width σ
The bell curve as a kernel: weights \propto e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}, scaled to sum to 1.

σ in pixels sets how far the averaging reaches. About 68 % of the weight lies within ±σ, 99.7 % within ±3σ.
So the kernel can be cut at 3σ to 4σ (our demos: 4σ). σ = 2 needs 2 \cdot 8 + 1 = 17 taps.
The 3×3 Gaussian of the filtering unit ([1\;2\;1]/4 in each direction) is a Gaussian with σ ≈ 0.85.
Larger σ: less noise, but edges get wider, corners round off, and edges that are close together merge.

There is no free lunch: every σ trades noise against detail. Choosing σ is choosing the scale of the edges you want (next unit: scale space).

title: Edges: Gaussian derivatives and Canny
text:
Separability: two 1D passes
A 2D Gaussian is a product: G_\sigma(x, y) = g_\sigma(x)\,g_\sigma(y).

Blur every row with the 1D kernel, then every column of the result. Same answer as the 2D kernel.
Cost per pixel with k taps: k^2 multiplications directly, 2k separably.
σ = 4: k = 33, so 1089 against 66.
Recall Sobel: a smoothing column [1\;2\;1]^\top times a derivative row [-1\;0\;1]. Also separable.


Ask: which other kernels are separable? The box filter (a row of ones times a column of ones), Sobel, all Gaussian derivatives. The Laplacian is not a single outer product, but a sum of two separable kernels (Lxx + Lyy).

title: Edges: Gaussian derivatives and Canny
text:
Derivative of a Gaussian
Smoothing then differentiating is one kernel (convolutions combine): the derivative of the Gaussian.


Shape: a positive and a negative lobe: “right side minus left side, with Gaussian weights”.
In 2D, G_x = a Gaussian derivative along x times a plain Gaussian along y: Sobel’s big brother, with a tunable σ.
Weights are scaled so that a ramp of slope 1 gives exactly 1: the response is the slope of the smoothed image, in grey levels per pixel.

title: Edges: Gaussian derivatives and Canny
section: The math: the derivative of a Gaussian
text:
The math: the derivative of a Gaussian
Smoothing is a convolution, L = G_\sigma * I. Differentiate under the integral:
\partial_x L(x) = \partial_x \int G_\sigma(x - u)\,I(u)\,du = \int \partial_x G_\sigma(x - u)\,I(u)\,du = (\partial_x G_\sigma) * I.

So the slope of the smoothed image is the image filtered with \partial_x G_\sigma; we never need \partial_x I itself (which does not exist for a noisy, sampled image).
With G_\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma}e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}: \quad\partial_x G_\sigma(x) = -\dfrac{x}{\sigma^2}\,G_\sigma(x).
Separability: G_\sigma(x, y) = g_\sigma(x)\,g_\sigma(y), hence \partial_x G_\sigma = g'_\sigma(x)\,g_\sigma(y): a 1D derivative kernel along rows, a 1D Gaussian along columns.
Same for any order: \partial_x^m\partial_y^n G_\sigma = g^{(m)}_\sigma(x)\,g^{(n)}_\sigma(y) (the Hessian unit uses m + n = 2).

title: Edges: Gaussian derivatives and Canny
section: The math: how much noise survives?
text:
The math: how much noise survives?
White noise of variance s^2 (independent pixels) through a kernel w has variance s^2\sum_k w_k^2.

\tfrac12[-1\;0\;1]: s^2(\tfrac14 + \tfrac14) = s^2/2, while a ramp of slope 1 still gives 1.
Derivative of a Gaussian (1D, normalised to slope 1): \sum_k w_k^2 \approx \dfrac{1}{4\sqrt\pi\,\sigma^3}: 0.14 at σ = 1, 0.018 at σ = 2. Doubling σ cuts the noise variance 8-fold.
In frequency (recall the Fourier unit): differentiating multiplies by i\omega, which boosts high frequencies, where white noise lives; the Gaussian multiplies by e^{-\sigma^2\omega^2/2}. The product i\omega\,e^{-\sigma^2\omega^2/2} is a band-pass: it peaks at \omega = 1/\sigma.

title: Edges: Gaussian derivatives and Canny
text:
Try it: smoothing before differentiating




Rows: the signal and its blur; the finite difference of the raw signal; the derivative-of-Gaussian response; the kernel itself, to scale, at the position you click. Tour: “finite difference on noise” (σ = 0.5): rows 2 and 3 look alike, noise everywhere. “σ = 2 cleans it”: the step at x = 48 is a clean bump of about 24 (the step of 120 spread over a Gaussian of σ = 2: 120/(2·√(2π)) ≈ 24). Slide σ up to 8: the two steps at 200 and 206 merge into one bump (“two close steps merge”). “A thin line gives two lobes”: a line is two edges, one up and one down. “Curvature”: order 2, the zero crossing sits exactly at the edge (next unit). The readout gives the taps and the cost of a 2D filter, direct against separable.

title: Edges: Gaussian derivatives and Canny
text:
Gradient: magnitude and direction
At every pixel, the two slopes L_x and L_y of the smoothed image form the gradient \nabla L = (L_x, L_y).

Magnitude \|\nabla L\| = \sqrt{L_x^2 + L_y^2}: the edge strength.
Direction θ: where brightness increases fastest. It points across the edge, from dark to bright.
Convention: x to the right, y down (rows), so L_y is the change going down; θ is counted counter-clockwise on the screen from the x axis.

Example: L_x = 3, L_y = -4 (brighter to the right and up): strength \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5, direction \operatorname{atan2}(4, 3) = 53°.
In the demo the direction is a colour (hue) and the magnitude its brightness.

title: Edges: Gaussian derivatives and Canny
section: The math: why look along the gradient?
text:
The math: why look along the gradient?
The slope of L in a direction given by a unit vector \mathbf u is the directional derivative
\partial_{\mathbf u} L = 
abla L \cdot \mathbf u = \|
abla L\|\cos\angle(
abla L, \mathbf u).

It is largest for \mathbf u \parallel 
abla L, with value \|
abla L\|; it is zero along the edge (\mathbf u \perp 
abla L).
So the profile across an edge is the profile along 
abla L. Non-maximum suppression (next slides) looks for the peak of \|
abla L\| along exactly this line.
With y down, the angle counter-clockwise on the screen is 	heta = \operatorname{atan2}(-L_y, L_x).

title: Edges: Gaussian derivatives and Canny
section: A gradient image is not yet “the edges”
text:
A gradient image is not yet “the edges”



The magnitude is a ridge several pixels wide (about 2σ): where exactly is the edge?
Noise and texture give small magnitudes everywhere.
A low-contrast edge can be weaker than the noise somewhere along it.

Canny’s answer (1986): thin the ridge to one pixel, then keep pixels by a two-threshold rule that uses connectivity.

Canny in four steps

Smooth with G_\sigma.
Gradient: magnitude and direction.
Non-maximum suppression (NMS): keep only the crest of the ridge.
Hysteresis: strong pixels seed, weak pixels survive only if connected to a seed.

title: Edges: Gaussian derivatives and Canny
text:
Non-maximum suppression
Keep a pixel only if its magnitude is at least as large as its two neighbours along the gradient direction.

Round θ to 0°, 45°, 90° or 135°: then the two neighbours are pixels (left/right, the diagonals, up/down).
The ridge becomes one pixel wide, at its crest: the best estimate of where the edge is.

A 3 × 3 piece of a magnitude image (vertical edge, gradient horizontal, so θ = 0°):



4
9
5


5
10
6


6
8
7



Centre: compare 10 with its left and right neighbours, 5 and 6: kept. The pixel left of it (5) would be compared with 10 and something smaller: removed.

title: Edges: Gaussian derivatives and Canny
text:
Hysteresis: two thresholds and connectivity
One threshold cannot work for a faint edge in noise: high enough to remove the noise is too high for the faint part of the edge.

Strong pixels (\ge t_\text{high}) are certainly edges: they are the seeds.
Weak pixels (t_\text{low} \le value < t_\text{high}) are kept only if they are connected (through other weak or strong pixels, 8 neighbours) to a seed.
Everything below t_\text{low} goes.

Picture it as a flood: start at the seeds and grow, one ring of neighbours at a time, through pixels above t_\text{low}. Faint stretches of a real edge hang on to its strong parts; isolated noise has nothing to hang on to.
The same idea comes back on the thresholding day, for faint filaments in any image.

title: Edges: Gaussian derivatives and Canny
section: Try it: Canny step by step
text:
Try it: Canny step by step




Synthetic 128 × 128 scene with noise 12: a rectangle, a disc, a staircase (two upward steps 4 pixels apart), a T-junction, and on the right a faint rectangle whose contrast fades from 45 (top) to 8 (bottom). Tabs show each stage; click a pixel to see its 3 × 3 magnitudes, the two neighbours NMS compares (cyan) and the verdict. Tour: “hysteresis closes the gap”: seeds only (red); press “grow 1 ring” a few times, then “play”: the flood creeps down the faint edge (pixel (96, 100) joins at ring 34). Default thresholds 3 and 10: 824 seeds, 338 weak pixels of which 128 are kept, 952 edge pixels. “One threshold” (10 and 10): only 824 pixels, the faint edge mostly gone; set both to 3: 1162 pixels, noise chains appear. “NMS thins the ridge”: the magnitude tab, pixel (46, 30): 20.99 against its neighbour 32.38: removed. “σ too small” (0.7): 4755 edge pixels, mostly noise. “σ too large” (4): the staircase’s two steps merge into one edge and the corners round off.

title: Edges: Gaussian derivatives and Canny
section: The math: Canny’s criteria, sub-pixel NMS
text:
The math: Canny’s criteria, sub-pixel NMS
Canny asked for the filter that best finds a step edge in white noise, with three criteria:

Good detection: high signal-to-noise ratio at the edge.
Good localisation: the response peaks close to the true edge.
One response per edge: few spurious maxima nearby.

Maximising the product of the first two under the third gives a filter that is very close to the derivative of a Gaussian (within about 20 % of the optimum), which is why it is used.
Sub-pixel NMS: instead of rounding θ, compare \|\nabla L\|(\mathbf p) with the magnitude interpolated bilinearly (images unit) at \mathbf p \pm \nabla L / \|\nabla L\|. Fitting a parabola through the three values even gives the edge position to a fraction of a pixel.

title: Edges: Gaussian derivatives and Canny
text:
Choosing σ and the thresholds







If …
you see …




σ too small
noise edges, ragged contours


σ too large
corners cut, close edges merge, T-junctions break, small objects vanish


t_\text{high} too high
gaps: whole faint edges lost


t_\text{low} too low
noise chains attached to real edges




Rule of thumb: t_\text{high}/t_\text{low} \approx 2 to 3.
The thresholds are in units of slope (grey levels per pixel) and depend on σ: larger σ, smaller magnitudes.
Image libraries call the whole pipeline “Canny”.

title: Edges: Gaussian derivatives and Canny
text:
Where this leads

Hough transform (detection elective): every edge pixel, with its direction θ, votes for the lines and circles it could belong to. Canny’s output is the edge list \{x, y, \theta, \text{strength}\}.
Morphological gradient (morphology day): dilation minus erosion, an edge strength without derivatives.
Snakes (curves elective): the edge strength is the force that pulls a contour onto the boundary.
Next unit: what “the right σ” means when an image has structures of many sizes: scale space.

title: Edges: Gaussian derivatives and Canny
text:
Summary

Smooth with a Gaussian of width σ, then differentiate: one kernel, the derivative of a Gaussian; separable, so cheap.
Gradient: magnitude = edge strength, direction = across the edge (counter-clockwise on the screen, y down).
Canny: smooth, gradient, non-maximum suppression (one-pixel crest along the gradient), hysteresis (strong seeds, weak pixels kept if connected).
σ trades noise against detail; t_\text{high} against gaps, t_\text{low} against noise chains.

title: Quiz: camera noise, SNR and PSNR
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A pixel collects on average 2500 photo-electrons. What is the shot noise, and what is the best possible SNR? How much more light would you need for twice the SNR?






Answer





Shot noise \sqrt{2500} = 50 electrons, so SNR = 2500/50 = 50. SNR grows as \sqrt N, so doubling it needs 4 times as much light (10 000 electrons, noise 100, SNR 100).




Q2. A camera has a full well of 10 000 electrons and a read noise of 10 electrons. Its manufacturer offers a 16-bit version. Is that useful?






Hint





Compare the full well with the read noise: how many distinguishable levels are there?









Answer





The dynamic range is 10\,000/10 = 1000 : 1, about 10 bits. A 16-bit ADC has a step of 10\,000/65\,535 \approx 0.15 electrons, so the read noise covers about 66 ADU: the lowest 6 bits only record noise. A 10- or 12-bit ADC would carry the same information. The 16-bit file is not wrong, just larger than it needs to be.




Q3. A camera with an 8-bit ADC has a gain of 118 electrons per ADU, so every reading below 59 electrons is stored as 0. It images a faint object of 20 electrons on a background of 5 electrons (read noise 1.5 electrons). What will you see?






Answer





Nothing: both are stored as 0. The object’s noise is only about \sqrt{20 + 1.5^2} \approx 4.7 electrons, far too small to push a reading of 20 past 59, so object and background give the same number in every pixel. The information is lost at the ADC and no later processing brings it back. With a smaller gain (more bits), the step would be below the noise, the noise would act as a dither, and averaging pixels or frames would recover the difference.




Q4. In a fluorescence image, is the noise in a bright nucleus larger or smaller than in the dark background, in electrons? And relative to the signal?






Answer





Larger in electrons: shot noise is \sqrt N, so more signal means more noise (signal-dependent noise). Smaller relative to the signal: the SNR \sqrt N grows with the light. A model with one Gaussian \sigma_n for the whole image ignores this.




Q5. Two denoising methods give PSNRs of 31 dB and 37 dB on the same 8-bit image. By what factor do their mean squared errors differ? And their RMS errors?






Hint





PSNR is 10\log_{10} of a ratio of squared quantities.









Answer





6 dB is a factor 10^{0.6} \approx 4 in MSE, so a factor of about 2 in RMS error. (Each 6 dB halves the RMS error.)




Q6. Why is a PSNR meaningless without the peak value, and what else does it not tell you?






Answer





PSNR = 10\log_{10}(\text{peak}^2/\text{MSE}): the same errors give a higher number with a larger peak (a 12-bit image scored with the 16-bit peak gains 24 dB). It also compares pixels one by one: it does not say where the errors are, or whether they form structure (bands, blocks) that the eye notices. Two images with the same PSNR can look very different.

title: Exercise: camera noise, SNR and PSNR
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute shot noise and the SNR of a pixel, and what averaging frames gains,
judge from a camera’s full well, read noise and ADC bits how many bits carry information,
say when the additive Gaussian noise model is reasonable,
compute a PSNR, and explain why the peak must be stated.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the interactive part. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: camera noise, SNR and PSNR
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute shot noise and the SNR of a pixel, and what averaging frames gains,
judge from a camera’s full well, read noise and ADC bits how many bits carry information,
say when the additive Gaussian noise model is reasonable,

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the interactive part. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: camera noise, SNR and PSNR
text:
By hand
B1. A camera has a full well of 15 000 electrons, a read noise of 3 electrons, and a 12-bit ADC whose range is matched to the full well. (a) What is the gain (electrons per ADU)? (b) What is the dynamic range, as a ratio, in dB (20\log_{10}) and in bits? (c) Is 12 bits enough? Compare one ADU with the read noise.
B2. One pixel collects on average 400 electrons, another 40 000. Give the shot noise and the SNR of each. You average 4 frames of the dim pixel: what happens to its SNR, and why?
B3. Noise model. For each case, is “additive Gaussian noise with one \sigma_n for the whole image” a reasonable model? (a) A dark-field image: almost all pixels near 5 electrons, read noise 3 electrons. (b) A fluorescence image with a background of 50 electrons and nuclei of 20 000 electrons. (c) A photo saved as a strongly compressed JPEG.
B4. An 8-bit image is corrupted by Gaussian noise with \sigma_n = 5 grey levels. (a) What are the MSE and the PSNR (peak 255)? (b) A denoiser halves the noise SD. What is the new PSNR, and by how many dB did it improve?
B5. A 12-bit camera image (values 0…4095) has noise of 80 ADU; it is saved in a 16-bit file. One paper reports its PSNR with peak 4095, another with peak 65 535. Compute both. Which one is right?
B6. The dim pixel of B2 (400 electrons) also has 3 electrons of read noise. What is its SNR in one frame? How many frames must you average to reach an SNR of at least 50?






Solutions





B1. (a) g = 15\,000 / 4095 \approx 3.66 electrons per ADU. (b) 15\,000/3 = 5000 : 1, which is 20\log_{10}5000 \approx 74.0 dB, or \log_2 5000 \approx 12.3 bits. (c) Just about. One ADU (3.66 electrons) is a little larger than the read noise (3 electrons), so the quantisation noise 3.66/\sqrt{12} \approx 1.06 electrons is not negligible. Added in variance it raises the dark noise from 3 to \sqrt{3^2 + 1.06^2} \approx 3.18 electrons, about 6 % more. A 13-bit ADC would make one ADU smaller than the read noise.
B2. Shot noise \sqrt{400} = 20 and \sqrt{40\,000} = 200 electrons; SNR 400/20 = 20 and 40\,000/200 = 200. 100 times more light gives 10 times the SNR. Averaging 4 frames of the dim pixel is like collecting 4 times the light (1600 electrons, noise 40): the SNR doubles, to 40. Averaging only helps because the noise differs from frame to frame.
B3. (a) Reasonable: read noise is close to Gaussian and, at a nearly constant 5 electrons, the shot noise (\sqrt5 \approx 2.2) is about the same everywhere; total \sigma_n \approx \sqrt{5 + 9} \approx 3.7 electrons. (b) Not with one \sigma_n: the shot noise is about \sqrt{50} \approx 7 electrons in the background and \sqrt{20\,000} \approx 141 in the nuclei. Gaussian within each region, but with a signal-dependent \sigma_n. (c) No: compression errors depend on the image content and are correlated between neighbouring pixels (blocks), not independent.
B4. (a) MSE = \sigma_n^2 = 25, PSNR = 10\log_{10}(255^2/25) = 34.2 dB. (b) \sigma_n = 2.5: MSE 6.25, PSNR = 40.2 dB, an improvement of 20\log_{10}2 = 6.0 dB.
B5. Peak 4095: 10\log_{10}(4095^2/80^2) = 34.2 dB. Peak 65 535: 58.3 dB, 24.1 dB more for the same image. The peak should be the largest value the data can take, 4095 here; the container (16-bit file) does not matter. Only PSNRs computed with the same peak can be compared.
B6. Noise \sqrt{400 + 3^2} = \sqrt{409} \approx 20.2 electrons, SNR = 400/20.2 \approx 19.8 (25.9 dB), a little below the pure shot-noise value 20. Averaging n frames multiplies the SNR by \sqrt n: 19.8\sqrt n \ge 50 needs n \ge 6.4, so 7 frames.




Math questions
B7. (math) With shot noise, read noise \sigma_r and quantisation (gain g) independent, the total noise is \sigma^2 = S + \sigma_r^2 + g^2/12. For the camera of B1, compute \sigma at S = 100 electrons. Above which signal does shot noise dominate the read noise? Show that the best possible SNR is \sqrt{N_\text{max}} (ignore read and quantisation noise at the full well).
B8. (math) Show that rounding to b bits (step 1 on the scale 0 \dots 2^b - 1, error uniform) gives \text{PSNR} = 20\log_{10}(2^b - 1) + 10\log_{10}12, and evaluate it for b = 4 and b = 8.
B9. (math) K_1, \dots, K_n are independent Poisson counts with mean N. Show that their average has mean N and variance N/n, and express the gain in SNR in dB.






Solutions (math)





B7. \sigma = \sqrt{100 + 9 + 1.06^2} \approx 10.5 electrons. Shot noise exceeds read noise when \sqrt S > \sigma_r, i.e. S > \sigma_r^2 = 9 electrons. At the full well the noise is \sqrt{N_\text{max}}, so \text{SNR} = N_\text{max}/\sqrt{N_\text{max}} = \sqrt{N_\text{max}}: about 122 for 15 000 electrons.
B8. The error is uniform on [-\tfrac12, \tfrac12], so MSE = 1/12 (quantisation unit). PSNR = 10\log_{10}\big((2^b - 1)^2 \cdot 12\big) = 20\log_{10}(2^b - 1) + 10\log_{10}12. For b = 4: 23.52 + 10.79 = 34.3 dB; for b = 8: 48.13 + 10.79 = 58.9 dB.
B9. \mathbb E[\bar K] = \frac1n\sum\mathbb E[K_i] = N; by independence \operatorname{Var}(\bar K) = \frac1{n^2}\sum\operatorname{Var}(K_i) = \frac{nN}{n^2} = \frac Nn. The SNR is N/\sqrt{N/n} = \sqrt{nN}, \sqrt n times that of one frame: 20\log_{10}\sqrt n = 10\log_{10}n dB (6.0 dB for 4 frames).

title: Exercise: camera noise, SNR and PSNR
text:
Explore
A simulated camera images the micrograph. The plot shows noise against signal, in electrons: shot noise, read noise, quantisation noise, their total, and points measured on simulated flat patches.



E1. Preset sCMOS 16 bit. How large is one ADU in electrons, and the quantisation noise? Which noise source dominates in the dark, and which in the bright? Do the measured points follow the model?
E2. Same, 8-bit ADC. What happens to the gain and the quantisation noise? Why are the measured points for dark patches drawn as red triangles (measured noise 0)? Is zero noise good news here?
E3. Compare low light, 8 bit and low light, 12 bit: how many different ADU values does the image use, and what do you see?
E4. Noisy, 16-bit ADC: how many ADU is the read noise? How many bits does the readout say are needed? What do the other bits store?






Solutions





E1. One ADU is 30\,000/65\,535 \approx 0.46 electrons, and the quantisation noise 0.13 electrons, far below the read noise of 1.5. In the dark the read noise dominates (the flat blue line), above a few electrons the shot noise \sqrt S takes over. The points sit on the total curve (e.g. 9.89 measured against 10.11 predicted at 100 electrons). The last point, at the full well, falls below: saturated pixels are all equal, so they have no noise left.
E2. One ADU is now about 118 electrons and the quantisation noise 34 electrons, far above the read noise. In a dark flat patch the true noise (a few electrons) is much smaller than one ADU, so every pixel rounds to the same number: the measured spread is 0. That is not good news. The signal differences below one ADU are not noisy, they are gone. The model g/\sqrt{12} also fails at 1000 electrons (measured about 59, predicted 46): it assumes the signal varies over many steps.
E3. 8 bits: only 4 different values in the image (the brightest pixel is 2.6 ADU), so the cell is a few flat patches. 12 bits: 48 values (brightest 41 ADU); the cell is recognisable, and noisy. In dim light the ADC’s step, not the sensor, decides what survives.
E4. The read noise is 10 electrons and one ADU is 10\,000/65\,535 \approx 0.15 electrons, so the read noise is about 66 ADU, around 2^6. The readout says 10 bits would do (\log_2 1000 \approx 10). The lowest ~6 bits of every pixel record read noise very precisely.

title: Exercise: camera noise, SNR and PSNR
text:
Where this leads
The noise model here, Poisson shot noise plus Gaussian read noise, and the SNR and PSNR defined here are used whenever the course measures noise: denoising with smoothness priors and wavelets, reconstruction of CT images, compression, and choosing exposure times in quantitative microscopy. The next unit is about storing and displaying the 12- and 16-bit numbers such cameras produce.

title: Box filters and local statistics
text:
About this lecture
Last unit: the integral image gives the sum over any rectangle from four lookups. Now we ask for it at every pixel.

Box filters of any size at the same cost per pixel, and four ways to compute them.
Repeated boxes look like a Gaussian: smoothing of any width at constant cost.
Local mean and standard deviation from two tables, and local contrast normalisation.
Numbers that get too big: how many bits the table needs, float32 rounding, and the trap in “mean of squares minus square of mean”.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Recalled, not re-taught: the box blur and border rules from the filtering unit (day 1); integer types, wrap-around, float32 and cancellation from the bit-depth day (day 3); the Gaussian from the edges day. The local thresholds that use the same mean and SD maps belong to the thresholding day.

title: Box filters and local statistics
text:
The box filter, recalled
From the filtering unit: the box blur replaces each pixel by the mean of the k \times k window around it (kernel “all ones \div\, k^2”).
Four ways to compute it, for a window of width k:








method
idea
additions per pixel




direct
add the k^2 pixels
k^2 - 1


separable
box along rows, then along columns
2(k-1)


running sum
slide along a row: add the pixel entering, subtract the one leaving; then the same down columns
4


integral image
build the table (3), then four lookups (3)
6



k = 51: 2600, 100, 4 and 6 additions per pixel.

title: Box filters and local statistics
section: Why the integral image wins anyway
text:
Why the integral image wins anyway
The running sum is a little cheaper, but only for one fixed square window. The integral image is built once and then gives:

every window size at the same cost: all scales of a feature stack from one table,
windows that change from pixel to pixel (larger in flat regions, smaller near edges),
rectangles of any shape, at any position, in any order (a detector asks for them at random),
a natural border rule: clip the window to the image and divide by the number of pixels actually inside. No dark frame (unlike padding with zeros), no copied edge pixels.

title: Box filters and local statistics
section: Try it: four ways to blur
text:
Try it: four ways to blur




Left: the micrograph blurred with a k × k box (window clipped at the border). Middle: additions per pixel against k, log scale; the dots are the current k. The readout times all four methods on this computer (median of three runs, after the slider rests; direct is skipped above k = 51). Tour: preset “direct at k = 51”: direct is two orders of magnitude slower than the others. Move k: red and orange grow, green and blue stay flat. “integral image: flat line” at k = 101. Point out that the timings are machine-dependent, the counts are not, and that all four images are identical.

title: Box filters and local statistics
text:
Repeated boxes look Gaussian


Box ∗ box = a triangle (width 3: weights 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, divided by 9). Three boxes: already a smooth bell.
Each pass adds the box’s variance; the shape tends to a Gaussian (the central limit theorem: a sum of independent uniform shifts).
Three passes are usually enough. In 2D, the square box becomes nearly round after 2–3 passes.
So: a Gaussian blur of any width at constant cost per pixel (3 \times 6 additions).

title: Box filters and local statistics
section: The math: variance of repeated boxes
text:
The math: variance of repeated boxes
A box of odd width k is the uniform distribution on \{-\tfrac{k-1}{2}, \dots, \tfrac{k-1}{2}\}: mean 0, variance \sigma_1^2 = \frac1k\sum_{j=-(k-1)/2}^{(k-1)/2} j^2 = \frac{k^2 - 1}{12}.
Convolving filters = adding independent random shifts, so variances add: n passes have \sigma^2 = n\,\frac{k^2-1}{12}. To approximate a Gaussian of a given \sigma with n boxes, choose k \approx \sqrt{12\sigma^2/n + 1} (Wells, 1986); e.g. \sigma = 3, n = 3: k \approx 6.1.
Fourier picture: the box’s transform is a sinc, n passes give \text{sinc}^n: close to a Gaussian near zero, with side lobes that shrink with n (the edges day’s Gaussian has none).

title: Box filters and local statistics
text:
Try it: repeated boxes



Tab “repeated boxes”. Bars: the 1D weights of n passes of a width-k box; red: the Gaussian with the same variance. Lower left: the 2D weights in 8 bands, with a red contour of that Gaussian; upper left: the points image after n passes (each point becomes the 2D weights). Tour: “one box: square artefacts”: each point becomes a square, difference to the Gaussian 45 %. n = 2: a pyramid (tent), 8 %. “three boxes”: 6 %, the bands are nearly circles. n = 4: 3.5 %.

title: Box filters and local statistics
section: Local mean and local standard deviation

title: Box filters and local statistics
text:
The math: the variance identity
For the n values in a window, with mean m = \frac1n\sum I: s^2 = \frac1n\sum (I - m)^2 = \frac1n\sum I^2 - 2m\cdot\frac1n\sum I + m^2 = \overline{I^2} - m^2.
Shift invariance: for any constant c, \operatorname{Var}(I - c) = \operatorname{Var}(I), so the tables can be built from I - c instead of I (useful below).
Exact two-pass alternative (no tables): compute m first, then \frac1n\sum (I - m)^2. It never goes negative, but costs O(k^2) per pixel.

title: Box filters and local statistics
text:
Local contrast normalisation
\frac{I - m}{s + \varepsilon}

Subtract the local mean, divide by the local standard deviation: a faint region and a bright, contrasty region look alike.
The window size decides what counts as “local”: larger than the objects, smaller than the illumination changes.
\varepsilon stops the noise in flat background from being blown up (there s is just the noise level).
The same two maps m and s give the local thresholds of Niblack and Sauvola: the thresholding day. The detector of unit 4 normalises every window by its s in the same way.

title: Box filters and local statistics
text:
Try it: local statistics



Synthetic image: six “cells” with contrasts 6 to 60 grey levels on a gradient, noise SD 3. Panels: input (orange line = the profile row; click to move it), local mean, local SD, contrast-normalised. Right: the profile with I, m and the band m ± s. Tour: “normalisation equalises the cells”: in the normalised image the faint cells look as strong as the bright ones. Window r: small windows make s follow the noise; large ones blur m. “ε = 0”: the flat background turns into amplified noise. “micrograph”: the SD map highlights membranes and texture.

title: Box filters and local statistics
text:
Numbers that get too big
The last table entry is the sum of the whole image. Bits needed: bit depth + \log_2(number of pixels).

8-bit, 1024 \times 1024: 8 + 20 = 28 bits; fits a 32-bit integer. The table of I^2: 16 + 20 = 36 bits; does not.
16-bit, 2048 \times 2048: 16 + 22 = 38 bits already for I.
Wrap-around can be fine (bit-depth day: unsigned integers wrap modulo 2^{32}): the table entries are wrong, but D - B - C + A is still the right rectangle sum as long as the rectangle’s sum fits in 32 bits. The errors cancel.
float32 stores integers exactly only up to 2^{24} \approx 1.7 \cdot 10^7. The sum of a 256 \times 256 8-bit image (\le 16\,711\,680) just fits; 512 \times 512 does not. Far from the top-left corner the entries are large and a small difference of two large rounded numbers is noisy.

title: Box filters and local statistics
text:
The cancellation trap
s^2 = \overline{I^2} - m^2 subtracts two large, nearly equal numbers (bit-depth day: catastrophic cancellation).

Bright, flat region: values 199, 200, 201. \overline{I^2} = 40\,000.67, m^2 = 40\,000: the answer, 0.67, is in the fifth digit.
With 4 significant digits: 40\,000 - 40\,000 = 0. With float32 tables over a large image: wrong, even negative variances.
Fixes:

subtract an offset (the global mean or mid-grey) before building the tables: the variance does not change, the numbers get small;
integer tables (exact, wrap-around allowed);
float64.

title: Box filters and local statistics
text:
Try it: precision



Tab “precision”: the same image plus 200 (bright), window 7 × 7. Panels: the SD from tables in the chosen number type, the exact SD, and the error (red = negative variance). Tour: float32, +200: largest error 22.7, 10 611 negative variances; errors grow towards the bottom right, where the table entries are largest. “subtract the offset”: largest error 1.32, none negative. Then 1024 × 1024 with the offset: errors again (the sum of squares exceeds 2^24 even after the shift). “32-bit integers”: the stored last entry has wrapped (4.26e9 instead of 1.16e11), yet the SD is exact.

title: Box filters and local statistics
section: The math: why wrapped sums are right
text:
The math: why wrapped sums are right
Unsigned 32-bit arithmetic computes everything modulo 2^{32}. Each stored entry is \tilde S = S \bmod 2^{32}, and \tilde D - \tilde B - \tilde C + \tilde A \equiv D - B - C + A \pmod{2^{32}}. If the true rectangle sum R = D - B - C + A satisfies 0 \le R < 2^{32}, the residue is R.
Rough float error bound: each float32 entry carries a rounding error of about 2^{-24}\times its size. An entry at (x, y) is about x\,y\,\bar I, so the error of a window mean is about 2^{-24}\,x\,y\,\bar I / k^2: it grows with the distance from the origin and shrinks with the window area. The variance error is that of \overline{I^2}, about 2^{-24}\,x\,y\,\overline{I^2}/k^2, compared with s^2 itself.

title: Box filters and local statistics
text:
Summary

Box filters of any size cost 6 additions per pixel with the integral image (direct: k^2 - 1); any window size, shape or position, with a natural border rule.
Repeated boxes ≈ Gaussian: variances add, n(k^2 - 1)/12; three passes are usually enough.
Two tables (I and I^2) give the local mean and standard deviation anywhere; (I - m)/(s + \varepsilon) normalises contrast.
The table needs bit depth + \log_2(pixels) bits; wrapped integer sums are still right; float32 rounds above 2^{24}.
\overline{I^2} - m^2 cancels: subtract an offset, or use integers or float64.

title: Quiz: learning
text:
Short questions on losses, gradient descent, backpropagation and overfitting. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Cross-entropy is -\ln p_\text{true class}; a gradient step is \mathbf w \leftarrow \mathbf w - \eta\nabla\mathcal L.

Q1. A network gives the true class probability 0.8 for one image and 0.05 for another. What is the cross-entropy of each?






Hint





-\ln p.









Answer





-\ln 0.8 = 0.22 and -\ln 0.05 = 3.00. The confident mistake costs about 13 times as much.




Q2. You train with full-batch gradient descent and the loss grows from step to step. What do you change first?






Hint





What sets the length of each step?









Answer





Lower the learning rate \eta: each step overshoots the valley and lands higher than it started.




Q3. 50,000 training images, mini-batches of 100. How many gradient steps is one epoch? What changes if you use batches of 10?






Hint





An epoch is one pass over all images.









Answer





500 steps. With batches of 10: 5,000 steps per epoch, each cheaper but noisier (the gradient estimate from 10 images varies more).




Q4. In the backward pass, a ReLU unit had z = -2 in the forward pass. What gradient does it pass back to its weights?






Hint





The local derivative of \max(0, z) at z < 0.









Answer





Zero: the ReLU’s local derivative is 0 for z < 0, so every gradient behind it is multiplied by 0. For this example the unit’s weights do not change. If that holds for every training example, the unit is dead.




Q5. Why is backpropagation so much cheaper than estimating each \partial\mathcal L/\partial w by changing w a little and recomputing the loss?






Hint





Count forward passes for a network with a million weights.









Answer





Finite differences need one extra forward pass per weight: a million forward passes. Backpropagation gets all million gradients from one forward and one backward pass, at about twice the cost of a forward pass, because it reuses the gradient of each node for everything behind it.




Q6. The training loss keeps falling, the validation loss has been rising for 50 epochs. What is happening, and which weights do you keep?






Hint





Learning curves.









Answer





The network is overfitting: it memorises the training examples, and gets worse on new ones. Keep the weights from the epoch with the lowest validation loss (early stopping), or regularise and train again.




Q7. Name three ways to reduce overfitting.






Hint





Penalty, noise, data.









Answer





Weight decay (a penalty on large weights), dropout (silence random units during training), more data or data augmentation. Also: a smaller network, early stopping.




Q8. (math) For softmax followed by cross-entropy, what is \partial\mathcal L/\partial z_k? Evaluate it for \mathbf p = (0.7, 0.2, 0.1) when the true class is the second.






Hint





Predicted minus wanted.









Answer





\partial\mathcal L/\partial z_k = p_k - y_k: (0.7, 0.2 - 1, 0.1) = (0.7, -0.8, 0.1). A step against it lowers z_1 and z_3 and raises z_2.

title: Exercise: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Loss \mathcal L
squared error (\hat y - y)^2 for numbers; cross-entropy -\ln p_\text{true class} for classes; averaged over the examples


Gradient step
w \leftarrow w - \eta\,\partial\mathcal L/\partial w for every weight; \eta = learning rate


Mini-batch, epoch
the gradient is computed on a random batch of examples; an epoch is one pass over all of them


Forward pass
compute every node’s value, from the input to the loss


Backward pass
compute \partial\mathcal L/\partial(\text{node}) from the loss back: each node’s gradient = sum over the nodes it feeds of (their gradient × the local derivative)


Local derivatives
z = wx + b: \partial z/\partial w = x, \partial z/\partial x = w, \partial z/\partial b = 1; ReLU: 1 if z > 0, else 0; (\hat y - y)^2: 2(\hat y - y)


Learning curves
training and validation loss against the training step
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Exercise: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
By hand
B1. Cross-entropy. (a) The network gives the true class the probability 0.9, 0.5 and 0.01. Compute the loss for each. (b) Three classes, probabilities (0.7, 0.2, 0.1). What is the loss if the true class is the first? The second?
B2. One weight, one data point: \mathcal L(w) = (y - wx)^2 with x = 2, y = 3 (the example of the previous unit). Start at w = 0 and take two steps with \eta = 0.1. Give w and \mathcal L after each step.
B3. Backpropagation by hand. The network z = w_1x + b_1, h = \text{ReLU}(z), \hat y = w_2h + b_2, \mathcal L = (\hat y - y)^2, with x = 2, y = 1, w_1 = 0.5, b_1 = 0, w_2 = 1.5, b_2 = 0. (a) Forward: compute z, h, \hat y and \mathcal L. (b) Backward: compute \partial\mathcal L/\partial\hat y, then \partial\mathcal L/\partial w_2, \partial\mathcal L/\partial b_2, \partial\mathcal L/\partial h, \partial\mathcal L/\partial z, \partial\mathcal L/\partial w_1 and \partial\mathcal L/\partial b_1. (c) Update all four weights with \eta = 0.1 and compute the new loss. Did it go down? Repeat with \eta = 0.05. (d) Now x = -1 (the rest unchanged). Forward and backward again. Which gradients are zero, and why? What does one update with \eta = 0.1 change?
B4. Learning curves of a small network (8 + 8 hidden units, 30 training and 30 validation points):


Which curve is which, and how can you tell without the labels?
At which step would you stop? What happens after it?
The validation set was used to choose the step. Which number do you report as the expected performance on new data, and on which data is it computed?

B5. 60,000 training images, mini-batches of 32. (a) How many gradient steps is one epoch? How many after 10 epochs? (b) Why not use all 60,000 images for every step?
B6. A sigmoid’s local derivative \varphi'(z) = \varphi(z)(1 - \varphi(z)) is at most 0.25 (at z = 0). (a) What is \varphi'(8)? Compare with ReLU’s local derivative for z = 8. (b) A gradient passes back through 10 sigmoid units in a chain (ignore the weights). By at most what factor is it multiplied? What does this mean for the first layers of a deep sigmoid network?






Solutions





B1. (a) -\ln 0.9 = 0.105, -\ln 0.5 = 0.693, -\ln 0.01 = 4.605. (b) -\ln 0.7 = 0.357; -\ln 0.2 = 1.609.
B2. \mathcal L'(w) = -2x(y - wx) = -4(3 - 2w). Step 1: \mathcal L'(0) = -12, w = 1.2, \mathcal L = (3 - 2.4)^2 = 0.36. Step 2: \mathcal L'(1.2) = -2.4, w = 1.44, \mathcal L = (3 - 2.88)^2 = 0.0144. Each step removes 80 % of the remaining distance to w = 1.5 (the factor 1 - 8\eta = 0.2).
B3. (a) z = 0.5 \cdot 2 + 0 = 1, h = 1, \hat y = 1.5, \mathcal L = 0.5^2 = 0.25. (b) \partial\mathcal L/\partial\hat y = 2(1.5 - 1) = 1. \partial\mathcal L/\partial w_2 = 1 \cdot h = 1, \partial\mathcal L/\partial b_2 = 1, \partial\mathcal L/\partial h = 1 \cdot w_2 = 1.5. The ReLU is on (z > 0): \partial\mathcal L/\partial z = 1.5. \partial\mathcal L/\partial w_1 = 1.5 \cdot x = 3, \partial\mathcal L/\partial b_1 = 1.5. (c) \eta = 0.1: w_1 = 0.5 - 0.3 = 0.2, b_1 = -0.15, w_2 = 1.4, b_2 = -0.1. New forward pass: z = 0.25, h = 0.25, \hat y = 0.35 - 0.1 = 0.25, \mathcal L = 0.75^2 = 0.5625: worse. Every weight moved downhill on its own, but together they overshoot: \hat y went from 1.5 past the target 1 to 0.25. With \eta = 0.05: w_1 = 0.35, b_1 = -0.075, w_2 = 1.45, b_2 = -0.05, z = 0.625, \hat y = 0.856, \mathcal L = 0.021. (d) z = -0.5, h = 0, \hat y = 0, \mathcal L = 1. \partial\mathcal L/\partial\hat y = -2, \partial\mathcal L/\partial b_2 = -2, \partial\mathcal L/\partial w_2 = -2 \cdot h = 0, \partial\mathcal L/\partial h = -2 \cdot 1.5 = -3, but the ReLU is off, so \partial\mathcal L/\partial z = 0 and \partial\mathcal L/\partial w_1 = \partial\mathcal L/\partial b_1 = 0. Only b_2 changes: b_2 = 0.2, \hat y = 0.2, \mathcal L = 0.64. The hidden unit learns nothing from this example.
B4. (a) The blue curve is the training loss: it keeps falling, towards 0.002, because the network is fitted to exactly these points. The red curve is the validation loss: it falls at first, then rises. (b) At the lowest validation loss, step 126 (validation loss 0.169). After it the network fits the noise of the 30 training points: the training loss goes on falling, but the validation loss rises (0.377 at step 2000). (c) Neither of these curves: the validation loss at step 126 is optimistic, because the step was chosen on it. Report the loss or accuracy of the chosen network on a separate test set that played no part in any choice (as on the random-forest day).
B5. (a) 60{,}000/32 = 1875 steps; 18,750 after 10 epochs. (b) Every step would cost 60,000 forward and backward passes. The gradient of 32 random images points roughly in the same direction for 1/1875 of the cost, so in the same time we take 1875 (noisy) steps instead of one exact one.
B6. (a) \varphi(8) = 0.99966, \varphi'(8) = 0.00034. The ReLU passes the gradient unchanged (derivative 1). (b) At most 0.25^{10} \approx 10^{-6}. The first layers of a deep sigmoid network get gradients a million times smaller than the last: they hardly learn (vanishing gradients). ReLU units that are on pass the gradient with factor 1.




Math questions
B7. (math) Softmax p_k = e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j} and cross-entropy \mathcal L = -\ln p_c for the true class c. Show that \partial\mathcal L/\partial z_k = p_k - y_k, where y_k = 1 if k = c and 0 otherwise.
B8. (math) A layer \mathbf z = W\mathbf a + \mathbf b followed by \mathbf a' = \varphi(\mathbf z). Given \boldsymbol\delta' = \partial\mathcal L/\partial\mathbf z' of the next layer \mathbf z' = W'\mathbf a' + \mathbf b', derive \boldsymbol\delta = \partial\mathcal L/\partial\mathbf z = (W'^\top\boldsymbol\delta') \odot \varphi'(\mathbf z) and \partial\mathcal L/\partial W = \boldsymbol\delta\,\mathbf a^\top.
B9. (math) \mathcal L = \frac1N\sum_n\ell_n. A mini-batch B of m examples is drawn uniformly at random (without replacement). Show that \mathbf g_B = \frac1m\sum_{n\in B}\nabla\ell_n is an unbiased estimate of \nabla\mathcal L.
B10. (math) Show that gradient descent on \mathcal L(\mathbf w) + \lambda\|\mathbf w\|^2 multiplies the weights by 1 - 2\eta\lambda before the usual step (“weight decay”). For the one-weight loss of B2 with \lambda > 0, what is the minimiser?






Solutions (math)





B7. (math) \mathcal L = -z_c + \ln\sum_j e^{z_j}. Then \partial\mathcal L/\partial z_k = -[k = c] + e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j} = p_k - y_k.
B8. (math) z'_i = \sum_j W'_{ij}a'_j + b'_i, so \partial\mathcal L/\partial a'_j = \sum_i \delta'_i W'_{ij} = (W'^\top\boldsymbol\delta')_j. Since a'_j = \varphi(z_j) depends only on z_j: \delta_j = \partial\mathcal L/\partial z_j = (W'^\top\boldsymbol\delta')_j\,\varphi'(z_j). Finally z_j = \sum_k W_{jk}a_k + b_j gives \partial\mathcal L/\partial W_{jk} = \delta_j a_k, i.e. the outer product \boldsymbol\delta\mathbf a^\top, and \partial\mathcal L/\partial b_j = \delta_j.
B9. (math) Each example is in B with probability m/N. So \mathbb E[\mathbf g_B] = \frac1m\sum_n P(n\in B)\nabla\ell_n = \frac1m\cdot\frac mN\sum_n\nabla\ell_n = \nabla\mathcal L.
B10. (math) The gradient is \nabla\mathcal L + 2\lambda\mathbf w, so \mathbf w \leftarrow \mathbf w - \eta\nabla\mathcal L - 2\eta\lambda\mathbf w = (1 - 2\eta\lambda)\mathbf w - \eta\nabla\mathcal L. For B2: \frac{d}{dw}[(3 - 2w)^2 + \lambda w^2] = -4(3 - 2w) + 2\lambda w = 0 gives w = 12/(8 + 2\lambda) = 6/(4 + \lambda): pulled from 1.5 towards 0.

title: Exercise: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Explore: backpropagation step by step
The network of B3 as a computational graph: orange boxes are weights, grey boxes are inputs, circles are operations. forward fills in every node’s value (blue), backward fills in \partial\mathcal L/\partial(\text{node}) from the loss back (red), with the local derivative on each edge. update takes one step with the learning rate \eta and shows the loss before and after. check compares each gradient with a finite difference. All numbers can be edited.



R1. Preset the by-hand exercise. Press forward, backward, update, and compare with your answers to B3. Press check: do backpropagation and finite differences agree?
R2. Preset dead ReLU (x = -1). Press backward. Which edges carry a zero, and where does the gradient stop? Press update a few times: what changes, and what never changes?
R3. Preset sigmoid saturates. Read the local derivative on the edge from z to h, and compare the gradients of w_1 and w_2. Press update: which weights move noticeably?
R4. Preset learning rate too large (\eta = 0.3). Press update once and read the loss. Then look at z: what has happened to the hidden unit? Press update four more times: does the loss go down, and how does the network now fit y?
R5. Preset 2–2–1 network. Press backward. Which weight has the largest gradient, and why? Press update with \eta = 0.05: what is the new loss?






Solutions





R1. The same numbers as B3: \mathcal L = 0.25; gradients w_1: 3, b_1: 1.5, w_2: 1, b_2: 1; after the update (\eta = 0.1) \mathcal L = 0.5625. The finite differences agree with backpropagation to many digits.
R2. The edge from z into the ReLU has local derivative ×0: \partial\mathcal L/\partial h = -3, but \partial\mathcal L/\partial z = 0, so w_1 and b_1 get 0. w_2 also gets 0, because its local derivative is h = 0. Only b_2 moves: 0 \to 0.2 (loss 0.64), then towards 1 with every further update. w_1, b_1, w_2 never change for this input.
R3. The edge z \to h has local derivative ×0.00034 (z = 8, the sigmoid is flat). \partial\mathcal L/\partial w_2 = 3.0 but \partial\mathcal L/\partial w_1 = 0.006, 500 times smaller. After one update with \eta = 0.1 the loss drops from 2.25 to 0.81, almost entirely through w_2 and b_2; w_1 moves by 0.0006.
R4. The loss goes from 0.25 to 1.69. The update made w_1 = -0.4 and b_1 = -0.45, so z = -1.25: the hidden unit is off (dead for this input). Further updates only change b_2: the loss falls (0.27, 0.043, 0.0069, 0.0011) because b_2 alone moves towards y = 1. The network now outputs a constant; the hidden unit no longer takes part.
R5. Loss 2.25 (\hat y = 3.5, y = 2). The largest gradient is \partial\mathcal L/\partial w_{22} = 12: it is \partial\mathcal L/\partial z_2 \cdot x_2 = 6 \cdot 2, where \partial\mathcal L/\partial z_2 = 3 \cdot v_2 = 6 (the output weight v_2 = 2 is the larger one) and x_2 = 2 is the larger input. After the update the loss is 1.3225.

title: Exercise: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
section: Explore: gradient descent on a landscape
text:
Explore: gradient descent on a landscape
The colours show a loss over two parameters (a, b) in bands (darker = lower; the white dot is the minimum). Each loss is the average over 40 training examples, so a mini-batch gradient is a real noisy estimate. Click to start a path (up to three), then 1 step or run 50 steps. The small plot shows the loss above the minimum, on a log scale.



G1. Presets too small and just right (the same start). Run each until the loss is within 0.001 of the minimum (0.092). How many steps does each need?
G2. Still on the bowl, raise \eta step by step from 0.3 (click the same start, or use diverges for \eta = 0.8). Above which \eta does the path diverge?
G3. Preset zig-zag across a narrow valley (\eta = 0.6). Describe the path. Then lower \eta to 0.03: what happens? Finally preset momentum in the valley (\eta = 0.03 with momentum).
G4. Preset SGD noise (batches of 4, \eta = 0.1). Compare the path with the full batch (set the batch size to 40, same \eta). Where does the mini-batch path end up after 200 steps? What changes with a smaller \eta?
G5. Preset two starts, two minima. Where does each path end, and with which loss?
G6. Preset one neuron’s real loss: the cross-entropy of one neuron p = \text{sigmoid}(ax + b) on 40 points of two overlapping classes. Describe the landscape. How many steps does \eta = 2 need, and \eta = 0.5?






Solutions





G1. \eta = 0.02: 192 steps; \eta = 0.3: 11 steps.
G2. \eta = 0.6 still converges (8 steps, with a small overshoot); at \eta = 0.8 the path jumps from side to side further each time and the loss explodes. The limit lies near \eta = 0.75: stability needs \eta < 2/\lambda_\text{max}, and the steepest curvature of this bowl is \lambda_\text{max} = 2.67, so 2/2.67 = 0.75.
G3. With \eta = 0.6 the path bounces from one wall of the valley to the other while it creeps along the valley floor; it gets within 0.001 of the minimum after 67 steps. With \eta = 0.03 there is no zig-zag, but progress along the flat floor is very slow: after 200 steps the loss is still 0.19 (minimum 0.064). With momentum, the same \eta = 0.03 gets there in 115 steps: the velocity builds up along the floor, while the back-and-forth across the valley cancels out. (The valley’s curvatures differ by a factor of about 40.)
G4. The mini-batch path wanders: each step uses only 4 of the 40 examples. It gets near the minimum about as fast as the full batch (within 0.001 after about 40 steps against 37), but it never settles: after 200 steps it is still jiggling around the minimum (loss 0.0924 against 0.0921). A smaller \eta makes the jiggle smaller but the approach slower (with \eta = 0.02 the loss is still 0.096 after 200 steps). In practice \eta is lowered during training for this reason.
G5. The left start (a = -0.3) ends in the deeper minimum at a = -1.03 (loss -0.254), the right start (a = +0.3) in the shallower one at a = 0.97 (loss +0.246). Gradient descent finds the bottom of the valley it starts in, not the deepest one.
G6. A long, flat, curved valley; the minimum is at (a, b) = (2.34, -0.61) with loss 0.325 (the classes overlap, so the loss cannot reach 0). Far from the minimum it rises steeply on one side and flattens on the other. \eta = 2 gets within 0.001 in 21 steps, \eta = 0.5 in 89. The real losses of networks have exactly this kind of flat and curved valleys, in millions of dimensions.

title: Exercise: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Explore: overfitting and its cures
The point classifier of the previous unit, now with the training controls: learning rate, batch size, validation share (hollow points are held out for validation and never used for training), weight decay \lambda and dropout. The plot shows the training loss (blue) and the validation loss (red); the readout gives the step with the lowest validation loss.



E1. Preset overfitting: 8+8 units, 60 noisy points (30 for training, 30 for validation). Train for about 2000 steps. Where is the validation loss lowest? What do the two losses do after that? Look at the decision boundary: how does it treat the noisy training points?
E2. Preset weight decay smooths it (\lambda = 0.003). Train again and compare both curves and the boundary with E1.
E3. Preset dropout (probability 0.4). What does the training curve look like, and why? What happens to the validation loss?
E4. Preset more data cures it (300 points). Compare the gap between the two curves with E1.
E5. Preset mini-batches of 8 (200 points, 100 for training). How many steps are one epoch? Compare the curves with the full batch (move the batch size slider to “all”).
E6. Presets learning rate too large (\eta = 1.5) and dead network (\eta = 5). Describe the loss curves and the hidden-unit thumbnails. What has happened?






Solutions





E1. The validation loss is lowest at step 126 (0.169, validation accuracy 90 %). After that the training loss falls towards zero (0.002 at step 2000) while the validation loss rises (0.72 at step 500, 0.38 at step 2000): the boundary bends around single noisy training points, making small islands that are wrong for new points. Early stopping would keep the step-126 network.
E2. The training loss stops at about 0.164 (it cannot go to zero: large weights are penalised), and the validation loss stays near 0.31 instead of climbing to 0.7. The boundary is smooth, without islands. (Its lowest validation loss, 0.185 at step 183, is not better than early stopping here; the gain is that it no longer matters much when you stop.)
E3. The training curve is noisy and stays high (about 0.23–0.32): every step trains a different random half-silenced network. The validation loss (computed with all units) stays low much longer: 0.18 after 2000 steps, against 0.38 without dropout.
E4. With 150 training points the two curves stay close (at step 1000: training 0.20, validation 0.18; at 4000: 0.13 and 0.24); the network cannot memorise 150 points with its 105 weights as easily as 30. More data is the most reliable cure.
E5. 100 training points in batches of 8: 12.5 steps per epoch. The mini-batch curve is jagged, the full-batch curve smooth; per step the full batch gets lower faster (at step 1000: 0.18 against 0.22 training loss), but each mini-batch step costs 1/12 as much.
E6. \eta = 1.5: the loss jumps up and down during the first steps (0.79, 0.65, 0.55, 0.45, 0.41, 0.44, 0.38, 0.39, 0.47, 0.56, …) and then gets stuck near 0.38; 14 of the 16 hidden units are dead (off for every training point; their thumbnails are blank). \eta = 5: after a few huge jumps (up to 6.4) again 14 of the 16 units are dead, the network outputs probability one half everywhere, and the loss sits at 0.693 = \ln 2 for ever: almost no gradient reaches the hidden weights any more.

title: Exercise: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Where this leads
Everything so far works for any input vector. For images, the next unit replaces the dense first layer by a convolutional layer: a bank of small kernels, learned with exactly this backpropagation, shared across the image. Data augmentation, the image-specific cure for overfitting, comes with it. The evaluation day (day 16) returns to the question of what makes a test set honest.

title: Back-projection and the Fourier slice theorem
text:
About this lecture
Last unit: the scanner measures a sinogram, one projection per angle. Now we try to get the image back.

Back-projection: smear every projection back along its own rays and add. Simple, and always blurred.
Why it blurs: a halo falling off like 1/r around every point.
The Fourier slice theorem: each projection hands us one line through the centre of the image’s 2D spectrum.
Direct Fourier reconstruction: fill the spectrum line by line and invert; why the gaps between the lines make it hard.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Recall from the fourier unit: the 2D spectrum, centre = slow waves, direction = orientation; filtering = multiplying the spectrum. Demos: backproj with the plain filter (the main demo of the next unit) and fourierslice.
crumbs: Back-projection and the Fourier slice theorem

title: Back-projection and the Fourier slice theorem
text:
Smearing back
We do not know where along a ray the attenuation sat. So spread each measured value evenly along its ray, for every ray of every angle, and add everything up. That is back-projection.

Back-projection of a single point with 1, 4, 16 and 180 angles.
One angle: a stripe through the point.
Four angles: a star; the arms cross only at the point.
180 angles: a bright centre in a halo that fades with distance.

The point is in the right place, but it now glows.
