Use two bins, [0.5, 0.75) and [0.75, 1]. For each bin compute the accuracy and the mean confidence; draw the reliability diagram.
Compute the ECE. Is the classifier over- or underconfident?
After temperature scaling with T > 1, what happens to the accuracy?

B7. Classical or deep? For each task, decide and give the main reason: (a) counting fluorescent beads of known size on a clean background, 30 images; (b) segmenting irregular cells in 10 000 phase-contrast images from many labs; (c) measuring the diameter of a calibration grid to check the microscope; (d) finding mitotic cells in histology, with 2000 annotated examples.






Solutions





B1. (a) Scores \mathbf q \cdot \mathbf k_j = 1, 0, 1. Weights e^1 : e^0 : e^1 normalised: 0.422, 0.155, 0.422. Output 0.422 \cdot 10 + 0.155 \cdot 0 + 0.422 \cdot 4 = 5.91. (b) T = \tfrac12: scores 2, 0, 2; weights 0.468, 0.063, 0.468; output 6.56. T = 2: scores 0.5, 0, 0.5; weights 0.384, 0.233, 0.384; output 5.37. (c) T \to 0: all weight on the best matches, tokens 1 and 3 equally: output (10 + 4)/2 = 7. T \to \infty: equal weights: (10 + 0 + 4)/3 = 4.67.
B2. (a) 16 \times 16: 32 \times 32 = 1024 tokens, 1024^2 = 1\,048\,576 weights. 8 \times 8: 64 \times 64 = 4096 tokens, 16\,777\,216 weights: 4 times more tokens, 16 times more weights. (b) A structure smaller than a patch is mixed with everything else in its patch; smaller patches keep it apart, at a cost growing with the square of the number of tokens.
B3. (a) (2L + 1) \times (2L + 1). Two pixels 200 apart are in one receptive field when 2L + 1 \ge 201: L = 100 layers (without pooling). (b) One: every token attends to every token. But attention does not know which tokens are neighbours: locality and position must come from the position code and be learned from data.
B4. (a) Frozen features + a probe (or light fine-tuning of the last layers): 20 images are too few to train or fully fine-tune a large network without overfitting, but enough for a linear probe on good features. (b) Fine-tuning (or even training from scratch): with 5000 images from the same microscope the network can adapt its features to the task; fine-tuning a pretrained network usually converges faster and better. (c) Fine-tuning with care, or training a smaller network from scratch: features pretrained on very different images may not transfer; check a probe on frozen features first as a baseline; if it is poor, the features do not fit.
B5. The network has been taught that hue does not matter: two views differing only in colour must have the same embedding. Colour information is suppressed, so a probe cannot separate the stains. Leave out hue (and colour jitter, greyscale conversion). Check also brightness and contrast if the stain intensity matters, and any augmentation that changes what you want to measure.
B6. (a) Bin [0.5, 0.75): 5 predictions, 3 correct: accuracy 0.6; mean confidence (0.55 + 0.60 + 0.65 + 0.70 + 0.72)/5 = 0.644. Bin [0.75, 1]: 5 predictions, 4 correct: accuracy 0.8; mean confidence (0.80 + 0.85 + 0.90 + 0.95 + 0.99)/5 = 0.898. Both points lie below the diagonal. (b) ECE = 0.5 \cdot |0.6 - 0.644| + 0.5 \cdot |0.8 - 0.898| = 0.022 + 0.049 = 0.071. Overconfident (confidence above accuracy in both bins; overall mean confidence 0.771 against accuracy 0.7). (c) Unchanged: dividing the logits by T never changes which class has the largest score; only the confidences move towards 0.5.
B7. (a) Classical: known shape and size, clean background, few images: threshold + labelling, or a blob detector; easy to check. (b) Deep (an instance route such as flows), pretrained or trained on many labs’ data: irregular shapes and large variation, and enough images. (c) Classical: the measurement’s bias must be understood and traceable; a fitted model of the grid is explainable; a network adds an unknown error. (d) Deep: subtle appearance, many examples; but test on data from other labs or scanners (domain shift) and check calibration before using its confidences.




Math questions
B8. (math) Show that self-attention without position codes is permutation-equivariant: \mathrm{Attn}(PX) = P\,\mathrm{Attn}(X) for every permutation matrix P.
B9. (math) Let \mathbf q, \mathbf k \in \mathbb R^d have independent entries with mean 0 and variance 1. Show that \mathbf q^\top\mathbf k has mean 0 and variance d. What happens to the softmax of scores with standard deviation \sqrt d when d is large?
B10. (math) Show that temperature scaling does not change the predicted class, and that for two classes it maps a confidence c > \tfrac12 to \sigma(\mathrm{logit}(c)/T). Compute the new confidence of 0.88 with T = 2.
B11. (math) Write the InfoNCE loss for a batch of 3 pairs with \tau = 0.5 and embeddings \mathbf z_1 = (1, 0), \mathbf z_2 = (0, 1), \mathbf z_3 = (0.6, 0.8); partners \mathbf z_1' = (0.8, 0.6), \mathbf z_2' = (0.6, 0.8), \mathbf z_3' = (0, 1). Compute the three losses and identify the loss as a cross-entropy.






Solutions (math)





B8. Q' = PXW_Q = PQ, and likewise K' = PK, V' = PV. Scores S' = Q'K'^\top/\sqrt d = PSP^\top: entry (i, j) of S' is entry (\pi(i), \pi(j)) of S. The row-wise softmax of PSP^\top is P\,\mathrm{softmax}(S)P^\top (each row is a permuted row of S, permuted within itself, and the softmax treats the entries of a row symmetrically). So \mathrm{Attn}(PX) = P\,\mathrm{softmax}(S)P^\top PV = P\,\mathrm{softmax}(S)V = P\,\mathrm{Attn}(X), using P^\top P = I.
B9. E[q_mk_m] = E[q_m]E[k_m] = 0, so E[\mathbf q^\top\mathbf k] = 0. \mathrm{Var}(q_mk_m) = E[q_m^2]E[k_m^2] = 1; the d terms are independent, so the variance is d. Scores spread by \sqrt d (e.g. 8 for d = 64): the largest score in a row dominates the softmax, which then puts nearly all weight on one token and has tiny gradients for the others. Dividing by \sqrt d restores variance 1.
B10. z_k/T is a strictly increasing function of z_k for T > 0, so the arg max is unchanged. Two classes: c = \sigma(z) with z = \mathrm{logit}(c) = \log\frac{c}{1-c}; after scaling c' = \sigma(z/T). c = 0.88: z = \log(0.88/0.12) = 1.99; c' = \sigma(0.996) = 0.73.
B11. Scores \mathbf z_i^\top\mathbf z_j'/\tau: \begin{bmatrix} 1.6 & 1.2 & 0 \\ 1.2 & 1.6 & 2.0 \\ 1.92 & 2.0 & 1.6 \end{bmatrix}. Row-wise softmax, diagonal entries: 0.534, 0.316, 0.258. Losses -\log: 0.627, 1.151, 1.353; mean 1.044. Each row is a 3-class classification (“which partner is mine?”) with logits \mathbf z_i^\top\mathbf z_j'/\tau and the correct class j = i: the loss is the cross-entropy of that classification. Pair 3 has the largest loss: its embedding is closer to partner 2 than to its own.

title: Exercise: attention, transformers and pretrained models
text:
Explore: attention on patches
A 64 \times 64 image cut into 8 \times 8 patches: 64 tokens. Click a patch (the query): its attention weights over all patches are shown in orange, the dashed blue square is what L stacked 3 \times 3 convolutions on the patch grid can see. The score is content weight × (similarity of hand-made features: brightness, contrast, edge orientation; or of the raw pixels) plus position weight × (closeness on the grid), with a temperature. The right panel is the image after one attention layer: every patch replaced by the weighted average of all patches. The weights are set by hand, not trained.



S1. Preset position only: a blur kernel. Which patches get the largest weights, and is the pattern the same for every query? What does the output look like? Why is this a convolution?
S2. Preset content only: similar patches, however far (query on a filament). Where does the weight go? How many patches are effectively attended? Click a cell patch and a background patch.
S3. Preset non-local means: denoise (noisy image, raw-patch similarity). What weight does the query keep for itself? Compare the filaments in the input and output. Move the temperature down to 0.1 and up to 2: what happens to the output?
S4. Preset temperature → 0: one patch. What is the output image, and why?
S5. Preset no position code: shuffling only reorders. Read the shuffle test. Now untick “no position code” and set a position weight of 1: what does the shuffle test show? Explain with B8.
S6. Preset a 3 × 3 conv needs many layers (query in a corner). How many conv layers on this 8 × 8 patch grid are needed before the corner sees the whole image?






Solutions





S1. The query (3, 3) keeps 32 % for itself and 12 % for each of its direct neighbours, decaying with grid distance: a bell-shaped kernel, the same for every query (away from the border). The output is a blocky blur of the image. The weights depend only on the offset between patches, not on what they contain: a convolution (math slide).
S2. On the other filament patches, wherever they are in the image (top weights about 9 % each, at (4, 1), (4, 6) and (2, 3)), and almost nothing on background or cells: about 15 effective patches. A cell patch attends to the other cells, a background patch to background. The weights follow the content, not the distance.
S3. 51 % on itself, the rest on similar patches (11 % and 7 % for the next two); about 8.5 effective patches. The output filaments and cells are smoother, because similar noisy patches are averaged and the noise partly cancels, while the structure (the same in all of them) stays. At T = 0.1 nearly all weight stays on the patch itself: hardly any denoising. At T = 2 the weights spread over many dissimilar patches: the output is washed out (structures averaged with background).
S4. The query (1, 6) gives 100 % to itself; every patch does the same: the output equals the input. With T \to 0 attention picks the best match, which (with position closeness and identical content) is the patch itself.
S5. With no position code the shuffle test reads 0.0: attention on the shuffled image equals the shuffled attention output. With a position weight the result depends on where patches sit on the grid, so shuffling changes the result (the test shows a large difference, e.g. 58.8 grey levels in the position preset). Without a position code the network sees a set of patches: B8.
S6. From the corner (0, 0), L layers see L patches to the right and down: the far corner (7, 7) needs L = 7 layers (a 15 \times 15 footprint). One attention layer already covers all 64 patches.

title: Exercise: attention, transformers and pretrained models
section: Explore: frozen features and a probe
text:
Explore: frozen features and a probe
A 128 \times 128 synthetic image: nuclei of any brightness among things that are not nuclei but can be as bright (debris spots, fibres, large soft cytoplasm-like regions); or the course micrograph. Three embeddings per pixel (on a 64 \times 64 grid): raw 9 \times 9 patches, the filter stack of the random-forest day, and learned features from a tiny encoder (7 k weights) trained without labels by a contrastive loss on synthetic images and the micrograph (its training script is next to the demo). Modes: click: similarity (cosine similarity to the clicked pixel), paint + probe (paint nucleus and background strokes; a logistic regression is trained on the frozen embeddings; Dice against the truth), click: prompt (similarity above a threshold, the connected piece containing the click). The another microscope sliders change the image after the probe was trained.



P1. Preset raw pixels: similarity = brightness. Where is the similarity to the bright nucleus high? Compare the mean similarity on nuclei and elsewhere with the presets for the learned features and (switch the embedding) the filter stack.
P2. Preset five strokes, learned features: two nucleus strokes (one bright, one dim nucleus) and three background strokes. Dice? Switch the embedding to raw and to filter stack, keeping the strokes. Which features need the fewest labels here?
P3. Add strokes where the probe is wrong (e.g. on a fibre or a soft bright region). How far can you push the Dice with each embedding?
P4. Preset a click → a mask (filter stack). Dice with the clicked nucleus? Switch to learned and raw features. Move the threshold: what happens when it is too low?
P5. Preset new microscope: probe kept (brightness × 0.5, blur 1.5, noise 8, probe trained on the original image). Dice with the learned features? With raw patches and with the filter stack? Why do all three survive the change of brightness here? Which change hurts most if you push the sliders further?
P6. Switch the image to the micrograph and click inside the nucleus in similarity mode with each embedding. Which one separates the nucleus from the cytoplasm?






Solutions





P1. Raw patches: high wherever the image is bright: on nuclei, but also on debris, fibres and the soft bright regions (mean similarity 0.23 on nuclei, 0.08 elsewhere: a weak separation). Learned features: 0.29 on nuclei, −0.05 elsewhere. Filter stack: 0.70 on nuclei, −0.25 elsewhere: on this image the hand-designed multiscale filters separate best.
P2. Learned features: Dice 0.55 with 69 labelled grid pixels. Raw: 0.39. Filter stack: 0.53. With five strokes, features that already encode “a compact blob of this size” (the stack, the learned features) do much better than raw pixels, where the probe can only learn “bright”, which the debris and soft regions are too.
P3. (Results depend on your strokes.) Background strokes on the soft bright regions and on fibres help the stack and the learned features most: their embeddings separate these structures from nuclei, so a few examples suffice. With raw patches the gain is small: a linear rule on raw grey levels cannot express “compact and sharp-edged”, and bright non-nuclei keep being confused with nuclei.
P4. Filter stack: 49 grid pixels, Dice 0.91 with that nucleus. Learned features: 30 pixels, Dice 0.65. Raw: 13 pixels, Dice 0.36. Too low a threshold lets the mask leak into neighbouring bright structures (it grows as long as they are connected); too high keeps only the centre of the nucleus. A click gives a mask; how far it reaches is a choice.
P5. Learned: 0.58 (0.55 before). Raw: 0.37 (0.39). Filter stack: 0.55 (0.53). Each embedding dimension is standardised over the image before the probe, so a global change of brightness cancels out for all three. Pushing the sliders further: strong noise (30) ruins the raw patches first (the probe on raw grey levels follows the noise), strong blur (3) costs the filter stack a little (edges and blob sizes change), while the learned encoder, trained with blur and noise augmentations, changes least. The augmentations decided what it ignores.
P6. The filter stack lights up the whole nucleus and little else: its smoothed intensities and texture at several scales describe “the even grey inside the envelope”. Raw patches give a speckled map: on this grainy micrograph a 9 \times 9 patch is dominated by grain, so a patch is similar mainly to itself. The tiny learned encoder gives a weak, streaky map: trained mostly on synthetic images, its features do not describe this kind of texture; a pretrained network is only as good as the match between its training images and yours.

title: Exercise: attention, transformers and pretrained models
text:
Explore: calibration
A simulated two-class classifier on 4000 test samples. Overconfidence multiplies its logits (1 = calibrated); temperature divides them; fit T on validation finds the temperature that minimises the negative log-likelihood on validation data from the training domain; domain shift moves the two test classes closer together after T was fitted. Left: histogram of the confidences; right: the reliability diagram (bars: accuracy per confidence bin; red: mean confidence in the bin).



C1. Preset calibrated. Compare accuracy and mean confidence, and read the ECE. Where do the bars lie?
C2. Preset overconfident network. What happens to the accuracy, the mean confidence, the ECE and the histogram?
C3. Preset temperature fixes it in-domain. Which T is fitted? What are the ECE and the accuracy now? Why did the accuracy not change?
C4. Preset shift: overconfident again. Accuracy, mean confidence, ECE? Press fit T on validation again: does it help? What would?
C5. Preset accuracy unchanged, calibration changed (overconfidence 0.4). Is this network over- or underconfident? Which T would fix it?






Solutions





C1. Accuracy 89.0 %, mean confidence 88.4 %, ECE 0.9 %: the bars lie on the diagonal (57, 63, 75, 89, 98 % correct in the five bins).
C2. Accuracy unchanged at 89.0 % (the predicted classes are the same), mean confidence 96.1 %, ECE 7.0 %. The histogram piles up near 1; the bars fall below the diagonal (e.g. 62 % correct among predictions with confidence 0.8–0.9).
C3. T = 2.86 (close to the overconfidence factor 3). ECE 0.4 %, mean confidence 88.9 %, accuracy 89.0 %: dividing all logits by the same positive number does not change which class has the larger logit.
C4. Accuracy 73.0 %, mean confidence 83.5 %, ECE 10.5 %: on shifted data the network is overconfident again although T was fitted. Fitting T on validation data does not change anything (the validation data are from the training domain). What helps: validation (and recalibration) data from the new domain, or retraining/fine-tuning with such data; and flagging inputs that look unlike the training data.
C5. Underconfident: confidence 75.1 % against accuracy 89.0 %, ECE 13.9 %; the bars lie above the diagonal. A temperature T < 1 (about 0.4) sharpens the probabilities and fixes it; fit T finds it.

title: Exercise: attention, transformers and pretrained models
text:
Where this leads
The last unit of the day uses everything here in reverse: networks that generate images (diffusion models), and what a generative prior does to a restored image. Calibration and domain shift return there as the question of which details in a restored image can be trusted.

title: Quiz: attention, transformers and pretrained models
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. In one sentence each: how does a 3 \times 3 convolution combine pixels, and how does self-attention combine tokens?






Hint





Where do the weights come from?









Answer





A convolution takes a weighted sum of the 9 neighbours with fixed learned weights that depend only on the relative position and are the same everywhere. Self-attention takes a weighted average of all tokens, with weights computed from the content (how well each token’s key matches the query) and normalised to sum to 1.




Q2. Scores 2, 0, 0 for three values 6, 3, 0. Compute the attention output.






Hint





Softmax: e^2, e^0, e^0 normalised.









Answer





Weights e^2/(e^2 + 2) = 0.787, and 0.106 twice. Output 0.787 \cdot 6 + 0.106 \cdot 3 + 0 = 5.04.




Q3. Why does a transformer without position codes not know where a patch is in the image?






Hint





Shuffle the patches.









Answer





Attention treats the tokens as a set: shuffling the input only shuffles the output in the same way (permutation equivariance). Nothing in the computation depends on the order, so the arrangement of the patches is invisible unless a position code is added to each token.




Q4. Halving the patch size of a transformer multiplies the number of attention weights per layer by how much?






Hint





Number of tokens, then its square.









Answer





Four times as many tokens, so 4^2 = 16 times as many weights.




Q5. You have 15 annotated images and a large pretrained network. Frozen features + a linear probe, or full fine-tuning? Why?






Hint





How many parameters are trained in each case?









Answer





Frozen features + a probe: only a few dozen parameters are trained, which 15 images can determine; full fine-tuning of millions of weights on 15 images overfits and can destroy the useful pretrained features.




Q6. A contrastive model was pretrained with strong brightness augmentation. Why is it a poor feature extractor for measuring the intensity of a stain?






Hint





What were the two views taught to agree on?









Answer





It was trained so that a crop and its brightened copy have the same embedding: brightness is exactly what it learned to ignore. The augmentations decide what the features are blind to.




Q7. A network says 0.99 for 1000 test images and is right on 920. Is it calibrated? What does temperature scaling with T > 1 do to its accuracy?






Hint





Compare confidence and accuracy.









Answer





No: confidence 0.99, accuracy 0.92: overconfident. Temperature scaling lowers the confidences but leaves the predicted classes, and so the accuracy (92 %), unchanged.




Q8. Temperature was fitted on validation data from microscope A. Will the network be calibrated on microscope B?






Hint





What changed between A and B?









Answer





Not necessarily: under domain shift the accuracy drops while the confidences need not, so the network is typically overconfident again. Calibration must be checked (and refitted) on data from B.




Q9. (math) Why is the dot product in attention divided by \sqrt d?






Hint





Variance of a sum of d independent products.









Answer





For queries and keys with independent unit-variance entries, \mathbf q^\top\mathbf k has variance d. Without scaling the scores grow with d and the softmax saturates (one token gets all the weight, gradients vanish); dividing by \sqrt d brings the variance back to 1.




Q10. Give two situations in which a classical method is the better choice than a deep network.






Hint





Data, prior knowledge, explanation.









Answer





For example: very few images or no annotations; a strong prior on the shape (circles, lines, a calibration grid) that a model fit uses directly; a measurement whose bias must be understood and explained; or when a simple classical pipeline already works on all the data.

title: From PCA to autoencoders
text:
About this lecture
Can we describe an image with a few numbers, and rebuild it from them?

An image is a point in a space with one axis per pixel. Images of one kind fill only a thin part of it.
PCA (unit Principal component analysis) finds the best flat summary. Seen again here: PCA is an autoencoder, an encoder (image → few numbers) and a decoder (few numbers → image).
Replace both straight maps by neural networks (unit Neural networks): an autoencoder that can follow curved families of images.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

This unit opens the VAE day. It recalls two earlier units in one slide each, PCA (Part I) and neural networks (the neural-networks day), and builds on them: “PCA is a linear autoencoder” and “only the bend makes an autoencoder more than PCA”. The source of the “PCA is a linear autoencoder” example is the VAE unit of the 3MB00A course, there with two genes instead of two pixels.

title: From PCA to autoencoders
text:
An image is a point
A 28 \times 28 image is a vector of 784 grey values: one point in \mathbb R^{784}.

Almost every point of that space looks like noise. Handwritten digits, or masks of cells, fill a tiny, connected region of it.
Moving along that region changes the image smoothly: a little thicker, a little more tilted, a little longer.
So a few numbers should be enough to say where in the region an image is.

Today, start with images of two pixels: a point in the plane, which we can draw.

The two-pixel image is the whole unit in miniature: everything we do in the plane works in 784 dimensions, we just cannot draw it. Ask: if you change one pixel of a digit at random, is it still a digit? Almost always yes; if you change all pixels at random, almost never. The region of real images is thin.

title: From PCA to autoencoders
text:
Recall: PCA and neural networks




PCA (unit Principal component analysis): two neighbouring pixels form a cloud along the diagonal. PC1 (blue), the direction of largest spread, is an eigenvector of the covariance matrix S. Keep the score along it; rebuild by going back along the line. Lost (red): the spread along the dropped directions, the sum of their eigenvalues.
Neural networks (unit Neural networks): a layer is a matrix, then a bend (ReLU); without the bend, layers collapse to one matrix. Training walks downhill on an error.


Two recall slides in one; skip quickly if both units were taught recently. The figure is the default state of the demo with the PCA button pressed: PC1 is (0.70, 0.71) for these data, the brightness of the pair; PC2 is the difference, a tiny edge. Same data as the pca2d demo’s “neighbouring pixels” preset.

title: From PCA to autoencoders
section: PCA is a linear autoencoder, by hand
text:
PCA is a linear autoencoder, by hand
Two pixels, mean subtracted. PC1 is the unit vector \mathbf u = (0.8,\ 0.6). Image \mathbf x = (3,\ 1).

Encode (image → one number): the score s = \mathbf u \cdot \mathbf x = 0.8 \cdot 3 + 0.6 \cdot 1 = 3.0.
Decode (number → image): \hat{\mathbf x} = s\,\mathbf u = 3.0 \cdot (0.8,\ 0.6) = (2.4,\ 1.8).
Error: \mathbf x - \hat{\mathbf x} = (0.6,\ -0.8), squared length 1.0.

With the mean added back: \text{encode}(\mathbf x) = \mathbf u^\top(\mathbf x - \bar{\mathbf x}), \ \text{decode}(s) = \bar{\mathbf x} + s\,\mathbf u.
With k components: k scores, and \hat{\mathbf x} = \bar{\mathbf x} + s_1\mathbf u_1 + \dots + s_k\mathbf u_k.

Encoder: project. Decoder: go back along the line. Every image on the PC1 line is rebuilt exactly; an image perpendicular to it has score 0 and is rebuilt as the mean image. In 784 dimensions, each u_k is itself an image (an “eigen-image”), and decoding adds eigen-images with the scores as weights.

title: From PCA to autoencoders
section: The math: no linear autoencoder beats PCA
text:
The math: no linear autoencoder beats PCA
The PCA unit showed that, for one unit direction \mathbf u, the mean squared reconstruction error of centred data is \operatorname{tr}S - \mathbf u^\top S\mathbf u, smallest at the top eigenvector, and that with k components the error is the sum of the dropped eigenvalues.

An autoencoder with a linear encoder E (k \times d) and a linear decoder D (d \times k), plus shifts, rebuilds every image inside the k-dimensional flat subspace spanned by the columns of D.
The best flat k-dimensional fit in squared error is the span of the first k PCs (Eckart–Young). So a trained linear autoencoder can do no better than PCA, and the best ones span the same subspace (Baldi & Hornik 1989), though not necessarily with orthogonal columns.


For the neighbouring-pixel data in the demo: S = [[0.0406, 0.0352], [0.0352, 0.0414]], eigenvalues 0.0762 and 0.0058, so the best one-number error is 0.0058 and keeping nothing (decode everything as the mean) costs tr S = 0.0820. At angle 0° (keep pixel 1 only) the error is tr S − S11 = 0.0820 − 0.0406 = 0.0414. The demo’s error-vs-angle plot is exactly tr S − uᵀSu.

title: From PCA to autoencoders
text:
The bottleneck must be narrow


Encoder: image → a few numbers z. Decoder: z → image. Train both so that \hat{\mathbf x} \approx \mathbf x for many images.
With as many numbers as pixels, the “autoencoder” just copies (PCA with all components: rotate, rotate back). It learns nothing.
A narrow bottleneck forces z to keep what varies most between images.


The digit is a real MNIST test image (a 7) encoded and decoded by the digit VAE of the unit Generating and exploring images; the reconstruction is blurrier than the input because two numbers cannot hold every detail of the stroke. MNIST: Y. LeCun, C. Cortes, C. J. C. Burges; CC BY-SA 3.0 as stated in the Keras documentation.

title: From PCA to autoencoders
section: When the images lie on a curve
text:
When the images lie on a curve




A bright spot moves past two pixels. One true number (its position), but the images lie on a curve.

PC1 is the best straight line, yet the spot at position -0.5 and the spot at 0.2 (noise-free scores 0.42 and 0.46) get almost the same score: the line folds the curve.
PCA needs two numbers to rebuild these images well.



The spot is a Gaussian (sd 0.5 pixel) at positions from −0.5 to 1.5, seen by pixels at 0 and 1; noise-free pixel values at position −0.5 are (0.607, 0.011), at 0.2 they are (0.923, 0.278). The PC1 score is about (p1 − p2)/√2 up to the mean, which rises from 0.42 at −0.5 to 0.61 at 0 and falls back through 0.46 at 0.2. Starting far left, pixel 1 rises then falls while pixel 2 rises: the dots run along a horseshoe. Mean squared error with PC1: 0.0170, against 0.2642 for keeping nothing. A trajectory in any image family (a cell elongating, a digit getting thicker) behaves like this: it is curved in pixel space.

title: From PCA to autoencoders
text:
An autoencoder follows the curve




Replace both straight maps by small neural networks (unit Neural networks):
\text{encoder: } 2 \to 16 \to 1, \qquad \text{decoder: } 1 \to 16 \to 2 \quad (\text{ReLU}).

Still one number per image, but the decoder draws a curve (green) instead of a line.
Error after 1500 training steps: 0.0006, against 0.0170 for PCA.
Without the bends, this network would be a linear autoencoder: PCA again.



Same data, same one-number bottleneck. The decoder curve is the set of all images the decoder can produce: a one-dimensional family, bent to follow the data. Training is the downhill walk of the neural-networks unit on the reconstruction error. Fixed seed; the demo reproduces exactly this curve.

title: From PCA to autoencoders
section: Try it: one number per image
text:
Try it: one number per image




Start at angle 0°: keep pixel 1 only, rebuild pixel 2 as its mean; error 0.0414. Drag u round: the error curve on the right is smallest at 45.3° (0.0058, the PCA button) and largest at −45° (0.0762, keeping only the edge). Click a dot to see it as a two-pixel image and its reconstructions. Then “moving spot”: PCA 0.0170; train the nonlinear autoencoder: 0.0006. Note the reconstructions on the curve.

title: From PCA to autoencoders
text:
From autoencoders to generating images
An autoencoder gives every image a place z in a small latent space, and a decoder that turns any z into an image.

Could we pick a new z and decode it, to make a new image?
A plain autoencoder only learns to rebuild its training images. Nothing says what lies between them in z, or where in z the images are.
The variational autoencoder (next unit) fixes this.

title: From PCA to autoencoders
text:
Summary







Idea
In one line




Image as a point
one axis per pixel; images of one kind fill a thin region


Encoder / decoder
image → few numbers z → image


PCA
the best linear autoencoder: encode = project, decode = mean + scores × eigen-images


Error of PCA
the spread of the images in the directions that were dropped


Bottleneck
must be narrow, or the network just copies


Autoencoder
encoder and decoder are networks: the decoder can follow a curve

title: Exercise: back-projection and the Fourier slice theorem
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

back-project a few projections by hand and recognise the ghosts and the halo,
explain why plain back-projection blurs every point with a 1/r halo,
use the Fourier slice theorem to predict which projection sees which pattern, and where it appears in the 2D spectrum,
explain why direct Fourier reconstruction needs interpolation and why its errors spread over the whole image.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the two demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: back-projection and the Fourier slice theorem
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Back-projection
every pixel receives the values of all rays through it, summed over all angles


Halo
plain back-projection of a point: a peak with a glow falling off like 1/r


Transpose
projection is A\mathbf x; back-projection is A^\top\mathbf y, not A^{-1}


Fourier slice theorem
1D spectrum of the projection at \theta = 2D spectrum along the central line at \theta


DFT convention
as in the Fourier unit: unnormalised forward DFT, frequency 0 (DC) in the centre
crumbs: Back-projection and the Fourier slice theorem

title: Exercise: back-projection and the Fourier slice theorem
text:
By hand
B1. Point masses A = (2, 0) (mass 1), B = (0, 1) (mass 2), C = (-1, -1) (mass 1). (a) Write down p_0 and p_{90°} (positions and heights of the bars). (b) Back-project both onto a 5 \times 5 grid with x and y from -2 to 2: each pixel gets p_0(x) + p_{90°}(y). Write the table. (c) Mark the true points. Which other pixels are as bright or brighter? Why do they appear?
B2. The halo. A point is back-projected from 180 angles. (a) How many smeared lines per unit length cross a circle of radius 5 pixels around the point? Of radius 20? (b) By what factor is the halo fainter at r = 20 than at r = 5? (c) Why does this make a bright disc look as if it were surrounded by a faint glow, and lower its contrast against the background?
B3. Back-project the row sums (3, 7) and column sums (4, 6) of the 2 \times 2 image \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}: each pixel gets its row sum plus its column sum. Compare with the image. What is right, what is wrong?
B4. Vertical stripes I = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12\cos(2\pi x/8) in a 64 \times 64 image. (a) What is the projection onto x (at 0°)? How many cycles does it have, and where are the peaks of its DFT (and how large, with the unnormalised DFT)? (b) What is the projection onto y (at 90°), and its DFT? (c) Mark both on a sketch of the 2D spectrum. Check that each projection’s spectrum is the slice at its angle.
B5. Predict, without computing: (a) Horizontal stripes with period 16 in a 64 \times 64 image: which projection shows them, and where are the dots in the 2D spectrum? (b) Stripes running diagonally (the grey value changes along the direction 45°): at which projection angle do they survive with full contrast? At which angle do they average away completely?
B6. Direct Fourier reconstruction of a 128 \times 128 image: the spectrum’s outer ring is 64 frequency steps from the centre. (a) With M spokes over 180°, how far apart are neighbouring spokes at the outer ring? (b) How many spokes are needed so that this gap is at most one frequency step? (c) Why does an interpolation error at one frequency show up over the whole reconstructed image?






Solutions





B1. (a) p_0: bars at \rho = 2 (height 1, A), 0 (2, B), -1 (1, C). p_{90°}: bars at \rho = 0 (1, A), 1 (2, B), -1 (1, C). (b) Rows from y = 2 (top) to -2, columns x = -2 \dots 2:

B = (0, 1): 4 (the maximum); A = (2, 0): 2; C = (-1, -1): 2. Four ghosts have value 3: (-1, 1), (2, 1), (0, 0), (0, -1), all brighter than A and C. Every pixel where a bright column meets a bright row lights up; with two angles the image cannot tell real points from crossings of their rays.

B2. (a) N lines cross a circle of radius r in 2N places, so per unit length 2N/(2\pi r) = N/(\pi r): 11.5 at r = 5, 2.9 at r = 20. (b) Four times fainter: the halo falls like 1/r. (c) Each point of the disc spreads part of its value into its surroundings; outside the disc these halos add up to a glow, and inside the disc the values are no longer flat. Neighbouring regions borrow brightness from each other, so contrast falls, worst for large slow structures.
B3. a = 3 + 4 = 7, b = 3 + 6 = 9, c = 7 + 4 = 11, d = 7 + 6 = 13. The order is right (a < b < c < d) and the differences between neighbours are right too, but every value is far too large: each pixel collects the whole sum of its row and of its column. Back-projection is not an inverse: it gives a blurred, unnormalised version. (The fourth unit returns to this: it is A^\top\mathbf b.)
B4. (a) Every column has 64 equal pixels: p_0(x) = 32 + 32\cos(2\pi x/8), 8 cycles over 64 pixels. DFT: DC = 64 \cdot 32 = 2048, peaks of 32 \cdot 64/2 = 1024 at \pm 8. (b) Every row contains whole periods: p_{90°}(y) = 64 \cdot \tfrac12 = 32, constant. DFT: only DC = 2048. (c) 2D DFT: 2048 at the centre, 1024 at (\pm 8, 0). The horizontal line through the centre (the 0° slice) contains -8, 0, 8, exactly the DFT of p_0; the vertical line (90°) contains only the DC term, exactly the DFT of p_{90°}.
B5. (a) They vary along y: the projection at 90° (row sums) shows a cosine with 64/16 = 4 cycles; the projection at 0° is constant. Dots at (0, \pm 4). (b) At 45° the rays run along the stripes, so each ray sees one grey value: full contrast. At 135° the rays cross the stripes and every ray averages over whole periods: the stripes vanish (up to the edges of the image).
B6. (a) The angular step is \pi/M, so the gap at radius 64 is 64\pi/M steps (2.2 for M = 90). (b) 64\pi/M \le 1 gives M \ge 201: about \tfrac{\pi}{2} \cdot 128. (This is the angle rule of the next unit.) (c) Every point of the spectrum is the amplitude of one plane wave that covers the whole image. A wrong value at one frequency adds a wrong wave everywhere, so local spectral errors become global image errors (ripples).




Math questions
B7. (math) Prove the Fourier slice theorem P_\theta(\omega) = F(\omega\,\mathbf n_\theta) for any \theta, starting from p_\theta(\rho) = \iint f(\mathbf x)\,\delta(\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf n_\theta - \rho)\,d\mathbf x.
B8. (math) Show that the back-projection of the sinogram of a point at the origin is 1/r: compute \int_0^\pi \delta(r\cos(\theta - \varphi))\,d\theta.
B9. (math) Use B8, linearity and the shift rule of the Radon transform to show \mathcal B\mathcal R f = f * \tfrac{1}{|\mathbf x|}.
B10. (math) Discrete version at 0°: an N \times N image I[y, x] (row y, column x) has column sums c[x] = \sum_y I[y, x]. Show that the DFT of c equals the row v = 0 of the 2D DFT of I.






Solutions (math)





B7. P_\theta(\omega) = \int p_\theta(\rho)e^{-2\pi i\omega\rho}d\rho = \iint f(\mathbf x)\Big(\int\delta(\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf n_\theta - \rho)e^{-2\pi i\omega\rho}d\rho\Big)d\mathbf x = \iint f(\mathbf x)e^{-2\pi i\omega\,\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf n_\theta}d\mathbf x = F(\omega\mathbf n_\theta) (swap the integrals, then use the sifting property of \delta).
B8. Substitute u = \theta - \varphi: \int\delta(r\cos u)\,du over an interval of length \pi. r\cos u has exactly one zero there (at u = \pm\pi/2), with derivative \mp r\sin u = \mp r, so the integral is 1/|r|.
B9. f = \iint f(\mathbf x')\,\delta(\mathbf x - \mathbf x')\,d\mathbf x' is a sum of shifted points. \mathcal R and \mathcal B are linear, and \mathcal R of a shifted point is the shifted sinusoid, whose back-projection is the shifted halo (the back-projection of g(\rho - \mathbf t\cdot\mathbf n_\theta, \theta) at \mathbf x is \mathcal Bg(\mathbf x - \mathbf t)). So \mathcal B\mathcal R f(\mathbf x) = \iint f(\mathbf x')\,\frac{1}{|\mathbf x - \mathbf x'|}\,d\mathbf x' = (f * \tfrac{1}{|\cdot|})(\mathbf x).
B10. F[u, 0] = \sum_y\sum_x I[y, x]\,e^{-2\pi i(ux + 0\cdot y)/N} = \sum_x\Big(\sum_y I[y, x]\Big)e^{-2\pi iux/N} = \sum_x c[x]\,e^{-2\pi iux/N}, the DFT of c. Exact, because the line v = 0 runs through grid points; at other angles the slice falls between them.

title: Exercise: back-projection and the Fourier slice theorem
text:
Explore: back-projection
Left: the sinogram, with the angle being back-projected marked in orange. Middle: the filter (here none) and the current projection. Right: the reconstruction, built up angle by angle. Angles in the scan sets how many projections are measured over 180°; back-projected how many of them are already smeared back; play adds them one after the other. The other filters belong to the next unit.



E1. Preset one point → star (4 angles). Where do the four arms cross? Set angles in the scan to 16 and then 180. Describe how the picture changes, and where the bright part ends up.
E2. With 180 angles, press clear and step with +1 angle a few times, then play. How does a single angle look in the reconstruction? When does the point first stand out?
E3. Preset plain: glow. Compare the reconstruction with the phantom you saw in the first unit. What is right, what is wrong? Why does the readout give no RMSE?






Solutions





E1. The arms cross only at the point, at (30, 20). With 16 angles the star has 16 arms; with 180 the arms merge into a bright spot surrounded by a halo that fades with distance (the auto contrast hides most of it; the outer parts of the image are not black). The spot sits where the point is: back-projection puts things in the right place, it just blurs them.
E2. One angle smears the projection into a stripe across the whole image (each bar of the projection becomes a band along its rays). After a few angles the stripes cross and the point is where they all meet; it stands out once several angles have been added, while the stripes far from it average into the halo.
E3. The shape is right: the skull, the ventricles and the small ellipses are in the right places. But everything is blurred and glows: the dark ellipses are not dark, the skull bleeds inwards and outwards, and the values are on a completely different scale (the halo adds up the whole image). Plain back-projection is not normalised (it is A^\top, not an inverse), so comparing its numbers with the phantom is meaningless.

title: Exercise: back-projection and the Fourier slice theorem
text:
Explore: the Fourier slice theorem
Slice theorem tab: drag on the image to turn the angle \theta (red line: the \rho direction; yellow: the rays). The middle panel is the 2D spectrum (log scale) with the slice at \theta in red. The plot shows the 1D spectrum of the projection (blue) and the 2D spectrum sampled along the red line (red, dashed), as log magnitude, real part or imaginary part. The readout gives their relative difference. Direct reconstruction tab: the projections’ spectra are placed on their spokes, interpolated onto the grid (nearest cell or bilinear), and inverted; the panels show the reconstruction, the gridded spectrum and the error.



E4. Preset stripes: one angle sees them, the other doesn’t (period 8). At \theta = 0°, where are the side peaks of the projection’s spectrum (in cycles per pixel)? Turn to 90°. What remains? Compare with B4.
E5. Choose tilted stripes. Find the angle at which the side peaks are largest, and their frequency. What is the period of the stripes?
E6. Preset projection ↔︎ slice match (Shepp–Logan). Read the relative difference at 0°, 30°, 45° and 90°. Why exactly zero at two of them? Switch to the real and the imaginary part: do they match too?
E7. Switch to direct reconstruction, preset spokes are sparse at the edge (24 spokes, bilinear). Look at the gridded spectrum: where is it empty? Compare the RMSE with filtered back-projection (readout).
E8. Preset nearest gridding: errors everywhere (90 spokes). Where is the error? Switch to bilinear: compare the RMSE and the fraction of grid cells filled. Then increase the spokes to 180 and 360. Does the direct method catch up with filtered back-projection?






Solutions





E4. At 0° the side peaks are at \pm 0.125 = 1/8 cycles per pixel (period 8), next to the large DC peak. At 90° only the DC peak remains: every row of the stripes averages to the same value. As in B4: the 0° slice of the 2D spectrum holds the stripe peaks, the 90° slice does not.
E5. At \theta = 30°, with side peaks near \pm 0.1 cycles per pixel: the stripes vary along the 30° direction with period 10. At 120° every ray crosses the stripes and averages over whole periods: the side peaks are gone.
E6. 0.00 % at 0° and 90°, 8.21 % at 30°, 8.72 % at 45°. At 0° and 90° the projection is exactly the column or row sums, and the slice runs along grid points of the 2D DFT, so the two are the same numbers (B10). At other angles the slice is interpolated between grid points and the projection itself is computed by interpolating between pixels: small differences, mostly at high frequencies. Real and imaginary parts match as well: the theorem holds for the complex spectrum, not only for magnitudes.
E7. The gridded spectrum is filled only along the 24 spokes; between them, especially far from the centre, it is empty (18.3 % of the cells filled). Missing high frequencies mean missing fine detail and streaky ripples. RMSE 0.112 (direct, bilinear) against 0.108 (filtered back-projection): with so few angles both suffer.
E8. With nearest-cell gridding the error is spread over the whole image as faint ripples, not only at the edges of the phantom: RMSE 0.079, 29.7 % of the cells filled. Bilinear gridding fills 58.3 % and gives 0.051. With 180 and 360 spokes (bilinear) the RMSE drops to 0.044, still above filtered back-projection (0.039): the interpolation error in the spectrum remains.

title: Exercise: back-projection and the Fourier slice theorem
text:
Where this leads
The spokes crowd at the centre of the spectrum: that is why plain back-projection over-weights slow waves. The next unit weights each projection’s spectrum by |\omega| before smearing back (filtered back-projection), and asks how many angles and photons a good reconstruction needs.

title: Quiz: back-projection and the Fourier slice theorem
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. What does back-projection do with one measured line integral?






Hint





We do not know where on the ray the attenuation was.









Answer





It adds the value to every pixel on that ray (with the same weights the projector used to sum them). Not knowing where along the ray the material was, it spreads it evenly. Doing this for all rays of all angles and adding gives the back-projection.




Q2. A single bright point is back-projected from 4 angles, then from 180. Describe both results.






Hint





Each angle contributes one stripe through the point.









Answer





4 angles: a star of four stripes crossing at the point. 180 angles: a bright peak at the point surrounded by a halo that fades like 1/r: the stripes overlap densely near the point and spread out with distance.




Q3. Is back-projection the inverse of projection? What is it instead?






Hint





Write projection as A\mathbf x.









Answer





No. Projection is a matrix A; back-projection is its transpose A^\top. A^\top A is not the identity but a blur (a 1/r kernel), so back-projecting a sinogram gives a blurred, unnormalised image.




Q4. Why does the plain back-projection of a large uniform disc look brighter in the middle than at its rim, and glow outside it?






Hint





Every point of the disc gets a halo.









Answer





Each point of the disc is blurred by the 1/r halo. A pixel in the middle receives halo contributions from disc points all around it; a pixel at the rim has disc on one side only; a pixel outside still receives the tails. So the middle is raised, the edge is soft and the surroundings glow.




Q5. State the Fourier slice theorem in one sentence, without formulas.






Answer





The 1D spectrum of the projection taken at angle \theta is the same as the 2D spectrum of the image along the straight line through its centre in the direction \theta.




Q6. An image contains only horizontal stripes (the grey value changes along y). Which projection angle shows the stripes, and which shows a constant? Where are the stripes in the 2D spectrum?






Hint





At 0° the rays are vertical.









Answer





At 90° the rays are horizontal and run along each stripe: the projection (row sums) shows the stripes. At 0° every column crosses all stripes and averages them: constant. In the 2D spectrum the stripes are two dots on the vertical axis, which is the 90° slice.




Q7. The theorem says projections fill the spectrum line by line. Why is “FFT each projection, place it on its line, inverse 2D FFT” not the standard method?






Hint





Where are the samples, and where does the inverse FFT need them?









Answer





The samples lie on spokes, dense near the centre and sparse far out; the inverse FFT needs them on a Cartesian grid. Interpolating from spokes to grid introduces errors, and an error at one frequency is a wave over the whole image: the errors spread everywhere instead of staying local.




Q8. How do the spokes of the Fourier slice theorem explain the halo of plain back-projection?






Answer





Every projection contributes a whole spoke through the centre, so the low frequencies near the centre are covered by every angle while the high frequencies far out are covered thinly. Back-projection adds all spokes with equal weight, so slow waves are over-represented, by a factor proportional to 1/|\omega|. In the image that is the 1/r halo.




Q9. (math) Prove the slice theorem for \theta = 0: \int p_0(x)\,e^{-2\pi iux}\,dx = F(u, 0).






Answer





p_0(x) = \int f(x, y)\,dy, so \int p_0(x)e^{-2\pi iux}dx = \iint f(x, y)e^{-2\pi i(ux + 0\cdot y)}\,dx\,dy = F(u, 0). The factor e^{-2\pi i\cdot 0\cdot y} = 1 lets the integral over y be done first.
crumbs: Back-projection and the Fourier slice theorem

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
About this lecture
The last unit built networks and said “training walks downhill”. This unit opens that box.

A loss says how wrong the network is: squared error for numbers, cross-entropy for classes.
Gradient descent steps downhill; the learning rate sets the step, a random mini-batch of examples estimates the slope.
Backpropagation computes the slope for every weight in one backward pass: the chain rule, organised.
Learning curves show overfitting; weight decay, dropout and more data fight it.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Suggested demo tour: gdescent (presets “just right”, “zig-zag”, “diverges”, “SGD noise”, “two starts”), then backprop (the by-hand preset: forward, backward, update, check; then “dead ReLU” and “sigmoid saturates”), then the playground with the training controls (overfitting presets). Adam, used without explanation on the VAE day, gets its one line on the math slide about mini-batches.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
section: The loss: how wrong is the network?
text:
The loss: how wrong is the network?
One number for all training examples, averaged; training makes it small.

Numbers (a brightness, a size): mean squared error, (\hat y - y)^2 averaged.
Classes: the network gives probabilities; the loss is cross-entropy, -\log p_{\text{true class}}.




probability given to the true class
0.99
0.9
0.5
0.2
0.01




cross-entropy -\ln p
0.01
0.11
0.69
1.61
4.61



A confident wrong answer costs far more than a hesitant one. 0.69 = \ln 2 is “50 : 50, no idea”.

Cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of the labels under the network’s probabilities: minimising it is maximum likelihood. Squared error on probabilities would also work but gives tiny gradients when the network is confidently wrong; cross-entropy gives the largest push exactly there (next math slide).
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
The math: softmax and cross-entropy
Scores \mathbf z, probabilities p_k = e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j}, true class c (one-hot \mathbf y):
\mathcal L = -\log p_c = -z_c + \log\sum_j e^{z_j}, \qquad \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial z_k} = p_k - y_k

The gradient is “predicted minus wanted”: no gradient when the network is right and sure, a gradient of almost -1 on the true score when it is sure and wrong.
Two classes with one sigmoid output p = 1/(1 + e^{-z}): \mathcal L = -[y\log p + (1 - y)\log(1 - p)], again \partial\mathcal L/\partial z = p - y.
Cross-entropy = negative log-likelihood of the training labels: minimising it is maximum likelihood.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Gradient descent: walk downhill
The loss is a landscape over all the weights. From the current weights, step a little in the steepest downhill direction; repeat.

Step length = learning rate \eta. Too small: it takes forever. Too large: it jumps across the valley, or out of it.
Recall the one-weight example of the last unit: \eta = 0.1, 0.125, 0.25, 0.5 gave losses 0.36, 0, 9, 81 after one step from 9.
A narrow valley makes a single \eta awkward: big enough for the gentle direction is too big for the steep one, so the path zig-zags.
Different starts can end in different valleys: different networks.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Try it: walking downhill




“too small” (η = 0.02): 192 steps to get within 0.001 of the minimum. “just right” (0.3): 11 steps. “zig-zag”: η = 0.6 in the narrow valley, the path bounces across the valley while it creeps along it. “momentum in the valley”: η = 0.03 with momentum gets there in about 115 steps; without momentum it is still far after 200. “diverges”: η = 0.8 on the bowl, the loss grows every step. “SGD noise”: batches of 4: a wandering path that ends jiggling around the minimum. “two starts, two minima”: the left start ends in the deeper minimum (loss −0.25), the right one in the shallower (+0.25). Click anywhere to add a path.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Mini-batches and epochs
The loss is an average over all training images, say 60,000. Its exact gradient needs all of them for every step: too slow.

Instead, take a random mini-batch (32 images), compute the gradient on it, step. A noisy but cheap estimate of the true slope.
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD): one step per mini-batch. One epoch = one pass through all the data: 60{,}000/32 = 1875 steps.
The noise is not just tolerated: it shakes the weights out of flat regions and narrow dips.
Momentum: keep part of the previous step, like a ball rolling downhill; it smooths zig-zags.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
The math: the update rules
\mathbf w \leftarrow \mathbf w - \eta\,\nabla_{\mathbf w}\mathcal L, \qquad \mathcal L(\mathbf w) = \frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N \ell_n(\mathbf w)

Mini-batch B of size m drawn uniformly: \mathbf g_B = \frac1m\sum_{n\in B}\nabla\ell_n has \mathbb E[\mathbf g_B] = \nabla\mathcal L (unbiased); its variance falls like 1/m.
Near a minimum the loss is a quadratic bowl with Hessian H; plain descent is stable only for \eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}(H), and the slow direction needs \approx 1/(\eta\lambda_{\min}) steps: elongated bowls are slow.
Momentum: \mathbf v \leftarrow \beta\mathbf v + \mathbf g, \mathbf w \leftarrow \mathbf w - \eta\mathbf v (typically \beta = 0.9).
Adam: momentum plus a separate step size per weight, dividing by a running average of \sqrt{g^2} (Kingma and Ba, 2015). The default in practice; the VAE day uses it.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
section: Backpropagation: the network as a graph
text:
Backpropagation: the network as a graph


Forward: values flow left to right (blue): z = w_1x + b_1, h = \text{ReLU}(z), \hat y = w_2h + b_2, \mathcal L = (\hat y - y)^2.
Backward: from the loss, each node passes on its gradient times its local derivative (red). Every weight gets \partial\mathcal L/\partial w.


Every node only needs to know its own local derivative: the multiply node knows ∂(wx)/∂w = x, the ReLU knows it passes or blocks, the loss knows 2(ŷ − y). The chain rule does the rest. The forward values must be kept, because the local derivatives need them.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Backprop by hand

Update with \eta = 0.1: w_1 = 0.2, b_1 = -0.15, w_2 = 1.4, b_2 = -0.1 → \mathcal L = 0.5625: worse! With \eta = 0.05: \mathcal L = 0.021.

Every weight moved in its own downhill direction, but together they overshoot: ŷ goes from 1.5 to 0.25, past the target 1. A smaller step works. The demo’s “update” button shows exactly these numbers.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
The math: backpropagation
Chain rule on the graph: \partial\mathcal L/\partial w = \sum_{\text{paths } w \to \mathcal L}\ \prod_{\text{edges}} local derivatives. Organised layer by layer, with \mathbf z^{(l)} = W^{(l)}\mathbf a^{(l-1)} + \mathbf b^{(l)}, \mathbf a^{(l)} = \varphi(\mathbf z^{(l)}) and \boldsymbol\delta^{(l)} = \partial\mathcal L/\partial\mathbf z^{(l)}:
\boldsymbol\delta^{(l-1)} = \big((W^{(l)})^\top\boldsymbol\delta^{(l)}\big) \odot \varphi'(\mathbf z^{(l-1)}), \qquad \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial W^{(l)}} = \boldsymbol\delta^{(l)}(\mathbf a^{(l-1)})^\top, \qquad \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\mathbf b^{(l)}} = \boldsymbol\delta^{(l)}

Start: \boldsymbol\delta^{(L)} = \mathbf p - \mathbf y (softmax + cross-entropy) or 2(\hat{\mathbf y} - \mathbf y) (squared error).
The backward pass is one matrix–vector product per layer, like the forward pass: the cost is about twice a forward pass, whatever the number of weights (Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams, 1986). Finite differences would need one forward pass per weight.

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Try it: forward, backward, update




Press forward (values appear node by node), backward (gradients, with each edge’s local derivative), update (the loss goes from 0.25 to 0.5625 with η = 0.1), check (finite differences agree). Then the presets: “dead ReLU” (x = −1: z < 0, the ReLU blocks, w1 and b1 get zero gradient), “sigmoid saturates” (z = 8: the sigmoid’s local derivative is 0.0003, w1 gets almost nothing), “learning rate too large” (η = 0.3: the loss jumps to 1.69). “2–2–1 network” shows the same with two hidden units.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
section: What the local derivatives tell us
text:
What the local derivatives tell us

ReLU passes the gradient (derivative 1) or blocks it (0). A unit that is off for every training example never gets a gradient again: a dead unit. A too large learning rate can kill many at once.
Sigmoid and tanh have derivatives near 0 when the input is large: a saturated unit passes almost nothing back. Through many such layers the gradient shrinks layer by layer: vanishing gradients.
That is why deep sigmoid networks were hard to train, and why ReLU took over around 2010.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Overfitting: recall, and learning curves

Day 14 (random forests): fit on training data, choose settings on validation data, report once on test data. A too flexible model fits the noise.

New here: plot the loss on both sets during training: the learning curves.
Training loss keeps falling. Validation loss falls, then rises: from there on the network memorises.
Early stopping: keep the weights from the step with the lowest validation loss.


The figure is the playground preset “overfitting”: 8 + 8 units on 60 noisy points, half of them for validation. The validation loss is lowest at step 126 (0.169); after 2000 steps the training loss is 0.002 and the validation loss 0.377. The test set must not be used for any of these choices, including when to stop.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Regularisation: making memorising harder

Weight decay: add \lambda\sum w^2 to the loss. Large weights make sharp, wiggly boundaries; small weights make smooth ones.
Dropout: during training, silence each hidden unit at random (say with probability 0.4). No unit can rely on a particular other unit; at test time all units are used.
More data, and data augmentation: train on shifted, rotated, brightened copies of the images (next unit).
And the simplest: a smaller network, or early stopping.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
section: The math: weight decay and dropout
text:
The math: weight decay and dropout

Weight decay: \mathcal L_\lambda(\mathbf w) = \mathcal L(\mathbf w) + \lambda\|\mathbf w\|^2, gradient \nabla\mathcal L + 2\lambda\mathbf w: every step also shrinks every weight by the factor 1 - 2\eta\lambda. The same penalty as ridge regression (Tikhonov regularisation, the deconvolution day).
Dropout: multiply each hidden output by m/(1 - q) with m \sim \text{Bernoulli}(1 - q); the expected output is unchanged, so nothing changes at test time (“inverted dropout”). It acts like averaging over the 2^{\#\text{units}} thinned networks (Srivastava et al., 2014).
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
section: Try it: overfitting and its cures
text:
Try it: overfitting and its cures




Hollow points are the validation set. “overfitting”: lowest validation loss 0.169 at step 126, then it rises while the training loss goes to 0.001. “weight decay smooths it”: the training loss stalls at 0.164 and the validation loss stays near 0.31: a smoother boundary. “dropout”: noisy training curve, the validation loss stays low much longer (0.18 at step 2000). “more data cures it”: 300 points, training and validation curves stay together. “mini-batches of 8”: a noisy curve. “learning rate too large”: the loss jumps, and 14 of the 16 hidden units die. “dead network”: η = 5, the loss sits at 0.693 = ln 2 for ever.

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Summary







Idea
In one line




Loss
squared error for numbers, cross-entropy -\log p_\text{true} for classes


Gradient descent
\mathbf w \leftarrow \mathbf w - \eta\nabla\mathcal L; \eta too small is slow, too large diverges


Mini-batch SGD
the gradient on 32 random examples; an epoch is one pass over the data


Backpropagation
forward values, then gradients backward, each node times its local derivative


Dead / saturated units
ReLU blocks, saturated sigmoids pass almost nothing: vanishing gradients


Learning curves
training loss falls, validation loss turns up: stop there


Regularisation
weight decay, dropout, more data, augmentation



Next: networks for images, where the first layer is a bank of learned convolution kernels.
