title: Exercise: linear classifiers
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Linear classifier
decide by the sign of f(\mathbf x) = \mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x + b: class +1 if f > 0, class -1 if f < 0


Labels
y = +1 or y = -1; a point is on its correct side when y\,f(\mathbf x) > 0


\mathbf w
the normal vector of the line (hyperplane), pointing to the +1 side


b
the offset: it shifts the line along \mathbf w


Signed distance
f(\mathbf x)/\|\mathbf w\|; positive on the +1 side


Scaling
(c\mathbf w, cb) with c > 0 gives the same line and the same distances; f is multiplied by c


Nearest class mean
\mathbf w = \boldsymbol\mu_+ - \boldsymbol\mu_-, line through the midpoint (\boldsymbol\mu_+ + \boldsymbol\mu_-)/2



Train/test splits, overfitting and cross-validation are recalled from the random forests day and not repeated here.

title: Exercise: linear classifiers
text:
By hand
B1. The classifier f(\mathbf x) = x_1 + 2x_2 - 4 and the points A = (1, 1), B = (3, 2), C = (0, 3), D = (2, 0.5). (a) Compute f for each point and classify it. (b) Compute the signed distance of each point to the line. Which points are closest? (c) Sketch the line (where does it cross the axes?) and the vector \mathbf w.
B2. Multiply \mathbf w and b of B1 by 3. What happens to the line, to the four values of f and to the four distances? And if you multiply by -1?
B3. Class +1: (3, 3), (4, 2), (5, 4). Class -1: (1, 1), (2, 0), (0, 2). (a) Compute the two class means and the nearest-class-mean classifier \mathbf w, b. (b) Check that it classifies all six training points correctly. (c) Classify the new points (2, 3) and (3, 1).
B4. A thresholding rule says “object if the intensity x > 100”. (a) Write it as a linear classifier (w, b) in one dimension. Is the answer unique? (b) The objects are now dark on a bright background: “object if x < 100”. Which (w, b)?
B5. XOR. Class -1: (0, 0) and (1, 1). Class +1: (1, 0) and (0, 1). Suppose a line f = w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + b classified all four correctly. Add up f(1, 0) + f(0, 1) and f(0, 0) + f(1, 1). What do you conclude? Which extra feature would make the problem linear?
B6. Objects are described by their area in pixels (typically 200 to 2000) and their mean intensity on a scale 0 to 1. A colleague proposes \mathbf w = (1, 1), b = -1000. (a) Which feature decides the class, in practice? Why? (b) Would nearest class mean or a distance-based method (1-NN) have the same problem? (This comes back in unit 4.)

Math questions
B7 (math). Show that the distance of \mathbf x to the hyperplane \mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x + b = 0 is |\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x + b|/\|\mathbf w\|. (Take a point \mathbf x_0 on the hyperplane and project \mathbf x - \mathbf x_0 on the unit normal.)
B8 (math). Show that the nearest-class-mean rule “\|\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu_+\| < \|\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu_-\|” is a linear classifier, and find \mathbf w and b.
B9 (math). The perceptron update for a misclassified point (\mathbf x, y) is \mathbf w \leftarrow \mathbf w + y\mathbf x, b \leftarrow b + y. Show that the new value of y\,f(\mathbf x) is larger than the old one, by exactly \|\mathbf x\|^2 + 1. Does that guarantee that the point is now correct?






Solutions





B1. (a) f(\text{A}) = 1 + 2 - 4 = -1 (class -1), f(\text{B}) = 3 + 4 - 4 = 3 (+1), f(\text{C}) = 0 + 6 - 4 = 2 (+1), f(\text{D}) = 2 + 1 - 4 = -1 (-1). (b) \|\mathbf w\| = \sqrt5 = 2.236. Distances: A -0.447, B +1.342, C +0.894, D -0.447. A and D are closest, on the -1 side, at the same distance. (c) The line crosses the x_1-axis at (4, 0) and the x_2-axis at (0, 2). \mathbf w = (1, 2) points up and to the right, perpendicular to the line, towards B and C.
B2. 3\mathbf w = (3, 6), 3b = -12: the same line. The values of f triple: -3, 9, 6, -3. The distances do not change: f and \|\mathbf w\| both triple. Multiplying by -1 keeps the line but swaps the sides: every point changes class, every distance changes sign.
B3. (a) \boldsymbol\mu_+ = (4, 3), \boldsymbol\mu_- = (1, 1). \mathbf w = (3, 2), midpoint (2.5, 2), b = -(3 \cdot 2.5 + 2 \cdot 2) = -11.5. (b) f = 3.5, 4.5, 11.5 for the +1 points and -6.5, -5.5, -7.5 for the -1 points: all correct. (c) f(2, 3) = 6 + 6 - 11.5 = 0.5: class +1, just. f(3, 1) = 9 + 2 - 11.5 = -0.5: class -1, just.
B4. (a) f(x) = x - 100: w = 1, b = -100. Not unique: any (c, -100c) with c > 0 is the same rule. (b) f(x) = 100 - x: w = -1, b = 100 (or any positive multiple).
B5. For a correct line: f(1, 0) > 0 and f(0, 1) > 0, so f(1, 0) + f(0, 1) = w_1 + w_2 + 2b > 0. Also f(0, 0) < 0 and f(1, 1) < 0, so f(0, 0) + f(1, 1) = w_1 + w_2 + 2b < 0. The same number cannot be both: no line classifies all four. With the product x_3 = x_1x_2 as a third feature, f = x_1 + x_2 - 2x_1x_2 - 0.5 gives -0.5, -0.5 for the class -1 points and +0.5, +0.5 for the class +1 points: linear in (x_1, x_2, x_3).
B6. (a) The area. f = area + intensity - 1000: the intensity changes f by at most 1, the area by hundreds or thousands. In practice the rule is “area > about 1000 px”, whatever the intensity. The numbers in \mathbf w must make up for the different units, and (1, 1) does not. (b) Yes: any method that measures distances between feature vectors (nearest mean, 1-NN, and the RBF kernel function of unit 3) is dominated by the feature with the largest range. A threshold on one feature, or a tree, is not. The cure (unit 4): standardise each feature.
B7. Take \mathbf x_0 with \mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x_0 = -b. The distance of \mathbf x to the hyperplane is the length of the component of \mathbf x - \mathbf x_0 along the unit normal \mathbf n = \mathbf w/\|\mathbf w\| (the component along the hyperplane does not change the distance): \mathbf n\cdot(\mathbf x - \mathbf x_0) = (\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x - \mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x_0)/\|\mathbf w\| = (\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x + b)/\|\mathbf w\|. Its absolute value is the distance; the sign tells the side.
B8. \|\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu_-\|^2 - \|\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu_+\|^2 = -2\boldsymbol\mu_-\cdot\mathbf x + \|\boldsymbol\mu_-\|^2 + 2\boldsymbol\mu_+\cdot\mathbf x - \|\boldsymbol\mu_+\|^2 = 2(\boldsymbol\mu_+ - \boldsymbol\mu_-)\cdot\mathbf x - (\|\boldsymbol\mu_+\|^2 - \|\boldsymbol\mu_-\|^2). It is positive exactly when \boldsymbol\mu_+ is closer. Divided by 2: \mathbf w = \boldsymbol\mu_+ - \boldsymbol\mu_-, b = -\tfrac12(\|\boldsymbol\mu_+\|^2 - \|\boldsymbol\mu_-\|^2) = -\mathbf w\cdot(\boldsymbol\mu_+ + \boldsymbol\mu_-)/2 (since \|\boldsymbol\mu_+\|^2 - \|\boldsymbol\mu_-\|^2 = (\boldsymbol\mu_+ - \boldsymbol\mu_-)\cdot(\boldsymbol\mu_+ + \boldsymbol\mu_-)). With the means of B3: b = -\tfrac12(25 - 2) = -11.5, as before.
B9. New value: y\left((\mathbf w + y\mathbf x)\cdot\mathbf x + b + y\right) = y(\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x + b) + y^2(\|\mathbf x\|^2 + 1) = y\,f(\mathbf x) + \|\mathbf x\|^2 + 1, since y^2 = 1. It increases, but not necessarily above 0: a badly wrong point may need several updates. And the update can make other points wrong.

title: Exercise: linear classifiers
text:
Explore
The demo shows two classes of points (blue = -1, red = +1) and a line with its normal vector \mathbf w (the arrow). Drag the arrow’s tip to turn \mathbf w, drag its foot to shift the line. The background is tinted by the sign of f; points on the wrong side are ringed (dashed). (w, b) × 2 and ÷ 2 scale \mathbf w and b together. Nearest class mean puts the line through the midpoint of the two means (the crosses); perceptron step makes one perceptron update with the next misclassified point (circled in yellow). Tick show signed distances to label each point with f/\|\mathbf w\|, and shade the 1-NN regions to see the nearest-neighbour classifier instead. Click to add points, drag them to move them.



L1. Preset by hand. Check your answers to B1 in the readout. Press (w, b) × 2 twice: what happens to the line, to f and to the distances? Compare with B2.
L2. Preset many lines are perfect. Turn and shift the line: find two quite different lines with 0 errors. Compare their smallest y \cdot f/\|\mathbf w\|. Then press nearest class mean: errors and smallest distance? Which of the lines would you trust most on new points, and why?
L3. Preset nearest mean is not the best line. Press nearest class mean: how many errors? Now drag the arrow until the line runs along the two clouds: can you reach 0 errors? Why does the nearest-mean line fail here?
L4. On the same preset, start again (reset line) and press perceptron step a few times. Describe how the line moves. (The perceptron needs 646 updates here before it stops; what is the smallest distance of the line it stops at? See the solution.)
L5. Preset one outlier. What is the smallest number of errors you can reach with a line? Tick shade the 1-NN regions: what does 1-NN do with the outlier?
L6. Presets XOR and ring around a blob. Try to find the best line. What is the fewest errors you can get? Which extra feature (a third axis) would help in each case?






Solutions





L1. f = -1, 3, 2, -1 and d = -0.45, +1.34, +0.89, -0.45 (A, B, C, D in the order of the readout). After two doublings (\mathbf w, b) = (4, 8, -16): the line does not move, f is 4 times larger (-4, 12, 8, -4), the distances are unchanged.
L2. Every line through the empty gap between the blobs has 0 errors, but the smallest distance varies: the starting line has 0 errors with a smallest distance of 0.58; the nearest-class-mean line has 0 errors with 0.99. A line that passes close to some training point (small smallest distance) is the one most likely to misclassify a new point that falls a little beyond it. This is the idea of the next unit: choose the line with the largest smallest distance.
L3. The nearest-mean line makes 9 errors of 60. A line along the clouds (roughly parallel to their long axes, in the narrow gap between them) has 0 errors. The two clouds are shifted along their length, so the line through the midpoint perpendicular to \boldsymbol\mu_+ - \boldsymbol\mu_- runs nearly across the clouds and cuts both. Nearest mean uses only the two means, not the shape of the clouds.
L4. Each step picks the next point on the wrong side and pulls the line towards classifying it correctly; the line often jumps far and many points flip side (after the first step 30 errors, then 6, then 30 again). It does converge here because the data are separable, but only after 646 updates, and it stops at the first line with 0 errors, whose smallest distance is only 0.015: it grazes a point. The perceptron finds a separating line, not a good one.
L5. At least 1 error: no line puts the outlier on the red side without misclassifying many blue points (the nearest-mean line also has 1 error). 1-NN classifies every training point correctly by construction: it draws a red island around the outlier, which will misclassify new blue points near it.
L6. XOR: the best line still has 14 errors of 60 (a line can at most cut off one corner cluster cleanly). The product x_1x_2 (with the origin in the middle of the square) separates the diagonals. Ring: no line beats calling everything blue, which gets the 17 inner (red) points wrong. The squared distance from the centre, (x_1 - 5)^2 + (x_2 - 5)^2, separates inside from outside with a single threshold. Both are the subject of unit 3.

title: Exercise: linear classifiers
text:
Where this leads
Among all lines with zero training errors, which is best? The next unit chooses the one with the widest margin: the support vector machine. Unit 3 then replaces the line by curves without giving up the linear algebra: kernel functions.

title: Quiz: linear classifiers
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A linear classifier decides by the sign of f(\mathbf x) = \mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x + b; labels are y = \pm 1.

Q1. Give one example each of a classification problem where the points are pixels, objects and image windows. What are the features?






Hint





What is measured for each pixel, each object, each window?









Answer





Pixels: nucleus / cytoplasm / background, with features from a stack of filtered images (smoothed intensity at several scales, edge strength, blob and texture responses). Objects: cell / debris, with features from the measurement table (area, mean intensity, form factor). Windows: “cell here” / “no cell”, with a descriptor of the patch (e.g. histograms of gradient directions). In all three each item becomes a point in a feature space with a label.




Q2. For f(\mathbf x) = 2x_1 - x_2 + 1, which side is class +1? What is the signed distance of (0, 3) to the line?






Hint





The distance is f/\|\mathbf w\|.









Answer





Class +1 is the side \mathbf w = (2, -1) points to (right and down). f(0, 3) = 0 - 3 + 1 = -2, \|\mathbf w\| = \sqrt5, distance -2/\sqrt5 = -0.894: the point lies on the -1 side, 0.894 from the line.




Q3. You multiply \mathbf w and b by 10. Which of these change: the line, the classification of each point, the value of f, the distance of each point to the line?






Hint





Write f/\|\mathbf w\| for the scaled classifier.









Answer





Only the value of f (ten times larger). The line f = 0, the signs (classes) and the distances f/\|\mathbf w\| are unchanged. So the value of f alone means nothing until the scale of (\mathbf w, b) is fixed.




Q4. The two class means are \boldsymbol\mu_+ = (2, 2) and \boldsymbol\mu_- = (0, 0). Give the nearest-class-mean line.






Hint





Perpendicular to \boldsymbol\mu_+ - \boldsymbol\mu_-, through the midpoint.









Answer





\mathbf w = (2, 2), midpoint (1, 1), b = -(2 + 2) = -4: f = 2x_1 + 2x_2 - 4, the line x_1 + x_2 = 2.




Q5. Two long, thin, parallel clouds are shifted mostly along their length. Why does the nearest-class-mean line do badly, even though a line with zero errors exists?






Hint





In which direction does \boldsymbol\mu_+ - \boldsymbol\mu_- point?









Answer





\boldsymbol\mu_+ - \boldsymbol\mu_- points mostly along the clouds, so the nearest-mean line, perpendicular to it, runs across both clouds and cuts them. The separating line runs along the clouds, through the narrow gap. Nearest mean only looks at the two means, not at the shape of the clouds.




Q6. Why can no line separate a nucleus (inside) from the cytoplasm around it when the features are the pixel’s (x, y) position, or two intensity features in which the cytoplasm surrounds the nucleus?






Hint





A line splits the plane into two half-planes. Can a half-plane contain the inside of a ring but not the ring?









Answer





A half-plane is convex and unbounded: if it contains the inner blob it also contains every point on the far side, including part of the ring, because the ring surrounds the blob in all directions. A ring around a blob needs a closed boundary (a circle), which a linear classifier on these two features cannot produce. Adding a feature such as the squared distance from the centre makes it linear again (unit 3).




Q7. Is the SVM generative or discriminative? And a classifier that fits one Gaussian per class and picks the more likely class?






Hint





Does the method describe how each class is distributed?









Answer





The SVM is discriminative: it only looks for a boundary. The Gaussian-per-class classifier is generative: it models each class and compares likelihoods (the minimum-error threshold of the thresholding day is the 1D case; the Gaussian mixtures day goes further).




Q8. (math) Show that f(\mathbf x)/\|\mathbf w\| is the same for (\mathbf w, b) and (c\mathbf w, cb) with c > 0.






Hint





\|c\mathbf w\| = |c|\,\|\mathbf w\|.









Answer





(c\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x + cb)/\|c\mathbf w\| = c(\mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x + b)/(c\|\mathbf w\|) = f(\mathbf x)/\|\mathbf w\| for c > 0. For c < 0 the sign flips: the same line, the sides swapped.

title: Convolutional networks
text:
About this lecture
A network for images should know two things about images: neighbouring pixels belong together, and a nucleus is a nucleus wherever it is. A convolutional layer builds in both.

A convolutional layer = a bank of small kernels, learned instead of designed. Each gives a feature map.
The same kernel everywhere (weight sharing): few weights, and shifting the input shifts the maps.
Pooling shrinks the maps; stacked layers see ever larger parts of the image (the receptive field).
Early layers find edges, later ones parts and objects. Augmentation teaches the invariances we want.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Suggested demo tour: convlayer (hand-made vs learned bank, shift, pooling), receptive (presets “three 3×3 = 7”, “with pooling”, “how deep to see a whole nucleus?”), cnnviewer (a digit through the trained network; “a 6 rotated to a 9”, rotation with and without augmentation, occlusion). Convolution itself is from the kernels unit of day 1: recall it in one sentence, do not re-teach it.

title: Convolutional networks
section: From hand-made features to learned ones
text:
From hand-made features to learned ones
Day 14 (random forests) gave every pixel a feature stack: Gaussian, derivative, LoG, Hessian filters at chosen scales (the edges day), then a classifier on top.

The filters were designed by us: interpretable, no training data needed.
A convolutional network learns the filters, and further layers that combine them, from labelled examples.
The trade-off: learned features adapt to the task, but they need examples (and checking).

title: Convolutional networks
section: Dense layers do not suit images
text:
Dense layers do not suit images
A 64 \times 64 grey image into a dense layer of 100 units: 4096 \times 100 + 100 = 409{,}700 weights.

Too many weights: each unit has a separate weight for every pixel.
No neighbourhood: the pixel order could be shuffled and the layer would not notice.
No shift: a nucleus in the top-left corner and the same nucleus in the bottom-right use completely different weights. Every position has to be learned separately.

title: Convolutional networks
section: A convolutional layer: a bank of kernels
text:
A convolutional layer: a bank of kernels
Recall (the kernels unit, day 1): a 3 \times 3 kernel slides over the image; each output pixel is the weighted sum of the 3 \times 3 neighbourhood.

A convolutional layer applies several kernels, say 8, each giving one output image: a feature map.
Then a bias and the ReLU, as in any layer: each map says “my pattern is here, this strongly”.
The kernel values are weights, learned by backpropagation like any others.
Networks actually compute the correlation (no flip); with learned kernels the flip does not matter.


Show the convlayer demo next. The hand-made bank has Sobel x and y, two diagonals, the Laplacian, a Gaussian, and two line detectors. The learned bank is layer 1 of the small digit network of cnnviewer: several of its kernels look like edge or stroke detectors in some direction.

title: Convolutional networks
text:
Try it: one convolutional layer




Start with the learned bank on a digit; switch to the hand-made bank and compare. Then “shift the input” (micrograph): every map shifts by the same amount. Then “pooling”: the maps at half size, still recognisable. Click a kernel and edit it (e.g. turn Sobel x into its negative: the other edge of each stroke lights up).

title: Convolutional networks
text:
Weight sharing
The same 9 weights at every position.

Weights per layer: 3 \cdot 3 \cdot C_\text{in} \cdot C_\text{out} + C_\text{out}, independent of the image size. One grey input, 8 kernels: 80 weights, for a 28 \times 28 or a 1000 \times 1000 image alike.
Translation equivariance: shift the input, and every feature map shifts the same way. A detector learned at one position works at all of them.
Compare: the dense layer of the last slide has 409,700 weights and no equivariance.

title: Convolutional networks
text:
The math: a convolutional layer
With input channels x_c and output channels y_{c'}:
y_{c'}[i, j] = b_{c'} + \sum_{c}\sum_{u,v} w_{c',c}[u, v]\; x_c[i + u,\ j + v]

It is a dense layer whose matrix is sparse (each output depends on a k \times k patch) and repeated (every row is the same kernel, shifted): a banded Toeplitz matrix in 1D.
Equivariance: with T_s = shift by s, \text{conv}(T_sx) = T_s\,\text{conv}(x) (up to borders). The ReLU acts pixel by pixel, so it keeps this. Stride and pooling break it for shifts that are not multiples of the stride.
Backprop through a convolution is again a correlation: \partial\mathcal L/\partial w_{c',c}[u, v] = \sum_{i,j}\delta_{c'}[i, j]\,x_c[i + u, j + v].

title: Convolutional networks
text:
Channels

A colour image has 3 channels; the output of a layer with 8 kernels has 8 channels.
A kernel of the next layer covers all input channels: it is 3 \times 3 \times 8, with 72 weights.
So layer 2 combines features: “a vertical edge here and a bright blob next to it”. Each output channel has its own kernel stack.
Counting: layer 2 with 16 output channels on 8 input channels: 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 8 \cdot 16 + 16 = 1168 weights.

title: Convolutional networks
text:
Pooling and stride

2×2 max pooling: keep the largest value of each 2 \times 2 block. The map shrinks to half width and height and keeps “the feature is somewhere here”, with a little tolerance to small shifts.
Stride 2: evaluate the kernel only at every second position: also halves the size.
Output size of a layer with kernel k, padding p, stride s on n pixels:

n_\text{out} = \left\lfloor\frac{n + 2p - k}{s}\right\rfloor + 1

n = 28, k = 3, p = 1, s = 1: 28 (padding keeps the size). k = 5, p = 0: 24. n = 64, k = 3, p = 1, s = 2: 32.

title: Convolutional networks
text:
The receptive field
The part of the input that one unit can see.

One 3 \times 3 layer: 3 pixels wide. Two: 5. Three: 7.
Three 3 \times 3 layers see as much as one 7 \times 7 layer, with 27 instead of 49 weights per channel pair, and two more nonlinearities.
Pooling multiplies the growth: after a 2 \times 2 pool, each further 3 \times 3 layer adds 4 input pixels instead of 2.
Deep layers see whole objects: that is where “nucleus” or “digit 6” can be decided.

title: Convolutional networks
text:
Try it: receptive fields




“three 3×3 layers = 7”, then “one 7×7 layer” (same field, readout shows 2320 weights per layer pair with 16 channels for 3×3, 12560 for 7×7: 6960 vs 12560). “with pooling”: conv, pool, conv, pool, conv sees 18 pixels (3, 4, 8, 10, 18). “how deep to see a whole nucleus?”: 8 layers with two pools see 32 pixels, more than a 20-pixel nucleus. “dilated: 1, 2, 4”: 15 pixels with only three layers. Click units in middle layers too.

title: Convolutional networks
text:
The math: receptive field recursion
Layer l with kernel k_l, stride s_l (pooling: k = s = 2), dilation d_l. Let r_l be the receptive field and j_l the jump: the distance in input pixels between neighbouring units of layer l.
r_l = r_{l-1} + d_l(k_l - 1)\,j_{l-1}, \qquad j_l = j_{l-1}\,s_l, \qquad r_0 = j_0 = 1

Conv 3, conv 3, pool, conv 3, conv 3: r = 3, 5, 6, 10, 14; j = 1, 1, 2, 2, 2.
Without pooling or stride, the field grows only linearly: r = 1 + 2L for L layers of 3 \times 3.

title: Convolutional networks
text:
What the layers learn


Layer 1 kernels: edges, lines, blobs in different directions. The only layer whose kernels can be looked at as pictures.
Deeper layers: corners and textures, then parts (a loop, a stroke ending), then whole objects (Zeiler and Fergus, 2014).
Ways to look inside: the feature maps for an input; the image patches that excite a unit most; occlusion: cover part of the image and watch the class probability.

title: Convolutional networks
section: A classification network, end to end
text:
A classification network, end to end
conv 3×3 (8) → ReLU → pool → conv 3×3 (16) → ReLU → pool → flatten → dense → softmax, trained with cross-entropy (previous unit).



layer
output
weights




conv, 1 → 8
8 \times 28 \times 28
80


conv, 8 → 16
16 \times 14 \times 14
1,168


dense, 16 \cdot 7 \cdot 7 = 784 → 10
10 scores
7,850



9,098 weights, 98.7 % correct on 10,000 test digits. A dense 784 → 100 → 10 network has 79,510.

title: Convolutional networks
section: Try it: inside a trained network
text:
Try it: inside a trained network




Draw a digit or pick one; look at the layer-1 maps (strokes in different directions) and layer-2 maps; click a layer-2 map to see its 9 favourite test patches. “shifted digit”: maps shift, the prediction stays 6. “a 6 rotated to a 9”: at 180° the network says 9, correctly! “rotation 30°”: without augmentation it says 4 (0.55), with rotation augmentation 6 (1.00). Weight sets epoch 0, 1, 3: random kernels and 10 % accuracy at epoch 0, 94 % after one epoch. “what is the network looking at?”: occlusion map of a 2.

title: Convolutional networks
text:
Data augmentation
Train on modified copies: shifted, rotated, flipped, brighter, darker, slightly deformed. The label stays the same.

The network learns the invariances we can name: “a rotated 2 is still a 2”.
Our digit network: on test digits rotated by 45°, 46.9 % correct without augmentation, 92.9 % with random rotations up to ±45° during training (and 97.2 % instead of 98.7 % on upright digits).
Choose with care: with full rotations a 6 and a 9 become the same class. For cells, rotations and flips are usually safe.
Compare the moments elective: there invariance is built into the features; here it is taught by examples.

title: Convolutional networks
text:
Summary







Idea
In one line




Convolutional layer
a bank of learned k \times k kernels, each giving a feature map; bias, ReLU


Weight sharing
same kernel everywhere: k^2C_\text{in}C_\text{out} + C_\text{out} weights, any image size


Equivariance
shift the input, the maps shift; pooling adds a little invariance


Output size
\lfloor(n + 2p - k)/s\rfloor + 1


Receptive field
grows by k - 1 per layer, faster after pooling


Hierarchy
edges → textures → parts → objects


Augmentation
teach invariances by training on modified copies



Next: from “what is in the image” to “which pixels belong to it”: segmentation networks.

title: Exercise: colocalisation
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute Pearson’s r, the overlap coefficient and Manders’ M1 and M2 for two small channels,
predict which of them change when a channel gets a background offset or a gain,
explain why thresholds decide M1 and M2, and how Costes’ method sets them,
recognise the classic pitfalls: the region, bleed-through, misalignment and resolution, and use shift and randomisation controls.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo.

title: Exercise: colocalisation
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Scatter plot
one point (A_i, B_i) per pixel of the region


Pearson r
\sum (A_i - \bar A)(B_i - \bar B) / \sqrt{\sum (A_i - \bar A)^2 \sum (B_i - \bar B)^2}


Overlap coefficient
\sum A_i B_i / \sqrt{\sum A_i^2 \sum B_i^2}


M1
\sum A_i over pixels with A_i > t_A and B_i > t_B, divided by \sum A_i over pixels with A_i > t_A


M2
the same with A and B (and t_A, t_B) swapped


Costes’ threshold
lower t_A (with t_B on the regression line) until the pixels below the thresholds have r \le 0


Randomisation
shuffle blocks of B, recompute r; compare with the observed r

title: Exercise: colocalisation
text:
By hand
Two 3 \times 3 channels (the region is all 9 pixels):
A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 & 8 \\ 1 & 6 & 9 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 5 & 8 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.
B1. (a) Compute the means \bar A and \bar B. (b) Compute \sum (A_i - \bar A)(B_i - \bar B), \sum (A_i - \bar A)^2 and \sum (B_i - \bar B)^2, and Pearson’s r. (c) Compute \sum A_i B_i, \sum A_i^2, \sum B_i^2 and the overlap coefficient.
B2. Thresholds t_A = t_B = 2 (“above” means > 2). (a) Which pixels are above in A, in B, in both? (b) Compute M1 and M2. Interpret them in words. (c) Compute M1 and M2 with t_A = t_B = -1 (no thresholds). Why are they both 1?
B3. The B channel gets a background offset: B' = B + 10. (a) Which of r and the overlap coefficient change? Compute the new overlap coefficient (\sum A_i B'_i = 454, \sum B_i'^2 = 1512). (b) Keep t_B = 2: what are M1 and M2 now, and why are they wrong? (c) Which t_B gives back the M1 and M2 of B2? (d) What would a gain, B'' = 2B with t_B = 4, change?
B4. A small structure inside a large one: A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 5 & 5 \\ 0 & 5 & 5 \\ 0 & 5 & 5 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad t_A = t_B = 0. Compute M1 and M2. Then compute r (it is 0.37) and say which of the three numbers best describes the situation.
B5. Explain, in one or two sentences each, why each of these makes two unrelated proteins look colocalised: (a) measuring r over the whole image including the dark background; (b) 30 % of dye A leaking into channel B; (c) both proteins being in vesicles smaller than the resolution limit.

Math questions
B6. (math) Show that r is unchanged when A is replaced by gA + c with g > 0, and that it changes sign for g < 0. Show that the overlap coefficient is unchanged by g > 0 but not by c.
B7. (math) Show that for B = aA (a > 0, no noise) and any t_A \ge 0 with t_B = a\,t_A, M_1 = M_2 = 1. What does this mean for the thresholds on the Costes line?
B8. (math) Show that the direction of the orthogonal regression line is the eigenvector of the 2 \times 2 covariance matrix of (A, B) with the largest eigenvalue, and derive the slope formula \big(s_{BB} - s_{AA} + \sqrt{(s_{BB} - s_{AA})^2 + 4 s_{AB}^2}\big)/(2 s_{AB}).






Solutions





B1. (a) \bar A = 30/9 = 3.33, \bar B = 24/9 = 2.67. (b) \sum (A - \bar A)(B - \bar B) = \sum AB - 9\bar A\bar B = 154 - 80 = 74; \sum (A - \bar A)^2 = 196 - 100 = 96; \sum (B - \bar B)^2 = 132 - 64 = 68. r = 74/\sqrt{96 \cdot 68} = 74/80.8 = \mathbf{0.916}. (c) \sum AB = 154, \sum A^2 = 196, \sum B^2 = 132: overlap = 154/\sqrt{196 \cdot 132} = 154/160.9 = \mathbf{0.957}.
B2. (a) A above 2: the pixels with values 8, 6, 9, 3. B above 2: 6, 5, 8 (at the positions of A’s 8, 6, 9). Both: the positions of A’s 8, 6 and 9. (b) M_1 = (8 + 6 + 9)/(8 + 6 + 9 + 3) = 23/26 = \mathbf{0.885}: 88 % of A’s signal lies where B is present (the 3 in the bottom-right corner has no B). M_2 = (6 + 5 + 8)/(6 + 5 + 8) = \mathbf{1}: all of B’s signal lies where A is present. (c) With t = -1 every pixel is above in both channels, so numerator and denominator are the same sums: M_1 = M_2 = 1. Without a threshold M1 and M2 say nothing.
B3. (a) r stays 0.916 (it subtracts the means). Overlap: 454/\sqrt{196 \cdot 1512} = 454/544.4 = \mathbf{0.834} (was 0.957): not offset-invariant. (b) Now every B' is above 2: M_1 = 26/26 = 1; M_2 = \sum B' over A-above pixels / \sum B' over all = (16 + 15 + 18 + 10)/114 = 59/114 = 0.518. Both are wrong: the offset made every pixel “positive” in B, so all of A counts as colocalised, and B’s background (now 10 per pixel) is counted as B signal. (c) Moving the threshold with the background: t_B = 12 gives back M_1 = 0.885, M_2 = 1. (d) A gain changes nothing if the threshold scales with it: r, overlap, M1 and M2 are the same (M2’s sums double in numerator and denominator).
B4. A above 0: the 9 and the 6, both where B = 5: M_1 = 15/15 = \mathbf 1. B above 0: six pixels with sum 30, of which two (sum 10) have A: M_2 = 10/30 = \mathbf{0.33}. All of A is inside B, but only a third of B contains A. r = 0.37 hides this asymmetry; M1 and M2 together describe it.
B5. (a) The background pixels are dark in both channels and the cells bright in both, so the scatter plot is a cloud stretched along the diagonal from (dark, dark) to (bright, bright): high r from the cell outline alone (demo: 0.51 against −0.08 inside the cells). (b) Wherever A is bright, B gets 0.3 × A on top: B now contains a copy of A’s pattern, so the channels correlate (demo with 40 %: r = 0.32 from −0.08). (c) Two vesicles closer than about 200 nm blur into one spot in both channels: the image cannot separate them, so they overlap in the image whether or not the proteins are in the same vesicle.









Solutions (math)





B6. gA + c has mean g\bar A + c, so (gA_i + c) - (g\bar A + c) = g(A_i - \bar A). Numerator scales by g, denominator by \sqrt{g^2} = |g|: r \mapsto \operatorname{sign}(g)\,r. Overlap: \sum (gA_i) B_i / \sqrt{g^2 \sum A_i^2 \sum B_i^2} is unchanged for g > 0; with c: \sum (A_i + c) B_i / \sqrt{\sum (A_i + c)^2 \sum B_i^2}, which differs in general (B3: 0.957 → 0.834) and tends to \sum B_i / \sqrt{n \sum B_i^2} as c \to \infty.
B7. With B_i = aA_i and t_B = a t_A: B_i > t_B \iff A_i > t_A. So the set of pixels above in A equals the set above in B, numerator and denominator of M_1 are the same sums, and likewise for M_2. On the Costes line the thresholds are “matched”: for perfectly colocalised channels M1 = M2 = 1 at every step, and any value below 1 comes from pixels off the line.
B8. Centre the data; a unit direction \mathbf u captures the variance \mathbf u^\top S \mathbf u, and the sum of squared perpendicular distances is \operatorname{tr} S - \mathbf u^\top S \mathbf u (times n). Minimising it maximises \mathbf u^\top S \mathbf u: the top eigenvector of S = \begin{bmatrix} s_{AA} & s_{AB} \\ s_{AB} & s_{BB} \end{bmatrix} (the PCA unit). Its eigenvalue \lambda = \tfrac12\big(s_{AA} + s_{BB} + \sqrt{(s_{BB} - s_{AA})^2 + 4 s_{AB}^2}\big); the eigenvector satisfies the first row of (S - \lambda I)\mathbf u = 0, (s_{AA} - \lambda) u_A + s_{AB} u_B = 0, so the slope u_B/u_A = (\lambda - s_{AA})/s_{AB} = \big(s_{BB} - s_{AA} + \sqrt{(s_{BB} - s_{AA})^2 + 4 s_{AB}^2}\big)/(2 s_{AB}).

title: Exercise: colocalisation
text:
Explore
The demo makes two synthetic channels inside two cells: structures in A; in B a fraction shared f of the same structures and the rest independent ones (or, with A inside B, large B structures that contain A’s small spots); a diffuse signal in the cells in both channels; bleed-through of A into B; a sideways shift of B; a background offset and noise. Left: the merge (A green, B magenta, white where both are bright) with the region (yellow: inside the cells). Middle: the 2D histogram over the region (logarithmic colour), the orthogonal regression line (dashed), and the thresholds t_A (green, vertical) and t_B (red, horizontal): drag them. Right: the readouts. Costes animates the threshold search; randomise shuffles 8 \times 8 blocks of B 50 times and shows the shuffled r against the observed one.



C1. Preset perfect colocalisation. Describe the scatter plot. Read r, the overlap coefficient, M1 and M2, and the Costes thresholds. Press Costes and watch the thresholds move: where do they stop, relative to the background blob?
C2. Preset independent: r ≈ 0. Describe the scatter plot. Why is Costes’ method not defined here, and what are M1 and M2 with the fallback thresholds? Press randomise: how many shuffled r are at least the observed one?
C3. Preset background inflates r: diffuse signal in both channels, region = whole image. Read r. Switch the region to inside cells. Explain the difference with the scatter plot.
C4. Preset M1 ≈ M2 ≈ 1 without thresholds (independent channels, t_A = t_B = 0). Read M1 and M2. Then press Costes. Compare with B2(c) and B3(b).
C5. Preset A inside B. Read M1, M2 and r. Which number tells you that A sits inside B? Set the thresholds to zero: what happens to M2, and why?
C6. Preset bleed-through fakes it (independent structures, 40 % of A leaks into B). Read r, M1 and M2, then randomise. Does the randomisation test protect you? Set the bleed-through to 0 and compare.
C7. Preset shift by 3 px: perfect colocalisation, B shifted 3 pixels. Read r. Set the shift to 1, 2 and 6 px. How fast does r fall, and what sets that speed?
C8. Back to the default (reset): shared f = 0.5. Set f to 0.25 and 0.75. Is r the fraction of shared structures?






Solutions





C1. A thin cloud along a line through the background blob with slope 1.00; r = 0.988, overlap 0.993, M1 = 0.940, M2 = 0.939. Costes’ thresholds stop at t_A = 13.9, t_B = 13.8, just above the background blob (offset 10, noise σ = 4): below them the remaining pixels are noise with no correlation.
C2. An L shape: bright A with dark B along the A axis, bright B with dark A along the B axis. r = -0.08 (structures that exclude each other slightly), so the regression line falls and there is no rising line to walk down. With the 75th-percentile thresholds, M1 = 0.20 and M2 = 0.18: the chance level, not zero. Randomisation: 47 of 50 shuffled r are at least −0.08: no evidence of colocalisation.
C3. Whole image: r = 0.51. Inside the cells: r = -0.08. Over the whole image the scatter plot has two clusters: the background at (10, 10) and the cells at about (40, 40) (diffuse signal 30 in both channels). The line through the two clusters gives a high r although the structures inside the cells are independent.
C4. M1 = 0.999, M2 = 0.997: with a background offset and noise, almost every pixel is above 0 in both channels, so “where the other channel is present” means everywhere. Costes is not defined for these anticorrelated channels; the fallback thresholds give 0.20 and 0.18. As in B2(c) and B3(b): without the right threshold, M1 and M2 measure nothing.
C5. M1 = 0.79, M2 = 0.32, r = 0.37. M1 high and M2 low: most of A lies where B is, but most of B has no A. r alone cannot tell this. With zero thresholds M2 becomes 0.995 (and M1 1.000): every pixel counts as A-positive, so all of B is “where A is”.
C6. r = 0.32, M1 = 0.70, M2 = 0.42, and none of 50 shuffles reaches 0.32: the test calls it significant. Randomisation only asks whether the overlap is more than chance for the two images as given; leakage puts a copy of A into B, which is real overlap in the images. With bleed-through 0, r goes back to −0.08. Only compensation (or sequential imaging) helps.
C7. r = 0.94 (1 px), 0.81 (2 px), 0.63 (3 px), 0.16 (6 px), from 0.99 without shift. The structures are blurred spots of a few pixels; once the shift is comparable with their size, they no longer overlap. Small structures make r very sensitive to chromatic misalignment; large ones (or the cell outline) make it insensitive.
C8. r = 0.26 at f = 0.25, 0.69 at 0.5, 0.94 at 0.75. It grows with f but is not equal to it: r measures how well a straight line explains B from A, which mixes the shared fraction with the intensities and the noise.

title: Exercise: colocalisation
text:
Where this leads
Colocalisation coefficients are per image or per cell; to compare conditions they become rows of the feature table and go through the same aggregation and statistics as every other measurement (the evaluation day: replicates, effect sizes). Bleed-through correction is the spectral unmixing elective; FRET and fluorescence lifetimes, which measure molecular proximity below the resolution limit, are planned as a fluorescence-quantification elective.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Quiz: colocalisation
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A merged green/magenta image shows many white spots. Why is that not enough to claim colocalisation?






Hint





What decides how bright each channel looks in the merge?









Answer





The colour depends on the display range chosen for each channel, on bleed-through, on misalignment and on resolution: spots can look white because one channel leaks into the other, or because two separate structures lie within one blurred spot. A claim needs coefficients over a defined region, thresholds, and controls.




Q2. Two channels are imaged with different gains and offsets on two days. Which of Pearson’s r and the overlap coefficient can be compared between the days?






Hint





Which one subtracts the means?









Answer





Pearson’s r: it subtracts the means and divides by the spreads, so offsets and (positive) gains cancel. The overlap coefficient uses the raw values, so a different offset changes it.




Q3. Why does including the dark background around cells raise Pearson’s r, even for independent structures?






Hint





Draw the scatter plot with two clusters.









Answer





The background pixels form a cluster that is dark in both channels; the cell pixels form one that is brighter in both (diffuse signal, autofluorescence). A line through the two clusters explains much of the variance, so r is high. It measures “both channels are in the cells”, not “the structures overlap”. Measure inside the cells.




Q4. Small vesicles of protein A all lie inside large compartments of protein B, which also contain much else. What do you expect for M1 and M2?






Hint





M1: how much of A is where B is.









Answer





M1 close to 1 (all of A is inside B), M2 small (most of B has no A). Pearson’s r would be moderate and hide the asymmetry (demo: M1 = 0.79, M2 = 0.32, r = 0.37).




Q5. Someone reports M1 = 0.98 and M2 = 0.97 for two unrelated proteins. What is the most likely mistake?






Hint





What is “above threshold” when the threshold is 0?









Answer





No (or too low) thresholds: with a background offset and noise, every pixel is above 0 in both channels, so all of A is “where B is” and vice versa. Thresholds above the background (for example Costes’) are essential.




Q6. The randomisation test gives p < 0.02 (none of 50 block-shuffled images reaches the observed r). Does that prove that the two proteins colocalise?






Hint





What would bleed-through do to the observed and the shuffled r?









Answer





No. It shows that the overlap in these two images is more than chance. Bleed-through, chromatic misalignment that happens to fit, or structures below the resolution limit all produce real overlap in the images without the proteins being together. The test cannot replace compensation, registration and biological controls.




Q7. Why does shifting one channel by 2–3 pixels make r drop sharply for small spots but hardly for large structures?






Hint





Compare the shift with the size of the structures.









Answer





After the shift, a spot of radius 2 px no longer overlaps its partner; a structure of radius 20 px still overlaps it almost entirely. r falls off over about the size of the structures (the autocorrelation width). This is also why chromatic misalignment matters most for small structures.




Q8. (math) For channels with B = aA + c + \varepsilon (noise \varepsilon independent of A, variance \sigma^2), express r in terms of a, \operatorname{var} A and \sigma^2. What happens when the noise grows?






Hint





\operatorname{cov}(A, B) = a \operatorname{var} A, \operatorname{var} B = a^2 \operatorname{var} A + \sigma^2.









Answer





r = \dfrac{a\operatorname{var}A}{\sqrt{\operatorname{var}A\,(a^2\operatorname{var}A + \sigma^2)}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 + \sigma^2/(a^2 \operatorname{var} A)}} (for a > 0). It falls towards 0 as the noise grows, although the colocalisation is perfect: r mixes colocalisation with signal-to-noise ratio. (Demo: 0.99 at noise σ = 4, 0.88 at σ = 15.)

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
text:
About this lecture
The last units read colour from images. Now the other direction: using colour to show data.

Pseudocolour and channel merges for fluorescence: a choice, not a fact.
Colour maps for a scalar image: sequential, diverging, qualitative. Lightness must change monotonically; the rainbow map invents edges.
Colour-blind viewers: a dichromat sees a projection of colour space; check figures with it.
Decorrelation stretch: PCA of the colour cloud brings out faint colour differences.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Every demo in the course uses the colour maps of this unit (viridis for sequential data, the blue–white–red map for signed data, the label palette for labels). Recall from the bit-depth day: window/level and lookup tables for high-bit data; the display range is part of the map.

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
section: Displaying a grey image is already a choice
text:
Displaying a grey image is already a choice
Recall (the bit-depth day): a lookup table maps each data value to a screen colour, after a display range (window/level).

The display range sets which values are black and white; values outside are clipped. Never let a display setting silently clip data that you measure.
A colour map is a lookup table with colours instead of greys: data value → position t \in [0, 1] → colour.
The data do not change; only how they look. But how they look decides what people see in them.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Colour for display: maps, merges & decorrelation

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
text:
Fluorescence: channels are grey images
A fluorescence image has one grey image per filter set (per dye). Colour is added for display:

Pseudocolour: each channel through its own ramp (black → green, black → magenta, …).
Merge: add the coloured channels. Where both are present the colours mix (green + magenta = white; red + green = yellow).
The colour of a channel says nothing about the dye’s emission colour unless you choose it to.
Red/green merges are invisible to about 8 % of men (red–green colour blindness): red, green and their mixture become similar yellows. Use magenta/green (or cyan/magenta/yellow) and also show the channels separately, in grey.

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
text:
Colour maps for scalar data








data
map
example




sequential (low → high)
lightness increases steadily
viridis, cividis, magma, grey


diverging (signed, around a centre)
lightest (or neutral) at the centre, two hues outwards
blue–white–red


qualitative (labels, classes)
distinct hues, no order
the label palette




The eye reads lightness as “how much”. A good sequential map has monotone lightness and roughly equal visible steps.
A diverging map puts its centre at the meaningful value (zero), so the display range must be symmetric around it.

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
text:
Lightness must be monotone




Jet (the classic rainbow) goes dark blue → bright cyan/yellow → dark red: its lightness rises to L^* = 97 at t = 0.62 and falls to 25.

Bands of fast lightness change look like edges that are not in the data; flat stretches hide real structure.
High values (dark red) look darker than middle values: the order is lost in greyscale or for colour-blind viewers.
Viridis and cividis rise steadily (from about 14 to 91).

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
section: The math: what makes a map perceptually uniform
text:
The math: what makes a map perceptually uniform
A colour map is a curve \mathbf c(t) in Lab, t \in [0, 1]. Perceived contrast between neighbouring data values is about
\Delta E \approx \left\|\frac{d\mathbf c}{dt}\right\| \Delta t .

Uniform: \|\mathbf c'(t)\| constant, so equal data steps give equal visible steps (arc length proportional to t).
Ordered: L^*(t) strictly monotone, so “more” always looks lighter (or always darker), also without hue.
Jet: L^{*\prime}(t) changes sign twice, and \|\mathbf c'\| varies strongly: false edges where it is large, flat zones where it is small. A map built by interpolating in Lab between anchors with increasing L^* (as the course’s maps are) is ordered by construction.

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
text:
Try it: colour maps




A smooth synthetic height field (no edges at all), the colour bar and its lightness profile. Tour: “jet invents edges”: sharp-looking boundaries at the cyan and yellow bands; L* from 12.9 up to 96.8 at t = 0.62 and down to 25.4. “viridis is monotone”: the same field reads as smooth hills. “signed data needs a diverging map”: data in [−3, 7] with viridis gives no clue where zero is; choose “diverging” and set the range to −7…7: zero is white. “red/green merge for a deuteranope”: both channels become yellows; choose “magenta + green”.

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
text:
Colour-blind viewers
About 8 % of men and 0.5 % of women have a red–green deficiency; most common is a weak or missing M (deutan) or L (protan) cone.

A dichromat has two cone types: two numbers per colour instead of three. Colours that differ only in the missing cone’s response look the same.
For a deuteranope, red and green both look like yellows of different lightness; for the rarer tritanope (no S cones) blue and green merge.
Check figures by simulating: the simulation is one 3 \times 3 matrix in linear RGB. Use maps whose order is carried by lightness (viridis, cividis) and magenta/green rather than red/green.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Colour for display: maps, merges & decorrelation

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
section: The math: a dichromat is a projection
text:
The math: a dichromat is a projection
In LMS a deuteranope does not have M. Replace it by a combination of the other two that keeps two anchor colours unchanged (white, and blue), i.e. M' = aL + bS with a, b from two equations:
D = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ a & 0 & b \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \text{in linear RGB: } S_\text{deutan} = T^{-1} D\, T,
with T = linear RGB → LMS.

D has rank 2 and D^2 = D: a projection onto a plane. Its null space is the direction (0, 1, 0) in LMS: changes of M alone are invisible.
Two colours look the same to the dichromat iff their difference lies in that null space, as in the metamers of the first unit.
(Brettel, Viénot and Mollon used two half-planes instead of one plane; a single matrix is the common simplification.)

Colour for display: maps, merges & decorrelation

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
text:
Decorrelation stretch
Recall PCA (day 1): the principal axes of a point cloud are the eigenvectors of its covariance matrix.

In most images R, G and B are strongly correlated: the colour cloud is a cigar along the grey axis. Brightness varies a lot, colour little.
Decorrelation stretch: rotate the cloud to its principal axes, equalise the variances, rotate back. The thin directions (colour differences) are stretched, the long one (brightness) compressed.
Faint colour differences become visible: faded stains, rock art, remote sensing. Colours become false; the stretch is for seeing, not for measuring.
PC1 alone is a data-driven greyscale: the direction in which this image varies most.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Colour for display: maps, merges & decorrelation

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
text:
The math: decorrelation stretch
Colour vectors \mathbf x_i (encoded RGB), mean \boldsymbol\mu, covariance S = U\Lambda U^\top with eigenvalues \lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \lambda_3.
\mathbf x_i' = \boldsymbol\mu + U\,\operatorname{diag}\!\left(\frac{\bar\sigma}{\sqrt{\lambda_k}}\right)U^\top(\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu), \qquad \bar\sigma^2 = \tfrac13(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3).

The new covariance is U\operatorname{diag}(\bar\sigma^2/\lambda_k)\Lambda U^\top = \bar\sigma^2 I: uncorrelated channels with equal variance, and the same total variance \operatorname{tr} S.
A tiny \lambda_3 means a huge gain \bar\sigma/\sqrt{\lambda_3}: noise along that axis is amplified as much. Values outside [0, 1] are clipped.
A fraction t \in [0, 1] of the stretch uses factors (\bar\sigma/\sqrt{\lambda_k})^t.

section: Try it: PCA of the colour cloud
text:
Try it: PCA of the colour cloud




The pixels of the synthetic H&E image in the sRGB cube, with the principal axes (±2 standard deviations; orange PC1, purple PC2, green PC3). Readout: σ along the axes 0.190, 0.070, 0.002; PC1 has 88.0 % of the variance; correlations R–G 0.74, R–B 0.99, G–B 0.84. The cloud is a flat sheet (two stains). Move “stretch” to 1: the sheet swells, the image gets garish but nuclei and stroma separate in colour; 14 % of the pixels are clipped. Then “objects”: a cigar along grey (PC1 (0.55, 0.64, 0.54), 77.2 %).

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
section: A checklist for colour in figures
text:
A checklist for colour in figures

Sequential data: a map with monotone lightness (viridis, cividis, magma); never jet for quantities.
Signed data: a diverging map, centred on zero with a symmetric range.
Labels: a qualitative palette; neighbouring labels must differ.
Merges: magenta/green (not red/green), plus the single channels in grey.
Always show a colour bar with the display range, and say if anything is clipped.
Check the figure in greyscale and with a dichromat simulation.

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
text:
Summary

Showing data in colour is a lookup table: display range + map. It changes what viewers see, not the data.
Sequential maps need monotone lightness; the rainbow map invents edges and loses the order. Diverging maps need a centred, symmetric range; qualitative palettes are for labels.
A dichromat sees a rank-2 projection of colour; simulate it to check figures; avoid red/green merges.
Decorrelation stretch = PCA of the colour cloud, variances equalised: faint colour differences become visible (false colours, for looking only).

title: Exercise: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute HSV coordinates, and handle hue as an angle (wrapping intervals, circular mean),
explain where hue is undefined and why a saturation floor is needed,
compute L^* and ΔE in CIELAB, and compare colour differences in Lab and in RGB,
choose a colour space and a rule (threshold, wedge, ball, clusters) for a colour segmentation.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute HSV coordinates, and handle hue as an angle (wrapping intervals, circular mean),
explain where hue is undefined and why a saturation floor is needed,
compute L^* and ΔE in CIELAB, and compare colour differences in Lab and in RGB,
choose a colour space and a rule (threshold, wedge, ball, clusters) for a colour segmentation.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Pixel cloud
every pixel is a point in a 3D colour space; a segmentation is a region of it


HSV
V = \max(R, G, B), S = (\max - \min)/\max, H = angle (0° red, 60° yellow, 120° green, 180° cyan, 240° blue, 300° magenta)


Hue of a grey
undefined (\max = \min)


Circular mean
angle of the mean of the unit vectors (\cos H, \sin H)


Normalised rgb
r = R/(R+G+B), g = G/(R+G+B)


CIELAB
L^* = 116 f(Y/Y_n) - 16, a^*, b^* from f(X/X_n), f(Y/Y_n), f(Z/Z_n), f(t) \approx t^{1/3}


ΔE
\Delta E^*_{ab} = \sqrt{\Delta L^{*2} + \Delta a^{*2} + \Delta b^{*2}}; about 1–2.3 is just noticeable


k-means
assign each pixel to the nearest centre, move each centre to its pixels’ mean, repeat

title: Exercise: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
By hand
B1. Compute H, S and V (with V in [0, 1]) of the codes (a) (255, 0, 0), (b) (0, 128, 0), (c) (200, 100, 50), (d) (128, 128, 128).
B2. (a) Compute the circular mean of the hues 350° and 10°, and their ordinary mean. Which colour is each? (b) What is the circular mean of 90° and 270°? What does that tell you? (c) Write the hue condition “red within ±20°” as one or two intervals of [0°, 360°).
B3. A surface has linear RGB (0.60, 0.10, 0.08) in the light and (0.30, 0.05, 0.04) in a shadow that halves the light. (a) Compute H, S, V for both. Which change? (b) Compute the normalised (r, g) for both. (c) Which of the rules “R > 0.4”, “H within ±20° of 0° and S > 0.4” keeps both?
B4. A grey wall has (R, G, B) = (0.50, 0.50, 0.50). Noise changes two pixels to (0.50, 0.52, 0.49) and (0.50, 0.49, 0.51). Compute their hue and saturation. What does this mean for a hue threshold?
B5. (a) Compute L^* for a grey with 18 % of white’s luminance, and for one with 50 %. (Use L^* = 116\,(Y/Y_n)^{1/3} - 16.) (b) Compute \Delta E^*_{ab} between (50, 20, 10) and (55, 17, 14). Visible? (c) In Lab, the yellow codes (255, 255, 0) and (255, 255, 40) are (97.1, -21.6, 94.5) and (97.2, -21.1, 89.9); the dark green codes (0, 80, 0) and (0, 120, 0) are (28.7, -37.2, 35.9) and (43.4, -49.4, 47.6). Compute the RGB distance and \Delta E^*_{ab} of each pair. What do you conclude?
B6. You must segment (i) yellow fruit on a table with soft shadows, (ii) all pixels that “look like” a reference skin colour, (iii) purple nuclei on a pink background. For each, propose a colour space and a rule, and say what could go wrong.






Solutions





B1. (a) H = 0°, S = 1, V = 1. (b) H = 120°, S = 1, V = 128/255 = 0.502. (c) \max = 200 (R), \min = 50, d = 150: V = 0.784, S = 150/200 = 0.75, H = 60° \cdot (100 - 50)/150 = 20° (orange). (d) S = 0, V = 0.502, H undefined (a grey).
B2. (a) Unit vectors (\cos 350°, \sin 350°) = (0.985, -0.174) and (0.985, 0.174): the mean is (0.985, 0), angle 0°: red. The ordinary mean is 180°: cyan, wrong. (b) The unit vectors (0, 1) and (0, -1) cancel: the mean vector is zero and the circular mean is undefined. Two opposite hues have no meaningful average (the length of the mean vector, 0, says the hues are maximally spread). (c) [340°, 360°) \cup [0°, 20°].
B3. (a) Light: \max = 0.60, \min = 0.08, d = 0.52: V = 0.60, S = 0.867, H = 60° \cdot (0.10 - 0.08)/0.52 = 2.3°. Shadow: V = 0.30, S = 0.867, H = 2.3°. Only V changes. (b) Both: r = 0.60/0.78 = 0.769, g = 0.10/0.78 = 0.128; the shadow gives 0.30/0.39 and 0.05/0.39, the same. (c) “R > 0.4” keeps the light part only. The hue/saturation rule keeps both.
B4. (0.50, 0.52, 0.49): \max = G, d = 0.03, H = 60°(0.49 - 0.50)/0.03 + 120° = 100°, S = 0.03/0.52 = 0.058. (0.50, 0.49, 0.51): \max = B, d = 0.02, H = 60°((0.50 - 0.49)/0.02 + 4) = 270°, S = 0.039. A noise of 1–2 % sends the hue from green to violet: on grey and dark pixels hue is meaningless, and a hue threshold selects some of them at random. A floor S > 0.2 (say) removes them.
B5. (a) 116 \cdot 0.18^{1/3} - 16 = 49.5; 116 \cdot 0.5^{1/3} - 16 = 76.1. A grey that looks halfway is only 18 % of the light. (b) \sqrt{5^2 + 3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{50} = 7.07: clearly visible. (c) Both pairs are 40 apart in RGB. Yellows: \sqrt{0.1^2 + 0.5^2 + 4.6^2} = 4.63; dark greens: \sqrt{14.7^2 + 12.2^2 + 11.7^2} = 22.40. The same RGB distance is a barely visible difference in the yellows and an obvious one in the dark greens: RGB distances do not measure perceived difference.
B6. (i) HSV: a hue wedge around yellow (about 40°–70°) with a saturation floor; robust to the shadows. Risk: the floor must be low enough for the shadowed fruit (in encoded values saturation drops slightly in deep shadow) and high enough to drop the table. (ii) Lab: a ball of radius ΔE around the reference; the radius sets what counts as “looks like”. Risk: lighting changes L^*, so a ball also rejects the same skin in shadow; a ball in a^*b^* only, or a larger radius along L^*, is more tolerant. (iii) Otsu on one channel that separates the stains (the red channel or a^*, see the colour-matrix demo of the last unit), or k-means with k = 2 or 3. Risk: unequal class sizes and stain variation between slides.




Math questions
B7. (math) Show that in CIELAB any grey (X, Y, Z) = k\,(X_n, Y_n, Z_n), k > 0, has a^* = b^* = 0, and that the white has L^* = 100. Which property of f do you use?
B8. (math) Show that the circular mean \bar H = \operatorname{atan2}(\sum\sin H_i, \sum\cos H_i) minimises \sum_i \big(1 - \cos(H_i - \theta)\big) over \theta (the sum of squared chord lengths, up to a factor). When is the minimiser not unique?
B9. (math) One step of k-means on the 1D values \{0, 1, 2, 8, 9, 10\} with centres starting at 0 and 1. Do the assignment and update steps until nothing changes. Then show, for general data, that the update step (centre = mean of its points) minimises the sum of squared distances of the points to their centre.






Solutions (math)





B7. With X/X_n = Y/Y_n = Z/Z_n = k, all three f values are f(k), so a^* = 500(f(k) - f(k)) = 0 and b^* = 0. White: k = 1, f(1) = 1, L^* = 116 - 16 = 100. Only that f is one and the same function for the three coordinates (and f(1) = 1).
B8. \sum_i(1 - \cos(H_i - \theta)) = n - \cos\theta\sum\cos H_i - \sin\theta\sum\sin H_i = n - R\cos(\theta - \bar H) with R\,(\cos\bar H, \sin\bar H) = (\sum\cos H_i, \sum\sin H_i). It is smallest when \cos(\theta - \bar H) = 1, at \theta = \bar H, provided R > 0. If R = 0 (the unit vectors cancel, e.g. 90° and 270°) every \theta gives the same value: no unique mean. And 1 - \cos\delta = \tfrac12\,(2\sin(\delta/2))^2 is half the squared chord.
B9. Centres 0 and 1. Assign: \{0\} to 0; \{1, 2, 8, 9, 10\} to 1. Update: centres 0 and 6. Assign: \{0, 1, 2\} to 0 (2 is closer to 0 than to 6), \{8, 9, 10\} to 6. Update: 1 and 9. Assign: unchanged. Done: centres 1 and 9. For a cluster with points \mathbf x_i, \sum_i\|\mathbf x_i - \mathbf c\|^2 is a convex quadratic in \mathbf c with gradient 2\sum_i(\mathbf c - \mathbf x_i); zero at \mathbf c = \frac1n\sum_i\mathbf x_i. So both steps lower (or keep) the total squared distance, and the algorithm stops after finitely many steps.

title: Exercise: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
Explore: the colour cloud
Left: an image (synthetic); right: its pixels as a point cloud (WebGL), each point in its own colour, inside the outline of the sRGB gamut in the chosen space. The black line is the grey axis. Drag the cloud to rotate it; front, top, 3/4 view reset the view. Choose a colour space: the cloud morphs from the old coordinates to the new ones. Click a pixel to see its coordinates in all spaces; a ball of the chosen radius around its colour (in the current space) selects points, and their pixels stay bright in the image. Brush: paint over the image, and the painted pixels light up in the cloud. Noise adds noise to the stored codes; shading darkens the image from left to right.



E1. Preset cube → HSV cone. The image contains every hue at every saturation and value. Describe the cloud in sRGB (click sRGB (encoded)) and then in HSV. Where are the greys, the pure colours, black?
E2. Switch the same image to CIELAB and Y′CbCr. Which way is up? Why is the CIELAB solid lopsided: where are yellow and blue?
E3. Preset shadows are rays through black (the red apple, in linear RGB). What shape do the apple’s pixels make, and why? Set shading to 0.6: what happens to the clouds of the other objects?
E4. Preset grey pixels scatter in hue (noise 0.03, the grey card selected). Where are the card’s pixels in HSV? Switch to CIELAB: where are they now? Which space is better behaved near grey?
E5. Reset, then click the red apple at pixel (60, 55) (the readout shows the pixel you clicked). Note its HSV and Lab. With ball radius 0.08, compare how many pixels are selected in sRGB, linear RGB, HSV and CIELAB. Why is a ball not the natural shape in HSV?
E6. Preset H&E: two stains, a sheet (in sRGB). Rotate the cloud. Is it a 3D blob, a 2D sheet or a 1D line? What would you expect for an image stained with only one dye?






Solutions





E1. In sRGB the chart fills the surface layers of the cube: the top half of the image (white to pure colours) covers the faces around the white corner, the bottom half (pure colours to black) the faces around the black corner. Greys lie on the diagonal from black to white. In HSV the cube becomes a cone with black at the tip: the greys are on the vertical axis, the pure colours on the rim at the top, hue goes around.
E2. In CIELAB and Y′CbCr the lightness axis (L^*, Y′) points up and greys stay on it. The CIELAB solid is lopsided: yellow is light (high L^*, large b^*) while blue is dark (low L^*, negative b^*), and saturated blue reaches far from the axis. Y′CbCr is a linear map of the encoded cube, so it stays a (tilted, sheared) parallelepiped.
E3. A straight line from near black up to the lit red (plus a curve towards white from the specular highlight): every apple pixel is the same red times a different amount of light. With shading 0.6 every object’s cloud stretches along its own ray towards black. A threshold on one channel cuts across these rays; a hue (angle) does not.
E4. The card (mean code about 99, V \approx 0.39) has saturations up to 0.32 (mean 0.125) once noise is added, and hues all around the circle (about equally many in each 60° sector). In the HSV cone they form a ring-shaped smear around the axis: their hue is random. In CIELAB they form a compact ball around the L^* axis (chroma \sqrt{a^{*2} + b^{*2}} 7.3 on average): the noise is just noise, with no special behaviour near grey. CIELAB is smooth near grey; HSV is singular there.
E5. The pixel has codes (162, 20, 22), HSV (359.3°, 0.873, 0.634) and Lab (34.4, 54.2, 38.5). Of the apple’s 2809 pixels the ball selects 985 in sRGB, 810 in linear RGB, 976 in HSV and 1321 in CIELAB, and nothing from other objects. In the HSV cone, V is the height, so the shadowed part of the apple is far away even though its hue and saturation are the same: the natural region in HSV is a wedge (a hue interval with a saturation floor, at any V), not a ball. CIELAB selects the most because its lightness is compressed (a cube root) relative to its opponent axes.
E6. A thin, curved 2D sheet: the pixels are mixtures of two stains in different amounts (plus white), so they have two degrees of freedom. (It is curved because absorption multiplies the light; in optical density it becomes flat, see the spectral unmixing elective.) With one dye the cloud would be a single curve from white to the dye’s darkest colour.

title: Exercise: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
Explore: colour segmentation
The image (click to set a reference colour), a 2D histogram of two chromatic coordinates (grey: all pixels, log counts; orange: the selected ones; the axes are written underneath), and the result: selected pixels at full brightness, or the k-means clusters in their mean colours. Methods: per-channel RGB thresholds; hue + floors (a hue interval that may wrap through 0°, minimum saturation and value); a ΔE ball around the reference colour (ΔE76 in Lab, ΔE2000, or plain RGB distance in code units); Otsu on one channel; k-means in RGB or Lab (step or run). Dice compares the result with the true red apple (1810 pixels) or the true nuclei of the synthetic scene.



S1. Preset R threshold fails in the shadow (R' \ge 120, G' \le 90, B' \le 90). Which part of the apple is found, and what is the Dice? Can you find RGB thresholds that do better?
S2. Preset hue survives the shadow. What is the hue interval, and the Dice? Where are the selected pixels in the H–S histogram?
S3. Preset red wraps around 0° (the chart of all hues). Which columns of the chart are selected, and why both edges?
S4. Preset grey and dark pixels speckle (noise 0.03, no floors). Which objects get selected by mistake? Raise S ≥ step by step: at which floor do the speckles disappear, and what is the Dice?
S5. Preset ΔE ball in Lab vs RGB distance (radius 25 around a lit apple pixel). Compare ΔE76, ΔE2000 and RGB distance at radius 25. Then increase the ΔE76 radius: what is the best Dice, and what happens if the radius is too large?
S6. Preset k-means in RGB vs in Lab (k = 4). Which clusters does RGB find, and what is the best cluster’s Dice? Switch to in Lab. Then try Otsu on a channel with a^*.






Solutions





S1. Only the lit upper half of the apple (1036 pixels): Dice 0.728. Lowering the thresholds to R' \ge 60 with G', B' \le 90 reaches 0.890 (1455 pixels, two of them table), but any fixed R' threshold trades the shadowed apple against dark non-red pixels: the shadow is a brightness change, and every RGB channel carries brightness.
S2. Hue in 340°–20° (shown as 0–20° ∪ 340–360°), S \ge 0.40, V \ge 0.10: 1728 pixels, Dice 0.977; only the specular highlight (white, low saturation) is missed. In the H–S histogram the selected pixels sit at the left and right edges (hue near 0° and 360°) and high saturation.
S3. The leftmost and rightmost columns of the chart (hues near 0° and near 360°), saturated rows only (1344 pixels). The interval wraps through 0°: it is the union of two intervals, which in the image are the two edges.
S4. With no floors, 3930 pixels are selected: 2096 table pixels (mostly in the dark shadow), 34 of the grey card and 17 of the dark stone, Dice 0.621. With S \ge 0.2: 456 table pixels remain, Dice 0.872. With S \ge 0.4: none, 1723 selected, Dice 0.973.
S5. At radius 25: ΔE76 Dice 0.761 (1111 pixels), ΔE2000 0.889 (1807, but 200 of them the dark stone), RGB distance 0.566 (715). ΔE76 at radius 60 reaches 0.986; at 80 the ball swallows the table (14 622 pixels, Dice 0.218). A ball in a lightness-including space must be wide enough to include the shadowed apple, which is far away in lightness; at some point it includes other things first.
S6. RGB, k = 4: clusters sized 5797, 968, 4119, 5500; the best matches the apple with Dice 0.422: the dark half of the apple joins the dark (shadowed) pixels, the lit half joins other bright saturated pixels. Lab: best cluster Dice 0.765: better, since a^* separates red, but L^* still splits by shadow. Otsu on a^*: threshold 21.2, Dice 0.943: one well-chosen number beats clustering in three.

Where this leads
Colour is now a set of coordinates in which a class can be a simple region. The next unit turns the question around: how to display data with colour (colour maps, channel merges, colour-blind viewers) and how PCA of the colour cloud brings out faint colour differences. A colour model per class becomes the data term of a graph cut (day 13), which adds smoothness to the pixel-wise decisions.

title: Quiz: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. HSV: V = \max, S = (\max - \min)/\max, H = angle around the grey axis (red 0°, green 120°, blue 240°). CIELAB: L^* lightness, a^* green–red, b^* blue–yellow; \Delta E^*_{ab} = Euclidean distance in Lab.

Q1. A red apple is half in shadow. Why does a threshold “R > 120” fail, while “hue near 0° and saturation > 0.4” works?






Hint





What does a shadow do to the three channels?









Answer





A shadow scales all three channels down by about the same factor. In the shadow R drops below 120, so the threshold cuts the apple in half. Hue and saturation depend only on the ratios of the channels, which the scaling keeps: the shadowed half has the same hue and saturation as the lit half.




Q2. What is the mean hue of two pixels with hues 350° and 10°? What does the ordinary average give?






Hint





Draw both on a circle.









Answer





Both are reds, 20° apart across 0°: the mean is 0°, red. The ordinary average (350 + 10)/2 = 180° is cyan, the opposite colour. Average the unit vectors (\cos H, \sin H) and take the angle of the result.




Q3. A hue mask for “red” applied to a noisy photo is full of speckles on a grey wall. Why, and what is the fix?






Hint





What is the hue of a grey pixel plus a little noise?









Answer





For grey the hue is undefined; with a little noise the channels differ slightly and the hue becomes the direction of the noise, which is random: some grey pixels get a “red” hue. Require a minimum saturation (and value): near-grey and dark pixels are then never selected.




Q4. Two colours differ by \Delta E^*_{ab} = 1. Two others differ by \Delta E^*_{ab} = 20. What do you expect to see?






Hint





What is a just-noticeable difference in Lab?









Answer





\Delta E \approx 1 is at the limit of what can be seen side by side: practically the same colour. \Delta E = 20 is an obvious difference. Lab was built so that distances roughly match perceived differences, so these statements hold anywhere in the space (approximately).




Q5. Two pairs of colours are each 40 code values apart in RGB: two bright yellows, and two dark greens. Which pair looks more different, and what does that say about distances in RGB?






Hint





Compare \Delta E: 4.6 and 22.4.









Answer





The dark greens (\Delta E = 22.4) look far more different than the yellows (\Delta E = 4.6). Equal distances in RGB are not equal visible differences, so a “ball” of fixed radius in RGB selects very different amounts of visible variation in different parts of the space.




Q6. What are a^* and b^* of any grey, and what is the Lab of the white point?






Hint





Lab is relative to the white.









Answer





Any grey has a^* = b^* = 0 (it is a scaled white, so the three ratios to the white are equal). The white is (L^*, a^*, b^*) = (100, 0, 0).




Q7. Why is “middle grey” (looks halfway between black and white) only about 18 % of white’s luminance?






Hint





L^* uses a cube root.









Answer





Perceived lightness grows roughly like the cube root of luminance. L^* = 50 (halfway) needs Y/Y_n with 116\,(Y/Y_n)^{1/3} - 16 = 50, i.e. Y/Y_n \approx 0.18. Conversely, 50 % luminance has L^* = 76: it looks fairly light.




Q8. k-means with k = 2 on the RGB values of a picture of a red apple half in shadow puts the shadowed half of the apple together with the dark background. Why might Lab do better, and why might it still fail?






Hint





What does the nearest-centre rule measure?









Answer





k-means gives each pixel to the nearest centre. In RGB the dark half of the apple is close to other dark pixels, because brightness dominates all three coordinates. In Lab the colour difference is carried by a^* (strongly positive for red), so the red pixels stay closer to each other. But L^* is still one of the three coordinates: a deep shadow can still move a pixel far from the lit apple. Dropping L^* (clustering in a^*b^* only) or using hue removes that.




Q9. (math) Show that HSV’s hue and saturation do not change when all three channels are multiplied by the same k > 0. What happens to V?






Hint





\max, \min and their difference all scale by k.









Answer





\max(kR, kG, kB) = k\max, likewise \min and d = \max - \min. S = kd/(k\max) = d/\max, and every case of H is a ratio like (kG - kB)/(kd) = (G - B)/d. Both unchanged; V = k\max scales by k.

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
text:
About this lecture
So far a colour image was “an M \times N \times 3 array”. Today: what the three numbers mean, and why there are three.

Light is a spectrum: power at every wavelength, far more than three numbers.
The eye (or a camera) reduces it to three responses: a linear map with a large blind spot.
Different spectra with the same three numbers: metamers. They are why screens work, and why cameras and eyes disagree.
CIE XYZ and the chromaticity diagram: a map of all colours; mixtures lie on straight lines; a display reaches a triangle.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Linear algebra used: matrix–vector product, rank, null space, change of basis, and (math slides only) the projector onto a null space. The demos assume an sRGB screen; a projector rarely is one, so every swatch in the demos comes with its numbers. Say this once at the start.

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
section: Colour is not in the light alone
text:
Colour is not in the light alone

Two lamps look the same white, yet a red apple looks different under them.
Two fabrics look identical to us, but different in a photo.
A colour-blind colleague cannot tell two cables apart that you can.

In each case different light gives the same colour to one observer and not to another. To understand why, follow the light from the lamp to the three numbers.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
text:
Light is a spectrum
The light reaching a point of the eye or the sensor is a spectrum s(\lambda): power at each wavelength from about 380 nm (violet) to 730 nm (deep red).

Daylight: smooth, power everywhere. A light bulb (a hot filament): rises towards the red. A white LED: a sharp blue peak plus a broad yellow hump. A laser: one line.
A surface reflects a fraction r(\lambda) of each wavelength; what we see from it is s(\lambda)\,r(\lambda): lamp times reflectance.
Sample the spectrum every 10 nm: 36 numbers. Real spectra need that many, or more.

So the input is a vector with 36 (or more) entries. The output of the eye is three numbers.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
text:
Three cone types




The retina has three kinds of cones: L (long), M (medium), S (short wavelengths).

Each cone adds up the light, weighted by its sensitivity curve: L = \sum_\lambda s(\lambda)\,\bar l(\lambda), and so on.
The curves are broad and overlap: L and M are almost the same.
A camera does the same with three filters R, G, B; its curves are different.



The cone curves here are the Hunt–Pointer–Estévez combination of the CIE colour-matching functions (right), so they are exactly a change of basis of them; real measured cone fundamentals look very similar. Each curve is scaled to peak 1 on the left. Point at 450–500 nm: S and M both respond; at 600 nm L and M both respond, L more.

From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
section: The math: colour vision is a 3 × 36 matrix
text:
The math: colour vision is a 3 × 36 matrix
Sample at 10 nm, \lambda_j = 380, 390, \dots, 730: a spectrum is \mathbf s \in \mathbb R^{36}, and
\mathbf c = \begin{pmatrix} L \\ M \\ S \end{pmatrix} = A\,\mathbf s, \qquad A = \begin{pmatrix} \bar l(\lambda_1) & \cdots & \bar l(\lambda_{36}) \\ \bar m(\lambda_1) & \cdots & \bar m(\lambda_{36}) \\ \bar s(\lambda_1) & \cdots & \bar s(\lambda_{36}) \end{pmatrix} \Delta\lambda .

The integral \int s(\lambda)\,\bar l(\lambda)\,d\lambda becomes a dot product of two vectors: row 1 of A times \mathbf s.
A is 3 \times 36 of rank 3: the eye is a linear map \mathbb R^{36} \to \mathbb R^3.
A camera: \mathbf c_\text{cam} = A_\text{cam}\,\mathbf s, another 3 \times 36 matrix. A surface under a lamp: \mathbf c = A\,\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf e)\,\mathbf r, lamp \mathbf e, reflectance \mathbf r.

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
section: Try it: from a spectrum to three numbers
text:
Try it: from a spectrum to three numbers




Top: the spectra (drag to draw). Middle: the three cone curves; the shaded areas are spectrum × sensitivity for A, whose sums are the numbers. Right: the colours and the numbers (each relative to daylight, so daylight gives 1, 1, 1). Tour: “daylight vs LED”: two very different spectra (the LED has a peak of 245 at 450 nm and almost nothing below 420), both 1.000, 1.000, 1.000 for the eye, and chromaticity 0.313, 0.329. Click “camera”: the LED becomes 0.905, 0.962, 0.900, the match is gone. Then “make a metamer” several times: B changes wildly, the numbers stay 1.022, 0.931, 0.591. Then “metameric failure under tungsten” (surfaces): click “daylight” (match), back to “tungsten” (0.602, 0.545, 0.353 against 0.589, 0.555, 0.302).
