From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
text:
Metamers
Many spectra give the same three numbers: they are metamers, and they look identical.

36 numbers in, 3 out: the eye throws away almost everything. Any change of the spectrum that all three cones are blind to goes unnoticed.
Those invisible changes form a huge set: wiggles that add a bit of light at some wavelengths and remove the same “cone-weighted” amount at others.
Why screens work: a display has only three primaries, yet it can produce a metamer of the light from (most) real scenes. The spectrum on the screen is nothing like the scene’s.
Constraint: a spectrum cannot be negative. A metamer must stay \ge 0 everywhere.

From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
section: The math: metamers live in the null space
text:
The math: metamers live in the null space
A\mathbf s_1 = A\mathbf s_2 \iff A(\mathbf s_2 - \mathbf s_1) = \mathbf 0 \iff \mathbf s_2 - \mathbf s_1 \in \ker A.

Rank–nullity: \dim\ker A = 36 - 3 = 33. Every spectrum has a 33-dimensional family of metamers (cut down by \mathbf s_2 \ge \mathbf 0).
Projector onto \ker A (for A of full row rank): P = I - A^\top (AA^\top)^{-1} A. Check: AP = A - AA^\top(AA^\top)^{-1}A = 0.
Making a metamer: take any vector \mathbf v, then \mathbf s_2 = \mathbf s_1 + t\,P\mathbf v, with t as large as the constraint \mathbf s_2 \ge \mathbf 0 allows. This is the demo’s make a metamer button.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
text:
When metamers break
A match holds for one observer under one light:

A different observer. A camera has A_\text{cam} \ne A, with a different blind set: a pair that matches for the eye differs in the photo.
A colour-blind observer. A deuteranope has no M cones: two numbers instead of three. More pairs match: everything that only the M cones could tell apart.
A different lamp (metameric failure). Two fabrics match in daylight; under a light bulb the lamp re-weights the wavelengths, and they no longer match.

Metamerism is the reason colour in images is never “the” colour of an object: it is the colour for this camera, under this light.

These are the demo presets “the camera disagrees”, “a dichromat sees more matches” (for the deuteranope 0.955, –, 0.812 for both; the eye sees M 0.972 vs 0.693) and “metameric failure under tungsten”. White balance, next unit, tries to undo the lamp; metameric failure shows why it can never be perfect.

From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
section: Colour matching: how the eye was measured
text:
Colour matching: how the eye was measured
Before cones could be measured, the eye was characterised by matching (Wright and Guild, 1920s):

An observer sees a test light on one half of a field and adjusts three primary lights (red, green, blue) on the other half until the two halves look the same.
Done for every wavelength: three colour-matching functions \bar r(\lambda), \bar g(\lambda), \bar b(\lambda), the amounts needed.
Surprise: for many test wavelengths no match is possible. One primary must be moved to the test side: a negative amount.

Three numbers per wavelength again: the matching functions describe the same three-dimensional information as the cones, in another basis.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
text:
CIE XYZ: a standard basis
The CIE (1931) chose a new basis of the same three-dimensional space with two convenient properties:

the three functions \bar x, \bar y, \bar z are never negative, so every real light has X, Y, Z \ge 0;
\bar y is the eye’s brightness sensitivity, so Y is the luminance: how bright the light looks.

The price: the XYZ “primaries” are not real lights. XYZ is a coordinate system for colours, the common reference for every device.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
section: The math: XYZ is a change of basis
text:
The math: XYZ is a change of basis
Cones, colour-matching functions and \bar x \bar y \bar z are three bases of the same row space of A:
\begin{pmatrix} \bar l \\ \bar m \\ \bar s \end{pmatrix} = T \begin{pmatrix} \bar x \\ \bar y \\ \bar z \end{pmatrix} \;\Rightarrow\; \begin{pmatrix} L \\ M \\ S \end{pmatrix} = T \begin{pmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{pmatrix}, \quad T = \begin{pmatrix} 0.4002 & 0.7076 & -0.0808 \\ -0.2263 & 1.1653 & 0.0457 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.9182 \end{pmatrix}.

T is invertible, so the null spaces agree: metamers for XYZ = metamers for the cones.
The same holds for \bar r\bar g\bar b: a matching experiment measures A up to an invertible 3 \times 3 matrix. Negative entries of \bar r\bar g\bar b just mean a basis that is not inside the cone of real lights.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
text:
Chromaticity: forget the brightness




Twice the light, same colour: divide out the brightness.
x = \frac{X}{X+Y+Z}, \qquad y = \frac{Y}{X+Y+Z}

Every colour becomes a point (x, y): the chromaticity diagram.
Monochromatic lights trace the horseshoe (the spectral locus, wavelengths marked); the straight purple line closes it.
All real colours lie inside. White (daylight D65) is near the middle, at (0.313, 0.329).



The colours of the figure are only approximate: outside the sRGB triangle the screen cannot show them, so they are drawn at the nearest colour the screen can show. That is also true on this projector. The axes are x and y, not the X and Y of XYZ: lower case = chromaticity.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
section: The math: a central projection, and mixtures on straight lines
text:
The math: a central projection, and mixtures on straight lines
(x, y, z) = (X, Y, Z)/(X+Y+Z) is the central projection of XYZ space onto the plane X + Y + Z = 1 (as homogeneous coordinates: scaling a colour does not move it).
Mixing two lights adds their XYZ: \mathbf C = \mathbf C_1 + \mathbf C_2. With S_i = X_i + Y_i + Z_i,
\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \frac{S_1}{S_1 + S_2}\begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ y_1 \end{pmatrix} + \frac{S_2}{S_1 + S_2}\begin{pmatrix} x_2 \\ y_2 \end{pmatrix}.

A convex combination: the mixture lies on the segment between the two chromaticities, at a position weighted by S_i (not by luminance Y_i).
Three primaries: all non-negative mixtures fill the triangle they span. Monochromatic lights are the extreme points, so the horseshoe region is convex.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
section: Gamuts: a display is a triangle
text:
Gamuts: a display is a triangle
A display mixes three primaries R, G, B with amounts between 0 and 1: it reaches exactly the triangle of their chromaticities, its gamut.

sRGB (most screens, the web): a modest triangle. Display P3 (newer phones and laptops): a larger green and red. Rec. 2020 (ultra-HD video): primaries almost on the horseshoe, as only lasers can produce.
No triangle with real primaries covers the horseshoe: some colours (saturated cyans, spectral greens) no display can show.
A colour outside the gamut needs a negative amount of a primary: it must be clipped or mapped inwards.

From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
text:
Try it: the chromaticity diagram




Tour: “mixing two lights”: A = 470 nm with Y = 0.3, B = 580 nm with Y = 0.6, share of B 0.5: the mixture sits at 0.189 of the way from A to B, not at 0.5, because A carries X+Y+Z = 5.28 against B’s 1.23. Ask: which share puts it halfway? (0.811.) Drag A or B around: the mixture stays on the line. Then “design a display”: “sRGB vs P3” (the test point T = (0.21, 0.71) is outside both), “a laser display” (T inside), “a primary outside the locus” (flagged: no light has that chromaticity).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
text:
Summary

Light is a spectrum; the eye and the camera reduce it to three numbers by weighted sums: a linear map of rank 3.
Metamers: different spectra with the same three numbers. They make displays possible, and break for another camera, a colour-blind viewer or another lamp.
CIE XYZ: a standard basis with X, Y, Z \ge 0 and Y = luminance; a change of basis of the cones.
Chromaticity (x, y) drops the brightness. Mixtures lie on straight lines; a display reaches a triangle, its gamut.
Next unit: what the numbers stored in an RGB image mean, and why they are not proportional to light.

By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

title: Exercise: compression and measurements, JPEG 2000, formats
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Lossy damage
content-dependent: dim spots, noise, texture, an 8-pixel grid; not independent noise


Bit depth
baseline JPEG is 8-bit; 12/16-bit data must be rescaled first


Blocking peaks
the size of neighbour differences repeats every 8 pixels: spectrum peaks at multiples of N/8


JPEG 2000
wavelet (no blocks); integer 5/3 lifting = exactly lossless; bit planes = cut the stream anywhere


Lossless ratio
typically 1.5–3 for noisy scientific images


OME-TIFF
multi-dimensional, 8/16/32-bit and float, lossless compression options (check that it is not JPEG)


HDF5, Zarr
chunked n-D arrays; each chunk compressed on its own; a region reads only its chunks


Chunks read
per dimension \lfloor (b-1)/c \rfloor - \lfloor a/c \rfloor + 1 for the region [a, b) and chunk size c; multiply

title: Exercise: compression and measurements, JPEG 2000, formats
text:
By hand
B1. A time-lapse experiment: 2048 × 2048 pixels, 16 bit, 30 z-slices, 2 channels, 500 time points. (a) How large is one frame, and the whole experiment, stored raw? (b) How large with a lossless codec at a ratio of 2.5? With JPEG at a ratio of 20? (c) What would you lose with the JPEG option, besides some quality?
B2. Choose a format (and lossless or lossy) and say why: (a) a 16-bit confocal z-stack that will be segmented and measured; (b) a figure panel for a paper; (c) the archive of a slide scanner, 50 000 slides of several gigapixels each, viewed by pathologists; (d) a 3D volume of 200 GB that colleagues browse over the network, region by region.
B3. A 12-bit camera image uses grey levels 0 to 4095. It is rescaled to 8 bits (0–255) before a JPEG is made. (a) How many 12-bit levels fall into one 8-bit level? What is the standard deviation of the rounding error, in 12-bit units? (b) Compare it with the Poisson noise of a background of 400 photons and of a dim spot peak of 60 photons above it. Is the bit-depth loss itself important here?
B4. A 2048 × 2048 × 100 stack (x, y, z), 16 bit, stored with chunks of 256 × 256 × 1. (a) How many chunks does reading the region x 100–611, y 300–811, z = 40 need? How many bytes are decoded, and how many are needed? (b) The same with chunks of 64 × 64 × 64. (c) Which chunk shape would you choose for a viewer that shows single z-slices? For an analysis that follows every pixel through z?
B5. In a 512 × 512 JPEG image, at which spatial frequencies (in cycles per image width) do you expect blocking peaks in the spectrum of the neighbour differences?
B6. A JPEG 2000 coefficient is 45 (binary 101101) and the decoder receives the bit planes from the top. After 1, 2 and 3 planes, which values are still possible, and what is the largest error if the decoder takes the middle of that range?






Solutions





B1. (a) 2048^2 \cdot 2 bytes = 8.39 MB per frame; 8.39 \text{ MB} \cdot 30 \cdot 2 \cdot 500 = 252 GB. (b) Lossless: about 101 GB. JPEG at 20: about 12.6 GB. (c) The 16-bit data become 8-bit, dim structures and their intensities change, noise and texture statistics change, and an 8-pixel grid is added: measurements on the JPEGs are not measurements of the sample.
B2. (a) OME-TIFF (or another multi-dimensional format) with lossless compression: 16 bit and all dimensions kept, exact values for measurement. (b) PNG (lossless, small for figures with flat areas); a JPEG copy at high quality is acceptable for display, if the measurements were done on the originals. (c) JPEG 2000 (or a pyramidal TIFF with JPEG/JPEG 2000 tiles) in a lossy setting validated for diagnosis: lossless would be several times larger, and pyramids and region access matter more than exact values. (d) A chunked format (Zarr / OME-Zarr, HDF5) with lossless chunk compression and a multiresolution pyramid, so a viewer fetches only the chunks of the visible region and level.
B3. (a) 4096/256 = 16 levels; the rounding error is uniform over one step of 16: standard deviation 16/\sqrt{12} = 4.6 12-bit levels. (b) Poisson noise: \sqrt{400} = 20 for the background, about \sqrt{460} = 21 at the dim spot. The rescaling error (4.6) is small compared with the noise here, so the bit depth loss alone is not the main problem; the JPEG quantisation afterwards is. With brighter, low-noise data or after a rescale of a small range to 8 bits, it can matter.
B4. (a) x: \lfloor 611/256 \rfloor - \lfloor 100/256 \rfloor + 1 = 2 - 0 + 1 = 3; y: \lfloor 811/256 \rfloor - \lfloor 300/256 \rfloor + 1 = 3 - 1 + 1 = 3; z: 1. 9 chunks, decoded 9 \cdot 256^2 \cdot 2 = 1.18 MB for 512^2 \cdot 2 = 0.52 MB needed. (b) x: \lfloor 611/64 \rfloor - \lfloor 100/64 \rfloor + 1 = 9 - 1 + 1 = 9; y: 12 - 4 + 1 = 9; z: \lfloor 40/64 \rfloor - \lfloor 40/64 \rfloor + 1 = 1. 81 chunks of 64^3: 81 \cdot 64^3 \cdot 2 = 42.5 MB decoded for the same 0.52 MB. (c) Slices: thin chunks (one or a few slices deep). Profiles through z: chunks that are deep in z (e.g. 64 \times 64 \times 100), so one chunk holds whole z-profiles; cubic chunks are the compromise when both happen.
B5. The pattern repeats every 8 pixels: 512/8 = 64 cycles per image width and its multiples, 128, 192 and 256 (the highest frequency), along both axes.
B6. 6-bit values 0–63. After the first plane (1): 32–63, middle 47.5, error up to 16 (here 2.5). After two planes (10): 32–47, middle 39.5, error up to 8 (here 5.5). After three (101): 40–47, middle 43.5, error up to 4 (here 1.5). Every plane halves the largest possible error: about 6 dB per plane, as in the JPEG unit.




Math questions
B7. (math) Show that the integer 5/3 lifting step of the lecture is exactly invertible for any integers, whatever the rounding (floor) does. Why would a version that first computes the real-valued wavelet coefficients and then rounds them not be invertible in general?
B8. (math) Prove the chunk-count formula for one dimension: the chunks k = \lfloor a/c \rfloor, \dots, \lfloor (b-1)/c \rfloor are exactly those that overlap [a, b). What is the worst-case read amplification of a region of size w with chunk size c in one dimension?
B9. (math) Spots of a fixed shape with integrated intensity I are smoothed by the codec, roughly like a blur that removes frequencies above f_c. Why does an aperture measurement of the integrated intensity change less than the peak height? When does it change anyway?






Solutions (math)





B7. Forward: d_n = x_{2n+1} - P_n with P_n = \lfloor (x_{2n} + x_{2n+2})/2 \rfloor, which depends only on even samples; then s_n = x_{2n} + U_n with U_n = \lfloor (d_{n-1} + d_n + 2)/4 \rfloor, which depends only on the d’s. The decoder knows all d_n, so it computes U_n exactly and gets x_{2n} = s_n - U_n; then it knows the even samples, computes P_n exactly and gets x_{2n+1} = d_n + P_n. Each step adds an integer function of values the decoder already has, so it can be subtracted again; the rounding inside P_n and U_n is reproduced exactly. Rounding the real-valued coefficients afterwards loses information: different integer images can round to the same coefficients, and the inverse of rounded coefficients is not an integer image in general.
B8. Chunk k covers [kc, (k+1)c). It overlaps [a, b) iff kc < b and (k+1)c > a, i.e. k \le \lfloor (b-1)/c \rfloor and k \ge \lfloor a/c \rfloor (for integers). The count is the difference + 1. A region of size w touches at most \lceil (w - 1)/c \rceil + 1 chunks, so up to (\lceil (w-1)/c \rceil + 1)\,c values are decoded for w needed: for w = 1 (a profile across the chunks’ long side) the amplification is c.
B9. The integrated intensity is the spot’s zero-frequency content (\hat f(0) of the spot), which a low-pass leaves unchanged; the peak height is \int \hat f over all frequencies, which loses everything above f_c. So an aperture large enough to hold the smoothed spot keeps the integral. It changes anyway when (1) the codec is not a pure low-pass: quantisation of a dim spot’s coefficients rounds them to zero or to a coarse step, and the DC of a block holding the spot is rounded too; (2) the smoothed spot spreads beyond the aperture, or into the background annulus, which then overestimates the background; (3) the spot is near the noise, where small coefficients become 0. That is why dim spots change by several percent while bright ones do not.

title: Exercise: compression and measurements, JPEG 2000, formats
section: Explore: what happens to the measurements
text:
Explore: what happens to the measurements
A synthetic 12-bit fluorescence image with known ground truth: 60 Gaussian spots (peaks 60–1500 above the cell) in a cell with a darker nucleus, Poisson noise. Choose lossless, JPEG at a quality (the image is first rescaled to 8 bits), or a wavelet codec at the same size as that JPEG. The same analysis runs on the original and on the decoded image: spot detection (detected yellow, missed true spots red), the integrated intensity of every spot (scatter: change against the original; red = dimmest third, blue = brightest third), background mean and noise, the share of high-frequency power, and the blocking index (spectrum peaks at multiples of 1/8). blocking spectrum shows that spectrum with the expected peak positions circled. The plot on the right follows one measurement over all JPEG qualities (log scale of bits per pixel; dashed: the original; orange: the current setting).



M1. Preset quality 95 looks perfect. Compare original and decoded by eye. Then read the numbers: file size and ratio, spots found, dim and bright spot changes, noise. Is the image “the same data”?
M2. Lower the quality to 90, 75, 50 and 30. Note size, spots found and false, dim-spot change and noise sd. Which measurement goes first? Which survives longest?
M3. Preset quality 10: spots lost. How many spots are found, how many false? Where are the false detections, and why?
M4. Preset blocking in the spectrum. Where are the peaks, and what is the blocking index? Compare with the original (lossless) and with the wavelet codec.
M5. Preset wavelet, same size as q 30. Compare all measurements with JPEG at quality 30 (same size). Which codec does less damage? Look at the decoded images: how do their errors look different?
M6. Preset lossless: identical. What is the ratio? Use the plot with noise sd and with HF power: from which JPEG quality on are these measurements within 5% of the original?






Solutions





M1. Quality 95: 17 200 bytes (7.6× smaller than the 131 072 raw bytes, 2.10 bits per pixel). All 60 spots found, no false ones; but the dim spots’ integrated intensities change by 3.2% on average (each spot up or down), the bright ones by 0.3%; noise sd 36.3 against 35.1. Visually identical, numerically not.
M2. Quality 90: 9 786 B, 60 found, dim 5.0%, noise 33.6. Quality 75: 4 206 B, 58 found, 0 false, dim 10.1%, noise 30.8. Quality 50: 2 480 B, 59 found, dim 13.6%, noise 29.8. Quality 30: 1 973 B, 56 found, 1 false, dim 24.7%, noise 30.2. The noise statistic and the high-frequency power change first (at 90 already −4% and −38%), then the dim spots’ intensities; the detection count holds until about quality 50, the bright spots’ intensities (within 1–4%) longest.
M3. 45 of 60 found and 129 false detections. The false ones lie at block borders and corners, in the dark surroundings and inside the cell: blocking adds steps between flat squares, and the difference-of-Gaussians filter responds to them like to small spots. The threshold was set on the original, where the background was only noise.
M4. Peaks on both axes at 32, 64, 96 and 128 cycles per image width (multiples of 256/8), circled; blocking index 136.5 at quality 30. The original (and lossless) has 0.9 (no peaks), the wavelet codec at the same size 0.7: no block grid.
M5. Wavelet at 1 973 B: 57 found, 0 false, dim spots 11.2%, noise 29.7, blocking index 0.7. JPEG at quality 30: 56 found, 1 false, dim spots 24.7%, noise 30.2, blocking index 136.5. The wavelet codec does less damage at the same size; its error is smooth blur and faint ripples around spots, while JPEG’s error is blocky. (The wavelet size is an entropy estimate, slightly optimistic compared with JPEG’s real Huffman code, so the comparison favours it a little.)
M6. Lossless: 55 586 bytes, 2.4× smaller, all numbers identical. Noise sd within 5% of 35.1 (33.3 to 36.9): qualities 95 and 100 (36.3 and 35.2); at 90 it is 33.6, 4.3% low, just inside; from 75 down (30.8) it is outside. High-frequency power within 5% of 1.08%: only quality 100 (1.11%); already at 95 it is 1.19% (+10%), at 90 0.67% (−38%). Texture measures are the most fragile.

title: Exercise: compression and measurements, JPEG 2000, formats
text:
Where this leads
The day’s chain is complete: entropy codes, prediction, transforms, quantisation, and their effect on data. Wavelet coding (the previous day) and JPEG 2000 replace the 8 × 8 blocks by a multiresolution transform; learned codecs (neural networks trained together with an entropy model) push the same rate–distortion trade-off further, with the same caution for scientific data: a codec that invents plausible detail is worse than one that blurs.

title: Quiz: compression and measurements, JPEG 2000, formats
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A JPEG at quality 95 of a fluorescence image looks identical to the original. Can you use it to measure spot intensities?






Hint





Which spots have most of their energy close to the noise and in high frequencies?









Answer





Not safely. In the demo every spot is still found at quality 95, but the integrated intensities of the dim spots change by about 3% on average (up or down, spot by spot), and the noise statistics change. Visual identity says nothing about the numbers; test the measurement itself, or use lossless storage.




Q2. Why does lossy compression damage dim spots more than bright ones?






Hint





What happens to coefficients that are not much larger than the quantisation step?









Answer





A dim spot adds only small coefficients, comparable to the noise and to the quantisation steps: they are rounded to zero or to a coarse level, so the spot is flattened, shifted or lost. A bright spot’s coefficients are many steps large, and their relative rounding error is small.




Q3. How can you tell that an image was once saved as a JPEG, even if it is now a TIFF?






Hint





What periodic structure does JPEG leave behind?









Answer





JPEG’s 8 × 8 blocks leave larger jumps between neighbouring pixels at every 8th row and column. The spectrum of the neighbour differences shows peaks at multiples of 1/8 cycle per pixel (in a 256-pixel image at 32, 64, 96, 128). Zoomed in, flat areas may also show blocks.




Q4. Why does JPEG 2000 show no blocking, even at low rates?






Hint





Which transform does it use, and on what?









Answer





It transforms the whole image (or large tiles) with a wavelet transform, whose basis functions overlap and come at many scales; there is no 8 × 8 grid whose blocks are coded independently. Its errors appear as blur and ringing around edges instead.




Q5. How can a wavelet transform be exactly lossless, when wavelet coefficients are normally real numbers?






Hint





Lifting, with rounding inside each step.









Answer





The reversible 5/3 transform is computed by lifting: each step adds a rounded function of samples the decoder already has (predict the odd samples from the even ones, update the even ones from the residuals). Integers stay integers, and the decoder subtracts exactly the same rounded values in reverse order. Without quantisation, the image comes back exactly.




Q6. A colleague saves a 16-bit confocal stack as a TIFF and is sure it is lossless. What should you check?






Hint





A TIFF is a container.









Answer





The compression inside the TIFF (none, LZW, Deflate and Zstandard are lossless; JPEG is lossy) and the bit depth (was it saved as 8-bit?). The file extension alone says neither.




Q7. A 3D volume is stored in chunks of 512 × 512 × 1. A viewer shows x–z slices. Why is it slow, and what chunk shape would help?






Hint





Which chunks does one x–z slice touch?









Answer





An x–z slice (one y, all x and z) passes through one chunk per z-slice and x-block: every chunk is decoded in full (512 × 512 values) to use one row of 512. Chunks that are deeper in z and thinner in y (e.g. 128 × 32 × 128), or cubic chunks, decode far less for x–z slices, at some cost for x–y slices.




Q8. (math) Each received bit plane of a JPEG 2000 coefficient halves the range of values it can still have. How many decibels of PSNR does one more bit plane buy, at most?






Hint





Halving the error amplitude divides the squared error by 4.









Answer





The error amplitude halves, the squared error is divided by 4: 10\log_{10} 4 = 6.02 dB per bit plane, the same 6 dB per bit as for a uniform quantiser.

title: Bleed-through and compensation
text:
About this lecture
A two-colour fluorescence image: nucleus labelled green, membrane labelled orange. The orange channel shows a faint ghost of the nucleus. Nothing orange is in the nucleus: the green dye’s light leaks into the orange channel.

Why dyes bleed through: broad emission spectra seen through finite filter bands.
Each dye gives one column of a mixing matrix: a pixel is \mathbf y = M\mathbf a.
A single-stained control measures a column.
Compensation undoes the mixing with M^{-1}; under- and over-compensation, and why similar dyes are hard.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

First unit of the spectral unmixing day (an elective after the colour day). Adapted from the earlier course’s flow-cytometry compensation unit: the cell becomes a pixel, the cytometer’s detectors become image channels. Linear algebra needed: a 2 × 2 inverse and the idea that the columns of a matrix are where the axes land (the images unit, day 1).

title: Bleed-through and compensation
section: Why a dye shows up in the wrong channel
text:
Why a dye shows up in the wrong channel


A dye emits over a broad range of wavelengths, with a long tail towards the red.
A channel’s filter lets through one band. Channel 1 is meant for dye 1, channel 2 for dye 2.
Dye 1’s tail reaches into channel 2’s band: a pixel with only dye 1 still gives a signal in channel 2. That is bleed-through (or crosstalk, spillover).
A second source: one laser can excite both dyes. The algebra below is the same.

title: Bleed-through and compensation
section: A channel adds up a band
text:
A channel adds up a band
The value a channel records is the dye’s spectrum times the filter’s transmission, added up over wavelength.
Five bins of 25 nm (500, 525, 550, 575, 600 nm), one unit of each dye:

Dye 1: channel 1 sees 0.2 + 1.0 = 1.2, channel 2 sees 0.3 + 0.1 = 0.4 (times 25 nm). Dye 2: channel 1 sees 0.1, channel 2 sees 1.6.
So one unit of dye 1 lands at (1.2,\ 0.4) in channel space, dye 2 at (0.1,\ 1.6).

title: Bleed-through and compensation
section: The math: the channel value as an integral
text:
The math: the channel value as an integral
With emission spectrum s_k(\lambda) of dye k (per unit amount) and transmission f_c(\lambda) of channel c (filter times detector sensitivity):
M_{ck} = \int s_k(\lambda)\, f_c(\lambda)\, d\lambda \;\approx\; \sum_i s_k(\lambda_i)\, f_c(\lambda_i)\, \Delta\lambda .

One column per dye: \mathbf m_k = (M_{1k}, \dots, M_{Nk})^\top, the dye as the channels see it.
A linear map from a spectrum to N numbers, the same as the camera of the colour day (three numbers from a spectrum).
Narrower f_c: smaller off-diagonal M_{ck}, but also a smaller M_{kk}: fewer photons for the dye’s own channel.

title: Bleed-through and compensation
text:
Try it: spectra and filters




Each column of the matrix is divided by its entry in the dye’s own channel, so the diagonal is 1 and the off-diagonal entries are the bleed-through fractions. Tour: “classic tail”: dye 1 → channel 2 is 20.4 %, dye 2 → channel 1 only 0.5 %: the tail goes to the red. Drag channel 2’s band to the right: the bleed-through drops. “Narrow filters”: 15.3 %, but each dye keeps only 20 % and 26 % of its photons in its own channel (61 % and 74 % before). “Two dyes 20 nm apart”: dye 1 → channel 2 is 1.02 (dye 1 is as bright in channel 2 as in its own channel), dye 2 → channel 1 is 0.15; det 0.85, κ 3.1. “8-bin spectral detector”: four dyes, every dye spreads over 2–3 bins; that is fine for least squares (next unit).

title: Bleed-through and compensation
text:
Fluorescence adds: the mixing matrix
Light from different dyes adds in each channel. A pixel with amounts a_1 of dye 1 and a_2 of dye 2 records
\mathbf y = a_1 \mathbf m_1 + a_2 \mathbf m_2 = M \mathbf a, \qquad M = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf m_1 & \mathbf m_2 \end{pmatrix}.

Rows of M = channels, columns = dyes (components). Column k is where one unit of dye k lands: “the columns of a matrix are where the axes land” (the images unit, day 1).
Scale each column by its own channel: the spillover matrix S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & s_{12} \\ s_{21} & 1 \end{pmatrix}. From the table: s_{21} = 0.4/1.2 = 0.33, s_{12} = 0.1/1.6 = 0.06.
The whole image: Y = MA, channels × pixels = (channels × dyes)(dyes × pixels). One matrix for all pixels.

title: Bleed-through and compensation
text:
Brightfield stains multiply
Absorbing stains (H&E, DAB) do not add light, they remove a fraction of it: two stains on top of each other multiply the transmitted light.

Take the logarithm first, the optical density -\log_{10}(I/I_0): then the stains add, and the same model \mathbf y = M\mathbf a holds.
The unit on stain separation (colour deconvolution) does exactly that; today stays with fluorescence.

title: Bleed-through and compensation
section: A single-stained control measures a column
text:
A single-stained control measures a column
Image a sample with only dye 1. Every pixel is a_1 \mathbf m_1: in the scatter plot of channel 2 against channel 1 the pixels lie on a line through the origin with slope s_{21}.

Four background-subtracted control pixels: (100, 27), (200, 48), (300, 77), (400, 98). The slope through the origin: \sum xy / \sum x^2 = 74\,600 / 300\,000 = 0.249.
Subtract the offset (dark level, background) first: an offset is a fake component with a flat spectrum and tilts the estimate.
A dim control gives a poor estimate: controls should be at least as bright as the sample.
One control per dye; with K dyes, K controls give the K columns.

title: Bleed-through and compensation
section: The math: the slope through the origin
text:
The math: the slope through the origin
The control pixels satisfy y_i \approx s\, x_i. Least squares: minimise E(s) = \sum_i (y_i - s x_i)^2.
\frac{dE}{ds} = -2 \sum_i x_i (y_i - s x_i) = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \hat s = \frac{\sum_i x_i y_i}{\sum_i x_i^2}.

No intercept: zero dye gives zero signal (after offset subtraction).
Noise in x (the dye’s own channel) biases a regression slope towards 0; bright controls keep that bias small.

title: Bleed-through and compensation
text:
Compensation: undo the matrix
If \mathbf y = S\mathbf a, then \mathbf a = S^{-1}\mathbf y. With s_{21} = 0.25, s_{12} = 0.02:
S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.02 \\ 0.25 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad S^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1.005 & -0.020 \\ -0.251 & 1.005 \end{pmatrix}.

The inverse has negative off-diagonal entries: “subtract 25 % of channel 1 from channel 2”, and a little the other way.
Compensation is one 2 \times 2 matrix applied to every pixel: the ghost of the nucleus disappears from channel 2.
It does not remove noise: the compensated values carry the noise of both channels, mixed through S^{-1}.

title: Bleed-through and compensation
text:
The math: the 2 \times 2 inverse
\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix}.
For S: \det S = 1 - s_{12}s_{21} = 1 - 0.02 \cdot 0.25 = 0.995, so S^{-1} = \frac{1}{0.995}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -0.02 \\ -0.25 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.

\det S is the area of the parallelogram spanned by the two columns. Well-separated dyes: a near-square, \det \approx 1, S^{-1} \approx I minus small corrections.
Similar dyes: nearly parallel columns, a thin parallelogram, \det \to 0 and entries of S^{-1} of size 1/\det.

title: Bleed-through and compensation
text:
Try it: compensate the image




A synthetic cell (seeded): dye 1 in the nucleus, dye 2 in the membrane, a few vesicles with both, Poisson noise. True spillover 0.25 and 0.05 (hidden). Left: channel 2 measured and compensated (buttons switch to channel 1 or the merge). Middle: channel 2 against channel 1 for every pixel. Right: after compensation with the guess. Tour: “no compensation”: the nucleus pixels (green) tilt up with slope 0.25, and the ghost is in channel 2. Raise s₂₁ slowly and ask the class when to stop: the green line flattens and the median comes down to the background. “Over”: the line tilts down, the nucleus gets a negative dye-2 signal and the ghost becomes a dark hole. “Reveal true S”. Point at Pearson’s r: 0.33 before, about 0 after. “Similar dyes”: the true S is (0.9, 0.9); even exact compensation smears the populations, and the background noise grows from about 5 to 31.

title: Bleed-through and compensation
section: Under, over, and the check without ground truth
text:
Under, over, and the check without ground truth

Under-compensated (guess too small): the single-stained population still tilts up; its median sits above the background.
Over-compensated (guess too large): it tilts down, below the background, into negative values.
A dye cannot emit negative light. Pixels of a single-stained population clearly below the background mean the spillover was set too high. A population that rises or falls with its own dye means the spillover is wrong.
In the demo (true s_{21} = 0.25): guess 0.15 leaves a median of 86 in channel 2 (background 11), guess 0.35 gives -66.

title: Bleed-through and compensation
section: The math: what a wrong guess leaves
text:
The math: what a wrong guess leaves
A pixel with only dye 1: \mathbf y = a\,(1,\ s)^\top (take s_{12} = 0). Compensating with the guess g:
\hat a_2 = y_2 - g\, y_1 = (s - g)\, a .

The dye-1 population lies on a line with slope exactly s - g: up when g < s, flat when g = s, down when g > s.
With both off-diagonals guessed (g_{12}, g_{21}): \hat{\mathbf a} = S_g^{-1} S \mathbf a; to first order in the errors the slope is still s_{21} - g_{21}.

title: Bleed-through and compensation
text:
Similar dyes: compensation amplifies noise
Two dyes with nearly the same spectrum: S_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.9 \\ 0.9 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \det S_2 = 0.19,
S_2^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 5.26 & -4.74 \\ -4.74 & 5.26 \end{pmatrix}.

A 10-unit error in channel 2 becomes errors of 47 and 53 in the two dyes. With S of the previous slides it stays 10.
The average is still right; individual pixels are not. In the demo the background noise grows from 4.6 to 31 after compensation.
Choosing dyes and filters that are far apart matters more than any algorithm. The next unit measures this with the condition number.

title: Bleed-through and compensation
text:
Bleed-through fakes colocalisation
Nucleus and membrane are different places, yet in the measured image the two channels correlate: every bright nucleus pixel is also a bit bright in channel 2.

In the demo: Pearson’s r between the channels inside the cell is 0.33 before compensation and −0.03 after.
Any measurement that compares channels (colocalisation, ratios, FRET) must compensate first. Colocalisation itself is taught on the measurements day (coloc/).
Physical remedies: narrower filters (cost: photons), sequential excitation (one laser at a time), dyes further apart.

title: Bleed-through and compensation
section: Aside: the same thing in flow cytometry
text:
Aside: the same thing in flow cytometry



Photo: Mark Fergus, CSIRO, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.


A flow cytometer measures thousands of cells per second, each a “pixel” with one value per detector.
Same spillover, same S^{-1}, one compensation per cell. This is where “compensation” got its name.
Spectral cytometers unmix 20 or more dyes with many detectors: the least squares of the next unit.



The demo has a data-mode=“cells” with the earlier course’s four simulated populations (unstained, dye 1, dye 2, both; true spillover 0.25 and 0.02), if you want to show the cytometry version: same sliders, same verdicts. With the true values the dye-1 population has slope −0.004 and median 105 in the other detector, the same as the unstained cells.

title: Bleed-through and compensation
text:
Summary

Broad emission spectra and finite filter bands: each dye shows up in several channels (bleed-through).
A channel value is spectrum × filter, added over wavelength; one dye gives one column of M; fluorescence adds: \mathbf y = M\mathbf a.
A single-stained control measures a column: the slope through the origin, after offset subtraction.
Compensation: \hat{\mathbf a} = M^{-1}\mathbf y. A single-stained population should lie flat at the background level; tilted up = under, tilted down and negative = over.
Similar dyes: \det M \to 0, the inverse is large and amplifies noise.
Bleed-through makes independent channels correlate: compensate before comparing channels.

title: Exercise: transform coding, the DCT and the KLT
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

apply a small DCT by hand and use Parseval to find the error of dropping coefficients,
explain energy compaction with the two-pixel rotation and the KLT (PCA of blocks),
predict which 8 × 8 DCT coefficients a flat block, an edge or a texture has,
explain why the DCT beats the DFT on blocks (no jump at the block edges),
compare whole-image and block transforms at the same number of kept coefficients.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demos.

title: Exercise: transform coding, the DCT and the KLT
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

apply a small DCT by hand and use Parseval to find the error of dropping coefficients,
explain energy compaction with the two-pixel rotation and the KLT (PCA of blocks),
predict which 8 × 8 DCT coefficients a flat block, an edge or a texture has,
explain why the DCT beats the DFT on blocks (no jump at the block edges),
compare whole-image and block transforms at the same number of kept coefficients.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demos.
crumbs: Transform coding, the DCT and the KLT

title: Exercise: transform coding, the DCT and the KLT
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Orthonormal transform
c = A x, x = A^\top c; rows of A are the basis vectors


Parseval
\sum_k c_k^2 = \sum_n x_n^2; dropping coefficients costs exactly their squares


2-point DCT
c_0 = (x_0 + x_1)/\sqrt2, c_1 = (x_0 - x_1)/\sqrt2: a 45° rotation


4-point DCT
rows (0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5), (0.653, 0.271, -0.271, -0.653), (0.5, -0.5, -0.5, 0.5), (0.271, -0.653, 0.653, -0.271)


8 × 8 DCT
C = D X D^\top; C_{00} = 8 \cdot block mean; (u, v) = (horizontal, vertical) frequency


KLT
eigenvectors of the covariance of the blocks (PCA), ordered by eigenvalue


DFT vs DCT
DFT: block repeated periodically (jumps at the edges); DCT: block mirrored (no jumps)
crumbs: Transform coding, the DCT and the KLT

title: Exercise: transform coding, the DCT and the KLT
text:
By hand
B1. Two neighbouring pixels (x_0, x_1) = (100, 104). (a) Compute the 2-point DCT. (b) Drop c_1 and transform back. What is the squared error, and how does it compare with c_1^2?
B2. Use the 4-point DCT matrix of the background table. (a) Transform (1, 1, 1, 1) and (1, 2, 3, 4). (b) Check that the second row has length 1 and is orthogonal to the fourth. (c) What is the sum of the squared coefficients of (1, 2, 3, 4), and of the squared pixel values?
B3. Keep only c_0 of (1, 2, 3, 4). What is the reconstruction, and what is its squared error? Check with Parseval. Then keep c_0 and c_1: what is the squared error now?
B4. Pairs of neighbouring pixels (mean removed) have the covariance S = \sigma^2 \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \rho \\ \rho & 1 \end{pmatrix}. (a) Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of S (the KLT). Compare with the 2-point DCT. (b) What fraction of the energy is in the first KLT coefficient for \rho = 0.95, and for \rho = 0?
B5. 8 × 8 blocks, after subtracting 128 from every pixel. (a) A flat block of value 200: which coefficients are non-zero, and what is C_{00}? (b) A block whose left four columns are 200 and right four columns 60: which coefficients can be non-zero? Which row of the 64 basis images do they belong to? (c) The same edge, but horizontal (top four rows 200, bottom four rows 60)? (d) Stripes 40 40 230 230 40 40 230 230 repeated in every row?
B6. The row 10 20 30 40 50 60 70 80. Sketch three periods of its periodic extension and of its mirrored extension. Which has jumps? Which transform will need more coefficients for this row, and why?
B7. A 256 × 256 image is cut into 8 × 8 blocks. How many blocks are there? If you keep the largest 1% of all block-DCT coefficients, how many is that per block on average? What must happen to some blocks?






Solutions





B1. (a) c_0 = 204/\sqrt2 = 144.25, c_1 = -4/\sqrt2 = -2.83. (b) With c_1 = 0: x = (c_0/\sqrt2, c_0/\sqrt2) = (102, 102). Squared error 2^2 + 2^2 = 8 = c_1^2. Nearly all of the energy is in c_0.
B2. (a) (1,1,1,1) \mapsto (2, 0, 0, 0): a constant has only the DC coefficient. (1,2,3,4) \mapsto (5, -2.230, 0, -0.159). (b) 0.653^2 + 0.271^2 + 0.271^2 + 0.653^2 = 1.000; 0.653 \cdot 0.271 + 0.271 \cdot (-0.653) + (-0.271) \cdot 0.653 + (-0.653)(-0.271) = 0. (c) 25 + 4.975 + 0 + 0.025 = 30 = 1 + 4 + 9 + 16.
B3. c_0 alone gives x = 5 \cdot (0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5) = (2.5, 2.5, 2.5, 2.5), the mean. Squared error 1.5^2 + 0.5^2 + 0.5^2 + 1.5^2 = 5 = c_1^2 + c_2^2 + c_3^2 = 4.975 + 0 + 0.025. Keeping c_0 and c_1: error = c_3^2 = 0.025: two coefficients describe the ramp almost perfectly.
B4. (a) \det(S - \lambda I) = 0 gives \lambda = \sigma^2(1 \pm \rho), with eigenvectors (1, 1)/\sqrt2 and (1, -1)/\sqrt2: exactly the rows of the 2-point DCT, for every \rho > 0. (b) \frac{1 + \rho}{2}: 97.5% for \rho = 0.95, 50% for \rho = 0 (uncorrelated pixels: no rotation helps).
B5. (a) Only C_{00} = 8 \cdot (200 - 128) = 576. (b) Every row of the block is the same, so all vertical frequencies are zero: only the top row v = 0. The row (72, 72, 72, 72, -68, -68, -68, -68) is antisymmetric about its centre except for its mean (2): C_{00} = 8 \cdot 2 = 16, and of the others only the odd u = 1, 3, 5, 7 (antisymmetric cosines). (c) The left column u = 0: C_{00} and C_{10}, C_{30}, C_{50}, C_{70} (rows of the coefficient table). (d) Again only the top row; the pattern has period 4 (half a cycle per 2 pixels), so the largest coefficient is near u = 4 (2 periods in 8 pixels); the demo shows u = 3 and u = 5 largest, with u = 1 and u = 7 smaller, because the stripes are not centred like a cosine.
B6. Periodic: … 70 80 | 10 20 … 80 | 10 20 …: a jump from 80 down to 10 at every edge (a sawtooth). Mirrored: … 20 10 | 10 20 … 80 | 80 70 …: continuous (a triangle wave). The DFT needs many coefficients for the jumps (slow 1/k decay); the DCT describes the ramp with two (B3).
B7. 32 \cdot 32 = 1024 blocks. 1% of 65 536 coefficients is 655: 0.64 per block. At least 369 blocks get no coefficient at all, not even their average (DC): they decode as flat grey (the level shift). JPEG avoids this by always coding the DC of every block.




Math questions
B8. (math) Show that the 8 × 8 2D DCT C = D X D^\top is orthonormal as a map from \mathbb R^{64} to \mathbb R^{64} if D is, and that its basis images are the outer products of rows of D.
B9. (math) Show that the KLT coefficients are uncorrelated, and that the expected squared error of keeping only the first k of them is \sum_{j > k} \lambda_j.
B10. (math) Derive the DCT from the DFT of the mirrored signal y = (x_0, \dots, x_{N-1}, x_{N-1}, \dots, x_0): show Y_k = 2 e^{i\pi k/2N} \sum_n x_n \cos\frac{\pi(2n+1)k}{2N}.
B11. (math) Show that the DFT coefficients of a jump decay like 1/k: compute the DFT of the sawtooth x_n = n, n = 0, \dots, N-1, for k \ne 0 (hint: \sum_n n z^n for z = e^{-2\pi i k/N}). What is |X_k| for small k/N?






Solutions (math)





B8. Write X as a vector x (row-major). C = D X D^\top is c = (D \otimes D)x, and (D \otimes D)^\top (D \otimes D) = (D^\top D) \otimes (D^\top D) = I. The basis image for (u, v) is row (v, u) of D \otimes D: the entries D_{v y} D_{u x}, the outer product of rows v and u of D.
B9. c_j = u_j^\top x, so E[c_i c_j] = u_i^\top E[x x^\top] u_j = u_i^\top S u_j = \lambda_j u_i^\top u_j = \lambda_j \delta_{ij}. Dropping c_{k+1}, \dots gives the error x - \hat x = \sum_{j > k} c_j u_j, with E\|x - \hat x\|^2 = \sum_{j > k} E[c_j^2] = \sum_{j > k} \lambda_j (Parseval in the orthonormal basis u_j).
B10. Y_k = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x_n e^{-i\pi nk/N} + \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x_n e^{-i\pi(2N-1-n)k/N}. The second exponent: e^{-2\pi i k} e^{i\pi(n+1)k/N} = e^{i\pi(n+1)k/N}. Factor out e^{i\pi k/2N}: e^{-i\pi nk/N} = e^{i\pi k/2N} e^{-i\pi(2n+1)k/2N} and e^{i\pi(n+1)k/N} = e^{i\pi k/2N} e^{i\pi(2n+1)k/2N}; their sum is e^{i\pi k/2N} \cdot 2\cos\frac{\pi(2n+1)k}{2N}.
B11. With z = e^{-2\pi i k/N} \ne 1 and z^N = 1: \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} n z^n = \frac{N z^N}{z - 1} - \frac{z(z^N - 1)}{(z-1)^2} = \frac{N}{z - 1}. So |X_k| = \frac{N}{|z - 1|} = \frac{N}{2\sin(\pi k/N)} \approx \frac{N^2}{2\pi k} for small k/N: decay like 1/k. The mirrored ramp (a triangle wave) has coefficients that decay like 1/k^2.

title: Exercise: transform coding, the DCT and the KLT
section: Explore: one block in three bases
text:
Explore: one block in three bases
Left: the image with the selected block (yellow; click to move it) and the energy in the best k coefficients, averaged over all blocks of the image, for the DCT (blue), the DFT (red) and the KLT (green). Middle: the block’s pixel values and its reconstruction from the kept coefficients. Right: the 64 coefficients of the block minus 128 (red positive, blue negative, grey dropped) and the 64 basis images (kept ones framed orange; click one to keep or drop it). Basis: DCT; DFT written as real cosine and sine basis images; KLT learnt from all 1024 blocks of the current image. Keep: the k largest coefficients of this block, the first k in zigzag order (eigenvalue order for the KLT), or by hand.



D1. Presets flat block: only DC, vertical edge and texture block. Check your answers to B5 (a), (b) and (d): which coefficients are non-zero, and what is C_{00}?
D2. Preset vertical edge with k largest. Lower k from 8 to 1. How much energy and what RMS error do 1, 2, 3 and 4 coefficients give? Which coefficient is kept first, and why not the DC?
D3. Preset ramp: DFT leaks, DCT does not (a steep ramp, DFT, first 3). Note the energy kept and the RMS error. Switch to the DCT. Then set k = 2 for both. Explain with B6.
D4. Preset a block of the cell (k = 6 largest). Compare the three bases. How many DCT coefficients do you need for an RMS error below about 11 grey levels? Why does this block need so many more than the synthetic blocks?
D5. Preset KLT looks like the DCT. Look at the KLT basis images: which DCT basis images do the first few resemble? Read the energy curves at k = 4 for the three bases. Then choose the test card image: how do the curves change, and why can the KLT now beat the DCT by much more?






Solutions





D1. Flat (200 everywhere): only C_{00} = 576. Vertical edge (200 | 60, edge in the middle): C_{00} = 16 and the top-row coefficients 507.4, −178.2, 119.1, −100.9 at u = 1, 3, 5, 7: five non-zero, all in the top row. Texture (40 40 230 230 …): C_{00} = 56, and u = 1, 3, 5, 7 in the top row: −285.3, −583.8, 390.1, 56.7.
D2. k = 1: 82.0% of the energy, RMS error 29.7; k = 2: 92.2%, 19.6; k = 3: 96.7%, 12.8; k = 4: 99.9%, 2.0 (the fifth, the DC of 16, gives 100%). The first kept coefficient is C_{01} = 507.4, the half cosine that follows the step; the DC is only 16 because the block mean (130) is close to the level shift 128.
D3. DFT, first 3: 74.8% of the energy, RMS error 12.65. DCT, first 3: 99.6%, 1.58. With k = 2 the numbers are the same (the third zigzag coefficient is a vertical frequency, zero for this block). The DFT sees a sawtooth with a jump at the block edge (B6) and spreads the energy over all horizontal frequencies; the DCT sees a continuous triangle wave and needs one cosine.
D4. DCT 60.7% (RMS 17.9), DFT 61.7% (17.7), KLT 63.2% (17.3): all similar and poor. With the DCT, k = 20 gives 85.8% and RMS 10.7. The micrograph block is grainy (electron-microscope texture and noise at the pixel scale); its energy is spread over many coefficients, while a flat block, a straight edge or regular stripes need one to five.
D5. The first KLT images look like the DCT’s DC, the two lowest horizontal and vertical cosines and then second-order patterns; the curves at k = 4: DCT 87.0%, DFT 85.6%, KLT 87.3%: the KLT is only a little better. On the test card: DCT 86.4%, DFT 88.8%, KLT 97.4%. The card has a few kinds of blocks (flat, one edge, the same stripes again and again), so its blocks lie in a low-dimensional subspace that the KLT learns; the DCT does not adapt to that. For natural, smooth images the KLT’s advantage is small, which is why a fixed basis (nothing to store) wins in practice.

title: Exercise: transform coding, the DCT and the KLT
text:
Explore: periodic or mirrored?
One row of 8 samples (drag the black points up or down). Top: its periodic extension, what the DFT assumes; middle: its mirrored extension, what the DCT assumes. Right: the size of the DFT (red) and DCT (blue) coefficients in frequency order, and the row rebuilt from the first k coefficients of each (dashed: the original).



R1. Preset ramp, k = 3: note the RMS errors. Compare the coefficient bars: how fast do they fall off for each transform?
R2. Preset step (20 20 20 20 80 80 80 80). Compare the errors for k = 2 and k = 4. Does the DCT still win clearly? Why is a step harder for the DCT than a ramp?
R3. Preset smooth bump with k = 2. Which transform wins now? Look at the periodic extension to explain it.
R4. Preset random: what does k change? What does that say about compressing noise?






Solutions





R1. k = 3: DCT 2.49, DFT 13.55. DCT: 127.3, −64.4, 0, −6.7, 0, −2.0, 0, −0.5: fast decay. DFT (real form): 127.3, −20.0, −48.3, −20.0, −20.0, −20.0, −8.3, −14.1: the coefficients stay large to the end, the signature of the jump.
R2. k = 2: DCT 12.69, DFT 28.06; k = 4: DCT 8.36, DFT 11.48. The DCT is still better, but neither is good: the jump now lies inside the block, and mirroring cannot remove it. Edges inside a block are expensive for every Fourier-type basis (they ring, as the next unit shows).
R3. k = 2: DFT 2.33, DCT 15.74 (with k = 3: DFT 1.46, DCT 1.19). The bump starts and ends at about the same height (30 and 40), so its periodic extension has almost no jump, and one DFT cosine-sine pair describes the hump; the DCT needs its second cosine (k = 2) for a shape that rises and falls. The DCT’s advantage is about the ends of the block.
R4. Almost nothing: the error drops from 25.6 (k = 1) to 25.3 (k = 4) for both. Noise has its energy spread evenly over all coefficients in every orthonormal basis; no transform compacts it.
crumbs: Transform coding, the DCT and the KLT

title: Exercise: transform coding, the DCT and the KLT
section: Explore: the whole image, three bases
text:
Explore: the whole image, three bases
The Fourier unit’s demo with a basis switch: DFT of the whole image (as there), DCT of the whole image, or 8 × 8 DCT (every block transformed separately; the coefficient picture groups them by frequency, one 32 × 32 tile per (u, v)). In the DCT bases only “no filter” and “keep largest” apply. The readout gives the share of coefficients kept, the share of the image’s variation they keep, and the RMS error.



F1. keep largest at 3% (as in the Fourier unit’s exercise). Note the variation kept and the RMS error for the three bases. Which is best?
F2. Now keep 1% and 10%. What happens to the 8 × 8 DCT at 1%? Look at the rebuilt image and use B7.
F3. In the 8 × 8 DCT picture, the top-left tile is a small copy of the image. Why?






Solutions





F1. 3%: DFT 81.3% of the variation, RMS 0.100; DCT 83.7%, 0.093; 8 × 8 DCT 81.5%, 0.099. The whole-image DCT is best: it has no wrap-around jump at the image border, which costs the DFT coefficients. The block DCT is as good as the whole-image DFT, despite its 1024 separate blocks.
F2. 1%: DFT 72.8% (0.120), DCT 75.5% (0.114), 8 × 8 DCT 64.5% (0.137). 655 coefficients for 1024 blocks: many blocks keep nothing and come out flat mid grey, others keep only their DC (flat at their mean): the image breaks into visible 8 × 8 squares. 10%: DFT 89.8% (0.074), DCT 91.8% (0.066), 8 × 8 DCT 91.2% (0.068).
F3. The (0, 0) tile holds the DC coefficient of every block, 8 \times (block mean − 0.5), at the block’s position: a 32 × 32 thumbnail of the image (one pixel per 8 × 8 block; shown as a magnitude, so it shows how far each block’s mean lies from mid grey). The other tiles show where in the image each frequency is strong, e.g. the edges of the nucleus in the low-frequency tiles.
crumbs: Transform coding, the DCT and the KLT

title: Exercise: transform coding, the DCT and the KLT
text:
Where this leads
The transform only rearranges the image. JPEG (next unit) quantises the 64 coefficients of each block with a table, coarse for high frequencies, reads them in zigzag order so the zeros come last, and entropy-codes them with run lengths and Huffman codes. The same “transform, then keep the important coefficients” idea is behind wavelet compression (JPEG 2000) and behind PCA-based shape and appearance models.
crumbs: Transform coding, the DCT and the KLT

title: Quiz: transform coding, the DCT and the KLT
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Orthonormal transform c = Ax, x = A^\top c; Parseval \|c\| = \|x\|.

Q1. A 64-pixel block becomes 64 DCT coefficients. Where does the compression come from, if not from the transform?






Hint





What do most of the 64 coefficients of a smooth block look like?









Answer





The transform only rearranges: most of the energy ends up in a few coefficients, the rest are close to zero. Quantisation then turns the small ones into exact zeros and stores the large ones coarsely, and entropy coding stores long runs of zeros in very few bits.




Q2. You drop three DCT coefficients with values 4, −3 and 0 from a block. What is the squared error of the rebuilt block?






Hint





Parseval.









Answer





4^2 + 3^2 + 0^2 = 25 (summed over the 64 pixels), because the DCT is orthonormal: the error in the coefficients equals the error in the pixels. You do not need to transform back to know it.




Q3. An 8 × 8 block contains a horizontal edge (bright top half, dark bottom half). Which coefficients are non-zero?






Hint





Does the block change from left to right?









Answer





Each row is constant, so all horizontal frequencies u > 0 are zero: only the left column u = 0 of the coefficient table, i.e. the DC and vertical frequencies. As in the vertical case, only the DC and the odd vertical frequencies v = 1, 3, 5, 7 for an edge exactly in the middle.




Q4. Why is the KLT, the best possible linear transform for compaction, not used in JPEG?






Hint





What would the decoder need to know?









Answer





The KLT depends on the image: its 64 basis vectors (4096 numbers) would have to be computed (an eigenproblem) and stored in the file, and there is no fast algorithm to apply it. For smooth natural images the fixed DCT is almost as good, needs nothing stored, and is fast.




Q5. Why does the DFT need more coefficients than the DCT for a block that is a smooth ramp?






Hint





What does the DFT assume about the signal outside the block?









Answer





The DFT treats the block as one period of a periodic signal: the ramp becomes a sawtooth with a jump at each block edge, and a jump needs many frequencies (coefficients fall off like 1/k). The DCT is the DFT of the mirrored block, which has no jump: its coefficients fall off like 1/k^2, and two describe the ramp.




Q6. For pure noise, which transform compacts the energy best: DCT, DFT or KLT?






Hint





What does the covariance matrix of independent noise look like?









Answer





None of them. Independent noise of equal variance has covariance \sigma^2 I: every orthonormal basis gives coefficients of the same variance \sigma^2, so the energy is spread evenly whatever the basis. Noise cannot be compacted, only removed (which is lossy).




Q7. What is the main price of transforming the image in independent 8 × 8 blocks?






Hint





What happens to the errors at the border between two blocks?









Answer





Each block is coded on its own, so its errors are independent of the neighbouring block’s: where coefficients are dropped or coarsely quantised, the pixel values jump at the block borders. This is blocking, the typical JPEG artefact at low quality, and it adds an 8-pixel periodic pattern to the image.




Q8. (math) Pairs of pixels have covariance \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \rho \\ \rho & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Show that the 2-point DCT diagonalises it, whatever \rho is.






Hint





Apply the matrix to (1, 1) and (1, -1).









Answer





\begin{pmatrix} 1 & \rho \\ \rho & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = (1 + \rho)\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} and \ldots\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} = (1 - \rho)\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}: the rows of the 2-point DCT, (1, 1)/\sqrt2 and (1, -1)/\sqrt2, are the eigenvectors for every \rho, so D S D^\top = \operatorname{diag}(1 + \rho, 1 - \rho).
crumbs: Transform coding, the DCT and the KLT

title: Linear deconvolution: inverse, Wiener, Tikhonov
text:
About this lecture
The image formation day ended with a problem: dividing by the transfer function undoes the blur exactly without noise, and explodes with it. Today’s answer, in three steps:

Give up where the data are hopeless: the truncated inverse.
Trust each frequency as much as its signal-to-noise ratio allows: the Wiener filter.
Say what we believe about the object as a penalty: Tikhonov regularisation.
Read every method as a gain curve, and predict the image from it.
Practicalities: the right PSF, and what the FFT does at the borders.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

First unit of the deconvolution day (day 5). It recalls the forward model, the OTF and the diagnosis “inversion is ill-posed” from the image formation day (day 4) in one slide and does not re-teach them. Notation: g = observed image, f = object, h = PSF, H = OTF (its Fourier transform), n = noise with standard deviation σn; λ = regularisation weight, as everywhere in the course. Not to be confused: “colour deconvolution” of stained slides (spectral unmixing elective) is unrelated despite the name.
Teacher note (not on a slide): simulating and restoring with the same discrete PSF on a periodic image is the “inverse crime” and flatters every method. The demo’s “realistic blur” option blurs a wider scene on a twice finer grid, so blur reaches in from outside the field and the PSF is not exactly the discrete one used for restoration.

title: Linear deconvolution: inverse, Wiener, Tikhonov
text:
Yesterday: dividing by H
From the image formation day: the observed image is the object blurred by the PSF, plus noise, g = h \ast f + n. In Fourier space each frequency is multiplied by the OTF: G = H F + N.

Inverse filter: \hat F = G / H = F + N/H. Without noise: perfect.
Where |H| is small, N/H is huge: noise of 0.1 % at a frequency with |H| = 0.001 becomes 100 %.
Beyond the cut-off H = 0: there is nothing to divide by, and no method can bring those frequencies back.

What must we add? Knowledge about the noise and about the object. Today: how, and (next unit) how much.

Recall only (owner: image formation day, unit “ill-posed”). The demo in inverse-only mode is the same one the image formation day used; here we go straight to the full demo. Gaussian σ = 2 px, phantom, σn = 0.1 % of the peak: RMSE of the inverse filter about 10⁶, half the pixels negative.

title: Linear deconvolution: inverse, Wiener, Tikhonov
section: Give up where the data are hopeless
text:
Give up where the data are hopeless
Truncated inverse: divide only where |H| > \varepsilon; set every other frequency to 0.

The simplest regularisation: frequencies the optics barely pass are dropped, not amplified.
ε small: noisy (weak frequencies still amplified up to 1/\varepsilon). ε large: blurred (good frequencies dropped too).
Price: the cut in frequency is sharp, and a sharp cut in frequency is a sinc in space (the Fourier unit): ringing, ripples parallel to every edge and around every bright spot.

Example, ε = 0.1: gains 1/H for H = 1, 0.5, 0.2 are 1, 2, 5; for H = 0.1 and below the gain is 0.

title: Linear deconvolution: inverse, Wiener, Tikhonov
section: Trust each frequency as much as its SNR allows
text:
Trust each frequency as much as its SNR allows
The Wiener filter multiplies frequency f by
W(f) = \frac{H^*(f)}{|H(f)|^2 + 1/\mathrm{SNR}(f)}
(H^*: complex conjugate; for a symmetric PSF H is real and H^* = H).

Where signal ≫ noise (|H|^2 \gg 1/\mathrm{SNR}): W \approx 1/H, invert.
Where noise ≫ signal: W \approx H\cdot\mathrm{SNR} \to 0, damp.
In between a smooth roll-off: much less ringing than a sharp cut.

With SNR = 100: H = 0.5 gives 0.5/(0.25 + 0.01) = 1.92 (the inverse: 2). H = 0.05 gives 0.05/(0.0025 + 0.01) = 4 instead of 20.

title: Linear deconvolution: inverse, Wiener, Tikhonov
text:
The math: the Wiener filter
Model per frequency: G = HF + N with F and N independent, zero mean, powers S_f = E|F|^2 and S_n = E|N|^2. Find the linear estimate \hat F = WG with the smallest expected error:
E|F - WG|^2 = |1 - WH|^2 S_f + |W|^2 S_n .
Setting the derivative with respect to W^* to zero: -(1 - WH)H^* S_f + W S_n = 0, so
W = \frac{H^* S_f}{|H|^2 S_f + S_n} = \frac{H^*}{|H|^2 + S_n/S_f}, \qquad \mathrm{SNR}(f) = S_f/S_n .
The error that remains at each frequency is \dfrac{S_f S_n}{|H|^2 S_f + S_n}: about S_n/|H|^2 where the signal dominates, and S_f (the whole signal is lost) where the noise dominates.

title: Linear deconvolution: inverse, Wiener, Tikhonov
text:
What Wiener needs to know
The filter needs the noise power and the signal power at every frequency.

Noise: the camera noise unit (day 3) showed how to measure it: σn from offset frames or a flat region. White noise has the same power S_n = \sigma_n^2 at every frequency (per pixel).
Signal: not known exactly; it is a model. Natural and microscope images have power falling roughly like 1/f^2: strong at low frequencies, weak at high ones.
So the SNR falls with frequency even where H does not. A flat model (one SNR for all frequencies) is a compromise: the best single value is the SNR at the frequencies that matter, not the image’s overall SNR.

title: Linear deconvolution: inverse, Wiener, Tikhonov
section: Try it: Wiener and the gain curve
text:
Try it: Wiener and the gain curve




Cell phantom, Gaussian σ = 2 px, σn = 1 %. Tour: “0.1% noise: inverse explodes” (RMSE 1.0e6, the red gain curve shoots up past 10⁴). “Truncated inverse: ringing” (beads + edge, Airy NA 1.0, ε = 0.1: RMSE 0.0393; ripples next to the edge and around the beads). “Wiener at the right SNR”: SNR 45 is the best on the sweep, RMSE 0.0244 against 0.0318 for the observed image. Point at the readout: the image’s true SNR (mean truth² / σn²) is 537, far from 45: the best flat SNR is a compromise. “Wiener with the wrong SNR” (2000): fine dots everywhere, RMSE 0.0641, 14 % negative pixels. “1/f² beats flat” on the motion-blurred star: 0.0714 against 0.0817 for the best flat SNR (161). “Motion blur”: the blue curve (cut along x) has deep dips; Wiener sets the gain to almost zero there instead of dividing.

title: Linear deconvolution: inverse, Wiener, Tikhonov
section: Fit the data, but not too wildly: Tikhonov
text:
Fit the data, but not too wildly: Tikhonov
Choose the image x that minimises
\underbrace{\|A x - g\|^2}_{\text{misfit: blur } x\text{, compare with the data}} \;+\; \lambda\,\underbrace{\|D x\|^2}_{\text{penalty}}

Energy penalty (D = identity): prefer small values. Roughness penalty (D = the Laplacian of the filtering unit): prefer smooth images.
λ small: the misfit wins, noise is fitted: noisy. λ large: the penalty wins: blurred.
With the energy penalty Tikhonov is Wiener with a flat spectrum, \lambda = 1/\mathrm{SNR}. With the roughness penalty the damping grows with frequency, like Wiener with a 1/f^2 signal model.
The pattern “data term + λ · penalty” is the general recipe of regularisation (next unit).

title: Linear deconvolution: inverse, Wiener, Tikhonov
text:
The math: Tikhonov
Minimise \|A\mathbf x - \mathbf g\|^2 + \lambda\|D\mathbf x\|^2. The gradient is 2A^\top(A\mathbf x - \mathbf g) + 2\lambda D^\top D\mathbf x; setting it to zero gives the normal equations
(A^\top A + \lambda D^\top D)\,\mathbf x = A^\top \mathbf g .
For a circular blur and a circular D every matrix is diagonal in the Fourier basis (A \to H, A^\top \to H^*, D \to \hat D), so each frequency is solved on its own:
\hat X(f) = \frac{H^*(f)\,G(f)}{|H(f)|^2 + \lambda|\hat D(f)|^2}.

Equal to Wiener when \lambda|\hat D|^2 = S_n/S_f; energy penalty: \hat D = 1, so \lambda = 1/\mathrm{SNR}.
At f = 0 (H(0) = 1): energy penalty gain 1/(1 + \lambda), the mean shrinks. The Laplacian has \hat D(0) = 0 (it kills constants), so the roughness penalty has gain exactly 1 at f = 0: it keeps the mean.

title: Linear deconvolution: inverse, Wiener, Tikhonov
text:
A two-pixel blur by hand
The two-pixel blur of the image formation day: A = \begin{bmatrix} 0.75 & 0.25 \\ 0.25 & 0.75 \end{bmatrix}. It keeps the sum of the pixels (gain 1) and halves their difference (gain 0.5). Data \mathbf g = (1, 0.5): sum part (0.75, 0.75), difference part (0.25, -0.25).
Tikhonov with the energy penalty multiplies each part by s/(s^2 + \lambda) (s = its gain):

title: Linear deconvolution: inverse, Wiener, Tikhonov
section: Three ways to read a restoration
text:
Three ways to read a restoration

Cell phantom, Gaussian blur σ = 2 px, 1 % noise. From the left: truth, observed, inverse filter (noise explodes), truncated inverse ε = 0.15, Wiener SNR 45, Tikhonov with the roughness penalty λ = 0.033.
Gain curve |W(f)|: how much of each frequency the filter keeps or amplifies.
Effective transfer |W H|: what optics + restoration together pass. Wider than the optics alone, never beyond the cut-off.
The image: predict it from the curves. A gain peak at high frequencies means fine dots; a sharp drop means ringing; an early roll-off means blur.


The numbers of the figure (RMSE against the truth, image values 0..1): observed 0.0318, inverse 1.0e7, truncated 0.0250, Wiener 0.0244, Tikhonov roughness 0.0237. Ask the class to predict, from the three curves of the demo, which image belongs to which method before showing the figure.

title: Linear deconvolution: inverse, Wiener, Tikhonov
section: Try it: Tikhonov, wrong PSF, borders
text:
Try it: Tikhonov, wrong PSF, borders




“Too much regularisation”: Tikhonov energy λ = 0.1, RMSE 0.0341, worse than the observed image (0.0318); the mean drops from 0.1575 to 0.1432 (the factor 1/(1 + λ) = 0.909). “Tikhonov = Wiener”: λ = 1/45 gives exactly the RMSE of Wiener SNR 45 (0.0244). “Roughness penalty”: λ = 0.033, RMSE 0.0237, mean kept. “Wrong PSF width” (×1.3, beads, Wiener SNR 85): dark rims around the beads (the darkest pixel near the single bead is −0.028 against a background of 0.05). Move “PSF used” to 0.8: no rims, but the beads stay blurred. “Periodic borders ring”: the scene continues past the border; with periodic borders the RMSE is 1.30 and stripes run across the image from the edge. Switch to “padded + tapered”: 0.0497.

title: Linear deconvolution: inverse, Wiener, Tikhonov
text:
Practicalities: the PSF

The PSF must be right: about 20 % too wide gives over-sharpening, dark rims (halos) and ringing; too narrow leaves blur. Unit 3 treats this fully.
Sampled at least at Nyquist (the image formation day): otherwise the blur is not a convolution of the pixels you have.
Normalised to sum 1, so that the restoration keeps the total intensity.
Measured (beads) or computed; measured PSFs are noisy and need care.

title: Linear deconvolution: inverse, Wiener, Tikhonov
text:
Practicalities: borders
FFT methods treat the image as periodic: the right edge continues at the left.

A bright object at the right edge “leaks” to the left in the model, and a jump in brightness between the left and right edges looks like a sharp edge to restore: ringing stripes from the border inwards.
In the real image the blur came in from outside the field of view, which the periodic model cannot know.
Fix: pad the image (continue its edge values) and taper to the mean towards the middle of the padding, so the periodic copies meet smoothly; restore; crop. This is the “wrap” border rule of the filtering unit, and how to avoid it.

title: Linear deconvolution: inverse, Wiener, Tikhonov
text:
Summary

The inverse filter 1/H is exact without noise and useless with it; beyond the cut-off nothing can be restored.
Truncated inverse: drop frequencies with |H| < \varepsilon; simple, but the sharp cut rings.
Wiener: gain H^*/(|H|^2 + 1/\mathrm{SNR}); inverts where the signal is strong, damps where noise dominates; needs a signal and noise model (1/f^2 is better than flat).
Tikhonov: minimise misfit + λ · penalty; energy penalty = Wiener with a flat spectrum; roughness penalty keeps the mean and damps high frequencies more.
Read a method by its gain curve and its effective transfer; predict the image from them.
Use the right PSF (sum 1, Nyquist), and pad and taper the borders.
