The outlier 200 vanishes; the step 10 → 50 stays sharp. The mean smears both.
But a line thinner than half the window is a minority in every window and disappears; corners are rounded.
crumbs: Denoising and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
section: The math: the median minimises the absolute deviation
text:
The math: the median minimises the absolute deviation
The mean minimises the sum of squared deviations \sum_i (x_i - m)^2; the median minimises the sum of absolute deviations
\operatorname*{arg\,min}_m \sum_i |x_i - m| .

The derivative of \sum_i|x_i - m| with respect to m is (\#\{x_i < m\}) - (\#\{x_i > m\}): zero (changing sign) when as many values lie below m as above it, the median.
An outlier moved from 200 to 2000 changes the squared cost hugely (and pulls the mean), but only adds to one side of the count: the median does not move.
This is the \ell^1 versus \ell^2 difference that also separates total variation from the roughness penalty (last unit).
crumbs: Denoising and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
text:
Bilateral: close and similar
Average the neighbours, but weight each by how close it is (σs, pixels) and how similar its value is (σr, grey levels):
w_{pq} = e^{-\|p - q\|^2/2\sigma_s^2}\; e^{-(I_p - I_q)^2/2\sigma_r^2} .

Across an edge the neighbours on the other side are dissimilar and get almost no weight: the edge stays sharp.
Three pixels 10, 10, 50 around a centre of 10, σr = 10: the 50 gets e^{-40^2/(2 \cdot 10^2)} = e^{-8} = 0.0003 of the weight of a 10.
Fails when the noise ≈ the edge height: noise then looks like edges and is kept, or σr is raised and edges blur. Large σr on a noisy ramp gives flat patches: a cartoon.
crumbs: Denoising and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
text:
Non-local means: similar patches
Average pixels whose whole patch (say 3 × 3 or 5 × 5 around them) looks like the patch around the pixel being denoised, wherever they lie in a search window:

Repetitive structure (a lattice, a texture, many similar cells) finds many good matches: strong averaging without blurring the pattern.
Unique fine detail has no match; with a large h (tolerance), it is averaged with dissimilar patches and fades.
Cost: (search window) × (pixels), with box sums for the patch distances.


Test image (step, ramp crossed by a 1-pixel line, dot lattice, one unique spot), noise σn = 20. From the left: truth, noisy, Gaussian σ = 1.5, median 3 × 3, bilateral (σs 2, σr 30), non-local means (patch 5 × 5, search 11 × 11, h = 20).
crumbs: Denoising and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
section: The math: bilateral and non-local means weights
text:
The math: bilateral and non-local means weights
Both are weighted means \hat I_p = \sum_q w_{pq} I_q \big/ \sum_q w_{pq}, with different weights:

Bilateral: w_{pq} = \exp\!\big(-\|p - q\|^2/2\sigma_s^2\big)\exp\!\big(-(I_p - I_q)^2/2\sigma_r^2\big) over a window of radius about 2\sigma_s.
Non-local means: w_{pq} = \exp\!\big(-d^2(P_p, P_q)/h^2\big), with d^2 the mean squared difference of the patches P_p, P_q, over a search window.
Per-offset computation: for each offset \delta in the search window, the squared differences (I_r - I_{r + \delta})^2 are summed over every patch with an integral image; the cost does not depend on the patch size.
With noise σn, even identical patches differ by d^2 \approx 2\sigma_n^2; so h must be of the order of σn or larger.
crumbs: Denoising and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
text:
Beyond these four

Total variation denoising: the TV penalty of the last unit with H = 1; keeps steps, staircases ramps (the Ising/MRF elective).
Wavelet shrinkage: a sparsity penalty, small coefficients set to zero (the wavelets elective).
Poisson noise depends on the signal: either use a method that knows it (Richardson–Lucy, Poisson data terms), or transform the image so the noise variance becomes constant first (camera noise unit).
Learned restoration: networks trained on noisy/clean pairs, or even on single noisy images, now beat all of these. Trained to “look right”, they can invent structure that was never in the data. The modern deep learning day shows when, with Wiener from this day as the honest baseline.
crumbs: Denoising and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
section: Method noise: what did the filter remove?
text:
Method noise: what did the filter remove?
Method noise = noisy − denoised. If the filter removed only noise, it looks like pure noise: no structure.

An edge, a line or the lattice visible in the method noise = signal the filter removed.
Gaussian σ = 3 on the test image (σn = 10): the method noise has RMS 9.9 in flat regions (≈ σn, fine) but jumps to +72 and −58 at the step: the edge was blurred away.
PSNR against a clean truth needs the truth; the method noise needs only the noisy image. Use it on real data.
crumbs: Denoising and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
text:
Try it: denoisers




PSNR (peak 255) noisy → denoised. “Gaussian blurs the step” (σn 20, σ 2): 22.1 → 21.6 dB, worse than doing nothing, because the lattice is wiped out; the best Gaussian σ is only 0.6 (25.8 dB). “Salt and pepper” (10 % of the pixels 0 or 255): median 3 × 3 15.3 → 22.7 dB, Gaussian σ 1: 21.9 dB, with grey smudges. “Median eats the thin line” (5 × 5, σn 5): the line pixel at (96, 32) drops from 211 to 133; PSNR falls from 34.1 to 21.6 dB. “Bilateral keeps edges” (σn 15, σs 2, σr 30): 33.7 dB, Gaussian σ 2: 21.7 dB. “Cartoon” (σn 50, σr 100): flat patches on the ramp. “Non-local means on texture” (σn 25, patch 3 × 3, search 15 × 15, h 25): 29.5 dB overall, 26.7 dB on the lattice quarter against 23.2 for bilateral. “Smears the unique spot” (patch 5 × 5, h 45): the spot falls from 220 to 129. “Method noise shows the removed edge”. “Best PSNR, wrong look” (micrograph crop, σn 25): Wiener SNR 3 23.4 dB, bilateral (1.5, 50) 23.3 dB: the PSNR prefers the blurred Wiener result by a hair.
crumbs: Denoising and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
section: A restored image is an estimate
text:
A restored image is an estimate

It depends on the PSF, the method, λ or the stopping point. Change any of them and the image changes.
It improves contrast and separation, but cannot recover what lies beyond the cut-off (image formation day: invisible objects stay invisible).
Its noise is no longer independent between pixels, and no longer Poisson: the camera noise unit’s rules for error bars do not apply to it.
So: what happens to the numbers we measure on it?
crumbs: Denoising and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
text:
What happens to measurements








measurement
after restoration
why




total intensity over a region larger than the PSF
kept (RL exactly; roughness-penalised Tikhonov exactly; Wiener and energy-penalised Tikhonov slightly shrink it)
flux is the f = 0 coefficient


peak intensity
rises, non-linearly, and depends on the iterations
light is moved into the centre


size (FWHM) near the resolution limit
shrinks with iterations to a floor set by the method, not by the object
restoration stops at the noise


separation of close objects
biased, most when the dip between them is weak



counts of objects
speckles and split objects add, ringing adds rims




In the demo (spots of flux 1 : 4, 3000 photons): RL after 100 iterations gives an integrated ratio of 4.00 but a peak ratio of 6.20; the raw image gives 3.86 and 4.13.
crumbs: Denoising and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
text:
The math: flux preservation
RL: \sum_j x_j^{\text{new}} = \sum_j x_j\sum_i A_{ij}\frac{y_i}{(A\mathbf x)_i} = \sum_i \frac{y_i}{(A\mathbf x)_i}\sum_j A_{ij}x_j = \sum_i y_i, every iteration (no background).
Linear filters: the total intensity is the f = 0 Fourier coefficient, \hat X(0) = \sum_j x_j, and the filter multiplies it by its gain at f = 0 (with H(0) = 1):

Wiener: \dfrac{1}{1 + 1/\mathrm{SNR}(0)}, slightly below 1;
Tikhonov, energy penalty: \dfrac{1}{1 + \lambda};
Tikhonov, roughness penalty: 1 exactly (\hat D(0) = 0).

Over a region rather than the whole image, flux is kept only approximately: light moves across the region’s boundary by about the PSF’s width, so the region must be larger than the PSF.
crumbs: Denoising and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
section: Try it: what may be measured
text:
Try it: what may be measured




A field with known truth, Airy PSF NA 1.0 (Rayleigh distance 4.88 px): top row, bead pairs at 0.8, 1.0, 1.2 and 1.5 × Rayleigh; middle, spots of flux 1 : 2 : 4; bottom, disks. The table compares raw, restored and truth; green within 10 %, yellow within 30 %, red worse. Tour (RL): “integrals hold” (3000 photons, k = 100): integrated ratio 4.00, peak ratio 6.20. “Peaks lie” (k = 316): peak ratio 6.53, integral 3.97. “Sizes shrink to a floor” (k = 1000): FWHM 1.93 px (raw 4.51, truth 1.45): it stops shrinking around 1.9 whatever the object. “Close pairs” (1000 photons, k = 100): the 1.2 × Rayleigh pair is 4.95 px apart in the raw image (truth 5.92), 5.85 after RL. “Extra spots” (1000 photons, k = 1000): 259 local maxima above the threshold instead of 11. “Wiener” (SNR 300): integral 4.27, peak 3.66, FWHM 3.53.
crumbs: Denoising and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
section: What to do, and what to report
text:
What to do, and what to report

Segment or detect on the restored image if it helps (better contrast, separated objects).
Measure intensities on the raw image (offset- and flat-field-corrected), inside the masks found.
Validate any measurement made on restored data with a known-truth test: beads, a phantom, the same microscope and noise.
Report the method, the PSF (measured or computed), λ or the number of iterations; show the raw data next to the result.
Never compare images restored with different settings, and keep the raw data.
Error bars and statistics of measurements: the evaluation day.
crumbs: Denoising and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
text:
Summary

With H = 1, Wiener and Tikhonov are low-pass denoisers. Gaussian blurs edges; median removes outliers, keeps steps, eats thin lines; bilateral keeps edges, cartoons at high noise; non-local means loves repetition, smears unique detail.
Method noise (noisy − denoised) should look like pure noise; structure in it is removed signal.
Learned restoration is better and can invent structure (modern deep learning day).
A restored image is an estimate: total intensity over a region larger than the PSF is kept; peaks, sizes, separations and counts change with the method and the stopping point.
Detect on the restored image, measure on the raw, validate with known truth, report everything.
crumbs: Denoising and what you may measure

title: Exercise: finding objects as boxes
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute the IoU of two boxes, and say how sensitive it is for small objects,
run greedy non-maximum suppression by hand and predict the effect of its threshold,
decide whether an object can be learned by a given set of anchors,
find the peaks of a centre heat map, and explain the failures of each approach in crowded images.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: finding objects as boxes
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute the IoU of two boxes, and say how sensitive it is for small objects,
run greedy non-maximum suppression by hand and predict the effect of its threshold,
decide whether an object can be learned by a given set of anchors,
find the peaks of a centre heat map, and explain the failures of each approach in crowded images.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: finding objects as boxes
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Box
[x_0, x_1] \times [y_0, y_1], a score, a class


IoU
intersection area / union area; for boxes the intersection is a box


Anchor
a template box at a grid position; it learns objects it overlaps with IoU \ge 0.5


Centre heat map
a bump at every object centre; objects = local maxima above a threshold


Greedy NMS
keep the best box, delete all boxes with IoU > t with it, repeat


Scoring
the evaluation day: matching at IoU \ge 0.5, TP/FP/FN, F1, matching accuracy, AP






NMS on touching elongated cells with t = 0.2: kept boxes in green with their scores, deleted boxes grey dashed, true boxes blue dashed. Four cells have no box left.

title: Exercise: finding objects as boxes
text:
By hand
B1. IoU of boxes. (a) A = [0, 4] \times [0, 4] and B = [2, 6] \times [2, 6]. (b) A and the same box shifted by one pixel to the right; and shifted by one pixel right and one down. (c) Two 2 \times 2 boxes shifted by one pixel. What does (b)–(c) tell you about IoU thresholds for small objects?
B2. Greedy NMS. Five candidate boxes with scores:



box
[x_0, x_1] \times [y_0, y_1]
score




b_1
[0, 10] \times [0, 10]
0.9


b_2
[1, 11] \times [0, 10]
0.8


b_3
[8, 18] \times [0, 10]
0.7


b_4
[9, 19] \times [1, 11]
0.6


b_5
[20, 26] \times [20, 26]
0.3



The true cells lie under b_1 and under b_3; b_5 is a false detection. (a) Compute the IoUs b_1b_2, b_1b_3, b_1b_4, b_2b_3, b_3b_4. (b) Run greedy NMS with t = 0.3 and with t = 0.7. Which boxes are kept? Count TP, FP and FN at IoU \ge 0.5 for both. (c) Run it with t = 0.1. What goes wrong? Which box represents the second cell now, and is it a good one? (d) Would a score threshold of 0.5 change any of the results?
B3. Anchors. (a) A 10 \times 10 anchor and a 4 \times 4 cell with the same centre: compute the IoU. Is the cell learned by this anchor at the matching threshold 0.5? (b) For which side lengths s does a square anchor with the same centre match the 4 \times 4 cell? (c) A thin rod 40 \times 4 (axis-aligned) and a 20 \times 20 anchor, same centre: IoU? A 2{:}1 anchor of the same area (28.3 \times 14.1)? What kind of anchor would match the rod?
B4. A 5 \times 5 centre heat map:
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 5 & 2 & 0 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 & 2 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}

Find the local maxima in a 3 \times 3 window (pixels outside the image are ignored).
Which of them remain with a threshold of 3.5? With a 5 \times 5 window and no threshold?
Which choice would you make if the objects are about 4 pixels apart? If the map is noisy?

B5. A colony of rod-shaped bacteria lying side by side, all tilted by 45°. (a) Why do the boxes of neighbouring bacteria overlap a lot, and how much of each box is background? (b) Explain why no NMS threshold both removes duplicates and keeps all bacteria. (c) Which instance route of the previous unit would you use instead?






Solutions





B1. (a) Intersection [2, 4]^2: 4; union 16 + 16 - 4 = 28; IoU = 0.143. (b) Right by one: intersection 3 \times 4 = 12, union 20, IoU 0.6. Right and down: 3 \times 3 = 9, union 23, IoU 0.39. (c) Intersection 1 \times 2 = 2, union 6, IoU 0.33. A shift of one pixel already fails the matching threshold 0.5 for a 2 \times 2 object, while a 40 \times 40 object hardly notices it. For small objects (spots, small cells) IoU thresholds are too strict; a distance between centres is a better matching rule.
B2. (a) b_1b_2: 9 \times 10 = 90, union 110, 0.818. b_1b_3: 2 \times 10 = 20, union 180, 0.111. b_1b_4: 1 \times 9 = 9, union 191, 0.047. b_2b_3: 3 \times 10 = 30, union 170, 0.176. b_3b_4: 9 \times 9 = 81, union 119, 0.681. (b) t = 0.3: keep b_1, delete b_2 (0.818); keep b_3 (0.111 with b_1), delete b_4 (0.681); keep b_5. Kept b_1, b_3, b_5: TP 2, FP 1 (b_5), FN 0. t = 0.7: keep b_1, delete b_2; keep b_3; b_4 survives (0.681 < 0.7); keep b_5. Kept b_1, b_3, b_4, b_5: TP 2, FP 2 (b_4 is a duplicate: it cannot be matched a second time), FN 0. (c) t = 0.1: keep b_1, delete b_2 and b_3 (0.111 > 0.1); b_4 survives (0.047 with b_1); keep b_5. The second cell is represented by b_4, a shifted duplicate; its IoU with the true cell (the box of b_3) is 0.68, so here it still counts as a TP, but the best box of the cell was deleted because it touched the first cell. (d) It removes b_5 before NMS: one FP fewer in every case; the duplicates and the lost box are unchanged.
B3. (a) Intersection 16, union 100, IoU 0.16: not matched; the cell is never learned by this anchor. (b) s \ge 4: IoU = 16/s^2 \ge 0.5 gives s \le 5.66. s \le 4: IoU = s^2/16 \ge 0.5 gives s \ge 2.83. So 2.83 \le s \le 5.66. (c) Square: intersection 20 \times 4 = 80, union 400 + 160 - 80 = 480, IoU 0.17. 2{:}1: intersection 28.3 \times 4 = 113, union 400 + 160 - 113 = 447, IoU 0.25. Neither matches; it would need an elongated anchor of about 40 \times 4 (aspect ratio 10:1) in the right orientation; a rod at 45° has a large square box (B5).
B4. (a) Four maxima: 5 (row 2, column 2), 3 (row 2, column 5), 4 (row 4, column 4), 3 (row 5, column 1). (b) Threshold 3.5: the 5 and the 4. 5 \times 5 window: the 5 and the 3 in the bottom-left corner (the 4 and the 3 at the right edge have the 5 or the 4 in their larger window). (c) Objects about 4 pixels apart: a 3 \times 3 window (a 5 \times 5 window would suppress true neighbours). Noisy map: a threshold and a larger window, accepting that close objects merge.
B5. (a) A rod at 45° fills only a small part of its box (two triangles of background), and the boxes of rods lying side by side overlap almost entirely even though the rods themselves do not touch much. (b) Duplicate boxes of one rod overlap by, say, 0.6–0.9; boxes of neighbouring rods overlap by a similar amount. Any t that deletes the duplicates also deletes the neighbours, and any t that keeps the neighbours keeps duplicates. (c) Flows (long, touching, possibly bent cells) or, for straight rods, a distance map; the evaluation then uses masks, not boxes.




Math questions
B6. (math) Derive the closed form of the IoU of two axis-aligned boxes and show that it is invariant to scaling both boxes by the same factor and to translating both.
B7. (math) Consider L = 1 - \mathrm{IoU}(A, B) as a function of the position of box B. Show that its gradient is zero whenever the boxes do not overlap. What does that mean for training with this loss alone?
B8. (math) Box widths are predicted as t_w = \log(w/w_a) relative to an anchor of width w_a. Show that predicting 2w and w/2 give the same squared error in t_w, and that a small error \delta in t_w is a relative error of about \delta in w. Why would w - w_a be a worse target?
B9. (math) Show that greedy NMS gives the same result if all scores are replaced by g(\text{score}) for any strictly increasing g, and that its cost is O(n^2) IoU evaluations for n candidates.






Solutions (math)





B6. The intersection of [a_0, a_1] \times [b_0, b_1] and [c_0, c_1] \times [d_0, d_1] is [\max(a_0, c_0), \min(a_1, c_1)] \times [\max(b_0, d_0), \min(b_1, d_1)] when both intervals are non-empty; its area is wh with w = \max(0, \min(a_1, c_1) - \max(a_0, c_0)) and h likewise. Union = |A| + |B| - wh (inclusion–exclusion). Translating both boxes adds the same constant to all coordinates: w, h and the areas are unchanged. Scaling all coordinates by s > 0 multiplies w and h by s, every area by s^2; the ratio is unchanged.
B7. If the boxes do not overlap, then w = 0 or h = 0, and this remains so for every small shift of B (the max with 0 is in its flat part), so the intersection is 0 in a neighbourhood and L = 1 there: the gradient is zero. A network trained with this loss alone gets no signal from boxes that miss the object, however close or far they are; hence regression losses on the coordinates (or IoU variants with a distance term).
B8. \log(2w/w_a) - \log(w/w_a) = \log 2 and \log((w/2)/w_a) - \log(w/w_a) = -\log 2: the same squared error (\log 2)^2. w = w_a e^{t_w}, so w(t_w + \delta) = w e^{\delta} \approx w(1 + \delta): relative error \delta. With w - w_a the same error of 5 pixels would be negligible for a large object and huge for a small one, the target range would depend on the object size, and nothing would keep the predicted width positive.
B9. NMS only uses the order of the scores (which box is “the best remaining”), and a strictly increasing g keeps the order (ties included). Each round keeps one box and compares it with the remaining ones: at most n - 1 + n - 2 + \dots = O(n^2) IoUs (fewer when many boxes are deleted early).

title: Exercise: finding objects as boxes
text:
Explore
The demo has four modes on a 128 \times 128 synthetic cell image. IoU: two boxes on a grid; drag a box to move it, its white corner to resize it. NMS: the candidate boxes of a simulated detector (5 jittered boxes per cell, scored by their overlap with the cell, plus 3 false boxes); step runs one round of greedy NMS (green: kept; grey dashed: removed, with its IoU; yellow: not yet decided), run all rounds; click a box and change its score with score ±. The readout uses the evaluation day’s matching at IoU \ge 0.5. Anchors: one anchor per grid cell (or three shapes); each object shows its best anchor and that IoU, in red if below 0.5. Heat map: a simulated centre heat map, its local maxima and their boxes.



E1. Preset IoU of two boxes. Check B1: drag B to reproduce (a), (b) and the shift by one pixel right and down. Where must B be for IoU = 1/7?
E2. Preset duplicates removed (sparse image, t = 0.5). How many candidates and how many boxes after NMS? Use step: how many duplicates does the first kept box remove? Compare F1 and matching accuracy with AP. Which number is hurt by the 3 false boxes, and how can the score threshold fix it?
E3. Still on the sparse image, set t to 0.3, 0.7 and 0.9. Write down the number of boxes and F1 each time. Why does AP hardly change?
E4. Preset touching cells: NMS deletes the neighbour (t = 0.2, true boxes shown). How many cells have no box after NMS? Step through the first round: what is deleted? Find the t with the best F1.
E5. Preset threshold too high: duplicates survive (t = 0.75). Number of boxes, FP, F1, AP? Explain why AP is high although F1 is low.
E6. Preset diagonal rod: a box is a poor shape. What fraction of the rod’s box is rod? What would a second box-based step (e.g. measuring the intensity inside the box) measure?
E7. Preset small cell: no anchor matches (stride 16, anchor size 20, one shape). Which objects can be learned? Try three shapes, then stride 8, then anchor size 8. Can one anchor setting match all five objects?
E8. Presets heat-map peaks = objects and noisy heat map: two peaks in one cell. Count peaks, TP, FP, FN. Then set the window to 7 \times 7 and compare. What is the price of the larger window?






Solutions





E1. A = [0, 4]^2, B = [2, 6]^2: intersection 4, union 28, IoU 0.143 (= 1/7). One right: 0.600; one right and one down: 0.391. IoU = 1/7 needs intersection 4 with two 4 \times 4 boxes, e.g. B at [2, 6]^2 (a 2 \times 2 overlap) or [0, 4] \times [3, 7] (4 \times 1).
E2. 48 candidates, 12 boxes after NMS (all 12 rounds). The first kept box removes 4 duplicates. TP 9, FP 3, FN 0: F1 0.86, matching accuracy 0.75; AP 1.00 (0.97 without NMS). The three false boxes have low scores: they come last in the ranking, so AP (which only asks whether the good boxes rank first) is not hurt, but F1 counts them. Setting the score threshold to 0.6 removes them: 10 boxes, F1 0.95.
E3. t = 0.3: 10 boxes, F1 0.95. t = 0.7: 34 boxes, F1 0.42. t = 0.9: 46 boxes, F1 0.33. The duplicates that survive have lower scores than the box kept for the same cell; in the ranking they come after all true detections, so AP stays 1.00 (0.97 at t = 0.9), while F1, which counts every box above the threshold, collapses.
E4. 10 boxes for 12 cells; 4 cells have no box (TP 8, FP 2, FN 4, F1 0.73). The first kept box deletes 9 boxes: its own duplicates and the boxes of its neighbours, whose IoU with it is about 0.3. F1 by t: 0.1: 0.76; 0.2: 0.73; 0.3: 0.75; 0.4: 0.89 (15 boxes, all 12 cells found, 3 FP); 0.5: 0.83; 0.75: 0.41.
E5. 46 boxes, TP 12, FP 34, F1 0.41, AP 0.98. Every cell’s best box is found (high scores first), and the 34 duplicates are ranked below them, so the precision–recall curve reaches recall 1 before the duplicates appear. AP measures ranking; F1 at a fixed operating point measures what a user would actually get.
E6. The rod fills 16 % of its box. A measurement inside the box (mean intensity, texture) would be dominated by background. A box says where an object is, not which pixels belong to it.
E7. One shape: only the large lower-right cell (IoU 0.67) is matched; the rod (0.17), the small cell (0.10) and the two other cells (0.39, 0.28) are not, because their centres fall between anchor centres or their size differs. Three shapes: still 1 of 5 (the elongated anchors fit no object here). Stride 8: 3 of 5 (0.76, 0.57, 0.67 for the three ordinary cells; rod and small cell still fail). Anchor size 8 with stride 8: only the small cell (0.64). No single setting matches all five: one needs several sizes, finer strides and elongated anchors in the right orientation.
E8. Heat-map peaks (crowded palisades, bump width 3, no noise): 12 peaks for 12 cells, TP 12, F1 1.00. Noisy heat map (sparse image, bump width 5, noise 0.2, 3 \times 3 window): 14 peaks for 9 cells, TP 9, FP 5, F1 0.78: some cells have two peaks. With a 7 \times 7 window: 10 peaks, FP 1, F1 0.95. The price: two true objects closer than about 3 pixels from each other’s centre window would also be merged into one peak.

title: Exercise: finding objects as boxes
text:
Where this leads
Boxes and heat maps are the outputs of detection networks; the next unit asks how a network can relate a pixel to the whole image (attention and transformers) and where networks come from that nobody trained on your images (pretraining). The scoring of detections is the evaluation day’s.

title: Quiz: finding objects as boxes
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Two 8 \times 8 boxes overlap in a 4 \times 8 strip. What is their IoU?






Hint





Union = area A + area B − intersection.









Answer





Intersection 32, union 64 + 64 - 32 = 96, IoU = 1/3.




Q2. Why does a detector produce several boxes for one object?






Hint





How many positions and anchors look at the same object?









Answer





Every grid position and anchor near the object, or every pixel near a heat-map peak, sees the object and proposes a box for it. Neighbouring positions give similar, overlapping boxes: duplicates that must be removed.




Q3. In greedy NMS with threshold t, what happens if t is too low? Too high?






Hint





t is the overlap above which a box is deleted.









Answer





Too low: boxes of true neighbouring objects overlap the kept box by more than t and are deleted (missed objects). Too high: duplicates of the same object overlap by less than t and survive (false positives).




Q4. A small spot of 3 \times 3 pixels is detected with a box shifted by one pixel. Is it a TP at IoU \ge 0.5?






Hint





Intersection 2 \times 3.









Answer





Intersection 6, union 9 + 9 - 6 = 12, IoU 0.5: just at the threshold. Shifted in both directions: 4/14 = 0.29, a miss. IoU thresholds are very strict for small objects.




Q5. Why can an object that matches no anchor never be detected by an anchor-based network?






Hint





Which anchors get the label “object” during training?









Answer





During training only anchors with IoU \ge 0.5 (or the best one) with an object are told “object” and learn its box correction. If no anchor overlaps the object enough, it is labelled background everywhere, and the network learns to ignore it.




Q6. How does a centre heat map find objects, and which earlier method uses the same step?






Hint





Peaks in a map.









Answer





Objects are the local maxima of the predicted map above a threshold (a pixel larger than all others in its window). The same peak picking finds lines and circles in the Hough accumulator.




Q7. AP is high but F1 is low. What does that tell you about the detections?






Hint





AP depends on the ranking, F1 on the boxes above a threshold.









Answer





The true detections have the highest scores (good ranking), but many low-scored false boxes (e.g. surviving duplicates) are kept at the chosen operating point. A higher score threshold or a lower NMS threshold would raise F1.




Q8. (math) Show that 1 - \mathrm{IoU} gives no gradient for two boxes that do not overlap.






Hint





What is the intersection for small shifts?









Answer





If the boxes do not overlap, the intersection is 0 and stays 0 for any small shift, so \mathrm{IoU} = 0 and 1 - \mathrm{IoU} = 1 in a whole neighbourhood: the derivative is zero.




Q9. Name the three meanings of “non-maximum suppression” in this course.






Hint





Edges, accumulators, boxes.









Answer





Canny (keep gradient values that are maximal across the edge), peak picking (keep local maxima of a Hough accumulator or heat map), and box NMS (delete boxes that overlap a better box by more than t).

title: Diffusion models and generated detail
text:
About this lecture
If a network can remove noise, can it make images from nothing? And if it restores my image, which details are real?

Forward: add a little noise, again and again, until only noise is left (the noise schedule).
Denoising is the core operation; sampling = repeated denoising, starting from pure noise.
Conditioning on a label or a measurement; guidance.
Restoration with a generative prior: the posterior mean is blurry but honest, a posterior sample is sharp and may be invented. What may still be measured.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Recalls the VAE day (latent variables, a decoder that outputs a mean gives blur, sampling new images), the cameranoise unit (noise, PSNR), and the deconvolution day (Wiener as the cautious classical restoration). Both demos are exact: the data are Gaussian mixtures, so the best denoiser and the exact posterior are known in closed form (diffusion2d also has small learned denoisers, trained offline; genrestore has none).

title: Diffusion models and generated detail
text:
Recall: generating with a VAE
From the VAE day: a generative model draws new images that look like the training images: samples from the distribution of the data, a cloud of points in a space with one axis per pixel.

The VAE: sample a latent code, decode it. Its decoder outputs a mean, so samples are blurry where the model is uncertain.
A diffusion model reaches the same goal by a different route: no encoder, no latent bottleneck; a single network that removes noise, applied many times.

title: Diffusion models and generated detail
section: The forward process: drowning the data in noise
text:
The forward process: drowning the data in noise
Take a training image, add a little Gaussian noise and shrink the signal a little; repeat many times. After enough steps nothing is left but noise.

The noise schedule says how fast: how much signal \sqrt{\bar\alpha} and how much noise \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha} remain at each time \tau from 0 (data) to 1 (noise).
In 2D: a cloud of points melts into one round Gaussian blob.
One step by hand: x_0 = 2, \sqrt{\bar\alpha} = 0.8, \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha} = 0.6, noise \varepsilon = -1: x_\tau = 0.8 \cdot 2 + 0.6 \cdot (-1) = 1.0.

title: Diffusion models and generated detail
text:
The math: the forward process
One step: \mathbf x_t = \sqrt{1 - \beta_t}\,\mathbf x_{t-1} + \sqrt{\beta_t}\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t. With \bar\alpha_t = \prod_{s \le t}(1 - \beta_s), the steps combine into one:
\mathbf x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,\mathbf x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon, \qquad \boldsymbol\varepsilon \sim \mathcal N(0, I),
so \mathbf x_t \mid \mathbf x_0 \sim \mathcal N(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\mathbf x_0, (1 - \bar\alpha_t)I) (sums of independent Gaussians are Gaussian; variances add). As \bar\alpha_t \to 0, \mathbf x_t \to \mathcal N(0, I) whatever \mathbf x_0 was. Signal-to-noise ratio \bar\alpha_t/(1 - \bar\alpha_t).
Schedules: linear (\beta rising linearly; in continuous time \bar\alpha = e^{-(0.1\tau + 9.95\tau^2)}) and cosine (\bar\alpha = \cos^2(\frac{\tau + s}{1 + s}\frac\pi2)/\cos^2(\frac{s}{1+s}\frac\pi2), s = 0.008), which removes the signal more evenly.

title: Diffusion models and generated detail
text:
Denoising is the core operation
Train a network that takes a noisy image and the noise level, and predicts the noise (equivalently the clean image).

Ordinary supervised learning with free labels: we added the noise ourselves, so we know it.
At high noise the best possible denoiser does not output a clean image: it outputs the average of all clean images compatible with the noisy one.
Data at \pm 1 (equally likely), x_\tau = 0.6\,x_0 + 0.8\,\varepsilon, observed x_\tau = 0.5: the best guess of x_0 is \tanh(0.6 \cdot 0.5/0.64) = 0.44: neither +1 nor -1, but a compromise leaning towards +1.

title: Diffusion models and generated detail
section: The math: the best denoiser is the score
text:
The math: the best denoiser is the score
Minimising \mathbb E\|\boldsymbol\varepsilon - \boldsymbol\varepsilon_\theta(\mathbf x_t, t)\|^2 over all functions gives the conditional mean \boldsymbol\varepsilon^\star = \mathbb E[\boldsymbol\varepsilon \mid \mathbf x_t], equivalently \hat{\mathbf x}_0 = \mathbb E[\mathbf x_0 \mid \mathbf x_t].
Tweedie’s formula: with p_t the density of \mathbf x_t,
\mathbb E[\mathbf x_0 \mid \mathbf x_t] = \frac{\mathbf x_t + (1 - \bar\alpha_t)\nabla\log p_t(\mathbf x_t)}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}}, \qquad \boldsymbol\varepsilon^\star = -\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\,\nabla\log p_t(\mathbf x_t).
A denoiser is an estimator of the score \nabla\log p_t: the direction in which the noisy data become more likely.
Mixture data (the demos): if \mathbf x_0 \sim \sum_k\pi_k\mathcal N(\boldsymbol\mu_k, \Sigma_k), then \mathbf x_t \sim \sum_k\pi_k\mathcal N(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\boldsymbol\mu_k, \bar\alpha_t\Sigma_k + (1 - \bar\alpha_t)I) and the score is \sum_k r_k(\mathbf x_t)\,C_k^{-1}(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\boldsymbol\mu_k - \mathbf x_t) with responsibilities r_k (“which component did this point come from”, as a probability). For \pm 1 data this gives the \tanh.

title: Diffusion models and generated detail
text:
Sampling = repeated denoising
Start from pure noise. At each step: estimate the clean image, move a little towards it, and (in the stochastic version) add back a bit less noise than before. After many steps a sample emerges.

The arrows (where the denoiser pushes) form a field that points towards the data at every noise level, coarse at high noise, fine at low noise.
Few steps: the samples land on the averages: between the blobs, off the data. Many steps: sharp samples on the data.
Deterministic sampling (no added noise) follows smooth paths; stochastic sampling jitters.

title: Diffusion models and generated detail
text:
The math: one sampling step
From \mathbf x_i at \bar\alpha_i to \bar\alpha_{i-1} > \bar\alpha_i, with \hat{\boldsymbol\varepsilon} = \boldsymbol\varepsilon_\theta(\mathbf x_i) and \hat{\mathbf x}_0 = (\mathbf x_i - \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_i}\,\hat{\boldsymbol\varepsilon})/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}:

Deterministic (DDIM): \mathbf x_{i-1} = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{i-1}}\,\hat{\mathbf x}_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_{i-1}}\,\hat{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}: keep the same noise direction, at the smaller noise level.
Stochastic (DDPM): sample the Gaussian q(\mathbf x_{i-1} \mid \mathbf x_i, \hat{\mathbf x}_0) with \alpha_i = \bar\alpha_i/\bar\alpha_{i-1}, \beta_i = 1 - \alpha_i: \text{mean } \frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{i-1}}\,\beta_i}{1 - \bar\alpha_i}\hat{\mathbf x}_0 + \frac{\sqrt{\alpha_i}\,(1 - \bar\alpha_{i-1})}{1 - \bar\alpha_i}\mathbf x_i, \qquad \text{variance } \frac{\beta_i(1 - \bar\alpha_{i-1})}{1 - \bar\alpha_i}.
With one step from pure noise both return \hat{\mathbf x}_0 = \mathbb E[\mathbf x_0]: the mean of the data.

title: Diffusion models and generated detail
section: Try it: noise in, data out
text:
Try it: noise in, data out




The data are Gaussian mixtures, so the exact score is known. Tour: “forward”: two moons, slide τ: at 0.4 the signal is 0.805, the noise 0.594. “noise in, data out”: 500 points, 100 stochastic steps: 48 % / 52 % on the two moons, 0 % off the data. Step through and watch the arrows: coarse at the start, fine at the end. “too few steps”: two blobs, 2 deterministic steps: the samples line up between the blobs, 38 % off the data. “learned score”: the rare blob (5 % of the data) gets 1 % of the samples with the briefly trained network. “perfect score of 20 points”: every sample lands on a training point (100 % within 0.05). “conditioning on one blob” and “strong guidance”: with w = 4 on “upper half” the samples crowd into the two upper blobs farthest from the lower half (55 195 195 55 instead of 135 123 124 118).

title: Diffusion models and generated detail
text:
Memorising or generalising?

The perfect denoiser of a finite training set knows only those images: its samples are copies of training images (the demo’s “20 points”: every sample within 0.05 of a training point).
Real networks are imperfect in a useful way: they smooth between training images and generate new ones. Small or under-trained networks also drop rare modes: a rare cell type in the training set may never be generated (the demo’s rare blob: 5 % of the data, 1 % of the samples).
Good to know when someone claims a generated image is “new” or “representative”.

title: Diffusion models and generated detail
text:
Conditioning and guidance

Give the denoiser extra input: a label (“dividing cell”), a text, or a measurement (a blurred image). Sampling then draws from the images that fit the condition.
Guidance: push harder towards the condition, w > 0. Samples become more typical of the condition and less diverse: they avoid anything that might also fit another condition.

title: Diffusion models and generated detail
text:
The math: conditioning by Bayes

abla\log p(\mathbf x \mid y) = 
abla\log p(\mathbf x) + 
abla\log p(y \mid \mathbf x)
(the normaliser p(y) does not depend on \mathbf x). A conditional score = unconditional score + the score of the measurement. For a linear measurement \mathbf y = A\mathbf x + \mathbf n, \mathbf n \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma_n^2 I): 
abla\log p(\mathbf y \mid \mathbf x) = A^	op(\mathbf y - A\mathbf x)/\sigma_n^2.
Guidance with weight w: 
abla\log p(\mathbf x) + (1 + w)
abla\log p(y \mid \mathbf x) = (1 + w)
abla\log p(\mathbf x \mid y) - w
abla\log p(\mathbf x), the score of p(\mathbf x)\,p(y \mid \mathbf x)^{1 + w}: points where the condition is most certain are favoured.

title: Diffusion models and generated detail
text:
Restoration with a generative prior
A degraded measurement (blurred, noisy, with holes) is compatible with many clean images.

Classical (Wiener or Tikhonov, the deconvolution day): assumes “smooth”; returns a blurry but cautious answer.
Generative prior: picks images that look like the training images: sharp, plausible, and possibly invented.
The posterior mean (average of all plausible restorations): blurry where uncertain, the lowest error on average.
A posterior sample (one plausible restoration): sharp everywhere; where the data are weak, its detail comes from the prior, not from the sample. Two samples disagree exactly there.

title: Diffusion models and generated detail
text:
The math: mean against sample
Scalar Gaussian prior x \sim \mathcal N(\mu, s^2), measurement y = x + n, n \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2). The posterior is Gaussian:
x \mid y \sim \mathcal N\Big(\mu + \frac{s^2}{s^2 + \sigma^2}(y - \mu),\ v\Big), \qquad v = \frac{s^2\sigma^2}{s^2 + \sigma^2}.

Mean: \mathbb E[(\hat x_{\text{mean}} - x)^2 \mid y] = v (the smallest possible).
Sample \tilde x drawn independently from the same posterior: \mathbb E[(\tilde x - x)^2 \mid y] = \mathrm{Var}(\tilde x - x) = v + v = 2v: twice the error of the mean, although it “looks like” real data (the perception–distortion trade-off).
Mixture prior (one narrow Gaussian per training image, the genrestore demo): the posterior is a mixture again, with weights \propto \pi_k\,\mathcal N(\mathbf y; A\boldsymbol\mu_k, A\Sigma_kA^\top + \sigma^2I) (“how well training image k explains the measurement”). With a blur that is diagonal in a cosine basis, everything is computed coefficient by coefficient.

title: Diffusion models and generated detail
section: Try it: which details are real?
text:
Try it: which details are real?




32 × 32 synthetic cells; prior = narrow Gaussians around 300 training cells, so the posterior is exact. Tour: “mild blur”: everything agrees; mean, samples and classical all count 2 nucleoli. “heavy blur” (σ 3.5, noise 0.08): the truth has 2 nucleoli; the samples show 1 or 2 (10 and 22 of 32), each sharp; the mean shows a smooth nucleus (0 nucleoli by the threshold) and has the best PSNR (30.5 dB, against 25.1 classical and 24.9 for the first sample). The disagreement map lights up inside the nucleus. “prior without dividing cells”: the dividing cell is restored as a single nucleus with a protrusion (the posterior trusts one protrusion cell 100 %). “unusual nucleus: made normal”: a ring-shaped nucleus comes out as a normal filled nucleus in mean and samples; the classical restoration keeps the ring. “three nucleoli”: all samples show 2. “inpainting”: a hole over the nucleus: samples show 0, 1 or 2 nucleoli (16, 11, 5).

title: Diffusion models and generated detail
text:
Hallucination in scientific images
A generative restoration can add a nucleolus, a protrusion, a membrane, a dividing cell that was not there, or remove a real one that the prior did not expect: an unusual phenotype is “corrected” towards normal. The last case is the most dangerous in biology and medicine: the interesting cell looks ordinary.

Higher PSNR (the cameranoise unit) does not mean the details are real: the posterior mean has the best PSNR and shows the fewest details.
A disagreement map (several samples, or several models) shows where the details come from the prior.

title: Diffusion models and generated detail
text:
What may be measured afterwards

Measure on the raw data, or on a restoration whose effect on that measurement was validated with ground truth.
Never count or measure structures smaller than the measurement can resolve on a generatively restored image.
Look at the disagreement between samples or models; do not trust details where they disagree.
Never train the prior on the condition you want to discover (and never without it).
Report the restoration method and show the raw data next to it.

Restoration for display or as a segmentation aid is different from restoration as data.

title: Diffusion models and generated detail
text:
Summary

Forward: \mathbf x_\tau = \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\,\mathbf x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha}\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon; the schedule says how fast the signal goes.
A network trained to denoise (free labels) estimates the average clean image, i.e. the score; sampling repeats denoising from pure noise; too few steps give averages.
A perfect denoiser of a finite set copies it; real ones generalise, and may drop rare modes.
Conditioning adds the measurement’s score; guidance trades diversity for typicality.
With a generative prior: the mean is blurry and honest, a sample sharp and possibly invented (twice the error). Measure on raw or validated data; check disagreement.

text:

title: Exercise: the DP principle
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Cost image C
one number per pixel; a path pays the sum of its pixels


Monotone path
one pixel per row, from the top row to the bottom row; each step goes one row down and at most one column sideways (↙ ↓ ↘)


Table M
M(i, j) = cost of the cheapest path from the top row to pixel (i, j)


Recursion
M(0, j) = C(0, j); M(i, j) = C(i, j) + \min\big(M(i-1, j-1), M(i-1, j), M(i-1, j+1)\big)


Pointer
which of the cells above gave the minimum


Backtracking
start at the smallest M of the last row and follow the pointers up


Tie rule (demo)
on a tie, straight wins, then left, then right



Pixels are written (row, column), counting from 0; row 0 is the top.

Math questions
B6. (math) Prove the principle of optimality for minimal monotone paths: if j_0, \dots, j_{n-1} is a cheapest path and 0 \le k < n-1, then j_0, \dots, j_k is a cheapest path from the top row to (k, j_k). Use it to prove by induction that the recursion gives M(i, j) = the cost of the cheapest path to (i, j).
B7. (math) (a) Show that the number of evaluations to fill an n \times m table (m \ge 2) is exactly (n-1)(3m-2). Check it for B2. (b) Show that the number of monotone paths P satisfies m \cdot 2^{n-1} \le P \le m \cdot 3^{n-1}.
B8. (math) Paths from the top-left to the bottom-right cell with steps right or down only. (a) Write the recursion for M and the order of filling. (b) Show that there are \binom{n + m - 2}{n - 1} such paths in an n \times m grid, and evaluate it for 5 \times 5.
B9. (math) Allow steps of up to \delta columns sideways with a penalty \alpha |d| for a step of d columns. Write the recursion and its cost in operations. Why does a large \alpha give straighter paths?






Solutions (math)





B6. Suppose j_0, \dots, j_k is not cheapest: some path j'_0, \dots, j'_k with j'_k = j_k costs less. Then j'_0, \dots, j'_k, j_{k+1}, \dots, j_{n-1} is a valid path (the step from j_k to j_{k+1} is unchanged) and costs less than the original, a contradiction. Induction: M(0, j) = C(0, j) is correct. If M(i-1, \cdot) is correct, a cheapest path to (i, j) passes through some (i-1, j+d), |d| \le 1, and by the principle its first part costs M(i-1, j+d); so the cheapest cost is C(i, j) + \min_d M(i-1, j+d), which is the recursion.
B7. (a) Rows 1, \dots, n-1 each have m - 2 interior cells with 3 candidates and 2 border cells with 2: 3(m-2) + 4 = 3m - 2 per row. For 5 \times 5: 4 \cdot 13 = 52. (b) With N(i, j) the number of paths to (i, j): every cell has at least 2 and at most 3 cells above it (for m \ge 2), so by induction 2^i \le N(i, j) \le 3^i. Summing over the m cells of the last row gives the bounds.
B8. (a) M(0, 0) = C(0, 0), M(i, j) = C(i, j) + \min\big(M(i-1, j), M(i, j-1)\big), with M = \infty outside the grid; fill row by row, left to right (both right-hand cells come earlier in this order). (b) A path makes n - 1 down-steps and m - 1 right-steps in some order: choose which n - 1 of the n + m - 2 steps go down. For 5 \times 5: \binom{8}{4} = 70.
B9. M(i, j) = C(i, j) + \min_{|d| \le \delta} \big(M(i-1, j+d) + \alpha|d|\big): 2\delta + 1 candidates per cell, about (2\delta+1)nm operations. A large \alpha makes every sideways step expensive, so the path changes column only where the costs of the image make it worth it: straighter, smoother paths. (\alpha = 0 and \delta = 1 is the case of B1.)

title: Exercise: the DP principle
text:
Explore
The demo shows the cost image C (left; light = cheap) and the table M (right). step fills one cell: the candidates in the row above are outlined in blue, the chosen minimum is shaded green and an arrow points back to it (show pointers keeps all arrows). next stage fills a whole row, fill all the table, backtrack follows the arrows from the best cell of the last row; the last frame adds the greedy path (red “g”). The readout counts cells, operations and paths. Click the upper half of a cost cell to raise it by 1, the lower half to lower it. moves → ↓ switches to paths from the top-left to the bottom-right cell.



E1. Preset by-hand exercise grid. Step through the first two rows and compare every entry and arrow with your table from B1. Then fill all and backtrack. What are the operations and the number of paths at the end?
E2. Preset greedy fails. Before stepping, guess the best path. Then end: what do the optimal and the greedy path cost, and why does greedy fail here?
E3. Preset two equal optima. Which path does the demo report? Find the second path with the same cost. Why does the table report only one of them, and how would you change the backtracking to find both?
E4. Preset a detour. The cheap channel of 1s runs down, right, up, right and down again. What does the best monotone path cost, and where does it go? Find a cheaper path by hand if you are allowed to move up, down, left and right. Why can no row-by-row table find it?
E5. Back to by-hand exercise grid, now with moves → ↓. What does the cheapest path from the top-left to the bottom-right cost, how many paths are there, and how many operations does the table take? Check the path count with B8.
E6. Back to by-hand exercise grid (moves ↙ ↓ ↘). Predict first, then check: raise C(0, 1) from 4 to 9 (five clicks on its upper half). Which path is now the cheapest, and what does it cost? Does the greedy path change?






Solutions





E1. The table and arrows match B1. At the end: 25 of 25 cells filled, 52 operations, 259 paths; optimal cost 10, greedy 19.
E2. Optimal 9: straight down the right column, 3 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 1. Greedy 20: it starts at the 1 in column 2 (the cheapest first pixel), then takes 2, and is then surrounded by 8s and 9s: 1 + 2 + 8 + 8 + 1. The cheapest first step leads into the most expensive region.
E3. The demo reports (0,2), (1,1), (2,0), (3,1), (4,2): cost 1 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 9. Its mirror image (0,2), (1,3), (2,4), (3,3), (4,2) also costs 9. At (4, 2) the two candidates M(3, 1) = M(3, 3) = 8 tie, and the pointer stores only one (left wins). To find all optimal paths, store all tied predecessors (a set of pointers per cell) and backtrack along every branch.
E4. The best monotone path costs 24: down the channel in column 1 to row 5 (six 1s), then through two 9s and out at the bottom left: (0,1), \dots, (5,1), (6,0), (7,0). Following the channel costs 19 (nineteen cells of cost 1): down column 1, right along row 5 to column 3, up column 3 to row 2, right along row 2 to column 6, and down column 6 to the bottom. A row-by-row table only allows one cell per row and moves downwards, so it cannot represent a path that goes back up; and even if it could, M of a cell in row 2 would depend on cells in row 5, which are filled later. There is no fixed row order: the live-wire unit solves this with Dijkstra’s algorithm.
E5. Cost 32, along (0,0), (1,0), (2,0), (2,1), (3,1), (3,2), (3,3), (3,4), (4,4); 70 paths, 40 operations (every cell except the first row and column has 2 candidates: 16 \cdot 2 + 8 \cdot 1 = 40). \binom{8}{4} = 70, as in B8.
E6. The old path loses its cheap start (it would now cost 15). The new optimum is 13: columns 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, that is 7 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 2: it starts at the 7 and joins the old path in row 1. Greedy is unchanged (it starts at the 3 in the top-right corner): 19. Only the cells whose cheapest path ran through (0, 1) change in M (most of the table); the right column, whose paths never touch (0, 1), is unchanged.

title: Exercise: the DP principle
text:
Where this leads
The table filled row by row works because a monotone path has a natural order. The next unit turns the table sideways: a closed boundary around a nucleus becomes a path through a polar image, with one radius per angle. After that, the live-wire unit drops the fixed order altogether (Dijkstra’s algorithm), and the fast marching unit makes the path continuous.

title: Quiz: the DP principle
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Paths go from the top row to the bottom row of a cost image, one row down per step and at most one column sideways; M(i, j) is the cost of the cheapest path to pixel (i, j).

Q1. State the principle of optimality for minimal paths in one sentence. Why does it let us keep only one number per pixel?






Hint





What could you do if a part of the best path were not the best way to its end pixel?









Answer





Every part of an optimal path is itself optimal: if the best path to the bottom passes through p, its part up to p is the cheapest path to p (otherwise we could swap in the cheaper part). So for continuing paths only the cheapest way to reach p matters, and one number per pixel, M(p), is enough.




Q2. Three cells above pixel (i, j) have M = 12, 9, 15, and C(i, j) = 4. What is M(i, j), and where does its pointer point?






Answer





M(i, j) = 4 + \min(12, 9, 15) = 13; the pointer points to the middle cell (straight up), the one with 9.




Q3. Why does the greedy path (cheapest first pixel, then always the cheapest pixel below) usually fail?






Answer





It decides each step by looking only at the next pixel. A cheap step can lead into an expensive region that cannot be left in time, because a path moves at most one column per row. DP avoids this by not committing to any step before the whole table is filled: the path is chosen from the end.




Q4. An image gets twice as many rows (same width). Roughly what happens to the number of paths, and to the work of DP?






Hint





About m \cdot 3^{n-1} paths, about 3nm operations.









Answer





The number of paths is roughly squared (divided by m): 3^{2n-1} instead of 3^{n-1}, so astronomically more. The DP work only doubles: it grows linearly with the number of pixels.




Q5. You need only the cost of the best path, not the path. How much memory does DP need? And if you need the path?






Answer





For the cost, one row of M is enough: each row is computed from the previous one only. For the path, you also need the pointers of every cell (or the whole table M), to backtrack from the end.




Q6. In the two-label chain of the graph-cut day (E = \sum_p D_p(L_p) + \lambda\,\#\{\text{label changes}\}), what are the stages, the states and the cost of a step? What is the “path”?






Answer





Stages: the pixels along the line. States: the two labels. Each pixel-and-label pays its data cost D_p(\ell), and a step that changes the label pays \lambda. The “path” is the labelling: one label per pixel. The same table, with 2 columns instead of m.




Q7. Why is one raster-order pass of the distance transform not enough, while one row-by-row pass is enough for monotone paths?






Answer





A monotone path only ever comes from above, so when row i is filled, everything it needs (row i-1) is final. For the distance transform, the shortest way to the nearest background pixel may come from below or from the right, which a top-to-bottom, left-to-right pass has not seen yet. Each pass is DP with a fixed order; neither order covers all paths.




Q8. (math) Paths go from the top-left to the bottom-right cell with steps right, down, or diagonally right-down. Write the recursion for M, and say in which order the table can be filled.






Answer





M(0, 0) = C(0, 0) and M(i, j) = C(i, j) + \min\big(M(i-1, j),\ M(i, j-1),\ M(i-1, j-1)\big), with M = \infty outside the grid. Row by row, left to right (or column by column): all three cells on the right-hand side come earlier. This is the table that aligns two signals (dynamic time warping).

title: Decision trees
text:
About this lecture
The first day of learning from examples. So far we wrote every rule by hand: a threshold, a filter, an energy. Now the rule is learned from examples that someone has labelled.

Classification = colouring a feature space: each pixel or object is a point.
A decision tree asks yes/no questions about one feature at a time.
It is grown greedily: the question that makes the two groups purest.
A tree grown too far memorises the training data: overfitting.
Training, validation and test data, and cross-validation: how to measure honestly.
Regression trees: the same idea for numbers.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

This day owns the classification basics for the whole course: feature space, training/validation/test data, overfitting, cross-validation. Later days (neural networks, evaluation, SVM, mixtures) recall them from here. The next unit makes forests from many trees; unit 3 classifies objects from measurements; unit 4 classifies pixels.

title: Decision trees
text:
Classification: colour the feature space

Measure a few numbers per pixel or per object: its features (intensity, local variance, area, …).
Each pixel or object is then a point, one axis per feature.
Training data: points whose class someone knows (nucleus / background, mitotic / not).
The classifier must colour the whole plane: every new point gets a class from where it lands.

The simplest way: give a new point the class of its nearest training point (nearest neighbour). Trees do it with a few questions instead.

Draw two clouds on the board, a new point between them. Nearest neighbour is mentioned only as the obvious baseline; it needs all training points at prediction time and depends on the units of the axes (a tree does not, see later).

title: Decision trees
text:
A decision tree

Eight pixels, two features: intensity I and local variance V (texture). Each node asks “is feature \le t?”; each leaf holds a class (or the class proportions). Every question cuts the plane along an axis: a tree is a set of axis-aligned rectangles. A tree with one question is a stump.

Read the tree: V ≤ 4.5 → background (3 smooth, dim pixels). Otherwise ask I ≤ 55: the left leaf still holds one of each, the right leaf three nuclei. The plane on the left is the same tree. Prediction is a handful of comparisons.

title: Decision trees
text:
Growing a tree

Take all training points in a node.
For every feature and every threshold between two neighbouring values: split the points into “≤” and “>”.
Keep the split whose two children are purest.
Repeat in each child (recursive partitioning), until a stopping rule says no.

This is greedy: each question is the best one now. The best first question is not always part of the best tree. With four quadrants coloured like a chessboard (XOR), no single cut helps, yet two cuts solve it.

The XOR preset in the demo shows this: the split scan at the root is almost flat (best impurity decrease 0.024 of a possible 0.5), but after three splits the training error is 1 of 120. Finding the best tree overall is computationally hopeless, hence greedy.

title: Decision trees
section: Impurity: how mixed is a node?
text:
Impurity: how mixed is a node?

0 when the node holds a single class; largest when the classes are equally mixed.
Gini impurity: the chance that two points drawn at random from the node (with replacement) have different classes. For two classes with shares p and 1 - p: 2p(1-p), at most 0.5.
Entropy: how many yes/no questions are still needed, on average, to name the class (at most 1 for two classes). It chooses almost the same splits; the full story is on the compression day.
A split is good when the weighted impurity of the children is much lower than the parent’s: the impurity decrease.

title: Decision trees
section: The math: impurity and its decrease
text:
The math: impurity and its decrease
Class shares p_k in a node. Gini, entropy and misclassification: G = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2 = \sum_{k \ne l} p_k p_l, \qquad H = -\sum_k p_k \log_2 p_k, \qquad M = 1 - \max_k p_k .
A split of n points into n_L and n_R: \Delta = I(\text{parent}) - \tfrac{n_L}{n}\, I(L) - \tfrac{n_R}{n}\, I(R) \;\ge\; 0 \quad\text{for concave } I . (The parent’s shares are the weighted mean of the children’s; Jensen’s inequality.) With H, \Delta is called the information gain.
M is a poor criterion: it is only piecewise linear, so many useful splits give \Delta = 0. Example: 400 + 400 points split into (300, 100) | (100, 300) or into (200, 400) | (200, 0). Both have \Delta M = 0.25; Gini prefers the second, which has a pure child (\Delta G = 0.167 against 0.125).

title: Decision trees
text:
Try it: grow a tree




Left: points (click to add, drag to move), the tree’s rectangles behind them, the split lines on top. Right: the tree, and for the selected node the split scan: impurity decrease against the threshold for a cut along x (blue) and y (green); click on a curve to force that cut. Tour: “two blobs”: one stump at x ≤ 0.48, best decrease 0.48, 1 of 100 training points wrong. “XOR”: the scan at the root is flat (0.024): next split three times, error drops to 1/120. “diagonal”: grow fully, a staircase of 13 leaves. “one mislabelled point”: a deep tree draws a thin sliver around it; min leaf size 3 removes it. “noisy overlap” with the error-vs-depth view: training error falls to 0.5 %, test error is lowest at depth 3 (20.9 %) and ends at 28.9 %.

title: Decision trees
text:
When to stop: overfitting

Grown until every leaf is pure, a tree memorises the training points: zero training error, jagged boundaries, a sliver around every mislabelled point.
Stopping rules: maximum depth, minimum points per leaf, minimum impurity decrease (or grow fully, then prune).
Training error falls with depth; test error on new data first falls, then rises: the U-shaped curve.
A deep tree is unstable: move a few points and you get a completely different tree (high variance). The next unit turns this weakness into a strength.


Numbers from the “noisy overlap” preset (200 training points, 1000 test points from the same two overlapping clouds): depth 1: 22.5 % / 22.8 %; depth 3: 17.5 % / 20.9 %; depth 12: 0.5 % / 28.9 %.

title: Decision trees
text:
Training, validation and test data

Training set: fits the model (grows the tree).
Validation set: chooses the settings (depth, leaf size) by comparing their errors.
Test set: touched once, at the very end, to report the error. If you choose anything with it, it has become a validation set and the reported error is optimistic.

Few labelled examples? k-fold cross-validation reuses them:

title: Decision trees
text:
Images are not independent samples

Neighbouring pixels in one painted stroke are near copies of each other; cells in one image share its staining and its illumination.
A random split by pixel puts near copies on both sides: the validation error looks far better than it will be on a new image.
Rule: split by image (or by region, or by stroke), never by pixel.

The pixel-classification unit shows the effect; the evaluation and statistics day treats data leakage in full.

title: Decision trees
text:
Regression trees: steps

Leaves hold a number (the mean of their points) instead of a class.
Splits reduce the spread: the sum of squared differences from the mean.
The fit is a staircase: a piecewise-constant function. Across a cell edge, a depth-2 tree gives four plateaus.
A small neural network (the neural-networks day) fits the same profile with bends instead of steps.

title: Decision trees
section: Try it: steps across a cell edge
text:
Try it: steps across a cell edge




The profile: 60 samples across a blurred, noisy edge from 40 to 160. Depth 1: one step at x = 0.449, means 46 and 155, training MSE 262.8. Depth 2: four plateaus 40, 75, 129, 158, training MSE 124.7, test MSE 141.4. The test error is lowest at depth 3 (130.1) and rises again (224.2 at depth 6): overfitting looks the same for numbers.

title: Decision trees
section: The math: search cost and regression
text:
The math: search cost and regression

Sort each feature once; sweep the thresholds from left to right, updating the class counts of the left child: O(d\, n \log n) per node for d features and n points.
Finding the tree with the fewest errors at a given size is NP-hard: hence the greedy growth.
Regression: a leaf predicts \bar y_{\text{leaf}}; the split criterion is the decrease of the sum of squared errors, \Delta = \sum_{i \in P}(y_i - \bar y_P)^2 - \sum_{i \in L}(y_i - \bar y_L)^2 - \sum_{i \in R}(y_i - \bar y_R)^2 , i.e. the variance reduction times n.

title: Decision trees
text:
What trees are good at

No scaling: only the order of a feature’s values matters. Measure area in µm² or in pixels, apply a logarithm: the same tree (with moved thresholds).
Mixed units: intensities, areas, ratios and yes/no features side by side.
Fast: a prediction is a handful of comparisons.
Readable, when small.

Weak points: axis-aligned staircases for oblique boundaries, and the instability of deep trees.

title: Decision trees
text:
Summary

Classification colours a feature space; training points are examples with known class.
A tree asks one-feature questions; its leaves are axis-aligned rectangles.
Grow greedily by the largest impurity decrease (Gini; entropy is almost the same).
Deep trees overfit: low training error, higher test error, unstable.
Choose settings on validation data or by cross-validation; report the test error once; split images, not pixels.
Regression trees fit steps.

title: Exercise: the 2D wavelet transform
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute one level of the 2D Haar transform of small blocks by hand and predict which subband an edge lights up,

text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Separable 2D DWT
one level of the 1D filter bank on every row, then on every column


Subbands
LL approximation; V high-pass along x (vertical edges); H high-pass along y (horizontal edges); D high-pass along both


2 \times 2 Haar block \begin{pmatrix} a & b\\ c & d\end{pmatrix}
LL = \tfrac12(a+b+c+d), V = \tfrac12(a-b+c-d), H = \tfrac12(a+b-c-d), D = \tfrac12(a-b-c+d)


Pyramid (Mallat layout)

Orthonormal transform

PSNR (8 bits)
10\log_{10}(255^2/\mathrm{MSE}) (camera noise unit)

title: Exercise: the 2D wavelet transform
text:
By hand
B1. Compute the four Haar subband values of each 2 \times 2 block: \text{(a)}\ \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 5\\ 5 & 5\end{pmatrix} \qquad \text{(b)}\ \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 8\\ 2 & 8\end{pmatrix} \qquad \text{(c)}\ \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2\\ 8 & 8\end{pmatrix} \qquad \text{(d)}\ \begin{pmatrix} 8 & 2\\ 2 & 8\end{pmatrix} Which band responds to which kind of edge?
B2. A 4 \times 4 image with a horizontal edge: the first three rows are all 1, the last row is all 9. (a) Compute one level of the 2D Haar transform (four 2 \times 2 subbands). Which bands are nonzero? (b) Now the edge lies one row higher: the first two rows are 1, the last two are 9. Which bands are nonzero after one level? After two levels? (c) What does this say about how the transform reacts to moving an edge by one pixel?
B3. A 256 \times 256 image, 4 levels. (a) How large is each subband at each level, and how many coefficients are there in total? (b) What fraction of the coefficients is in the final LL?
B4. Keeping a fraction of all coefficients of the micrograph (4 levels) gives these PSNR values (dB):



kept
Haar
db4
CDF 9/7
Fourier
8\times8 DCT




1 %
18.2
18.6
18.8

10.5


5 %
20.9

21.8

20 %

26.2




Which basis would you use, and how much better is it than Fourier at 5 %, in dB and as a ratio of MSEs?
Why does the DCT collapse at 1 %? (Hint: 655 coefficients for 1024 blocks.)
For the synthetic disc at 2 %, the values are Haar 47.6, db4 40.5, DCT 34.9, Fourier 29.8. Why is the ranking different from the micrograph?

B5. In an orthonormal transform of a 256 \times 256 image, the dropped coefficients have a total squared value of 10^6. What are the MSE and the PSNR? What happens to the PSNR if twice as much energy is dropped?
B6. You keep 5 % of the coefficients of a 256 \times 256 8-bit image. Estimate the number of bits if each kept coefficient is stored as an 8-bit value plus its position. What compression ratio is that? Name two things a real codec does to do better.






Solutions





B1. (a) LL = 10, V = H = D = 0. (b) LL = 10, V = \tfrac12(2 - 8 + 2 - 8) = -6, H = D = 0: a vertical edge (change along x) lights V. (c) LL = 10, H = \tfrac12(2 + 2 - 8 - 8) = -6, V = D = 0: a horizontal edge lights H. (d) LL = 10, D = \tfrac12(8 - 2 - 2 + 8) = 6, V = H = 0: a checkerboard (diagonal) pattern lights D. The sign tells the direction (here: brighter on the right gives a negative V, because V is left minus right).
B2. (a) Blocks (rows 1–2) are flat 1s: LL = 2, details 0. Blocks in rows 3–4 are \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 9 & 9\end{pmatrix}: LL = 10, H = \tfrac12(1 + 1 - 9 - 9) = -8, V = D = 0. Subbands: LL = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2\\ 10 & 10\end{pmatrix}, H = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0\\ -8 & -8\end{pmatrix}, V = D = 0. Only H has details. (b) Every 2 \times 2 block is flat (rows 1–2 all 1, rows 3–4 all 9): all level-1 details are 0, LL = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2\\ 18 & 18\end{pmatrix}. At level 2, LL is one block \begin{pmatrix}2 & 2\\ 18 & 18\end{pmatrix}: LL = 20, H = \tfrac12(2 + 2 - 18 - 18) = -16. (c) The same edge, moved by one row, appears at a different level with different values: the transform is not shift-invariant. Where an edge falls relative to the even–odd grid decides which coefficients see it.
B3. (a) Level 1: three bands of 128 \times 128 = 16\,384; level 2: three of 64 \times 64 = 4096; level 3: three of 1024; level 4: three of 256; final LL 16 \times 16 = 256. Total 3(16\,384 + 4096 + 1024 + 256) + 256 = 65\,536 = 256^2. (b) 256/65\,536 = 1/256 = 0.39\,\% (= 4^{-4}).
B4. (a) CDF 9/7 (or db4, 0.3 dB behind): 21.8 against 21.0 dB for Fourier, 0.8 dB, i.e. an MSE ratio of 10^{0.08} = 1.20: 20 % less squared error. The differences are small on this textured image; what you see differs more (blocks, ringing). (b) 655 coefficients for 1024 blocks: at least 369 blocks keep nothing, not even their average (DC), and become 0 (black). Real codecs always code every DC coefficient. (c) The disc is piecewise constant: flat regions and one smooth edge. Wavelets (Haar best: no smooth part needs vanishing moments) describe it with few coefficients along the edge; Fourier needs all frequencies for the edge. The micrograph is full of fine texture that no basis compresses well, which pulls all bases together.
B5. \mathrm{MSE} = 10^6/65\,536 = 15.26, \mathrm{PSNR} = 10\log_{10}(65\,025/15.26) = 36.3 dB. Twice the dropped energy doubles the MSE: 36.3 - 10\log_{10}2 = 33.3 dB (3 dB less).
B6. 0.05 \cdot 65\,536 = 3277 coefficients; each 8 bits of value plus \log_2 65\,536 = 16 bits of position: 3277 \cdot 24 = 78\,648 bits, against 65\,536 \cdot 8 = 524\,288 for the raw image: ratio 6.7. Real codecs quantise the values coarsely (fewer bits per value), code the positions jointly (large coefficients cluster along edges and across levels), and entropy-code the result. (Compression day.)




Math questions
B7. (math) Derive the four 2 \times 2 Haar formulas by applying the 1D step (a, b) \mapsto ((a+b)/\sqrt2, (a-b)/\sqrt2) first to both rows, then to both columns.
B8. (math) Let W be an orthogonal N \times N matrix (one 1D level or a full 1D transform). Show that X \mapsto WXW^\top preserves \sum_{ij} X_{ij}^2, and derive \mathrm{MSE} = \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{\text{dropped}} c^2.
B9. (math) Show that an L-level pyramid of an N \times N image (N divisible by 2^L) has exactly N^2 coefficients, using a geometric sum.
B10. (math) Show that a circular shift of an image by one pixel changes only the phases of its DFT coefficients. Then give a 1D two-sample example showing that the Haar detail coefficients are not invariant to a shift by one sample.






Solutions (math)





B7. Rows: (a, b) \mapsto \big(\tfrac{a+b}{\sqrt2}, \tfrac{a-b}{\sqrt2}\big), (c, d) \mapsto \big(\tfrac{c+d}{\sqrt2}, \tfrac{c-d}{\sqrt2}\big). Columns: the left column \big(\tfrac{a+b}{\sqrt2}, \tfrac{c+d}{\sqrt2}\big) gives LL = \tfrac{a+b+c+d}{2} (top) and H = \tfrac{a+b-c-d}{2} (bottom); the right column gives V = \tfrac{a-b+c-d}{2} and D = \tfrac{a-b-c+d}{2}.
B8. \sum_{ij}X_{ij}^2 = \operatorname{tr}(X^\top X), and \operatorname{tr}\big((WXW^\top)^\top WXW^\top\big) = \operatorname{tr}(W X^\top X W^\top) = \operatorname{tr}(X^\top X W^\top W) = \operatorname{tr}(X^\top X) (cyclic trace, W^\top W = I). The map is linear, so the error image X - \hat X maps to the dropped coefficients C - \hat C; its energy is preserved: \sum (x - \hat x)^2 = \sum_{\text{dropped}} c^2; divide by N^2.
B9. Level j has three bands of (N/2^j)^2 = N^2/4^j; the final LL has N^2/4^L. Total 3N^2\sum_{j=1}^{L} 4^{-j} + N^2 4^{-L} = 3N^2\cdot\frac{1 - 4^{-L}}{3} + N^2 4^{-L} = N^2.
B10. y_{m,n} = x_{m, n-1} (indices mod N) gives Y_{k,l} = e^{-2\pi i l/N}X_{k,l}: |Y_{k,l}| = |X_{k,l}|. Haar on 4 samples (0, 8, 8, 8): details \big(\tfrac{0-8}{\sqrt2}, 0\big) = (-5.66, 0). Shifted by one (circularly) to (8, 0, 8, 8): (5.66, 0). Shifted by two, (8, 8, 0, 8): (0, -5.66). The same edge moves between coefficients and changes sign; there is no simple relation like a phase factor, because the downsampling keeps only even positions.

title: Exercise: the 2D wavelet transform
text:
Explore
A 256 \times 256 image (the micrograph or a synthetic one) and its 2D wavelet transform. Panels: the image, the subbands (Mallat layout: grey LL in the corner, detail bands in blue/red, each scaled to its own largest value; with log |w| all bands in grey on a log scale), the reconstruction, and the error. keep K largest keeps a percentage of all coefficients (dropped ones are faded in the subband panel); zero bands lets you click subbands to remove them. compare shows the reconstructions from the same number of coefficients in the wavelet basis, the global Fourier basis and the 8 \times 8 block DCT. The plot gives PSNR against the percentage kept for the three. shift by 1 px moves the image one pixel to the right.



E1. Preset one level: three orientations (oriented bars, Haar, 1 level). In which band does each bar appear, and where? Compare with B1. Then set levels to 3.
E2. Preset pyramid of the cell (db2, 4 levels). Which band looks like a thumbnail? Which bands are the brightest in log |w| display, and which level has the most coefficients?
E3. Preset keep 3 %: Haar blocks. Read the PSNR and look at the reconstruction. Then select db4 and db8. What changes in the numbers and in the look of the errors?
E4. Preset wavelets vs Fourier vs DCT at 5 %. Read the three PSNRs. Move keep % to 1. What happens to the DCT reconstruction, and why (B4b)? Then choose CDF 9/7.
E5. Still in compare, choose the image disc and keep % = 2. Read the PSNRs. Select Haar: what is special at 3 %?
E6. Preset drop the finest level = blur (db4, 3 levels, the three level-1 bands removed). How many coefficients are kept, and what is the PSNR? Bring back V and H, keeping only D removed: PSNR? And only V removed? Then remove levels 1 and 2 entirely and compare with keep K largest at a similar percentage.
E7. Preset shift variance (square, Haar, 2 levels). By how much do the detail coefficients change? And the band energies? Choose the micrograph and db4, 3 levels.






Solutions





E1. The vertical bar’s left and right sides appear in V (top right), as two vertical lines of opposite colour; the horizontal bar’s top and bottom in H (bottom left); the diagonal bar in all three detail bands, strongest along its edges. Flat areas are white (0) everywhere. With 3 levels the coarser bands show the same structures at lower resolution, and only the edges that fall inside a coarser pattern appear there.
E2. The top-left LL (16 \times 16) is the thumbnail. In log |w| the LL and the coarse bands are brightest (largest values): the energy sits at coarse scales. Level 1 has the most coefficients (3 \times 128^2 = 49\,152, three quarters of all), mostly small.
E3. Haar at 3 %: 19.9 dB, and the reconstruction is made of visible rectangular blocks. db4: 20.4 dB, db8: 20.5 dB; the blocks disappear and the error turns into a smooth blur with faint ringing near strong edges.
E4. At 5 %: db4 21.5, Fourier 21.0, DCT 21.2 dB; Fourier rings everywhere, the DCT shows 8 \times 8 blocks. At 1 %: db4 18.6, Fourier 18.4, DCT 10.5 dB, with many black blocks: those blocks kept no coefficient, not even their average. CDF 9/7: 21.8 dB at 5 %, 18.8 at 1 %.
E5. Disc at 2 %: Haar 47.6, db4 40.5, DCT 34.9, Fourier 29.8 dB (with the demo’s 4 levels). With Haar at 3 % the readout says “∞ (exact)”: the disc (with its antialiased edge) has fewer than 3 % nonzero Haar coefficients, so keeping 3 % keeps all of them.
E6. 16 384 of 65 536 coefficients (25 %), 23.9 dB: the fine texture is gone, the image is blurred. Only D removed: 31.5 dB; only V removed: 27.5 dB (vertical edges become soft): the diagonal band carries the least energy. Levels 1 and 2 removed: 4096 coefficients (6.3 %), 20.3 dB, worse than keeping the largest 5 % (21.4 dB with 3 levels): choosing coefficients by size beats choosing them by band.
E7. Square, Haar, 2 levels: the detail coefficients change by 68 % (\|c_{\text{shifted}} - c\|/\|c\|), but the level-1 band energies stay the same (1.27 \cdot 10^6 in V). Micrograph, db4, 3 levels: 92 %, with level-1 V energy 7.58 \cdot 10^6 \to 7.35 \cdot 10^6. The energy per band hardly changes; the individual coefficients do.

title: Exercise: the 2D wavelet transform
text:
Where this leads
Sparsity is useful beyond compression. Noise does not become sparse in any basis: an orthonormal transform spreads white noise evenly over all coefficients. The next unit uses this to denoise by keeping the large coefficients and shrinking the small ones.
