title: Exercise: filter banks and Daubechies wavelets
text:
Explore: the filter bank
A signal of 64 samples goes through one level of the filter bank. Top: input (black) and output (orange). Left column: the low-pass and high-pass filtered signals (faint) and the kept samples, every second one (dots). Right column: each branch after upsampling and filtering; the two add up to the output. Grey lines mark the signal’s borders. Break it with drop the high-pass branch or wrong synthesis filters, and change the boundary rule. cascade repeats the step on the low branch (levels); basis functions shows \varphi and \psi built by the cascade algorithm (iterations). The readout gives the largest reconstruction error and the largest detail, inside the signal and overall.



E1. Preset perfect reconstruction (db4, HeaviSine). What is the largest reconstruction error? How many coefficients are there, and how do \Sigma x^2 and \Sigma a^2 + \Sigma d^2 compare?
E2. Preset Haar = unit 1 (two steps). All details are zero. Why? (The jumps are at samples 20 and 40.)
E3. Preset remove one branch: aliasing (db2, chirp). What is the reconstruction error now? Describe the output. Untick the box and tick wrong synthesis filters instead: what is the error? Then try Haar and db8 with the high branch dropped.
E4. Preset quadratic: db3 details vanish. Compare the largest detail inside for Haar, db2, db3, db4. Where is the largest detail overall, and why?
E5. Signal cubic: which is the first wavelet in the list whose inside details vanish? Is that what you expect?
E6. Preset periodic boundary: false edge (db4, ramp). Read the largest detail inside and overall. Switch to symmetric and zero: what changes, including the number of coefficients and the energies?
E7. Preset cascade: 4 levels (db2, HeaviSine). How many coefficients in total, and how many samples were filtered? Switch the boundary to zero.
E8. Preset basis functions (db2). Move iterations from 0 to 10. When does the shape stop changing visibly? Compare Haar, db2, db4 and db8 at 10 iterations: support and smoothness.






Solutions





E1. Max |x - \text{output}| = 1.8 \cdot 10^{-15}, i.e. rounding error. 32 + 32 = 64 coefficients; \Sigma x^2 = 604.988 = \Sigma a^2 + \Sigma d^2 (orthogonal transform, periodic border).
E2. The jumps sit between samples 19 and 20 and between 39 and 40: both fall between Haar pairs (0–1, 2–3, …), so every pair is flat and every difference is 0. The low branch alone reproduces the signal. (Shift a jump by one sample and one detail appears.)
E3. With the high branch dropped (db2): max error 1.18; the output is a smoothed chirp with spurious slow wiggles where the chirp is fast (the folded-down frequencies). Wrong synthesis filters: 1.97, worse than doing nothing. High branch dropped with Haar: 0.955, with db8: 1.19.
E4. Largest |d| inside: Haar 0.0435, db2 1.2 \cdot 10^{-3}, db3 8.3 \cdot 10^{-17}, db4 5.6 \cdot 10^{-17}. The quadratic has degree 2: db3 and db4 (3 and 4 vanishing moments) give zero; db2 almost (it kills the linear part, and a parabola is almost linear over 4 samples); Haar does not. Overall for db3, 0.0416 near the end (sample 60): the periodic border glues the parabola’s end to its start, which has a different slope.
E5. db4 (inside 8.3 \cdot 10^{-17}); db3 gives 1.0 \cdot 10^{-4}, db2 3.4 \cdot 10^{-3}. A cubic has degree 3, so it needs p \ge 4.
E6. Periodic: inside 1.4 \cdot 10^{-16}, overall 0.48 (at sample 58: the wrap-around jump from the top of the ramp to its bottom). Symmetric: overall 0.001, almost no border detail, but 35 + 35 = 70 coefficients and \Sigma a^2 + \Sigma d^2 = 21.343 \ne \Sigma x^2 = 20.836 (the extra coefficients see mirrored samples twice). Zero: overall 0.48 (the jump down to 0), also 35 + 35 coefficients, with \Sigma a^2 + \Sigma d^2 = 20.836. All three reconstruct to \sim 10^{-16}.
E7. Periodic: 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 details + 4 approximations = 64 coefficients; 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 = 120 samples filtered, less than 2N = 128. Zero border: 33 + 18 + 10 + 6 + 6 = 73 coefficients: each level keeps a few extra.
E8. At 0 iterations both are spikes, after 1 they are the filter taps themselves (\sqrt2 h, \sqrt2 g); the shape settles after about 5–6 iterations (the steps get finer, the outline stays). Supports: Haar [0, 1], db2 [0, 3], db4 [0, 7], db8 [0, 15]. Haar is a box, db2 is continuous with sharp corners, db4 and db8 are increasingly smooth and wide.

title: Quiz: filter banks and Daubechies wavelets
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Analysis: filter with a low-pass h and a high-pass g, keep every second sample; synthesis: upsample, filter, add.

Q1. In one level of the filter bank, a signal of N samples gives how many numbers? And after the full cascade?






Hint





Each branch keeps every second sample; only the low branch is split again.









Answer





One level: N/2 approximations + N/2 details = N. Full cascade: N/2 + N/4 + \dots + 1 details plus 1 approximation = N (periodic border). A change of basis keeps the count.




Q2. Keeping every second sample of a signal normally causes aliasing. Why does the reconstructed signal of a wavelet filter bank have none?






Hint





What happens to the folded part in the two branches?









Answer





Each branch alone is aliased, but for a matched (quadrature mirror) pair the folded-down part appears in the low and high branch with opposite signs, and they cancel when the branches are added on synthesis. Drop one branch, or use the wrong synthesis filters, and the aliasing stays.




Q3. Why does the DWT cost only \mathcal O(N) operations, while the FFT costs \mathcal O(N\log N)?






Hint





How much data does each level of the cascade process?









Answer





Each level filters only the low branch of the previous one: N + N/2 + N/4 + \dots < 2N samples, each with a fixed number L of multiplications. Total < 2LN. The FFT does \log_2 N passes over all N samples.




Q4. What does it mean that db3 has 3 vanishing moments? Give a signal whose db3 details are all zero (away from the borders).






Hint





Polynomials.









Answer





\sum_n n^m g_n = 0 for m = 0, 1, 2: the high-pass filter is blind to constants, ramps and parabolas. Any polynomial of degree at most 2, e.g. x_n = 3 - n + 0.5 n^2, gives zero details.




Q5. More vanishing moments make smooth regions sparser. Why is db8 not always better than db4?






Hint





How long is the filter?









Answer





db8 has 16 taps, db4 has 8. A jump (an edge) touches every coefficient whose filter covers it, so with a longer filter each edge creates more large coefficients. For signals with many jumps the shorter filter can win; for very smooth signals the longer one.




Q6. A signal is analysed with a periodic border. Its last few detail coefficients are large although the signal is smooth. What is going on, and what helps?






Hint





What does the filter see after the last sample?









Answer





The periodic border continues the signal with its own beginning: if the first and last samples differ, the filter sees a jump (a false edge) and produces large details there. A symmetric (mirror) border avoids the jump; it costs a few extra coefficients.




Q7. How are the Gaussian pyramid, the Laplacian pyramid and the DWT related?






Hint





Count the numbers stored.









Answer





All three go coarse to fine by smoothing and keeping every second sample. The Gaussian pyramid stores only the smoothed versions; the Laplacian pyramid stores the differences between levels, about 4/3 times as many numbers as pixels in 2D, and is not an orthogonal basis. The DWT stores exactly as many numbers as pixels and is an orthogonal change of basis.




Q8. (math) Show that db2’s high-pass g = (h_3, -h_2, h_1, -h_0) sums to zero, using h \propto (1+\sqrt3,\ 3+\sqrt3,\ 3-\sqrt3,\ 1-\sqrt3).






Hint





Add the four terms with their signs.









Answer





(1 - \sqrt3) - (3 - \sqrt3) + (3 + \sqrt3) - (1 + \sqrt3) = 1 - 3 + 3 - 1 + (-\sqrt3 + \sqrt3 + \sqrt3 - \sqrt3) = 0. A high-pass filter must give 0 on a constant signal: one vanishing moment.
crumbs: Multiresolution, filter banks and Daubechies wavelets

title: Floating point
text:
About this lecture

Analysis happens in floating point: what is stored, bit by bit, in float32, float16 (half) and bfloat16.
Floats are spaced unevenly: the gap between neighbours grows with the number. What that means for 16-bit images in half floats.
Special values: zero, infinity, NaN, tiny “subnormal” numbers.
Where rounding hurts: cancellation (a negative variance!) and summing millions of pixels.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

The previous unit recommended converting to float before arithmetic. This unit says what that buys and where it still goes wrong. Everything is base-2 scientific notation; the demos let students click bits and see sums drift.

title: Floating point
text:
Scientific notation, in base 2
6.02 \times 10^{23}: a few significant digits and an exponent. Floats do the same in base 2:
x = \pm\, 1.f_1 f_2 \dots f_m \;(\text{binary}) \times 2^{E}.

About 7 significant decimal digits in float32, 3 in float16, 2 in bfloat16.
bfloat16 keeps float32’s exponent range but very few digits (used in machine learning).

title: Floating point
section: Try it: the bits of a float
text:
Try it: the bits of a float




0.1 in float16: 0x2E66, exactly 0.0999755859375. 0.1 has no finite binary expansion, like 1/3 in decimal. Click +1 ulp a few times and watch the value step. Then click the exponent bits: each one doubles or halves. Presets: 2049 becomes 2048 in half; 65535 becomes infinity; switch to float32: 2049 is exact. Smallest subnormal: 6e-8. The plot: the gap between neighbouring floats against the value, a staircase; where it crosses “spacing 1”, integers stop being exact.

title: Floating point
text:
Floats are spaced unevenly
Between two powers of two there are always the same number of floats (2^m), evenly spaced. The next interval is twice as long, so the gaps double:



float16 near
1
1000
3000
65 000




gap to the next float
0.000 98
0.5
2
32




The relative gap is about the same everywhere: 2^{-10} to 2^{-11} for float16. This is machine epsilon, the gap above 1.
Rounding to the nearest float makes a relative error of at most half that: about 0.05 % for float16, 6 \times 10^{-8} for float32.
0.1 is not exactly a float (like 1/3 in decimal). In float16 it is 0.099 975 585 937 5.

title: Floating point
text:
Integers in floats
Every integer is exact as long as the gap is at most 1:



format

first one that is not




float32
2^{24} = 16\,777\,216
16 777 217


float16
2^{11} = 2048

A 16-bit image stored in half floats:

values up to 2048 survive; 2049 → 2048, 3001 → 3000, 40 001 → 40 000 (gap 32);
65 535 → infinity: the largest half float is 65 504.
Normalised to [0, 1] instead, the gap near 1 is 2^{-11}: about 11 bits. Half float is fine for 8- or 10-bit data, not for 16-bit.

title: Floating point
text:
Special values

±0: two zeros (the sign is kept, e.g. for 1/(-0) = -\infty).
±∞: overflow (65 535 in half), or 1/0.
NaN (“not a number”): 0/0, \infty - \infty, \sqrt{-1}. Any arithmetic with NaN gives NaN, and NaN ≠ NaN. One NaN pixel spreads through a blur to every pixel it touches; a mean over an image with one NaN is NaN.
Subnormals: below the smallest normal number (2^{-14} \approx 6 \times 10^{-5} in half) the spacing stops shrinking, so the floats run down evenly to 0. Tiny values lose relative precision gradually instead of dropping to 0 at once.

title: Floating point
text:
The math: IEEE 754 numbers
With sign s, stored exponent field E (e bits), fraction field F (m bits) and bias b = 2^{e-1} - 1 (15 for half, 127 for float32):
x = \begin{cases}(-1)^s\, 2^{E - b}\,(1 + F/2^m) & 0 < E < 2^e - 1 \text{ (normal)}\\ (-1)^s\, 2^{1 - b}\,(F/2^m) & E = 0 \text{ (zero, subnormal)}\\ \pm\infty \text{ if } F = 0, \text{ NaN otherwise} & E = 2^e - 1.\end{cases}

In [2^k, 2^{k+1}) the spacing is 2^{k - m}; the relative spacing is between 2^{-m-1} and 2^{-m}; \varepsilon = 2^{-m}.
Round to nearest, ties to even: \operatorname{fl}(x) = x(1 + \delta) with |\delta| \le \varepsilon/2.
Integers are exact while the spacing is \le 1: up to 2^{m+1}.

title: Floating point
text:
Cancellation
Subtracting two nearly equal numbers keeps their absolute error but not their size: the relative error explodes.

In half: 2049 - 2048 gives 0, because 2049 was already stored as 2048.
Textbook variance, \overline{x^2} - \bar x^2: two large, nearly equal numbers. For pixels 10 000, 10 001, 10 002 in float32 it gives 0 (the true value is 2/3): the sum of squares, 300 060 005, is stored as 300 060 000 (gap 32 there).
Fix: compute the mean first, then the squared deviations (two passes), or an update formula that does the same in one pass.

title: Floating point
text:
Summing many pixels
A running sum grows. Once the sum is large, the gap at the sum is larger than the pixel values: each addition rounds, and the small values lose their low bits.

float32: adding 1 to 2^{24} gives 2^{24}. A 2048 × 2048 image with mean 1000 sums to 4 \times 10^9: the naive float32 mean is off by 1 %.
float16: summing normalised pixel values (≈ 0.015 each) gets stuck at 64: from there, adding a pixel rounds back to the same sum.
Pairwise summation (add in a tree: pairs, pairs of pairs, …) keeps partial sums of similar size: error grows like \log n instead of n.
Kahan summation carries the rounding error of each addition into the next one: nearly exact.

title: Floating point
text:
Try it: summing 4 million pixels


Relative error of the sum against the number of pixels. float32 naive is exact up to 2^14 pixels, then drifts to 1 % at 4 million. Pairwise and Kahan stay near 1e-9. float16 naive gets stuck immediately; float16 pairwise is not bad, until “bright and flat”, where the sum of normalised values exceeds 65504 and becomes infinity. Variance: one pass gives a negative number; two passes with naive sums is still off because the mean is off; two passes with pairwise sums is right.

title: Floating point
section: The math: how errors grow when summing
text:
The math: how errors grow when summing
Each addition s_k = \operatorname{fl}(s_{k-1} + x_k) makes a relative error |\delta| \le u = \varepsilon/2. For n non-negative terms (to first order in u):
\text{naive: } |\hat s - s| \lesssim (n - 1)\,u \sum |x_i|, \qquad \text{pairwise: } \lesssim \lceil\log_2 n\rceil\, u \sum |x_i|, \qquad \text{Kahan: } \lesssim 2u \sum |x_i|.
The naive sum stalls when x_k < \tfrac12\operatorname{gap}(s_{k-1}): the addition rounds back to s_{k-1}. Kahan’s trick: after t = \operatorname{fl}(s + y), the quantity c = \operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(t - s) - y) is exactly the part of y that was lost (with the sign flipped); it is subtracted from the next term.

title: Floating point
text:
Rules of thumb

Do image arithmetic in float32; accumulate long sums (means, histograms of large stacks, integrals) in float64, or pairwise.
Compute variances from deviations from the mean, not from \overline{x^2} - \bar x^2.
Do not test two floats for exact equality; compare with a tolerance relative to their size.
Half floats: fine for display and for values of similar size; not for 16-bit raw data or long sums.
Check for NaN and ∞ after every step that can divide or overflow.

title: Floating point
text:
Summary

A float is \pm 1.f \times 2^E: a fixed number of significant bits, so precision is relative; the gap doubles at every power of two.
float32: 24 significant bits, integers exact to 2^{24}; float16: 11 bits, to 2048, max 65 504; bfloat16: 8 bits.
Special values: ±0, ±∞, NaN (spreads), subnormals.
Subtraction of near-equal values cancels significant bits; long sums drift or stall. Use two-pass variances and pairwise or compensated sums.

title: Exercise: forests on feature tables, and feature importance
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute the impurity importance of the features of a small tree,
compute permutation importances from errors before and after shuffling,
predict what correlated and duplicated features do to both importances,
explain why importance describes the model and not the biology,
(math) show why an exact copy halves the impurity importance.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo.

title: Exercise: forests on feature tables, and feature importance
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute the impurity importance of the features of a small tree,
compute permutation importances from errors before and after shuffling,
predict what correlated and duplicated features do to both importances,
explain why importance describes the model and not the biology,
(math) show why an exact copy halves the impurity importance.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo.

title: Exercise: forests on feature tables, and feature importance
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Feature table
one row per segmented object, one column per measurement


Impurity importance (MDI)
per feature: sum of \tfrac{n_t}{n}\Delta I_t over its splits, averaged over the trees


Permutation importance
rise of the OOB (or held-out) error when the feature’s column is shuffled


Correlated features
carry (almost) the same information: area, perimeter, equivalent diameter


Group permutation
shuffle several columns with the same permutation, so they stay consistent with each other









The math: the impurity importance of one tree adds up





Each split replaces the weighted impurity \tfrac{n_t}{n}I_t of a node by the weighted impurities of its two children; the difference is \tfrac{n_t}{n}\Delta I_t. Summed over all splits of a tree, the inner nodes cancel: the total importance is the root impurity minus \sum_{\text{leaves}}\tfrac{n_\ell}{n}I_\ell. For a tree grown until its leaves are pure, it is just the root impurity, shared among the features that did the splitting.

title: Exercise: forests on feature tables, and feature importance
text:
By hand
B1. A depth-2 tree on 100 cells, 50 interphase (I) and 50 mitotic (M). Node counts are written (I, M).

Root: split on texture into (45, 10) and (5, 40).
Left child (45, 10): split on area into (40, 2) and (5, 8).
Right child (5, 40): split on texture into (5, 5) and (0, 35).


Compute the Gini impurity of every node.
Compute \tfrac{n_t}{n}\Delta G for each of the three splits.
Give the impurity importance of texture and area, and their shares of the total.

B2. A forest is tested on 10 held-out cells: 1 is misclassified. Shuffling the texture column among the 10 cells (several times, on average) gives 4 errors; shuffling area gives 2; shuffling the noise feature gives 1. What are the permutation importances (as rises in error rate)?
B3. A table has area and equivalent diameter d = 2\sqrt{A/\pi}, and size matters for the classes. (a) Is equivalent diameter new information? Will a tree that splits on it ever separate cells differently than a split on area? (b) Predict the impurity importance of area when both are in the table, compared with area alone. (c) Predict the permutation importance of area when both are in the table. What happens to it if you remove the diameter column?
B4. You add a column of random numbers (uniform between 0 and 1) to the table and grow deep trees. Will its impurity importance be zero? Its permutation importance? Why the difference?
B5. The forest says texture is by far the most important feature for “mitotic”. A colleague concludes that texture is what causes or defines mitosis. What can and cannot be concluded?






Solutions





B1. (a) Root (50, 50): G = 0.5. (45, 10): 1 - (45/55)^2 - (10/55)^2 = 0.298. (5, 40): 0.198. (40, 2): 0.091. (5, 8): 0.473. (5, 5): 0.5. (0, 35): 0. (b) Root: \Delta G = 0.5 - 0.55 \cdot 0.298 - 0.45 \cdot 0.198 = 0.247; weight 100/100: 0.247. Left: \Delta G = 0.298 - \tfrac{42}{55}0.091 - \tfrac{13}{55}0.473 = 0.116; weight 55/100: 0.064. Right: \Delta G = 0.198 - \tfrac{10}{45}0.5 - 0 = 0.086; weight 45/100: 0.039. (c) Texture: 0.247 + 0.039 = 0.286 (82 %); area: 0.064 (18 %).
B2. Base error 0.1. Texture: 0.4 - 0.1 = 0.3. Area: 0.2 - 0.1 = 0.1. Noise: 0.1 - 0.1 = 0. (With only 10 cells these numbers are very noisy; in practice use many objects and several shuffles.)
B3. (a) No: d is an increasing function of A, so any split on d separates exactly the same cells as some split on A (B5 of the decision-trees exercise). It is the same feature in other units. (b) The trees use area or diameter about equally often for the same splits, so area gets roughly half of what it had alone (and diameter the other half). (c) Small: when area is shuffled, the trees that split on diameter still see the true size, and size is not lost. Remove the diameter column, and the forest has to use area; its permutation importance rises to the full importance of size.
B4. Impurity importance: not zero. Deep trees keep splitting small nodes until they are pure, and among the candidate features the noise column, with its many distinct values, often offers the best split in a small node by chance; the decreases are counted on the training data. Permutation importance on OOB data: about zero (possibly slightly negative), because shuffling the noise column does not change how well the forest predicts new objects.
B5. Only that this forest, on this data, relies on texture to tell the classes apart. Texture may be a consequence of mitosis (condensed chromatin), it may stand in for another, correlated feature, and features with low importance may carry the same information (they were simply not needed). Importance is a property of the model; causation needs experiments.




Math questions
B6. (math) Show that the impurity importances of all features in one tree add up to the root impurity minus \sum_{\text{leaves}}\frac{n_\ell}{n}I_\ell.
B7. (math) Feature j' is an exact copy of feature j. At each split the candidate features are a random subset of size m, and ties are broken at random. Argue that the expected impurity importances of j and j' are equal, and that their sum is about the importance j would have alone.
B8. (math) Show that permutation importance can be negative, and give a reason why a small negative value should be read as zero.






Solutions (math)





B6. Write W_t = \tfrac{n_t}{n}I_t. A split of node t into L and R contributes \tfrac{n_t}{n}\Delta I_t = W_t - W_L - W_R. Summing over all splits, every inner node other than the root appears once with + (as the parent of its split) and once with - (as a child of its parent’s split); the root appears only with +, the leaves only with -. The sum is W_{\text{root}} - \sum_{\text{leaves}} W_\ell = I_{\text{root}} - \sum_\ell \tfrac{n_\ell}{n}I_\ell.
B7. j and j' are interchangeable: every split on one has an identical split on the other with the same decrease, and the random candidate subsets treat them symmetrically. So any tree has the same probability as the tree with j and j' swapped, and the expected importances are equal. With the copy present, a split that j would have made alone is made by j or by j' (when at least one is a candidate), with the same decrease, so their sum is about \mathrm{MDI}_j alone. (Not exactly: with the copy, size is a candidate more often, which changes the trees a little. In the demo: area alone 42 %, area + copy 28 % + 23 %.)
B8. It is a difference of two error rates measured on a finite set; shuffling a useless column can by chance fix a few predictions as easily as break them, so the difference can be negative. Its size is about the sampling noise of the error rate (for n objects and error e, roughly \sqrt{e(1-e)/n}, 1.7 points for e = 0.13, n = 400): values within that range mean “no detectable importance”.

title: Exercise: forests on feature tables, and feature importance
text:
Explore
400 synthetic segmented cells, 200 interphase and 200 mitotic, with eight measured features: area, perimeter and equivalent diameter (three measures of size), intensity, texture, solidity, a continuous noise feature and a random yes/no feature (coin). Left: a scatter plot of any two features (choose x and y). Middle: for each feature in use, the impurity importance (share of the total Gini decrease, blue) and the permutation importance (rise of the OOB error in percentage points when its column is shuffled, orange; average of 5 shuffles). The forest has 100 trees; m is the number of features tried per split. Tick features on or off; add an exact copy of area appends a duplicate column; permute the size block together adds a bar for shuffling area, perimeter, diameter (and the copy) with one permutation.



E1. Preset texture decides. Read the OOB error and both importances of texture. Plot area against texture: why is texture so useful? Which features have a negative permutation importance, and what does that mean?
E2. Preset duplicate area: credit splits (area, intensity, solidity and the two noise features, plus an exact copy of area). Note both importances of area and of its copy. Untick add an exact copy of area: what are area’s importances now?
E3. Preset size block: permutation hides it (texture removed; area, perimeter, diameter in). Read the three impurity and permutation importances of the size features. Then tick permute the size block together. What does the block bar show? Is size important?
E4. Preset noise: impurity vs permutation. Compare the noise and coin features under both measures. Then remove texture: what happens to the noise feature’s impurity share, and why?
E5. With all eight features, set m to 1 and to 8 and compare the impurity importances of the three size features. Explain the 0 % of equivalent diameter at m = 8.






Solutions





E1. OOB error 12.8 %. Texture: impurity 48 %, permutation +24.0 points. In the scatter plot the classes overlap strongly in area but are almost separated by texture (class means 8.2 and 14.1). Negative permutation importance: area −0.7, perimeter −0.4, diameter −0.4, noise −0.1, coin −0.2. Shuffling these columns did not make the forest worse (by chance even slightly better): no detectable importance, here partly because the size information is held three times.
E2. With the copy: area 28 % and copy 23 % by impurity (51 % together); by permutation +5.9 and +3.3 points. Without the copy: area 42 % and +13.6 points. The impurity credit is split roughly in half; each permutation importance drops even more, because when one copy is shuffled the other still carries the size.
E3. Impurity: area 19 %, perimeter 22 %, diameter 16 %: together 57 %, the largest group. Permutation: −0.7, +1.8, +1.5 points: each looks almost useless. The block bar: +14.9 points. Size is important (with texture removed it is the main information); each single size feature is redundant given the other two. OOB error 24.0 %, almost twice that with texture.
E4. Texture decides: noise 4 % and coin 1 % by impurity, −0.1 and −0.2 by permutation. Without texture (the “size block” settings): noise 10 %, coin 2 % by impurity; +1.1 and +0.5 by permutation. Without a strong feature, the trees need many more splits to purify the nodes; in the small nodes deep in the trees the continuous noise feature, with 400 distinct values, often wins by chance. The yes/no coin offers only one threshold and wins rarely. Permutation stays near zero for both.
E5. m = 1: area 15 %, perimeter 12 %, diameter 15 % (the feature is a coin toss at every split, so the three share almost equally). m = 8: area 12 %, perimeter 6 %, diameter 0 %. With every feature a candidate at every split, area and diameter always offer exactly the same best split; the tie goes to the feature listed first (area), so diameter is never used. The split of credit between duplicates depends on details like this; it says nothing about the features themselves.

title: Exercise: forests on feature tables, and feature importance
text:
Where this leads
The last unit of the day applies the forest to every pixel of an image, with features computed by filters at several scales, and trains it from a few painted strokes. Feature importance returns there as “which filters does the forest use?”, and the OOB error meets a new trap: neighbouring pixels are not independent.

title: Quiz: forests on feature tables, and feature importance
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Your table has area in µm², intensity in camera counts (0–4095) and solidity (0–1). Do you need to standardise the columns before training a forest?






Hint





What does a split compare?









Answer





No. Each split compares one feature with its own threshold; the units and ranges of the other features play no role. (Distance-based classifiers such as nearest neighbour or the SVM do need it.)




Q2. How is the impurity importance of a feature computed, in one sentence?






Hint





Every split purifies its node a little.









Answer





Add up the impurity decreases of all splits that use the feature, each weighted by the fraction of the training objects reaching that node, and average over the trees.




Q3. Why is permutation importance usually computed on out-of-bag or held-out objects rather than on the training objects?






Hint





What is the training error of a forest of deep trees?









Answer





On the training objects the forest is almost perfect and partly memorised; shuffling a column measures how much the memorisation depends on it, not how much prediction on new objects does. On OOB or held-out objects the error rise is about generalisation.




Q4. Area has permutation importance 0.1 points, perimeter 0.3, equivalent diameter −0.2. Can you drop all three?






Hint





What happens when you shuffle one of three features that carry the same information?









Answer





Not without checking: the three are strongly correlated, so each can be shuffled without loss because the other two still carry the size. Shuffle them together (or drop all three and compare the OOB error). If that hurts, size matters, and one of them (any) should be kept.




Q5. A random noise column gets 8 % of the impurity importance. How can that be?






Hint





Where in the tree do these splits happen?









Answer





Deep trees split small nodes until they are pure. In a small node, a continuous noise feature with many distinct values offers many thresholds and often purifies the node best by chance. These decreases are counted on the training data, so noise collects a share. Its permutation importance on OOB data stays near zero.




Q6. Shuffling the area column creates cells with a large area and a small perimeter. Why is that a problem for permutation importance?






Hint





Did the forest ever see such cells?









Answer





Such objects do not exist in the data; the forest’s predictions for them are extrapolations that were never trained. The error rise then partly measures the behaviour on impossible objects, not the value of the feature. Permuting correlated features as a group avoids this.




Q7. (math) In a tree, a node with 40 objects and Gini 0.48 is split into children of 30 objects (Gini 0.2) and 10 objects (Gini 0). The training set has 200 objects. What does this split add to its feature’s impurity importance?






Hint





\tfrac{n_t}{n}\Delta G.









Answer





\Delta G = 0.48 - \tfrac{30}{40}0.2 - 0 = 0.33; weighted by 40/200 = 0.2: 0.066.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
About this lecture
Last unit: one deep tree fits its training data perfectly but is unstable: change a few points and the whole tree changes. Today we turn that into a strength (Breiman, 1996 and 2001).

Grow many trees, each on a bootstrap sample, and let them vote: bagging.
Averaging helps only as far as the trees make different mistakes.
Random forest: each split looks at a random subset of the features, so the trees differ more.
Out-of-bag error: a validation estimate for free.
Vote fractions as probabilities, and where they mislead.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: Bagging and random forests
section: One tree: low bias, high variance
text:
One tree: low bias, high variance

A tree grown fully follows every training point: on average it is in the right place (low bias), but it moves a lot with the particular sample of data (high variance).
Measurements have the same problem, and the same cure: average several of them.
But we have only one training set. How do we get many trees?


Recall from the decision-trees unit: on the noisy-overlap data one full tree has 0 % training error and 28.8 % test error. A shallower tree (depth 4) has 21.0 %: less variance, more bias. Averaging tries to get the low bias of deep trees with less of their variance.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
The bootstrap

Draw n points from the n training points with replacement.
Some points are drawn twice or three times, about a third are not drawn at all.
Each draw is a new, slightly different training set from the same data.
Bagging (bootstrap aggregating): grow one tree per bootstrap sample, let all trees vote.

title: Bagging and random forests
section: The math: one in three is left out
text:
The math: one in three is left out
The chance that one particular point is not chosen in one draw is 1 - \tfrac1n; the n draws are independent: P(\text{point not in the sample}) = \left(1 - \frac1n\right)^n \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} e^{-1} \approx 0.368 . n = 5: 0.328; n = 20: 0.358; n = 1000: 0.368. The expected number of distinct points in a bootstrap sample is n\,(1 - (1 - 1/n)^n) \approx 0.632\, n.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Try it: bootstrap samples




With n = 20 the first sample (seed fixed) leaves out 6 points and draws 4 points more than once (two of them three times). “draw 1000”: the out-of-bag fraction has mean 35.6 %, close to (1 − 1/20)^20 = 0.358; for large n it approaches 1/e = 0.368. With n = 5 the fraction jumps around a lot (standard deviation 13.9 percentage points over 1000 samples).

title: Bagging and random forests
section: Averaging helps only if the trees differ
text:
Averaging helps only if the trees differ

Average B predictions, each with the same spread.
If they are independent, the spread of the average shrinks without limit as B grows.
If they are correlated (they make similar mistakes), it shrinks only down to a floor set by the correlation.
Bagged trees on the same data are alike: the strongest feature is chosen at the root of almost every tree.

title: Bagging and random forests
section: The math: the variance of an average
text:
The math: the variance of an average
B predictors f_1, \dots, f_B, each with variance \sigma^2, every pair with correlation \rho: \operatorname{Var}\Big(\frac1B\sum_b f_b\Big) = \frac{1}{B^2}\Big(\sum_b \operatorname{Var} f_b + \sum_{b \ne c}\operatorname{Cov}(f_b, f_c)\Big) = \frac{B\sigma^2 + B(B-1)\rho\sigma^2}{B^2} = \rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{B}\,\sigma^2 .

B \to \infty leaves \rho\sigma^2: more trees cannot beat the correlation.
\sigma^2 = 1, \rho = 0.3: 1, 0.370, 0.307 for B = 1, 10, 100; floor 0.3.
To lower the floor, lower \rho, even at some cost in each tree’s own accuracy.
Squared error = bias² + variance + noise. Averaging leaves the bias unchanged and lowers only the variance.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Try it: averaging correlated predictors




Dots: simulated variance of the average of B predictors (2000 runs, fixed seed); line: the formula; dashed: the floor ρσ². With σ² = 1, ρ = 0.3: 0.370 at B = 10, 0.307 at B = 100 (simulated 0.375 and 0.312). With ρ = 0 the line keeps falling (0.010 at B = 100); with ρ = 0.5 it stops at 0.5.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Random forests: decorrelate the trees

At each split, look only at a random subset of m features (out of d) and choose the best split among those.
A typical choice: m \approx \sqrt d for classification.
The strongest feature is not always available, so other features get their turn: the trees become less alike, and their average better.
Everything else as in bagging: bootstrap samples, deep trees, vote.

m = d is plain bagging; m = 1 makes every split’s feature a coin toss.

title: Bagging and random forests
section: Try it: a forest in the plane
text:
Try it: a forest in the plane




Tour: “one deep tree overfits”: 0 % training, 28.8 % test error, hard edges everywhere. “100 bagged trees”: the map softens (colour strength = confidence), test 23.4 %, OOB 26.0 %; the error-vs-trees curve flattens after a few dozen trees. The six small maps are individual trees: each on its own bootstrap sample. “m = d: trees look alike” (two moons with the extra features x + y, x − y, d = 4): tree correlation 0.68, test 8.7 %. “m = 1”: correlation 0.62, test 9.2 % — lower correlation, but each tree is weaker; here the trade does not pay. “noise features”: 4 pure-noise features added; the forest’s test error is 1.9 % (3.2 % without them) and a single tree 3.0 %. “confident far from the data”: the corners are coloured with probability 1.00. “uncertainty on the boundary”: pale colours along the boundary between the moons.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Out-of-bag (OOB) error

Each training point was left out by about a third of the trees.
Let only those trees vote on it: that is a prediction for a point they never saw.
The error rate of these votes is the out-of-bag error: a validation estimate for free, without setting data aside.
It assumes the training points are independent. Pixels in a painted stroke are not: the pixel-classification unit shows how OOB then fools you.


In the demo the OOB error (solid curve) and the test error on 1000 fresh points (dashed) track each other: 26.0 % and 23.4 % for the bagged overlap data, 10.6 % and 8.7 % for the moons.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Probabilities from votes

70 of 100 trees say “nucleus”: P(\text{nucleus}) \approx 0.7. (Each tree votes with its leaf’s class shares; fully grown leaves are pure, so this is a vote count.)
The probability map: confident inside the classes, uncertain near the boundary. Useful for deciding where to look or where to label more.
Caveat: far from all training data, every tree extends its outermost rectangles, so the forest can be confident where it has never seen anything. A vote fraction is not a calibrated certainty.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
The settings

Number of trees B: more never hurts accuracy, only time. The OOB error curve flattens; stop there.
Depth / leaf size: forests usually grow deep trees; averaging takes care of the variance.
m: the one that matters most, but often fine at the default.
No feature scaling, little tuning: a reason forests are a common first choice for tables of measurements and for pixel classification.

title: Bagging and random forests
section: The math: a forest as adaptive neighbours
text:
The math: a forest as adaptive neighbours
The forest’s class probability at \mathbf x is the average of the trees’ leaf shares, \hat p_k(\mathbf x) = \frac1B\sum_{b=1}^B \hat p_{k,b}(\mathbf x) . Each leaf share is an average over the training points in the leaf of \mathbf x. So \hat p_k(\mathbf x) is a weighted vote of training points, with weight high for points that often share a leaf with \mathbf x: a nearest-neighbour rule whose notion of “near” is learned from the labels (it ignores features that never help to split).

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Summary

Bootstrap: n draws with replacement; about 1/e \approx 37\,\% of the points are left out of each sample.
Bagging: many deep trees on bootstrap samples, averaged: less variance, same bias.
Averaging B correlated predictors: variance \rho\sigma^2 + (1-\rho)\sigma^2/B; the correlation sets the floor.
Random forest: a random subset of m features at each split lowers the correlation.
OOB error for free; vote fractions as probabilities, but confident far from the data.
Boosting is the sequential, bias-reducing relative.

title: Exercise: images in frequency space
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

predict where a wave or a stripe pattern shows up in the spectrum, and why a real image has a spectrum with mirror pairs,
explain what a shift does to the spectrum,
find the frequency response of a kernel by trying it on a few waves, and say whether it is low-pass or high-pass,
predict aliasing when an image is sampled too coarsely,
choose between low-pass, high-pass, band-pass and notch filters for a given problem,
(math) compute a small DFT by hand, prove that the waves are orthogonal, and derive the mirror symmetry, the shift theorem and the frequency response in general.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the interactive parts. Questions marked (math) ask for derivations; do the others first.

title: Exercise: images in frequency space
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

explain what a shift does to the spectrum,

title: Exercise: images in frequency space
text:
By hand
B1. The 8 samples x = (1, 0, -1, 0, 1, 0, -1, 0) are one wave. How many cycles does it complete in the window? Its spectrum has exactly two non-zero coefficients. At which frequencies, and why two?
B2. Predict where the bright dots are in the centred spectrum of a 256 × 256 image of (a) vertical stripes (lines running up and down), 16 pixels apart; (b) horizontal stripes, 4 pixels apart; (c) the sum of the two images. Which dots lie further from the centre, and why?
B3. (Frequency response by numbers.) Filter three signals of length 8 with the blur \tfrac14\,(1, 2, 1) and with the second difference (1, -2, 1), wrapping around at the ends: the flat signal 1, 1, 1, \dots; the slow wave 1, 0, -1, 0, 1, 0, -1, 0; the fastest wave 1, -1, 1, -1, \dots. Each output is the input wave multiplied by a number: find it. Which filter is low-pass and which high-pass? Compare the number for the flat signal with the sum of the weights.
B4. (Shift.) Shift the wave x = (1, 0, -1, 0) one step to the right, wrapping around: y = (0, 1, 0, -1). Its DFT is X = (0, 2, 0, 2), and that of y is Y = (0, -2i, 0, 2i). Compare the sizes |X_k| and |Y_k|. What does a shift change, and what does it keep? What does this mean for the magnitude spectrum of a cell that moves within an image?
B5. (Aliasing.) A stripe pattern repeats every 3 pixels: \cos(2\pi n/3) for n = 0, 1, 2, \dots You halve the image by keeping every 2nd pixel. Write down the kept samples for n = 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. What period do you see in the small image, and what period does that correspond to in the original pixels? Could the small image have shown the true pattern at all? What should you have done before keeping every 2nd pixel?






Solutions





B1. One cycle every 4 samples, so 2 cycles in the window of 8: frequency 2. A real wave such as \cos is the sum of two complex waves, frequency +2 and frequency -2, so it has two coefficients: X_2 = X_6 = 4 (index 6 = 8 - 2 is frequency -2), all others 0. That is the mirror pair.
B2. (a) Vertical stripes change brightness from left to right: dots on the horizontal axis, at 256/16 = 16 cycles, (u, v) = (\pm 16, 0). (b) Horizontal stripes change from top to bottom: dots on the vertical axis at 256/4 = 64, (0, \pm 64). (c) The DFT is linear, so the spectrum of the sum is the sum of the spectra: all four dots. The dots of (b) are four times further out, because those stripes are four times finer (higher frequency). In every case the pair of dots lies perpendicular to the stripes and mirrored through the centre.
B3. Blur, each output is \tfrac14(\text{left} + 2\cdot\text{centre} + \text{right}). Flat: 1, 1, 1, \dots, multiplied by 1. Slow wave: 0.5, 0, -0.5, 0, \dots, multiplied by 0.5. Fastest: \tfrac14(-1 + 2 - 1) = 0 everywhere, multiplied by 0. Second difference, \text{left} - 2\cdot\text{centre} + \text{right}: flat: 0, multiplied by 0. Slow wave: -2, 0, 2, 0, \dots, multiplied by −2. Fastest: -1 - 2 - 1 = -4 at a +1, so -4, 4, -4, \dots, multiplied by −4. The blur keeps the flat signal, halves the slow wave and removes the fastest: low-pass. The second difference removes the flat signal and grows with the frequency (0, 2, 4 in size): high-pass. The number for the flat signal is the sum of the weights: \tfrac14(1 + 2 + 1) = 1 and 1 - 2 + 1 = 0.
B4. |X| = (0, 2, 0, 2) and |Y| = (0, 2, 0, 2): the sizes are the same. The shift changed the complex numbers (2 \to -2i and 2 \to 2i), that is the phase of each wave: it now peaks one step later. The magnitude spectrum is unchanged. So a cell that moves within the image has the same magnitude spectrum: the magnitudes say what structures are there, the phases say where.
B5. The kept samples are \cos(2\pi n/3) at n = 0, 2, 4, \dots: 1, -0.5, -0.5, 1, -0.5, -0.5, 1. They repeat every 3 samples of the small image, which is 6 original pixels: a false pattern twice as coarse as the real one. The small image has pixels 2 original pixels apart and needs at least two samples per cycle, so it can only show periods of 4 original pixels or more: a period of 3 cannot be represented, and it folds back as period 6. Blur (low-pass) the image first, to remove the pattern before keeping every 2nd pixel; then the small image shows a flat grey instead of a false pattern.




Math questions
B6. (math) (Orthogonality.) Show that for integers m, n \ge 1, \int_0^1 \sin(2\pi m t)\,\sin(2\pi n t)\,dt = \begin{cases} 0 & m \ne n,\\ \tfrac12 & m = n.\end{cases} (Use \sin a \sin b = \tfrac12[\cos(a - b) - \cos(a + b)].) If f(t) = \sum_n a_n \sin(2\pi n t), how do you get a_3 back from f?
B7. (math) Compute the DFT X_k = \sum_{n=0}^{3} x_n e^{-2\pi i kn/4} of x = (1, 0, -1, 0) for k = 0, 1, 2, 3. Which wave is x? Why are there two non-zero coefficients for a single wave? (Check your answer against B4.)
B8. (math) Show that for a real signal x, X_{N-k} = \overline{X_k}. Use this to explain why a single stripe pattern in an image gives a pair of dots in its 2D spectrum, mirrored through the centre.
B9. (math) (Shift theorem.) Let y_n = x_{n-m} (indices modulo N: the signal is shifted by m and wraps around). Show that Y_k = e^{-2\pi i km/N}\, X_k. What happens to |X_k|, and what to the phase? What does this mean for the magnitude spectrum of a cell that moves within the image? (Compare with B4.)
B10. (math) (Frequency response.) Filtering with the 1D kernel w = (w_{-1}, w_0, w_1) multiplies the wave e^{i\omega n} by \hat w(\omega) = w_{-1}e^{-i\omega} + w_0 + w_1 e^{i\omega}. Compute \hat w(\omega) for
(a) the blur \tfrac14(1, 2, 1) and (b) the second difference (1, -2, 1).
Evaluate both at \omega = 0 (a constant signal) and \omega = \pi (the fastest wave the grid can hold: +1, -1, +1, \dots). Which is low-pass, which high-pass? Relate \hat w(0) to the sum of the weights. Check your formulas against the numbers of B3, where the slow wave has \omega = \pi/2.






Solutions (math)





B6. \sin(2\pi m t)\sin(2\pi n t) = \tfrac12[\cos 2\pi(m-n)t - \cos 2\pi(m+n)t]. Over one period, \int_0^1 \cos(2\pi j t)\,dt = 0 for any integer j \neq 0 and = 1 for j = 0. If m \ne n both terms integrate to 0. If m = n, the first term is \tfrac12 \cdot 1 and the second 0, giving \tfrac12. So, multiplying f by \sin(2\pi \cdot 3 t) and integrating kills every term except n = 3: a_3 = 2\int_0^1 f(t)\sin(6\pi t)\,dt. This is a projection onto one basis vector.
B7. e^{-2\pi i k n/4} = (-i)^{kn}, and only n = 0 and n = 2 contribute: X_k = 1 - (-i)^{2k} = 1 - (-1)^k. So X = (0, 2, 0, 2). The signal x_n = \cos(2\pi n/4) is one cycle of a cosine. Since \cos\theta = \tfrac12(e^{i\theta} + e^{-i\theta}), it is made of frequency +1 and frequency -1, and index k = 3 = N - 1 is frequency -1.
B8. X_{N-k} = \sum_n x_n e^{-2\pi i (N-k)n/N} = \sum_n x_n e^{-2\pi i n}\, e^{2\pi i kn/N} = \sum_n x_n e^{2\pi i kn/N}, since e^{-2\pi i n} = 1. For real x_n this is the complex conjugate of X_k. A real stripe pattern is a cosine wave, which needs both e^{+i\theta} and e^{-i\theta}: frequencies (u, v) and (-u, -v), a pair of dots mirrored through the centre, with equal magnitude.
B9. Y_k = \sum_n x_{n-m} e^{-2\pi i kn/N}. Substitute p = n - m (the sum runs over all residues modulo N either way): Y_k = \sum_p x_p e^{-2\pi i k(p+m)/N} = e^{-2\pi i km/N} X_k. The factor has modulus 1, so |Y_k| = |X_k|: the magnitude is unchanged and only the phase changes, by -2\pi km/N. The magnitude spectrum of an image does not depend on where the cell is: it describes what structures are present, not where. (This is why the magnitude spectrum is useful as a texture feature, and also why the phase cannot be thrown away when rebuilding an image.)
B10. (a) \hat w(\omega) = \tfrac14(e^{-i\omega} + 2 + e^{i\omega}) = \tfrac14(2 + 2\cos\omega) = \tfrac12(1 + \cos\omega). \hat w(0) = 1: constants pass unchanged. \hat w(\pi) = 0: the fastest wave is removed completely. Low-pass. (b) \hat w(\omega) = e^{-i\omega} - 2 + e^{i\omega} = 2\cos\omega - 2 = -4\sin^2(\omega/2). \hat w(0) = 0: constants are removed. \hat w(\pi) = -4: the fastest wave is amplified 4 times (and flipped). High-pass; for small \omega, \hat w \approx -\omega^2, the frequency response of a second derivative (\tfrac{d^2}{dt^2}e^{i\omega t} = -\omega^2 e^{i\omega t}). In both cases \hat w(0) = \sum w, the sum of the weights.

title: Exercise: images in frequency space
text:
Explore: build a wave
The demo below adds up five waves, a_f \sin(2\pi f\,t) for f = 1, \dots, 5 cycles per window, over one window 0 \le t \le 1. Each slider sets one amplitude a_f and has the same colour as its thin line in the plot; the bold black line is the sum. (A sine is a cosine with phase \varphi = -\pi/2.) The bar chart shows the amplitude spectrum |a_f|: the amount of each frequency, which is what the Fourier transform of the black curve gives back.



W1. Choose pure tone. How many cycles does the sum complete in the window, and what does the spectrum look like? Now set that slider to −1. What changes in the plot, and what changes in the spectrum? Which of the three sinusoid parameters (frequency, amplitude, phase) did the sign change?
W2. Start from all zero, set a_1 = 1, then add a_3 \approx 0.33 and finally a_5 = 0.2 (or press square). Describe how the shape of the sum changes at each step. Roughly what height do the flat parts reach? Which frequencies would you have to add to make the edges steeper still?
W3. Press sawtooth and compare its spectrum with the one for square. Then change the signs of a_2 and a_4 to +1/2 and +1/4. What happens to the signal, and to the spectrum? (Compare with B4 and B9.) Finally, change only a_3 to -1/3. Does the signal still have the same shape? What information does the amplitude spectrum leave out?






Solutions





W1. The pure tone is \sin(2\pi\cdot 2\cdot t): two cycles in the window, and a single bar at f = 2 of height 1. With amplitude −1 the wave is flipped upside down, which is the same as sliding it half a cycle along: the phase changed by \pi. Frequency and the height |a| are the same, so the amplitude spectrum does not change.
W2. a_1 alone is one smooth swell. Adding the third harmonic flattens the tops and steepens the sides; adding the fifth flattens them further, with small ripples on the plateaus. The flat parts sit near \pm\pi/4 \approx \pm 0.79 (that is the limit of \sin x + \tfrac13\sin 3x + \tfrac15\sin 5x + \dots; with three terms the plateaus wiggle around this value). Steeper edges need higher odd harmonics: f = 7, 9, 11, \dots with amplitudes 1/7, 1/9, \dots. Sharp edges live at high frequencies.
W3. The square wave uses only the odd frequencies; the sawtooth uses all five, with heights 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5. Flipping the signs of a_2 and a_4 gives the same sawtooth, moved by half a window: shifting t by 1/2 multiplies \sin(2\pi f t) by (-1)^f, so it flips exactly the even frequencies. The spectrum is unchanged, as in B4 and B9: a time shift changes the phases, not the amplitudes. Flipping only a_3 is not a shift: the signal gets a clearly different shape, yet the bars are still the same. The amplitude spectrum leaves out the phase of each wave (here only its sign), so different signals can share the same amplitude spectrum. The full Fourier transform keeps the phase too, which is why the signal can be rebuilt from it.

title: Exercise: images in frequency space
text:
Explore: filter an image
The demo below is the lecture’s micrograph (a 256 × 256 crop). Left: the image; middle: its 2D spectrum, log of the magnitude, with frequency 0 in the centre; right: the image rebuilt from the coefficients you keep. Removed coefficients are shown dark red. The radial filters keep the coefficients whose distance r from the centre lies between a min radius and a max radius (the two blue circles; ∞ means no upper limit). The buttons are presets: low-pass sets min = 0, high-pass sets max = ∞, band-pass uses both. The box “keep average brightness (centre)” keeps the centre coefficient whatever the min radius is. The readout gives the share of coefficients kept, the share of the image’s variation they carry, and the RMS error of the rebuilt image (pixel values run from 0 to 1).



E1. Choose low-pass (min radius 0) and set the max radius to 5, 30 and 90. For each, note the percentage of coefficients kept and the percentage of the variation kept. What does that tell you about where the image’s content sits in the spectrum?
E2. Choose keep largest at 3%. Then go back to low-pass and find the max radius that also keeps about 3% of the coefficients. Which of the two has the smaller error? Look at where the kept coefficients lie in the spectrum in “keep largest” mode: why are the two results so similar?
E3. Choose high-pass (max radius ∞) with min radius 10. What is left of the cell? Why is the picture grey rather than black, although most of the low frequencies are gone? Untick keep average brightness (centre) to check your answer.
E4. Tick add stripe artefact and choose no filter: note the error. The stripe adds two bright coefficients to the spectrum, marked with yellow rings. Erase them by dragging over them. What happens to the error? Why are there two dots for one stripe? Then try removing the stripe with a low-pass filter instead, at max radius 15. Which approach is better here?
E5. Go back to low-pass with max radius 30, then raise the min radius from 0 to 5, so that only a ring between the two circles is kept. How many coefficients does that remove, and how much of the variation? What disappears from the image, and what is left? Compare with E1.






Solutions





E1. Radius 5 keeps 0.12% of the coefficients but already 53% of the variation; radius 30 keeps 4.3% of the coefficients and 81% of the variation; radius 90 keeps 39% and 96%. A tiny disc of low frequencies carries most of the variation: the broad light and dark regions. The many high-frequency coefficients each carry little; together they make the fine detail (and the grain). This is why a frequency basis compresses natural images well.
E2. Keep largest 3%: 81% of the variation, RMS error 0.100. Low-pass with max radius 25 also keeps 3.0% of the coefficients: 78% of the variation, error 0.109. Keeping the largest coefficients is slightly better, because it picks the coefficients that matter for this image, while the disc is fixed in advance. They are similar because most of the largest coefficients are low frequencies anyway: in “keep largest” mode the kept coefficients crowd around the centre, with a scatter of single ones further out.
E3. Only edges and fine texture remain: the outline of the nucleus, the membranes, the grain inside the cell. Large uniform regions all become the same grey, because their brightness is low-frequency content. The picture stays grey because the centre coefficient (frequency 0, the average brightness of the whole image) is kept by the “keep average brightness” box, even though it lies inside the min radius. Untick the box and the average of the rebuilt image drops from 0.66 to 0: the values vary around 0, the negative half is shown as black (about half the pixels), and the RMS error jumps from 0.18 to 0.69.
E4. With the stripe and no filter the error is 0.106 (the stripe itself). The stripe is a single 2D wave, so it adds a single bright pair of coefficients, about 19 units from the centre (16 across, 10 down, and its mirror image). Erasing them brings the error down to about 0.02; zeroing exactly the two coefficients would give 0.002, the brush also removes a few of the cell’s own coefficients around them. There are two dots because a real-valued wave is the sum of a frequency and its mirror image (+k and -k), the mirror symmetry of B1 and B8. A low-pass filter at max radius 15 also removes the stripe, but it removes the cell’s detail too: the error is 0.127, worse than leaving the stripe in. A notch removes exactly what you want to remove; a low-pass removes everything above a frequency.
E5. Raising the min radius from 0 to 5 removes very few coefficients: the kept share drops from 4.3% to 4.2% (only 68 of the 65 536 coefficients lie inside radius 5, not counting the centre, which is kept). But the variation kept drops from 81% to 29%, and the RMS error rises from 0.10 to 0.19. As in E1, the few lowest frequencies carry about half of the variation: they are the broad shading, such as the dark nucleus against the lighter cytoplasm. Without them the nucleus becomes the same mid grey as its surroundings, and what is left is structure of intermediate size: the outline of the nucleus, membranes and small organelles, but neither the overall shading (below the min radius) nor the fine grain (above the max radius). A band-pass picks out structures of one size range.

title: Exercise: images in frequency space
text:
Where this leads
Frequency-space features (peaks, orientation, texture energy in a ring) are a classic input for classifying textures. Larger blurs at many scales (a scale space) and the Laplacian of Gaussian come back when we detect objects. The next unit, principal component analysis, is another change of basis: not fixed waves, but directions learned from a set of images.

title: Quiz: images in frequency space
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Why does the discrete Fourier transform lose no information about an image?






Answer





It is a change of basis. An image of N pixels becomes N wave amounts: the same vector written in another coordinate system, as when you describe a point by different axes. Nothing is thrown away, and you can always go back exactly. (In formulas: X = Fx with an invertible matrix F, F^{-1} = \tfrac1N F^* because the waves are orthogonal, and x = F^{-1}X recovers the image.)




Q2. In the centred spectrum of a micrograph, where do you find the information about (a) the overall brightness, (b) the broad shape of the cell, (c) the fine texture and the noise?






Answer






The single centre coefficient, frequency (0, 0): it is N^2 times the mean grey level. (b) Close to the centre: low frequencies. (c) Far from the centre: high frequencies. Note that sharp real edges are high-frequency as well, so a low-pass filter that removes noise also blurs edges.





Q3. An image has a regular pattern of horizontal stripes (lines running left–right), 8 pixels apart, in a 256 × 256 image. Where are the bright dots in its spectrum?






Hint





The brightness changes when you move up and down, not left–right. How many cycles fit in the image?









Answer





On the vertical axis through the centre, at 256/8 = 32 cycles: the pair (u, v) = (0, \pm 32). The dots are perpendicular to the stripes, and come in a mirror pair because the image is real.




Q4. You blur an image by convolving with a 31 \times 31 Gaussian kernel. How else could you compute the same result, and why might it be faster?






Answer





By the convolution theorem: FFT the image and the (zero-padded) kernel, multiply the spectra, inverse FFT. Direct convolution costs about 31^2 \approx 960 multiplications per pixel; the FFT route costs \mathcal{O}(\log N) per pixel. (The Gaussian is also separable: a 31-tap pass along rows then along columns, 62 multiplications per pixel.) Beware: the FFT treats the image as periodic, so pad the image to avoid wrap-around at the border.




Q5. You reduce a photo of a brick wall to a quarter of its size by keeping every 4th pixel in each direction. A strange wavy pattern appears that is not on the wall. What happened, and how do you prevent it?






Answer





Aliasing. The new grid can only hold frequencies up to a quarter of the original Nyquist frequency; the fine brick pattern is above that and folds back as a false, coarser pattern (moiré). Low-pass filter (blur) the image first, so that what the coarse grid cannot represent is removed before sampling.




Q6. A detector adds a faint regular stripe to every image. Should you remove it with a low-pass filter or a notch filter? Why?






Answer





A notch. The stripe is a single wave, so in the spectrum it is one isolated pair of dots; zeroing just those (and their immediate neighbours) removes the stripe and leaves everything else. A low-pass filter would also remove every real structure finer than the stripe.




Q7. A cell sits in the left half of an image. In a second image, the same cell has moved 30 pixels to the right (on the same flat background). How do the two magnitude spectra |X_{u,v}| compare? What has changed in the full spectrum?






Hint





Shifting a wave slides its peaks along. Does it make the wave stronger or weaker?









Answer





The magnitude spectra are the same. Moving the image shifts every wave in it, which changes where its peaks are (its phase), not how strong it is. The magnitude spectrum describes what structures are present, not where; the position is stored in the phases. (Strictly this holds exactly for a shift that wraps around the image, which on a flat background is the same thing.)

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
About this lecture
k-means describes a group by one point and cuts the space with straight lines. Now each group gets a shape, a size and a weight: a Gaussian.

One Gaussian in 2D: a hill whose contour lines are ellipses, set by the covariance matrix \Sigma.
Mahalanobis distance: “how many standard deviations away”, in the direction you are going.
Covariance types: spherical, diagonal, full, tied.
The mixture as a recipe for making data; the hidden component of each point; responsibilities (soft labels) by Bayes’ rule.
The likelihood of a data set, and why one Gaussian is easy to fit and a mixture is not.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
From one dimension to two
In 1D the normal density is a bell: centre \mu, width \sigma. What matters is how many standard deviations x is from \mu: (x - \mu)/\sigma.
In 2D (two features per pixel) the density is a hill over the plane.

Its contour lines (points of equal density) are ellipses around the centre \boldsymbol\mu.
Round hill: both features vary equally and independently. Stretched hill: one direction varies more. Tilted hill: the features are correlated (bright in one channel, bright in the other).
All of this is in one 2 \times 2 matrix, the covariance \Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_1^2 & c \\ c & \sigma_2^2 \end{pmatrix}: variances on the diagonal, covariance c off it.

Notation: \Sigma for the covariance of a model component, S for a covariance computed from data.

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Reading an ellipse: an example




\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, centred at \mathbf 0.

Eigenvalues \lambda_1 = 6, \lambda_2 = 1; eigenvectors \mathbf v_1 = (2, 1)/\sqrt5, \mathbf v_2 = (-1, 2)/\sqrt5.
The 1σ ellipse: half-axis \sqrt6 = 2.45 along (2, 1), half-axis 1 across it. Tilted by 26.6°.
Check: \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = 7 = 5 + 2 (the trace), \lambda_1\lambda_2 = 6 = 5 \cdot 2 - 2^2 (the determinant).

The points P = (2, 1) and Q = (-1, 2) are both \sqrt5 = 2.24 from the centre. Is either of them unusual?

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Mahalanobis distance
Euclidean distance ignores the shape of the cloud. The Mahalanobis distance measures in standard deviations along the direction you are going:
d_M(\mathbf x)^2 = (\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu).

In 1D: d_M = |x - \mu|/\sigma, the familiar “how many sigmas”.
The 1σ ellipse is exactly d_M = 1; the 2σ ellipse d_M = 2.
In the example: P lies along the long axis, d_M(P) = \sqrt{5/6} = 0.91, inside the 1σ ellipse. Q lies along the short axis, d_M(Q) = \sqrt5 = 2.24: more than 2σ out. Same Euclidean distance, very different.

Use: “is this pixel (or object) unusual for this class?” (unit 4: anomalies).

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
section: The math: the density and its ellipses
text:
The math: the density and its ellipses
\mathcal N(\mathbf x \mid \boldsymbol\mu, \Sigma) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}\,|\Sigma|^{1/2}}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12 (\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu)\right)
In 1D the exponent is -\tfrac12 (x - \mu)^2/\sigma^2; \Sigma^{-1} replaces 1/\sigma^2.

\Sigma is symmetric positive definite: \Sigma = Q\Lambda Q^\top with orthonormal eigenvectors in Q and \Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_d). In the rotated coordinates \mathbf y = Q^\top(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu): d_M^2 = \sum_i y_i^2/\lambda_i.
So the density factorises into independent 1D normals with variances \lambda_i along the eigenvectors, and d_M = 1 is the ellipse with half-axes \sqrt{\lambda_i}. |\Sigma| = \prod_i\lambda_i.
Sampling: with \mathbf z standard normal (d independent \mathcal N(0, 1)), \mathbf x = \boldsymbol\mu + Q\Lambda^{1/2}\mathbf z has covariance Q\Lambda^{1/2}\Lambda^{1/2}Q^\top = \Sigma. (Any L with LL^\top = \Sigma, e.g. the Cholesky factor, works too.)
Example: \Sigma^{-1} = \frac16\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{pmatrix}; d_M(P)^2 = \frac16(8 - 8 + 5) = \frac56; d_M(Q)^2 = \frac16(2 + 8 + 20) = 5.

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Try it: one Gaussian




Preset “same Euclidean distance, different Mahalanobis”: Σ = [5 2; 2 2]. The readout gives λ1 = 6, λ2 = 1, the angle 26.6°, and for P = (2, 1): Euclidean 2.24, Mahalanobis 0.91, density 0.043; for Q = (−1, 2): Euclidean 2.24, Mahalanobis 2.24, density 0.005. Drag the square handles: the ellipse turns and stretches; the samples (300, fixed seed) follow. Switch Σ to “spherical”: circles, Mahalanobis = Euclidean / σ. “diagonal”: axis-aligned ellipses only.

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Covariance types
How much freedom each group’s shape gets. For K components in d dimensions, numbers per component:
