Total parameters = K - 1 weights + Kd means + covariance numbers. Colour pixels (d = 3), K = 3: spherical 2 + 9 + 3 = 14, diagonal 20, full 29, tied 17.
More freedom fits better, but needs more data and can overfit (unit 3).

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
section: A mixture is a recipe for data
text:
A mixture is a recipe for data
A Gaussian mixture with K components makes one data point like this:

pick a component k at random, with probability \pi_k (the weights, summing to 1);
draw \mathbf x from that component’s Gaussian \mathcal N(\boldsymbol\mu_k, \Sigma_k).

The density of the result is a weighted sum of hills:
p(\mathbf x) = \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k\,\mathcal N(\mathbf x \mid \boldsymbol\mu_k, \Sigma_k).
Image example: a pixel is background (weight 0.6, dark), cytoplasm (0.3, grey) or nucleus (0.1, bright), and its value scatters around the class mean.

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
The labels are hidden
We see the points, not which component made each one: the component is a hidden (latent) variable.

With colours (labels), fitting is easy: each class’s mean and covariance separately (this is supervised learning).
Without them, the clouds overlap and we must recover the recipe from the uncoloured points: unsupervised.
Fitting a mixture = finding \pi_k, \boldsymbol\mu_k, \Sigma_k that could have produced the data (unit 3).

In the demo: tick hide colours: this is what an algorithm gets.

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Responsibilities: soft labels
Given the parameters, which component made \mathbf x? Bayes’ rule, as on the thresholding day:
r_k(\mathbf x) = P(k \mid \mathbf x) = \frac{\pi_k\,\mathcal N(\mathbf x \mid \boldsymbol\mu_k, \Sigma_k)}{p(\mathbf x)}.

A soft label: “70 % component 1, 30 % component 2”. The r_k sum to 1.
The hard label is the component with the largest r_k.
1D example: \pi = (0.7, 0.3), \mu = (100, 160), \sigma = 20 for both. At x = 130 (halfway) the two densities are equal, so r_1 = 0.7: the weights decide. At x = 120: r_1 = 0.91; at x = 140: r_1 = 0.34.
The boundary (r_1 = r_2) is at 135.6, not at the midpoint 130: the more frequent class gets more room.

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Bayes boundaries: straight or curved
Where two components are equally probable, \pi_1\mathcal N_1(\mathbf x) = \pi_2\mathcal N_2(\mathbf x):

same covariance (tied): the boundary is a straight line (a plane), shifted by the weights. k-means’ bisector is the special case of equal weights and round, equal components.
different covariances: a curved boundary (a conic: ellipse, parabola or hyperbola). The wider component wins far away on both sides.
1D: \mathcal N(0, 1) and \mathcal N(3, 2^2), equal weights: the narrow component wins only for -3.42 < x < 1.42. Far to the left the wide one wins again.

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
section: The math: tied covariances give straight boundaries
text:
The math: tied covariances give straight boundaries
Take logs of \pi_1\mathcal N_1(\mathbf x) = \pi_2\mathcal N_2(\mathbf x) with \Sigma_1 = \Sigma_2 = \Sigma:
\log\pi_1 - \tfrac12(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu_1)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu_1) = \log\pi_2 - \tfrac12(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu_2)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu_2).
The normalising constants are equal and cancel; so does \mathbf x^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf x:
\mathbf x^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\boldsymbol\mu_1 - \boldsymbol\mu_2) = \tfrac12\left(\boldsymbol\mu_1^\top\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol\mu_1 - \boldsymbol\mu_2^\top\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol\mu_2\right) + \log\frac{\pi_2}{\pi_1}:
linear in \mathbf x. With \Sigma_1 \ne \Sigma_2 the term \tfrac12\mathbf x^\top(\Sigma_2^{-1} - \Sigma_1^{-1})\mathbf x survives: a quadratic boundary. In 1D with equal variances: x = \frac{\mu_1 + \mu_2}{2} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu_2 - \mu_1}\log\frac{\pi_1}{\pi_2}, the thresholding day’s equal-variance threshold. Example: 130 + \frac{400}{60}\log\frac{0.7}{0.3} = 135.6.

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Try it: a mixture




Preset “two overlapping components”: weights 0.6 and 0.4. The samples are coloured by the component that produced them; tick “hide colours”: that is what an algorithm sees. P at (0.3, 0.3): responsibilities 75 % / 25 %. Move the weight sliders: the bar changes although nothing moved. “same covariance: straight boundary” with the background “most probable component”: a straight line; change one weight and it shifts parallel. “different covariances: curved boundary”: the narrow component’s region is an island; the wide one wins on both sides.

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
section: The likelihood of a data set
text:
The likelihood of a data set
How well do parameters \theta explain the data? The likelihood: the probability density of the observed points, treated as a function of \theta:
p(\mathcal D \mid \theta) = \prod_i p(\mathbf x_i \mid \theta), \qquad \log p(\mathcal D \mid \theta) = \sum_i \log p(\mathbf x_i \mid \theta).

Maximum likelihood: choose the parameters that make the observed data most probable.
For one Gaussian the answer is in closed form: \boldsymbol\mu = the sample mean, \Sigma = the sample covariance S (divided by n).
For a mixture, \log p(\mathcal D) = \sum_i \log \sum_k \pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x_i): a log of a sum, and no closed form. If we knew the hidden labels, each component would be fitted by its own mean and covariance. That chicken-and-egg problem is unit 3.

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
section: The math: maximum likelihood for one Gaussian
text:
The math: maximum likelihood for one Gaussian
\log p(\mathcal D) = -\frac{nd}{2}\log 2\pi - \frac n2\log|\Sigma| - \frac12\sum_i(\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu).

Gradient in \boldsymbol\mu: \Sigma^{-1}\sum_i(\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu) = 0 \Rightarrow \hat{\boldsymbol\mu} = \frac1n\sum_i\mathbf x_i.
In \Sigma^{-1} =: P (using \partial\log|P|/\partial P = P^{-1} and \partial\,\mathbf a^\top P\mathbf a/\partial P = \mathbf a\mathbf a^\top): \frac n2 P^{-1} - \frac12\sum_i(\mathbf x_i - \hat{\boldsymbol\mu})(\mathbf x_i - \hat{\boldsymbol\mu})^\top = 0 \Rightarrow \hat\Sigma = \frac1n\sum_i(\mathbf x_i - \hat{\boldsymbol\mu})(\mathbf x_i - \hat{\boldsymbol\mu})^\top = S.
With known labels the mixture splits into K such problems, plus \hat\pi_k = n_k/n. With hidden labels the \log\sum_k couples everything.

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Generative and discriminative
The same 2D point cloud, two ways of learning from it:

With labels (random-forests day, SVM elective): learn a boundary between the classes directly. Discriminative: says nothing about where points come from.
Without labels (this day): learn a model of how the points were made, a mixture. Generative: it gives a density p(\mathbf x), can draw new points, can say “this point is unlikely under every class”, and its Bayes boundaries come for free.

Generative models need more assumptions (here: Gaussian groups). When the assumptions hold, few data suffice; when they do not, a discriminative boundary is usually more accurate.

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Summary

A 2D Gaussian is a hill with elliptical contours: axes = eigenvectors of \Sigma, half-lengths \sqrt{\lambda_i} (1σ).
Mahalanobis distance d_M^2 = (\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu): standard deviations in the direction of \mathbf x.
Covariance types: spherical, diagonal, full, tied: more freedom, more parameters.
A mixture: pick a component with probability \pi_k, then draw from its Gaussian; the component is hidden.
Responsibilities r_k(\mathbf x) = \pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x)/p(\mathbf x): soft labels; boundaries straight for tied covariances, curved otherwise.
Likelihood \sum_i\log p(\mathbf x_i): one Gaussian has a closed-form fit; a mixture does not (next unit).

title: Exercise: geodesic active contours
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

turn an image into an edge-stopping function g by hand, and say where a front slows down,
explain why a braking balloon does not stop on its own, and what the advection term adds,
predict what the parameters \sigma, k, c, \varepsilon, a do, and when the front leaks or gets stuck,
use one curve to segment several objects (outside-in) or grow seeds (inside-out),
(math) compute the first variation of the edge-weighted length for a circle, and find equilibria.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: geodesic active contours
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

turn an image into an edge-stopping function g by hand, and say where a front slows down,
explain why a braking balloon does not stop on its own, and what the advection term adds,
predict what the parameters \sigma, k, c, \varepsilon, a do, and when the front leaks or gets stuck,
use one curve to segment several objects (outside-in) or grow seeds (inside-out),
(math) compute the first variation of the edge-weighted length for a circle, and find equilibria.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: geodesic active contours
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Edge strength
\lvert\nabla I_\sigma\rvert: gradient magnitude of the image smoothed with a Gaussian of width \sigma


Edge-stopping function
g = 1/(1 + \lvert\nabla I_\sigma\rvert^2/k^2): 1 in flat regions, small on edges; g = 0.5 at strength k, 0.1 at 3k


Braking balloon
outward speed F = g\,(c - \varepsilon\kappa); c > 0 inflates, c < 0 shrinks


Geodesic active contour
minimise \oint g\,ds; adds an advection along -\nabla g (strength a), into the edge


Level set form
\phi_t = -g c\lvert\nabla\phi\rvert + \varepsilon g\kappa\lvert\nabla\phi\rvert + a\,\nabla g\cdot\nabla\phi (\phi < 0 inside)









The math: first variation of the weighted length





Moving each point of a closed curve outward by a small \delta(s) changes L_g = \oint g\,ds by \oint(g\kappa + \nabla g\cdot\mathbf n)\,\delta\,ds: the length element grows by \kappa\delta\,ds and the weight changes by \nabla g\cdot\mathbf n\,\delta. Steepest descent: F = -(g\kappa + \nabla g\cdot\mathbf n), which in level set form is \phi_t = g\kappa|\nabla\phi| + \nabla g\cdot\nabla\phi.

title: Exercise: geodesic active contours
text:
By hand
B1. A 1D edge. The pixels 0, 0, 0, 10, 10, 10. (a) Smooth with [1\ 2\ 1]/4 (repeat the border pixels). (b) Compute |\nabla I| with central differences \tfrac12(I_{i+1} - I_{i-1}) and g for k = 2. (c) A front moves with speed g (balloon c = 1). Where is it slowest? Does it fall below 0.1 anywhere? Which k would be needed for that? (d) Compute -g' (central differences) at each pixel. On which side of the edge does it point right, and on which left?
B2. Strong and weak edges. A step of height h blurred by a Gaussian of width \sigma has a largest slope of h/(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}). In the demo’s test image the objects are 130 grey levels above the background, but one disk fades to only 25 above it on one side; \sigma = 1.5, k = 8. (a) Compute g at the centre of the strong edge and of the weak edge. (b) A braking balloon with c = 0.3 (no advection) reaches the strong edge. How long does it need to creep through a 3-pixel-wide band where g \approx 0.06?
B3. Balloon against curvature. In a flat region (g = 1, no advection), a circle of radius r moves with F = c - \varepsilon/r. (a) For which radius does it stand still? What happens to circles slightly smaller or larger? (b) You click seed circles of radius 8 with c = 0.3, \varepsilon = 0.3. Do they grow? And with c = 0.05, \varepsilon = 1?
B4. Predict. Describe in one sentence what happens to the segmentation of a noisy image when you (a) set \sigma = 0, (b) make \sigma very large, (c) make k very large, (d) make |c| very large, (e) set a = 0, (f) make \varepsilon very large.
B5. Outside-in and inside-out. An image has 5 bright cells, two of which touch. (a) You start with one big box and c < 0. How many curves do you expect at the end, and what could make it 4? (b) You click 2 seeds in each cell and use c > 0. What happens to the two seeds in one cell?






Solutions





B1. (a) 0, 0, 2.5, 7.5, 10, 10. (b) |\nabla I| = 0, 1.25, 3.75, 3.75, 1.25, 0; g = 1, 0.72, 0.22, 0.22, 0.72, 1. (c) Slowest on the two middle pixels, at 22% speed. It never falls below 0.1: that needs |\nabla I| > 3k, so k < 3.75/3 = 1.25 (with k = 1: g = 0.066). (d) -g' = 0.14, 0.39, 0.25, -0.25, -0.39, -0.14: positive (pointing right) on the left half, negative (pointing left) on the right half. From both sides it points to the edge between pixels 3 and 4.
B2. (a) Strong: slope 130/(1.5\sqrt{2\pi}) = 34.6 grey levels per pixel, g = 1/(1 + (34.6/8)^2) = 0.051. Weak: slope 6.6, g = 0.59: the front hardly notices it. (The demo, with noise and the shapes’ curvature, measures about 0.06 and 0.44.) (b) Speed 0.06 \cdot 0.3 = 0.018 pixels per unit time: 3/0.018 \approx 170 time units. The braking balloon only delays; given time, it crosses every edge.
B3. (a) F = 0 at r^* = \varepsilon/c. Smaller circles have \varepsilon/r > c and shrink (and vanish), larger ones grow: an unstable equilibrium. (b) r^* = 0.3/0.3 = 1: radius 8 grows. With c = 0.05, \varepsilon = 1: r^* = 20, so seeds of radius 8 shrink and disappear before they can reach any edge.
B4. (a) Noise makes g small almost everywhere: the front sticks near its start. (b) Edges blur into each other and weak edges disappear: objects merge, small ones are lost, boundaries are rounded. (c) g \approx 1 even on real edges: the front passes through them. (d) It leaks through every weak edge and overshoots corners. (e) Only braking: the front slows at edges but keeps creeping and eventually crosses them. (f) Curves become round and short: concave parts are cut off, small objects vanish.
B5. (a) Five, one per cell, if the touching cells are separated by an edge strong enough; if the boundary between the two touching cells is weak (or \sigma large), they stay together in one curve: 4. (b) They grow and merge into one curve when their fronts meet: the topology adapts.




Math questions
B6. (math) Let g depend only on the distance \rho from a point, and let C be the circle of radius r around it. (a) Write L_g(r) = \oint g\,ds. (b) Compute dL_g/dr and show it equals \oint(g\kappa + \nabla g\cdot\mathbf n)\,ds. (c) For g(\rho) = 1 - 0.9\,e^{-(\rho - 10)^2/8} (a ring-shaped edge at \rho = 10), is the circle r = 10 a stationary point? Is it a minimum of L_g among circles?
B7. (math) Show that the advection term a\,\nabla g\cdot\nabla\phi in \phi_t corresponds to an outward normal speed F = -a\,\nabla g\cdot\mathbf n. Explain with this why a front just outside an edge moves inward, and one just inside moves outward.
B8. (math) The time-step limit for the advection part is \Delta t\,\max(|v_x| + |v_y|) \le \Delta x with \mathbf v = -a\nabla g. Why does a larger a, or a sharper edge (smaller \sigma), force a smaller time step?






Solutions (math)





B6. (a) L_g = 2\pi r\,g(r). (b) dL_g/dr = 2\pi(g + r g') = \oint(g/r + g')\,ds over the circle of length 2\pi r; with \kappa = 1/r and \nabla g\cdot\mathbf n = g'(r) this is \oint(g\kappa + \nabla g\cdot\mathbf n)\,ds. (c) At r = 10: g' = 0, g = 0.1: dL_g/dr = 2\pi \cdot 0.1 > 0, so it is not stationary: the length term still wants to shrink it. The minimum among circles is slightly inside the valley, where g + r g' = 0, i.e. g' = -g/r: here at r = 9.955 (found numerically). A balloon c > 0 can compensate this small inward shift. This is the shrinking bias of length terms, as for snakes and graph cuts.
B7. \phi_t + F|\nabla\phi| = 0 with \phi_t = a\nabla g\cdot\nabla\phi gives F = -a\nabla g\cdot\nabla\phi/|\nabla\phi| = -a\nabla g\cdot\mathbf n. Just outside an edge, g increases outward (\nabla g\cdot\mathbf n > 0): F < 0, inward. Just inside, g increases inward (\nabla g\cdot\mathbf n < 0): F > 0, outward. Both move towards the valley.
B8. |\mathbf v| = a|\nabla g|: doubling a doubles the speed, and a sharper edge makes g drop from 1 to near 0 over fewer pixels, so |\nabla g| is larger. Faster transport must still move at most one pixel per step.

title: Exercise: geodesic active contours
text:
Explore: edge-based segmentation
A 128 \times 128 image: a synthetic test image (three disks, the lower-left one fading on its right side, and a C shape; noise adjustable) or the micrograph. image / g switches the view to the edge-stopping function (white = 1, black = 0); −∇g arrows shows the advection direction. Start shapes: big box, or click the image to add start circles (radius 8). The yellow curve is the front; “pieces” counts its closed curves, and for the test image “wrong” counts pixels that differ from the true objects. \phi is reinitialised every 20 steps.



E1. Preset shrink-wrap (c = -0.3, \varepsilon = 0.3, a = 5, \sigma = 1.5, k = 8). Play. Note the step at which the front splits into 3 and into 4 pieces, and the final number of wrong pixels. Look at the g view and the arrows: where is g smallest, and where do the arrows point?
E2. Same preset, but set the advection a = 0 and reset. What happens, and why (compare B2(b))?
E3. Same preset with a = 5 again, but balloon c = -0.6. Watch the lower-left disk. How many pieces remain, and why?
E4. Preset leak through the weak edge (c = 1, a = 1, a seed inside the lower-left disk of 531 pixels). How many pixels are inside after 100 steps? Then try c = 0.3 with a = 1, and c = 0.3 with a = 3. Which settings hold the front?
E5. Preset C shape: no balloon (c = 0, \varepsilon = 1, a = 2, start: a circle around the C). Where does the front stop? Compare its area with that of the C itself (1020 pixels). Then set c = -0.3 and reset.
E6. Preset noise, no smoothing (noise 25, \sigma = 0). Look at the g view. What does the front do? Set \sigma = 2 and reset.
E7. Preset micrograph: nucleus (\sigma = 1.5, k = 4, c = 0.3, a seed in the nucleus). Where does the front stop? Try k = 8, and k = 2, each from a reset. Explain with B4.






Solutions





E1. (Δt = 0.195.) Around step 800 the front has split into 3 pieces, by step 1200 (t \approx 235) into 4: one per object. It then stays put with 79 wrong pixels (2376 inside; the true objects have 2455 pixels). g is darkest on the object boundaries (about 0.06), about 1 elsewhere (median 0.97); the weak right side of the lower-left disk is only grey (about 0.44). The arrows point into the dark rims from both sides.
E2. With a = 0 (Δt = 0.667) the front slows at the edges but never stops: it creeps through them into the objects, and by t \approx 530 nothing is left inside. Exactly as in B2(b): g > 0 everywhere, so a braking balloon only delays.
E3. At first four pieces (step 800), but the stronger push breaks through the weak side of the lower-left disk and eats it: 3 pieces by step 1600, 598 wrong pixels. The weak edge only holds while the advection beats g c.
E4. After 100 steps 1315 pixels are inside: the front has escaped through the weak side and floods the background (10795 pixels after 300 steps). With c = 0.3, a = 1 it still leaks, more slowly (2102 pixels after 300 steps). With c = 0.3, a = 3 it stops at 527 pixels, the disk.
E5. The front wraps the C but bridges the opening with an almost straight segment and stops with about 1600 pixels inside (after 4000 steps): the C plus most of its inner hole. With c = -0.3 the balloon pushes it into the slot: 979 pixels after 2000 steps, close to the C alone.
E6. In the g view the whole image is speckled dark (median g about 0.12): every noisy pixel is an “edge”. The box hardly moves (13194 pixels inside after 1200 steps). With \sigma = 2 the noise is smoothed away: 4 pieces and 392 wrong pixels after 600 steps (later the weak disk is lost again: 3 pieces).
E7. With k = 4 the front grows through the textured nucleus and stops at the dark nuclear envelope (about 2570 pixels). With k = 8 the envelope no longer counts as a strong enough edge: the front passes it in places and spreads into the cytoplasm (about 4240 pixels). With k = 2 the texture inside the nucleus already counts as edges: the front stops after a few steps (237 pixels). (B4(c) and (a).)

title: Exercise: geodesic active contours
text:
Where this leads
Edge-based contours only look at local differences: noise, blur and weak edges are their enemies, and the result depends on \sigma, k and the balloon. The next unit asks a global question instead: which curve splits the image into two regions that are each as uniform as possible? That is the Chan–Vese model, a level set cousin of the graph-cut energy.

title: Quiz: geodesic active contours
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Edge-stopping function g = 1/(1 + |\nabla I_\sigma|^2/k^2); speed F = g(c - \varepsilon\kappa) plus advection along -\nabla g.

Q1. With k = 10, what is g where |\nabla I_\sigma| = 0, 10 and 30?






Hint





Plug in: 1/(1 + (m/k)^2).









Answer





1, 0.5 and 0.1. Flat regions let the front move at full speed; an edge three times stronger than k slows it to 10%.




Q2. Why smooth the image (σ > 0) before computing g?






Hint





What does the gradient of pure noise look like?









Answer





Differences of neighbouring noisy pixels are large, so without smoothing g is small at many pixels inside flat regions: the front gets stuck on noise. Smoothing averages the noise away while keeping large-scale edges (at the cost of blurring nearby edges together).




Q3. A balloon front (F = g c, no advection) reaches an edge where g = 0.05. Does it stop?






Hint





Is the speed zero?









Answer





No: it slows to 5% of c but keeps creeping, and after enough time it crosses the edge. Only g = 0 exactly would stop it. The advection term of geodesic active contours pulls it back into the edge.




Q4. In which direction does -\nabla g point on each side of an edge?






Hint





g has a valley at the edge.









Answer





Towards the edge from both sides: g decreases towards the bottom of the valley, so -\nabla g points downhill, into the edge. A front on either side is pushed onto it.




Q5. What is the edge-weighted length \oint g\,ds of a curve that runs exactly along an edge where g = 0.05, compared with a curve of the same length in a flat region?






Hint





Each bit of curve costs g times its length.









Answer





5% of it. Along edges the curve is “short” in the image’s metric, so the shortest closed curve (a geodesic) prefers to follow edges.




Q6. A curve shrinks onto a C-shaped object from outside, with no balloon. Why does it not enter the slot of the C?






Hint





What drives the part of the curve that bridges the opening?









Answer





The bridging part is straight (\kappa = 0) and lies in a flat region (g \approx 1, \nabla g \approx 0): no curvature, no advection, no balloon: nothing moves it. A negative balloon c pushes it into the slot.




Q7. Starting from one curve around three separate objects, how many curves do you get, and who decides that?






Hint





Recall unit 2.









Answer





Three (one per object, if the parameters are right). The zero level of \phi splits by itself when it passes between the objects; neither the user nor the algorithm has to count the objects.




Q8. Why does a large balloon leak through a weak part of an edge but not through a strong part?






Hint





Compare g c with the advection there.









Answer





On a weak edge g is not small (0.44 in the demo) and \nabla g is shallow, so the balloon’s push g c beats the advection that pulls the front back; on a strong edge g \approx 0 and the valley is steep. Once the front passes the weak spot, it spreads into the region behind it.

title: The generalised Hough transform
text:
About this lecture
Lines and circles have formulas. A key, a leaf, a letter, a cell of a particular shape do not. The generalised Hough transform (Ballard, 1981) stores the shape as a table instead, and keeps the voting.

The R-table: for each edge direction, the vectors from the edge to a reference point.
Voting with the table: every edge point votes for where the reference point would be.
The circle with gradient voting is a generalised Hough transform.
Rotation and scale as extra dimensions, and what they cost.
Occlusion, clutter, and how this compares with other ways to find a shape.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Third unit of the Hough day. Builds on the circle unit (gradient voting: the gradient tells the edge point where the centre is). Pixel coordinates, y down; angles on the screen counter-clockwise, as for the gradient direction on the edges day.

title: The generalised Hough transform
text:
A shape without a formula
Gradient voting for circles worked because an edge point knew where the centre was: at distance r along its gradient.
For any fixed shape the same holds, just without a formula:

Choose a reference point inside the shape (any point; the centroid is a natural choice).
From an edge point of the shape, the reference point is at some vector \mathbf v: a direction and a distance.
Which vector depends on where on the boundary the point is. The only local clue we have is the edge direction.

So: remember, for each edge direction, which vectors lead to the reference point.

title: The generalised Hough transform
text:
The R-table

Built once from a template image: for every edge point, store the vector to the reference point under its gradient direction (in bins, e.g. 36 bins of 10°). A direction can hold several vectors: all sides facing the same way share one entry.

title: The generalised Hough transform
text:
Voting with the R-table
In a new image, for every edge point \mathbf p with gradient direction \theta:

Look up the bin of \theta in the R-table.
For every vector \mathbf v in it, add one vote at \mathbf p + \mathbf v.

Where the shape is present, the votes of all its edge points land on the same reference point: a peak. Each vote that belongs to a “wrong” vector of the same direction lands elsewhere and spreads out.
Small example: a 4 × 4 square, reference at its centre, 4 direction bins. Each side has 3 edge points, so each bin holds 3 vectors. A translated copy: each of its 12 edge points casts 3 votes (36 in total); the centre gets 12, no other position more than 4.

title: The generalised Hough transform
section: Try it: the R-table and its votes
text:
Try it: the R-table and its votes




Left: the template with its edge points (from the same Canny settings as the scene) and the R-table as arrows to the reference point (+), coloured by direction bin; below, the table itself. Middle: scene, edges, detections drawn as the template outline at the found pose. Right: accumulator. Tour: “square, 4 bins”: 120 table entries, about 30 per side; the accumulator shows a cross through each square (each side’s 30 vectors spread its votes along a line), with the peak at the centre: scores 1.00 and 0.99 (fraction of the template’s edge points). Then “translation only” with the key (36 bins): 0.90 and 0.74. Drag the reference point: the detections stay, the peaks move with it. Drag a vertex of the template: the match gets worse. Click a scene edge point: its votes (magenta), one per vector in its bin.

title: The generalised Hough transform
section: The circle is a special case
text:
The circle is a special case
Take a disc of radius r as the template, with its centre as the reference point. Every edge direction occurs exactly once on the boundary, and the vector from that point to the centre has length r and points along the gradient.

The R-table holds one vector per direction: length r, along the gradient.
Voting with it is exactly gradient voting for circles with a known radius and known polarity.

The general method contains the special case. In the demo (“circle template”), the table has 136 entries spread over 36 bins (2 to 5 per bin, from the digital edge), all of length 18.

title: The generalised Hough transform
text:
Rotation and scale
A rotated copy of the shape has rotated gradient directions and rotated vectors: the unrotated table looks up the wrong bins and votes in the wrong places. It is missed.

Search over rotations \phi and scales s: for each (\phi, s), rotate and scale the table (shift the direction index by \phi, rotate and scale every vector), vote into its own accumulator slice.
The accumulator becomes 4D: (x, y, \phi, s). A detection gives position, angle and size.
Cost: every edge point does one lookup per (\phi, s). 36 angles × 5 scales = 180 times the work and memory of translation only.
Remedy: coarse to fine. Search all poses in a downsampled image (a Gaussian pyramid, the edges day), then refine only near the candidates at full resolution.

title: The generalised Hough transform
section: The math: the GHT with rotation and scale
text:
The math: the GHT with rotation and scale
A copy of the template rotated by \phi and scaled by s maps each template vector \mathbf v to s R(\phi)\mathbf v and each gradient direction \theta to \theta + \phi. An edge point \mathbf x with direction \theta therefore votes, for each (\phi, s), for the reference points
\mathbf c = \mathbf x + s\,R(\phi)\,\mathbf v \qquad \text{for all } \mathbf v \in T\big[\theta - \phi\big],
where T[\cdot] is the R-table bin. (In the course’s pixel convention, y down and angles counter-clockwise on the screen, R(\phi) = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\phi & \sin\phi \\ -\sin\phi & \cos\phi \end{pmatrix}.) Cost: N_\text{edge} \cdot N_\phi \cdot N_s lookups and on average |T|/N_\text{bins} votes per lookup; memory N_x N_y N_\phi N_s cells. A similarity transform (shift, rotation, scale) is the same one that aligns shapes in Procrustes analysis (the snakes and shape-model elective).

title: The generalised Hough transform
text:
Occlusion and clutter

Occlusion: votes from the visible part still meet at the reference point. Half the boundary hidden gives roughly half the peak. The threshold is then a minimum visible fraction of the boundary.
Clutter: random edges vote randomly and raise the floor, as for lines.
Similar shapes are the real danger: a shape that shares long pieces of boundary with the template collects many votes at a nearby point. With a low threshold it becomes a false positive.

In the demo the score is the number of edge points that vote within a pixel of a cell, divided by the number of template edge points: about 1 for a perfect, fully visible copy.

title: The generalised Hough transform
text:
Try it: rotation search




“rotated: missed”: the second key is rotated by 60°; without a rotation search only the upright key is found (0.90). “rotation search: found”: 36 rotations; both keys found, the rotated one at 60° with 0.91; the work goes from 721 lookups to 25,956 (36 times) and from 4,682 votes to 129,925. Other poses of the same keys give weak peaks (0.31 to 0.40). “scale search”: copies at 0.8 and 1.2; 5 scales find both (0.54 and 0.93). “occluded copy still found”: a disc hides part of the first key; its score drops from 0.90 to 0.58, still above 0.5. “similar shape”: a stretched key gives 0.31; with the threshold at 0.3 it is reported: a false positive.

title: The generalised Hough transform
section: The math: the GHT as matched filtering
text:
The math: the GHT as matched filtering
Merge all direction bins into one: every edge point now votes with every template vector. The vote count at \mathbf c becomes
H(\mathbf c) = \sum_{\mathbf x} E(\mathbf x) \sum_{\mathbf v \in T} [\mathbf x + \mathbf v = \mathbf c] = \sum_{\mathbf q} E(\mathbf c + \mathbf q)\, E_T(\mathbf q),
with \mathbf q = -\mathbf v running over the template’s edge points relative to the reference point. That is the correlation of the scene’s edge map E with the template’s edge map E_T: template matching on edge maps (the FFT registration day uses the same correlation on intensities, normalised). The direction bins make it selective: only edge points with the right direction may vote with a given vector, so far fewer accidental matches.

title: The generalised Hough transform
text:
Finding a shape: the options










finds
needs
tolerates




GHT

Active shape models (snakes elective)

a starting pose

Moment invariants (moments elective)

a segmentation
