title: Prediction, dictionaries and lossless formats
text:
The math: why prediction helps

The decoder knows \hat x (a function of decoded pixels), so x \mapsto e = x - \hat x is invertible given the past: lossless.
Cost per pixel \approx H(e), the entropy of the residual histogram. For a Gaussian-like histogram with standard deviation \sigma (in grey levels), H \approx \log_2\!\big(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi e}\big) = \log_2 \sigma + 2.05 bits: halving the spread saves one bit.
Left predictor on a smooth signal: e_i = x_i - x_{i-1} \approx \partial x/\partial t; planar a + b - c is exact on any plane x = \alpha + \beta i + \gamma j.
Noise floor: if x = s + n with independent noise of variance \sigma_n^2 and a perfect predictor of s from noisy neighbours, the residual still contains n_i - n_{i-1}: variance \ge \sigma_n^2, and 2\sigma_n^2 for the left predictor. On pure noise, prediction adds \log_2\sqrt2 = 0.5 bit.

title: Prediction, dictionaries and lossless formats
text:
Try it: prediction




Smooth image, left predictor: entropy 7.08 → 3.28 bits/pixel, DEFLATE 44 457 → 31 212 bytes (of 65 536). Average is best here (3.11). Switch to “cell”: only 7.68 → 6.78 (left), 6.45 (average): the micrograph is grainy, the grain cannot be predicted. “Noise kills prediction”: smooth image + noise 10: residual entropy 5.89. “Flat field” with noise: the residuals have a HIGHER entropy than the pixels (+0.5 bit). “Edges are what remains”: shapes with the planar predictor; the residual image shows only the outlines. Click a pixel on an edge and compare MED with average. “12-bit spots”: 8.42 → 7.29 bits (MED), but DEFLATE on 2-byte values does poorly (82 742 → 79 341 of 131 072 bytes).

(ideal ratio = stored bits per pixel / residual entropy.) Lossless ratios for real microscopy data are typically 1.5–3×, not 10×. The 12-bit image gains mostly because its 16-bit storage has 4 empty bits.

title: Prediction, dictionaries and lossless formats
text:
Lossless formats: PNG and JPEG-LS

PNG: each row picks one filter (None, Sub = left, Up, Average, Paeth), then the filtered bytes go through DEFLATE. 1 to 16 bits per channel.
JPEG-LS (LOCO-I, 1990s): MED prediction, then the residuals are context-modelled (the local gradients choose a probability model) and coded with simple Golomb–Rice codes; also a near-lossless mode (error ≤ a set bound). Used in medical imaging.
Lossless JPEG 2000 (reversible integer wavelet, last unit of the day) and JPEG-XL lossless (several predictors, context modelling, an arithmetic-type coder) do somewhat better.
All of them: predict or transform first, then entropy-code what is left.

title: Prediction, dictionaries and lossless formats
text:
Dictionary coding: repeats are cheap


LZ77 (Ziv and Lempel 1977): replace a repeat by a pointer (go back d, copy \ell symbols) into a sliding window of recent data. LZW (GIF, TIFF) builds a table of strings instead.
DEFLATE = LZ77 + Huffman: zip, gzip, PNG, TIFF. Modern successors (e.g. Zstandard) are faster and stronger, used in chunked array formats.
They need exact repeats. Noisy pixel values rarely repeat exactly, which is why PNG predicts first, and why DEFLATE on 16-bit values (two bytes) is poor.

title: Prediction, dictionaries and lossless formats
text:
Summary

Neighbours are alike: store the residual e = x - \hat x of a prediction from decoded neighbours; the decoder repeats the prediction, so it is exact.
Residual histograms are narrow and centred at 0: much lower entropy than the pixels.
Edges and noise are what prediction cannot remove; noise sets the floor (pure noise: prediction even costs 0.5 bit).
PNG: row filters + DEFLATE; JPEG-LS: MED + context modelling.
Dictionary methods (LZ77, DEFLATE) exploit exact repeats.
Next: instead of predicting pixel by pixel, change the basis so that a few coefficients carry the image.

title: Exercise: least-squares unmixing
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

solve a small unmixing problem with more channels than components by the normal equations, and check that the residual is orthogonal to the spectra,
predict from the spectra how much noise unmixing amplifies (the condition number), and choose filters,
use the residual map to detect a missing component,
explain when weighted least squares helps.

title: Exercise: least-squares unmixing
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Model
\mathbf y \approx M\mathbf a: N channels, K < N components, spectra as columns of M


Least squares
minimise \|\mathbf y - M\mathbf a\|^2: the closest mixture


Normal equations
M^\top M\,\hat{\mathbf a} = M^\top\mathbf y; pseudo-inverse M^+ = (M^\top M)^{-1}M^\top, \hat{\mathbf a} = M^+\mathbf y


Residual
\mathbf r = \mathbf y - M\hat{\mathbf a}, orthogonal to every column: M^\top\mathbf r = \mathbf 0


Condition number
\kappa = \sigma_\text{max}/\sigma_\text{min} (singular values of M = square roots of the eigenvalues of M^\top M)


Noise of the estimate
\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf a}) = \sigma_n^2 (M^\top M)^{-1} for independent channel noise \sigma_n


Weighted LS
\hat{\mathbf a} = (M^\top W M)^{-1}M^\top W\mathbf y, W = \operatorname{diag}(1/\text{expected count})

title: Exercise: least-squares unmixing
text:
By hand
B1. Three channels, two dyes: M = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.2 \\ 0.5 & 0.5 \\ 0.1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} and a measured pixel \mathbf y = (1.3, 0.9, 1.2). (a) Compute M^\top M and M^\top\mathbf y. (b) Solve the 2 \times 2 system for \hat{\mathbf a}. (c) Compute the fit M\hat{\mathbf a} and the residual \mathbf r. Check that \mathbf r is orthogonal to both columns. (d) The pixel was made from \mathbf a = (1, 1). What would the noise-free pixel have been? How large is the residual compared with the noise you can infer?
B2. Two pairs of spectra on three channels: near-parallel \mathbf m_1 = (1, 0.9, 0.5), \mathbf m_2 = (0.9, 1, 0.5); well separated \mathbf m_1 = (1, 0.1, 0.5), \mathbf m_2 = (0.1, 1, 0.5). (a) For each pair compute M^\top M and its eigenvalues. (A 2 \times 2 matrix \begin{pmatrix} p & q \\ q & p \end{pmatrix} has eigenvalues p \pm q with eigenvectors (1, 1) and (1, -1).) (b) The singular values of M are the square roots of these eigenvalues. Compute \kappa for each pair. (c) Channel 1 reads one unit too high. How much does each abundance move? (The first column of M^+ is (5.23, -4.77) for the near-parallel pair and (0.88, -0.23) for the separated pair; check one entry.) (d) Which combination of the two abundances is well determined for the near-parallel pair, and which is not?
B3. Two dyes are sampled in six bins: dye 1 = (0.1, 0.6, 1.0, 0.6, 0.3, 0.1), dye 2 = (0, 0.1, 0.4, 0.9, 1.0, 0.5). You can build two channels from the bins in three ways: A: bin 2 and bin 5; B: bin 3 and bin 4; C: bins 1–3 and bins 4–6. (a) Write M for each set (channel value = sum over its bins). (b) Which set has the smallest bleed-through between the channels? Which collects the most photons? (c) The condition numbers are 2.08 (A), 3.22 (B) and 2.34 (C), and the noise on the abundances, per unit channel noise, is (1.76, 1.18), (1.49, 1.77) and (0.68, 0.55). Which set would you choose, and why is \kappa alone not the whole story?
B4. Four detectors, two dyes, with reference spectra \mathbf m_1 = (1, 0.45, 0.10, 0.02) and \mathbf m_2 = (0.02, 0.30, 1, 0.40). A pixel records \mathbf y = (104, 58, 61, 24). (a) Why does M^{-1} not exist? (b) Compute M^\top M and M^\top\mathbf y, and solve for \hat{\mathbf a} (two decimals). (c) The pixel was made from (100, 50) plus small errors. Compare.
B5. An unmixed image looks clean, but the residual map is at about 1.4 times the noise level in the cytoplasm and at 1.0 in the nucleus. Give two possible causes and how you would distinguish them.
B6. A photon-starved pixel has expected counts of 4 in one channel and 400 in another. What is the standard deviation of each count? Which channel should weigh more in the fit, and by what factor?

Math questions
B7. (math) Derive the normal equations by setting the gradient of \|\mathbf y - M\mathbf a\|^2 to zero. Then derive them a second time from the requirement that the residual be orthogonal to every column.
B8. (math) Show that P = MM^+ is symmetric and idempotent (P^2 = P), and that (I - P)M = 0. What do these say about a pixel that is an exact mixture?
B9. (math) Show that \operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf a}) = \sigma_n^2 (M^\top M)^{-1} when the channel noise is independent with variance \sigma_n^2. For the near-parallel pair of B2, compute the standard deviations of \hat a_1 + \hat a_2 and \hat a_1 - \hat a_2 in units of \sigma_n.
B10. (math) Write the log-likelihood of \mathbf a for independent Gaussian channels with variances v_c, and show that its maximum is the weighted least-squares solution with W = \operatorname{diag}(1/v_c).






Solutions





B1. (a) M^\top M = \begin{pmatrix} 1 + 0.25 + 0.01 & 0.2 + 0.25 + 0.1 \\ 0.55 & 0.04 + 0.25 + 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1.26 & 0.55 \\ 0.55 & 1.29 \end{pmatrix}, M^\top\mathbf y = (1.3 + 0.45 + 0.12,\ 0.26 + 0.45 + 1.2) = (1.87, 1.91). (b) \det = 1.26 \cdot 1.29 - 0.55^2 = 1.3229; \hat a_1 = (1.29 \cdot 1.87 - 0.55 \cdot 1.91)/1.3229 = 1.029, \hat a_2 = (1.26 \cdot 1.91 - 0.55 \cdot 1.87)/1.3229 = 1.042. (c) M\hat{\mathbf a} = (1.238, 1.036, 1.145), \mathbf r = (0.062, -0.136, 0.055). \mathbf m_1 \cdot \mathbf r = 0.062 - 0.068 + 0.0055 = 0.000 and \mathbf m_2 \cdot \mathbf r = 0.0124 - 0.068 + 0.055 = 0.000 (up to rounding). (d) M(1, 1)^\top = (1.2, 1.0, 1.1): the noise was (0.1, -0.1, 0.1). The residual (|\mathbf r| = 0.16) is the part of that noise perpendicular to the plane; the part within the plane moved the estimate from (1, 1) to (1.03, 1.04).
B2. (a) Near-parallel: M^\top M = \begin{pmatrix} 2.06 & 2.05 \\ 2.05 & 2.06 \end{pmatrix}, eigenvalues 4.11 (along (1, 1)) and 0.01 (along (1, -1)). Separated: \begin{pmatrix} 1.26 & 0.45 \\ 0.45 & 1.26 \end{pmatrix}, eigenvalues 1.71 and 0.81. (b) Near-parallel: \sigma = 2.03 and 0.10, \kappa = 20.3. Separated: \sigma = 1.31 and 0.90, \kappa = 1.45. (c) Near-parallel: \hat{\mathbf a} moves by (5.23, -4.77): a unit error becomes errors of about 5 in opposite directions. Separated: (0.88, -0.23). Check, near-parallel: M^+ = (M^\top M)^{-1}M^\top, first column = (M^\top M)^{-1}(1, 0.9)^\top = \frac{1}{0.0411}(2.06 - 1.845,\ -2.05 + 1.854) = (5.23, -4.77). (d) The sum \hat a_1 + \hat a_2 is well determined (large eigenvalue along (1, 1)); the difference is not (eigenvalue 0.01 along (1, -1)). The two errors in (c) nearly cancel in the sum.
B3. (a) A: \begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & 0.1 \\ 0.3 & 1.0 \end{pmatrix}; B: \begin{pmatrix} 1.0 & 0.4 \\ 0.6 & 0.9 \end{pmatrix}; C: \begin{pmatrix} 1.7 & 0.5 \\ 1.0 & 2.4 \end{pmatrix} (rows = channels, columns = dyes). (b) A has the smallest bleed-through relative to the dyes’ own signals: dye 1 into channel 2 0.3/0.6 = 50 %, dye 2 into channel 1 0.1/1.0 = 10 % (B: 60 % and 44 %; C: 59 % and 21 %). C collects by far the most photons (2.7 and 2.9 per unit dye, against 0.9/1.1 for A and 1.6/1.3 for B). (c) C: its \kappa (2.34) is almost as good as A’s, and because it collects about three times more light its absolute noise gain is the smallest (0.68 and 0.55). \kappa measures only the shape of M (how unequal its stretches are), not its size: a matrix twice as large has the same \kappa but half the noise on \hat{\mathbf a}. For a choice of filters, compare the noise on the abundances you care about.
B4. (a) M is 4 \times 2, not square. (b) M^\top M = \begin{pmatrix} 1.2129 & 0.263 \\ 0.263 & 1.2504 \end{pmatrix}, M^\top\mathbf y = (136.68, 90.08), \hat{\mathbf a} = (101.71, 50.65). (c) Close to (100, 50): the four detectors average the errors (3, -2, 1, 2) that were added to the noise-free pixel (101, 60, 60, 22). The residual is (1.28, -2.96, 0.18, 1.71).
B5. (1) A missing component in the cytoplasm (autofluorescence, an unexpected dye): its spectrum cannot be made from the reference spectra. (2) A wrong reference spectrum for a component that lives in the cytoplasm (for example a dye whose spectrum shifted there). Look at the residual spectrum of the cytoplasm pixels: a broad, smooth shape that also appears in an unstained control points to autofluorescence; a residual shaped like the difference of two similar curves (positive on one flank, negative on the other) points to a shifted reference.
B6. Poisson: sd = \sqrt{\text{mean}}, so 2 and 20 counts. The dim channel’s absolute error is ten times smaller: weight 1/4 against 1/400, a factor 100 (the squared ratio of the standard deviations).
B7. E(\mathbf a) = \mathbf y^\top\mathbf y - 2\mathbf a^\top M^\top\mathbf y + \mathbf a^\top M^\top M\mathbf a, \nabla E = -2M^\top\mathbf y + 2M^\top M\mathbf a = 0, so M^\top M\hat{\mathbf a} = M^\top\mathbf y. Orthogonality: \mathbf m_k^\top(\mathbf y - M\hat{\mathbf a}) = 0 for every k is M^\top(\mathbf y - M\hat{\mathbf a}) = \mathbf 0, the same equations. (The closest point of a subspace is the one whose difference is perpendicular to it.)
B8. P^\top = M\big((M^\top M)^{-1}\big)^\top M^\top = P since M^\top M is symmetric. P^2 = P as in quiz Q8. (I - P)M = M - M(M^\top M)^{-1}M^\top M = M - M = 0. For an exact mixture \mathbf y = M\mathbf a: P\mathbf y = \mathbf y (fit = pixel), residual (I - P)\mathbf y = 0, and M^+\mathbf y = \mathbf a exactly.
B9. \hat{\mathbf a} = M^+\mathbf y is linear in \mathbf y, so \operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf a}) = M^+\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf y)M^{+\top} = \sigma_n^2 (M^\top M)^{-1}M^\top M(M^\top M)^{-1} = \sigma_n^2(M^\top M)^{-1}. For the near-parallel pair, (M^\top M)^{-1} has eigenvalues 1/4.11 along (1, 1) and 1/0.01 along (1, -1). \operatorname{Var}(\hat a_1 + \hat a_2) = \sigma_n^2 (1, 1)(M^\top M)^{-1}(1, 1)^\top = \sigma_n^2 \cdot 2/4.11, sd = 0.70\,\sigma_n; \operatorname{Var}(\hat a_1 - \hat a_2) = \sigma_n^2 \cdot 2/0.01, sd = 14.1\,\sigma_n.
B10. \log L(\mathbf a) = -\tfrac12\sum_c (y_c - (M\mathbf a)_c)^2/v_c + \text{const} = -\tfrac12(\mathbf y - M\mathbf a)^\top W(\mathbf y - M\mathbf a) + \text{const}. Its gradient M^\top W(\mathbf y - M\mathbf a) vanishes at M^\top WM\hat{\mathbf a} = M^\top W\mathbf y, the WLS solution; the Hessian -M^\top WM is negative definite, so it is a maximum.

title: Exercise: least-squares unmixing
text:
Explore: unmix a lambda stack
A synthetic cell (seeded, 128 \times 128) with four components: nucleus (blue), mitochondria (green), membrane (magenta) and a diffuse autofluorescence with a broad spectrum (orange). It is recorded as a lambda stack of 3–32 contiguous channels between 480 and 700 nm, with Poisson noise; photons is the expected total count of a pixel with abundance 1. Top: the true and the unmixed pseudocolour merge, and the residual (in units of the expected photon noise: about 1 = noise only). Bottom: the four abundance maps (red = negative), or the true ones. Right: the four spectra over the channel bins (dashed = not in M); below, the clicked pixel: dots = measured, black line = fit, coloured bands = each component’s contribution. Methods: one channel per dye (each dye read in its brightest channel, as if there were no bleed-through), least squares, weighted LS. The readout gives \kappa(M), the noise amplification per component compared with the same dye measured alone, the RMSE of each map against the truth, the share of negative abundances and the mean residual.



L1. Preset one channel per dye. Which map is worst, and why? Look at the mitochondria map: what else do you see in it?
L2. Preset least squares removes it. Compare the RMSEs with L1. Click a nucleus pixel and a mitochondrion: how do the coloured bands explain the measured dots?
L3. Preset two dyes 6 nm apart. What happens to the nucleus and mitochondria maps, the RMSE and the noise amplification? Which maps are unaffected?
L4. With the dyes still 6 nm apart, set 8 channels, then 32 (preset 32 channels: no rescue). How much does the noise amplification change? Then move the peaks back to 45 nm apart.
L5. Preset forgot the autofluorescence. Where does the residual light up? What happens to the other maps? Then add it as a component.
L6. Set 3 channels with all four components in M. What does the demo say, and why?
L7. Preset photon-starved: WLS vs LS (20 photons). Compare the RMSEs of weighted and ordinary least squares, and the share of negative abundances.






Solutions





L1. The autofluorescence map (RMSE 0.30): its brightest channel is also bright for the other dyes, so it shows the whole cell. The mitochondria map (RMSE 0.069) contains the nucleus too: dye 1’s light in the mitochondria dye’s channel. This is bleed-through again, now with four dyes.
L2. RMSEs 0.017, 0.023, 0.024 and 0.062 (against 0.035, 0.069, 0.058, 0.298): the maps are clean. In a nucleus pixel the blue band carries almost everything and the black fit follows the dots; in a mitochondrion the green band dominates, with some orange autofluorescence underneath. The dots scatter around the black line: that scatter is the photon noise, the residual.
L3. The nucleus and mitochondria maps become grainy: RMSE 0.071 and 0.074 (were 0.017 and 0.023), noise amplification 4.9 and 5.1 (was 1.3 and 1.7), \kappa = 10.2. Membrane and autofluorescence are hardly affected (noise × 1.5 and 1.7): only the two similar spectra trade off against each other.
L4. Noise amplification for nucleus and mitochondria: 5.7 and 5.9 with 8 channels, 4.9 and 5.1 with 16, 4.7 and 4.9 with 32; the RMSE barely moves (0.069/0.073 at 32 channels). Finer sampling helps a little; the photons are the same. With 45 nm separation the amplification drops back to 1.3 and 1.7.
L5. The residual rises in the cytoplasm (1.37 times the noise on average, against 1.04 in the nucleus): the autofluorescence spectrum cannot be built from the three narrow dyes. Its light leaks into the other maps (mitochondria RMSE 0.054, membrane 0.057). With the autofluorescence added, the residual is about 1 everywhere and the RMSEs return to 0.017–0.062.
L6. “3 channels < 4 components: no unique solution”. Three equations cannot determine four unknowns: M^\top M is singular, and infinitely many mixtures fit exactly. You need at least as many channels as components (and in practice more, for noise).
L7. Ordinary LS: RMSE 0.077, 0.105, 0.108, 0.271; weighted LS: 0.072, 0.095, 0.100, 0.244, a modest gain (6–10 %). About 20 % of the abundance values are negative with either method: the constraints of the next unit address that.

title: Exercise: least-squares unmixing
text:
Where this leads
Least squares lets the abundances go negative and needs the spectra in advance. The next unit, endmembers, adds the constraints (non-negative, sum to one) with their geometry, cones and simplices, and asks how to find the spectra when no reference is available.

title: Quiz: least-squares unmixing
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A pixel with N channel values is \mathbf y \approx M\mathbf a, with the K component spectra as the columns of M (N > K); least squares gives \hat{\mathbf a} = M^+\mathbf y, M^+ = (M^\top M)^{-1}M^\top.

Q1. Why can’t you simply invert M when there are 16 channels and 4 dyes?






Hint





What shape is M? How many equations per pixel?









Answer





M is 16 \times 4: not square, no inverse. Each pixel gives 16 equations for 4 unknowns; with noise they cannot all hold. Least squares takes the 4 abundances whose mixture is closest to the measured spectrum.




Q2. Geometrically, what is the least-squares fit M\hat{\mathbf a} of a pixel, and what is the residual?






Hint





Think of 3 channels and 2 dyes: the set of all mixtures is a plane.









Answer





The fit is the orthogonal projection of the pixel onto the column space of M (all mixtures of the spectra): the nearest explainable spectrum. The residual is the perpendicular part, \mathbf y - M\hat{\mathbf a}, orthogonal to every component spectrum.




Q3. Why is unmixing a 512 \times 512 image with 32 channels cheap, even though every pixel needs its own least-squares fit?






Hint





What does M^+ depend on?









Answer





M^+ depends only on the reference spectra, not on the pixel: compute it once (K \times 32), then every pixel’s abundances are one small matrix–vector product, \hat{\mathbf a} = M^+\mathbf y. The whole image is one matrix product M^+Y.




Q4. After unmixing, the residual map is at the noise level everywhere except in the cytoplasm, where it is clearly higher. What would you suspect, and how would you test it?






Hint





The residual is what no combination of your reference spectra can explain.









Answer





A component is missing from M, present in the cytoplasm only: typically autofluorescence (or an unexpected dye, or an offset). Look at the residual spectrum of those pixels, add a spectrum of that shape as an extra column (from an unstained control, for example) and check that the residual drops to the noise level.




Q5. Two dyes have nearly the same spectrum. Which is better determined: the sum of their abundances or the difference? Why?






Hint





What happens to the measured spectrum if you add a little of dye 1 and remove the same amount of dye 2?









Answer





The sum. Trading dye 1 for dye 2 hardly changes the measured spectrum, so the data cannot pin down the difference: noise moves it a lot. The total amount of light, and hence the sum, is well measured. In the math: M^\top M has a small eigenvalue with eigenvector \approx (1, -1).




Q6. A colleague says “with 32 channels instead of 8 we can separate any two dyes”. Is that right?






Hint





Do finer bins create new photons? Do they change the shapes?









Answer





No. Finer bins over the same range sample the shapes better and help a little (in the demo, noise × 5.7 → 4.7 for dyes 6 nm apart), but they add no photons, and two identical shapes stay inseparable however finely you sample them (\kappa = \infty). What helps more: dyes further apart, more photons.




Q7. In a photon-starved image, why give a channel with 4 expected counts more weight than one with 400?






Hint





For Poisson counts the variance equals the mean.









Answer





The channel with 400 counts has variance 400 (sd 20); the one with 4 counts has variance 4 (sd 2). In absolute terms the dim channel’s error is ten times smaller, so it deserves more weight: weighted least squares uses w_c = 1/\text{expected count}. (In relative terms the dim channel is noisier: 50 % against 5 %.)




Q8. (math) Show that P = M(M^\top M)^{-1}M^\top satisfies P^2 = P. What does that mean for a pixel that is already a perfect mixture?






Hint





Multiply out; the middle M^\top M cancels one inverse.









Answer





P^2 = M(M^\top M)^{-1}(M^\top M)(M^\top M)^{-1}M^\top = M(M^\top M)^{-1}M^\top = P. Projecting twice changes nothing: a pixel that already lies in the column space, \mathbf y = M\mathbf a, has P\mathbf y = \mathbf y, its abundances are recovered exactly and its residual is zero.

title: Marching cubes
text:
About this lecture
Marching squares drew the boundary \{I = c\} of a 2D image as curves. The same idea in a volume gives a surface made of triangles: marching cubes (Lorensen & Cline, 1987), the standard way to turn a 3D image into a 3D model.

A cell is a cube of 8 voxels: 256 cases, which symmetry reduces to 23 or 15.
The triangle table, and how to generate it from marching squares on the cube’s faces.
Ambiguous faces, cracks, and how to avoid them; marching tetrahedra.
Normals from the image gradient: smooth shading for free.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Builds directly on the previous unit (marching squares, crossing points, saddle cells, the asymptotic decider) and on volumes3d/ (spacing, trilinear interpolation). Rendering (projection, shading) is the 3D-graphics day’s; here it is a pointer. Corner numbering convention of the course: k = x + 2y + 4z, printed on the exercise sheet.

title: Marching cubes
section: The same idea, one dimension up
text:
The same idea, one dimension up





A cell = the cube between 8 neighbouring voxel centres. Corner k = x + 2y + 4z.
Each corner above or below c: an 8-bit case index, 2^8 = 256 cases.
An edge with corners on opposite sides is crossed once; the crossing point by linear interpolation, t = (c - I_a)/(I_b - I_a), as in 2D.
The crossing points are connected by triangles: up to 5 per cube.

title: Marching cubes
text:
Shared edges: one closed mesh

A cube edge is shared by up to 4 cubes, and each computes the same crossing point. Store the point once per grid edge and let all triangles index it: a mesh with shared vertices, not a soup of loose triangles.
With a consistent rule on every face, the triangles of neighbouring cubes meet edge to edge: the surface is closed (watertight), apart from where it leaves the volume. Pad the volume with background to close it.
One pass over the cells: n^3 cubes for an n^3 volume. The output grows with the area of the surface, about n^2 triangles, not with the volume.
For a smooth surface: about 2 triangles per vertex, and about 3 triangles per unit of area (in voxel units).

title: Marching cubes
text:
256 cases, but only 15 shapes


Rotations: turning the cube turns the case into another case with the same surface, turned. The cube has 24 rotations; they group the 256 cases into 23 classes.
Complement: swapping inside and outside gives the same surface with the normals flipped. Rotations + complement: 15 classes (the table of Lorensen & Cline). As we will see, the complement step is not innocent.

title: Marching cubes
text:
The math: counting classes (Burnside)
The number of classes = the average number of cases left unchanged by a rotation. A case is unchanged when all corners in each cycle of the corner permutation have the same state: 2^{\#\text{cycles}} cases.

\frac{256 + 6 \cdot 4 + 3 \cdot 16 + 8 \cdot 16 + 6 \cdot 16}{24} = \frac{552}{24} = 23.
With the complement as well (48 symmetries; a complement-rotation fixes a case when every cycle has even length and alternates), the same count gives 15.

title: Marching cubes
text:
Generating the triangle table
The table lists, for each of the 256 cases, which edges the triangles connect. We do not copy it; we generate it:

The surface meets each face of the cube in a marching-squares contour: run marching squares on the 6 faces (with a rule for saddle faces).
Every crossed edge belongs to two faces, so the face segments chain into closed loops around the cube.
Triangulate each loop as a fan (a polygon of m points gives m - 2 triangles).


Case 1 (one corner above): one loop of 3 points, 1 triangle. Case 3 (an edge): a loop of 4, 2 triangles.
The face rule is all the table “knows”: change the rule, and you get a different table.

title: Marching cubes
text:
Try it: one cube




Click corners to flip them (orange = above c). Readouts: bits, case index, class among 15 and among 23, the rotation to the representative (“rotate to its representative” animates it). Tour: “one corner” (case 1, one triangle); click corner 1 too: case 3, two triangles, a quad. “Values: vertices slide”: corners 0.9, 0.35, 0.6, … with c = 0.5; move c and the selected corner’s value: the vertices slide along the edges (on edge 0–1, t = 0.73). “The 15 classes”: step through them; class 9 (case 23) is a hexagon. “An ambiguous face”: case 9, face −z tinted; switch separate/join: 2 triangles or 4.

title: Marching cubes
text:
Ambiguous faces and cracks

A face with diagonal corners above is a 2D saddle: the surface may separate or join the two bright corners on that face. 6 of the 15 classes contain such a face (120 of the 256 cases).
The face is shared with the neighbouring cube. If the two cubes choose differently, their triangles end at different points on that face: a crack (a hole) in the surface.
The 15-class table makes exactly this mistake (Dürst, 1988): using the complement swaps “separate” for “join” in cases with many corners above, so neighbours can disagree.
Fixes:

one consistent rule for all faces (e.g. always separate; 23 classes, no complement): closed, but sometimes the wrong topology;
the asymptotic decider on each face (Nielson & Hamann, 1991): consistent, because both cubes see the same 4 face values, and usually the right topology;
ambiguities inside the cube (tunnels) need more cases (Chernyaev’s 33 cases, 1995; Lewiner et al., 2003).

title: Marching cubes
text:
Try it: a crack




Two cubes share the +x face of the left one, which is ambiguous (corners 1 and 7 above). The left cube separates, the right cube joins: their segments on the shared face differ, and the red lines are the 4 crack edges (edges with a triangle on one side only). Set the neighbour’s rule to separate, or both to decider: the crack closes. Then “tetrahedra instead”.

title: Marching cubes
text:
Marching tetrahedra

Split each cube into tetrahedra (5 or 6) and run the same idea per tetrahedron: 4 corners, 2^4 = 16 cases.
Up to symmetry only 3: nothing (all in or all out), one corner separated (1 triangle), two and two (a quad, 2 triangles).
Never ambiguous: no tetrahedron has a face with diagonal corners (its faces are triangles).
Costs: more triangles (often 2–4 times), thin triangles, and a directional bias from the chosen diagonals; the split must match between neighbouring cubes (the 5-tetrahedron split alternates between neighbours).

title: Marching cubes
section: The math: why a tetrahedron is unambiguous
text:
The math: why a tetrahedron is unambiguous

Inside a tetrahedron with corners \mathbf p_0, \dots, \mathbf p_3 every point is \sum \lambda_i \mathbf p_i with barycentric weights \lambda_i \ge 0, \sum\lambda_i = 1. The natural interpolant is f = \sum \lambda_i I_i, which is linear (affine) in \mathbf x.
The level set \{f = c\} of an affine function is a plane. A plane cuts a tetrahedron in nothing, a triangle or a quadrilateral, always connected: no choice to make.
On a shared triangular face, f is the same affine function seen from both sides, so neighbours agree automatically.
The cube’s trilinear interpolant is not affine (its xy, yz, xz, xyz terms bend the level set): that is where the ambiguity comes from.

title: Marching cubes
text:
Normals from the image
To shade a surface we need its normal at every vertex. A level set has one for free:

Moving along the surface, I stays equal to c; moving across it, I changes fastest. So the normal points along the gradient \nabla I.
For a bright object, \nabla I points inwards (towards higher values): the outward normal is \mathbf n = -\nabla I / \lVert\nabla I\rVert.
Compute \nabla I at the voxels by central differences (or Sobel, kernels/), interpolate it trilinearly to each vertex, normalise.
Result: smooth shading from a coarse mesh, because the normals come from the image, not from the facets.

title: Marching cubes
text:
The math: gradient normals

If \mathbf x(s) is any curve on the surface, I(\mathbf x(s)) = c, so \nabla I \cdot \mathbf x'(s) = 0: the gradient is perpendicular to every tangent direction.
Central differences with spacing: \partial_x I \approx \dfrac{I[i+1] - I[i-1]}{2\Delta x}, and likewise with \Delta y, \Delta z. Divided by voxels instead, the z component is \Delta z/\Delta x times too large and the normals tilt.
At a vertex \mathbf v on an edge: \nabla I(\mathbf v) \approx trilinear interpolation of the 8 voxel gradients around it (or linear along the edge).
Face normals instead: \mathbf n = (\mathbf b - \mathbf a) \times (\mathbf c - \mathbf a) per triangle; constant per facet, so the mesh looks faceted. Shading with normals (Lambert, Phong) is the 3D-graphics day.

title: Marching cubes
text:
When gradient normals fail

Noise: the gradient of a noisy image points in random directions; the surface looks speckled. Blur first.
Flat regions: where \lVert\nabla I\rVert \approx 0 (a plateau touching c), the direction is undefined.
Binary images (a 0/1 mask): central differences give only a few directions (combinations of -1, 0, 1), so the normals are as blocky as the mask. Blur the mask slightly first (last unit).
Wrong spacing in the differences: tilted normals, wrong lighting.

title: Marching cubes
section: Try it: marching cubes on a volume
text:
Try it: marching cubes on a volume




48³ volumes, extracted on every change. Tour: “two blobs merge”: lower c from 0.6; at c = 0.49 the two components become one (their saddle value is 0.499); χ drops from 4 to 2. “A torus has a hole”: 1 component, χ = 0. “Noise”: 4324 components (thousands of tiny surfaces); “blur first” (σ = 1.5): one surface again. “Faceted vs gradient normals” with wireframe: the same triangles, shaded two ways. “Wrong z spacing”: the ellipsoid volume drops by 0.4 (7609 → 3044). “Cracks”: the complement rule on a noisy sphere gives 296 boundary edges (red); the decider gives none. Switch to 6 tetrahedra: about 3 times the triangles.

title: Marching cubes
text:
Summary

Marching cubes: per cube of 8 voxels, case index (256) → crossed edges → triangles; vertices by linear interpolation, shared between cubes: a closed, indexed mesh in one pass.
Symmetry: 24 rotations → 23 classes; with the complement → 15.
The triangle table = marching squares on the 6 faces + chaining into loops + fans; the face rule decides it.
Ambiguous faces must be resolved the same way by both neighbours (consistent rule or asymptotic decider), or the surface cracks. Marching tetrahedra is never ambiguous, at the cost of more triangles.
Normals \mathbf n = -\nabla I/\lVert\nabla I\rVert from the image give smooth shading; blur noisy and binary images first.

score a candidate shift with SSD, cross-correlation (CC) and normalised cross-correlation (NCC), by hand for short signals,

title: Exercise: finding a shift by sliding and scoring
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Shift t
where image B must be placed on image A so that they agree: B(x) \approx A(x + t)


Overlap
the pixels x of B for which x + t lies inside A; only these are compared


SSD
sum of squared differences of the pixel pairs; small is good


CC
sum of products of the pixel pairs; large is good


NCC
the correlation coefficient of the pixel pairs in the overlap; between −1 and 1, large is good


Cost
one multiply-add per pixel pair; all shifts of two images with N pixels each: about N^2

title: Exercise: finding a shift by sliding and scoring
text:
By hand
B1. The template B = (1, 3, 1) is placed at the positions t = 0, 1, \ldots, 5 of A = (0, 1, 3, 1, 0, 2, 6, 2) (B’s first pixel on A’s pixel t). (a) Compute CC and SSD at every position. (b) Compute NCC at t = 1, t = 3 and t = 5. (For t = 3: the pixels of A are (1, 0, 2).) (c) Which position does each score choose? A contains B twice. Which score would you use for a mosaic whose tiles differ in exposure?
B2. A = (0, 1, 0, 0, 5, 5, 5) and the template B = (0, 1, 0), positions t = 0 \ldots 4. (a) Compute CC at every position. Where is its maximum, and where is the copy of B? (b) What is NCC at t = 4? What does that tell you about NCC in flat regions?
B3. A = (1, 2, 3) and B = (3, 5, 7), full overlap. Compute SSD and NCC. Write B as aA + b. Which of the two scores says “same pattern”?
B4. Cost. Two tiles of 2048 \times 2048 pixels overlap by about 10 % of their width (205 columns); the stage puts them within \pm 20 pixels of the nominal position, in both directions. (a) How many multiply-adds does a comparison at every shift cost? How long at 10^9 multiply-adds per second? (b) How many if you only compare the expected overlap strip (205 \times 2048 pixels) at the 41 \times 41 shifts the stage allows? (c) What do you risk with (b)?
B5. A grating with a period of 12 pixels is registered with NCC, every shift between −40 and 45. Predict where the NCC curve reaches 1. What extra information would decide the true shift?
B6. You look for small round cells of radius 5 px with a template of 15 \times 15 px. Predict what NCC gives at (a) a cell of the same size but twice as bright, (b) a cell of radius 10 px, (c) an empty, flat background region, (d) a dark hole of radius 5 px in a bright background.






Solutions





B1. (a)

B has mean 5/3 and deviations (-\tfrac23, \tfrac43, -\tfrac23). At t = 1 the pixels of A are B itself: NCC = 1. At t = 5, (2, 6, 2) = 2B: the same deviations times 2, NCC = 1. At t = 3, (1, 0, 2) has mean 1 and deviations (0, -1, 1); the sum of products of deviations is 0 - \tfrac43 - \tfrac23 = -2, the squared lengths are \tfrac{24}{9} and 2, so NCC = -2/\sqrt{48/9} = -0.866. (The others: -0.189 at t = 0, 2, 4.)
CC chooses t = 5 (22 against 11 for the exact copy): it prefers the bright copy. SSD chooses t = 1 (0 against 11). NCC scores both copies 1. For tiles with different exposure, NCC: a change of gain or offset does not matter to it, while SSD would penalise the true shift.

B2. (a) CC = 1, 0, 0, 5, 5: the maximum (5) is in the bright region at t = 3 and 4, while the copy of B is at t = 0 (CC 1, SSD 0). (b) At t = 4 the pixels of A are (5, 5, 5): flat, with zero spread, so NCC is 0/0, undefined. Flat regions carry no pattern; NCC cannot (and should not) say they match. Implementations return 0 or skip them.
B3. SSD = 2^2 + 3^2 + 4^2 = 29. B = 2A + 1, so NCC = 1: the same pattern with more contrast and an offset. SSD says “different”, NCC says “same pattern”.
B4. (a) All shifts of two N-pixel images cost about N^2: (2048^2)^2 = 1.8 \cdot 10^{13} multiply-adds, about 4.9 hours. (b) 41^2 = 1681 shifts of about 205 \cdot 2048 = 4.2 \cdot 10^5 pixels: 7 \cdot 10^8 (exactly 6.7 \cdot 10^8, counting the slightly smaller overlaps of the shifted strips), less than a second. (c) If the stage is worse than you assumed, the true shift is outside the window, and the best score in the window is a wrong shift. Check the score: a low NCC means “not found”, not “found here”.
B5. At every shift that is a multiple of 12 away from the true one: if the true shift is 9, at -39, -27, -15, -3, 9, 21, 33, 45. A defect or the edge of the grating inside the overlap, or the nominal stage position (take the peak nearest to it), decides.
B6. (a) NCC about 1 (a gain does not matter). (b) Lower: the template sees only part of the big cell, a bright patch filling most of the window; NCC is positive but well below 1, and the best position may be off-centre. (c) Undefined or close to 0: no pattern (in practice the noise gives small random values). (d) Close to −1: the same pattern with the contrast inverted. A detector keeps the positive peaks above a threshold.




Math questions
B7. (math) Show that over the overlap \Omega_t, \mathrm{SSD}(t) = E_A(t) + E_B(t) - 2\,\mathrm{CC}(t) with E_A(t) = \sum_{\Omega_t} f(x+t)^2 and E_B(t) = \sum_{\Omega_t} g(x)^2. For a template that always lies completely inside A, which of the two energies depends on t? What does that mean for SSD vs CC?
B8. (math) (a) Show that |\mathrm{NCC}| \le 1, with equality exactly when g = af + b on the overlap (a \ne 0). (b) Show that NCC does not change when g is replaced by ag + b with a > 0. What happens for a < 0?
B9. (math) Show that all shifts of two signals of length N (every shift with a non-empty overlap) cost N^2 multiply-adds in total, and that a window |t| \le w costs (2w+1)N - w(w+1). Give the 2D versions for N \times N images.






Solutions (math)





B7. Expand (f - g)^2 = f^2 + g^2 - 2fg and sum over \Omega_t. For a template inside A, \Omega_t is always the whole template, so E_B is a constant; but E_A(t) is the energy of the part of A under the template and changes with t. SSD = E_A(t) + \text{const} - 2\,\mathrm{CC}(t): minimising SSD is maximising \mathrm{CC}(t) - E_A(t)/2, which punishes bright regions. Maximising CC alone rewards them (B2).
B8. (a) Let \mathbf u, \mathbf v be the mean-free overlap vectors of f and g. NCC = \mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v / (\|\mathbf u\|\|\mathbf v\|), and Cauchy–Schwarz gives |\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v| \le \|\mathbf u\|\|\mathbf v\|, with equality iff \mathbf v = a\mathbf u, i.e. g - \bar g = a(f - \bar f), g = af + b. (b) ag + b has mean a\bar g + b, so its mean-free vector is a\mathbf v: numerator and denominator both scale by |a| up to the sign of a, NCC becomes \operatorname{sign}(a)\,NCC. For a < 0 (inverted contrast) NCC changes sign: a perfect match scores −1.
B9. Shift t overlaps N - |t| samples. \sum_{t=-(N-1)}^{N-1}(N - |t|) = N + 2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}k = N + N(N - 1) = N^2. For the window: \sum_{|t| \le w}(N - |t|) = (2w+1)N - 2\cdot\frac{w(w+1)}{2} = (2w+1)N - w(w+1). In 2D the overlap (N - |t_x|)(N - |t_y|) is a product, so the double sum is the square of the 1D sum: N^4 for all shifts, \big((2w+1)N - w(w+1)\big)^2 for the window; for N = 1024, w = 32: 65504^2 = 4.29 \cdot 10^9.

title: Exercise: finding a shift by sliding and scoring
text:
Explore: sliding and scoring
Image A (blue, 64 samples) and image B (red) placed at the shift t; the shaded band is the overlap. Below, the score of every shift: SSD (red), CC (green) and NCC (blue), each scaled to its own range in all three mode; the bold part has been “visited” by B so far, the dots mark each score’s best shift, the dotted green line the true shift. SSD and CC are averaged over the overlap (so that long and short overlaps compare fairly); the readout gives the sums and counts the multiply-adds. gain, offset and ramp change B’s brightness; min. overlap limits the shifts.



E1. Preset by hand: (1,3,1). Move the shift from 0 to 5 and check your table of B1. Which shift does each score choose?
E2. Preset a matching bump: B is a 16-sample piece of A. Slide B from left to right. Which shift does each score choose? How many multiply-adds did the whole search cost?
E3. Preset brighter copy: SSD fails (B as long as A, gain 1.6, offset 40). Where are the best shifts of SSD, CC and NCC? Compare SSD per pixel at the true shift and at SSD’s best shift. Set the gain back to 1 and the offset to 0: what changes?
E4. Preset bright blob: CC fails. Where does CC put its peak, and why there? Do SSD and NCC agree with the truth?
E5. Preset periodic: many peaks, score NCC. List the shifts where NCC reaches 1. Which one does the readout report as best, and why that one?
E6. Preset tiny overlap: NCC noisy (noise 15, overlaps down to 2 samples). Where is NCC’s best shift, and how large is the overlap there? Raise min. overlap to 16. What does NCC choose now, and what is its value at the true shift?
E7. Preset micrograph profile: A is a row of the course micrograph. Which score fails here? Look at the profile: why?






Solutions





E1. The readout gives the sums of B1: CC 6, 11, 6, 3, 12, 22; SSD 9, 0, 9, 10, 27, 11; NCC −0.189, 1, −0.189, −0.866, −0.189, 1. Best: SSD 1, CC 5, NCC 1 (both copies score 1; the first one is reported).
E2. All three find the true shift 22. The search covers 65 shifts (min. overlap 8) and costs 968 multiply-adds.
E3. SSD chooses 48 (wrong), CC 10 (one off), NCC 9 (the truth, NCC 1.000). SSD per pixel is 9462.6 at the truth but only 1598.3 at 48, where B’s bright parts happen to lie on bright parts of A. With gain 1 and offset 0 B is an exact copy, SSD is 0 at the truth and all three agree.
E4. CC puts its peak at 42, where B lies on the bright blob: the products are large because A is large there. SSD and NCC find the truth, 12.
E5. NCC is 1 at -39, -27, -15, -3, 9, 21, 33, 45: every 12 samples. The readout reports −3, the first of the equal maxima from the left: the choice between equal peaks is arbitrary. (The true shift is 9.)
E6. NCC’s best is at 62, where the overlap is only 2 samples: two pairs of numbers always have a correlation of ±1. With min. overlap 16 NCC chooses 9, the true shift, with NCC 0.874 (less than 1 because of the noise).
E7. CC chooses −28; SSD and NCC find 9. The micrograph is bright (around 170) with dark structures: CC is largest where B’s bright parts lie on bright parts of A, not where the dark structures match.

Explore: template matching
Drag the yellow template box over the image. The right panel shows the NCC of the template at every position (top-left corner of the box; red positive, blue negative, grey where the template does not fit). Cyan boxes mark the local maxima above the threshold.



E8. Preset dark granules: a 20 \times 20 template on a dark granule of the micrograph. What is the NCC at the template’s own position, and how high are the next best matches? Lower the threshold to 0.3: what kind of places are added?
E9. Preset nuclei (synthetic): 18 nuclei, a 32 \times 32 template on the one at the top left. How many matches are there at threshold 0.5? Which nuclei are missed, and what do they have in common? Lower the threshold to 0.3: how many nuclei are found now?






Solutions





E8. NCC is 1.00 at (99, 59), the template’s own position (it is a copy of itself). The next best are (203, 10), (225, 162) and (79, 207), all with NCC about 0.5: dark specks with some likeness, but no real copies of the granule. At 0.3 many more dark or textured places pass the threshold: NCC rewards any similar local pattern, so the threshold sets the trade-off between missed and false matches.
E9. At 0.5 there are 14 matches, one on each of 14 nuclei (NCC from 1.00 for the template itself down to 0.57). Three of the four missed nuclei touch a neighbour, so the template window also contains part of the other nucleus; the fourth, at the bottom edge, is cut by the border and the template cannot be centred on it. At 0.3 there are 16 matches, on 16 of the 18 nuclei. Of the last two, one (touching its neighbour at the bottom left) scores only 0.27; the other, at the right (NCC 0.35), lies within half a template of a better match on its touching neighbour, and the search keeps only the higher of two nearby maxima. Template matching assumes isolated objects of one size and shape; touching and elongated objects score lower.

text:
Where this leads
Trying every shift costs about N^2 operations for two images of N pixels. The next unit computes the cross-correlation for all shifts at once with three FFTs, at a cost of about N \log N. After that, normalising the spectrum turns the broad CC peak into a sharp spike: phase correlation.

title: Quiz: finding a shift by sliding and scoring
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. The shift t of image B is where B must be placed on image A so that they agree; a score compares the pixels of A and B that lie on top of each other.

Q1. Name three situations in microscopy where two images differ by a shift. What is the unknown in each case?






Hint





Think of large samples, long experiments and several detectors.









Answer





Overlapping tiles of a mosaic (the stage position is not exact), drift between frames of a time-lapse (the sample or the stage creeps), and colour channels recorded with different filters or cameras. In each case the unknown is one vector t = (t_x, t_y): how far B must be moved to lie on A.




Q2. Image B is image A with every grey level doubled. At the true shift, what are SSD and NCC? Which of the two still finds the shift reliably?






Hint





SSD compares grey levels; NCC compares patterns.









Answer





SSD at the true shift is \sum (f - 2f)^2 = \sum f^2, not 0, and another shift where B’s bright pixels lie on A’s bright pixels can score lower. NCC is exactly 1 at the true shift: it removes the means and divides by the spreads, so a gain (and an offset) does not matter. NCC finds the shift.




Q3. Image A contains a very bright blob that B does not contain. Why can plain cross-correlation (sum of products) put its peak on the blob?






Hint





What happens to a sum of products when one factor is large everywhere in a region?









Answer





CC adds up A \cdot B over the overlap. Wherever B lands on the bright blob, the products are large simply because A is large there, whether or not the patterns match. CC measures “bright on bright” as much as “same pattern”. NCC removes the mean of the overlap and divides by its spread, so a bright but featureless region scores no better than any other.




Q4. (math) Show that \mathrm{SSD}(t) = \sum f^2 + \sum g^2 - 2\,\mathrm{CC}(t) over the overlap. When does minimising SSD give the same shift as maximising CC?






Hint





Expand the square. Which terms depend on t?









Answer





(f - g)^2 = f^2 + g^2 - 2fg, summed over the overlap. The two energies \sum f(x+t)^2 and \sum g(x)^2 are over the overlap, so in general they change with t. Only when they are (nearly) the same for every candidate shift, e.g. for circular shifts where the overlap is always the whole image, or for a small template inside a region of even brightness, do SSD and CC pick the same shift.




Q5. Why is NCC unreliable when the overlap is only a few pixels?






Hint





What is the correlation coefficient of two random pairs of numbers?









Answer





NCC is a correlation coefficient estimated from the pixels of the overlap. With 2 pixels it is always \pm 1; with a handful it is often close to \pm 1 by chance. A search over all shifts then finds a “perfect” match at the edge. Require a minimum overlap (a fraction of the image), or restrict the shifts to those the stage allows.




Q6. A periodic pattern (a grating, a crystal, a regular grid of wells) is registered. What does the NCC curve look like, and what is the consequence?






Hint





Shift the pattern by one period.









Answer





It has a peak every period, all of nearly the same height: shifting by one period gives the same picture. The score cannot tell which peak is the true shift. Only something that breaks the periodicity (a defect, the border of the pattern, a prior from the stage position) can decide.




Q7. Two 1024 \times 1024 tiles are compared at every possible shift. Roughly how many multiply-adds is that? And within a window of \pm 32 pixels?






Hint





All shifts of two N-pixel images cost about N^2; a window of S shifts about N \cdot S.









Answer





N = 1024^2 \approx 10^6 pixels, so all shifts cost about N^2 = 1024^4 \approx 1.1 \cdot 10^{12} multiply-adds: about 18 minutes at 10^9 per second. The window has 65^2 = 4225 shifts of about 10^6 pixels each: 4.3 \cdot 10^9, about 4 seconds.




Q8. What is the difference between template matching and registering two tiles?






Hint





Look at the sizes of the two images and at what you do with the score map.









Answer





The score is the same (usually NCC). In registration both images are large and overlap partly; you want one shift, the best peak. In template matching the template is small and lies completely inside the image at every position; you want all peaks above a threshold, one per copy of the template.

title: Graphs, cuts and maximum flow
text:
About this lecture
Last time: segmentation = the labelling with the smallest energy. Next time we will see that this is a minimum cut of a graph. Today: how to find one.

Directed graphs with capacities, a source s and a sink t.
An s–t cut and its cost.
A flow, and why no flow can be larger than any cut.
Augmenting paths in the residual graph: Ford–Fulkerson.
The max-flow / min-cut theorem: the largest flow equals the smallest cut, and the algorithm hands us that cut.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: Graphs, cuts and maximum flow
text:
Graphs with capacities

Nodes V, directed edges (u, v), each with a capacity c(u, v) \ge 0.
Two special nodes: the source s and the sink t.
Think of pipes: c(u, v) is how much water per second the pipe from u to v can carry.

Example used in the demo:

title: Graphs, cuts and maximum flow
text:
s–t cuts
An s–t cut splits the nodes into two sets, S \ni s and T \ni t. Its cost is the total capacity of the edges from S to T:
c(S, T) = \sum_{u \in S,\; v \in T} c(u, v).

Edges from T back to S do not count.
Every path from s to t must cross from S to T at least once: removing the cut edges disconnects t from s.
With n nodes there are 2^{n-2} cuts (each node other than s, t goes left or right).

Example: S = \{s\} costs 10 + 10 = 20; S = \{s, b\} costs c(s,a) + c(b,d) = 10 + 9 = 19.

title: Graphs, cuts and maximum flow
text:
Flows
A flow assigns f(u, v) to every edge with

capacity: 0 \le f(u, v) \le c(u, v),
conservation: at every node other than s and t, flow in = flow out.

Its value |f| is the net flow out of s, which equals the net flow into t.
No flow is larger than any cut: every unit of water from s to t has to pass through the cut edges, and they carry at most their capacities. So the largest flow is at most the smallest cut. The surprise is that they are equal.

title: Graphs, cuts and maximum flow
section: Augmenting paths and the residual graph
text:
Augmenting paths and the residual graph
Given a flow f, the residual graph says how the flow can still change:

a forward arc u \to v with residual capacity c(u, v) - f(u, v) (room left),
a backward arc v \to u with residual capacity f(u, v) (flow that can be undone).

An augmenting path is a path from s to t in the residual graph. Its bottleneck b is its smallest residual capacity. Push b along it: add b on forward arcs, subtract b on backward arcs. The flow stays valid and grows by b.

title: Graphs, cuts and maximum flow
text:
Why backward arcs are needed
Four nodes, all capacities 1: s\!\to\!a, s\!\to\!b, a\!\to\!b, a\!\to\!t, b\!\to\!t. Maximum flow: 2.

Suppose we first push 1 along s \to a \to b \to t.
Now s\!\to\!a and b\!\to\!t are full. Using only forward arcs, t is unreachable: stuck at 1.
In the residual graph there is the backward arc b \to a: the path s \to b \to a \to t pushes 1 more, and cancels the flow on a \to b.

Backward arcs let the algorithm change its mind, so the order in which paths are found does not matter for the result.

title: Graphs, cuts and maximum flow
text:
Ford–Fulkerson

Start with f = 0.
Find a path from s to t in the residual graph. If there is none, stop.
Push its bottleneck along it; go to 2.


With integer capacities each step adds at least 1, so it stops.
Edmonds–Karp: choose the shortest path (breadth-first search). Then the number of steps is at most O(|V|\,|E|), whatever the capacities.
In the example: s\,a\,c\,t (4), s\,a\,d\,t (6), s\,b\,d\,t (4), s\,b\,d\,c\,t (5): flow 19.

title: Graphs, cuts and maximum flow
text:
Max-flow = min-cut
Theorem (Ford & Fulkerson, 1956): the largest possible flow equals the cost of the smallest cut.

When no augmenting path is left, colour the nodes you can still reach from s in the residual graph: that set is S, the rest is T.
Every edge from S to T is then full, and no flow comes back from T to S: the flow is exactly the cut.
So Ford–Fulkerson gives both answers at once: the maximum flow, and a minimum cut.
In the example: S = \{s, b\}, cut c(s,a) + c(b,d) = 10 + 9 = 19 = flow.

title: Graphs, cuts and maximum flow
text:
The math: why flow = cut
Any flow \le any cut. Summing “flow out − flow in” over the nodes of S (0 everywhere except |f| at s), the edges inside S cancel:
|f| = \sum_{S \to T} f(u, v) - \sum_{T \to S} f(u, v) \;\le\; \sum_{S \to T} c(u, v) = c(S, T).
Equality at the end. Let S = the nodes reachable from s in the final residual graph.

An edge u \to v from S to T is full, f = c: otherwise the forward arc would make v reachable.
An edge v \to u from T to S carries no flow: otherwise its backward arc u \to v would make v reachable.
So both sums above are at their extremes: |f| = c(S, T), and this flow and this cut are both optimal.

title: Graphs, cuts and maximum flow
text:
Try it: augmenting paths




Edges show flow / capacity. “Next augmenting path” finds the shortest path in the residual graph (orange) and pushes its bottleneck. Tour: step through the example: 4, 6, 4, 5. Tick “show the residual graph” after step 2: grey arcs are room left, red ones flow that can be undone. Press next once more after the last path: no path left, the source side is shaded blue, the cut edges are red and dashed: flow 19 = cut 19. Point out that a→b goes from T to S and is not counted. Then “needs a back-edge”: the second path runs b→a backwards and cancels the first path’s flow on a→b. “Two minimum cuts”: the algorithm returns the cut nearest s; the toggle shows the one nearest t. Clicking an edge lets you change its capacity: raise b→d to 12 and the flow becomes 20.

title: Graphs, cuts and maximum flow
text:
Minimum cuts in practice

The minimum cut need not be unique. The reachable set from s gives the cut nearest s; the nodes that can still reach t give the one nearest t.
Image graphs have one node per pixel: millions of nodes, but only a few edges each.
Boykov–Kolmogorov (2004): grows search trees from s and t and reuses them between augmentations. Not the best worst case, but very fast on image graphs.
Push–relabel: pushes excess flow locally, node by node, instead of along whole paths; easy to run in parallel.
Undirected edges (as in images) are two directed edges, one each way.

title: Graphs, cuts and maximum flow
text:
Summary

An s–t cut separates s from t; its cost is the capacity of the edges from S to T.
Any flow \le any cut. Max-flow = min-cut.
Ford–Fulkerson: push flow along augmenting paths in the residual graph; backward arcs undo flow.
When no path is left, the nodes reachable from s form a minimum cut.
Next: segmentation energies as cuts, so that one max-flow gives the best segmentation.

title: Exercise: maximum margin and support vectors
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

find the maximum-margin line, its street width and its support vectors for a few points by hand,
decide whether a given line is the max-margin line,
predict what the slack penalty C does to the street, with and without outliers,
compute and compare the hinge, 0–1, logistic and squared losses.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the two demos.

title: Exercise: maximum margin and support vectors
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Street
the region -1 \le f(\mathbf x) \le 1 around the line f = 0; its width is 2/\|\mathbf w\|


Margin constraint
y_i f(\mathbf x_i) \ge 1: every training point on its side, outside the street


Max-margin line
the widest street, i.e. the smallest \|\mathbf w\| that satisfies all constraints


Support vectors
the training points on the edge of the street (soft margin: on, inside, or on the wrong side)


Slack
\xi_i = \max(0, 1 - y_i f(\mathbf x_i)): how far a point falls short of the street’s edge


Soft margin
minimise \tfrac12\|\mathbf w\|^2 + C\sum_i \xi_i; small C: wide street, many violations; large C: narrow street


Losses of m = y f
0–1: [m \le 0]; hinge: \max(0, 1 - m); logistic: \log_2(1 + e^{-m}); squared: (1 - m)^2



A recipe for a few points in 2D: find the closest pair of points of opposite classes (or the closest point and edge between the two groups). The max-margin line is the perpendicular bisector of that pair; check that no point lies inside the resulting street.

Math questions
B7 (math). Show that the distance between the lines \mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x + b = 1 and \mathbf w\cdot\mathbf x + b = -1 is 2/\|\mathbf w\|.
B8 (math). Show that at the optimum of the soft-margin problem, \xi_i = \max(0, 1 - y_i f(\mathbf x_i)), and derive the unconstrained form \tfrac12\|\mathbf w\|^2 + C\sum_i \max(0, 1 - y_i f(\mathbf x_i)).

For the lecture’s example, blue (0, 0), (0, 2), red (2, 1), (3, 0), the next unit will show that the solution has the form \mathbf w = \sum_i \alpha_i y_i\mathbf x_i with \sum_i \alpha_i y_i = 0. Check that \alpha = (0.25,\ 0.25,\ 0.5,\ 0) (in the order of the points) gives \mathbf w = (1, 0) and satisfies \sum_i \alpha_i y_i = 0. Which point has \alpha = 0, and why?






Solutions





B1. (a) The blue points lie on the segment x_1 = 1, 1 \le x_2 \le 3. The closest point of that segment to (4, 2) is (1, 2), at distance 3 (inside the segment, not an end point). (5, 4) is farther from everything blue. (b) The perpendicular bisector of (1, 2) and (4, 2): the line x_1 = 2.5. The street is 1 \le x_1 \le 4, width 3. No point lies inside it. Support vectors: (1, 1), (1, 3) and (4, 2), on the edges. (c) f = w_1(x_1 - 2.5) with f(4, 2) = 1: w_1 = 1/1.5 = 2/3. So \mathbf w = (2/3, 0), b = -5/3, and the width is 2/\|\mathbf w\| = 3. y f: (1, 1): -1 \cdot (2/3)(1 - 2.5) = 1; (1, 3): 1; (4, 2): 1; (5, 4): (2/3)(2.5) = 5/3 = 1.67.
B2. (a) Distances to x_2 = 1: (0, 0): 1, (1, 0): 1, (0, 2): 1, (2, 3): 2. The street 0 \le x_2 \le 2 is empty, width 2. Yes (see (c)). (b) No: it is 0.8 from the blue points and 1.2 from (0, 2). Its street is only 2 \cdot 0.8 = 1.6 wide; shifting it to the middle, x_2 = 1, widens it to 2. (c) No. Any street that separates (0, 0) from (0, 2) lies between them, so its width is at most their distance, 2. The line x_2 = 1 reaches that, so it is the max-margin line (\mathbf w = (0, 1), b = -1).
