It is XOR. With s = x_1 + x_2: out = s for 0 \le s \le 1, 2 - s for s \ge 1, and 0 for s < 0. So out > \tfrac12 exactly where \tfrac12 < x_1 + x_2 < \tfrac32: a band between two parallel lines, one per hidden unit.
B12. (a) e^2 = 7.389, e^1 = 2.718, e^0 = 1, sum 11.107: p = (0.665, 0.245, 0.090). (b) The same, (0.665, 0.245, 0.090): every e^{z_k} gets the factor e^{100}, which cancels. (Computed directly, e^{102} would overflow in many programs, which is why software subtracts the largest score first.) (c) p_1 = e^s/(e^0 + e^s) = 1/(e^{-s} + 1), the sigmoid of s.
B13. 784 \cdot 100 + 100 = 78{,}500 and 100 \cdot 10 + 10 = 1{,}010: 79,510 numbers. Every hidden unit has its own weight for every pixel, so nothing it learns about a stroke at one position carries over to the same stroke one pixel to the right: shifting the digit changes almost every input, and the network must learn each position separately, from many examples. Convolutional layers (unit 3 of this day) share the same small kernel across all positions.





Math questions
B14. (math) Show that a network with ReLU hidden units and a linear output is a continuous, piecewise linear function of its input: the input space splits into regions in which the network is an affine map \mathbf x \mapsto M\mathbf x + \mathbf c.
B15. (math) A network with one input x, one hidden layer of n ReLU units and a linear output. Show that its output, as a function of x, has at most n kinks. Can two units give the same kink position?
B16. (math) Show that after one step w_\text{new} - 1.5 = (1 - 8\eta)(w - 1.5). For which \eta does every step bring w closer to the best value?






Solutions (math)





B14. (math) Fix an input \mathbf x and record which hidden units are on (z > 0). In the set of inputs with the same on/off pattern, each ReLU is either the identity or zero, so every layer is an affine map (a matrix times the input plus a shift, with some rows zeroed), and a composition of affine maps is affine. The patterns split the input space into finitely many regions bounded by the hyperplanes z_j = 0 (for deeper layers, pieces of such hyperplanes). Continuity: every layer is continuous (ReLU is continuous), so the composition is.
B15. (math) Unit k computes \max(0, a_kx + b_k), which bends only at x = -b_k/a_k (and not at all if a_k = 0). The output \sum_k c_k\max(0, a_kx + b_k) + d is linear between consecutive bend points, so it can only change slope at these at most n positions. Two units can have the same bend position; then the network has fewer than n distinct kinks (and a kink disappears if the slope changes cancel).
B16. (math) w_\text{new} = w + 4\eta(3 - 2w) = w + 8\eta(1.5 - w), so w_\text{new} - 1.5 = (w - 1.5) - 8\eta(w - 1.5) = (1 - 8\eta)(w - 1.5). The distance shrinks at every step when |1 - 8\eta| < 1, i.e. 0 < \eta < 0.25. For 0.125 < \eta < 0.25 it zigzags across the valley but still converges.

title: Exercise: neural networks
text:
Explore
The demo fits a small network (1 \to H \to 1) to a line scan across two nuclei of different brightness (synthetic data with noise). Grey dots are the pixels, the red curve is the network, the faint orange curves are the hidden units’ hinges (each times its output weight) and the orange triangles mark where they bend. Below: the loss against the training step. train 500 steps runs gradient descent; new start puts the hinges back at their (fixed-seed) starting positions.



E1. With 3 hidden units, press train 500 steps six times. Where do the three hinges end up? Which features of the profile does the network get, and which does it miss?
E2. Compare the presets one hinge, 3 hinges and 12 hinges: read the final loss of each. The noise in the data has variance 0.03^2 = 0.0009. Which network is close to the best you can hope for? Can a network do better than the noise level on these data, and would that be good?
E3. Preset no bend: 12 hidden units, but no ReLU. Describe the fit and compare its loss with a flat line at the mean intensity (loss 0.0728). Explain with the collapse argument from the lecture.
E4. Preset learning rate too large. What happens to the loss, and to the hinges at the end? What does the fit look like?






Solutions





E1. After 3000 steps the three hinges sit at about 0.04, 0.27 and 0.47 on the 0–1 axis: the left foot, the top and the right foot of the bright nucleus. The network makes a tent over the bright nucleus and a flat line (about 0.33) to the right of it: the dimmer nucleus is missed. Three hinges are not enough for two plateaus with four edges. Loss 0.0203.
E2. Final losses after 3000 steps: one hinge 0.0588, 3 hinges 0.0203, 12 hinges 0.00186. Only the 12-hinge network is close to the noise variance 0.0009. A network with very many units could push the loss below 0.0009 by following the noise from pixel to pixel; that would be overfitting: it would fit these 100 pixels better but a new line scan of the same nuclei worse.
E3. The fit stays a straight, slightly tilted line, loss 0.0652, barely better than the flat line at the mean (0.0728). Without the bend, twelve hidden units and the output layer collapse to one matrix: \text{out} = (CA)x + \text{shift}, a straight line, however many units there are.
E4. The loss jumps around instead of falling smoothly, and after 500 steps it sits at 0.0728, exactly the loss of the flat mean line: every hinge has been thrown off the data (no unit is switched on anywhere between 0 and 1), so the network outputs a constant. The steps were so large that they overshot into a region where the ReLUs are off and the gradient is zero, and the network can no longer recover (“dead units”). A smaller learning rate avoids this.

title: Exercise: neural networks
text:
Explore: classifying points
The demo trains a small network to classify points in the plane. The points are coloured by class; the background shows the network’s decision (colour = predicted class, stronger = more confident). Choose the number of hidden layers (0–2), the units per layer and the activation \varphi. Each thumbnail shows one hidden unit: orange where it is active (strong = large output). play trains, step takes one gradient step, reset goes back to the start weights, new start draws other start weights. Click to add points of the chosen class, drag points to move them. With no hidden layer and two classes the network is one neuron: drag the round handle to move its line and the dark tip to turn it (the arrow is \mathbf w).



P1. Preset one neuron, by hand. The line starts vertical through the centre (\mathbf w = (1, 0), b = 0). Read the loss and accuracy. Turn and move the line so that it separates the two blobs as well as possible. Then drag the tip further out without moving the line: what happens to the loss, and why? Finally press play: where does training put the line, and what happens to \|\mathbf w\|?
P2. Preset one neuron on XOR fails. Press play. What loss and accuracy does the neuron reach? Compare the loss with \ln 2 = 0.693.
P3. Preset 2 hidden units solve XOR. Press play and watch the two thumbnails. What does each hidden unit do, and what does the output region look like? Then press new start a few times (play each time). Does training always succeed?
P4. Preset no nonlinearity: still a line: 8 hidden units, but no bend, on a circle inside a ring. Train. What does the boundary look like and what accuracy is reached? Explain with the collapse argument.
P5. Preset circle: 3 ReLU units. Train and describe the shape of the region inside. Why 3 units at least? Try 2 units.
P6. Preset spiral needs depth (two layers of 8). Train and compare the thumbnails of layer 1 with those of layer 2. Then set hidden layers to 1 and train again.
P7. Preset 3 classes with softmax, no hidden layer. What do the boundaries between the regions look like? Why?






Solutions





P1. The start line splits the blobs fairly well already: loss 0.535, accuracy 98 %. A line between the blobs, perpendicular to the line joining their centres, does about as well in accuracy. Making \mathbf w longer without moving the line makes every probability more confident: the loss falls while all points are on the right side (for example \mathbf w = (1, 1): 0.461, (4, 4): 0.154, (8, 8): 0.070, same line through the centre), but a point on the wrong side is punished harder and harder, so with overlapping classes the loss eventually rises again. Training puts the line between the blobs (accuracy 98 %, loss 0.032 after 1000 steps) and keeps growing \mathbf w, to about (16.8, 6.5) after 1000 steps: the few points in the overlap stay wrong, and the rest become ever more certain.
P2. The loss drops to 0.691 and stays; accuracy 50 %. 0.693 = \ln 2 is the loss of always answering “50 : 50”. The best a single line can do here is to give up: whatever line it draws, half of each class is on the wrong side.
P3. After about 50 steps the loss is below 0.03 and the accuracy 100 % (0.002 after 1000 steps). Each hidden unit is a half-plane (a ReLU of one line); the output region of one class is the band between the two lines (as in B11), which contains the two corners of that class. With other start weights (new start: start seeds 2 to 6) the network gets stuck at 75 % every time: one corner stays wrong. With the second start, one hidden unit is off on every point (“dead”: its gradient is zero, so it never comes back); with the others, both units are active but their lines sit where they can only fix three of the four corners, and no small step improves the loss. Small networks are sensitive to the start; larger ones much less (try 4 units).
P4. The boundary stays a straight line; accuracy 74 % (the line cuts off part of the ring), loss 0.569. Without a bend, W^{(2)}(W^{(1)}\mathbf x + \mathbf b^{(1)}) + \mathbf b^{(2)} is a single affine function of \mathbf x, however many units: one line.
P5. The inner region is a rounded triangle: three lines, one per hidden unit, cut off the corners; accuracy 100 % after about 200 steps (loss 0.016). A bounded region needs at least 3 lines in the plane (two lines give a wedge or a band, which is open on one side). With 2 units the accuracy stays around 74 %.
P6. Layer-1 thumbnails are half-planes (one line each). Layer-2 units combine them: their thumbnails are polygons and stripes. Together they follow the spiral: 100 % after about 500 steps. With a single layer of 8 units the network needs much longer and stays around 75–90 % (it oscillates between these values for thousands of steps): 8 lines are too few to cut the spiral into the right pieces.
P7. The boundaries are straight lines meeting in a point: with no hidden layer each class score is linear, z_k = \mathbf w_k^\top\mathbf x + b_k, and the boundary between classes k and j is where z_k = z_j, a line. Softmax only turns the scores into probabilities; it does not bend the boundaries.

title: Exercise: neural networks
text:
Where this leads
The next unit opens the black box of training: losses for classes, gradient descent with mini-batches, and backpropagation, which computes all the gradients in one backward pass. The rest of the neural-networks day uses the same “matrix, bend, matrix” with whole images as input (a 784-number vector for a 28\times28 image), many layers and many training examples: losses for classification, backpropagation, and convolutional networks that segment images. Later, the autoencoder units squeeze an image through a few numbers and rebuild it; without the bend such a network is exactly PCA.

title: Quiz: neural networks
text:
Short questions on neurons, layers, the ReLU bend, softmax and training. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A layer computes \text{ReLU}(A\mathbf x + \mathbf b) with \text{ReLU}(s) = \max(0, s) on each entry; training steps the weights against the gradient of a loss.

Q1. Compute \text{ReLU}\big((2,\ -3,\ 0,\ 0.5)\big).






Hint





Entry by entry: negatives become 0, the rest pass through.









Answer





(2,\ 0,\ 0,\ 0.5).




Q2. A colleague stacks ten layers, each a matrix plus a shift, with no ReLU in between. Can this network fit a curved intensity profile better than a single layer?






Hint





What is C(A\mathbf x + \mathbf b) + \mathbf d?









Answer





No. C(A\mathbf x + \mathbf b) + \mathbf d = (CA)\mathbf x + (C\mathbf b + \mathbf d): one matrix and one shift. However many layers, the result is a straight-line (linear) map. Only the bend between layers allows curves.




Q3. A network with one input x has three ReLU hidden units and one linear output. What does its output look like as a function of x?






Hint





Each hidden unit is \max(0, a_k x + b_k).









Answer





A continuous, piecewise straight line with at most three bends, one where each unit switches on (x = -b_k/a_k). Between the bends it is straight. More units allow more bends.




Q4. You train with gradient descent and the loss jumps up and down and grows. What is the first thing to change?






Hint





What controls the size of each step?









Answer





Lower the learning rate \eta. Steps that are too large overshoot the bottom of the valley and land higher on the other side; if each overshoot is larger than the last, the loss grows.




Q5. How many numbers (weights and shifts) does a layer from a 28\times 28 image to 64 hidden units have?






Hint





The matrix is 64 \times 784; one shift per hidden unit.









Answer





784 \cdot 64 + 64 = 50{,}240.




Q6. Why do neural networks for images need many training images?






Hint





Compare the number of weights with the number of examples.









Answer





They have very many weights (hundreds of thousands). With few images, many different weight settings fit them equally well, including ones that just memorise the training images and fail on new ones. Many examples (or a penalty, or a smaller network) pin the weights down; checking on images not used for training shows whether it worked.




Q7. A neuron has weights \mathbf w = (1, -1) and bias b = 0. Which points are on its positive side: (2, 1), (1, 2), (3, 3)? What is its decision line?






Hint





Compute x_1 - x_2.









Answer





(2, 1): +1, positive. (1, 2): -1, negative. (3, 3): 0, exactly on the line. The decision line is the diagonal x_1 = x_2; \mathbf w points to the side below it.




Q8. Why can a single neuron not compute XOR, while a network with two hidden units can?






Hint





Draw the four corners of the unit square and their XOR values.









Answer





One neuron splits the plane with one straight line, and no line puts (1,0) and (0,1) on one side and (0,0) and (1,1) on the other. Two hidden units give two lines; the output combines them (for example, “between the two lines”), which separates the corners.




Q9. A three-class network outputs the scores (1, 1, 1). What are the softmax probabilities? And for (5, 1, 1)?






Hint





p_k = e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j}.









Answer





Equal scores give equal probabilities, (1/3, 1/3, 1/3). For (5, 1, 1): e^4 = 54.6 times larger for the first class, so p = (54.6, 1, 1)/56.6 = (0.965, 0.018, 0.018).




Q10. (math) The neuron \varphi(\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x + b) with \mathbf w = (3, 4), b = -10. How far is its decision line from the origin? What changes if \mathbf w and b are both multiplied by 10?






Hint





Distance |b|/\|\mathbf w\|.









Answer





\|\mathbf w\| = 5, so the distance is 10/5 = 2. Multiplying both by 10 keeps the line (and the distance); only the steepness of a sigmoid output across the line increases tenfold.

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
About this lecture
A segmentation is usually used to count and measure objects. Pixel scores (the thresholding day) do not see objects. Today we score objects:

IoU of two objects, and what an IoU of 0.5 looks like.
Matching predicted to true objects, one to one, at an IoU threshold \tau: true positives, false positives, false negatives.
Precision, recall, F1 of objects, and F1 as a function of \tau.
Splits and merges: the errors that cost most.
Scored predictions: the precision–recall curve and average precision, and a naming trap.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.
crumbs: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
section: Recall: pixel scores cannot see objects
text:
Recall: pixel scores cannot see objects
From the thresholding day: compare a predicted mask with the true mask pixel by pixel. TP, FP, FN pixels; Dice = 2\,TP/(2\,TP + FP + FN), IoU (Jaccard) = TP/(TP + FP + FN).

Two touching nuclei predicted as one object: almost every pixel is right (Dice 0.96), but the count is 1 instead of 2, and the area of “the nucleus” is doubled. We have to decide which predicted object is which true object.
crumbs: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
IoU of two objects
The intersection over union of a true object G and a predicted object P: the overlap divided by the area covered by either.


IoU 1: identical. IoU 0: no overlap.
IoU 0.5 is already sloppy: the same disc shifted by about half its radius.
Small objects lose IoU fast: a one-pixel shift of a disc of radius 3 px gives IoU 0.65; of radius 20 px, 0.94.
crumbs: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
The math: IoU and Dice
For pixel sets A (truth) and B (prediction):
\text{IoU}(A, B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}, \qquad \text{Dice}(A, B) = \frac{2|A \cap B|}{|A| + |B|}.
With |A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|, writing J for IoU and D for Dice:
D = \frac{2J}{1 + J}, \qquad J = \frac{D}{2 - D}.
Both are monotone in each other, so they rank results the same way; IoU is the stricter number (IoU 0.5 ⇔ Dice 0.67, IoU 0.9 ⇔ Dice 0.95).
Disc of radius r shifted by d: |A \cap B| = 2r^2\arccos\frac{d}{2r} - \frac d2\sqrt{4r^2 - d^2}. For d \ll r the overlap loses about 2rd and the union gains 2rd, so IoU \approx 1 - \frac{4d}{\pi r}: the loss per pixel of shift scales with 1/r.
crumbs: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
section: The math: matching is forced above 0.5
text:
The math: matching is forced above 0.5
Claim. If B_1 \cap B_2 = \emptyset, then IoU(A, B_1) > \frac12 and IoU(A, B_2) > \frac12 cannot both hold.
Proof. IoU(A, B) > \frac12 means |A \cap B| > \frac12|A \cup B| \ge \frac12|A|. Two disjoint predictions would cover more than \frac12|A| + \frac12|A| = |A| pixels of A: impossible. \square
The same holds with the roles of truth and prediction swapped (true objects do not overlap either). So for \tau > \frac12 each row and each column of the IoU table has at most one entry \ge \tau, and the matching is unique.
At exactly \frac12 it fails: A cut into two equal halves B_1, B_2 gives IoU \frac12 with both.
crumbs: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
section: Below 0.5: greedy can lose a match
text:
Below 0.5: greedy can lose a match


Greedy: take the largest IoU first, then the next largest among free objects, … Here: G1–P1 (0.44); then G2 and P2 have no free partner. 1 match.
Optimal: the assignment with the most matches (then the largest total IoU): G1–P2, G2–P1. 2 matches.
Image libraries call the optimal solver the “Hungarian algorithm”. Above \tau = 0.5 both give the same answer.
crumbs: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
section: The math: matching as a linear assignment problem
text:
The math: matching as a linear assignment problem
Unknowns x_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}: true object i is matched to prediction j. Weights
M_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 + \varepsilon\,\text{IoU}_{ij} & \text{IoU}_{ij} \ge \tau \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad (\varepsilon \text{ small: count matches first, then IoU}).
\max_x \sum_{i,j} M_{ij}\,x_{ij} \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_j x_{ij} \le 1,\ \ \sum_i x_{ij} \le 1,\ \ x_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}.

The constraint matrix is totally unimodular: the linear-programming relaxation 0 \le x_{ij} \le 1 already has an integer optimum (stated without proof).
The Hungarian algorithm solves it exactly in O(n^3) for n objects (pad the table with zeros to a square).
With M_{ij} = \text{IoU}_{ij} instead, it maximises the total IoU; that can prefer fewer, better matches.
crumbs: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
section: Precision, recall and F1 of objects
text:
Precision, recall and F1 of objects
The pixel formulas, but each object counts one, big or small:
\text{precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} \quad \text{("how many of my objects are real")} \text{recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} \quad \text{("how many real objects did I find")} \text{F1} = \frac{2\,TP}{2\,TP + FP + FN}
The table above at \tau = 0.5: precision 2/4 = 0.5, recall 2/3 = 0.67, F1 = 4/7 = 0.57. At \tau = 0.3: G2–P2 also matches, F1 = 6/7 = 0.86.
crumbs: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
F1 as a function of \tau

Sweep \tau from 0.1 to 0.95. Sloppy outlines (blue): F1 0.88 at 0.5, 0.25 at 0.8. Merged pairs (red): a lower plateau (0.69 at 0.5) but tight outlines, so 0.38 at 0.8. Their pixel Dice says the opposite (0.86 vs 0.97). Report the curve, or at least two \tau values, never one number.
crumbs: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
The math: F1 against \tau
Write n_G and n_P for the numbers of true and predicted objects. Every object is either matched or not, so FP = n_P - TP and FN = n_G - TP:
\text{F1}(\tau) = \frac{2\,TP(\tau)}{2\,TP(\tau) + FP(\tau) + FN(\tau)} = \frac{2\,TP(\tau)}{n_G + n_P}.
The denominator does not depend on \tau; F1 is the number of matches, scaled. Raising \tau only removes allowed pairs, so the largest possible number of matches cannot grow: \text{F1}(\tau) is non-increasing. (Also for greedy matching: at a higher \tau it walks the same list of pairs, just stops earlier.)
The matching accuracy TP/(TP + FP + FN) = TP/(n_G + n_P - TP) moves with F1: \text{acc} = \text{F1}/(2 - \text{F1}), the same relation as IoU and Dice.
crumbs: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
Splits, merges, misses, specks
Read from the IoU table:

Split: one true object, two predictions with IoU around 0.4 each. At \tau = 0.5: 1 FN + 2 FP.
Merge: two true objects, one prediction. At best 1 TP + 1 FN; often (IoU < 0.5 with both) 2 FN + 1 FP.
Missed dim objects: FN. Spurious specks: FP.

One merge costs more F1 than many slightly wrong outlines. Count splits and merges and report them on their own: they say what to fix (the seeds of a watershed, a threshold, a minimum size).
Watershed segmentation (the watershed day) produces exactly these errors when its markers are wrong.
crumbs: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
Try it: matching objects




Synthetic nuclei, 16 true objects (white outlines). Predictions are filled green (TP) or red (FP); missed true objects have dashed orange outlines. Tour: “a typical result” at τ = 0.5: TP 12, FP 2, FN 4, F1 0.80, pixel Dice 0.86; two merges are labelled. “Dice high, count wrong”: Dice 0.97, but 5 merges, F1 0.69. “Sloppy outlines”: F1 0.88 at 0.5, drag τ to 0.8: 0.25. “One split”: TP 15, FP 2, FN 1. “Greedy loses a match” (τ = 0.3): switch the IoU table on the exercise page, or compare greedy (TP 15) and optimal (TP 16) with the buttons. “Specks”: precision 0.57, F1 0.73, but the PR tab shows AP 1.00: the specks have low scores. “vs a second annotator”: the grey band is above annotator B’s agreement with A.

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
Scores and average precision
Many methods give each object a confidence score. Sort the predictions by score and walk down the list; each one is a TP or an FP (at \tau). After each step write down (recall, precision).


4 true objects, 5 predictions by score: TP, TP, FP, TP, FP.

Average precision (AP) = area under the precision–recall curve, with precision made “never decreasing from the right”: 0.25 \cdot 1 + 0.25 \cdot 1 + 0.25 \cdot 0.75 = 0.6875.



Low-scored specks come last: they lower precision at the end of the list but hardly change AP. Averaging AP over \tau = 0.5, 0.55, \dots, 0.95 also rewards good outlines.
crumbs: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
The math: average precision
Predictions sorted by decreasing score; after the first k of them, P_k = TP_k / k and R_k = TP_k / n_G.
Interpolated precision: P^{\text{interp}}(R_k) = \max_{k' \ge k} P_{k'} (the best precision at this or a higher recall).
\text{AP} = \sum_k (R_k - R_{k-1})\,P^{\text{interp}}(R_k), \qquad R_0 = 0.
Only steps that add a TP raise the recall, so FPs at the end of the list (R_k = R_{k-1}) add nothing. AP over thresholds: \frac{1}{10}\sum_{\tau \in \{0.5, 0.55, \dots, 0.95\}} \text{AP}(\tau).
For AP the matching is done in score order: each prediction takes the free true object with the largest IoU \ge \tau.
crumbs: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
section: A naming trap: “AP” is two different things
text:
A naming trap: “AP” is two different things
Many cell-segmentation papers report “AP at \tau” meaning
\frac{TP}{TP + FP + FN} \quad \text{at one } \tau, \text{ without any scores.}
That is not the area under a precision–recall curve. In the example: AP (area) = 0.6875, but TP/(TP+FP+FN) = 3/(3 + 2 + 1) = 0.5.
In this course we call TP/(TP + FP + FN) the matching accuracy, and say that papers sometimes call it AP. Always check the definition before comparing numbers between papers.
crumbs: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
Two practical rules

Border objects: an object cut by the image border cannot match well. Decide once whether objects touching the border count, and apply the same rule to truth and prediction (the unbiased counting frame of the labelling day is one consistent choice).
Report enough to reproduce: \tau (or the F1-vs-\tau curve), the matching rule, how many objects, and the numbers of splits and merges, next to any single score.
crumbs: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
Summary

IoU of two objects: overlap / union. IoU 0.5 is already sloppy; small objects lose IoU fast.
Matching: one to one, IoU \ge \tau. TP = matched pairs, FP = unmatched predictions, FN = unmatched true objects; no TN.
Above \tau = 0.5 the matching is forced; below, use the optimal assignment, not greedy.
Object precision, recall, F1: the pixel formulas, counting objects. Report F1 against \tau.
Splits and merges cost most; count them.
AP = area under the precision–recall curve of scored predictions; TP/(TP+FP+FN) is the matching accuracy, which some papers also call AP.

title: Exercise: Legendre moments and reconstruction
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

explain why reconstructing an image from monomial moments is an ill-conditioned linear system (the Gram matrix),
run Gram–Schmidt on 1, x, x^2 and recognise the Legendre polynomials,
approximate a function by Legendre polynomials and see that this is an orthogonal projection,
describe how a reconstruction from moments differs from a Fourier low-pass, and what pixels do to orthogonality,
(math) prove the best-approximation property and convert geometric to Legendre moments.

title: Exercise: Legendre moments and reconstruction
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Inner product
\langle g, h\rangle = \int_{-1}^1 g h\,dx (or \sum_i g_i h_i \Delta x on a grid)


Gram matrix
G_{jk} = \langle b_j, b_k\rangle of the basis functions; diagonal iff the basis is orthogonal


Condition number
\kappa(G) = largest/smallest eigenvalue; about \log_{10}\kappa digits are lost when solving G a = m


Legendre polynomials
P_0 = 1, P_1 = x, P_2 = \tfrac12(3x^2 - 1), (n+1)P_{n+1} = (2n+1)xP_n - nP_{n-1}, \int P_n^2 = \frac{2}{2n+1}


Coefficients
a_n = \frac{2n+1}{2}\langle f, P_n\rangle; in 2D a_{pq} = \frac{(2p+1)(2q+1)}{4}\iint P_p P_q I


Reconstruction
\hat f_N = \sum_{n \le N} a_n P_n (2D: \sum_{p+q \le N} a_{pq} P_p P_q), the orthogonal projection
crumbs: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction

title: Exercise: Legendre moments and reconstruction
text:
By hand
B1. Gram–Schmidt on 1, x, x^2 over [-1, 1]. (a) Compute \langle 1, 1\rangle, \langle x, 1\rangle, \langle x^2, 1\rangle, \langle x^2, x\rangle. (b) q_0 = 1. Compute q_1 = x - \frac{\langle x, q_0\rangle}{\langle q_0, q_0\rangle} q_0 and q_2 = x^2 - (\dots)q_0 - (\dots)q_1. (c) Scale q_2 so that its value at x = 1 is 1 and compare with P_2.
B2. The 3 \times 3 Gram matrix of 1, x, x^2 on [-1, 1]. (a) Write it down. Why is it not diagonal? (b) Compute the cosine of the angle between 1 and x^2. (c) Write the Gram matrix of P_0, P_1, P_2.
B3. Approximate f(x) = |x| on [-1, 1] by P_0, P_1, P_2. (a) Compute a_0 = \tfrac12\int |x|\,dx, a_1 and a_2 = \tfrac52\int |x| P_2\,dx. (Use symmetry: \int_{-1}^1 |x| g = 2\int_0^1 x g for even g.) (b) Write \hat f_2(x) as a polynomial in x, evaluate it at x = 0 and x = \pm 1, and sketch it with |x|. (c) The relative error \|\hat f - f\|/\|f\| is 0.5 with P_0 alone and 0.125 with P_0, P_1, P_2. Why does adding P_1 not help here?
B4. The cosine between x^8 and x^{10} on [-1, 1] is 0.994. What angle is that? What is the cosine between x^9 and x^{10}, and why?
B5. The condition number of the monomial Gram matrix on [-1, 1] is 9.4 \times 10^6 at degree 10 and 3.1 \times 10^{14} at degree 20; on [0, 1] it is 5.2 \times 10^{14} at degree 10. How many of the 16 significant digits of a double are left in each case? What does this say about the choice of coordinates?
B6. Count: how many Legendre moments are there up to order 20, and up to 40? What fraction of the pixels of a 128 \times 128 image are they?
B7. Four pixels on [-1, 1] have their centres at x = -\tfrac34, -\tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac34 (\Delta x = \tfrac12). Compute the sampled inner product \sum_i P_0(x_i) P_2(x_i)\,\Delta x. Is it 0? What does that mean for Legendre moments of a 4 \times 4 image?

Math questions
B8. (math) Verify \int_{-1}^1 P_n^2\,dx = \frac{2}{2n+1} for n = 0, 1, 2, and use the recurrence to compute P_3 and P_4.
B9. (math) Express a_{20}, a_{11} and a_{02} in terms of the geometric moments m_{pq} (on [-1, 1]^2).
B10. (math) Let b_0, \dots, b_N be orthogonal and \hat f = \sum_k \frac{\langle f, b_k\rangle}{\langle b_k, b_k\rangle}b_k. Show that f - \hat f is orthogonal to every b_j, and that \|f - g\| \ge \|f - \hat f\| for every g in their span.
B11. (math) Show that the Gram matrix of 1, x, \dots, x^N on [0, 1] is the Hilbert matrix H_{jk} = \frac{1}{j+k+1}, and that on [-1, 1] the entries with j + k odd are 0. Why does the zero pattern not save the [-1, 1] matrix from being ill-conditioned?






Solutions





B1. (a) \langle 1, 1\rangle = 2, \langle x, 1\rangle = 0, \langle x^2, 1\rangle = 2/3, \langle x^2, x\rangle = 0. (b) q_1 = x - 0 = x. q_2 = x^2 - \frac{2/3}{2}\cdot 1 - \frac{0}{2/3}x = x^2 - \frac13. (c) q_2(1) = \frac23, so q_2 / \frac23 = \frac32 x^2 - \frac12 = \frac12(3x^2 - 1) = P_2.
B2. (a) G = \begin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 0 & 2/3 \\ 0 & 2/3 & 0 \\ 2/3 & 0 & 2/5 \end{psmallmatrix}. Not diagonal because 1 and x^2 are both even and positive: \langle 1, x^2\rangle = 2/3 \ne 0. (b) \frac{2/3}{\sqrt{2 \cdot 2/5}} = 0.745 (an angle of 42°). (c) \operatorname{diag}(2, 2/3, 2/5).
B3. (a) a_0 = \tfrac12 \cdot 2\int_0^1 x\,dx = \tfrac12. a_1 = 0 (|x| is even, P_1 odd). a_2 = \tfrac52 \cdot 2\int_0^1 x \cdot \tfrac12(3x^2 - 1)\,dx = \tfrac52\left(\tfrac34 - \tfrac12\right) = \tfrac58. (b) \hat f_2 = \tfrac12 + \tfrac58 \cdot \tfrac12(3x^2 - 1) = \tfrac{3}{16} + \tfrac{15}{16}x^2. \hat f_2(0) = 0.1875, \hat f_2(\pm 1) = 1.125: a parabola that misses the corner at 0 (too high) and overshoots at the ends. (c) |x| is even, so its coefficient on the odd P_1 is 0: adding P_1 adds nothing. (The 400-sample demo gives the same 0.5 and 0.125.)
B4. \arccos 0.994 = 6.1°: nearly parallel. x^9 \cdot x^{10} = x^{19} is odd: the cosine is exactly 0. Monomials are orthogonal across parity, nearly parallel within it.
B5. \log_{10} 9.4 \times 10^6 \approx 7: about 9 digits left. \log_{10} 3.1 \times 10^{14} \approx 14.5: 1–2 digits left. On [0, 1] at degree 10 already about 1–2 left. Coordinates in [-1, 1] (centred) are much better than [0, 1], but even there monomials of high degree are unusable; an orthogonal basis needs no system at all.
B6. 231 and 861; 1.4 % and 5.3 % of 16384.
B7. P_2(\pm\tfrac34) = \tfrac12(3 \cdot \tfrac{9}{16} - 1) = \tfrac{11}{32}, P_2(\pm\tfrac14) = \tfrac12(\tfrac{3}{16} - 1) = -\tfrac{13}{32}. Sum: \tfrac12 \cdot 2\left(\tfrac{11}{32} - \tfrac{13}{32}\right) = -\tfrac{1}{16} = -0.0625 \ne 0. On 4 pixels the sampled P_0 and P_2 are not orthogonal: a Legendre moment computed by sampling mixes in a little of the other orders, and the reconstruction is not an exact projection. The fewer pixels and the higher the order, the worse.









Solutions (math)





B8. \int 1 = 2; \int x^2 = 2/3; \int \tfrac14(3x^2 - 1)^2 = \tfrac14(\tfrac{18}{5} - 4 + 2) = \tfrac25. Recurrence with n = 2: 3P_3 = 5xP_2 - 2P_1 = \tfrac52(3x^3 - x) - 2x, so P_3 = \tfrac12(5x^3 - 3x). With n = 3: 4P_4 = 7xP_3 - 3P_2, so P_4 = \tfrac18(35x^4 - 30x^2 + 3).
B9. a_{20} = \tfrac{5 \cdot 1}{4}\iint P_2(x) I = \tfrac54\left(\tfrac32 m_{20} - \tfrac12 m_{00}\right); a_{02} = \tfrac54\left(\tfrac32 m_{02} - \tfrac12 m_{00}\right); a_{11} = \tfrac{3 \cdot 3}{4} m_{11} = \tfrac94 m_{11}.
B10. \langle f - \hat f, b_j\rangle = \langle f, b_j\rangle - \sum_k \frac{\langle f, b_k\rangle}{\langle b_k, b_k\rangle}\langle b_k, b_j\rangle = \langle f, b_j\rangle - \langle f, b_j\rangle = 0. For g in the span, \hat f - g is in the span too, so \|f - g\|^2 = \|(f - \hat f) + (\hat f - g)\|^2 = \|f - \hat f\|^2 + \|\hat f - g\|^2 (cross term 0).
B11. \int_0^1 x^{j+k}dx = \frac{1}{j+k+1}; \int_{-1}^1 x^{j+k}dx = \frac{1 - (-1)^{j+k+1}}{j+k+1}, which is 0 for j + k odd. The zeros split the problem into an even and an odd block, but within each block (e.g. 1, x^2, x^4, \dots) the functions are again nearly parallel: each block is ill-conditioned on its own.
crumbs: Better bases: Legendre moments and reconstruction

title: Exercise: Legendre moments and reconstruction
text:
Explore: monomials and Legendre in 1D
The interval [-1, 1] with 400 samples. Top left: the basis functions up to degree N: monomials, Legendre polynomials, or the Gram–Schmidt view (the next monomial, its projection onto the functions already orthogonalised, and what is left). Top right: the Gram matrix of the shown functions as cosines (\langle b_j, b_k\rangle / \|b_j\|\|b_k\|, 1 = same direction) and its condition number \kappa. Bottom: a signal fitted with degree N by both bases (monomials through the Gram system, Legendre by projection), and the error against N, in 64-bit or 32-bit arithmetic.



P1. Preset monomials look alike (N = 10). Read the cosines of (x^8, x^{10}), (x^9, x^{10}) and (1, x^2) in the Gram matrix, and \kappa. Switch to Legendre: what are the cosines and \kappa now, and where does that \kappa come from?
P2. Preset Gram–Schmidt to P₃: press Gram–Schmidt step to go back to step 1 and step through. At step 3, what is subtracted from x^2? Compare with B1. Watch the Gram matrix change.
P3. Choose the signal |x| and Legendre, and set N = 0, 2 and 4. Compare the errors with B3.
P4. Preset fit a step (N = 12). Compare the two errors. Raise N to 30: from which N do the two errors differ? Switch to 32-bit: from which N now?
P5. Preset monomials break down (the bump, N = 24). Read both errors. Explain the error-vs-N plot for the monomials in 64-bit and in 32-bit.






Solutions





P1. \cos(x^8, x^{10}) = 0.99, \cos(x^9, x^{10}) = 0.00, \cos(1, x^2) = 0.75 (the grid values agree with B2 and B4); \kappa = 9.5 \times 10^6. Legendre: the identity matrix (all off-diagonal cosines 0), \kappa = 21: the Gram matrix is diagonal with entries 2/(2n+1), from 2 down to 2/21, so \kappa is just the ratio of the longest to the shortest basis function. Normalised Legendre polynomials would have \kappa = 1.
P2. At step 3, the projection of x^2 onto 1 is the constant 1/3 (the projection onto x is 0); the remainder x^2 - 1/3, scaled to 1 at x = 1, is P_2. After step k the top-left k \times k block of the Gram matrix is diagonal; after step 4 the whole matrix is (\kappa = 7 for P_0 \dots P_3).
P3. 0.5000, 0.1250 and 0.0625: N = 2 matches B3 exactly.
P4. At N = 12 both 0.1749. In 64-bit they agree to four digits up to N \approx 20 (0.1352 against 0.1353) and differ from about N = 24 (0.1312 against 0.1238); at 30: 0.1358 against 0.1131. In 32-bit the monomial fit departs from N \approx 13 (0.1727 against 0.1533 at N = 16).
P5. Monomials 0.147, Legendre 0.017. In 64-bit the monomial error follows the Legendre one until N \approx 22, then jumps around: the Gram system (\kappa \approx 10^{14} and more) has lost all its digits, so the coefficients are dominated by rounding error. In 32-bit (7 digits) this happens already at N \approx 13. The Legendre fit needs no system and keeps improving.

title: Exercise: Legendre moments and reconstruction
section: Explore: rebuild an image from its moments
text:
Explore: rebuild an image from its moments
A 64 \times 64 image is rebuilt from its moments up to order N (slider) with four bases: monomials (least squares through the Gram system; coordinates in [-1, 1] or [0, 1]; computed only up to N = 32), Legendre, Zernike (on the inscribed disc, the next unit) and a Fourier low-pass that keeps the same number of coefficients (lowest frequencies first). Under each panel: the number of coefficients and the relative error against the input; the plot shows the error against N for all four. The display range is the input’s range \pm 30\,\%, so overshoots are visible. pixels chooses how the Legendre polynomials meet the pixel grid: sampled at the centres, averaged over each pixel, or the discrete orthogonal polynomials. noise adds Gaussian noise (the error is still measured against the clean input).



E1. Preset low orders = blurry ellipse (nucleus, N = 2). How many coefficients, and what do the reconstructions look like? Raise N to 20. Which basis has the smallest error at N = 2 and at N = 20?
E2. Preset monomials explode (letter E, N = 14, monomial coordinates [0, 1]). Compare the monomial and Legendre errors. Switch the monomial coordinates to [-1, 1]. Then look at the monomial curve in the error plot for both choices.
E3. Preset Legendre vs Fourier ringing (square, N = 16). Compare the errors and the ripples of Legendre and Fourier. Where are the ripples strongest?
E4. Choose micrograph and N = 40. Read the Legendre error with point samples, pixel-integrated and discrete (exact). Look at the Legendre curve in the plot for point samples. Explain.
E5. Preset noise in high orders (nucleus, \sigma = 0.3, N = 40). Find the N with the smallest error for Legendre, Zernike and Fourier. Why does the error rise again?






Solutions





E1. 6 coefficients; every reconstruction is a blurry blob (Legendre and monomials a smooth hill, error 0.685; Zernike 0.571; Fourier 0.564). At N = 20 (231 coefficients): Legendre 0.226, Zernike 0.185, Fourier 0.175; the dent of the nucleus is visible. Fourier is slightly best at both; Legendre and monomials agree (same space, well-conditioned at this N).
E2. Monomials on [0, 1]: error 2.430, the image is a mess of large values; Legendre 0.366. With [-1, 1]: 0.365, the same as Legendre. In the plot the [0, 1] curve departs from about N = 12 (0.482 against 0.419) and jumps around; the [-1, 1] curve follows Legendre up to about N = 24 (0.316 against 0.312) and then departs (0.566 at N = 25, 0.361 against 0.290 at N = 28). Both bases span the same polynomials; only the rounding errors of the ill-conditioned Gram system differ.
E3. Legendre 0.254, Zernike 0.242, Fourier 0.227. Both overshoot next to the edges (Legendre values from −0.142 to 1.144, Fourier from −0.137 to 1.180). The Legendre ripples run parallel to the image border and get closer together towards it; the Fourier ripples are evenly spaced and continue across the border (the Fourier basis treats the image as periodic). The largest single error is at the square’s corners for both.
E4. Point samples 0.349, pixel-integrated 0.099, discrete 0.094. With point samples the error falls to about 0.160 at N = 16–20 and then rises (0.218 at 30): the sampled polynomials are less and less orthogonal on the grid as the order grows, and the micrograph is bright up to the image border, where the high-order polynomials are largest. The pixel-integrated and discrete bases keep improving.
E5. Legendre: smallest at N = 24 (0.268), 0.340 at N = 40; Zernike: N = 18 (0.257), 0.421 at 40; Fourier: N = 22 (0.238), 0.318 at 40. Low orders capture the shape; the noise is spread over all orders, so high orders add more noise than shape. As with a low-pass filter, stopping early is a denoiser.

title: Exercise: Legendre moments and reconstruction

Where this leads
Legendre moments live on a square, and a rotated image mixes them in a complicated way. The next unit moves to the disc and polar coordinates: Zernike polynomials are orthogonal there, and their magnitudes do not change at all when the image rotates.

title: Quiz: Legendre moments and reconstruction
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Inner product on [-1, 1]: \langle g, h\rangle = \int_{-1}^1 g h\,dx; Legendre polynomials P_0 = 1, P_1 = x, P_2 = \tfrac12(3x^2 - 1).

Q1. Why are x and x^2 orthogonal on [-1, 1], but 1 and x^2 not?






Hint





Even times odd is odd.









Answer





x \cdot x^2 = x^3 is odd, so its integral over the symmetric interval is 0. 1 \cdot x^2 = x^2 is positive everywhere (except at 0): \int_{-1}^1 x^2\,dx = 2/3 \ne 0.




Q2. The cosine of the angle between x^8 and x^{10} on [-1, 1] is 0.994. What does that mean for the moments m_8 and m_{10} of a 1D signal, and for getting the signal back from them?






Hint





Two nearly parallel vectors measure almost the same component.









Answer





They are almost the same measurement: m_{10} adds very little information to m_8. To separate the contributions of x^8 and x^{10} to the signal, one has to take a small difference of two large, nearly equal numbers: rounding errors in the moments are amplified enormously (an ill-conditioned system).




Q3. The Gram matrix of the monomials up to degree 10 on [-1, 1] has condition number about 10^7. Roughly how many of the 16 significant digits of a double survive in the coefficients of the reconstruction?






Hint





About \log_{10}\kappa digits are lost.









Answer





About 7 digits are lost, so about 9 remain. At degree 20 (\kappa \approx 3 \times 10^{14}) only 1–2 remain: the reconstruction becomes noise.




Q4. Gram–Schmidt on 1, x, x^2: what do you subtract from x^2, and what is the result after scaling to the value 1 at x = 1?






Hint





x^2 is already orthogonal to x. Its component along 1 is its average over the interval.









Answer





Subtract the projection onto 1: \frac{\langle x^2, 1\rangle}{\langle 1, 1\rangle} = \frac{2/3}{2} = \frac13. Then x^2 - \frac13, scaled by \frac32: P_2 = \frac12(3x^2 - 1).




Q5. You have reconstructed an image from its Legendre moments up to N = 10, and now add order 11. Which coefficients must be recomputed? And with monomials?






Hint





Orthogonal projection: each coefficient is \langle I, b_k\rangle / \langle b_k, b_k\rangle.









Answer





Legendre: none; only the 12 new coefficients of order 11 are added. Each coefficient depends only on its own basis function. Monomials: all coefficients change, because the new monomials are not orthogonal to the old ones and the whole Gram system has to be solved again.




Q6. Legendre moments up to order N and geometric moments up to order N: which contains more information about the image?






Hint





Is P_p a combination of monomials of degree at most p, and conversely?









Answer





Neither: each set is a fixed invertible (triangular) linear transformation of the other. They differ in how well they are conditioned, not in information.




Q7. A 64 \times 64 image is rebuilt from its moments up to order 40 with Legendre polynomials sampled at the pixel centres. The error first falls with N, then rises again. Why, and what are two remedies?






Hint





Are the sampled polynomials orthogonal on the grid?









Answer





The integral is replaced by a sum over pixel centres, and the sampled P_n are only approximately orthogonal on the grid; the error grows with the order, so the “projection” is no longer a projection. Remedies: integrate each P_n over the pixel (exact for an image constant on each pixel), or use discrete orthogonal polynomials (Tchebichef), which are exactly orthogonal on the grid.




Q8. How many Legendre moments are there up to order 20, and what fraction of the pixels of a 128 \times 128 image is that?






Hint





(N+1)(N+2)/2.









Answer





21 \cdot 22/2 = 231; 231/16384 = 1.4\,\%.




Q9. (math) Show that \int_{-1}^1 P_2(x)^2\,dx = 2/5.






Hint





P_2^2 = \tfrac14(9x^4 - 6x^2 + 1).









Answer





\tfrac14\left(9 \cdot \tfrac25 - 6 \cdot \tfrac23 + 2\right) = \tfrac14\left(\tfrac{18}{5} - 4 + 2\right) = \tfrac14 \cdot \tfrac85 = \tfrac25, in agreement with \frac{2}{2n+1} for n = 2.

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
About this lecture
Last unit: a threshold t splits the histogram into background and object, and a good t sits in a valley. Now the computer chooses t from the histogram alone.

Otsu: make both classes as tight as possible; equivalently, push their means apart.
Isodata: two means and their midpoint, repeated; 1D k-means.
Minimum error: model the histogram as two normal distributions and put t where they cross (Bayes).
Which method is biased when one class is small or wide, and in which direction.
Briefly: the triangle and maximum-entropy methods, and three classes.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Choosing the threshold: Otsu & minimum error

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Two classes

A threshold t splits the grey levels into class 0 (background, i \le t) and class 1 (object, i > t). Each class has

a weight \omega_0, \omega_1: the fraction of pixels in it (\omega_0 = P(t), \omega_1 = 1 - \omega_0),
a mean \mu_0, \mu_1 and a variance \sigma_0^2, \sigma_1^2 of its grey levels.

Worked example (8 grey levels, 20 pixels): h = (2, 5, 3, 1, 1, 2, 4, 2), mean \mu = 3.3, variance \sigma_T^2 = 5.81. At t = 3: \omega_0 = 0.55, \mu_0 = 1.27, \mu_1 = 5.78.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Choosing the threshold: Otsu & minimum error

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Otsu: tight classes, far apart
Otsu (1979): a good split makes each class tight around its own mean.

Measure the spread within the classes: \sigma_W^2 = the weighted average of the two class variances. Choose t to make it smallest.
The total spread of all pixels, \sigma_T^2, does not depend on t. It splits into within + between: the spread of the pixels around their class mean, plus the spread of the class means around the overall mean.
So making the classes tight is the same as making the class means far apart: maximise the between-class variance \sigma_B^2 = \omega_0\omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2.
\sigma_B^2 is large when the means are far apart and both classes are substantial: a class with 1 % of the pixels contributes little, however far away it is.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Choosing the threshold: Otsu & minimum error

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
The math: within + between
With p_i the normalised histogram, class 0 = \{i \le t\}: \sigma_T^2 = \sum_i (i - \mu)^2 p_i = \sum_{k=0}^{1}\sum_{i \in k} \big((i - \mu_k) + (\mu_k - \mu)\big)^2 p_i . Expand the square. The cross term 2(\mu_k - \mu)\sum_{i \in k}(i - \mu_k)p_i vanishes, because the deviations from a class’s own mean sum to zero. What remains: \sigma_T^2 = \underbrace{\omega_0\sigma_0^2 + \omega_1\sigma_1^2}_{\sigma_W^2} + \underbrace{\omega_0(\mu_0 - \mu)^2 + \omega_1(\mu_1 - \mu)^2}_{\sigma_B^2}. \sigma_T^2 is fixed, so \arg\min_t \sigma_W^2 = \arg\max_t \sigma_B^2. With \mu = \omega_0\mu_0 + \omega_1\mu_1: \mu_0 - \mu = \omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1) and \mu_1 - \mu = \omega_0(\mu_1 - \mu_0), so \sigma_B^2 = \omega_0\omega_1^2(\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2 + \omega_1\omega_0^2(\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2 = \omega_0\omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2 .
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Choosing the threshold: Otsu & minimum error

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
section: The math: one pass over the histogram
text:
The math: one pass over the histogram
With the running sums P(t) = \sum_{i \le t} p_i and M(t) = \sum_{i \le t} i\,p_i of the last unit: \omega_0 = P, \mu_0 = M/P, \mu_1 = (\mu - M)/(1 - P), and \mu_1 - \mu_0 = \frac{\mu P - M}{P(1 - P)} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sigma_B^2(t) = \frac{\big(\mu\,P(t) - M(t)\big)^2}{P(t)\,\big(1 - P(t)\big)} .

Build the histogram: O(N) for N pixels. Then one pass over the L grey levels evaluates \sigma_B^2 at every t: O(L).
For 256 grey levels the search is free; even for 16-bit data it is 65 536 evaluations.
Undefined where a class is empty (P = 0 or 1).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Choosing the threshold: Otsu & minimum error

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Choosing the threshold: Otsu & minimum error

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Try it: Otsu by hand




The bars are the worked example; drag a bar to change its count, move t with the slider or by clicking a row. The stacked bar under the plot shows total = within + between: the total stays at 5.81 while t moves. Tour: move t from 0 to 6 and watch the star (best t) and the stacked bar. “isodata step” from 5.5: 4.17 → 3.75 → 3.53, the same split as Otsu. “two equal peaks”: t* = 3 by symmetry. “isodata stuck”: three groups of levels; isodata from 6.5 stops at 4.58 (split 4, σ_B² = 3.33) while Otsu’s best is t = 0 (4.05).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Choosing the threshold: Otsu & minimum error

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
section: Isodata: two means and their midpoint
text:
Isodata: two means and their midpoint
Ridler & Calvard (1978): start with any t, then repeat

split at t and compute the two class means \mu_0, \mu_1;
move t to their midpoint (\mu_0 + \mu_1)/2;

until t stops moving.

Every pixel joins the nearer mean, then the means are recomputed: this is k-means with k = 2 in one dimension.
The worked example from t = 5.5: 4.17 \to 3.75 \to 3.53, which splits at 3, the same as Otsu.
It can stop at a different fixed point: with three groups of grey levels (levels 0, 3–4 and 7), isodata from 6.5 stops at 4.58 (split \{0, 3, 4\} vs \{7\}), while Otsu’s best split is \{0\} vs the rest. Isodata finds a local optimum; Otsu searches all t.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Choosing the threshold: Otsu & minimum error

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
section: The math: Otsu’s optimum is an isodata fixed point
text:
The math: Otsu’s optimum is an isodata fixed point
Continuous grey levels with density p(x): P' = p(t), M' = t\,p(t). Write D = \mu P - M = P(1 - P)(\mu_1 - \mu_0), so \sigma_B^2 = D^2 / (P(1 - P)) and D' = (\mu - t)\,p(t). Setting the derivative to zero (with p(t) \ne 0, D \ne 0): 2(\mu - t)\,P(1 - P) = D(1 - 2P) \;\Longrightarrow\; t = \mu - \tfrac12 (1 - 2P)(\mu_1 - \mu_0). Insert \mu = P\mu_0 + (1 - P)\mu_1: t = \frac{\mu_0 + \mu_1}{2}. Every stationary point of \sigma_B^2(t), the maximum included, is a fixed point of isodata. The converse fails: a fixed point can be a local maximum or even a minimum of \sigma_B^2.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Choosing the threshold: Otsu & minimum error

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Two classes as probabilities: Bayes
Treat the grey level x of a pixel as random. Class k has prior probability \omega_k (its share of the pixels) and a distribution f_k(x) of grey levels.

Bayes’ rule: the probability that a pixel with grey level x is object is proportional to \omega_1 f_1(x); that it is background, to \omega_0 f_0(x). “Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior.”
Decide object where \omega_1 f_1(x) > \omega_0 f_0(x): this rule makes the fewest errors.
For a threshold t: the errors are the background tail above t plus the object tail below t. Moving t trades one tail for the other; the total is smallest where the two weighted curves cross.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Choosing the threshold: Otsu & minimum error

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Where the curves cross

Background \mu_0 = 50 (90 % of the pixels), objects \mu_1 = 150 (10 %), both with \sigma = 20.

The crossing is at 108.8, not at the midpoint 100: the rarer class gets less room. Error 0.35 %, against 0.62 % at the midpoint.
Shaded: the two tails that a threshold at the crossing gets wrong.
Equal variances, equal weights: the crossing is the midpoint, as in isodata.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Choosing the threshold: Otsu & minimum error

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
The math: the minimum-error threshold
The error of the rule “object if x > t”: E(t) = \omega_0 \int_t^\infty f_0(x)\,dx + \omega_1 \int_{-\infty}^t f_1(x)\,dx, \qquad E'(t) = -\omega_0 f_0(t) + \omega_1 f_1(t) = 0 . For normal f_k take logarithms: \ln\omega_0 - \ln\sigma_0 - \frac{(t - \mu_0)^2}{2\sigma_0^2} = \ln\omega_1 - \ln\sigma_1 - \frac{(t - \mu_1)^2}{2\sigma_1^2}.

Equal variances: the t^2 terms cancel, and t = \frac{\mu_0 + \mu_1}{2} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu_1 - \mu_0}\,\ln\frac{\omega_0}{\omega_1} . Example: 100 + \frac{400}{100}\ln 9 = 108.8.
Unequal variances: a quadratic in t with up to two roots. The wider class wins in both tails: far out on either side its density is larger.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Choosing the threshold: Otsu & minimum error

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Minimum error from the histogram
We do not know \omega_k, \mu_k, \sigma_k. Kittler & Illingworth (1986): for every candidate t,

fit a normal distribution to each side of the split (weight, mean and variance of the pixels on that side),
measure how well the two fitted curves explain the histogram,
keep the t with the best fit, and threshold there.

When the histogram really is two normal peaks, this lands near the crossing, even for unequal weights or widths. When it is not (clipped values, a long tail, three groups), the fit can go badly wrong.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Choosing the threshold: Otsu & minimum error

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
The math: Kittler–Illingworth
The criterion is the average negative log-likelihood of the pixels under the fitted mixture, with each pixel assigned to its side of t: J(t) = -\sum_i p_i \ln\big(\omega_{k(i)}\, f_{k(i)}(i)\big) = \tfrac12\ln 2\pi + \tfrac12 + \sum_k \omega_k \ln\sigma_k - \sum_k \omega_k \ln\omega_k , using \sum_{i \in k} p_i (i - \mu_k)^2 = \omega_k\sigma_k^2. Dropping constants and doubling: J(t) = 1 + 2(\omega_0\ln\sigma_0 + \omega_1\ln\sigma_1) - 2(\omega_0\ln\omega_0 + \omega_1\ln\omega_1), \qquad t^* = \arg\min_t J(t). Like Otsu, one pass with running sums (now also \sum_{i \le t} i^2 p_i). A class with almost zero variance gives \ln\sigma \to -\infty: guard against empty or one-level classes.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Choosing the threshold: Otsu & minimum error

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
section: Who is biased, and which way
text:
Who is biased, and which way
Otsu and isodata use only the means. In effect they assume equal variances and similar weights.

Small object class (10 % of the pixels): Otsu moves into the larger class. On the curves above it chooses 98.5 instead of 108.8; at 3 % objects it falls to 60.5, inside the background peak.
Much wider background: Otsu again moves into the wider class.
Minimum error follows the crossing as long as the two-Gaussian model fits.
Heavy overlap: every threshold has a large error; the grey level alone cannot decide. Neighbours must help (graph cuts, day 13).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Choosing the threshold: Otsu & minimum error

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
section: Try it: two Gaussians, six thresholds
text:
Try it: two Gaussians, six thresholds




The image (right) is drawn from the mixture: blob-shaped objects with fraction ω₁, each pixel’s grey level sampled from its class. Top: histogram (grey), weighted densities (blue, orange), every method’s threshold (dashed); the selected one is solid, its error tails shaded. Below: its criterion curve. Table: threshold and error rate under the model. Tour: “equal, well separated”: all at 125 except the triangle. “unequal weights” (ω₁ = 0.1): Otsu 85 with 19.9 % error, Bayes 114.6 (3.4 %), min-error 123 (4.1 %). “unequal variances”: two Bayes crossings, 40.8 and 105.4. “small object (3 %)”: Otsu 62 (40.6 %), triangle 91, Kapur 93, min-error 98, Bayes 94.1, all about 1.4 %. “heavy overlap”: the best possible error is 21.9 %. Shrink the image to 32² to see how noisy small histograms make every method.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Choosing the threshold: Otsu & minimum error

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
section: Other criteria: triangle and maximum entropy
text:
Other criteria: triangle and maximum entropy

Triangle (Zack et al., 1977): draw a line from the histogram’s peak to the far end of its long tail; the threshold is where the histogram lies farthest below that line. Made for a unimodal histogram with a few bright object pixels (fluorescent spots), where there is no valley and Otsu fails.
Maximum entropy (Kapur et al., 1985): choose t so that the grey levels within each class are as spread out as possible (the entropies H_0 + H_1 of the two class distributions p_i/\omega_k are largest).
Another criterion, another answer: there is no single “correct” threshold. The choice is a choice of model of the histogram.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Choosing the threshold: Otsu & minimum error

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Three classes: multi-level Otsu
\sigma_B^2 = \sum_k \omega_k(\mu_k - \mu)^2 for K classes; for three, try all pairs t_1 < t_2 (about 32 000 for 256 levels).




The micrograph with three-class Otsu: t₁ = 120, t₂ = 188 (dark material in purple, the middle grey levels in orange, the bright background unmarked). Two-class Otsu (untick “3 classes”) gives 163 with η = σ_B²/σ_T² = 0.76. The middle class mixes cytoplasm and nucleus: their grey levels overlap, so no threshold separates them.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Choosing the threshold: Otsu & minimum error

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Summary

Otsu: total variance = within + between; minimise the within-class variance \Leftrightarrow maximise \sigma_B^2 = \omega_0\omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2. One pass over the histogram.
Isodata: t \leftarrow (\mu_0 + \mu_1)/2, repeated; 1D 2-means. Otsu’s optimum is one of its fixed points; it may stop at another.
Bayes / minimum error: decide object where \omega_1 f_1 > \omega_0 f_0; the best threshold is where the weighted densities cross. Equal variances: midpoint shifted by \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu_1 - \mu_0}\ln\frac{\omega_0}{\omega_1}.
Kittler–Illingworth fits two Gaussians at every t and keeps the best fit.
Otsu and isodata are biased into the larger or wider class; triangle for a unimodal histogram with a tail; three classes by multi-level Otsu.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Choosing the threshold: Otsu & minimum error

title: Exercise: principal component analysis
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

treat small images as points, centre them, and compute their covariance matrix,
find the principal components of a 2 × 2 covariance and say what they mean for the images,
project an image onto the first components and rebuild it, and give the error,
choose a number of components from a scree plot, and say when PCA misleads,
compare PCA with the Fourier basis: fixed versus learned from the data.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the interactive part. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: principal component analysis
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

treat small images as points, centre them, and compute their covariance matrix,
