Give the confusion matrix (TP, FP, FN, TN with N as positive), the accuracy and the Dice coefficient of N and of B.
The forest’s OOB error on the painted pixels was 0.5 %. Why is it so much lower than the error here?

B4. Which feature family, at which scale, should separate: (a) nuclei (bright, about 30 px across) from background; (b) a thin bright membrane (2 px wide) from the cytoplasm on both sides; (c) a granular region from a smooth region with the same mean brightness; (d) a dim nucleus from slightly brighter background that ramps up across the image?
B5. A forest trained on strokes from image 1 reaches 97 % on a fully annotated region of image 1, and 81 % on image 2. Give two reasons, and what you would paint next.






Solutions





B1. (a) Box: the 3 \times 3 block 15, 40, 80, 50, 90, 95, 85, 96, 98 sums to 649: b = 72.1. g_x = (95 - 50)/2 = 22.5, g_y = (96 - 40)/2 = 28, g = \sqrt{22.5^2 + 28^2} = 35.9. \ell = 40 + 96 + 50 + 95 - 360 = -79. (b) Tree 1: 72.1 > 60 → N. Tree 2: 35.9 > 30 → B. Tree 3: -79 \le -50 → N. P(\text{N}) = 2/3, label N. (c) Pixel (row 2, column 2) = 15: box over rows 1–3, columns 1–3: 10 + 12 + 14 + 12 + 15 + 40 + 14 + 50 + 90 = 257, b = 28.6; g_x = (40 - 12)/2 = 14, g_y = (50 - 12)/2 = 19, g = 23.6; \ell = 40 + 12 + 50 + 12 - 60 = 54. Votes: B, N, B: P(\text{N}) = 1/3, label B. (d) The centre sits on the edge of a bright object (dark top-left, bright bottom-right): bright on average and brighter than its neighbours, but with a strong gradient. The edge tree reads “boundary” as background, the others “inside”. Boundary pixels are where the votes split and the uncertainty is high.
B2. (a) Majority background: P(\text{nucleus}) = 2/10 = 0.2. (b) Weight each class by 1/n_c (here w = 0.525 and 10.5, ratio 20), or sample the same number of pixels per class (e.g. all 20 nucleus pixels and 20 random background pixels, which throws data away). With the weights: P(\text{N}) = 2 \cdot 10.5/(2 \cdot 10.5 + 8 \cdot 0.525) = 0.83. (c) Yes: background pixels that resemble the 20 nucleus pixels are now called nucleus more often. Balancing trades errors of the small class for errors of the large one; it does not add information.
B3. (a) TP = 4, FP = 2 (row 1 column 3, row 3 column 2), FN = 1 (row 2 column 2), TN = 9. Accuracy 13/16 = 0.8125. Dice N = 8/(8 + 2 + 1) = 0.727; Dice B = 18/(18 + 3) = 0.857. (b) OOB votes are cast on painted pixels, whose neighbours (near copies) were in the bootstrap samples, and which sit where painting was easy. The held-out region contains boundaries, dim objects and other hard pixels that no stroke came near.
B4. (a) Intensity (smoothed) at a medium scale, or blobs (LoG) at σ ≈ 30/(2√2) ≈ 10. (b) Ridges (Hessian eigenvalue) at a small scale, σ ≈ 1: a bright line has a strongly negative eigenvalue across it. (c) Texture (structure tensor) or edges (gradient magnitude) at a small scale: smoothing removes the texture, so intensity at large σ cannot tell them apart. (d) Large-scale intensity to capture the ramp, together with small-scale intensity, so that the tree can compare the pixel with its surroundings; or paint background on both ends of the ramp.
B5. Image 2 may differ in staining, illumination or noise (the features shift), and it may contain structures never painted in image 1. Strokes from image 1 also share its specific neighbourhoods. Paint a few strokes on image 2 where it is wrong or uncertain, retrain on both images, and evaluate on a third, or on an annotated region not used for training.




Math questions
B6. (math) Show that weighting every sample of class k by w_k in the Gini impurity gives exactly the impurity of the data in which each sample of class k is replicated w_k times (for integer w_k), so both choose the same splits. Which weights balance 400 background and 20 nucleus pixels?
B7. (math) A stroke of 200 pixels is so smooth that consecutive pixels have correlation \rho = 0.95 in every feature. Treating the correlation as that of an AR(1) sequence, the effective number of independent samples is about n\frac{1-\rho}{1+\rho}. Compute it, and explain what it means for the OOB error.






Solutions (math)





B6. In a node with n_k samples of class k, the weighted shares are p_k = w_k n_k/\sum_l w_l n_l. Replicating each sample of class k w_k times gives w_k n_k samples of class k and the same shares. Gini depends only on the shares, and the weighted sizes \sum_l w_l n_l of the children are the sizes of the replicated children, so every split has the same impurity decrease in both settings: the same splits win. Balancing: w_k = n/(K n_k): 420/(2 \cdot 400) = 0.525 and 420/(2 \cdot 20) = 10.5 (any pair with ratio 20 works).
B7. 200 \cdot 0.05/1.95 \approx 5.1: the stroke is worth about 5 independent pixels, not 200. The bootstrap and the OOB estimate count 200; nearly every OOB pixel has near copies in the bag, so OOB measures the error on near copies of training pixels, and is far too optimistic.

title: Exercise: pixel classification with a forest
text:
Explore
Left: the image with the painted labels. Choose a label and paint with the mouse (brush sets the size; erase, undo, clear). The forest retrains when you lift the mouse (untick train after each stroke to train only with train). Middle: the result: segmentation (colour = most probable class), probability of a chosen class, uncertainty (1 - \max P), one feature channel (step through all of them), or the ground truth (test image only). Right: presets, the classifier (random forest or single tree) and its settings, the feature families and scales used, balance classes, and hold out the right part (the strokes right of the yellow line are not used for training; the region is evaluated). The readout lists the painted (and used) pixels per class, the OOB accuracy on the painted pixels, and on the test image the accuracy, Dice per class and the confusion matrix against the ground truth (rows: truth; columns: prediction; in % of the pixels of the whole image or the held-out region).
The test image: background (illumination rising to the right), smooth nuclei (some dim) and granular cells that are as bright as the nuclei but textured. The micrograph has no ground truth.



E1. Preset two strokes (one nucleus stroke, one background stroke). How many pixels are painted? Accuracy and Dice of the nucleus class? What happens to the granular cells, and why can the forest not do otherwise? Paint one stroke of granular cell across a granular cell and watch the result.
E2. Preset intensity only (strokes for all three classes, only the intensity channels): accuracy, Dice of nucleus and granular cell, and the share of granular-cell pixels called nucleus. Then preset full stack (all 42 channels): the same numbers. Use the features view to find a channel in which the granular cells differ clearly from the nuclei.
E3. Preset small scales only (σ ≤ 1.6). Accuracy and Dice compared with the full stack? Look at the segmentation: where are the extra errors?
E4. Preset only bright nuclei painted. Compare the nucleus row of the confusion matrix (how much of the image is nucleus called background?) with the full stack preset. Look at the dim nuclei in the segmentation. Then paint a short nucleus stroke on one dim nucleus.
E5. Preset huge background strokes. How many pixels per class are painted, and how many are used (the training set is capped at 4000)? Read the nucleus row of the confusion matrix and the Dice of the nucleus. Tick balance classes: what changes in the nucleus row, in the background row and in the accuracy?
E6. Preset OOB vs held-out region (strokes on both sides; those right of the yellow line are held out). Compare the OOB accuracy, the accuracy on the painted pixels in the held-out region, and the accuracy against the ground truth in that region. Which number would you report? Untick hold out the right part: what does the accuracy in the right part (now trained on) become?
E7. Preset uncertainty: where to paint (no granular stroke). Where is the uncertainty high? Is it high on the granular cells? Paint where the map tells you to, and then where the truth view tells you to.
E8. Switch the classifier to single tree on the full stack preset. Accuracy and Dice compared with the forest? Look at the segmentation of the granular cells.
E9. Preset micrograph: nucleus (nucleus and background strokes). Describe the result: where is it wrong? Then preset micrograph: + cytoplasm. Which parts of the cell become cytoplasm? Where would you paint next?






Solutions





E1. 220 background and 116 nucleus pixels. Accuracy 87.4 %, Dice nucleus 0.57. The granular cells are classified as nucleus (8.5 % of all pixels: the granular row of the confusion matrix is 0.4 / 8.5 / 0.0): the forest only knows two classes and granular cells are bright like nuclei. A classifier can only output classes it was shown. A granular stroke adds the class; with the base strokes (E2) its Dice reaches 0.86.
E2. Intensity only (6 channels): accuracy 91.3 %, Dice nucleus 0.65, granular 0.68; 3.8 % of the image is granular cell called nucleus (granular row 0.0 / 3.8 / 5.1). Full stack (42 channels): 96.3 %, Dice nucleus 0.85, granular 0.86; granular row 0.1 / 0.0 / 8.7. Channels that separate them: the gradient or the structure-tensor eigenvalue μ1 at small σ (σ = 0.7–1.6): bright speckle inside the granular cells, nearly flat inside the nuclei.
E3. Small scales only (21 channels): 94.8 % (full stack 96.3 %), Dice nucleus 0.78 (0.85), granular 0.83 (0.86). The extra errors: an orange speckle of “nucleus” in the brighter background on the right (0.9 % of the image, against 0.2 %), and more nucleus pixels called granular (2.2 % against 1.6 %). Without the large scales a pixel only knows its immediate surroundings: a bright background pixel on the right looks like a dim nucleus pixel, and the forest cannot see that it lies far from any object.
E4. Only bright nuclei: nucleus row 1.2 / 6.4 / 2.0, i.e. 1.2 % of the image is nucleus called background (full stack: 0.7 %); Dice nucleus 0.80 (0.85). Parts of the dim nuclei (16 % of their interior, against 2 % with a dim stroke) become background: they are darker than anything painted as nucleus. One stroke on a dim nucleus brings them back.
E5. Painted: 4772 background, 37 nucleus, 45 granular; used (capped, same fraction per class): 3959, 30, 42. Without balancing: nucleus row 4.1 / 3.5 / 2.0 (more nucleus pixels called background than found), Dice nucleus 0.53, accuracy 92.6 %. Balanced: nucleus row 3.3 / 3.9 / 2.4, Dice 0.58; but the background row changes from 81.6 / 0.0 / 0.0 to 79.1 / 0.0 / 2.5, and the accuracy drops to 91.8 %. Balancing helps the small classes and costs the large one; the real cure is better strokes for the small classes.
E6. OOB accuracy 100.0 %; painted pixels in the held-out region 99.8 % right (650 pixels); full ground truth in the region 95.9 %. Report the last one: OOB is fooled by neighbouring pixels, and the painted pixels in the region are easy ones (stroke centres). Trained on all strokes: the accuracy in the right part rises to 96.9 %, but that number is no longer an independent test.
E7. High uncertainty on the rims of all objects and on the background in the right part of the image, which is brighter than any painted background (the background strokes are on the left). Not on the granular cells: they are classified confidently as nucleus (8.4 % of the image is granular cell called nucleus). The uncertainty map shows where the classes it knows meet, not what it has never seen. Paint background on the right; for the granular cells you need the truth (or your eyes) to add a class.
E8. Single tree: accuracy 94.6 %, Dice nucleus 0.78, granular 0.74 (forest: 96.3 %, 0.85, 0.86). Every granular cell gets a thick nucleus-coloured rim: 3.5 % of the image is granular cell called nucleus. One tree uses only a few channels (mean depth 3) and draws one hard boundary in them; the forest averages many trees that use different channels and gets the rims right.
E9. With nucleus and background only: the nucleus is found, but so is much of the cytoplasm and other dark material (it is neither the light background nor anything else the forest knows). With the cytoplasm strokes, the cytoplasm around the nucleus and the cell processes become cytoplasm; the nucleus is mostly nucleus, with its lower part and its envelope partly called cytoplasm. Paint nucleus in the lower part of the nucleus and cytoplasm or background where the result is uncertain (the uncertainty view).

title: Exercise: pixel classification with a forest
text:
Where this leads
The forest on a hand-made stack is the strong baseline from a few strokes. The SVM elective plugs a support-vector machine into the same demo, where feature standardisation and by-stroke cross-validation become essential. The neural-networks day replaces the hand-made stack by filters that a network learns itself (U-Net), at the price of many more labels. The evaluation day measures segmentations object by object and makes the “split by image” rule precise.

title: Quiz: pixel classification with a forest
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. What is a pixel’s feature vector in pixel classification, and where do the training points come from?






Hint





One number per channel of the stack.









Answer





The values of the pixel in every channel of the feature stack (each filter family at each scale): typically a few dozen numbers describing its brightness, edges, blobs, ridges and texture around it. The training points are the painted pixels, with the class of the stroke they belong to.




Q2. Why use several scales σ for each filter family?






Hint





How large are the structures, and how far does a pixel need to “see”?









Answer





Structures come in different sizes: a 2-pixel membrane, a 30-pixel nucleus, a texture of fine grains. Small scales capture fine detail and texture; large scales capture context (is this pixel inside a large bright object?). The forest picks whichever channels help; it does not need to be told the right scale.




Q3. The OOB accuracy on your painted pixels is 99.9 %. Why should you not believe it?






Hint





What is next to an out-of-bag pixel?









Answer





Neighbouring pixels in a stroke are near copies; an OOB pixel’s neighbours were in the bootstrap sample, so the trees have effectively seen it. Moreover, the strokes are where labelling was easy. Evaluate on a held-out region (or image) with full labels.




Q4. The uncertainty map is dark (confident) inside a group of cells you never painted. Does that mean they are classified correctly?






Hint





What can the forest say about a class it has never seen?









Answer





No. The forest can only choose among the classes it was shown; if the unknown cells resemble one of them, all trees agree on it and the map is confident. Uncertainty is high where known classes meet, not where something new appears. Look at the image (or the truth) and add a class or strokes.




Q5. Name the feature family you would rely on to separate a granular region from a smooth region of the same mean brightness.






Hint





Smoothing removes the difference.









Answer





Texture (structure-tensor eigenvalues) or edges (gradient magnitude) at small σ: the granular region has strong local gradients everywhere, the smooth one does not. Smoothed intensity at large σ is the same for both.




Q6. You paint 5000 background pixels and 50 nucleus pixels. What happens to ambiguous pixels, and what are two remedies?






Hint





Who wins the majority in a mixed leaf?









Answer





Mixed leaves are dominated by background, so ambiguous pixels (dim nuclei, rims) are called background. Remedies: weight each class by 1/n_c (balance), or sample the same number of pixels per class; better still, paint more nucleus strokes on the hard cases.




Q7. How can a graph cut improve a pixel classification?






Hint





What does the forest ignore about neighbouring pixels’ labels?









Answer





The forest labels each pixel on its own, so its result can be speckled. A graph cut uses -\log P(\text{class} \mid \text{features}) as the data term and adds a smoothness term that makes neighbours prefer the same label: isolated wrong pixels disappear and boundaries become clean.




Q8. (math) 300 background and 30 nucleus pixels. Give the balancing weights w_k = n/(K n_k) and the weighted P(\text{nucleus}) of a leaf with 6 background and 3 nucleus pixels.






Hint





n = 330, K = 2.









Answer





w_{\text{bg}} = 330/600 = 0.55, w_{\text{nuc}} = 330/60 = 5.5. Leaf: P(\text{nucleus}) = 3 \cdot 5.5/(3 \cdot 5.5 + 6 \cdot 0.55) = 16.5/19.8 = 0.83 (unweighted: 3/9 = 0.33).

title: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates
text:
About this lecture
Last unit: the cheapest path from the top to the bottom of a cost image, exactly, by filling a table row by row. Today the same table finds a closed boundary around a nucleus.

A boundary around a centre is one radius per angle, if the object is star-shaped.
Unwrap the image to polar coordinates: the closed curve becomes a path from left to right.
A cost that is low on the edge, with the right polarity, and a smoothness limit.
The catch: the path must close. Three ways to handle it.
Where it fails, and DP for snakes.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Prerequisites: the DP table of the previous unit; inverse mapping and bilinear interpolation from the Images unit (day 1), recalled on one slide; the snake energy from the snakes day (first day of this elective chain), quoted on one slide.
crumbs: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates

title: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates
text:
The problem
A fluorescent nucleus, blurred, noisy, with a weak part of its boundary and a brighter neighbour touching it.

A threshold that keeps the weak part leaks into the background; one that avoids the leak cuts the nucleus. And it merges the neighbour.
Snakes and level sets (the previous two days) need a starting curve and descend locally: they can stop at the wrong edge.
We know something about the shape: it is a blob around a centre. Can we use that to get the best boundary, not just a nearby one?
crumbs: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates

title: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates
text:
Star-shaped objects
An object is star-shaped around a centre c if every ray from c leaves the object exactly once.

Every convex shape is star-shaped around any of its points; a nucleus usually is around its middle.
Then the boundary is a function: one radius r(\theta) for each angle \theta.
Finding a closed curve becomes finding one number per angle: a chain, exactly what DP handles.

Not star-shaped: a bean seen from a point in one of its lobes, a dumbbell, a cell with long protrusions. We come back to them.
crumbs: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates

title: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates
section: Unwrapping: the image in polar coordinates
text:
Unwrapping: the image in polar coordinates

Sample the image along K rays at radii 0, 1, 2, \dots The rays become columns: angle across, radius down. The circle-like boundary becomes a path from left to right, one radius per column.
crumbs: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates

title: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates
text:
The math: unwrapping
Centre c = (c_x, c_y), angles \theta_k = 2\pi k / K, radii r = 0, 1, \dots, R-1:
P(k, r) = I\big(c_x + r\cos\theta_k,\ c_y + r\sin\theta_k\big).
The sample point is not a pixel centre, so I is read by bilinear interpolation (the inverse mapping of the Images unit): with x = x_0 + f_x, y = y_0 + f_y, 0 \le f_x, f_y < 1,
I(x, y) = (1 - f_y)\big[(1-f_x) I_{x_0, y_0} + f_x I_{x_0+1, y_0}\big] + f_y\big[(1-f_x) I_{x_0, y_1} + f_x I_{x_0+1, y_1}\big],\quad y_1 = y_0 + 1.
The y-axis points down, so \theta increases clockwise on the screen. Mapping back: a path r_k is the closed polygon c + r_k(\cos\theta_k, \sin\theta_k).
crumbs: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates

title: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates
text:
A cost along each ray
Along a ray, a bright nucleus on a dark background goes bright → dark at the boundary: the intensity drops. Use the radial derivative \partial P / \partial r:

bright → dark (bright inside): cost = +\partial P/\partial r, very negative at the boundary;
dark → bright: cost = -\partial P/\partial r;
either: cost = -|\partial P/\partial r|.
A thin dark line (a nuclear envelope in an electron micrograph): the second derivative, low in the middle of the line.

The sign selects the edge we want. A plain gradient magnitude cannot tell the outer edge of the nucleus from the inner edge of a brighter neighbour; the radial derivative can. Smooth the image a little first (a Gaussian, as in the Filtering unit), or the noise dominates the derivative.
crumbs: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates

title: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates
section: Smoothness: how far may the radius jump?
text:
Smoothness: how far may the radius jump?
Without a limit, the path picks the best edge on every ray independently, and jumps between edges (and noise).

Hard limit: |r_{k+1} - r_k| \le \delta pixels between neighbouring angles.
Soft penalty: add \alpha\,|r_{k+1} - r_k| for every pixel of change.

This is the previous unit turned sideways: the angles are the stages (rows of the table), the radii are the states (columns), the steps go up to \delta columns sideways, with a penalty.
Note: \delta is per angle step. With more angles (K larger) the same \delta allows a steeper boundary.
crumbs: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates

title: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates
text:
The math: the recursion
Cost C(k, r) for angle k = 0, \dots, K-1 and radius r \in [r_{\min}, r_{\max}]:
M(0, r) = C(0, r), \qquad M(k, r) = C(k, r) + \min_{|d| \le \delta} \big(M(k-1, r+d) + \alpha |d|\big).
The best open path ends at \arg\min_r M(K-1, r) and is read off by backtracking. Work: (2\delta + 1) candidates per cell, O(K R \delta) in total: for K = 360, R = 100, \delta = 3 about 250 000 operations.
The energy that is minimised is
E(r_0, \dots, r_{K-1}) = \sum_k C(k, r_k) + \alpha \sum_{k} |r_{k} - r_{k-1}|, \qquad |r_k - r_{k-1}| \le \delta,
a data term plus a smoothness term, as on the graph-cut day, but over a chain.
crumbs: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates

title: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates
text:
Closing the curve
Angle 0° and angle 360° are the same ray, so the path must satisfy |r_0 - r_{K-1}| \le \delta too. The table of the previous slide does not know that.

Open (ignore it): the result often has a visible jump at 0°.
Exact: fix the start radius r_0, run DP, and accept only end radii within \delta of r_0. Do this for every start radius and keep the best closed path. R times the work, still a few milliseconds.
Unroll (the common heuristic): repeat the angles three times (0° \dots 1080°), run DP once, and keep the middle copy. The ends of the long path are far away, so the middle usually closes. Not guaranteed, and not guaranteed optimal.
crumbs: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates

title: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates
section: The math: why the exact closure is exact
text:
The math: why the exact closure is exact
Every closed path has some start radius s = r_0. For fixed s, set M_s(0, r) = C(0, r) if r = s and \infty otherwise, run the recursion, and close:
E^*_s = \min_{|r - s| \le \delta} \big(M_s(K-1, r) + \alpha|r - s|\big).
E^*_s is the cheapest closed path that starts at s (the principle of optimality, with the extra closing step). The best closed path is \min_s E^*_s. Work: R runs, O(K R^2 \delta): for K = 360, R = 100, \delta = 3 about 25 million operations, a few tens of milliseconds.
Faster exact methods exist (branch and bound over the start radius, Appleton & Sun 2003). Unrolling costs only 3 runs, but a counterexample where its middle copy does not close is in the exercise.
crumbs: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates

title: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates
section: Try it: boundaries in polar coordinates
text:
Try it: boundaries in polar coordinates




Left: the image, the centre (drag it), every few rays (red: angle 0), the annulus [r min, r max] and the contour. Middle: the unwrapped image (angle across, radius down) with the path; switch to the cost (blue = cheap) or the table M. Tour: “nucleus: done” (δ = 1, α = 0.1, exact: gap 0, cost −58.67). Closure “open”: gap 7 px at angle 0. “no smoothness” (δ = 8, α = 0): the path jumps out to the outer edge of the brighter neighbour (radius 94 at 0°), because that edge is stronger: the cost is lower (−69.99), so the energy prefers it, and only the smoothness limit stops it. “open path: jump at 0°” (δ = 2): gap 15 px. “bad centre”: the bean seen from its left lobe; “centre → centroid” a few times moves the centre but the right lobe stays outside. “wrong polarity”: dark → bright finds nothing useful near the boundary. “micrograph nucleus”: dark line cost on the nuclear envelope; on the left it follows the parallel cell membrane instead.
crumbs: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates

title: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates
text:
Where it fails

Not star-shaped: a ray that crosses the boundary twice can only report one crossing. The bean seen from one lobe loses the other lobe.
Wrong centre: even a convex nucleus looks distorted from a centre near its edge: the angles are spread unevenly, and \delta limits the slope.
A brighter edge on the same ray: the neighbour’s outer edge, a parallel membrane. If it is cheaper and reachable within the smoothness limit, the optimum is that edge: the energy is wrong, not the optimisation.

Remedies: a centre from a seed click or from the peak of the distance transform (morphology day) of a rough mask; an annulus r_{\min} \le r \le r_{\max}; iterate (new centre = centroid of the result, then run again); the right polarity.
crumbs: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates

title: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates
section: Global, but in a small family
text:
Global, but in a small family
Three ways to find a nucleus boundary, three kinds of guarantee:








Method
Optimises
Guarantee




Graph cuts (graph-cut day)
a 2D labelling, binary, submodular
global minimum


Snakes, level sets (previous days)
a curve, by local descent
a local minimum near the start


Polar DP (today)
one radius per angle
global minimum among star-shaped curves around c



Polar DP needs no starting curve, only a centre, and is never trapped by a nearby weak edge. The price is the restriction: star-shaped around a known centre.
crumbs: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates

title: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates
text:
DP for snakes
Recall from the snakes day: a snake is a closed curve of n points v_i with an energy of an internal part (elasticity, rigidity) and an image part. Gradient descent moves it to a nearby local minimum.
DP version (Amini, Weymouth & Jain 1990): let each point move only within a small window of m candidate positions around its current place.

With only the elastic term \sum_i |v_{i} - v_{i-1}|^2, the energy links each point to the next one only: a closed chain, so DP finds the best move of all points at once. Repeat until nothing moves.
Polar DP is the special case “each point moves along its ray”.
The rigidity (bending) term links three consecutive points: the states become pairs of positions, m^2 per stage, and the work grows to about n m^3.
crumbs: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates

title: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates
text:
The math: DP snakes
Candidate positions v_i \in W_i (|W_i| = m). First-order energy
E = \sum_i \big[E_{\text{img}}(v_i) + \alpha\,|v_i - v_{i-1}|^2\big]
is a chain: M_i(v) = E_{\text{img}}(v) + \min_{u \in W_{i-1}} \big(M_{i-1}(u) + \alpha|v - u|^2\big), m^2 work per point, O(nm^2) in total (times m for the exact closure, as before).
With the bending term \beta\,|v_{i+1} - 2v_i + v_{i-1}|^2 (as on the snakes day) each term involves three points. Use the pair (v_{i-1}, v_i) as the state: M_i(v_{i-1}, v_i) = \min_{v_{i-2}} \big(M_{i-1}(v_{i-2}, v_{i-1}) + \dots\big): m^2 states, m candidates each, O(nm^3).
crumbs: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates

title: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates
text:
Summary

A star-shaped boundary around a centre is one radius per angle: a chain.
Unwrap the image (bilinear sampling along rays); the boundary becomes a left-to-right path.
Cost from the radial derivative, with the right polarity; smoothness by a step limit \delta and a penalty \alpha.
DP gives the global optimum of this restricted problem; closing the curve needs the exact method (all start radii) or the unroll heuristic.
Fails for non-star-shaped objects, bad centres, and brighter edges on the same rays. The same idea optimises snakes (DP over a window per point).
crumbs: Closed boundaries: DP in polar coordinates

title: Exercise: image formation and the PSF
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Forward model
image = sample(object ∗ PSF) + noise: what the instrument does to the truth


PSF h
the image of a point; normalised to sum 1


OTF H
Fourier transform of the PSF; contrast kept at each frequency; H(0) = 1


MTF
\lvert H\rvert, the magnitude of the OTF


NA
numerical aperture, n\sin\alpha (half-angle \alpha of the light cone, refractive index n)


Cut-off
2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda: the OTF is zero beyond it


Rayleigh distance
0.61\lambda/\mathrm{NA}, the radius of the first dark ring of the Airy pattern


Abbe distance
\lambda/2\mathrm{NA}, the finest grating period that passes


Gaussian approximation
\sigma = 0.21\lambda/\mathrm{NA}

title: Exercise: image formation and the PSF
text:
By hand
B1. A row of pixels (0, 0, 3, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0) is blurred with the PSF (1, 2, 1)/4 (outside the row, take 0). (a) Compute the blurred row. (b) Check that the total brightness is unchanged. Why must it be? (c) Can you still see from the blurred row that the object had a single bright point on the left and two neighbouring points on the right?
B2. Compute the Rayleigh distance, the Abbe distance and the cut-off frequency (in cycles/µm) for (a) a water objective, NA 1.2, at λ = 488 nm; (b) a dry objective, NA 0.75, at λ = 600 nm.
B3. Two objectives, NA 1.4 and NA 1.2, image blue light (450 nm). Which of them resolves two points 200 nm apart by the Rayleigh criterion?
B4. Use the OTF curve of the lecture (NA 1.4, 520 nm; right panel of the Airy figure). (a) Read off the contrast kept for gratings of period 1 µm, 400 nm and 250 nm. (b) What happens to a grating of period 180 nm?
B5. A 100 nm fluorescent bead is imaged with an NA 0.3 and an NA 1.4 objective (same wavelength). The two images look alike, but one is much larger. Why do they have the same shape? How much larger is the NA 0.3 image?
B6. During an exposure the stage drifted by 0.5 µm along x. (a) What does the PSF look like (ignoring diffraction)? (b) Which grating periods along x vanish completely? (c) What happens to a grating with stripes running along x (its frequency is along y)?
B7. In a defocused image of a striped test chart, the stripes in one region look inverted. A colleague concludes the camera’s colour table is wrong. Explain what actually happened.






Solutions





B1. (a) Each pixel becomes \tfrac14 left neighbour + \tfrac12 itself + \tfrac14 right neighbour: (0,\ 0.75,\ 1.5,\ 0.75,\ 0,\ 0.25,\ 0.75,\ 0.75,\ 0.25). (b) Object total 3 + 1 + 1 = 5; blurred total 0.75 + 1.5 + 0.75 + 0.25 + 0.75 + 0.75 + 0.25 = 5. The PSF sums to 1: every point’s light is spread over its neighbours, none is lost (no light falls off the ends here). (c) Yes, here: the left blob is symmetric with peak 1.5, the right one is flat-topped (0.75, 0.75) and wider. With a wider PSF the two right points would merge into a single blob: that is the resolution question of the next unit.
B2. (a) Rayleigh 0.61 \cdot 488/1.2 = 248 nm; Abbe 488/2.4 = 203 nm; cut-off 2.4/0.488 = 4.92 cycles/µm. (b) Rayleigh 0.61 \cdot 600/0.75 = 488 nm; Abbe 600/1.5 = 400 nm; cut-off 1.5/0.6 = 2.5 cycles/µm.
B3. NA 1.4: 0.61 \cdot 450/1.4 = 196 nm < 200 nm: resolved. NA 1.2: 0.61 \cdot 450/1.2 = 229 nm > 200 nm: not resolved by Rayleigh’s criterion.
B4. (a) The cut-off is 5.4 cycles/µm. Period 1 µm = 1 cycle/µm: about 0.77. Period 400 nm = 2.5 cycles/µm: about 0.43. Period 250 nm = 4 cycles/µm: about 0.15. (From the formula: 0.765, 0.431, 0.150.) (b) Period 180 nm = 5.6 cycles/µm, beyond the cut-off: contrast 0. The grating is not in the image at all.
B5. A 100 nm bead is much smaller than both PSFs, so in both cases the image of the bead is essentially the PSF itself, an Airy pattern. The Airy pattern of a perfect lens always has the same shape; only its scale \lambda/\mathrm{NA} changes. At NA 0.3 it is 1.4/0.3 = 4.7 times larger (first dark ring at 1.06 µm instead of 227 nm at 520 nm).
B6. (a) A short line of length 0.5 µm along x, uniform brightness (constant speed). (b) The OTF along x is \mathrm{sinc}(Lk) with zeros at k = 1/L, 2/L, \dots = 2, 4, 6, … cycles/µm: periods 500 nm, 250 nm, 167 nm, …. Each of these is averaged over exactly a whole number of periods during the motion. (c) Nothing: moving along the stripes does not change what each pixel sees. The OTF along y is 1 (apart from the lens’s own blur).
B7. Not the colour table: defocus. The OTF of a defocused lens becomes negative at some frequencies. A stripe pattern with such a frequency is imaged as 1 + H\cos(\dots) with H < 0: shifted by half a period, so bright and dark swap. Only the stripes in that frequency band are inverted; coarser stripes keep their sign.




Math questions
B8. (math) The pupil of a lens is a disc of radius \rho_0 = \mathrm{NA}/\lambda in frequency space, and the incoherent OTF is the autocorrelation of the pupil, H(\mathbf k) \propto \int P(\boldsymbol\rho)\,P(\boldsymbol\rho + \mathbf k)\,d\boldsymbol\rho. (a) Explain why H(\mathbf k) = 0 for |\mathbf k| > 2\rho_0. (b) Compute H for a one-dimensional “pupil” P(\rho) = 1 for |\rho| \le \rho_0 (a slit), normalised so that H(0) = 1. What shape is it?
B9. (math) Show that a PSF with h(-\mathbf x) = h(\mathbf x) has a real OTF. Give an example of a symmetric PSF whose OTF is negative somewhere.
B10. (math) Motion blur over a length L along x: h(x) = \tfrac1L for |x| \le L/2, else 0. (a) Compute H(k) and its zeros. (b) The image of the grating 1 + \cos(2\pi k x) is 1 + H(k)\cos(2\pi kx). For L = 1 µm, what is the image of a grating with period 700 nm?






Solutions (math)





B8. (a) P(\boldsymbol\rho)P(\boldsymbol\rho + \mathbf k) is non-zero only where the disc and its copy shifted by -\mathbf k overlap. Two discs of radius \rho_0 whose centres are more than 2\rho_0 apart do not overlap: H = 0 for |\mathbf k| > 2\rho_0 = 2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda. (b) The overlap of two intervals of length 2\rho_0 shifted by k has length 2\rho_0 - |k| for |k| \le 2\rho_0. Normalised: H(k) = 1 - |k|/(2\rho_0), a triangle, falling linearly from 1 to 0 at the cut-off. (The circular pupil gives the curved version \tfrac2\pi(\arccos s - s\sqrt{1 - s^2}), which also starts with a straight fall.)
B9. H(\mathbf k) = \int h(\mathbf x)\,e^{-2\pi i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}d\mathbf x. Its complex conjugate is \int h(\mathbf x)\,e^{2\pi i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}d\mathbf x; substituting \mathbf x \to -\mathbf x and using h(-\mathbf x) = h(\mathbf x) gives H(\mathbf k) back. A number equal to its conjugate is real. Example: the uniform line of B10, H = \mathrm{sinc}(Lk), negative between 1/L and 2/L; or a uniform disc (geometric defocus), whose OTF 2J_1(x)/x is negative between its first two zeros.
B10. (a) H(k) = \frac1L\int_{-L/2}^{L/2}e^{-2\pi ikx}dx = \frac{e^{-i\pi Lk} - e^{i\pi Lk}}{-2\pi i L k} = \frac{\sin(\pi Lk)}{\pi Lk}, zero at k = m/L, m = \pm1, \pm2, \dots (b) Period 700 nm: k = 1.43 cycles/µm, \pi L k = 4.49, H = \sin(4.49)/4.49 = -0.217. The image is 1 - 0.217\cos(2\pi kx): the grating with 22 % of its contrast, inverted.

title: Exercise: image formation and the PSF
text:
Explore
The demo computes the PSF of an ideal lens from its pupil on a 256 × 256 grid of 40 nm pixels (a 10 µm field), and blurs a test object with it. Panels: the PSF (2.6 µm wide; tick “log scale” to see the rings), the OTF as an image up to ±8 cycles/µm with the cut-off circle 2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda in red (tick “signed” to see negative values in blue), the object and its image. The plot shows the OTF along the horizontal frequency axis with the curve of an ideal in-focus lens (dashed). The PSF menu adds defocus, motion blur, or the Gaussian approximation. The micrograph is treated as the true object with 40 nm pixels (it is itself already a blurred image).



E1. Preset oil objective, NA 1.4. Write down the Rayleigh distance, the Abbe distance, the cut-off and the PSF FWHM. Check the FWHM against 0.51\lambda/\mathrm{NA}. Where does the blue curve reach zero?
E2. Lower the NA to 0.3 (preset dry objective). By what factor do the FWHM and the cut-off change? Compare with the ratio of the NAs. What happens to the micrograph?
E3. Choose the Siemens star as object. Its 16 bright spokes have period 2\pi r/16 at radius r. At NA 1.4 and at NA 0.3, estimate the radius of the grey disc in the middle where the spokes disappear, and predict it from the Abbe distance.
E4. Preset blue vs red (NA 0.8, bar groups with periods 160–800 nm, finest top left). Which groups show bars at 450 nm? Move λ to 650 nm: which groups disappear? Use the Abbe distance to explain.
E5. Preset defocus: contrast reversal (NA 0.7, 2 µm out of focus). In which frequency range is the OTF negative? Find a spoke of the star that changes from bright to dark along its length. Then set the defocus to 0: does any part of the OTF stay negative?
E6. Preset motion blur (1 µm along x). Where are the zeros of the OTF, and how negative does it get? Change the motion length to 0.5 µm and the angle to 90°: where are the zeros now, and which spokes of the star are affected?
E7. Preset Gaussian approximation. Compare its FWHM with the Airy PSF’s (switch the PSF menu to “lens”). Where do the two OTF curves differ most? What does the Gaussian OTF do beyond the cut-off?






Solutions





E1. Rayleigh 227 nm, Abbe 186 nm, cut-off 5.38 cycles/µm, PSF FWHM 192 nm. 0.51 \cdot 520/1.4 = 191 nm: they agree (the demo measures on 40 nm pixels). The blue curve follows the dashed ideal curve and reaches zero at the red line, 5.38 cycles/µm.
E2. At NA 0.3: FWHM 891 nm and cut-off 1.15 cycles/µm. The FWHM grows by 891/192 = 4.6 and the cut-off falls by 5.38/1.15 = 4.7, both the ratio of the NAs, 1.4/0.3 = 4.7. The micrograph keeps only its coarse structure (the nucleus outline); the fine granules are gone, and the red circle in the OTF panel has shrunk to a small disc.
E3. The spokes vanish where their period 2\pi r/16 drops below the Abbe distance: r = 16 \cdot \lambda/(2\mathrm{NA})/(2\pi). NA 1.4: 16 \cdot 186/(2\pi) = 0.47 µm, about 12 pixels; NA 0.3: 16 \cdot 867/(2\pi) = 2.2 µm, about 55 pixels, a quarter of the field. Inside that radius the star is uniformly grey.
E4. At 450 nm (Abbe 450/1.6 = 281 nm) the groups with periods 320 nm (faint, tick “stretch”) and 400 nm and above show bars; 160–240 nm are grey. At 650 nm (Abbe 650/1.6 = 406 nm) the 320 nm and 400 nm groups disappear too; 480 nm is still faintly visible. Their frequency is now beyond the cut-off. The readout’s cut-off moves from 3.56 to 2.46 cycles/µm.
E5. The OTF is negative from about 0.55 to 2.3 cycles/µm (most negative about −0.06 near 0.7 cycles/µm), then slightly positive until the cut-off 2.69 cycles/µm. On the star these frequencies lie between radii of about 1.1 and 4.6 µm: a spoke that is bright near the rim becomes dark in that band. With defocus 0 the OTF is positive everywhere up to the cut-off: the in-focus lens never reverses contrast.
E6. Zeros at 1 and 2 cycles/µm (every 1/L); the curve dips to about −0.14 near 1.4 cycles/µm. With 0.5 µm the zeros move to 2 and 4 cycles/µm (fewer within the cut-off). At 90° the motion is vertical: the stripes in the OTF image turn by 90°, the curve along the horizontal axis is the lens’s own OTF again, and now the horizontal spokes of the star (whose stripes vary along y) lose contrast instead of the vertical ones.
E7. FWHM 186 nm for the Gaussian, 192 nm for the lens. The OTF curves differ most at low frequencies (at 1 cycle/µm: 0.89 for the Gaussian against 0.77) and near the cut-off; around 3–4 cycles/µm they nearly agree. Beyond the cut-off the Gaussian OTF is small but not zero (0.03 at 5.4 cycles/µm): it lets through a little of what a real lens cannot pass. In log scale the Gaussian PSF has no rings.

text:
Where this leads
The OTF says which frequencies the optics deliver. The next unit asks the practical questions that follow: when are two points resolved, how large may a pixel be (Nyquist for a microscope), why is the PSF longer along the optical axis, and how do we measure a PSF with beads.

title: Quiz: image formation and the PSF
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Notation: PSF = image of a point, OTF = its Fourier transform, NA = numerical aperture, λ = wavelength.

Q1. Why is the image of a fluorescent sample a sum of PSFs, one per point of the object, weighted by its brightness?






Hint





Do the light waves from two different molecules interfere?









Answer





Fluorescent molecules emit independently (incoherent light), so their waves do not interfere on average: the intensities add. Each point contributes a copy of the PSF, scaled by its brightness and shifted to its position. A weighted sum of shifted copies of one kernel is a convolution: image = object ∗ PSF.




Q2. A grating of period 300 nm is imaged with an NA 1.4 objective at 520 nm. The OTF at that frequency is 0.27. What does the image of the grating look like?






Hint





The OTF multiplies the contrast of each stripe pattern.









Answer





The same stripes, same period and position, with 27 % of the original contrast: a pattern 1 + \cos becomes 1 + 0.27\cos. The mean brightness is unchanged (H(0) = 1).




Q3. Which improves the resolution more: halving the wavelength, or doubling the NA?






Hint





Look at 0.61\lambda/\mathrm{NA}.









Answer





Both halve 0.61\lambda/\mathrm{NA}: the same improvement. In practice neither is free: NA is limited to about 1.4–1.5 (it cannot exceed the refractive index of the immersion medium), and the wavelength is set by the fluorescent dye.




Q4. A grating of period 150 nm lies under an NA 1.4 objective (λ = 520 nm). Is it blurred, or is it gone? Would a better camera help?






Hint





Compare its frequency with 2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda.









Answer





Its frequency, 6.7 cycles/µm, is above the cut-off 2 \cdot 1.4/0.52 = 5.4 cycles/µm. The OTF is exactly zero there: the grating does not reach the camera at all, so the image is the same as without the grating. No camera can record what the lens did not pass.




Q5. In a defocused image of a striped test pattern, one band of stripes appears inverted (dark where the pattern is bright). Why?






Hint





What does a negative OTF value do to 1 + \cos?









Answer





The OTF of a defocused lens becomes negative at some frequencies. A stripe pattern at such a frequency is imaged as 1 + H\cos with H < 0: the stripes are shifted by half a period, bright and dark swap. Stripes at other frequencies keep their sign.




Q6. A camera moved by 2 µm (in the sample plane) along x during the exposure. Which stripe patterns along x vanish completely?






Hint





The OTF of a line of length L is a sinc with zeros at k/L.









Answer





Those with frequencies 1/L, 2/L, \dots = 0.5, 1, 1.5, … cycles/µm along x, i.e. periods 2 µm, 1 µm, 667 nm, …: each such stripe is averaged over exactly a whole number of periods. Stripes along y (frequency in y only) are not affected.




Q7. The Gaussian approximation of the PSF uses \sigma = 0.21\lambda/\mathrm{NA}. What does it get right, and what does it miss?






Hint





Compare the profile and the OTF of the two.









Answer





It matches the central disc: almost the same width (FWHM 0.49 against 0.51 λ/NA) and almost the same OTF at low and middle frequencies. It misses the rings of the Airy pattern and the hard cut-off: a Gaussian OTF is never exactly zero, so it pretends that very fine detail passes a little.




Q8. (math) Show that a PSF normalised to \int h(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x = 1 has H(\mathbf 0) = 1, and say what that means for the image.






Hint





Put \mathbf k = 0 into the Fourier integral.









Answer





H(\mathbf k) = \int h(\mathbf x)\,e^{-2\pi i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\,d\mathbf x, so H(\mathbf 0) = \int h(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x = 1. Frequency 0 is the mean brightness (the total light): blur redistributes the light but does not change its total.




Q9. (math) Why is the OTF of a perfect lens zero beyond 2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda, and not beyond \mathrm{NA}/\lambda, the radius of the pupil?






Hint





The intensity PSF is |a|^2; what is the Fourier transform of a product?









Answer





The amplitude PSF a contains frequencies up to \mathrm{NA}/\lambda (the pupil). The intensity h = a\,a^* is a product, so its spectrum is the autocorrelation of the pupil: the overlap of the disc with a shifted copy, non-zero for shifts up to the disc’s diameter, 2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda.
crumbs: Image formation and the point spread function

title: Quantisation and bit depth
text:
About this lecture

A digital image loses information twice: where it is measured (sampling) and which values it can store (quantisation).
How many grey levels b bits give, and what rounding to them does: banding, and an error of predictable size.
Dithering: why adding noise on purpose makes an image look better.
How the error shrinks with each extra bit: about 6 dB per bit.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

The images lecture said “typically 8 or 16 bits”. This lecture asks what that choice costs and when it matters. The plan: picture and demo first, the variance formula afterwards. The next unit (camera noise) asks how many bits the measurement itself can fill, and owns the noise models, SNR and PSNR; this lecture’s SNR is only the rounding one.

title: Quantisation and bit depth
text:
Two ways to lose information
A camera measures a continuous brightness f(x, y) and stores a matrix of whole numbers:









Sampling
Quantisation




what is cut
positions: f is read only at grid points
values: each reading is rounded to one of a few levels


controlled by
pixel size, optics
bit depth b


typical damage
lost fine detail, aliasing
banding in smooth regions, lost faint differences


treated in
the Fourier unit
this lecture

title: Quantisation and bit depth
text:
Bits and levels
With b bits a pixel can take 2^b values, 0, 1, \dots, 2^b - 1:



bits b
1
2
8
10
12
14
16




levels 2^b
2
4
256
1024
4096
16 384
65 536




Spread over the same range (say black to white), the step between neighbouring levels is \Delta = \text{range}/(2^b - 1).
One more bit → twice as many levels → half the step.
8 bits: the step is 1/255 of the range. 12 bits: 1/4095, a 16 times finer step.

title: Quantisation and bit depth
text:
Try it: quantise an image




Start on the ramp at 4 bits: 16 visible bands. Slide the bits down to 1 and up to 8; at 6 bits most people stop seeing bands on a projector. Point at the error image: a sawtooth, between −Δ/2 and +Δ/2, and the histogram is flat. Then “4 bits: banding” on the smooth blobs: contour lines appear that are not in the scene. Then “4 bits + dither”: the bands are gone, replaced by fine grain, and the histogram becomes a triangle. Then the micrograph at 2 bits with error diffusion: only 4 grey levels, but it still looks like the cell.

title: Quantisation and bit depth
section: What the rounding error looks like
text:
What the rounding error looks like

Rounding moves each value to the nearest level, so the error is between −Δ/2 and +Δ/2.
In a smooth region the error is a sawtooth: the image jumps in steps of \Delta where it should change gradually. The eye sees the jumps as contour lines: banding (posterisation).
In a busy or noisy region, the error looks like random noise, evenly spread between −Δ/2 and +Δ/2.
Its typical size is about 0.29\,\Delta (root mean square). The demo’s readout shows it: at 4 bits, RMS error 0.0192 of the range.
One more bit halves the error. In decibels: about 6 dB per bit.

title: Quantisation and bit depth
section: The math: the error of rounding
text:
The math: the error of rounding
Model the error e as uniform on [-\Delta/2, \Delta/2], with density 1/\Delta. Then
\mathbb E[e] = 0, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(e) = \int_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2} e^2\,\frac{1}{\Delta}\,de = \frac{1}{\Delta}\left[\frac{e^3}{3}\right]_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2} = \frac{\Delta^2}{12}.
So \text{RMS} = \Delta/\sqrt{12} \approx 0.289\,\Delta. Here the signal-to-noise ratio in decibels compares variances: \text{SNR} = 10\log_{10}(\sigma^2_\text{signal}/\sigma^2_\text{noise}) (SNR and PSNR in general: camera-noise unit). For a signal spread evenly over the full range R = (2^b - 1)\Delta, \sigma^2_\text{signal} = R^2/12, so
\text{SNR} = 10\log_{10}\,(2^b - 1)^2 \approx 20\,b\log_{10}2 \approx 6.02\,b \text{ dB}.
(For a full-scale sine wave, the textbook value is 6.02\,b + 1.76 dB.) The model holds when the signal changes by many steps across the image; on a perfectly flat region the error is one constant number, not noise.

title: Quantisation and bit depth
text:
Dithering: add noise before rounding
Rounding a smooth gradient gives bands, because many neighbouring pixels round the same way.

Random dither: add a little noise (up to ±Δ/2) to every pixel before rounding. A pixel 75 % of the way from one level to the next now rounds up 75 % of the time. On average, the grey value is right.
The bands turn into fine grain. The total error is a bit larger (a triangle instead of a box, RMS \times\sqrt2), but it no longer follows the image, and the eye averages grain away.
Error diffusion (Floyd–Steinberg): round a pixel, then pass its error on to the neighbours not yet visited. The local average stays right. This is how a printer shows grey with only black ink.

title: Quantisation and bit depth
section: The math: why random dither is unbiased
text:
The math: why random dither is unbiased
Measure in units of \Delta, write a value as x = k + f with k an integer and 0 \le f < 1, and add u uniform on [-\tfrac12, \tfrac12). Then x + u rounds up to k + 1 exactly when u \ge \tfrac12 - f, which has probability f:
\mathbb E[\operatorname{round}(x + u)] = (1 - f)\,k + f\,(k + 1) = k + f = x.
No bias, for every x: the expected output is a straight line, not a staircase. The price: the error is 1 - f with probability f and -f with probability 1 - f, so \mathbb E[e^2] = f(1-f); averaged over f, \int_0^1 f(1-f)\,df = \tfrac16. So the error variance is \Delta^2/6, twice that of plain rounding.

title: Quantisation and bit depth
text:
Summary

b bits give 2^b levels; rounding to them makes an error of at most half a step (typically 0.29 steps): about 6 dB per bit.
In smooth regions the error shows as banding; dithering trades the bands for fine, unbiased noise.
Next: where the numbers come from. A camera counts electrons, and the count is noisy: how many bits are worth storing?

title: Exercise: projections and the sinogram

turn a transmitted fraction I/I_0 into a line integral of the attenuation, and back,

title: Exercise: projections and the sinogram
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Attenuation \mu
fraction of photons removed per cm (about 0.2 cm⁻¹ for soft tissue, more for bone)


Measurement
-\ln(I/I_0) = sum (integral) of \mu along the ray


Line (\theta, \rho)
all points with x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = \rho; origin at the image centre, y up, \theta \in [0°, 180°)


Projection p_\theta(\rho)
the line integrals of all parallel lines at angle \theta; \theta = 0°: column sums, 90°: row sums


Sinogram
the projections side by side: \theta across, \rho up


A point (x, y)
lands at \rho = x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = r\cos(\theta - \varphi)

title: Exercise: projections and the sinogram
text:
By hand
B1. Beer–Lambert with numbers. (a) A beam crosses 20 cm of water-like tissue (\mu = 0.2 cm⁻¹). Which fraction of the photons arrives? (b) The beam crosses 18 cm of tissue and 2 cm of bone (\mu = 0.5 cm⁻¹). What is -\ln(I/I_0), and I/I_0? Does it matter whether the bone comes first or last? (c) A detector reads I/I_0 = 0.05. What is the line integral of \mu along that ray? (d) Why does a CT scanner take the logarithm of the measured intensity before doing anything else?
B2. Three point masses: A = (2, 0) with mass 1, B = (0, 1) with mass 2, C = (-1, -1) with mass 1. (a) Draw the projections at 0°, 45°, 90° and 135° as bar plots on a \rho axis. (b) Check that every projection sums to the same number. Which number, and why?
B3. The sinogram of B2. (a) Give each point’s sinusoid as \rho = r\cos(\theta - \varphi): its amplitude r and the angle \varphi where it peaks. (b) Sketch the three curves for \theta from 0° to 180°. (c) At which angles do two curves cross, and at which \rho? What does a crossing mean for the measurement?
B4. Where in the sinogram is (a) a point at the image centre, (b) a point at (0, -3)? (c) A sinogram shows a sinusoid with amplitude 5 that peaks at \theta = 90°. Where is the point?
B5. You have measured p_{20°}(\rho). Without measuring again, what is p_{200°}(\rho)? Why does a parallel-beam scanner turn only half a turn?
B6. A uniform disc of radius 3 cm with \mu = 0.2 cm⁻¹, centred at the origin. (a) The ray at \rho crosses the disc along a chord of length 2\sqrt{9 - \rho^2}. Compute p_0(\rho) at \rho = 0, 1, 2, 2.5, 3 and sketch it. (b) Does the projection depend on \theta? What is the area under it? (c) The disc moves to (2, 0). Sketch p_0 and p_{90°} now. Describe its sinogram.
B7. A 3 \times 3 binary image has row sums (1, 2, 1) (top to bottom) and column sums (1, 2, 1) (left to right). (a) Find two different binary images with these sums. (b) Which small change of an image never changes its row and column sums? (c) Does a third projection at 45° always tell the images apart?






Solutions





B1. (a) I/I_0 = e^{-0.2 \cdot 20} = e^{-4} = 0.018: under 2 %. (b) -\ln(I/I_0) = 18 \cdot 0.2 + 2 \cdot 0.5 = 3.6 + 1.0 = 4.6, so I/I_0 = e^{-4.6} = 0.010. The order does not matter: the fractions multiply, and multiplication does not care about order (after the logarithm: a sum). (c) -\ln 0.05 = 3.00. (d) Because then each reading is a sum of the unknowns along the ray (linear in \mu). Everything later (back-projection, filtering, linear systems) needs that linearity.
B2. (a) \rho = x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta:

Each projection is three bars of heights 1, 2, 1 at these positions. (b) Each sums to 1 + 2 + 1 = 4, the total mass: a projection only moves mass sideways onto the detector, every point lands somewhere exactly once.
B3. (a) A: r = 2, \varphi = 0° (peaks at 0°). B: r = 1, \varphi = 90°. C: r = \sqrt2 = 1.41, \varphi = -135°, i.e. the curve 1.41\cos(\theta + 135°) peaks at 225° and has its minimum, -1.41, at 45°. (c) Set the two \rho equal: A and B cross at \theta = 63.4° (\tan\theta = 2), \rho = 0.89; A and C at 108.4°, \rho = -0.63; B and C at 153.4°, \rho = 0.45. At a crossing both points lie on the same ray: that projection cannot tell them apart, it shows one bar with their summed mass.
B4. (a) r = 0: the flat line \rho = 0. The centre of rotation is the only point that never moves on the detector. (b) \rho = -3\sin\theta: zero at 0°, -3 at 90°. (c) r = 5, \varphi = 90°: the point (0, 5).
B5. p_{200°}(\rho) = p_{20°}(-\rho): the same rays, walked in the opposite direction, so the profile is mirrored. Turning from 180° to 360° measures nothing new.
B6. (a) p_0(\rho) = 0.4\sqrt{9 - \rho^2}: 1.20, 1.13, 0.89, 0.66, 0 at \rho = 0, 1, 2, 2.5, 3: a half-ellipse. (b) A disc looks the same from every direction: every projection is this half-ellipse. Area: \mu \cdot \pi R^2 = 0.2 \cdot 9\pi = 5.65, the total of the image. (c) p_0 is the same half-ellipse centred at \rho = 2; p_{90°} is centred at \rho = 0 (the disc’s y is 0). In the sinogram the band follows the sinusoid of the centre, \rho = 2\cos\theta.
B7. (a) For example \begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&1\\0&1&0\end{bmatrix} and \begin{bmatrix}0&1&0\\1&0&1\\0&1&0\end{bmatrix}. Five binary images have exactly these sums. (b) Swapping a 2 \times 2 checkerboard: in two rows and two columns, change \begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix} into \begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}. Every row and column keeps its sum. (c) No, not always: it removes some ambiguities but not all. With more angles fewer images agree with all the data. (The fourth unit counts this with the rank of a matrix.)




Math questions
B8. (math) Derive I = I_0\exp(-\int\mu\,ds) from dI/ds = -\mu(s) I. Which assumption about the photons does the equation make?
B9. (math) From \mathcal R f(\rho, \theta) = \int f(\rho\,\mathbf n_\theta + s\,\mathbf n^\perp_\theta)\,ds, prove (a) the shift rule f(\mathbf x - \mathbf t) \mapsto \mathcal R f(\rho - \mathbf t\cdot\mathbf n_\theta, \theta), (b) the symmetry \mathcal R f(-\rho, \theta + \pi) = \mathcal R f(\rho, \theta), (c) \int \mathcal R f\,d\rho = \iint f.
B10. (math) Show that the projection of a uniform disc (value \mu, radius R, centre 0) is 2\mu\sqrt{R^2 - \rho^2}, and check that its integral over \rho is \mu\pi R^2.
B11. (math) A point mass m at \mathbf x_0 is f = m\,\delta(\mathbf x - \mathbf x_0). Use the first form of the definition, \iint f\,\delta(\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf n_\theta - \rho)\,d\mathbf x, to show that its Radon transform is m\,\delta(\rho - \mathbf x_0\cdot\mathbf n_\theta), and write \mathbf x_0\cdot\mathbf n_\theta as r\cos(\theta - \varphi).






Solutions (math)





B8. Separate variables: dI/I = -\mu(s)\,ds, integrate from the source (I_0) to the detector: \ln I - \ln I_0 = -\int\mu\,ds. The equation says every photon has the same chance per unit length of being removed, independent of the others: one energy (otherwise \mu depends on the photon) and no scattered photons reaching the detector.
B9. (a) \int f(\rho\mathbf n + s\mathbf n^\perp - \mathbf t)\,ds; write \mathbf t = (\mathbf t\cdot\mathbf n)\mathbf n + (\mathbf t\cdot\mathbf n^\perp)\mathbf n^\perp and substitute s' = s - \mathbf t\cdot\mathbf n^\perp: \int f((\rho - \mathbf t\cdot\mathbf n)\mathbf n + s'\mathbf n^\perp)\,ds' = \mathcal R f(\rho - \mathbf t\cdot\mathbf n, \theta). (b) \mathbf n_{\theta + \pi} = -\mathbf n_\theta and \mathbf n^\perp_{\theta + \pi} = -\mathbf n^\perp_\theta: \mathcal R f(-\rho, \theta + \pi) = \int f(\rho\mathbf n - s\mathbf n^\perp)\,ds, the same integral with s \to -s. (c) (\rho, s) \mapsto \rho\mathbf n + s\mathbf n^\perp is a rotation (Jacobian 1), so \iint \mathcal R f\,d\rho = \iint f(\rho\mathbf n + s\mathbf n^\perp)\,ds\,d\rho = \iint f\,dx\,dy.
B10. By symmetry take \theta = 0: the line x = \rho meets the disc for |y| \le \sqrt{R^2 - \rho^2}, so \int f\,dy = 2\mu\sqrt{R^2 - \rho^2}. With \rho = R\sin u: \int_{-R}^R 2\mu\sqrt{R^2 - \rho^2}\,d\rho = 2\mu R^2\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^2 u\,du = \mu\pi R^2.
B11. \iint m\,\delta(\mathbf x - \mathbf x_0)\,\delta(\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf n_\theta - \rho)\,d\mathbf x = m\,\delta(\mathbf x_0\cdot\mathbf n_\theta - \rho) (sifting property). With \mathbf x_0 = r(\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi): \mathbf x_0\cdot\mathbf n_\theta = r(\cos\varphi\cos\theta + \sin\varphi\sin\theta) = r\cos(\theta - \varphi).

title: Exercise: projections and the sinogram
text:
Explore
The demo shows a 128 \times 128 object on the left, with the rays of the current angle (yellow, the arrow shows the beam direction) and the detector (blue bar). The middle panel is the projection p_\theta(\rho); the right panel is the sinogram, filled in up to the current angle. Click in the object to drop a point mass (its mass is set by the slider); every point gets a coloured sinusoid on the sinogram, a dashed line in the projection and a dot on the detector. Drag moves the object shifts the whole object instead. 0°–360° extends the sinogram to a full turn. The readout gives the sum of the current projection, the total of the image, and each point’s current \rho. Distances are in pixels.



E1. Preset three points by hand (one unit of B2 = 16 pixels). Read \rho of the three points at 0°, 45° and 90° (use 0° and +45°) and compare with B2. What is the sum of each projection?
E2. Play the sinogram from 0°. At which angle do the red and green curves (A and B) cross? What do you see in the projection at that angle? Compare with B3.
E3. Preset the centre does not move. Which curve is flat? For the other two points, read their positions in the readout and predict the amplitude and the angle of the peak of their sinusoids. Check with the slider.
E4. Preset 180°–360° mirrors 0°–180°. Compare the sinogram column at 30° with the one at 210° (move the slider). What exactly is the relation? Which point has the largest amplitude, and why?
E5. Preset every column has the same sum. Read the sum of the projection at 0°, 30° and 45° and the total of the image. Are they equal? Why could they differ in the last digits on a pixel grid?
E6. Preset shift the object: drag the disc about 20 pixels to the right. How does the sinogram change? At which angles does the band move most, and at which not at all?
E7. Presets Shepp–Logan sinogram and a real image. In the Shepp–Logan sinogram, which feature of the phantom makes the two bright outer bands? Why are they brightest where they are tangent to the outline? Add a point mass of 8 inside the micrograph and find its curve.






Solutions





E1. At 0°: A 32, B 0, C −16 pixels (2, 0, −1 units). At 45°: 22.6, 11.3, −22.6 (1.41, 0.71, −1.41). At 90°: 0, 16, −16 (0, 1, −1). Every projection sums to 4.0, the total.
E2. They cross at about 63°: there the two point masses lie on the same ray (A at \rho = 14.5, B at 14.3 pixels at 63°), and the projection shows one peak holding both masses, 1 + 2 = 3, instead of two separate bars.
E3. The point at the centre has the flat curve \rho = 0. The point at (40, 0) has amplitude 40 and peaks at 0°; the point at (-20, 30) has amplitude \sqrt{20^2 + 30^2} = 36.1 and peaks at \varphi = 123.7° (at 124° the readout gives \rho = 36.0).
E4. The column at 210° is the column at 30° upside down: p_{\theta + 180°}(\rho) = p_\theta(-\rho), the same rays walked the other way. The point mass at (36, 36) is farthest from the centre (r = 50.9), so its sinusoid has the largest amplitude.
E5. Total 1936.0; projection sums 1936.0 at 0°, 1936.8 at 30°, 1936.0 at 45°. Equal up to 0.04 %. At 0° and 90° the rays run exactly through pixel centres; at other angles the linear interpolation between pixels distributes each pixel’s value over neighbouring rays not quite evenly, so the sum is exact only on average.
E6. Every sinusoid moves by t_x\cos\theta + t_y\sin\theta: with \mathbf t = (20, 0) the band moves up by 20 at 0°, not at all at 90°, and down by 20 at 180°. The sinogram is bent, not slid.
E7. The bright outer bands come from the skull: the dense outer ring of the phantom. A ray that just grazes the ring runs a long way inside it (tangent), so its line integral is largest there. The point mass adds a thin sinusoid of its own on top of the micrograph’s sinogram: linearity.

title: Exercise: projections and the sinogram
text:
Where this leads
The sinogram is all the scanner gives us. The next unit tries the most natural inversion, smearing every projection back over the image (back-projection), and finds out why it blurs; the Fourier slice theorem explains what is missing. Later units fix the blur with a filter and then treat reconstruction as a linear system.

title: Quiz: projections and the sinogram
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Lines are x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = \rho, origin at the image centre, y up, \theta \in [0°, 180°).

Q1. Why does a CT scanner work with -\ln(I/I_0) rather than with the measured intensity I?






Hint





How do the attenuations of two layers combine?









Answer





Each layer removes a fraction of the photons, so the transmitted fractions multiply. The logarithm turns the product into a sum of \mu along the ray: a line integral, linear in the unknown attenuation. All reconstruction methods rely on that linearity.




Q2. 10 cm of water-like tissue (\mu = 0.2 cm⁻¹): what fraction of the photons gets through? And with 1 cm of bone (\mu = 0.5 cm⁻¹) added?






Hint





I/I_0 = e^{-\sum \mu\,\Delta s}.









Answer





e^{-2} = 0.135, about 14 %. With the bone: e^{-2.5} = 0.082; the bone alone would pass e^{-0.5} = 0.61, and the two fractions multiply: 0.135 \cdot 0.61 = 0.082.




Q3. What does the projection at \theta = 0° of an image look like, in terms of its pixels? And at \theta = 90°?






Hint





At \theta = 0° the lines are x = \rho.









Answer





At 0° the rays are vertical: the projection is the column sums, left to right with increasing \rho. At 90° the rays are horizontal: the row sums, with the top row at the largest \rho (because y points up).




Q4. A sinogram contains a sinusoid with amplitude 30 pixels whose maximum is at \theta = 60°. Where is the point?






Hint





\rho = r\cos(\theta - \varphi).









Answer





At distance r = 30 from the centre in direction \varphi = 60°: (30\cos 60°, 30\sin 60°) = (15, 26).




Q5. Why is a half turn (180°) enough for a parallel-beam scanner?






Hint





Compare the rays at \theta and at \theta + 180°.









Answer





The line at (\theta + 180°, \rho) is the line at (\theta, -\rho): the same set of points. So p_{\theta + 180°}(\rho) = p_\theta(-\rho); the second half turn repeats the first, mirrored.




Q6. The sums of the projections of a scan are 512.3 at most angles but 480.1 at a few neighbouring angles. What might have happened?






Hint





Which number should every projection share?









Answer





Every projection should sum to the total of the object. A drop at a few angles means those projections lost part of the object: for example, the object stuck out of the field of view at those angles (truncation), or detector elements failed, or the source fluctuated. The consistency check catches it.




Q7. You move an object 10 pixels up (in +y). How does its sinogram change?






Hint





Each point moves by \mathbf t\cdot(\cos\theta, \sin\theta) on the detector.









Answer





Every point’s curve moves by 10\sin\theta: not at all at 0° (vertical rays do not see a vertical shift), by +10 at 90°, and back to 0 at 180°. The whole sinogram is bent by this sinusoid; it is not simply shifted.




Q8. Row sums and column sums of a binary image are known. Why can’t you always reconstruct the image from them?






Hint





Look for a change that keeps every row and column sum.









Answer





Swapping a 2 \times 2 checkerboard pattern \begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix} \leftrightarrow \begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix} (in any two rows and two columns) leaves all row and column sums unchanged. Different images give the same two projections; more angles are needed to tell them apart.




Q9. (math) Show that every projection of f has the same integral \int p_\theta(\rho)\,d\rho.






Answer





\int p_\theta(\rho)\,d\rho = \iint f(\rho\,\mathbf n_\theta + s\,\mathbf n_\theta^\perp)\,ds\,d\rho. The map (\rho, s) \mapsto \rho\,\mathbf n_\theta + s\,\mathbf n_\theta^\perp is a rotation with Jacobian 1, so the double integral is \iint f\,dx\,dy, independent of \theta.

title: Hypothesise and verify: RANSAC
text:
About this lecture
The Hough transform finds a model by voting into a grid over its parameters. That needs a grid, and the grid grows with every parameter. RANSAC (Fischler & Bolles, 1981) does the opposite: guess a model from a few points and check how many others agree.

Why least squares fails with outliers.
The RANSAC loop: minimal sample, exact fit, count inliers, keep the best, refit.
How many guesses are needed: a formula with the inlier fraction.
Choosing \varepsilon, several models, and the randomised Hough transform as a bridge.
Voting or guessing? When to use which.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Last unit of the Hough day. Needs: the line unit’s normal form; least squares from linear algebra (recalled in one line); PCA from the pca unit for the total-least-squares refit (math slide). All random choices in the demo come from a fixed seed (slider), so a run can be repeated.

title: Hypothesise and verify: RANSAC
text:
Least squares and outliers
Fit a line to points of which 30 % are outliers (points that do not belong to the line at all):


Least squares minimises the sum of squared distances. An outlier 30 px away costs as much as 900 points 1 px away: a few outliers pull the line towards them (orange, dashed).
The Hough transform solves this by voting: outliers vote, but for scattered bins. It needs a grid in parameter space.
Another idea: guess and check.

title: Hypothesise and verify: RANSAC
text:
RANSAC: guess and check
Repeat N times:

Pick a minimal sample at random: as few points as determine the model. 2 for a line, 3 for a circle.
Fit the model exactly through them.
Count the points within a distance \varepsilon of the model: the inliers.
Keep the model with the most inliers so far.

At the end, refit by least squares on the inliers of the best model only.
A sample of two points that are both on the line gives (nearly) the right line, and then many points agree. A sample that contains an outlier gives a wrong line that few points agree with.

title: Hypothesise and verify: RANSAC
section: Try it: RANSAC step by step
text:
Try it: RANSAC step by step




60 points, half of them on a line (θ = 63°, ρ = 58), seeded. Press “restart”, then “one sample” repeatedly: the red points are the sample, the red band ±ε (2 px), the bars the inlier count of each sample, the blue step line the best so far. Seed 1: samples 2 and 3 are all-inlier (29 inliers each), sample 14 (30 inliers) becomes the best. “run all”: refit on its 31 inliers (29 of them true), θ = 63.4°, ρ = 58.1; least squares on all points (orange) gives θ = 75.8°. Right: the chance of at least one all-inlier sample, 99 % after 17 samples for w = 0.5, s = 2. Change the seed to see other runs: with seed 4 the very first sample is a good one.

title: Hypothesise and verify: RANSAC
text:
Refit on the inliers
The best sample’s model goes exactly through two (or three) points, which are noisy. The final model should use all the inliers:

Take the inliers of the best model.
Fit by least squares to them only: now there are no outliers to pull it away.
Optionally recount the inliers of the refitted model, and refit once more.

For a line, the natural least-squares fit measures perpendicular distances (the same distance as the inlier test), not vertical ones: the line through the centroid along the direction of largest spread, which is PCA of the inlier points (the PCA unit).

title: Hypothesise and verify: RANSAC
text:
The math: least-squares refits

Line, total least squares: minimise \sum_i (\mathbf n^\top \mathbf p_i - \rho)^2 over unit normals \mathbf n and \rho. Setting the derivative in \rho to zero gives \rho = \mathbf n^\top \bar{\mathbf p} (the line passes through the centroid). What is left is \mathbf n^\top S\,\mathbf n with the scatter matrix S = \sum_i (\mathbf p_i - \bar{\mathbf p})(\mathbf p_i - \bar{\mathbf p})^\top; its minimum over unit \mathbf n is the eigenvector of the smaller eigenvalue (PCA). The result is the line unit’s (\theta, \rho), with \mathbf n = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta).
Circle, algebraic fit: (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2 is x^2 + y^2 = 2ax + 2by + c with c = r^2 - a^2 - b^2, linear in (a, b, c). Stack one row (2x_i, 2y_i, 1) per point, solve the 3 \times 3 normal equations, then r = \sqrt{c + a^2 + b^2}.
Robust variants: MSAC scores a model by \sum_i \min(d_i^2, \varepsilon^2) instead of the inlier count, so that among models with equal counts the one closer to its inliers wins.

title: Hypothesise and verify: RANSAC
text:
How many guesses?
Let w be the fraction of inliers and s the sample size.

One random point is an inlier with probability w; a whole sample of s points with probability w^s.
w = 0.5, s = 2: one sample in 4 is all-inlier. s = 3: one in 8.
After N samples, the chance that at least one was all-inlier is 1 - (1 - w^s)^N.
For 99 %:




inlier fraction w
sample size s
samples N




0.5

N does not depend on the number of points; it explodes when w is small or s is large.

title: Hypothesise and verify: RANSAC
section: The math: the number of iterations
text:
The math: the number of iterations
Samples are drawn independently (with replacement between samples). A sample is all-inlier with probability w^s (for many points; without replacement inside a sample it is slightly less, e.g. \tfrac{20}{100}\cdot\tfrac{19}{99} instead of 0.2^2). The probability that none of N samples is all-inlier is (1 - w^s)^N. Requiring it to be at most 1 - p:
(1 - w^s)^N \le 1 - p \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad N \ge \frac{\log(1 - p)}{\log(1 - w^s)}.
w = 0.5, s = 2, p = 0.99: \log 0.01 / \log 0.75 = 16.0, so N = 17. For small w^s, \log(1 - w^s) \approx -w^s and N \approx 4.6 / w^s: halving w multiplies N by 2^s. In practice w is unknown: start pessimistic and lower N each time a better model shows a larger inlier fraction (adaptive RANSAC).

title: Hypothesise and verify: RANSAC
text:
Choosing ε, and several models

\varepsilon too small: true points with a little noise fall outside the band; the counts are low and noisy, and the best model is decided by chance. Rule of thumb: 2 to 3 times the noise of the inliers.
\varepsilon too large: outliers count as inliers, and two nearby lines merge into one model between them. (Demo: “ε too large”.)
Not enough iterations: no all-inlier sample, and the best model is a chance alignment of outliers.
Several models in the data: RANSAC finds the one with most inliers. Sequential RANSAC: remove its inliers and run again. The Hough transform finds all of them in one pass.

title: Hypothesise and verify: RANSAC
text:
Randomised and probabilistic Hough
Two bridges between voting and guessing:

Randomised Hough transform (Xu, Oja & Kultanen, 1990): pick a minimal sample, fit the model, and cast one vote for that parameter value. The accumulator is sparse (a list of the cells that got votes), so it works for more parameters than a full grid.
Probabilistic Hough transform (Kiryati, Eldar & Bruckstein, 1991; progressive version: Matas, Galambos & Kittler, 2000): vote with a random subset of the edge points and stop as soon as a peak is clearly above the rest; remove the points of that line and continue. Image libraries call this “probabilistic Hough” and return line segments.

title: Hypothesise and verify: RANSAC
text:

title: Hypothesise and verify: RANSAC
text:
Try it: 80 % outliers




100 points, 20 on the line, 80 outliers. With 17 iterations (enough for w = 0.5) the chance of an all-inlier sample is only 50 %; with seed 1 none of the 17 samples is all-inlier, and the “best” model is a chance alignment of 10 points (4 of them true). The Hough accumulator of the same points (purple, dotted) has its peak at θ = 63°, ρ = 58.2 with 22 votes: the true line. Raise the iterations to 113, the 99 % value: with seed 1 the best model now appears at iteration 18 (22 inliers; its sample is an inlier plus an outlier that happens to lie 0.87 px from the line). The two all-inlier samples (91 and 93) consist of points close together, so their lines are poorly determined (8 and 7 inliers). The refit gives θ = 62.1°, ρ = 58.7, with 24 inliers, 18 of them true.

title: Hypothesise and verify: RANSAC
text:
Where RANSAC is standard

Fitting a transform between two images from matched feature points (registration, panoramas, stitching): an affine transform has 6 parameters (3 point pairs), a homography 8 (4 pairs). A grid over 6 or 8 parameters is hopeless; RANSAC with a few hundred samples is routine. This application belongs to the planned Motion elective, after the FFT registration day.
Two-view geometry (the fundamental matrix from 7 or 8 point pairs) in reconstructing 3D from images.
Geometric primitives in 3D point clouds: planes (3 points), spheres, cylinders.
Whenever a few gross errors would ruin a least-squares fit.

title: Hypothesise and verify: RANSAC
text:
Summary

Least squares is pulled by outliers: one far point outweighs many near ones.
RANSAC: minimal sample → exact fit → count inliers within \varepsilon → keep the best → refit on its inliers.
Iterations for success probability p: N = \log(1 - p)/\log(1 - w^s): 17 for a line at 50 % inliers, 113 at 20 %.
\varepsilon about 2–3 × the noise; too large merges nearby models; sequential RANSAC for several models.
Voting wins with few parameters, many instances and huge outlier fractions; guessing wins with many parameters.

title: Exercise: from triangles to shaded pixels
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

decide with edge functions whether a pixel centre lies inside a triangle, and compute its barycentric coordinates and interpolated depth,
fill a small z-buffer and explain why the result does not depend on the drawing order,
explain the top-left rule and back-face culling,
compute a perspective-correct interpolation, and say why depth precision depends on the near plane,
compute Lambert, Phong and Blinn–Phong shading at a point, and say what flat, Gouraud and per-pixel shading miss,
transform a normal correctly with M^{-\top}.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.
