title: Quiz: neighbours, parents and children
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Two papers report “4.9 neighbours per cell” and “1.2 neighbours per cell” for the same kind of tissue. Name a reason other than biology.






Hint





How was “neighbour” defined?









Answer





Different definitions: “expand until adjacent” (a Voronoi tessellation, about 5–6 inside a dense pattern) against “the segmented cells touch” (depends on how far the cell bodies were grown). In the demo the same 40 cells give 4.90 and 1.15. Connectivity (4 or 8), a distance r, and the border rule change the number too.




Q2. Why does “expand until adjacent” give every isolated cell at least one neighbour?






Hint





What happens to the background pixels?









Answer





Every background pixel is given to the nearest object, so the regions fill the whole image and every region borders some other region (unless there is only one object). Distance plays no role: two cells 200 µm apart are neighbours if nothing lies between them.




Q3. A pattern of cells has Clark–Evans ratio R = 0.6. What does that mean? And R = 1.8?






Hint





R = observed mean nearest-neighbour distance / that of a random pattern of the same density.









Answer





R = 0.6: nearest neighbours are on average 40 % closer than in a random pattern: the cells are clustered. R = 1.8: they are further apart than random: a regular pattern (cells keep their distance, as in an epithelium). Small deviations from 1 can come from the objects’ size (they cannot overlap) and from the image border.




Q4. Why do objects at the image border have fewer neighbours, and why is removing them not a good fix?






Hint





What happens to the objects next to the removed ones?









Answer





Part of their surroundings lies outside the image, so their neighbours there are not seen. Removing them makes their inner neighbours the new outer layer, which now misses neighbours instead. A guard zone fixes it: measure only objects away from the border, but let every object count as a neighbour.




Q5. A curved spot wraps around the edge of a nucleus; most of its pixels are inside. Which parent does it get by largest overlap, and by centroid?






Hint





Where is the centroid of a crescent?









Answer





By overlap: the nucleus. By centroid: possibly none, because the centroid of a crescent lies in the hollow of the curve, which may be outside the nucleus. The overlap rule (with the overlap fraction recorded) is the safer choice for irregular children.




Q6. With nuclei as parents, 10 % of the spots have no parent; with whole cells as parents, none. Which number do you report as “spots per cell”?






Hint





Where are the spots without a nucleus?









Answer





They are in the cytoplasm. If the question is about the cell, use cells as parents (all spots count); if it is about the nucleus, use nuclei and report the cytoplasmic spots separately. Silently dropping children without a parent biases the counts.




Q7. (math) For random points with density \rho = 0.01 per µm², what mean nearest-neighbour distance do you expect? A sample has mean 8 µm: what is R?






Hint





E[D] = 1/(2\sqrt\rho).









Answer





E[D] = 1/(2 \cdot 0.1) = 5 µm. R = 8/5 = 1.6: regular.




Q8. (math) Why is the mean number of Voronoi neighbours of points in the plane below 6?






Hint





The neighbour graph is planar; use Euler’s formula.









Answer





The neighbour graph (the Delaunay triangulation) is planar. With V vertices, E edges and F faces, V - E + F = 2 and 3F \le 2E give E \le 3V - 6, so the mean degree 2E/V \le 6 - 12/V < 6. Far from the border it approaches 6.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
About this lecture
Image analysis turns images into measurements: areas, intensities, counts, hundreds of features per cell. The usual question behind them: does a treatment change a feature?

The new statistics, by simulation: standard error, p-value, confidence interval.
The unit of replication, and pseudoreplication: why 1000 cells from one dish are one replicate.
Do it right: aggregate per experiment, paired designs, the SuperPlot.
Effect sizes with confidence intervals; multiple comparisons across many features.
Batch and plate effects, and designs that are confounded beyond repair.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
The data are hierarchical
A typical imaging experiment:
cells within images within wells within experiments (days, animals, patients)

Variation exists at every level: cells differ, fields differ, wells differ, and days differ: a new batch of cells, medium, stain, a refocused microscope.
The day-to-day variation is usually the largest, and it is shared by every cell measured that day.
Treatment and control are compared within this hierarchy. Which differences count as evidence?

title: From measurements to claims
section: A mean wobbles: the standard error
text:
A mean wobbles: the standard error
Measure n values with spread SD and take their mean. Repeat the whole experiment: the mean comes out a little different each time.

The wobble of the mean is its standard error: \text{SE} = \text{SD}/\sqrt n. Four times as many values halve it.
This holds for independent values. If they share a common deviation (the same day), it does not shrink below that shared part.

The difference of two means (treated − control) has \text{SE} = \sqrt{\text{SE}_1^2 + \text{SE}_2^2}.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
The p-value, by simulation
Suppose the treatment does nothing. How often would chance alone give a difference at least as large as the one observed?

Four experiments per condition, experiment means with SD 1: the difference of the two means wobbles with SE 0.71. An observed difference of 1.6 or more (either sign) comes up in 2.3 % of the simulated null experiments: p = 0.023.
A small p says “chance alone rarely does this”. It says nothing about how large or important the effect is.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
The confidence interval
Estimate ± 2 SE is a 95 % confidence interval: the range of true effects compatible with the data.

Observed 1.6 with SE 0.71: about 0.2 to 3.0. The effect is probably positive, but could be small or large.
The interval excludes 0 exactly when p < 0.05 (roughly); but it also shows the size and the uncertainty of the effect.
With few replicates the factor 2 is too small: it grows to 2.78 for 5 values and 4.30 for 3 (math slide).

title: From measurements to claims
section: The math: t statistic and t-distribution
text:
The math: t statistic and t-distribution
One sample x_1, \dots, x_n with mean \bar x and sample SD s: \text{SE} = s/\sqrt n and
t = \frac{\bar x - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt n}.
If the x_i are independent and normal with mean \mu_0, t follows Student’s t-distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom: like the standard normal, but with heavier tails, because s is itself estimated from few values. 95 % interval: \bar x \pm t_{0.975,\,n-1}\, s/\sqrt n, with t_{0.975} = 4.30 (2 df), 2.78 (4 df), 2.07 (22 df), 1.96 (\infty).
Two groups (Welch): t = (\bar y - \bar x)/\sqrt{s_x^2/n_x + s_y^2/n_y}, degrees of freedom from the Welch–Satterthwaite formula. Paired data: a one-sample test on the differences d_i = y_i - x_i.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
The unit of replication
The unit of replication is the level at which the treatment was applied independently: the experiment, the animal, the well if wells were treated separately. Not the cell.

1000 cells from one dish are 1000 measurements of one replicate: they share the dish, the day, the stain.
Treating cells as n (pseudoreplication) makes the SE far too small, and p-values tiny even when there is no effect.
In the demo below (3 experiments per condition, 100 cells each, day-to-day SD 1, cell-to-cell SD 2, no effect), the cells-as-n test gives p < 0.05 in 69 % of repeated experiments, instead of 5 %.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
The math: the two-level model
y_{ec} = \mu + \tau\,T_e + u_e + \varepsilon_{ec} for cell c of experiment e, with u_e \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2) (day) and \varepsilon_{ec} \sim N(0, \sigma^2) (cell), all independent.
Mean of the m cells of experiment e: \text{Var}(\bar y_e) = \sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2/m. Mean of all E\,m cells of a condition:
\text{Var}(\bar y) = \frac{\sigma_u^2}{E} + \frac{\sigma^2}{E\,m}, \quad\text{while cells-as-}n \text{ assumes } \frac{\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2}{E\,m}.
Ratio = 1 + (m - 1)\rho, the design effect, with the intra-class correlation \rho = \sigma_u^2/(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2). Effective number of cells: n_{\text{eff}} = E\,m/(1 + (m-1)\rho) \to E/\rho as m \to \infty. More cells cannot beat the number of experiments.

title: From measurements to claims
section: The math: how often cells-as-n is fooled
text:
The math: how often cells-as-n is fooled
Under no effect, the cells-as-n statistic z = (\bar y_1 - \bar y_0)/\sqrt{2(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2)/(Em)} is normal with mean 0 but variance 1 + (m-1)\rho, not 1. It rejects when |z| > 1.96:
P(\text{false positive}) = 2\,\Phi\!\left(-\frac{1.96}{\sqrt{1 + (m - 1)\rho}}\right).
\rho = 0.1: m = 10: 0.16; m = 100: \sqrt{10.9} = 3.30, 2\Phi(-0.59) = 0.55; m = 1000: 0.85. (Large-E approximation; with few experiments the t-test version behaves alike, as the demo shows.)

title: From measurements to claims
text:
Do it right

Aggregate per replicate: one number per experiment (mean or median of its cells), and test those E numbers. Correct false-positive rate, and the effect is unchanged.
Pair the design: control and treated in every experiment, compare within each. The day-to-day variation cancels; often far more power.
Mixed-effects models do the same with all cells kept (a pointer: they model u_e explicitly).
Show it as a SuperPlot: cells as small dots coloured by experiment, experiment means as big markers, the statistics on the big markers.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
Try it: cells, experiments, pairs




Tour: “1000 cells, no effect” (3 experiments per condition, independent): cells as n: effect 0.65, p = 2.6e-31; experiments as n: same estimate, CI −2.27 to 3.57, p = 0.49. Over 1000 repetitions (exercise page): cells-as-n rejects in 89 %, experiments-as-n in 4 %. “More cells does not help” (true effect 1): power of the correct analysis 12.5 % with 1000 cells. “More experiments does”: 10 experiments of 20 cells: 46 %. “Paired design wins”: paired p = 0.023, unpaired means p = 0.43; power 84 % vs 14 %. “Confounded with the day”: no treatment effect, but all treated experiments in a later batch shifted by 1.5: estimate 2.53, even the experiment-level test gives p = 0.029.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
More cells or more experiments?
The SE of the effect, with experiments as the unit, against the number of cells per experiment (3 experiments per condition, day-to-day SD 1, cell-to-cell SD 2):



cells per experiment

Beyond a few dozen cells the true SE flattens out at \sigma_u\sqrt{2/E}: the day-to-day variation dominates.
More experiments shrink it like 1/\sqrt E. A paired design removes \sigma_u altogether.
Cells-as-n claims an SE that keeps shrinking: ever smaller p-values for the same evidence.

title: From measurements to claims
section: The math: pairing removes the day
text:
The math: pairing removes the day
Paired design: both conditions in each experiment e. Difference of the experiment means:
D_e = \bar y_{e,T} - \bar y_{e,C} = \tau + (u_e - u_e) + (\bar\varepsilon_{e,T} - \bar\varepsilon_{e,C}), \qquad \text{Var}(D_e) = \frac{2\sigma^2}{m}.
The day effect u_e cancels. Unpaired comparison of experiment means: \text{Var} = 2(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2/m) per pair of experiments. Pairing wins whenever \sigma_u^2 > 0; it loses a little only through the degrees of freedom (E - 1 instead of 2E - 2) when \sigma_u is close to 0, or if the pairing is not real (control and treated not sharing the day).

title: From measurements to claims
section: Effect size and confidence interval first
text:
Effect size and confidence interval first
“Treated cells were significantly larger (p < 0.0001, n = 2400)” says nothing useful:

How much larger? “12 % larger (95 % CI 4 to 20 %)” says what matters.
What is n? “n = 4 independent experiments, 600 cells each” names the unit of replication.
p < 0.0001 with 2400 cells as n is pseudoreplication; with enough cells any tiny difference becomes “significant”.

For comparing features with different units, a standardised effect: the difference divided by the SD (of experiment means, or of cells, say which).

title: From measurements to claims
text:
Many features: multiple comparisons
Image-based profiling measures hundreds of features. Test 300 features with no real effect at \alpha = 0.05: about 15 “hits” by chance.


Under no effect, p-values are uniform: a flat histogram (left: 15 below 0.05, all false). Real effects add a spike near 0 (right: 30 real features).
Bonferroni: test each at \alpha/m. Controls the chance of any false hit. Strict: left 0 hits; right 13 hits, all real.
Benjamini–Hochberg (BH): controls the fraction of false hits among the hits (the false discovery rate). Right: 24 hits, 2 of them false.
Picking the best-looking feature after the fact is the same mistake as tuning on the test set.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
The math: Bonferroni and Benjamini–Hochberg
m tests, all null, independent, level \alpha: P(\text{at least one false hit}) = 1 - (1 - \alpha)^m: 0.64 for m = 20, 0.99996 for m = 200.
Bonferroni. Reject when p_i \le \alpha/m. By the union bound, without any independence assumption: P\Big(\bigcup_{i \text{ null}} \{p_i \le \alpha/m\}\Big) \le \sum_{i \text{ null}} \frac{\alpha}{m} \le \alpha.
Benjamini–Hochberg at level q: sort p_{(1)} \le \dots \le p_{(m)}; find the largest k with p_{(k)} \le k\,q/m; reject the k smallest. Then E[\text{false hits}/\max(\text{hits}, 1)] \le q (for independent or positively dependent tests; stated without proof). Example: 0.001, 0.004, 0.012, 0.02, 0.03, 0.2, … with m = 10: lines 0.005, 0.010, 0.015, 0.020, 0.025: k = 4.

title: From measurements to claims
section: Try it: many features on a plate
text:
Try it: many features on a plate




A 384-well plate, 300 features. Tour: “300 null features”: 15 uncorrected hits, Bonferroni and BH 0. “10 % real”: uncorrected 43 (14 false), Bonferroni 13 (all real), BH 24 (2 false). “gradient + treated on the left”: a left-to-right gradient, treated wells on the left half: 281 of 300 features “significant” at 0.05, 249 even after Bonferroni, none of them real. The plate map of the smallest-p feature shows the gradient. “Randomised layout”: the same gradient, random layout: no hits after correction (37 uncorrected).

title: From measurements to claims
text:
Batch and plate effects
Day, plate, row and column, the edge wells (evaporation), the order of imaging (focus drift, bleaching): all change the measurements.

If all controls are on day 1 and all treated on day 2, the treatment effect is confounded with the day: no statistics can separate them. More cells, more wells, any test: it stays an experiment about days.
The cures are in the design: every batch contains every condition; randomise the plate layout; controls on every plate; image in a randomised or balanced order.
Then normalise against the controls of each plate (the measurements day shows how) and analyse per plate or per experiment.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
A reporting checklist

n at every level (experiments, wells, images, cells), and which one is the unit of replication.
How values were aggregated (mean or median per well, per experiment).
Effect size with a confidence interval, not only a p-value.
Correction for multiple testing, and how many features were tested.
The design: pairing, randomisation, plate layout, batches.
How the image analysis was validated: the split (the leakage unit), who annotated (the agreement unit).
Images and analysis parameters available.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
Summary

Standard error = the wobble of an estimate; p-value = how often chance alone gives a result this extreme; 95 % CI ≈ estimate ± 2 SE.
The unit of replication is the independently treated unit (experiment, animal, well), not the cell. Cells as n gives false positives far above 5 %.
Aggregate per replicate, or pair the design; show a SuperPlot. More experiments help, more cells hardly.
Report effect sizes with CIs.
Many features: about \alpha m false hits; correct with Bonferroni (any false hit) or Benjamini–Hochberg (false discovery rate).
Batch and plate effects confounded with the treatment cannot be fixed afterwards: randomise and balance the design.

title: Exercise: resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

say when two points are resolved (Rayleigh, Sparrow) and why noise changes the answer,
compute the pixel size in the sample plane and check it against Nyquist, \lambda/4\mathrm{NA},

describe how a PSF is measured from beads, and correct for the bead size,
(math) derive the Sparrow distance of a Gaussian, the axial Nyquist step, and the bead-size correction.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the three demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations.

title: Exercise: resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Rayleigh distance
0.61\lambda/\mathrm{NA}; two equal points show a dip of about 26 %


Sparrow distance
0.47\lambda/\mathrm{NA} (Airy), 2\sigma (Gaussian); the dip just vanishes


Pixel in the sample plane
camera pixel ÷ total magnification


Lateral Nyquist
\Delta x \le \lambda/4\mathrm{NA}


Axial Nyquist
\Delta z \le \lambda/\big(2n(1 - \cos\alpha)\big), \sin\alpha = \mathrm{NA}/n; about n\lambda/\mathrm{NA}^2 for small NA


Axial extent of the PSF
about 2n\lambda/\mathrm{NA}^2 (small NA); 2.5–6 times the lateral


Bead-size correction
\text{FWHM}_\text{meas}^2 \approx \text{FWHM}_\text{PSF}^2 + (0.53D)^2, bead diameter D


Averaging N beads
noise ÷ \sqrt N



Unless stated otherwise, λ = 520 nm, immersion oil n = 1.518, and a camera with 6.5 µm pixels.

title: Exercise: resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF
text:
By hand
B1. For each objective, compute the pixel size in the sample plane, compare it with Nyquist, and give the number of pixels across the Rayleigh distance. (a) 100× / 1.4 oil; (b) 63× / 1.4 oil; (c) 40× / 0.95 dry; (d) 20× / 0.75 dry.
B2. A widefield microscope in a teaching lab has a camera with 2048 × 2048 pixels of 6.5 µm and four objectives: 10× / 0.45, 20× / 0.8, 40× / 1.3 oil and 60× / 1.4 oil. Make a table: pixel in the sample, Nyquist pixel, Nyquist met?, width of the field of view. Which objective would you choose to count cells in a large tissue section, and which to measure the width of microtubules?
B3. Two points are 300 nm apart. (a) Express the distance in units of \lambda/\mathrm{NA} for NA 1.4 and for NA 0.95 (dry). (b) Are they resolved by Rayleigh’s criterion in each case? (The dips are 71 % and 11 %.)
B4. Two molecules at the Rayleigh distance, imaged with 65 nm pixels. About 9 % of each molecule’s photons land in its peak pixel. (a) With 20 photons per molecule, how many photons are in the peak pixel and how large is the Poisson noise there? (b) Suppose the dip (26 % of the peak) must be at least 3 times the noise of a pixel, 0.26N_p \ge 3\sqrt{N_p}, to be seen reliably. How many photons N_p does the peak pixel need, and how many photons per molecule is that?
B5. A widefield z-stack is taken with an NA 1.4 oil objective and steps of 1 µm. (a) What is the axial Nyquist step? (b) What happens to a 100 nm bead halfway between two planes?
B6. Use the rule of thumb 2n\lambda/\mathrm{NA}^2 for the axial extent and 0.61\lambda/\mathrm{NA} for the lateral, for NA 0.8 (air, n = 1) and NA 1.4 (oil). What is the ratio axial/lateral in each case? Which objective gives the more “isotropic” voxels?
B7. The true PSF has an FWHM of 191 nm. (a) What FWHM do you measure with 100 nm beads, and with 200 nm beads? (b) A colleague measured 230 nm with 200 nm beads. Estimate the true FWHM.
B8. One bead’s profile has a noise of 10 % of its peak. How many beads must you average to bring it to 2 %? What else must be done before averaging, and why?






Solutions

Counting cells in a large section: the 10× or 20×; nuclei are many micrometres wide, so undersampling the optics does not matter, and the field is large. Microtubule widths (25 nm, far below the resolution) can only be measured as the PSF width; at least the 60× is needed, ideally with an extra magnifier to reach Nyquist, and even then the measured width is about the PSF’s FWHM, not the microtubule’s.
B3. (a) NA 1.4: \lambda/\mathrm{NA} = 371 nm, so d = 0.81\lambda/\mathrm{NA}. NA 0.95: \lambda/\mathrm{NA} = 547 nm, d = 0.55\lambda/\mathrm{NA}. (b) NA 1.4: yes, well above 0.61 (dip 71 %). NA 0.95: below the Rayleigh distance (334 nm) but above Sparrow (0.47 \cdot 547 = 257 nm): a small dip (11 %), not resolved by Rayleigh’s criterion.
B4. (a) 0.09 \cdot 20 \approx 1.8 photons, noise \pm\sqrt{1.8} = \pm 1.3 photons, about 75 %. The 26 % dip drowns. (b) 0.26\sqrt{N_p} \ge 3 gives N_p \ge (3/0.26)^2 = 133 photons in the peak pixel, i.e. about 133/0.09 \approx 1500 photons per molecule.
B5. (a) \sin\alpha = 1.4/1.518 = 0.922, \cos\alpha = 0.387; \Delta z \le 520/(2 \cdot 1.518 \cdot 0.613) = 279 nm. The 1 µm step is 3.6 times too large. (b) It is 0.5 µm from both planes. The axial FWHM is about 0.5 µm (half-width 0.26 µm), so at 0.5 µm the bead’s peak brightness has dropped to a few per cent (about 4 %): it appears in the stack only as a faint, spread-out blob, or not at all.
B6. NA 0.8: axial 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 520/0.64 = 1625 nm, lateral 397 nm, ratio 4.1. NA 1.4: axial 2 \cdot 1.518 \cdot 520/1.96 = 805 nm, lateral 227 nm, ratio 3.5. The high-NA objective gives the more isotropic voxels: the axial extent falls with \mathrm{NA}^2, the lateral only with NA. (The exact calculation in the demo gives FWHM ratios of 3.5 and 2.7: the rule overestimates the axial extent at high NA.)
B7. (a) \sqrt{191^2 + 53^2} = 198 nm (+4 %); \sqrt{191^2 + 105^2} = 218 nm (+14 %). (b) \sqrt{230^2 - (0.53 \cdot 200)^2} = \sqrt{230^2 - 105^2} \approx 204 nm.
B8. Noise falls as 1/\sqrt N: 10\,\%/\sqrt N = 2\,\% gives N = 25 beads. Before averaging, subtract each bead’s background (otherwise the average sits on a pedestal and looks too wide), and centre each bead with sub-pixel accuracy (otherwise the average is blurred by the random offsets of the beads relative to the pixel grid).




Math questions
B9. (math) Two equal Gaussian spots, h(x) = e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}, at \pm d/2. Show that the midpoint of h(x - d/2) + h(x + d/2) is a maximum for d < 2\sigma and a minimum for d > 2\sigma. With \sigma = 0.21\lambda/\mathrm{NA}, compare with the Sparrow distance of the Airy pattern, 0.47\lambda/\mathrm{NA}.
B10. (math) The widefield OTF extends along the axis to k_z = \frac{n}{\lambda}(1 - \cos\alpha). (a) Derive the axial Nyquist step. (b) Evaluate it for a water objective, NA 1.2, n = 1.33, at 520 nm. (c) Show that for small NA it is about n\lambda/\mathrm{NA}^2.
B11. (math) (a) Show that the variances of two normalised, centred profiles add under convolution: \mathrm{Var}(f \ast g) = \mathrm{Var}(f) + \mathrm{Var}(g). (b) A uniform sphere of radius R is viewed along z. Show that its brightness profile along x (integrated over y and z) is proportional to R^2 - x^2, with variance R^2/5. (c) Derive the bead-size correction (0.53D)^2 from (a) and (b), treating the profiles as Gaussians for the FWHM.






Solutions (math)





B9. I(x) = h(x - d/2) + h(x + d/2) is symmetric, so I'(0) = 0, and I''(0) = h''(-d/2) + h''(d/2) = 2h''(d/2). For the Gaussian h''(x) = \big(x^2/\sigma^4 - 1/\sigma^2\big)h(x), negative for |x| < \sigma and positive for |x| > \sigma. So I''(0) < 0 (a maximum, one peak) for d < 2\sigma and > 0 (a minimum, a dip) for d > 2\sigma. With \sigma = 0.21\lambda/\mathrm{NA}: 2\sigma = 0.42\lambda/\mathrm{NA}, a little below the Airy value 0.47: the Gaussian’s tails differ from the Airy rings, so the criterion moves slightly.
B10. (a) The image is band-limited along z to |k_z| \le k_{z,\max}; two samples per period of the finest component: \Delta z \le 1/(2k_{z,\max}) = \lambda/\big(2n(1 - \cos\alpha)\big). (b) \sin\alpha = 1.2/1.33 = 0.902, \cos\alpha = 0.431: \Delta z \le 520/(2 \cdot 1.33 \cdot 0.569) = 344 nm. (c) \cos\alpha = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2\alpha} \approx 1 - \tfrac12\sin^2\alpha = 1 - \mathrm{NA}^2/(2n^2), so 2n(1 - \cos\alpha) \approx \mathrm{NA}^2/n and \Delta z \le n\lambda/\mathrm{NA}^2.
B11. (a) For profiles with \int f = \int g = 1 and zero mean, f \ast g is the density of the sum of two independent random variables with densities f and g; variances of independent variables add. (Directly: \int x^2 (f \ast g)(x)\,dx = \iint (y + t)^2 f(y)g(t)\,dy\,dt = \mathrm{Var}f + 2\cdot 0 \cdot 0 + \mathrm{Var}g.) (b) At position x the sphere’s cross-section is a disc of radius \sqrt{R^2 - x^2}, area \pi(R^2 - x^2). Normalised: p(x) = \tfrac{3}{4R^3}(R^2 - x^2) on [-R, R]. \int x^2 p = \tfrac{3}{4R^3}\big(\tfrac{2R^5}{3} - \tfrac{2R^5}{5}\big) = \tfrac{3}{4R^3}\cdot\tfrac{4R^5}{15} = R^2/5. (c) Measured variance = PSF variance + R^2/5. For Gaussians FWHM = 2.355\,\sigma, so \text{FWHM}_\text{meas}^2 = \text{FWHM}_\text{PSF}^2 + 2.355^2 R^2/5 = \text{FWHM}_\text{PSF}^2 + (1.053R)^2 = \text{FWHM}_\text{PSF}^2 + (0.53D)^2.

title: Exercise: resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF
text:
Explore: two points on pixels
Two points (or a sinusoidal grating) imaged by an ideal lens and recorded on a pixel grid. The image shows the pixels of a 2 × 1 µm field; the plot shows the profile through both points: blue the optical image (no pixels, no noise), red the recorded pixels. The readout gives the dip in the optical image and in the pixels, and the Nyquist pixel. Tick photon noise for seeded Poisson noise.



P1. Preset Rayleigh. What is the dip in the optical image and in the pixels? Lower the distance until the dip disappears and compare with the Sparrow distance.
P2. Preset Rayleigh, 20 photons. How many photons are in the peak pixel? Is the dip in the pixels meaningful? Raise the photons to 2000: what is the dip in the pixels now? Compare with B4.
P3. Back to Rayleigh (no noise). Increase the pixel size: 93 nm (Nyquist), 150 nm, 200 nm. What happens to the dip in the pixels?
P4. Preset undersampled: aliasing (grating of period 300 nm, 200 nm pixels). What period do the pixels show? Lower the pixel size to 150 nm and then 100 nm. When does the true period come back?
P5. Preset oversampled: noisier pixels (300 nm apart, 500 photons, 20 nm pixels). How many photons are in the peak pixel, and how noisy is it? Change the pixel to 65 nm.
P6. At d = 227 nm (Rayleigh for 520 nm), change the wavelength to 450 nm and 650 nm. What happens to the dip, and why?






Solutions





P1. Dip 26.8 % in the optical image and 25.6 % in the 40 nm pixels (each pixel averages over 40 nm, which fills the dip a little). The dip disappears at about 176 nm, the Sparrow distance 0.47 \cdot 520/1.4 = 175 nm in the readout.
P2. About 2 photons in the peak pixel (the readout’s “peak pixel ≈ 2.0 photons”); with noise \pm\sqrt2 the pixel profile is mostly noise, and the “dip in the pixels” (100 % in this seed: the middle pixel happened to receive 0 photons) means nothing. With 2000 photons the peak pixel holds about 167 photons (noise ±8 %) and the dip in the pixels is 23 %, close to the noise-free 22.7 % on 65 nm pixels: clearly resolved, as B4 predicts for more than about 1500 photons.
P3. Pixel dip 20.1 % at 93 nm, 4.0 % at 150 nm, and at 200 nm no dip at all: the middle pixel now collects light from both points and is the brightest. The optical image still has its 26.8 % dip; the coarse pixels destroy it.
P4. With 200 nm pixels the pixel values repeat every 3 pixels: an apparent period of 600 nm (the readout: “looks like period 600 nm”). At 150 nm the pixels are exactly half the period and the 300 nm period is recorded (2 pixels per period); at 100 nm it is clearly recorded. The grating passes the optics with 26.6 % contrast; it is the pixels that alias it.
P5. With 20 nm pixels the peak pixel holds about 6.5 photons (noise ±39 %): the profile is ragged. With 65 nm pixels about 50 photons (±14 %), and the dip (67 % noise-free) is clear. The same photons over 10 times fewer pixels.
P6. At 450 nm the dip grows to 51 %; at 650 nm it nearly vanishes (0.6 %). The Rayleigh distance scales with λ: 196 nm for blue, 283 nm for red, so 227 nm is comfortably resolved in blue and just at Sparrow-like merging in red.
crumbs: Resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF

title: Exercise: resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF
text:
Explore: the axial PSF
The xz slice of the PSF of an ideal lens (optical axis vertical), and the same PSF recorded as a stack with planes every Δz. The plot shows the profiles across (blue) and along (red) the axis; red dots mark the planes.



A1. Preset NA 1.4: lateral and axial FWHM, their ratio, and the axial Nyquist step. Compare with B5 and B6.
A2. Preset NA 0.5 (air). How do the FWHMs and the ratio change? What z-step does Nyquist ask for?
A3. Preset z-step too large (1 µm at NA 1.4). How many planes fall within the axial FWHM? Shift the z-step to 300 nm and then 250 nm.
A4. Preset out-of-focus light (log). Describe the shape. Then preset confocal: what changes in the image and in the FWHMs?






Solutions





A1. Lateral 191 nm, axial 515 nm, ratio 2.7; axial Nyquist 279 nm. The first axial minimum is at about \lambda/n(1 - \cos\alpha) = 558 nm, smaller than the rule of thumb’s 805 nm: at high NA the rule overestimates the axial extent.
A2. At NA 0.5 in air: lateral 535 nm, axial 3.44 µm, ratio 6.4; axial Nyquist 1.94 µm. The axial extent grows like 1/\mathrm{NA}^2, the lateral like 1/\mathrm{NA}: low-NA PSFs are long needles.
A3. With 1 µm steps, at most one plane falls inside the 515 nm FWHM (here the one at the focus; a point between planes would fall between them), and the plot shows the dots jumping from the peak straight to the near-zero tails. The readout says 3.6× too large. At 300 nm the dots trace the curve coarsely (still 1.1× too large); at 250 nm the step is within Nyquist.
A4. An hourglass: two cones of light opening above and below the focus, each plane carrying the same total light, spread wider and wider. In the confocal PSF the cones are gone (the product of two PSFs squares the faint out-of-focus values away), and both FWHMs shrink: 138 nm and 369 nm.

title: Exercise: resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF
section: Explore: measuring a PSF from beads
text:
Explore: measuring a PSF from beads
A simulated bead slide: 30 beads (40 nm unless changed), NA 1.4, 520 nm, 65 nm pixels, seeded photon noise and a uniform background. The demo subtracts the background (median of each bead’s patch border), finds each bead’s centre with sub-pixel accuracy, shifts it to the patch centre and averages the first N beads (orange boxes). Panels: one raw bead, the average, and the true PSF (a point as these pixels record it, FWHM 195 nm; the optical Airy FWHM is 191 nm).



E1. Preset one bead, noisy. What FWHM is measured, and how far from the true one? How many photons are in the bead’s peak pixel?
E2. Move beads averaged from 1 to 30 and note the FWHM. How much does it scatter for N \le 5, and for N \ge 20? Compare with the \sqrt N rule.
E3. Preset forgot the background. What is the measured FWHM, and what does the profile show? Tick subtract the background.
E4. Preset beads too large (200 nm beads, 2000 photons, 30 beads). Compare the measured FWHM with your prediction from B7. Then try 300 and 400 nm.
E5. With 30 beads and background subtraction, set the background to 50 photons per pixel. Does the average still converge? What does that say about how well the background must be known?






Solutions





E1. 204 nm, +4.6 % from the true 195 nm; the peak pixel holds about 54 photons on a background of 10, and the averaged image of one bead is lumpy (the noise is shifted along with it).
E2. For N = 1 to 5 the FWHM jumps between 188 and 206 nm (−3.4 % to +5.8 %); from about 13 beads on it stays between 193 and 195 nm, within 1 % of the true value (30 beads: 194 nm, −0.4 %). Noise of one bead ÷ \sqrt{30} = 0.18: the scatter shrinks roughly five-fold, as observed.
E3. 223 nm (+14.3 %): the profile sits on a pedestal (the background, normalised along with the PSF), so the peak is low and the half-maximum is reached far out. With subtraction: 194 nm again.
E4. 215 nm with 200 nm beads, 10.6 % too wide; B7 predicts 218–222 nm (with a PSF of 191–195 nm). With 300 nm beads 255 nm, with 400 nm beads 316 nm (+62 %): the measurement now mostly reports the bead.
E5. With a background of 50 photons per pixel (more than a bead’s own peak, about 44 photons above the background) the average gives 180 nm, 7.5 % too narrow: the noisy background estimate and the higher noise bias the centring and the subtraction. Without subtraction it would be 473 nm. The background must be known well, and the beads must be bright compared with it.

title: Exercise: resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF
text:
Where this leads
We now know what the microscope does to an object: blur by the PSF, sampling, noise. The last unit of the day asks the natural question: if we know the PSF, can we run the model backwards and get the object back?
crumbs: Resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF

title: Quiz: resolution, sampling and measuring the PSF
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Numbers use green light, λ = 520 nm.

Q1. Two points are 0.61λ/NA apart. What does the profile through them look like? And at 0.47λ/NA?






Hint





Rayleigh and Sparrow.









Answer





At 0.61λ/NA (Rayleigh) the peak of each point lies on the first dark ring of the other: two peaks with a dip of about 26 % between them. At 0.47λ/NA (Sparrow) the dip has just vanished: the profile is flat at the midpoint, a single broad peak.




Q2. Two molecules are exactly at the Rayleigh distance, but each delivers only 20 photons. Are they resolved?






Hint





How many photons land in the brightest pixel, and how large is the Poisson noise there?









Answer





In practice no. With 65 nm pixels about 9 % of a point’s photons land in its peak pixel: about 2 photons, with noise \pm\sqrt2 \approx \pm 1.4, i.e. ±70 %. A 26 % dip is far below that noise. The Rayleigh criterion assumes a noise-free image; with few photons, noise decides what can be resolved.




Q3. A 60× / 1.4 oil objective is used with a camera of 6.5 µm pixels. Is the image Nyquist sampled at 520 nm?






Hint





Pixel in the sample plane = camera pixel ÷ magnification; Nyquist = λ/4NA.









Answer





Pixel in the sample: 6500/60 = 108 nm. Nyquist: 520/(4 \cdot 1.4) = 93 nm. Slightly undersampled (by 1.17×): the finest detail the lens passes, near the cut-off, can alias. A 1.5× extra magnifier (72 nm) would fix it.




Q4. Why not simply use pixels much smaller than Nyquist, to be safe?






Hint





What happens to the number of photons per pixel?









Answer





The optics deliver no detail beyond the cut-off, so smaller pixels add none. But the same photons are spread over more pixels: each pixel is noisier (shot noise relative to the signal grows, and every pixel adds its own read noise). Files grow and acquisitions slow down; for live samples, more light per useful pixel means more bleaching.




Q5. A widefield z-stack is taken with an NA 1.4 objective and 1 µm steps. What goes wrong?






Hint





Axial Nyquist at NA 1.4 is about 280 nm; the PSF is about 0.5 µm long (FWHM).









Answer





The z-step is about 3.6 times too large. A small object halfway between two planes (0.5 µm from each) appears in neither at full brightness: on the axis the PSF has dropped to about 4 % of its peak there. Axial detail is aliased or lost, and deconvolution cannot recover it afterwards.




Q6. What is the “missing cone” of a widefield microscope, and what does it mean for the image?






Hint





Where in 3D frequency space is the widefield OTF zero?









Answer





The 3D OTF of a widefield microscope is zero in a cone around the k_z axis: structures that vary slowly sideways but change along z (a uniform layer, a large flat sheet) are not transmitted in their z-variation. In the image, out-of-focus light from such structures is spread over neighbouring planes, not removed: widefield has no optical sectioning. A confocal pinhole fills the cone.




Q7. You measure a PSF with 200 nm beads and get an FWHM of 230 nm. Is the PSF really that wide?






Hint





\text{FWHM}_\text{meas}^2 \approx \text{FWHM}_\text{PSF}^2 + (0.53D)^2.









Answer





No: the bead itself adds about 0.53 \cdot 200 = 105 nm in quadrature. \sqrt{230^2 - 105^2} \approx 204 nm. Use smaller beads (100 nm or less) so that the correction is small.




Q8. Why average many beads instead of measuring one very carefully?






Hint





What happens to independent noise when you average N copies?









Answer





Each bead’s image is noisy; after background subtraction and sub-pixel centring, averaging N of them keeps the PSF and reduces the noise by \sqrt N (30 beads: to 18 %). A single bead can only be made less noisy with more photons, which bleaches it.




Q9. (math) Show that for a Gaussian PSF with standard deviation σ, two equal points are just at the Sparrow limit when they are 2σ apart.






Hint





The midpoint curvature of h(x - d/2) + h(x + d/2) is 2h''(d/2).









Answer





h(x) = e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2} has h''(x) = (x^2/\sigma^4 - 1/\sigma^2)\,h(x), zero at x = \sigma. The midpoint curvature 2h''(d/2) changes sign at d/2 = \sigma: below d = 2\sigma the midpoint is a maximum (one peak), above it a minimum (a dip).

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
About this lecture
Last unit: colour is three numbers, a linear map of a spectrum. Today: what the three numbers in an RGB file are.

RGB is a device space: “full red” means this display’s red.
Stored values are gamma-encoded: not proportional to light. Blurring, resizing and averaging must be done on linear values.
Changing colour space is a 3 × 3 matrix: RGB → XYZ, → luminance, → Y′CbCr (with chroma subsampling).
White balance: undoing the lamp with a diagonal matrix, and when that fails.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Recall from the bit-depth day (highbit/): an 8-bit photograph stores sRGB codes, not light. Today explains why those codes exist. Everything here is linear algebra on 3-vectors, except the transfer curve, a function of one variable.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
RGB: gamma, linear maps & white balance

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
RGB is a device space
“(255, 0, 0)” means: full drive of this display’s red primary. Without knowing the primaries and the white, it is not a colour.

sRGB fixes everything: the three primaries (the triangle of the last unit), the white point D65, and a transfer curve from stored values to light.
An untagged 8-bit image, a web page and the browser canvas are assumed to be sRGB.
A wide-gamut photo (Display P3) with the same numbers is a different, more saturated colour.
A camera’s raw data and a microscope’s detector are linear and in the camera’s own RGB: each sensor has its own three curves.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
RGB: gamma, linear maps & white balance

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
Gamma encoding




The stored value is not proportional to the light. The display decodes it with a curve close to a power 2.4.

Why: perceived lightness is roughly the cube root of light. Equal steps of stored value are roughly equal visible steps, so 8 bits suffice without banding in the darks.
Stored 128 is only 21.6 % of white’s light. Half of white’s light is stored as 188.
JPEG photos are encoded; raw camera data and microscope images are linear.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
RGB: gamma, linear maps & white balance

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
section: The math: the sRGB transfer function
text:
The math: the sRGB transfer function
Stored value C \in [0, 1] (the 8-bit code divided by 255), linear light C_\text{lin} \in [0, 1]:
C_\text{lin} = \begin{cases} C / 12.92, & C \le 0.04045 \\[2pt] \left(\dfrac{C + 0.055}{1.055}\right)^{2.4}, & C > 0.04045 \end{cases} \qquad C = \begin{cases} 12.92\,C_\text{lin}, & C_\text{lin} \le 0.0031308 \\[2pt] 1.055\,C_\text{lin}^{1/2.4} - 0.055, & \text{else.} \end{cases}

A short straight piece near black (no infinite slope at 0), then a power 2.4 with an offset. Overall it is close to a pure power 2.2.
128/255 = 0.502 \to 0.216; 188/255 = 0.737 \to 0.503; C_\text{lin} = 0.5 \to C = 0.735, code 187.5.
Decode with a 256-entry lookup table; encode by the formula (or a finer table).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
RGB: gamma, linear maps & white balance

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
section: Why it matters: light adds, codes do not
text:
Why it matters: light adds, codes do not
Blur, resampling, averaging and mixing add up light. Done on encoded values they are wrong:

Black + white: the average of 0 and 255 is 128 in codes, but the average light is 0.5, code 188. A fine black/white stripe pattern looks like 188 from a distance, not 128.
Blurred highlights lose their glow; small bright lights shrink and dim.
Red meets green: blurring on codes gives a dark, muddy seam (codes 111, 144, 0 at the border instead of 176, 198, 0).
Downsampling fine bright detail on a dark background darkens the image.

Rule: decode → operate → encode. In quantitative work, never measure intensities on gamma-encoded exports.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
RGB: gamma, linear maps & white balance

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
section: Try it: blur in linear light
text:
Try it: blur in linear light




Same blur twice: on the stored codes (middle) and decode → blur → encode (right); the profile is along the dashed row. Tour: “black + white = 128 or 188?”: the blurred stripes come out 128 (codes) and 188 (light). Squint at the input: which uniform patch matches the stripes? (On a well-behaved screen, the bottom one, 188; a projector may disagree.) Mean luminance: codes lose 32.9 %, linear keeps it. “red meets green”: a dark seam on codes (luminance profile dips to 107, below both the red at 127 and the green at 220). “blurred lights”: codes lose 62.8 % of the light. “downsampling ×4” on thin lines: −69.0 %.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
RGB: gamma, linear maps & white balance

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
Linear maps between colour spaces
In linear RGB a colour is a mix of the display’s three primaries:
\text{colour} = R \cdot \text{(red primary)} + G \cdot \text{(green primary)} + B \cdot \text{(blue primary)}.
So XYZ is a matrix times linear RGB; for sRGB:
\begin{pmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.4124 & 0.3576 & 0.1805 \\ 0.2126 & 0.7152 & 0.0722 \\ 0.0193 & 0.1192 & 0.9505 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} R \\ G \\ B \end{pmatrix}.

Columns: the XYZ of each primary at full drive. Middle row: the luminance weights; green carries 72 % of the brightness, blue only 7 %.
Display A → display B: M_B^{-1}M_A, a change of basis. Colours outside B’s gamut get components < 0 or > 1: they must be clipped (or mapped inwards).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
RGB: gamma, linear maps & white balance

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
section: The math: the matrix from primaries and white point
text:
The math: the matrix from primaries and white point
Primary k with chromaticity (x_k, y_k) has XYZ proportional to \mathbf p_k = (x_k/y_k,\; 1,\; (1 - x_k - y_k)/y_k). Unknown: its brightness s_k. Require that R = G = B = 1 gives the white \mathbf w (with Y_w = 1):
M = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf p_R & \mathbf p_G & \mathbf p_B \end{pmatrix}\operatorname{diag}(s_R, s_G, s_B), \qquad \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf p_R & \mathbf p_G & \mathbf p_B \end{pmatrix}\mathbf s = \mathbf w .

One 3 \times 3 linear system for the three scales; the scales are the middle row of M (the luminance weights), since the middle entry of every \mathbf p_k is 1.
sRGB: primaries (0.64, 0.33), (0.30, 0.60), (0.15, 0.06), white (0.3127, 0.3290) give the matrix on the previous slide.
The display-design demo of the last unit computes exactly this.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
RGB: gamma, linear maps & white balance

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
section: Converting to grey is a choice
text:
Converting to grey is a choice
One colour image, four greys:

Luminance Y = 0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B on linear RGB: the physically right brightness.
Luma Y' = 0.299R' + 0.587G' + 0.114B' on encoded values: the video standard, an approximation.
Channel mean (R + G + B)/3: treats the eye as equally sensitive to blue. Simple, often wrong.
One channel: often the best for analysis. In stained tissue or fluorescence, pick the channel with the contrast you need.

Test: red letters on a green background of equal luminance vanish in the luminance image but not in the mean. “Greyscale” is a projection, and you choose its direction.

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
Opponent channels and Y′CbCr
The visual system recodes the cone signals into one brightness and two colour-difference channels (red–green, blue–yellow), and it sees the colour differences with less detail.
Y′CbCr (JPEG, video) does the same with a matrix on encoded R′G′B′:

Y′: luma; Cb ∝ B′ − Y′, Cr ∝ R′ − Y′, stored around 128.
Chroma subsampling (4:2:0): keep Cb and Cr at half resolution in both directions. Half the data, almost invisible. Subsampling Y′ the same way is obvious.
Same idea as the low-pass filtering in the Fourier unit: drop the detail the eye does not use.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
section: The math: Y′CbCr as an affine map
text:
The math: Y′CbCr as an affine map
\begin{pmatrix} Y' \\ C_b \\ C_r \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.299 & 0.587 & 0.114 \\ -0.1687 & -0.3313 & 0.5 \\ 0.5 & -0.4187 & -0.0813 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} R' \\ G' \\ B' \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 128 \\ 128 \end{pmatrix}

Rows 2 and 3 are (to rounding) 0.564\,(B' - Y') and 0.713\,(R' - Y'): the coefficients of each row sum to zero, so every grey has C_b = C_r = 128.
Invertible: decoding is the inverse matrix after removing the offset. 4:2:0 stores 1 + 2 \cdot \tfrac14 = 1.5 values per pixel instead of 3.
Because it acts on encoded values, Y′ is luma, not luminance.

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
section: Try it: colour as a matrix
text:
Try it: colour as a matrix




Y′CbCr channels of the synthetic objects scene (Cb, Cr with 128 as mid-grey). Tour: “subsample chroma by 4”: hard to see any change; mean ΔE*ab 2.18, at 1.125 bytes per pixel. “subsample luma by 4”: blocky edges at once, although the mean ΔE is smaller (1.87): the eye is far more sensitive to brightness detail than mean ΔE suggests. Then “greyscale” → “the isoluminant test”: luminance gives 117.3 for both letter and background; switch to mean (78.8 vs 45.7). “any matrix” → “P3 → sRGB”: 15.3 % of the pixels fall outside [0, 1].

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
White balance: undoing the lamp
The same white paper is orange under a light bulb and blue in shade; our eyes adapt and still call it white (colour constancy). A camera does not.

Camera responses: \mathbf c = A\,\operatorname{diag}(\text{lamp})\,\mathbf r. We want the colours under a reference light (daylight, D65).
von Kries (1902): scale each channel separately, \mathbf c' = D\,\mathbf c with D = \operatorname{diag}(w_\text{ref}/w), where w is the response to a white under the current lamp. A diagonal matrix.
Apply it to linear values: on encoded values a scaling of light is not a scaling of codes.
Works best in a basis close to the cones (or “sharpened” cone-like channels, as in the Bradford transform).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
Estimating the white
The correction needs w, the camera’s response to white under this lamp:

Grey world: assume the scene averages to grey; w = the mean of each channel. Fails when one colour dominates: a forest turns grey-magenta.
White patch (max-RGB): assume the brightest values are white. Fails with a clipped highlight, which is “white” whatever the lamp.
A grey card (or a known white area) in the image: the most reliable.
In microscopy: the blank-field reference (light with no specimen) is a per-pixel white balance; the same idea as flat-field correction.

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
section: The math: diagonal in which basis?
text:
The math: diagonal in which basis?
Diagonal scaling in a basis given by an invertible B (rows: XYZ → cone-like channels), written in linear RGB:
\mathbf c' = M_{\text{XYZ}\to\text{RGB}}\,B^{-1}\,\operatorname{diag}\!\left(\frac{B M\,\mathbf w_\text{ref}}{B M\,\mathbf w}\right) B\,M\,\mathbf c, \qquad M = M_{\text{RGB}\to\text{XYZ}} .

B = I (on RGB): the camera channels; B = cone matrix: von Kries; B = Bradford’s “sharpened” matrix: narrower channels, usually the most accurate diagonal.
Exact only if the lamp change acts diagonally in that basis, which needs narrow-band channels. Broad, overlapping sensitivities (and metameric failure) leave an error.
With a known chart: fit a full 3 \times 3 matrix by least squares, \min_M \sum_i \|M\mathbf c_i - \mathbf t_i\|^2, i.e. M = TC^\top(CC^\top)^{-1}.

text:
Try it: white balance




A chart of 24 patches with known reflectance spectra (synthetic), rendered under the lamp; truth = the same chart under daylight. ΔE*ab ≈ 2 is just noticeable. Tour: “tungsten 2800 K”: no correction, mean ΔE 44.1. Grey card (click the third grey), cones: 7.61; Bradford: 5.31; encoded: 14.99. “grey world in a forest”: 22.6 (magenta cast); white patch there: 6.08. “white patch fooled by a highlight”: 24.6. “narrow-band LED”: grey card 10.6, and even the 3×3 fit leaves 4.66.

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
Forward pointer: stains absorb
Brightfield microscopy is different: stains absorb light. The transmitted light is I = I_0 \cdot 10^{-(\text{absorbance})}, a product, not a sum.

Take the optical density -\log_{10}(I/I_0) per channel: then two stains add up linearly again.
Separating hematoxylin and eosin is then a 3 \times 3 (or 3 \times 2) linear problem: the spectral unmixing elective (stain unmixing).

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
Summary

RGB numbers are device values; sRGB fixes the primaries, the white and the transfer curve.
Stored values are gamma-encoded: decode before blurring, resizing, averaging or measuring (128 + black/white: the light says 188).
Colour spaces are related by 3 × 3 matrices: RGB → XYZ (columns = primaries), luminance (its middle row), Y′CbCr (plus an offset; chroma can be subsampled).
White balance is a diagonal matrix on linear values, best in a cone-like basis; estimate the white by grey world, white patch or a grey card, and know how each fails.

title: Exercise: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

run Richardson–Lucy by hand for two steps and check that it keeps the total and stays non-negative,
explain semi-convergence and choose when to stop, depending on the number of photons,
say what 3D deconvolution does for widefield and confocal stacks, and why it cannot fill the missing cone,
predict the effect of a wrong PSF, and why blind deconvolution needs constraints,
derive RL from the Poisson likelihood (math).

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

explain semi-convergence and choose when to stop, depending on the number of photons,

predict the effect of a wrong PSF, and why blind deconvolution needs constraints,
