title: Quiz: from a peak to a mosaic
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. The shift of tile B relative to tile A is where B sits on A; tiles are N \times N.

Q1. Two 100 \times 100 tiles give an unpadded phase-correlation peak at (80, 10). Which four shifts can it mean? Which overlaps do they have?






Hint





Subtract the tile size in x, in y, or in both.









Answer





(80, 10), (-20, 10), (80, -90) and (-20, -90). Overlaps: 20 \cdot 90 = 1800 px (18 %), 80 \cdot 90 = 7200 (72 %), 20 \cdot 10 = 200 (2 %), 80 \cdot 10 = 800 (8 %). NCC on each overlap decides; the 2 % candidate is too small to judge.




Q2. Why do stitching programs often test the four candidates instead of zero-padding the tiles?






Hint





Compare the cost of the two ways.









Answer





Padding makes every FFT about four times larger (in 2D) and the overlap becomes a smaller part of the padded image. Testing four candidates by NCC costs one small computation per candidate on the overlap pixels only, and also gives a confidence for the pair.




Q3. The correlation samples around a peak are (0.5, 0.9, 0.7). Estimate the sub-pixel position with a parabola.






Hint





\delta = \dfrac{c_{-1} - c_{+1}}{2(c_{-1} - 2c_0 + c_{+1})}.









Answer





\delta = \dfrac{0.5 - 0.7}{2(0.5 - 1.8 + 0.7)} = \dfrac{-0.2}{-1.2} = \tfrac16 \approx 0.17 px to the right of the middle sample, towards the larger neighbour.




Q4. What is “pixel locking”, and which method avoids it?






Hint





Plot the error of the parabola against the true fraction of a pixel.









Answer





The parabola (and the centroid) estimates are pulled towards whole pixels: their error is zero at fractions 0 and 0.5 and largest in between, an S-shaped curve, because the true peak is not a parabola. A histogram of many estimates then piles up near whole pixels. The upsampled DFT evaluates the exact interpolated correlation on a fine grid and has no such bias (only the grid spacing).




Q5. Three tiles in a row: measured shifts d_{12} = 100, d_{23} = 102, d_{13} = 199. Chaining gives x_3 = 202 from the first two, but the direct measurement says 199. What does least squares (equal weights, x_1 = 0) give?






Hint





Minimise (x_2 - 100)^2 + (x_3 - x_2 - 102)^2 + (x_3 - 199)^2.









Answer





Setting the derivatives to zero: 2x_2 - x_3 = -2 and -x_2 + 2x_3 = 301, so x_2 = 99, x_3 = 200. Each measurement is off by 1: residuals -1, -1, +1. The discrepancy of 3 around the loop is shared by all three pairs.




Q6. One pair of a mosaic was registered wrongly by 100 px. What happens with chaining along a path through that pair, and with global least squares?






Hint





Who depends on that pair in each case?









Answer





Chaining: every tile after the bad pair moves by 100 px. Global least squares: the other paths around the loop disagree with the bad pair, so the solution follows the majority; the bad pair is left with a large residual (here about 100 px), which flags it. If its confidence is low, it gets little weight in the first place. Then drop it and solve again.




Q7. A time-lapse drifts slowly while the cells inside change their shape. Register every frame to the first frame or to the previous frame?






Hint





What makes each choice fail?









Answer





To the first frame, errors do not accumulate, but late frames may no longer resemble the first one when the sample changes. To the previous frame, consecutive frames resemble each other, but the errors of all steps add up (a random walk). With a changing sample, register to the previous frame or to key frames, and keep the step errors small (sub-pixel estimation, low noise).




Q8. (math) Why is the matrix of the normal equations of global alignment singular, and how is that fixed?






Hint





What happens to the energy if every tile is moved by the same amount?









Answer





The energy depends only on differences x_j - x_i; adding the same constant to every position does not change it. So the graph Laplacian L has L\mathbf 1 = 0: the constant vector is in its null space. Fixing one tile (x_1 = 0, i.e. deleting its row and column) removes this freedom; for a connected graph the reduced matrix is invertible.

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
text:
About this lecture
Fibres, wood grain, fingerprints, muscle, collagen: what is the dominant orientation in a small window, and how sure are we? And where are the corners?

Averaging gradients fails; averaging \nabla L\,\nabla L^\top works.
The structure tensor J: a 2 × 2 matrix per pixel, with two scales σ and ρ.
J is the covariance matrix of the gradients in the window (recall PCA).
Its eigenvalues give orientation, coherence, and edge / corner / flat.
Corners (Harris) as interest points.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.
crumbs: The structure tensor: orientation and corners

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
section: The question: orientation in a window
text:
The question: orientation in a window

At one pixel the gradient points across the local edge. But in a textured region, we want one orientation for a whole window, and a measure of how well defined it is.
Uses: fibre orientation maps (collagen, muscle, cytoskeleton), fingerprint ridge flow, wood grain, flow-like textures; also “is there an edge, a corner, or nothing here?”
First idea: average the gradient vectors in the window.
crumbs: The structure tensor: orientation and corners

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
section: First try: average the gradients. It fails.
text:
First try: average the gradients. It fails.


On a bright line the gradients on the two sides point in opposite directions (towards the line from both sides) and cancel: the average is ≈ 0, although the orientation is perfectly clear.
Same on stripes: every bright stripe has two sides.
Fix: average something that does not care about the sign. The outer product \nabla L\,\nabla L^\top is the same for \mathbf g and -\mathbf g: a direction counted as an axis, not an arrow.
crumbs: The structure tensor: orientation and corners

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
text:
The structure tensor
J = G_\rho * \begin{pmatrix} L_x^2 & L_xL_y \\ L_xL_y & L_y^2 \end{pmatrix}

Two scales: the gradient is taken at scale σ (against noise, as in Canny); the products are averaged with a Gaussian window of width ρ (how large a region we summarise).
Every entry is an average of products of gradients: symmetric, 2 × 2, at every pixel.
It is the covariance matrix of the gradient vectors in the window (without subtracting the mean, which is the point): plot the window’s gradients as a point cloud, and J is its ellipse. The same picture as in the PCA unit.
crumbs: The structure tensor: orientation and corners

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
section: Reading J: three kinds of clouds
text:
Reading J: three kinds of clouds


Edge (or oriented texture): gradients all along one axis: a long thin cloud, one large eigenvalue \mu_1, \mu_2 \approx 0.
Corner: gradients in two directions in the same window: a round, large cloud, two large eigenvalues.
Flat: tiny cloud, both eigenvalues ≈ 0.
crumbs: The structure tensor: orientation and corners

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
text:
Orientation and coherence
With eigenvalues \mu_1 \ge \mu_2 \ge 0:

The eigenvector of \mu_1 is the dominant gradient direction, across the stripes. The structure’s orientation is perpendicular to it.
Coherence \Big(\dfrac{\mu_1 - \mu_2}{\mu_1 + \mu_2}\Big)^2: 1 = perfectly oriented, 0 = no preferred direction (isotropic texture, or a corner).
Energy \mu_1 + \mu_2: how much is going on at all.
Display: hue = orientation, saturation = coherence, brightness = energy.

Example: J = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{pmatrix}: \mu = 3.5 \pm 2.5, i.e. 6 and 1; coherence (5/7)^2 = 0.51.
crumbs: The structure tensor: orientation and corners

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
section: The math: why the outer product works
text:
The math: why the outer product works
The squared slope in a direction \mathbf u (unit vector) is
(
abla L\cdot\mathbf u)^2 = \mathbf u^	op
abla L\,
abla L^	op\mathbf u, \qquad	ext{averaged over the window: } E(\mathbf u) = \mathbf u^	op J\,\mathbf u.

E(\mathbf u) is the energy of change in direction \mathbf u. Maximise over unit \mathbf u: J\mathbf u = \mu\mathbf u (Rayleigh quotient, the same algebra as PCA’s largest variance direction). The maximum \mu_1 is along the first eigenvector, the minimum \mu_2 along the second.
(
abla L\cdot\mathbf u)^2 is the same for 
abla L and -
abla L: opposite gradients add instead of cancelling.
Without the window (ρ = 0), J = 
abla L\,
abla L^	op has rank 1: \mu_2 = 0 at every pixel. Every pixel is an “edge”; only the window can see two directions at once.
crumbs: The structure tensor: orientation and corners

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
text:
The math: the doubled angle
Write the gradient as \nabla L = r(\cos\phi, \sin\phi). Then
J_{xx} - J_{yy} = \langle r^2(\cos^2\phi - \sin^2\phi)\rangle = \langle r^2\cos2\phi\rangle, \qquad 2J_{xy} = \langle r^2\,2\sin\phi\cos\phi\rangle = \langle r^2\sin2\phi\rangle.

So J averages the vectors r^2(\cos2\phi, \sin2\phi): the doubled angle. Opposite gradients (\phi and \phi + 180°) have the same doubled angle and add up.
The dominant gradient direction: \theta = \tfrac12\operatorname{atan2}(2J_{xy},\, J_{xx} - J_{yy}) (image coordinates, y down); the orientation of the structure is \theta + 90°.
Coherence: \dfrac{\mu_1 - \mu_2}{\mu_1 + \mu_2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{(J_{xx} - J_{yy})^2 + 4J_{xy}^2}}{J_{xx} + J_{yy}}, the length of the averaged doubled-angle vector relative to the average r^2.
crumbs: The structure tensor: orientation and corners

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
text:
Try it: the structure tensor




Left: the image with one ellipse of J per 16-pixel cell (tabs: orientation map, Harris corners). Middle: the window around the clicked pixel with its gradient arrows (yellow) and their mean (red), and the gradient cloud with the ellipse of J. Tour, square image, σ = 1, ρ = 3: “edge” (32, 64): J = [740 0; 0 0], μ2 = 0, coherence 1. “Corner” (32, 32): μ1 = 447, μ2 = 285, coherence 0.05, the cloud is a fan in two directions. “Flat”: nothing. “Averaging gradients cancels”: stripes at 30°, naive mode: the map is black; the mean gradient at (64, 64) is 0.48 against √μ1 = 32.1. “ρ = 0”: the corner pixel has μ2 = 0 and the Harris response is never positive: no corners. “Rotating stripes”: the hue follows the turning stripes; orientation 106°, 120°, 0°, 60°, 74° across the image at x = 16, 32, 64, 96, 112.

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
section: Edge, corner, flat: Harris and Förstner
text:
Edge, corner, flat: Harris and Förstner










\mu_1
\mu_2





flat
small
small



edge / oriented
large
small



corner
large
large
gradients in two directions in one window




Harris corner response: R = \det J - k\,(\operatorname{tr} J)^2 = \mu_1\mu_2 - k(\mu_1 + \mu_2)^2, k \approx 0.04 to 0.06: positive at corners, negative at edges, ≈ 0 in flat regions. No eigenvalues needed.
Förstner / Shi–Tomasi: the smaller eigenvalue \mu_2 itself.
Corners are local maxima of R above a threshold.
Example (k = 0.05): edge J = \mathrm{diag}(10, 0.1): R = 1 - 0.05 \cdot 10.1^2 = -4.1; corner \mathrm{diag}(10, 8): R = 80 - 16.2 = 63.8; flat \mathrm{diag}(0.1, 0.1): R = 0.008.
crumbs: The structure tensor: orientation and corners

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
section: The math: Harris from shifting a window
text:
The math: Harris from shifting a window
How much does a window change when shifted by a small \mathbf h?
E(\mathbf h) = \sum_{\mathbf x} w(\mathbf x)\,\big(I(\mathbf x + \mathbf h) - I(\mathbf x)\big)^2 \approx \sum_{\mathbf x} w(\mathbf x)\,(\nabla I^\top\mathbf h)^2 = \mathbf h^\top J\,\mathbf h \quad(\text{first-order Taylor}).

Flat: E \approx 0 for every shift. Edge: E large across the edge, ≈ 0 along it (\mu_2 \approx 0). Corner: E large for every direction of \mathbf h, i.e. \mu_2 large.
\det J = \mu_1\mu_2 and \operatorname{tr}J = \mu_1 + \mu_2, so Harris’s R is large only if both eigenvalues are, without computing them.
This is why corners are good interest points: a corner’s window cannot be shifted in any direction without changing, so it can be found again, uniquely, in a shifted image.
crumbs: The structure tensor: orientation and corners

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
text:
Interest points

A corner can be found again in a shifted or rotated image: that is what tracking and feature-based registration match.
Modern keypoint detectors and descriptors (SIFT, ORB and others) combine a detector (corners, or DoG blobs from the scale-space unit) with a description of the window around each point, so that points can be matched between images.
Pointer: the motion elective (registration, tracking) builds on this.

Try it: textures and corners




“ρ too small or too large”: two textures (30° and 120°) meeting at x = 64, noise 25, ρ = 1: the orientation map is speckled with noise; raise ρ to 3: clean; to 8: the boundary between the two textures becomes a wide band of low coherence (at x = 62 the coherence is 0.01 for ρ = 8). “Corners of a checkerboard” (ρ = 2): 35 corners: the 21 inner corners of the checkerboard, and corners of the square, the triangle and the checkerboard’s right border. title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
text:
Uses

Orientation maps of fibres: collagen in tissue, actin, muscle; fingerprint analysis.
Coherence-enhancing diffusion and other anisotropic filters: smooth along the orientation, not across it (pointer).
Corners for registration and tracking.
A feature channel for pixel classifiers: the eigenvalues of J (and of the Hessian) at several scales are standard features on the random-forest day.
crumbs: The structure tensor: orientation and corners

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
text:
Summary

Averaging gradients cancels on lines and stripes; averaging \nabla L\,\nabla L^\top does not.
Structure tensor J = G_\rho * (\nabla L\,\nabla L^\top): gradient at scale σ, window ρ; the covariance matrix of the window’s gradients.
Eigenvector of \mu_1: dominant gradient direction (orientation = perpendicular); coherence ((\mu_1 - \mu_2)/(\mu_1 + \mu_2))^2.
Flat: both small; edge: one large; corner: both large. Harris \det J - k(\operatorname{tr}J)^2, or \mu_2.
Corners are interest points: a window that changes under every shift.

title: Exercise: measuring surfaces
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute the area and volume of a small triangle mesh, and compare them with voxel counts and voxel faces,
explain why voxel faces overestimate area at every resolution, and why marching cubes converges,
use the Euler characteristic and boundary edges to check a mesh’s topology,
reason about the choice of c, smoothing, anisotropic spacing, surfaces of binary masks, and mesh size.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: measuring surfaces
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute the area and volume of a small triangle mesh, and compare them with voxel counts and voxel faces,
explain why voxel faces overestimate area at every resolution, and why marching cubes converges,
use the Euler characteristic and boundary edges to check a mesh’s topology,
reason about the choice of c, smoothing, anisotropic spacing, surfaces of binary masks, and mesh size.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: measuring surfaces
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Triangle area
\tfrac12\lVert(\mathbf b - \mathbf a)\times(\mathbf c - \mathbf a)\rVert


Enclosed volume
\sum \tfrac16\,\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c) over the triangles (closed, outward-oriented mesh)


Voxel estimates
volume = voxels inside × voxel volume; area = exposed voxel faces × face area


Euler characteristic
\chi = V - E + F; one closed surface with g holes: 2 - 2g; components add


Boundary edge
an edge with a triangle on one side only (a crack, or where the surface leaves the volume)


Half-way level
a symmetric blur of a step from a to b passes (a+b)/2 at the true edge

title: Exercise: measuring surfaces
text:
By hand
B1. One bright voxel. A voxel of value 1 has six face neighbours of value 0 (and all other voxels are 0); c = 0.5. (a) Where are the vertices of the marching-cubes surface? What shape is it, with how many triangles? (b) Compute its area. (Each triangle is equilateral; what is its side?) (c) Compute its volume, e.g. as 8 tetrahedra with a corner at the centre. (d) Compare with the voxel count (volume) and the exposed voxel faces (area).
B2. Same voxel. For which c does the octahedron have volume 1, the volume of the voxel? (The vertex on an edge from 1 to 0 lies at distance 1 - c from the centre.) What is its area then?
B3. Pixel edges in 2D. Take all pixels whose centres lie within distance 3 of the centre of one pixel (a digital disk of radius 3). (a) How many pixels are there? Compare with \pi \cdot 3^2. (b) Count the exposed pixel edges (each of length 1) and compare with 2\pi \cdot 3. (c) Show that for this convex shape the pixel-edge perimeter equals the perimeter of its bounding box. What does that give for a large disk of radius r, compared with 2\pi r?
B4. Euler characteristic. Compute \chi and say what it tells you: (a) the octahedron of B1; (b) the surface of a cube made of 12 triangles (8 vertices, 18 edges); (c) the octahedron with one triangle removed (how many boundary edges?); (d) a mesh of two separate spheres; (e) a torus made of a 6 \times 4 grid of quads, each split into two triangles.
B5. Choosing c. (a) A nucleus has grey value 200, the background 20, and the image is blurred symmetrically. Which c puts the surface at the true boundary of a large, flat part of the nucleus? (b) The nucleus is small (radius 2 voxels) and the blur is \sigma = 1.5 voxels. Will the surface at that c be too large or too small? Why? (c) Measuring the volume at c = 0.45, 0.5, 0.55 (normalised values) gives 2163, 2115, 2068 for one object and 1750, 1525, 1318 for another. Which measurement do you trust more, and why?
B6. Spacing. A spherical nucleus of radius 5 µm is imaged with \Delta x = \Delta y = 0.2 µm and \Delta z = 0.5 µm. (a) The vertex positions are computed with \Delta z = 0.2 µm by mistake. What shape do you get, and what are its volume and area? (The surface area of a flattened spheroid with semi-axes 5, 5, 2 is 200.0 µm².) Compare with the true sphere. (b) The positions are correct but the gradient normals ignore \Delta z. What is wrong now, and what is still right?
B7. Mesh size. A surface of area 10^6 voxel² is extracted (about 3 triangles per voxel², 2 triangles per vertex). (a) Estimate the number of triangles and vertices. (b) Each coordinate and each index takes 4 bytes. How much memory does the mesh need with shared vertices, and as a triangle soup (3 separate vertices per triangle)? (c) Vertex clustering with a cell of 3 voxels reduces the triangles about 10-fold on smooth surfaces. Why can it change the topology?
B8. Binary masks. A large flat surface tilted slightly against the voxel grid is extracted from a 0/1 mask at c = 0.5. (a) Where do all the vertices lie on their edges? What does the surface look like? (b) Why does its area stay too large however fine the voxels are? (c) Name two remedies.






Solutions





B1. (a) The 6 edges from the voxel to its face neighbours are crossed at t = 0.5: vertices at distance 0.5 from the centre along \pm x, \pm y, \pm z. They form an octahedron: 8 triangles. (b) Each side joins e.g. (0.5, 0, 0) and (0, 0.5, 0): length \sqrt{0.5} = 0.707. An equilateral triangle of side s has area \tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}s^2 = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\cdot 0.5 = 0.2165; times 8: \sqrt3 = 1.732. (c) Each of the 8 tetrahedra (centre plus one face) has three perpendicular edges of length 0.5: volume \tfrac16 \cdot 0.5^3 = \tfrac1{48}; total \tfrac{8}{48} = \tfrac16 = 0.167. (d) Voxel count: volume 1; voxel faces: area 6. The octahedron is much smaller (a single voxel is all boundary); for large objects the volume estimates agree.
B2. With vertices at distance r = 1 - c: volume 8 \cdot \tfrac16 r^3 = \tfrac43 r^3 = 1, so r = (3/4)^{1/3} = 0.909 and c = 0.091. Area 8 \cdot \tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}(r\sqrt2)^2 = 4\sqrt3\,r^2 = 5.72, still less than the 6 faces.
B3. (a) 29 pixels (rows of 1, 5, 5, 7, 5, 5, 1 pixels, i.e. offsets with x^2 + y^2 \le 9), against \pi \cdot 9 = 28.27. (b) 28 exposed edges, against 2\pi \cdot 3 = 18.85: 1.49 times too long. (c) Walking around a convex pixel shape, the boundary moves right as often as the bounding box is wide, and so on: the horizontal steps add up to twice its width, the vertical ones to twice its height. Here 2(7 + 7) = 28. For a large disk the box is 2r \times 2r: perimeter 8r, against 2\pi r, a factor 4/\pi = 1.27, at any resolution.
B4. (a) 6 - 12 + 8 = 2: one closed surface without holes. (b) 8 - 18 + 12 = 2: the same. (c) 6 - 12 + 7 = 1, with 3 boundary edges: the surface has a hole (a crack). (d) 2 + 2 = 4: two closed surfaces. (e) V = 24, E = 3 \cdot 24 = 72, F = 48: \chi = 0, one hole (a torus).
B5. (a) c = (20 + 200)/2 = 110. (b) Too small. At the boundary of a small ball the blur averages over a neighbourhood that lies mostly outside (the boundary curves away), so the value there is below 110, and the level 110 lies further inside: the partial-volume effect. (c) The first: changing c by ±0.05 changes its volume by about ±2 %, so the result hardly depends on c. The second changes by about ±14 %: its volume is mostly a choice of c (a heavily blurred or small object).
B6. (a) The z coordinates shrink by 0.2/0.5 = 0.4: a flattened spheroid with semi-axes 5, 5, 2 µm. Volume \tfrac43\pi \cdot 5 \cdot 5 \cdot 2 = 209.4 µm³ instead of 523.6 (exactly 0.4 times), area 200.0 µm² instead of 4\pi \cdot 25 = 314.2 (0.64 times). (b) The normals are tilted (their z component is 2.5 times too large before normalising), so the shading is wrong; the vertex positions, area and volume are still right.
B7. (a) About 3 \times 10^6 triangles and 1.5 \times 10^6 vertices. (b) Shared: vertices 1.5 \times 10^6 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 B = 18 MB, triangles 3 \times 10^6 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 B = 36 MB, together 54 MB. Soup: 3 \times 10^6 \cdot 3 \cdot 12 B = 108 MB, twice as much (and the connectivity is lost). (c) It merges all vertices in a cell, regardless of the surface: two sheets of the surface that pass through the same cell (a thin plate, two objects close together) are glued together, and small holes or thin parts collapse. The result can be non-manifold, and \chi can change.
B8. (a) Every crossed edge goes from 1 to 0, so t = 0.5: every vertex at an edge midpoint. The surface is a staircase of terraces following the voxels, with flat steps. (b) As with voxel faces, the steps get smaller with finer voxels but there are more of them; the excess area per unit of true area stays (in the demo about 8 % for a sphere). (c) Blur the mask slightly (σ ≈ 1 voxel) before extraction, or compute a signed distance function from the mask and extract its zero level; or smooth the mesh afterwards (which shrinks it).




Math questions
B9. (math) Derive V = \sum\tfrac16\,\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c) from the divergence theorem with \mathbf F = \mathbf x/3, and show that it does not depend on the choice of origin when the mesh is closed.
B10. (math) Show that replacing a surface patch with normal \mathbf n by voxel faces multiplies its area by |n_x| + |n_y| + |n_z|, and that the average of |n_x| over the unit sphere is \tfrac12. Conclude the factor \tfrac32 for a sphere, and derive 4/\pi in 2D.
B11. (math) (a) For a closed triangle mesh show 2E = 3F and hence F = 2(V - \chi). (b) Show that a torus built from an m \times n grid of quads (each split into 2 triangles, wrapping around in both directions) has \chi = 0.
B12. (math) (a) Show that a step from a to b, blurred by a symmetric kernel, passes (a + b)/2 at the step. (b) Use the coarea formula \frac{dV}{dc} = -\oiint_{\{I = c\}} \frac{dA}{\lVert\nabla I\rVert} to explain why a blurred edge makes the volume more sensitive to c.






Solutions (math)





B9. \nabla\cdot(\mathbf x/3) = 1, so V = \oiint \tfrac13\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf n\,dA. On a flat triangle with unit normal \mathbf n = (\mathbf b - \mathbf a)\times(\mathbf c - \mathbf a)/(2\,\text{area}), every point has \mathbf x\cdot\mathbf n = \mathbf a\cdot\mathbf n. So the triangle contributes \tfrac13\,\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf n\cdot\text{area} = \tfrac16\,\mathbf a\cdot\big((\mathbf b - \mathbf a)\times(\mathbf c - \mathbf a)\big) = \tfrac16\,\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c) (the terms with \mathbf a\times vanish in the triple product). Shifting all points by \mathbf t adds \tfrac13\,\mathbf t\cdot\oiint\mathbf n\,dA = 0, because the vector area of a closed surface is zero.
B10. The voxel faces approximating the patch are its projections onto the three coordinate planes, with areas |n_x|\,dA, |n_y|\,dA, |n_z|\,dA. On the unit sphere with n_x = \cos\theta: \langle|\cos\theta|\rangle = \frac{1}{4\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^\pi |\cos\theta|\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi = \frac{2\pi \cdot 1}{4\pi} = \tfrac12. Sum of three: \tfrac32. In 2D, (|\cos\phi| + |\sin\phi|) averaged over the circle: 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\cos\phi|\,d\phi = 2\cdot\frac{4}{2\pi} = \frac4\pi.
B11. (a) Every triangle has 3 edges and every edge of a closed mesh belongs to exactly 2 triangles: 3F = 2E. Then \chi = V - \tfrac32F + F = V - \tfrac12F, i.e. F = 2(V - \chi). (b) V = mn grid points; each quad contributes 3 new edges (one horizontal, one vertical, one diagonal) when the grid wraps around: E = 3mn; F = 2mn. \chi = mn - 3mn + 2mn = 0.
B12. (a) I(x) = a + (b - a)\int_{-\infty}^{x}g(s)\,ds; with g symmetric, \int_{-\infty}^0 g = \tfrac12, so I(0) = (a + b)/2. (b) Raising c by dc moves each surface point inwards by dc/\lVert\nabla I\rVert, removing a shell of volume \oiint dc/\lVert\nabla I\rVert\,dA. Blur lowers \lVert\nabla I\rVert at the edge (the same step spread over a wider distance), so the same dc moves the surface further: a steeper volume-against-c curve.

title: Exercise: measuring surfaces
section: Explore: voxel faces vs marching cubes
text:
Explore: voxel faces vs marching cubes
A disk (2D) and a ball (3D) of radius R pixels/voxels, as a grey image (each pixel ≈ the fraction of it inside, as a camera would record it) or a binary mask. Left: the disk with the pixels above ½, the pixel-edge boundary (red), the marching-squares contour (blue) and the true circle (dashed). Middle: relative errors against R on log–log axes, the dots at the current R. Right: the numbers.



R1. Preset voxel faces overestimate area (R = 6, grey). Read the area from voxel faces and from marching cubes, and the volume from voxel count and marching cubes. Compare with 4\pi R^2 and \tfrac43\pi R^3. Compare the 2D pixel-edge perimeter with B3.
R2. Preset marching cubes converges (R = 16). What happens to the four errors between R = 6 and R = 16? Which one does not improve, and why (B10)?
R3. Switch to binary mask and move R. What happens to the marching-cubes (and marching-squares) error now? Explain with B8.






Solutions





R1. Voxel faces 674 against 4\pi \cdot 36 = 452.4 (+49.0 %); marching cubes 449.4 (−0.7 %). Volume: 903 voxels (−0.2 %) and marching cubes 889.8 (−1.7 %) against 904.8. In 2D, 48 pixel edges against 37.7 (+27.3 %) = the bounding box 2(12 + 12), as in B3; marching squares 37.7 (−0.1 %).
R2. At R = 16: voxel faces still +50.1 %; marching cubes area +0.07 %, voxel count +0.09 %, marching-cubes volume −0.23 %. The face count does not improve: the staircase factor |n_x| + |n_y| + |n_z| does not depend on the voxel size. The other errors fall roughly like 1/R to 1/R^2 (the volume curves jump about because of how the boundary voxels happen to fall).
R3. With a binary mask every vertex sits at an edge midpoint. The marching-cubes area stays about 7–8 % too large (+7.4 % at R = 6, +8.3 % at R = 16), and the marching-squares perimeter about 6 % (+5.6 % and +5.8 %): the terraces do not go away with resolution. The volumes are still good: the mask has the right amount of inside.

title: Exercise: measuring surfaces
text:
Explore: volume against c
The volume enclosed by the marching-cubes surface as a function of c (click in the plot or use the slider), for a ball of radius 8 voxels that was binary and then blurred with \sigma, or for the nuclei stack of volumes3d/ (values scaled to background 0, nuclei about 1; true total volume 79.2 µm³). Right: a slice and its contour at the current c.



I1. Preset a plateau in volume vs c (\sigma = 0.5). Read the volume at c = 0.5 and the change for c \pm 0.05. How close is it to \tfrac43\pi\cdot8^3?
I2. Preset heavy blur: c decides the volume (\sigma = 2.5). The same questions. Why is the volume at c = 0.5 so much smaller now (B5)?
I3. Switch to the nuclei stack. Read the volume at c = 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7 and compare with 79.2 µm³. Which c would you report, and how would you justify it?






Solutions





I1. 2115.5 voxels³ against \tfrac43\pi\cdot512 = 2144.7 (−1.4 %); c \pm 0.05 changes it by about 2.3 %. A flat part of the curve: the measurement is robust.
I2. 1524.5 (−28.9 %), and c \pm 0.05 changes it by about 14 %. The blur (\sigma = 2.5 on a radius of 8) spreads the ball’s brightness outwards; at the true radius the value is well below 0.5, so the half-way surface lies inside (partial volume), and the gentle slope of the blurred edge makes the volume sensitive to c.
I3. About 94.4 µm³ at c = 0.3, 77.2 at c = 0.5 and 62.2 at c = 0.7 (blur 0.5 voxels). c = 0.5, half-way between background and nuclei, is closest to 79.2 (−2.5 %), as expected for objects much larger than the blur; report c together with the result, and the spread over a reasonable range of c.

title: Exercise: measuring surfaces
text:
Explore: binary masks and decimation
A tilted ellipsoid (semi-axes 16, 9, 11 voxels; true volume 6635 voxels³) extracted from a grey image, a binary mask, or the mask blurred with \sigma = 1. The cluster cell size decimates the mesh by vertex clustering. Face normals, so facets and terraces show; drag to rotate.



D1. Preset terraces from a binary mask. Compare the area and volume with the grey-level image and the blurred mask. Which inputs agree on the volume, and which on the area?
D2. Preset decimate 10×. How many triangles are left, and how much do area and volume change? Increase the cell size to 6: what happens to \chi and the non-manifold edges?
D3. With a cell size of 3, compare the decimated binary mask with the decimated grey image. Does decimation remove the terraces?






Solutions





D1. Binary mask: area 1932.9, volume 6632.5. Grey image: area 1779.4, volume 6605.2. Blurred mask: area 1758.2, volume 6479.8. All three volumes are within 2.5 % of 6635; the binary mask’s area is 8.6 % larger than the grey image’s (terraces). Blurring the mask removes the terraces but shrinks the object (−2.3 % volume): blur rounds a convex object inwards.
D2. 508 triangles instead of 5332 (10.5 times fewer), area −2.1 %, volume −4.3 %: the coarse mesh cuts off the curved parts. At cell size 6: 138 triangles, area −7.2 %, volume −16.7 %, \chi = 4 and 3 non-manifold edges: vertices from different parts of the surface were merged into the same cell, and the mesh is no longer a single closed surface.
D3. With cell size 3 the binary mask gives 544 triangles and its area drops to 1759.5, close to the grey image’s decimated 1741.2: the merged vertices average over the steps, so the coarse mesh no longer follows the terraces. Decimation smooths at the scale of its cells (with the shrinkage seen in D2).

title: Exercise: measuring surfaces
text:
Where this leads
Optional further reading: dual methods (surface nets, dual contouring) place one vertex per cell instead of per edge, need no case table, and handle label images naturally. Instead of extracting a surface, a volume can also be rendered directly (projections, volume rendering with a transfer function): the 3D-graphics day, which also shows how the meshes of this day are drawn on the screen.

title: Quiz: measuring surfaces
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Meshes are closed and oriented with outward normals unless said otherwise.

Q1. Why must a mesh be closed to compute its volume by summing signed tetrahedra?






Hint





What cancels in the sum?









Answer





The tetrahedra from the origin to the triangles overlap; only for a closed surface do the parts outside the object cancel between the near and far side, leaving exactly the enclosed volume. With a hole, part of the boundary is missing and the sum depends on where the origin is.




Q2. A sphere is digitised at a very fine resolution. Which estimate is good and which is bad: volume from the voxel count, area from the exposed voxel faces?






Hint





Does a staircase get closer to a slope when its steps get smaller?









Answer





The voxel count converges to the true volume. The face count stays about 1.5 times the true area at any resolution: smaller steps, but the same total length of steps per unit of slope.




Q3. A mesh has V = 1000, E = 3000, F = 2000. What is \chi, and what could the surface be?






Hint





\chi = V - E + F; a closed surface with g holes has \chi = 2 - 2g.









Answer





\chi = 0: for example one torus (one hole), or one sphere (+2) plus a surface with two holes (-2). Count the components to tell.




Q4. Two objects have the same true volume. Object A is large with sharp edges, object B small and blurred. Which one’s measured volume depends more on c?






Hint





How far does the surface move when c changes a little?









Answer





B. A blurred edge has a small gradient, so a small change of c moves the surface a long way, and a small object has a large fraction of its volume near the surface. A’s volume-against-c curve has a plateau; B’s is steep.




Q5. You smooth a mesh with many iterations of Laplacian smoothing. What happens to its volume, and why?






Hint





Where is the mean of a vertex’s neighbours on a convex surface?









Answer





It shrinks. On a convex surface the mean of a vertex’s neighbours lies inside the surface, so every step moves the vertices inwards; repeated, the whole mesh contracts (a sphere shrinks towards a point).




Q6. A confocal stack has \Delta z = 3\Delta x. The volume of a cell is computed from a mesh whose vertices were placed with \Delta z = \Delta x. By what factor is the volume wrong?






Hint





Only one coordinate is scaled.









Answer





All z coordinates are 3 times too small, so the volume is 3 times too small (a factor 1/3).




Q7. Why does a mesh from a binary mask (0/1) at c = 0.5 look terraced, and why does this inflate its area?






Hint





Where on each edge does the vertex go?









Answer





All edge values are 1 and 0, so every vertex is at an edge midpoint: the vertices follow the voxel staircase instead of the smooth boundary. The steps add area, like voxel faces but less (about 8 % for a sphere), at any resolution.




Q8. (math) Compute the signed volume \tfrac16\,\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c) of the tetrahedron with \mathbf a = (1, 0, 0), \mathbf b = (0, 1, 0), \mathbf c = (0, 0, 1) and the origin. What happens if you swap \mathbf b and \mathbf c?






Hint





\mathbf b\times\mathbf c for two unit axis vectors.









Answer





\mathbf b\times\mathbf c = (1, 0, 0), so \tfrac16\,\mathbf a\cdot(1, 0, 0) = \tfrac16. Swapping \mathbf b and \mathbf c reverses the orientation: -\tfrac16.

title: Texture: co-occurrence matrices
text:
About this lecture
The last unit measured the pixel values of an object as a bag of numbers. Texture is about how the values are arranged: fine or coarse, oriented or not, regular or random.

Histogram features cannot see arrangement: we need pairs of pixels.
The grey-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM): a 2D histogram of a pixel and its neighbour at a fixed offset.
Haralick features: contrast, homogeneity, ASM/energy, entropy, correlation.
The choices that change the numbers: distance, angle, number of grey levels, quantisation range.
Briefly: Gabor filters, local binary patterns, granularity.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Second unit of the measurements day. The GLCM is introduced as a 2D histogram; the same object comes back in the colocalisation unit (two channels instead of an image and its shifted copy). Entropy is owned by the compression elective and gets one line here. Grey levels are numbered from 0.

Same histogram, different texture

Left: smoothed noise. Right: the same pixel values, shuffled. Same mean, standard deviation, median, quartiles: every statistic of the last unit is identical.

Left: neighbours are similar. Right: neighbours are unrelated.

title: Texture: co-occurrence matrices
text:
The co-occurrence matrix

Quantise the image to L grey levels 0, \dots, L-1.
Choose an offset: distance d and angle (0° = to the right, 90° = up).
For every pixel whose partner at that offset is also inside the image (or object), add 1 to cell (level of the pixel, level of the partner).
Usually symmetric: count each pair both ways. Divide by the total: a joint probability p(i, j).

Two 4 \times 4 images with 8 zeros and 8 ones, offset 1 to the right:



image

(0,1) and (1,0)
(1,1)




checkerboard 0 1 0 1 / 1 0 1 0 / …
0

8

8



Same histogram, different matrices: all mass off the diagonal for the checkerboard, mostly on it for the halves.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Texture: co-occurrence matrices
text:
The math: the GLCM
For a quantised image q, offset \mathbf d = (d_x, d_y) and region \Omega:
P_{\mathbf d}(i, j) = \#\{\mathbf x : \mathbf x \in \Omega,\ \mathbf x + \mathbf d \in \Omega,\ q(\mathbf x) = i,\ q(\mathbf x + \mathbf d) = j\}.

Symmetric version P_{\mathbf d} + P_{\mathbf d}^\top = P_{\mathbf d} + P_{-\mathbf d}: the offsets \mathbf d and -\mathbf d are merged, so 0° and 180° give the same matrix.
p = P / \sum P is the joint distribution of (q(\mathbf X), q(\mathbf X + \mathbf d)) for a random pixel \mathbf X: the 2D histogram of the image against its own copy shifted by -\mathbf d.
The marginals p_x(i) = \sum_j p(i, j) are (nearly) the grey-level histogram: the histogram is inside the GLCM, the arrangement is in how the mass spreads around the diagonal.
Angles on a pixel grid (Haralick 1973): 0°, 45°, 90°, 135° with offsets (d, 0), (d, -d), (0, -d), (-d, -d), y pointing down.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Texture: co-occurrence matrices
text:
Features: statistics of the matrix
Each feature summarises where the mass of p(i, j) lies:

Contrast: the mean of (i - j)^2: large when neighbours differ. Checkerboard 1, halves 0.33.
Homogeneity: the mean of 1/(1 + (i - j)^2): large when the mass is near the diagonal. 0.5 and 0.83.
ASM (angular second moment) = \sum p^2, and energy = \sqrt{\text{ASM}}: large when few pairs dominate. 0.5 and 0.28.
Entropy = -\sum p \log_2 p: the expected surprise of a pixel pair, in bits (entropy itself is the compression elective’s topic). 1.0 and 1.92.
Correlation: the Pearson correlation of a pixel with its partner. −1 and +0.33.

Haralick listed 14 features; the others (sum and difference averages, variances and entropies, information measures of correlation) are mostly strongly correlated with these five.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Texture: co-occurrence matrices
text:
The math: Haralick features
With \mu = \sum_{i,j} i\,p(i,j) and \sigma^2 = \sum_{i,j} (i - \mu)^2 p(i,j) (the same for rows and columns of a symmetric p):
\text{contrast} = \sum_{i,j} (i - j)^2 p, \quad \text{homogeneity} = \sum_{i,j} \frac{p}{1 + (i-j)^2}, \quad \text{ASM} = \sum_{i,j} p^2, \text{entropy} = -\sum_{i,j} p \log_2 p, \qquad \text{correlation} = \frac{\sum_{i,j} (i - \mu)(j - \mu)\, p}{\sigma^2}.

For symmetric p: \text{contrast} = E[(I - J)^2] = 2\sigma^2 - 2\operatorname{cov}(I, J) = 2\sigma^2(1 - \text{correlation}).
\text{ASM} \le 1 with equality iff all pairs fall into one cell (a constant patch); 0 \le \text{entropy} \le \log_2 L^2.
Correlation is undefined for a constant patch (\sigma = 0).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Texture: co-occurrence matrices
text:
A familiar object, twice

The GLCM is the 2D histogram of an image against its shifted copy. The colocalisation unit draws the same picture with two channels instead.
Correlation at offset \mathbf d is the autocorrelation of the image at lag \mathbf d (the Fourier day): how similar the image is to itself shifted by \mathbf d.
Plotting a feature against d is therefore a cheap look at the scale of the texture: correlation falls off over about the size of the grains.

Demo, smoothed noise (σ = 4 px), 8 levels: correlation 0.95 at d = 1, 0.73 at d = 4, 0.28 at d = 8. White noise: about 0 at every d.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Texture: co-occurrence matrices
text:
Try it: the co-occurrence matrix




Tour: “same histogram, different texture”: A has its mass along the diagonal (38 of 64 cells used), B (shuffled) fills the whole matrix; contrast 0.51 against 10.59, correlation 0.95 against −0.01. Then “fine vs coarse”: move d from 1 to 8; the contrast of the smoothed noise grows (0.18 → 2.29), that of white noise stays near 10.3. “period = d”: stripes with period 8; at d = 8 the contrast is 0 and correlation 1, at d = 4 contrast is maximal and correlation −0.98. The polar plot shows contrast against angle at the current d.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Texture: co-occurrence matrices
text:
Choices that change the numbers

Distance d: the scale of the texture you look at. Stripes with period 8: contrast 0 at d = 8 and d = 16, maximal at d = 4 and d = 12.
Angle: oriented textures give different matrices per angle. Report each angle, or average the four for rotation invariance.
Number of levels L: 8–256. Too many levels for a small object: the matrix is mostly empty. Disc of radius 6 (200 pairs), L = 64: entropy 6.80 bits, against 9.01 on the whole patch.
Quantisation range: each object’s own min–max, or one fixed range. Per-object min–max makes a dim, low-contrast cell look like a bright one: it destroys comparisons between objects.
Symmetric or not, and which pairs count: only pairs with both pixels inside the object.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Texture: co-occurrence matrices
text:
The math: angles and rotation

Rotating the image by 90° maps the offset (d, 0) to (0, -d) (or its negative): the four standard angles are permuted. The average over the four angles is therefore invariant to rotations by multiples of 90° (and nearly to 45°).
For an angle \theta that is not a multiple of 45°, the offset (d\cos\theta, -d\sin\theta) is not on the grid. Rounding it changes both the direction and the length; interpolating the partner pixel blurs the values. Either way, only four (or eight) directions are exact.
With L levels and N pairs, at most \min(L^2, N) cells are non-zero, so \text{entropy} \le \log_2 \min(L^2, N): on a small object the entropy measures N, not the texture.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Texture: co-occurrence matrices
text:
Naming traps
The same name, different formulas, depending on the program:







name
formulas in use




homogeneity / inverse difference moment
\sum p/(1 + (i-j)^2)


inverse difference
\sum p/(1 + \lvert i-j \rvert), sometimes also called homogeneity


energy
\sqrt{\text{ASM}}, or ASM itself


entropy
\log_2 (bits) or \ln (nats)


sum variance
with the sum average or (a misprint in the original paper) the sum entropy



Grey levels numbered from 0 or from 1 change the sum average. Always state the formula, d, angle, L and the range together with the numbers.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Texture: co-occurrence matrices
text:
Other texture descriptors

Gabor filter bank: convolve with a Gaussian window times a wave (the Fourier day: a band-pass filter tuned to one frequency and orientation). The mean energy of each filter’s output is one feature; a bank of 4 orientations × 4 frequencies gives 16.
Local binary patterns (LBP): compare each pixel’s 8 neighbours with it (1 if brighter or equal) and read the 8 bits as a code 0–255. The histogram of codes over the object is the feature vector. Taking the smallest of the 8 rotations of each code makes it rotation invariant; “uniform” codes (at most two 0/1 changes around the circle) are edges, corners and flat spots.
Granularity: how much of the signal disappears in openings of growing size (the granulometry of the morphology day).
Learned features: the activations of a trained network act as texture descriptors (the neural network days).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Texture: co-occurrence matrices
text:
The math: Gabor and LBP
Gabor kernel with frequency f, orientation \theta, width \sigma: g(x, y) = e^{-(x^2 + y^2)/2\sigma^2}\, e^{2\pi i f (x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta)}. Its Fourier transform is a Gaussian centred at f(\cos\theta, \sin\theta): it passes one patch of the spectrum. Feature: \frac{1}{|\Omega|}\sum_\Omega |I * g|^2.
LBP at pixel c with neighbours n_0, \dots, n_7 clockwise from the top-left: \mathrm{LBP} = \sum_{k=0}^{7} s(n_k - c)\, 2^{7-k}, \qquad s(t) = [t \ge 0]. Invariant to any increasing grey-level map (offset, gain, gamma): only the order of values matters. Rotation-invariant code: \min_r \mathrm{rot}_r(\mathrm{LBP}) over the 8 circular shifts.

title: Texture: co-occurrence matrices
text:
Summary

Texture is the arrangement of values; the histogram cannot see it.
The co-occurrence matrix counts pairs (level at \mathbf x, level at \mathbf x + \mathbf d): a 2D histogram of the image against its shifted copy.
Contrast and homogeneity say how far pairs are from the diagonal, ASM/entropy how concentrated they are, correlation how linearly related.
The numbers depend on d (scale), the angle, the number of levels and the range: fix them, report them, and do not rescale each object to its own min–max.
Gabor energies, LBP histograms and granularity are other texture columns.

title: Exercise: segmentation networks
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute the per-pixel cross-entropy and the soft Dice of a probability map, and explain why they disagree under class imbalance,
upsample a signal by hand (nearest neighbour, transposed convolution),
follow sizes, channels and weights through a small U-Net, and say what its receptive field is,
read the errors of a segmentation, compare it with a threshold, and recognise when the input is outside the training range.

The questions under By hand and Explore are for everyone. The Math questions (derive, prove) are for students who want the full treatment.

title: Exercise: segmentation networks
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute the per-pixel cross-entropy and the soft Dice of a probability map, and explain why they disagree under class imbalance,
upsample a signal by hand (nearest neighbour, transposed convolution),
follow sizes, channels and weights through a small U-Net, and say what its receptive field is,

The questions under By hand and Explore are for everyone. The Math questions (derive, prove) are for students who want the full treatment.

title: Exercise: segmentation networks
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Encoder–decoder
convolutions and pooling down to small maps, then upsampling and convolutions back to full size


U-Net
an encoder–decoder with skip connections: encoder maps copied to the decoder and concatenated (channels add up)


Transposed convolution
each input value stamps a scaled copy of the kernel into the output, s positions apart: output length (n - 1)s + k - 2p


Per-pixel cross-entropy
-\frac1N\sum_i\big[g_i\ln p_i + (1 - g_i)\ln(1 - p_i)\big], g_i \in \{0, 1\} the true mask


Soft Dice
D = 2\sum_i p_ig_i/(\sum_i p_i + \sum_i g_i); Dice loss = 1 - D


Dice, IoU (masks)
2\,\text{TP}/(2\,\text{TP} + \text{FP} + \text{FN}), \text{TP}/(\text{TP} + \text{FP} + \text{FN})

title: Exercise: segmentation networks
text:
By hand
B1. A 3 \times 3 probability map and its true mask:
p = \begin{bmatrix} 0.9&0.8&0.1\\ 0.7&0.6&0.2\\ 0.1&0.2&0.1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad g = \begin{bmatrix} 1&1&0\\ 1&1&0\\ 0&0&0 \end{bmatrix}

Compute the mean per-pixel cross-entropy.
Compute the soft Dice. Then threshold at 0.5 and compute the ordinary Dice of the mask.
A 20 \times 20 image contains one nucleus of 20 pixels (5 %). A network outputs p = 0.01 everywhere. Compute the pixel accuracy (threshold 0.5), the cross-entropy, the soft Dice and the Dice of the mask. Which of these numbers notices that the network is useless?

B2. Upsampling the 1D signal (1, 2, 3) by a factor 2. (a) Nearest neighbour. (b) Nearest neighbour followed by the correlation with (\tfrac14, \tfrac12, \tfrac14) (zeros beyond the ends, keep 6 values). (c) A transposed convolution with stride 2 and kernel (\tfrac12, 1, \tfrac12) (7 values). What kind of interpolation is it? (d) Which kernel, with stride 2, gives exactly nearest-neighbour upsampling?
B3. The U-Net of the demo on a 1 \times 64 \times 64 input (all convolutions 3 \times 3 with padding 1): encoder 1: conv 1→8, conv 8→8; pool; encoder 2: conv 8→16, conv 16→16; pool; bottleneck: conv 16→32, conv 32→32; upsample, concatenate with encoder 2, conv →16, conv 16→16; upsample, concatenate with encoder 1, conv →8, conv 8→8; 1 \times 1 conv 8→1. (a) Give the size (channels × height × width) after every block, including the two concatenations. (b) Count the weights of every layer and in total. (c) Without skip connections the two decoder convolutions after upsampling get only 32 and 16 channels. How many weights fewer?
B4. Receptive field of the same network. (a) Compute the receptive field of one bottleneck unit (conv, conv, pool, conv, conv, pool, conv, conv). (b) Can it see a whole nucleus of 20 pixels? (c) Upsampling does not enlarge the field, but the decoder’s convolutions do. Roughly how large is the field of one output pixel?
B5. A U-Net segments 7 nuclei perfectly, but 3 pairs of them touch. How many objects does connected-component labelling (day 9) find in the mask? Name two ways to get 7.
B6. The U-Net’s probability map as the data term of a graph cut (day 13): D_p(\ell) = -\ln p_p(\ell). Compute D_p(\text{object}) and D_p(\text{background}) for a pixel with p = 0.9, and for one with p = 0.5. What will the smoothness term decide?






Solutions





B1. (a) Object pixels: -\ln 0.9 - \ln 0.8 - \ln 0.7 - \ln 0.6 = 0.105 + 0.223 + 0.357 + 0.511; background pixels: -\ln 0.9 - \ln 0.8 - \ln 0.9 - \ln 0.8 - \ln 0.9 = 3 \cdot 0.105 + 2 \cdot 0.223. Total 1.958, mean over 9 pixels 0.218. (b) \sum p_ig_i = 0.9 + 0.8 + 0.7 + 0.6 = 3.0, \sum p_i = 3.7, \sum g_i = 4: D = 6/7.7 = 0.779. At threshold 0.5 the mask equals g exactly (TP 4, FP 0, FN 0): Dice 1. The soft Dice still rewards making the probabilities more confident. (c) Accuracy 380/400 = 95 %. Cross-entropy (380 \cdot 0.01005 + 20 \cdot 4.605)/400 = 0.240: below the 0.693 of a coin toss, so it does not look alarming. Soft Dice 2 \cdot 0.01 \cdot 20/(4 + 20) = 0.017; mask Dice 0. Only the Dice numbers show that not a single nucleus pixel is found.
B2. (a) (1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3). (b) (0.75, 1.25, 1.75, 2.25, 2.75, 2.25). (c) 1 \cdot (\tfrac12, 1, \tfrac12) at positions 0–2, 2 \cdot (\ldots) at 2–4, 3 \cdot (\ldots) at 4–6: (0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 1.5): linear interpolation (with half values at the open ends). (d) The kernel (1, 1) with stride 2: each value is stamped twice, side by side.
B3. (a) 8 \times 64 \times 64 → pool 8 \times 32 \times 32 → 16 \times 32 \times 32 → pool 16 \times 16 \times 16 → 32 \times 16 \times 16 → upsample 32 \times 32 \times 32 → concatenate 48 \times 32 \times 32 → 16 \times 32 \times 32 → upsample 16 \times 64 \times 64 → concatenate 24 \times 64 \times 64 → 8 \times 64 \times 64 → 1 \times 64 \times 64. (b) 9C_\text{in}C_\text{out} + C_\text{out}: 80, 584, 1168, 2320, 4640, 9248 (encoder and bottleneck), 6928, 2320, 1736, 584 (decoder), 8 + 1 = 9 (the 1 \times 1 conv): 29,617. (c) 9 \cdot 16 \cdot 16 = 2304 fewer in the first (48 \to 32 input channels) and 9 \cdot 8 \cdot 8 = 576 in the second (24 \to 16): 2880 fewer, 26,737 in total.
B4. (a) r = 3, 5, 6, 10, 14, 16, 24, 32: 32 pixels (jump 4). (b) Yes, 32 > 20. (c) After the bottleneck, two convolutions at jump 2 add 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 8, two at jump 1 add 4: about 44 pixels (the paths through the skip connections see less).
B5. 4 objects (3 merged pairs + 1 single). Split them: train with a third class “boundary between touching nuclei” and label the interiors; or use the distance transform and the watershed on the mask (days 8–10); or networks that predict separate objects directly (day 18).
B6. p = 0.9: D(\text{object}) = -\ln 0.9 = 0.105, D(\text{background}) = -\ln 0.1 = 2.303: a strong preference. p = 0.5: both \ln 2 = 0.693: no preference, so the neighbours (through the smoothness term) decide.




Math questions
B7. (math) Derive \partial D/\partial p_j for the soft Dice. Evaluate it for B1 at an object pixel and at a background pixel. Which pixels does a gradient step on the Dice loss push up, and which down?
B8. (math) Let A be the matrix of a 1D strided convolution (kernel k, stride s, no padding) and T the transposed convolution with the same kernel. Show that \langle A\mathbf x, \mathbf y\rangle = \langle\mathbf x, T\mathbf y\rangle for all \mathbf x, \mathbf y, i.e. T = A^\top.
B9. (math) Weighted cross-entropy with weights w_1 for object pixels and w_0 for background pixels. If the object share is f, show that choosing w_c \propto 1/(\text{share of class } c) makes both classes contribute equally to the loss of a network that outputs the constant p. Give the weights for f = 0.05, normalised so that w_0 = 1.






Solutions (math)





B7. (math) With I = \sum_i p_ig_i and S = \sum_i p_i + \sum_i g_i: D = 2I/S, \partial I/\partial p_j = g_j, \partial S/\partial p_j = 1, so \partial D/\partial p_j = (2g_jS - 2I)/S^2. For B1: S = 7.7, I = 3: object pixels (15.4 - 6)/59.29 = 0.159, background pixels -6/59.29 = -0.101. The Dice loss 1 - D has the opposite gradient: a step pushes object pixels up and background pixels down, with the same size for every object pixel, however confident it already is.
B8. (math) (A\mathbf x)_i = \sum_u k_u x_{is + u}, so \langle A\mathbf x, \mathbf y\rangle = \sum_i\sum_u k_ux_{is + u}y_i. The transposed convolution stamps: (T\mathbf y)_t = \sum_i\sum_u [is + u = t]\,k_uy_i, so \langle\mathbf x, T\mathbf y\rangle = \sum_t x_t\sum_{i,u}[is + u = t]k_uy_i = \sum_{i,u}k_ux_{is+u}y_i. The two sums are equal.
B9. (math) For a constant output p the loss is -\big[w_1f\ln p + w_0(1 - f)\ln(1 - p)\big]: the classes contribute with the factors w_1f and w_0(1 - f), equal when w_1/w_0 = (1 - f)/f. With w_c \propto 1/\text{share}: w_1 = c/f, w_0 = c/(1 - f), so w_1f = w_0(1 - f) = c. For f = 0.05: w_0 = 1, w_1 = 0.95/0.05 = 19. The minimum of this weighted loss over constant outputs is then at p = \tfrac12 instead of p = f.

title: Exercise: segmentation networks
text:
Explore: a U-Net segments nuclei
A tiny U-Net (8, 16 and 32 channels, 29,617 weights) was trained on 4000 synthetic 64 \times 64 fluorescence-like images: nuclei of different sizes and brightness, some touching, an illumination gradient and noise. The demo draws new images from the same generator (new image). Panels: the input, the nucleus probability of every pixel, the mask at the threshold, the errors against the true mask (white = correct nucleus, red = false positive, blue = false negative) with Dice and IoU, and Otsu’s threshold (thresholding day) as the baseline. Click a block of the architecture to see its feature maps. The sliders move the input away from the training images: extra noise, a stronger illumination gradient, a brightness factor, larger or smaller nuclei. Weight sets: U-Net (trained with per-pixel cross-entropy), no skip connections, and trained with Dice loss.



U1. Preset a typical image. Read Dice, IoU and the error counts of the U-Net and the Dice of Otsu. Where are the U-Net’s errors? Move the threshold from 0.1 to 0.9: how much does Dice change?
U2. Preset U-Net vs Otsu on uneven illumination (the same image with an illumination gradient of 100 grey levels). Compare the two error images. Why does Otsu fail, and why not the U-Net?
U3. Click the five blocks of the architecture. How many maps of which size does each have? What do the bottleneck maps look like compared with those of encoder 1?
U4. Preset no skips: small nuclei (nuclei half the usual size). Compare the Dice of no skip connections and U-Net on this image, and the number of uncertain pixels (0.1 < p < 0.9). Then press back to training conditions and compare the two weight sets on a few new images. When do the skip connections matter?
U5. Preset touching nuclei merge. How many nuclei are there (readout), and how many separate white regions does the mask have? Is that an error of the network?
U6. Preset too noisy: outside the training range (extra noise with standard deviation 30). What happens to the U-Net and to Otsu? Try 15.
U7. Preset dimmer microscope: domain shift (the whole image ×0.5). Compare the U-Net with Otsu, and with the same image at brightness 1. Lower the threshold: does it help much? Then try brightness 2.
U8. Preset Dice loss: probabilities near 0 or 1. Compare the probability maps and the readouts (cross-entropy, soft Dice, uncertain pixels) of trained with Dice loss and U-Net. Move the threshold from 0.1 to 0.9 for both.






Solutions





U1. U-Net: Dice 0.986, IoU 0.972, TP 446, FP 2, FN 11; Otsu: 0.975. The few errors lie on the nucleus boundaries (blue rims: the U-Net’s nuclei are a little too small), where even the truth is a matter of half pixels. Dice is 0.980 at threshold 0.1, 0.986 at 0.5, 0.974 at 0.9: the probabilities are close to 0 or 1 except at the boundaries, so the threshold matters little.
U2. Otsu (threshold 81) labels the whole bright right side as nucleus: Dice 0.349 (a large red region). One global threshold cannot separate nuclei from a background that is brighter on one side than the dim nuclei on the other. The U-Net sees each nucleus in its neighbourhood (a bright blob is brighter than its surroundings) and was trained on images with gradients up to 100: Dice 0.987, the same as without the gradient.
U3. Encoder 1: 8 maps of 64 \times 64; encoder 2: 16 of 32 \times 32; bottleneck: 32 of 16 \times 16; decoder 2: 16 of 32 \times 32; decoder 1: 8 of 64 \times 64. Encoder-1 maps look like filtered versions of the image (edges, blobs, background); the bottleneck maps are coarse blobs that mark where the nuclei are, with blocky outlines.
U4. On this image: no skips Dice 0.936 (FP 27, 41 uncertain pixels), U-Net 0.954 (FP 19, 28 uncertain pixels): without skips the small nuclei come out too large and blurred. On typical images the difference is small (validation Dice 0.965 against 0.968): these smooth, fairly large blobs can be located from the 16 \times 16 bottleneck maps. Skip connections matter for small objects and fine boundaries; over 40 test images with half-size nuclei the Dice is 0.904 without and 0.925 with skips.
U5. 7 nuclei, but the mask has 4 connected regions: several nuclei touch. The network did what it was trained for (Dice 0.986): label pixels as nucleus or not. Separating touching nuclei needs another step (B5).
U6. Noise 30 (training noise was 3–10): the U-Net drops to Dice 0.943 and its mask breaks into 9 pieces (specks in the background, holes); Otsu drops to 0.729. At noise 15 both are still good (0.978 and 0.951). The network degrades gracefully here, but its errors are of a new kind (scattered specks).
U7. At brightness ×0.5 the U-Net misses most of the nuclei: Dice 0.269 (TP 143, FN 776), while Otsu still reaches 0.705. At brightness 1 the same image gives 0.951. Lowering the threshold to 0.1 helps little (0.335): the probabilities themselves are low, the network has never seen nuclei this dim. At brightness ×2: 0.930. A network can be beaten by a simple threshold as soon as the input leaves its training range; it gives no warning. Augmenting the brightness during training, or normalising the images, would help.
U8. The Dice-trained network gives almost only probabilities near 0 or 1: 16 uncertain pixels against 285 for the cross-entropy network. Its Dice hardly depends on the threshold (0.904–0.906 from 0.1 to 0.9); the cross-entropy network peaks at 0.5 (0.909) and drops to 0.851 at 0.1 and 0.856 at 0.9. The Dice-trained network’s cross-entropy is high (0.491 against 0.108): where it is wrong it is confidently wrong. Its probabilities are not calibrated: “0.99” does not mean “right 99 % of the time”.

title: Exercise: segmentation networks
text:
Where this leads
The evaluation day (day 16) asks how to measure segmentations honestly: object-level matching, test sets from new sources, and the statistics of comparing methods. Modern deep learning (day 18) splits touching nuclei with networks, uses pretrained models that need fewer annotations, and generates images; the VAE day (day 17) shows networks that learn to make images rather than label them. Learned image restoration (denoising, deconvolution with networks) is discussed on the deconvolution day.

title: Quiz: segmentation networks
text:
Short questions on encoder–decoders, U-Nets, per-pixel losses and evaluation. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Dice = 2|P \cap G|/(|P| + |G|), IoU = |P \cap G|/|P \cup G|.

Q1. Why can a classification network with a dense last layer not simply be used to segment an image?






Hint





What does it output, and for which input size?









Answer





It outputs one set of class probabilities for the whole image, and its dense layer fixes the input size. A segmentation network must output one probability per pixel, for any image size: it has to be convolutional all the way, with a decoder that returns to full resolution.




Q2. What do the skip connections of a U-Net carry, and what goes wrong without them?






Hint





What did pooling throw away?









Answer





They copy the sharp, full-resolution feature maps of the encoder to the decoder. Without them the decoder only has the coarse bottleneck maps: it knows roughly where objects are, but boundaries and small objects come out blurred or misplaced.




Q3. Nuclei cover 3 % of the pixels. A network predicts “background” everywhere. What are its pixel accuracy and its Dice?






Hint





|P| = 0.









Answer





Accuracy 97 %, Dice 0 (no true positives). Accuracy rewards the large background class; Dice looks only at the objects.




Q4. Upsample (4, 8) by a factor 2 with nearest neighbour, then with a transposed convolution with stride 2 and kernel (\tfrac12, 1, \tfrac12).






Hint





Each input value stamps the scaled kernel, two positions apart.









Answer





Nearest: (4, 4, 8, 8). Transposed: 4 \cdot (\tfrac12, 1, \tfrac12) at positions 0–2 and 8 \cdot (\tfrac12, 1, \tfrac12) at positions 2–4: (2, 4, 2 + 4, 8, 4) = (2, 4, 6, 8, 4): linear interpolation between 4 and 8, with a half value at the far end.




Q5. A U-Net trained on images from one microscope gives Dice 0.95 on held-out images from it, and 0.6 on images from a new microscope. What is this called, and what would you do?






Hint





Training range.









Answer





Domain shift: the new images (brightness, noise, blur, stain) lie outside what the network has seen. Annotate a few images from the new microscope and add them to the training set (fine-tune), augment brightness and noise more strongly during training, and always test on images from the setting where the network will be used.




Q6. The U-Net gives a perfect mask of two touching nuclei. Why is the nucleus count still wrong?






Hint





Connected components of the mask.









Answer





A semantic mask only says “nucleus or not” per pixel: two touching nuclei form one connected component, which labelling counts as one object. They have to be split, for example with a “boundary” class, the distance transform and the watershed (days 8–10), or with a network that outputs separate objects (day 18).




Q7. (math) Soft Dice D = 2\sum p_ig_i/(\sum p_i + \sum g_i). A pixel outside the object (g_j = 0) has its probability p_j raised. Does D go up or down? Show it from the formula.






Hint





Only the denominator depends on p_j.









Answer





Down: with g_j = 0 the numerator does not change and the denominator grows, \partial D/\partial p_j = -2\sum_i p_ig_i/(\sum_i p_i + \sum_i g_i)^2 \le 0. False positives are penalised, and more strongly the better the overlap already is.

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
About this lecture
A trained VAE gives us a decoder from a small latent space to images, and an encoder back. Today we use it.

Generate: draw z from the prior, decode.
Interpolate: walk in z from one image to another; the midpoint is not the pixel average.
Explore: what the latent space has learned about digits and about cell shapes.
Apply: denoising, anomaly detection, morphology spaces. And the limits: blurry images, nonsense far from the data.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Two trained VAEs, both 784 → 192 → 2 → 192 → 784, both run live in the demo: one on MNIST handwritten digits (adapted from the 3MB00A course), one on synthetic cell masks (four kinds: round, elongated, dividing, with a protrusion). The synthetic masks are honestly labelled as such; a VAE on real nucleus crops is the obvious next step and works the same way.
crumbs: Generating and exploring images with a VAE

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
section: Generating: decode a draw from the prior
text:
Generating: decode a draw from the prior

Decoding a 15 \times 15 grid of points z \in [-3, 3]^2: almost every point gives a digit-like image, and neighbours are similar. Only the bottom middle, where no training digit lies, decodes to smudges. To make a new image: draw z \sim \mathcal N(0, I) and decode.

This is the classic picture of a 2D VAE. Point out: 0s on the left, 1s on the right and bottom right, 7s at the top, 6 and 5 between 0 and the middle, the crowded middle with 3, 8, 2, 9, 4. Between regions the images morph: a 7 becomes a 9, a 6 becomes a 0. The bottom middle (around z = (0, −2.5)) decodes to smudges: almost no digits are encoded there (1 of the 1000 test digits of the latent map has z₂ < −2 and |z₁| < 1), so the decoder was never trained there. The prior N(0, I) puts 86.5% of its draws inside radius 2 (1 − e^{−2}); the edges of this grid (|z| up to 3) are rarely drawn and decode to exaggerated versions of the outermost shapes.
crumbs: Generating and exploring images with a VAE

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Walking through latent space

Top: decode 7 equally spaced points on the line from the centre of the 1s to the centre of the 7s, z(t) = (1 - t)\,z_A + t\,z_B. Bottom: fade the two end images into each other, pixel by pixel, (1 - t)\,x_A + t\,x_B.

The latent walk passes through plausible shapes (here via a 9-like stroke).
The pixel fade is a double exposure: a faint 1 and a faint 7 on top of each other.


A straight line in latent space is a curve in pixel space, as with the moving spot in the autoencoder unit. The pixel average of two images is almost never an image of the same kind. The centres are the medians of the 1000 test-digit centres per class, as the demo’s “walk 1 → 7” preset uses: (2.46, 0.00) and (0.94, 1.21).
crumbs: Generating and exploring images with a VAE

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Midpoint vs average, by hand
A decoder that draws a bright bar on a 3-pixel image at position z: pixel i gets \max(0,\ 1 - |z - i|), i = 0, 1, 2.




z = 0
z = 1
z = 2




decoded
(1, 0, 0)
(0, 1, 0)
(0, 0, 1)




Latent midpoint of z = 0 and z = 2: z = 1, the bar in the middle, (0, 1, 0).
Pixel average of the two images: (0.5,\ 0,\ 0.5), two half-bright bars.

A linear decoder (PCA) would give the average; a curved decoder moves the bar.

This is the image version of the 3MB00A argument with a transient progenitor gene: the middle pixel is dark at both ends but bright at the midpoint. Ask the class for z = 0.5: (0.5, 0.5, 0): the bar halfway between pixels 0 and 1, smeared over both.
crumbs: Generating and exploring images with a VAE

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
section: What the latent space has learned
text:
What the latent space has learned

Similar images are neighbours: in the digit VAE, 4 next to 9, and 3, 5, 8 together in the middle.
Two numbers are too few to keep ten digits apart: a vote among the 15 nearest test digits in z finds the right digit for 68% of test images.
The axes mean nothing by themselves: the KL penalty looks the same if the latent space is rotated, so “z_1” is not “thickness”. Read directions from decoded images, not from the axis labels.
Distances are only roughly meaningful, as in any nonlinear map.


The 68% is a leave-one-out 15-nearest-neighbour vote among the first 4000 MNIST test digits, computed with the demo’s weights. With a larger latent space (10–20 dimensions) the classes separate much better, but then we cannot draw the map. Contrast with PCA, where components are ordered by variance and orthogonal.
crumbs: Generating and exploring images with a VAE

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Try it: digits




Draw a digit and press Encode, or press “example ▸” for real MNIST test digits (20 of them, two of each). The cross is the cloud centre, the orange ellipse its ±2 sd. Drag z. Tick “decoded grid”. “walk 1 → 7” shows the latent walk. “sample from the prior” makes 7 new digits. “far outside” (3.3, −3.3) still decodes to a stroke: the decoder always answers, even where the prior almost never draws (density 0.00002 of that at 0).
crumbs: Generating and exploring images with a VAE

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
section: Cell shapes: a morphology latent space
text:
Cell shapes: a morphology latent space




The same network trained on synthetic cell masks (28 \times 28): round, elongated, dividing, with a protrusion, at random sizes and orientations.

The map organises size (large round cells on the left), elongation and orientation (right) and dividing cells (bottom).
A walk in z is a smooth change of shape; a generated mask is a plausible new cell.
Thin protrusions are lost: two numbers cannot also hold their direction. Their reconstruction error is the highest of the four kinds.

A nonlinear relative of the point distribution model (PCA of landmark shapes), learned straight from pixels.


Synthetic data, made by the training script with a fixed seed (no external images): wobbly ellipses, dumbbells and discs with a thin bar. Mean squared pixel error of the reconstructions on 2000 test masks: 0.0129 overall; by kind round 0.0071, elongated 0.0113, dividing 0.0116, protrusion 0.0218. Real use: VAEs and related autoencoders on cell and nucleus images give “morphology spaces” in which drug treatments or cell states form regions (e.g. Ruan & Murphy 2019; Zaritsky et al. 2021). If the Shape models unit came first, compare: the point distribution model is linear and needs landmarks; the VAE is nonlinear and works on the mask directly.
crumbs: Generating and exploring images with a VAE

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Denoising




Columns: clean mask, with noise added (sd 0.3 per pixel), decoded from the code of the noisy mask.

The decoder can only draw cell-like images, so it cannot draw the noise.
Mean squared error against the clean mask: noisy input 0.045, 0.048, 0.047; decoded 0.009, 0.018, 0.016.
But it draws its own version of a cell: details the model never learned (a protrusion, a precise outline) are replaced by typical ones.

Denoising by “project onto what the model can draw”: the nonlinear cousin of keeping a few PCA components.


Rows are test masks 2 (round), 7 (dividing) and 11 (protrusion) of the demo’s examples, noise from a fixed seed as in the demo’s “noise on input” slider at 0.3. Not every case works: for example 4 (an elongated cell) the noisy code lands in the wrong place and the output error, 0.110, is worse than the noisy input’s 0.047. For the digit model the decoded image is usually worse than the noisy input in squared error (its reconstructions are already blurry), although it looks cleaner.
crumbs: Generating and exploring images with a VAE

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Anomaly detection

Top: input masks. Bottom: their reconstructions. Four normal test cells, then a ring, two cells and a square.

Normal cells (the 12 test examples of the demo): error 0.004–0.023. On 2000 test masks, 99% have error below 0.045.
Ring 0.172, two cells 0.253: far above, flagged as unusual. Their codes land far outside the prior’s circle.
Square 0.030: below the threshold. It is close enough to a round cell to be rebuilt as one. The detector only sees what the model cannot draw.


Errors are mean squared pixel errors between the mask and the decoded cloud centre, computed with the demo code. Reading: a threshold at the 99th percentile of normal errors flags about 1% of normal cells as false alarms (20 of 2000). In practice: flag unusual cells, out-of-focus images, debris or segmentation failures in a screen. The encoder centres: ring (−6.30, 3.49), two cells (−4.18, −0.36): both outside the plotted square of the demo, far in the prior’s tail.
crumbs: Generating and exploring images with a VAE

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Try it: cell shapes




“example ▸” steps through 12 test masks (three per kind) and then the three anomalies; the error is shown under the encoder input. Draw a filled blob to make your own cell (the brush is wide). Raise “noise on input” to see denoising. “walk round → dividing” morphs a round cell into a dividing one.
crumbs: Generating and exploring images with a VAE

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
β-VAE: tidier space, blurrier images
Weight the KL more, \beta > 1:

Clouds are pulled harder to the prior: more overlap, a smoother latent space, and often directions that match one factor each (size, elongation, …): “disentangled”.
The decoder must serve wider clouds with one image each: blurrier, more average images.
\beta < 1: sharper reconstructions, but the gaps of a plain autoencoder start to return.

There is no free lunch: \beta trades image quality for latent-space quality.

Higgins et al. (2017), β-VAE: learning basic visual concepts with a constrained variational framework, ICLR. The elbo1d demo shows the same trade-off in one dimension: β = 5 pulls the best cloud from (1.2, 0.447) to (0.667, 0.745) and the reconstruction term rises from 0.58 to 2.5. Our two image VAEs were trained with β = 1.
crumbs: Generating and exploring images with a VAE

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Limits

Blurry outputs: the decoder outputs the average of all images that fit a given z (next slide). Fine detail and sharp edges are smeared.
Far from the data the decoder guesses: it always outputs an image, plausible or not. Generated images are only as good as the training images.
Small latent spaces lose detail (protrusions); large ones are hard to look at.
Sharper generators: GANs (a generator trained against a classifier that tries to tell real from fake) and diffusion models (learn to remove noise step by step, then start from pure noise). Both build on the same idea: a learned map from random numbers to images.
crumbs: Generating and exploring images with a VAE

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
section: The math: why VAE images are blurry
text:
The math: why VAE images are blurry
Suppose several different images x are all encoded near the same z. The decoder outputs one image c for that z, chosen to minimise the expected squared error:
\mathbb E\big[\|x - c\|^2\big] = \|c - \mathbb E[x]\|^2 + \mathbb E\big[\|x - \mathbb E[x]\|^2\big] \quad\Rightarrow\quad c^* = \mathbb E[x \mid z].

The best output is the conditional mean: an average of sharp images is a blurry image.
The same holds for cross-entropy on pixel “ink”: the best ink probability is the average ink.
The wider the clouds (larger \beta), the more images share each z, and the blurrier the mean.
crumbs: Generating and exploring images with a VAE

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Summary







Idea
In one line




Generate
z \sim \mathcal N(0, I), decode


Interpolate
walk z(t) = (1-t)z_A + tz_B; the midpoint is a new shape, not a double exposure


Latent structure
similar images nearby; classes overlap in 2D; axes have no fixed meaning


Morphology space
a VAE on cell masks orders cells by size, elongation, division


Denoising
decode the code of a noisy image: only what the model can draw survives


Anomaly
high reconstruction error = unlike the training images (if the model cannot draw it)


Limits
blurry (conditional mean), unreliable far from the data; GANs and diffusion go further
crumbs: Generating and exploring images with a VAE

title: Exercise: the variational autoencoder
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

explain what the encoder’s cloud and the prior do, and why the decoder is fed random draws,
draw a point of a cloud with the reparameterisation z = \mu + \sigma\varepsilon,
compute the KL divergence of a Gaussian cloud to the prior, and the two terms of the VAE loss for a small example,
predict how the best cloud moves when the image or \beta changes.

The questions under By hand and Explore are for everyone. The Math questions (derive, prove) are for students who want the full treatment.

By the end of this exercise you should be able to:
